pattern-arrays-hashing.title: Arrays & Hashing — the pattern
signals: find a pair or complement that sums to target
count frequencies or detect duplicates
group items sharing a key, like anagrams
nested loops feel obvious but O(n) is wanted
variants: hash set for seen or duplicates
hash map value → index
frequency counter
group by canonical key
pattern-arrays-hashing.hook: Trade a little memory for speed: a hash map turns 'search again' into one instant lookup.
pattern-arrays-hashing.ask: Arrays and hashing means storing what you have seen in a hash set or map, so each later question is answered in constant time instead of a rescan.
pattern-arrays-hashing.exampleWhy: Worked example Two Sum: 2 at index 3 plus 4 at index 5 makes 6.

brute.idea: Answer every question by rescanning the array: nested loops compare each element with every other one.
steps: Fix one element i
Rescan the others for what i needs
Repeat for every i
brute.whySlow: It repeats the same search for every element: 10,000 numbers means about 50 million pair checks.

optimal.insight: Each rescan asks the same question: have I seen X? Store everything seen in a hash map once, and every such question becomes an O(1) lookup.
steps: Decide what to remember: value, count, index or group key
Walk the input once
Ask the map your question before inserting
Insert or update the current element's entry

codeNotes.note: What we need to have seen
Answer read straight from the map

pitfalls: Inserting before checking lets an element match itself, e.g. target = 2n.
Using a list for 'seen' makes each lookup O(n), losing the speedup.

say.intro: Okay, arrays and hashing. This is the pattern behind half the easy questions you'll see. The idea is simple. Remember what you've seen in a hash map, so you never search for it again. Our example is Two Sum. The target is six. Two plus four gives six, at indices three and five.
say.brute: Without the pattern, what do people do? They rescan. For each number, they loop over everything else, looking for its partner. Two nested loops. It's correct. But notice we keep asking the same question, over and over. Have I seen this value before? Ten thousand numbers means about fifty million checks. That's n squared, and interviewers will push you past it.
say.insight: Here's the core idea. If you keep asking, have I seen this, store the answers once. A hash map answers in constant time. And the recipe is always the same. First, decide what to remember. A value, a count, or an index. Then walk the input once. Ask your question before inserting. Then record the current element. One pass, done.
say.anim: We start with an empty hash map to remember numbers we've already seen. At index zero, value three, we need five more to hit target six, but map is empty, so we store three. At index one, value five, we need one, not found yet, so we add five to the map. At index two, value eight, we need negative two, missing, so eight gets stored too. At index three, value two, we need four, still missing, so two joins the map. At index four, value eleven, we need negative five, not present, so eleven is stored. At index five, value four, we need two, and two is already in our map at index three. That lookup instantly finds the match, returning indices three and five as the final answer.
say.code: Here's the template. First, an empty map from value to index. That's what we chose to remember. Then one pass with enumerate. We work out what we need, the difference. We ask the map, have we seen it? If yes, return both indices. Otherwise, record the current number. Notice the order. Check first, insert second, so nothing pairs with itself.
say.outro: Linear time, linear space. Reach for a hash map when you hear pairs that sum to a target, counting or duplicates, grouping by a key, or when nested loops feel obvious.

lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container the interview platform expects for our method.
The twoSum method takes a list of numbers and a target, and returns the two indices that add up to it.
We create an empty hash map called prevMap that will remember each value we have seen and its index.
We loop through the list once, getting both the index i and the number n at each step.
We compute diff, the partner value needed so that it plus the current number equals the target.
We check whether diff is already in prevMap, which is a constant time lookup instead of rescanning.
If found, we return the stored index of diff together with the current index i, solving the problem.
Otherwise we store the current number with its index in prevMap so later numbers can find it as their partner.

pattern-two-pointers.title: Two Pointers — the pattern
signals: sorted array plus a pair or triplet target
palindrome, or compare from both ends
in place with O(1) extra space
maximize area or width between two lines
variants: opposite ends squeezing inward
fast and slow, same direction
fix one, two-pointer the rest (3Sum)
pattern-two-pointers.hook: Two indices moving toward each other turn an n-squared pair search into one linear sweep.
pattern-two-pointers.ask: Two pointers means keeping two indices into the same sequence and moving one per step, using order to rule out positions you never need to revisit.
pattern-two-pointers.exampleWhy: Worked example Two Sum II: 3 at position 2 plus 11 at position 6 is 14.

brute.idea: Check every pair with two nested loops, ignoring the order the input already gives you.
steps: Fix the left element i
Try every right element j > i
Check the pair condition
brute.whySlow: 30,000 sorted numbers means about 450 million pairs, though sorting already marks most as hopeless.

optimal.insight: On sorted data, comparing the pair to the goal tells you which pointer is hopeless. Move it inward; every move discards one candidate forever.
steps: Place pointers at both ends, or both at the start
Evaluate the pair under the two pointers
Move the pointer that cannot be part of an answer
Stop when they meet or the condition is met

codeNotes.note: Too big: the largest is hopeless
Too small: the smallest is hopeless

pitfalls: Squeezing from both ends needs sorted input; sort first or use a hash map.
Use l < r, not l <= r, or an element pairs with itself.

say.intro: Okay, two pointers. Instead of one index walking the array, we keep two. And we move them toward each other, using the order of the data to decide who moves. Our example is Two Sum Two. The list is sorted, and the target is fourteen. Three plus eleven works, at positions two and six.
say.brute: Without the pattern, you try every pair. Fix a left number, then try every number to its right. It works. But it throws away the best clue you have. The order. With thirty thousand numbers, that's about four hundred fifty million pairs. And the sorting already tells us most of them are hopeless.
say.insight: Here's the core idea. Look at the pair under the two pointers, and compare it to the goal. That comparison tells you which pointer can never be part of an answer. So move that one inward. Each move throws out a candidate forever. The recipe: place the pointers, evaluate the pair, move the hopeless one, and stop when they meet.
say.anim: We start with pointer l at index 0 and r at index 6, ends of the sorted array. Adding numbers at l and r gives curSum 16, which is more than target 14. Since the sum is too big, we move r left to shrink the pair's total. Now curSum is 12, less than target, so the pair is too small. We move l right instead, increasing the sum toward the target. With l at 1 and r at 5, curSum equals target 14 exactly. The loop stops and we return the one-based indices of these pointers. The final answer returned is index pair 2 and 6.
say.code: Here's the template. Pointers start at both ends. We loop while left is less than right, so they never cross. We evaluate the pair. Sum too big? The largest number is hopeless, so right moves in. Too small? The smallest is hopeless, so left moves in. Otherwise we've found it, and we return one based positions.
say.outro: Linear time, constant space. Reach for two pointers when you see a sorted array with a pair target, a palindrome check, an in place constant space ask, or the widest container between two lines.

lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container this problem's method lives in.
The twoSum method takes a sorted list called numbers and a target, and returns the two matching positions.
We set left to zero and right to the last index, so the pointers start at opposite ends.
We loop while left is less than right, so the two pointers never cross or reuse the same element.
We add the numbers at the left and right pointers to get the current sum.
If the current sum is greater than the target, the right value is too big for any partner.
So we move right one step inward, discarding that large value for good.
Otherwise, if the current sum is less than the target, the left value is too small for any partner.
So we move left one step inward, discarding that small value for good.
Otherwise the sum equals the target, so we have found the pair we wanted.
We return left plus one and right plus one, because the problem expects one-based positions.

pattern-sliding-window.title: Sliding Window — the pattern
signals: longest or shortest contiguous substring or subarray
at most k distinct or k replacements
window of size k: max, sum or average
contains a permutation or anagram of t
variants: variable window: shrink while invalid
fixed-size window of k
count-matching window (anagram, min window)
monotonic deque for window max
pattern-sliding-window.hook: Contiguous stretch questions? Slide a window instead of restarting, and each element is touched at most twice.
pattern-sliding-window.ask: Sliding window means keeping a contiguous range between a left and right pointer, growing it on the right and shrinking it on the left while updating its state incrementally.
pattern-sliding-window.exampleWhy: Worked example: in abcabcbb the longest run with no repeated letter is abc, length 3.

brute.idea: Restart from every left edge and rebuild the window's state from scratch, rescanning characters already checked.
steps: Pick every start index i
Extend j while building a fresh set
Stop at the first repeat, record length
brute.time: O(n · min(n, a)), a = alphabet size
brute.whySlow: Each restart throws away a window it just built and rescans it; large alphabets make it n².

optimal.insight: When the window breaks, only its left part is to blame. Keep the right edge and shrink from the left until valid, updating state incrementally.
steps: Expand: add s[r] to the window state
While the window is invalid, remove s[l] and move l
Window valid: record r - l + 1 as a candidate
Both edges only move right, so total work is linear

codeNotes.note: Remove the left element from state
Add the new element to state

pitfalls: Shrink with while, not if: one step may not restore validity.
Update state on both edges; forgetting the removal corrupts the window.

say.intro: Okay, sliding window. Whenever a question asks about a contiguous stretch, a substring or a subarray, think of a window. The right edge grows, the left edge shrinks, and neither ever goes back. Our example is the longest substring without repeating letters. In a b c a b c b b, that's a b c. Length three.
say.brute: Without the pattern, you restart from every position. Build a fresh set, walk right until a letter repeats, record the length, then start over from the next position. It works. But each restart throws away a window we just built, and rescans the same letters. With a big alphabet, that's n squared.
say.insight: Here's the core idea. When the window breaks, why throw it all away? Only the left part is to blame. So keep the right edge, and shrink from the left until it's valid again. The recipe: expand right and add to your state. While it's invalid, remove from the left. Then record the answer. Each element enters once and leaves once.
say.anim: We start with an empty character set, left pointer at zero, scanning the string abcabcbb. Right pointer moves through a, b, c, adding each new letter since none repeat yet, res grows to 3. At r equals 3, s of r is a, already in the set, so we shrink from the left. Right keeps advancing, each repeat of a, b, or c triggers removal from the left to restore validity. More repeats force left to jump forward several times, shrinking the window down to just one character. Near the end, repeated b characters keep shrinking the window as left catches up to right. The loop finishes, and the function returns the final result. The longest substring without repeating characters has length 3.
say.code: Here's the template. A set holds the window's state, the letters inside. The right edge expands on every loop. Is the window invalid now? Then we shrink with a while loop, removing the left letter and moving left forward. Once it's valid, we add the new letter. And we record the window size, right minus left plus one.
say.outro: Linear time. Reach for a sliding window when you hear longest or shortest contiguous substring, at most k of something, a window of size k, or contains a permutation.

lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container for the method we are about to write.
This method takes a string s and returns the length of its longest substring without repeating characters.
We create an empty set called charSet to track which characters are currently inside our window.
We set the left pointer l to zero, so the window starts at the beginning of the string.
We set res to zero, which will hold the longest valid window length we have seen.
We move the right pointer r across every index of s, growing the window one character at a time.
While the new character at r is already in charSet, the window is invalid because of a duplicate.
To fix it, we remove the character at the left pointer from charSet, since the left part is to blame.
Then we advance l by one, shrinking the window from the left while keeping the right edge fixed.
Once the duplicate is gone, we add the character at r to charSet so the window state stays current.
We update res with the larger of itself and the current window size, which is r minus l plus one.
After scanning the whole string, we return res as the length of the longest substring without repeats.

pattern-stack.title: Stack — the pattern
signals: matching or nested brackets
next greater or next smaller element
evaluate an expression or undo history
most recent unresolved item settles first
variants: matching stack (parentheses)
monotonic stack (next greater)
evaluation stack (RPN)
min stack with paired values
pattern-stack.hook: Last in, first out: perfect when the newest unresolved item is the next one to settle.
pattern-stack.ask: The stack pattern keeps unfinished items in last-in-first-out order, so each new element settles the most recent pending ones first: brackets, expressions, next greater element.
pattern-stack.exampleWhy: Worked example Daily Temperatures: 75 on day 2 waits four days for 76; the last two never warm up.

brute.idea: For every element, scan forward again to find what resolves it, rereading the same elements many times.
steps: For each day i
Scan forward j = i+1, i+2, ...
First warmer day: record j - i
brute.whySlow: Falling temperatures make every scan run to the end: 100,000 days means about 5 billion checks.

optimal.insight: Keep unresolved items on a stack. Each new element settles the most recent pending ones: pop while it resolves the top. Every item is pushed and popped once.
steps: Walk the input once, left to right
While the current element resolves the top, pop and record
Push the current element; it is now pending
Leftovers on the stack never got resolved

codeNotes.note: Step 3: current item is now pending

pitfalls: Check the stack is non-empty before peeking or popping.
Store indices, not just values, when the answer is a distance.

say.intro: Okay, the stack pattern. Last in, first out. It shines whenever the most recent unfinished thing is the next one to settle. Our example is Daily Temperatures. For each day, how long until it gets warmer? Seventy five waits four days for seventy six. The last two days never warm up, so they get zero.
say.brute: Without the pattern, every day scans forward on its own until it finds a warmer day. It's correct. But what if temperatures keep falling? Then every scan runs to the end, rereading the same days again and again. That's n squared. A hundred thousand days means about five billion checks.
say.insight: Here's the core idea. Keep the unresolved items on a stack. When a new element arrives, which pending items can it settle? Only the most recent ones, sitting on top. So pop while it resolves the top, and record answers. Then push the new one. Every item goes on once and comes off once. That's linear time.
say.anim: We start with results all zero and an empty stack to track pending temperatures. Temperature 73 at index 0 goes onto the stack, waiting for a warmer day. At index 1, temperature 74 beats 73, so we pop it and set its wait to 1. Now 75 beats 74, popping index 1 again and recording a wait of 1 day. 71 and 69 can't beat 75, so they just get pushed onto the stack. At 72, both 69 and 71 resolve, getting waits of 1 and 2 days respectively. 76 finally beats everything left, popping 72 and 75, giving waits 1 and 4. The loop ends, and the final answer is 1, 1, 4, 2, 1, 1, 0, 0.
say.code: Here's the template. Answers default to zero, for days never resolved. The stack holds pending days, with temperatures decreasing. For each day, while it's warmer than the top, it resolves that day. So we pop it, and record its wait, today's index minus its index. Then today becomes pending, so we push it.
say.outro: Linear time and space. Reach for a stack when you see matching brackets, next greater or smaller element, expression evaluation, or when the most recent unresolved item comes first.

lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which holds the method that solves the daily temperatures problem.
This method takes the list of temperatures and returns how many days each day waits for a warmer one.
We create a result list of zeros, one per day, since days with no warmer future stay zero.
We start an empty stack that holds pending days as pairs of temperature and index, still waiting for a warmer day.
We loop through every day, getting both its index i and its temperature t.
While the stack has items and today is warmer than the top pending day, we can resolve that day.
We pop the most recent pending day, getting its temperature and its index.
We record the wait for that popped day as today's index minus its index.
We push today's temperature and index onto the stack, since today now awaits its own warmer day.
After all days are processed, we return the result list, leaving zeros for days that never found a warmer one.

pattern-binary-search.title: Binary Search — the pattern
signals: sorted array: find a target or boundary
required O(log n) time
smallest or largest value that still works
rotated sorted array
variants: exact match in a sorted array
first or last true boundary
binary search on the answer
rotated array: pick the sorted half
pattern-binary-search.hook: If one check rules out half the candidates, a million items take about twenty steps.
pattern-binary-search.ask: Binary search keeps a range that must contain the answer and halves it with one comparison at the middle, whenever the data or answer space is sorted or monotonic.
pattern-binary-search.exampleWhy: Worked example Binary Search: 24 sits at index 8 of the sorted list.

brute.idea: Scan every candidate one by one, ignoring that sorted order tells you where the target cannot be.
steps: Walk i from 0 to n - 1
nums[i] == target? return i
Reached the end? return -1
brute.whySlow: It ignores the sorting: 10,000 numbers can take 10,000 checks instead of about 14.

optimal.insight: In a sorted or monotonic space, one comparison at the middle proves a whole half cannot hold the answer. Discard it; log n checks remain.
steps: Set l and r so the answer is surely inside
Compute the middle m and test it
Throw away the half that cannot contain the answer
Stop when found or the range is empty

codeNotes.note: Step 1: inclusive range holds the answer

pitfalls: Use l <= r with inclusive bounds, or you miss single-element ranges.
Move to m - 1 or m + 1, never m, or it may loop forever.

say.intro: Okay, binary search. If one check can rule out half of your candidates, you don't need to look at them all. A million items takes about twenty steps. Our example is the classic. A sorted list of ten numbers, and the target twenty four. It sits at index eight.
say.brute: Without the pattern, you scan left to right until you hit the target. Simple, and correct. But it ignores the sorting completely. Ten thousand numbers can take ten thousand checks, when about fourteen would do. And whenever an interviewer says sorted, or asks for log time, they're hinting at exactly this.
say.insight: Here's the core idea. Keep a range that surely contains the answer. Check the middle. Middle too big? Then everything to its right is too big too. So one comparison throws away half. The recipe: set the range, test the middle, discard the hopeless half, and stop when found or empty. It even works on answer values, as long as they're monotonic.
say.anim: We start with left at 0 and right at 9, spanning the whole array. Middle index m is 4, value 9, which is less than target 24, so we search right. Left moves to 5, shrinking the search space to the upper half. Now middle index m is 7, value 20, still less than 24, so left moves again. Left becomes 8, narrowing the range to just two elements. Middle index m is 8, and nums at 8 equals target 24, a match found. The function returns index 8, confirming that is where 24 lives.
say.code: Here's the template. Left and right mark an inclusive range. We loop while the range still has candidates. We compute the middle, as left plus half the gap. Middle too big? Discard the right half, so right becomes middle minus one. Too small? Left becomes middle plus one. Equal? Return it. If the range empties, return minus one.
say.outro: Log time, constant space. Reach for binary search when you see a sorted array, a log time requirement, the smallest value that still works, or a rotated sorted array.

lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which wraps the search method the problem asks us to implement.
The search method takes a sorted list called nums and a target value, and returns the target's index.
We set left to zero and right to the last index, so the range covers the whole list.
We loop while left is at most right, meaning the range still holds at least one candidate.
We compute the middle as left plus half the gap, which avoids overflow that adding left and right could cause.
If the middle value is larger than target, the target can only sit in the left half.
So we move right to just before the middle, discarding the middle and everything after it.
Otherwise, if the middle value is smaller than target, the target can only sit in the right half.
So we move left to just after the middle, discarding the middle and everything before it.
Otherwise the middle value equals the target, so we have found what we were looking for.
We return the middle index right away, since that is the position of the target.
If the loop ends with an empty range, the target is absent, so we return negative one.

pattern-linked-list.title: Linked List — the pattern
signals: reverse, reorder or merge a list in place
detect a cycle or find the middle
remove the nth node from the end
O(1) extra space on a linked list
variants: in-place reversal (prev, curr, next)
fast and slow pointers
dummy head for merging and deletion
list plus hash map (LRU, copy)
pattern-linked-list.hook: No indexes, only arrows. Master a few pointer moves and every list problem becomes choreography.
pattern-linked-list.ask: The linked list pattern means rewiring next pointers in place with a few named references, using tricks like dummy heads, fast and slow pointers, and saving next first.
pattern-linked-list.exampleWhy: Worked example Reverse Linked List: 1→2→3→4→5 becomes 5→4→3→2→1 by flipping every arrow.

brute.idea: Treat the list like an array: copy the values out, process them, then write them back.
steps: Walk the list, copying values into an array
Walk again, popping values from the end
Overwrite each node's value
brute.whySlow: It needs O(n) extra memory and two passes, and never relinks nodes, which interviewers expect.

optimal.insight: Rewire pointers in place with a few named references. Before overwriting any next pointer, save what it pointed to, or the rest is lost.
steps: Name the pointers you need: prev, curr, maybe a dummy
Save curr.next before changing any link
Rewire the link, then advance every pointer
Return the right head: often prev or dummy.next

pattern-linked-list.optimalCode:
# Definition for singly-linked list.
# class ListNode:
#     def __init__(self, x):
#         self.val = x
#         self.next = None


class Solution:
    def reverseList(self, head: ListNode) -> ListNode:
        prev, curr = None, head

        while curr:
            temp = curr.next
            curr.next = prev
            prev = curr
            curr = temp
        return prev

codeNotes.note: Advance curr into the saved rest
Step 4: prev is the new head

pitfalls: Overwriting next before saving it loses the rest of the list.
Empty or single-node lists break head logic; a dummy head removes special cases.

say.intro: Okay, linked lists. There are no indexes here, only arrows from node to node. So the whole pattern is pointer work. Rewire the arrows in place, carefully, with a few named references. Our example is Reverse Linked List. One, two, three, four, five becomes five, four, three, two, one.
say.brute: Without the pattern, people treat the list like an array. Copy every value out, then walk again and write them back in reverse. It works. But it needs a whole extra array, and two passes. And here's the catch. It never actually relinks a node. Interviewers want to see you move pointers, not values.
say.insight: Here's the core idea. Keep a few named pointers, and rewire as you walk. But careful. The moment you overwrite a next pointer, the rest of the list is gone. So the recipe: name your pointers. Save next before changing anything. Rewire the link. Advance every pointer. Then return the right head. Save, flip, advance.
say.anim: We start with prev set to none and curr pointing at the head, node one through five. Before rewiring, temp saves curr's next, node two, so we don't lose the rest of the list. Curr's next now points back to prev, flipping node one's arrow to none. Prev and curr both advance, prev becomes node one and curr becomes node two. The same steps repeat: temp saves node three, then node two's next flips to point at node one. This continues through node four, building a growing reversed chain, four to three to two to one. At node five, temp becomes none, its next flips to point at four, completing the reversal. Curr is now none, the loop ends, and prev is returned as the new head, five four three two one.
say.code: Here's the template. Prev starts as None, and current at the head. Inside the loop, first we save the rest in temp. Then we flip the arrow, pointing current back at prev. Prev moves up to current, and current steps into the saved rest. When current runs out, prev is the new head. Return it.
say.outro: Linear time, constant space. Reach for these pointer moves when you see reverse or reorder in place, detect a cycle, remove the nth from the end, or constant extra space on a list.

lineNotes: This comment explains that we are given a singly linked list node class, where each node has a value and a next pointer.
The commented class header shows that ListNode is the type used to represent each node in the list.
The constructor takes a value x, which will be stored as the value of the new node.
The node stores its value in a field called val, which holds the data for that node.
The next pointer starts as none, so a fresh node points to nothing until we link it.
We define the Solution class that holds the method for solving this problem.
The reverseList method takes the head of a linked list and will return the head of the reversed list.
We set prev to none and curr to head, so curr walks the list while prev builds the reversed part.
We loop as long as curr is a real node, stopping once we walk past the end.
We save the next node in temp first, because overwriting the next pointer would otherwise lose the rest of the list.
Now we point the next of curr back at prev, which flips this one link in the reversed direction.
We move prev forward to curr, since curr is now the head of the reversed portion.
We move curr to temp, the saved next node, so we continue with the unreversed remainder.
When the loop ends, prev sits on the old tail, which is the new head, so we return it.

pattern-trees.title: Trees — the pattern
pattern-trees.hook: Almost every tree question is one recursive function: ask your children, combine their answers, return.
pattern-trees.ask: Tree DFS solves a problem at a node by solving it for the left and right subtrees, then combining those answers.
pattern-trees.exampleWhy: The path 1 → 3 → 5 → 7 touches four nodes, and no root-to-leaf path is longer.

brute.idea: Treat the tree like a flat list: collect every node, then search from the root again to measure each one.
steps: Collect every node with a stack
For each node, search from root to find its depth
Keep the largest depth found
brute.whySlow: With 10,000 nodes we run 10,000 separate searches — up to 100 million visits, reusing nothing.

optimal.insight: A subtree is just a smaller tree, so the same function solves it. Define a node's answer from its children's answers; each node is visited once.
steps: Base case: an empty node returns a neutral value
Recurse into the left and right subtrees
Combine the children's answers with this node
Need context from above? Pass it down as a parameter

codeNotes.note: Step 1: base case, fell off the tree
Neutral value for an empty subtree
Step 2: same function on both subtrees

pitfalls: Missing the empty-node base case, so the code crashes on None children.
Deep skewed trees can overflow recursion; switch to an explicit stack or BFS queue.
signals: you are given the root of a binary tree
depth, height, diameter, or path sum
compare, validate, or match subtrees
level by level, or right side view
BST with sorted order or kth smallest
variants: bottom-up DFS: return values to the parent
top-down DFS: pass state to the children
BFS level order with a queue
BST: use ordering to prune a side

say.intro: Okay, trees. Almost every tree question has the same shape. You write one recursive function. It asks the left child, asks the right child, and combines the answers. Interviewers love it because it tests whether you trust recursion. Our example is maximum depth. The longest path here, one, three, five, seven, has four nodes.
say.brute: Without the pattern, people treat the tree like a list. Collect every node with a stack. Then, for each node, search down from the root to find how deep it sits. Keep the biggest. It works. But each search can walk the whole tree again. With ten thousand nodes, that's a hundred million visits. That's n squared, because nothing gets reused.
say.insight: Here's the thing. A subtree is just a smaller tree. So the same function solves it. That's the whole pattern. First, a base case. An empty node returns something neutral, like zero. Then recurse into the left and right subtrees. Then combine their answers with the current node. Need info from above, like a running max? Pass it down as a parameter.
say.anim: We start at root node 1, checking if it exists before exploring its children. Recursion dives left into node 2, then into node 4, each solved by the same function. Node 4 has no children, so both sides return 0 and node 4 returns depth 1. Node 2 combines its children's depths and returns 2 back up the call chain. Now we explore the right side, node 3, going into node 5 and its child node 7. Node 7 has no children, giving node 5 a depth of 2 after combining results. Node 6 is checked similarly, having no children, so it returns depth 1. Node 3 returns depth 3, and root node 1 combines both sides for final answer 4.
say.code: Here's the template. If the node is empty, we've hit the base case. Return the neutral value, zero, because an empty tree adds no depth. Next, call the same function on both subtrees. Finally, combine. Here that's one for this node, plus the larger child. Swap that combine line, and you get diameter, balance checks, or path sums.
say.outro: Linear time, height space. Spot trees when you hear: a root is given, depth or paths, comparing subtrees, level by level, or sorted order in a BST. Then ask the children, and trust the recursion.

lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which holds the method that computes the depth of a binary tree.
The maxDepth method takes the root of a tree and returns its maximum depth as an integer.
This is the base case check: we ask whether the current node is empty, meaning we walked past a leaf.
An empty tree has depth zero, so we return zero and the recursion stops here.
Otherwise the depth is one for this node plus the larger depth of its left and right subtrees, each solved recursively.

pattern-heap-priority-queue.title: Heap / Priority Queue — the pattern
pattern-heap-priority-queue.hook: Need the top k, or the next smallest, over and over? A heap answers in log time.
pattern-heap-priority-queue.ask: A heap is a structure that always keeps the smallest (or largest) item on top, with log-time push and pop.
pattern-heap-priority-queue.exampleWhy: Sorted descending: 6, 5, 5, 4, ... The fourth value is 4.

brute.idea: Rescan for the best item every time: find the max, delete it, repeat k - 1 times. Or sort everything.
steps: Find the max with a full scan
Remove it; repeat k - 1 times
Return the max of what is left
brute.whySlow: Each removal rescans the list. With 100,000 numbers and k = 50,000 that is billions of steps.

optimal.insight: Keep only the items that could still matter. For the k largest, a size-k min-heap: its top is the weakest survivor, evicted in log k.
steps: Pick min-heap or max-heap (negate values for max in Python)
Push each new item onto the heap
If the heap grows past k, pop the top
Read the answer from the top, heap[0]

codeNotes.note: Step 1: min-heap of the best k
Step 2: push every item, log k
Evict the smallest, it cannot win
Step 4: top is the kth largest

pitfalls: Python's heapq is a min-heap only; negate values to simulate a max-heap.
Kth largest wants a MIN-heap of size k, not a max-heap of everything.
signals: kth largest or kth smallest
top k, k closest, k most frequent
repeatedly take the biggest or smallest
median of a data stream
schedule tasks by priority or time
variants: size-k min-heap for top k
max-heap via negated values
two heaps for a running median
heap of (priority, item) tuples

say.intro: Okay, heaps, also called priority queues. A heap always keeps the smallest item on top. Pushing or popping costs only log n. Interviewers love it, because so many problems secretly ask, what's the best item right now? Our example finds the fourth largest number. Reading from the top: six, five, five, four. So it's four.
say.brute: Without a heap, people rescan. Find the maximum with a full pass, delete it, and repeat k minus one times. Then the max of what's left is the answer. It's correct. So what's wrong? Every removal rescans the whole list. That's n times k. With a hundred thousand numbers and a big k, that's billions of steps.
say.insight: Here's the trick. Only keep what could still matter. For the k largest, keep a min heap of size k. Why a min heap? Its top is the weakest survivor, the first one to kick out. And the recipe works everywhere. Pick min or max. Push each item. If the heap grows past k, pop the top. Then read the answer off the top.
say.anim: We start with an empty heap, aiming to find the fourth largest number. Numbers three, two, three, and one are pushed, filling the heap to size four. Pushing two makes the heap too big, so the smallest item gets popped out. Four is pushed, then the weakest survivor is evicted again to keep size four. Five enters, bumping out the smallest, keeping only the four largest values seen. Another five pushes in, and the smallest element is popped once more. Finally six is pushed, evicting the smallest to maintain the top four largest. The heap's top, four, is returned as the fourth largest number overall.
say.code: Start with an empty min heap. For each number, push it in. That costs log k. Now check the size. More than k? Pop the top, which evicts the smallest. It can't be in the top k anymore. After the loop, the heap holds exactly the k largest. And the top, index zero, is the kth largest. Change what you push, and this same loop finds k closest points.
say.outro: n log k time, k space. Reach for a heap when you hear: kth largest, top k, k closest, always take the biggest, a running median, or scheduling by priority.

lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which holds the method that finds the kth largest number in a list.
The method takes the list nums and the integer k, and returns the kth largest value as an integer.
We start with an empty list called heap, which will act as a min-heap holding our best candidates.
We loop over every number n in nums, considering each one as a possible member of the top k.
We push n onto the heap, and the heap keeps its smallest item on top in log time.
If the heap now holds more than k items, then one of them can no longer be among the k largest.
We pop the smallest item, which is the weakest survivor, so the heap never grows beyond size k.
After the loop, the heap holds the k largest numbers, and its top is the smallest of them, which is the kth largest.

pattern-backtracking.title: Backtracking — the pattern
pattern-backtracking.hook: Generate every combination, permutation, or board? Backtracking is one recipe: choose, explore, undo.
pattern-backtracking.ask: Backtracking builds a candidate one choice at a time, recursing on each choice and undoing it afterwards, so every option is explored exactly once.
pattern-backtracking.exampleWhy: Three numbers, each in or out, gives 2³ = 8 subsets.

brute.idea: Make choices in any order with no fixed decision sequence, then throw away the duplicates at the end.
steps: From each selection, try adding every unused index
Record the sorted selection in a set
Turn the set into the answer list
brute.whySlow: Each subset of size k is built k! times. At n = 10 that is about 10 million paths for only 1,024 subsets.

optimal.insight: Fix the order of decisions. At each step make one choice, recurse, then undo it. That walks a decision tree whose every leaf is a distinct answer.
steps: Define dfs(i): the next decision to make
Base case: record a copy of the current state
For each option: choose it, recurse, then undo it
Prune branches that already break a constraint

pattern-backtracking.optimalCode:
class Solution:
    def subsets(self, nums: List[int]) -> List[List[int]]:
        res = []

        subset = []

        def dfs(i):
            if i >= len(nums):
                res.append(subset.copy())
                return
            # decision to include nums[i]
            subset.append(nums[i])
            dfs(i + 1)
            # decision NOT to include nums[i]
            subset.pop()
            dfs(i + 1)

        dfs(0)
        return res

codeNotes.note: Step 2: every decision made, a leaf
Record a copy, not the live list
Step 1: start at the first decision

pitfalls: Appending the path itself instead of a copy — later pops erase every saved answer.
Forgetting to undo a choice, so state leaks into sibling branches.
signals: return all subsets, combinations, or permutations
generate every valid arrangement
place items under constraints, like N-Queens
find a word path in a grid
n is tiny, around 10 to 20
variants: include or exclude each item (subsets)

used-set for permutations
sort, then skip duplicates

say.intro: Okay, backtracking. Whenever a problem says return all the subsets, combinations, or arrangements, this is the tool. We build an answer one choice at a time. Interviewers love it because it shows clean recursion and clean state. Our example: every subset of one, two, three. Each number is in or out, so eight subsets.
say.brute: Without the pattern, people grow selections in any order. Add any unused number, then any other, and so on. Sort each one, and drop it in a set to remove repeats. It finds every subset. But here's the catch. It builds the same subset many times, once per ordering. At ten numbers, that's about ten million paths for roughly a thousand answers.
say.insight: Here's the fix. Fix the order of decisions. Walk the numbers left to right, making one choice at a time. The recipe is always the same. Choose. Recurse. Undo. When you hit the bottom, record a copy. And if a branch already breaks a rule, prune it early. That walks a decision tree where every leaf is a different answer.
say.anim: We start with nums one two three, an empty subset, and an empty results list. We include one, then two, then three, building subset one two three by making choices. At index three we stop and save subset one two three into results, our first leaf. We undo three, backtrack, and now skip it, saving subset one two as another leaf. Back at one, we skip two instead, try three, saving one three, then just one. We undo one entirely and explore starting from two, repeating the include and skip choices. Finally we try starting from only three, saving three alone and then the empty set. All branches explored, giving the final answer: eight subsets from empty to one two three.
say.code: Our helper decides about index i. If i reaches the end, every decision is made. So we record a copy of the subset. Why a copy? Later pops would erase it. Then we choose. Append the number, and recurse on i plus one. Then we undo it with a pop. That's the backtrack. Then we recurse again without it. We start at index zero.
say.outro: n times two to the n, which matches the output size. Spot backtracking when you hear: all subsets, all combinations, permutations, placing items under rules, or a tiny n. Choose, recurse, undo.

We create subset as an empty working list that holds our current choices as we explore.

If i has reached the length of nums, every number has been decided, so we are at a leaf.
At a leaf we append a copy of subset to res, since subset will keep changing later.
We return to stop recursing and let the caller backtrack to an earlier decision.
This comment marks the first branch, where we choose to include the current number.
We append the number at index i to subset to make the include choice.
We recurse on the next index to explore every way to finish the decisions with this number included.
This comment marks the second branch, where we choose to leave the current number out.
We pop the number off subset to undo the include choice, which is the backtracking step.
We recurse on the next index again to explore every completion with this number excluded.
We start the search by calling dfs at index zero with an empty subset.
We return res, which now holds all subsets, one for each leaf of the decision tree.

pattern-tries.title: Tries — the pattern
pattern-tries.hook: When a problem keeps asking about prefixes, stop comparing whole words and share the letters instead.
pattern-tries.ask: A trie is a tree where each edge is one letter, so words with a common prefix share a path and lookups cost only the word length.
pattern-tries.exampleWhy: "app" is only a prefix of apple until we insert it; then search("app") flips from false to true.

brute.idea: Store whole words in a plain list, and scan or slice every stored word for each query.
steps: insert: append the word to a list
search: compare against every stored word
startsWith: check each word's beginning
brute.whySlow: With 30,000 calls and thousands of stored words, every query rescans everything: hundreds of millions of character comparisons.

optimal.insight: Words sharing a prefix share a path. Store one node per letter; any query walks only its own letters, so cost depends on length, not word count.
steps: Node: one child per letter, plus an end-of-word flag
Insert: walk the letters, create missing children, mark the end
Lookup: walk the letters, fail early on a missing child
Exact word checks the end flag; a prefix needs only the path

codeNotes.note: Marks where a full word ends
Step 4: exact word needs the end flag

pitfalls: search must check the end flag; reaching the last node only proves a prefix exists.
Forgetting to step curr down to the child, so every letter hangs off the root.
signals: prefix, starts with, or autocomplete
many words searched against one input
wildcard search with dots
find all dictionary words in a grid
variants: insert, search, startsWith
DFS through the trie for wildcards
trie plus grid backtracking (Word Search II)

say.intro: Okay, tries, also called prefix trees. A trie stores words letter by letter, so words that start the same share a path. Interviewers love it for autocomplete and word search questions. Our example inserts apple, then asks about app. It's only a prefix, until we insert app itself.
say.brute: Without a trie, people keep a plain list of words. Insert appends. Search compares against every word. Starts with checks the front of every word. It's correct. So what's the problem? Every query pays for the number of words times their length. With tens of thousands of calls, that's hundreds of millions of character comparisons.
say.insight: Notice that apple and app share three letters. So why store them twice? Store letters, not words. Each node has one child per letter, plus a flag that says a word ends here. Insert walks the letters, creating missing nodes. Lookup walks the same way, and stops early on a missing child. So cost depends on word length, never on how many words exist.
say.anim: We create a new trie with an empty root node to start. Inserting apple, we walk letter by letter, creating new child nodes as needed. After inserting all letters, the final node for apple is marked as end of word. Searching apple, we follow the same path and find the end flag true, so it returns true. Searching app follows the same letters but stops at a node where end is false, returning false. Checking startsWith app just walks the path and confirms the nodes exist, returning true. Now we insert app itself, marking its final node's end flag as true. Searching app again now reaches a node with end true, so the final answer is true.
say.code: Each node has twenty six slots, one per letter, and an end flag. Insert turns each letter into a slot index. Missing child? Create it, then step down. At the end, mark the word. Search does the same walk, but returns the end flag, because the word must finish there. Starts with only needs the path to exist, so it returns true.
say.outro: Time proportional to the word length, per operation. Spot a trie when you hear: prefix, starts with, autocomplete, wildcard search, or many words searched at once.

pattern-graphs.title: Graphs — the pattern
pattern-graphs.hook: Grids, prerequisites, friendships: all graphs. One visited set plus DFS or BFS cracks most of them.
pattern-graphs.ask: Graph traversal explores nodes along their edges with DFS or BFS, marking each node visited so it is processed exactly once.
pattern-graphs.exampleWhy: The top-left L shape, the right-hand pair, and the lone cell at the bottom are three separate islands.

brute.idea: Ignore the graph structure: sweep the whole grid repeatedly, letting touching cells share the smaller label until nothing changes.
steps: Label each land cell with a unique number
Sweep: neighbours both take the smaller label
Repeat sweeps until no label changes
Count distinct labels
brute.whySlow: A 300 by 300 winding island may need tens of thousands of full sweeps of 90,000 cells each.

optimal.insight: Model cells or items as nodes and connections as edges. Start a traversal from each unvisited node; one traversal covers exactly one connected component.
steps: Model nodes and edges: grid neighbours or an adjacency list
Keep a visited set so nothing is processed twice
Loop over all nodes; DFS or BFS from each unvisited one
Do the per-component work: count, measure, or record

codeNotes.note: Not an edge: water stops the search

Check bounds before indexing; only four directions connect unless stated.
signals: a grid of land, water, or cells
connected, reachable, islands, or regions
prerequisites or dependencies between items
fewest steps in an unweighted graph
clone or copy a graph
variants: DFS flood fill on a grid
multi-source BFS (rotting oranges)

say.intro: Okay, graphs. Grids, course prerequisites, friend networks. They're all nodes joined by edges. Interviewers love graphs because one tool, a traversal with a visited set, cracks most of them. Our example counts islands. In this three by four grid, land cells touching sideways form one island. There are three.
say.brute: Without the pattern, people try repeated sweeps. Give every land cell its own label. Then sweep the whole grid again and again, letting touching cells share the smaller label, until nothing changes. Count the labels. It works. But a long, winding island can need thousands of full sweeps. That's quadratic in the number of cells.
say.insight: Here's the shift. See the grid as a graph. Each land cell is a node, joined to its land neighbours. Now the recipe. Keep a visited set. Loop over every node. Find one that's unvisited? Start a depth first or breadth first search from it. That one search covers its whole connected piece. Then do your work, like counting it.
say.anim: We start with the grid loaded and begin scanning each cell for unvisited land. At row zero column zero we find a one, so islands becomes one and we explore from there. The depth first search spreads to neighboring ones, marking zero one and one zero as visited. Scanning continues and a new unvisited one appears at row zero column three, so islands becomes two. That search floods into one three, since connected cells belong to the same island. Later another unvisited one at row two column one starts a third traversal, making islands three. The remaining cells are either water or already visited, so no more islands are found. The function returns three, matching the expected total number of islands.
say.code: We keep a visited set. The search stops at the grid edge, at water, or at a cell we've seen. Otherwise, we mark this cell visited. Then we spread in all four directions. Those neighbours are the edges. The main loop scans every cell. Unvisited land means a new component. So we bump the count, and launch the search. One search equals one island.
say.outro: Linear in nodes plus edges. Spot graphs when you hear: a grid of cells, connected or reachable, islands or regions, prerequisites, or fewest steps. Then traverse with a visited set.

pattern-advanced-graphs.title: Advanced Graphs — the pattern
pattern-advanced-graphs.hook: When edges have weights, plain BFS gives wrong answers. Dijkstra swaps the queue for a min-heap.
pattern-advanced-graphs.ask: Advanced graph problems add weights or ordering; Dijkstra's shortest path handles weights by always finalizing the closest unfinished node next, using a min-heap.
pattern-advanced-graphs.exampleWhy: Node 2 is fastest via 3 (1+2=3), then node 4 via 2 at time 4. The slowest node finishes at 4.

brute.idea: Ignore which node is closest: relax every edge, round after round, n - 1 times, until distances settle (Bellman-Ford).
steps: dist[k] = 0, others infinity
Repeat n - 1 times: relax every edge
Answer is the largest distance, or -1
brute.whySlow: With 100 nodes and 6,000 edges, that is 600,000 relaxations, mostly wasted on already-settled nodes.

optimal.insight: With non-negative weights, the unfinished node with the smallest known distance can never get closer. Pop it from a min-heap, finalize it, relax its edges.
steps: Build an adjacency list of (neighbour, weight)
Push (0, source) onto a min-heap
Pop the closest; skip it if already finalized
Finalize it; push neighbours with distance plus weight
Read the answer from finalized distances; unreached means -1

Dijkstra fails with negative weights or hop limits; use Bellman-Ford rounds instead.
signals: weighted edges: cost, time, or distance
cheapest or fastest path between nodes
connect all points at minimum cost
an ordering derived from comparison rules
minimise the worst step along a path

say.intro: Okay, advanced graphs. Now edges have weights, like time or cost. A plain breadth first search no longer finds the best path. Interviewers love this because it tests Dijkstra, Prim, and friends. Our example: a signal leaves node one. Node three hears it at one, node two at three, node four at four. So the answer is four.
say.brute: Without the pattern, people relax everything blindly. That's Bellman Ford. Start every distance at infinity, except the source at zero. Then relax every edge, again and again, n minus one rounds. If an edge offers a shorter time, take it. It's correct. But it costs V times E. Most rounds just recheck nodes that settled long ago.
say.insight: Here's the key. With no negative weights, the unfinished node with the smallest known distance can never get closer. Why? Every other route already costs more. So the recipe is simple. Keep a min heap of distance and node. Pop the closest. Already finished? Skip it. Otherwise, lock it in, and push its neighbours with distance plus weight.
say.anim: We first build an adjacency list from the times array, mapping each node to its outgoing edges. The heap starts with node one at distance zero, and visit is empty. We pop node one, mark it visited, then push its neighbors two and three with distances four and one. Next we pop node three, the smallest distance one, finalize it, and relax its edges to two and four. Now node two pops with distance three, becomes finalized, and pushes neighbor four at distance four. A duplicate entry for node two is skipped since it's already visited. Node four finally pops with distance four, gets finalized, completing all nodes. All nodes are visited, so the function returns the final answer, four.
say.code: First, build an adjacency list with weights. The heap starts with distance zero at the source. Pop the closest entry. Already visited? It's stale, so skip it. Otherwise, mark it, and record its time. That time is now final. Then push each unvisited neighbour with time plus edge weight. At the end, if every node was reached, return the last time. If not, minus one.
say.outro: E log V time. Spot advanced graphs when you hear: weighted edges, cheapest or fastest path, connect everything at minimum cost, ordering from rules, or minimise the worst step.

pattern-1-d-dynamic-programming.title: 1-D Dynamic Programming — the pattern
signals: maximum or minimum total over a sequence
count the number of ways to reach n
each step depends on the previous one or two
take it or skip it, with a restriction
can this string or amount be built from pieces

pattern-1-d-dynamic-programming.hook: Exponential recursion collapses into one pass once you store each answer by index.
pattern-1-d-dynamic-programming.ask: Solve a sequence problem by defining best(i) as the answer for the first i items, building each from a few earlier answers.
pattern-1-d-dynamic-programming.exampleWhy: Houses hold 2, 7, 9, 3, 1; no two neighbours robbed. Best plan takes 2, 9 and 1 for 12.

brute.idea: Write the natural recursion: at each item, try every choice and recurse on what remains. Correct, but it re-solves the same suffixes again and again.
steps: Define best(i) for the rest of the list
Try each choice: take or skip
Recurse and keep the best
No caching: same i solved many times
brute.whySlow: Each house doubles the call tree. With 100 houses that is around 2^100 calls for only 100 distinct states.

optimal.insight: The recursion has only n distinct states, one per index. Store each answer once, in index order, so every state reads finished smaller states.
steps: Define the state: dp[i] = best answer using the first i items
Write the recurrence from a few earlier states
Set base cases, then fill i from small to large
Keep only the states the recurrence still needs

Base cases and fill order matter: never read a state before it is computed.

say.intro: Okay, so this is one dimensional dynamic programming. The answer for position i is built from answers at a few earlier positions. Interviewers love it because the naive recursion is exponential, and one small idea makes it linear. Our example is House Robber. Houses with two, seven, nine, three, one. No two neighbours. The best is twelve.
say.brute: So what do people try first? Recursion. At each house, either rob it and jump two ahead, or skip it and move one ahead. Take the better result. That's correct. So what's the catch? The same suffix gets solved over and over. Every house doubles the call tree. A hundred houses means two to the hundred calls, for only a hundred real questions.
say.insight: Here's the thing. There are only n different questions. What's the best answer up to house i? So answer each one once, in order. Here's the recipe. One, define the state. Two, write the recurrence. For us, skip this house, or take it plus the best from two back. Three, set base cases and fill left to right. Four, keep only what you still need.
say.anim: We start with prev2 and prev1 both zero, tracking best robbed amounts so far. At house value 2, cur becomes max of zero and zero plus two, so two. Next house is seven, cur becomes max of two and zero plus seven, so seven. Now prev2 is two and prev1 is seven, moving to house value nine. Cur becomes max of seven and two plus nine, giving eleven, skipping adjacent house. With house three, cur stays eleven since robbing it wouldn't beat current best. Last house is one, cur becomes max of eleven and eleven plus one, twelve. The loop ends and the function returns prev1, giving final answer twelve.
say.code: Now the code. The two previous states start at zero. Those are our base cases, no houses yet. Then we fill the states in index order, one house at a time. The recurrence is one line. Skip this house and keep the previous best, or take it plus the best from two back. Then we slide both states forward. Only the last two matter. At the end, the final state is our answer.
say.outro: Linear time, constant space. Listen for these signals. A best total over a sequence. Counting ways to reach n. Each step depending on the last one or two. And take it or skip it with a rule.

lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container the problem expects for our method.
The rob method takes a list of house values called nums and returns the largest total we can steal.
We start prev2 and prev1 at zero, representing the best totals for zero houses and for the house before.
We loop through each house value n in order, so every state reads answers that are already finished.
The best for this house is the larger of skipping it, prev1, or robbing it and adding n to prev2.
We slide the window forward, so prev2 becomes old prev1 and prev1 becomes the new best, cur.
After the loop, prev1 holds the best total for all houses, so we return it.

pattern-2-d-dynamic-programming.title: 2-D Dynamic Programming — the pattern
signals: two strings or sequences compared together
grid paths: count or minimise moves
choose items with a capacity or target
minimum edits to turn one into another
count subsequences matching a pattern
variants: two strings: dp[i][j] over suffixes or prefixes
grid walking: cell from top and left
knapsack: items by remaining amount
interval DP: dp over ranges l..r
pattern-2-d-dynamic-programming.hook: When the recursion needs two indices, the memo becomes a grid you fill cell by cell.
pattern-2-d-dynamic-programming.ask: Solve a problem whose state needs two numbers, like positions in two strings, by filling a table where each cell uses nearby cells.
pattern-2-d-dynamic-programming.exampleWhy: a, c and e appear in order in both "abcde" and "ace", so the longest common subsequence has length 3.

brute.idea: Recurse on two indices: compare the current characters, and on a mismatch try skipping from either string. Correct, but each mismatch branches twice.
steps: State is a pair (i, j)
Match: 1 plus recurse on (i + 1, j + 1)
Mismatch: best of skipping either side
No caching: pairs recomputed many times
brute.whySlow: Two 1,000-character strings can branch about 2^2000 times, yet only a million distinct (i, j) pairs exist.

optimal.insight: Every call is just a pair (i, j), so there are only m·n states. Lay them out as a grid and fill it so each cell's neighbours are already done.
steps: Define dp[i][j] using both indices
Recurrence: each cell reads a few neighbour cells
Add a border row and column for base cases
Fill in an order where neighbours come first; read the corner

codeNotes.match: dp = [[0 for j in range(len(text2) + 1)] for i in range(len(text1) + 1)]
codeNotes.note: Grid plus zero border: base cases
Mismatch: best of right or below
Corner cell holds the full answer

pitfalls: Off-by-one: the table is (m+1) by (n+1) so empty suffixes have a row.
Wrong fill order reads cells that are not computed yet.

say.intro: Okay, so this is two dimensional dynamic programming. It's the same idea as one dimensional, but the state needs two numbers. Positions in two strings. A row and a column. Interviewers love it because so many classics are secretly one grid. Our example: the longest common subsequence of a b c d e and a c e. That's three.
say.brute: So what do people try first? A recursion on two positions. Compare the current letters. If they match, count one and move both forward. If not, try skipping a letter from either string, and keep the better. It works. But every mismatch branches twice. Two thousand letters in total? That's two to the two thousand calls, for only a million real pairs.
say.insight: Here's the thing. Every call is just a pair, i and j. So there are only m times n questions. Put them in a grid. Here's the recipe. One, define the cell using both indices. Two, write how a cell reads its neighbours. Three, add a border for the base cases. Four, fill in an order where neighbours are ready, then read the corner.
say.anim: We build a grid dp sized for text1 and text2, all zeros to start. At i equals 4, j equals 2, letters e and e match, so dp becomes one plus the diagonal. When letters differ, we take the max of the cell to the right and below, filling row four. Moving to i equals 3, matching rules keep propagating best lengths leftward across the row. At i equals 2, matching c with c gives dp value two, building on earlier matches. Row one fills similarly, comparing neighbors since b and c don't match text2 letters. Finally at i equals 0, matching a with a adds one to get three in the corner. The function returns dp of zero zero, giving the final answer three.
say.code: Now the code. We build the grid with a border of zeros. Those are the base cases, empty suffixes. Then we loop i and j backwards, so the cells we need are always filled. If the letters match, the cell is one plus the diagonal. If not, it's the larger of the cell to the right and the cell below. Finally, the top left corner is the answer.
say.outro: m times n time and space. Listen for the signals. Two strings compared. Paths through a grid. Items against a capacity. Minimum edits. Or counting matching subsequences.

lineNotes: We define a solution class that holds the method for solving the longest common subsequence problem.
The method takes two strings and returns the length of their longest common subsequence as an integer.
We build a grid with one extra row and column of zeros, so empty suffixes give a length of zero.
We loop the first string's position from the last character down to the first, so later rows are filled first.
For each row we loop the second string's position from the end to the start, so right neighbors are ready.
We check whether the current characters of both strings match at these two positions.
On a match, we extend the best answer from the next positions in both strings by one.
Otherwise the characters do not match, so we must skip one of them.
We take the larger of skipping a character in the second string or skipping one in the first.
The top-left cell holds the answer for both full strings, so we return it.

pattern-greedy.title: Greedy — the pattern
signals: can you reach the end
minimum number of jumps, stops or groups
a best choice at each step looks obvious
one pass with a running max or total
dynamic programming works but feels too slow
variants: track the farthest reach so far
work backward from the goal
reset a running sum when it goes negative
process in sorted order, take smallest first
pattern-greedy.hook: Sometimes the locally best move is provably safe, and one pass beats exploring every path.
pattern-greedy.ask: Make the best choice available at each step, never undoing it, when you can prove a local best choice never ruins the final answer.
pattern-greedy.exampleWhy: From index 0 jump to 2, leap three to 5, then step to 6. Both zeros are jumped over.

brute.idea: Explore every option: from each reachable index, mark every index its jump can land on, then check whether the end got marked.
steps: Index 0 is reachable
From each reachable i, mark i+1 .. i+nums[i]
Is the last index marked?
brute.whySlow: Each reachable index can mark up to n others: 10,000 indices means up to 50 million marks.

optimal.insight: If index i can reach the goal, reaching i is just as good as reaching the goal. So pull the goal back to i the moment it can, and never reconsider.
steps: Name the one quantity worth tracking: goal, reach or running sum
Scan once in the right direction
At each item, make the locally best update
Prove it: the choice never blocks a better answer

codeNotes.note: Did the goal reach the start?

pitfalls: Greedy needs a proof; if a local choice can backfire, use DP instead.
Track the right quantity: >= goal, not == goal, since overshooting is fine.

say.intro: Okay, so this is greedy. At every step, you make the best local move, and you never take it back. Interviewers love it because the code is tiny, but you have to explain why it's safe. Our example is Jump Game. Each number is your maximum jump. Two, zero, three, one, zero, two, one. Can we reach the end? Yes.
say.brute: So what do people try first? Explore everything. Index zero is reachable. From each reachable index, mark every spot its jump can land on. At the end, is the last index marked? That's correct. But each index can mark a long range. So it's n squared. With ten thousand numbers, that's tens of millions of marks.
say.insight: Here's the thing. If some index can reach the goal, getting there is as good as getting to the goal. So pull the goal back to it, and never look again. Here's the recipe. One, pick the single quantity to track. Two, scan once in the right direction. Three, make the locally best update. Four, convince yourself it can't block a better answer.
say.anim: We start with the array and set goal to the last index, six. At index five, five plus two reaches six, so goal pulls back to five. At index four, four plus zero only reaches four, so goal stays unchanged. At index three, three plus one reaches four, but not five, so goal stays. At index two, two plus three reaches five, so goal shifts back to two. At index one, one plus zero can't reach two, so goal remains two. At index zero, zero plus two reaches goal two, so goal becomes zero. Goal equals zero, meaning the start can reach the end, so it returns true.
say.code: Now the code. The goal starts at the last index. That's the one quantity we track. Then a single scan, walking backward. At each index, can it reach the goal or jump past it? If so, that's our greedy move. The goal becomes this index, and we never undo it. At the end, we just ask, did the goal reach the start?
say.outro: Linear time, constant space. Listen for the signals. Can you reach the end. Minimum jumps or groups. An obvious best move. A running max. Or a DP that feels too slow.

lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container the interview platform expects for our method.
The canJump method takes the list nums, where each value is the maximum jump length from that index, and returns true or false.
We start by setting goal to the last index, since that is where we need to end up.
We walk backward from the second to last index down to zero, checking each position as a possible launch point.
If index i plus its jump length nums at i reaches or passes the current goal, then i can reach the goal.
Since i can reach the goal, we move the goal back to i and never reconsider that choice.
After the loop, the answer is true only if the goal has been pulled all the way back to index zero.

pattern-intervals.title: Intervals — the pattern
signals: list of start and end pairs
merge or insert overlapping ranges
fewest removals to stop overlaps
how many meetings at the same time
which interval covers this point
variants: sort by start, merge into last
sort by end, keep earliest finishing
split starts and ends, sweep events
min-heap of end times for rooms
pattern-intervals.hook: Sort by start, and every overlap lines up next to its neighbour. Then one sweep does it.
pattern-intervals.ask: Handle ranges with a start and end by sorting them, then sweeping once while comparing each range to the last one you kept.
pattern-intervals.exampleWhy: [1,3] and [2,6] overlap and become [1,6]; [8,10] and [15,18] touch nothing.

brute.idea: Compare every pair of intervals. Whenever two overlap, merge them and start scanning again, until no pair overlaps.
steps: Scan all pairs for an overlap
Merge that pair, restart the scan
No overlaps left: sort and return
brute.whySlow: Up to n merges, each rescanning n² pairs: 10,000 intervals means around a trillion checks.

optimal.insight: Once sorted by start, an interval can only overlap the last one you kept, because everything earlier already ended. So one comparison per interval is enough.
steps: Sort by start (or by end, for keep-most problems)
Keep a result list seeded with the first interval
Compare each interval only with the last kept one
Overlap: extend or drop; gap: append

codeNotes.note: Sort by start: overlaps become neighbours
Only the last kept can overlap

pitfalls: Decide if touching counts: [1,4] and [4,5] overlap here, so use <=.
Extend with max, not the new end: [1,10] then [2,3] stays [1,10].

say.intro: Okay, so this is the intervals pattern. You get ranges, each with a start and an end. Meetings, bookings, time slots. Interviewers love it because one sort turns a messy tangle into a single clean sweep. Our example is Merge Intervals. Eight to ten, one to three, fifteen to eighteen, two to six. Merge the overlaps.
say.brute: So what do people try first? Compare every pair. If two intervals overlap, merge them and start the search over. Keep going until nothing overlaps. Does it work? Yes. But each merge can rescan every pair, and there can be n merges. That's cubic. Ten thousand intervals means around a trillion checks.
say.insight: Here's the thing. Sort by start. Now a new interval can only overlap the last one you kept. Why? Everything earlier already ended. Here's the recipe. One, sort, usually by start. Two, seed the result with the first interval. Three, compare each one only with the last kept. Four, overlap means extend or drop. A gap means append.
say.anim: First the intervals get sorted by start, giving one, three then two, six then eight, ten then fifteen, eighteen. Output starts with the first interval, one to three, as our baseline. Start is two, end is six; since two is less than lastEnd three, they overlap. The last interval merges into one, six, extending its end. Next start is eight, but lastEnd is six, so eight does not overlap. Eight, ten gets appended as a brand new separate interval. Similarly fifteen exceeds lastEnd ten, so fifteen, eighteen is appended too. The function returns the merged result: one six, eight ten, and fifteen eighteen.
say.code: Now the code. First we sort by start, so overlaps become neighbours. We seed the output with the first interval. Then for each interval, grab the end of the last kept block. Only that one can overlap. If our start is at most that end, we extend it with the max. Why max? One interval might contain the other. Otherwise there's a gap, so we append a new block.
say.outro: n log n time, from the sort. Listen for the signals. Start and end pairs. Merging or inserting ranges. Fewest removals. Meetings at once. Which range covers a point.

lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container for the merge method that the problem expects.
The merge method takes a list of intervals, each with a start and end, and returns the merged list.
We sort the intervals by their start value so any overlap can only involve the most recently kept interval.
We seed the output with the first interval, so there is always a last kept interval to compare against.
We loop over every interval, unpacking each one into its start and its end.
We read the end of the last kept interval, which is the only one the current interval could overlap.
If the current start is at or before that last end, the two intervals overlap and must be merged.
We extend the last kept interval's end to the larger of the two ends, so containment is handled correctly.
Otherwise the current interval begins after the last one ended, meaning there is a gap between them.
In that case we append the current interval as a new separate entry in the output.
After the sweep, we return the output holding all the merged, non-overlapping intervals.

pattern-math-geometry.title: Math & Geometry — the pattern
signals: rotate, flip or spiral a matrix
do it in place, constant extra space
digits of a number, carry or overflow
power, square or cycle of numbers
points and squares on a plane
variants: layer by layer with shrinking bounds
index mapping like (r, c) to (c, n-1-r)
digit-by-digit math with carry
fast power by repeated squaring
pattern-math-geometry.hook: No fancy data structure: just find the index formula and move things exactly where they belong.
pattern-math-geometry.ask: Solve a grid or number problem by finding the exact formula for where each value goes, then applying it directly, often in place.
pattern-math-geometry.exampleWhy: Rotating clockwise, the left column read bottom to top (15,13,2,5) becomes the new top row.

brute.idea: Simulate the geometry with spare space: build a fresh grid, put each value at its rotated spot, then copy it all back.
steps: Make an empty n by n grid
Place matrix[r][c] at new[c][n-1-r]
Copy the new grid back into matrix
brute.whySlow: Time is fine, but it ignores the in-place rule: a 1000 by 1000 image needs a million extra cells.

optimal.insight: A 90 degree turn moves values in cycles of four corners. Work out the four index formulas, save one value, shift three, drop it in: no extra grid.
steps: Draw a small case and find the index mapping
Split the work into layers or cycles with clear bounds
Apply the mapping with one temp value
Shrink the bounds and repeat until they meet

codeNotes.note: Apply the mapping corner by corner
Shrink bounds to the next layer

pitfalls: Index offsets: work a 3 by 3 by hand before coding, e.g. bottom - i.
Overwriting a value you still need; save it first or use a marker.

say.intro: Okay, so this is math and geometry. No clever data structure here. You find the exact formula for where things go, and apply it directly. Interviewers love it because it tests careful index thinking under pressure. Our example is Rotate Image. Turn this four by four grid clockwise, in place. The left column becomes the top row.
say.brute: So what do people try first? Just simulate it with spare room. Build a brand new grid. The value at row r, column c lands at row c, column n minus one minus r. Then copy it all back. The time is fine. So what's the catch? It breaks the in place rule. A big image costs a million extra cells.
say.insight: Here's the thing. In a ninety degree turn, values move in cycles of four corners. So we only need one spare value. Here's the recipe. One, draw a small case and find the index mapping. Two, split the work into layers with clear bounds. Three, apply the mapping with one temp. Four, shrink the bounds and repeat until they meet.
say.anim: We start with the outer ring, left at zero and right at three, rotating layer by layer. We save the top left value, five, before overwriting it in the cycle. Bottom left's thirteen moves to top left, and the chain shifts three more values around the ring. Now i is one, so we grab one, cycle the next four corner positions, and place five correctly. With i at two, nine gets swapped around, finishing the outer ring rotation. The outer layer is done, so left and right shrink inward to rotate the inner square. Inside, four is saved and rotated among the remaining four positions, completing that smaller ring. Left meets right, the loop ends, giving the final rotated matrix with fifteen, thirteen, two, five as the top row.
say.code: Now the code. Left and right mark the outer layer. Each offset i is one four way cycle. We save the top left, since it's the only value overwritten. Then we apply the mapping corner by corner. Bottom left moves up, bottom right moves left, top right moves down. The saved value closes the cycle. Finally, we shrink the bounds to the next layer.
say.outro: n squared time, constant space. Listen for the signals. Rotate, flip or spiral a matrix. Do it in place. Digits and carries. Powers and cycles. Points on a plane.

lineNotes: We define a Solution class, as the problem setup requires, to hold the rotate method.
The rotate method takes a square matrix and turns it ninety degrees clockwise in place, returning nothing.
We set left to zero and right to the last index, marking the outermost square layer.
We loop while left is less than right, peeling one layer at a time moving inward.
For each layer we loop over the positions along its top edge, one fewer than the layer's side length.
We set top to left and bottom to right, since the layer is a square with equal sides.
We save the top left value of this four-corner cycle in a temporary variable, because it will be overwritten.
We move the bottom left value up into the top position, which is the first step of the clockwise shift.
We move the bottom right value into the bottom left position, shifting along the cycle.
We move the top right value down into the bottom right position, continuing the cycle.
We drop the saved top left value into the top right position, completing the four-way swap.
After finishing a layer we shrink right by one to move to the next inner layer.
We grow left by one so both boundaries step inward, and the loop continues with the smaller square.

pattern-bit-manipulation.title: Bit Manipulation — the pattern
signals: every element appears twice except one
constant extra space, linear time
count the 1 bits
add without plus or minus
find the missing number in 0..n
variants: XOR to cancel pairs
n & (n - 1) drops the lowest set bit
shift and mask to read each bit
