carry with AND, sum with XOR
pattern-bit-manipulation.hook: Numbers are just bits. A few bit rules replace whole hash maps and extra loops.
pattern-bit-manipulation.ask: Work on the binary form of numbers with AND, OR, XOR and shifts, using bit rules to cancel, count or combine values in constant space.
pattern-bit-manipulation.exampleWhy: 4, 1 and 2 each appear twice; only 5 appears once, so the answer is 5.

brute.idea: Ignore the bits and count directly: for each number, scan the whole list to count its copies, and return the one seen once.
steps: Pick nums[i]
Count its occurrences in the list
Count is 1? return it
brute.whySlow: With 30,000 numbers that is up to 900 million comparisons. A hash map is faster but breaks O(1) space.

optimal.insight: x XOR x is 0, x XOR 0 is x, and XOR ignores order. So XOR everything: every pair cancels, and only the single number is left.
steps: Find the bit rule that fits: cancel, count, or carry
Start from the identity value, like 0 for XOR
Fold every number in with one bit operation
What survives is the answer

pitfalls: Python ints are unbounded: mask with 0xFFFFFFFF for 32-bit negative tricks.
Operator precedence: wrap bit expressions in parentheses, e.g. (n & 1) == 1.

say.intro: Okay, so this is bit manipulation. Every number is just a row of bits. A few simple rules about AND, OR and XOR can replace whole hash maps. Interviewers love it because the answers are tiny and use constant space. Our example is Single Number. Every value appears twice, except one. Here, that's five.
say.brute: So what do people try first? Count directly. Take each number, and scan the whole list to count its copies. The one that shows up once is the answer. That's n squared. Thirty thousand numbers means nearly a billion comparisons. A hash map is linear. But it uses linear memory, and the problem asks for constant.
say.insight: Here's the thing. A number XOR itself is zero. Anything XOR zero stays the same. And order doesn't matter. So XOR everything, and every pair cancels. Here's the recipe. One, find the bit rule that fits. Cancel, count, or carry. Two, start from its identity value. Three, fold every number in. Four, what survives is the answer.
say.anim: We start with res at zero, ready to scan the list of numbers. We xor each number into res, so duplicates cancel each other out over time. After folding in four, one, and two, res becomes seven temporarily. Xoring the repeated one and two again cancels them back out, dropping res to four. Now we xor in five, the only number without a matching pair, giving res five. Folding in the second four cancels it completely, leaving res at five. All numbers processed, so the function returns the final res value. The single number appearing only once is five, matching the expected output.
say.code: Now the code. We start the result at zero, because anything XOR zero is itself. Then we fold in every number, one pass. Each step XORs the number into the result. That's the bit rule doing the work. Pairs cancel to zero. When the loop ends, only the single number survives, so we return it.
say.outro: Linear time, constant space. Listen for the signals. Everything twice except one. Constant space. Counting one bits. Adding without plus. Or a missing number.

lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container the interview platform expects for our method.
The singleNumber method takes a list of integers where every value appears twice except one, and returns that one.
We start res at zero, because XOR with zero leaves any value unchanged, making it a safe starting point.
We loop through every number in the list, visiting each one exactly once for linear time.
We XOR res with the current number, so matching pairs cancel to zero regardless of the order they appear.
After the loop only the unpaired number remains in res, so we return it using constant extra space.

pattern-prefix-sum.name: Prefix Sum
pattern-prefix-sum.title: Prefix Sum — the pattern
signals: sum of a subarray or range
many range-sum queries on fixed data
count subarrays with sum equal to k
negative numbers rule out a sliding window
variants: prefix array for range queries
prefix sum + hash map of counts
prefix modulo k for divisibility
2-D prefix sums for rectangles
pattern-prefix-sum.hook: Precompute running totals once, and any range sum becomes a single subtraction.
pattern-prefix-sum.ask: Prefix sum means storing the running total up to each index, so the sum of any range i..j is prefix[j+1] minus prefix[i].
pattern-prefix-sum.exampleWhy: Worked example Subarray Sum Equals K: [3,4], [7], [7,2,-3,1] and [1,4,2] each sum to 7.

brute.idea: Recompute every range sum from scratch: fix a start, stretch the end, and add numbers one by one.
steps: Pick a start i
Extend end j, adding nums[j]
Check the range sum against k
brute.whySlow: Every range re-adds numbers already summed: 20,000 numbers means about 200 million ranges.

optimal.insight: A range sum is the difference of two running totals. Keep the running total and remember earlier totals; a range ending here sums to k exactly when an earlier total equals current minus k.
steps: Seed with the empty prefix: total 0
Walk once, adding each number to the running total
Answer the range question with current minus an earlier prefix
Record the current prefix for later indices

codeNotes.note: Step 1: the empty prefix, seen once
Step 3: ranges ending here that sum to k
Step 4: record this prefix after checking

pitfalls: Forgetting the empty prefix {0: 1} misses ranges that start at index 0.
Reaching for a sliding window: with negative numbers, shrinking no longer works.

say.intro: Okay, prefix sums. This one shows up everywhere, from range queries to Google's subarray questions. Keep a running total, and any range sum becomes one subtraction. Our example: count subarrays summing to seven. Three plus four. Seven alone. Seven, two, minus three, one. And one, four, two. Four of them.
say.brute: Without the pattern, people fix a start, then stretch the end, adding numbers as they go. It works. But look at what's happening. The same numbers get added again and again, once for every range that contains them. Twenty thousand numbers means around two hundred million ranges. That's n squared, and it falls over.
say.insight: Here's the trick. The sum from i to j is just the running total at j, minus the running total before i. So keep the running total, and remember the earlier ones. The recipe: seed with an empty prefix of zero. Walk once, adding each number. Ask, did an earlier total equal current minus k? Then record the current total.
say.anim: We start with a running total of zero, and a map remembering that total zero has appeared once. Adding three makes prefix three, no earlier total matches three minus seven, so count stays zero. Adding four makes prefix seven, which matches zero plus k, so count becomes one. Prefix grows to fourteen, matching an earlier seven, so count rises to two. Prefix dips to thirteen after adding negative three, no match found, count unchanged. Prefix returns to fourteen again, matching the earlier seven, count becomes three. Finally prefix reaches twenty, matching thirteen minus seven, pushing count to four. The loop ends and the function returns four as the total subarrays summing to seven.
say.code: Here's the template. The map starts with zero, seen once. That's the empty prefix. Then one pass. Add the number to the running total. Now the key line. Look up prefix minus k, and add how many times we've seen it. Finally, record the current prefix. Check before you record, so a range is never empty.
say.outro: Linear time, linear space. Reach for prefix sums when you hear subarray or range sums, many range queries, counting sums equal to k, or negative numbers that break a sliding window.

lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container for the method that solves the subarray sum problem.
The method subarraySum takes a list of numbers and a target k, and returns how many subarrays sum to k.
We start a dictionary called seen with prefix total zero appearing once, so subarrays starting at index zero are counted.
We set both prefix and count to zero, tracking the running total and the number of matching subarrays.
We loop over each number x in nums, extending the running total one element at a time.
We add x to prefix so it holds the sum of everything up to the current position.
We add to count how many earlier totals equal prefix minus k, since each one marks a subarray ending here that sums to k.
We record the current prefix in seen, increasing its count by one, so later positions can match against it.
After scanning every element, we return count as the total number of subarrays whose sum equals k.

pattern-kadane-s-algorithm.name: Kadane's Algorithm
pattern-kadane-s-algorithm.title: Kadane's Algorithm — the pattern
signals: maximum or minimum sum of a contiguous subarray
best profit from one buy and one sell
extend the run or restart from here
maximum subarray in a circular array
variants: max subarray sum
min subarray sum (flip the max)
max product: track max and min
circular: total minus min subarray
pattern-kadane-s-algorithm.hook: One running sum and one rule, drop the past when it hurts, finds the best subarray in a single pass.
pattern-kadane-s-algorithm.ask: Kadane's algorithm tracks the best subarray ending at each index: either extend the previous one or start fresh, keeping the overall best.
pattern-kadane-s-algorithm.exampleWhy: Worked example Maximum Subarray: 4, -1, 2, 1 sums to 6, and no other run beats it.

brute.idea: Try every start, extend the end with a running sum, and keep the best total seen.
steps: Pick a start i
Extend j rightward, adding nums[j]
Track the best total
brute.whySlow: Each start redoes work the previous start already did: 100,000 numbers means about 5 billion slices.

optimal.insight: The best subarray ending here either extends the best one ending just before, or starts fresh at this element. A negative running sum can only hurt, so drop it. It is DP with a single variable.
steps: Track cur: the best sum ending at this index
For each element, extend or restart: max(x, cur + x)
Update the global best
Return the best after one pass

codeNotes.note: Step 1: start from the first element, not 0

pitfalls: Starting best at 0 returns 0 when every number is negative.
For products, track both max and min: a negative number flips them.

say.intro: Okay, Kadane's algorithm. It's the classic answer to maximum subarray, and interviewers love it because it's one tiny loop with a real idea inside. Our example has nine numbers with mixed signs. The best run is four, minus one, two, one. That sums to six.
say.brute: Without the pattern, you try every start. Then you stretch the end, keeping a running sum, and remember the biggest. It's correct. But each start redoes work the previous start already did. A hundred thousand numbers means about five billion pairs. That's n squared.
say.insight: Here's the idea. The best subarray ending right here has only two options. Extend the best one ending just before, or start fresh with this number. If the running sum went negative, it only drags you down, so drop it. The recipe: track current, pick extend or restart, update the global best, and finish in one pass.
say.anim: We start with best and cur both set to the first element, negative two. At x equals one, cur becomes max of one and negative one, so cur is one. At x equals negative three, extending hurts, so cur drops to negative two. At x equals four, starting fresh beats extending, so cur jumps to four, the new best. Adding two and one keeps extending, pushing cur up to six, our new best. A negative five drags cur down to one, but best stays at six. Adding four brings cur to five, still below the current best of six. The loop ends, and the function returns the best value, six.
say.code: Here's the template. Current and best both start at the first number, not zero. Then loop over the rest. The key line: current is the max of x alone, or current plus x. That's restart or extend. Then best takes the max with current. Return best. Two variables, one pass, constant space.
say.outro: Linear time, constant space. Reach for Kadane whenever you hear maximum or minimum subarray sum, one buy and one sell, extend or restart, or a circular max subarray.

lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container this problem's method lives in.
The method maxSubArray takes a list of integers called nums and returns the largest sum of any contiguous subarray.
We start both best and cur at the first element, since any subarray must include at least one number.
We loop over every remaining element, treating each one as x, the possible end of a subarray.
We set cur to the larger of x alone or cur plus x, dropping a negative running sum by starting fresh.
We update best to the larger of itself and cur, so it remembers the top sum seen at any index.
We return best, which now holds the maximum subarray sum across the entire list.

pattern-matrix-traversal.name: Matrix Traversal
pattern-matrix-traversal.title: Matrix Traversal — the pattern
signals: visit cells in spiral, diagonal or zigzag order
rotate, transpose or flip a 2-D grid
modify a matrix in place
walk along rows, columns or diagonals
variants: shrinking boundaries (spiral)
direction vectors with turns
diagonals: r + c or r - c constant
in-place layer swaps (rotate)
pattern-matrix-traversal.hook: Grids look scary, but most matrix questions are careful index walking with clear boundaries.
pattern-matrix-traversal.ask: Matrix traversal means visiting the cells of a 2-D grid in a deliberate order, row by row, by diagonals or in a spiral, by moving boundaries or direction vectors.
pattern-matrix-traversal.exampleWhy: Worked example Spiral Matrix: 1-4 across the top, 8 and 12 down, 11-9 back, 5 up, then 6 and 7.

brute.idea: Simulate a robot: keep a direction and a visited grid, turning whenever the next cell is off the edge or already seen.
steps: Start at the top-left heading right
Record the cell and mark it visited
If the next cell is blocked, turn clockwise
Stop after visiting every cell
brute.whySlow: Same time, but a visited grid as big as the input and fiddly turn logic: a 1000 by 1000 grid costs a million extra flags.
brute.code:
class Solution:
    def spiralOrder(self, matrix: List[List[int]]) -> List[int]:
        rows, cols = len(matrix), len(matrix[0])
        seen = [[False] * cols for _ in range(rows)]
        dirs = [(0, 1), (1, 0), (0, -1), (-1, 0)]
        r = c = d = 0
        res = []
        for _ in range(rows * cols):
            res.append(matrix[r][c])
            seen[r][c] = True
            nr, nc = r + dirs[d][0], c + dirs[d][1]
            if not (0 <= nr < rows and 0 <= nc < cols) or seen[nr][nc]:
                d = (d + 1) % 4
                nr, nc = r + dirs[d][0], c + dirs[d][1]
            r, c = nr, nc
        return res

optimal.insight: The unvisited part is always a rectangle. Describe it with four boundaries: top, bottom, left, right. Walk one edge, then shrink that boundary. The boundaries remember what is visited, so no extra grid is needed.
steps: Set boundaries: top, bottom, left, right
Walk one edge with a plain for loop
Shrink the boundary you just finished
Re-check the boundaries before walking back

codeNotes.match: while left < right and top < bottom:
codeNotes.note: Loop while the rectangle is non-empty

codeNotes.match: if not (left < right and top < bottom):

pitfalls: Skipping the re-check after two edges double-counts a lone middle row or column.
Mixing up rows and columns: matrix[r][c], with r bounded by len(matrix).

say.intro: Okay, matrix traversal. Google loves grid questions, and many are really about walking indexes in the right order. Spiral, diagonal, rotate. Our example is a three by four grid. Read it in a spiral: one to four, down to twelve, back to nine, then five, six, seven.
say.brute: Without a plan, people simulate a robot. Keep a direction, keep a visited grid, and turn right whenever you'd hit an edge or a cell you've seen. It works. But you need a second grid as big as the input, plus fiddly turning logic. A thousand by thousand grid means a million extra flags, and plenty of off-by-one bugs.
say.insight: Here's the cleaner way. The part you haven't visited is always a rectangle. Describe it with four boundaries: top, bottom, left, right. The recipe: walk one edge with a plain loop. Shrink that boundary. Repeat for each side. And re-check the boundaries before walking back, because a single row or column can remain.
say.anim: We start with boundaries left zero, right four, top zero, bottom three around the matrix. We walk the top row, collecting one, two, three, four into the result. Top moves down to one, so that row is now excluded from future passes. We walk the right column downward, adding eight and twelve, then shrink right to three. We walk the bottom row backward, adding eleven, ten, and nine, then shrink bottom. We walk the left column upward, adding five, then shrink left to one. With a smaller rectangle left, we grab the last top row values, six and seven. The rectangle collapses, the loop breaks, and the final spiral order is returned.
say.code: Here's the template. Four boundaries, with right and bottom exclusive. While the rectangle isn't empty, walk the top row and move top down. Walk the right column and move right in. Then the key check. If the rectangle is gone, stop. Otherwise walk the bottom row backwards, then the left column upwards, shrinking each one.
say.outro: Linear in cells, constant extra space. Reach for this when you hear spiral, diagonal or zigzag order, rotate or transpose a grid, change a matrix in place, or walk rows and columns.

lineNotes: We define a Solution class that holds the method for solving the spiral traversal problem.
The spiralOrder method takes a matrix of integers and returns its values in spiral order as a list.
We start with an empty result list that will collect the values in the order we visit them.
We set left to zero and right to the number of columns, so right is exclusive.
We set top to zero and bottom to the number of rows, so bottom is also exclusive.
We keep looping while the unvisited rectangle still has at least one column and one row.
This comment says the next loop collects every value along the current top row.
We walk i from left up to right, moving across the top row of the remaining rectangle.
Each value at the top row and column i is appended to the result.
We move the top boundary down by one because that row is now fully visited.
This comment says the next loop collects the values down the current right column.
We walk i from the new top down to bottom, moving along the rightmost remaining column.
Each value at row i in the last column of the rectangle is appended to the result.
We move the right boundary inward by one because that column is now visited.
After shrinking, we check whether the rectangle has become empty, which would make the next two passes repeat cells.
If no rows or columns remain, we break out of the loop early.
This comment says the next loop collects the bottom row, read from right to left.
We walk i backward from the last remaining column down to left, covering the bottom row in reverse.
Each value in the bottom row at column i is appended to the result.
We move the bottom boundary up by one because that row is finished.
This comment says the final loop collects the left column, read from bottom to top.
We walk i backward from the new bottom row up to top, moving up the leftmost column.
Each value at row i in the left column is appended to the result.
We move the left boundary inward by one, finishing a full lap, then the loop checks the smaller rectangle.
Once the rectangle is empty, we return the result list holding every value in spiral order.

pattern-sliding-window-fixed-size.name: Sliding Window — Fixed Size
pattern-sliding-window-fixed-size.title: Sliding Window — Fixed Size — the pattern
signals: subarray or substring of length exactly k
max, average or count over every k-window
k consecutive elements
each window reuses most of the last
variants: running sum over k elements
character counts over k letters
anagram or permutation in a window
distinct elements in every k-window
pattern-sliding-window-fixed-size.hook: When the window size is fixed, slide it: add the number coming in, subtract the one going out.
pattern-sliding-window-fixed-size.ask: A fixed-size sliding window keeps a running summary of exactly k consecutive elements and updates it in O(1) as the window moves one step.
pattern-sliding-window-fixed-size.exampleWhy: Worked example Maximum Average Subarray I: 12, -5, -6, 50 sums to 51, and 51 / 4 = 12.75.

brute.idea: For every start index, add up the next k numbers from scratch and keep the largest sum.
steps: Pick a start i
Sum nums[i] to nums[i + k - 1]
Keep the largest sum; divide by k
brute.whySlow: Neighbouring windows share k - 1 numbers, yet each is re-added: up to 2.5 billion additions for n = 100,000.

optimal.insight: Neighbouring windows share k - 1 elements. When the window moves, exactly one element enters and one leaves. Update the summary with just those two, and every window costs O(1).
steps: Build the first window of size k
Slide: add nums[i], remove nums[i - k]
Update the answer after each slide
Return the best seen

pitfalls: Off-by-one on the leaving element: it is nums[i - k], not nums[i - k + 1].
Forgetting to count the very first window before sliding.

say.intro: Okay, the fixed-size sliding window. Whenever a problem says exactly k in a row, this is your tool. Picture a frame of width k sliding along the array. Our example: the best average of four consecutive numbers. Twelve, minus five, minus six, fifty. That's fifty-one, over four. Twelve point seven five.
say.brute: Without the pattern, people take every start and add up the next k numbers from scratch. It's correct. But neighbouring windows share almost everything. Moving one step, you re-add k minus one numbers you just added. With a hundred thousand numbers and a big k, that's billions of additions. That's n times k.
say.insight: Here's the core idea. When the frame moves one step, exactly one number comes in, and exactly one goes out. So update with just those two. The recipe: build the first window. Then slide. Add the new number, subtract the one leaving. Update the answer after each slide, and return the best.
say.anim: We sum the first four numbers, one, twelve, negative five, negative six, giving window two. Best starts equal to this initial window value, two. At index four, fifty enters and one leaves, growing window to fifty one. Best updates to fifty one, the new maximum sum found. At index five, three enters and twelve leaves, shrinking window to forty two. At index six, negative two enters and negative five leaves, window becomes forty five. At index seven, negative four enters and negative six leaves, window becomes forty seven. Best stays fifty one, divided by k four gives final answer twelve point seven five.
say.code: Here's the template. First, sum the first k numbers. That's our starting window, and our best so far. Then loop from k to the end. The key line: add nums i, subtract nums i minus k. One in, one out. Update best. Finally divide by k. Notice the leaving index is i minus k, exactly k steps behind.
say.outro: Linear time, constant space. Reach for a fixed window when you hear length exactly k, max or average over every k-window, k consecutive elements, or windows that mostly overlap.

lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container the problem expects for our method.
The method findMaxAverage takes the list nums and the window size k, and returns the largest average as a float.
We compute the sum of the first k numbers once, which gives us the first window's total.
We set best to that first window sum, since it is the only window we have seen so far.
We loop index i from k to the end of nums, so each step moves the window right by one.
We update the window sum by adding the entering element at i and subtracting the leaving element k steps back.
We keep best as the larger of itself and the current window sum, tracking the maximum sum seen.
Finally we divide the best sum by k to get the maximum average, dividing only once at the end.

pattern-monotonic-queue-deque.name: Monotonic Queue (Deque)
pattern-monotonic-queue-deque.title: Monotonic Queue (Deque) — the pattern
signals: max or min of every sliding window
window limit on max minus min
best value among the last k DP states
subarray sum at least k with negatives
variants: decreasing deque for window max
increasing deque for window min
two deques for a max - min limit
deque over prefix sums
pattern-monotonic-queue-deque.hook: Keep a deque of candidates in decreasing order, and the window's maximum is always waiting at the front.
pattern-monotonic-queue-deque.ask: A monotonic queue is a deque of indices whose values stay sorted, so the max or min of a sliding window is read from the front in O(1).
pattern-monotonic-queue-deque.exampleWhy: Worked example Sliding Window Maximum: the six windows of size 3 have maxima 3, 3, 5, 5, 6, 7.

brute.idea: For each window position, scan all k numbers in it and take the largest.
steps: For each start i
Scan nums[i] to nums[i+k-1]
Append the maximum
brute.whySlow: Each step rescans almost the same numbers: with n = 100,000 and k = 50,000, that is billions of comparisons.

optimal.insight: When a bigger number arrives, every smaller number before it can never be a window max again: it leaves sooner and is smaller. Throw them out. What remains is decreasing, so the front is the max; pop it only when it slides out.
steps: Store indices in a deque, values kept decreasing
Pop from the back while the new value beats them
Pop from the front when its index leaves the window
Read the answer from the front

codeNotes.note: Step 1: deque of indices, values decreasing
Step 2: smaller values can never win again
The new index joins at the back
Step 3: front index slid out of the window
Step 4: the front is the window max

pitfalls: Storing values instead of indices, so you cannot tell when the front has left the window.
Reaching for a heap: it works, but costs O(n log n) and needs lazy deletion.

say.intro: Okay, the monotonic queue. It's the go-to answer whenever you need the max or min of every sliding window, and Google asks it a lot. Our example: windows of size three over eight numbers. The maxima come out three, three, five, five, six, seven.
say.brute: Without the pattern, people scan each window to find its max. For every start, look at all k numbers. It's correct. But each step throws away what it learned and rescans almost the same numbers. With a hundred thousand numbers and k of fifty thousand, that's billions of comparisons. That's n times k.
say.insight: Here's the core idea. When a bigger number arrives, every smaller one before it is useless. It leaves the window sooner, and it's smaller. So throw it out. The recipe: keep indices in a deque, values decreasing. Pop the back while the new value beats them. Pop the front when it slides out. The front is your answer.
say.anim: We start with an empty deque and window size three, scanning the array left to right. At index one, value three is bigger, so it pops the smaller one and the deque holds just one. Index two adds negative one, giving a decreasing deque of one and two, window not full yet. Index three adds negative three, window size three reached, so the front value three becomes the first max. At index four, value five pops both smaller entries, becoming the new front and next max. Index five's three is smaller, so it just appends, keeping five as the max. Index six's six pops smaller entries again, becoming the new maximum for its window. Index seven's seven pops everything else, becoming the final window's maximum. The final sliding window maximums are three, three, five, five, six, and seven.
say.code: Here's the template. The deque holds indices, not values, so we know when they expire. For each new number, pop from the back while those values are smaller or equal. Then append our index. If the front index fell out of the window, pop it from the front. Once the first window is full, the front is the max. Each index enters once, leaves once.
say.outro: Linear time, order k space. Reach for a monotonic queue when you hear max or min of every window, a limit on max minus min, the best of the last k DP states, or sums with negatives.

lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container the interview platform expects for our method.
The method takes the list nums and window size k, and returns the maximum of each sliding window.
We create an empty deque that will hold indices whose matching values are kept in decreasing order.
We start an empty result list that will collect the maximum of each completed window.
We loop through nums, getting both the index i and the value x at each step.
While the deque is not empty and its last value is at most x, that old value is now useless.
We pop those smaller indices from the back, since they leave sooner and are smaller than x, so they can never be a maximum.
We append the current index, which keeps the deque values decreasing from front to back.
If the front index has fallen outside the window ending at i, it is expired and needs removal.
We pop the expired index from the front of the deque.
Once i reaches k minus one, the first full window exists, so we can start recording answers.
We append the value at the front index, because the front always holds the current window's maximum.
After processing every element, we return the list of window maximums.

pattern-monotonic-stack.name: Monotonic Stack
pattern-monotonic-stack.title: Monotonic Stack — the pattern
signals: next greater or next smaller element
how many days until a warmer day
span or visibility over previous elements
largest rectangle bounded by heights
variants: decreasing stack for next greater
increasing stack for next smaller
indices on the stack for distances
circular array: loop twice
pattern-monotonic-stack.hook: A stack that stays sorted answers 'what is the next bigger element?' for everyone in one pass.
pattern-monotonic-stack.ask: A monotonic stack keeps unanswered elements in sorted order; when a new element breaks that order, it is the answer for everything it pops.
pattern-monotonic-stack.exampleWhy: Worked example Next Greater Element I: in [1,3,4,2], 1 is followed by 3, while 4 and 2 have nothing bigger after them.

brute.idea: For each value, find it in the array, then scan to the right for the first bigger value.
steps: Locate x in nums2
Scan right for a bigger value
Record it, or -1
brute.whySlow: Every query rescans the same stretch: 1,000 queries over 1,000 numbers is a million comparisons, n² on a full array.

optimal.insight: Elements still waiting for a bigger value form a decreasing stack. When a bigger value arrives, it is the answer for every smaller value on top, so pop them and record it. Each element is pushed once and popped once.
steps: Keep a stack of items still waiting for an answer
For each new item, pop while it beats the top
Record the new item as each popped item's answer
Push the new item; leftovers get the default

codeNotes.note: Step 1: values still waiting for an answer
Step 3: x answers every popped value
Step 4: x now waits its turn

pitfalls: Getting the comparison backwards: pop on smaller for next greater, on larger for next smaller.
Pushing values when you need distances or positions: push indices instead.

say.intro: Okay, the monotonic stack. Any time a question asks for the next bigger or next smaller element, think of this. Our example: for four, one and two, find the next greater value in the second array. Four and two have nothing bigger after them. One is followed by three.
say.brute: Without the pattern, people find each number, then scan to the right until something bigger shows up. It's correct. But every query rescans the same stretch of numbers, again and again. A thousand queries over a thousand numbers is a million comparisons. That's n times m, and on a full array, n squared.
say.insight: Here's the core idea. Numbers still waiting for a bigger value form a decreasing stack. When a bigger one arrives, it's the answer for every smaller number on top. The recipe: keep waiters on a stack. Pop while the new item beats the top. Record it as their answer. Push the new item. Leftovers get the default.
say.anim: We start with nums1 as 4,1,2 and nums2 as 1,3,4,2, using an empty stack and map. X is 1, the stack is empty, so we simply push 1 onto the stack. X is 3, and since 1 is smaller, we pop it and record its next greater value as 3. Stack is empty now, so we push 3 onto the stack to wait for something bigger. X is 4, so 3 is popped and mapped to 4 since it is the next greater value. Stack is empty again, so we push 4, waiting for a bigger number ahead. X is 2, which is smaller than 4, so we just push 2 onto the stack. Finally we look up each value in nums1, giving the result minus one, three, minus one.
say.code: Here's the template. A map for answers, and an empty stack of waiting values. Walk the array once. The key loop: while the stack isn't empty and the top is smaller than x, pop it, and x becomes its answer. Then push x to wait its turn. Finally, look up each query, defaulting to minus one. Every value is pushed once, popped once.
say.outro: Linear time, linear space. Reach for a monotonic stack when you hear next greater or smaller element, days until warmer, spans over previous elements, or the largest rectangle under heights.

lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container for the method that solves the next greater element problem.
This method takes nums1, a list of query values, and nums2, the list in which we look for next greater values.
We create an empty dictionary called nxt that will map each number to its next greater element.
We create an empty stack that holds numbers still waiting to find a bigger value after them.
We walk through every number x in nums2 from left to right, treating each as a possible answer.
While the stack has items and its top is smaller than x, that top has just found its answer.
We pop the smaller top and record x as its next greater element in the dictionary.
After popping smaller values, we push x onto the stack so it can wait for its own bigger value.
For each value in nums1 we look up its next greater element, using negative one when none exists, and return that list.

pattern-in-place-linked-list-reversal.name: In-place Linked List Reversal
pattern-in-place-linked-list-reversal.title: In-place Linked List Reversal — the pattern
signals: reverse a list, or part of it
reverse every k nodes or swap pairs
do it in place, O(1) extra space
compare the second half with the first half
variants: reverse the whole list
reverse a sublist between left and right
reverse in groups of k
reverse the second half, then compare or weave
pattern-in-place-linked-list-reversal.hook: Three pointers flip any stretch of a list in place, with zero extra memory.
pattern-in-place-linked-list-reversal.ask: In-place reversal means walking a linked list with prev, cur and next pointers, turning each arrow around as you go, then stitching the reversed piece back in.
pattern-in-place-linked-list-reversal.exampleWhy: Worked example Reverse Linked List II: flip positions 2 to 4 of 1→2→3→4→5 to get 1→4→3→2→5.

brute.idea: Copy the values into an array, reverse the slice there, then write the values back into the nodes.
steps: Walk the list, copy values to an array
Reverse the slice in the array
Walk again, overwrite node values
brute.whySlow: It needs O(n) extra memory and swaps values, not nodes; interviews forbid both when nodes carry data.

optimal.insight: Reversing a list only means turning each next arrow around. Save the next node first, flip the arrow, slide forward. Then reconnect the two ends.
steps: Use a dummy and walk to the node before the section
Loop: save next, point cur back at prev
Slide prev and cur one step forward
Reconnect: old first node to cur, before-node to prev

pattern-in-place-linked-list-reversal.optimalCode:
class Solution:
    def reverseBetween(self, head: Optional[ListNode], left: int, right: int) -> Optional[ListNode]:
        dummy = ListNode(0, head)
        before = dummy
        for _ in range(left - 1):
            before = before.next

        prev, cur = None, before.next
        for _ in range(right - left + 1):
            nxt = cur.next
            cur.next = prev
            prev, cur = cur, nxt

        before.next.next = cur
        before.next = prev
        return dummy.next

codeNotes.note: Dummy handles reversing from the head
Step 1: stop just before the section
Step 2: save next before breaking it

pitfalls: Flipping cur.next before saving it loses the rest of the list.
Forgetting to reconnect the reversed piece leaves a cut or a cycle.

say.intro: Okay, in place linked list reversal. You flip the arrows of a list as you walk it. No extra memory at all. Interviewers love it because pointer order is easy to get wrong. Our example reverses positions two to four of one through five. We get one, four, three, two, five.
say.brute: So what do people try first? Copy the values into an array. Reverse the slice there. Then walk the list again and write the values back. It works. So what's the catch? It costs linear extra memory. And it swaps values, not nodes. If each node carries real data, that's cheating. Interviewers will ask you to do it in place.
say.insight: Here's the thing. Reversing a list just means turning every arrow around. The recipe never changes. First, walk to the node just before the section. A dummy node helps. Then loop. Save the next node. Point the current node back at the previous one. Slide both pointers forward. Finally, stitch the two ends back in.
say.anim: We start with list one through five, adding a dummy node before the head. Before moves forward once, landing on node one, just before the reversal zone. Prev starts as none and cur points to node two, ready to reverse. We save node three as next, then flip node two's arrow back to prev. Now prev is two, cur is three, and the loop repeats the same flip. Node four flips next, pointing back at three, continuing the chain reversal. After the loop, we reconnect node two's tail to five and link four as new start. The final list reads one, four, three, two, five, matching the expected output.
say.code: Here's the template. A dummy node, so reversing from the head is no special case. We step to the node just before the section. Inside the loop, we save next first. Then we flip the arrow back to prev. Then prev and cur both slide forward. After the loop, the old first node points to cur, and the node before points to prev.
say.outro: Linear time, constant space. Reach for it when you hear reverse a list or part of it, reverse in groups or swap pairs, in place, or compare halves.

lineNotes: We define the Solution class that holds the method for reversing a section of a linked list.
The method takes the head of the list plus the left and right positions that bound the section to reverse.
We create a dummy node pointing at head so that reversing from position one needs no special handling.
We start a pointer called before at the dummy node, aiming to land just ahead of the section.
We loop left minus one times so before can walk up to the node preceding position left.
Each step moves before forward by one node along the list.
We set prev to nothing and cur to the first node of the section, the one after before.
We loop for the number of nodes in the section, which is right minus left plus one.
We save the next node of cur in nxt first, so we do not lose the rest of the list.
We flip the arrow by pointing cur's next back at prev, which reverses this single link.
We slide forward by moving prev to cur and cur to the saved nxt.
The original first section node, still reachable as before's next, now becomes the tail and is linked to cur, the node after the section.
We connect before's next to prev, the new head of the reversed section, stitching the front back in.
We return dummy's next, which is the true head of the list even if the first node changed.

pattern-fast-slow-pointers.name: Fast & Slow Pointers
pattern-fast-slow-pointers.title: Fast & Slow Pointers — the pattern
signals: detect a cycle in a list or sequence
find the middle node in one pass
repeated function values, like happy numbers
constant extra space, no visited set
variants: cycle detection: do they meet?
cycle start: reset one pointer to head
middle node: fast hits the end
array as implicit list (find duplicate)
pattern-fast-slow-pointers.hook: Two runners at different speeds find cycles and middles with constant memory.
pattern-fast-slow-pointers.ask: Fast and slow pointers move two pointers through a sequence, one step and two steps at a time; their meeting or spacing reveals cycles, middles and loop entries.
pattern-fast-slow-pointers.exampleWhy: Worked example Linked List Cycle: node 6 links back to node 3, so a cycle exists.

brute.idea: Remember every node you visit in a hash set. If you ever see a node twice, there is a cycle.
steps: Walk the list one node at a time
Stop if the node is already in the set
Otherwise add it and keep walking
brute.whySlow: Time is fine, but the set stores every node: 10,000 nodes means 10,000 extra entries, and O(1) space is the follow-up.

optimal.insight: Inside a cycle the fast pointer gains one step per move, so it must land on the slow one. If there is no cycle, fast simply falls off the end.
steps: Start slow and fast at the head
While fast can move: slow one step, fast two
Check the meeting or stop condition each move
Fast reaching the end means no cycle; middle is slow

codeNotes.note: Step 1: both start at the head
Fast can still take two steps
Step 4: fast fell off, no cycle

pitfalls: Check fast and fast.next before jumping two, or you crash on short lists.
Compare nodes, not values: equal values in different nodes are not a meeting.

say.intro: Okay, fast and slow pointers. Two pointers race through a list. One takes one step, the other takes two. Interviewers love it because it finds cycles and middles with no extra memory. Our example has six nodes, and node six links back to node three. So there's a cycle. The answer is true.
say.brute: So what do people try first? A visited set. Walk the list and remember every node. If you ever see one twice, that's a cycle. It's correct, and it's linear time. So what's the catch? The set holds every node. Ten thousand nodes, ten thousand entries. And the follow up is always the same. Can you do it in constant space?
say.insight: Here's the idea. Think of two runners on a circular track. The fast one gains one step every move. So once both are in the loop, the gap shrinks to zero. They must meet. No loop? Fast just runs off the end. The recipe: start both at the head. Move slow one, fast two. Check your condition each move.
say.anim: We start with slow and fast both pointing at node one, the list's head. The loop begins, checking that fast and its next node both exist. Slow moves one step to node two, while fast jumps two steps to node three. Next round, slow advances to node three, fast leaps ahead to node five. Now slow reaches node four, and fast wraps around back to node three. Slow moves to node five, and fast also lands exactly on node five. Since slow equals fast, the pointers have met inside a cycle. The function returns true, confirming the linked list contains a cycle.
say.code: Here's the template. Both pointers start at the head. The loop runs while fast can still take two steps. Slow moves one. Fast moves two. Then we ask, are they on the same node? If yes, there's a cycle. If the loop ends, fast fell off the end, so there's no cycle.
say.outro: Linear time, constant space. Listen for detect a cycle, find the middle, repeating values like happy numbers, or no extra space allowed.

lineNotes: We define a Solution class that holds the method for detecting a cycle in a linked list.
The method hasCycle takes the head of a linked list and returns true if the list loops back on itself.
We start both slow and fast at the head so they begin the race from the same node.
We keep looping only while fast and the node after fast exist, since otherwise fast has fallen off the end.
Each round we move slow forward by exactly one node.
We move fast forward by two nodes, so it gains one step on slow every round.
If slow and fast ever land on the same node, the faster pointer has lapped the slower one inside a cycle.
In that case we return true, because meeting is proof that a cycle exists.
If the loop ends, fast reached the end of the list, so there is no cycle and we return false.

pattern-bucket-sort.name: Bucket Sort
pattern-bucket-sort.title: Bucket Sort — the pattern
signals: top k most frequent, or sort by frequency
keys are bounded small integers, like counts
better than n log n is asked
values fit a known range from 0 to n
variants: buckets indexed by frequency
counting sort over a small value range
range buckets for max gap or near duplicates
cap keys at n, like H-index
pattern-bucket-sort.hook: When the keys are small whole numbers, you can sort without comparing anything.
pattern-bucket-sort.ask: Bucket sort drops each item into a slot indexed by its key, like its count, then reads the slots in order. When keys are bounded by n, that beats n log n.
pattern-bucket-sort.exampleWhy: Worked example Top K Frequent: 5 appears four times, 3 three times, so the top two are 5 and 3.

brute.idea: Count each distinct value, then sort the pairs by count with a normal comparison sort and take the first k.
steps: Collect the distinct values
Count each one
Sort pairs by count, take k
brute.whySlow: Counting with a rescan per value is n squared, and even with a hash map the comparison sort still costs n log n.

optimal.insight: A frequency can only be between 1 and n. So use the count itself as an array index: bucket i holds every value seen exactly i times. No comparisons needed.
steps: Compute each item's key, here its count
Make n + 1 buckets, one per possible key
Drop each item into the bucket of its key
Read buckets from high to low until you have k

codeNotes.note: Step 1: the key is the count
Step 2: one bucket per possible count
Step 3: drop value in its bucket
Step 4: read from high to low
Stop once we hold k items

pitfalls: Allocate n + 1 buckets; a value seen n times needs index n.
Bucket sort only works when keys are bounded; huge ranges waste memory.

say.intro: Okay, bucket sort. Instead of comparing items, you drop each one into a slot numbered by its key. Then you read the slots in order. Interviewers love it because it beats n log n. Our example: top two frequent numbers. Five shows up four times, three shows up three times. So the answer is five and three.
say.brute: So what do people try first? Count each distinct value. Then sort the values by count and take the first k. If you count by rescanning, that's n squared. Even with a hash map, the sort costs n log n. So what's the catch? The interviewer asks, can you beat n log n? A comparison sort can't. We need a different trick.
say.insight: Here's the thing. A count can only be between one and n. That's a tiny, bounded range. So use the count itself as an array index. Bucket i holds every value seen exactly i times. The recipe: compute each key. Make one bucket per possible key. Drop items in. Then read the buckets from high to low.
say.anim: We start counting how many times each number appears in the input list. After scanning all numbers, five appeared four times, three appeared three times, one and two once each. We create buckets indexed by frequency, so counts can map directly to positions. Five goes into bucket four, three goes into bucket three, one and two go into bucket one. Now we scan buckets from highest frequency down, searching for the most frequent numbers. At bucket four we find five, so five gets added to our result list. At bucket three we find three, and the result now has two elements, matching k. The function returns the two most frequent numbers, five and three.
say.code: Here's the template. First we count, so the key is the frequency. Then we make n plus one empty buckets, one per possible count. Each value drops into the bucket of its count. Now we read from the highest bucket down. We collect values, and the moment we hold k of them, we return.
say.outro: Linear time, linear space. Listen for top k frequent, sort by frequency, small bounded keys like counts, or an explicit ask to beat n log n.

lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container the problem expects for our method.
The method topKFrequent takes the list nums and an integer k, and returns the k most frequent values.
We start with an empty dictionary called count to track how many times each number appears.
We loop over every number n in the input list nums.
We add one to the stored count for n, defaulting to zero when n has not been seen yet.
We build a list of empty buckets, one for each possible frequency from zero up to the length of nums.
We loop over each number and its frequency in the count dictionary.
We append the number to the bucket whose index equals its frequency, so no comparisons are needed.
We create an empty result list to collect the answers as we find them.
We walk the bucket indexes from the highest possible frequency down to one, so most frequent values come first.
For each frequency, we look at every number stored in that bucket.
We append that number to the result list since it is among the most frequent so far.
We check whether the result now holds exactly k numbers.
Once we have k numbers, we return the result immediately and stop scanning.

pattern-counting-custom-sorting.name: Counting & Custom Sorting
pattern-counting-custom-sorting.title: Counting & Custom Sorting — the pattern
signals: arrange items to form the largest or smallest result
sort by frequency, then by value
order is defined by a rule, not numeric value
values come from a tiny range, like three colours
variants: pairwise comparator (a+b vs b+a)
multi-field key: (-count, value)
counting sort over a small range
sort by one rule, then greedy scan
pattern-counting-custom-sorting.hook: The whole problem is choosing the right order; after that, one sort does all the work.
pattern-counting-custom-sorting.ask: Counting and custom sorting means defining exactly how two items should be ordered, with a key, a comparator or a count table, then letting one sort produce the answer.
pattern-counting-custom-sorting.exampleWhy: Worked example Largest Number: ordering 3, 30, 34, 5 as 5, 34, 3, 30 gives the biggest number, 534330.

brute.idea: Try every possible order of the numbers, glue each one into a string, and keep the biggest result.
steps: Generate every permutation
Join each into one string
Keep the largest string seen
brute.whySlow: There are n factorial orders: 100 numbers give about 10^158 permutations, far beyond any time limit.

optimal.insight: Whichever of two pieces should come first is a local question: put a before b exactly when a+b beats b+a. That rule is consistent, so one sort with it is optimal.
steps: Turn items into the form you compare
Write the order rule: a key or a pairwise comparator
Sort once with that rule
Scan the sorted result and fix edge cases

codeNotes.note: a first if a+b is bigger
Step 3: one sort does the work

pitfalls: Plain string sort fails: 3 vs 30 needs the a+b vs b+a test.
A comparator returns negative, zero or positive, not a boolean.

say.intro: Okay, counting and custom sorting. Many problems are really one question. In what order should these things go? Define that order, and one sort solves it. Google asks this a lot. Our example: arrange three, thirty, thirty four and five into the biggest number. The answer is five, thirty four, three, thirty.
say.brute: So what do people try first? Try every order. Glue each permutation into one string and keep the biggest. It's correct. So what's the catch? There are n factorial orders. Four numbers give twenty four. A hundred numbers give more permutations than atoms in the universe. We need to know the right order without trying them all.
say.insight: Here's the thing. Which of two pieces goes first? Just test both. Put a before b when a then b beats b then a. That rule is consistent, so sorting with it is optimal. The recipe: put items in the form you compare. Write the order rule, as a key or a comparator. Sort once. Then fix edge cases.
say.anim: We start by converting each number to a string, like turning five into a text piece. Now we sort the strings using a custom comparison instead of normal order. Comparing thirty and three, three hundred three beats thirty three, so three comes first. Comparing thirty four and thirty, three hundred forty beats thirty thirty four, so thirty four wins. More comparisons check combined strings, always picking the order that forms a bigger number. Even five gets compared against thirty four, again choosing the larger concatenated result. After sorting, strs becomes five, thirty four, three, thirty, giving the biggest arrangement. Joining these pieces together produces the final answer, five three four three three zero.
say.code: Here's the template. First turn the numbers into strings, because that's what we compare. Then the order rule. If a plus b is bigger, a goes first. If smaller, b goes first. Then one sort, with the comparator wrapped as a key. Last, the edge case. If the biggest piece is zero, the whole answer is just zero.
say.outro: That's n log n. Listen for arrange to make the largest result, sort by frequency then value, order defined by a rule, or values from a tiny range.

lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container the judge expects for our method.
The method largestNumber takes a list of integers and returns the biggest possible number as a string.
We convert every number to a string so we can compare and join them by concatenation.
We define a comparator named compare that decides which of two strings should come first.
If putting a before b makes a bigger combined string than b before a, a should come first.
In that case we return negative one, telling the sort to place a ahead of b.
If putting b before a makes the bigger combined string, then b should come first.
So we return positive one, telling the sort to place b ahead of a.
If both orders give the same string, we return zero because their order does not matter.
We sort the strings using this comparator, wrapped by cmp_to_key so the sort function can use it.
After sorting, if the first string is zero, then every number must be zero.
In that case we return a single zero instead of a string like several zeros in a row.
Otherwise we join the sorted strings together into one string, which is the largest possible number.

pattern-quickselect.name: QuickSelect
pattern-quickselect.title: QuickSelect — the pattern
signals: kth largest or kth smallest element
k closest, k smallest, top k
order inside the top k does not matter
average O(n) wanted, beat n log n
variants: Lomuto partition, pivot at the end
Hoare partition, two pointers inward
random pivot for expected linear time
median of medians for worst-case linear
pattern-quickselect.hook: Find the k smallest in average linear time by only sorting the half you need.
pattern-quickselect.ask: QuickSelect partitions around a pivot like quicksort, then recurses into only the side that holds position k, so the k smallest items end up first.
pattern-quickselect.exampleWhy: Worked example K Closest Points: squared distances 2, 8 and 9 belong to (1,1), (2,-2), (0,-3).

brute.idea: Repeatedly scan for the closest remaining point, take it out, and do this k times.
steps: Compute every squared distance
Scan all remaining points for the minimum
Remove it and repeat k times
brute.whySlow: Each pick rescans everything: 10,000 points with k = 5,000 means about 50 million checks.

optimal.insight: One partition puts the pivot at its final sorted index p. If p is k-1 we are done; otherwise the answer lies wholly on one side, so throw the other side away.
steps: Pick a pivot in the range lo to hi
Partition: smaller items left, pivot lands at index p
If p equals the target index, stop
Otherwise shrink the range to the side holding the target

codeNotes.note: Step 1: pivot is the last item
Pivot lands at its final index p
Step 4: keep only the right side

pitfalls: A fixed pivot hits n squared on sorted input; randomize it in real code.
Target index is k - 1 (or n - k for kth largest): off-by-one is common.

say.intro: Okay, QuickSelect. It's quicksort's lazy cousin. You partition around a pivot, but then you only chase the side you need. Interviewers love it because it beats a heap on average. Our example: the three points closest to the origin. Those are one one, two minus two, and zero minus three.
say.brute: So what do people try first? Pick the closest point. Remove it. Pick the closest again. Do that k times. It's correct. So what's the catch? Every pick rescans everything. Ten thousand points with k of five thousand means about fifty million checks. And a full sort is n log n, even though we never needed the order inside the top k.
say.insight: Here's the thing. One partition drops the pivot at its final sorted spot. Call it p. If p is the target, we're done. If not, the answer is entirely on one side. Throw the other side away. The recipe: pick a pivot. Partition smaller items left. Check p against the target. Shrink to one side and repeat.
say.anim: We start with six points and need the three closest to the origin, using quickselect partitioning. The pivot is the last point, two, negative two, with squared distance eight. Points closer than the pivot get swapped toward the front, building up the partition boundary p. After partitioning, p equals one, not two, so we search the right side next, setting lo to two. Now pivot is five, negative one with distance twenty six, and partitioning continues from index two to five. This partition lands p at five, too high, so we shrink hi to four and retry. New pivot zero, negative three has distance nine, and partitioning swaps points two and three again. Now p equals two, matching k minus one, so the answer is one one, two negative two, zero negative three.
say.code: Here's the template. The pivot is the last item in the range. We sweep the range, moving every smaller item to the left. Then the pivot swaps into its final index p. If p is the target index, return the first k. If p is too small, keep only the right side. Otherwise keep only the left side.
say.outro: Average linear time, worst case n squared. Listen for kth largest or smallest, k closest, top k, order inside the k not mattering, or beat n log n.

lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the wrapper the problem expects for our method.
The kClosest method takes a list of points and a number k, and returns the k closest points to the origin.
We define a small helper called dist that measures how far a point is from the origin.
It returns x squared plus y squared, skipping the square root since ordering stays the same.
We set lo to zero and hi to the last index, so the search window starts as the whole list.
We loop forever, narrowing the window each pass until the pivot lands exactly at its final index.
We pick the last point in the window as the pivot and record its distance.
We set p to lo, which marks where the next smaller-than-pivot point will be placed.
We scan every index in the window from lo up to, but not including, hi.
We check whether this point is closer to the origin than the pivot.
If it is closer, we swap it into position p, growing the group of closer points.
We then move p forward by one to make room for the next closer point.
We swap the pivot into position p, so everything left of it is closer and everything right is not.
If p equals k minus one, the pivot sits at the last spot of the k closest, so we are done.
We return the first k points, which are now the k closest in some order.
If p is less than k minus one, we still need more points from the right side.
So we set lo to p plus one, discarding the left side and the pivot, which are already among the answer.
Otherwise p is too far right, meaning the k closest all lie to its left.
So we set hi to p minus one, throwing away the pivot and everything farther than it.

pattern-recursion.name: Recursion
pattern-recursion.title: Recursion — the pattern
signals: the input contains a smaller copy of itself
lists or trees defined node by rest
answer for n built from answer for n-1
naturally nested or self-similar structure
variants: linear: handle head, recurse on the rest
return value builds the answer bottom-up
pass state down as parameters
multiple branches (trees, Fibonacci)
pattern-recursion.hook: Solve one tiny step yourself and trust the same function to handle everything that is left.
pattern-recursion.ask: Recursion solves a problem by handling the smallest piece directly and calling the same function on a smaller version of the rest, until a base case stops it.
pattern-recursion.exampleWhy: Worked example Merge Two Sorted Lists: 1→4→7 and 2→3→6 merge into 1→2→3→4→6→7.

brute.idea: Ignore the structure: dump every value from both lists into an array, sort it, and build a fresh list.
steps: Copy all values from both lists
Sort the combined array
Build a brand-new list from it
brute.whySlow: It throws away that both lists are already sorted, paying n log n plus new nodes instead of one linear merge.

optimal.insight: The merged list starts with the smaller head, and what follows is just the merge of everything else: the same problem, one node smaller. Trust the call to solve it.
steps: Write the base case: the smallest input answers itself
Do one step of work on the current piece
Call the same function on the smaller rest
Combine your step with the returned result

codeNotes.note: Step 1: base case, one list empty
Step 3: recurse on the smaller rest

pitfalls: Missing or wrong base case means infinite recursion and a stack overflow.
Each call must shrink the input; very deep inputs can exceed the stack.

say.intro: Okay, recursion. You solve one tiny step yourself. Then you hand the rest to the same function, on a smaller input. Interviewers love it because it turns messy loops into a few clean lines. Our example merges one, four, seven with two, three, six. We get one through seven, without five.
say.brute: So what do people try first? Ignore the structure. Dump every value from both lists into an array. Sort it. Build a brand new list. It works. So what's the catch? Both lists were already sorted, and we threw that away. We pay n log n for the sort, plus a whole new set of nodes.
say.insight: Here's the thing. The merged list starts with the smaller of the two heads. And what comes after it? Just the merge of everything else. Same problem, one node smaller. So trust the function to solve it. The recipe: write the base case first. Do one step of work. Call yourself on the smaller rest. Combine the result.
say.anim: We start comparing heads one and two, with list one holding four and seven next. One is smaller, so it recurses on four, seven against two, three, six. Two is now smaller, so it recurses on four, seven against three, six. Three is smaller next, recursing on four, seven against just six. Four is smaller now, recursing on seven against six. Six is smaller, recursing on seven against an empty list, ending the chain. With list two empty, recursion stops and returns list one, the lone seven. Each call now links its node and returns, rebuilding the list upward: six then seven. Finally one links to the rest, giving the fully merged list one, two, three, four, six, seven.
say.code: Here's the template. Base case first. If one list is empty, the answer is the other list. Then one step of work. Which head is smaller? Then the leap of faith. Its next becomes the merge of the rest. We return that head, with the merged rest hanging off it. The other branch is the mirror image.
say.outro: Linear time, plus a linear call stack. Reach for recursion when the input holds a smaller copy of itself, lists or trees, or answer n builds from answer n minus one.

lineNotes: We define a Solution class that holds the method for merging two sorted linked lists.
The merge method takes the heads of two sorted lists and returns the head of one merged sorted list.
If the first list is empty, there is nothing to interleave, so we handle this base case first.
We simply return the second list, since merging nothing with it leaves it unchanged.
If the second list is empty, this is the mirrored base case that stops the recursion.
We return the first list, because it is already the complete merged result.
We compare the two head values, and when the first is smaller or equal, its node must come first.
We attach to the first node the merge of its remaining nodes and the whole second list, trusting the recursion.
We return the first node as the head of this merged piece, now linked to the sorted rest.
Otherwise the second head is smaller, so we link it to the merge of the first list and the rest of the second.
We return the second node as the head, since it leads the merged result here.

pattern-divide-and-conquer.name: Divide and Conquer
pattern-divide-and-conquer.title: Divide and Conquer — the pattern
signals: problem splits into same-shaped halves
answer for the whole built from answers for parts
an exponent, range or array can be halved
need log n or n log n via recursion
variants: halve and reuse, like fast power
split, recurse both, merge, like merge sort
pick a root, recurse on each side
recurse into one side only, like quickselect
pattern-divide-and-conquer.hook: Split the problem in half, solve the half once, stitch it back: n steps shrink to log n.
pattern-divide-and-conquer.ask: Divide and conquer means breaking a problem into smaller copies of itself, solving those recursively, then combining their answers into the answer for the whole.
pattern-divide-and-conquer.exampleWhy: Worked example Pow(x, n): 2 to the 13th is 8192.

brute.idea: Multiply x by itself n times in one long loop, never reusing a product already computed.
steps: Start the result at 1
Multiply by x, n times
Invert at the end if n is negative
brute.whySlow: n can be about two billion, so one answer costs two billion multiplications.

optimal.insight: x^n is x^(n/2) squared, times one extra x if n is odd. Solve the half once, reuse it: n halves per level, so log n levels.
steps: Define a base case small enough to answer directly
Split the input into smaller subproblems of the same shape
Solve each subproblem recursively
Combine the sub-answers into the answer for the whole

codeNotes.note: Divide: solve the half-size problem once
Negative n: solve positive, then invert

pitfalls: Calling solve(n // 2) twice instead of reusing it brings the cost back to O(n).
Forgetting the odd leftover or the negative exponent breaks half the inputs.

say.intro: Okay, divide and conquer. Got a big problem? Cut it into smaller copies of itself. Solve those, then glue the answers together. Interviewers love it because it turns slow loops into log time. Our example is Pow of x and n. Two to the thirteenth. The answer is eight thousand one hundred ninety two.
say.brute: Without the pattern, what do people write? A loop. Start at one, multiply by two, thirteen times. It works. But n can be around two billion. That's two billion multiplications for a single number. And notice the waste. Two to the twelfth is just two to the sixth, times itself. We keep rebuilding products we already had.
say.insight: Here's the core idea. Two to the thirteenth is two to the sixth, squared, times one extra two. So solve the half-size problem once, and reuse it. Every level halves n, so we need only about log n levels. And the recipe works everywhere. Pick a base case. Split into smaller copies. Solve them recursively. Then combine the answers.
say.anim: We start computing 2 raised to the power 13 using recursive halving. The function keeps calling itself with n halved, reaching n equals 1, then 0. At n equals 0 it hits the base case and returns 1. Back at n equals 1, half squared gives 1, then times x makes res 2. At n equals 3, half squared is 4, times x gives res 8. At n equals 6, squaring 8 gives 64, with no extra multiply since n is even. Finally at n equals 13, squaring 64 and multiplying by x gives res 8192. Since n is positive, the final answer returned is 8192.
say.code: Here's the template. First, the base case. Zero means the answer is one. Then divide. We solve n over two, just once. Then combine. Square the half. If n is odd, multiply one more x for the leftover. Finally, call it on the absolute value, and flip it for negative exponents. Notice we store the half. Calling it twice would undo the whole speedup.
say.outro: Log time, log stack. Reach for divide and conquer when the problem splits into same-shaped halves, the whole is built from its parts, or something can be halved.

lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container for the method we are asked to write.
The method myPow takes a base x and an integer exponent n and returns x raised to n.
We define a helper called solve that computes x to the power n for a nonnegative exponent recursively.
This checks the base case, where the exponent has shrunk all the way down to zero.
Any number to the power zero is one, so we return one point zero and stop recursing.
We recursively solve for half the exponent using integer division, computing that smaller power only once and reusing it.
We square the half result, since x to the n is x to the half, times itself.
If n is odd, integer division dropped one factor of x, so we need to put it back.
In the odd case we multiply the result by x one more time to make up the missing factor.
We return the result for this level to the caller, which will use it as its half.
We call solve on the absolute value of n, so the recursion only ever handles nonnegative exponents.
For a negative exponent we return the reciprocal of the result, otherwise we return the result directly.

pattern-merge-sort.name: Merge Sort
pattern-merge-sort.title: Merge Sort — the pattern
signals: sort in guaranteed n log n without a built-in
sort a linked list
count inversions or pairs i < j with a condition
merge two or k sorted sequences
variants: top-down recursive merge sort
bottom-up iterative merge sort
merge sort on a linked list
count pairs during the merge step
pattern-merge-sort.hook: Sort two halves, then zip them together. That merge step reappears in a dozen interview problems.
pattern-merge-sort.ask: Merge sort splits an array in half, sorts each half recursively, then merges the two sorted halves with two pointers into one sorted array.
pattern-merge-sort.exampleWhy: Worked example Sort an Array: [5,2,8,1,9,3] becomes [1,2,3,5,8,9].

brute.idea: Insertion sort: take each element in turn and slide it left past every larger element until it fits.
steps: Take the next element
Shift larger elements one place right
Drop it into the gap
brute.whySlow: On 50,000 reverse-sorted numbers it makes about 1.25 billion shifts: every element passes every other.

optimal.insight: Merging two already-sorted lists is linear: compare the two fronts, take the smaller. Halving gives log n levels, each merged in linear time.
steps: Stop when a piece has at most one element
Split at the midpoint
Sort each half recursively
Merge: compare fronts, take the smaller, append leftovers

codeNotes.match: while i < len(left) and j < len(right):
codeNotes.note: Merge: two pointers on the fronts
Take the smaller; <= keeps it stable

pitfalls: Using < instead of <= in the merge breaks stability for equal keys.
Forgetting to append one half's leftovers silently drops elements.

say.intro: Okay, merge sort. It's the cleanest divide and conquer there is. Split the array in half. Sort each half. Then merge them. Interviewers love it because the merge step shows up everywhere, from linked lists to counting inversions. Our example is five, two, eight, one, nine, three. Sorted, that's one, two, three, five, eight, nine.
say.brute: Without the pattern, what do people reach for? Insertion sort. Take each number and slide it left past everything bigger. It's correct, and it's fine for tiny arrays. But here's the catch. On a reversed array, every element walks past every other one. Fifty thousand numbers means over a billion shifts. That's n squared.
say.insight: Here's the core idea. Merging two lists that are already sorted is cheap. Just compare the two front elements, and take the smaller. That's linear. And halving gives only log n levels. So the recipe is always the same. Stop at one element. Split at the middle. Sort both halves. Then merge with two pointers.
say.anim: We start with the unsorted list five, two, eight, one, nine, three, ready to split in half. The algorithm keeps splitting down to single elements, like five, two, and eight, which are already sorted. Now it merges two and eight by comparing fronts, taking two first, then appending the rest. Merging five with two, eight compares fronts again, building the sorted list two, five, eight. The right half one, nine, three splits similarly down to single elements for merging. Merging one with three, nine compares values, producing the sorted sequence one, three, nine. Finally the two sorted halves, two five eight and one three nine, merge by comparing fronts each step. The final merged result is one, two, three, five, eight, nine, fully sorted.
say.code: Here's the template. First, the base case. One element or none is already sorted. Then we find the middle. We sort the left half and the right half recursively. Now the merge. Two pointers walk both halves. We take the smaller front, using less than or equal, so equal values keep their order. Finally, we append whatever is left over.
say.outro: n log n time, linear extra space. Reach for merge sort when you need a guaranteed sort, a sorted linked list, inversion counting, or merging sorted sequences.

lineNotes: We define the Solution class that holds our sorting method for this problem.
The sortArray method takes a list of numbers and will return it sorted in ascending order.
We define a helper called merge sort that recursively sorts whatever array it is given.
First we check whether the array has one element or none, since that is already sorted.
In that base case we simply return the array unchanged, which stops the recursion.
We compute mid as the length of the array divided by two, rounded down, to find the split point.
We recursively sort the first half of the array and store the sorted result as left.
We recursively sort the second half of the array and store the sorted result as right.
We create an empty list called merged to collect the combined sorted output.
We set two pointers, i and j, to zero so they point at the front of left and right.
We loop while both halves still have unused elements, so we can compare their fronts.
We compare the current front of left with the front of right, using less than or equal to keep the sort stable.
If left's front is smaller or equal, we append it to merged.
Then we advance the left pointer i to the next element.
Otherwise the front of right is strictly smaller, so we handle that case.
We append the front element of right to merged.
Then we advance the right pointer j to the next element.
When the loop ends, one half may have leftovers, so we append the rest of left, which is already sorted.
Likewise we append whatever remains of right, and at most one of these two leftovers is nonempty.
We return the fully merged sorted list for this level of recursion.
Finally we call merge sort on the original nums and return the sorted result.

pattern-binary-search-on-the-answer.name: Binary Search on the Answer
pattern-binary-search-on-the-answer.title: Binary Search on the Answer — the pattern
signals: minimize the maximum or maximize the minimum
smallest speed, capacity or time that still works
answer lies in a numeric range, not an index
a check gets easier as the answer grows
variants: find the minimum feasible value
find the maximum feasible value
minimize the largest part when splitting
real-valued search to a precision
pattern-binary-search-on-the-answer.hook: Can't compute the answer directly? Guess it, check it, and binary search the guesses.
pattern-binary-search-on-the-answer.ask: Binary search on the answer means searching over possible answer values, not array positions, when a yes-or-no check only gets easier as the answer grows.
pattern-binary-search-on-the-answer.exampleWhy: Worked example Koko: piles [3,6,7,11], 8 hours. Speed 4 takes 1+2+2+3 = 8 hours; speed 3 takes 10.

brute.idea: Try every candidate answer from the smallest upward, and return the first one that passes the check.
steps: Start at the smallest possible answer
Run the feasibility check
Step up by one until it passes
brute.whySlow: A pile can hold a billion bananas, so up to a billion checks, each scanning every pile.

optimal.insight: Feasibility is monotonic: if speed k works, every faster speed works too. Answers read no, no, ..., yes, yes, so binary search finds the first yes.
steps: Bound the answer: lowest and highest possible values
Write a check: does this candidate work?
Binary search for the first value that passes
When the check passes, keep it and search smaller

codeNotes.note: Integer ceiling: hours for this pile

pitfalls: Pair the loop with the updates: l <= r with r = k loops forever.
Float ceiling can round wrong on huge values; use (p + k - 1) // k.

say.intro: Okay, binary search on the answer. Sometimes there's no sorted array to search. But the answer itself is a number in a range. So we guess it, and check the guess. Our example is Koko eating bananas. Piles of three, six, seven and eleven, and eight hours. The slowest speed that works is four.
say.brute: Without the pattern, what do people try? Every speed, starting at one. Speed one takes twenty seven hours. Too slow. Speed two, speed three, still too slow. Speed four finally fits in eight hours. It's correct. But a pile can hold a billion bananas. That's up to a billion guesses, and each one scans every pile.
say.insight: Here's the core idea. If speed four works, speed five works too. Eating faster never hurts. So the answers look like no, no, no, then yes forever. That's sorted, and binary search finds the first yes. The recipe is the same every time. Bound the range. Write a yes or no check. Then binary search for the boundary.
say.anim: We start with speed range from 1 to 11, the largest pile. We try the middle speed, 6, checking if Koko can finish in time. Eating each pile at speed 6 takes 6 hours total, within the 8 hour limit, so 6 works. We narrow the range to 1 through 6 and test 3, the new midpoint. At speed 3, eating takes 10 hours, too slow, so we rule it out. Range shrinks to 4 through 6, testing midpoint 5 next. Speed 5 takes exactly 8 hours, so it works and we lower the range to 4 through 5. Testing speed 4, it also finishes in exactly 8 hours, so it still works. The range closes to a single value, and the answer is 4.
say.code: Here's the template. First, the check. Given a speed, add up the hours for each pile, rounding up with integer math. It's a yes if the total fits in h.
