Next, bound the answer, from one to the biggest pile. Now binary search. Test the middle. If it passes, keep it by moving the right edge there. If not, the answer is bigger, so move left past it.
say.outro: n log m time, constant space. Reach for this when you hear minimize the maximum, smallest speed or capacity that works, or a check that gets easier as the answer grows.

lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which holds the method that solves the banana eating problem.
The method minEatingSpeed takes the piles and the hour limit h, and returns the slowest speed that still finishes in time.
We define a helper called canFinish that checks whether eating at speed k finishes all piles within the allowed hours.
We start an hours counter at zero to total up the time needed at this speed.
We loop over every pile, since each pile is eaten separately and costs its own hours.
Each pile takes its size divided by k rounded up, which we get with the add k minus one trick.
We return true when the total hours is at most h, meaning speed k is fast enough.
We set left to one and right to the largest pile, since the answer must lie between those speeds.
We keep searching while left is less than right, which means more than one candidate speed remains.
We pick the middle speed k between left and right as the candidate to test.
We test whether eating at speed k finishes in time.
If it works, k might be the answer, so we shrink right down to k and keep it.
Otherwise the speed is too slow, so the first working speed must be higher.
We move left to k plus one, discarding k and every slower speed since they all fail.
When left meets right, that value is the first speed that works, so we return it.

pattern-tree-bfs-level-order.name: Tree BFS (Level Order)
pattern-tree-bfs-level-order.title: Tree BFS (Level Order) — the pattern
signals: level by level, or row by row
rightmost, leftmost or largest value per level
minimum depth or nearest node
width of each level
link nodes at the same depth
variants: level-size snapshot loop
zigzag: reverse alternate levels
right side view: last node per level
width via node position indices
pattern-tree-bfs-level-order.hook: A queue visits a tree one level at a time. It's the go-to for anything about rows or depth.
pattern-tree-bfs-level-order.ask: Tree BFS uses a queue to visit nodes level by level: everything at depth zero, then depth one, and so on, enqueuing children as you go.
pattern-tree-bfs-level-order.exampleWhy: Worked example Level Order: the rows are [1], [2,3], [4,5,6], [7].

brute.idea: For each depth d, run a fresh DFS from the root and collect only the nodes at depth d.
steps: Pick a depth d
DFS from the root, keeping depth-d nodes
Repeat until a depth comes back empty
brute.whySlow: Each level restarts at the root: a skinny 10,000-node tree costs about 50 million visits.

optimal.insight: A queue is first-in, first-out, so children line up behind their whole level. Snapshot the queue's length when a level starts, and you pop exactly one level.
steps: Seed a queue with the root
While the queue is not empty, record its size
Pop that many nodes and process each
Push their children to form the next level

pitfalls: Re-reading the queue length while children are added mixes two levels together.
A list with pop(0) costs O(n) per pop; use a deque.

say.intro: Okay, tree BFS, also called level order. Instead of diving deep, we sweep the tree one row at a time. Any question about levels, rows, or the nearest node points here. Our example is level order traversal. The rows are one, then two and three, then four, five, six, then seven.
say.brute: Without the pattern, what do people try? Depth by depth. To get row zero, run a DFS from the root. For row one, start over from the root again. And again for every row. It's correct. But each row walks the whole top of the tree again. On a deep, skinny tree, that's n times the height. Close to n squared.
say.insight: Here's the core idea. A queue is first in, first out. So children always line up behind the rest of their level. At the start of each level, count what's in the queue. Pop exactly that many. That's one row. The recipe: seed the queue with the root. Snapshot its size. Pop that many, processing each. Push their children.
say.anim: We start with root node 1, and the queue is empty before we push it. Node 1 is dequeued, its value is recorded, and its child 2 is queued. The queue now holds 2 and 3, marking the start of the next level. Nodes 2 and 3 are popped, their values collected, and children 4 and 5 queued. Level two finishes as result becomes 1, then 2 and 3 together. Nodes 4, 5, and 6 are processed this round, pushing only child 7 onward. Finally node 7 is popped alone, forming the last level by itself. The final breadth first order is 1, then 2 3, then 4 5 6, then 7.
say.code: Here's the template. A deque, seeded with the root if there is one. While the queue isn't empty, we start a new level. We loop exactly the current length of the queue. That number is frozen before children arrive. Pop a node from the front, and record its value. Push its left and right children. When the inner loop ends, one full level goes into the result.
say.outro: Linear time, space for the widest level. Reach for BFS when you hear level by level, rightmost per row, minimum depth, or level width.

lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which holds the method for performing a level order traversal of a binary tree.
The levelOrder method takes the root of a tree and returns a list of lists, one per level.
We start with res as an empty list that will collect the values of each level.
We create an empty double-ended queue, which gives us fast removal from the front for first-in, first-out order.
We check that the root exists, so an empty tree does not put a missing node in the queue.
If the root exists, we enqueue it, so the traversal begins with depth zero.
We keep looping while the queue still has nodes, meaning there are more levels to process.
At the start of each level, we create an empty list called val to hold that level's values.
We loop exactly as many times as the queue's length right now, which snapshots the current level's size.
We pop the node at the front of the queue, taking the oldest waiting node of this level.
We append that node's value to the val list for the current level.
We check whether the node has a left child that needs to be visited later.
If so, we enqueue the left child, where it waits behind the rest of the current level.
We likewise check whether the node has a right child.
If so, we enqueue the right child, so the next level stays in left-to-right order.
After the level is fully popped, we append its val list to res as one level of output.
Once the queue is empty, every level has been processed, so we return the result.

pattern-tree-dfs-pre-in-post-order.name: Tree DFS (Pre / In / Post Order)
pattern-tree-dfs-pre-in-post-order.title: Tree DFS (Pre / In / Post Order) — the pattern
signals: path, depth or height in a tree
compare or combine left and right subtrees
carry a running value from root to leaves
every root-to-leaf path
a node's answer depends on its children
variants: preorder: pass state down
postorder: return values up
inorder: sorted order in a BST
global best updated during recursion
pattern-tree-dfs-pre-in-post-order.hook: Make each recursive call return what its parent needs, and most tree problems fall in one pass.
pattern-tree-dfs-pre-in-post-order.ask: Tree DFS visits every node by recursing into its children. Preorder does the work before the children, inorder between them, postorder after, using what the children returned.
pattern-tree-dfs-pre-in-post-order.exampleWhy: Worked example Diameter: the longest path, from 8 to 9 through node 2, has 6 edges.

brute.idea: At every node, recompute the heights of both subtrees from scratch with a separate recursion.
steps: Visit each node
Compute left and right heights from scratch
Keep the best sum
brute.whySlow: Heights are recomputed for every ancestor: a 10,000-node chain costs about 50 million visits.

optimal.insight: Let each call return what its parent needs, here the height. In postorder a node already has both children's answers, so updating the best costs O(1).
steps: Pick the order: pass state down (pre) or results up (post)
Return a base value for an empty node
Recurse into the left and right children
Combine the children's results, update the answer, return upward

codeNotes.note: Global best, updated during the walk
Return the height the parent needs

pitfalls: Returning the diameter instead of the height gives the parent the wrong value.
Very deep skewed trees can hit Python's recursion limit; know the stack version.

say.intro: Okay, tree DFS. Preorder, inorder, postorder. They're all the same recursion. The only question is when you do the work. Before the children, between them, or after. Our example is diameter of a binary tree. The longest path runs from eight to nine, through node two. Six edges.
say.brute: Without the pattern, what do people write? At every node, they call a separate height function on the left and on the right. Add them up, keep the best. It works. But here's the catch. The same heights get recomputed for every ancestor. On a long, skinny tree, that's ten thousand nodes times ten thousand. n squared.
say.insight: Here's the core idea. Make each call return what its parent needs. Here, that's height. In postorder, a node already holds both children's heights. So the path through it is just left plus right. The recipe: pick the order. Handle the empty node. Recurse left and right. Then combine, update the answer, and return upward.
say.anim: We start at the root, node one, with res initialized to zero to track the best diameter. The recursion dives left through nodes four, six, and eight, reaching the bottom of the tree. Null children return zero, so node eight computes height one with left and right both zero. Node six combines its children to get height two, updating res to one along the way. Node four merges left height two and right zero, pushing res up to two. Moving to node five's subtree, nodes nine and seven each return height one upward. Node five sees left three and right three, raising res to six, the biggest path so far. Back at the root, left four and right one don't beat six, so res stays six, the final answer.
say.code: Here's the template. A shared best answer, starting at zero. Then the recursive function. Base case first. An empty node has height zero. Recurse left, then right. Now we're in postorder, so both answers are in hand. Left plus right is the longest path through this node. Update the best. Finally, return one plus the taller side. That's the height the parent needs.
say.outro: Linear time, a stack as deep as the tree. Reach for DFS when you hear paths, depth or height, comparing left and right subtrees, or root to leaf.

lineNotes: We define a Solution class that holds the method for finding the diameter of a binary tree.
The method takes the root of the tree and returns the diameter as an integer.
We start res at zero to track the longest path found so far, measured in edges.
We define a helper function dfs that recurses through the tree and returns the height of each subtree.
We declare res as nonlocal so the helper can update the outer best answer.
If the current node is empty, we have reached past a leaf.
An empty node has height zero, which serves as the base case for the recursion.
We recurse into the left child first and store its height as left.
We then recurse into the right child and store its height as right, so both answers are ready postorder.
The longest path bending at this node is left plus right, so we update res if that is larger.
We return one plus the taller child height, giving the parent this subtree's height.
We kick off the traversal by calling dfs on the root of the tree.
Finally we return res, which holds the largest diameter seen at any node.

pattern-bst-ordered-set.name: BST / Ordered Set
pattern-bst-ordered-set.title: BST / Ordered Set — the pattern
signals: the input is a binary search tree
k-th smallest, successor or predecessor
validate or search a sorted tree
floor, ceiling or values in a range
sorted container with fast insert and delete
variants: inorder walk equals sorted order
search: go left or right by comparing
validate with min and max bounds
ordered set: floor, ceiling, range queries
pattern-bst-ordered-set.hook: A BST is a sorted list in disguise: walk it in order, or compare once to skip a whole side.
pattern-bst-ordered-set.ask: A binary search tree keeps smaller values left and larger values right, so an inorder walk gives sorted order and each comparison discards a whole subtree.
pattern-bst-ordered-set.exampleWhy: Worked example Kth Smallest in a BST: inorder gives 1,2,3,4,5,6, so with k = 3 the answer is 3.

brute.idea: Ignore the ordering: collect every value with any traversal, sort the list, and index into it.
steps: Visit every node in any order
Sort all collected values
Return the k-th one
brute.whySlow: It reads and sorts all 10,000 nodes even when k is 1 and the answer is the leftmost node.

optimal.insight: The BST rule makes inorder (left, node, right) visit values in sorted order. Count nodes as inorder pops them, and stop at the k-th.
steps: Lean on the invariant: left smaller, right larger
Go left first to reach the smallest values
Visit nodes in sorted order with an inorder walk
Stop early, or prune a side using one comparison

codeNotes.note: Stack holds the path back up
Then the larger values on the right

pitfalls: Checking only parent-child pairs misses deeper violations; pass min and max bounds down.
Duplicates break the strict left-smaller rule; ask how equal keys are stored.

say.intro: Okay, binary search trees and ordered sets. A BST keeps smaller values on the left and bigger ones on the right. That one rule makes it a sorted list in disguise. Our example is kth smallest element in a BST. With k equal to three, the inorder walk goes one, two, three. So the answer is three.
say.brute: Without the pattern, what do people do? They ignore the ordering. Collect every value with any traversal, sort the list, then pick the k-th. It's correct. But we read all ten thousand nodes and sort them, even when k is one and the answer sits at the far left. We threw away the order the tree already gave us.
say.insight: Here's the core idea. Left subtree, then node, then right subtree. That's inorder, and in a BST it visits values in sorted order. So just count as you go, and stop at the k-th. The recipe works across BST problems. Lean on the invariant. Go left for small values. Walk in order, or prune a side with one comparison. Stop as early as you can.
say.anim: We start at root node 5, with k equal to 3, looking for the third smallest value. We dive left repeatedly, pushing 5, 3, and 2 onto the stack, chasing the smallest node. We reach node 1, the leftmost node, and push it onto the stack too. We pop node 1, decrement k to 2, and since k isn't zero we move right. We pop node 2 next, decrement k to 1, still not zero, so we continue. We pop node 3, decrement k to 0, meaning we found the target node. The inorder traversal returns node 3's value as the third smallest element.
say.code: Here's the template, an iterative inorder walk. A stack holds the path. Push the current node and slide left, as far as we can. That reaches the smallest value first. Then pop. That's the next value in sorted order. Count it down from k. If k hits zero, that's our answer. Otherwise, step to the right child, and repeat.
say.outro: Height plus k time, height space. Reach for BST tricks when you hear binary search tree, k-th smallest, successor, values in a range, or a sorted set with fast updates.

lineNotes: We define a Solution class with a method that finds the kth smallest value in a binary search tree.
The method takes the tree root and k, and returns the kth smallest value.
We create an empty stack to remember ancestors whose left subtrees we are still exploring.
We set curr to the root so the walk begins at the top of the tree.
We keep looping while there are saved nodes on the stack or a current node still to explore.
We run an inner loop that keeps going as long as curr points to a real node.
We push the current node onto the stack so we can return to it after its left side.
We move curr to its left child, heading toward the smallest values first.
With no more left children, we pop the stack to get the next node in sorted order.
We decrease k by one because we have just visited one more value in sorted order.
We check whether k has reached zero, meaning this node is the kth smallest.
If so, we return the value of the current node as the answer.
Otherwise we move curr to the right child, so larger values get visited after this node.

pattern-two-heaps.name: Two Heaps
pattern-two-heaps.title: Two Heaps — the pattern
signals: median of a growing stream of numbers
split values into a lower and upper half
pick the best item among those now unlocked
need max of one group and min of another
variants: running median: keep the halves balanced
sliding-window median with lazy deletion
unlock-then-pick: cost heap feeds profit heap
free vs busy resources (meeting rooms III)
pattern-two-heaps.hook: Keep the low half in a max-heap and the high half in a min-heap; the middle sits on top.
pattern-two-heaps.ask: Split a changing collection into two halves: a max-heap for the smaller values and a min-heap for the larger ones, so the values at the boundary are always one peek away.
pattern-two-heaps.exampleWhy: Add 5, 2, 8, 1. After 5 and 2 the median is 3.5; after 8 it is 5; after 1 it is 3.5 again.

brute.idea: Keep every number in one list and sort it whenever the middle is needed. Correct, but it re-sorts data that barely changed.
steps: Append each new number to a list
On every query, sort the whole list
Read the middle one or two values
brute.time: add O(1), query O(n log n)
brute.whySlow: With 50,000 calls each sorting up to 50,000 numbers, that is billions of operations.

optimal.insight: You only ever need the largest of the low half and the smallest of the high half. Two heaps keep exactly those on top, with log n updates.
steps: Max-heap holds the smaller half, min-heap the larger half
Push into the low heap, then move its top across
Rebalance so the sizes differ by at most one
Answer from the two heap tops only

codeNotes.note: Low half max-heap, high half min-heap
New value enters the low half
Odd count: low top is the median
Even count: average the two tops

pitfalls: Python heapq is a min-heap: negate values for the max-heap, and negate back when reading.
Route every new value through one heap first, or a large value can land in the low half.

say.intro: Okay, so this is the two heaps pattern. You split your data into a low half and a high half. A max heap holds the low half. A min heap holds the high half. Now the middle is always sitting on top. Our example is the running median. We add five, two, eight, and one.
say.brute: So what do people try first? Keep every number in one list. Whenever someone asks for the median, sort it and read the middle. That's correct. So what's the catch? You re-sort the whole list for every query, even though only one number changed. Fifty thousand queries on fifty thousand numbers is billions of operations.
say.insight: Here's the thing. You never need the full order. You only need the biggest of the small half and the smallest of the big half. A heap keeps exactly that on top. Here's the recipe. One, a max heap for the low half, a min heap for the high half. Two, push into the low heap, then pass its top across. Three, rebalance the sizes. Four, answer from the tops.
say.anim: We start with two empty heaps, small for low numbers and large for high numbers. Adding five pushes it into small, then balances by moving it through large and back. Adding two goes into small first, then large stays balanced since sizes already match. With two numbers split evenly, the median averages the tops of both heaps, giving three point five. Adding eight pushes through small and large, then rebalances so small keeps its extra top. Now small has more elements, so the median is just its top value, five. Adding one keeps the heaps balanced again after pushing through small and large. Final median averages both heap tops again, giving the answer three point five.
say.code: Now the code. Two lists used as heaps. Small is the low half, stored negated so it acts like a max heap. Large is the high half. Every new number enters the low half first. Then the low half's largest crosses over. That keeps every low value below every high value. If the high side got bigger, move one back. For the median, an odd count means the low top. Even means average both tops.
say.outro: Log n per add, constant per query. Listen for these signals. A running median. A lower half balanced against an upper half. Or picking the best item among those you've just unlocked.

lineNotes: We define a MedianFinder class that will keep track of a running stream of numbers and report the median.
The constructor sets up the two heaps that will hold the lower and upper halves of the data.
We create small as a max-heap, stored as negated values, and large as a min-heap, both starting empty.
The addNum method takes a new number and inserts it so the two halves stay balanced.
We push the negated number onto small, so it enters the lower half as a max-heap entry.
We pop the largest value from small and move it into large, ensuring every low value is no bigger than any high value.
If large now holds more elements than small, the halves are unbalanced and we need to fix it.
We pop the smallest from large and push it back into small, so small is never smaller than large.
The findMedian method returns the median using only the top of each heap.
If small has more elements than large, the total count is odd and the median sits in small.
We return the top of small, negating it back, since that is the largest of the lower half and the middle value.
Otherwise the counts are equal, so we average the top of small and the top of large to get the median.

pattern-top-k-elements.name: Top K Elements
pattern-top-k-elements.title: Top K Elements — the pattern
signals: k largest, smallest, or closest items
k most frequent elements or words
kth largest in an array or stream
best k by some score
variants: min-heap of size k for the k largest
max-heap of size k for k smallest or closest
kth element = heap top after the scan
bucket sort or quickselect for average O(n)
pattern-top-k-elements.hook: To find the k best, never sort everything. Keep a heap of just k and evict the weakest.
pattern-top-k-elements.ask: To pick the k largest (or most frequent, or closest) items, keep a min-heap of size k. Whenever it grows past k, pop the weakest, so the heap always holds the current top k.
pattern-top-k-elements.exampleWhy: 5 appears four times, 3 three times, 1 and 2 once each. The two most frequent values are 5 and 3.

brute.idea: Score every item, sort all of them by score, and slice off the first k. Correct, but it fully orders items you are about to throw away.
steps: Count how often each value appears
Sort every distinct value by its count
Take the first k
brute.whySlow: Sorting all d distinct values costs d log d even when k is 2; on a stream you would re-sort after every arrival.

optimal.insight: Only the k best matter, and the one at risk is the weakest of them. A min-heap of size k keeps that weakest on top, so each newcomer either replaces it or leaves.
steps: Compute a score for each item
Push (score, item) onto a min-heap
If the heap holds more than k, pop the smallest
What survives is the top k

codeNotes.note: Score first, so the heap orders by it
Evict the weakest of the k + 1

codeNotes.match: return [num for c, num in sorted(heap, reverse=True)]

pitfalls: For the k largest use a MIN-heap capped at k; a max-heap of everything costs n log n.
Push a tuple with the score first; pushing the bare item orders by the wrong key.

say.intro: Okay, so this is the top k elements pattern. Whenever a problem asks for the k largest, the k most frequent, or the k closest, think heap of size k. Interviewers love it because sorting works, but they want better. Our example is top k frequent. Nine numbers, k is two. The answer is five and three.
say.brute: So what do people try first? Count every value, sort all of them by count, and take the first k. That's correct. So what's the catch? You fully order items you're about to throw away. With a million distinct values and k of two, you sort a million things to keep two. And on a stream, you'd re-sort every time.
say.insight: Here's the thing. To keep the k best, you only need to watch the weakest of them. A min heap of size k keeps that weakest one on top. Here's the recipe. One, score every item. Two, push the score and the item onto a min heap. Three, if the heap holds more than k, pop the smallest. Four, whatever survives is your top k.
say.anim: We start counting how often each number appears in the array. After processing most numbers, five appears three times and three appears twice. Counting finishes: five appears four times, three three times, one and two once each. We build a min-heap of size two, pushing five with count four first. Three with count three joins the heap alongside five. One gets pushed in, growing the heap beyond size two. Since the heap exceeds size two, the weakest entry, one, gets popped off. Two tries next but also gets pushed then popped, since its count is smallest. Sorting the final heap gives the top two frequent elements, five and three.
say.code: Now the code. First we score every item, here by counting. Then for each value we push its count first, then the value, so the heap orders by count. If the heap now holds more than k, we pop. The weakest of the k plus one leaves. At the end the survivors are the top k, and we sort just those k for the answer.
say.outro: n log k instead of n log n. Listen for these signals. The k largest or smallest. The k most frequent. The kth largest in an array or a stream. Or the k closest points.

lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container for the method that solves the top k frequent problem.
This method takes a list of numbers and an integer k, and returns the k most frequent numbers.
We start with an empty dictionary called count that will map each number to how often it appears.
We loop through every number in the input list so each one gets counted.
For each number we add one to its tally, starting from zero if we have not seen it before.
We create an empty list called heap, which will serve as our min-heap holding at most k entries.
We loop over each distinct number and its count, so every candidate gets a chance to enter the heap.
We push a pair of count and number onto the heap, so the heap orders items by frequency with the smallest on top.
If the heap now holds more than k items, we know one must be dropped.
We pop the smallest entry, the least frequent one, so the heap always keeps only the current top k.
We sort the remaining pairs from highest count down and return just the numbers, giving the k most frequent elements.

pattern-k-way-merge.name: K-Way Merge
pattern-k-way-merge.title: K-Way Merge — the pattern
signals: merge k sorted lists or arrays
kth smallest across several sorted rows
smallest range covering one value from each list
matrix with sorted rows and columns
variants: merge everything into one output
stop at the kth pop (kth smallest)
track the current max too (smallest range)
divide and conquer: merge pairs repeatedly
pattern-k-way-merge.hook: k sorted lists? The next smallest overall is always one of k heads, and a heap picks it.
pattern-k-way-merge.ask: Merge k sorted sequences by keeping only the current front of each in a min-heap: pop the smallest, output it, then push the next element from that same sequence.
pattern-k-way-merge.exampleWhy: Four sorted lists hold ten values. Taking the smallest front each time gives 0,1,1,2,3,4,4,5,6,7.

brute.idea: Ignore that each list is already sorted. Pour every value into one array, sort it, and build a brand new list.
steps: Collect all N values from every list
Sort the combined array
Build a fresh output list
brute.whySlow: Ignores that each list is already sorted: N log N instead of N log k, plus N freshly allocated nodes.

optimal.insight: Each list is sorted, so the next output must be one of the k list heads. A min-heap of those k heads finds it in log k per value.
steps: Push the first element of every list onto a min-heap
Pop the smallest and append it to the output
Push the next element from that same list
Repeat until the heap is empty

codeNotes.note: Value first; list index breaks ties

pitfalls: Include a tie-breaker like the list index; comparing two nodes directly raises an error.
Skip empty lists when seeding, and push a successor only when it exists.

say.intro: Okay, so this is the k way merge pattern. You have k sorted lists, and you want one sorted stream. Interviewers love it because it shows up everywhere. Log files, search results, sorted matrix rows. Our example merges four sorted linked lists. Ten values in, zero through seven out, in order.
say.brute: So what do people try first? Pour every value into one big array, sort it, and build a new list. That's correct. So what's the catch? It throws away the fact that each list is already sorted. You pay n log n to sort, when the order inside each list was free. And you allocate every node again.
say.insight: Here's the thing. Each list is sorted. So the next smallest value overall must be one of the k front values. Keep just those fronts in a min heap. Here's the recipe. One, push every list's head. Two, pop the smallest and output it. Three, push the next node from that same list. Four, repeat until the heap is empty.
say.anim: We start by pushing each list's first value into a min-heap, tagged with its list index. After all four heads are pushed, the heap holds zero, one, one, and two as candidate smallest values. A dummy head is created, and the loop pops the smallest value, zero, attaching it to the output. Next the smallest is one from list zero, so it's appended and its successor four is pushed in. Popping continues: one from list one joins the chain, then its next value three enters the heap. Two comes off next, extending the merged list, and six is pushed from that same list. The heap keeps giving the next smallest, three, four, four, five, six, then seven, each time replaced by its successor. Once the heap empties, the final merged list reads zero, one, one, two, three, four, four, five, six, seven.
say.code: Now the code. We seed the heap with every list's head. Each entry is the value first, then the list index to break ties. Then we pop the smallest head overall, and append it to the output. If that node has a next, we push it, so its list stays represented. When the heap is empty, every node has been placed.
say.outro: n log k time, k extra space. Listen for these signals. Merging k sorted lists or arrays. The kth smallest across sorted rows. And the smallest range covering every list.

lineNotes: We define the Solution class that holds our method for merging k sorted linked lists.
The method takes a list of list heads and returns the head of one merged sorted list.
We start with an empty heap that will always hold the current front node of each list.
We loop over the input lists with their index, so each node can be tagged with its list number.
We only consider a list if its head exists, skipping any empty lists.
We push the value, the list index and the node, where the index breaks ties so nodes are never compared.
We create a dummy starting node and a tail pointer that both begin there to build the output.
We keep going as long as the heap still has candidate nodes to output.
We pop the smallest front node, which must be the next value in the merged order.
We attach that node to the end of the merged list by linking the tail's next to it.
We move the tail forward to this node so the next attachment goes after it.
If the popped node has a successor, that successor is now the new front of its list.
We push that next node with its value and the same list index so it competes with the other fronts.
When the heap is empty, we return the node after dummy, which is the real head of the merged list.

pattern-data-structure-design.name: Data Structure Design
pattern-data-structure-design.title: Data Structure Design — the pattern
signals: design a class supporting these operations
each operation in O(1) average time
get random, least recently used, or timestamps
implement your own cache, set, or map
variants: array plus hash map (index + lookup)
hash map plus doubly linked list (LRU)
hash map of sorted lists (time-based store)
stack storing extra state (min stack)
pattern-data-structure-design.hook: No single structure does every operation fast. Combine two, each covering the other's weakness.
pattern-data-structure-design.ask: Design a class whose operations each hit a time target by pairing simple structures, usually an array or list plus a hash map, and keeping them in sync on every update.
pattern-data-structure-design.exampleWhy: Insert 10, 20, 30; remove 10; inserting 20 again fails; remove 30. Only 20 is left, so getRandom returns 20.

brute.idea: Use one plain list for everything. Membership checks and removals scan or shift the list, so each operation can cost linear time.
steps: insert: scan for val, append if missing
remove: scan for val, delete it, shifting the rest
getRandom: random index into the list
brute.whySlow: Membership checks and middle deletions scan or shift the list: 200,000 calls on a large set is billions of moves.

optimal.insight: Give each operation the structure that makes it O(1): an array for random index access, a hash map from value to index for lookup. Swap-with-last makes deletion O(1).
steps: List each operation with its target cost
Pick one structure per operation's need
Link them: the map stores positions in the array
Update every structure on every write

codeNotes.note: Map: value to its array slot
Insert: record the slot, then append
Remove: move the last value into the hole
Random pick straight from the array

pitfalls: Every write must update every structure; one stale map entry breaks later removals.
When val is itself the last item, update the map before deleting val's key.

say.intro: Okay, so this is data structure design. The interviewer hands you a class with a few operations, and a speed target for each. Google loves these, because no single structure is enough. You have to combine them. Our example is a randomized set. Insert, remove, and get random, all in constant time.
say.brute: So what do people try first? One plain list. Insert appends. Remove searches and deletes. Get random picks an index. That's correct. So what's the catch? Checking if a value is there scans the list. Deleting from the middle shifts everything after it. Two hundred thousand calls on a big set is billions of moves.
say.insight: Here's the thing. Each operation needs a different superpower. Random pick needs an array. Fast lookup needs a hash map. So use both. Here's the recipe. One, list each operation and its target. Two, pick a structure for each need. Three, link them. Here the map stores array positions. Four, update both on every write. And to delete fast, swap with the last slot.
say.anim: We start with an empty array for values and an empty map from value to index. Inserting 10, 20, and 30 appends each to the array and records its index in the map. Removing 10 swaps it with the last value, 30, then pops the array for constant time deletion. Inserting 20 again fails since it is already present, so insert returns false. Removing 30 swaps it with the last value, 20, updates the index, then pops it off. Finally getRandom picks randomly from the array, which now only contains 20, returning 20.
say.code: Now the code. An array for random access, and a map from value to its slot. Insert records the slot, then appends. Remove is the clever part. We take the last value and move it into the hole. Then we fix that value's slot in the map, so the two stay in sync. Pop the end, delete the old key. Get random just picks from the array.
say.outro: Constant time per operation. Listen for these signals. Design a class with these operations. Each one in constant time. Random picks, caches, or lookups by timestamp.

lineNotes: We import the random module so we can pick a uniformly random element later.
We define the RandomizedSet class, which supports insert, remove and random pick, each in constant time.
The constructor sets up the two structures that we will keep in sync.
The vals list holds every value, giving us fast random access by position.
The index dictionary maps each value to its position in the list, giving fast lookup.
Insert takes a value and returns whether it was newly added.
We check the dictionary to see whether the value is already present.
If it is already there, we return false and change nothing.
We record the value's future position, which is the current length of the list, in the dictionary.
We append the value to the end of the list so both structures agree.
We return true to signal that the insert succeeded.
Remove takes a value and returns whether it was actually removed.
If the value is not in the dictionary, there is nothing to remove.
So we return false right away.
We look up the position of the value we want to delete.
We grab the last element of the list, which will fill the hole.
We overwrite the deleted slot with the last element, avoiding a costly shift of items.
We update the dictionary so the moved last element points to its new position.
We pop the final list entry, which is now a duplicate, keeping removal constant time.
We delete the removed value from the dictionary; this order also handles the case where the value was last.
We return true to show the removal succeeded.
getRandom returns a random element currently in the set.
Since the list holds exactly the current values, random choice on it gives each one equal probability.

pattern-graph-dfs.name: Graph DFS
pattern-graph-dfs.title: Graph DFS — the pattern
signals: count connected components or groups
can node B be reached from node A
detect a cycle in a graph
clone, explore, or flood fill a graph
variants: count components: launch per unvisited node
flood fill on a grid
cycle detection with three colours
iterative DFS with an explicit stack
pattern-graph-dfs.hook: Build the adjacency list, keep a visited set, and dive. Most graph questions start right here.
pattern-graph-dfs.ask: Explore a graph by going as deep as possible along one path before backtracking, marking nodes visited so each is handled once. Use it to find reachable nodes or connected components.
pattern-graph-dfs.exampleWhy: Six nodes. Edges join 0, 1, 2 in a triangle and link 3 with 4. Node 5 is alone. That makes 3 components.

brute.idea: Without a traversal, people relabel: every node starts with its own label, and edges are swept repeatedly until connected nodes share the smallest label.
steps: label[i] = i for every node
Sweep edges: both ends take the smaller label
Repeat until stable, then count distinct labels
brute.whySlow: A long chain listed in the wrong order needs one sweep per node: 2,000 sweeps of 5,000 edges.

optimal.insight: One DFS from an unvisited node marks its entire component, and the shared visited set means no node is explored twice. So just count DFS launches.
steps: Build an adjacency list from the edges
Keep one visited set shared by all searches
DFS: mark the node, recurse into unvisited neighbours
Launch from each unvisited node; count or collect

codeNotes.note: Adjacency list, one slot per node
Unvisited start means a new component

pitfalls: Mark a node visited as soon as you enter it, or cycles recurse forever.
Very deep graphs can hit Python's recursion limit; switch to an explicit stack.

say.intro: Okay, so this is graph depth first search. Start at a node, go as deep as you can, then backtrack. A visited set makes sure every node is handled once. Interviewers love it because so many graph questions reduce to it. Our example counts connected components. Six nodes, four edges. The answer is three.
say.brute: So what do people try without a traversal? Give every node its own label. Sweep all the edges, and let both ends take the smaller label. Repeat until nothing changes, then count the labels. That's correct. So what's the catch? A long chain in the wrong order needs one full sweep per node. Thousands of sweeps over thousands of edges.
say.insight: Here's the thing. One depth first search from a fresh node reaches its entire component. And the visited set means nothing is explored twice. So just count how many times you launch. Here's the recipe. One, build an adjacency list. Two, keep one visited set. Three, mark a node, then dive into unvisited neighbours. Four, launch from each unvisited node.
say.anim: We build an adjacency list from the edges, connecting nodes zero through four. Count starts at zero, and we begin checking each node from zero to five. Node zero is unvisited, so depth first search starts, marking zero visited. The search spreads to neighbors one and two, visiting them as part of the same component. Component one is done, count becomes one, and we move to already visited nodes one and two. Node three is unvisited, so a new search runs, visiting three and four together. Count becomes two, then node five starts its own search as a lone component. All nodes are visited, count reaches three, and the function returns three components.
say.code: Now the code. First, an adjacency list with one slot per node. The graph is undirected, so every edge goes in both directions. In the search, we mark the node visited the moment we enter. Then we dive only into neighbours we haven't seen. Back in the main loop, an unvisited node means a brand new component. So we launch a search and add one.
say.outro: Linear in nodes plus edges. Listen for these signals. Counting components or groups. Can one node reach another. Detecting a cycle. Cloning or flood filling a graph.

lineNotes: We define a Solution class that holds the method for counting connected components in an undirected graph.
The method takes the number of nodes n and a list of edges, and returns the number of components.
We build an adjacency list with one empty list for each node from zero up to n minus one.
We loop over every edge, unpacking its two endpoints into a and b.
We add b to the neighbor list of a so a can reach b.
We also add a to the neighbor list of b, since the graph is undirected and edges go both ways.
We create an empty visited set that is shared across all searches so no node is explored twice.
We define a helper function dfs that explores everything reachable from a given node.
On entering a node, we mark it visited right away so it is never processed again.
We loop through every neighbor of the current node to continue exploring deeper.
We check whether that neighbor has not been visited yet, which also prevents infinite loops on cycles.
For an unvisited neighbor we recurse, going as deep as possible before backtracking.
We start the component counter at zero.
We iterate over every node label so that nodes in disconnected pieces are all considered.
If the node has not been visited, it belongs to a brand new component we haven't touched.
We launch a DFS from that node, which marks its entire component as visited.
We increment the count by one, since each DFS launch corresponds to exactly one component.
After checking all nodes, we return the total number of components found.

pattern-graph-bfs-shortest-path-unweight.name: Graph BFS (Shortest Path, Unweighted)
pattern-graph-bfs-shortest-path-unweight.title: Graph BFS (Shortest Path, Unweighted) — the pattern
signals: minimum number of steps or moves
shortest path in a grid or maze
fewest transformations from start to target
minutes until every cell is reached
variants: single source to one target
multi-source BFS (rotting oranges, 01 matrix)
level-by-level loop to count minutes
implicit graph of states (word ladder)
pattern-graph-bfs-shortest-path-unweight.hook: When every step costs the same, the first time BFS reaches a node is the shortest way there.
pattern-graph-bfs-shortest-path-unweight.ask: Find the fewest steps between two points when every move costs one, by exploring outward in rings: everything one step away, then two, using a queue and marking nodes as they are enqueued.
pattern-graph-bfs-shortest-path-unweight.exampleWhy: Cells with 0 are open. Best route: right, diagonal, down, diagonal into the corner, touching 5 cells.

brute.idea: Explore every simple path with depth first search, and keep the shortest one that reaches the target. Correct, but you must finish all paths to be sure.
steps: DFS from the start in all 8 directions
Never revisit a cell on the current path
At the target, record the length
Backtrack and try every other branch
brute.whySlow: The number of simple paths grows exponentially. Even a 10 by 10 open grid has astronomically many.

optimal.insight: A FIFO queue hands out nodes in order of distance. So the first time BFS reaches a node, it used the fewest steps; mark it then and never revisit.
steps: Push the start with its distance and mark it
Pop from the front of the queue
If it is the target, return its distance
Push unvisited neighbours at distance + 1, marking them now

codeNotes.note: Queue starts at the source, distance 1
FIFO: nearer cells come out first

codeNotes.match: if r == n - 1 and c == n - 1:

codeNotes.note: Mark on push, never queue twice

pitfalls: Mark nodes visited when you enqueue them, not when you pop, or the queue fills with duplicates.
BFS gives shortest paths only when every edge costs the same; weighted graphs need Dijkstra.

say.intro: Okay, so this is breadth first search for shortest paths. When every move costs the same, BFS explores in rings. Everything one step away, then two, then three. Interviewers love it because shortest path questions hide everywhere. Our example is a grid. Find the fewest cells from the top left to the bottom right, moving in eight directions.
say.brute: So what do people try first? Depth first search over every possible path, keeping the shortest one that reaches the corner. That's correct. So what's the catch? DFS commits to one long path before trying others. To be sure you found the shortest, you have to explore all of them. And the number of paths explodes, even on a ten by ten grid.
say.insight: Here's the thing. A queue hands out cells in order of distance. So the first time we reach any cell, that's already the shortest way there. Mark it, and never look again. Here's the recipe. One, push the start and mark it. Two, pop from the front. Three, if it's the target, return the distance. Four, push unvisited neighbours one step farther, marking them now.
say.anim: We start at cell zero zero, marked visited, queued with distance one. BFS pops zero zero, checks neighbors in all eight directions for unvisited open cells. Cell zero one gets marked visited and queued with distance two, since it's reachable. Next, cells zero two and one two are discovered and queued at distance three. Now cells two one and two two are marked visited, queued with distance four. Finally cell three three, the bottom right corner, is reached and queued at distance five. Popping that node, since it's the target, BFS returns the shortest path length five.
say.code: Now the code. The queue starts with the top left cell, at distance one. We mark it right away. Each loop pops from the front, so nearer cells always come out first. If it's the bottom right, that first arrival is the answer. Otherwise we check all eight neighbours. Each open one gets marked as we push it, one step farther.
say.outro: Linear in the number of cells. Listen for these signals. Minimum steps or moves. Shortest path in a grid or maze. Fewest transformations to a target. Or minutes until everything is reached.

lineNotes: We define a Solution class that holds the method for this shortest path problem.
The method takes a square grid of zeros and ones and returns the fewest cells on a clear path.
We store the grid size as n, since the grid is square.
If the start or the destination cell is blocked by a one, no path can exist.
So we return negative one right away in that blocked case.
We create a queue seeded with the start cell at row zero, column zero, with path length one.
We mark the start as visited by setting it to one, so we never enqueue it again.
We loop as long as the queue still has cells waiting to be explored.
We pop the oldest cell from the front, getting its row, column, and distance so far.
We check whether this cell is the bottom right corner, our destination.
Since the queue hands out cells in distance order, this first arrival is the shortest, so we return its distance.
We loop over row offsets of negative one, zero, and one to look at neighbors.
We loop over column offsets likewise, so together we cover all eight directions.
We compute the neighbor's row and column by adding the offsets to the current position.
We only continue if the neighbor is inside the grid and is an open, unvisited cell.
We mark that neighbor as visited right when enqueuing, so no other cell can queue it again.
We enqueue the neighbor with distance one larger than the current cell's distance.
If the queue empties without reaching the destination, no path exists, so we return negative one.

pattern-multi-source-bfs.name: Multi-source BFS
pattern-multi-source-bfs.title: Multi-source BFS — the pattern
signals: several sources spreading at the same time
distance from every cell to the nearest X
minimum minutes until everything is infected
fill each empty room with distance to a gate
start from the border or from all targets
variants: count layers for elapsed time
write distances into the grid
seed from border cells, reverse the flow
multi-source BFS, then heap or binary search
pattern-multi-source-bfs.hook: When many starting points spread at once, one BFS from all of them beats a search from each.
pattern-multi-source-bfs.ask: Multi-source BFS puts every starting cell into the queue at distance zero, then expands layer by layer, so each cell is reached first by its nearest source.
pattern-multi-source-bfs.exampleWhy: Rot spreads from both corners at once: four oranges turn at minute one, the last two at minute two.

brute.idea: Handle each fresh orange on its own: run a separate BFS from it to the nearest rotten orange. The answer is the largest of those distances.
steps: For each fresh orange, start a new BFS
Stop at the first rotten orange reached
Answer is the largest such distance
An orange that reaches none means -1
brute.whySlow: Every fresh orange re-explores the grid. A 100 by 100 grid means up to 10,000 searches of 10,000 cells each.

optimal.insight: Put every source in the queue before starting. BFS layers then grow from all sources together, so each cell is first reached by its nearest source, exactly once.
steps: Scan the grid; queue every source, count the targets
Pop one full layer at a time
Claim unvisited neighbours and queue them
Count layers until no targets remain
Leftover targets are unreachable: return -1

codeNotes.note: Step 1: every source starts at distance zero
Count the targets still to reach
Step 2: one full layer per minute
Step 3: claim it so it is queued once
Step 4: one layer equals one minute

pitfalls: Running BFS from one source at a time loses the nearest-source guarantee and costs far more.
Mark cells when queued, not when popped, or one cell gets queued twice.

say.intro: Okay, multi source BFS. Sometimes the spreading starts in many places at once. Fire, rot, signals. Instead of searching from each start, you search from all of them together. Google loves this on grids. Our example is Rotting Oranges. Rotten oranges sit in two corners. After two minutes, every orange is rotten.
say.brute: Without the pattern, people take each fresh orange on its own. Run a search from it, out to the nearest rotten orange. The answer is the longest of those trips. It's correct. But every fresh orange explores the grid all over again. On a hundred by hundred grid, that's ten thousand searches, each touching up to ten thousand cells.
say.insight: So flip it around. Don't search from the targets. Search from the sources, all at once. Put every rotten orange in the queue before you start. Now each layer is one minute, and every cell is reached first by its nearest source. The recipe. Queue every source and count the targets. Pop one whole layer. Claim fresh neighbours. Count layers. Anything left means minus one.
say.anim: We start with a grid of oranges, counting rotten and fresh ones. Both rotten oranges at corners get queued immediately, since BFS starts from all sources at once. Scanning continues, fresh now counts six, and the second rotten orange joins the queue too. BFS begins minute zero, processing both rotten oranges together from the queue. Neighboring fresh cells turn rotten, fresh count drops, and new rotten cells enter the queue. Minute one finishes, with fresh down to two and four new rotten oranges queued. By this point every fresh orange has turned rotten, so fresh reaches zero. The BFS layers finish and the function returns two minutes as the final answer.
say.code: Here's the template. First, scan the grid. Every rotten orange goes in the queue, and we count the fresh ones. Then, while fruit is still fresh, we pop exactly one layer. Each fresh neighbour is marked rotten right away, so it's queued only once. Lower the count and queue it. One layer done means one more minute. Anything still fresh? Return minus one.
say.outro: Linear in the grid size. Reach for multi source BFS when you hear: many starts spreading at once, distance to the nearest something, minutes until everything is infected, or start from the border.

lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container the problem expects for our method.
The method orangesRotting takes the grid and returns the minutes until no fresh orange remains, or negative one.
We read the number of rows and columns from the grid so we can check boundaries later.
We create a double ended queue that will hold every rotten orange as a BFS source.
We start a counter for fresh oranges so we know when everything has rotted.
We loop over every row of the grid to scan for starting cells.
Inside each row we loop over every column to visit each cell.
We check whether the current cell holds a rotten orange, which is a source.
Each rotten orange goes into the queue at the start, so all sources begin together at distance zero.
Otherwise we check whether the cell holds a fresh orange.
We count that fresh orange so we can later tell whether all of them rotted.
We set the minutes counter to zero, since the sources are already rotten at time zero.
We keep expanding while rotten oranges remain to spread and fresh oranges still exist.
We process exactly the current queue size, which is one full layer, equal to one minute.
We pop the next rotten orange from the front of the queue and read its row and column.
We try the four neighbor directions: down, up, right and left.
We compute the neighbor's row and column by adding the direction offsets.
We make sure the neighbor is inside the grid and holds a fresh orange.
We mark the neighbor rotten so no other source can reach it again.
We reduce the fresh count because this orange just rotted.
We add the newly rotten orange to the queue so it spreads in the next layer.
After finishing the whole layer, we add one minute to the timer.
If no fresh oranges remain we return the minutes, otherwise some were unreachable and we return negative one.

pattern-topological-sort.name: Topological Sort
pattern-topological-sort.title: Topological Sort — the pattern
signals: prerequisites, dependencies, or must happen before
find a valid build or course order
detect a cycle in a directed graph
derive an order from pairwise rules
process a task once all inputs are ready
variants: Kahn's BFS with in-degrees

say.intro: Okay, topological sort. Whenever things depend on other things, like courses, builds, or tasks, you need an order where everything comes after what it needs. Google asks this constantly. Our example is Course Schedule Two. Six courses. Two needs zero and one. Three and four need two. Five needs three and four. So zero through five works.
say.brute: Without the pattern, people sweep. Go through every course, and take any whose prerequisites are all done. Then sweep again, and again, until nothing is left. If a sweep finds nothing new, there's a cycle. It's correct. But each sweep rechecks every prerequisite of every course. A chain of two thousand courses means two thousand sweeps, and billions of checks.
say.insight: Here's the trick. For each course, keep a count of unfinished prerequisites. That's its in degree. A course is ready exactly when the count hits zero. And finishing a course only changes the courses that depend on it. So the recipe. Count in degrees. Queue everything at zero. Pop one, add it to the order, and decrement its neighbours. Whoever hits zero joins the queue.
say.anim: We build an adjacency list and in degree counts for six courses. Each prerequisite pair updates adjacency and increases the dependent course's in degree. After processing all edges, courses zero and one have zero in degree, so they start the queue. We pop course zero, add it to order, and decrease in degree for course two. Popping course one drops course two's in degree to zero, so it joins the queue. Processing course two finishes courses three and four's remaining prerequisite, queuing both. Finishing courses three and four finally zeroes out course five's in degree, queuing it. Course five is popped last, giving the final topological order zero one two three four five.
say.code: First, build edges from each prerequisite to the course that needs it, and count in degrees. Then queue every course with nothing blocking it. Pop one and append it to the order. Decrement each neighbour's count. If it reaches zero, its last blocker is gone, so queue it. Finally, if the order is missing courses, they were stuck in a cycle, so return an empty list.
say.outro: V plus E time. Reach for topological sort when you hear: prerequisites or dependencies, find a valid order, detect a cycle in a directed graph, or an order built from rules.

pattern-union-find.hook: Two tiny operations, find and union, answer 'are these connected?' in nearly constant time as edges arrive.

pattern-union-find.exampleWhy: Edges 1-2, 2-3 and 3-4 already join 1 and 4, so edge 1-4 closes a cycle.

say.intro: Okay, union find. Also called disjoint set union. It answers one question, fast. Are these two things in the same group? And it keeps answering as new connections arrive. Our example is Redundant Connection. Edges one two, two three, three four. Then one four closes a loop. So that's the extra edge.
say.brute: Without the pattern, people search. Before adding each edge, run a depth first search from one end. Can it already reach the other end? If yes, this edge is redundant. It's correct. But every check can walk the whole graph again. A thousand edges means up to a million steps. And we're finding full paths, when all we need is yes or no.
say.insight: Here's the key. We only care about groups, not paths. So give each group a root, and every node points toward it. The recipe. Start with every node as its own root. Find follows parents up to the root, and shortcuts the path as it goes. Union finds both roots. Same root? Already connected. Otherwise, hang the smaller tree under the bigger one.
say.anim: We start with each node as its own parent, every group size one. Processing edge one two, we find roots one and two separately. Roots differ, so we union them, attaching two under one. Next edge two three finds roots one and three, still different, so we merge again. Edge three four follows the same pattern, roots one and four merge into one group. Now edge one four is checked, both nodes already point to root one. Since ra equals rb, this edge would create a cycle, union fails. The redundant connection found is edge one four, our final answer.
say.code: Here's the template. The parent list starts with every node pointing at itself. Find walks up to the root, and the line inside points each node at its grandparent. That's path compression. Union finds both roots. If they match, return false, they were already connected. Otherwise, attach the smaller tree under the larger and add up the sizes. In the main loop, the first failed union is our answer.
say.outro: Nearly constant time per operation. Reach for union find when you hear: already connected, edges arriving one by one, merging groups, or an edge that creates a cycle.

say.intro: Okay, minimum spanning trees. You need to connect everything, cities, servers, points, for the smallest total cost. No loops, no waste. Our example is Min Cost to Connect All Points. Five points, and each link costs the Manhattan distance. The cheapest way to wire them all costs twenty.
say.brute: Without the pattern, people grow the network by brute force. Start at point zero. Every round, check every pair, one point inside and one outside, and add the cheapest link. It's correct. But each round rescans everything from scratch. With a thousand points, that's hundreds of millions of distance checks.
say.insight: Here's the key. The cheapest edge joining two separate groups is always safe. Some minimum tree uses it. That's Kruskal's algorithm. The recipe. List every edge with its cost. Sort them, cheapest first. For each edge, ask union find, are both ends already in one group? If yes, skip it, it would make a loop. If not, merge and pay. Stop at n minus one edges.
say.anim: We start with five points and will compute every pairwise distance between them. Each distance gets stored as an edge, like four between points zero and one. All edges are now sorted by distance, and union find starts with everyone separate. Smallest edge, distance three between one and three, joins them, cost becomes three. Next edge distance four merges zero into the group, cost rises to seven. Edge distance four between three and four has different roots, so cost grows to eleven. Edge zero to three is skipped since both already share the same root, avoiding a cycle. The final edge distance nine joins the last group, giving total cost twenty.
say.code: Here's the template. First, every pair of points becomes a candidate edge, with its distance. Sort them, cheapest first. Then a small find function with path compression. Now walk the edges. If both ends share a root, skip it, it would close a loop. Otherwise merge the groups and add the cost. Once we've used n minus one edges, the tree is complete.
say.outro: N squared log n here. Reach for a minimum spanning tree when you hear: connect all points, minimum total cost of wires or roads, or everything reachable with no waste.

say.intro: Okay, shortest paths. Edges have weights, like price or time, and you want the cheapest route. Dijkstra and Bellman Ford both use the same move, called relaxing an edge. Our example is Cheapest Flights within K Stops. Four cities, at most one stop. The best fare from zero to three is seven hundred.
say.brute: Without the pattern, people try every route. Depth first search from the source, along every flight, counting stops. And we keep re-pricing the same cities over and over.
say.insight: Here's the key. Keep one best known cost per city. Relaxing an edge asks, is going through u cheaper for v? If so, update v. The only question is the order. No limits and no negative weights? Dijkstra pops the cheapest city from a heap. A stop limit? Bellman Ford relaxes every edge once per round. After round i, costs are best using at most i flights.

Edge one to two relaxes, making node two cost two hundred through node one. Edge one to three relaxes too, giving node three a cost of seven hundred. After two rounds, final prices are zero, one hundred, two hundred, seven hundred, so answer is seven hundred.

At the end, an unreached city means minus one.
say.outro: K times E time. Reach for shortest paths when you hear: weighted edges, cheapest or fastest route, at most k stops, negative weights, or minimise the worst step.

say.intro: Okay, Eulerian paths. Can you travel every edge exactly once? Like drawing a shape without lifting your pen. Interviewers hide it as tickets, dominoes, or pairs to chain. Our example is Reconstruct Itinerary. Four tickets, starting at JFK, smallest airport names first. The answer is JFK, NRT, JFK, KUL, SFO.
say.brute: Without the pattern, people backtrack. From JFK, take the smallest unused ticket, and keep going. Stuck before every ticket is used? Undo, and try the next one. It works. Here, flying to KUL first strands us at SFO, with the NRT tickets unused. Every wrong turn is found only at a dead end, so the retries can grow exponentially.
say.insight: Here's the clever bit, Hierholzer's algorithm. When a greedy walk gets stuck, that airport has to be the end of the route. So never undo. Just write each airport down the moment it runs out of tickets, and reverse the list at the end. Leftover loops get spliced in automatically. The recipe. Sort neighbours. Walk and delete edges. Append when stuck. Reverse.
say.anim: We build an adjacency map from tickets, sorted in reverse so popping gives smallest destination first. JFK now points to NRT and KUL, ready for the greedy walk to begin. Starting the depth first search at JFK, we pop and visit KUL, then SFO. SFO has no outgoing flights, so it gets stuck and appended first to route. KUL also runs out of edges, so it's appended next, right after SFO. Back at JFK, we pop NRT, then JFK again, before both run dry and get appended. NRT then JFK finish their edges too, each appended as they get stuck. Reversing the post-order route gives the final itinerary: JFK, NRT, JFK, KUL, SFO.
say.code: Here's the template. Sort the tickets in reverse, so popping from the end gives the smallest airport. The depth first search keeps flying while this airport has tickets. Popping a ticket deletes it, so each one is used once. When nothing is left, append the airport. That's post order. Finally, reverse the list, and that's the itinerary.
say.outro: E log E time. Reach for an Eulerian path when you hear: use every edge, ticket, or domino exactly once, rebuild a route from pairs, or draw it without lifting the pen.

say.intro: Okay, so this is zero one knapsack. You have items, and each one gets a single decision. Take it, or leave it. Never twice. Interviewers love it because it hides inside subset sums, partitions and plus minus puzzles. Our example: can one, five, eleven, five split into two equal halves? Yes. Eleven versus one plus five plus five.
say.brute: So what do people try first? Every subset. For each number, branch. Take it, or skip it. If some branch lands exactly on half the total, we're done. It's correct. But it doubles with every item. Two hundred numbers? Two to the two hundred subsets. And yet the amount left over only has a few thousand possible values.
say.insight: Here's the thing. All that matters is how much capacity is left. So here's the recipe. One, pick the capacity, here half the total. Two, let each cell answer the question for that capacity, and seed zero. Three, for each item, sweep capacity from high to low. Four, combine skip with take. Five, read the target cell.
say.anim: We sum the numbers to get total twenty two, then set target to eleven, half the total. We build a dp array of size twelve, marking only capacity zero as reachable. Processing num equals one, we sweep capacities from eleven down to one, updating dp from lower values. After item one, dp shows capacity zero and one reachable, so progress is building toward eleven. Now num equals five, sweeping down, dp at five and six become true, reflecting new reachable sums. Item eleven is too big for most capacities, so its inner loop barely updates anything. Processing the second five, dp at nine and ten also turn true, nearing our target. Finally dp at target eleven is true, so the function returns true, confirming equal partition exists.
say.code: Now the code. The target is half the total. We seed cell zero as true, because an empty subset makes zero. Then for each number, we loop capacity backwards. Why backwards? So this number is only ever used once. Each cell is true if skipping works, or taking does. Finally, we return the target cell.
say.outro: n times target time, target space. Listen for the signals. Each item once. An exact subset sum. Equal halves. Plus or minus signs. Best value under a weight limit.

lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container the problem expects for our method.
The method canPartition takes a list of numbers and returns whether it can be split into two equal-sum subsets.
We compute the total sum of all numbers, since equal halves must each be exactly half of this total.
If the total is odd, no two whole-number halves can be equal, so we must check that first.
In that odd case we immediately return false because a fair split is impossible.
Otherwise we set target to half the total, turning the problem into finding a subset that sums to target.
We build a row of booleans indexed by capacity from zero to target, all starting as false.
We mark capacity zero as true, because the empty subset always makes a sum of zero.
We loop over each number, deciding once per item whether to take it or skip it.
We walk capacity from target down to the number's value, going downward so each number is used at most once.
A capacity is reachable if it already was, or if capacity minus this number was reachable before taking it.
Finally we return whether the target sum is reachable, which tells us if a valid partition exists.

pattern-unbounded-knapsack.name: Unbounded Knapsack
pattern-unbounded-knapsack.title: Unbounded Knapsack — the pattern
signals: unlimited supply of each coin or item
build an amount from reusable pieces
fewest coins or squares to make n
count combinations, order does not matter
variants: count combinations: coins outer, amount inner
count permutations: amount outer, coins inner
minimum pieces: dp[a] = 1 + min over items
one row, capacity looped forwards
pattern-unbounded-knapsack.hook: Same knapsack, one change: items never run out, so the loop direction flips.
pattern-unbounded-knapsack.ask: Build a target from items you may reuse any number of times, filling a row indexed by amount from small to large.
pattern-unbounded-knapsack.exampleWhy: 5, 2+2+1, 2+1+1+1 and 1+1+1+1+1 — four combinations of coins 1, 2, 5 that make 5.

brute.idea: At each coin, either use it again and stay on it, or move on to the next coin; count the branches that land exactly on the amount.
steps: State: coin index and amount so far
Use this coin again: stay on it
Or move on to the next coin
Count branches that hit the amount
brute.whySlow: Amount 5000 with a few coins explodes into astronomically many branches, yet there are only k·5001 distinct states.

optimal.insight: Reuse means a cell may build on a cell already updated for the same item. So loop the amount forwards, and put items in the outer loop so each combination is counted once.
steps: Index the row by amount; seed dp[0]
Outer loop over items, inner loop over amount
Loop amount upwards so an item can repeat
dp[a] adds or mins with dp[a - item]
Answer at dp[target]

codeNotes.note: Seed: one way to make zero
Add ways that end with this coin

pitfalls: Swapping the loops counts orderings (1+2 and 2+1 separately) instead of combinations.
Looping amount backwards silently turns it into 0/1 knapsack.

say.intro: Okay, so this is unbounded knapsack. Same idea as zero one, but items never run out. Use a coin once, twice, ten times. Interviewers love it because coin change and its cousins are everywhere. Our example: how many ways make five from coins one, two and five? Four.
say.brute: So what do people try first? Branch at every coin. Use it again and stay put, or move on to the next coin. Count every branch that lands on exactly five. It works. But each step splits in two. An amount of five thousand? The branches explode. Yet there are only coins times amount real states.
say.insight: Here's the thing. Reusing a coin means a cell can build on one we just updated. So the loop runs forwards. Here's the recipe. One, a row by amount, seed zero. Two, items outside, amounts inside. Three, sweep amounts upwards. Four, each cell adds the cell one item back. Five, read the target.
say.anim: We start with amount five and coins one, two, five, and an empty dp array. Dp zero is set to one, representing one way to make zero amount. Using coin one, every amount from one to five gets exactly one way, filling dp with ones. Now using coin two, we build on earlier updated cells, so dp two and four jump to two and three. Finally coin five adds one more way, updating dp five from three to four. The loops finish and we return dp at amount five, the final answer. The result is four ways to make change for five using coins one, two, and five.
say.code: Now the code. One row, indexed by amount. Cell zero starts at one, there's one way to make nothing. Coins go in the outer loop, so we count combinations, not orders. The amount loops forwards, so a coin can be used again. Each cell adds the ways from one coin back. Then return the last cell.
say.outro: Coins times amount time, linear space. Listen for the signals. Unlimited supply. Building an amount from reusable pieces. Fewest coins. Or counting combinations.

lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the wrapper this problem expects for our method.
The change method takes a target amount and a list of coin values, and returns the number of combinations.
We create a row dp with one slot per amount from zero up to the target, all starting at zero.
We set dp at zero to one, because there is exactly one way to make nothing: use no coins.
We put coins in the outer loop so each combination is counted once, regardless of the order of coins.
For each coin we walk amounts forward starting at the coin value, since smaller amounts cannot use this coin.
We add the ways to make the amount minus the coin, and going forward lets the same coin be reused.
We return dp at the target amount, which holds the total number of coin combinations that make it.

pattern-longest-increasing-subsequence.name: Longest Increasing Subsequence
pattern-longest-increasing-subsequence.title: Longest Increasing Subsequence — the pattern
signals: longest subsequence with an ordering rule
chain items where each beats the last
nest envelopes or boxes inside each other
each element divides or extends the previous
variants: dp[i] = best chain ending at i
sort first, then LIS on one key
patience sorting with binary search, n log n
hash map by value for fixed difference
pattern-longest-increasing-subsequence.hook: Ask one question per index: what is the longest chain that ends right here?
pattern-longest-increasing-subsequence.ask: Find the longest subsequence obeying an ordering rule by storing, for each index, the best chain that ends there.
pattern-longest-increasing-subsequence.exampleWhy: 0, 1, 2, 3 is strictly increasing with length 4; nothing longer exists.

brute.idea: Walk the array and, at each number, either skip it or take it if it beats the last number taken; keep the longest result.
steps: Remember the index of the last taken number
Skip the current number
Or take it if it is bigger
Return the longer choice
brute.whySlow: 2,500 numbers mean 2^2500 subsequences, but only 2,500 places a chain can end.

optimal.insight: A chain is defined by where it ends. If dp[j] is the best chain ending at j, then dp[i] is one more than the best dp[j] that may come before i.
steps: dp[i] = best chain ending at index i
Start every dp[i] at 1: the item alone
For each earlier j that fits the rule, extend
Answer is the max over all dp[i]

codeNotes.note: Every item alone is a chain of one
Look at every earlier end point

pitfalls: Returning dp[-1] instead of max(dp): the best chain need not end at the last item.
Using <= when the rule is strictly increasing (or vice versa).

say.intro: Okay, so this is longest increasing subsequence. Pick items in order, skipping freely, so each one beats the last. Interviewers love it because envelopes, divisible sets and chains are all secretly this. Our example: zero, one, zero, three, two, three. The answer is four. Zero, one, two, three.
say.brute: So what do people try first? Walk the array. At each number, skip it, or take it if it's bigger than the last one we took. Keep the longer result. It's correct. But every number doubles the work. Twenty five hundred numbers? Two to the twenty five hundred. Yet a chain can only end in twenty five hundred places.
say.insight: Here's the thing. A chain is defined by where it ends. So ask, for each index, what's the longest chain ending right here? Here's the recipe. One, a cell per index. Two, start each at one, the item alone. Three, look back at every earlier item that fits, and extend its chain. Four, take the max of all cells.
say.anim: We start with dp all ones, since every number alone is a chain of length one. At i equals one, j equals zero, zero is less than one, so dp of one becomes two. At i equals three, we compare against zero, one, and zero again, growing dp of three up to three. At i equals four, comparing against earlier smaller values raises dp of four to three. At i equals five, dp of five climbs using dp of three or four, reaching four. Final dp array is one, two, one, three, three, four, the best chain ending at each index. The max of dp is four, so the longest increasing subsequence length is four.
say.code: Now the code. Every cell starts at one. For each index, we look at every earlier index. If the earlier number is smaller, the rule holds. Then this cell can be that chain plus one, if that's better. Finally, the best chain could end anywhere, so we return the max.
say.outro: n squared time, linear space. Listen for the signals. Longest subsequence with an order rule. Chains. Nesting envelopes. Each item extending the last.

lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container the interview platform expects for our method.
The method lengthOfLIS takes a list of numbers and returns the length of the longest increasing subsequence.
We create a dp list the same size as nums, starting every entry at one since each number alone is a chain.
We loop over each index i, treating it as the possible end of an increasing chain.
For each i, an inner loop visits every earlier index j that could come before it in a chain.
We check whether the number at j is smaller than the number at i, so it can extend the chain.
If so, dp at i becomes the larger of its current value or dp at j plus one.
Finally we return the largest dp value, since the best chain may end at any index.

pattern-grid-dp.name: Grid DP
pattern-grid-dp.title: Grid DP — the pattern
signals: move only right or down
count paths from corner to corner
cheapest path through a grid of costs
largest square or shape of ones
variants: count paths: add top and left
min or max cost: best of top and left
obstacles: blocked cells become zero
roll to one row for linear space
