pattern-grid-dp.hook: When moves only go right or down, every cell depends on just the cell above and the cell to its left.
pattern-grid-dp.ask: Fill a table the same shape as the grid, where each cell combines the answers of the cells you could have come from.
pattern-grid-dp.exampleWhy: The path 1, 3, 1, 1, 1 along the top then down the right side sums to 7.

brute.idea: From each cell, recursively try going down and going right, and keep the cheaper path to the bottom-right corner.
steps: At the target, return its value
Otherwise recurse down and right
Add this cell to the cheaper result
brute.whySlow: Every cell is re-solved along every path that reaches it: a 20 by 20 grid has billions of paths but only 400 cells.

optimal.insight: A cell can only be entered from above or from the left. Fill the grid top to bottom, left to right, and both of those are always ready.
steps: dp has the same shape as the grid
Seed the start cell
First row and column have one way in
Every other cell: its value plus best of top and left
Answer in the bottom-right cell

pitfalls: Forgetting the first row and column, which have only one neighbour to come from.
Filling in the wrong order, so top or left is not computed yet.

say.intro: Okay, so this is grid DP. You move through a grid, only right or down, and want a count or a best cost. Interviewers love it because it's the cleanest picture of dynamic programming there is. Our example: the cheapest path through one three one, one five one, four two one. That's seven.
say.brute: So what do people try first? From every cell, try going down, try going right, and keep the cheaper. It's correct. But the same cells get solved again and again, once for every path through them. A twenty by twenty grid has billions of paths. And only four hundred cells.
say.insight: Here's the thing. You can only enter a cell from above or from the left. So fill top to bottom, left to right, and both are always ready. Here's the recipe. One, a table shaped like the grid. Two, seed the start. Three, edges have one way in. Four, every other cell adds the best of top and left. Five, read the corner.
say.anim: We start with a three by three grid and an empty dp table of zeros. At row zero, column zero, dp just copies the grid value, giving one. Still on row zero, each cell adds the grid value to the cell on its left, reaching four then five. Moving to row one, column zero only has a cell above, so two comes from one plus one. For other cells, dp takes the smaller of the cell above or to the left before adding the grid value, giving seven and six. Row two repeats this rule, always picking the cheaper path from above or the left. The last cells fill in as eight and seven, tracking the cheapest route down and across. The function returns the bottom right cell, giving a minimum path sum of seven.
say.code: Now the code. We make a table the same shape as the grid. The start cell is just its own value. On the top row or left column, there's only one way in, so we add that neighbour. Everywhere else, we add the smaller of top and left. Finally, return the bottom right corner.
say.outro: m times n time and space. Listen for the signals. Moves only right or down. Counting paths. Cheapest route through costs. Or the largest square of ones.

lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container that the problem expects for our method.
The minPathSum method takes a grid of costs and returns the smallest total along a path.
We read the number of rows and columns from the grid so we know the table dimensions.
We build a dp table of zeros with the same shape as the grid to hold best path costs.
We loop over every row from top to bottom so earlier rows are always finished first.
Inside each row we loop over columns from left to right so left neighbors are ready.
We check for the top left corner, which is the starting cell with no previous cell.
At the start, the cheapest cost is simply the grid value at that cell.
If we are in the first row, the only way in is from the left.
So the cost here is the grid value plus the best cost of the cell to the left.
If we are in the first column, the only way in is from above.
So the cost here is the grid value plus the best cost of the cell above.
Otherwise we can arrive from either above or from the left, so we must choose.
We add the grid value to the smaller of the cost from above and the cost from the left.
Finally we return the dp value at the bottom right corner, which is the minimum total path cost.

pattern-string-dp-lcs-edit-distance.name: String DP (LCS / Edit Distance)
pattern-string-dp-lcs-edit-distance.title: String DP (LCS / Edit Distance) — the pattern
signals: two strings compared character by character
minimum insert, delete or replace operations
longest common subsequence or supersequence
does a pattern with wildcards match
is one string woven from two others
variants: LCS: match adds one, else best skip
edit distance: match free, else 1 + min of three
counting matches: distinct subsequences
pattern matching: wildcard and regex
pattern-string-dp-lcs-edit-distance.hook: Two strings, two pointers, and one question per pair of prefixes: how do these last characters relate?
pattern-string-dp-lcs-edit-distance.ask: Compare two strings with a table where dp[i][j] answers the question for the first i characters of one and the first j of the other.
pattern-string-dp-lcs-edit-distance.exampleWhy: horse → rorse (replace h) → rose (delete r) → ros (delete e): 3 operations.

brute.idea: Recurse on two positions: if the letters match move both on for free, otherwise try insert, delete and replace and keep the cheapest.
steps: One word used up: the rest are inserts or deletes
Letters match: move both, no cost
Otherwise try all three edits
Keep the cheapest, plus one
brute.whySlow: Each mismatch branches three ways; two 500-letter words give 3^1000 calls for only 250,000 prefix pairs.

optimal.insight: Every subproblem is a pair of prefixes (i, j). Put them in an (m+1) by (n+1) table; each cell only looks at its diagonal, top and left neighbours.
steps: dp[i][j] = answer for first i and first j characters
Border row and column: one string empty
Last characters match: take the diagonal
Otherwise combine top, left and diagonal
Answer in dp[m][n]

codeNotes.note: Table of prefix pairs, with a border

pitfalls: Indexing word1[i] instead of word1[i - 1]: cell i means the first i characters.
Leaving the border at zero — empty versus non-empty still costs edits.

say.intro: Okay, so this is string DP. Two strings, compared character by character. Longest common subsequence, edit distance, wildcard matching. Interviewers love it because one table solves a whole family. Our example: turn horse into ros. Three edits. Replace h, delete r, delete e.
say.brute: So what do people try first? Recurse on two positions. If the letters match, move both on for free. If not, try insert, delete and replace, and keep the cheapest. It works. But every mismatch branches three ways. Two five hundred letter words? Three to the thousand calls. For only a quarter million prefix pairs.
say.insight: Here's the thing. Every question is just a pair of prefixes. So lay them in a table. Here's the recipe. One, a cell for the first i and first j characters. Two, a border for when one string is empty. Three, if the last letters match, take the diagonal. Four, if not, combine top, left and diagonal. Five, read the bottom corner.
say.anim: We compare horse and ros, building a table of prefix lengths five by three. First column and row fill with zero to five and zero to three, base conversion costs. Now for each letter pair we check if characters match, like h versus r. Since they differ, we take one plus the smallest neighboring cost, filling row one. At row two, o matches o, so dp just copies the diagonal value one. Row four handles s matching s, copying diagonal twos and threes forward smoothly. After filling all rows, the bottom right cell holds the final edit distance. The function returns three, the minimum edits turning horse into ros.
say.code: Now the code. The table has an extra row and column for empty prefixes. The border is just the length, delete or insert everything. Then we compare the last characters of each prefix. A match is free, so we copy the diagonal. Otherwise it's one plus the cheapest of delete, insert or replace. Then return the bottom right cell.
say.outro: m times n time and space. Listen for the signals. Two strings compared. Minimum edits. Common subsequences. Wildcard patterns. Or weaving two strings into one.

lineNotes: We define a Solution class, as the problem platform expects, to hold our edit distance method.
The method minDistance takes word1 and word2 and returns the minimum number of edits to turn one into the other.
We store the lengths of word1 and word2 in m and n so we can size the table.
We build an m plus one by n plus one table of zeros, where each cell covers a pair of prefixes.
This loop walks every row index from zero through m to fill the first column.
Turning the first i letters of word1 into an empty string takes i deletions, so we set that cell to i.
This loop walks every column index from zero through n to fill the first row.
Turning an empty string into the first j letters of word2 takes j insertions, so we set that cell to j.
Now we move through each row from one to m, covering every nonempty prefix of word1.
Inside each row we move through each column from one to n, covering every nonempty prefix of word2.
We compare the current last characters, using index minus one because the table is shifted by one.
If the characters match, no edit is needed, so we copy the diagonal value from the shorter prefixes.
Otherwise the characters differ, so we must spend one edit and choose the cheapest option.
We add one to the minimum of the top, left and diagonal neighbours, which stand for delete, insert and replace.
The bottom right cell holds the answer for the full words, so we return it.

pattern-interval-dp.name: Interval DP
pattern-interval-dp.title: Interval DP — the pattern
signals: answer for a range l..r of the array
merge, cut or burst pieces of a row
order of operations changes the cost
palindromes inside a substring
two players taking from either end
variants: split point k: dp[l][k] + dp[k][r] + cost
shrink from ends: dp[l+1][r] vs dp[l][r-1]
last action in the range, not first
fill by increasing interval length
pattern-interval-dp.hook: When the answer for a whole row depends on how you split it, solve every sub-range — shortest ones first.
pattern-interval-dp.ask: Let dp[l][r] be the answer for the range l..r, and build it from smaller ranges by trying every split point inside.

brute.idea: Try every order: pick any balloon to pop next, collect its coins, and recurse on the remaining list; keep the best total.
steps: Empty list: zero coins
Try popping each balloon next
Coins: left times it times right
Recurse on the rest, keep the max
brute.whySlow: Every pop order is a different branch: 300 balloons have 300! orders, but only about 45,000 ranges.

optimal.insight: Choose which balloon in (l, r) bursts LAST. Its neighbours are then the fixed walls l and r, and the two sides become independent smaller intervals.
steps: dp[l][r] = best answer for the range l..r
Pad or seed the smallest ranges
Loop range length from short to long
Try every split k: left + right + cost of k
Answer in dp[0][n-1]

codeNotes.note: Try every split: k bursts last

pitfalls: Choosing the FIRST action in the range: its neighbours keep changing, so sides are not independent.
Looping l and r in plain order instead of by length, reading ranges not yet solved.

say.intro: Okay, so this is interval DP. The answer for a range depends on how you split it. Bursting balloons, cutting sticks, palindromes, games from both ends. Interviewers love it because it looks impossible until you see it. Our example: balloons three, one, five. Best total? Thirty five.
say.brute: So what do people try first? Try every order. Pick a balloon, pop it, collect left times it times right, and recurse on the rest. Keep the best. It works. But every order is a new branch. Three hundred balloons? Three hundred factorial orders. Yet there are only about forty five thousand ranges.
say.insight: Here's the thing. Pick the balloon that bursts last in a range. Its neighbours are then the fixed walls, and the two sides don't touch. Here's the recipe. One, a cell per range. Two, seed the tiny ranges. Three, go from short ranges to long. Four, try every split point. Five, read the whole range.
say.anim: Balloons are padded with ones on both sides, giving the array one, three, one, five, one. We start with small gaps, bursting balloon at index one last between walls one and three, scoring three. Next gap between walls one and three, bursting middle balloon gives fifteen coins, stored in the table. Then bursting balloon at index three between walls one and five scores five, filling another small interval. Now length three combines smaller results, testing each balloon as the last burst, reaching thirty for left zero. For the next window, trying balloons as last burst gives thirty, the best combination so far. Finally the full interval from zero to four tries each possible last balloon, picking the best total. The algorithm returns thirty five, the maximum coins obtainable by bursting all balloons optimally.
say.code: Now the code. We pad the row with ones as walls. Each cell holds the best inside a range. We loop by length, so smaller ranges are always ready. For each range, we try every balloon k as the last one. Its coins plus the best of each side. Finally, the full range is the answer.
say.outro: n cubed time, n squared space. Listen for the signals. A range of the array. Merging, cutting or bursting. Order changes the cost. Palindromes. Or players taking from both ends.

lineNotes: This line declares the Solution class that holds our method, as the platform expects.
We define maxCoins, which takes the list of balloon values and returns the maximum coins collectable.
We pad nums with a one on each end, so the edge balloons have virtual neighbours worth one.
We store the padded length as n, which sizes our table and bounds our loops.
We build an n by n table of zeros, where dp at left and right is the best score strictly between those walls.
We loop over interval length from two upward, so smaller intervals are always solved before the larger ones using them.
For each length, we slide the left wall across every position that still leaves room for a right wall.
We compute right as left plus length, fixing the two walls of the current interval.
We try every balloon k strictly between the walls as the one that bursts last in this interval.
If k bursts last, its neighbours are the walls, so its coins are left value times k value times right value.
We update dp for this interval with the best of its current value or the left side plus these coins plus the right side.
We return dp from zero to n minus one, the best total for the whole padded range.

pattern-tree-dp.name: Tree DP
pattern-tree-dp.title: Tree DP — the pattern
signals: optimize a choice made at every tree node
a parent and its child cannot both be picked
longest path or diameter through any node
subtree answer built from the children's answers
variants: return a pair: take or skip
update global best, return one branch
three states: covered, camera, needs cover
pattern-tree-dp.hook: When a subtree's answer comes from its children's answers, one post-order pass solves the whole tree.
pattern-tree-dp.ask: Tree DP means every node returns a small summary of its subtree, often several states like take or skip, and the parent combines its children's summaries.
pattern-tree-dp.exampleWhy: House Robber III: rob 4 and 5, the root's children, for 9. Robbing the root gives only 8.

brute.idea: Plain recursion with no stored answers: from each node, re-solve deeper subtrees every time you need them.
steps: Rob the node, recurse into the four grandchildren
Skip the node, recurse into the two children
Return the better of the two
brute.whySlow: Each node is re-solved by its parent and by its grandparent; on a long chain that repeats Fibonacci-style, exponentially.

optimal.insight: Solve each subtree once, bottom-up. Each node returns every state its parent may need, like robbed and not robbed, combined in constant time.
steps: Define the states a subtree must report upward
Post-order DFS: get both children's states first
Combine the children's states into this node's states
Read the answer from the root's states

codeNotes.note: Step 4: best of the root's states

pitfalls: Returning one number loses information; the parent needs every state it combines.
For diameter or max path, update a global best but return one branch upward.

say.intro: Okay, tree DP. This is dynamic programming where the table is the tree itself. Each node answers a question about its own subtree, using only its children's answers. Our example is House Robber Three. You can't rob a house and its direct child on the same night. The best haul here is nine, robbing four and five.
say.brute: So what does everyone try first? Plain recursion. At each node, either rob it and jump to the four grandchildren, or skip it and recurse into the two children. It's correct. But look closer. Every node gets solved by its parent, and again by its grandparent. That doubling repeats all the way down. On a long chain, the work grows exponentially.
say.insight: Here's the trick. Never ask a subtree twice. Instead, have each node hand up everything its parent could need. Here, that's two numbers. Best if I'm robbed, and best if I'm not. And the recipe works for any tree DP. Define the states. Visit the children first, post-order. Combine their states into yours. Then read the answer at the root.
say.anim: We start at root node 3, about to recurse into its left subtree. The recursion dives down through node 4 and node 1, hitting null children returning zero zero. Node 1 computes with_node as 1 and without_node as 0, then returns upward. Node 3 at depth two returns three zero, letting node 4 combine results into four and four. Now we explore node 5's subtree, processing its child node 1 similarly, getting one and zero. Node 5 combines its child results, computing with_node five and without_node one, then returns. Back at root, with_node becomes eight and without_node becomes nine, combining both subtrees. The final answer is nine, the maximum amount that can be robbed.
say.code: Here's the template. The helper returns a pair, robbed and not robbed. An empty subtree gives zero and zero. Then we recurse into both children first. That's post-order. If we rob this node, both children must be skipped, so we add their second values. If we skip it, each child picks its own best. Finally, return the larger of the root's pair.
say.outro: Linear time, height space. Think tree DP when choices live on tree nodes, parents and children conflict, paths run through any node, or a subtree's answer comes from its children.

lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which holds the method that solves the house robber problem on a binary tree.
The rob method takes the root of the tree and returns the largest amount we can steal.
We define a helper called dfs that returns a summary pair for the subtree rooted at a node.
If the node is empty, there is nothing to rob, so we handle this base case first.
An empty subtree returns zero for both robbing and not robbing its root, which keeps parent math simple.
We recursively solve the left child first, getting its pair of robbed and not robbed totals.
We do the same for the right child, so both children are solved exactly once.
If we rob this node, we must skip both children, so we add their not robbed totals to the node value.
If we skip this node, each child is free, so we add the better option from the left and from the right.
We return both states as a pair so the parent can choose whichever it needs.
At the top, the answer is the larger of robbing or skipping the root.

pattern-bitmask-dp.name: Bitmask DP
pattern-bitmask-dp.title: Bitmask DP — the pattern
signals: n is tiny, at most 15 to 20
visit or assign every item exactly once
shortest route through all nodes
best ordering or pairing of a small set
variants: TSP style: mask plus last item
assignment: mask of used workers
subset DP over prime or letter masks
BFS over (node, visited mask)
pattern-bitmask-dp.hook: Twenty items have a million subsets. Store each subset as one integer and run DP over them.
pattern-bitmask-dp.ask: Bitmask DP records which items are already used as the bits of one integer, so a state like used-set plus last item fits in a table instead of n factorial orderings.
pattern-bitmask-dp.exampleWhy: Order 0,1,2 costs |0-0| + |1-2| + |2-1| = 2, the minimum, and it is lexicographically smallest.

brute.idea: Try every ordering of the items with permutations, score each one, and keep the cheapest.
steps: Generate all n factorial orderings
Score each ordering from scratch
Keep the cheapest; the first one wins ties
brute.whySlow: Fourteen items means about 87 billion orderings, and orders sharing a prefix are rescored from scratch.

optimal.insight: The future depends only on which items are used and where you stand, not their order. Encode the used set as bits: 2^n times n states, not n factorial.
steps: Let bit i of mask mean item i is used
State: the mask plus any extra, like the last item
Transition: pick an unused bit j, recurse on mask | 1 << j
Base case at the full mask; memoize every state

codeNotes.note: All bits set: every item used
Step 2: used set plus last item
Step 4: full mask closes the cycle

codeNotes.match: best = min(best, abs(last - nums[nxt]) + dp(mask | 1 << nxt, nxt))
codeNotes.note: Step 3: set the bit, recurse, keep min
Mark the chosen item as used

pitfalls: Only feasible for n up to about 20; check the constraints before using 2^n states.
Mask alone fails when cost depends on the last item; add it to the state.

say.intro: Okay, bitmask DP. When a problem wants the best ordering of a small set, the real state is which items you've already used. And a set of up to twenty items fits inside one integer. Our example: order zero, one, two so a cyclic cost is smallest. Here, zero, one, two costs just two.
say.brute: So what's the naive move? Try every ordering. Generate all permutations, score each, keep the best. It's correct. But n factorial grows brutally. Fourteen items is about eighty seven billion orders. And notice the waste. Orders that share a prefix get scored from scratch each time, even though the remaining choices are identical.
say.insight: Here's the key idea. Once you know which items are used and where you stand, the order you used them in no longer matters. So the state is a mask plus the last item. That's two to the n times n states, not n factorial. The recipe: one bit per item. Pick an unused bit, set it, recurse. Stop at the full mask, and memoize.
say.anim: We start with nums 1, 0, 2 and build a permutation using bitmask dynamic programming. Perm begins with just index 0, and mask marks only item 0 as used. For each next index, we compute dp over remaining masks to find the cheapest continuation. When mask reaches full, dp returns the cost closing back to the first element, here 1. Back at mask 1, dp compares branches and settles on best cost 2 for last equals 0. Index 1 gives matching cost, so perm becomes 0 and 1, mask updates to 3. Now checking from last equals 1, nxt 2 matches the dp value and gets appended. Mask reaches full, loop ends, and the final permutation returned is 0, 1, 2.
say.code: Here's the template. Full is all bits set, every item used. The cached helper takes the mask and the last item. When the mask is full, we pay to close the cycle. Otherwise, for each unused bit, we add the step cost, set that bit, and recurse, keeping the minimum. To rebuild, start at item zero, and keep marking the first choice that matches the optimal cost.
say.outro: Exponential, but in a tiny n. Think bitmask DP when n is at most twenty, every item is used once, you need a route through all nodes, or the best ordering of a small set.

lineNotes: We define the Solution class that holds the method for this problem.
The method findPermutation takes the list nums and returns the permutation that gives the smallest cyclic score.
We store n as the number of items in nums.
We build full as a mask with all n bits set, meaning every item has been used.
The cache decorator memoizes results so each state of used set and last item is computed only once.
The function dp takes a mask of used items and the last item placed, and returns the minimum remaining cost.
If the mask equals full, every item is placed, so we are ready to close the cycle.
To close the cycle we add the distance from the last item's value back to the value at the first position.
We start best as infinity so any real cost will replace it.
We loop over every candidate next item index from zero to n minus one.
We only consider an item if its bit in the mask is not set, meaning it is unused.
We try that item, adding the step cost plus the recursive cost with its bit set, and keep the minimum.
We return the smallest cost found among all choices for this state.
To rebuild the answer, we start the permutation with zero and a mask that marks only item zero as used.
We keep building until the mask shows all items have been placed.
We take the last placed item as the current position.
We scan candidate next items in increasing order so the first match is lexicographically smallest.
We pick an unused item whose step cost plus its future cost equals the optimal cost for the current state.
We append that item to the permutation since it lies on an optimal path.
We mark the item as used by setting its bit in the mask.
We break out of the loop because we only need the first valid choice at each step.
We return the finished permutation.

pattern-digit-dp.name: Digit DP
pattern-digit-dp.title: Digit DP — the pattern
signals: count integers in [lo, hi] with a digit rule
n as large as 10^9 or 10^18
digit sums, digit counts, or forbidden digits
numbers whose digits satisfy a property
variants: tight flag for the upper bound
started flag for leading zeros
range answer as f(hi) - f(lo - 1)
extra state: digit sum or remainder
pattern-digit-dp.hook: Counting numbers up to ten to the eighteen? Walk the digits, not the numbers.
pattern-digit-dp.ask: Digit DP counts the numbers from 0 to n with some digit property by building them digit by digit, tracking the position, a small summary, and whether we still match n's prefix.
pattern-digit-dp.exampleWhy: From 1 to 121 the digit 1 is written 55 times, counting both ones in 11 and all three in 111.

brute.idea: Loop over every number from 1 to n, turn it into a string, and count its ones.
steps: Loop x from 1 to n
Count the ones in x
Add them to a running total
brute.whySlow: n can be a billion: a billion string conversions, though numbers sharing a prefix behave identically after it.

optimal.insight: Once your prefix drops below n's prefix, later digits are free 0 to 9, so states repeat. Memoize on position, summary so far, and a tight flag.
steps: Turn n into its list of digits
State: position, summary so far, tight flag
Next digit goes up to n's digit if tight, else 9
Stay tight only when you pick n's digit; memoize

codeNotes.note: Step 1: n as a digit list
One full number built: its ones

codeNotes.match: total += dp(pos + 1, ones + (d == 1), tight and d == limit)
codeNotes.note: Step 4: stay tight only on n's digit
Start tight at the first digit

pitfalls: Leading zeros matter for rules like distinct digits; add a started flag.
For a range [lo, hi], answer f(hi) minus f(lo - 1).

say.intro: Okay, digit DP. Some problems ask you to count numbers up to a huge n, maybe ten to the eighteen, that have some digit property. You can't loop that far. So we build the numbers digit by digit instead. Our example: how many times is the digit one written from one to a hundred twenty one? Fifty five.
say.brute: So what's the obvious way? Loop over every number, turn it into a string, and count its ones. It's correct. But n can be a billion. That's a billion conversions. And here's the waste. Once a number's prefix is smaller than n's prefix, the remaining digits can be anything. Huge groups of numbers behave exactly alike, and we count each one separately.
say.insight: Here's the idea. Fill in digits left to right, and track three things. The position. A small summary, like ones so far. And a tight flag. Tight means we've matched n exactly so far, so the next digit is capped. Once we go below, every digit is free, and states start repeating. So memoize them. That's the recipe for any digit DP.
say.anim: We start with n equals 121, splitting it into digits 1, 2, 1. The recursion begins at position 0, with zero ones counted and tight still true. Once tight becomes false, the digit loop runs freely from 0 to 9 at each position. Deeper calls accumulate counts of ones, building totals like 11 and 20 at earlier positions. Back at position 0, tight is true again, so digits only loop up to the limit 2. Branch by branch, totals climb through 21 and 32 as ones counts combine across positions. The last branch with tight true finishes, returning 35 up through the recursion chain. All branches combine, and the final count of digit one occurrences is 55.
say.code: Here's the template. First, n becomes a list of digits. The helper takes the position, the ones so far, and tight. When we run out of digits, we've built one number, so report its ones. The limit is n's digit if tight, otherwise nine. For each digit, recurse, adding one if it's a one. We stay tight only if we picked exactly the limit. Start tight at position zero.
say.outro: About ten times digits squared work. Reach for digit DP when you count integers in a range, n is up to ten to the eighteen, or the rule is about digit sums, counts, or forbidden digits.

lineNotes: We define the Solution class that holds our method, as the problem format expects.
The method countDigitOne takes n and returns the total count of digit one across all numbers from zero to n.
We convert n into a list of its digits so we can place them one position at a time.
The cache decorator memoizes results, so repeated states of position, ones count, and tight flag are computed only once.
The function dp takes the current position, the ones counted so far, and whether we still match the prefix of n.
When position reaches the length of digits, the number is fully built, so we are at the base case.
At that point we return the ones count, which adds this number's count of one digits to the overall total.
The limit for this digit is the digit of n if we are tight, otherwise any digit up to nine.
We start a running total of ones counted across all numbers built from this state.
We loop over every digit choice from zero up to and including the limit.
We recurse to the next position, adding one to ones if d is one, and staying tight only if we hit the limit.
After trying all digit choices, we return the accumulated total for this state.
We start the search at position zero with no ones counted and the tight flag on, and return its result.

pattern-state-machine-dp.name: State Machine DP
pattern-state-machine-dp.title: State Machine DP — the pattern
signals: buy, sell, cooldown, or fee rules
at most k transactions
allowed moves depend on your current mode
adjacent choices restrict each other
variants: hold / sold / rest with cooldown
one hold and free state per transaction
letter-to-letter rules, like vowel chains
pattern-state-machine-dp.hook: Holding, just sold, resting: name the states, draw the arrows, and the DP writes itself.
pattern-state-machine-dp.ask: State machine DP keeps one best value per state, like holding a stock or resting, and at each step updates every state from the arrows that lead into it.
pattern-state-machine-dp.exampleWhy: Buy at 1, sell at 4, cool down, buy at 0, sell at 5: 3 + 5 = 8.

brute.idea: Recurse day by day, trying buy, sell, or wait from each state, with no caching, so every action sequence is explored.
steps: Each day, branch on buy, sell or wait
After a sale, skip one day
Return the best total over all branches
brute.whySlow: Branches double every day: 5,000 days means 2^5000 sequences, yet only three states exist per day.

optimal.insight: Each day you are in one of a few states: holding, just sold, or resting. Keep the best profit per state, updated from yesterday through the allowed arrows.
steps: List the states you can be in after each step
Draw the arrows: which actions move between states
Each new state = best over its incoming arrows
Update all states together; answer is the best final state

codeNotes.match: prev_hold, prev_sold, prev_rest = hold, sold, rest

codeNotes.note: Step 3: keep holding, or buy from rest

pitfalls: Updating in place mixes today with yesterday; snapshot the old values first.
Start impossible states at minus infinity, not zero, or you sell before buying.

say.intro: Okay, state machine DP. Some problems have modes. You're holding a stock, or you just sold, or you're resting. The trick is to name those modes and track the best score in each one. Our example: stock trading with a one day cooldown after every sale. The best profit here is eight.
say.brute: So how do people start? They recurse. Each day, try buying, selling, or waiting, and explore every sequence of actions. It works on tiny input. But every day multiplies the branches. Five thousand days is hopeless. And yet, on any given day, you can only be in three situations. All those branches collapse into just three numbers.
say.insight: Here's the core idea. Draw the machine. Holding can stay holding, or sell into sold. Sold must move to rest. That's the cooldown. Rest can stay, or buy into holding. The recipe: list the states, draw the arrows, and set each state to the best of its incoming arrows. Update them all together, once per day.
say.anim: We start with hold at negative infinity, and sold and rest both at zero. Price is 3: hold becomes negative three, since buying costs three with no prior profit. Price is 1: hold improves to negative one, a cheaper share to hold. Price is 4: selling now would only give sold equals three, so rest stays small. Price is 0: hold jumps to three, buying cheaply using rest profit from before. Price is 5: selling the held share gives sold equals eight, the best so far. Finally we compare sold and rest, and the maximum profit returned is eight.
say.code: Here's the template. Three variables, one per state. Hold starts at minus infinity, since we can't own anything yet. Each day, we snapshot yesterday's values first. Hold either keeps holding or buys from rest. Sold can only come from hold, plus today's price. Rest takes the better of resting or finishing a cooldown. At the end, the answer is sold or rest, never holding.
say.outro: Linear time, constant space. Think state machine DP when you see buy, sell, cooldown or fee rules, a cap on transactions, or choices that depend on your current mode.

lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container this problem's method lives in.
The maxProfit method takes the list of prices and returns the best total profit with a cooldown after selling.
Hold starts at negative infinity because before any purchase it is impossible to already own a share.
Sold starts at zero, meaning the state of having just sold today, with no profit yet and cooldown next.
Rest starts at zero, meaning we own nothing, are free to buy, and have made no profit so far.
We loop over each price p, treating each day as one step of the state machine.
We save yesterday's three values first so every update this day uses old values, not partly changed ones.
Hold is the better of staying in hold, or buying today from rest and paying the price p.
Sold comes only from holding yesterday and selling today, so we add today's price p to previous hold.
Rest is the better of staying rested, or coming off yesterday's sale, since the cooldown day ends in rest.
At the end we return the better of sold or rest, because holding a share unsold can never be best.

pattern-probability-dp.name: Probability DP
pattern-probability-dp.title: Probability DP — the pattern
signals: probability, chance, or expected value
dice, coins, cards, or random moves
number of ways after n random steps
answers within 10^-5 are accepted
variants: count ways, divide by total at the end
push probability forward each step
expected value, solved backward from the end
pattern-probability-dp.hook: Dice, coins, random moves: push probability forward through states instead of listing every outcome.
pattern-probability-dp.ask: Probability DP tracks how much probability, or how many ways, sits in each state, and moves that mass forward one random step at a time, splitting it across the outcomes.
pattern-probability-dp.exampleWhy: Two six-sided dice reach 7 in 6 ways out of 36: a probability of one sixth.

brute.idea: List every sequence of outcomes, all k^n of them, and count the ones that hit the target.
steps: Enumerate every roll sequence
Sum each sequence
Count the ones equal to target
brute.whySlow: Thirty 30-sided dice give 30^30 sequences, yet running sums only take about a thousand values.

optimal.insight: Outcomes that land on the same state behave identically afterwards. Merge them: keep the mass per state, ways or probability, and push it forward each step.
steps: Define the state after each random step
Put all the mass, probability 1, on the start
Push each state's mass to every outcome, times its chance
Read the target state's mass after the last step

codeNotes.note: Step 2: all mass on sum zero
Step 1: one random step per die
Fresh array for the next step
No mass here, nothing to push
Step 3: push mass to each face

pitfalls: For a probability multiply by 1/k per outcome; for ways, add and take the modulo.
Reusing one array lets mass move twice in a step; build a fresh one.

say.intro: Okay, probability DP. Whenever a problem has dice, coin flips, or random moves, and asks for a chance or a number of ways, this is your tool. Our example: roll two six-sided dice. How many ways sum to seven? Six, out of thirty six. That's a probability of one sixth.
say.brute: So what's the naive approach? List every outcome. With n dice of k faces, that's k to the n sequences. Sum each one and count the hits. For two dice it's fine. For thirty dice, it's astronomical. And here's the waste. Rolling two then five, and five then two, land on the same running sum. After that, they behave exactly the same.
say.insight: Here's the core idea. Don't track outcomes, track states. Merge everything that lands on the same state, and keep its mass, either ways or probability. The recipe: define the state. Put all the mass on the start. Each step, push every state's mass to each outcome. For probability, multiply by one over k. Finally, read the target's mass.
say.anim: We want ways to roll two dice summing to seven, with faces one through six. Dp starts with mass one at sum zero, meaning before any rolls we are at zero. For each face value, we push that mass forward into new sums, like one plus one. After finishing sum zero, new holds one way each for sums one through six. Dp becomes that spread row, and we start the second roll from these six states. Now each prior sum spreads its mass again, accumulating ways like two at sum three. Mass keeps merging into new, sum six now reaching five accumulated ways. After both rolls, dp at target seven gives six, the final answer.
say.code: Here's the template. The array starts with one way at sum zero. Then one round per die, that's the random step. Each round builds a fresh array. If a sum has no mass, skip it. Otherwise push its ways to every face, staying within the target, with the modulo. After the last die, return the mass at the target. Divide by k to the n for the probability.
say.outro: n times target times k work. Think probability DP when you see chance or expected value, dice, coins or random moves, or counting outcomes after many random steps.

lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container the problem expects for our method.
The method takes the number of dice n, faces per die k, and the target sum, and returns a count.
We set MOD to one billion seven, since the number of ways can grow huge and must be reduced.
We start dp with one way to reach sum zero and zero ways for every other running sum.
We loop once for each die, pushing the mass forward by one random roll each time.
We create a fresh new array of zeros so this die's results do not mix with the previous ones.
We walk through every current running sum t from zero up to the target.
If no ways reach this sum, there is nothing to push forward, so we check for zero.
We skip that sum and move on, saving needless work.
For each sum with ways, we try every face value f from one up to k.
We only continue if adding the face keeps the sum within the target, since larger sums can never come back.
We add the ways from sum t into the new sum t plus f, taking the remainder by MOD.
After all sums are processed, we replace dp with new, so the next die starts from these merged counts.
After all dice are rolled, dp at target holds the number of ways to hit the target, which we return.

pattern-memoization-top-down-dp.name: Memoization (Top-down DP)
pattern-memoization-top-down-dp.title: Memoization (Top-down DP) — the pattern
signals: natural recursion repeats the same subcalls
a choice at each step: take, skip, split
huge n but few reachable states
bottom-up fill order is hard to see
variants: dict memo keyed by arguments
functools cache decorator
memo on (index, remaining) tuples
pattern-memoization-top-down-dp.hook: Write the recursion you'd say out loud, add a cache, and exponential work becomes tiny.
pattern-memoization-top-down-dp.ask: Memoization means writing the natural recursive solution, then storing each subproblem's answer the first time it is computed, so every repeated call becomes a lookup.

brute.idea: Recurse on every choice each day: eat one, eat half, or eat two thirds, with no memory of amounts already solved.
steps: From k, try k - 1, k/2 and k/3
Take the minimum, plus one day
Re-solve every repeated k from scratch
brute.whySlow: Many paths reach the same amount and each re-solves it; the eat-one chain alone is n deep, n up to 2·10^9.

optimal.insight: The answer for k never changes, so cache it by its arguments. Eating k mod 2 or k mod 3 singly before dividing leaves only about log² n reachable states.
steps: Write the recursion: state as arguments, choices as calls
Return base cases directly
Check the memo before computing
Store the result before returning

codeNotes.note: Step 2: base cases seeded in the memo
Step 3: compute only on a miss
Eat k mod 2 singly, then halve
Eat k mod 3 singly, then a third

pitfalls: Lists as arguments are unhashable; key the memo on indices or tuples.
Deep recursion can hit Python's limit of about 1,000 frames.

say.intro: Okay, memoization. Top-down DP. You write the recursion exactly as you'd explain it out loud. Then you add a cache. That's it. Our example: you have ten oranges. Each day, eat one, or half if it's even, or two thirds if it divides by three. Fewest days to finish? Four.
say.brute: So what's the first attempt? Plain recursion. From k oranges, try eating one, try halving, try the two thirds move, and take the best. It's correct. But draw the call tree. The same amounts show up along many different paths, and each one is solved from scratch again. Plus, the eat one chain alone is n calls deep, and n can be two billion.
say.insight: Here's the idea. The answer for k never changes. So the first time you solve it, store it. Next time, it's a lookup. The recipe: the arguments are the state. Return base cases. Check the memo first. Store before returning. And a bonus. Eat the leftover k mod two singly, then halve. Now only about log squared n states are ever reached.
say.anim: We start with a memo cache holding base cases, zero maps to zero and one maps to one. We call days of ten, which isn't cached yet, so we branch into halving and thirding. Recursion dives down through five, then two, then one, reusing cached results as it unwinds. Days of two gets computed as two, combining a halve cost of one and a third cost of two. Days of five resolves to four, picking the cheaper branch between halving and thirding. Days of three resolves to two, since dividing by three needs only one extra step. Combining halve four and third three, days of ten becomes one plus three, equaling four. The final cached answer for ten is four, matching the expected output.
say.code: Here's the template. The memo starts with the base cases, zero and one. The helper's argument is the state, k. If k isn't in the memo, we compute it. Option one: eat k mod two singly, then halve. Option two: eat k mod three singly, then keep a third. Store one plus the better option. Then return straight from the memo.
say.outro: About log squared n states here. Reach for memoization when the natural recursion repeats subcalls, you choose at each step, n is huge but few states are reachable, or bottom-up order is unclear.

lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container for the method that the problem asks us to write.
The minDays method takes n oranges and returns the minimum number of days needed to eat them all.
We create a memo dictionary seeded with base cases: zero oranges need zero days and one orange needs one day.
We define an inner helper called days that computes the answer for k oranges using recursion.
We only compute k if it is not already in memo, so repeated calls become simple lookups.
For halving, we eat k mod 2 oranges one at a time, then recurse on k divided by two.
For thirding, we eat k mod 3 oranges singly, then recurse on k divided by three.
We store in memo for k one day plus the cheaper of the halving and thirding options.
We return the cached answer for k, whether it was just computed or already stored.
We start the recursion by calling days with n and return its result as the final answer.

pattern-string-matching-kmp-rolling-hash.name: String Matching (KMP / Rolling Hash)
pattern-string-matching-kmp-rolling-hash.title: String Matching (KMP / Rolling Hash) — the pattern
signals: find a pattern inside a longer text
first or all occurrences of a substring
rotated, repeated or periodic strings
longest prefix that is also a suffix
compare many equal-length substrings quickly
variants: KMP failure table (longest prefix-suffix)
rolling hash (Rabin-Karp) over a window
Z-function for prefix matches
pattern + '#' + text concatenation trick
pattern-string-matching-kmp-rolling-hash.hook: Never re-read the text: a tiny table tells you where to resume after every mismatch.
pattern-string-matching-kmp-rolling-hash.ask: Find where a pattern occurs in a text in linear time, by precomputing how much of the pattern still matches after a mismatch.
pattern-string-matching-kmp-rolling-hash.exampleWhy: The needle aabaaac first appears inside aabaaabaaac starting at index 4.

brute.idea: Try every start position in the text and compare the pattern letter by letter. After a mismatch, slide by one and start comparing from scratch.
steps: For each start i in the text
Compare the pattern against the text from i
Return i on a full match
On a mismatch, shift by one and restart
brute.whySlow: Text aaa…ab with pattern aa…ab re-reads almost m letters at every start: 10^4 × 10^4 = 10^8.

optimal.insight: After a mismatch, the matched part is a known prefix of the pattern. Its longest border (prefix that is also a suffix) says how much still matches.
steps: Build lps: longest proper border of every pattern prefix
Scan the text once, counting letters matched so far
On a mismatch, fall back to the border; never move back in the text
When the count reaches m, report a match at i - m + 1

codeNotes.note: Border length for every pattern prefix
Disagree: fall back to a shorter border

pitfalls: Borders must be proper: build lps from i = 1, or every border becomes the whole prefix.
Rolling hash can collide: confirm the substring on a hash hit, or use two moduli.

say.intro: Okay, so this is string matching. Find a pattern inside a longer text. Sounds trivial, right? But the naive way can be quadratic, and interviewers love asking how to make it linear. Our example: find a a b a a a c inside a longer text. The answer is index four.
say.brute: So what do people try first? Line the pattern up at every start in the text and compare letter by letter. On a mismatch, slide over by one and start again from scratch. It's correct. So what's the catch? We throw away everything we just matched. With lots of repeated letters, every start re-reads almost the whole pattern. That's n times m.
say.insight: Here's the thing. When a mismatch hits, the part we matched is a prefix of the pattern. We already know it. So precompute, for every prefix, its longest border. That's a prefix that is also a suffix. The recipe. One, build that border table. Two, scan the text once, counting matched letters. Three, on a mismatch, fall back to the border instead of restarting. Four, a full count means a match.
say.anim: We start building the lps array for the pattern aabaaac, tracking its longest matching prefix-suffix lengths. As i advances, k resets using lps whenever characters mismatch, avoiding redundant comparisons. By the time i reaches 6, the lps array becomes 0,1,0,1,2,2,0, capturing self similarity. Now we scan the haystack aabaaabaaac, matching characters while increasing j using the pattern. At i equals 6, a mismatch on b sends j back to 2 using the lps shortcut. Matching resumes smoothly, with j climbing back up through 3, 4, 5, and 6 as characters align. At i equals 10, the final character c completes the pattern, making j equal to 7. The function returns 4, the starting index where needle first fully matches haystack.
say.code: Now the code. First, the border table, one slot per pattern prefix. While the next letter disagrees, we fall back to a shorter border. If it agrees, the border grows, and we record it. Then the text loop. The text pointer only moves forward. On a mismatch, the matched count resumes from its border. And when it reaches the pattern length, the match started at i minus m plus one.
say.outro: Linear time, n plus m. Listen for these signals. Find a pattern in a text. First or all occurrences. Rotated or repeated strings. A prefix that is also a suffix. And comparing many equal-length substrings.

lineNotes: We define a Solution class, the standard wrapper for this interview problem.
The strStr method returns the first index where needle appears in haystack, or negative one if it never does.
We store the length of the needle in m, since we will use it often.
We create the lps table of zeros, holding the longest border length for each needle prefix.
We set k to zero, the length of the current border we are extending.
We loop i from one to the end of the needle, filling the table left to right.
While k is positive and the characters differ, we cannot extend the current border, so we fall back.
We set k to the table value just before k, which is the next shorter border.
If the characters now match, the current border can be extended by one.
We increase k by one to record the longer border.
We store k as the border length for the prefix ending at i.
We set j to zero, the number of needle characters currently matched in the haystack.
We scan each haystack character with its index i, never moving backward in the text.
While some match exists and the character mismatches the next needle character, we need a shorter match.
We set j to the border length of the matched part, keeping what still matches without rescanning text.
If the haystack character equals the needle character at j, the match grows.
We increase j by one to count the extended match.
If j equals m, the whole needle has matched ending at the current position.
We return i minus m plus one, which is the starting index of that match.
If the scan finishes with no full match, we return negative one.

pattern-segment-tree-fenwick-tree.name: Segment Tree / Fenwick Tree
pattern-segment-tree-fenwick-tree.title: Segment Tree / Fenwick Tree — the pattern
signals: range sum, min or max with updates
count smaller or larger elements seen so far
many queries mixed with point updates
pairs or inversions with an order condition
values need rank compression first
variants: Fenwick tree (BIT) for prefix sums
segment tree for min, max or custom merge
lazy propagation for range updates
BIT over value ranks for counting
pattern-segment-tree-fenwick-tree.hook: When the array keeps changing, prefix sums break. A Fenwick tree updates and queries in log n.
pattern-segment-tree-fenwick-tree.ask: Keep an array that supports both point updates and prefix or range queries in logarithmic time, using a tree of partial sums.
pattern-segment-tree-fenwick-tree.exampleWhy: Right of 5 sit 2, 1 and 3, so 3. Right of 2 only 1. Right of 6: 1 and 3.

brute.idea: For each element, scan everything to its right and count the smaller values. Every query re-reads data we already looked at.
steps: For each index i
Scan every j to the right of i
Count values smaller than nums[i]
Store the count
brute.whySlow: With 10^5 numbers that is about 5·10^9 comparisons; each suffix is recounted from scratch.

optimal.insight: Store sums of power-of-two blocks; index i covers a block sized by its lowest set bit. Any prefix splits into log n blocks, and any update touches log n blocks.
steps: Map values or positions to indices 1..m (compress if needed)
Query a prefix: add tree[i], then drop the lowest bit
Update a point: add to tree[i], then climb by the lowest bit
Combine prefix queries into ranges or counts

codeNotes.note: Query drops the lowest set bit
Count smaller values seen so far
Add this value to the tree

pitfalls: Fenwick is 1-indexed: index 0 never climbs, since 0 & -0 is 0.
Query r - 1 for strictly smaller; querying r also counts equal values.

say.intro: Okay, so this is the segment tree and Fenwick tree family. They answer range questions on an array that keeps changing. Plain prefix sums can't handle updates. Interviewers love these for counting problems. Our example: for each number, count the smaller numbers to its right. Five, two, six, one, three gives three, one, two, zero, zero.
say.brute: So what do people try first? For every number, scan everything to its right and count the smaller ones. Simple, and correct. So what's the catch? That's n squared. A hundred thousand numbers means billions of comparisons. And notice, we keep recounting the same suffix again and again. We want a running tally we can update and query fast.
say.insight: Here's the thing. A Fenwick tree stores sums of blocks sized by powers of two. Any prefix splits into at most log n blocks. Any update touches at most log n blocks. The recipe. One, map values to indices one to m. Two, to query, add a block and drop the lowest bit. Three, to update, add and climb by the lowest bit. Four, combine prefix queries into your answer.
say.anim: We rank the distinct values, giving each number a compact index for the tree. The Fenwick tree starts empty, all zeros, ready to track counts as we scan right to left. At index three, value three has rank one; querying rank zero gives zero smaller elements seen so far. We update rank one, adding one into tree positions one, two, and four. At index two, value six has rank five; querying up to rank four returns two, since two smaller values exist. At index one, value two has rank two; query returns one, counting the single smaller value already seen. At index zero, value five has rank four; querying up to rank three gives three smaller elements. The final result array is three, one, two, zero, zero, matching the expected output.
say.code: Now the code. First we compress values into ranks, one to m. Update adds to a slot, then climbs by adding the lowest set bit. Query sums a slot, then drops the lowest set bit. Then we walk the array right to left. For each value, we query everything with a smaller rank. That's our count. Then we add this value to the tree.
say.outro: n log n time. Listen for these signals. Range sums with updates. Counting smaller elements seen so far. Many queries mixed with changes. And pairs with an order condition.

lineNotes: We define a Solution class, as the problem platform expects, to hold our method.
The countSmaller method takes nums and returns, for each position, how many smaller numbers appear to its right.
We map each distinct value to a rank starting at one, so values fit into small Fenwick tree indices.
We store m as the number of distinct values, which is the size of our tree.
We create the tree array of zeros with an extra slot, since Fenwick indexing starts at one.
The update helper adds a delta at rank i and pushes it up through all covering blocks.
We loop while the index stays within the tree size m.
We add delta to the partial sum stored at this index.
We jump to the next block covering this index by adding its lowest set bit.
The query helper returns the count of inserted values with rank up to i.
We start the running total at zero before gathering block sums.
We loop while the index is positive, since index zero means nothing is left to add.
We add the block sum stored at this index into the total.
We strip the lowest set bit to move to the previous disjoint block.
We return the accumulated prefix count.
We prepare the result list with zeros, one slot per input number.
We scan the array from right to left, so the tree holds only elements to the right.
We look up the rank of the current number.
We query the prefix up to rank minus one, which counts strictly smaller numbers already seen on the right.
We record this number in the tree by adding one at its rank.
We return the finished list of counts.

pattern-line-sweep.name: Line Sweep
pattern-line-sweep.title: Line Sweep — the pattern
signals: maximum overlap at any moment
how many intervals cover a point
rooms, cars or seats in use
many range updates, read final values once
things happen only at start and end times
variants: sorted start/end events (+1 / -1)
difference array over small coordinates
sweep with a heap of active items
sweep to find gaps or cut points
pattern-line-sweep.hook: Stop checking every pair of intervals. Turn them into events and walk the timeline once.
pattern-line-sweep.ask: Turn each interval into a start event and an end event, sort them by time, and sweep left to right keeping a running count of what is active.
pattern-line-sweep.exampleWhy: At time 8, meetings 0-30, 5-10 and 8-16 all run; no moment ever needs four rooms.

brute.idea: For every meeting's start time, count how many meetings are running at that moment. Overlap always peaks at some start, so the busiest start is the answer.
steps: Take each meeting's start time t
Count meetings with s ≤ t < e
Keep the maximum count
brute.whySlow: With 10^4 meetings that is 10^8 containment checks; every moment rescans every meeting.

optimal.insight: The active count only changes at starts and ends. Sort those events once; adding +1 at a start and -1 at an end gives the count at every moment.
steps: Turn each interval into (start, +1) and (end, -1)
Sort events by time; ends before starts on ties
Sweep, adding each delta to a running count
Record the answer (peak, check or cut) as you go

pitfalls: Tie order matters: when an end and a start share a time, process the end first.
Decide whether intervals are half-open; it changes how ties at endpoints count.

say.intro: Okay, so this is line sweep. Instead of comparing intervals with each other, we walk along the timeline once and watch what's active. Interviewers love it for overlap questions. Our example: five meetings. Zero to thirty, five to ten, fifteen to twenty, eight to sixteen, and twenty five to thirty five. How many rooms? Three.
say.brute: So what do people try first? Pick each meeting's start time. Then count how many meetings are running at that moment. The busiest moment is the answer. That works, because overlap always peaks at some start. So what's the catch? Every moment rescans every meeting. That's n squared. Ten thousand meetings means a hundred million checks.
say.insight: Here's the thing. The number of running meetings only changes at a start or an end. Nothing happens in between. So the recipe. One, turn each interval into two events. Plus one at its start, minus one at its end. Two, sort the events by time, ends first on ties. Three, sweep, adding each change to a running count. Four, record what you need as you go.
say.anim: We start with five meeting intervals and build start and end events for each. All events are sorted by time, mixing starts and ends chronologically. We sweep through events, adding one for a start and tracking active meetings. By time eight, three meetings overlap, pushing active count to three, our new best. At time ten a meeting ends, dropping active count back down to two. Another start at fifteen bumps active back up to three meetings overlapping again. As meetings end one by one, active count decreases back toward zero. The sweep finishes and the function returns three, the maximum rooms needed.
say.code: Now the code. Each meeting adds two events. Its start takes a room with plus one. Its end frees a room with minus one. Then we sort. Tuples sort by time, and minus one comes before plus one on ties. So a room frees up before the next meeting grabs it. Then the sweep. Add each change to the active count, and keep the peak.
say.outro: n log n time. Listen for these signals. Maximum overlap at any moment. How many intervals cover a point. Rooms, cars or seats in use. And range updates you only read at the end.

lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the wrapper this problem expects for our method.
The method minMeetingRooms takes a list of meeting intervals and returns the minimum number of rooms needed.
We start with an empty list called events to hold every start and end moment.
We loop over each interval, unpacking it into its start time and end time.
For each meeting we add a start event with plus one, meaning one more room is in use.
We also add an end event with minus one, meaning a room becomes free at that time.
We sort events by time, and ties put minus one first, so a meeting ending frees its room before another starts.
We set active to zero, since before the sweep no meetings are running.
We set best to zero to remember the largest number of overlapping meetings seen so far.
We sweep through the sorted events in order, reading each event's time and its delta.
We add the delta to active, so the count rises at starts and falls at ends.
We update best to the larger of itself and active, capturing the peak overlap.
We return best, which is the peak number of simultaneous meetings and so the rooms needed.

pattern-number-theory-gcd-sieve-modulo.name: Number Theory (GCD, Sieve, Modulo)
pattern-number-theory-gcd-sieve-modulo.title: Number Theory (GCD, Sieve, Modulo) — the pattern
signals: count or list primes up to n
greatest common divisor or least common multiple
return the answer modulo 10^9 + 7
a huge exponent or power
divisibility, factors or remainders
variants: Euclid: gcd(a, b) = gcd(b, a % b)
Sieve of Eratosthenes for all primes ≤ n
fast modular exponentiation by squaring
factorization by trial division up to √n
pattern-number-theory-gcd-sieve-modulo.hook: Primes, GCDs and huge powers each have a classic trick that turns slow loops into near-instant math.
pattern-number-theory-gcd-sieve-modulo.ask: Use a few number facts (Euclid's GCD, the prime sieve, modular arithmetic) to answer prime, divisor and big-number questions without brute-force checks.
pattern-number-theory-gcd-sieve-modulo.exampleWhy: Primes below 30 are 2, 3, 5, 7, 11, 13, 17, 19, 23 and 29: ten of them.

brute.idea: Test each number on its own by trying every divisor up to its square root. Correct, but every number repeats divisions the others already did.
steps: For each x from 2 to n - 1
Try divisors d from 2 up to √x
Count x if no divisor works
brute.whySlow: For n = 5·10^6 that is about 10^10 divisions; the same small primes are retried for every x.

optimal.insight: Flip the question: instead of asking each number for a divisor, let each prime cross out its own multiples. Every composite is crossed out by a smaller prime.
steps: Name the fact the problem needs: sieve, GCD or modular rule
Sieve: each prime p crosses out multiples from p² upward
GCD: replace (a, b) with (b, a % b) until b is 0
Modulo: reduce after every multiply to keep numbers small

codeNotes.match: for m in range(p * p, n, p):
codeNotes.note: Start at p²; smaller ones done

pitfalls: Start crossing out at p², and stop the outer loop at √n.
Take the modulo after every multiply, not only at the end.

say.intro: Okay, so this is number theory. Primes, greatest common divisors, and answers modulo a big number. Each has a classic trick, and interviewers expect you to know them. Our example: count the primes below thirty. Two, three, five, seven, and so on up to twenty nine. That's ten.
say.brute: So what do people try first? Test each number on its own. Try every divisor up to its square root. If nothing divides it, it's prime. That's correct. So what's the catch? Every number redoes the same work. We keep dividing by two, by three, by five, over and over. For millions of numbers, that's billions of divisions.
say.insight: Here's the thing. Flip the question. Don't ask each number for a divisor. Let each prime cross out its own multiples. That's the sieve. The same spirit runs through the pattern. For a greatest common divisor, swap a and b for b and a mod b. For huge answers, reduce after every multiply. The recipe: name the fact, then let it do the work in bulk.
say.anim: We start with n equal to thirty and build a list assuming every number is prime. Starting at p equals 2, we cross out its multiples: 4, 6, 8, 10, and onward. Now p equals 3, a surviving prime, so we cross out 9, 12, 15, 18, 21, 24, 27. P equals 4 is already crossed out, so it gets skipped entirely. P equals 5 is still prime, so we cross out its first new multiple, 25. The loop ends since remaining primes square past thirty, so we sum the true flags. The final count of primes below thirty is ten.
say.code: Now the code. We start by assuming every number is prime, except zero and one. The outer loop only goes up to the square root of n. Bigger primes have nothing left to cross out. We skip numbers already crossed out. Each prime crosses out from its square, in steps of p. Smaller multiples were handled by smaller primes. Finally, count the survivors.
say.outro: n log log n time. Listen for these signals. Count primes up to n. A greatest common divisor. An answer modulo ten to the nine plus seven. Huge exponents. And divisibility or remainders.

lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which holds the method that counts primes strictly less than n.
The countPrimes method takes n and returns how many prime numbers are smaller than n.
If n is less than three, there are no primes below it, so we handle that edge case first.
In that case we return zero immediately, since the smallest prime, two, is not below n.
We build a list of n flags, all true, assuming every number from zero to n minus one is prime.
We mark zero and one as not prime, because primes start at two.
We loop p from two up to the integer square root of n minus one, since larger factors pair with smaller ones.
We only act when p is still marked prime, because multiples of a composite were already crossed out by its prime factors.
For this prime p, we walk through its multiples starting at p squared, since smaller multiples were crossed out by smaller primes.
We mark each of those multiples as not prime, since each has p as a divisor.
Finally we sum the flags, counting each true as one, which gives the number of primes below n.

pattern-game-theory-minimax.name: Game Theory (Minimax)
pattern-game-theory-minimax.title: Game Theory (Minimax) — the pattern
signals: two players take turns
both players play optimally
can the first player win
take from either end, or take 1 to k
maximize your score minus the opponent's
variants: score margin: my take minus their best
win/lose states: win if a move leaves a loss
interval DP over a shrinking range
math shortcut once the pattern is seen (Nim)
pattern-game-theory-minimax.hook: Two perfect players sounds like a two-sided mess. Score it as one number and it is plain recursion.
pattern-game-theory-minimax.ask: Model the game as states. The player to move picks the move that is best for them, assuming the opponent then plays perfectly; memoize each state.
pattern-game-theory-minimax.exampleWhy: Player 1 takes 1; whichever end player 2 takes, 233 is exposed. 234 beats 12.

brute.idea: Play out every possible game: at each turn try both ends, carry both players' scores, maximize the final gap on player 1's turn and minimize it on player 2's.
steps: Recurse with the range, both scores and the turn
Player 1 maximizes the final difference
Player 2 minimizes it
Nothing cached: every move order is replayed
brute.whySlow: Each turn doubles the tree: 20 numbers give about a million move orders, yet only 210 distinct ranges.

optimal.insight: Whoever moves faces the same kind of game; only what remains matters. Score it from the mover's view: my take minus the opponent's best result on the rest.
steps: Define the state: what remains (here, the range i..j)
Score a state as the mover's best margin
Try each move: gain minus the next state's score
Memoize; the answer is score(start) compared with 0

codeNotes.note: My gain minus their best reply
A tie counts as a win

pitfalls: Subtract the opponent's result; adding it treats the opponent as your teammate.
Read the tie rule: here a draw still counts as a win for player 1.

say.intro: Okay, so this is game theory, or minimax. Two players take turns, both play perfectly, and you must predict the winner. It looks scary, but it's just recursion with one clever score. Our example: one, five, two hundred thirty three, seven. Players take from either end. Can player one win? Yes.
say.brute: So what do people try first? Play out every possible game. At each turn, try both ends. Track both players' scores. Player one maximizes the final gap, player two minimizes it. That's correct. So what's the catch? Every turn doubles the tree. Twenty numbers means about a million move orders. But there are only two hundred ten distinct ranges.
say.insight: Here's the thing. Whoever moves faces the same kind of game. Only what's left matters. So score it from the mover's view. My take, minus the best my opponent can do on what remains. The recipe. One, define the state. Two, score it as the mover's best margin. Three, try each move: gain minus the next state's score. Four, memoize.
say.anim: We start with the array one, five, two thirty three, seven, and cache our results. Recursion dives down until i exceeds j, meaning no elements remain to pick. At the base, taking seven alone gives take left seven and take right seven, so best is seven. For the pair five and two thirty three, taking two thirty three wins with score two thirty three. Combining these, picking one from the left gives a net score of two twenty six for that subgame. Working outward, each player always takes the move maximizing their score minus the opponent's best reply. Finally for the whole array, take right gives two twenty nine, beating take left's negative two twenty seven. The final score is nonnegative, so predictTheWinner returns true, confirming player one wins.
say.code: Now the code. The cache makes sure each state is solved once. The state is just the remaining range, i to j. When nothing is left, the margin is zero. Taking the left end gives that number, minus the opponent's best on the rest. Same for the right end. The mover picks the larger. Player one wins if the final margin is zero or more.
say.outro: n squared time. Listen for these signals. Two players taking turns. Both playing optimally. Can the first player win. And taking from the ends, or up to k at a time.

lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container this problem's method lives in.
The method predictTheWinner takes the list of scores and returns whether player one can at least tie.
We add a cache decorator so each subarray state is computed only once, avoiding repeated work.
The helper best takes left index i and right index j, describing the remaining slice of numbers.
If i has passed j, no numbers remain, which is the base case of the game.
In that empty case the score difference is zero, since nobody can gain anything more.
Taking the left number gives its value minus the opponent's best advantage on the remaining slice starting after i.
Taking the right number gives its value minus the opponent's best advantage on the slice ending before j.
The mover picks the larger of the two options, giving their best score difference against perfect play.
We start with the full list and return true if player one's final difference is zero or more.

pattern-combinatorics.name: Combinatorics
pattern-combinatorics.title: Combinatorics — the pattern
signals: count the number of ways or arrangements
choose k items from n
grid paths moving only right or down
answer modulo 10^9 + 7
count far too large to enumerate
variants: binomial C(n, k) by multiplicative formula
Pascal's rule C(n, k) = C(n-1, k-1) + C(n-1, k)
multiplication principle for independent choices
factorials with modular inverses
pattern-combinatorics.hook: Stop enumerating. If you can name what is being chosen, one formula counts it.
pattern-combinatorics.ask: Count arrangements directly with formulas (the multiplication principle, factorials, n choose k) instead of listing every arrangement one by one.
pattern-combinatorics.exampleWhy: Every path is 4 downs and 4 rights in some order: choose which 4 of the 8 moves go down, 70 ways.

brute.idea: Walk every path recursively: from each cell go right or go down, and count a path whenever it reaches the last row or column. Correct, but it touches every single path.
steps: Start at the top-left cell
Recurse right and recurse down
Count 1 on the last row or column
Sum the two branches
brute.whySlow: The path count explodes: a 17 × 17 grid already has over 600 million paths to walk.

optimal.insight: Every path is the same multiset of moves: m-1 downs and n-1 rights. A path is just a choice of which slots hold the downs, so the count is C(m+n-2, m-1).
steps: Name the objects being arranged or chosen
Spot the structure: order, repetition, independent choices
Map it to a formula: product, factorial or C(n, k)
Compute safely: multiply then divide, or mod with inverses

codeNotes.note: Choose the smaller side: fewer steps
Build C(total, k) factor by factor

pitfalls: Multiply before dividing; each partial result is itself a binomial, so the division is exact.
Off by one: an m by n grid needs m - 1 downs, not m.

say.intro: Okay, so this is combinatorics. Counting arrangements with a formula, instead of listing them. Interviewers love it because the brute force is exponential, and the formula is one short loop. Our example: a five by five grid. Move only right or down, from the top left to the bottom right. How many paths? Seventy.
say.brute: So what do people try first? Walk every path. From each cell, branch right and branch down. Count one whenever you reach the edge. That's correct. So what's the catch? We visit every single path, and the count explodes. A seventeen by seventeen grid already has over six hundred million paths. We're counting by touching each one.
say.insight: Here's the thing. Every path uses the same moves. Four downs and four rights, just in a different order. So a path is a choice. Which four of the eight slots hold the downs? That's eight choose four. The recipe. One, name what's being chosen. Two, spot the structure. Three, map it to a formula. Four, compute it safely.
say.anim: We start with a five by five grid, so m and n are both five. Total moves needed is eight, the sum of downs and rights required. K becomes four, the smaller count, and result starts at one. The loop begins, multiplying result by a shrinking fraction each step. After i equals one, result updates to five, building the combination. At i equals two, result grows to fifteen, counting more paths. At i equals three, result climbs to thirty five paths so far. At i equals four, result reaches seventy, completing the combination formula. The function returns seventy, the total unique paths through the grid.
say.code: Now the code. Total is the number of moves in any path. We choose the smaller side, so the loop is short. Then we build the binomial one factor at a time. Multiply first, then divide. After each step the result is itself a binomial, so the division is always exact. At the end, that's the number of paths.
say.outro: Linear in the smaller side. Listen for these signals. Count the ways. Choose k from n. Grid paths moving right and down. Answers modulo a big prime. And counts too big to list.

lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container the problem expects for our method.
The method uniquePaths takes the grid height m and width n and returns the number of distinct paths.
Total is the number of moves in every path, which is m plus n minus two.
We set k to the smaller of the downs and rights counts, since choosing the smaller side keeps the computation short.
Result starts at one, which is the empty product and the base value for building n choose k.
We loop i from one up to k, building the binomial coefficient one factor at a time.
Each step multiplies result by the next numerator term and divides by i, and the division stays exact because the running value is itself a binomial coefficient.
We return result, which now equals total choose k, the number of unique paths.

pattern-randomized-reservoir-sampling.name: Randomized & Reservoir Sampling
pattern-randomized-reservoir-sampling.title: Randomized & Reservoir Sampling — the pattern
signals: return a random element with equal probability
pick an index proportional to its weight
sample k items from a stream of unknown length
getRandom in constant time
expected time with a random pivot
variants: weighted pick: prefix sums + binary search
reservoir: keep item i with probability k/i
array + hash map for O(1) getRandom
random-pivot quickselect
pattern-randomized-reservoir-sampling.hook: Interviewers ask for 'random' to test whether every outcome gets exactly the right probability.
pattern-randomized-reservoir-sampling.ask: Randomized sampling turns one uniform random number into a choice with exactly the required odds, using prefix ranges, swaps or a reservoir, instead of building every outcome.
pattern-randomized-reservoir-sampling.exampleWhy: Worked example Random Pick with Weight: weights 2, 5, 3 own ranges 1–2, 3–7, 8–10, so index 1 wins half the time.

brute.idea: Make the odds literal: copy each index into a big pool as many times as its weight, then pick a uniform slot.
steps: Repeat index i w[i] times in a pool
Draw a uniform slot in the pool
Return the index stored there
brute.time: O(sum of w) build, O(1) pick
brute.whySlow: Ten thousand weights of up to 100,000 each means a pool of a billion entries.
