The total moves from negative three up through negative one as left advances, never reaching zero. Now a is negative one, with left at two and right at five, giving total zero. That triple negative one, negative one, two gets recorded, then pointers move inward. Another zero total is found, adding negative one, zero, one to the results. The next a value repeats negative one, so that iteration is skipped to avoid duplicates. Once a becomes positive one, the loop breaks, returning the final answer with two triples.
say.code: Here's the code. First we sort. That enables the pointers and the dedup. Then we loop over each value. If it's positive, we stop, since no zero sum is left. If it matches the previous value, skip it as a duplicate. Now it's Two Sum Two on the rest. When we find a zero triple, record it and move both pointers. Then skip repeated second values.
say.outro: Quadratic time, beating cubic. Pattern: two pointers. Fix one element, then reduce what's left to a problem you already know.

3sum.title: 3Sum
lineNotes: We define a Solution class that holds the method for solving the problem.
The threeSum method takes a list of integers and returns a list of triples that sum to zero.
We start with an empty result list to collect every valid triple we find.
We sort the numbers so we can use two pointers and skip duplicates easily.
This comment says we fix the first value a and move it from left to right.
We loop over every index i, treating the value there as the first number of a triple.
We store the current first value in a, which will be the smallest in its triple.
This comment explains that in a sorted triple a is smallest, so a positive a makes a zero sum impossible.
If a is greater than zero, no triple starting here or later can sum to zero.
So we break out of the loop entirely, since all remaining values are positive too.
This comment says we skip repeated values of a so we do not produce duplicate triples.
If this is not the first index and a equals the previous value, we have already handled it.
We continue to the next index, skipping this duplicate first value.
This comment says we now use two pointers on the rest of the array to find pairs summing to negative a.
We place left just after i, at the start of the remaining portion.
We place right at the last index, the largest value in the array.
We loop while the pointers have not met, so each pair uses two different positions.
We compute total as a plus the values at left and right.
If the total is too large, we need a smaller sum.
So we move right one step inward to a smaller value.
Otherwise, if the total is too small, we need a larger sum.
So we move left one step inward to a larger value.
Otherwise the total is exactly zero, so we have found a valid triple.
This comment says we record the triple and then move both pointers inward.
We append a, the left value, and the right value to the result as a new triple.
We move left forward one step to look for the next pair.
We move right back one step as well, since the old right value cannot pair again with the same a.
This comment says we skip repeated left values to avoid duplicate triples.
While left is still before right and its value equals the previous one, we have a duplicate pair.
We advance left past each repeated value until we reach a new one.
After all first values are processed, we return the collected list of distinct triples.

container-with-most-water.hook: Two walls, one tank. The shorter wall is always the one worth giving up.
container-with-most-water.ask: Given wall heights along a line, pick two walls that, with the floor between them, hold the most water. Water height is the shorter wall; width is the distance between them. Return that maximum area.
container-with-most-water.exampleWhy: Walls at index 1 (height 8) and index 8 (height 7): min 7 · width 7 = 49.

brute.idea: Try every pair of walls, compute min height times distance, and keep the largest.
steps: Pick a left wall i
Try every right wall j > i
Area = min height · (j - i)
Keep the maximum
brute.whySlow: With 100,000 walls that is about 5 billion pairs.

optimal.insight: Start widest. The shorter wall limits the area, and any narrower tank using it can only be worse, so discard it and move that pointer inward.
steps: l at the first wall, r at the last
Record min height · width
Move the shorter wall's pointer inward
Stop when they meet

codeNotes.note: Left is the bottleneck: drop it
Right is shorter or equal: drop it

pitfalls: Moving the taller wall can never help; justify why in the interview.
Width is r - l, not r - l + 1.

say.intro: Okay, Container With Most Water. Each number is a wall's height. Pick two walls. The water they hold is the shorter height times the distance between them. Here, walls of height eight and seven stand seven apart. Seven times seven is forty nine. That's the biggest. Let's find it.
say.brute: The brute force way tries every pair of walls, computes each area, and keeps the largest. Simple, and clearly correct. But there are about n squared over two pairs. With a hundred thousand walls, that's around five billion areas. So we need a smart way to prune.
say.insight: Here's the thing. Start with the widest tank, the first and last walls. The shorter wall caps the water. Now, any other tank using that short wall would be narrower, and still capped by it. Could it ever win? No. So we safely throw away the shorter wall and move inward. Nothing better ever gets skipped.
say.anim: We start with left at index zero and right at index eight, the widest span. Width is eight, and the shorter wall is height one, giving an area of eight. Since the left wall is shorter, we move left inward to discard it. Now width is seven and both walls are eight, giving area forty nine, our new max. Right wall tied, so we move right inward instead this time. Width shrinks to six, shorter wall three, area eighteen, not better than forty nine. Width five with wall eight gives area forty, still less than our best. Pointers keep closing in, but no area beats forty nine, so that's the final answer.
say.code: Here's the code. Left and right start at the ends, the widest possible container. While they haven't met, we compute the area. That's the shorter wall times the width. We keep the max. Now, if the left wall is the bottleneck, we drop it by moving left forward. Otherwise, the right side is shorter or equal, so we drop it instead.
say.outro: Linear time, constant space. Pattern: two pointers. At every step, drop the side that can't lead to a better answer. And say why out loud.

container-with-most-water.title: Container With Most Water
container-with-most-water.optimalCode:
class Solution:
    def maxArea(self, height: List[int]) -> int:
        left = 0
        right = len(height) - 1
        max_area = 0

        # Start with the widest container and narrow it down
        while left < right:
            width = right - left
            shorter_wall = min(height[left], height[right])
            area = shorter_wall * width
            max_area = max(max_area, area)

            # Move the pointer at the shorter wall inward
            if height[left] < height[right]:
                left += 1
            else:
                right -= 1

        return max_area
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container for our method as the problem expects.
The method maxArea takes the list of wall heights and returns the largest water area as an integer.
We set left to zero so the left pointer begins at the first wall.
We set right to the last index of height so the right pointer begins at the final wall.
We set max_area to zero, which will track the best area we have found so far.
This comment says we begin with the widest possible container and then shrink it step by step.
We loop while left is less than right, so the two pointers always mark two different walls.
The width is the distance between the pointers, found by subtracting left from right.
The shorter wall is the smaller of the two heights, since water can only rise to the lower wall.
The area is the shorter wall height multiplied by the width between the walls.
We update max_area to the larger of its current value and the area we just computed.
This comment explains that we move whichever pointer sits on the shorter wall, moving it inward.
If the left wall is shorter than the right wall, the left wall is the limiting side.
So we move left one step inward, because keeping that short wall could never give a bigger area.
Otherwise the right wall is shorter or equal, so it is the one we should discard.
We move right one step inward, hoping to find a taller wall that improves the area.
When the pointers meet, we have checked every useful pair and return the maximum area found.

trapping-rain-water.hook: A hard problem with a tiny solution: water over each bar depends on its shorter tallest side.
trapping-rain-water.ask: Given bar heights of an elevation map, each bar one unit wide, compute how many units of rain water are trapped between the bars after it rains.
trapping-rain-water.exampleWhy: Water fills the dips: 1 unit at index 2, 1 at 4, 2 at 5, 1 at 6 and 1 at 9, totalling 6.

brute.idea: For each bar, scan left for the tallest bar and scan right for the tallest bar. Water above it is the smaller minus its height.
steps: For each index i
Scan left and right for the maxima
Add min(leftMax, rightMax) - height[i]
brute.whySlow: Every bar rescans the whole map: 20,000 bars means about 400 million reads.

optimal.insight: Water at a bar is min(leftMax, rightMax) - height. If leftMax < rightMax, the left max is the binding limit, so advance l and settle that bar with leftMax alone.
steps: Pointers at both ends with running maxima
Smaller max decides which side moves
Advance it and update that side's max
Add max minus height to the total

codeNotes.note: Left side is the true limit
Never negative: max includes this bar
Mirror case for the right side

pitfalls: Prefix and suffix max arrays give O(n) with O(n) space; a fine stepping stone.
Update the max before adding water, avoiding negatives.

say.intro: Okay, Trapping Rain Water. Bars of different heights stand side by side, and rain falls on them. How much water gets trapped in the dips? In our map, water pools in five spots. One, one, two, one, and one unit. That's six in total.
say.brute: The brute force way looks at each bar on its own. Scan left for the tallest bar. Scan right for the tallest bar. The water above this bar is the smaller of those two, minus the bar's own height. It's correct. But every bar rescans the whole map. So it's n squared.
say.insight: Here's the key. Water at a bar is the smaller of its left max and right max, minus its height. Now put pointers at both ends. If the left max is smaller than the right max, which side is the real limit? The left. Whatever's in between. So we step left inward and settle that bar using the left max alone.
say.anim: We start with the height array and set left and right pointers at the ends. Left max is 0 and right max is 1, since right max is bigger we move right first. Left max is smaller, so left advances to index 1, trapping zero water there. Right pointer moves to index 10, right max becomes 2, no water trapped yet. Left keeps advancing through lower bars, updating left max as it goes. Right max grows to 3 at index 7, trapping water equal to right max minus height. Now left max binds, so left pointer moves forward adding water at each step. Pointers meet and the loop ends, giving a total trapped water answer of 6.
say.code: Here's the code. Left and right start at the ends, and we track the tallest bar seen from each side. While they haven't met, if the left max is smaller, the left side is the true limit. So we move left forward. We update the max first, then add the water. Why is that never negative? Because the max includes this bar. Otherwise we mirror it on the right.
say.outro: Linear time, constant space. Pattern: two pointers. Always move the side whose limit you already know for sure, and settle it.

trapping-rain-water.title: Trapping Rain Water
trapping-rain-water.optimalCode:
class Solution:
    def trap(self, height: List[int]) -> int:
        if not height:
            return 0

        # 1. Set up two pointers and running maxima from each side
        left = 0
        right = len(height) - 1
        left_max = height[left]
        right_max = height[right]
        total_water = 0

        # 2. Move the pointer on the side with the smaller max
        while left < right:
            if left_max < right_max:
                # 3. Left side is the limiting height, advance left pointer
                left += 1
                left_max = max(left_max, height[left])
                total_water += left_max - height[left]
            else:
                # 4. Right side is the limiting height, advance right pointer
                right -= 1
                right_max = max(right_max, height[right])
                total_water += right_max - height[right]

        return total_water
lineNotes: We define a class named Solution, as the problem platform expects.
The trap method takes the list of bar heights and returns the total trapped water as an integer.
If the height list is empty, there are no bars to hold any water.
In that empty case we return zero right away.
This comment says we begin with two pointers and the tallest bar seen from each side.
We set left to zero, the first bar on the left end.
We set right to the last index, the bar on the right end.
We start left max as the height of the leftmost bar.
We start right max as the height of the rightmost bar.
We set total water to zero, since nothing has been counted yet.
This comment says we always move the pointer on the side whose max is smaller.
We loop while left is less than right, so the two pointers move toward each other until they meet.
If left max is smaller than right max, the left side is the limit on water height.
This comment explains that the left side limits the water, so we can safely process the left bar.
We move the left pointer one bar to the right.
We update left max to include the new bar if it is taller than before.
We add left max minus this bar's height, which is the water this bar holds, using left max alone.
Otherwise right max is smaller or equal, so the right side is the limiting height.
This comment says the right side limits the water, so we process the right bar instead.
We move the right pointer one bar to the left.
We update right max to include the new bar if it is taller than before.
We add right max minus this bar's height, which is the water trapped above that bar.
After the pointers meet, we return the total water collected.

best-time-to-buy-and-sell-stock.hook: One buy, one sell, best profit. Just remember the cheapest price seen so far.
best-time-to-buy-and-sell-stock.ask: Given a list of daily stock prices, choose one day to buy and a later day to sell. Return the largest possible profit, or 0 if no profitable trade exists.
best-time-to-buy-and-sell-stock.exampleWhy: Buy at price 1 (index 1), sell at price 6 (index 4): profit 5. Selling before buying is not allowed.

brute.idea: Try every buy day with every later sell day and keep the best difference.
steps: Pick a buy day i
Try every sell day j > i
Keep the max of prices[j] - prices[i]
brute.whySlow: With 100,000 days that is about 5 billion buy and sell pairs.

optimal.insight: For a sell on day j, the best buy is the lowest price before it. Track that running minimum, so each day's best profit is one subtraction.
steps: Keep lowest price seen so far
New lower price? update lowest
Profit if sold today = price - lowest
Keep the maximum profit

pitfalls: Profit can be zero, never negative; start res at 0.
Global min minus global max fails when the min comes later.

say.intro: Okay, Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock. You get daily prices. You can buy once, and sell once, later. What's the biggest profit? If every trade loses, the answer is zero. With seven, one, five, three, six, four, you buy at one, sell at six. Profit five.
say.brute: The brute force way pairs every buy day with every later sell day, and keeps the biggest difference. It's correct, and it never sells before buying. But that's about n squared over two pairs. A hundred thousand days means roughly five billion pairs. Way too slow.
say.insight: Think about it this way. If I sell today, what's the best day to have bought? Simply the cheapest day before today. So as we walk the prices, we only need to remember the lowest price so far. Today's best profit is today's price minus that. And the answer is the best of those.
say.anim: We start with lowest price set to seven, and max profit at zero. On day one, price equals seven, so profit today stays zero, no improvement. Price drops to one, so lowest price updates to one, the new floor. Price rises to five, giving profit today of four, our new max profit. Price three gives only two profit, since lowest price is still one. Price six yields profit today of five, becoming the new max profit. Final price four gives profit three, which does not beat five. The loop ends and the function returns the final answer, five.
say.code: Here's the code. The result starts at zero, and lowest starts at the first price. That's the cheapest buy so far. We loop over every price. Found a cheaper buy day? Update lowest. Then we check the best profit selling today, price minus lowest, and keep the larger. If prices only fall, the result just stays zero.
say.outro: Linear time, constant space. Pattern: sliding window, where the left edge always sits on the cheapest day so far.

best-time-to-buy-and-sell-stock.title: Best Time to Buy And Sell Stock
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container the problem expects for our method.
This method takes the list of prices and returns the best profit as an integer.
This comment says we need to remember the lowest price seen so far, since that is the best day to buy.
We start the lowest price at the first day's price, since nothing earlier exists to compare against.
We start the max profit at zero, which is the answer if no profitable trade exists.
We walk through each day's price in order, so every buy candidate comes before the sell day.
This comment reminds us to check whether today's price is a new low to buy at.
If today's price is below the lowest price so far, we have found a better buy day.
We update the lowest price to today's price so later days compare against the cheaper buy.
This comment explains that selling today earns today's price minus the lowest price seen.
We compute profit today by subtracting the lowest price from today's price, which is the best sale ending today.
This comment says we want to keep track of the largest profit seen across all days.
If profit today beats the best profit so far, we have found a better trade.
We then record profit today as the new max profit.
After checking every day, we return the max profit, which stays zero when prices only fall.

longest-substring-without-repeating-char.hook: The textbook sliding window: grow on the right, shrink on the left, never look back.
longest-substring-without-repeating-char.ask: Given a string, find the length of the longest stretch of consecutive characters where no character repeats.
longest-substring-without-repeating-char.exampleWhy: "abc" has three distinct letters; any longer stretch would repeat an a, b or c.

brute.idea: Start a substring at every index and extend it to the right until a character repeats. Track the longest run found.
steps: Pick a start index i
Extend j while s[j] is unseen
Record j - i as a candidate
brute.time: O(n · min(n, a)), a = alphabet size
brute.whySlow: Each start rescans up to a characters: with 95 printable characters that is up to 95x the work of one pass, and n² for large alphabets.

optimal.insight: When s[r] repeats, every start before the old copy is also broken. So slide the left edge forward past the duplicate instead of restarting.
steps: Keep a set of letters inside window [l, r]
Add s[r]; if it is already present, drop s[l] and move l
Repeat until s[r] is unique, then add it
Window size r - l + 1 is a candidate answer

codeNotes.note: Window is unique again; include s[r]

pitfalls: Answer is a length, not the substring itself.
Empty string returns 0; spaces and symbols count as characters too.

say.intro: Okay, Longest Substring Without Repeating Characters. We want the longest stretch of back to back characters where nothing repeats. Take a b c a b c b b. The best we can do is a b c. So the answer is three. Any longer stretch repeats a letter.
say.brute: The brute force way starts at every position and walks right, keeping a set of letters, until something repeats. Record that length, then restart from the next position. It's correct. But each restart rescans letters we just checked. Each scan is capped by the alphabet size. With a large alphabet, that's n squared.
say.insight: Here's the thing. When a letter repeats, do we really need to restart? No. Any window still holding the older copy is broken. So we just slide the left edge forward until that copy falls out. Both edges only ever move right. Each letter goes in once and comes out once. That's linear time.
say.anim: We start with the string abcabcbb, an empty seen set, and left at zero. Right moves through a, b, and c, adding each new letter since none repeat yet, growing longest to 3. At right equals 3, s of right is a, already in seen, so the while loop triggers. We remove a from seen and slide left forward to 1, breaking the old window. Right reaches 4, b repeats, so left slides again, removing b and advancing to 2. This repeating pattern continues as c, b repeat, each time sliding left past the duplicate instead of restarting. Near the end, repeated b's force left to slide all the way up to 7. The loop finishes and returns the longest window found, which is 3.
say.code: Here's the code. A set holds the letters currently inside the window. For each right index, is the new letter a duplicate? Then we shrink from the left. We evict the leftmost letter and move left forward, until it's gone. Now the window is unique again, so we add the new letter. And we update the best window length so far, right minus left plus one.
say.outro: Linear time, and space bounded by the alphabet. Pattern: sliding window. Grow on the right, shrink on the left, and never go backwards.

longest-substring-without-repeating-char.title: Longest Substring Without Repeating Characters
longest-substring-without-repeating-char.optimalCode:
class Solution:
    def lengthOfLongestSubstring(self, s: str) -> int:
        seen = set()
        left = 0
        longest = 0

        # Expand the window one character at a time with right
        for right in range(len(s)):
            # If the new character is already in the window, shrink from the left
            while s[right] in seen:
                seen.remove(s[left])
                left += 1
            # Add the new character and update the best length seen so far
            seen.add(s[right])
            windowLength = right - left + 1
            if windowLength > longest:
                longest = windowLength

        return longest
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container the problem expects for our method.
This method takes a string s and returns the length of its longest substring with no repeated characters.
We create an empty set called seen to track which characters are currently inside our window.
We set left to zero, marking the start of the current window at the beginning of the string.
We set longest to zero, since we have not found any valid window yet.
This comment says we grow the window one character at a time by moving the right edge.
We loop right across every index of s, so each character gets a turn as the new window end.
This comment explains that if the new character already sits in the window, we must shrink from the left.
While the character at right is already in seen, the window has a duplicate and must be fixed.
We remove the character at left from seen, dropping the leftmost character out of the window.
We move left one step forward, so the window now starts after the removed character.
This comment says that once the window is clean, we add the new character and check for a new best.
We add the character at right to seen, since it is now safely part of the window.
We compute windowLength as right minus left plus one, which is the number of characters in the window.
We check whether this window is longer than the best length recorded so far.
If it is longer, we update longest to the new window length.
After scanning the whole string, we return longest as the answer.

longest-repeating-character-replacement.hook: A sliding window with a sneaky shortcut: the max count never needs to go down.
longest-repeating-character-replacement.ask: You have a string of capital letters and may change at most k characters. Return the length of the longest stretch you can make all one letter.
longest-repeating-character-replacement.exampleWhy: Change the A in "BABB" (or the B in "AABA") to get four equal letters using one change.

brute.idea: Try every substring. It can be made uniform if its length minus its most common letter count is at most k.
steps: Fix a start i, extend end j
Track letter counts and the top count
If length - top ≤ k, record length
brute.whySlow: With 100,000 letters there are about 5 billion substrings to check - far too many.

optimal.insight: Valid means length minus top letter count ≤ k. A longer answer needs a bigger top count, so a stale max is safe: slide the window instead of shrinking it.
steps: Extend r and count s[r]
Update maxf, the highest count ever seen
If length - maxf > k, slide: drop s[l], move l
Final window length is the answer

codeNotes.note: Window size holds the best length

pitfalls: Use if, not while: the window slides, it never shrinks below the best size.
maxf is never decreased - that is intentional, not a bug.

say.intro: Okay, Longest Repeating Character Replacement. You can change up to k letters in the string. How long a run of one letter can you make? Here k is one. Look at B A B B. Change that lone A, and you get four B's in a row. So the answer is four.
say.brute: The brute force way checks every substring. When does a substring work? When its length minus its most common letter count is at most k. Why? Because those other letters are exactly the ones we'd change. Extending from each start with running counts is still n squared. For a long string, that's billions of checks.
say.insight: Here's the trick. We only care about windows longer than our best so far. And a longer valid window needs a bigger top count. So we keep max frequency as the highest count ever seen, even if it goes stale. When the window breaks the rule, we slide it forward instead of shrinking it. The answer never gets worse.
say.anim: We start with string AABABBA, k equals 1, left at zero, and an empty count map. As right moves through A's and B's, the count map tracks letters and max frequency updates to track the top count. By right equals 3, max frequency becomes 3 with three A's, window length 4, still valid. At right 4, window length hits 5 but max frequency stays 3, so it's invalid now. The window slides forward, decrementing the left character and moving left to 1 instead of shrinking the answer. More B's arrive, triggering another invalid window, so left slides again to 2. One more slide pushes left to 3, keeping the window size fixed at four. Final answer is length seven minus left three, giving the longest replacement substring length of 4.
say.code: Here's the code. First, we count the new letter. Then we update max frequency, the best single letter count so far. Now, are there too many letters to change? That's window length minus max frequency, compared with k. If so, we drop the leftmost letter's count and move left by one. Notice it's an if, not a while. The window slides and never shrinks. So at the end, the window size holds the answer.
say.outro: Linear time, and constant space for twenty six letters. Pattern: sliding window, with a clever window that only grows or slides.

longest-repeating-character-replacement.title: Longest Repeating Character Replacement
lineNotes: We define a class named Solution, which is the container the problem expects for our method.

permutation-in-string.hook: Order does not matter, only counts do - so a fixed-size sliding window solves it in one pass.
permutation-in-string.ask: Given two lowercase strings s1 and s2, return true if some rearrangement of s1 appears as a contiguous block inside s2.
permutation-in-string.exampleWhy: s2 contains "ba", which is a rearrangement of "ab".

brute.idea: Slide over every block of s2 with the same length as s1, sort it, and compare with sorted s1.
steps: Sort s1 once
For each start i, sort s2[i:i+m]
Equal? return True
brute.whySlow: With s1 of 5,000 and s2 of 10,000 letters, it sorts 5,000 blocks of 5,000 letters: hundreds of millions of steps.

optimal.insight: Two strings are permutations exactly when all 26 letter counts match. Sliding the window changes just two counts, so track how many of the 26 counts currently match.
steps: Count s1 and the first window of s2
matches = letters whose counts agree
Slide: add s2[r], remove s2[l], adjust matches
matches == 26 means a permutation is here

codeNotes.note: Letter counts for s1 and the window
How many letters agree right now

pitfalls: Check the last window after the loop - it is easy to miss.
If s1 is longer than s2, return False immediately.

say.intro: Okay, Permutation in String. Does any rearrangement of s one appear as a block inside s two? Here s one is a b. And s two is e i d b a o o o. See the block b a? That's a b, rearranged. So the answer is true.
say.brute: The brute force way looks at every block of s two with the same length as s one. Sort it, and compare with sorted s one. It works. But neighbouring blocks share almost every letter, and we re-sort each one from scratch. That's n times m log m, mostly wasted effort. We can reuse work.
say.insight: Here's the key. What is a permutation, really? Just the same letter counts. So we keep a count array for s one, and one for the current window. Now, sliding by one changes only two counts. So we track how many of the twenty six letters currently match, and update that in constant time. Linear overall.
say.anim: We check s1 'ab' against s2 'eidbaooo' for a permutation window match. We build letter counts for s1 and for the first window of s2, letters e and i. Now we compare all 26 counts, counting how many letters already match between windows. Matches climbs quickly since most letters have zero count in both, reaching 22 matches. We slide the window right, adding a new letter and removing the leftmost one each step. Each slide updates matches up or down depending on whether counts now align exactly. After sliding to left equals 3, matches reaches the full 26, meaning counts align perfectly. The function returns true, confirming s2 contains a permutation of s1.
say.code: Here's the code. We fill letter counts for s one and the first window. Then we count how many letters agree right now. In the loop, if all twenty six match, we've found a permutation. Otherwise, a letter enters on the right, and we adjust matches. A letter leaves on the left, and we adjust again. Then left moves forward. After the loop, we check the final window too.
say.outro: Linear time, constant space. Pattern: fixed size sliding window with counts. The same idea finds all anagrams in a string. Compare counts, never sort.

minimum-window-substring.hook: The boss of sliding windows: expand until valid, then squeeze until it breaks.
minimum-window-substring.ask: Given strings s and t, return the shortest block of s that contains every character of t, counting repeats. Return an empty string if none exists.
minimum-window-substring.exampleWhy: "BANC" holds an A, a B and a C in just four letters; every other covering block is longer.

brute.idea: For each start l, extend r until the window covers t, record its length, then move to the next start.
steps: Fix a start l
Grow r, counting letters, until t is covered
Keep the shortest covering window
brute.space: O(|s|) for the best substring copy
brute.whySlow: With s of 100,000 chars, restarting from each l is billions of steps.

optimal.insight: Track have = how many distinct letters of t are fully satisfied. Grow right until have == need, then shrink left while still valid, recording the smallest window.
steps: Count what t needs
Expand r; when a letter's count is met, have += 1
While have == need: record window, drop s[l], move l
Return the shortest recorded window
optimal.space: O(k), k = distinct letters seen (at most 52)

codeNotes.match: if c in countT and window[c] == countT[c]:
if s[l] in countT and window[s[l]] < countT[s[l]]:
codeNotes.note: Dropped a needed letter; now invalid

pitfalls: t may repeat letters: compare counts, not just presence.
Return "" when no window covers t.

say.intro: Okay, Minimum Window Substring. Find the shortest block of s that contains every character of t, repeats included. Here t is A B C. Now look near the end of s. B A N C. All three letters, in just four characters. Every other covering block is longer.
say.brute: The brute force way picks every starting point and extends right, counting letters, until the window covers t. Record it, then try the next start. Correct? Yes. But we keep recounting the same letters again and again. That's roughly n squared. For a long string, billions of steps.
say.insight: Here's the trick. Use two pointers, plus a counter called have. It's the number of distinct letters of t that are fully satisfied. Grow the right edge until have equals need. Then shrink from the left while the window stays valid, recording the smallest size. Each pointer only moves forward. So it's linear.
say.anim: We build needCount from t, needing three distinct letters A, B, and C. Right expands through the string, adding letters to windowCount as it goes. At right equals five, have reaches three, meaning the window now satisfies t. The first valid window spans index zero to five, giving best length six. Left shrinks, dropping A below needed count, so have drops back to two. Expanding further, at right equals ten, have becomes three again with a bigger window. Left keeps advancing, shrinking the valid window and updating the best length each time. Window shrinks to length five, then four, as left passes O, D, and E. Final shrinking confirms the smallest valid window, giving answer BANC.
say.code: Here's the code. First we count what t requires. Have counts satisfied letters, need counts letters required. For each right index, we add the letter. If its count just reached the target, it became satisfied, so have goes up. While the window is valid, we try shrinking from the left. We record the new shortest window. Then we drop the left letter. Lost a needed letter? Have goes down, and the window is invalid again.
say.outro: Linear in the two string lengths. Pattern: variable size sliding window. Expand to become valid, then shrink to become minimal.

sliding-window-maximum.hook: A deque that keeps only the candidates that could ever be a maximum.
sliding-window-maximum.ask: Given a list of numbers and a window size k, slide the window from left to right one step at a time and report the largest number in each window.

brute.idea: For each window position, scan all k numbers in it and take the largest.
steps: For each start i
Scan nums[i] to nums[i+k-1]
Append the maximum
brute.whySlow: With n = 100,000 and k = 50,000, that is billions of comparisons.

optimal.insight: If a newer number is bigger, every older smaller number can never be a maximum again. Drop them, so the deque stays decreasing and its front is the max.
steps: Pop smaller values from the back
Push the new index
Drop the front if it left the window
Once the window is full, the front is the max

codeNotes.note: Indices, values decreasing front to back
Smaller older values are useless now
Front slid out of the window

pitfalls: Store indices, not values, so you can tell when the front leaves the window.
Each index is pushed and popped at most once - that is why it is O(n).

say.intro: Okay, Sliding Window Maximum. We slide a window of size k across a list, one step at a time. For each window, report the biggest number. Here k is three. The six windows give three, three, five, five, six, and finally seven. That's our answer.
say.brute: The brute force way scans all k numbers at every window position and takes the largest. Simple, and correct. But neighbouring windows share almost all their numbers, and we rescan them every time. That's n times k. On the largest inputs, billions of comparisons.
say.insight: Here's the thing. When a bigger number arrives, can any smaller number before it ever be the max again? No. The bigger one will outlive it in every future window. So we keep a deque of indices, with values decreasing from front to back. And the front is always the current maximum.
say.anim: We start with nums and a window size of three, building a deque of indices. Three is bigger than one, so index zero pops out, leaving only index one. Window fills with indices one and two, and the front value three becomes our first max. Negative one joins the deque, window stays decreasing, and three stays the max again. Five is huge, so it pops everything smaller, becoming the new front and max. Three gets added after five, keeping the deque decreasing, max stays five. Six pops five and three off the back, becoming the new maximum. Seven pops six too, giving a final result of three, three, five, five, six, seven.
say.code: Here's the code. The deque holds indices, with values decreasing front to back. For each right index, smaller older values are useless now, so we pop them off the back. Then we push the new index. Has the front slid out of the window? Then we pop it from the front. Once the window is full, the front holds the window max, so we record it. Each index is pushed and popped once.
say.outro: So the whole thing is linear time. Pattern: sliding window with a monotonic deque. Use it for any rolling maximum or minimum.

sliding-window-maximum.title: Sliding Window Maximum
sliding-window-maximum.optimalCode:
class Solution:
    def maxSlidingWindow(self, nums: List[int], k: int) -> List[int]:
        result = []
        window = collections.deque()  # stores indices, values decreasing
        left = 0
        right = 0

        while right < len(nums):
            # 1. Pop smaller values from the back
            while window and nums[window[-1]] < nums[right]:
                window.pop()
            # 2. Push the new index
            window.append(right)

            # 3. Drop the front if it left the window
            if left > window[0]:
                window.popleft()

            # 4. Once the window is full, the front is the max
            if right + 1 >= k:
                result.append(nums[window[0]])
                left += 1

            right += 1

        return result
lineNotes: We define a Solution class that holds the method for solving the sliding window maximum problem.
The method takes the list of numbers and window size k, and returns a list of window maximums.
We start with an empty result list that will collect the maximum of each window.
We create a deque that stores indices, keeping their values in decreasing order so the front is always the maximum.
We set left to zero, marking the start of the current window.
We set right to zero, marking the new element we are about to add.
We loop while right is still inside the list, processing one new number each step.
This comment says the first step is removing smaller values from the back of the deque.
While the back index holds a value smaller than the new number, that older value can never be a maximum.
We pop that smaller index off the back to keep the deque decreasing.
This comment says the next step is adding the new index to the deque.
We append the index at right, since it is now the newest candidate for the maximum.
This comment says we must remove the front index if it has slid out of the window.
If left has passed the front index, that front element is no longer inside the window.
We pop it from the front so the deque only holds indices in the current window.
This comment says that once the window is full, the front of the deque holds the maximum.
When right plus one reaches k, we have a full window and can record an answer.
We append the value at the front index of the deque, which is the window's maximum.
We move left forward by one so the window slides on the next step.
We advance right by one to bring the next number into consideration.
After processing every number, we return the list of window maximums.

valid-parentheses.hook: The problem that teaches you why stacks exist: the last bracket opened must close first.
valid-parentheses.ask: Given a string of only brackets - round, square and curly - return true if every opener is closed by the same type, in the correct order.
valid-parentheses.exampleWhy: Each closer matches the most recent unclosed opener: ( with ), [ with ], ( with ), then { with }.

brute.idea: Repeatedly delete any adjacent matched pair like (), [] or {}. If the string becomes empty, it was valid.
steps: Find an adjacent pair (), [] or {}
Remove it and rescan
Valid if nothing is left
brute.whySlow: Each pass removes at most three pairs and rebuilds the string, so 10,000 brackets cost tens of millions of character copies.

optimal.insight: A closer must match the most recently opened unclosed bracket. Last in, first out is exactly a stack.
steps: Openers: push onto the stack
Closer: top must be its matching opener
Match? pop. Mismatch or empty? return False
Valid only if the stack ends empty

codeNotes.note: Each closer maps to its opener

codeNotes.match: if not stack or stack[-1] != bracketMap[c]:

pitfalls: A lone closer with an empty stack must return False, not crash.
Leftover openers like "((" are invalid - check the stack is empty.

say.intro: Okay, Valid Parentheses. You get a string of round, square, and curly brackets. Is every opener closed by the same type, in the right order? In our example, every closer matches the latest opener still waiting. So the answer is true. One mismatch anywhere, and it's false.
say.brute: The brute force way keeps deleting matched pairs that sit right next to each other. Like an open and close round bracket. If the string shrinks to nothing, it was valid. It works. But every pass rebuilds the whole string. That's n squared. Ten thousand brackets means tens of millions of copies.
say.insight: Here's the key. A closing bracket must match the most recent opener that's still open. Most recent first. What does that sound like? Last in, first out. That's a stack. Push every opener. When a closer arrives, the top of the stack must be its partner. If it isn't, the string is invalid.
say.anim: We start with an empty stack and the string of brackets to check. The first three characters are openers, so brace, bracket, and parenthesis get pushed onto the stack. Now char is a closing parenthesis, it matches the top of stack which is open parenthesis, so we pop it. Char is a closing bracket, matching the open bracket on top, so that gets popped too, leaving just brace. Another open parenthesis is pushed, then its closer matches and pops it right back off. Finally the closing brace matches the remaining open brace, popping it and emptying the stack. With the stack empty after processing every character, the function returns true as the final answer.
say.code: Here's the code. A map links each closer to its opener. We loop over the characters. Is it an opener? Then we remember it by pushing it. Otherwise, it's a closer. If nothing is open, or the top is the wrong type, return false. If it matches, we pop, closing the latest opener. Finally, any leftover openers mean invalid. So we return true only if the stack is empty.
say.outro: Linear time, linear space. Pattern: stack. Whenever the latest thing you opened must close first, reach for a stack. Real parsers use it too.

valid-parentheses.title: Valid Parentheses
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container the interview platform expects for our method.
The method isValid takes the string s and returns a boolean saying whether the brackets are balanced.
We build a dictionary that maps each closing bracket to the opening bracket it must pair with.
We start with an empty stack that will hold openers still waiting to be closed.
This comment says we will examine every character of the string one at a time.
We loop over the string, handling one character per iteration from left to right.
This comment says that any opener gets pushed onto the stack to wait for its closer.
If the character is not a key in matching, it must be an opener.
We push that opener onto the stack so it becomes the most recent unclosed bracket.
We continue to the next character since an opener needs no further checking right now.
This comment says a closer must line up with the opener currently on top of the stack.
If the stack is empty or its top is not the matching opener, the order is broken.
In that case we immediately return false because the closer has no valid partner.
Otherwise the top matches, so we pop it off, marking that pair as properly closed.
This comment says the string is valid only if no opener is left unmatched at the end.
We return true only when the stack is empty, meaning every opener found its closer.

min-stack.hook: Get the minimum in constant time - even after pops - by remembering history.
min-stack.ask: Design a stack with push, pop, top, and getMin, where getMin returns the smallest value currently in the stack. Every operation must run in constant time.
min-stack.exampleWhy: After pushing 5,3,7,2 the min is 2. Popping 2 makes the min 3 again; the top is 7.

brute.idea: Use a plain list as the stack, and compute getMin by scanning every element.
steps: push, pop, top use the list end
getMin scans the whole list
Return the smallest value
brute.whySlow: With 30,000 calls on a deep stack, each getMin can scan 30,000 values - hundreds of millions of steps.

optimal.insight: The minimum only depends on what is below. Store, beside each value, the minimum of the stack up to that level; popping restores the old minimum.
steps: Keep a second stack, minStack, in sync
On push, store min(val, current min)
On pop, pop both stacks
getMin reads the top of minStack

codeNotes.match: val = min(val, self.minStack[-1] if self.minStack else val)

pitfalls: A single min variable fails: after popping the min you cannot recover the previous one.
Push onto minStack on every push, so both stacks stay the same height.

say.intro: Okay, Min Stack. Design a stack with push, pop, top, and get min, all in constant time. We push five, three, seven, and two. The min is two. Now pop the two. The min goes back to three. And the top is seven.
say.brute: The simple approach uses one list. Push, pop, and top all work at the end. For get min, we scan every element and keep the smallest. It's correct. So what's the catch? Get min becomes linear. Tens of thousands of calls on a deep stack adds up to hundreds of millions of steps.
say.insight: Here's the thing. The minimum at any moment depends only on the values at or below the top. So beside each value, we store the minimum of everything up to that level. When we pop, the level below already knows its own minimum. Nothing ever gets recomputed. We just trade a little memory for speed.
say.anim: We start with two empty stacks, one for values and one for running minimums. Pushing five adds it to both stacks, since it is the first value, minimum is five. Pushing three compares it to current minimum five, three is smaller, so minimum becomes three. Pushing seven compares it to minimum three, seven is bigger, so minimum stays three. Pushing two compares it to minimum three, two is smaller, so new minimum becomes two. Getting the minimum now returns two, the top of the min stack. Popping removes two from both stacks, restoring the previous minimum of three underneath. Now getMin returns three and top returns seven, the final answers shown.
say.code: Here's the code. We keep a main stack and a min stack. Each min stack entry is the minimum at or below that level. On push, we append the value, then the smaller of the value and the current min. That's the new min at this level. On pop, we pop both together, so the old min comes back. Top reads the main stack. Get min just reads the top of the min stack.
say.outro: Constant time for every operation, linear space. Pattern: stack, with a helper stack storing each level's answer beside its data.

min-stack.title: Min Stack
lineNotes: We define a class called MinStack that supports push, pop, top, and getMin, all in constant time.
The constructor runs when a new MinStack is created to set up its internal storage.
We create an empty list called stack to hold the actual values in order.
We create a second empty list called minStack that will hold the running minimum at each level.
The push method takes a value and adds it to the structure.
This comment says the first step is putting the new value on the main stack.
We append the value to the main stack so it becomes the new top.
This comment says we next need to figure out the smallest value now in the stack.
We check whether the min stack has anything in it, meaning the stack is not empty.
If it has entries, we read the last one, which is the minimum before this push, into currentMin.
We compare the new value against that current minimum to see if it is smaller.
If the value is smaller, it becomes the new minimum.
Otherwise we fall into the other case where the value is not smaller.
The old minimum stays as the new minimum since the value did not beat it.
If the min stack is empty, we take the other path for the very first element.
With nothing below, the first value is automatically the minimum, so newMin equals val.
This comment says the computed minimum must be recorded on the min stack.
We append newMin to the min stack so both stacks always have the same height.
The pop method removes the top element from the structure.
This comment reminds us to pop both stacks together so they stay aligned.
We pop the main stack, discarding the top value.
We pop the min stack too, which restores the minimum that held before that value was pushed.
The top method returns the most recent value without removing it.
We simply return the last item of the main stack.
The getMin method returns the smallest value currently stored.
We return the last item of the min stack, which is the minimum for the whole current stack.

evaluate-reverse-polish-notation.hook: No parentheses, no precedence rules - just a stack. This is how calculators really think.
evaluate-reverse-polish-notation.ask: Evaluate an arithmetic expression written in postfix order, where each operator comes after its two operands. Division truncates toward zero. Return the integer result.

brute.idea: Repeatedly find the first operator, apply it to the two tokens before it, and splice the result back into the list.
steps: Scan for the first operator
Combine it with the two tokens before it
Replace those three tokens, repeat
brute.whySlow: Each operator triggers a rescan and list rebuild, so 10,000 tokens cost tens of millions of steps.

optimal.insight: In postfix, an operator always applies to the two most recent values. Most recent first means a stack: push numbers, pop two on each operator, push the result.
steps: Number: push it
Operator: pop a (top), then b
Push b op a - order matters for - and /
The last value left is the answer

codeNotes.note: a was on top: compute b minus a

pitfalls: Python // floors (-7 // 2 = -4); the problem wants truncation (-3).
Pop order: the first pop is the right operand for - and /.

say.intro: Okay, Evaluate Reverse Polish Notation. Each operator comes right after its two operands. No brackets, no precedence rules. In our example, thirteen divided by five is two. Four plus two is six. Six times two is twelve. And that's the answer.
say.brute: A naive approach finds the first operator, combines it with the two tokens just before it, and splices the result back in. Then it scans again from the start. It works. But every operator means a fresh rescan and a rebuilt list. That's n squared.
say.insight: Here's the key. In postfix, an operator always applies to the two most recent unused values. Most recent first? That's a stack. Push every number. When an operator arrives, pop two values, combine them, and push the result back for later operators. One pass, no rescanning.
say.anim: We start with an empty stack and the tokens four, thirteen, five, divide, plus, two, multiply. Four, thirteen, and five are numbers, so each gets pushed onto the stack in turn. Now token is divide, so we pop five and thirteen, the two most recent values. We divide thirteen by five, getting two, and push it back onto the stack. Token is plus, so we pop two and four, add them, and push six. Two is pushed next, giving a stack of six and two before the multiply. Multiply pops six and two, multiplies them, and pushes twelve onto the stack. Only twelve remains on the stack, so the final answer returned is twelve.
say.code: Here's the code. We loop over the tokens. For plus and times, order doesn't matter, so pop two and push the result. For minus, a was on top, so we compute b minus a. Divide works the same way, but we truncate toward zero, not floor. Anything else is a plain number, so we push it. At the end, one value remains. That's the answer.
say.outro: Linear time, linear space. Pattern: stack. And watch division. It must round toward zero, and Python's floor division gets that wrong.

evaluate-reverse-polish-notation.title: Evaluate Reverse Polish Notation
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container the problem expects for our method.
The method evalRPN takes a list of string tokens and returns the final integer result.
We start with an empty stack that will hold numbers waiting for an operator.
We loop through each token in order, from left to right, as postfix requires.
This comment says that when a token is an operator, we need the two most recent values.
We check whether the token is plus, minus, times, or divide, meaning it is an operator.
We pop the top of the stack into second, since it was pushed most recently and is the right operand.
We pop again into first, which is the left operand of the operation.
This comment reminds us that order matters, especially for subtraction and division.
If the token is plus, we are in the addition case.
We set result to first plus second.
Otherwise, if the token is minus, we handle subtraction.
We set result to first minus second, keeping the left operand first.
Otherwise, if the token is times, we handle multiplication.
We set result to first times second.
Otherwise the operator must be division.
We divide as a float and convert to int, which truncates toward zero as the problem demands.
This comment says the computed result goes back onto the stack for later operators.
We push result onto the stack so it can serve as an operand later.
Otherwise, the token is not an operator, so it must be a number.
This comment says numbers are simply pushed onto the stack.
We convert the token string to an integer and push it onto the stack.
After all tokens are processed, exactly one value remains on the stack, which is the answer, so we return it.

daily-temperatures.hook: The gateway to monotonic stacks: answer 'next warmer day' for everyone in one pass.
daily-temperatures.ask: Given daily temperatures, for each day return how many days you must wait for a warmer temperature. If no warmer day comes, the answer is 0.
daily-temperatures.exampleWhy: 75 on day 2 waits until 76 on day 6, so four days; 76 and the last 73 never see a warmer day.

brute.idea: For each day, scan forward until you find a warmer day and record the distance.
steps: For each day i
Scan j = i+1 onward
First warmer day: res[i] = j - i
brute.whySlow: With 100,000 days that never warm up, each scan runs to the end - about 5 billion checks.

optimal.insight: Keep the days still waiting for a warmer day on a stack; their temperatures never rise toward the top. A new warmer day resolves every cooler day on top at once.
steps: Walk days left to right
While today is warmer than the stack top, pop it
Its answer is today's index minus its index
Push today; it waits too

codeNotes.note: Today is warmer than waiting day

pitfalls: Use strictly warmer (>), not ≥ - equal temperatures do not count.
Days left on the stack keep their default answer 0.

say.intro: Okay, Daily Temperatures. For each day, how many days until it gets warmer? If that never happens, the answer is zero. Seventy five, on day two, waits four days, until seventy six. And the last two days never see a warmer day. So both get zero.
say.brute: The brute force way scans forward from each day until it finds a warmer one, and records the distance. It's correct. But what if temperatures keep falling? Then every scan runs all the way to the end. That's n squared. A hundred thousand days means about five billion checks.
say.insight: Here's the trick. Keep a stack of days still waiting for a warmer day. Their temperatures never rise from bottom to top. Now, when a warmer day arrives, it's the answer for every cooler day on top. So we pop them all, and fill in their waits at once. Each day gets its answer exactly once.
say.anim: We start with temperatures listed and an answer array full of zeros. Day zero, seventy three degrees, gets pushed onto the empty stack to wait. Day one is warmer, so day zero pops off, getting a wait time of one. Day two is even warmer, popping day one, giving it a wait time of one too. Days three and four are cooler, so indices three and four just get pushed. Day five warms up, popping day four then day three, giving waits two and one. Day six is hottest yet, popping day five and day two, with waits one and four. Days six and seven never find warmer days, so their answers stay zero, final output one one four two one one zero zero.
say.code: Here's the code. The result starts as all zeros. The stack holds days still waiting, with temperatures decreasing. For each day, while today is warmer than the waiting day on top, we pop it. Its answer is the days waited, today's index minus its index. Then today joins the waiting list, so we push it. Anything left on the stack keeps its zero.
say.outro: Each day is pushed and popped at most once, so it's linear. Pattern: monotonic stack, the go to tool for next greater element questions.

daily-temperatures.title: Daily Temperatures
daily-temperatures.optimalCode:
class Solution:
    def dailyTemperatures(self, temperatures: List[int]) -> List[int]:
        answer = [0] * len(temperatures)
        stack = []  # stores indices of days waiting for a warmer day

        # 1. Walk through each day left to right
        for today in range(len(temperatures)):
            # 2. Resolve every cooler day waiting on the stack
            while stack and temperatures[today] > temperatures[stack[-1]]:
                previousDay = stack.pop()
                # 3. Its answer is today's index minus its index
                answer[previousDay] = today - previousDay
            # 4. Push today; it waits too
            stack.append(today)

        return answer
lineNotes: We define a class named Solution, which is the container for the method that solves this problem.
This method takes the list of temperatures and returns a list of waiting days for each day.
We create the answer list filled with zeros, one per day, so days with no warmer future stay zero.
We start an empty stack that will hold indices of days still waiting for a warmer day.
The comment says we walk through the days from left to right, handling each one in order.
We loop with today as the index of each day in the temperatures list.
The comment explains that a warmer today can settle every cooler day waiting on the stack.
While the stack has days and today is warmer than the day on top, we keep resolving the top day.
We pop the top index off the stack and call it previousDay, since today has answered its wait.
The comment says the wait length is just the gap between today's index and that earlier index.
We store today minus previousDay in the answer at previousDay, which is how many days it waited.
The comment says today is pushed too, because it now needs its own warmer day.
We append today's index to the stack, keeping temperatures on it from rising toward the top.
After all days are processed, we return the answer list, with zeros left for days that never found a warmer one.

car-fleet.hook: Physics disguised as a stack problem: sort by position, and arrival times tell the story.
car-fleet.ask: Cars drive toward a target on a one-lane road and cannot pass. A faster car that catches a slower one joins it as a fleet. How many fleets arrive?
car-fleet.exampleWhy: Cars at 10 and 8 meet at time 1; cars at 5 and 3 merge (time 7); the car at 0 arrives alone.

brute.idea: Sort cars by position. A car leads its own fleet if it would arrive later than every car ahead of it.
steps: Sort by position, closest to target first
For each car, compute the max time of cars ahead
Slower than all of them? new fleet
brute.time: O(n²) (after an O(n log n) sort)
brute.whySlow: Rescanning all cars ahead for each car is about 5 billion checks with 100,000 cars.

optimal.insight: Going from the car nearest the target backward, a car arriving no later than the fleet ahead catches it and merges; only slower arrival times start new fleets.
steps: Pair positions with speeds, sort descending
Compute each car's arrival time
Push it; if ≤ the fleet ahead, pop (merged)
Stack size = number of fleets

codeNotes.note: Each remaining time is a fleet

pitfalls: Use float division for times; integer division merges cars wrongly.
Catching up exactly at the target still counts as one fleet (≤).

say.intro: Okay, Car Fleet. Cars drive toward a target on a single lane, and nobody can overtake. So a fast car that catches a slower one just tails it. That's a fleet. In this example, five cars end up arriving as three separate fleets.
say.brute: A simple approach sorts the cars by position, closest to the target first. When does a car start a new fleet? Only if it arrives later than every car ahead of it. But checking all the cars ahead, for every car, is n squared. A hundred thousand cars means about five billion checks.
say.insight: Here's the thing. Work out each car's arrival time as if it drove alone. Then go from the front of the road backwards. If a car would arrive no later than the fleet ahead, it must catch up and merge. Only a strictly later arrival starts a new fleet. And a stack holds each fleet's arrival time.
say.anim: We start pairing each car's position with its speed into a list called cars. After sorting, cars are ordered closest to target first: ten, eight, five, three, zero. Car at position ten takes one time unit to reach target, starting fleets with one point zero. Car at eight also arrives at time one, catching the fleet ahead, so it merges and gets removed. Car at five arrives at time seven, slower, so it starts a new separate fleet. Car at three arrives at time three, catching the fleet ahead, so it merges away. Car at zero arrives at time twelve, too slow to catch up, forming its own fleet. Three fleets remain, so the final answer returned is three.
say.code: Here's the code. We zip positions with speeds, and sort so the car closest to the target comes first. For each car, we push its time to reach the target alone. That's target minus position, over speed. Now, does it catch the fleet ahead? If its time is less than or equal to the one below, it merges, so we pop it. At the end, each remaining time is a fleet.
say.outro: Sorting makes it n log n. Pattern: stack. Sort first, then let the stack absorb every car that catches up. Think in times.

car-fleet.title: Car Fleet
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container the problem expects for our method.
The carFleet method takes the target distance, the list of car positions, and the list of speeds, and returns the fleet count.
This comment says our first step is to pair each car's position with its own speed.
We start with an empty list called cars to hold those position and speed pairs.
We loop over every index in the position list so each car gets visited once.
For each index we append a pair of that car's position and speed to cars.
This comment says we next sort the cars so the one closest to the target comes first.
We sort cars in reverse order, so the largest position, nearest the target, comes first.
This comment explains that we now process cars from the one nearest the target backward.
We create an empty list called fleets that will hold the arrival time of each fleet ahead.
We loop through each car, unpacking its position and speed, starting from the front of the road.
We compute arrival time as the remaining distance to the target divided by the car's speed.
We tentatively add this arrival time to fleets, treating the car as its own new fleet.
This comment says that if the car catches the fleet ahead, it should merge into it.
If there are two fleets and this car arrives no later than the one ahead, it will catch up.
In that case we pop the last time, since the car merges and the fleet ahead keeps its slower time.
Finally we return the length of fleets, which is the number of distinct fleets reaching the target.

largest-rectangle-in-histogram.hook: A hard stack classic: each bar learns how far it can stretch the moment a shorter bar shows up.
largest-rectangle-in-histogram.ask: Given bar heights of a histogram, each bar one unit wide, find the area of the largest rectangle that fits entirely inside the bars.
largest-rectangle-in-histogram.exampleWhy: Bars 5 and 6 side by side give height 5 times width 2, area 10.

brute.idea: Try every left bar, extend right, and track the minimum height so far; area is min height times width.
steps: Pick a left index i
Extend j, tracking the shortest bar
Area = shortest x (j - i + 1)
brute.whySlow: With 100,000 bars that is about 5 billion pairs to try.

optimal.insight: A bar's rectangle extends right until a shorter bar appears. Keep bars in non-decreasing height on a stack; a shorter bar pops them and finalizes their widths.
steps: Stack holds (start index, height), heights increasing
Shorter bar arrives: pop taller bars, score height x width
New bar inherits the start of the last popped bar
Leftover bars extend to the end

codeNotes.note: Taller bar can no longer extend
Its rectangle ends just before i
New bar extends back to here

pitfalls: Do not forget the bars left on the stack after the loop.
Extending start backward is the subtle part - it counts the popped bars' width.

say.intro: Okay, Largest Rectangle in Histogram. Each bar is one unit wide. Find the biggest rectangle that fits entirely inside the bars. Look at the bars of height five and six. Together they give height five, width two. So the answer is ten.
say.brute: The brute force way picks every left bar and extends to the right, tracking the shortest bar so far. The area is that shortest height times the width. Keep the best. It's correct. But it's n squared. A hundred thousand bars means about five billion pairs.
say.insight: Here's the key. A bar's rectangle keeps stretching right until a shorter bar shows up. So keep a stack of bars with increasing heights. When a shorter bar arrives, every taller bar on top is finished. Pop it and score it. And here's the clever part. The new bar inherits the popped bar's start.
say.anim: We start with the histogram two one five six two three, max area at zero and an empty stack. At index one height one is shorter, so bar height two pops off, giving area two. Bars five then six push onto the stack since heights keep increasing. At index four height two pops six for area six, then pops five for area ten. Remaining bars one, two and three stay on the stack as the loop ends. We sweep the leftover stack, computing areas for heights one, two and three to the end. The largest rectangle found has area ten, matching the expected answer.
say.code: Here's the code. The stack holds a start index and a height. For each bar, while the top is taller, it can no longer extend. So we pop it. Its rectangle ends just before here, so we score its height times that width. And the new bar extends back to its start. Then we push the new bar with its earliest start. Finally, the remaining bars reach the end, so we score them too.
say.outro: Each bar is pushed and popped at most once, so it's linear time. Pattern: monotonic stack. One of the hardest to master, and most rewarding.

largest-rectangle-in-histogram.title: Largest Rectangle In Histogram
lineNotes: We define a class named Solution, which holds the method that solves the histogram problem.
The method takes the list of bar heights and returns the largest rectangle area as an integer.
We start the best area seen so far, maxArea, at zero.
We create an empty stack that stores pairs of a starting index and a height, kept in non-decreasing height.
We loop over every bar, getting its index i and its height h.
We set start to the current index, assuming this bar's rectangle can only extend left to itself for now.
While the stack has bars and the top bar is taller than the current one, that top bar can no longer extend right.
We pop the top bar, getting the index where its rectangle starts and its height.
We compute the popped bar's area as its height times the distance from its start to i, and keep the larger area.
We move start back to the popped index, since the current shorter bar can extend left over that taller bar's span.
We push the current bar onto the stack with its adjusted start index and its height.
After the loop, the bars left on the stack extend all the way to the right end, so we go through each.
For each remaining bar, we compute height times the distance from its start to the end of the histogram, updating maxArea.
We return maxArea as the largest rectangle area found.

binary-search.hook: The algorithm every other search builds on - halve the problem every single step.
binary-search.ask: Given a sorted list of distinct numbers and a target, return the index of the target, or -1 if it is not there. Aim for logarithmic time.
binary-search.exampleWhy: 24 sits at index 8 in the sorted list.

brute.idea: Check every element from left to right until you find the target.
steps: Walk i from 0 to n - 1
nums[i] == target? return i
Reached the end? return -1
brute.whySlow: It ignores the sorting: 10,000 numbers can take 10,000 checks instead of about 14.

optimal.insight: Because the list is sorted, one comparison with the middle tells you which half cannot contain the target. Discard that half every step.
steps: Search range [l, r] starts as the whole list
Look at the middle m
Too big: r = m - 1. Too small: l = m + 1
Equal: return m; empty range: return -1

codeNotes.note: Overflow-safe habit; Python ints never overflow
Target is in the left half
Target is in the right half

pitfalls: Use l <= r with inclusive bounds, or you miss single-element ranges.
Move to m - 1 or m + 1, never m, or it may loop forever.

say.intro: Okay, Binary Search. You get a sorted list of distinct numbers and a target. Return the target's index, or minus one if it's missing. Here the list has ten numbers. The target is twenty four. It sits at index eight.
say.brute: The brute force way checks every element from left to right until it hits the target. Simple, and correct. But it completely ignores that the list is sorted. Ten thousand numbers could take ten thousand checks, when about fourteen would do. Interviewers want the log time answer here.
say.insight: Here's the thing. Because the list is sorted, one comparison with the middle tells us which half can't hold the target. Middle too big? Then everything to its right is too big as well. So every comparison throws away half of what's left. That's log time. Fourteen looks for ten thousand numbers.
say.anim: We start with left at 0 and right at 9, covering the whole array. Middle lands on index 4, where the value 9 is less than target 24. Since nine is too small, we discard the left half and move left to 5. Now middle is index 7, holding value 20, still less than 24. We move left to 8, narrowing the search range further. Middle becomes index 8, where nums of middle equals 24, matching target. The function returns middle, giving the final answer 8.
say.code: Here's the code. Left and right mark an inclusive search range. While the range still has elements, we compute the middle. Writing it as left plus half the gap is an overflow safe habit, though Python ints never overflow. Middle too big? The target is in the left half, so move right in. Too small? It's in the right half, so move left in. Otherwise return the middle. If the range empties, return minus one.
say.outro: Log time, constant space. Pattern: binary search, the foundation for every halving trick you'll meet. Know it cold.

binary-search.title: Binary Search
lineNotes: We define a class called Solution, which is the container for our search method.
The search method takes a sorted list of numbers and a target, and returns the index of the target.
This comment says we begin by treating the whole list as the range where the target might be.
We set left to zero, the first index of the list.
We set right to the last index, which is the length of nums minus one.
This comment says we keep shrinking the range for as long as it still contains something.
The loop runs while left is not past right, meaning at least one candidate index remains.
We compute middle as left plus half the gap, which avoids overflow and lands in the center of the range.
This comment explains that a middle value too big means look left, and too small means look right.
If the middle value is greater than the target, the target must lie in the left half.
So we move right to just before middle, discarding the middle and everything after it.
Otherwise, if the middle value is less than the target, the target must lie in the right half.
So we move left to just after middle, discarding the middle and everything before it.
If neither comparison held, the middle value equals the target.
This comment simply marks that reaching this branch means we found the target.
We return middle, the index where the target sits.
If the loop ends with an empty range, the target is absent, so we return negative one.

search-a-2d-matrix.hook: A grid that is secretly one sorted list - binary search it twice, or once.
search-a-2d-matrix.ask: Each row of the matrix is sorted, and each row starts after the previous row ends. Return true if the target is in the matrix, in logarithmic time.
search-a-2d-matrix.exampleWhy: 16 lies in the middle row, at column 2.

brute.idea: Scan every cell of the matrix and compare it with the target.
steps: Loop over each row
Loop over each value in the row
Equal to target? return True
brute.whySlow: A 100 x 100 matrix needs up to 10,000 checks; binary search needs about 14.

optimal.insight: Rows are sorted and stacked in order, so first binary search for the one row whose range contains the target, then binary search inside it.
steps: Binary search rows by first and last value
Target above the row's last? go down; below its first? go up
No row left? return False
Binary search within the found row

codeNotes.note: Target lies in a lower row
Target lies in a higher row
Normal binary search in that row

pitfalls: Alternative: one flat sorted list, where index i maps to row i // n.
Do not confuse this with Search a 2D Matrix II, where rows overlap.

say.intro: Okay, Search a Two D Matrix. Each row is sorted, and each row starts after the previous row ends. Is the target anywhere in the matrix? Our target is sixteen. It's in the middle row, third column. So the answer is true.
say.brute: The brute force way checks every cell, row by row, until it finds the target. It's correct. But it throws away all the ordering we were given. A hundred by hundred matrix could take ten thousand checks, when binary search needs about fourteen. And the problem asks for log time.
say.insight: Think about it this way. Read the rows left to right, top to bottom, and you get one long sorted list. So first, we binary search the rows. Compare the target with each row's first and last values to find the only row that could hold it. Then we binary search inside that row. Two log searches.
say.anim: We start with a sorted matrix and target sixteen, setting up row and column counts. Binary search begins on rows, with top zero and bottom two to find the right range. Middle row index one is checked, and sixteen fits between its first and last values. Target row is set to one, since row ten eleven sixteen twenty contains our target. Now we binary search inside row one, starting left zero and right three. Middle index one holds eleven, smaller than sixteen, so left moves up to two. Next middle index two holds sixteen, matching the target exactly. The function returns true, confirming sixteen exists in the matrix.
say.code: Here's the code. Top and bottom bound the rows. If the target is bigger than the middle row's last value, it lies in a lower row. If it's smaller than the first value, it lies in a higher row. Otherwise we stop. If no rows remain, no row can contain it, so return false. Then we run a normal binary search in that row, returning true when we find the target.
say.outro: Log of rows plus log of columns. Pattern: binary search, applied twice here, or once on a flattened view of the grid.

lineNotes: We define the Solution class that holds the search method for this problem.
The searchMatrix method takes the matrix and the target value and returns true or false.
We store the number of rows in the matrix as num rows.
We store the number of columns, using the length of the first row, as num cols.
