We set bottom to the last row index, which is num rows minus one.
We set target row to negative one, meaning no candidate row has been found yet.
We loop while the range of rows between top and bottom is not empty.
We pick the middle row by averaging top and bottom with integer division.
If the target is bigger than the last value of the middle row, the row must be lower down.
So we move top to just below the middle row, discarding the middle row and everything above.
Otherwise, if the target is smaller than the first value of the middle row, it must be higher up.
So we move bottom to just above the middle row, discarding it and everything below.
Otherwise the target falls within this row's range, so this is the only row that could contain it.
We record the middle row as target row.
We break out of the row search since we found the candidate row.
This comment notes that if the loop ended without a row, the target is absent.
We check whether target row is still negative one, meaning no row's range held the target.
In that case we return false immediately.
This comment says step three is a binary search inside the chosen row.
We set left to zero, the first column of the row.
We set right to the last column index, which is num cols minus one.
We loop while the column range between left and right is not empty.
We compute the middle column by averaging left and right with integer division.
If the target is larger than the middle value in the row, the target must be to the right.
So we move left to just after the middle column.
If the target is smaller than the middle value, it must be to the left.
So we move right to just before the middle column.
Otherwise the middle value equals the target, which is exactly what we wanted.
We return true because we found the target.

koko-eating-bananas.hook: Binary search on the answer, not the array - the trick behind many hard-looking problems.
koko-eating-bananas.ask: Koko eats from one pile per hour, up to k bananas, and has h hours. Find the smallest whole-number speed k that lets her finish every pile in time.
koko-eating-bananas.exampleWhy: At speed 4 she needs 1+2+2+3 = 8 hours. At speed 3 she needs 10 hours - too slow.

brute.idea: Try speeds 1, 2, 3, ... and return the first one whose total hours fit within h.
steps: For k = 1 upward
Hours = sum of ceil(pile / k)
First k with hours ≤ h is the answer
brute.whySlow: Piles can hold a billion bananas, so trying every speed means up to a billion passes over the piles.

optimal.insight: Faster speed never takes more hours, so 'fits in h' flips from false to true once. Binary search speeds 1..max(piles) for that flip point.
steps: Search speeds l = 1 to r = max(piles)
Try k = middle; total hours = sum of ceil(p / k)
Fits: record k, try slower (r = k - 1)
Too slow: go faster (l = k + 1)

codeNotes.note: Hours for this pile, rounded up

pitfalls: Round hours up: a pile of 7 at speed 4 takes 2 hours.
Never search above max(piles); faster than that cannot save time.

say.intro: Okay, Koko Eating Bananas. Each hour, Koko picks one pile and eats up to k bananas from it. She has h hours. What's the slowest speed that still finishes? With eight hours, speed four takes exactly eight hours. Speed three takes ten. So the answer is four.
say.brute: The brute force way tries speed one, then two, then three, and returns the first speed that fits. Each try sums the hours across every pile. It works. But a single pile can hold a billion bananas. So we might test a billion speeds, each one scanning every pile.
say.insight: Here's the key. Does eating faster ever make Koko finish later? Never. So as speed rises, the answer to does it fit flips from no to yes exactly once. That's a sorted run of no's, then yes's. And what do we do with sorted things? Binary search them. From speed one up to the biggest pile.
say.anim: We start with piles three, six, seven, eleven, and eight hours to finish eating. Left starts at one, right at eleven, the largest pile, our search range. We try speed six, eating each pile and summing hours, totaling six hours. Six hours fits within eight, so answer becomes six and we try slower speeds. Next we try speed three, but total hours climb to ten, too slow. Since that fails, we search faster speeds, moving left up to four. Speed four needs eight hours, exactly fitting, so answer updates to four. The search converges and returns four, the minimum eating speed that works.
say.code: Here's the code. The speeds worth trying run from one up to the largest pile. We take the middle as our candidate speed. Then we add up the hours, rounding each pile up. Fast enough? Record that speed and try slower. Too slow? Search faster speeds. When the range is empty, we return the best speed recorded.
say.outro: n times log of the largest pile. Pattern: binary search on the answer. When feasibility only flips once, search the answer itself.

This comment says we test the middle speed of the current range.

Since this speed works, we record it as the best answer found so far.
We move right below speed to look for a smaller speed that might still work.
Otherwise the speed was too slow and Koko could not finish in time.
So we move left above speed, searching only the faster speeds.
When the search ends, we return answer, which holds the smallest speed that fit within h hours.

find-minimum-in-rotated-sorted-array.hook: A sorted array got rotated - one comparison with the right end still tells you which half to keep.
find-minimum-in-rotated-sorted-array.ask: A sorted list of distinct numbers was rotated, so it may start in the middle and wrap around. Return the smallest number in logarithmic time.
find-minimum-in-rotated-sorted-array.exampleWhy: Originally [0,1,2,4,5,6,7], rotated four times; the minimum 0 sits right where the values drop.

brute.idea: Scan every element and keep the smallest.
steps: Start with the first value
Compare with every other value
Return the smallest
brute.whySlow: It ignores the sorted structure: 5,000 numbers take 5,000 checks instead of about 13.

optimal.insight: Compare mid with the right end. If mid is bigger, the drop and minimum lie right of mid; otherwise mid..end is sorted, so the minimum is mid or left.
steps: Range [start, end]; remember the smallest mid seen
nums[mid] > nums[end]: minimum is right, start = mid + 1
Otherwise: mid is a candidate, search left
Answer = min(best seen, nums[start])

codeNotes.note: Rotation drop is to the right
Right side sorted; mid already recorded

pitfalls: Compare with the right end, not the left - it handles the un-rotated case cleanly.
If the array is not rotated at all, the answer is simply nums[0].

say.intro: Okay, Find Minimum in Rotated Sorted Array. A sorted list got rotated, so it wraps around somewhere. Find the smallest number, in log time. Here we have four, five, six, seven, then zero, one, two. The minimum is zero. And notice, it sits right at the wrap point.
say.brute: The brute force way scans every element and keeps the smallest. Correct, and linear. But it ignores the sorted structure completely. Five thousand numbers means five thousand checks, when binary search needs about thirteen. And the problem explicitly asks for log time.
say.insight: Here's the trick. Compare the middle with the right end. Middle bigger? Then the list must drop somewhere to the right, so the minimum is over there. Not bigger? Then the middle to the end is sorted, so the minimum is the middle or to its left. Either way, half is gone.
say.anim: We start with the rotated array, setting left to 0 and right to 6. The loop begins since left is less than right, tracking the smallest value seen. Mid becomes 3, pointing to value 7, which updates smallest seen to 7. Since nums at mid, 7, is bigger than nums at right, 2, minimum lies to the right. Left moves to 4, mid becomes 5, pointing to value 1, updating smallest seen to 1. Now nums at mid is not greater than nums at right, so minimum lies left of mid. The loop ends as left equals right, both pointing to value 0. Comparing smallest seen, 1, with nums at left, 0, the final answer is 0.
say.code: Here's the code. Each middle might be the minimum, so we record it. Is the middle bigger than the end? Then the rotation drop is to the right, so we discard the sorted left part and move start past the middle. Otherwise the right side is sorted, and the middle is already recorded. So we move end just left of it. Finally, we check the last remaining cell.
say.outro: Log time, constant space. Pattern: binary search on a rotated array. Compare with the right end, and the unrotated case just works.

find-minimum-in-rotated-sorted-array.title: Find Minimum In Rotated Sorted Array

We check whether the number at mid is greater than the number at right, which signals the drop is right of mid.
Since mid cannot be the minimum, we move left to mid plus one and discard the left half.

We move right to mid minus one, safe because mid was already recorded in smallest_seen.
This comment notes that we finish by comparing the best candidate seen with the value at the final left position.
We return the smaller of smallest_seen and the number at left, covering the case where the loop ends on an unvisited element.

search-in-rotated-sorted-array.hook: Binary search still works on a broken sorted array — if you ask the right question at every step.
search-in-rotated-sorted-array.ask: A sorted list of distinct numbers was rotated at some unknown point. Find the index of target in logarithmic time, or return -1 if it is not there.
search-in-rotated-sorted-array.exampleWhy: The list was rotated after 10; the value 3 sits at index 8.

brute.idea: Ignore the rotation entirely and scan the list from left to right until we hit the target.
steps: Check each index i in order
nums[i] equals target? return i
Reached the end? return -1
brute.whySlow: Linear in n, but the problem demands O(log n): 5,000 items can take 5,000 checks instead of about 13.

optimal.insight: Cut at mid and one half is always fully sorted. Check if target lies in that sorted half's range; if yes go there, else go to the other half.
steps: Compute mid; return it if it is the target
nums[l] ≤ nums[mid] means the left half is sorted
Target inside the sorted half's range? search that half
Otherwise discard it and search the other half

codeNotes.note: Left half is the sorted one

codeNotes.match: if target > nums[mid] or target < nums[l]:
if target < nums[mid] or target > nums[r]:

pitfalls: Use ≤ in nums[l] <= nums[mid]: when l equals mid, that one-element half is sorted.

say.intro: Search in Rotated Sorted Array. Picture a sorted list that someone cut and swapped around. It climbs, drops, then climbs again. We need the target's index in log time, or minus one. Here, the target three sits at index eight.
say.brute: Okay, so the easy way? Ignore the rotation completely. Walk left to right and stop when you hit the target. That's correct. But it's linear, and the problem asks for log time. Five thousand numbers could take five thousand checks, instead of about thirteen. Your interviewer will push back.
say.insight: Here's the thing. Cut the list at the middle, and at least one half is always perfectly sorted. Why? The drop can only live on one side. For the sorted half, we know its smallest and largest values. So we can check in one step if the target fits in there. If it does, go there. If not, it's in the other half.
say.anim: We start searching the rotated array for target 3, with left at 0 and right at 9. Mid is 4, pointing to value 9, which is not the target. The left half is sorted, but 3 isn't between 5 and 9, so we move left past mid. Now left is 5 and we recompute mid as 7, landing on value 2. This time the right half is sorted, and 3 fits between 2 and 4, so we move left forward. With left now 8, the new mid is also 8, pointing to value 3. That matches the target exactly, so we return this index. The search finds target 3 at index 8, giving the final answer 8.
say.code: We keep left and right, and compute the midpoint. If mid is the target, return it. Now, if the left value is at most the mid value, the left half is sorted. If the target falls outside that left range, we go right. Otherwise go left. The else branch mirrors this for the sorted right half. And if the window empties, return minus one.
say.outro: Log time, constant space. The pattern is binary search. On a rotated array, always ask two things. Which half is sorted? And does the target fit inside it?

time-based-key-value-store.hook: A key-value store with time travel — and the timestamps arrive already sorted for free.
time-based-key-value-store.ask: Build a store where set saves a value for a key at a timestamp, and get returns the value set at the latest timestamp not after the given one, or an empty string.
time-based-key-value-store.exampleWhy: At time 5 the newest value is b, set at 4. Time 0 is before everything, and bar was never set.

brute.idea: Store each key's values in a list. On get, scan the whole list and keep the value with the largest timestamp not after the query.
steps: set: append value and timestamp
get: scan every entry for the key
Track the best timestamp ≤ query
brute.whySlow: 100,000 sets then 100,000 gets on one key: every get scans the whole list, about ten billion checks.

optimal.insight: Timestamps for set are strictly increasing, so each key's list is already sorted by time. Binary search for the last timestamp ≤ the query.
steps: set: append [value, timestamp] to the key's list
get: binary search that list
If mid's timestamp ≤ query, record it and go right
Otherwise go left; return the last recorded value

codeNotes.note: Appends stay sorted: timestamps only increase
Valid candidate: not in the future
Record it, then look for later
Too late: search the left part

pitfalls: Missing key or query earlier than all timestamps must return the empty string, not crash.

say.intro: Time Based Key Value Store. Set saves a value for a key at a timestamp. Get asks, what was the value at that moment? Here, at time five the answer is b, since b was set at time four. Before time one, there's nothing, so we return an empty string.
say.brute: The simple version keeps a list of value and timestamp pairs per key. On every get, we scan the whole list and keep the best timestamp that isn't after the query. Works fine. But what if one key gets a hundred thousand sets, then a hundred thousand gets? That's about ten billion checks.
say.insight: So what's the catch we're missing? Read the constraints. Timestamps for set always increase. That means each key's list is already sorted, just from appending. And finding the last entry at or before some time in a sorted list? That's a textbook binary search. Log time per get.
say.anim: We start with an empty key store ready to hold timestamped values. We set foo to a at time one, creating a new list for foo. We append b at time four, then c at time seven, into foo's list. Getting foo at time five, binary search checks mid value b at time four, a valid candidate. Search narrows further, confirming b is the best match, returning b as the answer. Getting foo at time seven, search moves right and finds c at time seven, returning c. Getting foo at time zero, no timestamp qualifies, so result stays empty string. Getting bar at time three finds no entries at all, so the final answer is empty string.
say.code: Set just appends, and the list stays sorted because timestamps only grow. Get starts with an empty string as the default answer. In the binary search, if the mid timestamp isn't in the future, it's a valid candidate. We record it, then move right to look for a later one. If it's too late, we search the left part.
say.outro: Constant time set, log time get. The pattern is binary search, on data the problem quietly keeps sorted for you. Always read the constraints.

median-of-two-sorted-arrays.hook: The famous hard one: find a median without merging, by binary searching a cut instead of a value.
median-of-two-sorted-arrays.ask: Given two sorted arrays, return the median of all their numbers combined. It must run in logarithmic time in the total size.
median-of-two-sorted-arrays.exampleWhy: Merged there are eleven numbers: 1,3,7,8,9,11,15,18,19,21,25. The sixth, 11, is the middle one.

brute.idea: Merge the two sorted arrays like merge sort does, then read the middle element or average the middle two.
steps: Two pointers merge into one sorted list
Odd length: take the middle element
Even length: average the middle two
brute.whySlow: Linear time and memory; the problem demands O(log(m + n)), so touching every element is too much.

optimal.insight: Picking how many items the left half takes from the smaller array fixes the rest. Binary search that count until both left maxes ≤ both right mins.
steps: Binary search a cut i in the smaller array A
Cut B at j so the left side holds half the items
If Aleft > Bright move left; if Bleft > Aright move right
Valid cut: median comes from the four border values

codeNotes.note: B's cut forced by A's cut

codeNotes.match: Aleft = A[i] if i >= 0 else float("-infinity")
if Aleft <= Bright and Bleft <= Aright:
codeNotes.note: Every left value ≤ every right value

pitfalls: Always binary search the shorter array, or j can go out of range.
Use plus or minus infinity sentinels when a cut sits at an array edge.

say.intro: Median of Two Sorted Arrays. A famous hard one. We get two sorted arrays and need the median of everything combined, in log time. Here we have eleven numbers in total. So the median is the sixth smallest, which is eleven.
say.brute: Okay, the natural first move. Merge the two arrays, just like the merge step in merge sort. Then read the middle value, or average the middle two. Clean and correct. But it's linear in time and memory. The problem wants log time, so we can't even afford to touch every element.
say.insight: Think about cuts, not values. The median splits everything into a left half and a right half. Now, if we pick how many items the left half takes from the smaller array, the count from the other array is forced. So there's only one thing to search for. The cut is right when every left value is at most every right value.
say.anim: We start with array A of five numbers and array B of six numbers to merge. Total length is eleven and half is five, setting up the binary search bounds. First guess sets cut index i to two in A, with j to one in B. Aleft is eight, Aright is nine, Bleft is eleven, Bright is eighteen for this partition. Since Aleft exceeds Bright, the cut is too far right, so we move left in A. New cut index i becomes three, pairing with j equal to zero in B. Now Aleft is nine, Aright fifteen, Bleft seven, Bright eleven, a valid partition. Total length is odd, so the median is the smaller of Aright and Bright, giving eleven.
say.code: First, we search the smaller array, so swap if needed. Pick a cut in A, and B's cut is forced by it. Past the edges, we use infinities, so empty sides just work. If every left value fits under every right value, we're done. An odd total returns the smallest right value. Even averages the middle two. And if we took too many from A, move the cut left.
say.outro: Log time in the smaller array, constant space. The pattern is binary search, but on a partition instead of a value. Practise drawing the cuts.

For an even total, we average the largest left value and the smallest right value.
Otherwise, if Aleft is larger than Bright, A's left part has reached too far.

This comment says our cut in A is too far left, so we move right.

reverse-linked-list.hook: The linked list rite of passage: three pointers, one pass, and no extra memory.
reverse-linked-list.ask: Given the head of a singly linked list, reverse the list so every arrow points the other way, and return the new head.
reverse-linked-list.exampleWhy: The old tail 5 becomes the new head, and every next pointer is flipped.

brute.idea: Copy all the values into an array, then walk the list again and write the values back in reverse order.
steps: Walk the list, pushing each value onto an array
Walk again, popping values from the end
Overwrite each node's value
brute.whySlow: Two passes and an extra array of 5,000 values; it also swaps values instead of truly relinking nodes.

optimal.insight: Walk the list once and flip each node's next to point at the node behind it. Save the forward pointer first so the rest of the list is not lost.
steps: Keep prev = None and curr = head
Save curr.next in temp
Point curr.next back at prev
Advance prev and curr; return prev at the end

codeNotes.note: New tail will point to None
Save the rest before breaking it
Step forward into the saved rest
prev ends on the new head

pitfalls: Forgetting to save next before flipping loses the rest of the list.
Return prev, not curr — curr ends as None.

say.intro: Reverse Linked List. We get the head of a singly linked list, and we flip it so every arrow points the other way. One, two, three, four, five becomes five, four, three, two, one. This one shows up inside tons of harder problems.
say.brute: The simple approach copies every value into an array. Then we walk the list again, popping from the end of the array and writing values back. It works. But it needs a whole extra array, and two passes. And here's the catch. It only swaps values. Interviewers want you to actually relink the nodes.
say.insight: So can we flip the arrows in place, in one walk? Yes. Point each node's next back at the node behind it. But careful. The moment you flip that arrow, you lose your way to the rest of the list. So before flipping, save the forward pointer. That's the whole trick.
say.anim: We start with previous as none and current pointing at node one, head of the list. Before rewiring, we save next node as two through five, so we don't lose the rest. Node one's next is flipped to point at previous, then previous and current both move forward. Now current is node two, and we repeat, saving three through five before reversing two's pointer. Current is node three now, its next flips back to two, extending the reversed chain. Current reaches node four, its pointer reverses too, building five, four, three, two, one. Finally current is node five, next node becomes none, and its pointer reverses last. Current becomes none, the loop ends, and we return the reversed list five four three two one.
say.code: Prev starts as None, because the new tail points to nothing. In the loop, we first save the rest of the list in temp. Then we flip the arrow, pointing current back at prev. Then we step forward into the saved rest. When current falls off the end, prev is sitting on the new head. Return it.
say.outro: Linear time, constant space. The pattern is linked list pointer work. Remember the rhythm. Save, flip, advance.

reverse-linked-list.title: Reverse Linked List
reverse-linked-list.optimalCode:
class Solution:
    def reverseList(self, head: ListNode) -> ListNode:
        # 1. Start with no previous node
        previous = None
        current = head

        # 2. Walk through the list one node at a time
        while current:
            # 3. Save the next node before we overwrite the pointer
            next_node = current.next

            # 4. Reverse the pointer, then move both forward
            current.next = previous
            previous = current
            current = next_node

        return previous
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which holds the method that will reverse the linked list.
This method takes the head of a singly linked list and will return the head of the reversed list.
This comment says we begin with no previous node, because the new tail must point to nothing.
We set previous to none, since the original first node will become the last and point at nothing.
We set current to head, so we begin walking the list from its first node.
This comment says we will visit the list one node at a time, flipping as we go.
We loop while current is a real node, stopping once we walk past the end of the list.
This comment reminds us to save the next node before we overwrite the pointer and lose it.
We store the node after current in next_node so the rest of the list stays reachable.
This comment says each step reverses one pointer and then advances both trackers.
We point the next of current back at previous, which flips this one arrow.
We move previous up to current, since current is now the head of the reversed portion.
We move current to next_node, advancing to the next original node we saved earlier.
When the loop ends, previous sits on the old last node, which is the new head, so we return it.

merge-two-sorted-lists.hook: The merge step of merge sort, done with pointers — and a dummy node that kills every edge case.
merge-two-sorted-lists.ask: Given the heads of two sorted linked lists, splice them together into one sorted list and return its head.
merge-two-sorted-lists.exampleWhy: Repeatedly taking the smaller front node from either list gives one sorted list.

brute.idea: Dump every value from both lists into an array, sort it, and build a brand new list from the sorted values.
steps: Collect values from both lists
Sort the array
Build a new list from it
brute.whySlow: Sorting throws away the fact both lists are already sorted, and it allocates new nodes.

optimal.insight: The smallest remaining value is always at the front of one of the two lists. Repeatedly splice the smaller front node onto a tail pointer.
steps: Start a dummy node and a tail pointer
Attach the smaller of the two front nodes
Advance that list and the tail
When one list ends, attach the other's remainder

codeNotes.note: Dummy head avoids special-casing the first node
Tail moves to the node just attached

pitfalls: Either list may be empty — the dummy node and the final 'or' handle it.

say.intro: Merge Two Sorted Lists. We get two linked lists, each already sorted, and we splice them into one sorted list. Here, one two four seven and one three four five eight become nine nodes, all in order. Equal values just sit side by side.
say.brute: The lazy way? Pour every value into an array, sort it, and build a brand new list. It works. But sorting costs n log n, and it totally ignores that both lists are already sorted. Plus it allocates a whole new set of nodes, when we could just reuse the ones we have.
say.insight: Here's the thing. Both lists are sorted, so the smallest remaining value is always at the front of one of them. So just compare the two fronts. Take the smaller one, attach it to our result, and step forward in that list. Repeat. Each node gets touched exactly once.
say.anim: We start with a dummy node and a tail pointer, ready to build the merged list. Both lists start with value one, so list2's node is attached first and its pointer advances. Now list1's one is smaller, so it gets spliced onto the tail next. List1's two is attached, since it is smaller than list2's three. List2's three is smaller than list1's four, so it joins the merged chain. List2 keeps winning with four, five, getting attached before list1's four catches up. Eventually list1 runs out after attaching five, seven, leaving only list2's eight remaining. The leftover eight is spliced on, giving the final merged list one, one, two, three, four, four, five, seven, eight.
say.code: We start with a dummy head, so the first node needs no special case. While both lists have nodes, pick the smaller front node and attach it. Then the tail moves to the node we just attached. When one list runs out, attach whatever's left of the other, in one step. Finally, skip the dummy and return the next node.
say.outro: Linear time, constant extra space. The pattern is two pointers on linked lists, plus the dummy head trick. Merge sort uses exactly this step.

merge-two-sorted-lists.title: Merge Two Sorted Lists

linked-list-cycle.hook: A tortoise and a hare prove a loop exists using zero extra memory.
linked-list-cycle.ask: Given the head of a linked list, return true if following next pointers ever brings you back to a node you already visited, meaning the list loops.
linked-list-cycle.exampleWhy: pos 2 means the tail 6 points back to node 3, so walking never ends.

brute.idea: Walk the list and remember every node in a hash set. Meeting a node already in the set means a cycle.
steps: Walk node by node
Node already in the set? cycle
Reach None? no cycle
brute.whySlow: Linear memory: 10,000 nodes means 10,000 stored references. The follow-up asks for O(1) memory.

optimal.insight: Move one pointer one step and another two steps. Inside a loop the fast one closes the gap by one each step, so it must land on the slow one.
steps: slow and fast both start at head
slow moves 1 step, fast moves 2
They meet? there is a cycle
fast hits the end? no cycle

codeNotes.note: Fast reaching the end means no cycle
Caught up: must be a loop

pitfalls: Check fast and fast.next before jumping two steps, or you crash on None.
Compare nodes, not values — values can repeat.

say.intro: Linked List Cycle. Given the head of a linked list, does it loop back on itself? Here, the last node, six, points back to node three. So walking the list would never end, and the answer is true.
say.brute: The straightforward way is to remember every node in a hash set. Hit a node that's already in the set? We've gone in a circle. Reach the end? No cycle. That's linear time. But it's also linear memory, ten thousand stored nodes for ten thousand nodes. And the follow-up asks for constant memory.
say.insight: So how do we detect a loop with no memory? Two runners. Slow moves one step, fast moves two. With no cycle, fast just falls off the end. With a cycle, both end up circling the loop. Now notice, fast gains exactly one step per move. So the gap shrinks by one each time. It can't jump over slow. They have to meet.
say.anim: We start with both slow and fast pointers at node 1, the list head. Slow moves one step to node 2, while fast jumps ahead two steps to node 3. Next round, slow advances to node 3, and fast leaps to node 5. Fast wraps around the cycle, now sitting at node 3 while slow reaches node 4. Slow steps to node 5, and fast, still looping, lands back on node 3. Slow moves to node 5 again, and this time fast also arrives at node 5. Since slow and fast now point to the same node, a cycle is confirmed. The function returns true, correctly detecting the cycle in the linked list.
say.code: Both runners start together at the head. The loop keeps going while fast and its next node exist. If fast reaches the end, there's no cycle, and we return false. Inside, slow takes one step, and fast takes two. If they're now the same node, fast caught up, so it must be a loop. Return true.
say.outro: Linear time, constant space. The pattern is fast and slow pointers, Floyd's tortoise and hare. A must-know.

linked-list-cycle.title: Linked List Cycle

We keep looping while fast and the node after it exist, since reaching the end means no cycle.
Each round, slow moves forward by exactly one node.
Fast moves forward by two nodes, so it gains one step on slow each round.
If slow and fast now point to the same node, they have met inside a loop.
In that case we return true because the list must contain a cycle.
If the loop ends because fast ran off the end, there is no cycle, so we return false.

reorder-list.hook: Three classic linked list moves — find the middle, reverse, merge — combined into one problem.
reorder-list.ask: Rearrange a linked list in place so it goes first, last, second, second-to-last, and so on, alternating from both ends.
reorder-list.exampleWhy: Take 1 from the front, 6 from the back, then 2, then 5, then 3, then 4.

brute.idea: Copy every node into an array so we can index both ends, then relink with two indices moving toward each other.
steps: Store all nodes in an array
i from the front, j from the back
Link nodes[i] to nodes[j], then nodes[j] to nodes[i+1]
brute.whySlow: Needs an O(n) array — 50,000 node references — just to reach the back of the list.

optimal.insight: The back half, read backwards, is just the second half reversed. So split at the middle, reverse the second half, then interleave the two lists.
steps: Slow and fast pointers find the middle
Cut the list and reverse the second half
Merge: alternate one node from each half

codeNotes.note: Slow stops at end of first half
Second half starts after the middle
Reverse the second half in place
Interleave: front node, then back node

pitfalls: Forget to cut slow.next and you create a cycle during the merge.

say.intro: Reorder List. We rearrange a linked list in place so it goes first, last, second, second to last, and so on. One through six becomes one, six, two, five, three, four. And we change the links, not the values.
say.brute: So what makes this hard? We can't walk backwards in a singly linked list. The easy fix is to copy every node into an array. Then two indices, one at each end, relink the nodes as they move inward. Linear time, sure. But that's fifty thousand stored references for a big list. Your interviewer will ask for constant space.
say.insight: Look closely at the order we want. The back half, read backwards, is just the second half reversed. So, three moves. Find the middle. Reverse the second half in place. Then zip the two halves together, one node from each. Each move is a problem you already know, and none needs extra memory.
say.anim: We start with the list one through six, using slow and fast pointers to find the middle. Slow and fast both advance, slow reaching three while fast jumps to six, marking the midpoint. The list splits: first half ends at three, second half starts at four, five, six. We reverse the second half step by step, building six, five, four from the original order. Now previous holds the reversed second half, six then five then four, ready to merge. Merging begins, weaving nodes from first half and reversed second half one at a time. After merging several nodes, the list now reads one, six, two, five, three, building the final order. The merge finishes and the list becomes one, six, two, five, three, four, our reordered answer.
say.code: Slow and fast pointers stop slow at the end of the first half. The second half starts right after it. Then we cut the list in two. Next, we reverse the second half in place, with the usual three pointers. Finally, interleave. Link a front node to a back node, then that back node to the next front node. Save the next pointers first.
say.outro: Linear time, constant space. The pattern is linked lists. Find the middle, reverse, then merge.

reorder-list.title: Reorder List
reorder-list.optimalCode:
class Solution:
    def reorderList(self, head: ListNode) -> None:
        # 1. Find the middle of the list using slow and fast pointers
        slow = head
        fast = head.next
        while fast and fast.next:
            slow = slow.next
            fast = fast.next.next

        # 2. Cut the list in half and reverse the second half
        second = slow.next
        slow.next = None
        previous = None
        while second:
            next_node = second.next
            second.next = previous
            previous = second
            second = next_node

        # 3. Merge the two halves by alternating nodes
        first = head
        second = previous
        while second:
            first_next = first.next
            second_next = second.next
            first.next = second
            second.next = first_next
            first = first_next
            second = second_next
lineNotes: We define the Solution class that holds the method for this problem.
The reorderList method takes the head of the list and changes it in place without returning anything.
This comment says the first step is finding the middle using a slow pointer and a fast pointer.
We start slow at the head of the list.
We start fast one node ahead at head next, so that for even lengths slow ends at the end of the first half.
We keep looping while fast and the node after it both exist.
Each round slow moves forward one node.
Each round fast moves forward two nodes, so when fast finishes slow sits at the middle.
This comment says we now cut the list in half and reverse the second half.
We set second to the node right after slow, which is the start of the back half.
We set the next of slow to nothing, which cuts the first half off from the second.
We set previous to nothing, since the reversed list will start with an empty tail.
We loop through the second half until we run out of nodes.
We save the next node of second first so we do not lose the rest of the list.
We point the next of second back at previous, which reverses that link.
We move previous forward to the current second node.
We move second forward to the saved next node to continue reversing.
This comment says the last step is merging the two halves by alternating nodes.

We set second to previous, which is now the head of the reversed second half.

We save the next node of first before we change its link.
We save the next node of second before we change its link.
We point the next of first to second, placing a back node right after a front node.
We point the next of second to the saved first next, linking back into the front half.
We advance first to its saved next node.
We advance second to its saved next node and repeat until the second half is used up.
reorder-list.optimalCodeOriginal:
class Solution:
    def reorderList(self, head: ListNode) -> None:
        # find middle
        slow, fast = head, head.next
        while fast and fast.next:
            slow = slow.next
            fast = fast.next.next

        # reverse second half
        second = slow.next
        prev = slow.next = None
        while second:
            tmp = second.next
            second.next = prev
            prev = second
            second = tmp

        # merge two halfs
        first, second = head, prev
        while second:
            tmp1, tmp2 = first.next, second.next
            first.next = second
            second.next = tmp1
            first, second = tmp1, tmp2

remove-nth-node-from-end-of-list.hook: Counting from the end of a list you can only walk forward — solved with a fixed-gap pair of pointers.
remove-nth-node-from-end-of-list.ask: Given a linked list and a number n, remove the n-th node counting from the end, and return the head of the list.
remove-nth-node-from-end-of-list.exampleWhy: Counting back from 7: 7 is first, 6 second, 5 third. So 5 is removed.

brute.idea: Walk the list once to count its length L. The target is node L - n from the front; walk again and unlink it.
steps: First pass: count length L
Second pass: stop just before index L - n
Skip over the target node
brute.whySlow: Same big-O but two full passes; the follow-up explicitly asks for a single pass.

optimal.insight: Put right n nodes ahead of left. Move both together; when right falls off the end, left sits exactly before the node to delete.
steps: left starts at a dummy before head
Move right n steps ahead
Move both until right is None
Unlink left.next

codeNotes.note: Lets us delete the head too
Open a gap of n nodes

pitfalls: Without a dummy node, removing the head (n equals length) needs a special case.

say.intro: Remove Nth Node From End of List. We get a linked list and a number n, and we delete the n-th node from the end. Here n is three. Counting back from seven, that's five. So the list becomes one, two, three, four, six, seven.
say.brute: The obvious way takes two passes. First, walk the whole list to count its length. Then the target is length minus n steps from the front, so walk again and unlink it. That's linear, and honestly fine. But the follow-up asks something sharper. Can you do it in one pass?
say.insight: Here's the trick. Use two pointers with a fixed gap between them. Send the right pointer n steps ahead. Then move both together, one step at a time. Why does that work? When right falls off the end, left is exactly one node before the target. The gap does the counting for us.
say.anim: We start with the list one through seven, and n equals three, plus a dummy node before head. Right begins at node one, and we advance it three steps ahead, landing on node four. Now left and right move together, step by step, keeping that three node gap between them. Left moves to node two while right moves to node five, maintaining the same spacing. Left reaches node four as right reaches the last node seven, still three apart. Right falls off the end to none, so left now sits right before the target node five. Left's next pointer skips over node five, unlinking it from the list entirely. The final list returned is one, two, three, four, six, seven, matching the expected output.
say.code: Left starts at a dummy node before the head. That lets us delete the head too. Move right n steps forward, opening a gap of n nodes. Then both move together, and the gap stays fixed, until right is None. Now left's next is the target, so we skip over it. Return the dummy's next.
say.outro: Linear time, one pass, constant space. The pattern is two pointers with a fixed gap, plus a dummy node for safety.

remove-nth-node-from-end-of-list.title: Remove Nth Node From End of List
remove-nth-node-from-end-of-list.optimalCode:
class Solution:
    def removeNthFromEnd(self, head: ListNode, n: int) -> ListNode:
        # 1. Set up a dummy node before head so left can remove the very first node too
        dummy = ListNode(0, head)
        left = dummy
        right = head

        # 2. Move right n steps ahead of left
        count = n
        while count > 0:
            right = right.next
            count -= 1

        # 3. Move both pointers together until right falls off the end
        while right:
            left = left.next
            right = right.next

        # 4. left now sits right before the node to delete, so unlink it
        left.next = left.next.next
        return dummy.next
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container the interview platform expects for our method.
This method takes the head of the list and a number n, and returns the head after removal.
This comment explains that a dummy node before head lets us handle deleting the very first node.
We create a dummy node with value zero whose next points at head, giving us a safe starting anchor.
We set left to the dummy node, so left begins one step behind the real head.
We set right to head, so right starts one node ahead of left.
This comment says we first push right forward by n steps to create the needed gap.
We copy n into a counter called count so we can decrement it without changing n.
We loop as long as count is greater than zero, stepping right forward each time.
Each pass moves right to the next node, widening the gap between left and right.
We decrease count by one so the loop stops after exactly n moves.
This comment explains that both pointers now advance together until right runs off the list.
We keep looping while right still points to a real node, meaning it has not fallen off the end.
We move left forward one node, keeping the gap of n nodes intact.
We move right forward one node as well, bringing it closer to the end.
This comment notes that left now sits just before the target node, ready to be unlinked.
We skip over the target by pointing left's next to the node after it, deleting it from the list.
We return the dummy's next, which is the true head even if the original head was removed.
remove-nth-node-from-end-of-list.optimalCodeOriginal:
class Solution:
    def removeNthFromEnd(self, head: ListNode, n: int) -> ListNode:
        dummy = ListNode(0, head)
        left = dummy
        right = head

        while n > 0:
            right = right.next
            n -= 1

        while right:
            left = left.next
            right = right.next

        # delete
        left.next = left.next.next
        return dummy.next

copy-list-with-random-pointer.hook: Deep-copy a list whose random pointers can jump anywhere — even to nodes you have not copied yet.
copy-list-with-random-pointer.ask: Each node has a next pointer and a random pointer to any node or null. Build a completely new copy of the list with the same structure, using only new nodes.
copy-list-with-random-pointer.exampleWhy: Each pair is a value and the index its random points to. The copy must match exactly, built from new nodes.

brute.idea: Copy nodes into an array. For each original random, find its index by scanning from the head, then point the copy at that index.
steps: Create copies in order and link next
For each node, scan from head to find random's index
Point copy's random at copies[index]
brute.whySlow: Every random lookup rescans the list: 1,000 nodes means up to a million steps.

optimal.insight: A hash map from each old node to its copy makes every pointer lookup O(1). First pass creates all copies; second pass wires next and random through the map.
steps: Map None to None
Pass one: create a copy of every node in the map
Pass two: copy.next = map[old.next]
copy.random = map[old.random]; return map[head]

codeNotes.note: None maps to None: no special cases
Pass one: every node gets a twin

pitfalls: Wiring random in the first pass fails: its target copy may not exist yet.

say.intro: Copy List with Random Pointer. Each node has a next pointer, plus a random pointer that can point anywhere, or nowhere. We build a fully separate deep copy with the same shape. Brand new nodes only.
say.brute: A naive way makes all the copies in an array first. Then, for each random pointer, scan from the head to find which index it points to, and wire the copy there. It works. But every lookup can walk the whole list. A thousand nodes could mean a million steps. That's n squared.
say.insight: So what's the real problem here? Translating an old node into its copy. A hash map from each old node to its twin does that instantly. Now, if we make all the copies first, every pointer can be wired with one lookup. Even one pointing far ahead in the list. Two clean passes.
say.anim: We start with a linked list of nodes seven, thirteen, eleven, ten, and one. A hash map starts with just none mapped to none, so lookups never fail. In the first pass we walk the list, creating a fresh copy node for each original. Each original node, like seven, thirteen, eleven, ten, one, gets its own new copy stored in the map. Now current resets to head, starting the second pass to wire up pointers. For each node we look up its copy, then set the copy's next and random using the map. This repeats for thirteen, eleven, ten, and one, linking all the copied nodes correctly. The function returns the copied head, producing an identical structure: seven, thirteen, eleven, ten, one.
say.code: The map starts with None mapped to None, so we need no special cases. Pass one gives every node a twin, stored in the map. Pass two wires each copy's next through the map. Then its random, whose target already exists. Finally, return the copy of the head.
say.outro: Linear time, linear space. The pattern is a hash map from old nodes to their new copies. It's exactly the same idea as cloning a graph.

copy-list-with-random-pointer.title: Copy List With Random Pointer

meta.name: copyRandomList

copy-list-with-random-pointer.optimalCode:
class Solution:
    def copyRandomList(self, head: "Node") -> "Node":
        # 1. Map None to None, so lookups never fail
        oldToCopy = {None: None}

        # 2. First pass: create a copy of every node
        current = head
        while current:
            oldToCopy[current] = Node(current.val)
            current = current.next

        # 3. Second pass: wire up next and random pointers
        current = head
        while current:
            copy = oldToCopy[current]
            copy.next = oldToCopy[current.next]
            copy.random = oldToCopy[current.random]
            current = current.next

        # 4. Return the copy of the head
        return oldToCopy[head]

The method copyRandomList takes the head of the original list and returns the head of the new copied list.
