We create the dictionary oldToCopy and seed it with none mapped to none.
This comment says the first pass creates a new copy node for every original node.
We set current to head so we can walk the original list from the start.
We loop as long as current is not none, visiting each original node once.
We create a new node with the same value as current and store it in the map under current.
We advance current to the next original node to continue the first pass.
This comment says the second pass connects the next and random pointers on the copies.
We reset current back to head so we can walk the original list again.
We loop again over every original node until current becomes none.
We look up the copy of current in the map and name it copy.
We set the copy's next to the copy of current's next, which is none at the tail.
We set the copy's random to the copy of current's random, so the structure is mirrored with only new nodes.
We move current forward to the next original node to keep wiring.
This comment says we finish by returning the copy of the original head.
We return the mapped copy of head, which is none for an empty list or the new list's head.

add-two-numbers.hook: Grade-school addition with a carry — on linked lists stored backwards, so it is actually easy.
add-two-numbers.ask: Two non-negative numbers are stored as linked lists of digits, ones digit first. Add them and return the sum as a linked list in the same reversed format.
add-two-numbers.exampleWhy: 942 plus 9465 is 10407; written ones digit first that is 7,0,4,0,1.

brute.idea: Turn each list into an integer, add the integers, then turn the sum back into a list of digits.
steps: Rebuild each number from its digits
Add the two numbers
Peel off digits with mod 10 into a list
brute.whySlow: Lists can hold 100 digits; that overflows 64-bit integers in most languages. Only Python's big ints hide it.

optimal.insight: Ones digits come first, which is exactly the order we add by hand. Add digit by digit, carrying the tens into the next position.
steps: Walk both lists together
Digit sum = v1 + v2 + carry
Write sum % 10, carry sum // 10
Keep going while either list or the carry remains

codeNotes.match: while l1 or l2 or carry:
codeNotes.note: Final carry adds one more digit

codeNotes.match: l1 = l1.next if l1 else None

pitfalls: Forgetting the final carry drops the leading 1 (e.g. 5 + 5 must give [0,1]).

say.intro: Add Two Numbers. Two numbers are stored as linked lists of digits, ones digit first. We add them and return the sum the same way. Here, nine hundred forty two plus nine thousand four hundred sixty five is ten thousand four hundred seven.
say.brute: The tempting shortcut? Turn each list into an integer, add them, and turn the sum back into digits. In Python, that works. But lists can be a hundred digits long. In Java or C plus plus, that overflows every built in integer type. So an interviewer won't accept it. We need real digit by digit math.
say.insight: Now, notice the digits come ones first. That's exactly the order we add by hand, right to left. So walk both lists together. Add the two digits plus the carry. Write down the ones digit, and carry the tens to the next spot. Just like grade school.
say.anim: We start with two digit lists, two and five leading, plus a dummy head node and zero carry. First digits two and five sum to seven, with no carry, so seven is appended to the result. Next digits four and six add up to ten, writing zero and carrying one into the next step. Nine plus four plus the carried one equals fourteen, so we write four and carry one again. First list is exhausted, so zero plus nine plus carry one equals ten, writing zero and carrying one. Both lists are empty now, but carry one remains, so we append a final one digit. With no digits or carry left, the loop ends and we return the built list. The final answer reads seven, zero, four, zero, one, matching the expected output.
say.code: We loop while either list or the carry remains, because a final carry adds one more digit. A shorter list just counts as zeros. Add up the column, and the tens part carries over. Then append a node holding the ones digit. Finally, advance both lists safely, so we never step past the end.
say.outro: Linear time in the longer list. The pattern is simulating grade school addition. Never forget that last carry. Test five plus five.

add-two-numbers.title: Add Two Numbers
add-two-numbers.optimalCode:
class Solution:
    def addTwoNumbers(self, l1: ListNode, l2: ListNode) -> ListNode:
        dummy = ListNode()
        current = dummy
        carry = 0

        # Walk both lists together while either has digits or there is a carry
        while l1 or l2 or carry:
            value1 = l1.val if l1 else 0
            value2 = l2.val if l2 else 0

            # Digit sum = v1 + v2 + carry
            total = value1 + value2 + carry
            digit = total % 10
            carry = total // 10

            # Write sum % 10, carry sum // 10
            current.next = ListNode(digit)
            current = current.next

            # Move to next nodes if they exist
            if l1:
                l1 = l1.next
            if l2:
                l2 = l2.next

        return dummy.next
lineNotes: We define a Solution class that holds the method for solving this problem.
The method takes the heads of two linked lists, each holding digits with the ones digit first.
We create a dummy node to anchor the result list so we never special-case the head.
We set current to the dummy node, and it will always point at the tail of the result.
We start the carry at zero because the ones position has nothing carried into it.
This comment says we keep walking while either list has digits left or a carry remains.
The loop continues while l1 or l2 has a node or carry is nonzero, so a final carry gets its own digit.
We read the digit from l1 if that node exists, otherwise we treat it as zero.
We do the same for l2, so a shorter list simply contributes zeros.
This comment reminds us that each digit sum is the two digits plus the carry.
We add value1, value2 and the carry to get the total for this position.
The new digit to store is the total mod ten, which is the ones place of the sum.
The new carry is the total divided by ten using integer division, either zero or one.
This comment restates that we write the remainder and carry the quotient.
We attach a new node holding the digit to the end of the result list.
We advance current to that new node so the next digit gets appended after it.
This comment says we should step forward in each input list, but only where a node exists.
We check whether l1 still has a node before trying to move along it.
If it does, we move l1 to its next node.
We check whether l2 still has a node as well.
If so, we move l2 to its next node.
We return the node after dummy, which is the real head of the summed list.
add-two-numbers.optimalCodeOriginal:
class Solution:
    def addTwoNumbers(self, l1: ListNode, l2: ListNode) -> ListNode:
        dummy = ListNode()
        cur = dummy

        carry = 0
        while l1 or l2 or carry:
            v1 = l1.val if l1 else 0
            v2 = l2.val if l2 else 0

            # new digit
            val = v1 + v2 + carry
            carry = val // 10
            val = val % 10
            cur.next = ListNode(val)

            # update ptrs
            cur = cur.next
            l1 = l1.next if l1 else None
            l2 = l2.next if l2 else None

        return dummy.next

find-the-duplicate-number.hook: An array secretly is a linked list with a cycle — and the duplicate is where the loop begins.
find-the-duplicate-number.ask: An array of n + 1 numbers holds values from 1 to n, so one value repeats. Find it without changing the array and using only constant extra memory.
find-the-duplicate-number.exampleWhy: Values run 1 to 9 across ten slots, so something repeats; 9 appears three times.

brute.idea: Compare every pair of positions. The first equal pair gives the duplicate. No extra memory, array untouched.
steps: Pick nums[i]
Compare with every nums[j] after it
Equal? return it
brute.whySlow: With 100,000 numbers that is about 5 billion comparisons.

optimal.insight: Treat i → nums[i] as a next pointer. The duplicate d has two indices pointing at index d, so d is where the cycle starts. Find it with Floyd.
steps: Index 0 is the head; nums[i] is the next pointer
Slow moves 1 hop, fast 2, until they meet
Start slow2 at 0; move slow and slow2 one hop each
They meet at the cycle entrance: the duplicate

codeNotes.note: One hop along the implicit list

pitfalls: The first meeting point is inside the cycle, not the duplicate — phase two is required.
Sorting or a set breaks the 'do not modify / O(1) space' rules.

say.intro: Find the Duplicate Number. We have n plus one numbers, all between one and n. So some value has to repeat. Find it without changing the array, with constant extra memory. Here, the repeat is nine.
say.brute: No extra memory, and no sorting allowed. So the obvious move is to compare every pair. Take each number, check it against every number after it, and return the first match. Correct, but n squared. For a hundred thousand numbers, that's about five billion checks.
say.insight: Here's the clever part. Treat each value as a pointer to an index. From index i, jump to the index stored there. Two slots hold the same value, so two arrows point at the same index. That forces a loop. And the duplicate is exactly where the loop begins. So this is really a linked list cycle problem, hidden in an array.
say.anim: We start with slow and fast pointers both at index zero in the array. Slow moves one step while fast moves two steps, following each number as a pointer. They keep chasing, slow reaching one and fast jumping to six, tracing the hidden cycle. Eventually slow and fast both land on eight, meaning they entered the cycle together. A second pointer slow2 starts over at zero to find the cycle's entrance. Both slow and slow2 now advance one step at a time toward each other. Slow and slow2 both reach nine, marking the start of the cycle. The function returns nine, the duplicate number found in the array.
say.code: Phase one is Floyd's chase. Slow takes one hop along this hidden list, and fast takes two, until they meet. Phase two starts a second runner from the head, at index zero. Both move one hop at a time, and they meet at the cycle entrance. Why? The head and the meeting point sit equally far from that entrance.
say.outro: Linear time, constant space, array untouched. The pattern is fast and slow pointers, on a linked list hidden inside an array.

find-the-duplicate-number.title: Find The Duplicate Number
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container the problem expects for our method.
The method findDuplicate takes the array nums and returns the single repeated number.
We start both slow and fast pointers at index zero, treating the array as a linked list of next pointers.
We begin a loop that runs until the two pointers meet inside the cycle.
Slow moves one step by jumping to the value stored at its current index.
Fast moves two steps by following the next pointer twice, so it gains one step on slow each round.
If slow and fast land on the same index, they have met somewhere inside the cycle.
We break out of the loop, since meeting proves a cycle exists and the duplicate causes it.
We create slow2 at index zero to start the second phase, which finds the cycle entrance.
We begin a second loop that moves both pointers one step at a time until they meet.
Slow keeps advancing one step from the meeting point inside the cycle.
Slow2 advances one step from the start of the array.
When slow and slow2 are equal, they have reached the cycle's starting index.
We return that index, which is the duplicate number because two indices point to it.

lru-cache.hook: The most-asked design problem: two data structures glued together so every operation is O(1).
lru-cache.ask: Build a cache with a fixed capacity. get returns a key's value or -1. put inserts or updates a key, and if over capacity, evicts the least recently used key.
lru-cache.exampleWhy: get(1) makes key 1 recent, so put(3) evicts 2. Then put(4) evicts 1, the oldest by then.

brute.idea: Keep a dict for values and a plain list for usage order. Each access removes the key from the list and appends it at the end.
steps: Dict holds key → value
List holds keys, oldest first
On access: list.remove(key), append(key)
Over capacity: evict list[0]
brute.whySlow: list.remove and pop(0) are linear; capacity 3,000 with 200,000 calls means hundreds of millions of shifts.

optimal.insight: A hash map finds a node in O(1); a doubly linked list moves or removes a known node in O(1). Map keys to list nodes and you get both.
steps: Map key → node in a doubly linked list
Left sentinel side = least recent, right side = most recent
get/put: unlink the node and reinsert at the right
Over capacity: remove left.next from list and map

codeNotes.note: Sentinels: no null checks at the ends
Insert just before right: most recent
Touching a key makes it most recent
Least recently used sits by left

pitfalls: Store the key inside the node, or you cannot delete the evicted entry from the map.
get must also refresh recency, not only put.

say.intro: LRU Cache. We build a cache with a fixed capacity. Get returns a value, or minus one. Put adds or updates a key. When it's too full, we evict the key used least recently. And every operation has to be constant time.
say.brute: A first try uses a dictionary for values and a plain list for usage order. Each access removes the key from the list and appends it at the end. Eviction pops the front. So what's wrong? Removing from the middle of a list is linear. With a big capacity and lots of calls, that's hundreds of millions of shifts.
say.insight: Think about what needs to be fast. Finding a key, and moving it within the usage order. A hash map finds things instantly. A doubly linked list can unlink and move a node instantly, once you're holding it. So map each key straight to its node. And each node also stores its key. We'll see why.
say.anim: We start with capacity two and two dummy nodes linking an empty list. Put one one and put two two insert new nodes at the right end. Get one moves that node to the most recently used end, returning one. Put three three fills capacity, evicting key two as least recently used. Get two now returns negative one since that node was removed. Put four four evicts key one, the next least recently used node. Get one returns negative one because it was already evicted earlier. Get three returns three and get four returns four, matching the expected output.
say.code: Two sentinel nodes mark the ends, so there are no null checks. Remove unlinks a node in constant time by joining its neighbours. Insert places a node just before the right end, the most recent spot. Touching a key in get or put makes it most recent. Over capacity, the least recently used sits next to the left sentinel. Evict it, and delete its key. That's why nodes store keys.
say.outro: Constant time per operation. The pattern is a hash map plus a doubly linked list. The classic design combo. Know it cold.

lru-cache.title: LRU Cache
lineNotes: We define a Node class to represent one entry in the doubly linked list.
The constructor stores the key and value so a node can be traced back to its map entry.
We keep the key and value together on the node, which lets eviction delete the right map entry later.
Previous and next links start empty and get set once the node is placed in the list.
Next we define the LRUCache class that combines a hash map with the linked list.
The constructor takes the capacity, the maximum number of keys the cache may hold.
We save the capacity as cap to compare against the cache size later.
The cache dictionary maps each key to its node, giving constant time lookup.
We create two dummy nodes, left for the least recent end and right for the most recent end.
We link the dummy nodes to each other so the empty list has a valid start and end.
This comment says the next helper removes a node from the list.
The remove helper takes a node that is already in the list.
We grab the node's neighbors on both sides so we can connect them.
We point the neighbors at each other, which unlinks the node in constant time.
This comment says the next helper inserts a node at the right end, marking it most recent.
The insert helper takes a node to place just before the right dummy.
We find the current last real node and the right dummy as the two neighbors.
We make both neighbors point to the new node, one forward and one backward.
We set the node's own links to point to its two neighbors, completing the insertion.
The get method looks up a key and returns its value or negative one.
First we check whether the key exists in the map.
If found, we unlink its node from its current position in the list.
Then we reinsert it at the right end, marking it as most recently used.
We return the node's value.
If the key was missing, we return negative one.
The put method inserts or updates a key with a value.
We check whether the key already has a node in the cache.
If so, we remove the old node from the list so it can be replaced.
We create a fresh node with the new value and store it in the map under the key.
We insert this new node at the right end as the most recently used entry.
If the cache now holds more keys than its capacity, we need to evict one.
This comment explains we must drop the least recently used node from both the list and the map.
The least recently used node is the one right after the left dummy.
We remove that node from the linked list.
We delete its key from the map so the cache size returns to capacity.

merge-k-sorted-lists.hook: Merging two lists is easy. Merging k lists fast needs one idea borrowed straight from merge sort.
merge-k-sorted-lists.ask: Given k linked lists, each sorted, merge them all into one sorted linked list and return its head.
merge-k-sorted-lists.exampleWhy: All ten values from the four lists, laid out in one sorted chain.

brute.idea: Pour every value from every list into one array, sort it, and build a new linked list from the result.
steps: Collect values from all k lists
Sort the array
Build a new list
brute.whySlow: Ignores that each list is already sorted: N log N instead of N log k, plus N freshly allocated nodes.

optimal.insight: Merge lists in pairs, round after round, like merge sort. Each round touches all N nodes once and halves the list count, so only log k rounds.
steps: Pair up lists: 0 with 1, 2 with 3, ...
Merge each pair with the two-list merge
Repeat on the merged lists until one remains

codeNotes.note: Each round halves the list count
Take lists two at a time

codeNotes.match: l2 = lists[i + 1] if (i + 1) < len(lists) else None
codeNotes.note: Odd one out merges with None

pitfalls: Merging one by one into a growing result is O(N·k), not O(N log k).
Handle an empty input list and empty inner lists.

say.intro: Merge K Sorted Lists. We get k linked lists, each already sorted, and merge them all into one sorted list. Here, four short lists become ten values in order, from zero up to seven.
say.brute: The quick hack? Collect every value from every list, sort them, and build a fresh list. That's n log n time, plus new nodes for everything. And it throws away the fact that each list was already sorted. Merging lists one at a time into a growing result is no better.
say.insight: So let's borrow from merge sort. Merge the lists in pairs. Now k lists become k over two, then k over four, and so on. Why is that fast? Each round touches every node once, and there are only log k rounds. So n log k total, which beats a full sort.
say.anim: We start with four sorted lists and will merge them in pairs, round by round. First we merge list one, four five, with list one three four, comparing nodes as we go. Smaller values get linked into the merged list, building one four one one three four four five. Next pair, two six and zero seven, merges into zero two six seven. Round one done, now we merge the two resulting lists together. We keep comparing remaining nodes, attaching four, four, five, six, seven in order. The second merge finishes, producing one fully sorted combined list. Final answer: zero one one two three four four five six seven, fully merged and sorted.
say.code: Each round of the outer loop halves the number of lists. We take the lists two at a time. If there's an odd one out, it merges with None. Each pair uses the standard two list merge, always taking the smaller front node. When one side runs out, attach the leftover tail. Repeat until one list remains.
say.outro: N log k time. The pattern is divide and conquer on linked lists. A min heap of the k front nodes gets the same bound.

merge-k-sorted-lists.title: Merge K Sorted Lists
lineNotes: We define the Solution class that holds our method for merging many sorted linked lists.
The main method takes a list of list heads and will return the head of one merged list.
First we guard against an empty or missing input, since there would be nothing to merge.
In that case we simply return None because the merged result is an empty list.
We keep looping while more than one list remains, since each round shrinks the count.
We start a fresh empty collection to hold the lists produced by this round of pairwise merges.
We step through the lists two at a time so every pair gets merged together.
We take the list at the current index as the first list of the pair.
The second list is the next one if it exists, otherwise None for an odd leftover list.
We merge the pair with our helper and add the combined list to the new collection.
After the round, the merged lists replace the old ones, roughly halving how many we have.
When one list remains, it contains every node in sorted order, so we return its head.
This helper merges two sorted linked lists into a single sorted list.
We create a dummy node so we never need a special case for the head.
The tail pointer starts at the dummy and always marks the end of the merged list.
We loop as long as both lists still have nodes to compare.
If the first list's value is smaller, it should come next in the merged list.
We attach the first list's current node after the tail.
Then we advance the first list to its next node.
Otherwise the second list's value is smaller or equal, so it goes next.
We attach the second list's current node after the tail.
Then we advance the second list to its next node.
Either way, we move the tail forward onto the node we just attached.
If the first list still has nodes, all of them are larger, so we attach the remainder directly.
We link the tail to the rest of the first list without copying anything.
Likewise, if the second list still has nodes, we attach its remainder.
We link the tail to the rest of the second list, since it is already sorted.
We return the node after the dummy, which is the true head of the merged list.

reverse-nodes-in-k-group.hook: Reverse a linked list — but in chunks of k, stitching every chunk back in place. Pure pointer surgery.
reverse-nodes-in-k-group.ask: Reverse the nodes of a linked list k at a time and return the new head. If fewer than k nodes remain at the end, leave them as they are.
reverse-nodes-in-k-group.exampleWhy: Groups 1,2,3 and 4,5,6 get reversed; 7,8 is shorter than 3, so it stays.

brute.idea: Copy all values into an array, reverse each full chunk of k in the array, then write values back into the nodes.
steps: Collect values into an array
Reverse each complete block of k
Write values back node by node
brute.whySlow: Same O(n) time, but O(n) extra memory, and rewriting values breaks the rule that only the links may change.

optimal.insight: Treat each group as a small list reversal, but start prev at the node after the group, so the reversed group links to the rest automatically. Then reattach the front.
steps: From groupPrev, step k nodes to find kth
No kth? fewer than k left, stop
Reverse the group with prev starting at kth.next
Link groupPrev to kth; old first node becomes new groupPrev

codeNotes.note: Is there a full group ahead?
Reversed group points into the rest
Old first node ends the group

pitfalls: Check a full group exists before reversing, or the short tail gets flipped.

say.intro: Reverse Nodes in K Group. We reverse a linked list k nodes at a time, and leave a short leftover group alone. With k of three, one through eight becomes three two one, six five four, then seven, eight.
say.brute: A simple approach copies the values into an array. Reverse each full block of k there, then write the values back into the nodes. Linear time, sure. But it uses linear extra memory. And the problem says only the links may change, not the values. So we need real pointer surgery.
say.insight: Here's the thing. Each group is just a normal list reversal. The trick is where prev starts. Start it at the node right after the group. Then the reversed group already points into the rest of the list. After that, connect the node before the group to its new front, the old k-th node. Then repeat.
say.anim: We start with the list one through eight, and a dummy node points to the head. Walking forward three steps from groupPrev finds node three as the end of the first group. Now we reverse this group, flipping each node's pointer back to the previous one. The group becomes three, two, one, now pointing forward into four, five, six. GroupPrev jumps to node one, ready to process the next group of three. The same reversal happens again, turning four, five, six into six, five, four. Getting the kth node from here fails since only seven and eight remain, so we stop. The final reversed list is three, two, one, six, five, four, seven, eight.
say.code: First, check if there's a full group ahead. If the k-th node is missing, stop. Then reverse the group, with prev starting at the node after it, so the group points into the rest. Inside is the standard in-place flip. Then the node before the group points at the k-th node, its new front. The old first node now ends the group, so it becomes the next anchor.
say.outro: Linear time, constant space. The pattern is linked list reversal, group by group, with careful stitching. Draw it out first.

reverse-nodes-in-k-group.title: Reverse Nodes In K Group
reverse-nodes-in-k-group.optimalCode:
class Solution:
    def reverseKGroup(self, head: ListNode, k: int) -> ListNode:
        dummy = ListNode(0, head)
        groupPrev = dummy

        while True:
            # 1. Find the kth node from groupPrev, if any
            kthNode = self.getKth(groupPrev, k)
            if not kthNode:
                break
            groupNext = kthNode.next

            # 2. Reverse the group between groupPrev and groupNext
            prevNode = groupNext
            currNode = groupPrev.next
            while currNode != groupNext:
                nextNode = currNode.next
                currNode.next = prevNode
                prevNode = currNode
                currNode = nextNode

            # 3. Reattach the reversed group to the rest of the list
            oldFirst = groupPrev.next
            groupPrev.next = kthNode
            groupPrev = oldFirst

        return dummy.next

    def getKth(self, curr, k):
        # 4. Walk k steps forward, return None if list is too short
        while curr and k > 0:
            curr = curr.next
            k -= 1
        return curr
lineNotes: We define a Solution class that holds the method for reversing a linked list in groups.
The reverseKGroup method takes the head of the list and the group size k.
We create a dummy node pointing to head so the first group has a node before it.
We set groupPrev to the dummy, marking the node just before the current group.
We loop forever, processing one group per pass until there are too few nodes left.
This comment says the first step is to find the kth node after groupPrev, if one exists.
We call getKth to walk k steps from groupPrev and get the last node of this group.
If no kth node exists, fewer than k nodes remain, so we stop reversing.
We break out of the loop and leave the remaining nodes untouched.
We save groupNext, the node right after the group, which the reversed group must link to.
This comment says the second step is reversing the nodes between groupPrev and groupNext.
We start prevNode at groupNext so the reversed group's first node ends up linked to the rest.
We set currNode to the first node of the group, which is the node after groupPrev.
We keep reversing until currNode reaches groupNext, meaning the whole group has been processed.
We remember the next node before we overwrite the current link.
We point currNode backward to prevNode, flipping one link in the group.
We advance prevNode to currNode so it becomes the new reversed front.
We move currNode forward to the saved next node and continue the reversal.
This comment says the third step is hooking the reversed group back into the list.
We save oldFirst, the original first node of the group, which is now the group's tail.
We point groupPrev to kthNode, which is now the front of the reversed group.
We move groupPrev to oldFirst, the tail of this group, ready for the next group.
After the loop we return dummy next, the head of the fully processed list.
The getKth helper finds the node k steps ahead of a given node.
This comment says we walk k steps forward and return None if the list is too short.
We keep stepping while curr exists and steps remain.
We move curr to its next node, advancing one step.
We decrease k by one to count the step we just took.
We return curr, which is the kth node or None if we ran out of nodes.
reverse-nodes-in-k-group.optimalCodeOriginal:
class Solution:
    def reverseKGroup(self, head: ListNode, k: int) -> ListNode:
        dummy = ListNode(0, head)
        groupPrev = dummy

        while True:
            kth = self.getKth(groupPrev, k)
            if not kth:
                break
            groupNext = kth.next

            # reverse group
            prev, curr = kth.next, groupPrev.next
            while curr != groupNext:
                tmp = curr.next
                curr.next = prev
                prev = curr
                curr = tmp

            tmp = groupPrev.next
            groupPrev.next = kth
            groupPrev = tmp
        return dummy.next

    def getKth(self, curr, k):
        while curr and k > 0:
            curr = curr.next
            k -= 1
        return curr

invert-binary-tree.hook: The tree problem that famously stumped an engineer at Google — it is really just one swap per node.
invert-binary-tree.ask: Given the root of a binary tree, mirror it: every node's left and right children trade places, all the way down. Return the root.
invert-binary-tree.exampleWhy: Each node's children swap, so the level order reads right to left: 7 before 2, then 9,6,3,1.

brute.idea: Build a brand new mirrored tree: copy each node, using the mirror of its right subtree as the left child and vice versa.
steps: Copy the current node's value
New left = mirror of old right
New right = mirror of old left
brute.whySlow: Same time, but allocates a full second tree — 100 extra nodes — when the swap can happen in place.

optimal.insight: A mirrored tree is a tree where every node has its children swapped. So swap at the root, then let recursion do the same to each subtree.
steps: Empty node? return None
Swap left and right children
Recurse into both children
Return root

pitfalls: Swapping only values, or only at the root, does not mirror the subtrees.

say.intro: Invert Binary Tree. We mirror a binary tree, so every node's left and right children trade places, all the way down. Here, four with children two and seven becomes four with seven and two. And every level below flips too.
say.brute: One safe approach builds a brand new tree. For every node, make a copy whose left child is the mirror of the old right side, and vice versa. It works, and it's linear. But we're allocating a whole second tree we don't need. Why not just swap in place?
say.insight: Think about it this way. A mirror image is just every node with its two children swapped. So swap the children at the root. Then trust recursion to do the same thing to each subtree. Every node gets visited once, and we reuse the original nodes. The order of the two calls doesn't even matter.
say.anim: We start at root node four, checking that it is not empty before inverting. Node four swaps its children, so left becomes seven and right becomes two. Recursion moves to node seven, swapping its children six and nine. Node nine has no children, so both recursive calls simply return none. Node six also has no children, returning quickly back up the tree. Node seven now returns fully inverted, with nine on left and six on right. Now node two swaps its children one and three, then recursion handles each leaf. Finally node four returns the fully inverted tree: four, seven, two, nine, six, three, one.
say.code: The base case is an empty subtree, so return None. Otherwise, swap the left and right children in place, in one line. Then mirror the new left subtree. Then mirror the new right subtree. Finally, return the root, which now sits on top of the mirrored tree.
say.outro: Linear time, with recursion as deep as the tree is tall. The pattern is tree depth first search. One simple action at every node.

invert-binary-tree.title: Invert Binary Tree
invert-binary-tree.optimalCode:
class Solution:
    def invertTree(self, root: Optional[TreeNode]) -> Optional[TreeNode]:
        # 1. Empty node, nothing to invert
        if root is None:
            return None

        # 2. Swap left and right children
        left_child = root.left
        right_child = root.right
        root.left = right_child
        root.right = left_child

        # 3. Recurse into both children
        self.invertTree(root.left)
        self.invertTree(root.right)

        # 4. Return the root of the inverted tree
        return root
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container this problem's method lives in.
The invertTree method takes the root of a tree, which may be empty, and returns the inverted root.
This comment says the first case is an empty node, where there is nothing to invert.
We check whether the root is none, which is the base case that stops the recursion.
For an empty node we simply return none, since there is nothing to mirror.
This comment says the next step is swapping the left and right children of the current node.
We save the current left child in left child so it is not lost during the swap.
We save the current right child in right child for the same reason.
We point the root's left side at the old right child, which is half of the swap.
We point the root's right side at the old left child, completing the swap.
This comment says we now recurse into both children so the whole tree gets mirrored.
We recursively invert the new left subtree, which flips every node beneath it.
We recursively invert the new right subtree the same way.
This comment says we finish by returning the root of the now inverted tree.
We return the root, which now sits atop a fully mirrored tree.

maximum-depth-of-binary-tree.hook: The hello-world of tree recursion: one line of code, but it teaches how every tree problem thinks.
maximum-depth-of-binary-tree.ask: Given the root of a binary tree, return its maximum depth: the number of nodes on the longest path from the root down to any leaf.
maximum-depth-of-binary-tree.exampleWhy: The path 1 → 3 → 5 → 7 touches four nodes, and no root-to-leaf path is longer.

brute.idea: List every node, then for each one search down from the root to find how deep it sits. The deepest node gives the answer.
steps: Collect every node with a stack
For each node, search from root to find its depth
Keep the largest depth found
brute.whySlow: With 10,000 nodes we run 10,000 separate searches over the tree — up to 100 million visits.

optimal.insight: A tree's depth is one (for the root) plus the deeper of its two subtrees' depths. Ask each child, trust the answer, add one.
steps: Empty tree has depth zero
Recursively get the left and right depths
Return one plus the larger of the two

codeNotes.note: Base case: fell off the tree
An empty subtree adds no depth
This node plus its deeper child

pitfalls: Depth counts nodes, not edges — a single node has depth 1, an empty tree 0.
Recursion depth equals tree height; a 10,000-node chain may need an iterative BFS.

say.intro: Maximum Depth of Binary Tree. We get the root of a tree and return how many nodes sit on its longest root to leaf path. Here, the path one, three, five, seven has four nodes. Nothing is longer, so the answer is four.
say.brute: Okay, a brute force idea. List every node. Then for each one, run a fresh search from the root to find how deep it sits, and keep the max. It's correct. But every search can walk the whole tree. With ten thousand nodes, that's up to a hundred million visits. That's n squared.
say.insight: Here's the thing. A tree's depth is just one, for the root, plus the deeper of its two subtrees. So ask the left child for its depth. Ask the right child. Trust both answers, and add one. And an empty subtree? It just answers zero. Every node gets visited exactly once.
say.anim: We start at root node one, checking if the tree is empty before recursing. We dive left to node four, whose children are null, so its depth is zero plus one, giving one. Back at node two, left depth one beats right depth zero, so it returns depth two. Now node one explores its right subtree, node three, recursing into node five and node seven. Node seven has no children, returning depth one, which makes node five's depth two. Node six also has no children, giving node three a right depth of two and left depth two, so depth three. Finally node one compares left depth two and right depth three, picking the larger. Adding one gives a final maximum depth of four for the whole tree.
say.code: The code is tiny. If the root is empty, we fell off the tree. Return zero, because an empty subtree adds no depth. Otherwise, return one for this node, plus the max of the left and right depths. That's it.
say.outro: Linear time, space equal to the height. The pattern is depth first search on trees. Define the answer using the children, then trust the recursion.

Compute left and right heights from scratch
Their sum is a candidate diameter
brute.whySlow: Heights are recomputed for each node: on a 10,000-node chain that is about 50 million visits.

At each node, left plus right is the path bending there
Update a global best with that sum
Return one plus the taller side to the parent

Height handed up to the parent

say.intro: Diameter of Binary Tree. We want the longest path between any two nodes, counted in edges. Here, the path from eight up to two and down to nine has six edges. And notice, it bends at node two, not at the root.
say.brute: The brute force treats every node as the spot where the path bends. The best path through it is left height plus right height. So we compute those heights from scratch, for every node. On a chain of ten thousand nodes, that's about fifty million visits. n squared.
say.insight: Now, notice something. The heights we keep recomputing are exactly what one bottom up pass gives us. So write one depth first search that returns each node's height to its parent. And while it's there, it checks left plus right as a candidate diameter. Two jobs, one visit per node.
say.anim: We start at the root, node one, with res initialized to zero to track the best diameter. The recursion dives left down nodes two, four, six, and eight, reaching leaves first. At node eight with no children, left and right heights are zero, so it returns height one. Node six combines left one and right zero, updates res to one, returns height two. After the left subtree, node two now has left height three, so recursion explores its right side. Node five returns height two, letting node two compare left three and right three. Node two sets res to six, since left and right heights sum to six, the biggest path so far. After checking node three on the right, the final answer returned is six, the tree's diameter.
say.code: We keep the best diameter seen anywhere, starting at zero. The helper returns zero for an empty node. Otherwise, it gets the height of the left subtree, and of the right. Left plus right is the path that bends at this node, so update the best. Then hand one plus the taller side up to the parent.
say.outro: Linear time, space equal to the height. The pattern is tree depth first search. Return one value upward, and track the real answer on the side.

balanced-binary-tree.hook: Looks like a height check, but doing it naively re-measures the same subtrees again and again.
balanced-binary-tree.ask: Given a binary tree, return true if it is height-balanced: at every node, the heights of the left and right subtrees differ by at most one. Otherwise return false.
balanced-binary-tree.exampleWhy: At the root, the left subtree has height 3 but the right has height 1 — a gap of 2.

Gap above one? return False
Recurse into both children

brute.whySlow: Every ancestor re-measures the same subtrees: even a balanced 5,000-node tree costs about 60,000 visits instead of 5,000.

optimal.insight: Go bottom-up. Each call returns two facts — am I balanced, and how tall am I — so a parent decides using its children's answers, never re-measuring.
steps: Empty node: balanced, height zero
Get both children's pair
Balanced if both are and heights differ by at most one
Return balanced flag and one plus taller height

pitfalls: Checking only the root's two heights is wrong — every node must be balanced.
An empty tree counts as balanced.

say.intro: Balanced Binary Tree. A tree is balanced if, at every node, the left and right heights differ by at most one. Here, the root's left side is three levels tall, but its right side is just one. A gap of two. So the answer is false.
say.brute: The brute force goes top down. At each node, measure both heights from scratch and compare them. Then repeat on both children. It works. But every ancestor re-measures the same deep nodes. Even a balanced tree of five thousand nodes costs about sixty thousand visits, instead of five thousand.
say.insight: So flip the direction. Go bottom up. Let every call return two facts at once. Am I balanced, and how tall am I? Then a parent combines its children's answers in one step. Balanced only if both kids are balanced, and their heights are within one. No height is ever measured twice.
say.anim: We start at the root, node 1, and recurse down its left side to node 4. Node 4's children are empty, so each returns balanced true with height zero. Node 4 combines these: balanced true, height one, since the difference is zero. Node 3 checks its other child, node 4 again, which also returns balanced with height one. Node 3's two subtrees both have height one, so node 3 is balanced with height two. Moving to node 2's right side, node 3 here has empty children, giving balanced height one. Node 2 sees heights two and one, a difference of one, so it stays balanced with height three. At the root, left height three versus right height one gives a difference of two, breaking balance. The final answer returned is false, since the tree is not height balanced.
say.code: An empty tree is balanced, with height zero. Otherwise, the children report first, so this is post-order. This node is balanced if both sides are fine, and their heights are close. Then we pass both facts up. The flag, and one plus the taller height. The answer is the root's flag.
say.outro: One pass, linear time, a stack as deep as the tree. The pattern is post-order depth first search, returning two facts from one call.

balanced-binary-tree.title: Balanced Binary Tree
balanced-binary-tree.optimalCode:
class Solution:
    def isBalanced(self, root: Optional[TreeNode]) -> bool:
        def dfs(node):
            # 1. Empty node: balanced, height zero
            if not node:
                return True, 0

            # 2. Get both children's pair
            left_balanced, left_height = dfs(node.left)
            right_balanced, right_height = dfs(node.right)

            # 3. Balanced if both are and heights differ by at most one
            height_diff = abs(left_height - right_height)
            balanced = left_balanced and right_balanced and height_diff <= 1

            # 4. Return balanced flag and one plus taller height
            height = 1 + max(left_height, right_height)
            return balanced, height

        is_balanced, _ = dfs(root)
        return is_balanced
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container the problem expects for our method.
The isBalanced method takes the root of the tree and returns true or false.
We define a helper called dfs that visits a node and reports balance and height together.
This comment says an empty node counts as balanced with height zero, which is our base case.
We check whether the current node is missing, meaning we have walked past a leaf.
For a missing node we return true for balanced and zero for height.
This comment says we first collect the answer pair from both children before deciding anything.
We recurse on the left child and store whether it is balanced and how tall it is.
We do the same on the right child, getting its balanced flag and its height.
This comment says the node is balanced only if both children are and their heights are close.
We compute height diff as the absolute difference between the left and right heights.
The node is balanced only if left is balanced, right is balanced, and height diff is at most one.
This comment says we also return the height, which is one plus the taller child.
We set height to one plus the larger of the two child heights, counting this node.
We return the balanced flag and height so the parent can use them without re-measuring.
We call dfs on the root and keep only the balanced flag, ignoring the height with an underscore.
We return that flag as the final answer to whether the whole tree is balanced.

same-tree.exampleWhy: The shapes match and four values agree, but the last leaf is 5 in one tree and 6 in the other.

brute.idea: Write each tree out as a full list, using a marker for empty children, then compare the two lists.
steps: Serialize tree p in preorder with null markers
Serialize tree q the same way
Compare the two lists
brute.whySlow: It always walks both whole trees and stores them, even when the roots already differ.

optimal.insight: Two trees are equal exactly when their roots match and their left subtrees are equal and their right subtrees are equal. Walk both together, stopping at the first mismatch.
steps: Both empty: equal
Both present with equal values: compare left pair and right pair
Anything else: not equal

say.intro: Same Tree. We get two binary trees and say whether they're identical. Same shape, same value in every spot. Here, the shapes match, but the last leaf is five in one tree and six in the other. So the answer is false.
say.brute: A simple first approach. Flatten each tree into a list in preorder, with a marker wherever a child is missing. Then compare the lists. The markers make the shape count. It's correct. But it always walks both whole trees and stores everything, even when the roots already differ.
say.insight: Think recursively. Two trees are equal exactly when the roots match, the left subtrees are equal, and the right subtrees are equal. So walk both trees in lockstep. Two empty nodes? Match. One empty, or different values? Instant false. And we stop right there.
say.anim: We start comparing root nodes, both valued 1, so we check their children next. Now comparing the left children, both valued 2, matching so far. Next we compare their left children, both valued 4, still equal. Both children here are empty, so this branch returns true immediately. The subtree rooted at 4 matches completely, returning true. Now we compare nodes 5 and 6, but their values differ. Since the values mismatch, this call returns false right away. That false propagates all the way up, so the trees are not the same.
say.code: If both ran out together, that's a match, so return true. If both exist and hold the same value, check the children. The left pair and the right pair must both match. In every other case, the shape or value differs, so return false. And the and short circuits, so a left mismatch skips the right side.
say.outro: Linear time, a stack as deep as the tree, and an early exit on the first mismatch. The pattern is walking two trees in lockstep.

say.intro: Subtree of Another Tree. We get a big tree and a small tree. Does the small one appear inside the big one, exactly, all descendants included? Here, node four has children one and two, and nothing more. That's a match, so the answer is true.
say.brute: A brute force. Turn the small tree into a string, with markers for empty children. Then for every node in the big tree, turn its whole subtree into a string too, and compare. It's correct. But every node rebuilds a string of everything beneath it. On a long chain, that's millions of visits.
say.insight: Here's the thing. Any match has to start at some node of the big tree. So walk the big tree, and at each node, ask the Same Tree question. Why is that cheap? Same Tree stops at the first mismatch. So most checks end after one or two comparisons.

Both sides matched completely, so same tree returns true for node 4. The subtree check succeeds, confirming the final answer is true.

say.intro: Lowest Common Ancestor of a Binary Search Tree. Given two nodes, find the deepest node with both of them below it. A node counts as below itself. Here, three and five are both children of four. So the answer is four.
say.brute: The general approach ignores the ordering. Search for the path from the root to p. Do the same for q. Then walk both paths together, and the last shared node wins. It works on any tree. But it might explore all hundred thousand nodes, and store two long paths.
say.insight: So why not use the ordering? Smaller values live on the left, larger ones on the right. If p and q are both smaller than this node, the answer must be to the left. Both larger? Go right. And the moment they split to different sides, or one equals this node, we've found it.
say.anim: We start at the root, node six, searching for nodes three and five. Six is greater than both three and five, so we move left. Now root is node two, and we check if both targets are smaller. Two is smaller than both three and five, so we move right. Root becomes node four, with p at three and q at five. Four is not smaller than both, nor greater than both targets. This split means node four is the lowest common ancestor, so we return it. The function returns node four as the final answer.
say.code: We walk down one path with a single pointer, no recursion. If both targets are bigger than the current value, the answer is to the right, so move right. If both are smaller, move left. Otherwise they split, or one equals the current node. Return it.

say.brute: A brute force. For depth zero, then one, then two, run a fresh depth first search that keeps only nodes at that exact depth. Stop when a depth comes back empty. It's correct. But we rescan the whole tree once per level. A chain of two thousand nodes means about two million visits.
say.insight: Breadth first search with a queue already visits nodes in exactly this order. So what's the catch? Knowing where one level ends. Here's the trick. At the start of each round, read the queue's length. Exactly that many nodes belong to this level. Any children we add wait for the next round.
say.anim: We start with root node 1, and the queue is empty before we add it. The queue now holds node 1, so level size is fixed at one. We process node 1, record its value, and enqueue its children 2 and 3. Result now shows level one as just the value 1. Level size is now two, so we process nodes 2 and 3, collecting values and enqueuing 4, 5, and 6. Result now has two levels, and the queue holds 4, 5, and 6 for the next round. We process 4, 5, and 6, gathering their values and enqueuing node 7 for later. Finally we process node 7 alone, finishing with result [[1],[2,3],[4,5,6],[7]].
say.code: A first in, first out queue drives the search, starting with the root. Each round, we freeze its length, so we handle exactly one level. Pop the oldest node first, left to right, and save its value. Its children get appended, and they wait for the next round. Then the finished level goes into the result.
say.outro: Linear time, linear space for the queue. The pattern is breadth first search. Freeze the queue length each round.

We record that node's value in the current level's list.

We append the left child to the back of the queue for the next round.
Then we check whether the node has a right child.
We append the right child behind the left one, still waiting for the next round.

binary-tree-right-side-view.hook: Not just the right edge — a deep left branch can peek out when the right side runs short.
binary-tree-right-side-view.ask: Imagine standing to the right of a binary tree. Return the values you can see from top to bottom: for each level, the rightmost node in that level.
binary-tree-right-side-view.exampleWhy: Levels are [1], [2,3], [4,5], [7]. Node 7 sits under the left branch, but it is alone on its level.

brute.idea: For depth 0, 1, 2 and so on, run a full DFS collecting nodes at exactly that depth, and keep the last one seen.
steps: DFS the whole tree for target depth d
Last node seen at depth d is visible
Stop when a depth has no nodes
brute.whySlow: One full scan per level — a 100-node chain has 100 levels, so roughly 5,000 visits instead of 100.

optimal.insight: BFS processes each level left to right, so the last real node popped in a level is exactly what you see from the right.
steps: BFS with a queue, one level per round
Remember the last non-null node popped this round
Append its value after the round ends

codeNotes.note: Latest real node — rightmost so far
Rightmost of this level is visible

pitfalls: Following only right children fails: here 7 hangs off the left branch.
Skip levels made only of None placeholders.

say.intro: Binary Tree Right Side View. Picture standing to the right of a tree. Top to bottom, which values can you see? The rightmost node on each level. Here that's one, three, five, and then seven. And seven actually hangs on the left side.
say.brute: A brute force. For each depth, run a full depth first search that collects only nodes at that depth, and keep the last one. Stop when a depth is empty. It's correct. But it rescans the whole tree once per level. On a tall, skinny tree, that's n squared.
say.insight: Breadth first search already handles each level from left to right. So the last real node we pop in a level is exactly the one you'd see from the right. And here's why levels matter. If the right side of the tree ends early, a deep left node still shows up. Just like seven here.
say.anim: We start with root node 1, and the queue holds just that single node. Processing this level of size one, node 1 is popped and becomes the last node seen. Its children 2 and 3 are queued, and since 1 was last, it is added to the result. Next level has two nodes; popping 2 then 3, with their children 4, 5, and nulls queued. Node 3 was popped last this level, so 3 joins the result, now showing 1 and 3. Level size is four now, processing nodes 4, 5, and two nulls, tracking last real node. Node 5 becomes last_node here, and after the nulls, 5 gets appended to the result. Only node 7 remains in the next level, popped and set as last_node, then appended. Final result shows the right side view as 1, 3, 5, and 7.
say.code: The queue holds nodes, and it may hold None too. Each round, we count the nodes in the current level. Each real node popped becomes the rightmost so far. It pushes both its children, even if they're None. After the round, the rightmost real node of this level is visible, so we append its value.
say.outro: Linear time and space. The pattern is breadth first search. The answer is just the last real node of every level.

count-good-nodes-in-binary-tree.hook: Each node only needs one number from its ancestors — pass it down and the problem collapses.
count-good-nodes-in-binary-tree.ask: A node is good if no node on the path from the root down to it has a larger value. Given a binary tree, return how many good nodes it has. The root is always good.
count-good-nodes-in-binary-tree.exampleWhy: Good: root 3, then 4, then 5, and the lower 3 (path 3, 1, 3). The 1s have a 3 above them.

brute.idea: For every node, search from the root again to find the largest value on its path. The node is good if it is at least that large.
steps: Visit every node with a stack
Search from root to it, tracking the path maximum
Count it if its value is at least that maximum
brute.whySlow: Each of up to 100,000 nodes triggers its own search from the root — billions of steps in the worst case.

optimal.insight: Whether a node is good depends only on the maximum value above it. Carry that running maximum down as a parameter, so every node is judged in O(1).
steps: Start DFS at the root with maxVal = root.val
Node good if its value ≥ maxVal
Update maxVal and pass it to both children
Sum the counts coming back up

codeNotes.note: maxVal = largest value above this node
Good if nothing above is bigger
Add good nodes from each side

pitfalls: Use ≥, not >: a node equal to the path max is still good.
The max is per path — do not share one global max across branches.

say.intro: Count Good Nodes in Binary Tree. A node is good if nothing on the path from the root down to it is bigger. We count them. Here, both threes, four and five are good. The two ones have a three above them. So four.
say.brute: The brute force checks each node on its own. For every node, start at the root again, search down to it, and track the biggest value along the way. If the node's at least that big, count it. Correct. But every node triggers its own search. That's n squared, billions of steps in the worst case.
say.insight: Think about it this way. A node's fate depends on one number, the largest value above it. So carry that number down as we go. Each node compares itself to it, decides instantly, updates the max, and hands it to both children. Each branch gets its own copy, so paths never interfere.
say.anim: We start the depth first search at the root, node 3, carrying max value 3 downward. Root equals its max so it counts as good, giving count 1 so far. Moving left to node 1, it is less than max 3, so it is not good. Next, node 3 under it equals the running max 3, so it counts as good too. At node 4, it exceeds the old max, becoming good and updating max to 4. Node 1 under it is less than max 4, so it is skipped as not good. Finally node 5 beats max 4, so it is counted as good, updating max to 5. All counts combine back up the tree, giving a final total of four good nodes.
say.code: The helper takes a node and the largest value above it. An empty node adds zero. The node is good if nothing above it is bigger. Then update the max, because the children see this node too. Add the good nodes from each side, and return the total. The root is always good, since it starts as its own max.
say.outro: Linear time, space equal to the height. The pattern is depth first search, passing state down instead of searching back up.

validate-binary-search-tree.hook: Checking each node against its children looks right — and is the classic wrong answer.
validate-binary-search-tree.ask: Given a binary tree, return true if it is a valid binary search tree: for every node, all values in its left subtree are smaller, and all values in its right subtree are larger. Otherwise return false.
validate-binary-search-tree.exampleWhy: 2 is a fine left child of 7, but it sits in 5's right subtree, where everything must exceed 5.

brute.idea: For every node, gather every value in its left subtree and right subtree, and check each one against the node.
steps: Visit every node
Collect all values in its left and right subtrees
Any left value ≥ node, or right value ≤ node? False
brute.whySlow: Every node re-collects its whole subtree: a 10,000-node chain means about 50 million values copied.

optimal.insight: Every node must fit inside an open interval set by its ancestors. Going left lowers the upper bound to the parent; going right raises the lower bound.
steps: Root may be anything: bounds minus infinity to infinity
Node outside (left, right)? return False
Left child gets (left, node.val)
Right child gets (node.val, right)

codeNotes.note: Allowed open interval for this node

pitfalls: Comparing a node only with its direct children misses this example's 2.
Duplicates are invalid: use strict < on both sides.

say.intro: Validate Binary Search Tree. Every node's left subtree must hold only smaller values, and its right subtree only larger ones. Here, two is a fine left child of seven. But it lives inside five's right subtree, where everything must beat five. So, false.
say.brute: A brute force. At every node, collect all values on its left and check they're smaller. Then collect all values on its right and check they're bigger. That's literally the definition, so it's correct. But each node re-collects its whole subtree. On a tall tree, that's n squared.
say.insight: So what's the catch with just checking parent and child? It misses grandparents. So flip the view. Instead of a node checking everything below, let it inherit a range from above. Going left, the parent becomes the new upper bound. Going right, the new lower bound. Each node just checks it fits inside.
say.anim: We start validating the tree at root node 5, allowed range negative infinity to infinity. Node 3 must fit between negative infinity and 5, which it does, so we continue left. Node 1 checks against bounds and its empty children return true immediately. Back at node 3, we now check its right child, node 4, which must be greater than 3. Moving to node 8, range opens up from 5 to infinity, looking fine so far. Node 7 checks its left child, node 2, which must be greater than 7 but fails. Node 7 is now invalid, so node 8's left side becomes invalid too. The errors bubble up to the root, giving the final answer false.
say.code: The helper takes a node and its allowed open range. An empty node is valid. If the value is outside its range, it's invalid, return false. Going left, the upper bound tightens to this value. Going right, the lower bound tightens. The root starts unbounded, from minus infinity to infinity.
say.outro: Linear time, and space equal to the height. The pattern is depth first search, pushing limits down from the ancestors instead of checking only children.

For the right child, we set the lower bound to the current node value and keep the same upper bound.

kth-smallest-element-in-a-bst.hook: In a BST, in-order traversal reads the values already sorted — so just count to k.
kth-smallest-element-in-a-bst.ask: Given the root of a binary search tree and a number k, return the k-th smallest value in the tree, counting from 1.
kth-smallest-element-in-a-bst.exampleWhy: Sorted, the values are 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6. The third smallest is 3.

brute.idea: Ignore the ordering: collect every value, sort the list, and return the item at position k minus one.
steps: DFS to collect all values
Sort the list
Return vals[k - 1]
brute.whySlow: It visits and sorts all 10,000 nodes even when k = 1 and the answer is on the far left.

optimal.insight: In-order traversal of a BST (left, node, right) visits values in sorted order. Do it iteratively and stop at the k-th node popped.
steps: Push nodes while walking as far left as possible
Pop: this is the next smallest value
Decrement k; at zero, return it
Move to the right child and repeat

codeNotes.note: Ancestors still waiting to be visited
Next smallest value in sorted order
Popped k nodes: this is the answer

pitfalls: k is 1-indexed: decrement before checking for zero.
Follow-up: with frequent inserts, store subtree sizes in each node.

say.intro: Kth Smallest Element in a BST. Given a binary search tree and a number k, return the k-th smallest value. Here, the sorted values are one through six. With k of three, the answer is three.
say.brute: The brute force ignores the search tree property. Walk the whole tree, dump every value in a list, sort it, and take position k minus one. Correct, and n log n isn't terrible. But it touches every node, even when k is one and the answer sits at the far left.
say.insight: Here's the thing. A binary search tree is already sorted, if you read it in order. Left subtree, then the node, then the right subtree. So we do that walk, counting as we go, and stop at the k-th node. And using our own stack makes stopping early really easy.
say.anim: We start at root node five, looking for the third smallest value using an empty stack. We push nodes five, three, two, and one while moving left, building the stack in order. Curr is now none, so we pop node one off the stack first, since it's smallest. K decreases to two, not zero yet, so we move to node one's right child, none. Next we pop node two, decrementing k to one, still not our target. We pop node three next, decrementing k to zero, meeting our stopping condition. Since k equals zero, we return curr's value, which is three, the final answer.
say.code: The stack holds ancestors still waiting to be visited. First, dive left toward smaller values, pushing as we go. Then pop. That's the next smallest value in sorted order. Count it down. If we've popped k nodes, this is the answer. Otherwise, explore the larger side, its right child, and dive left again from there.
say.outro: Height plus k time, height space. The pattern is in-order traversal of a binary search tree. Read it sorted, and stop when you have enough.

kth-smallest-element-in-a-bst.title: Kth Smallest Element In a Bst
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which holds the method that finds the k-th smallest value in the tree.
The method kthSmallest takes the root of the binary search tree and the number k, and returns an integer.
We start with an empty stack that will remember nodes whose left subtrees we are still exploring.
We set curr to the root so the traversal begins at the top of the tree.
We keep looping while there are nodes on the stack or a current node to explore, meaning work remains.
This inner loop runs as long as curr is a real node, pushing us down the left side.
We push the current node onto the stack so we can come back to it after finishing its left subtree.
We move curr to its left child, since smaller values in a binary search tree live on the left.
Once no left child remains, we pop the top node, which is the next smallest unvisited value.
We decrease k by one because we have just visited one more node in sorted order.
If k has reached zero, this popped node is exactly the k-th smallest value.
So we return the value of the current node immediately, without traversing the rest of the tree.
Otherwise we move to the right child, so its subtree, which holds larger values, gets visited next.

construct-binary-tree-from-preorder-and-.hook: Two flat lists, one unique tree. The trick is reading which list tells you what.
construct-binary-tree-from-preorder-and-.ask: You are given the preorder and inorder traversals of a binary tree with unique values. Rebuild the tree and return its root.
construct-binary-tree-from-preorder-and-.exampleWhy: Preorder starts with root 1. In inorder, 4, 2, 5 sit left of 1 and 3, 6 sit right.

brute.idea: For an inorder window, the subtree root is the first preorder value that appears in that window. Find it by scanning, split the window, recurse.
steps: Scan preorder for the first value inside this window
Make it the root and find it in the window
Recurse on the left part and the right part
brute.whySlow: Each node scans preorder with a linear membership test: up to tens of billions of steps for 3,000 nodes.

optimal.insight: Preorder's first value is the root. Its position mid in inorder says the left subtree has mid nodes — so the next mid preorder values are the left subtree.
steps: Root = preorder[0]
Find root in inorder at index mid
Left: preorder[1 : mid + 1] with inorder[:mid]
Right: the remaining slices of both lists

codeNotes.match: if not preorder or not inorder:

codeNotes.note: Preorder always starts with the root
Next mid preorder values form the left
Everything after belongs to the right

pitfalls: index() and slicing make this O(n²); a value→index hash map plus pointers gives O(n).
It relies on unique values — duplicates make the split ambiguous.

say.intro: Construct Binary Tree from Preorder and Inorder Traversal. We get two lists for the same tree and rebuild it. Preorder starts with one, so one is the root. In inorder, four, two and five sit to its left. Three and six sit to its right.
say.brute: A brute force works window by window. For any slice of inorder, the subtree's root is the first preorder value that shows up in that slice. So scan preorder, testing membership each time. Then split and recurse. It's correct. But all that scanning makes it cubic in the worst case.
say.insight: Here's the thing. Each list tells us something different. Preorder's first value is always the root. Inorder tells us sizes. If the root sits at index mid, the left subtree has exactly mid nodes. So the next mid values in preorder are the left subtree. Everything after is the right.
say.anim: We start with the full preorder and inorder lists, ready to build the tree. Root becomes 1, and we find it at index 3 in inorder, splitting left and right subtrees. Recursing left, root becomes 2, found at index 1 in its inorder slice. Node 4 has no left or right children, so it returns as a leaf. Back at node 2, we build its right child, which becomes node 5, also a leaf. Now we build the right subtree of root 1, starting with node 3 at mid 0. Node 3's right child becomes 6, which has no children itself. All recursive calls return, reconstructing the tree rooted at 1 with children 2 and 3, matching the expected output.
say.code: No values left means an empty subtree, so return None. Preorder always starts with the root, so build it from the first value. Find its index, mid, in inorder. The left subtree has mid nodes. So the next mid preorder values build the left. Everything after belongs to the right.
say.outro: Quadratic as written, linear with a hash map of inorder positions. The pattern is divide and conquer on trees. Remember, preorder gives roots. Inorder gives sizes.

construct-binary-tree-from-preorder-and-.title: Construct Binary Tree From Preorder And Inorder Traversal
lineNotes: We define a Solution class that holds the method for rebuilding the tree.
The buildTree method takes the preorder and inorder lists and returns the root of the rebuilt tree.
If either list is empty, there are no nodes left to place, so we hit the base case.
In that case we return None, which marks an empty subtree.
The first value in preorder is always the root, so we create a tree node from it.
We find that root value's position in inorder, called mid, which tells us how many nodes are in the left subtree.
The left subtree uses the next mid preorder values and the inorder values before mid, and we build it recursively.
The right subtree uses the remaining preorder values and the inorder values after mid, and we build it recursively.
Finally we return the root, which now has its left and right subtrees attached.

binary-tree-maximum-path-sum.hook: A Hard that is really Diameter in disguise — once you split what you return from what you record.
binary-tree-maximum-path-sum.ask: A path is any chain of connected nodes, used at most once each, and it need not pass through the root. Given a binary tree, return the largest possible sum of node values along any path.
binary-tree-maximum-path-sum.exampleWhy: 15 → 20 → 7 sums to 42. Adding -10, 9 or -5 would only lower it.

brute.idea: Try every node as the top of the path. For each, compute the best downward chain into each child from scratch, and keep the best total.
steps: Visit every node as the path's peak
Recompute best downward chains into both children
Peak + positive chains is a candidate
brute.whySlow: Downward chains are recomputed for every peak: a 30,000-node chain means about 450 million visits.

optimal.insight: A parent can only extend one branch of a child, but a path may bend once. Return the best single chain upward, and record the bent sum on the side.
steps: DFS returns each node's best downward chain
Drop negative child chains: treat them as zero
Record node + left + right as a bent path
Return node + the larger chain to the parent

codeNotes.note: Best path so far; works if all negative
A negative chain is better skipped
Parent may extend only one side

pitfalls: Initialize the answer to root.val, not 0 — an all-negative tree must return its largest value.
Never return the split sum upward; that would fork the path.

say.intro: Binary Tree Maximum Path Sum. A path is any chain of connected nodes, and it doesn't have to touch the root. We want the biggest sum. Here, fifteen, twenty and seven make forty two. Adding minus ten, nine, or minus five only makes it worse.
say.brute: The brute force treats every node as the peak of the path. For each peak, compute the best chain down into each child from scratch, skip negative ones, and add them up. It's correct. But those chains get recomputed over and over. On a long chain, that's hundreds of millions of visits.
say.insight: So what's the catch? A path can only bend once, at its peak. That means a parent can only extend one side of its child. So each call returns its best single chain downward. And on the side, it records the bent path, node plus left plus right. Negative chains? Drop them. They only hurt.
say.anim: We start at the root, value negative ten, and set best to negative ten. We dive into node nine, whose children are empty, so both chains are zero. Node nine's bent sum is nine, bigger than best, so best updates to nine. Now we explore node twenty's subtree, reaching leaves fifteen and negative five under node six. Node fifteen has no children, its bent sum is fifteen, and best updates to fifteen. Node seven also has no children, giving a bent sum of seven, less than best. Node twenty combines chains fifteen and seven, making a bent sum of forty two, the new best. After finishing the root, the final maximum path sum returned is forty two.
say.code: The best path starts at the root's value, so all negative trees still work. For each node, get the left and right chains. A negative chain is better skipped, so clip it at zero. The path bending at this node is node plus both chains, so update the best. Then return node plus the larger chain, since the parent may extend only one side.
say.outro: Linear time, height-sized stack. The pattern is post-order depth first search. It's Diameter, but with values.

binary-tree-maximum-path-sum.title: Binary Tree Maximum Path Sum
lineNotes: We define a Solution class that holds the method for solving the maximum path sum problem.
