If the node is empty, there is nothing to add, so we handle the base case here.
An empty node contributes a chain sum of zero to its parent.
This comment explains that negative child chains are dropped, because including them would only lower the sum.
We get the left chain by recursing left and taking the larger of that result and zero.
We do the same on the right side, ignoring the right chain if it is negative.
This comment says we record the path that bends at this node, using both child chains.
The bent sum is the node value plus the left chain plus the right chain, forming a path through this node.
We compare the bent sum against the best answer recorded so far.
If the bent sum is larger, we update the best answer to it.
This comment notes that only one branch can be extended upward, so we return the node plus one chain.
We return the node value plus the larger of the two chains, since a parent can only continue one branch.
We start the recursion from the root, which fills in the best answer as it goes.
Finally we return the best path sum that was recorded during the traversal.

serialize-and-deserialize-binary-tree.hook: One traversal plus explicit null markers pins down any tree, duplicates and all.
serialize-and-deserialize-binary-tree.ask: Design two functions: serialize turns a binary tree into a string, and deserialize turns that string back into exactly the same tree. Any format is allowed, as long as the round trip works.
serialize-and-deserialize-binary-tree.exampleWhy: Serialize writes "1,2,N,N,3,4,N,N,5,N,N"; deserialize reads it back into the identical tree.

brute.idea: Store two traversals, preorder and inorder, without null markers, then rebuild by finding each root in the inorder list and slicing.
steps: Write preorder and inorder values, joined by a bar
Deserialize: first preorder value is the root
Find it in inorder, slice both lists, recurse
brute.whySlow: Breaks on repeated values (the root's inorder position is ambiguous), stores every value twice, and index plus slicing per node is quadratic.

optimal.insight: Preorder alone is ambiguous, but preorder with an N for every empty child is not: the reader always knows when a subtree ends.
steps: Serialize: preorder DFS, write N for each missing child
Join with commas
Deserialize: read values in the same order
N means None; otherwise build node, then left, then right
optimal.time: O(n) with an index; O(n²) as written (pop(0))

codeNotes.note: Consume tokens in the same order
Marker means this subtree is empty

pitfalls: vals.pop(0) is O(n) per call; use an index or deque to keep deserialize truly O(n).
Without null markers, one traversal cannot tell different shapes apart.

say.intro: Serialize and Deserialize Binary Tree. We design two functions. One turns a tree into a string. The other turns that string back into the exact same tree. Here, the tree one through five goes into a string and comes back identical.
say.brute: A first idea, borrowed from the last problem. Store two traversals, preorder and inorder, then rebuild by finding each root and slicing. It works. But it stores everything twice, it's n squared, and it breaks when values repeat. Why? The root's spot in inorder becomes ambiguous.
say.insight: Here's the thing. One preorder walk is enough, if we also write a marker, the letter N, for every empty child. Now the string pins down the shape exactly. Reading it back, each token says either here's a node, or this branch ends. Duplicates don't matter, because we never search for a value.
say.anim: We start serializing the tree rooted at node 1, building a result list. Preorder visits node 1 then node 2, appending their values to the list. Node 2 has no children, so two N markers mark its empty left and right. Back at node 1, we move to its right subtree, visiting nodes 3, 4, and 5. Each leaf gets two N markers, giving the full sequence 1,2,N,N,3,4,N,N,5,N,N. Deserializing splits that string back into values and rebuilds nodes in the same order. Recursive calls recreate node 1, then node 2 with two null children, then node 3 with children 4 and 5. The final rebuilt tree matches the original: 1,2,3,null,null,4,5.
say.code: Serialize marks empty children explicitly with N. It's preorder, so each node is written before its children. Then join everything into one comma separated string. Deserialize consumes tokens in the same order. A marker means this subtree is empty. Otherwise, make the node, rebuild its left fully, then its right. Popping from the front is linear, so use an index.
say.outro: Linear time and space with an index. The pattern is preorder depth first search, with null markers so the shape is never ambiguous.

serialize-and-deserialize-binary-tree.title: Serialize And Deserialize Binary Tree
lineNotes: We define a Codec class that holds both the serialize and deserialize methods for the tree.
The serialize method takes the root of the tree and will produce a single string.
We start with an empty list called res to collect the tokens in preorder.
We define a helper function dfs that visits each node recursively in preorder.
If the current node is empty, we handle the null case, which must be recorded.
We append the letter N to res so the reader knows an empty child sits here.
We return right away, since an empty node has no children to visit.
Otherwise we append the node's value, converted to a string, to record the current node first.
We recurse into the left child next, which keeps the preorder of root, then left, then right.
We then recurse into the right child, finishing the full preorder with markers.
We kick off the traversal from the root of the tree.
We join all tokens with commas into one string and return it.
The deserialize method takes the string produced earlier and rebuilds the tree.
We split the string on commas to get a list of tokens in the original preorder.
We define a helper dfs that builds one subtree by consuming tokens from the front.
We pop the first token off the list, which is always the next node in preorder.
If that token is N, this position is an empty child.
So we return None, ending this subtree without consuming anything more.
Otherwise we create a new tree node, converting the token back into an integer value.
We build the left subtree recursively, which consumes exactly the tokens belonging to the left side.
We then build the right subtree from the tokens that remain, mirroring the serialization order.
We return the finished node so the caller can attach it as a child.
We start the rebuild and return the root of the reconstructed tree.

kth-largest-element-in-a-stream.hook: You never need the whole stream sorted — only the top k, and a tiny heap guards them.
kth-largest-element-in-a-stream.ask: Design a class that starts with k and a list of numbers. Each call to add inserts one new number and returns the k-th largest number seen so far.
kth-largest-element-in-a-stream.exampleWhy: With k = 3, after adding 3 the top three are 8, 5, 4, so 4. Adding 10 makes them 10, 8, 5.

brute.idea: Keep every number in a list. On each add, append, sort the whole list, and read the k-th from the end.
steps: Store all numbers
add: append the value and sort
Return nums[-k]
brute.whySlow: With 10,000 adds on 10,000 numbers, each re-sorts up to 20,000 values — hundreds of millions of steps.

optimal.insight: Only the k largest values matter. Keep exactly those in a min-heap: its smallest element, the root, is the k-th largest overall.
steps: Heapify nums, pop until only k remain
add: push the new value
Size above k? pop the smallest
Return the heap's root

codeNotes.note: Turn the list into a min-heap
Trim down to the k largest
One too many: evict the smallest

pitfalls: Use a min-heap, not a max-heap: you must evict the smallest of the top k.
nums may start with fewer than k values; only pop when size exceeds k.

say.intro: Kth Largest Element in a Stream. We build a class with a number k and a starting list. Each time a new number arrives, we return the k-th largest so far. Here k is three, so we report the third biggest value each time.
say.brute: The brute force keeps every number in a list. On each add, append, sort everything, and read the k-th from the end. Short and correct. But every add pays for a full sort. Ten thousand adds on a growing list? That's hundreds of millions of steps.
say.insight: Think about it this way. Do we ever care about anything below the top k? No. So keep only the k largest, in a min heap. The heap's root is the smallest of those k. And that's exactly the k-th largest overall. New value comes in. Heap too big? Throw out the smallest.
say.anim: We start with k equal to three and nums containing four, five, eight, two. Heapify arranges nums into a min-heap, now ordered as two, four, eight, five. Since the heap has more than k elements, we pop the smallest, two, away. Now the heap holds four, five, eight, exactly the three largest values so far. Adding three pushes it in, but popping removes it since it's smallest, returning four. Adding five pushes it, pops the smallest four, and the heap now returns five. Adding ten pushes it, pops the smallest five, but heap top is still five. Adding nine pushes it, pops five, leaving eight as the new third largest. Finally adding four pushes then pops it right away, keeping eight as the answer.
say.code: The constructor turns the list into a min heap. Then it trims down to the k largest by popping. In add, admit the new value with a push. If there's one too many, evict the smallest. Then return the root, which is the k-th largest. Each add costs just log k time, however long the stream gets.
say.outro: Log k per add, k space. The pattern is heaps. For the top k largest, keep a min heap of size k.

kth-largest-element-in-a-stream.title: Kth Largest Element In a Stream
lineNotes: We define a class called KthLargest that will track the k-th largest number as values stream in.
The constructor takes k and a starting list of numbers to initialize our tracking structure.
We store the numbers as our min-heap and remember k, so we can enforce the size limit later.
We heapify the list in place, turning it into a valid min-heap so the smallest value sits at the root.
While the heap holds more than k items, we keep trimming, since only the k largest values matter.
Each pop removes the current smallest value, which cannot be among the k largest, so the heap shrinks toward size k.
The add method takes one new value from the stream and must return the current k-th largest.
We push the new value onto the min-heap, which keeps the heap property intact automatically.
If the heap now has more than k elements, the extra smallest one needs to be discarded.
We pop the smallest element, leaving exactly the k largest values seen so far in the heap.
The root of the heap is the smallest of the k largest, which is exactly the k-th largest overall, so we return it.

last-stone-weight.hook: A tiny smash-the-rocks game that shows exactly when a max heap pays off.
last-stone-weight.ask: Each turn, take the two heaviest stones and smash them. Equal stones both vanish; otherwise the smaller vanishes and the bigger shrinks by the smaller's weight. Return the last stone's weight, or 0 if none remain.
last-stone-weight.exampleWhy: 8 and 7 leave 1; 4 and 2 leave 2; 2 and 1 leave 1; 1 and 1 vanish. One stone of weight 1 remains.

brute.idea: Simulate literally: every turn, sort the stones to find the two heaviest, smash them, and put any leftover back.
steps: Sort the stones each turn
Pop the two heaviest
Push back the difference if nonzero
brute.whySlow: Up to n turns, each re-sorting the whole list: n² log n total, versus n log n with a heap.

optimal.insight: We only ever need the two largest. A max heap hands us the largest in O(log n) and absorbs the leftover in O(log n) — no full re-sort.
steps: Negate stones so Python's min heap acts as a max heap
Heapify once in O(n)
Pop two, push back the difference if nonzero
Return the last stone, or 0

codeNotes.note: Negate: min heap becomes max heap
Build the heap in linear time

pitfalls: Python only has a min heap: negate values, and remember the difference stays negative.
Handle the empty heap: return 0 when every stone is destroyed.

say.intro: Okay, Last Stone Weight. Every turn, we grab the two heaviest stones and smash them together. Same weight? Both disappear. Otherwise, the bigger one survives, shrunk by the smaller one's weight. In our example, four smashes leave a single stone of weight one. So we return one.
say.brute: The obvious move is to just simulate it. Each turn, sort all the stones. Grab the two heaviest from the end and smash them. Drop any leftover back into the list. That works, and it's easy to explain. So what's the catch? We re-sort everything on every single turn. That adds up to about n squared log n.
say.insight: Here's the thing. We never care about the full order. We only want the two biggest, over and over, while new stones keep showing up. That's exactly what a max heap is for. It hands us the largest in log n time. And it takes the leftover back just as cheaply. One wrinkle: Python's heap is a min heap. So we store negative weights.
say.anim: Stones are negated into a max heap, so the heap's smallest value acts as the largest stone. The heap holds negated weights, with eight and seven ready to be popped as the top two. We pop the two heaviest stones, eight and seven, since they differ their difference one gets pushed back. Now four and two are popped, their difference two is pushed back into the heap. Two and one are popped next, leaving a difference of one pushed back in. The last two equal stones, both weight one, smash and cancel each other out completely. Only one stone remains in the heap, so the loop stops. The final remaining stone weight is returned as one, the answer.
say.code: First, we negate every stone, so the min heap acts like a max heap. Then we heapify the list in linear time. We loop while two or more stones remain. We pop the heaviest, then the second heaviest. If they differ, a leftover survives. So we push back their difference, which stays negative. After the loop, we append a zero, so an empty heap still works. Then we return the absolute value of the top.
say.outro: n log n time, linear space. The pattern is the heap. Whenever you keep needing the biggest item from a changing pile, reach for one.

last-stone-weight.title: Last Stone Weight
last-stone-weight.optimalCode:
class Solution:
    def lastStoneWeight(self, stones: List[int]) -> int:
        # 1. Negate stones so the min heap behaves like a max heap
        maxHeap = [-stone for stone in stones]
        heapq.heapify(maxHeap)

        # 2. Repeatedly smash the two heaviest stones
        while len(maxHeap) > 1:
            first = -heapq.heappop(maxHeap)
            second = -heapq.heappop(maxHeap)

            # 3. Push back the leftover weight if any
            if first != second:
                remaining = first - second
                heapq.heappush(maxHeap, -remaining)

        # 4. Return the last stone's weight, or 0 if none remain
        if len(maxHeap) == 0:
            return 0
        return -maxHeap[0]
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container the interview platform expects for our method.
The method lastStoneWeight takes the list of stone weights and returns a single integer for the final stone.
This comment explains that Python only has a min heap, so negating weights makes the largest stone come out first.
We build maxHeap by negating each stone, so the heaviest stone becomes the most negative, smallest value.
Heapify rearranges that list into a valid heap in linear time, which is faster than pushing each stone separately.
This comment says we keep smashing the two heaviest stones until the game ends.
The loop continues while at least two stones remain, since a smash needs a pair.
We pop the smallest negative value and negate it, giving the weight of the heaviest stone as first.
We pop again and negate, giving the second heaviest stone as second, which is never larger than first.
This comment notes that any leftover weight from a smash must go back into the heap.
If first and second differ, the smash leaves a stone; if they match, both vanish and we push nothing.
The leftover weight is first minus second, which is the bigger stone reduced by the smaller one.
We push the negated leftover back so the heap keeps ordering stones by heaviest first.
This comment says that after the loop we report the last stone's weight, or zero if none remain.
If the heap is empty, every stone was destroyed in matching smashes.
So we return zero in that case, as the problem requires.
Otherwise exactly one stone remains, and we negate the heap's top element to recover its true weight.

k-closest-points-to-origin.hook: Find the nearest k points without sorting everything — a heap does the selecting.
k-closest-points-to-origin.ask: Given points on a plane and a number k, return the k points closest to the origin, measured by straight-line distance. Any order is accepted.
k-closest-points-to-origin.exampleWhy: Squared distances are 18, 26, 20, 2, 9, 8. The three smallest are 2, 8 and 9.

brute.idea: Repeat k times: scan every remaining point, pick the one with the smallest distance, and remove it.
steps: Scan all remaining points
Take the closest one
Remove it and repeat k times
brute.whySlow: With 10,000 points and k = 5,000, that is about 50 million distance comparisons.

optimal.insight: Compute every squared distance once, heapify in O(n), then the closest point is always at the top: k pops cost O(k log n).
steps: Store [distance², x, y] for each point
Heapify the list in linear time
Pop the top k times
Collect the popped points

codeNotes.note: Squared distance: no square root needed
Distance first so the heap orders by it

pitfalls: Skip the square root: comparing squared distances gives the same order.
Alternative: a max heap of size k gives O(n log k) and O(k) space.

say.intro: Okay, K Closest Points to Origin. We get a bunch of points and a number k. We return the k points nearest the origin. Here we have six points, and k is three. The answer is one one, then two minus two, then zero minus three.
say.brute: The simplest idea? Repeat a selection k times. Scan every remaining point and find the closest one. Add it to the answer, then remove it. Each pass is a full linear scan. So the total is n times k. With ten thousand points and k of five thousand, that's fifty million comparisons.
say.insight: Notice we keep asking the same question. Which remaining point is closest? A min heap keyed by distance answers that instantly. The smallest is always sitting on top. We build it once in linear time. Then each pop costs only log n. And here's a small trick. Skip the square roots. Squared distances sort in exactly the same order.
say.anim: We start with six points and need the three closest to the origin. For each point we compute squared distance, like eighteen for point three,three, storing it in the heap list. After processing all points, the heap holds distance, x, y triples in input order. Heapify rearranges the list so the smallest distance, two, sits at the top. We pop the smallest distance, two, giving point one,one, and add it to results. Next pop gives distance eight, point two,negative two, appended to the growing result. Third pop gives distance nine, point zero,negative three, completing three closest picks. The final answer is one,one, two,negative two, and zero,negative three.
say.code: For each point, we compute x squared plus y squared. No square root needed. We append the distance first, then x and y, so the heap orders by distance. Then we heapify the list in linear time. Now, while k is still positive, we pop the closest remaining point. We record its x and y, and we decrease k by one. Once k hits zero, we stop and return the collected points.
say.outro: n plus k log n time, and linear space. The pattern is the heap. For any top k or closest k problem, let a heap do the picking.

k-closest-points-to-origin.title: K Closest Points to Origin
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the wrapper the interview platform expects for our answer.
The kClosest method takes a list of points and a number k, and returns the k nearest points.
We start with an empty list that will become our min heap of distance entries.
We loop over every point in the input, unpacking each one into its x and y coordinates.
We compute the squared distance from the origin, skipping the square root since ordering stays the same.
We append a list holding the distance, x, and y, so the distance leads and drives the heap ordering.
We heapify the list in place, which builds a valid min heap in linear time.
We create an empty result list to collect the chosen closest points.
We loop while k is above zero, so we pop exactly k points.
We pop the smallest entry from the heap, which is the closest remaining point, and unpack its distance and coordinates.
We append just the x and y of that point to the result, dropping the distance.
We decrease k by one to track how many points we still need.
We return the result list holding the k closest points to the origin.

kth-largest-element-in-an-array.hook: Kth largest without fully sorting — shrink a heap until the answer sits on top.
kth-largest-element-in-an-array.ask: Given a list of numbers and k, return the value that would sit in position k if the list were sorted from largest to smallest. Duplicates count separately, so in 5, 5, 4 the second largest is 5.
kth-largest-element-in-an-array.exampleWhy: Sorted descending: 6, 5, 5, 4, ... The fourth value is 4.

brute.idea: Remove the maximum k minus 1 times. The maximum of what remains is the kth largest.
steps: Find the max with a full scan
Remove it; repeat k - 1 times
Return the max of what is left
brute.whySlow: Each removal rescans the list. With 100,000 numbers and k = 50,000 that is billions of steps.

optimal.insight: Min-heapify, then pop the smallest until only k numbers remain. Those are the k largest, and the smallest of them, the top, is the answer.
steps: Heapify the list in place (O(n))
Pop the minimum while more than k remain
The heap now holds the k largest
Its top is the kth largest

codeNotes.note: Min heap built in place, linear time

pitfalls: A size-k min heap built while scanning gives O(n log k) and O(k) space.
Quickselect averages O(n) but degrades to n² on bad pivots — mention it.

say.intro: Kth Largest Element in an Array. We get a list of numbers and a value k. We return the kth largest, and duplicates count separately. Here k is four. Reading from the top, we get six, five, five, then four. So the answer is four, even though five shows up twice.
say.brute: A simple first try is to peel off the top. Find the maximum and delete it. Do that k minus one times. Then the maximum of what's left is our answer. So what's wrong with it? Every deletion rescans the whole list. That's n times k work. On big inputs, that's billions of steps.
say.insight: Let's flip the question around. Instead of hunting for big numbers, throw away the small ones. Put everything in a min heap. Then pop the smallest until exactly k numbers remain. What survives? The k largest values. And the smallest of those survivors sits right on top. That top value is the kth largest.
say.anim: We start by heapifying the array into a min-heap, smallest value bubbles to the top. With k equal to four, we keep popping the smallest element while the heap is larger than four. The one gets popped first, leaving the next smallest value at the top. Popping continues, removing two, then another two, shrinking the heap each time. After popping the small values, the heap holds three, five, four, five, six. One more pop removes the three, leaving exactly four numbers in the heap. Now only four elements remain, the k largest values from the original array. The top of the heap, four, is returned as the fourth largest element.
say.code: First, we heapify the list in place. That's linear time and no extra memory. While the list holds more than k numbers, we keep going. Why? We only want to keep the k largest. Each time, we pop the current smallest and throw it away. When the loop stops, only the top k are left. So we return index zero. That's the top of the heap, and the smallest of the top k.
say.outro: A linear heap build, plus log n per pop. The pattern is the heap. For kth largest, keep the big ones, drop the small ones, and read the top.

kth-largest-element-in-an-array.title: Kth Largest Element In An Array
kth-largest-element-in-an-array.optimalCode:
import heapq

class Solution:
    def findKthLargest(self, nums: List[int], k: int) -> int:
        # 1. Turn the list into a min-heap in place
        heapq.heapify(nums)
        # 2. Remove the smallest elements until only k remain
        while len(nums) > k:
            heapq.heappop(nums)
        # 3. The heap now holds the k largest numbers
        # 4. Its top is the smallest of those, the kth largest overall
        return nums[0]
lineNotes: We import the heapq module, which gives us a min-heap built on top of an ordinary list.
We define a Solution class, which is the wrapper this problem expects for our method.
The method findKthLargest takes the list of numbers and k, and returns the kth largest value.
This comment says step one is to turn the list into a min-heap right where it sits.
Heapify rearranges nums in place so the smallest number is at the front, in linear time.
This comment says step two is to throw away the smallest elements until only k remain.
We loop as long as the heap holds more than k numbers, since extras must be removed.
Each pop removes the current smallest number, so the larger values survive in the heap.
This comment notes that after the loop the heap holds exactly the k largest numbers.
This comment explains that the top of the heap is the smallest of those k, which is the kth largest overall.
We return the first element of nums, the heap top, which is the answer.
kth-largest-element-in-an-array.optimalCodeOriginal:
class Solution:
    def findKthLargest(self, nums: List[int], k: int) -> int:
        heapify(nums)
        while len(nums) > k:
            heappop(nums)
        return nums[0]

task-scheduler.hook: A CPU scheduling puzzle where greedily running the most frequent task wins.
task-scheduler.ask: Each task takes one time unit. The same task must wait at least n units before running again; the CPU may idle. Return the fewest time units needed to finish every task.
task-scheduler.exampleWhy: A B idle A B idle A B: each A is three units after the last A, and likewise for B.

brute.idea: Simulate tick by tick. At each tick, scan the remaining tasks, pick the ready task with the most copies left, and count copies by rescanning.
steps: Advance time by one
Scan remaining tasks for the ready one with most copies
Run it, or idle if none is ready
brute.whySlow: Every tick rescans and recounts all m remaining tasks. With 10,000 tasks that is hundreds of millions of operations.

optimal.insight: Always run the ready task with the most copies left, so big ones never pile up at the end. Max heap picks it; a queue holds cooldowns.
steps: Count tasks; put counts in a max heap
Each tick: pop the biggest count, run one copy
If copies remain, park it in a queue with its ready time
When its ready time arrives, push it back to the heap
If the heap is empty, jump time to the next ready task

codeNotes.note: How many copies of each task
Run one copy of the biggest

pitfalls: Only counts matter, not letters — the heap stores counts alone.
Closed form: max(len(tasks), (maxCount - 1)(n + 1) + numberOfMaxTasks).

say.intro: Okay, Task Scheduler. Each task takes one unit of time. Two copies of the same task need a cooldown of n units between them. And the CPU is allowed to sit idle. With three As, three Bs, and a cooldown of two, the best schedule takes eight units. A, B, idle, A, B, idle, A, B.
say.brute: The direct approach simulates tick by tick. At each tick, we scan every remaining task. We count how many copies of each are left. Then we run the ready task with the most copies. If nothing is ready, the CPU idles. It's correct. But every tick rescans and recounts the whole list. That gets very slow, very fast.
say.insight: Here's the greedy idea. Always run the ready task with the most copies left. Why? Because frequent tasks are the ones that force idles if they pile up at the end. A max heap of counts gives us that task instantly. And tasks that are cooling down wait in a queue. Each one is tagged with the exact time it's ready again.
say.anim: We have three A tasks and three B tasks, with a cooldown of two between repeats. The max heap stores negative counts, negative three and negative three, to pick the biggest task first. At time one, we run a task, popping negative three and leaving it at negative two, needing cooldown. At time two, we run the other task, then both wait in the cooldown queue until ready again. At time three, no task is ready, so time jumps ahead to the next cooldown finish. A task returns from cooldown, runs again, and goes back into cooldown until time six. By time six and seven, tasks keep cycling through cooldown since only one copy remains each. At time eight everything finishes, so the least number of intervals needed is eight.
say.code: First, we count how many copies of each task we have. We store those counts negated, so the heap acts as a max heap. Each tick, time ticks up by one. If the heap is empty, we skip ahead to the queue front's ready time. Otherwise, we pop the biggest count and run one copy. If copies remain, it cools down until time plus n. Once that's over, it goes back on the heap.
say.outro: Linear in the number of tasks, since the heap holds at most twenty six counts. The pattern is heap plus queue. Greedy by frequency, with a queue for cooldowns.

task-scheduler.title: Task Scheduler
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the wrapper this problem's method lives in.
The method leastInterval takes the list of tasks and the cooldown n, and returns the minimum total time.
This comment says the first step is counting how many times each task occurs.
We build a counter that maps each task to its number of occurrences.
We make a max heap by storing negated counts, since Python's heap only gives the smallest value.
We heapify that list so the task with the most copies left sits on top.
We start the clock at time zero before any task has run.
We create a cooldown queue that holds pairs of remaining count and the time the task becomes ready.
This comment says we now simulate the schedule one time unit at a time.
We keep looping while any task is ready in the heap or still waiting in the cooldown queue.
We advance the clock by one unit for this step.
This comment says that if nothing is ready, we skip ahead to the next ready time.
If the heap is empty, every remaining task is cooling down, so the CPU would idle.
We jump the time straight to when the first cooling task becomes ready, skipping the idle units.
Otherwise at least one task is ready, so we run one this turn.
We pop the most frequent task and add one to its negative count, meaning one copy is done.
If the remaining count is still negative, copies remain, so the task must cool down.
We push the task onto the cooldown queue with its ready time set to now plus n.
This comment says tasks that finished cooling should return to the heap.
If the oldest cooling task becomes ready exactly at the current time, we should release it.
We pop it from the queue and push its remaining count back onto the max heap.
When everything is finished, we return the total time elapsed.

design-twitter.hook: A mini Twitter feed: merging many sorted timelines is a heap problem in disguise.
design-twitter.ask: Build a tiny Twitter. Users post tweets, follow and unfollow others, and ask for their news feed: the 10 most recent tweets from themselves and everyone they follow, newest first.
design-twitter.exampleWhy: User 1 follows 2, so the feed merges 3, 6, 5 newest first. After unfollowing, tweet 6 disappears.

brute.idea: For a feed, gather every tweet from the user and their followees into one list, sort it by time, and take the first 10.
steps: Collect all tweets of user and followees
Sort them, newest first
Return the first 10 ids
brute.whySlow: A user following 500 accounts with 1,000 tweets each sorts 500,000 tweets just to show 10.

optimal.insight: Each user's tweets are already time-sorted. A feed merges k sorted lists, and we need only 10: a heap of each list's newest unread tweet.
steps: Stamp each tweet with a decreasing counter so smaller means newer
Seed a min heap with each followee's newest tweet
Pop the newest, add it to the feed
Push that user's next older tweet; stop at 10
optimal.time: post/follow O(1); getNewsFeed O(f log f)

codeNotes.note: Global clock; goes negative for min heap
Your own tweets are in your feed
Push that user's next older tweet

pitfalls: Unfollowing someone you don't follow must not crash — guard the remove.
A user must see their own tweets even with zero followees.

say.intro: Design Twitter. We support posting, following, unfollowing, and a news feed. The feed is the ten newest tweets from you and everyone you follow. Here, user one follows user two. So the feed shows three, six, five. After unfollowing, it shows just three and five.
say.brute: The easy version stores every tweet with a timestamp. To build a feed, we dump every tweet from you and all your followees into one list. We sort it by time and keep the first ten. Correct? Yes. But think about it. Follow five hundred busy accounts, and you sort half a million tweets. All that, just to show ten.
say.insight: Here's the thing. Each person's tweets are already stored in time order. So a feed is really just merging a few sorted lists. And we only need the first ten items. So we put each followee's newest tweet into a heap. Pop the newest overall. Then push the next older tweet from that same person. Ten pops and we're done.
say.anim: We post tweet 5 for user 1 and tweet 6 for user 2, each timestamped by a counter. User 1 posts tweet 3, then follows user 2, joining their tweet streams. Getting user 1's feed builds a heap with the newest tweet from each followed user. Tweet 3 from user 1 and tweet 6 from user 2 enter the heap, sorted by recency. Popping the heap repeatedly merges these sorted lists, picking the newest tweet each time. Tweets 3, then 6, then 5 get pulled out in order, since the heap always gives the smallest count. The feed returns 3, 6, 5, the ten most recent tweets merged from both users. After user 1 unfollows user 2, a new feed request only pulls from user 1's own tweets. This time the heap merge yields just tweets 3 and 5, the final answer.
say.code: A global clock goes more negative with every tweet. That way, the smallest stamp is always the newest. Each user's tweets are appended in order, so they stay sorted by time. For a feed, we first make sure you follow yourself. Then we seed the heap with each followee's newest tweet and its index. We only ever take ten. And after each pop, if that person has an older tweet, we push it in.
say.outro: A feed costs f log f for f followees, no matter how many tweets exist. The pattern is the heap, merging k sorted lists. Remember it for any timeline question.

find-median-from-data-stream.hook: Two heaps facing each other make the median an O(1) lookup, forever.
find-median-from-data-stream.ask: Numbers arrive one at a time. Support adding a number and asking for the median of everything so far: the middle value, or the average of the two middle values when the count is even.

brute.idea: Keep every number in a plain list. To find the median, sort the list and read the middle.
steps: addNum: append to the list
findMedian: sort the whole list
Read the middle one or two values
brute.time: add O(1), median O(n log n)
brute.whySlow: With 50,000 calls each sorting up to 50,000 numbers, that is billions of operations.

optimal.insight: The median sits at the boundary between halves. Keep the lower half in a max heap, the upper half in a min heap; their tops are the middle.
steps: small: max heap of the lower half
large: min heap of the upper half
Insert on the correct side
Rebalance so sizes differ by at most one
Median = bigger heap's top, or average of both tops

codeNotes.note: Bigger than upper half's min: goes up
Lower half too big: move its max
Upper half too big: move its min
Even count: average the two tops

pitfalls: Python heaps are min heaps: store the lower half negated and un-negate on read.
Even count: average the two tops as a float, not integer division.

say.intro: Find Median from Data Stream. Numbers arrive one at a time. At any moment, someone can ask for the median. After five and two arrive, the median is three point five. Add eight, and it becomes five. Add one, and we're back to three point five.
say.brute: The simple design keeps everything in a plain list. Adding is instant. When someone asks for the median, we sort the list and read the middle. Or we average the middle two. So what's the problem? Every median query costs n log n. Fifty thousand queries on fifty thousand numbers? That's billions of steps.
say.insight: Think about it this way. The median only cares about the middle. So split the numbers into a lower half and an upper half. Keep the lower half in a max heap, and the upper half in a min heap. Keep their sizes within one of each other. Now the two tops sit right at the middle. The median is always one peek away.
say.anim: We start with two empty heaps, small for the lower half and large for the upper half. Adding five, since large is empty it goes into small as negative five. Adding two, it also goes into small, making small hold two and five. Small now has one more element than large, so we move its top, five, into large to rebalance. With equal sizes, the median averages both tops, two and five, giving three point five. Adding eight, since it beats large's top five, it pushes into large directly. Now large has one extra element, so its top, five, becomes the median. Finally adding one goes into small, rebalancing keeps sizes equal, and the median averages to three point five.
say.code: The lower half is stored negated, the upper half as is. If a number is bigger than the upper half's minimum, it goes up. Otherwise, it goes into the lower half. If the lower half gets two bigger, we move its max across. If the upper half gets two bigger, we move its min across. For the median, an even count means averaging the two tops. Otherwise, we read the bigger heap's top.
say.outro: Log n per insert, constant time per median. The pattern is two heaps. Use it whenever you need a running middle from a stream.

find-median-from-data-stream.title: Find Median From Data Stream

We define the MedianFinder class to hold the two halves of the data stream.
The constructor sets up the two empty heaps we will need.

We create small as an empty list, which will hold the lower half as negated numbers.
We create large as an empty list, which will hold the upper half in natural order.
The addNum method accepts one new number from the stream and stores it.

If the upper half exists and the number is bigger than its smallest value, the number belongs in the upper half.
We push the number onto the large min heap.
Otherwise the number belongs in the lower half, so we take the else branch.
We push the negated number onto small so the largest lower value stays on top.
This comment says we now rebalance so the heap sizes differ by at most one.
If small has more than one extra element compared with large, it is too heavy.
We pop the largest value from small and negate it back to its true value.
We push that value into large, moving the boundary element across.
Otherwise, if large has more than one extra element, it is too heavy.
We pop the smallest value from large, which is the lowest of the upper half.
We push its negation onto small, moving it into the lower half.
The findMedian method returns the median of all numbers added so far.
This comment explains the median is the top of the bigger heap or the average of both tops.
If small holds more elements, the median is its top, so the count is odd.
We negate the top of small to recover the real value and return it.
If large holds more elements, the count is odd and the middle lives in large.
We return the smallest value in large, which is the median.
When both heaps are equal in size, we average the two tops, negating small's top, to get the median.

subsets.hook: The purest backtracking problem: every element gets a yes or no decision.
subsets.ask: Given a list of distinct numbers, return every possible subset, including the empty set and the whole list. No subset may appear twice.
subsets.exampleWhy: Three numbers, each in or out, gives 2³ = 8 subsets.

brute.idea: Grow selections by adding any unused index in any order, then deduplicate by sorting each selection.
steps: From each selection, try adding every unused index
Record the sorted selection in a set
Turn the set into the answer list
brute.whySlow: Each subset of size k is built k! times. At n = 10 that is about 10 million paths for only 1,024 subsets.

optimal.insight: Order doesn't matter in a subset, so decide elements in index order: for each one, branch on include or exclude. Every leaf of that binary tree is a unique subset.
steps: dfs(i): decide about nums[i]
Include it, recurse on i + 1
Undo, exclude it, recurse on i + 1
At i = n, copy the current subset into the answer

codeNotes.note: Copy, or later pops erase it

pitfalls: Append subset.copy(), not subset — otherwise every entry is the same, emptied list.
There are 2^n subsets, so O(n·2^n) is optimal: output size forces it.

say.intro: Okay, Subsets. Given a list of distinct numbers, return every possible subset. That's everything from the empty set up to the whole list, with no repeats. For one, two, three, each number is either in or out. So we get two times two times two. Eight subsets.
say.brute: A naive way starts from nothing. Then it keeps adding any unused number, in any order. Each selection gets sorted and stored in a set, which removes repeats. It does find every subset. But here's the catch. It builds each subset many times over. At ten numbers, that's about ten million paths for roughly a thousand answers.
say.insight: A subset has no order. So why choose in every possible order? Instead, walk the numbers from left to right. For each one, make exactly one decision. Include it, or skip it. That gives a binary tree of depth n. And every leaf is a different subset. No duplicates, and no wasted work.
say.anim: We start with an empty result list and an empty subset, exploring include or exclude choices for each number. We include one, then two, then three, building subset one two three, which gets saved as a complete subset. Backtracking, we pop three off, keeping one and two, and save that smaller subset too. We backtrack further, excluding two, include three instead to get subset one three, saved to results. Popping again leaves just one alone, which also counts as a valid subset. Now we exclude one entirely, restart with two, then two three, then two alone, saving each. Excluding two as well, we try three alone, then the empty subset, finishing all branches. The final answer holds all eight subsets: full set down to the empty set.
say.code: Our helper decides about the number at index i. If i has reached the end, we've decided every element. That's a leaf. So we append a copy of the subset. Why a copy? Because later pops would erase it. Otherwise, branch one includes the number, and we recurse on i plus one. Then we pop it, to undo that choice. Branch two recurses on i plus one without it. We start from index zero.
say.outro: n times two to the n, which matches the size of the output. The pattern is backtracking. Include, recurse, undo, then exclude and recurse.

subsets.title: Subsets
subsets.optimalCode:
class Solution:
    def subsets(self, nums: List[int]) -> List[List[int]]:
        res = []

        subset = []

        def dfs(i):
            if i >= len(nums):
                res.append(subset.copy())
                return
            # decision to include nums[i]
            subset.append(nums[i])
            dfs(i + 1)
            # decision NOT to include nums[i]
            subset.pop()
            dfs(i + 1)

        dfs(0)
        return res
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which holds the method that LeetCode will call to generate the subsets.
The subsets method takes a list of distinct numbers and returns a list of lists, one for each subset.
We create res as an empty list that will collect every finished subset.
We create subset as an empty working list that tracks the choices made along the current path.
We define a recursive helper dfs, where i is the index of the element we are currently deciding on.
If i has reached the length of nums, every element has been decided, so we are at a leaf.
At a leaf we append a copy of subset to res, since subset keeps changing later.
We return to stop recursing and backtrack to the previous decision.
This comment marks the first branch, where we choose to include the current number.
We add nums at index i to subset, committing to include it on this branch.
We recurse with i plus one to decide on the remaining elements with that number included.
This comment marks the second branch, where we choose to leave the current number out.
We pop the last element, undoing the include choice so subset is back to its earlier state.
We recurse again with i plus one, now exploring every subset that excludes nums at index i.
We kick off the search by calling dfs at index zero with an empty subset.
We return res, which now holds all subsets, each produced by exactly one path of include or exclude choices.

combination-sum.hook: Unlimited reuse makes this tricky; one index trick keeps combinations from repeating.
combination-sum.ask: Given distinct positive candidates and a target, return every unique combination that sums to the target. A number may be used any number of times; order within a combination doesn't matter.
combination-sum.exampleWhy: 2+2+2+2, 2+3+3 and 3+5 all make 8; nothing else does.

brute.idea: Try every count for every candidate — from as many as fit down to zero — and keep combos whose sum hits the target.
steps: For candidate i, try each count up to target // c
Recurse to the next candidate
At the end, keep it if the sum equals target
brute.whySlow: It never stops early: with 30 candidates and target 40, the count combinations explode into the billions.

optimal.insight: Branch on: use candidates[i] again (stay at i), or never use it again (move to i + 1). Moving only forward prevents reordered duplicates; stop once the total overshoots.
steps: dfs(i, cur, total)
total == target: record a copy
Past the end or over target: stop
Include candidates[i] and stay at i
Undo, then skip to i + 1

codeNotes.match: if i >= len(candidates) or total > target:
codeNotes.note: Out of candidates or overshot: prune

pitfalls: Staying at i allows reuse; recursing with i + 1 everywhere would forbid it.
Sorting first lets you break the loop early once a candidate exceeds the remainder.

say.intro: Combination Sum. We get distinct positive numbers and a target. We list every combination that adds up to the target. And we can reuse any number as often as we like. With two, three, and five, and a target of eight, there are three answers. Four twos. Two, three, three. And three, five.
say.brute: The brute force tries every count of every number. Up to four twos, up to two threes, up to one five. Then it checks each complete combination's sum, only at the very end. So what's wrong? It never stops early. Even when the total is already too big, it keeps going. With many candidates, that explodes.
say.insight: Here's the trick. At each step, make a two way choice. Either use the current number again, and stay on it. Or decide never to use it again, and move right. Why does that help? We only ever move right. So the same combination can't show up in a different order. And once the total passes the target, we cut that branch.
say.anim: We start with candidates two, three, five and a target of eight. The code keeps reusing candidate two, building current list two, two, two, two until total hits eight. Total equals target, so two, two, two, two gets added to the results. Backtracking tries two, two, three, three, which also sums to eight and gets saved. Moving forward past two, the search tries two, three, five but overshoots past eight. Starting fresh from three, combination three, five sums exactly to eight and is added. Starting from five alone, five plus five overshoots eight, so that branch returns empty. Final answer: two,two,two,two; two,three,three; and three,five.
say.code: If the total equals the target, we've hit it. So we record a copy. If we ran out of candidates, or overshot, we prune and return. Otherwise, we add the current number and recurse on the same index. Staying at i is what allows reuse. Then we pop it, to backtrack. Finally, we recurse on the next index, with the same total. That means we never use this number again.
say.outro: Exponential in the worst case, but pruned hard. The pattern is backtracking. Stay on an index to reuse it. Move right to avoid duplicates.

combination-sum.title: Combination Sum
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container the interview platform expects for our method.
The combinationSum method takes the list of candidates and the target, and returns a list of combinations.
We start with an empty result list that will collect every valid combination we find.
We define a recursive helper called dfs that tracks the current index, the current combination, and its running total.
If the running total equals the target, we have found a valid combination.
We append a copy of the current combination to the results, so later changes to it do not affect the saved answer.
We return immediately, since adding more positive numbers could only overshoot the target.
We stop this branch if the index runs past the candidates or the total has exceeded the target.
In the first branch, we add the candidate at the current index to the current combination.
We recurse staying at the same index, so this candidate can be used again, and we add its value to the total.
We backtrack by removing that candidate, restoring the combination to its earlier state.
In the second branch, we move to the next index without using this candidate again, which avoids reordered duplicates.
We kick off the search from index zero with an empty combination and a total of zero.
After the search finishes, all valid combinations are stored in the result list.
We return the result list containing every unique combination that sums to the target.

combination-sum-ii.hook: Same as Combination Sum, but with duplicate inputs — the real test is skipping repeats.
combination-sum-ii.ask: Given candidates that may contain duplicates and a target, return every unique combination summing to the target. Each element can be used at most once, and no combination may repeat.
combination-sum-ii.exampleWhy: Sorted: 1,2,2,2,5. 1+2+2 = 5 and 5 alone. Picking different 2s must not produce repeats.

brute.idea: Sort, try every subset with a bitmask, keep those summing to target, and dedupe with a set.
steps: Sort the candidates
Enumerate all 2^n subsets
Keep sum == target; dedupe with a set
Sort the unique combos
brute.whySlow: With 100 candidates there are 2^100 subsets — and many are duplicates thrown away after building them.

optimal.insight: Sort so equal values sit together. At each level, try each distinct value once: skipping a value equal to the one just tried kills duplicate branches before they start.
steps: Sort the candidates
backtrack(cur, pos, target)
Loop i from pos; skip if same as previous value tried
Take candidates[i], recurse with i + 1
Prune when target goes to zero or below

codeNotes.note: Same value at this level: skip

pitfalls: Skip duplicates per level, not globally — [1,1,6] uses both 1s legitimately.
Forgetting to sort makes the prev check useless.

say.intro: Combination Sum Two. This time the input can have duplicates. And each element can be used at most once. With two, five, two, one, two, and a target of five, there are two answers. One, two, two. And five on its own. Picking different twos must not create repeated answers.
say.brute: The brute force sorts the numbers first. Then it tries every subset using a bitmask. It keeps the ones that hit the target, and throws them into a set to remove duplicates. That's two to the n subsets. And lots of duplicate combinations get fully built, only to be thrown away.
say.insight: So how do we stop duplicates before they happen? Sort first, so equal numbers sit side by side. Now, at each level of the search, try each distinct value only once. If the next candidate equals the one we just tried, it would grow the exact same branch. So we skip it. Duplicates never even get generated.
say.anim: The array is sorted into one, two, two, two, five, so duplicates sit together. We start exploring with one, then add two and another two, remaining drops to zero. One, two, two sums to five, so that combination is saved into results. Backtracking undoes choices, skips the duplicate two, and tries one plus five, which overshoots. Next the search starts fresh with two, building two, two, two, which overshoots target too. Skipping repeated twos avoids duplicate branches, then two plus five also overshoots remaining. At the top level duplicate twos are skipped, leaving just five to try alone. Five alone equals target, giving final answer one two two and five.
say.code: First, we sort the candidates, so duplicates become neighbours. When the remaining target hits zero, we record a copy. Below zero, we just stop. Then we loop over the candidates. If a value equals prev, the one we just tried at this level, we skip it. Otherwise, we add it and recurse from i plus one. That way, each element is used once. After we pop it, we remember it as prev.
say.outro: Exponential in the worst case, but no duplicate work. The pattern is backtracking with sort and skip. Use it whenever the input has repeats.

combination-sum-ii.title: Combination Sum II
combination-sum-ii.optimalCode:
class Solution:
    def combinationSum2(self, candidates: List[int], target: int) -> List[List[int]]:
        # 1. Sort so equal values sit together
        candidates.sort()

        result = []

        def backtrack(current, start, remaining):
            # 2. Found a valid combination
            if remaining == 0:
                result.append(current.copy())
                return
            if remaining < 0:
                return

            previous = -1
            # 3. Try each distinct value once at this level
            for i in range(start, len(candidates)):
                if candidates[i] == previous:
                    continue
                # 4. Take candidates[i], recurse, then undo the choice
                current.append(candidates[i])
                backtrack(current, i + 1, remaining - candidates[i])
                current.pop()
                previous = candidates[i]

        backtrack([], 0, target)
        return result
lineNotes: We define the Solution class that holds our method for solving the combination sum problem.
The method takes the candidate numbers and a target, and returns a list of unique combinations that hit the target.
This comment says we sort first so that equal values end up sitting next to each other.
We sort the candidates in place, which makes duplicate detection a simple comparison with the previous value.
We create an empty result list that will collect every valid combination we find.
We define a helper called backtrack that tracks the current combination, the starting index, and the remaining amount needed.
This comment marks the base case where a valid combination has been found.
If the remaining amount is exactly zero, the current combination sums to the target.
We append a copy of the current combination to the result so later changes do not alter it.
We return immediately since no further numbers should be added to a completed combination.
If the remaining amount has gone negative, we have overshot the target.
We return to abandon this branch, since adding more positive numbers cannot fix the overshoot.
We set previous to negative one as a sentinel meaning no value has been tried yet at this level.
This comment explains that at each level we try each distinct value only once.
We loop over indices from start to the end, so each element is used at most once per combination.
If this value equals the one we just tried at this level, it would repeat an identical branch.
We skip it with continue, which prunes the duplicate branch before it begins.
This comment says we take the candidate, recurse, then undo the choice.
We add the current candidate to the combination, choosing it for this position.
We recurse starting at the next index, with the remaining amount reduced by the chosen value.
We pop the candidate off the combination to undo the choice and restore the earlier state.
We record this value as previous so any equal value following it at this level gets skipped.
We kick off the search with an empty combination, starting index zero, and the full target remaining.
We return the result list holding all unique combinations that sum to the target.

permutations.hook: Every ordering of a list — a backtracking classic you must write in two minutes.
permutations.ask: Given a list of distinct numbers, return every possible ordering of them. Any order of the answers is accepted.
permutations.exampleWhy: Three distinct numbers have 3! = 6 orderings, and each appears exactly once.

brute.idea: Build every length-n sequence allowing repeats, filling positions from the back, then keep only sequences with no repeated value.
steps: Fill each slot with any of the n values
Try values rotating after the last one placed
Keep sequences whose values are all distinct
brute.whySlow: n^n grows far faster than n!: at n = 6 that is 46,656 sequences for only 720 answers.

optimal.insight: A permutation is one element followed by a permutation of the rest. Take each element out in turn, permute the rest recursively, and append the removed element.
steps: Base case: one number has one permutation
Pop the first number n
Recursively permute the remaining numbers
Append n to each of those, add to result
Put n back at the end, rotating the list

codeNotes.note: Restore it at the back: list rotates

pitfalls: The usual alternative: backtrack with a used array or swaps — know one by heart.
Return copies; reusing the same list object corrupts results.

say.intro: Permutations. Given a list of distinct numbers, return every possible ordering, each exactly once. For one, two, three, that's three factorial. Six orderings. And any order of the answers is fine.
say.brute: A blunt brute force fills every slot with any number, repeats allowed. Then it throws away sequences that repeat a value. The problem? That's n to the n sequences, not n factorial. At six numbers, that's over forty six thousand candidates. And we keep just seven hundred and twenty of them.
say.insight: Think about it recursively. Every permutation is some first choice, plus a permutation of what's left. So take each number out in turn. Ask for all permutations of the rest. Then attach the removed number to each one. Here's a neat bit. Putting the number back at the end rotates the list. So the next loop picks a different number. No used array needed.
say.anim: We start with nums equal to one, two, three, and an empty result list. We pop out the first element, one, leaving nums as two, three to permute recursively. Recursion keeps pulling out elements, like two, until only one number remains as the base case. Each returned permutation gets the removed number appended, building three, two, one first. Rotating nums and repeating, we also build two, three, one before combining with one. Appending one to each sub permutation gives three, two, one and two, three, one in the result. The process repeats for three as the removed element, generating two, one, three and one, two, three. Finally all six permutations are returned, matching the expected full permutation list.
say.code: The base case is easy. One number means one permutation. Otherwise, we loop once per number. We take the front number out. Then we recursively get all permutations of the rest. To each of those, we append the number we removed. We add them all to the result. Finally, we put the number back at the end. That's what rotates the list for the next round.
say.outro: n factorial times n, which matches the size of the output. The pattern is backtracking. Choose one number, solve the rest, and combine the results.

permutations.title: Permutations
permutations.optimalCode:
class Solution:
    def permute(self, nums: List[int]) -> List[List[int]]:
        result = []

        # 1. Base case: only one number, only one permutation
        if len(nums) == 1:
            return [nums[:]]

        # 2. Try each number as the one we pull out
        for i in range(len(nums)):
            first = nums.pop(0)

            # 3. Recursively permute the rest of the numbers
            remaining_perms = self.permute(nums)

            # 4. Append the removed number to each of those permutations
            for perm in remaining_perms:
                perm.append(first)
            result.extend(remaining_perms)

            # 5. Put the number back at the end, rotating the list
            nums.append(first)

        return result
lineNotes: This defines the Solution class that holds our permutation method, as the problem platform expects.
The permute method takes a list of distinct numbers and returns a list of all their orderings.
We start with an empty result list that will collect every permutation we build.
This comment says the base case is a single number, which has exactly one permutation.
We check whether nums has just one element, which stops the recursion.
We return a list holding a copy of nums, so callers can safely modify it later.
This comment says we will try every number as the one we pull out.
We loop once for each position, so every element gets a turn as the removed one.
We pop the front number off nums and call it first, leaving the rest behind.
This comment says we now permute the remaining numbers recursively.
We call permute on the shortened nums to get all orderings of the remaining numbers.
This comment says the removed number gets attached to each smaller permutation.
