subsets-ii.hook: Subsets with duplicate values — learn the skip trick that removes repeats at the source.
subsets-ii.ask: Given numbers that may contain duplicates, return every possible subset, but with no duplicate subsets. Two subsets with the same values count as the same.
subsets-ii.exampleWhy: Choosing the first 2 or the second 2 gives the same subset, so only 6 unique subsets, not 8.

brute.idea: Sort, generate all 2^n subsets by bitmask, and keep only the ones not seen before.
steps: Sort the numbers
Enumerate all 2^n masks
Build each subset; skip if already seen
brute.whySlow: Ten equal numbers give only 11 distinct subsets, but it still builds all 1,024 and throws most away.

optimal.insight: Sort. When you decide to exclude a value, exclude all its copies at once: skip ahead past equal neighbours. Then each multiset is generated exactly once.
steps: Sort so duplicates are adjacent
Include nums[i], recurse on i + 1
Undo; skip every copy of nums[i]
Recurse on the first different value

codeNotes.note: Record a copy at a leaf

codeNotes.match: while i + 1 < len(nums) and nums[i] == nums[i + 1]:

pitfalls: Sort first — the skip only works when duplicates are adjacent.
Skip only on the exclude branch; the include branch may still take the next copy.

say.intro: Subsets Two. It's the same as Subsets, but now the input can have duplicates. And we must never return the same subset twice. One, two, two would give eight subsets by position. But two pairs of them are identical. So we get six unique subsets.
say.brute: The brute force sorts, then builds every subset with a bitmask. It keeps a set of subsets it has already seen, and skips repeats. Correct? Sure. But it's wasteful. Ten equal numbers have just eleven distinct subsets. Yet this builds over a thousand of them, and throws almost all away.
say.insight: Sort first, so equal values sit together. Now, where do duplicates come from? The exclude branch. Skipping the first two but taking the second looks exactly like taking the first. So here's the fix. When we exclude a value, we exclude every copy of it at once. We jump past all its equal neighbours. That one skip removes every duplicate.
say.anim: We start by sorting the array into one, two, two, then begin backtracking from an empty list. The algorithm always tries including the current number first, building up one, then one two, then one two two. At index three we've used every element, so one two two gets saved as a complete subset. Now we backtrack and try excluding instead, skipping past duplicate twos to avoid repeats, giving us one two. Excluding the second element too, skipping its duplicate, leaves just one, which also gets recorded. Back at index zero we try excluding the first one entirely, moving on to just the twos. Including both twos gives two two, then excluding the second duplicate gives just two, both saved. Finally skipping both twos together, thanks to the duplicate skip rule, leaves the empty set. The final answer is one two two, one two, one, two two, two, and the empty list.
say.code: First, we sort, so duplicates become neighbours. At a leaf, when i reaches the end, we record a copy of the subset. Otherwise, we include this value and recurse on i plus one, then pop it. Now the exclude side. We advance i while the next value equals this one. That skips every equal copy. Then we continue with the next decision, starting from the first different value.
say.outro: n times two to the n in the worst case. The pattern is backtracking with sorting, skipping duplicates on the exclude branch. It pairs nicely with Combination Sum Two.

subsets-ii.title: Subsets II
subsets-ii.optimalCode:
class Solution:
    def subsetsWithDup(self, nums: List[int]) -> List[List[int]]:
        result = []
        nums.sort()

        def backtrack(index, current):
            if index == len(nums):
                result.append(current[:])
                return

            # 1. Include nums[index] and recurse
            current.append(nums[index])
            backtrack(index + 1, current)
            current.pop()

            # 2. Exclude nums[index]; skip all its duplicates
            next_index = index
            while next_index + 1 < len(nums) and nums[next_index] == nums[next_index + 1]:
                next_index += 1

            # 3. Recurse on the first different value
            backtrack(next_index + 1, current)

        backtrack(0, [])
        return result
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container the interview platform expects for our method.
This method takes a list of numbers that may contain duplicates and returns all unique subsets.
We start with an empty result list that will collect every unique subset we build.
We sort the numbers so that equal values sit next to each other, which makes skipping duplicates easy.
We define a recursive helper called backtrack that takes the current index and the subset built so far.
When the index reaches the length of nums, we have decided on every element and hold a complete subset.
We append a copy of the current subset to the result, so later changes do not alter the saved one.
We return to stop recursing, since there are no more elements to decide on.
This comment introduces the first branch, where we choose to include the number at the current index.
We add the number at the current index to the current subset, committing to include it.
We recurse on the next index to decide about the remaining numbers with this number included.
We pop the number off so the current subset goes back to its earlier state for the exclude branch.
This comment introduces the second branch, where we exclude this value and all of its copies together.
We set next_index to the current index as the starting point for scanning past equal values.
While the next number exists and equals the one at next_index, we are still inside a run of duplicates.
We advance next_index by one so it ends on the last copy of the repeated value.
This comment says we now continue from the first number that differs from the excluded value.
We recurse from just past the last duplicate, so excluding one copy means excluding all, which prevents repeated subsets.
We kick off the search at index zero with an empty current subset.
We return the result, which now holds every unique subset exactly once.
subsets-ii.optimalCodeOriginal:
class Solution:
    def subsetsWithDup(self, nums: List[int]) -> List[List[int]]:
        res = []
        nums.sort()

        def backtrack(i, subset):
            if i == len(nums):
                res.append(subset[::])
                return

            # All subsets that include nums[i]
            subset.append(nums[i])
            backtrack(i + 1, subset)
            subset.pop()
            # All subsets that don't include nums[i]
            while i + 1 < len(nums) and nums[i] == nums[i + 1]:
                i += 1
            backtrack(i + 1, subset)

        backtrack(0, [])
        return res

generate-parentheses.hook: Generate only valid strings — two counters prune every bad branch before it grows.
generate-parentheses.ask: Given n, return every string of n pairs of parentheses that is well formed: every closing bracket matches an earlier opening one.
generate-parentheses.exampleWhy: With three pairs there are exactly five balanced strings.

brute.idea: Build every string of length 2n from open and close brackets, then check each one for balance.
steps: Generate all 2^(2n) bracket strings
Repeatedly delete "()" pairs from each
Keep strings that reduce to empty
brute.whySlow: At n = 8 that is 65,536 strings to check for only 1,430 valid ones.

optimal.insight: A prefix stays valid while opens ≤ n and closes ≤ opens. Add '(' only if open < n, ')' only if closed < open; every path ends valid.
steps: Track open and closed counts
Add '(' if open < n
Add ')' if closed < open
When both equal n, record the string

codeNotes.note: Used all pairs: a valid string
A close has something to match

pitfalls: The count is the nth Catalan number, about 4^n/(n·sqrt(n)) — say so for complexity.
Using a shared list then joining avoids building many intermediate strings.

say.intro: Generate Parentheses. Given a number n, list every well formed string of n bracket pairs. Well formed means every close bracket matches an earlier open one. For three pairs, there are exactly five such strings. The first is three opens, then three closes.
say.brute: The brute force builds every string of six brackets. That's sixty four of them. Then it checks each one for balance at the end. But most of those strings are invalid. At eight pairs, it checks sixty five thousand strings. And only about fourteen hundred of them are valid.
say.insight: What if we never built an invalid prefix in the first place? Keep two counts: opens used, and closes used. You can add an open while opens are below n. You can add a close only while closes are below opens. Why does that work? Every close always has an open to match. Follow those two rules, and every path ends in a valid string.
say.anim: We start with n equal to three and an empty result list to collect valid combinations. The algorithm greedily adds open parentheses first, building up to three opens before any closes. Once opens reach three, it adds closing brackets, completing the first valid string, three opens then three closes. It backtracks, undoing choices, then tries closing earlier to explore new branches like open open close open close close. The recursion keeps balancing opens and closes, only closing when it won't exceed the open count, finding open open close close open close. Further backtracking explores open close open open close close, then open close open close open close, each a new valid pattern. All branches are exhausted once opens and closes balance out at three each in every remaining path. The final result holds five valid combinations: open open open close close close, open open close open close close, open open close close open close, open close open open close close, and open close open close open close.
say.code: When opens and closes both equal n, we've used every pair. So we join the stack and record the string. If opens are still below n, there are opens left to place. We push an open, recurse, and pop. If closes are below opens, a close has something to match. So we push a close, recurse, and pop it to undo the choice. We start with zero of each.
say.outro: The work grows with the number of valid strings, the Catalan numbers. The pattern is backtracking, with rules that prune bad branches early.

generate-parentheses.title: Generate Parentheses
generate-parentheses.optimalCode:
class Solution:
    def generateParenthesis(self, n: int) -> List[str]:
        result = []
        current = []

        def backtrack(openCount, closedCount):
            # Base case: used n open and n closed, so the string is complete
            if openCount == n and closedCount == n:
                result.append("".join(current))
                return

            # Add an open bracket if we have not used all n of them
            if openCount < n:
                current.append("(")
                backtrack(openCount + 1, closedCount)
                current.pop()

            # Add a close bracket only if it would still match an open one
            if closedCount < openCount:
                current.append(")")
                backtrack(openCount, closedCount + 1)
                current.pop()

        backtrack(0, 0)
        return result
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container for our method as the problem expects.
The method generateParenthesis takes n, the number of pairs, and returns a list of well formed strings.
We start with an empty result list that will collect every finished valid string.
We keep current as a list of characters, the string we are building one bracket at a time.
We define a helper backtrack that tracks how many open and closed brackets we have placed so far.
This comment says that once we have used n opens and n closes, the string is complete.
We check whether both counts equal n, which means current is a full valid combination.
We join the characters in current into one string and save it in result.
We return so this path stops and the search goes back to try other choices.
This comment says we may add an open bracket only while we have not used all n.
We check that openCount is still less than n before placing another open bracket.
We append an open bracket to current to extend the prefix.
We recurse with openCount increased by one, exploring everything that can follow this choice.
We pop the open bracket off current to undo the choice so we can try the other branch.
This comment says a close bracket is allowed only if it matches an earlier unmatched open one.
We check that closedCount is less than openCount, so the prefix never has more closes than opens.
We append a close bracket to current to extend the prefix.
We recurse with closedCount increased by one, exploring all completions after this close bracket.
We pop the close bracket to backtrack and restore current for the caller.
We start the search with an empty string, so both counts begin at zero.
We return result, which now holds every well formed combination of n pairs.

word-search.hook: Grid DFS with backtracking: walk the word letter by letter and undo your steps.
word-search.ask: Given a grid of letters and a word, return true if the word can be traced through adjacent cells, moving up, down, left or right, without using any cell twice.
word-search.exampleWhy: A B C across the top, down to C, down to E, left to D.

brute.idea: From every start cell, walk every path of word length through unused neighbours, and only compare letters once the path is complete.
steps: Start at every cell
Extend the path in all four directions
At full length, compare the path to the word
brute.whySlow: Same worst-case bound as the optimal, but it never prunes: each path is walked to full length before any letter is compared.

optimal.insight: Check the letter at each step: the moment a cell doesn't match word[i], abandon that path. Mark cells on the current path and unmark when backtracking.
steps: Try every cell as a start
dfs(r, c, i): fail if off-grid, wrong letter, or used
Mark the cell, try four neighbours with i + 1
Unmark on the way back

codeNotes.note: Mark: no reuse on this path

pitfalls: Unmark the cell after exploring, or other paths can't use it.
Reversing the word to start from the rarer letter avoids worst-case timeouts.

say.intro: Okay, Word Search. We get a grid of letters and a word. Can we trace the word through neighbouring cells? We move up, down, left, or right, and never reuse a cell. Here, A B C C E D works. Across the top, down twice, then one step left. So we return true.
say.brute: The brute force walks every path of the word's length, from every cell. Only at the very end does it check the letters. On paper, its worst case matches the optimal. But here's the catch. It pays that worst case every time. Even on paths that went wrong at the very first letter.
say.insight: So check as you go. At each step, we know exactly which letter we need next. Wrong letter? Abandon that path right away. We also keep a set of cells on the current path, so we never reuse one. And when we back up, we remove the cell. That way, other paths can still use it. That's backtracking.
say.anim: We start searching the grid for the word ABCCED, scanning every cell as a start. At row zero col zero we find letter A matching word index zero, so we mark it. Neighbors up and down are tried, but only moving right finds B at index one. The path continues right to C, down to C again, then down to E, marking each cell. From there moving right to D completes the word, since index six equals word length. Each recursive call returns true, unwinding and removing cells back up the call stack. All marks are cleared and the final result bubbles up as true. The function returns True, confirming ABCCED exists in the board.
say.code: In the search, if the index reaches the end of the word, we matched every letter. Return true. Off the grid, on a used cell, or the wrong letter? Prune, and return false. Otherwise, we mark the cell, try all four neighbours, then free the cell again. One trick before searching. If the first letter is more common than the last, we reverse the word. So we start from the rarer end.
say.outro: Grid size times four to the word length, in the worst case. The pattern is backtracking on a grid. Mark, explore, then unmark.

word-search.title: Word Search
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container this problem's method lives in.
The exist method takes the board and the word, and returns true if the word can be traced.
We store the number of rows in the board for later boundary checks.
We store the number of columns, using the first row, for the same boundary checks.
We create an empty set called path to remember which cells are used on the current path.
This comment explains that dfs tries to match the word from index i starting at a given cell.
We define dfs, which takes a row, a column, and the index i of the letter we need next.
If i equals the length of the word, every letter has matched, so we have found the word.
We return true here to signal success back up through the recursion.
If the row or column falls outside the board, this path has walked off the grid.
We return false because there is no cell to match there.
If this cell is already in path, we would be reusing a cell, which is not allowed.

If the cell's letter does not match the needed letter at index i, this path cannot work.
We return false immediately, pruning the search the moment a letter mismatches.
This comment says we mark the current cell as used while exploring from it.
We add the current row and column to path so deeper calls cannot reuse it.

First we try moving down one row, looking for the next letter at index i plus one.
If that fails, we try moving up one row with the same next index.
If that fails too, we try moving one column to the right.
Finally we try moving one column to the left, and the group of options ends.
We close the parenthesis, so found now holds whether any direction completed the word.
This comment explains that we unmark the cell when backtracking so other paths may use it.
We remove the current cell from path, restoring the state before we explored it.
We return found, telling the caller whether this branch led to a full match.
This comment says we try every cell on the board as a possible starting point.
We loop over every row index of the board.
Inside that, we loop over every column index to visit each cell.
We start dfs at this cell with index zero, checking whether the whole word can be built from here.
If any start succeeds, we return true right away.
If no starting cell leads to a match, we return false at the end.

palindrome-partitioning.hook: Cut a string every possible way — but only keep cutting after palindromic pieces.
palindrome-partitioning.ask: Given a string, split it into pieces so that every piece reads the same forwards and backwards. Return every possible way to do that.
palindrome-partitioning.exampleWhy: "aa" and "bb" are palindromes, single letters always are; "aab" or "abb" are not.

brute.idea: Generate every way to cut the string into pieces, then keep only the partitions where all pieces are palindromes.
steps: Choose every possible first piece
Recurse on the rest, building all 2^(n-1) partitions
At the end, check every piece
brute.whySlow: Same O(n·2^n) worst case (a string of all a's), but it always builds all 32,768 partitions at n = 16, even after a bad first piece.

optimal.insight: Choose the first piece, but only recurse if that piece is a palindrome. Invalid branches die at the first bad piece instead of being built and checked later.
steps: dfs(i): partitions of s[i:]
Try every end j for the next piece
If s[i..j] is a palindrome, take it and recurse at j + 1
At the end of the string, record a copy

codeNotes.note: Backtrack to try a longer piece

pitfalls: Precomputing a palindrome table with DP makes each check O(1).
Append part.copy(); appending part itself records an empty list later.

say.intro: Palindrome Partitioning. We split a string into pieces where every piece is a palindrome. And we return every way to do it. For a a b b, there are four ways. All single letters. The two bs joined. The two as joined. Or both pairs joined.
say.brute: The brute force cuts the string in every possible way. That's two to the n minus one partitions. Only then does it check every piece. Its worst case matches the optimal, since a string of identical letters makes every split valid. But on normal strings, it still builds them all. Even when the first piece was never a palindrome.
say.insight: So check each piece as you cut it. From position i, try every possible next piece. Not a palindrome? Don't go any deeper. If it is, take it, and solve the rest of the string recursively. Now here's the nice part. Every path that reaches the end is automatically valid. No final check needed.
say.anim: We start with the string aabb, splitting it into every possible set of palindrome pieces. At index zero, single letter a is checked and confirmed a palindrome, so it gets added. Now part holds a and a, continuing deeper since each piece is palindromic. Single letters b and b pass too, building part into a, a, b, b, a full partition. We reached the end, so a, a, b, b is saved into results. Backtracking, the code tries merging bb as one palindrome piece, saving a, a, bb. Further back, starting fresh with aa as one piece, it then finds b, b and aa, bb too. Checks like a versus b fail palindrome tests, so those branches are skipped early. Final answer: all four valid partitions, a a b b, a a bb, aa b b, and aa bb.
say.code: If i has reached the end, we've used the whole string. So we record a copy of the parts. Otherwise, we try every possible end j for the next piece. If s from i to j is a palindrome, we append it and recurse from j plus one. Then we pop it, so we can try a longer piece. The palindrome check itself uses two pointers. They move inward, comparing as they go.
say.outro: n times two to the n in the worst case. The pattern is backtracking. Prune each choice before you recurse on it.

letter-combinations-of-a-phone-number.hook: Old phone keypads meet backtracking: one letter per digit, every combination.
letter-combinations-of-a-phone-number.ask: Each digit from 2 to 9 maps to letters, like a phone keypad. Given a string of digits, return every letter string you could type, one letter per digit.
letter-combinations-of-a-phone-number.exampleWhy: 2 is a, b or c; 3 is d, e or f: 3 x 3 = 9 combinations.

brute.idea: Pool the letters of all the digits, try every string of the right length from that pool, and keep those where each letter belongs to its digit.
steps: Pool every digit's letters together
Build every length-n string from the pool
Keep strings where each letter matches its digit
brute.whySlow: With 4 digits the pool has up to 16 letters: 65,536 strings for at most 256 answers.

optimal.insight: Only ever try the letters of the current digit. Position i has 3 or 4 choices, so the search tree is exactly the answer tree.
steps: backtrack(i, curStr)
If curStr is full length, record it
For each letter of digits[i], recurse on i + 1
Empty input returns an empty list

codeNotes.note: Typo q before p: output order only
New string, so no undo needed

pitfalls: Empty digits must return [], not [""].
7 and 9 have four letters, so the bound is 4^n, not 3^n.

say.intro: Letter Combinations of a Phone Number. Each digit from two to nine maps to letters, like an old phone keypad. Given some digits, return every letter string you could type. Two, three gives nine combinations. They run from a d through to c f.
say.brute: A blunt brute force pools all the letters from all the digits. It tries every string of the right length from that pool. Then it keeps the ones where each letter belongs to its digit. With four digits, that's about sixty five thousand strings. And there are at most two hundred fifty six real answers.
say.insight: Here's the thing. Why ever consider a letter the current digit can't produce? At position i, only branch on that digit's three or four letters. Now every leaf of the search tree is a valid answer. Nothing gets thrown away. So the total work is just proportional to the size of the output.
say.anim: We start with digits two three and build a map from digits to their letters. Backtracking begins at position zero with an empty string so far. At position zero we try letter a, then move to position one with curStr a. Adding letter d gives ad, which is length two, so it's saved to results. Back at position one, we try e and f, adding ae and af to results. Now we try letter b, pairing it with d, e, and f to get bd, be, bf. Finally letter c combines with d, e, and f, adding cd, ce, and cf. The final answer is ad, ae, af, bd, be, bf, cd, ce, and cf.
say.code: We store the keypad in a dictionary. One quirk: seven is typed as q, p, r, s. That only changes the output order. With one letter per digit, we record the string. Otherwise, we loop over just this digit's letters. For each one, we recurse with the next index and the longer string. That's a brand new string, so no undo is needed. And if the input is empty, we return an empty list.
say.outro: n times four to the n. The pattern is backtracking. Branch only on the valid choices, and every leaf is an answer.

n-queens.hook: Place n queens so none attack each other: the textbook case for pruning a search tree early.
n-queens.ask: Put n queens on an n by n chessboard so no two share a row, column, or diagonal. Return every valid board, each row written as a string of dots with one Q.
n-queens.exampleWhy: On a 4 by 4 board exactly two layouts work, and they are mirror images of each other.

brute.idea: Each row holds one queen in a different column, so try every column ordering (n! of them), then check all row pairs for a shared diagonal.
steps: Generate every permutation of the columns
Check each pair of rows for a diagonal clash
Keep permutations with no clash as boards
brute.whySlow: It finishes boards already doomed at row two. For n = 9 that is 362,880 boards, each checked pair by pair.

optimal.insight: Place queens row by row and abandon a square the moment it is attacked. Three sets (columns, r+c, r-c) make the attack check O(1).
steps: Go row by row, trying each column c
Skip c if its column or either diagonal is already taken
Mark column, r+c and r-c, place Q, recurse into the next row
Undo the marks and the Q when the recursion returns
Reaching row n means a full solution: copy the board

say.intro: Okay, N Queens. We place n queens on an n by n chessboard, so no two attack each other. Then we return every valid board. With four queens on a four by four board, there are exactly two answers. And they're mirror images of each other.
say.brute: Let's start with brute force. Every row needs exactly one queen. And no two queens can share a column. So we try every ordering of the columns. That's n factorial boards. For each one, we check every pair of rows for a diagonal clash. It's correct. But it happily finishes boards that were already broken at row two.
say.insight: So check as you go. Place queens one row at a time. The moment a square is attacked, skip it, and never explore below it. How do we make that check instant? Three sets. Used columns, used r plus c values, and used r minus c values. Why those? Every square on one diagonal shares the same value.
say.anim: We start with an empty four by four board and empty tracking sets for attacks. A queen is placed at row zero column zero, recording its column and diagonals. Backtracking tries columns in row two, skipping any attacked by placed queens. Placing queens hits a dead end, so the algorithm removes queens and backtracks upward. A full valid arrangement is found and saved as the first solution string. Backtracking continues exploring other branches, finding a second complete valid placement. The search resumes from earlier rows, testing remaining column possibilities before finishing. Final answer returned: two solutions, each showing queens safely placed on the board.
say.code: We keep three sets: columns, plus one for each diagonal direction. Along one, r plus c stays constant. Along the other, r minus c does. If the row equals n, every row is filled, so we record a copy of the board. Otherwise, we try each column. Attacked? Skip it. Safe? Mark all three sets, place the queen, and solve the next row. Then unmark, so the next column starts clean.
say.outro: Roughly n factorial time, and n squared space for the board. The pattern is backtracking. Choose, explore, un-choose, and cut dead branches early.

n-queens.optimalCode:
class Solution:
    def solveNQueens(self, n: int) -> List[List[str]]:
        columns = set()
        diagonal_sum = set()
        diagonal_diff = set()
        result = []
        board = []
        for i in range(n):
            board.append(["."] * n)

        def backtrack(row):
            # 1. If we placed a queen in every row, save a copy of the board
            if row == n:
                solution = []
                for boardRow in board:
                    solution.append("".join(boardRow))
                result.append(solution)
                return

            # 2. Try each column in this row
            for col in range(n):
                diagSum = row + col
                diagDiff = row - col
                # 3. Skip this square if it is attacked by a placed queen
                if col in columns or diagSum in diagonal_sum or diagDiff in diagonal_diff:
                    continue

                # 4. Place the queen, mark its lines, and recurse into the next row
                columns.add(col)
                diagonal_sum.add(diagSum)
                diagonal_diff.add(diagDiff)
                board[row][col] = "Q"

                backtrack(row + 1)

                # 5. Undo the placement before trying the next column
                columns.remove(col)
                diagonal_sum.remove(diagSum)
                diagonal_diff.remove(diagDiff)
                board[row][col] = "."

        backtrack(0)
        return result

class Solution:
    def solveNQueens(self, n: int) -> List[List[str]]:
        col = set()
        posDiag = set()  # (r + c)
        negDiag = set()  # (r - c)

        res = []
        board = [["."] * n for i in range(n)]

        def backtrack(r):
            if r == n:
                copy = ["".join(row) for row in board]
                res.append(copy)
                return

            for c in range(n):
                if c in col or (r + c) in posDiag or (r - c) in negDiag:

                posDiag.add(r + c)
                negDiag.add(r - c)
                board[r][c] = "Q"

                backtrack(r + 1)

                col.remove(c)
                posDiag.remove(r + c)
                negDiag.remove(r - c)
                board[r][c] = "."

        backtrack(0)
        return res

say.intro: Implement Trie, also called a prefix tree. We support three operations. Insert a word. Search for an exact word. And starts with, which asks if any stored word begins with a prefix. In our example, app is just a prefix of apple. That is, until we insert app itself.
say.brute: The simplest version keeps a plain list of words. Insert just appends. Search compares the query against every stored word. Starts with checks the beginning of every word. So what's the problem? Each query costs the number of words times their length. With tens of thousands of calls, that's hundreds of millions of character comparisons.
say.insight: Notice that apple and app share their first three letters. So why store them twice? Store letters, not words. Build a tree where each node is one letter. Words with a common prefix share the same path. Now a query just walks its own letters from the root. The cost depends on the word's length. Never on how many words exist.
say.anim: We start by creating the trie root node, an empty container with twenty six child slots. Inserting apple, we walk each letter, creating new nodes for a, p, p, l, e as needed. After insertion, the final e node is marked end true, meaning apple is a complete word. Searching apple walks the same path letter by letter, reaching the e node marked end, so it returns true. Searching app follows a, p, p but that node's end is false, so it returns false. StartsWith app just checks the path exists without checking end, so it returns true. Inserting app again marks that same p node's end flag true, completing the word app. Now searching app walks to that node, finds end true, and the final output matches null, null, true, false, true, null, true.
say.code: Each node has twenty six child slots, one per letter. It also has an end flag, marking where a full word ends. Insert walks the word, turning each letter into a slot index. Missing child? We create it. Then we mark the end. Search does the same walk, then returns the end flag, since a word must end there. Starts with is the same walk. If the path exists, that's enough, so we return true.
say.outro: Every operation runs in time proportional to the word length. The pattern is the trie. Whenever a problem talks about prefixes, reach for one.

say.intro: Design Add and Search Words. We store words, then search for them. But the search can contain dots, and a dot matches any single letter. We add bad, dad, and mad. Searching pad fails. Bad succeeds. Dot a d matches three words. And b dot dot matches bad.
say.brute: The brute force keeps a plain list. To search, we loop over every stored word. We skip any with a different length. Then we compare letter by letter, letting a dot match anything. It works. But every search touches every word. Even when the first letter could have ruled almost all of them out.
say.insight: So put the words in a trie, and shared prefixes get stored once. A normal letter just follows one child. Now, what about a dot? We don't know which letter it stands for. So we try every child, and recurse on the rest of the query. If any branch ends on a word, the answer is true. And queries have at most two dots, so the branching stays small.

Searching b dot dot follows b, then dots match a and d, confirming a word, so the final results are false, true, true, true.
say.code: Adding a word is a standard trie insert. We grow nodes for missing letters, then mark the last one as a word. Search uses a helper that matches the word from an index, starting at a node. say.outro: Linear time for plain words, with branching only at the dots. The pattern is a trie plus depth first search. It's great for any wildcard matching.

max-area-of-island.hook: Number of Islands with one change: the flood fill now returns a size instead of nothing.
max-area-of-island.ask: A grid has 1s for land and 0s for water. An island is land connected up, down, left or right. Its area is its number of cells. Return the largest area, or 0 if there is no land.
max-area-of-island.exampleWhy: Islands have areas 3, 4 and 1. The right-hand island has four cells, so the answer is 4.

brute.idea: From every land cell, run a fresh flood fill with its own visited set to measure that cell's island, and keep the maximum.
steps: For every land cell
Flood-fill its island from scratch
Area = cells reached; keep the biggest
brute.whySlow: A 50 by 50 grid of all land floods 2,500 cells from each of 2,500 starts: over six million steps.

optimal.insight: Share one visited set across all floods. Each island is then measured exactly once: DFS returns 1 for the cell plus the areas returned by its four neighbours.
steps: Scan every cell, calling DFS on it
DFS returns 0 for water, out of bounds, or visited
Otherwise mark visited and return 1 plus four neighbour calls
Keep the maximum returned area

codeNotes.match: return 1 + dfs(r + 1, c) + dfs(r - 1, c) + dfs(r, c + 1) + dfs(r, c - 1)
codeNotes.note: This cell plus its neighbours' areas

pitfalls: Mark a cell visited before recursing, or neighbours will count each other twice.
Very large islands can hit Python's recursion limit; an explicit stack avoids it.

say.intro: Max Area of Island. Ones are land, zeros are water, and land connects up, down, left, and right. An island's area is its number of cells. We want the biggest one. In our grid, the islands have areas three, four, and one. So the answer is four.
say.brute: The brute force goes like this. From every land cell, run a brand new flood fill, with its own visited set. Count what it reaches, and keep the max. It's correct. So what's the catch? Every cell of a big island measures that same island again. On a fifty by fifty grid of land, that's millions of wasted steps.
say.insight: Use one shared visited set, just like Number of Islands. Now each island gets flooded exactly once. The only new idea? Make the flood fill return a number. A cell returns zero if it's water, off the grid, or already visited. Otherwise, it returns one, for itself. Plus whatever its four neighbours return.
say.anim: We start with a four by four grid of land and water cells, rows and columns set to four. The scan begins at row zero, col zero, with an empty visited set and depth first search exploring outward. The search marks cells like zero zero and one zero visited, growing area as it floods this first island. After exploring neighbours, this island finishes with current area three, becoming the new max area. A new flood explores another island, visiting cells like two three, three three, and one three. This second island returns current area four, larger than before, so max area updates to four. Remaining scans at row two and three find isolated or already visited cells, adding nothing new. After scanning the whole grid, the function returns four as the maximum island area found.
say.code: The visited set is shared across every flood fill. In the search, if we're off the grid, on water, or already visited, we return zero. Water adds nothing. Otherwise, we mark the cell. Then we return one, plus the areas from all four neighbours. The main loop calls the search on every cell, and keeps the max. Cells already flooded just return zero. So no island gets counted twice.
say.outro: Each cell is visited once, so it's linear in the grid size. The pattern is flood fill, where the search returns a value instead of just marking.

max-area-of-island.title: Max Area of Island
max-area-of-island.optimalCode:
class Solution:
    def maxAreaOfIsland(self, grid: List[List[int]]) -> int:
        rows = len(grid)
        cols = len(grid[0])
        visited = set()

        # DFS returns 0 for water, out of bounds, or visited cells
        def dfs(row, col):
            if row < 0 or row == rows or col < 0 or col == cols:
                return 0
            if grid[row][col] == 0 or (row, col) in visited:
                return 0
            # Otherwise mark visited and return 1 plus four neighbour calls
            visited.add((row, col))
            area = 1
            area += dfs(row + 1, col)
            area += dfs(row - 1, col)
            area += dfs(row, col + 1)
            area += dfs(row, col - 1)
            return area

        # Scan every cell, calling DFS on it
        max_area = 0
        for row in range(rows):
            for col in range(cols):
                current_area = dfs(row, col)
                # Keep the maximum returned area
                if current_area > max_area:
                    max_area = current_area
        return max_area

clone-graph.hook: Deep-copying a graph with cycles: the trick is never copying the same node twice.
clone-graph.ask: Given one node of a connected undirected graph, return a deep copy: brand-new nodes with the same values, wired to each other exactly like the original.
clone-graph.exampleWhy: A square: 1-2-3-4-1. The copy's node 1 must link to new nodes 2 and 4, never the originals.

brute.idea: First collect every original node into a list, then create one copy per node, then wire each copy's neighbours by searching the list for each neighbour's position.
steps: Walk the graph, collecting nodes in a list
Make one new node per original
For each edge, find the neighbour's index by linear search
brute.whySlow: Without a map, every membership check and index lookup scans the whole list: about V times E work.

optimal.insight: A hash map from original node to its copy does two jobs: it finds any node's copy in O(1), and it marks nodes already copied, which stops cycles.
steps: DFS from the given node
Already in the map? Return its copy
Otherwise create the copy and store it in the map first
Recursively clone each neighbour and append the result

codeNotes.note: Seen before: reuse, which breaks cycles

codeNotes.match: return dfs(node) if node else None

pitfalls: Store the copy in the map BEFORE visiting neighbours, or a cycle recurses forever.
Handle the empty graph: input node can be None.

say.intro: Clone Graph. We're handed one node of a connected graph. We return a deep copy. That means new nodes, same values, wired up exactly like the original. Our example is a square. One, two, three, four, and back to one. So there are cycles everywhere.
say.brute: A brute force without any map works in three steps. Walk the graph and collect every node in a list. Make one new node per original. Then, for every edge, find the neighbour's position by scanning the list, and connect the matching copies. It works. But every lookup scans the whole list. That's roughly nodes times edges.
say.insight: Here's the thing. One hash map solves both problems. It maps each original node to its copy. So we find any copy in constant time. And it remembers what we've already cloned. When a cycle leads back to a node, we reuse its copy. No infinite loop. The key? Store the copy before visiting neighbours.
say.anim: We start at node 1, which connects to nodes 2 and 4, and create an empty map. A copy of node 1 is made and stored in the map before visiting its neighbors. Visiting neighbor 2, we create its copy too, since it is not in the map yet. Node 2 already has node 1 mapped, so it reuses that copy instead of recursing again. The same pattern continues for node 3, creating a new copy and recording it in the map. Node 4 is copied last, and its neighbors 1 and 3 are found already cloned in the map. As recursion unwinds, each copy returns upward, linking neighbors back together correctly. The final result is node 1 connected to nodes 2 and 4, a fully cloned graph.
say.code: We start with a map from each original node to its copy. The helper first checks the map. If we've seen this node before, we reuse its copy. That's what breaks cycles. Otherwise, we make a new node with the same value. And we register it in the map before recursing. Then we clone each neighbour, and wire the clone in. Finally, we call the helper on the input. An empty graph just returns none.
say.outro: Every node and edge is handled once, so it's linear. The pattern is a hash map from old to new. Register before you recurse.

walls-and-gates.hook: Distance to the nearest of many targets? Start the BFS from all targets at once.
walls-and-gates.ask: A grid has walls (-1), gates (0) and empty rooms (a huge number meaning infinity). Fill each empty room, in place, with its step distance to the nearest gate. Unreachable rooms stay infinite.
walls-and-gates.exampleWhy: Two gates. The room at row 1, column 1 is 2 steps from either gate, and the bottom-right room is 3 steps away.

brute.idea: For every empty room, run its own BFS outward until it reaches any gate; the BFS depth is the distance.
steps: For each empty room
BFS outward, avoiding walls
First gate reached gives the distance
brute.whySlow: A 250 by 250 grid has 62,500 rooms, each possibly searching the whole grid: billions of steps.

optimal.insight: Reverse the search: queue every gate at distance 0 and BFS once. Layers expand one step at a time, so a room's first visit gives its nearest-gate distance.
steps: Queue every gate and mark it visited
Pop a whole layer, writing the current distance into each cell
Push unvisited, non-wall neighbours
Increase the distance after each layer

codeNotes.note: Queue a neighbour if it is open
Every gate is a BFS source
Next layer is one step further

pitfalls: BFS from rooms to gates repeats work; start from the gates instead.
Mark cells visited when queued, not when popped, to avoid duplicates.

say.intro: Walls and Gates. Our grid has walls, gates, and empty rooms marked with infinity. We fill every room, in place, with its distance to the nearest gate. Here there are two gates. The farthest room, in the bottom right corner, ends up three steps away.
say.brute: The brute force runs a separate breadth first search from every empty room. It spreads outward until it hits any gate. That depth is the room's answer. It's correct. But each room might search almost the whole grid. With tens of thousands of rooms, we repeat the same work billions of times.
say.insight: Let's reverse the direction. Instead of every room looking for a gate, let all the gates search at once. Put every gate in one queue, at distance zero. Then run a single breadth first search. It spreads in layers, one step at a time. So the first wave to reach a room comes from its nearest gate.
say.anim: We start with a grid of gates, walls, and empty rooms marked with a huge number. We scan the grid, finding gates at positions like row zero col two and row two col zero, queuing them. With both gates queued at distance zero, we begin popping them and exploring their neighbors. Neighbors like row one col two and row zero col three get visited and queued for distance one. Distance becomes one, and we write that value into rooms like row zero col three and row one col two. Distance climbs to two, filling rooms such as row one col zero and row two col two with value two. At distance three, the last room row two col three finally gets filled in, completing the grid. The queue is empty, giving the final answer: distances two, negative one, zero, one, one, two, one, negative one, zero, negative one, two, three.
say.code: A small helper queues a neighbour, but only if it's open. Out of bounds, already seen, or a wall? Walls block the wave, so we skip it. Every gate becomes a starting point. Then we process one distance layer at a time. For each cell, we write the current distance, then try its four neighbours. The first arrival is always the shortest. After each layer, the distance goes up by one.
say.outro: Each cell enters the queue once, so it's linear in the grid size. The pattern is multi source breadth first search. Many targets? Start from all of them.

rotting-oranges.hook: A simulation that looks minute-by-minute is really just BFS layers in disguise.
rotting-oranges.ask: In a grid, 0 is empty, 1 is a fresh orange, 2 is rotten. Each minute, rotten oranges rot their fresh neighbours up, down, left and right. Return the minutes until none are fresh, or -1 if impossible.
rotting-oranges.exampleWhy: Rot spreads from the top-left corner; the bottom-right orange is four steps away, so it rots in minute four.

brute.idea: Simulate literally: each minute, rescan the whole grid, collect fresh oranges touching a rotten one, rot them all, and repeat until nothing changes.
steps: Scan every cell for fresh oranges next to rot
Rot them all together; count a minute
Stop when no change; any fresh left means -1
brute.whySlow: A long snake of oranges takes about m·n minutes, and every minute rescans all m·n cells.

optimal.insight: Only newly rotten oranges can spread. Queue all initially rotten oranges and run multi-source BFS; each BFS layer is exactly one minute.
steps: Count fresh oranges; queue every rotten one
Process the queue one layer at a time
Rot each fresh neighbour, queue it, decrement fresh
Each finished layer adds one minute
Fresh left over means -1

codeNotes.note: Track how many still need to rot
Rot it now so it is not queued twice

pitfalls: No fresh oranges at the start means answer 0, not -1.
Loop on fresh > 0, or you count an extra minute after the last rot.

say.intro: Rotting Oranges. The grid holds empty cells, fresh oranges, and rotten ones. Every minute, each rotten orange rots its fresh neighbours. How many minutes until nothing fresh is left? Or minus one, if some orange can never rot. In our example, the far corner rots at minute four.
say.brute: The brute force simulates it literally. Each minute, scan the whole grid. Find every fresh orange touching a rotten one, and rot them all at once. Stop when nothing changes. It works. But a long snake of oranges can take a minute per cell. And every minute rescans the entire grid. That's quadratic.
say.insight: Only oranges that just turned rotten can spread anything new. So why rescan the rest? Put every rotten orange in a queue. Run breadth first search from all of them at once. The queue naturally forms layers. And each layer is exactly one minute. We also count fresh oranges, so we know if any are left.
say.anim: We start with a grid containing one rotten orange, marked two, and several fresh ones. Scanning the grid, fresh count climbs to six while the rotten orange at zero zero joins the queue. Breadth first search begins, processing the single rotten orange layer by layer, one minute per layer. Its neighbors at zero one and one zero turn rotten, fresh count drops to four, minute becomes one. Next layer spreads rot to zero two and one one, fresh count falls to two, minute two. The following layer rots one two and two one, leaving just one fresh orange, minute three. Finally the last fresh orange at two two rots, bringing fresh count down to zero. All oranges are rotten now, and the function returns four minutes as the final answer.
say.code: First pass: we count how many fresh oranges still need to rot. Every rotten orange goes into the queue, so they all start together. Then we loop while fresh oranges remain and the queue isn't empty. We freeze this minute's layer by taking the queue length. Each fresh neighbour rots right away, so it's never queued twice. After each layer, we add a minute. Any fresh orange left? Return minus one.
say.outro: Every cell is processed once, so it's linear in the grid size. The pattern is multi source breadth first search. Each layer is one tick of time.

pacific-atlantic-water-flow.hook: Instead of asking where water from each cell goes, ask which cells each ocean can reach.
pacific-atlantic-water-flow.ask: Each cell has a height. Rain flows to a neighbour of equal or lower height. The Pacific touches the top and left edges; the Atlantic touches the bottom and right. Return cells whose water can reach both oceans.
pacific-atlantic-water-flow.exampleWhy: Heights spiral upward from 1. Only the cells holding 1 and 2 cannot drain downhill to the bottom or right edge.

Keep cells that touch both
brute.whySlow: A 200 by 200 grid is 40,000 searches of up to 40,000 cells each: 1.6 billion steps.

optimal.insight: Reverse the flow. Start from each ocean's edge cells and climb uphill (to equal or higher neighbours). Two searches mark every cell each ocean can reach; answer is the overlap.

DFS uphill from bottom and right edges into the atl set
A neighbour is reachable if it is at least as high
Return cells present in both sets

say.intro: Pacific Atlantic Water Flow. Each cell has a height, and rain flows to any neighbour that's equal or lower. The Pacific touches the top and left edges. The Atlantic touches the bottom and right. Which cells drain into both? Here, every cell except the one and the two.
say.brute: The brute force asks every cell separately. From each cell, search downhill to every neighbour that's no higher. Note whether we touch a Pacific edge, and an Atlantic edge. It's correct. But each search can cover the whole grid. So a two hundred by two hundred grid takes over a billion steps.
say.insight: Turn the question around. Instead of following water down from every cell, start at the oceans and climb up. From every Pacific edge cell, search uphill to neighbours that are equal or higher. That marks everything the Pacific can reach. Then do the same for the Atlantic. Two searches in total. The answer is the cells marked by both.
say.anim: We start with a three by three grid of heights, ready to explore both oceans. A depth first search climbs uphill from Pacific edge cells, marking visited cells as it goes. By frame nine, the pacific search has spread to cover almost the whole grid, since it keeps climbing higher ground. With Pacific done, pacific now holds most cells, and we start the same search for the Atlantic edges. The Atlantic search grows outward from bottom and right edges, adding cells like one zero and two zero. Atlantic search keeps climbing uphill neighbours, eventually reaching cells like one one and two two. Now we compare both sets, collecting cells present in both pacific and atlantic into result. The final answer lists seven cells where water can reach both oceans, matching the expected output.
say.code: Two sets hold the cells each ocean can reach. The search stops at a visited cell, or off the grid. It also stops if the cell is lower than the previous height. Remember, we're flowing in reverse, so we only climb. Otherwise, we add the cell and recurse four ways. The top edge seeds the Pacific, the bottom edge the Atlantic. The side columns work the same way. Finally, we keep cells reachable from both.
say.outro: Two linear searches instead of one per cell. The pattern is reverse search. When many sources flow to a few targets, start from the targets.

surrounded-regions.hook: Finding what to capture is hard. Finding what is safe is easy: it touches the border.
surrounded-regions.ask: A board has X and O cells. A region of connected O cells is captured, flipped to X, if it does not touch the board's edge. Modify the board in place.
surrounded-regions.exampleWhy: The three O cells in the middle are enclosed and flip. The right pair and the bottom O touch the edge, so they stay.

brute.idea: For every O cell, run its own search through connected O cells to see whether it can reach the border. If not, it is captured.
steps: For each O, search its connected O cells
Reaching the edge means safe
Flip every O that could not escape
brute.whySlow: A 200 by 200 board full of O repeats a 40,000-cell search from each of 40,000 cells.

optimal.insight: A region survives only if it touches the border. So flood-fill from border O cells, tagging them safe; every O left untagged must be surrounded.
steps: DFS from every border O, turning its region into T
Flip every remaining O to X: those are surrounded

say.intro: Surrounded Regions. The board has X cells and O cells. Any group of connected O cells that doesn't touch the edge is surrounded. We flip it to X, in place. Here, the three O cells in the middle get captured. The groups on the edge survive.
say.brute: The brute force checks each O cell on its own. From that cell, search through connected O cells. Can we reach the border? If not, the cell is trapped, and we flip it. It works. But on a board full of O cells, we repeat a huge search from every single one. That's quadratic.
say.insight: Let's flip the question. Deciding what's captured is awkward. But deciding what's safe is easy. A region is safe exactly when it touches the border. So start flood fills only from O cells on the border. Tag everything they reach as safe, for now. Afterwards, any untagged O must be surrounded. So we capture it.

Then comes a second pass. Any O that's still untagged is surrounded. So we capture it, turning it into X. Finally, a third pass restores every T back to O. That's three simple passes over the board.
say.outro: Each cell is touched a few times, so it's linear. The pattern is flood fill from the border. When a question is awkward, solve its opposite.

course-schedule.hook: Prerequisites form a graph. You can finish everything exactly when that graph has no cycle.
course-schedule.ask: There are numCourses courses. Each pair [a, b] means you must take b before a. Return true if you can finish every course, false if the requirements are impossible.

All its prerequisites taken? Take it
Repeat until a pass changes nothing

optimal.insight: Courses are nodes, prerequisites are edges. It is impossible exactly when there is a cycle. DFS finds one when it reaches a course already on the current path.

say.intro: Course Schedule. We have some courses, and each pair says one course must come before another. Can we finish them all? Here we have five courses. Course two needs four. Four needs three. And three needs two. That loop can never start. So the answer is false.
say.brute: The brute force acts like a student. Scan the course list, and take any course whose prerequisites are all done. Keep making passes until one takes nothing new. Then check whether everything got taken. It's correct. But every pass rescans every prerequisite pair. And a long chain of courses needs one full pass per course.
say.insight: Think of courses as nodes and prerequisites as edges. When is finishing impossible? Exactly when this graph has a cycle. Depth first search finds cycles by tracking the current path. If we reach a course already on the path, we've looped. And once a course is proven finishable, we remember it. So it's never explored twice.
say.anim: We build a prerequisite map, giving each of the five courses an empty list. Now we fill it in: course one needs zero, two needs one, three needs two, four needs three, and two also needs four. We start depth first search from course zero, which has no prerequisites and finishes instantly. Course one depends on zero, which is already done, so course one finishes too. Now we dive into course two, visiting one, then four, then three, building a chain on the current path. Course three needs course two, but two is still being visited, meaning we found a cycle. This cycle forces every call in the chain to return false, three, four, and two all fail. The final answer is false, since these five courses cannot all be finished.
say.code: We map each course to its prerequisites. If the course is already in visiting, we're back on the current path. That's a cycle, so return false. If its list is empty, it has no prereqs, or it's already proven. Return true. Otherwise, we add the course to the visiting path. We recurse into each prerequisite, failing on any failure. Then we remove it from the path. And we clear its list, as a memo.
say.outro: Each course and edge is handled once, so it's linear. The pattern is cycle detection, using depth first search on a directed graph.

graph-valid-tree.hook: A tree is just a graph that is connected and has no cycles. Check both in one DFS.
graph-valid-tree.ask: Given n nodes labelled 0 to n - 1 and a list of undirected edges, return true if these edges form a valid tree: every node connected, with no cycles.
graph-valid-tree.exampleWhy: Four edges join all five nodes, and there is no loop: node 0 branches to 1, 2 and 3, and 1 leads to 4.

brute.idea: A tree has exactly n - 1 edges and no cycle. Add edges one by one; before each, search earlier edges to see if its ends already connect.
steps: Edge count must be n - 1
For each edge, search earlier edges from one end
Reaching the other end means a cycle: false
brute.whySlow: Each edge launches a search that rescans the edge list for every node it visits: billions of steps for 2,000 nodes.

optimal.insight: One DFS from node 0 checks both rules. Revisiting a node through any edge except the one we came from means a cycle; afterwards, every node must have been visited.
steps: Build an undirected adjacency list
DFS from 0, passing the parent we came from
Skip the parent; any other visited neighbour means a cycle
At the end, the visited count must equal n

Do not walk back along the same edge
Pass ourselves as the child's parent

pitfalls: Skip the parent edge: in an undirected graph it always leads back to a visited node.
No cycle is not enough: the graph must also be connected.

say.intro: Graph Valid Tree. We get n nodes and a list of undirected edges. Do they form a tree? A tree means two things. Every node is connected. And there are no cycles. Our five nodes and four edges branch out from zero without a loop. So, true.
say.brute: The brute force uses a fact about trees. They have exactly n minus one edges. And an edge between already connected nodes makes a cycle. So we add edges one by one. Before each, we search the earlier edges, to see if its two ends already connect. It's correct. But each search rescans the edges over and over.
say.insight: One depth first search from node zero checks both rules at once. As we walk, we remember the node we just came from. Why? In an undirected graph, that edge leads straight back. So we skip it. If any other neighbour is already visited, we've found a cycle. And when the search ends, the visited set must hold all n nodes.
say.anim: We start with five nodes and four edges, building an undirected adjacency list first. Each edge adds both directions, so node 0 ends up connected to 1, 2, and 3. The full adjacency list is built, and now the depth first search begins from node 0. We visit node 0, then move to neighbor 1, marking it visited too. From node 1, we skip node 0 since it is the parent, avoiding a false cycle. We dive into node 4, visiting it, then skip parent 1 and return true. Back at node 0, we explore neighbors 2 and 3 next, visiting each one. All five nodes are visited with no cycles, so the graph is a valid tree, true.
say.code: We build an adjacency list. It's undirected, so each edge goes in both directions. The search takes a node and its parent. If the node is already visited, we've reached it again. That's a cycle. Otherwise, we mark it and loop over its neighbours. We never walk back along the parent edge. For every other neighbour, we recurse, passing ourselves as its parent. Finally, we need two things. No cycle, and every node connected.
say.outro: Linear in nodes plus edges. The pattern is depth first search with a parent pointer. Connected and no cycles, both checked in one pass.

number-of-connected-components-in-an-und.hook: Union-Find in its purest form: start with n groups and merge one edge at a time.
number-of-connected-components-in-an-und.ask: Given n nodes labelled 0 to n - 1 and a list of undirected edges, return how many connected components the graph has: separate groups of nodes linked by edges.
number-of-connected-components-in-an-und.exampleWhy: Nodes 0, 1, 2 form one group, 3 and 4 another, and 5 sits alone. The edge 2-0 joins nodes already linked.

brute.idea: Give each node its own label. Repeatedly sweep the edges, letting both ends take the smaller label, until nothing changes. Count the distinct labels.
steps: label[i] = i for every node
Sweep edges: both ends take the smaller label
Repeat until stable, then count distinct labels
brute.whySlow: A long chain listed in the wrong order needs one sweep per node: 2,000 sweeps of 5,000 edges.

optimal.insight: Start with n separate components. Each edge that joins two different roots merges them, reducing the count by one; an edge inside one group changes nothing.
steps: Every node is its own parent; count = n
find: follow parents to the root, compressing the path
union: different roots? Attach the smaller tree under the larger
Subtract 1 for each successful union

codeNotes.note: Each node starts as its own root
Union by size keeps trees shallow
Each real merge removes one component

pitfalls: Isolated nodes with no edges still count as components.
Compare roots, not the nodes themselves, before merging.

say.intro: Number of Connected Components. We have n nodes and some undirected edges, and we count the separate groups. With six nodes, zero, one, and two form a group. Three and four form another. Five is alone. So, three components. And the edge from two back to zero adds nothing new.
say.brute: The brute force spreads labels. Every node starts with its own number. We sweep through the edges, and both ends take the smaller label. Keep sweeping until nothing changes. Then count the distinct labels. It's correct. But a long chain can need one sweep per node. And every sweep rescans every edge.
say.insight: Union find is built exactly for this. Start by assuming n separate components. For each edge, find the root of each end. Different roots? Merge the two groups, and subtract one from the count. Same root? The edge is inside a group, so nothing changes. Path compression and union by size keep each find almost constant.
say.anim: We start with six nodes, each its own parent, so count begins at six. Processing edge zero and one, both find themselves as their own roots. Roots zero and one differ, so we merge them and count drops to five. Next edge one and two finds root zero for one and root two for two. Different roots again, so they merge, shrinking count further down to four. Edge three and four have distinct roots three and four, merging them, count becomes three. Finally edge two and zero both resolve to root zero, already the same group. No merge happens there, so the final answer stays three connected components.
say.code: Each node starts as its own root. Find walks up toward the root. Along the way, it points each node at its grandparent, skipping a level. That's path compression. Union finds both roots. If they match, the edge adds nothing, so it returns zero. Otherwise, we hang the smaller tree under the larger one. That keeps trees shallow. The answer starts at n. And each real merge removes one component.
say.outro: Nearly linear time, thanks to path compression and union by size. The pattern is union find. Counting groups as edges arrive is exactly its job.

say.brute: The obvious way? Keep an adjacency list of the edges so far. Before adding a new edge, run a depth first search from one end. Can we already reach the other end? Then this edge is the culprit. It works. But every edge might trigger a search of the whole graph. That's n squared overall.

word-ladder.hook: A shortest path problem in disguise: words are nodes, one-letter changes are edges.
word-ladder.ask: Change the begin word into the end word one letter at a time. Every word along the way must be in the word list. Return how many words are in the shortest such sequence, or zero if impossible.
word-ladder.exampleWhy: hit → hot → dot → dog → cog uses five words, and no shorter chain exists.

brute.idea: Breadth-first search, but find neighbors by comparing the current word against every word in the list, letter by letter.
steps: Pop a word from the queue
Compare it with every unvisited list word
Differ by one letter? Visit and enqueue it
Hit endWord? Return the level
brute.whySlow: With 5,000 words, each pop scans all 5,000 others: 25 million comparisons times word length.

optimal.insight: Words one letter apart share a wildcard pattern, like h*t. Bucket words by pattern once, then neighbors are a lookup instead of a scan.
steps: For each word and position, add it to the bucket for that pattern
BFS from beginWord, one level per ladder step
Neighbors are all words in the word's pattern buckets
First time we pop endWord, return the level

codeNotes.note: Neighbors come straight from the bucket

pitfalls: The answer counts words, not moves, so start the level count at 1.
Mark words visited when enqueued, or the queue explodes with duplicates.

say.intro: Word Ladder. Turn hit into cog, changing one letter at a time. Every word along the way must be in the list. The shortest chain? Hit, hot, dot, dog, cog. That's five words, so we return five. And if there's no chain at all, we return zero.
say.brute: Think of each word as a node. Two words share an edge if they differ by one letter. Shortest chain? That's breadth first search. So what's the catch? Finding neighbors. We compare the current word against every other word, letter by letter. Five thousand words means about twenty five million comparisons. Times the word length. Way too slow.
say.insight: Here's the trick. Two words are one letter apart exactly when they fit the same wildcard pattern. Hot and dot both fit star o t. So, up front, we drop every word into buckets keyed by its patterns. Now a word's neighbors are just the words sharing its buckets. No more scanning the whole list.
say.anim: We start checking that cog is actually in the word list before anything else. Now every word gets bucketed by its wildcard patterns, like hot matching star ot and h star t. All words including hit get indexed this way, building a pattern lookup table for fast neighbor search. Breadth first search begins from hit, exploring patterns like h star t to find neighbor hot. At length three, dot and lot expand, discovering new neighbors dog and log through shared patterns. At length four, dog and log are processed, each revealing cog as a neighbor through pattern star og. The queue now holds cog, so length increases to five before the final check. Word equals cog, so the ladder length of five is returned as the final answer.
say.code: First, if the end word isn't in the list, return zero. Then build the pattern buckets, including the begin word. The queue starts with the begin word and a count of one. We process one whole level at a time. Pop the end word? Return the count. That first arrival is the shortest. Otherwise, queue every unvisited neighbor from the buckets. Then bump the count for the next level.
say.outro: About n times word length squared. Pattern: graphs. Breadth first search finds shortest paths in unweighted graphs. The real trick is building the edges cleverly.

network-delay-time.hook: A signal spreads through weighted edges. The answer is simply the last node Dijkstra settles.
network-delay-time.ask: A signal starts at node k and travels along one-way edges, each with a travel time. Return how long until every node has received it, or minus one if some node never does.
network-delay-time.exampleWhy: Node 2 is fastest via 3 (1+2=3), then node 4 via 2 at time 4. The slowest node finishes at 4.

brute.idea: Bellman-Ford: start with infinite distances, then relax every edge again and again, n - 1 times, until shortest times settle.
steps: dist[k] = 0, others infinity
Repeat n - 1 times: relax every edge
Answer is the largest distance, or -1
brute.whySlow: With 100 nodes and 6,000 edges, that is 600,000 relaxations, mostly wasted on already-settled nodes.

optimal.insight: The node with the smallest known arrival time can never be reached sooner. A min-heap hands us that node next, so each node is finalized once.
steps: Push (0, k) onto a min-heap
Pop the earliest node; skip it if already visited
Mark it visited; its time is final
Push each unvisited neighbor with time plus edge weight
Answer is the last time popped, if all n were visited

pitfalls: Nodes are labeled 1 to n, not 0 to n - 1.
Skip stale heap entries; a node may be pushed several times.

say.intro: Network Delay Time. A signal leaves node one and travels along weighted, one way edges. How long until every node hears it? Node three hears it at time one. Node two at three, by going through node three. Node four at four. The slowest node decides. So the answer is four.
say.brute: One option is Bellman Ford. Every distance starts at infinity, except the start, which is zero. Then we relax every edge, n minus one times. If an edge gives a shorter time, take it. It's correct. But it costs V times E work. And most passes just recheck nodes that settled long ago.
say.insight: So here's Dijkstra's idea. There are no negative weights. That means the unvisited node with the smallest known time can never be reached faster. Why? Any other route is already slower. So pop it from a min heap, lock its time in, and offer its neighbors new times. Each node is finalized once. The last one finalized is our answer.
say.anim: We build a graph from the edges, mapping each source node to its destinations and weights. The heap starts with node 1 at time zero, and visited is empty. We pop node 1, mark it visited, and push neighbors 2 and 3 with times 4 and 1. Node 3 pops next with time 1, since it's the smallest, and we push neighbor 2 at time 3 and 4 at time 6. Node 2 pops at time 3, gets visited, and pushes neighbor 4 at time 4. We skip the duplicate entry for node 2, since it's already visited. Node 4 pops at time 4 and becomes visited, completing all four nodes. All nodes are visited, so the function returns the final answer, 4.
say.code: We build an adjacency list with travel times. The heap starts with time zero at node k. Pop the earliest entry. Already visited? It's stale, so skip it. Otherwise, mark it and record its time. That's the latest finalized arrival. Then push each unvisited neighbor with time plus edge weight. At the end, did we reach all n nodes? Return the last time. If not, minus one.
say.outro: E log V time, linear space. Pattern: advanced graphs, Dijkstra's shortest path. Non negative weights and earliest arrival? Reach for a min heap.

reconstruct-itinerary.hook: Use every ticket exactly once. Greedy alone gets stuck; post-order DFS fixes it elegantly.
reconstruct-itinerary.ask: Given airline tickets as from-to pairs, build the trip starting at JFK that uses every ticket exactly once. If several trips work, return the one that comes first alphabetically.
reconstruct-itinerary.exampleWhy: ATL comes before SFO, and this trip uses all five tickets. JFK, SFO, ... is valid too, but later alphabetically.

brute.idea: Backtracking: from the current airport, try unused tickets in alphabetical order. If we get stuck before using all tickets, undo and try the next.
steps: Sort tickets by destination
Try each unused ticket out of the current airport
Path uses all tickets? Done
Dead end? Un-use the ticket and backtrack
brute.whySlow: Each dead end forces undoing work; with 300 tickets the number of tried orderings can explode exponentially.

optimal.insight: Always fly the smallest ticket. When an airport has no tickets left, it must be the end of what remains, so add it after its children: post-order, then reverse.
steps: Build sorted destination lists per airport
DFS from JFK, always taking the smallest remaining ticket
Remove each ticket as it is used
When an airport is out of tickets, append it to res
Reverse res for the itinerary
optimal.time: O(E log E) ideal; O(E²) as written

pitfalls: Greedy alone can strand you in a dead end; the post-order append handles it.
pop(0) and the list copies cost O(degree); reverse-sort and pop() from the end for true O(E log E).

say.intro: Reconstruct Itinerary. We get a pile of airline tickets. We must use every one exactly once, starting from JFK. If several trips work, we pick the alphabetically smallest. Here, that's JFK, Atlanta, JFK, San Francisco, Atlanta, San Francisco.
say.brute: The obvious approach is backtracking. Sort the tickets. From the current airport, try unused tickets in alphabetical order. Stuck before using them all? Undo the last ticket and try the next one. The first complete trip we find is the smallest. It's correct. But dead ends can make it exponential in the number of tickets.
say.insight: Here's the trick. Always fly the smallest ticket, and never undo. What if we get stuck? Then that airport must be the very end of the trip. So it belongs last. Think about it this way. We add an airport to the result only after everything reachable from it is used up. That builds the trip backwards. Flip it, and we're done.
say.anim: We build a map of destinations for each airport from the ticket list. Each airport's destination list gets sorted so we always try the smallest city first. Starting at JFK, we follow the smallest unused ticket, popping it as we go. We dive deeper through ATL, JFK, and SFO, consuming tickets until an airport runs dry. SFO has no tickets left, so it's appended first, beginning the post order list. ATL, SFO, JFK, and ATL again get appended as their ticket lists empty out. After reversing this post order list, we get the full travel sequence. The final itinerary is JFK, ATL, JFK, SFO, ATL, SFO.
say.code: Each airport gets a sorted list of destinations, smallest first. The search takes the first destination and removes that ticket. Then it flies there and keeps going. When an airport has nothing left, we append it. That's the post order step. After the search from JFK, we reverse the result. Used every ticket? Return it. Otherwise, an empty list. One quirk: popping from the front can make a busy hub quadratic.
say.outro: This is Hierholzer's algorithm for an Euler path. Pattern: advanced graphs. Need to use every edge exactly once? Think post order search.
