min-cost-to-connect-all-points.hook: Connect every point as cheaply as possible: a textbook minimum spanning tree with Prim's algorithm.
min-cost-to-connect-all-points.ask: Given points on a grid, connecting two points costs their Manhattan distance: the x gap plus the y gap. Return the minimum total cost so every point is connected, directly or through others.

brute.idea: Grow a tree from point 0. Each round, scan every pair of (in-tree, out-of-tree) points and add the cheapest link.
steps: Start with point 0 in the tree
Scan all in-tree x out-tree pairs
Add the cheapest link to the tree
Repeat until all points are in
brute.whySlow: With 1,000 points, n rounds each scanning up to n² pairs is about a billion distance checks.

optimal.insight: The cheapest edge leaving the current tree is always safe to add. A min-heap of candidate edges finds it without rescanning every pair.
steps: Build all pairwise distances as an adjacency list
Heap starts with (0, point 0)
Pop the cheapest; skip if already in the tree
Add its cost, mark visited, push its edges to unvisited points

codeNotes.note: Pay for the cheapest new link

pitfalls: Skip popped points already in the tree, or you double count.
Dense graph: Prim with a plain min-distance array is O(n²), beating the heap.

say.intro: Min Cost to Connect All Points. Linking two points costs their Manhattan distance. That's the horizontal gap plus the vertical gap. We must connect every point, directly or through others, as cheaply as possible. Here, four links costing four, three, four and nine give twenty. Nothing cheaper works.
say.brute: A simple approach: grow a tree from point zero. Each round, check every pair with one point inside and one outside. Then add the cheapest link. We need n rounds, and each round can check n squared pairs. That's n cubed. For a thousand points? About a billion distance checks.
say.insight: Here's the thing. This is a minimum spanning tree. The cheapest edge leaving our tree is always safe to take. Why? Because any spanning tree has to cross that boundary somewhere. That's Prim's algorithm. And instead of rescanning every pair each round, we keep candidate edges in a min heap. The cheapest one always sits on top.
say.anim: We start with five points and build a table of distances between every pair. Prim's algorithm begins at point zero, with a heap holding just cost zero. Point zero is visited, and its edges to points one, two, three, and four get pushed. The cheapest edge, cost four to point one, gets taken next, raising total cost to four. Point three joins next at cost three, since its edge was the cheapest available. Point four joins at cost four, bringing total cost up to eleven. Finally point two joins at cost nine, completing the tree with total cost twenty. The algorithm returns twenty, the minimum cost to connect all five points.
say.code: First, we compute every pairwise Manhattan distance into an adjacency list. The heap starts with cost zero at point zero. It joins for free. While points are still unvisited, pop the cheapest entry. Already visited? That's a stale edge, so skip it. Otherwise, pay its cost and mark it visited. Then offer edges to every unvisited point. Finally, return the total.
say.outro: n squared log n time. Pattern: advanced graphs, minimum spanning tree. Need to connect everything cheaply? Reach for Prim's or Kruskal's algorithm.

swim-in-rising-water.hook: The cost of a path is its highest cell, not its sum. Dijkstra still works with one tweak.
swim-in-rising-water.ask: Each cell of an n by n grid has a height. At time t, you can swim through any cell with height at most t. Starting top-left, return the earliest time you can reach the bottom-right.
swim-in-rising-water.exampleWhy: Path 0 → 6 → 1 → 4 → 3 peaks at 6. Every path down the left side must cross 7 or 8.

brute.idea: Try each time t = 0, 1, 2, ... and flood-fill from the start through cells ≤ t. The first t that reaches the corner wins.
steps: Pick the next time t
DFS from (0,0) through cells with height ≤ t
Corner reached? Return t
brute.whySlow: A 50 by 50 grid has 2,500 possible times, each needing a 2,500-cell flood fill: over six million visits.

optimal.insight: Path cost is the maximum height on it. Always expand the cell with the lowest required time so far, using a min-heap; the first time we pop the corner is optimal.
steps: Heap starts with (grid[0][0], 0, 0)
Pop the cell with the smallest time so far
Is it the bottom-right? Return its time
Push unvisited neighbors with max(time, their height)

codeNotes.note: Start time is the first cell's height

codeNotes.match: if r == N - 1 and c == N - 1:

codeNotes.note: Cost is the path's highest cell

pitfalls: Start time is grid[0][0], not zero.
Use max, not sum: you wait for the water, you do not pay per cell.

say.intro: Swim in Rising Water. The water rises one unit per second. You can swim through any cell no higher than the water. How soon can we get from top left to bottom right? The path along the top and right peaks at six. Going down the left needs at least seven. So the answer is six.
say.brute: The obvious approach? Try every time. Zero, one, two, and so on. For each one, flood fill from the start through cells already underwater. The first time we reach the corner is the answer. But that can mean n squared different times. Each costs n squared work. On a fifty by fifty grid, that's millions of visits.
say.insight: Now, notice. A path's cost isn't its sum. It's its highest cell. And Dijkstra still works with that change. We keep a min heap ordered by the highest cell needed so far. We always expand the cheapest. Stepping into a neighbor costs the max of our time and its height. So the first time we pop the corner, it's optimal.
say.anim: We start at the top left cell, time zero, grid value zero, added to the heap. We explore neighbor at row zero col one, its height six becomes the new time. We explore neighbor at row one col zero, height two, smaller than six, pushed too. We pop the smallest time entry, two, and expand its unvisited neighbors next. Popping time six now, we expand from row zero col one, finding col two with height six. We keep popping the lowest times, exploring row one col two and row two col two. Finally we pop and reach the bottom right corner, returning the answer six.
say.code: The start time is the first cell's height. We push it and mark it visited. Then pop the lowest time. Is it the bottom right corner? Return it. First arrival is optimal. Otherwise, look at each neighbor in bounds and not yet visited. Mark it when we push it, so it's never pushed twice. Its time is the max of ours and its height.
say.outro: n squared log n time. Pattern: advanced graphs, a Dijkstra variant. When a path costs its maximum, not its sum, the heap still works.

swim-in-rising-water.title: Swim In Rising Water
swim-in-rising-water.optimalCode:
import heapq
from typing import List

class Solution:
    def swimInWater(self, grid: List[List[int]]) -> int:
        n = len(grid)
        seen = set()
        directions = [(0, 1), (0, -1), (1, 0), (-1, 0)]

        # 1. Start the heap with the top-left cell
        heap = [(grid[0][0], 0, 0)]
        seen.add((0, 0))

        # 2. Always expand the cell with the smallest time so far
        while heap:
            time, row, col = heapq.heappop(heap)

            # 3. If we reached the bottom-right, this is the answer
            if row == n - 1 and col == n - 1:
                return time

            # 4. Push unvisited neighbors with the updated max height
            for dr, dc in directions:
                newRow = row + dr
                newCol = col + dc
                if newRow < 0 or newCol < 0 or newRow >= n or newCol >= n:
                    continue
                if (newRow, newCol) in seen:
                    continue
                seen.add((newRow, newCol))
                newTime = max(time, grid[newRow][newCol])
                heapq.heappush(heap, (newTime, newRow, newCol))

We create an empty seen set so we never push the same cell onto the heap twice.
We list the four directions we can move: right, left, down, and up.
This comment says we begin by putting the top-left cell into the heap.
The heap starts with one entry holding the top-left height as time, plus its row and column of zero.
We mark the top-left cell as seen right away so it is never added again.
This comment says we always expand the cell with the smallest time so far.
We loop as long as the heap has cells waiting to be explored.
We pop the cell with the lowest time, getting its time, row, and column.
This comment says reaching the bottom-right corner means we have our answer.
We check whether the popped cell is the bottom-right corner of the grid.
Since the heap pops the smallest time first, this time is optimal, so we return it.
This comment says we now push unvisited neighbors using the updated maximum height.
We loop over each of the four directions, getting a row step and a column step.
We compute the neighbor's row by adding the row step to the current row.
We compute the neighbor's column by adding the column step to the current column.
We check whether the neighbor falls outside the grid on any side.
If it is out of bounds, we skip it and move on to the next direction.

If so, we skip it, because its earliest time was already recorded when first added.
We mark the neighbor as seen so no other path pushes it again.
The neighbor's time is the larger of our current time and its height, since a path costs its highest cell.

alien-dictionary.hook: Sorted words leak the alphabet. Each adjacent pair reveals at most one letter rule; topological sort does the rest.

pitfalls: Only the first differing letter of a pair counts; later letters say nothing.
Word then its own prefix, like abc before ab, is invalid.

say.intro: Alien Dictionary. An alien language uses our letters, but in a different order. We get its words already sorted. Can we recover the alphabet? Neighboring words tell us t before f, w before e, r before t, and e before r. Chain those together. The answer is w, e, r, t, f.
say.brute: First we collect a rule from each pair of adjacent words. Then a slow way to order them. Scan every letter, looking for one whose predecessors are all placed. Place it, and scan again. Nothing qualifies? The rules contradict. It works, but it rechecks every rule each pass. With twenty six letters, that's clumsy rather than slow. Topological sort touches each rule once.
say.insight: Think about it this way. Each rule is a directed edge from one letter to another. Any valid alphabet is a topological order of that graph. And only the first difference between two words tells us anything. The letters after it don't. What if the rules form a cycle? Then no order exists, so we return an empty string.
say.anim: We build a node for every unique letter across all five words first. Comparing wrt and wrf, the first difference is at index one, so t points to f. Comparing wrf and er, the first letters differ, giving edge w points to e. Comparing er and ett, letters differ at index one, so r points to t. Comparing ett and rftt, first letters differ, adding edge e points to r. Now depth first search explores w to e to r to t to f, marking each visiting. Each letter finishes with no cycle found, appending in order f, t, r, e, w. Reversing that post order gives the final alien alphabet, wertf.
say.code: Every letter becomes a node. For each adjacent pair, a longer word before its own prefix is invalid. Otherwise, the first difference gives one edge. The search marks letters on the current path. Meet one again? That's a cycle. When a letter finishes, after all its successors, we unmark it and append it. Finally, reverse the list. That's the topological order.
say.outro: Linear in the total number of characters. Pattern: advanced graphs, topological sort. Ordering things from pairwise rules? Think topo sort.

The method alienOrder takes the list of words and returns the alphabet order as a string.

We store the current word as firstWord.
We store the next word as secondWord.

If the first word is longer and the shorter word is its prefix, the ordering is invalid.
In that invalid prefix case we return an empty string right away.

If the letters at this position differ, we have found the first differing letter pair.
We add an edge from the first word's letter to the second word's letter, meaning it must come earlier.

The state dictionary records whether each letter is currently being visited or fully done.
The order list will collect letters in post-order as their searches finish.
The hasCycle flag starts false and turns true if we find a cycle.
We define a recursive helper dfs that explores from one letter.
The nonlocal declaration lets the helper modify the outer hasCycle variable.

If that state is visiting, the letter is on the current path, which means a cycle.

cheapest-flights-within-k-stops.hook: Cheapest is not enough: you have a stop limit. Bellman-Ford with k + 1 rounds handles both.
cheapest-flights-within-k-stops.ask: Given flights with prices, find the cheapest way from src to dst using at most k stops in between. Return the price, or minus one if no such route exists.
cheapest-flights-within-k-stops.exampleWhy: 0 → 1 → 3 costs 700 with one stop. 0 → 1 → 2 → 3 costs only 400 but needs two stops.

brute.idea: DFS every route from src, counting stops. Stop exploring past k stops, and keep the cheapest price that reaches dst.
steps: DFS from src with cost and stops used
Reached dst? Record the cost
Too many stops? Abandon this route
Return the cheapest recorded cost
brute.whySlow: Every node can branch to many flights at each stop; with 100 cities and k = 10 that explodes.

optimal.insight: After round i of relaxing every edge, prices hold the cheapest cost using at most i flights. Copy prices each round so one round adds only one flight.
steps: prices[src] = 0, others infinity
Repeat k + 1 times: copy prices to tmp
Relax every flight from old prices into tmp
Replace prices with tmp
Return prices[dst], or -1

codeNotes.note: Zero flights: only src is reachable
Read old round, write new round

pitfalls: Without the copy, one round can chain several flights and break the stop limit.
Plain Dijkstra on price alone can discard a pricier route with fewer stops.

say.intro: Cheapest Flights Within K Stops. Find the cheapest route from city zero to city three, with at most one stop. Zero, one, two, three costs just four hundred. But that's two stops. So the best legal route is zero, one, three, for seven hundred.
say.brute: The obvious approach is depth first search. Explore every route from the source, and count the stops. Gone past k stops? Abandon the route. Keep the cheapest price that reaches the destination. So what's the catch? Every stop can branch into many flights. The number of routes grows exponentially with k. That won't scale.
say.insight: Here's the thing. Bellman Ford fits perfectly. After one round of relaxing every flight, we know the cheapest prices using at most one flight. After two rounds, at most two. So we run exactly k plus one rounds. One key detail. Read from last round's prices, and write into a copy. That way, one round never chains two flights together.
say.anim: We initialize prices as infinity for all nodes except source zero, which starts at zero. Round zero begins, copying prices so this round adds only one more flight. Flight zero to one costs one hundred, so new prices becomes zero, one hundred, infinity, infinity. Node two and node three stay unreachable since their source prices are still infinity. Round one starts, copying prices zero, one hundred, infinity, infinity as the baseline. Edge one to two adds cost one hundred, giving new price two hundred at node two. Edge one to three adds six hundred, making new price seven hundred at node three. After both rounds, the cheapest price to destination three is returned as seven hundred.
say.code: Prices start at infinity, with zero at the source. With zero flights, only the source is reachable. We loop k plus one times, because k stops means k plus one flights. Each round, copy the prices. Read the old round, write the new one. If a flight makes its destination cheaper, update the copy. Then commit it. Finally, return the destination price, or minus one.
say.outro: k times E time, linear space. Pattern: advanced graphs, Bellman Ford. Limited number of edges? Count rounds instead of reaching for Dijkstra.

cheapest-flights-within-k-stops.title: Cheapest Flights Within K Stops
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container the interview platform expects for our method.
This line begins the method findCheapestPrice, which takes the city count, the flights, the source, the destination, and the stop limit.
The parameters continue here: n cities, the flights list, src, dst, and k, the maximum number of stops allowed.
The method returns an integer, either the cheapest price or minus one when no valid route exists.
This comment says we start with the source costing zero and every other city unreachable.
We create a prices list of length n where every city starts at infinity, meaning not yet reachable.
We set the price of the source city to zero, since we begin there without paying anything.
This comment explains that we repeat k plus one times, because k stops means at most k plus one flights.
We loop k plus one times, and each round allows paths to use one more flight than before.
This comment says we copy prices so each round extends paths by only a single flight.
We make new_prices as a copy of prices, so updates this round do not chain into extra flights.
We go through every flight, unpacking its source, destination, and cost.
We check whether the source city is still unreachable in the previous round's prices.
If it is unreachable, we skip this flight, since nothing can be extended from there.

We check whether this new cost beats the best known price for the destination in new_prices.

After all flights are processed, we replace prices with new_prices, locking in the cheapest costs using one more flight.

climbing-stairs.hook: The gateway to dynamic programming, and secretly the Fibonacci sequence.
climbing-stairs.ask: You are climbing a staircase with n steps. Each move climbs one step or two steps. In how many different ways can you reach the top?
climbing-stairs.exampleWhy: Ways to reach step 5 plus ways to reach step 4: 8 + 5 = 13.

brute.idea: Recurse: the last move was either one step or two, so ways(n) = ways(n - 1) + ways(n - 2), computed from scratch every time.
steps: n is 1 or 2? Return n
Otherwise return ways(n - 1) + ways(n - 2)
brute.whySlow: The same subproblems are recomputed over and over; n = 45 needs over a billion calls.

optimal.insight: ways(i) depends only on the two previous values. Build upward from the bottom and keep just those two numbers.
steps: Small n: the answer is n
Keep the last two counts: 2 and 3
Each step: new = previous two added
Shift the window forward

pitfalls: Plain recursion times out around n = 40; memoize or iterate.
Watch off-by-one: ways(1) = 1, ways(2) = 2.

say.intro: Climbing Stairs. You can climb one step or two at a time. How many different ways can you reach the top of six steps? The answer is thirteen. Let's see why.
say.brute: Think about your very last move. You got to step n from step n minus one, or from step n minus two. So the ways to reach n are those two counts added together. Plain recursion gets that right. But it recomputes the same steps again and again. The calls double with every step. That's exponential.
say.insight: Here's the key. Each count only depends on the two counts right before it. One, two, three, five, eight. Look familiar? It's the Fibonacci sequence. So instead of recursing down from the top, we build up from the bottom. We keep just the last two values. No recursion, no table, constant memory. This is dynamic programming at its simplest.
say.anim: We start with n equal to six, which is more than three, so we continue. We initialize n1 to two and n2 to three, our base step counts. At i equals four, temp becomes five, the sum of n1 and n2. We shift forward, setting n1 to three and n2 to five. At i equals five, temp becomes eight, then n1 and n2 update to five and eight. At i equals six, temp becomes thirteen, combining n1 eight and n2 five. We update n1 to eight and n2 to thirteen, finishing the loop. The function returns n2, giving the final answer thirteen.
say.code: If n is three or less, the answer is just n. Otherwise, we start with two and three. Those are the ways to reach steps two and three. For each step from four up to n, the new count is the last two added. Then we slide the window forward one step. Finally, return the second value. That's the ways to reach step n.
say.outro: Linear time, constant space. Pattern: one dimensional dynamic programming. Find the recurrence first. Then keep only the values you actually need.

climbing-stairs.title: Climbing Stairs
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container the problem expects for our method.
The method climbStairs takes the number of steps n and returns how many distinct ways reach the top.
For small staircases of three steps or fewer, we check for a base case first.
In those cases the number of ways equals n itself, so we return n directly.
We start with n1 as two ways for two steps and n2 as three ways for three steps.
We loop from step four up to n, building each answer from the two before it.
The ways to reach this step equal the sum of the previous two, stored in temp.
We slide the window forward by setting n1 to the old n2.
Then n2 becomes the new total from temp, so we only ever keep two values.
After the loop finishes, n2 holds the number of ways for n steps, and we return it.

min-cost-climbing-stairs.hook: Climbing Stairs with a price tag: same two-choice recurrence, now minimizing instead of counting.
min-cost-climbing-stairs.ask: Each step has a cost you pay when you stand on it. You may start on step zero or step one, and climb one or two steps each move. Return the minimum total cost to get past the last step.
min-cost-climbing-stairs.exampleWhy: Stand on steps 0, 2, 4 and 6, each costing 1, and hop over both 100s. Total 4.

brute.idea: Recurse from each step: pay its cost, then take the cheaper of jumping one or two steps. Try both starts.
steps: Past the end? Cost 0
Else cost[i] + min(go(i + 1), go(i + 2))
Answer: min(go(0), go(1))
brute.whySlow: Each call branches twice and repeats subproblems; 1,000 steps means an astronomical number of calls.

optimal.insight: The cheapest way from step i is its cost plus the cheaper of the next two steps. Fill it in backward from the top, in place.
steps: Append 0 for the top
Walk backward from the third-last index
cost[i] += min(cost[i + 1], cost[i + 2])
Answer: min(cost[0], cost[1])

codeNotes.note: Pay here, then cheaper next move
Start on step zero or one

pitfalls: The top is past the last index; you do not pay to land there.
Remember you may start from step one for free.

say.intro: Min Cost Climbing Stairs. Each step costs money when you stand on it. You can start on step zero or step one. Then climb one or two steps at a time. The top, past the last step, is free. Here, we hop over both hundreds and pay just four.
say.brute: The obvious way is recursion. From step i, pay its cost, then take the cheaper of a one step or two step jump. Try starting on step zero and step one, and keep the smaller. It's correct. But it branches twice at every step, and redoes the same steps endlessly. A thousand steps? Completely hopeless.
say.insight: Now, notice. The cheapest cost from step i only depends on the next two steps. So let's work backwards from the top. Each cell becomes its own cost plus the cheaper of the two cells after it. And here's a bonus. We can overwrite the input array. No extra memory at all. Just one backward pass.
say.anim: We start with the cost array, and append a zero for the top step. Index starts at five, the third-last position, ready to walk backward. At index five, cost becomes one plus the minimum of its next two steps. At index four, cost one becomes two, adding the cheaper neighbor cost. At index three, cost becomes three, combining with the smaller next step. At index two, cost becomes three again, using the cheapest path forward. At index one, cost jumps to one hundred three, reflecting its high original cost. At index zero, cost becomes four, and the loop finally ends. Comparing cost zero and cost one, the minimum four is returned as the answer.
say.code: We append a zero. That's the top, and it costs nothing. Then we loop backward, starting from the third last index. Each cell adds the minimum of the next two cells. In other words, pay here, then take the cheaper next move. Now every cell holds the cheapest way to finish from there. We can start on step zero or one, so return the smaller.
say.outro: Linear time, constant extra space. Pattern: one dimensional dynamic programming. Same shape as climbing stairs, but minimizing instead of counting.

min-cost-climbing-stairs.title: Min Cost Climbing Stairs
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container the problem expects for our method.
This method takes the list of step costs and returns the minimum total cost as an integer.
The first comment says we need a top step beyond the last stair, so we model it with zero cost.
We append zero to the cost list, creating the top platform that costs nothing to stand on.
The second comment says we start the backward walk at the third-last index of the extended list.
We set index to the length of cost minus three, which is the last real step whose two successors both exist.
We loop while index is at least zero, moving backward through every real step.
The comment reminds us that the cost at a step is its own cost plus the cheaper of the next two steps.
We add the smaller of the next step and the one after to this step's cost, storing the result in place.
We decrease index by one to move to the previous step.
The final comment says we may begin on either step zero or step one.
We return the smaller of cost at zero and cost at one, since each now holds the cheapest total from there.

house-robber.hook: Rob or skip, house by house. Two running numbers capture every possible plan.
house-robber.ask: Houses on a street each hold some money. You cannot rob two neighboring houses, or the alarm goes off. Return the most money you can steal.
house-robber.exampleWhy: Rob houses with 2, 9 and 1: no two are adjacent, total 12. Taking 7 blocks both 2 and 9.

brute.idea: At each house, either rob it and jump two ahead, or skip it and move one ahead. Recurse on both and take the max.
steps: Past the end? Return 0
Rob: nums[i] + best(i + 2)
Skip: best(i + 1)
Return the larger
brute.whySlow: Each house doubles the branches with repeated subproblems; 100 houses is far beyond any time limit.

optimal.insight: The best up to house i is either the best up to i - 1 (skip it) or the best up to i - 2 plus this house (rob it). Two numbers suffice.
steps: rob1 = best two houses back, rob2 = best one back
For each house: max(house + rob1, rob2)
Slide: rob1 = rob2, rob2 = new best
Return rob2

codeNotes.note: Best two back, best one back
Rob this house, or skip it

pitfalls: Greedy every-other-house fails: [2,1,1,2] needs houses 0 and 3.
Empty or one-house streets must still work.

say.intro: House Robber. Each house on the street holds some money. But rob two neighbors, and the alarm goes off. What's the most you can take? Here, robbing two, nine and one gives twelve. Notice the seven. It looks juicy, but it blocks both neighbors. Taking it costs us more.
say.brute: At every house, you have two choices. Rob it and jump two houses ahead. Or skip it and move to the next one. We recurse on both and keep the better total. It works. But the same subproblems get solved again and again. The work roughly doubles with every house. A hundred houses? Hopeless.
say.insight: Here's the key. The best total up to this house is one of two things. Either the best up to the previous house, because we skip this one. Or the best from two houses back, plus this house. That's it. So we only ever need two numbers, sliding along the street.
say.anim: We start with rob1 and rob2 both at zero, tracking best totals as we scan houses. At house worth 2, robbing gives 2 while skipping gives 0, so current best is 2. At house worth 7, robbing gives 7 versus skipping's 2, updating current best to 7. At house worth 9, robbing gives 11 versus skipping's 7, so best becomes 11. At house worth 3, robbing gives 10 but skipping keeps 11, so best stays 11. At house worth 1, robbing gives 12 beating skip's 11, making current best 12. With all houses considered, the function returns rob2 as the final answer. The maximum amount that can be robbed without alerting police is 12.
say.code: Both totals start at zero. Those are the best two back and the best one back. For each house, we rob it or skip it. The new best is the larger of this house plus the total two back, or the total one back. Then we slide the window forward. When the loop ends, the second total is the best for the whole street.
say.outro: Linear time, constant space. Pattern: one dimensional dynamic programming. Take it or skip it. Then remember only the last two answers.

house-robber.title: House Robber
house-robber.optimalCode:
class Solution:
    def rob(self, nums: List[int]) -> int:
        # 1. rob1 = best total two houses back, rob2 = best total one house back
        rob1 = 0
        rob2 = 0

        # 2. For each house, decide to rob it or skip it
        for money in nums:
            best_if_rob = money + rob1
            best_if_skip = rob2
            current_best = max(best_if_rob, best_if_skip)

            # 3. Slide the window forward by one house
            rob1 = rob2
            rob2 = current_best

        # 4. rob2 holds the best total after considering all houses
        return rob2
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container this problem's method lives in.
The rob method takes the list of house values called nums and returns the maximum money as an integer.
This comment explains that rob1 tracks the best total from two houses back and rob2 tracks the best from one house back.
We start rob1 at zero because before any houses exist, there is no money to have collected.
We start rob2 at zero as well, since the best total with no houses considered is nothing.
This comment says that for each house we choose between robbing it and skipping it.
We loop through every house, naming its value money, so each house is decided in street order.
If we rob this house, we add its money to rob1, because the neighbor just before it must be skipped.
If we skip this house, our best total simply stays equal to rob2, the best through the previous house.
We take the larger of robbing and skipping, which gives the best total up to the current house.
This comment says we now slide our two-number window forward by one house.
We move rob1 up to the old rob2, so it now represents two houses back for the next house.
We set rob2 to current best, so it now represents the best total through this house.
This comment notes that after the loop, rob2 contains the answer covering every house.
We return rob2, the maximum money we can steal without robbing two neighboring houses.

house-robber-ii.hook: Same robbery, but the street is a circle: the first and last houses are now neighbors.
house-robber-ii.ask: Houses are arranged in a circle, each with some money. You cannot rob two adjacent houses, and the first and last houses are adjacent too. Return the most money you can steal.
house-robber-ii.exampleWhy: 2, 9 and 1 is no longer allowed since 1 and 2 touch. Best is 2 + 9 = 11.

brute.idea: Try every rob-or-skip choice, remembering whether house 0 was robbed. If it was, the last house is forbidden.
steps: Recurse: rob house i or skip it
Track whether house 0 was robbed
At the last house, block it if house 0 was taken
Return the max total
brute.whySlow: Every house branches into two choices; 100 houses means about 2^100 paths.

optimal.insight: The first and last houses can never both be robbed. So solve the straight-line problem twice: once without the last house, once without the first.
steps: Run House Robber on nums[1:]
Run House Robber on nums[:-1]
Also consider nums[0] alone, for one house
Return the largest

codeNotes.note: Drop first or last; one house case
Rob this house or skip it

pitfalls: With one house, both slices are empty; the nums[0] term rescues it.
Slicing copies the list; pass indices to keep O(1) space.

say.intro: House Robber Two. Same rules, but now the houses form a circle. So the first and last houses are neighbors too. On a straight street, two, nine and one gave twelve. But now that one and that two touch. Alarm. So the best is two plus nine, which is eleven.
say.brute: The obvious way tries every rob or skip choice, house by house. It also remembers whether we robbed the very first house. If we did, the last house is off limits. At the end, keep the best total. It's correct. But two choices per house makes it exponential. A hundred houses? It never finishes.
say.insight: Here's the thing. The circle only adds one rule. The first and last houses can't both be robbed. So at least one of them gets skipped. That means we solve the ordinary straight street twice. Once without the last house. Once without the first. Then take the better answer. Plus one special case: a single house.
say.anim: We start with houses holding 2, 7, 9, 3, and 1, arranged in a circle. First we solve ignoring the last house, using the sublist 2, 7, 9, 3. The helper sweeps through, tracking best totals as previous and current update each step. After processing house 9, current reaches 11, the best so far for this range. Without the last house, the maximum achievable total comes out to 11. Next we solve ignoring the first house, using the sublist 7, 9, 3, 1. This time the running total ends lower, returning 10 as the best result. Comparing 11 and 10, the final answer for robbing the circular houses is 11.
say.code: The main method takes the max of three things. The first house alone, for the one house case. The helper without the first house. And the helper without the last house. The helper is plain House Robber. Two rolling totals. At each house, rob it or skip it. Then it returns the second total, the best for that straight street.
say.outro: Linear time. Linear space as written, because slicing copies the list. Pattern: one dimensional dynamic programming. Circle causing trouble? Split it into two straight lines.

house-robber-ii.title: House Robber II
lineNotes: We define a class called Solution, which holds the methods for this problem.
The rob method takes the list of house values and returns the maximum money we can steal.
This comment says a single house is a special case, because the circle logic would otherwise exclude it.
We check whether the list has exactly one house.
If so, we simply return that house's money, since there are no neighbors to conflict with.
This comment explains the first of two scenarios, where the last house is skipped.
We run the straight-line helper on every house except the last and store the result as withoutLast.
This comment explains the second scenario, where the first house is skipped.
We run the helper on every house except the first and store the result as withoutFirst.
This comment says we pick the better of the two scenarios.
We return the larger of withoutLast and withoutFirst, which guarantees the first and last houses are never both robbed.
The helper method solves the ordinary straight-line house robber problem for a given list of houses.
We set previous to zero, representing the best total from two houses back.
We set current to zero, representing the best total up to the previous house.
We loop through each house's money value in order.
The new best is the larger of robbing this house plus previous, or skipping it and keeping current.
We shift previous forward so it now holds the old current best.
We update current to the new best total we just computed.
After the loop ends, we return current, the maximum money obtainable from this straight row of houses.

longest-palindromic-substring.hook: Every palindrome has a center. Expand from all 2n - 1 of them instead of checking every substring.
longest-palindromic-substring.ask: Given a string, return its longest contiguous piece that reads the same forwards and backwards.
longest-palindromic-substring.exampleWhy: abba reads the same both ways. Its center sits between the two b's, an even-length palindrome.

brute.idea: Check every substring: reverse it and compare. Keep the longest palindrome found.
steps: Pick every start i and end j
Is s[i..j] equal to its reverse?
Longer than the best? Keep it
brute.whySlow: A 1,000-character string has half a million substrings, each costing up to 1,000 to check.

optimal.insight: A palindrome mirrors around its center. Grow outward from each center while the ends match; check odd centers (i, i) and even centers (i, i + 1).
steps: For each index i
Expand from (i, i) for odd lengths
Expand from (i, i + 1) for even lengths
Record any longer palindrome in shared self.res

codeNotes.match: while left >= 0 and right < len(s) and s[left] == s[right]:

codeNotes.note: Longer than the best so far?

pitfalls: Forgetting even-length centers misses answers like abba.
Manacher's algorithm is O(n), but expand-around-center is the expected answer.

say.intro: Longest Palindromic Substring. Find the longest contiguous piece that reads the same forwards and backwards. In c a b b a d, that's a b b a. Now, notice its length is even. Its middle sits between the two b's. Keep that in mind.
say.brute: The obvious approach? Check every substring. For each start and end, reverse the piece and compare. Keep the longest match. There are about n squared substrings. Each check costs up to n. So that's n cubed. For a thousand characters, about a billion operations. Way too slow.
say.insight: Let's flip the question around. Every palindrome has a center, and it mirrors outward from there. So instead of checking substrings, we stand at each center and expand. Both ends match? Keep going. They differ? Stop. And there are two kinds of centers. On a letter for odd lengths. Between two letters for even lengths. Together they cover every palindrome.
say.anim: We start with the string cabbad and an empty result to track the longest palindrome. At index zero, expanding around the single letter c gives a palindrome of length one. At index one, expanding around a and around b both give single letter matches. Expanding around index two, the two b letters match, extending to the palindrome bb, length two. Expanding outward further, a matches a and b matches b, forming abba with length four. Later centers at indices two through five only produce single letters, nothing longer. The loop finishes checking every center, and the longest palindrome found is abba.
say.code: For every index, we call the helper twice. Once with both pointers on i, the odd center. Once with right one step ahead, the even center. The helper expands while both ends match. Longer than the best so far? Record it. Then step both ends outward. One quirk: the helper returns the shared best. So the last call's result is the overall best.
say.outro: n squared time, constant space. Pattern: palindromes. The simplest solution expands around every possible center, odd and even.

Then we expand around the gap between i and the next index, which finds even length palindromes.
After all centers are tried, we return the longest palindrome stored in result.

palindromic-substrings.hook: Same expand-around-center trick, but now every successful expansion is one more palindrome.
palindromic-substrings.ask: Given a string, count how many of its substrings are palindromes. Substrings at different positions count separately, even if they contain the same letters.
palindromic-substrings.exampleWhy: Four single letters, plus aba and aa: six palindromes.

brute.idea: Check every substring by comparing it with its reverse, and count the matches.
steps: Pick every start i and end j
Is s[i..j] equal to its reverse?
Yes? Add one to the count
brute.whySlow: With 1,000 characters, half a million substrings each cost up to 1,000 to check.

optimal.insight: Each palindrome has one center. Expanding from a center, every step where the ends still match is exactly one new palindrome.
steps: For each index i
Expand from (i, i) and count matches
Expand from (i, i + 1) and count matches
Sum all the counts

codeNotes.match: while l >= 0 and r < len(s) and s[l] == s[r]:

pitfalls: Count positions, not distinct strings: aaa has six palindromes.
Do not forget even-length centers.

say.intro: Palindromic Substrings. Count every substring that reads the same forwards and backwards. Copies at different positions count separately. In a b a a, each of the four letters is a palindrome on its own. Add a b a, and a a. That's six in total.
say.brute: The obvious approach? List every substring, and check it against its reverse. If they match, add one. There are about n squared substrings. Each check costs up to n. So it's n cubed overall. For a thousand characters, around a billion operations. Way too slow.
say.insight: Here's the thing. Every palindrome has exactly one center. So let's stand at each center and expand outward. Each step where both ends still match? That's one more palindrome. The first mismatch ends that center for good. Just like the longest palindrome problem, we check odd centers on letters, and even centers between letters. Nothing missed, nothing double counted.
say.anim: We start counting palindromic substrings in abaa, with count set to zero. At index zero, expanding around a single center matches, giving one palindrome, the letter a. Checking the even center between index zero and one fails since a and b differ, adding zero. At index one, centered on b, it matches once, then expanding further fails, so count becomes three. At index two, centered on a, expansion succeeds once more, raising count to four. The even center between index two and three also matches once, bringing count to five. Finally index three, the last a, matches itself once, pushing count to six. After checking every center, the total palindromic substrings found in abaa is six.
say.code: We loop over each index. First, add the count from the odd center, with both pointers on i. Then add the even center, with right one step ahead. The helper starts a local count at zero. While the pointers are in bounds and the ends match, it's still a palindrome. So each expansion adds one. Then both ends step outward.
say.outro: n squared time, constant space. Pattern: expand around center, a close cousin of dynamic programming. Same trick as the longest palindrome problem.

palindromic-substrings.optimalCode:
class Solution:
    def countSubstrings(self, s: str) -> int:
        count = 0

        # 1. For each index, try it as a center
        for i in range(len(s)):
            # 2. Expand from a single character center (odd length)
            count += self.expandAndCount(s, i, i)
            # 3. Expand from a between-characters center (even length)
            count += self.expandAndCount(s, i, i + 1)

        # 4. Sum of all counts is the answer
        return count

    def expandAndCount(self, s, left, right):
        count = 0
        while left >= 0 and right < len(s) and s[left] == s[right]:
            count += 1
            left -= 1
            right += 1
        return count

decode-ways.hook: Looks like a string puzzle, behaves like Climbing Stairs, with zeros as the trap.
decode-ways.ask: Letters are encoded as numbers: A is 1, B is 2, up to Z as 26. Given a string of digits, count how many ways it can be decoded back into letters.

brute.idea: From position i, take one digit or a valid two-digit code, and recurse on the rest. Count the ways that reach the end.
steps: Reached the end? One way
Leading zero? Zero ways
Take one digit, recurse
If 10 to 26, take two digits, recurse
brute.whySlow: Strings like 111...1 branch twice almost everywhere; 100 digits is about 2^100 calls.

optimal.insight: The number of ways from position i only depends on i. Cache it: ways(i) = ways(i + 1) + ways(i + 2) when a two-digit code fits.
steps: dp[len(s)] = 1: empty tail decodes one way
A 0 at position i gives zero ways
Single digit: add ways(i + 1)
Valid 10 to 26: add ways(i + 2)
Store in dp and return

pitfalls: Zero cannot stand alone: 06 decodes zero ways, but 10 and 20 are valid.
27 and above are not letters; only 10 to 26 pair up.

say.intro: Decode Ways. Letters are encoded as numbers. A is one, B is two, all the way to Z at twenty six. Given a string of digits, how many ways can we decode it? One two two six has five. For example, twelve, two, six. Or one, twenty two, six.
say.brute: The obvious approach? From each position, decode one digit and recurse. If the next two digits make ten to twenty six, try that too. Count the paths that reach the end. A lone zero is a dead end. So what's the catch? No caching. It branches twice per digit. A hundred ones means an astronomical number of calls.
say.insight: Here's the key. The number of ways from position i depends only on i. Not on how we got there. So cache it. Ways from i is ways from i plus one. Plus ways from i plus two, if a valid two digit code fits. Look familiar? It's Climbing Stairs, with zeros as the trap. Each position is solved once.
say.anim: We start with the string one two two six, and set up a cache called dp. Dp at position four is one, representing the empty tail with one way to decode. At position three the digit is six, so single decode gives ways equal to one. At position two, digit two pairs with six forming twenty six, a valid two digit code. Ways becomes two here, combining single and double digit decodings, stored as dp of two. At position one, digit two pairs with two forming twenty two, another valid two digit code. At position zero, digit one always allows a two digit pair, giving ways equal to five. The function returns dp of zero, giving the final answer of five decoding ways.
say.code: The empty suffix has exactly one decoding, so the cache starts with that. In the search, already solved? Reuse it. Nothing can start with zero, so a zero gives zero ways. Otherwise, decode one digit and recurse. If the next two digits make ten to twenty six, take both and recurse too. Cache the sum for i, and return it. The bottom up loop after the return never runs.
say.outro: Linear time and space. Pattern: one dimensional dynamic programming. Branching choices over a string? Memoize by index, then maybe go bottom up.

coin-change.hook: Greedy fails here: grabbing the biggest coin first gives three coins when two will do.
coin-change.ask: You have unlimited coins of some values and a target amount. Return the fewest coins that add up to the amount exactly, or -1 if no combination works.
coin-change.exampleWhy: 3 + 3 = 6 uses two coins. Greedy takes 4, then 1, then 1 — three coins.

brute.idea: Try every coin as the last one used, recursively solve the smaller amount, and keep the best. The same sub-amounts get solved again and again.
steps: fewest(a) tries each coin c ≤ a
Recurse on a - c and add one coin
Keep the minimum; amount 0 costs 0
brute.whySlow: Amount 10,000 with a few coins means exponentially many paths re-solving the same amounts.

optimal.insight: fewest(a) = 1 + min over coins of fewest(a - c). Smaller amounts are subproblems, so fill a table from 0 up and solve each amount once.
steps: dp[a] = fewest coins for amount a, start at 'infinity'
dp[0] = 0: zero coins make zero
For each a and coin c: dp[a] = min(dp[a], 1 + dp[a - c])
Still 'infinity' at the end means impossible: -1

codeNotes.note: Coin c on top of best smaller

codeNotes.match: return dp[amount] if dp[amount] != amount + 1 else -1

pitfalls: Greedy by largest coin is wrong: coins 1, 3, 4 with amount 6 breaks it.
Return -1, not the sentinel, when the amount cannot be formed.

say.intro: Coin Change. Given some coin values and a target, find the fewest coins that add up to it exactly. Coins one, three and four. Amount six. The answer is two: three plus three. Now, grab the four first, and you're stuck needing three coins. So greedy fails here.
say.brute: The brute force asks one question. Which coin do I use last? Try each one, then solve the smaller amount that's left. Keep the minimum. It's correct. So what's the catch? It solves the same amounts over and over. With an amount in the thousands, the paths explode exponentially.
say.insight: Here's the key. The best answer for any amount is one coin, plus the best answer for what's left. Every smaller amount is a subproblem. Solve it once, and store it. So we build a table from zero upward. Each entry just reads earlier entries. No amount is ever computed twice.
say.anim: We start with coins one, three, four and amount six, setting infinity as seven. The dp table fills with placeholder sevens, except dp of zero which stays zero. For amount one, using coin one gives candidate one, better than infinity. For amount two, coin one gives candidate two, updating dp of two. For amount three, coin one gives three, but coin three gives just one, the best so far. For amount four, trying each coin, coin four gives candidate one, the new minimum. For amount five, testing coins one, three and four, dp of five settles at two. Finally for amount six, coin three gives candidate two, beating other options, so coin change returns two.
say.code: We fill the table with amount plus one. That acts as infinity. Entry zero is zero coins, our base case. Then we walk the amounts, smallest first. For each coin that fits, try one plus the best answer for what remains. At the end, is the last entry still the sentinel? Then it's unreachable, so return minus one. Otherwise, return it.
say.outro: Amount times coins time, linear space. Pattern: one dimensional dynamic programming, unbounded knapsack. Greedy looks tempting? Hunt for a counterexample first.

Otherwise we return dp at the amount, which is the fewest coins needed.

maximum-product-subarray.hook: A negative number can turn the worst product into the best one, so track the minimum too.
maximum-product-subarray.ask: Given a list of integers, find the contiguous run of numbers whose product is largest, and return that product.

brute.idea: Try every starting index, extend the run one number at a time, multiply as you go, and track the largest product seen.
steps: Fix a start i
Extend j to the right, multiplying
Keep the max product
brute.whySlow: With 20,000 numbers that is about 200 million multiplications.

optimal.insight: The best product ending here is n, n·prevMax or n·prevMin — a negative n flips max and min. Keep both and update in one pass.
steps: Keep curMax and curMin for runs ending at the previous number
Candidates: n, n·curMax, n·curMin
curMax = biggest candidate, curMin = smallest
Update the answer with curMax

codeNotes.note: Answer must be a real subarray

codeNotes.match: curMax = max(n * curMax, n * curMin, n)
codeNotes.note: Extend a run, or restart at n

pitfalls: Forgetting tmp: curMin would then use the already-updated curMax.
Zeros reset everything; keeping n alone as a candidate handles that.

say.intro: Maximum Product Subarray. Find the contiguous stretch with the largest product. Our numbers are two, minus five, minus two, minus four, three. The best stretch is minus two, times minus four, times three. That's twenty four. It beats the twenty from the first three numbers.
say.brute: The obvious way? Try every start, then extend to the right, multiplying as you go. Track the best product. Simple and correct. But it's quadratic. Twenty thousand numbers means about two hundred million multiplications. Way too slow. And notice, it throws away every product when it moves to the next start.
say.insight: Here's the twist. A negative number flips the sign. So the smallest product so far can become the largest one step later. That means we keep two values for runs ending here. The max, and the min. Each new number either extends one of them, or starts fresh on its own. No restarting from scratch.
say.anim: We start with curMax, curMin, and answer all set to the first number, two. At index one, number is negative five, so products with curMax and curMin are compared. Since negative five flips things, curMax becomes negative five and curMin becomes negative ten. At index two, number is negative two, multiplying curMin gives a big candidate, twenty. CurMax jumps to twenty because multiplying two negatives gave a large positive product. At index three, number is negative four, but curMax drops to eight this time. Finally at index four, number is three, giving candidateMax twenty four, the new best. The loop ends and the function returns twenty four as the maximum product subarray.
say.code: The answer starts at the first number, so it's a real subarray. The running max and min start at one, the empty product. For each number, we save the old max before it's overwritten. The new max is the biggest of the number times max, times min, or the number alone. That's extend a run, or restart. The new min takes the smallest of those. Then update the best ever.
say.outro: Linear time, constant space. Pattern: one dimensional dynamic programming, a cousin of Kadane's algorithm. With products, track the minimum too.

maximum-product-subarray.title: Maximum Product Subarray
maximum-product-subarray.optimalCode:
class Solution:
    def maxProduct(self, nums: List[int]) -> int:
        # 1. Start with the first number as our running max/min and answer
        curMax = nums[0]
        curMin = nums[0]
        answer = nums[0]

        # 2. Walk through the rest of the numbers
        for i in range(1, len(nums)):
            number = nums[i]

            # 3. Compute candidates before overwriting curMax
            candidateMax = max(number, number * curMax, number * curMin)
            candidateMin = min(number, number * curMax, number * curMin)

            curMax = candidateMax
            curMin = candidateMin

            # 4. Update the best answer seen so far
            answer = max(answer, curMax)

        return answer
lineNotes: This defines the Solution class that holds our method for the maximum product subarray problem.
The method maxProduct takes a list of integers called nums and returns the largest product of any contiguous run.
This comment says we begin by seeding the running maximum, minimum and answer with the first number.
We set curMax to the first number, since the best product ending at index zero is just that number.
We set curMin to the first number too, because a negative later could turn the smallest product into the largest.
We set answer to the first number so a single element list returns correctly and we have a baseline.
This comment says we now walk through the remaining numbers after the first one.
The loop runs index i from one to the end of nums, since index zero is already handled.
We read the current value at index i into number to keep the following lines readable.
This comment warns us to compute both new candidates before overwriting curMax, since both need the old value.
The new maximum is the best of starting fresh at number, or extending the old max or the old min.
The new minimum is the smallest of number alone, or number times the old max or old min.
Now that both candidates are computed safely, we store the new maximum in curMax.
We store the new minimum in curMin, ready for the next iteration where a negative may flip things.
This comment says we now update the best answer seen so far using the new running maximum.
We set answer to the larger of itself and curMax, recording the best product of any subarray ending here.
After the loop finishes, we return answer, the largest product found across all contiguous subarrays.
maximum-product-subarray.optimalCodeOriginal:
class Solution:
    def maxProduct(self, nums: List[int]) -> int:
        # O(n)/O(1) : Time/Memory
        res = nums[0]
        curMin, curMax = 1, 1

        for n in nums:

            tmp = curMax * n
            curMax = max(n * curMax, n * curMin, n)
            curMin = min(tmp, n * curMin, n)
            res = max(res, curMax)
        return res

word-break.hook: Splitting a string looks like a search problem, but each suffix only needs to be solved once.
word-break.ask: Given a string and a dictionary of words, return true if the string can be cut into a sequence of dictionary words. Words may be reused.
word-break.exampleWhy: cats + and + dog, or cat + sand + dog: both use only dictionary words.

brute.idea: From the current position, try every word that matches there and recurse on the rest. Succeed when the position reaches the end.
steps: At index i, try each dictionary word
If it matches, recurse from i + len(word)
Reaching the end means True
brute.whySlow: Input like 'aaaa...ab' with words 'a', 'aa' re-explores the same suffixes; 300 characters never finishes.

optimal.insight: Whether s[i:] can be split depends only on i. dp[i] is True if some word matches at i and dp[i + len(word)] is True. Fill from the end.
steps: dp[i] means the suffix starting at i is breakable
dp[len(s)] = True: the empty suffix
For i from right to left, try each word matching at i
dp[i] copies dp[i + len(w)]; stop once True

codeNotes.match: if (i + len(w)) <= len(s) and s[i : i + len(w)] == w:
codeNotes.note: Word fits and matches at i

pitfalls: Greedy longest match fails: after 'cats' you may need to back off to 'cat'.
Break once dp[i] is True so a later word cannot overwrite it.

say.intro: Word Break. Can a string be chopped into dictionary words? Take cats and dog, written as one word. Our dictionary has cat, cats, and, sand and dog. Can we do it? Yes. Cats, and, dog. Words can be reused as often as you like. So the answer here is true. Actually, in two different ways.
say.brute: The brute force stands at a position and tries every word that matches there. Then it recurses on the rest. Reach the end, and you win. So what's the problem? Repetition. Cat then sand, or cats then and. Both leave us at dog. Each leftover suffix gets solved again. Bad inputs blow up exponentially.
say.insight: Here's the key. Whether a suffix can be broken only depends on where it starts. So we store one true or false per starting index. Index i is good if some word matches at i, and the spot right after that word is also good. We work backwards from the end. Each index is solved once.
say.anim: We start with the string catsanddog and our dictionary of five words, building a dp array. Dp has eleven slots, all false except the empty suffix at the end, and we begin checking from index nine. At index seven, the word dog matches and dp of ten is true, so dp of seven becomes true. At index four, the word and matches and dp of seven is true, so dp of four becomes true. At index three, the word sand matches and dp of seven is true, so dp of three becomes true. At index zero, the word cat matches and dp of three is true, so dp of zero becomes true. Dp of zero is true, meaning the whole string can be split, so the function returns true.
say.code: We make one slot per suffix start, one longer than the string. The empty suffix is trivially fine, so the end is true. Then we walk i from right to left, so shorter suffixes come first. For each word, does it fit and match at i? Then inherit the answer from just past the word. Once i is true, break. Finally, return index zero.
say.outro: About n times words times word length. Pattern: one dimensional dynamic programming over suffixes. Recursion keeps repeating a suffix? Cache it.

longest-increasing-subsequence.hook: Subsequences explode exponentially, yet each index only needs one number: the best chain starting there.
longest-increasing-subsequence.ask: Given a list of integers, return the length of the longest subsequence whose values strictly increase. A subsequence keeps the original order but may skip elements.
longest-increasing-subsequence.exampleWhy: 0, 1, 2, 3 is strictly increasing with length 4; nothing longer exists.

brute.idea: For every element, take it or skip it, taking only if it beats the last taken value. Return the longest chain any choice produces.
steps: At index i, always try skipping it
Take it only if bigger than the last taken
Return the longer choice
brute.whySlow: 2,500 numbers give 2 to the 2,500 take-or-skip patterns — hopeless.

optimal.insight: The longest increasing chain starting at i is 1 plus the best LIS[j] over later j with a bigger value. Compute from the right.
steps: LIS[i] = longest increasing subsequence starting at i
Start every LIS[i] at 1
Walk i from right to left; check every j after i
If nums[i] < nums[j]: LIS[i] = max(LIS[i], 1 + LIS[j])
Answer is the max over all i

codeNotes.note: Each number alone has length one
Right to left: later answers ready
Extend the best chain from j

pitfalls: Strictly increasing: equal values cannot chain.
Mention the O(n log n) follow-up using binary search on tails.

say.intro: Longest Increasing Subsequence. Pick numbers in order, skipping any you like, so each one beats the last. How long can that chain get? For zero, one, zero, three, two, three, the answer is four. Zero, one, two, three. We skip the second zero and the first three.
say.brute: The brute force decides, for every number, take it or skip it. It only takes a number if it beats the last one taken. So it explores every subset. That's two to the n. A few dozen numbers is already slow. A few thousand? Impossible. And it forgets every answer it already worked out.
say.insight: Let's flip the question. Each index stores the longest chain that starts there. That chain is the number itself, plus the best chain from some later, bigger number. Now think about it. If we fill from the right, every answer we need is already known. No subsets listed. Each index just reads stored answers.
say.anim: We start with nums and set every LIS value to one, since each number alone counts. At index four, comparing with index five, three is less than three fails, so LIS stays two from before. At index three, value three beats values at four and five, but LIS stays at one since those aren't bigger. At index two, zero is less than three and three, so LIS becomes three, chaining through later elements. At index one, value one is less than values at two, three and four, building LIS up to three. At index zero, zero beats everything after it, so LIS becomes four, the best possible chain. Finally we take the max of all LIS values, giving the answer four.
say.code: Every entry starts at one, since each number alone has length one. We loop i from right to left, so later answers are ready. For every j after i, can the number at j follow the number at i? If so, extend the best chain from j. One plus entry j, if that's bigger. Finally, return the max entry. The best chain can start anywhere. Two loops, so n squared.
say.outro: n squared time, linear space. Pattern: one dimensional dynamic programming. In an interview, mention the n log n binary search version too.

longest-increasing-subsequence.title: Longest Increasing Subsequence
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container the interview platform expects for our method.
The method lengthOfLIS takes a list of integers called nums and returns the length of the longest strictly increasing subsequence.
We create a list called LIS with one entry per number, starting at one because each element alone is a chain.
We loop i from the last index down to zero, so every later answer is ready before we need it.
For each i, an inner loop j checks every position to the right of i as a possible next element.
We only consider j when the value at i is strictly smaller than the value at j, keeping the chain increasing.
We update LIS at i to the larger of its current value or one plus LIS at j, extending the best chain.
Since the best chain may start anywhere, we return the maximum value in LIS as the final answer.

partition-equal-subset-sum.hook: Splitting into two equal halves is really one question: can some subset hit half the total?
partition-equal-subset-sum.ask: Given a list of positive integers, return true if you can split them into two groups with equal sums.
partition-equal-subset-sum.exampleWhy: The total is 22. {11} and {1, 5, 5} both sum to 11.

brute.idea: The target is half the total. Recursively include or exclude each number and check whether some choice reaches the target exactly.
steps: Odd total: impossible
For each number, include it or skip it
Remaining hits 0: True
brute.whySlow: 200 numbers mean up to 2 to the 200 include-or-skip patterns.

optimal.insight: We never care which numbers form a sum, only which sums are reachable. Keep a set of reachable sums; it holds at most total + 1 values.
steps: Odd total: return False
Reachable sums start as {0}
Each number turns every sum t into t and t + num
Any t + num equal to half: return True

codeNotes.note: Odd total can never split evenly

pitfalls: Check the odd total first; it rules out many inputs instantly.
Build into a new set so the same number is never used twice.

say.intro: Partition Equal Subset Sum. Can we split the numbers into two groups with the same total? We have one, five, eleven and five. The total is twenty two. Put eleven on one side. One, five and five on the other. Eleven each. So the answer is true.
say.brute: First, an odd total can never split evenly. Return false. Otherwise, we need a subset that sums to half. The brute force includes or excludes every number, recursively. That's two to the n. Two hundred numbers? Hopeless. And here's the waste. Many subsets reach the same partial sum, yet each is explored separately.
say.insight: Here's the thing. We never need to know which numbers made a sum. Only which sums are reachable. So we keep a set of reachable sums. Each new number either joins a sum or it doesn't. And the set can never hold more than the total. So the work stays polynomial. Total sums, times n numbers.
say.anim: We start with the array one, five, eleven, five, and compute its total sum. Total is twenty two, which is even, so splitting equally is still possible. Target becomes eleven, half the total, and we start tracking reachable sums from zero. Processing number one, we add it to zero, giving reachable sums zero and one. Processing number five, we expand reachable sums to include zero, one, five, and six. Processing number eleven, adding it to zero gives newSum eleven, matching our target. Since newSum equals target, the function immediately returns true, confirming a valid split exists.
say.code: An odd total can never split evenly, so return false. The empty subset sums to zero, so the set starts with zero. Each half must hit the target, half the total. For each number, build a new set. For every reachable sum, does adding the number hit the target? Then we've found one half, and we're done. Otherwise, keep the sum with and without the number. That's the next layer.
say.outro: Numbers times total, in time. Space up to the total. Pattern: zero one knapsack. Any partition problem? Reframe it as reaching a target sum.

partition-equal-subset-sum.title: Partition Equal Subset Sum
partition-equal-subset-sum.optimalCode:
class Solution:
    def canPartition(self, nums: List[int]) -> bool:
        total = sum(nums)
        # 1. Odd total can never be split evenly
        if total % 2 == 1:
            return False

        target = total // 2
        reachable = set()
        reachable.add(0)

        # 2. Try adding each number to every sum we can already make
        for num in nums:
            nextReachable = set()
            for t in reachable:
                newSum = t + num
                # 3. If we hit the target exactly, we found a valid split
                if newSum == target:
                    return True
                nextReachable.add(newSum)
                nextReachable.add(t)
            reachable = nextReachable

        # 4. No combination reached the target
        return False
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container the interview platform expects for our method.
The method canPartition takes the list of numbers and returns true or false depending on whether an equal split exists.
We compute the total sum of all the numbers, since both groups must add up to half of it.
This comment says an odd total can never be divided into two equal whole-number halves.
We check whether the total leaves a remainder of one when divided by two, meaning it is odd.
In that odd case we return false right away, because no equal split is possible.
Otherwise we set target to half the total, which is the sum one group must reach.
We create an empty set called reachable to hold every subset sum we can currently build.
We add zero to the set, because choosing no numbers at all gives a sum of zero.
This comment explains that each number gets added onto every sum we can already make.
We loop through each number in the list, deciding for each whether it joins the group.
We start a fresh set called nextReachable so we do not modify reachable while iterating over it.
We go through every sum t that was reachable before considering this number.
We compute newSum by adding the current number to the existing sum t.
This comment says that hitting the target exactly means we have found a valid split.
We check whether newSum equals the target sum we need.
If it does, we return true immediately, since the other numbers must then make up the other half.
We record newSum as reachable, covering the case where this number is included.
We also keep the old sum t, covering the case where this number is skipped.
After processing the number, we replace reachable with nextReachable so the next number builds on updated sums.
This comment notes that if we finish the loop, no subset ever reached the target.
We return false because after considering every number, the target sum was never reachable.

unique-paths.hook: Counting grid paths by hand explodes, but each cell just adds two neighbours.
unique-paths.ask: A robot starts at the top-left of an m by n grid and may only move right or down. Count the distinct paths to the bottom-right corner.
unique-paths.exampleWhy: In 3 rows by 4 columns the robot makes 2 downs and 3 rights in any order: 5 choose 2 = 10.

brute.idea: From each cell, recursively count paths going down plus paths going right. Any cell on the last row or column has exactly one path.
steps: paths(r, c) = paths(r + 1, c) + paths(r, c + 1)
Last row or column: one path
Start from the top-left
brute.whySlow: A 100 by 100 grid means roughly 2 to the 200 calls, re-counting identical cells.

optimal.insight: Paths from a cell = paths from the cell below + paths from the cell to the right. Fill rows from the bottom, keeping only one row.
steps: Bottom row is all 1s
Move up a row; the rightmost column stays 1
Each cell = its right neighbour + the cell below
The top-left cell holds the answer

codeNotes.note: Climb up one row at a time

pitfalls: Mention the closed form: choose m-1 downs out of m+n-2 moves.
Keep m (rows) and n (columns) straight when sizing the row array.

say.intro: Unique Paths. A robot sits in the top left corner of a grid. It can only step right or down. How many different routes reach the bottom right? For three rows and four columns, there are ten. Why? It's two downs and three rights, in any order.
say.brute: The brute force is recursion. From any cell, the paths are the paths going down plus the paths going right. And any cell on the last row or column has exactly one path. It's correct. But the same cells get counted again and again. That's exponential. A big grid takes forever.
say.insight: Here's the key. Every cell's count is just the cell below, plus the cell to its right. So we fill the grid backwards from the bottom right. But wait, it gets better. We only ever need the row directly below. So one array of length n is enough. Each cell is computed once, and memory stays at one row.
say.anim: We start with a grid of 3 rows and 4 columns, initializing the bottom row to all ones. Moving up one row, we create a new row, still starting as all ones. Filling from right to left, each cell becomes its right neighbor plus the cell below it. After this pass, the new row is 4, 3, 2, 1, replacing the old row. We move up again, building another new row using the same rule. This row finishes as 10, 6, 3, 1, representing paths from the second row. With no more rows to process, we look at the top-left cell. The function returns 10, the total number of unique paths.
say.code: We start with a row of ones. That's the bottom row, one path each. Then we climb up one row at a time. Each new row starts as ones, because the last column is always one. We walk j leftward from the second last column. Each cell is its right neighbour plus the cell below. Then swap rows. Finally, return the first entry, the top left count.
say.outro: Rows times columns time, linear space. Pattern: two dimensional dynamic programming on a grid. It's Pascal's triangle in disguise.

unique-paths.title: Unique Paths
lineNotes: This defines the Solution class that holds our method, as the problem format expects.
The method uniquePaths takes the grid height m and width n and returns the number of distinct paths.
This comment says the bottom row starts as all ones, since from there only rightward moves remain.
We create row as a list of n ones, representing path counts for each cell in the bottom row.
This comment says we move up one row at a time, and the rightmost column always stays one.
We loop m minus one times, because the bottom row is already built and we need the remaining rows.
We start a new row filled with ones, so the rightmost cell is already correct with one path.
This comment explains each cell equals the cell to its right plus the cell directly below it.
We walk columns from second to last down to zero, so the right neighbor is always computed first.
Each new cell adds its right neighbor in newRow to the cell below it, which is the same column in row.
We replace row with newRow, so the next iteration treats this finished row as the one below.
This comment notes that the top-left cell of the final row holds our answer.
We return the first entry of row, which counts all paths from the top-left to the bottom-right.

longest-common-subsequence.hook: The DP grid behind diff tools and DNA alignment: two strings, one table.
longest-common-subsequence.ask: Given two strings, return the length of their longest common subsequence: characters appearing in both, in the same order, not necessarily next to each other.
longest-common-subsequence.exampleWhy: a, c, e appear in that order in both strings, so the length is 3.

brute.idea: Compare the current characters. If equal, take it and advance both; otherwise try skipping one character from either string and keep the better.
steps: Match: 1 + lcs(i + 1, j + 1)
No match: max of skipping either side
Either string used up: 0
brute.whySlow: Two 1,000-character strings branch twice per mismatch — around 2 to the 2,000 calls.

optimal.insight: lcs(i, j) depends only on the suffixes starting at i and j. There are only m·n pairs, so store them in a grid filled from the bottom-right.
steps: dp[i][j] = LCS of text1[i:] and text2[j:]
Extra row and column of zeros: empty suffixes
Match: 1 + diagonal dp[i + 1][j + 1]
Mismatch: max of right and below

codeNotes.match: dp = [[0 for j in range(len(text2) + 1)] for i in range(len(text1) + 1)]

codeNotes.note: Skip one side, keep the best

pitfalls: Subsequence, not substring: matched characters need not be adjacent.
Space can drop to O(min(m, n)) by keeping just two rows.

say.intro: Longest Common Subsequence. Given two strings, find the longest sequence of characters that appears in both. In order, but gaps are allowed. For a b c d e, and a c e, the answer is three. The letters a, c and e. We just skip b and d.
say.brute: The brute force compares the current characters. Do they match? Count one, and move ahead in both strings. If not, try skipping a character in either string. Keep the better result. So what's the catch? Every mismatch branches twice. That's exponential in the combined length. Two thousand character strings would outlast the universe.
say.insight: Now, notice. Every recursive call is just a pair of positions. i in the first string, and j in the second. That's only m times n pairs. So store each answer in a grid. Fill it from the bottom right, so the cells we need are always ready. Each cell then takes constant time.
say.anim: We start with text1 abcde and text2 ace, building a grid of zeros for all suffix pairs. At i equals 4, j equals 2, characters e and e match, so we add one to the diagonal value. When characters mismatch, like d versus e, we take the max of the neighboring cells instead. Moving to i equals 3, c and e still mismatch, so values just carry over from neighbors. At i equals 2, j equals 1, c matches c, giving dp value two from the diagonal plus one. Row by row, matches at b and a build longer chains, propagating counts upward. Finally at i equals 0, j equals 0, a matches a, giving three from the diagonal plus one. The function returns dp of zero zero, confirming the longest common subsequence length is three.
say.code: We build a grid with a zero border, one extra row and column. Then loop i and j backwards. Do the characters match? Then take it and move diagonally. The cell is one plus the diagonal. If not, skip one side and keep the best. That's the max of the cell to the right and the cell below. The top left is the answer for both whole strings.
say.outro: m times n time and space. Pattern: two dimensional dynamic programming on two strings. It's the template for edit distance and more.
