lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container the problem expects for our method.
This method takes two strings, text1 and text2, and returns the length of their longest common subsequence.
We store the length of text1 in length1 so we can size the grid and drive loops.
We store the length of text2 in length2 for the same reason.
This comment says we need an extra row and column of zeros to represent empty suffixes.
We build a grid of zeros with length1 plus one rows and length2 plus one columns, so the borders act as base cases.
This comment explains we fill from bottom-right so every smaller subproblem is already computed when needed.
The outer loop walks i from the last index of text1 down to zero, shrinking the suffix backward.
The inner loop walks j from the last index of text2 down to zero, covering every suffix pair.
This comment says that when characters match, we extend the diagonal answer by one.
We check whether the current characters of text1 at i and text2 at j are equal.
On a match, we set the cell to one plus the diagonal cell, since both characters join the subsequence.
The else branch handles the case where the two current characters differ.
This comment says on a mismatch we take the better result from skipping a character in either string.
We set the cell to the larger of the cell to the right and the cell below, representing skipping from text2 or text1.
Finally we return the top-left cell, which holds the answer for the full strings.

best-time-to-buy-and-sell-stock-with-coo.hook: Stock trading with a mandatory rest day: model it as a tiny state machine and cache it.
best-time-to-buy-and-sell-stock-with-coo.ask: Given daily stock prices, maximise profit with as many buy-then-sell trades as you like, holding at most one share, but after selling you must skip the next day.
best-time-to-buy-and-sell-stock-with-coo.exampleWhy: Buy at 1, sell at 2, cool down, buy at 0, sell at 2: profit 1 + 2 = 3.

brute.idea: Each day, either rest or act: buy if not holding, sell if holding. Selling jumps two days ahead. Recursively try every choice.
steps: State: day i, buying or selling
Rest: move to day i + 1
Buy pays the price; sell earns it and skips a day
brute.whySlow: 5,000 days with two choices each — about 2 to the 5,000 paths.

optimal.insight: Profit from day i onward depends only on (day, holding or not). That is just 2n states, so memoize each one.
steps: dfs(i, buying) = best profit from day i in that state
Cooldown option: dfs(i + 1, same state)
Buy: dfs(i + 1, selling) - price
Sell: dfs(i + 2, buying) + price — the cooldown
Cache each (i, buying)

pitfalls: Selling must jump to i + 2; that is where the cooldown lives.
Base case uses i >= len(prices) because i + 2 can overshoot.

say.intro: Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock with Cooldown. Trade as often as you like, one share at a time. But after any sale, you must sit out a day. Prices are one, two, three, zero, two. The best profit is three. That's two trades, with a rest in between.
say.brute: The brute force tries everything. Each day, you either rest or act. Buy if you hold nothing. Sell if you hold a share. A sale jumps two days ahead, for the cooldown. Two choices per day, so the recursion tree grows exponentially. Five thousand days? More paths than atoms in the universe.
say.insight: Here's the thing. The future only depends on two facts. Which day it is, and whether you're holding a share. That's just two states per day. So cache the best profit for each day and state. Every state gets solved exactly once. And with two choices per state, the total work is linear.
say.anim: We start with prices one two three zero two, and an empty cache to store results. Recursion dives forward, day by day, always starting in the buying state. At day five we hit the base case, returning zero since no days remain. At day four buying gives zero profit, but selling there yields two, which gets cached. Working backward, day three buying and selling both resolve to a best profit of two. At day two, selling beats buying, giving a best profit of three, cached for reuse. Day one buying stores profit two, but selling there computes four using cached future values. Finally day zero buying returns three, so the final maximum profit is three.
say.code: The cache maps a day and a state to the best profit. Past the last day? Return zero. Seen this state? Reuse it. Doing nothing today is always an option. If we're buying, pay today's price and switch state. If we're selling, add today's price, then skip tomorrow by jumping two days. Keep the best, cache it, and return. We start on day zero, ready to buy.
say.outro: Linear time and space. Pattern: dynamic programming on a state machine. Draw the states first, and the transitions almost write themselves.

best-time-to-buy-and-sell-stock-with-coo.title: Best Time to Buy And Sell Stock With Cooldown

The maxProfit method takes the list of daily prices and returns the best total profit.
We create an empty cache dictionary to remember answers for each day and holding state.
We define a helper called dfs that returns the best profit from a given day onward in a given state.
This comment says we stop when no trading days remain.
If the day is past the last price, there is nothing left to do.
So we return zero profit for that base case.
Before computing, we check whether this day and state pair was already solved.
If it was, we return the stored answer and avoid repeating work.
This comment introduces the first choice, which is to simply skip today and keep our state.
We set best to the profit from skipping today, moving to the next day with the same buying flag.
If buying is true, we hold no share and may purchase one.
This comment explains that buying today leads to a state where we must sell later.
Buying subtracts today's price and continues from tomorrow with buying set to false.
We check whether buying beats the current best.
If so, we update best to the buying profit.
Otherwise we are holding a share and can consider selling.
This comment notes that selling forces a one day cooldown afterward.
Selling adds today's price and jumps two days ahead, skipping the cooldown day, with buying set to true.
We compare the selling profit against the current best.
If selling is better, we update best accordingly.
We store the computed best in the cache for this day and state.
We return best as the answer for this state.
We start the search on day zero with buying true, since we hold nothing initially, and return the result.

coin-change-ii.hook: Counting combinations, not orderings: keeping the coin index in the state prevents double counting.
coin-change-ii.ask: Given coin values and an amount, return how many different combinations of coins add up to the amount. Coins are unlimited and order does not matter.

brute.idea: At coin i, either use it again or move on to the next coin for good. Count every branch that lands exactly on the amount.
steps: Use coin i: add it, stay on i
Skip: move to coin i + 1
Exact amount: count 1
brute.whySlow: Amount 5,000 with a coin of 1 makes recursion thousands deep and exponentially wide.

optimal.insight: The state is just (coin index, running total). Only k·a of them exist, so cache each; never revisiting earlier coins stops reorders being counted.
steps: dfs(i, a) = ways to finish from total a using coins i onward
Hit amount: 1; overshoot or out of coins: 0
Ways = use coin i again + skip to coin i + 1
Memoize (i, a)

codeNotes.match: cache[(i, a)] = dfs(i, a + coins[i]) + dfs(i + 1, a)
codeNotes.note: Use coin again, or move on

pitfalls: Looping coins inside amounts counts orderings: 1+2 and 2+1 twice.
Amount 0 has exactly one way: use no coins.

say.intro: Coin Change Two. Count the combinations of coins that make an amount. Coins are unlimited, and order doesn't matter. For amount five, with coins one, two and five, there are four. Five. Two, two, one. Two, one, one, one. And five ones.
say.brute: The brute force stands on one coin and makes a choice. Use this coin again? Or move on to the next coin for good? Count the branches that land exactly on the amount. Why no double counting? Because we never go back to earlier coins. But the tree is exponential. Small amounts get recounted again and again.
say.insight: Here's the key. Every call is described by just two numbers. Which coin we're on, and the total so far. That's only coins times amount states. Cache each one, and the exponential tree collapses into a table we fill once. Same table idea as Coin Change. We're just counting instead of minimising.
say.anim: We start with amount five and coins one, two, five, and an empty cache. The search tries using coin one repeatedly, pushing total up through one, two, three. When total hits five it matches amount, counting one valid way to make change. Branches exceeding five or running out of coins return zero, marking dead ends. Results for index and total pairs like four and three get cached to avoid recomputation. Cached subproblems like total three with coins from index one now resolve instantly to two. The recursion keeps combining use and skip choices, filling the cache for every state. Finally dfs from index zero total zero returns four, the total ways to make change.
say.code: The cache maps a coin index and a running total to a count. Hit the amount exactly? That's one combination. Overshoot, or run out of coins? Zero. Already solved this state? Reuse it. Otherwise, the ways are: use this coin again, plus move on to the next. Store it and return. We start at the first coin, total zero. The bottom up versions after the return never run.
say.outro: Coins times amount, for time and space. Pattern: unbounded knapsack counting. Put the coin index in the state to count combinations, not orderings.

target-sum.hook: Plus or minus on every number: two to the n sign patterns, but far fewer distinct running totals.
target-sum.ask: Put a plus or minus sign in front of each number. Count how many sign choices make the whole expression equal the target.
target-sum.exampleWhy: Four pluses and one minus sum to 3, and the minus can go on any of the five ones.

brute.idea: Recursively try plus and minus for each number, and at the end count 1 if the total equals the target.
steps: At index i, branch: add or subtract nums[i]
At the end, total == target counts 1
Sum both branches
brute.whySlow: 20 numbers already mean a million sign patterns, and the totals repeat heavily.

optimal.insight: Ways from here depend only on (index, running total). Totals lie between -sum and +sum, so at most n·(2·sum + 1) states — cache them.
steps: backtrack(i, total) = ways to finish from here
End of list: 1 if total equals target, else 0
Ways = plus branch + minus branch
Store each (i, total) in dp

codeNotes.note: Cache: state to number of ways

codeNotes.match: dp[(i, total)] = backtrack(i + 1, total + nums[i]) + backtrack(

pitfalls: Zeros double the count: +0 and -0 are different sign choices.
Follow-up: reduce to counting subsets that sum to (sum + target) / 2.

say.intro: Target Sum. Put a plus or a minus in front of every number. How many sign patterns hit the target? We have five ones, and a target of three. So we need exactly one minus. It can sit on any of the five ones. The answer is five.
say.brute: The brute force branches twice at every number. Plus, or minus. At the end, it counts one if the total equals the target. Simple and correct. But it's two to the n. Twenty numbers is about a million leaves. Thirty numbers? About a billion. Too slow.
say.insight: Now, notice. Lots of sign patterns reach the same running total at the same index. And from there, the future is identical. So the state is just the index and the total. Cache it. The number of distinct states is tiny next to the full tree. Why? Running totals only range from minus the sum to plus the sum.
say.anim: We start with an empty cache and numbers all ones, aiming for a total of three. The recursion explores adding or subtracting each number, branching deeply before any caching happens. At index five with total three, this matches the target, so it returns one way. Results for state index four, total four get stored in the cache for reuse later. Later calls reuse cached states like index four total two, avoiding redundant recomputation. Combining add and subtract ways at index two total two gives three stored in cache. At index one total one, four ways are returned using previously cached subproblems. All branches combine back to the start, giving a final answer of five ways.
say.code: The cache maps an index and a running total to a number of ways. Once every number has a sign, did we land on the target? Then one, otherwise zero. Already solved this state? Reuse it. Otherwise, take the plus branch, then the minus branch, and add their ways. Store the sum, and return it. We start at index zero, total zero.
say.outro: Numbers times total sum, in time and space. Pattern: memoized dynamic programming, where choices become states. Look for the states that repeat.

target-sum.title: Target Sum
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container this problem's method lives in.
This method takes the list of numbers and a target, and returns how many sign assignments hit the target.
The first step is to remember answers for each pair of index and running total so we never recompute them.
We create an empty dictionary called cache to hold those remembered answers.
We define a recursive helper called backtrack that takes the current index and the running total so far.
Next comes the base case, which is when every number has been given a sign.
We check whether the index has reached the length of nums, meaning no numbers remain.
If the total equals the target, this sign combination is valid.
So we return one, counting this single successful way.
Otherwise the total missed the target.
So we return zero, since this combination contributes no valid ways.
Before doing any work, we check whether this index and total pair was already solved.
If it was, we return the stored answer immediately and skip the repeated recursion.
Now we explore both choices for the current number, plus and minus.
We recurse with the next index after adding the current number, and call the count add ways.
We recurse with the next index after subtracting the current number, and call the count subtract ways.
Then we save the combined result for this state so future visits can reuse it.
The number of ways from here is add ways plus subtract ways, stored in the cache under this state.
We return that cached value to the caller, passing the count up the recursion.
Finally we start the search at index zero with a total of zero and return its result.

interleaving-string.hook: Two strings shuffled like a deck of cards; the trick is that only two positions matter.
interleaving-string.ask: Given strings s1, s2 and s3, return true if s3 can be formed by interleaving all of s1 and s2 while keeping each string's own character order.
interleaving-string.exampleWhy: aaxaby = a(s1) a(s2) x(s2) a(s1) b(s1) y(s2): every character used once, in order.

brute.idea: Take the next character of s3 from s1 or from s2, whichever matches, and recurse. Succeed when both strings are used up.
steps: Lengths must add up
Take from s1 if it matches s3[i + j]
Or take from s2 if it matches
brute.whySlow: With 100-character strings full of repeats both branches keep matching: up to 2 to the 200 paths.

optimal.insight: Position in s3 is always i + j, so the state is just (i, j). dp[i][j] says whether the remaining suffixes interleave; fill the grid backwards.
steps: dp[i][j]: can s1[i:] and s2[j:] form s3[i + j:]?
Both used up: dp[m][n] = True
True if s1[i] matches s3[i + j] and dp[i + 1][j]
Or s2[j] matches s3[i + j] and dp[i][j + 1]

codeNotes.match: if i < len(s1) and s1[i] == s3[i + j] and dp[i + 1][j]:
codeNotes.note: Take the next char from s1

codeNotes.match: if j < len(s2) and s2[j] == s3[i + j] and dp[i][j + 1]:

pitfalls: Greedy fails when both strings offer the same character; you must try both.
Check the length sum first, or indexing s3 can go out of range.

say.intro: Interleaving String. Can the third string be built by weaving the first two together? Each one must keep its own order. Here, a a b and a x y weave into a a x a b y. So the answer is true. And notice those leading a's. They could come from either string.
say.brute: The brute force looks at the next character of the target. Does string one's next character match? Try taking it. Does string two's match? Try that too. Recurse until both are used up. So what's the catch? When both strings offer the same letter, it branches twice. Worst case, exponential. Repeated letters make it explode.
say.insight: Here's the key. Say we've used i characters from string one, and j from string two. Then we're always at position i plus j in the target. So the whole state is just i and j. We make a grid of true or false, and fill it from the bottom right. Each cell then takes constant time.
say.anim: We start with strings aab, axy, and target aaxaby, checking lengths first. The dp grid is initialized, with dp at the last cell set true as the base case. At i equals 3, j equals 3, we check position 5, but canTake stays false here. Moving backwards, dp values get filled in based on matching characters from s1 or s2. We continue sweeping i from 2 down, recomputing canTake using s2 matches at each position. At i equals 1, matching s2's character lets canTake become true, updating dp accordingly. Now at i equals 0, we keep testing s1 and s2 characters against s3 to fill remaining cells. Finally dp at zero, zero is true, so isInterleave returns true for this example.
say.code: First, the lengths must add up. Then we build a grid of falses. Both strings fully used is a success, so the bottom right is true. We fill from the bottom right, looping i and j backwards. Can we take the next character from string one? Check it matches, and the cell below is true. Or take it from string two, using the cell to the right. Return the top left.
say.outro: m times n time and space. Pattern: two dimensional dynamic programming over two string positions. Two pointers define the state? Think grid.

The method isInterleave takes the three strings and returns whether s3 is a valid interleaving of s1 and s2.
We store the length of s1 in length1 so we can use it repeatedly.
We store the length of s2 in length2 for the same reason.
We store the length of s3 in length3 to compare against the combined input lengths.
This comment says a quick length check comes first, since the totals must match.
If length1 plus length2 does not equal length3, no interleaving can exist.
So we return false immediately without doing any further work.
This comment explains that dp at i and j tells whether the suffixes of s1 and s2 can form the matching suffix of s3.
We build a grid of false values with length1 plus one rows and length2 plus one columns, covering the empty suffix cases.
The base case is that two empty suffixes trivially form an empty suffix of s3, so that cell is true.
This comment says we fill the grid backwards, starting from the ends of both strings.
The outer loop walks i from length1 down to zero so later suffixes are solved first.
The inner loop walks j from length2 down to zero, so cells to the right and below are ready.
We check whether we are at the bottom right corner, which is already set.
We skip that corner using continue, so we do not overwrite the base case.
The current position in s3 is always i plus j, since that many characters have been consumed.
We start with canTake false, assuming no valid way until we find one.
This comment says we try taking the next character from s1 first, then from s2.
If s1 has a character left, it matches s3 at position, and the rest works from the next row, then taking it is valid.
In that case we mark canTake as true.
Similarly, if s2 has a character left, it matches s3 at position, and the next column works, then taking it is valid.
That also sets canTake to true.
We record the result for this cell in the grid for later cells to rely on.
Finally, we return the top left cell, which answers whether the full strings interleave to form s3.

longest-increasing-path-in-a-matrix.hook: A graph problem disguised as a grid: strictly increasing means no cycles, so memoized DFS just works.
longest-increasing-path-in-a-matrix.ask: Given a grid of integers, return the length of the longest path that moves up, down, left or right and strictly increases at every step.
longest-increasing-path-in-a-matrix.exampleWhy: 1 → 2 → 6 → 9: start bottom middle, step left, then climb the left column. Length 4.

brute.idea: From every cell, DFS into each bigger neighbour and return the longest path found. Take the best over all starting cells.
steps: Start a DFS from every cell
Move only to strictly bigger neighbours
Length = 1 + longest neighbour path
brute.whySlow: On a 200 by 200 grid, each cell is re-solved from every start that reaches it — exponential blow-up.

optimal.insight: The longest path from a cell never depends on how you arrived; increasing paths cannot loop back. So compute each cell once and cache it.
steps: dfs(r, c) = longest increasing path starting at (r, c)
Off grid or not bigger than previous: 0
Answer = 1 + best of four neighbours
Cache in dp; run from every cell, take the max

codeNotes.match: if r < 0 or r == ROWS or c < 0 or c == COLS or matrix[r][c] <= prevVal:

pitfalls: No visited set needed: strict increase already prevents cycles.
Equal neighbours do not count; stop on <= prevVal.

say.intro: Longest Increasing Path in a Matrix. From any cell, step up, down, left or right. But always to a strictly bigger number. How long can the path get? In this three by three grid, it's four. One, two, six, nine. It starts bottom middle, then climbs the left column.
say.brute: The brute force runs a depth first search from every cell. It only moves into bigger neighbours, and returns the longest path. It's correct. But the same cell's best path is recomputed from every start that reaches it. That blows up exponentially. A two hundred by two hundred grid? It would never finish.
say.insight: Here's the thing. The longest path from a cell doesn't depend on how you got there. Values strictly increase, so a path can never loop back. That means each cell's answer is fixed. Compute it once, cache it, reuse it everywhere. Each cell is solved once. And each solve only looks at four neighbours.
say.anim: We start with a three by three grid of values to explore for increasing paths. Dfs begins at cell zero zero, value nine, with no cache yet. Cell zero zero has no bigger neighbors, so its longest path length is cached as one. Moving to cell zero two, value four leads into six, eight, giving a path length of two. Cell one zero, value six, climbs upward into nine, caching a length of two. At row two col zero, value two climbs through six then nine, reaching length three. From value one, the path goes one, two, six, nine, caching the best length of four. After checking every cell, the longest increasing path found is four.
say.code: The cache maps a cell to its longest path. The search takes a cell and the previous value. Off the grid, or not increasing? Return zero. Already solved this cell? Return it. Otherwise, try each of the four neighbours. The answer is one plus the best. Cache it before returning. Finally, take the best over all starting cells. Strict increase means no visited set needed.
say.outro: Each cell is solved once, so m times n time. Pattern: memoized depth first search, dynamic programming on a graph with no cycles.

We create an empty dictionary dp to cache the best path length starting from each cell.

We define dfs with a row, a column, and the previous value we stepped from.
This comment notes that leaving the grid or failing to strictly increase ends the path.
If the row or column is outside the grid, we are off the matrix.
Going off the grid contributes zero length, so we return zero.
If the current value is not strictly greater than the previous value, the step is invalid.
An invalid step also returns zero, since the path cannot continue through this cell.
We check whether this cell's answer is already cached in dp.
If cached, we return it immediately, which avoids recomputing and keeps the work linear in cells.
This comment says we explore all four neighbors and keep the best result.
We start best at one, because the cell itself counts as a path of length one.
We explore the cell below, passing the current value, and add one for this cell.
We explore the cell above the same way, adding one for the current cell.
We explore the cell to the right, again adding one for the current cell.
We explore the cell to the left, adding one for the current cell.
We set best to the largest of the single cell path and the four directional options.
We cache best for this cell, since its longest path never depends on how we arrived.
We return best to the caller as the longest path starting here.
This comment says we launch dfs from every cell and keep the maximum, relying on the cache.
We initialize longest to zero to track the overall best path found.
We loop over every row of the grid.
We loop over every column within that row, so each cell gets visited as a start.
We call dfs from this cell with a previous value of negative one, so any cell value is allowed.
We update longest if this starting cell gives a longer path than we have seen.
After trying every start cell, we return the longest path length found.

distinct-subsequences.hook: Counting every way to pick t out of s: the count can be huge, but the states are few.
distinct-subsequences.ask: Given strings s and t, count how many different ways you can delete characters from s so that what remains equals t.
distinct-subsequences.exampleWhy: Five different sets of positions in babgbag spell b, a, g in order.

brute.idea: Walk s. You can always skip the current character; if it matches the current letter of t, you can also use it. Count paths that finish t.
steps: t finished: count 1; s finished first: 0
Always try skipping s[i]
If s[i] == t[j], also try using it
brute.whySlow: With s of length 1,000, every character offers skip or use — astronomically many paths.

optimal.insight: The count depends only on (i, j), positions in s and t. Fill an (m + 1)·(n + 1) table from the end: match means use + skip.
steps: cache[(i, j)] = ways s[i:] forms t[j:]
Empty t: 1 way; empty s with t left: 0
Match: use it + skip it
No match: skip it only

codeNotes.note: s ran out with t left

codeNotes.match: cache[(i, j)] = cache[(i + 1, j + 1)] + cache[(i + 1, j)]

pitfalls: Both strings empty counts as 1 way, not 0.
Counts get huge: fine in Python, use 64-bit or modulo elsewhere.

say.intro: Distinct Subsequences. Count the ways to delete characters from s so that what's left is exactly t. Our s is b a b g b a g, and t is bag. There are five different ways. Each way picks a different set of letter positions in s.
say.brute: The brute force walks through s. At each character, you can always skip it. And if it matches the next letter of t, you can also use it. Finished t? Count one. Ran out of s first? Count zero. Two branches per character means exponential time. Long strings with lots of repeats make it explode.
say.insight: Here's the key. The number of ways only depends on two positions. Where we are in s, and where we are in t. So we build a table with one cell per pair, and fill it from the end. Each cell is just the use count plus the skip count. Constant time per cell. So the work is polynomial.
say.anim: We start with s equal to babgbag and t equal to bag, building a lookup table. Base cases fill in first: matching an empty t always counts as one way, for every position. Then positions with leftover letters in t but no letters left in s get zero ways. Now we scan backward through s and t, comparing characters at each pair of positions. When letters match, like s of g and t of g, we add using and skipping counts together. When letters differ, we simply copy the count from skipping the current s character. At the very start, i is zero and j is zero, finishing the full table. The final cached value at position zero zero gives the answer, five distinct subsequences.
say.code: First, the base cases. An empty t can be formed exactly one way. If s ran out with t left, that's zero. Then we loop i and j backwards. Do the characters match? Then we use it, plus skip it. Add both counts. No match? We can only skip. Finally, return the count at zero, zero. That's the ways for the whole strings.
say.outro: s times t, in time and space. Pattern: two dimensional dynamic programming on two strings. To count ways, add up each branch.

distinct-subsequences.title: Distinct Subsequences
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container the interview platform expects for our method.
The numDistinct method takes strings s and t and returns how many distinct ways s can produce t.
We create an empty dictionary called cache to hold the answer for each pair of positions in s and t.
We loop over every position i in s, including the position just past its end.
When t is fully used, there is exactly one way to finish, which is to delete everything remaining in s.
Next we loop over every position j in t, since those need separate base cases.
When s is used up but t still has characters left, there are zero ways, so we store zero.
We now fill the table backward, with i walking from the last index of s down to zero.
Inside that, j walks from the last index of t down to zero, so smaller subproblems are ready first.
We check whether the current characters of s and t are equal, since a match gives us an extra choice.
On a match we add the ways of using this character, moving both forward, and the ways of skipping it in s.
Otherwise the characters differ, so we handle that case separately.
With no match, we must skip the character in s, so we copy the count from the next position in s.
Finally we return the value at position zero in both strings, which is the total number of distinct subsequences.

edit-distance.hook: The algorithm behind spell checkers: three operations, one beautifully small recurrence.
edit-distance.ask: Given two words, return the minimum number of single-character inserts, deletes or replacements needed to turn the first word into the second.
edit-distance.exampleWhy: horse → rorse (replace h) → rose (delete r) → ros (delete e): 3 operations.

brute.idea: Compare the current characters. Equal: advance both for free. Otherwise try insert, delete and replace, each costing one, and keep the cheapest.
steps: One word used up: cost is the other's remaining length
Match: advance both for free
Else 1 + min(insert, delete, replace)
brute.whySlow: Two 500-letter words branch three ways per mismatch — far beyond any time limit.

optimal.insight: Every call is just (i, j), a suffix of each word. Only m·n pairs exist, so fill a grid from the bottom-right; each cell reads three neighbours.
steps: dp[i][j] = edits to turn word1[i:] into word2[j:]
Last row and column: remaining length
Match: copy the diagonal
Else 1 + min(below, right, diagonal)

codeNotes.note: word1 used up: insert the rest
word2 used up: delete the rest

pitfalls: Initialise the border; it encodes pure inserts or deletes.
Below is delete, right is insert, diagonal is replace — know which is which.

say.intro: Edit Distance. What's the fewest single letter inserts, deletes or replacements to turn one word into another? Horse becomes r o s in three steps. Replace the h with r. Delete the r. Then delete the e.
say.brute: The brute force compares the current letters. Do they match? Move on, for free. If not, try all three operations, each costing one, and recurse. When one word runs out, the cost is whatever's left of the other. Three branches per mismatch. That's exponential. Two words of five hundred letters? You'd wait forever.
say.insight: Here's the thing. Every call is just two positions, one in each word. There are only m times n of them. So we store them in a grid. Each cell reads three neighbours. Below means delete. Right means insert. And the diagonal means replace. Constant time per cell, so the whole grid costs m times n.
say.anim: We start with horse and ros, building a grid to track edit distances between suffixes. The last row and column fill with remaining lengths, the base cases for empty suffixes. Now we fill from bottom right to top left, comparing characters at each position. When letters match, like s and s, we simply copy the diagonal value, no edit needed. When letters differ, we take one plus the minimum of below, right, and diagonal neighbors. This process continues row by row, each cell combining results from cells already solved. Finally the top left cell, representing the full words, holds the answer. The function returns 3, the minimum edit distance between horse and ros.
say.code: Once word one is used up, we insert the rest. Once word two is used up, we delete the rest. So the last row and column hold the remaining lengths. Then we loop backwards. Same letter? No cost. It's a free move along the diagonal. Otherwise, delete, insert, or replace. One plus the cheapest of the three. The top left is the cost for the whole words.
say.outro: m times n time and space. Pattern: two dimensional dynamic programming on two strings. This is the classic Levenshtein distance.

edit-distance.title: Edit Distance
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container LeetCode expects for this problem.
The minDistance method takes two words and returns the fewest edits needed to turn the first into the second.
We store the length of word1 in length1 so we can size the grid and loop bounds.
We store the length of word2 in length2 for the same reason.
This comment says we will build a grid with one extra row and column for empty suffixes.
We create the grid filled with zeros, with length1 plus one rows and length2 plus one columns.
This comment explains that the last row and column hold base cases equal to the remaining length.
We loop over every column index in the last row, including the empty suffix position.
When word1 is exhausted, we must insert every remaining character of word2, so the cost is length2 minus j.
We loop over every row index to fill the last column.
When word2 is exhausted, we must delete every remaining character of word1, so the cost is length1 minus i.
This comment says we now fill the grid from the bottom-right toward the top-left.
We walk i backward from the last character of word1 down to zero, so smaller suffix answers are ready first.
For each row we walk j backward from the last character of word2 down to zero.
We check whether the current characters of word1 at i and word2 at j are equal.
This comment notes that a match costs nothing extra and just reuses the diagonal.
On a match we copy the diagonal cell, since both characters are skipped with no edit.
Otherwise the characters differ, so we need one edit and must pick the cheapest option.
This comment says a mismatch costs one plus the minimum of below, right and diagonal.
Below is the cost after deleting a character from word1, so we read the cell one row down.
Right is the cost after inserting a character into word1, so we read the cell one column over.
Diagonal is the cost after replacing the character, so we read the cell down and over.
We set the cell to one plus the cheapest of the three choices, counting the edit we just made.
The top-left cell covers both full words, so we return it as the minimum edit distance.

burst-balloons.hook: Thinking about the first balloon to pop is a dead end. Think about the last one instead.
burst-balloons.ask: Bursting a balloon earns its value times its current left and right neighbours (1 past either end). Burst every balloon in the best order and return the maximum coins.

brute.idea: Try every balloon as the next one to burst, recurse on the remaining list, and keep the best total. That explores every ordering.
steps: Pick any balloon to burst now
Earn left · it · right
Recurse on the shorter list
brute.whySlow: 300 balloons have 300 factorial orders, and changing neighbours make naive caching useless.

optimal.insight: Pick the LAST balloon to burst between walls l and r. Its neighbours are then exactly l and r, so both sides become independent subproblems.
steps: Pad with 1 on both ends
cache[(l, r)] = best for balloons strictly between l and r
Try each pivot as the last burst: l·p·r + both sides
Grow the interval width from 2 up to the full array

codeNotes.note: Pivot is the last to burst
Plus the best of each side

pitfalls: Choosing the FIRST balloon breaks independence; neighbours keep changing.
Intervals are exclusive: the walls l and r are not burst.

say.intro: Burst Balloons. Popping a balloon earns its value, times its current left and right neighbours. Past the edges, count a one. Pick the order that earns the most coins. For three, one, five, pop one first, then three, then five. That's thirty five. Pop three first, and you earn far less.
say.brute: The brute force tries every balloon as the next pop, then recurses on what's left. That's every ordering. n factorial. And it's worse than that. Caching is awkward, because each pop changes the neighbours. So the subproblems never separate cleanly. A few hundred balloons? Completely out of reach.
say.insight: Here's the trick. Flip time around. Think about the last balloon to pop in a range. When it pops, everything inside is already gone. So its neighbours are the range's walls. And the two sides never touch each other. They're independent subproblems. So we solve every interval, shortest first. Each tries every pivot inside it. That's cubic time.
say.anim: We pad the balloons with walls of one on each side, giving one, three, one, five, one. We start with small intervals of width two, checking left zero and right two, bursting pivot one for three coins. Interval zero to two stores best value three, then we try left one, right three with pivot two. Bursting pivot two between one and three gives fifteen coins, the best for that interval. Next interval left two right four tries pivot three, giving only five coins stored. Now width three begins, interval zero to three tries pivot one, scoring thirty coins. Interval one to four is checked next, pivot two then three, settling on thirty coins stored. Finally the full interval zero to four tries each pivot, finding thirty five as the best combination. The algorithm returns the maximum coins achievable, which is thirty five.
say.code: We put virtual ones at both ends. That way, the edges never need special cases. Then short intervals first. We loop the width from two upward, then every left edge. Each pivot is the last to burst. Its neighbours are the walls. So it earns left times pivot times right. Plus the best of each side, from the cache. Keep the max. Return the whole padded range.
say.outro: Cubic time, quadratic space. Pattern: interval dynamic programming. When the first choice tangles everything, think about the last one instead.

The method maxCoins takes the list of balloon values nums and returns the maximum coins as an integer.

We build balloons by putting a one before and after nums, so edge balloons have valid neighbours.

We set right as left plus width, giving the other wall of this interval.

If pivot bursts last, its neighbours are the walls, so we multiply left, pivot, and right values.
We add the best coins from the left sub-interval, defaulting to zero if it holds no balloons.
We add the best coins from the right sub-interval, which is independent of the left one.
We check whether this pivot's total beats the best found so far for the interval.
If it does, we update best for this interval to this larger total.
This comment says we store the best result for this interval.
We save the best value in the dictionary keyed by the pair left and right for later larger intervals.
We return the stored answer for the full padded range from zero to the last index.

regular-expression-matching.hook: Dots and stars turn string matching into a branching puzzle — and a beautiful 2-D DP.
regular-expression-matching.ask: Given a string s and a pattern p, return true if p matches all of s. A dot matches any single character; a star means zero or more copies of the character before it.
regular-expression-matching.exampleWhy: c* matches zero c's, a* matches "aa", then b matches b — the whole string is covered.

brute.idea: Plain recursion on (i, j): if a star follows p[j], either skip the pair or consume one matching character; otherwise match one character and advance both.
steps: If the pattern is used up, s must be too
Star next: skip x* or eat one char
Otherwise match one char, move both
brute.whySlow: Each star branches twice and the same (i, j) states are recomputed; patterns like a*a*a*a* explode exponentially.

optimal.insight: The answer for suffixes s[i:] and p[j:] depends only on (i, j). There are just (m+1)·(n+1) such pairs, so fill a table from the ends backward.
steps: cache[i][j] = does s[i:] match p[j:]?
Base case: both empty → True
Star next: skip the pair, or match one char and stay on j
Else: char match and cache[i+1][j+1]
Answer is cache[0][0]

codeNotes.match: match = i < len(s) and (s[i] == p[j] or p[j] == ".")

codeNotes.note: Eat one char, keep the star

pitfalls: Check for a star at j + 1 before testing a plain match.
Row i = len(s) still matters: x* can match the empty string.

say.intro: Okay, so this is Regular Expression Matching. A dot matches any single character. A star means zero or more copies of the character before it. Our string is a a b. Our pattern is c star, a star, b. Does it match? Yes. Zero c's, then two a's, then the final b.
say.brute: The obvious first try is plain recursion. We keep one position in the string and one in the pattern. When a star comes next, we branch. Either skip the starred pair completely, or eat one matching character and keep the star. Otherwise, match one character and move both. So what's the catch? The branches keep recomputing the same states. It explodes exponentially.
say.insight: Here's the thing. What does each call really ask? Does the rest of the string, from i, match the rest of the pattern, from j? That's it. Just two numbers. So there are only about m times n different questions. We answer each one exactly once and store it in a table. And we fill the table from the ends backward, so every answer we need is already there.
say.anim: We start with string aab and pattern c star a star b, building a match table. The base case marks both strings empty as a match, true at the last cell. For row three, past the end of s, we check each pattern position from right to left. Star patterns let us skip two pattern characters, copying results from further right. At row two, s has a, matching pattern a before the star, so char matches true. At row one, s has a, the star lets a repeat, setting cache true by reusing row below. At row zero, s has a, matching again, combining skip and repeat options as true. Finally cache at zero zero is true, confirming aab matches c star a star b.
say.code: Now the code. We build the table, and mark empty string against empty pattern as true. Then, for every cell, we first ask: do the current characters match? If a star comes next, we can use it zero times by skipping the pair. Or, when the characters match, we eat one character and keep the star. Otherwise, it's a plain match. We need the characters to match and the diagonal cell to be true.
say.outro: So that's m times n time and space. The pattern is two dimensional dynamic programming. When a recursion keeps repeating the same states, cache them in a table.

regular-expression-matching.title: Regular Expression Matching
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container the interview platform expects for our method.
The method isMatch takes a string s and a pattern p and returns whether the pattern matches the entire string.
We store the length of the string in string_length so we can use it for table sizes and bounds checks.
We store the length of the pattern in pattern_length for the same reason.
This comment explains that cache at i and j records whether the suffix of s from i matches the suffix of p from j.
We build a table of false values with one extra row and column, so empty suffixes have their own entries.
This comment states the base case, where an empty string and an empty pattern match each other.
We set the bottom right cell to true, since both suffixes are empty at that point.
We loop i from the string length down to zero, so rows below are already filled when we need them.
Inside, we loop j from the last pattern index down to zero, so cells to the right are ready.
We compute char_matches, which is true only if characters remain in s and the current pattern character equals it or is a dot.
This comment says that when a star follows, we either skip the starred pair or use it to match one character.
We check whether the next pattern character exists and is a star, meaning the current character is repeatable.
For the zero-copies option, we copy the answer from two columns right, skipping the character and its star.
If the current character matches, we can also consume one string character and stay on the same pattern position.
We set the cell to true if either skipping works or matching one character and staying on j works.
This comment says that without a star, the characters must match and the rest must match too.
Without a star, we only proceed when the current characters match.
In that case the cell takes the value of the diagonal cell, which covers both suffixes moving one step forward.
Finally we return the top left cell, which says whether the whole string matches the whole pattern.

maximum-subarray.hook: One running sum and one rule — drop it when it goes negative — beats checking every subarray.
maximum-subarray.ask: Given a list of integers, find the contiguous slice with the largest sum and return that sum. The slice must contain at least one number.
maximum-subarray.exampleWhy: The slice [4,-1,2,1] adds up to 6, and no other contiguous slice does better.

brute.idea: Try every start index, extend the slice one element at a time keeping a running sum, and record the best sum seen.
steps: Pick a start i
Extend j rightward, adding nums[j]
Track the best total
brute.whySlow: With 100,000 numbers that is about 5 billion slices to sum.

optimal.insight: A prefix with a negative sum can only drag down whatever follows it. So whenever the running sum dips below zero, throw it away and start fresh (Kadane).
steps: Keep a running total
Add each number, update the best answer
If total < 0, reset it to 0

codeNotes.note: Start best at first element (handles all-negative)
Record the best slice so far
Drop it, start a new slice

pitfalls: Initialize res to nums[0], not 0 — an all-negative array must return its largest element.

say.intro: Okay, so this is Maximum Subarray. You get a list of numbers, some of them negative. Find the contiguous slice with the biggest sum, and return that sum. In our example, the best slice is four, minus one, two, one. That adds up to six. Nothing beats it.
say.brute: The obvious first move is to try every starting point. From each start, stretch the slice right, one number at a time. Keep a running sum, and remember the best total. Does it work? Sure. But it's n squared. With a hundred thousand numbers, that's around five billion slices.
say.insight: Here's the thing. Say the slice we're building has a negative sum. What good is it? None. It can only drag down whatever comes next. Any future slice is better off without it. So the moment our running total drops below zero, we throw it away. We start fresh at the next number. That's Kadane's algorithm.
say.anim: We start with best sum set to the first number, negative two. Running total begins at zero before we scan each number in the list. Adding negative two makes running total negative two, which is not bigger than best sum. Since running total is negative, we reset it to zero to avoid dragging future sums down. Adding four gives running total four, which beats best sum, so best sum updates to four. After adding two and one, running total climbs to six, a new best sum. Subtracting five drops running total to one, but best sum stays at six. After scanning all numbers, the function returns the final best sum of six.
say.code: Now the code. We start the best answer at the first number. Why not zero? Because an all negative list must return its largest number. Then, for each number, we add it to the running total. We update the best if the total beats it. And if the total drops below zero? That prefix only hurts. So we reset it to zero and start a new slice.
say.outro: So that's linear time and constant space. The pattern is greedy, the famous Kadane's algorithm. Whenever a prefix only hurts you, drop it and start over.

maximum-subarray.title: Maximum Subarray
lineNotes: We define a class called Solution, which is the wrapper the interview platform expects for our method.
This method takes a list of integers called nums and returns the largest sum of any contiguous slice.
This comment says we begin by treating the first number as the best answer found so far.
We set best_sum to the first element, which is safe because the slice must contain at least one number.
This comment explains that we will track a running total while scanning through the list.
We set running_total to zero, meaning we begin with an empty current slice before looking at any number.
We loop over every number in nums, one at a time, from left to right.
We add the current number to running_total, extending the current slice to include it.
This comment says we should record the running total whenever it beats the best answer.
We check whether running_total is greater than best_sum, meaning the current slice is the best so far.
If so, we copy running_total into best_sum to remember this new record.
This comment explains that a negative running total can only hurt later sums, so we discard it.
We check whether running_total has dropped below zero after updating the best answer.
If it is negative, we reset running_total to zero so the next slice starts fresh.
After scanning everything, we return best_sum, the largest contiguous slice sum we found.

jump-game.hook: Instead of exploring every jump forward, walk backward and drag the finish line toward you.
jump-game.ask: You start at index zero of a list. Each value is the maximum number of steps you may jump forward from there. Return true if you can reach the last index.
jump-game.exampleWhy: Jump 0 → 2, then 2 → 5 (three steps), then 5 → 6. The zeros at 1 and 4 are jumped over.

brute.idea: Mark which indices are reachable. From every reachable index, mark every index within its jump range.
steps: Index 0 is reachable
From each reachable i, mark i+1 .. i+nums[i]
Is the last index marked?
brute.whySlow: Each reachable index can mark up to n others: 10,000 indices means up to 50 million marks.

optimal.insight: If i can reach the goal, reaching i is as good as reaching the goal. So walk backward, moving the goal to i whenever i + nums[i] ≥ goal.
steps: Goal starts at the last index
Scan i from right to left
If i + nums[i] reaches goal, move goal to i
Success if goal ends at 0

codeNotes.note: Initially we must reach the end
Can i jump to the goal?
Then i becomes the new goal
Did the goal reach the start?

pitfalls: Use >= not ==: overshooting the goal is fine.
A single-element list is already at the end: return true.

say.intro: Okay, so this is Jump Game. Each number tells you the farthest you may jump forward from that spot. You start at the first index. Can you reach the last one? Here, yes. Jump to index two. Leap three spots to index five. Then step to the end. Both zeros get skipped.
say.brute: The obvious approach marks reachable spots. Index zero is reachable. Then, walking left to right, every reachable index marks everything in its jump range. At the end, is the last index marked? That works. But each index can mark a huge range. So the worst case is n squared.
say.insight: Think about it this way. Walk backward instead. If some index can reach the goal, then getting to that index is just as good as getting to the goal. Right? So we walk from right to left. Each time an index can reach the current goal, we pull the goal back to it. Does the goal end up at zero? Then we can win.
say.anim: We start with the array and set goal to the last index, six. At index five, five plus zero reaches goal six, so goal moves to five. At index four, four plus zero can't reach goal five, so goal stays. At index three, three plus one can't reach goal five either. At index two, two plus three reaches five, so goal becomes two. At index one, one plus zero can't reach goal two, so it stays. At index zero, zero plus two reaches goal two, so goal becomes zero. Goal equals zero, meaning the start can reach the end, so it returns true.
say.code: Now the code. The goal starts at the last index, since that's where we must get. Then we walk backward, from the second last index. Can i plus its jump reach the goal, or go past it? Overshooting is fine. If so, i becomes the new goal. When the loop ends, we just ask: did the goal reach index zero?
say.outro: So that's linear time and constant space. The pattern is greedy, working from the end. Don't explore every path. Just drag the finish line toward you.

jump-game.title: Jump Game
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container the interview platform expects for our method.
The method canJump takes the list nums and returns true or false depending on whether the last index is reachable.
We start by setting goal to the last index of nums, since that is where we need to end up.
We loop i backward from the second to last index down to zero, checking each position as a possible jumping point.
If i plus the jump length at i reaches or passes the current goal, then position i can get us to the goal.
In that case we move goal back to i, because reaching i is now just as good as reaching the old goal.
At the end, if goal has been pulled all the way back to index zero, the start can reach the end, so we return true.

jump-game-ii.hook: Minimum jumps looks like shortest path — but a window-by-window BFS needs no queue at all.
jump-game-ii.ask: You start at index zero; each value is the maximum jump length from there. The end is always reachable. Return the fewest jumps needed to reach the last index.
jump-game-ii.exampleWhy: 0 → 1 → 4 → 5 → 8: four jumps. No path with three jumps reaches index 8.

brute.idea: Dynamic programming: dp[j] is the fewest jumps to reach j. From each i, relax every index it can jump to.
steps: dp[0] = 0, others infinity
From each i, update dp[j] for j in reach
Return dp at the last index
brute.whySlow: Each index relaxes up to 1,000 cells: 10,000 indices means ten million updates, versus one linear scan.

optimal.insight: Indices reachable in exactly k jumps form one contiguous window [l, r]. The next window ends at the farthest point any index in it can reach. Count windows.
steps: Window [l, r] = indices reachable with res jumps
Scan window, find farthest reach
Next window is r+1 .. farthest; res += 1
Stop when r reaches the end

codeNotes.note: Until the window covers the end
Next window starts after this one

pitfalls: Each index is scanned once overall, so the nested loop is still O(n).
A one-element list needs zero jumps.

say.intro: Okay, so this is Jump Game Two. Each number is the longest jump you can make from that spot. And the end is always reachable. The question now is, what's the fewest jumps to get there? Here, the best route is zero, one, four, five, eight. That's four jumps.
say.brute: The obvious first try is dynamic programming. Keep the fewest jumps needed to reach every index. The first one costs zero. From each index, update every spot it can land on with one more jump. Does it work? Yes. But each index touches its whole jump range. Most of those updates are wasted. That's n times the jump length.
say.insight: Here's the thing. Think breadth first search. All the indices you can reach in exactly one jump form one contiguous window. No gaps. The next window starts right after it. And where does it end? At the farthest point any index in the current window can reach. So the answer is just how many windows we need before one covers the end.
say.anim: We start with the array and jumps, left, and right all set to zero. The window covers just index zero, checking how far it can reach. Index zero with value two reaches as far as index two, so farthest becomes two. We move the window to indices one through two and count one jump. Scanning indices one and two, farthest updates to four, so window becomes three to four. Scanning indices three and four, farthest reaches six, expanding window to five and six. Scanning indices five and six, farthest jumps to nine, covering the rest of the array. The window now reaches the last index, so the loop ends with four jumps, the final answer.
say.code: Now the code. We start with a window of just index zero. Zero jumps reach only there. While the window doesn't reach the end, we scan every index in it. We track the farthest reach. The next window starts right after this one, and ends at that reach. And each new window costs one more jump. Every index is scanned once in total.
say.outro: So that's linear time and constant space. The pattern is greedy, which here is really breadth first search, level by level. No queue needed.

jump-game-ii.title: Jump Game II
jump-game-ii.optimalCode:
class Solution:
    def jump(self, nums: List[int]) -> int:
        jumps = 0
        left = 0
        right = 0

        # Keep expanding the window until it covers the last index
        while right < len(nums) - 1:
            # Find the farthest index reachable from current window
            farthest = 0
            for i in range(left, right + 1):
                farthest = max(farthest, i + nums[i])

            # Move to the next window and count this jump
            left = right + 1
            right = farthest
            jumps += 1

        return jumps
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container the problem expects for our jump method.
The jump method takes the list nums of maximum jump lengths and returns the minimum number of jumps as an integer.
We start the jumps counter at zero because we have not taken any jump yet.
We set left to zero, so the current window of reachable indices begins at the start.
We set right to zero too, since with zero jumps we can only stand at index zero.
This comment says we keep growing the window of reachable indices until it includes the last index.
The loop runs while right is less than the last index, meaning the end is not yet reachable.
This comment explains that next we search the current window for the farthest index it can reach.
We reset farthest to zero before scanning, so it tracks the best reach for this window only.
We loop over every index i from left through right, all reachable with the current number of jumps.
For each index we compare farthest with i plus nums at i, keeping the largest reach seen.
This comment says we now shift to the next window and record that one more jump was used.
The next window starts just after the old one, so left becomes right plus one.
The next window ends at farthest, the furthest index reachable with one additional jump.
We increase jumps by one, since moving to this new window costs exactly one jump.
Once the window covers the last index, we return the number of windows counted as the answer.

gas-station.hook: Simulating every starting station is quadratic — two pointers closing a loop find the start in one pass.
gas-station.ask: Stations sit on a circle. At station i you gain gas[i], and driving to the next costs cost[i]. Starting with an empty tank, return the station that lets you go all the way around, or minus one.
gas-station.exampleWhy: Starting at station 3, the tank goes 3, 6, 4, 2, 0 — it never goes negative and returns home.

brute.idea: Try each station as the start and simulate the full trip, stopping early if the tank goes negative.
steps: Pick a start s
Drive n legs, updating the tank
Tank negative? try the next start
brute.whySlow: With 100,000 stations, up to 10 billion legs simulated.

optimal.insight: Grow one wrapping segment from start to end. Net gas negative? The trip must begin earlier: move start back. Otherwise extend end. When they meet, the circle is covered.
steps: start = last station, end = 0
Net gas negative → move start back, add that station
Otherwise add station end and move end forward
When start meets end: success if net ≥ 0

codeNotes.note: Segment begins at the last station

pitfalls: If total gas < total cost, no start works: the pointers cross and we return -1.
The tank starts with the last station's net gas, not zero.

say.intro: Okay, so this is Gas Station. Stations sit in a circle. At each one you collect some gas. Driving to the next costs some gas. You start with an empty tank. Which station lets you drive all the way around? Here, station three works. The tank never once goes negative.
say.brute: The obvious first try is every station as the start. From there, simulate the whole trip. Add gas, subtract cost at each leg. Give up as soon as the tank goes negative. Does it work? Sure. But for each of n starts we may drive n legs. That's n squared.
say.insight: Here's the thing. Let's grow one stretch of road that wraps around the circle. It runs from a start station to an end station, and we track its net gas. Is it negative? Then the trip must begin earlier, so move the start one station back. Otherwise, there's gas to spare, so extend the end forward. When the two meet, we've covered the whole circle.
say.anim: We begin with start at station four and end at station zero. Total net gas starts at three, since start and end have not met yet. We extend the segment forward, adding station zero's gas, total becomes one. Extending again through station one, total drops to negative one. Since total is negative, the trip must begin earlier, so start moves back to three. Adding station three's gas, total rises back to two, now non negative. Extending forward once more through station two, total settles at zero. Now start and end both equal three, so the circle is fully covered, answer is three.
say.code: Now the code. The segment begins at the last station, so the tank starts with that station's net gas. While the total is negative, we begin earlier. Move the start back and add its net gas. If the start meets the end, the whole circle is covered. Return the start. Otherwise, we have enough gas, so add station end and extend forward. If the pointers cross first, return minus one.
say.outro: So that's linear time and constant space. The pattern is greedy with two pointers on a circle. If total gas covers total cost, a start always exists.

gas-station.title: Gas Station
gas-station.optimalCode:
class Solution:
    def canCompleteCircuit(self, gas: List[int], cost: List[int]) -> int:
        # 1. Start the segment at the last station, end at the first
        start = len(gas) - 1
        end = 0
        total = gas[start] - cost[start]

        while start >= end:
            # 2. If net gas is negative, the trip must begin earlier
            while total < 0 and start >= end:
                start -= 1
                total += gas[start] - cost[start]

            # 3. If start and end meet, we have covered the whole circle
            if start == end:
                return start

            # 4. Otherwise extend the segment forward
            total += gas[end] - cost[end]
            end += 1

        return -1
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container the problem expects for our method.
This method takes the gas and cost lists and returns the starting station index, or minus one.
This comment says we begin with a segment that starts at the last station and ends at the first.
We set start to the last index of the gas list, so the segment begins at the final station.
We set end to zero, so the forward side of the segment begins at the first station.
Total begins as the net gas of the last station, its gas minus its cost.
We loop while start is still at or after end, meaning the segment has not yet used every station.
This comment says that when net gas is negative, the trip has to begin at an earlier station.
While total is negative and stations remain, we keep trying to fix the deficit by moving start backward.
We move start back by one station, making the segment begin earlier.
We add the new start station's net gas, gas minus cost, into the running total.
This comment says that when start and end meet, every station is covered and the circle is complete.
If start equals end, the segment spans the whole circle, so a valid answer exists.
We return start, since beginning there keeps the tank from going negative all the way around.
This comment says that with a nonnegative total, we should grow the segment from the front.
We add the net gas of the station at end, since the segment now includes it.
We advance end by one, moving the forward boundary of the segment.
If the loop finishes without the segment closing, no starting station works, so we return minus one.

hand-of-straights.hook: The smallest card has no choice — it must start a group. That forced move solves everything.
hand-of-straights.ask: Given a hand of card values and a group size, can you split all the cards into groups of that size where each group is consecutive values?

brute.idea: Sort the hand. Repeatedly take the smallest card and remove the next groupSize consecutive values from the list one by one.
steps: Sort the cards
Smallest card starts a group
Remove each needed value; missing → False
brute.whySlow: Each list search and removal is O(n); with 10,000 cards that is about 100 million operations.

optimal.insight: The smallest remaining card can only be the start of a group. Count cards, keep distinct values in a min-heap, and build groups from the minimum.
steps: Count each value
Min-heap of distinct values
From the minimum, take one of each next value
A value hitting zero must be the heap minimum

codeNotes.note: Smallest card must start a group

pitfalls: Check len(hand) % groupSize first — a quick false.
When a count hits zero below an unfinished smaller value, fail.

say.intro: Okay, so this is Hand of Straights. You hold some cards. Can you split them all into groups of a fixed size, where each group is a run of consecutive values? Here, with groups of three, yes. The nine cards make one two three, two three four, and six seven eight.
say.brute: The obvious first try is to sort the cards. Then repeatedly take the smallest card, and remove the next few consecutive values from the list, one by one. If a value is missing, we fail. Does it work? Yes. But every search and removal scans the whole list. That's n squared. With ten thousand cards, about a hundred million operations.
say.insight: Here's the thing. Look at the smallest card left in your hand. Can it sit in the middle of a run? No. Nothing smaller is left to come before it. So it has no choice. It must start a group. That forced move solves everything. We count the cards, keep the distinct values in a min heap, and always build the next group from the minimum.
say.anim: Nine cards split into groups of three, so the length check passes. We count each card, building a frequency map like two twos and two threes. Distinct values are heaped into a min-heap, giving one through eight sorted. Starting at one, we consume one, two, three, decrementing counts as we go. Next the smallest remaining value two starts a new group of two, three, four. Now six starts a group, consuming six, seven, eight successfully. All counts hit zero and the heap empties completely. The function returns true, confirming the hand forms valid consecutive groups.
say.code: Now the code. First, the sizes must divide evenly. If not, it's a quick false. Then we count every card value, and heapify the distinct ones. The smallest card must start a group. For each value in its run, is it missing? That's a gap, so fail. Otherwise decrement its count. And if a count hits zero, it must be the heap minimum. If not, a smaller card is stranded.
say.outro: So that's n log n time and linear space. The pattern is greedy with a min heap. When one choice is forced, let it lead the way.

hand-of-straights.title: Hand of Straights
lineNotes: We define the Solution class with a method that checks whether the hand can be split into consecutive groups.
The method takes the hand of cards and the group size, and returns true or false.
This comment marks step one: count how many times each card value appears.
If the number of cards does not divide evenly by group size, full groups are impossible.
So we return false right away in that case.
We start with an empty dictionary to hold counts per card value.
We loop over every card in the hand.
For each card we add one to its count, starting from zero if unseen.
This comment marks step two: we need a min-heap holding the distinct card values.
We build a list from the distinct values, which are the keys of the count dictionary.
We heapify that list so the smallest value sits at the front.
This comment says we build groups starting from the smallest remaining value.
We keep going while the heap still holds values with cards remaining.
The smallest value in the heap must start a group, so we call it start.
We walk through each value from start up to start plus group size, exclusive, which is one full group.
If a needed value is missing or used up, the group cannot be completed, so we must fail.
We return false because the consecutive run is broken.
Otherwise we use one copy of this value by decreasing its count.
This comment notes that a value running out must be the current heap minimum.
We check whether this value's count just reached zero.
If it ran out but is not the heap minimum, a smaller value would be left stranded without a valid group.
So we return false in that case.
When the value is the minimum and exhausted, we pop it from the heap so the next smallest becomes the front.
If every group was formed successfully and the heap empties, we return true.

merge-triplets-to-form-target-triplet.hook: Merging takes the max, so one bad triplet poisons everything — throw those out, then just check coverage.
merge-triplets-to-form-target-triplet.ask: You may repeatedly merge two triplets by taking the max in each position. Given a list of triplets and a target, return true if some merge sequence can make a triplet equal to the target.
merge-triplets-to-form-target-triplet.exampleWhy: Merging [2,5,3] and [1,7,5] gives [2,7,5]. [1,8,4] can never be used: its 8 would overshoot.

brute.idea: Try every subset of triplets, merge the chosen ones by position-wise max, and check if any merge equals the target.
steps: Enumerate each non-empty subset
Merge: max in each of 3 positions
Equals target? return True
brute.whySlow: With 100,000 triplets, 2^100000 subsets — hopeless beyond about 20 triplets.

optimal.insight: Max never decreases, so a triplet exceeding the target anywhere is unusable. Merging all safe ones is harmless: just check each target position is hit by some safe triplet.
steps: Skip triplets exceeding the target anywhere
For safe ones, note positions equal to target
True if all 3 positions are covered

codeNotes.match: if t[0] > target[0] or t[1] > target[1] or t[2] > target[2]:

codeNotes.note: This safe triplet hits position i

pitfalls: Do not skip a safe triplet that misses one position — it may supply another.

say.intro: Okay, so this is Merge Triplets to Form Target Triplet. Merging two triplets keeps the larger value in each position. Can some sequence of merges produce exactly the target? Here, merge two five three with one seven five. We get two seven five. That's the target, so the answer is true.
say.brute: The obvious first try is every possible subset of triplets. Merge each subset, taking the max in every position, and compare with the target. Does it work? Sure. But there are two to the n subsets. It collapses beyond about twenty triplets. And the real input can have a hundred thousand.
say.insight: Here's the thing. Merging takes the max. And a max can never go back down. So what about a triplet that's bigger than the target anywhere? It's poison. We can never use it. Every other triplet is safe. Merging all of them never overshoots. So we just ask, is each target position hit exactly by some safe triplet?
say.anim: We start with an empty seen set and target two, seven, five. Triplet two, five, three is safe, and position zero matches, so seen becomes zero. Triplet one, eight, four exceeds target at position one, so it's skipped entirely. Triplet one, seven, five is safe, matching positions one and two, filling seen to zero, one, two. Triplet two, three, one is safe too, matching only position zero, already seen. All three positions zero, one, two are now covered in seen. The function returns true, confirming the target triplet can be formed.
say.code: Now the code. We keep a set of target positions we've already hit. For each triplet, does any value overshoot the target? Then it's unusable, so skip it. Otherwise it's safe. We look at its three values, and add every position where it equals the target. At the end, are all three positions covered?
say.outro: So that's linear time and constant space. The pattern is greedy. Throw out everything that could hurt you, then safely take everything else.

merge-triplets-to-form-target-triplet.title: Merge Triplets to Form Target Triplet
lineNotes: We define the Solution class that holds the method for this problem.
The method takes the list of triplets and the target triplet, and returns true or false.
We create an empty set called seen to record which target positions some safe triplet has matched.
This comment says we first throw away any triplet that is too large in any position.
We loop over every triplet in the list one at a time.
If the triplet exceeds the target in any of the three positions, it is unsafe because max could never come back down.
For an unsafe triplet we continue, skipping it so it never contributes to any merge.
This comment says that for safe triplets we now record which positions equal the target value.
For each of the three positions we check the safe triplet, one index at a time.
If the triplet's value at this position equals the target's value, this triplet can supply that exact number.
We add that position to seen, since merging can then reach the target value there without overshooting.
This comment says the answer is true only when every one of the three positions has been covered.
We return whether seen holds all three positions, meaning merging the safe triplets can produce the target.

partition-labels.hook: Each letter's last appearance tells you exactly where a piece is allowed to end.
partition-labels.ask: Split a string into as many pieces as possible so that each letter appears in at most one piece. Return the lengths of the pieces in order.
partition-labels.exampleWhy: "aba" holds every a, "cdcd" every c and d, "efe" every e and f: lengths 3, 4, 3.

brute.idea: Grow each piece from its start; for every character inside it, scan from the right to find its last occurrence and stretch the end there.
steps: Start a piece at i
For each char in the piece, scan for its last index
Stretch end; close piece when reached
brute.whySlow: Every character triggers a scan of the string — 500 characters means up to 250,000 comparisons instead of 500.

optimal.insight: Precompute each letter's last index. Walking left to right, the current piece must extend to the furthest last index of any letter seen in it; when i reaches that, cut.
steps: Record last index of every letter
Walk i, goal = max(goal, last[s[i]])
When i == goal, close the piece and record its length

codeNotes.note: Piece must reach this letter's end
Every letter inside is finished: cut

pitfalls: Return lengths, not the substrings.
Space is O(1): at most 26 letters in the map.

say.intro: Okay, so this is Partition Labels. Cut a string into as many pieces as you can, so no letter shows up in two pieces. Return each piece's length. In our example we get a b a, then c d c d, then e f e. So the answer is three, four, three.
say.brute: The obvious first try grows each piece from its start. For every character in the piece, scan from the right end of the string to find its last appearance. Then stretch the piece to reach it. When we reach the piece's end, we cut. Does it work? Yes. But every character triggers a full scan. That's n squared.
say.insight: Here's the thing. Each letter's last appearance tells you exactly where a piece is allowed to end. So precompute it. Now walk left to right. The current piece must stretch at least to the last appearance of every letter inside it. So keep the furthest one as a goal. When our position reaches the goal, nothing inside can escape. We cut right there.
say.anim: We scan the string once to record the last index where each letter appears. By the end, letters like a and c map to their final positions, like two and five. Now we walk through again, tracking a goal that extends to the furthest last index seen. At index zero, letter a pushes goal to two, since a last appears there. When index reaches goal at two, we close the first piece with length three. Next piece grows through c and d, extending goal to six, then closing with length four. The last piece spans e and f, goal reaches nine, closing with length three. The final partition lengths are three, four, and three.
say.code: Now the code. First, one pass maps each letter to its last index. Then we walk the string again. At each position, the piece must reach this letter's end, so we push the goal out to the furthest last index. We grow the current length by one. When the index equals the goal, every letter inside is finished. So we record the length and start a new piece.
say.outro: So that's linear time, and constant extra space, since there are only twenty six letters. The pattern is greedy. Cut as early as the last occurrences allow.
