valid-parenthesis-string.hook: Each star could be three things — but tracking just a min and max of open brackets covers them all.
valid-parenthesis-string.ask: A string has open brackets, close brackets and stars. Each star can act as an open bracket, a close bracket, or nothing. Return true if some choice makes the brackets balanced.
valid-parenthesis-string.exampleWhy: Treat the first star as empty and the second as an open bracket: "(()())" is balanced.

brute.idea: Recursively try all three meanings for every star, tracking the open-bracket count; fail if it goes negative.
steps: Open count below zero → dead end
At a star, branch three ways
At the end, open count must be 0
brute.whySlow: With 100 characters that could be 3^100 branches — astronomically many.

optimal.insight: All the choices give a contiguous range of possible open counts. Track only its min and max: a star widens the range by one each way.
steps: ( raises both min and max
) lowers both
* lowers min, raises max
max < 0 → fail; clamp min at 0
Valid if min ends at 0

codeNotes.note: Too many closes in every choice

pitfalls: Clamp leftMin at 0 — a negative open count is not a valid state.
Check leftMax < 0 inside the loop, not just at the end.

say.intro: Okay, so this is Valid Parenthesis String. We have open brackets, close brackets, and stars. Each star can be an open bracket, a close bracket, or nothing. Can we choose so everything balances? Here, yes. The first star becomes nothing. The second becomes an open bracket.
say.brute: The obvious first try is recursion. Try all three meanings for every star, counting open brackets as we go. If the count goes negative, that's a dead end. At the end, the count must be zero. Does it work? Sure. But every star triples the work. That's three to the n branches.
say.insight: Here's the thing. Do we care which choice we made? Not really. We only care how many brackets could still be open. And all the possible counts form one range, with no gaps. So we track just two numbers, the smallest and largest open count. A star stretches the range by one in each direction. And the minimum never drops below zero.
say.anim: We start tracking the range of open bracket counts, both min and max at zero. The first character is an open paren, so both min and max open increase to one. Next is a star, treated as flexible, so min open drops and max open rises to two. Another open paren arrives, pushing min and max open up to one and three. A close paren appears, decreasing both min and max open down to zero and two. Another star widens the range again, but min open dips below zero and resets to zero. Two more close parens shrink the range, each time clamping min open back to zero. After processing all characters, min open equals zero, so the string is valid, returning true.
say.code: Now the code. Both counts start at zero, the range of possible open counts. An open bracket raises both. A close lowers both. A star could close or open, so it lowers the min and raises the max. If the max goes negative, there are too many closes in every choice. Return false. If the min goes negative, reset it to zero. At the end, is zero open achievable?
say.outro: So that's linear time and constant space. The pattern is greedy. When choices multiply, track the range of possibilities, not every single one.

insert-interval.hook: The list is already sorted — so one pass with three cases beats re-sorting everything.
insert-interval.ask: You get a sorted list of non-overlapping intervals and one new interval. Insert it, merging any overlaps, and return the list still sorted and non-overlapping.
insert-interval.exampleWhy: [4,8] overlaps [3,5], [6,7] and [8,10]; together they merge into [3,10].

brute.idea: Append the new interval, sort everything by start, then do a full merge-intervals pass.
steps: Append newInterval
Sort by start
Merge overlapping neighbours
brute.whySlow: It re-sorts 10,000 intervals that were already sorted — about 130,000 comparisons instead of 10,000.

optimal.insight: Walking the sorted list, each interval is entirely before, entirely after, or overlapping the new one. Copy before, absorb overlaps into it, and stop at the first one after.
steps: New ends before current: emit new, then the rest
New starts after current: emit current
Otherwise overlap: widen the new interval
If loop ends, append the new interval

pitfalls: Touching intervals like [3,5] and [5,7] overlap: use strict < and > tests.
Empty input: just return [newInterval].

say.intro: Okay, so this is Insert Interval. We have a sorted list of intervals that don't overlap, plus one new interval. Insert it, merge anything it overlaps, and keep the list sorted. In our example, four to eight swallows three to five, six to seven, and eight to ten. That leaves three to ten.
say.brute: The obvious first try just throws the new interval into the list. Sort everything by start. Then run a standard merge pass. Does it work? Sure, and it's short. So what's the catch? It pays n log n to sort a list that was already sorted. We'd be wasting the one gift the problem gave us.
say.insight: Here's the thing. Because the list is sorted, every interval falls into one of three cases. Is it completely before the new one? Copy it over. Completely after? Then the new interval goes right here, and the rest is untouched. Otherwise it overlaps. So we absorb it, widening the new interval to cover both.
say.anim: We start with five intervals and a new interval of four to eight. Interval one to two ends before four, so it's copied straight into result. Interval three to five overlaps, merging newInterval into three to eight. Interval six to seven also overlaps, stretching newInterval's end to eight. Interval eight to ten overlaps too, expanding newInterval to three to ten. Interval twelve to sixteen starts after ten, so merging stops and newInterval is added. The remaining interval twelve to sixteen is copied unchanged after the merge. Final result is one to two, three to ten, and twelve to sixteen.
say.code: Now the code. We loop over the intervals. Does the new one end before the current one starts? Then it fits entirely before. Append it, and return it with the rest, untouched. Does it start after the current one ends? Then copy the current one. Otherwise, they overlap. We absorb it, taking the smaller start and the larger end. If we finish the loop, the new interval goes last.
say.outro: So that's linear time, and linear space for the output. The pattern is intervals. Before, after, or overlapping. Three cases cover everything.

insert-interval.title: Insert Interval
insert-interval.optimalCode:
class Solution:
    def insert(
        self, intervals: List[List[int]], newInterval: List[int]
    ) -> List[List[int]]:
        result = []
        index = 0
        total = len(intervals)

        # 1. Copy all intervals that end before the new interval starts
        while index < total and intervals[index][1] < newInterval[0]:
            result.append(intervals[index])
            index += 1

        # 2. Merge all intervals that overlap with the new interval
        while index < total and intervals[index][0] <= newInterval[1]:
            newInterval[0] = min(newInterval[0], intervals[index][0])
            newInterval[1] = max(newInterval[1], intervals[index][1])
            index += 1
        result.append(newInterval)

        # 3. Copy all intervals that start after the new interval ends
        while index < total:
            result.append(intervals[index])
            index += 1

        return result
lineNotes: We define a class called Solution to hold the method, as the problem format expects.
The insert method is declared, taking the sorted intervals and the new interval to add.
Its parameters are the list of intervals and newInterval, each given as a pair of start and end.
It returns a list of intervals, still sorted and with no overlaps.
We start with an empty result list that will collect the final merged intervals in order.
We set index to zero so we can walk through the intervals from the beginning.
We store the number of intervals in total so the loop checks stay short and clear.
This comment introduces phase one, copying every interval that finishes before the new one begins.
While intervals remain and the current one ends before the new start, it cannot overlap, so we keep going.
We append that earlier interval unchanged to the result.
We advance index to look at the next interval.
This comment introduces phase two, merging every interval that overlaps with the new interval.
While the current interval starts at or before the new end, it must overlap, since it does not end before the new start.
We set the new start to the smaller of the two starts, stretching the merged interval leftward if needed.
We set the new end to the larger of the two ends, stretching the merged interval rightward if needed.
We move index forward, having absorbed this interval into the new one.
Now the fully merged new interval is appended to the result, in its correct sorted position.
This comment introduces phase three, copying the intervals that start after the new interval ends.
While any intervals remain, they all come after the merged one and cannot overlap it.
We append each remaining interval unchanged to the result.
We advance index until every interval has been copied.
We return the result, which is sorted and free of overlaps.

merge-intervals.hook: Sort by start, and overlapping intervals line up next to each other — one sweep merges them all.
merge-intervals.ask: Given a list of intervals in any order, merge every group that overlaps and return the resulting non-overlapping intervals.
merge-intervals.exampleWhy: [1,3] and [2,6] overlap and become [1,6]; [8,10] and [15,18] touch nothing.

brute.idea: Repeatedly search for any pair of intervals that overlap, merge that pair, and restart, until no pair overlaps.
steps: Scan all pairs for an overlap
Merge the pair, restart the scan
No overlaps left: sort and return
brute.whySlow: Up to n merges, each rescanning n² pairs: 10,000 intervals means around a trillion checks.

optimal.insight: After sorting by start, an interval can only overlap the last merged one. If its start is at most the last end, extend that end; otherwise begin a new block.
steps: Sort by start
Seed output with the first interval
Start ≤ last end → extend the last end
Else append a new interval

codeNotes.note: Only the last block can overlap

pitfalls: Use max for the new end — [1,10] then [2,3] must stay [1,10].
[1,4] and [4,5] overlap: use <=.

say.intro: Okay, so this is Merge Intervals. We get intervals in any order, and we merge every group that overlaps. In our example, one to three and two to six overlap. So they combine into one to six. Eight to ten and fifteen to eighteen touch nothing. They stay as they are.
say.brute: The obvious first try keeps hunting for any pair that overlaps. When it finds one, it merges that pair and starts the search over. Eventually no pair overlaps, and it stops. Does it work? Yes. But each merge can rescan every pair, and there can be n merges. That's cubic time.
say.insight: Here's the thing. Sort the intervals by start. Now anything that overlaps sits side by side. So a new interval can only overlap the last block we built. Why? Because everything earlier already ended before that block. If its start is no later than the block's end, stretch the block. Otherwise there's a gap, so begin a new block. One sweep does it.
say.anim: We start by sorting intervals by their start value, giving one, two, eight ten, fifteen eighteen order. Merged begins with the first interval, one to three, as our seed block. Now we check interval two to six against the last merged block, one to three. Since two is less than or equal to three, these intervals overlap and get extended. The last block becomes one to six after extending its end to six. Next, eight to ten starts after six, so no overlap, and it's appended as new. Then fifteen to eighteen starts after ten, so it also becomes a separate new block. The final merged result returned is one six, eight ten, and fifteen eighteen.
say.code: Now the code. First we sort by start, so overlaps become neighbours. Then for each interval, we grab the end of the last block. Only that block can overlap. Is our start at most that end? Touching counts. Then extend the end, using the larger of the two ends. Why the max? Because one interval might contain the other. Otherwise, there's a gap, so append a new block.
say.outro: So that's n log n time, dominated by the sort. The pattern is intervals. Sort by start, then sweep once, merging into the last block.

We sort the intervals in place using each pair's first number, its start, as the sorting key.
Second step: we begin the answer with a starting point taken from the sorted input.
We seed the merged list with the first interval, since nothing before it can overlap.
We loop over every remaining interval, unpacking each one into a start and an end.
We read the start and end of the most recent merged interval to compare against the current one.
Third step: if the current start is not past the last end, the two intervals overlap.
We check whether the current start is at most the last end, which signals an overlap.
On overlap we stretch the last merged end to the larger of the two ends, absorbing the current interval.
Otherwise the current interval begins after the last one ends, so there is a gap.

We append the current interval as a new block at the end of the merged list.
After processing every interval, we return the merged list of non-overlapping intervals.

non-overlapping-intervals.hook: Removing the fewest intervals means keeping the most — and the greedy keeps whoever ends first.
non-overlapping-intervals.ask: Given a list of intervals, return the minimum number you must remove so that the rest do not overlap. Intervals that only touch at an endpoint are fine.
non-overlapping-intervals.exampleWhy: Keep [1,2], [2,3], [3,4]; removing [1,3] and [2,5] leaves no overlaps.

brute.idea: Sort, then DP: best[i] is the longest non-overlapping chain ending at interval i. Answer is n minus the longest chain.
steps: Sort intervals
best[i] = 1 + max best[j] where j ends ≤ start i
Return n - max(best)
brute.whySlow: Every interval looks back at all earlier ones: 100,000 intervals means 5 billion checks.

optimal.insight: When two intervals overlap, one must go. Keep the one that ends earlier: it leaves the most room for everything after, so it is never a worse choice.
steps: Sort by start
No overlap: advance prevEnd
Overlap: count a removal
Keep whichever ends first: prevEnd = min

pitfalls: Use >= : [1,2] and [2,3] do not overlap.
Return removals, not the number kept.

say.intro: Okay, so this is Non Overlapping Intervals. What's the fewest intervals you must remove so the rest never overlap? Touching at an endpoint is fine. In our example, we keep one to two, two to three, and three to four. We remove the other two. So the answer is two.
say.brute: A slower but correct approach is dynamic programming. Sort the intervals. For each one, find the longest chain of non overlapping intervals ending there, by checking every earlier one. The answer is n minus the longest chain. Does it work? Yes. But it's n squared. That's around five billion checks for a hundred thousand intervals.
say.insight: Here's the thing. Removing the fewest means keeping the most. Whenever two intervals overlap, one has to go. Which one? Keep the one that ends sooner. Why? It leaves the most room for everything to its right. So keeping it is never worse than keeping the other. That one greedy rule gives the minimum in a single pass.
say.anim: We start by sorting intervals by their start time for easy comparison. PreviousEnd is set to 2, the end of the first interval, and removeCount is zero. Checking interval one to three: its start, 1, is less than previousEnd, 2, so they overlap. We remove one interval, keeping the earlier end since 2 is smaller than 3. Next interval two to three starts at 2, which matches previousEnd, so no overlap, advance to 3. Interval two to five overlaps since start 2 is less than previousEnd 3, so we remove it too. Finally, interval three to four starts at 3, no overlap, so previousEnd becomes 4. The loop ends and the function returns removeCount, which is 2.
say.code: Now the code. We sort the intervals, so we process them left to right. We track the end of the last interval we kept. Does the next one start at or after that end? Touching is fine, so keep it and move the end. Otherwise they overlap, so count one removal. Then keep the smaller of the two ends. That means keeping the interval that finishes first.
say.outro: So that's n log n time and constant extra space. The pattern is intervals with a greedy twist. When two clash, keep whoever ends first.

meeting-rooms.hook: Can one person attend everything? After sorting, only neighbours can clash.
meeting-rooms.ask: Given a list of meeting time intervals, each a start and end, return true if one person could attend all of them, meaning no two meetings overlap.
meeting-rooms.exampleWhy: Sorted: [0,3],[3,5],[5,8],[9,11],[12,14]. Each ends no later than the next starts.

brute.idea: Compare every pair of meetings; if any two overlap, attending all is impossible.
steps: Pick meeting i
Check every later meeting j
Overlap? return False
brute.whySlow: With 10,000 meetings that is about 50 million pair checks.

optimal.insight: Sort by start time. If any two meetings overlap, then some pair of neighbours overlaps — so only compare each meeting with the one just before it.
steps: Sort meetings by start
Compare each with the previous one
Previous ends after this starts → False

pitfalls: Back-to-back meetings like [3,5] and [5,8] are fine — use strict >.
Empty list: return true.

say.intro: Okay, so this is Meeting Rooms. You get a list of meetings, each with a start and an end. Can one person attend all of them? That means no two may overlap. In our example, yes. Once sorted, every meeting ends before, or exactly when, the next one starts.
say.brute: The obvious first try compares every pair of meetings. Do they overlap? That happens when each one starts before the other ends. If any pair overlaps, return false. Does it work? Sure. But it's n squared. With ten thousand meetings, that's around fifty million comparisons.
say.insight: Here's the thing. Sort the meetings by start time. Now, take any two meetings that clash. What about the meetings between them? They all start before the first one ends. So the first one clashes with its very next neighbour. That means we only compare neighbours. Does the previous meeting end after the current one starts?
say.anim: We start by sorting the meetings by their start times for easy comparison. Now intervals are ordered: zero to three, three to five, five to eight, nine to eleven, twelve to fourteen. At index one, we compare previous zero to three with current three to five, no overlap. At index two, previous three to five and current five to eight also don't overlap. At index three, previous five to eight and current nine to eleven are fine too. At index four, previous nine to eleven and current twelve to fourteen still don't overlap. No overlaps found anywhere, so the loop finishes and returns true. The final answer is true, meaning all meetings can be attended.
say.code: Now the code. First we sort by start time, so any clash becomes a pair of neighbours. Then we loop from the second meeting on, checking each adjacent pair. Does the previous meeting run past this one's start? Then they clash, so return false. Ending exactly when the next begins is fine. If no clash shows up, return true.
say.outro: So that's n log n time for the sort, then one linear scan. The pattern is intervals. Sort first, and only neighbours can clash.

This comment says the next step is checking each meeting against the one right before it.
We loop an index from one up to the last position, since the first meeting has no predecessor to compare with.
We grab the previous meeting, the one just before the current index in the sorted list.
We grab the current meeting at the index we are examining.
This comment explains the overlap rule: if the previous meeting ends after the current one starts, they collide.
We check whether the previous end time is greater than the current start time, which means the two meetings overlap.
On finding an overlap, we return false immediately because one person cannot attend every meeting.
If the loop finishes with no overlaps found, every neighbouring pair is fine, so we return true.

meeting-rooms-ii.hook: Forget which meeting is in which room — just count how many are running at the busiest moment.
meeting-rooms-ii.ask: Given meeting time intervals, return the minimum number of conference rooms needed so that every meeting has a room.
meeting-rooms-ii.exampleWhy: At time 8, meetings [0,30], [5,10] and [8,16] all run at once — three rooms. Never more.

brute.idea: Peak overlap always happens at some meeting's start. For each start time, count how many meetings are running then.
steps: For each meeting start t
Count meetings with start ≤ t < end
Return the largest count
brute.whySlow: With 10,000 meetings that is 100 million interval checks.

optimal.insight: Rooms needed = the most meetings running at once. Turn each meeting into a +1 at its start and a -1 at its end, sort, and sweep a running count.
steps: Make events: (start, +1), (end, -1)
Sort by time; ends before starts on ties
Sweep, adding each event to count
Answer is the maximum count

pitfalls: A meeting ending at 10 frees its room for one starting at 10: ends first.

say.intro: Okay, so this is Meeting Rooms Two. Given a set of meetings, what's the fewest conference rooms that fit them all? No two meetings can share a room at the same time. Here, at time eight, three meetings are running at once. That's the peak, so we need three rooms.
say.brute: The obvious first try uses one fact. The busiest moment is always at some meeting's start. So for every start time, count how many meetings are running then, and keep the max. Does it work? Yes. But each start checks every meeting. That's n squared. About a hundred million checks for ten thousand meetings.
say.insight: Here's the thing. Do we care which meeting sits in which room? No. The answer is just the most meetings running at once. So split each meeting into two events. Plus one when it starts. Minus one when it ends. Sort the events, and sweep with a running count. The highest point it reaches is the answer.
say.anim: We start with five meetings and build events marking each start and end time. Each meeting becomes two events, a plus one at its start and minus one at its end. Now all ten events get sorted by time, with endings breaking ties before starts. We sweep through, adding one at time zero and five, raising current rooms to two. At time eight a third meeting starts, pushing current rooms up to three, our peak. As meetings end at ten, sixteen, and twenty, current rooms drops back down gradually. meeting-rooms-ii.title: Meeting Rooms II
meeting-rooms-ii.optimalCode:
class Solution:
    def minMeetingRooms(self, intervals: List[List[int]]) -> int:
        # 1. Make events: (time, +1) for start, (time, -1) for end
        events = []
        for start, end in intervals:
            events.append((start, 1))
            events.append((end, -1))

        # 2. Sort by time; on ties, ends (-1) come before starts (+1)
        events.sort(key=lambda event: (event[0], event[1]))

        # 3. Sweep through events, keeping a running count of rooms in use
        current_rooms = 0
        max_rooms = 0
        for time, change in events:
            current_rooms += change
            if current_rooms > max_rooms:
                max_rooms = current_rooms

        # 4. The maximum count seen is the answer
        return max_rooms

rotate-image.optimalCode:
class Solution:
    def rotate(self, matrix: List[List[int]]) -> None:
        """
        Do not return anything, modify matrix in-place instead.
        """
        l, r = 0, len(matrix) - 1
        while l < r:
            for i in range(r - l):
                top, bottom = l, r

                # save the topleft
                topLeft = matrix[top][l + i]

                # move bottom left into top left
                matrix[top][l + i] = matrix[bottom - i][l]

                # move bottom right into bottom left
                matrix[bottom - i][l] = matrix[bottom][r - i]

                # move top right into bottom right
                matrix[bottom][r - i] = matrix[top + i][r]

                # move top left into top right
                matrix[top + i][r] = topLeft
            r -= 1
            l += 1

spiral-matrix.hook: No clever math here: just four walls that close in. Get the boundaries right and it is easy.
spiral-matrix.ask: Given a grid of numbers, return all of them in spiral order: across the top, down the right side, back along the bottom, up the left, then repeat inward.

brute.code:
class Solution:
    def spiralOrder(self, matrix: List[List[int]]) -> List[int]:
        rows, cols = len(matrix), len(matrix[0])
        seen = [[False] * cols for _ in range(rows)]
        dirs = [(0, 1), (1, 0), (0, -1), (-1, 0)]
        r = c = d = 0
        res = []
        for _ in range(rows * cols):
            res.append(matrix[r][c])
            seen[r][c] = True
            nr, nc = r + dirs[d][0], c + dirs[d][1]
            if not (0 <= nr < rows and 0 <= nc < cols) or seen[nr][nc]:
                d = (d + 1) % 4
                nr, nc = r + dirs[d][0], c + dirs[d][1]
            r, c = nr, nc
        return res

happy-number.hook: A number game that secretly hides a linked list cycle. Floyd's tortoise and hare saves the day.
happy-number.ask: Repeatedly replace a number with the sum of the squares of its digits. If you eventually reach 1, the number is happy. If you loop forever, it is not.

say.intro: Okay, so this is Happy Number. Replace a number with the sum of the squares of its digits. Again and again. If you reach one, it's happy. If you loop forever, it's not. Nineteen goes to eighty two, then sixty eight, then one hundred, then one. So nineteen is happy.
say.brute: The obvious first move is a hash set. Remember every number we've seen. Reach one? Return true. See a number again? We're stuck in a loop, so return false. Does it work? Sure, and it's fast. But it stores the whole path. And the follow up asks for constant memory.
say.insight: Here's the twist. Every number has exactly one next number. So the sequence behaves like a linked list. And since the numbers stay small, it must end in a cycle. Slow moves one step to eighty two, while fast takes two steps, reaching one hundred. Fast continues advancing twice per round, now landing on one after squaring digits. Slow updates again to sixty eight, still chasing the faster pointer. Slow advances to one hundred, fast stays at one, since one always maps to one. Now slow reaches one too, matching fast exactly inside the cycle. Since they meet at one, the function returns true, confirming nineteen is happy.
say.code: Now the code. Slow starts at n, and fast starts one step ahead. We run until the two pointers meet. Each round, slow moves once, and fast moves twice. When they meet, we ask one question. Is the meeting point one? Then it's happy. And the helper? It sums the digit squares, squaring the last digit each time and peeling it off.
say.outro: So that's logarithmic time and constant space. The pattern is math plus fast and slow pointers. Cycle detection works on any one next value sequence.

happy-number.title: Happy Number
happy-number.optimalCode:
class Solution:
    def isHappy(self, n: int) -> bool:
        # 1. slow starts at n, fast starts one step ahead
        slow = n
        fast = self.sumSquareDigits(n)

        # 2. move slow once and fast twice each round
        while slow != fast:
            slow = self.sumSquareDigits(slow)
            fast = self.sumSquareDigits(fast)
            fast = self.sumSquareDigits(fast)

        # 3. they meet inside the final loop
        # 4. happy only if that loop is just the number 1
        if fast == 1:
            return True
        return False

    def sumSquareDigits(self, n):
        total = 0
        while n > 0:
            digit = n % 10
            total += digit * digit
            n = n // 10
        return total

We loop until slow and fast become equal, which means they have met inside a cycle.
Each round, slow advances one step by replacing itself with its sum of squared digits.
Fast advances its first step by taking the sum of squared digits of itself.
Fast advances a second step in the same round, so it moves twice as quickly as slow.
This comment notes that the two pointers must meet somewhere inside the final cycle.
This comment says the number is happy only if that cycle consists solely of the number 1.
If the meeting point is 1, the sequence reached the self-looping happy ending.
So we return true because the number is happy.
Otherwise the cycle is some other loop, so we return false because the number is not happy.
The helper sumSquareDigits computes the next number in the sequence from the current one.
We start a running total at zero to accumulate the squared digits.
We loop while n is positive, peeling off one digit at a time.
The digit is the remainder of n divided by ten, which is its last digit.
We add the square of that digit to the total.
We drop the last digit by dividing n by ten with integer division.
After all digits are processed, we return the total as the next number in the sequence.

plus-one.hook: Grade-school addition, one digit at a time. The only twist is a carry that ripples, maybe off the edge.
plus-one.ask: A big number is given as a list of its digits, most significant first. Add one to it and return the new list of digits.
plus-one.exampleWhy: 299 plus 1 is 300: both nines roll over to zero and the carry bumps the 2 to 3.

brute.idea: Glue the digits into one integer, add one, then split it back into digits.
steps: Build the integer digit by digit
Add one
Turn it back into a digit list
brute.whySlow: With 100 digits the number overflows 64-bit in most languages; Python big-ints hide quadratic work.

optimal.insight: Adding one only changes the trailing nines and the digit before them. Walk from the end: nines become zero and carry; the first non-nine just increases and we stop.
steps: Reverse so the ones digit comes first
Nine? set to 0, keep the carry
Otherwise add one and clear the carry
Ran out of digits with a carry? append 1

codeNotes.note: Loop only while a carry remains

pitfalls: All nines, like 999, must grow to 1000; do not forget the new digit.

say.intro: Okay, so this is Plus One. A very large number is stored as a list of digits, most significant first. We add one to it. For two, nine, nine, the answer is three, zero, zero. See why? Both nines roll over to zero, and the carry lands on the two.
say.brute: The obvious shortcut is to glue the digits into a real integer. Add one. Then split it back into digits. In Python that runs, because integers can grow. But with a hundred digits, most languages overflow. And the interviewer wants to see you handle the digits yourself, the way you'd add on paper.
say.insight: Think about it this way. How do you add one by hand? Only the trailing nines change, plus the digit just before them. So walk from the right. A nine becomes zero and passes the carry along. The first digit that isn't a nine just goes up by one. And we stop. What if every digit was nine? Then we need a new leading one.
say.anim: We start with digits two nine nine, reversed to nine nine two for easy carrying. Carry is set to one, and we begin scanning from index zero. The digit at index zero is nine, so it becomes zero and carry stays. Index one is also nine, so it turns to zero, carry still remains. Index two holds two, not nine, so we add one making it three. Carry becomes zero, meaning the addition is finished, no more changes needed. The loop stops since carry is zero, so we reverse the digits back. The final result is three, zero, zero, confirming the plus one worked.
say.code: Now the code. First, we reverse the list, so the ones digit comes first. We keep a carry called one, and loop only while a carry remains. A nine rolls over to zero, and the carry continues. Any other digit goes up by one, absorbing the carry. And if every digit was nine, we append a new leading one. Then we reverse back and return.
say.outro: So that's linear time, and linear space here, since we reverse copies. The pattern is math on digit arrays. Stop the moment the carry is absorbed.

powx-n.hook: Computing x to the n with only about log n multiplications: the idea behind fast modular exponentiation.
powx-n.ask: Compute x raised to the power n, where x is a decimal number and n is an integer that may be negative or huge. Do not use a built-in power function.
powx-n.exampleWhy: Two multiplied by itself thirteen times is 8192.

brute.idea: Multiply x into a running product |n| times. If n is negative, take one over the result.
steps: Start with result 1
Multiply by x, |n| times
Negative n? return 1 / result
brute.whySlow: n can be about two billion, so that means two billion multiplications for a single call.

optimal.insight: x to the n equals (x squared) to the n over 2, times one extra x when n is odd. Each step halves n, so only about log n steps.
steps: Recurse on x*x with n // 2
Base case: n is 0, return 1
If n is odd, multiply by one extra x
For negative n, return 1 over the result

codeNotes.note: Anything to the zero is one
Square the base, halve the exponent

codeNotes.match: return x * res if n % 2 else res
return res if n >= 0 else 1 / res

pitfalls: Negative n: use abs(n), then reciprocal; in Java, -2^31 overflows when negated.
Do not recurse twice on n/2; that loses the speedup.

say.intro: Okay, so this is Pow x n. We compute x to the power n ourselves, no built in power function. And n can be negative, or as big as two billion. In our example, two to the thirteenth is eight thousand one hundred ninety two.
say.brute: The obvious first move is to multiply x into a running product, n times. If n was negative, take one over the result. Does it work? Sure. But it's linear in n. With n near two billion, that's two billion multiplications for one answer. It'll time out.
say.insight: Here's the thing. X to the n equals x squared, to the power n over two. If n is odd, multiply by one extra x. Every step halves the exponent. So thirteen becomes six, then three, then one, then zero. Instead of thirteen multiplications, we do a handful. And two billion? Only about thirty one steps.
say.anim: We start computing two to the power thirteen using fast recursive squaring. Base squares to four with exponent six, then sixteen with exponent three, halving each time. Exponent keeps shrinking until base is sixty five thousand five hundred thirty six and exponent hits zero. Zero exponent returns one, the base case ending the recursive descent. Climbing back up, odd exponent one multiplies base two fifty six by one, giving two fifty six. Next level, odd exponent three multiplies sixteen by two fifty six, yielding four thousand ninety six. Exponent six is even, so four thousand ninety six passes through unchanged. Finally odd exponent thirteen multiplies two by four thousand ninety six, giving final answer eight thousand one hundred ninety two.
say.code: Now the code. The helper starts with the base case. Anything to the zero is one. Otherwise, we square the base and halve the exponent, recursing just once. Notice, only once. That's what keeps it fast. If the exponent was odd, we multiply in one extra x. Outside, we call the helper with a positive exponent. And for a negative power, we take the reciprocal.
say.outro: So that's logarithmic time and logarithmic stack space. The pattern is fast exponentiation by repeated squaring. It shows up everywhere, even in modular arithmetic.

powx-n.title: Pow(x, n)

The method myPow takes a decimal x and an integer n and returns x raised to the power n.
We define an inner helper function that handles only non-negative exponents using the repeated squaring idea.

If the base is zero, we check this first because every positive power of zero is zero.
In that case we return zero right away, with no further recursion needed.
If the exponent is zero, we have reached the bottom of the recursion.
We return one, since anything raised to the power zero is one.
This comment says we recurse on the squared base with the exponent cut in half.
We call helper with base times base and exponent divided by two, rounding down, so the problem shrinks quickly.
This comment says that when the exponent is odd, one leftover base factor must be multiplied in.
We check whether the exponent leaves a remainder of one when divided by two, meaning it is odd.
For an odd exponent, the halving dropped one factor, so we multiply the half result by base.
For an even exponent the halving was exact, so we simply return the half result.
This comment says negative exponents are handled by computing with the absolute value and then taking a reciprocal.
We compute the power for the absolute value of n, so the helper never sees a negative exponent.
If n is zero or positive, the computed result is already the answer.
So we return result directly in that case.
For negative n, we return one divided by result, since x to the negative n is the reciprocal.

multiply-strings.optimalCode:
class Solution:
    def multiply(self, num1: str, num2: str) -> str:
        if num1 == "0" or num2 == "0":
            return "0"

        # 1. Reverse both strings so index 0 is the ones place
        reversed_num1 = num1[::-1]
        reversed_num2 = num2[::-1]
        result = [0] * (len(num1) + len(num2))

        # 2. Multiply every digit pair and add into the correct place
        for i in range(len(reversed_num1)):
            digit1 = int(reversed_num1[i])
            for j in range(len(reversed_num2)):
                digit2 = int(reversed_num2[j])
                result[i + j] += digit1 * digit2

                # 3. Push the carry into the next place
                carry = result[i + j] // 10
                result[i + j] = result[i + j] % 10
                result[i + j + 1] += carry

        # 4. Reverse back, skip leading zeros, join into a string
        result = result[::-1]
        start = 0
        while start < len(result) - 1 and result[start] == 0:
            start += 1

        digits = []
        for digit in result[start:]:
            digits.append(str(digit))
        return "".join(digits)
multiply-strings.hook: Long multiplication from school, turned into a neat array trick: digit i times digit j lands at i plus j.
multiply-strings.ask: Two non-negative whole numbers are given as strings, possibly hundreds of digits long. Return their product as a string, without converting the whole strings to integers.
multiply-strings.exampleWhy: 25 times 11 is 275: 25 times 1 is 25, plus 25 times 10 is 250.

brute.idea: Multiplication is repeated addition. Add num1 to a running string total, num2 times, using digit-by-digit string addition.
steps: Start the total at "0"
Add num1 to the total with carry, column by column
Repeat num2 times
brute.whySlow: num2 can have 200 digits, so its value is astronomically large. Repeated addition would never finish.

optimal.insight: In long multiplication, digit at place i times digit at place j always lands in place i + j. One result array of length n + m collects everything.
steps: Reverse both strings so index 0 is the ones place
Add num1[i]·num2[j] into res[i+j]
Push the carry into res[i+j+1]
Reverse, skip leading zeros, join

codeNotes.note: Product has at most n + m digits
Place i times place j lands at i + j
Carry spills to the next place

pitfalls: Return "0" early; otherwise stripping zeros leaves an empty string.
Result length is at most n + m digits: size the array once.

say.intro: Okay, so this is Multiply Strings. Two whole numbers arrive as strings, maybe two hundred digits long. We return their product as a string, without converting to big integers. In our small example, twenty five times eleven is two hundred seventy five. We'll trace it digit by digit.
say.brute: A first idea is that multiplication is just repeated addition. Write a string adder that adds column by column with a carry. Then add num one to a running total, num two times. Does it work? Sure. But num two could have two hundred digits. That loop would never finish.
say.insight: Here's the thing. Go back to long multiplication on paper. The digit in place i, times the digit in place j, always lands in place i plus j. Always. So we make one array of length n plus m. We drop every digit product into its slot, and push the tens carry one place over. No partial rows, and no string additions.
say.anim: We start multiplying twenty five by eleven, neither is zero, so we continue. Both strings get reversed to fifty two and eleven, so index zero is the ones place. A result array of four zeros is created, one slot for each possible digit place. Digit one is five, and we multiply it by digit two, one, landing in place zero. Next five times the tens digit one lands in place one, giving result five, five, zero, zero. Now digit one is two, multiplying by one again and adding into place one and two. The array becomes zero, two, seven, five, then we reverse it and skip the leading zero. Joining the remaining digits gives the final answer, two hundred seventy five.
say.code: Now the code. First, if either number is zero, return zero right away. Otherwise we'd strip every digit and return an empty string. Then we size the result array once, n plus m digits. For every pair of digits, add the product at place i plus j. The tens carry spills into the next place. Finally, we strip the leading zeros and join the digits.
say.outro: So that's n times m time, and n plus m space. The pattern is math. Simulate long multiplication, where place i times place j lands at i plus j.

detect-squares.hook: Counting squares sounds geometric, but fix one corner as the diagonal and a hash map does the rest.
detect-squares.ask: Build a structure that stores points (duplicates allowed). For a query point, count how many ways to pick three stored points that form an axis-aligned square of positive area with it.
detect-squares.exampleWhy: Query (11,10) with (3,10),(11,2),(3,2) makes one square. After adding (11,2) again, there are two.

brute.idea: Store points in a list. For a query, try every stored point as the opposite diagonal corner, and scan the whole list to count the other two corners.
steps: Pick a stored point as the diagonal
Check it forms a square with the query
Scan all points for each of the other two corners
Multiply the two counts, add up
brute.whySlow: At most 3,000 calls: with 1,500 stored points, a single count does over two million checks.

optimal.insight: The query point plus a diagonal corner fully determine the square. Then the other two corners are fixed, so a point-count hash map gives their multiplicities in O(1).
steps: add: bump the count for that point and keep it in a list
count: try each stored point as the diagonal
Skip if not a true diagonal (equal dx, dy, nonzero)
Add count(x,py) times count(px,y)

codeNotes.note: Each stored point as the diagonal

codeNotes.match: if (abs(py - y) != abs(px - x)) or x == px or y == py:
codeNotes.note: Need a square with positive area
Other two corners via hash lookup

pitfalls: Duplicates multiply: two copies of a corner mean two different squares.
Reject zero-area squares where the diagonal shares the query's x or y.

say.intro: Okay, so this is Detect Squares. We add points, and duplicates are allowed. For a query point, we count the axis aligned squares it forms with three stored points. Here, three corners plus the query make one square. Add a second copy of one corner, and that query finds two.
say.brute: The obvious first try picks every stored point as the opposite corner. For each one, it rescans the whole list to count the two remaining corners. Does it work? Yes. But that's n squared per query. With fifteen hundred stored points, one query does over two million checks.
say.insight: Here's the thing. Once you pick the diagonal corner, the square is fully decided. Its other two corners are known exactly. So keep a hash map from each point to how many times it was added. Now those two corners are instant lookups. And their counts just multiply. Why multiply? Because each duplicate makes a different square.
say.anim: We start with empty point counts and an empty points list for our detector. We add three points: three ten, eleven two, and three two, tracking their counts. Now we query eleven ten, checking each stored point as a diagonal corner. For point three ten, delta x is eight but delta y is zero, so it's skipped. Point three two gives delta x and delta y both eight, forming a valid square, adding one. Querying fourteen eight finds no matching diagonal deltas, so the count returns zero. We add another point at eleven two, increasing its stored count to two. Querying eleven ten again now finds two matching squares, since eleven two appears twice, giving a final count of two.
say.code: Now the code. Add bumps a counter for the point, so duplicates count separately, and appends it to a list. Count loops over the stored points, trying each as the diagonal. Are the x gap and the y gap different? Or would the square be flat? Then skip it. We need positive area. Otherwise, we look up the other two corners in the hash map, and add the product of their counts.
say.outro: So that's constant time add and linear time count. The pattern is geometry with hashing. Fix the diagonal, then look up everything else.

detect-squares.title: Detect Squares
detect-squares.optimalCode:
class DetectSquares:
    def __init__(self):
        # 1. Keep a count of each point and a list of all points added
        self.pointCount = defaultdict(int)
        self.points = []

    def add(self, point: List[int]) -> None:
        self.pointCount[tuple(point)] += 1
        self.points.append(point)

    def count(self, point: List[int]) -> int:
        totalSquares = 0
        queryX, queryY = point
        # 2. Try every stored point as the diagonal corner
        for x, y in self.points:
            deltaX = abs(queryX - x)
            deltaY = abs(queryY - y)
            # 3. Skip points that cannot form a diagonal with the query point
            if deltaX != deltaY or deltaX == 0:
                continue
            # 4. Multiply counts of the other two corners needed for the square
            totalSquares += self.pointCount[(x, queryY)] * self.pointCount[(queryX, y)]
        return totalSquares
lineNotes: We define a class called DetectSquares that will store points and answer square counting queries.
The constructor sets up the starting state for the structure when it is created.
This comment says we track how many times each point appears, plus a list of every point added.
We create pointCount as a default dictionary of integers so unseen points count as zero.
We create an empty list called points that will hold every added point, duplicates included.
The add method takes a point and stores it in our structure.
We increase the count for this point's tuple form by one, since lists cannot be dictionary keys.
We also append the point to the points list so duplicates appear as separate diagonal candidates.
The count method takes a query point and returns how many squares it can form with stored points.
We start totalSquares at zero to accumulate the number of valid squares.
We unpack the query point into queryX and queryY for easy use below.
This comment says we will try each stored point as the possible diagonal corner opposite the query.
We loop over every stored point, reading its x and y coordinates, with duplicates visited once each.
We compute deltaX as the absolute horizontal distance between the query and this point.
We compute deltaY as the absolute vertical distance between the query and this point.
This comment says we must skip points that cannot be a diagonal corner of a square.
If the distances differ or are zero, the shape is not a positive area square, so we move on.
The continue statement skips to the next stored point when the diagonal check fails.
This comment says the other two corners are fixed, so we multiply their stored counts.
We add the product of counts at the two remaining corners, which gives all ways to complete this square.
We return totalSquares as the final number of squares formed with the query point.

single-number.hook: Every number appears twice except one. A single XOR pass makes all the pairs vanish.
single-number.ask: In a list where every number appears exactly twice except one, find the number that appears once. Use linear time and constant extra memory.
single-number.exampleWhy: 4, 1 and 2 each appear twice; only 5 appears once.

brute.idea: For each number, count how many times it appears by scanning the whole list. Return the one with count one.
steps: Pick nums[i]
Count its occurrences in the list
Count is 1? return it
brute.whySlow: With 30,000 numbers that is up to 900 million comparisons.

optimal.insight: XOR of a number with itself is 0, XOR with 0 changes nothing, and order does not matter. XOR everything: pairs cancel, the single number remains.
steps: Start with res = 0
XOR every number into res
Pairs cancel to 0, leaving the unique number

pitfalls: A hash set also works in O(n) but uses O(n) memory, which the problem forbids.

say.intro: Okay, so this is Single Number. Every value in the list appears exactly twice, except one. Find that one, in linear time and constant extra memory. In our example, four, one and two all come in pairs. So the answer is five. It's the only number without a partner.
say.brute: The obvious first try takes each number and counts how often it shows up, by scanning the whole list again. Whichever appears once is the answer. That's n squared. Nearly a billion comparisons for thirty thousand numbers. A hash set would be linear. But it uses linear memory, and the problem forbids that.
say.insight: Here's the thing. Think XOR. A number XOR itself is zero. Anything XOR zero stays the same. And XOR doesn't care about order. So we can pretend all the pairs sit right next to each other. What happens if we XOR everything together? Every pair cancels out. And the lonely number is all that's left.
say.anim: We start with res at zero and our list of numbers to scan. We XOR four with res, giving res the value four. Next we XOR one in, updating res to five. XORing two gives res seven, then XORing one again cancels it back to six. XORing two again cancels that pair too, dropping res to four. XORing five brings res to one, then XORing the second four cancels it, leaving res five. All duplicate pairs have canceled out, leaving only the unique number. The function returns five, the single number in the list.
say.code: Now the code. We start the result at zero. Why zero? Because anything XOR zero is itself. Then we make one pass over the list. We XOR each number into the result, and duplicates cancel each other out. When the loop ends, only the single number survives. So we return the result.
say.outro: So that's linear time and constant space. The pattern is bit manipulation. When things come in pairs and you need the odd one out, think XOR.

single-number.title: Single Number
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container this problem's method lives in.
The singleNumber method takes a list of integers called nums and returns the one number that appears only once.
We start res at zero, because XOR with zero changes nothing, so it is a safe starting value.
We loop through every number n in nums, visiting each element exactly once for linear time.
We XOR n into res, so numbers that appear twice cancel to zero and the single number survives.
After the loop, res holds the lone number, and we return it using only constant extra memory.

number-of-1-bits.hook: Counting set bits by checking all 32 is fine. Brian Kernighan's trick only visits the ones.
number-of-1-bits.ask: Given a positive integer, return how many 1 bits it has in binary. This is also called the Hamming weight.
number-of-1-bits.exampleWhy: 1000 in binary is 1111101000, which has six 1 bits.

brute.idea: Check each of the 32 bit positions: shift and test the lowest bit, counting the ones.
steps: Look at the lowest bit with n & 1
Add it to the count
Shift n right; repeat 32 times
brute.whySlow: Always 32 iterations, even when only a handful of bits are set; it visits every zero too.

optimal.insight: n - 1 flips the lowest 1 bit to 0 and the zeros below it to 1. So n & (n - 1) erases exactly the lowest set bit.
steps: While n is not zero
n &= n - 1 removes the lowest set bit
Count one per removal

codeNotes.note: Stop once every 1 bit is gone

pitfalls: In Java the input is signed; use unsigned shift >>> or the n & (n-1) loop.

say.intro: Okay, so this is Number of One Bits. Given a positive integer, count how many ones appear in its binary form. That's also called the Hamming weight. One thousand in binary is one one one one one zero one zero zero zero. That has six ones.
say.brute: The obvious first move checks all thirty two bit positions. Shift the number right, look at the lowest bit with AND one, and add it to the count. Does it work? Sure. So what's the catch? It always takes thirty two steps. Even when there are only a couple of ones. It visits every zero too.
say.insight: Here's a classic trick. What happens when you subtract one from n? The lowest one bit flips to zero. And the zeros below it turn into ones. So n AND n minus one wipes out exactly that lowest set bit. Everything above it stays put. Repeat until n is zero. The number of rounds is the answer.
say.anim: We start with n equal to 1000 and res initialized to 0. Each loop, n and n minus 1 erases the lowest set bit, now n is 992. Res increments to 1, counting that cleared bit, and the loop continues. N keeps shrinking, 960 then 896 then 768, as each bit gets erased. Res climbs to 4, then n becomes 512 after another bit clears. The final bit clears, n becomes 0, and res reaches 6. With n now 0, the while loop condition fails and we exit. The function returns res, giving a final answer of 6.
say.code: Now the code. We loop while n isn't zero. That way, we stop once every one bit is gone. Inside, we set n to n AND n minus one, which erases the lowest set bit. Then we add one to the count, one per erased bit. When n hits zero, we return the count. So the loop runs once per one bit, never more.
say.outro: So that's time proportional to the number of ones, and constant space. The pattern is bit manipulation. The n AND n minus one trick is worth memorising.

number-of-1-bits.title: Number of 1 Bits
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container the problem expects for our method.
The method hammingWeight takes the integer n and will return how many one bits it contains.
We start the result counter res at zero because we have not counted any set bits yet.
We loop as long as n is nonzero, meaning at least one set bit remains.
Setting n to n and n minus one erases exactly the lowest set bit, shrinking the problem each time.
Each time we erase a set bit, we add one to res to count it.
Once n becomes zero, every one bit has been counted, so we return res.

counting-bits.hook: Count bits for every number up to n without recounting: each answer reuses a smaller one.
counting-bits.ask: Given n, return a list where position i holds the number of 1 bits in i, for every i from 0 to n.
counting-bits.exampleWhy: For example 7 is 111 with three ones, and 8 is 1000 with one.

brute.idea: For every i from 0 to n, count its bits from scratch by shifting it right until it is zero.
steps: For each i
Shift i right, adding the lowest bit
Store the count
brute.whySlow: For n = 100,000 every number is re-counted bit by bit: about 1.7 million operations instead of 100,000.

optimal.insight: With offset the largest power of two ≤ i, i is that top bit plus i - offset, already solved. So dp[i] = 1 + dp[i - offset].
steps: dp[0] = 0, offset = 1
When i doubles offset, i is a new power of two
dp[i] = 1 + dp[i - offset]

codeNotes.note: dp[i] = number of ones in i
Reached a new power of two
Top bit plus the remainder's answer

pitfalls: Another clean recurrence: dp[i] = dp[i >> 1] + (i & 1).
Remember position 0, so the list has n + 1 entries.

say.intro: Okay, so this is Counting Bits. For every number from zero up to n, count its one bits. Return all the counts in a list. For n equals eight, the counts run zero, one, one, two, one, two, two, three. And eight is one followed by three zeros, so it has just one.
say.brute: The obvious first try recounts every number from scratch. Shift it right, adding up its bits one at a time. Each number has about log n bits, so that's n log n in total. Does it work? Sure. But we keep redoing work. Every number contains a smaller number we've already counted.
say.insight: Here's the thing. Take the biggest power of two that fits in i. Call it the offset. Then i is just that single top bit, plus a smaller number, i minus offset. And we already know the answer for that smaller number, right? So the count for i is one, plus the count for i minus offset. That's dynamic programming.
say.anim: We start with an array dp of nine zeros, for numbers zero through eight. Offset is one, and at i equals one, dp of one becomes one plus dp of zero. At i equals two, offset doubles to two, since it matches the new power of two. At i equals three, dp of three uses offset two, giving one plus dp of one, so two. At i equals four, offset updates again to four, the next power of two boundary. For i five through seven, dp builds using offset four, reusing earlier solved values. At i equals eight, offset updates to eight, since eight is the next power of two. The final bit counts array is zero, one, one, two, one, two, two, three, one.
say.code: Now the code. We make a dp list of size n plus one. Entry i will hold the number of ones in i. The offset starts at one. For each i, have we reached a new power of two? That's when i equals double the offset. Then the highest bit moves up, so the offset becomes i. And dp of i is one, for the top bit, plus dp of i minus offset.
say.outro: So that's linear time, in a single pass. The pattern is bit manipulation meets dynamic programming. Build each answer from a smaller one you already have.

counting-bits.title: Counting Bits
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container the interview platform expects for our method.
The method countBits takes the number n and returns a list of bit counts for zero through n.
We create a list called dp of length n plus one, filled with zeros, so dp at zero is already correct.
We set offset to one, which tracks the largest power of two that is at most the current number.
We loop i from one up to n inclusive, filling in each answer using earlier results.
When twice the offset equals i, we have reached a new power of two, so the offset must grow.
We update offset to i, making it the new largest power of two not exceeding i.
The count for i is one for the top bit plus the already computed count for i minus offset.
We return the finished dp list holding the number of one bits for every value from zero to n.

reverse-bits.hook: Mirror a 32-bit number end to end using only shifts and masks, no strings attached.
reverse-bits.ask: Treat the input as a 32-bit unsigned number. Reverse the order of its bits, so bit 0 becomes bit 31 and so on, and return the resulting number.

brute.idea: Write the number as a 32-character binary string, reverse the string, and parse it back as a number.
steps: Build the 32 bits as text, padding with zeros
Reverse the text
Parse the text back into a number
brute.whySlow: Same step count, but it builds and parses strings; when called millions of times that overhead dominates.

optimal.insight: Bit i of the input belongs at position 31 - i of the answer. Read it with a shift and mask, then OR it into place; no strings needed.
steps: For i from 0 to 31
Read bit i: (n >> i) & 1
OR it into res at position 31 - i

codeNotes.note: Write it at the mirror position

pitfalls: Always loop 32 times; stopping when n is 0 drops the leading zeros.
Follow-up: cache byte reversals, or swap halves, quarters, pairs with masks.

say.intro: Okay, so this is Reverse Bits. We take a thirty two bit number and mirror its bits. The lowest bit becomes the highest, and the highest becomes the lowest. In our example, the input has six zeros at the top. So the answer ends with six zeros, and it's a much bigger number.
say.brute: The obvious first try writes the number as a thirty two character binary string. Reverse the string. Parse it back into a number. Does it work? Sure, and it's easy to explain. But it builds text and converts back and forth. The interviewer will push you to stay in pure bit operations. Especially for millions of calls.
say.insight: Here's the thing. Bit i of the input belongs at position thirty one minus i in the answer. That's all. So how do we read bit i? Shift the number right by i, and mask with one. Then shift that bit left into its mirror spot, and OR it into the result. No strings at all. Just shifts and masks.
say.anim: We start with n as 43261596 and res initialized to 0. At i equals 0, bit is 0, so res stays unchanged after shifting into position 31. By i equals 2, bit 1 is placed at position 29, growing res to 536870912. Each loop extracts one bit with a shift and mask, then ors it into its mirrored spot. After many iterations, res has climbed to 964173824 as bits accumulate in reverse order. Near the end, res reaches 964176192, nearly all 32 bits reversed and placed. The loop finishes and the function returns 964176192, the bit reversed result.
say.code: Now the code. The result starts at zero. We loop exactly thirty two times. Why not stop when n hits zero? Because the leading zeros must be mirrored too. Each round, we read bit i with a right shift and AND one. Then we write it at the mirror position. Shift it left by thirty one minus i, and OR it into the result.
say.outro: So that's constant time and constant space, always thirty two steps. The pattern is bit manipulation. Read with shift and mask, write with shift and OR.

reverse-bits.title: Reverse Bits
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container for the method that reverses the bits.
The reverseBits method takes the integer n, treated as a 32-bit unsigned number, and returns its bit-reversed value.
We start the result at zero, so every bit position is empty until we place bits into it.
We loop over each of the 32 bit positions of the input, one index at a time.
We shift n right by i and mask with one, which extracts the bit at position i.
We shift that bit left to position thirty-one minus i and OR it into the result, mirroring its place.
After all 32 bits are placed, we return the result as the reversed number.

missing-number.hook: One number from zero to n is missing. Pair indexes against values and the gap reveals itself.
missing-number.ask: You get n distinct numbers taken from the range 0 to n, so exactly one number in that range is missing. Return it.
missing-number.exampleWhy: n is 9, so the range is 0 to 9. Every number appears except 8.

brute.idea: Try each candidate from 0 to n and scan the list to see whether it is there. The first one not found is missing.
steps: For each candidate c from 0 to n
Scan the list for c
Not found? return c
brute.whySlow: With 10,000 numbers that is up to 100 million comparisons.

optimal.insight: Sum of 0..n minus sum of the list is the missing number. Adding each index and subtracting each value builds that difference in one pass.
steps: Start res at n (the one index with no slot)
For each i, add i and subtract nums[i]
Everything present cancels; the missing value remains

codeNotes.note: n itself has no matching index

pitfalls: XOR of all indexes and values works the same way and never overflows.

say.intro: Okay, so this is Missing Number. We get n different numbers, taken from the range zero to n. So exactly one number in that range is missing. Find it. In our example there are nine numbers. The range is zero to nine. And eight is the one that never shows up.
say.brute: The obvious first try checks every candidate from zero to n. For each, scan the whole list. Is it there? The first candidate we can't find is the answer. That's n squared. Around a hundred million checks for ten thousand numbers. Sorting or a hash set would help, but costs time or memory.
say.insight: Think about it this way. Add up everything from zero to n. Subtract everything in the list. What's left over? Only the missing number. And we can do that in one pass. For each index, add the index and subtract the value. We start with n itself. Why? Because n is the one expected number with no index of its own.
say.anim: We start with the array of nine numbers missing one value from zero to nine. Result is initialized to nine, since that index has no slot in the array. We loop through each index, adding the index and subtracting its value. After processing index zero, result drops to zero since nine was subtracted. As the loop continues, result keeps shifting as indices and values cancel out. Near the end, result fluctuates between negative and positive as more terms combine. On the final index eight, result updates to nine before the last subtraction. The loop finishes with result equal to eight, the missing number in the sequence.
say.code: Now the code. The result starts at the length of the list, which is n. That's because n has no matching index. Then we make one pass over the indexes. For each index i, we add i and subtract the number at i. Expected in, actual out. Every number that's present cancels against its index. So only the missing value survives, and we return it.
say.outro: So that's linear time and constant space. The pattern is math and bit tricks. XOR of indexes and values works too, since pairs cancel.

missing-number.title: Missing Number
missing-number.optimalCode:
class Solution:
    def missingNumber(self, nums: List[int]) -> int:
        n = len(nums)
        # 1. Start result at n, the one index with no slot in nums
        result = n

        # 2. For each index, add the index and subtract the value at that index
        for i in range(n):
            result += i
            result -= nums[i]

        # 3. Everything present cancels out, leaving the missing number
        return result
lineNotes: We define a class called Solution, which holds the method that solves the missing number problem.
The method missingNumber takes the list nums of distinct numbers and returns the single integer missing from the range.
We store the length of nums in n, which is also the largest number in the full range.
This comment explains that n needs special handling because no index in nums ever equals n.
We start result at n so the top number of the range is already counted in the sum of indices.
This comment says that at each position we add the index and subtract the value found there.
We loop i across every index from zero up to n minus one, visiting each position once.
We add the current index i to result, building up the sum of the expected numbers.
We subtract the value at index i from result, removing each number that is actually present.
This comment notes that matching indices and values cancel, so only the missing number remains.
We return result, which now equals the expected sum minus the actual sum, which is the missing number.

sum-of-two-integers.hook: Add two numbers without using plus or minus. You are about to rebuild a hardware adder.
sum-of-two-integers.ask: Return the sum of two integers a and b, but you are not allowed to use the plus or minus operators.

brute.idea: A ripple-carry adder: walk all 32 bit positions, computing each sum bit and the carry like a circuit, then fix the sign.
steps: For each of 32 bits, read bit x and bit y
Sum bit = x ^ y ^ carry
New carry from x & y or carry & (x ^ y)
If bit 31 is set, convert back to negative
brute.whySlow: Same O(32) bound; it just always runs all 32 rounds, while the carry loop stops once carries vanish: three rounds for 5 + 7.

optimal.insight: XOR adds bits without carrying; AND shifted left is the carry. So a + b = (a ^ b) + ((a & b) << 1). Repeat until no carry.
steps: Partial sum = a ^ b
Carry = (a & b) << 1
Add them again the same way
Stop when carry is 0

codeNotes.match: if not a or not b:

codeNotes.note: Sum without carry, plus the carry
Mixed signs need special handling in Python

codeNotes.match: return add(a, b)  # a*b >= 0 or (-a) > b > 0

pitfalls: Python ints are unbounded: a positive plus a bigger negative, like 3 and -1, recurses forever.
Hence the sign branches; in Java or C++ the plain carry loop just works.

say.intro: Okay, so this is Sum of Two Integers. Add a and b, but you can't use the plus or minus operators. So we rebuild addition from bit operations, like the adder circuits in a processor. In our example, five plus seven should give twelve. In binary, that's one one zero zero.
say.brute: One approach mimics a ripple carry adder circuit. Walk all thirty two bit positions. At each one, the sum bit is the XOR of the two input bits and the carry. The new carry comes from AND and OR. Does it work? Yes, even for negatives. But it always does thirty two rounds. Even for tiny numbers like ours.
say.insight: Here's the thing. XOR adds two numbers, but forgets every carry. And AND? It finds exactly where both bits are one. That's where a carry happens. Shift it left by one, and it moves to the right column. So the sum equals the XOR plus the shifted AND. Repeat until the carry is zero. Just like carrying on paper.
say.anim: We start with a equal to five and b equal to seven, using a mask to keep thirty two bits. XOR gives a partial sum of two, while AND shifted left gives a carry of ten. Now a becomes two and b becomes ten, since there is still a carry to add. Looping again, XOR of two and ten gives eight, with a carry of four. Now a is eight and b is four, continuing because the carry is nonzero. This time XOR gives twelve, and the AND shifted left produces zero carry. With b now zero, the loop ends since there is no carry left. The sign bit check passes since a is positive, so the function returns twelve.
say.code: Now the code. The helper stops when either number is zero. There's nothing left to carry, so it returns the other. Otherwise, it recurses on the XOR, the sum without carry, and the shifted AND, the carry. Then there's a branch for mixed signs. Why? Python integers never overflow, so we rewrite those cases using positives. Same signs go straight to the helper.
say.outro: So that's at most thirty two rounds, and constant space. The pattern is bit manipulation. XOR gives the sum without carries. AND shifted left gives the carries.

sum-of-two-integers.title: Sum of Two Integers
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container this problem's method lives in.
The getSum method takes two integers a and b and returns their sum without using plus or minus.
We set mask to thirty-two one bits, so we can simulate a thirty-two bit integer in Python.
This comment says we keep adding without carrying until no carry remains.
The loop continues while b, limited to thirty-two bits, is not zero, meaning a carry is still pending.
Partial sum is a xor b, which adds each bit without carry, trimmed to thirty-two bits.
Carry is a and b shifted left by one, since matching one bits carry into the next position, masked to thirty-two bits.
We replace a with the partial sum, which becomes the running result.
We replace b with the carry, which still has to be added into the result.
This comment says that if the thirty-two bit result represents a negative number, we must convert it back.
If the top bit, the sign bit, is set, the result is negative in thirty-two bit two's complement.
We flip the lower thirty-two bits with xor against mask, then invert everything, which gives Python's proper negative value.
We return a, the final sum as a normal Python integer.

reverse-integer.hook: Reversing digits is easy. Doing it while proving you never overflow 32 bits is the real test.
reverse-integer.ask: Reverse the digits of a signed 32-bit integer. If the reversed value falls outside the 32-bit range, return 0. Pretend you cannot store 64-bit numbers.
reverse-integer.exampleWhy: Digits 1230 reversed give 0321, the leading zero drops, and the minus sign stays: -321.

brute.idea: Turn the absolute value into a string, reverse it, parse it back, restore the sign, then check the 32-bit range.
steps: Reverse the digits as text
Parse back and reapply the sign
Outside 32-bit range? return 0
brute.whySlow: The range check happens after building a value that may not fit in 32 bits, which the rules forbid.

optimal.insight: Build the answer as res * 10 + digit, but first check res against MAX // 10 and MIN // 10, so overflow is caught before it happens.
steps: Pop the last digit, truncating toward zero
Would res * 10 + digit leave the range? return 0
Otherwise push the digit onto res
Stop when x is 0

codeNotes.note: Drop the digit, truncate toward zero

codeNotes.match: if res > MAX // 10 or (res == MAX // 10 and digit > MAX % 10):
if res < MIN // 10 or (res == MIN // 10 and digit < MIN % 10):
codeNotes.note: Same check on the negative side
Push the digit onto the answer

pitfalls: Python's % and // round toward negative infinity; use fmod and int division.
In Python MIN // 10 floors to -214748365; safe only because 10-digit inputs start with 1 or 2.

say.intro: Okay, so this is Reverse Integer. Reverse the digits of a thirty two bit integer. If the result would overflow, return zero. The catch? Pretend you can't store anything bigger than thirty two bits. Here, minus one two three zero becomes minus three two one. The trailing zero just disappears.
say.brute: The obvious first try turns the number into a string. Reverse it, parse it back, and restore the sign. Then check the range. In Python, that runs fine. So what's wrong? It builds a number that might not fit in thirty two bits, before checking it. That's exactly what the problem forbids.
say.insight: Here's the thing. Build the answer one digit at a time. Multiply by ten, then add the next digit. The trick is to check before multiplying, not after. Is the result already bigger than the max divided by ten? Then the next step must overflow. So return zero right there. The same check against the min protects negatives.
say.anim: We start with x equal to negative 1230, and set up the integer bounds. Negative is marked true, then x becomes its absolute value, 1230. Result starts at zero, and we loop while x is not zero. We pop the last digit, zero, leaving x as 123, then check overflow safely. Result becomes zero, then we repeat, popping digit three, making result 3. Next loop pops digit two, updating result to 32, still safe from overflow. Final loop pops digit one, giving result 321 as x reaches zero. Since negative was true, result flips to negative 321, the final answer.
say.code: Now the code. Each loop takes the last digit with fmod, which keeps the sign. Then we drop that digit, dividing x by ten and truncating toward zero. Why not Python's own mod and floor division? They round the wrong way for negatives. Next, we check overflow before multiplying, against max divided by ten. Then the same check on the negative side. If it's safe, we push the digit onto the answer.
say.outro: So that's logarithmic time in the value, and constant space. The pattern is math with overflow checks. Check before the risky operation, never after.

reverse-integer.title: Reverse Integer
reverse-integer.optimalCode:
class Solution:
    def reverse(self, x: int) -> int:
        MIN = -2147483648  # -2^31
        MAX = 2147483647   # 2^31 - 1

        # 1. Handle sign separately so we can truncate toward zero
        negative = x < 0
        x = abs(x)

        result = 0
        while x != 0:
            # 2. Pop the last digit
            digit = x % 10
            x = x // 10

            # 3. Check overflow before pushing the digit onto result
            if result > MAX // 10 or (result == MAX // 10 and digit > MAX % 10):
                return 0

            # 4. Push the digit onto result
            result = result * 10 + digit

        if negative:
            result = -result

        return result
lineNotes: We define a class named Solution, which is the container the interview platform expects for our method.
The reverse method takes an integer x and returns the reversed integer, or zero when it overflows.
MIN holds the smallest signed 32-bit value, negative two to the power of thirty-one, as our lower boundary.
MAX holds the largest signed 32-bit value, two to the power of thirty-one minus one, as our upper boundary.
This comment says we handle the sign separately, so integer division truncates toward zero instead of flooring negatives.
We record whether x is negative in a boolean called negative, so we can restore the sign later.
We replace x with its absolute value so the loop only has to deal with nonnegative digits.
We start result at zero, and it will accumulate the reversed digits.
The loop keeps running as long as x still has digits left to pop off.
This comment announces that we pop the last digit of x in the next two lines.
The digit is x modulo ten, which gives the last digit of the current number.
We floor divide x by ten to drop that last digit and shrink the number.
This comment says we must check for overflow before pushing the digit, since we cannot store larger numbers.
If result already exceeds MAX divided by ten, or equals it with a digit above MAX's last digit, the next step would overflow.
In that overflow case we immediately return zero, as the problem requires.
This comment says the next line pushes the digit onto the result.
We shift result one place left by multiplying by ten and add the digit, safely within range.
After the loop ends, if the original number was negative, we need to put the sign back.
We negate result so the reversed value carries the original negative sign.
Finally we return the reversed result, which is guaranteed to fit in the 32-bit range.

palindrome-number.hook: No strings allowed: flip half the digits with arithmetic and compare the two halves.
palindrome-number.ask: Given an integer x, return true if it reads the same forwards and backwards, and false otherwise. Negative numbers are never palindromes because of the minus sign.
palindrome-number.exampleWhy: Reversing the digits of 12321 gives 12321 again, so it is a palindrome.

brute.idea: Turn the number into a string, reverse the string, and check whether the two strings are equal.
steps: Convert x to a string
Build the reversed string
Return whether they match
brute.whySlow: Same O(d) time over d digits, but it builds two extra strings and dodges the no-strings follow-up interviewers ask.

optimal.insight: Reverse only the last half of the digits using mod and divide. Stop when the reversed half catches up with the remaining half.
steps: Reject negatives and numbers ending in 0, except 0
Pop the last digit and push it onto rev
Stop once rev is at least the remaining x
Compare x with rev, or with rev without its middle digit
