codeNotes.note: Minus sign or trailing zero: impossible

codeNotes.match: return x == rev or x == rev // 10

pitfalls: Reversing the whole number can overflow in fixed-width languages; half avoids it.
Numbers like 10 end in zero and must be rejected up front.

say.intro: Okay, so this is Palindrome Number. We get an integer. Does it read the same forwards and backwards? Our example is one two three two one. Flip it, and you get the exact same number. So the answer is true. And negatives? Always false, because the minus sign only shows up on one side.
say.brute: The obvious move is to turn the number into a string. Reverse the string, then compare. That works, and it's linear in the number of digits. So it isn't actually slower. Here's the catch, though. It builds two extra strings. And the follow up asks you to do it without converting to a string at all.
say.insight: Here's the thing. We only need to reverse half the number. Peel the last digit off x with mod ten. Push it onto a reversed number. Keep going. When does it stop? When the reversed half catches up with what's left of x. That's the middle. Now we just compare the two halves.
say.anim: We start with x equal to twelve thousand three hundred twenty one, checking it's not negative. Rev is initialized to zero, ready to build the reversed half of the digits. The loop runs since x exceeds rev, peeling off the last digit each time. After one step, rev becomes one and x shrinks to one thousand two hundred thirty two. Continuing, rev grows to twelve as x shrinks to one hundred twenty three. Next iteration, rev becomes one hundred twenty three while x drops to twelve. Now x is twelve, which is not greater than rev, so the loop stops. Comparing x to rev divided by ten, both equal twelve, so the number is a palindrome, returning true.
say.code: Let's walk the code. First, reject negatives. Also reject anything ending in zero, unless it's zero itself. Then we loop while x is still bigger than rev. That's how we stop at the middle. Each round, we tack the last digit of x onto rev. Then we chop that digit off x. Finally, return true if x equals rev. Or if it equals rev with the middle digit dropped. That handles odd lengths.
say.outro: Logarithmic time, constant space. The pattern is math. Peel digits with mod and divide, instead of reaching for strings.

palindrome-number.title: Palindrome Number
lineNotes: We define a Solution class that holds the method for checking whether an integer is a palindrome.
The method isPalindrome takes an integer x and returns a boolean answer.
We reject negatives and numbers ending in zero, except zero itself, since those can never read the same backwards.
In those cases we immediately return false.
We start rev at zero, which will hold the reversed second half of the digits.
We loop while x is still greater than rev, meaning we have not yet processed half the digits.
We take the last digit of x and append it to rev by shifting rev left one place.
We drop the last digit from x using integer division by ten.
For even length x equals rev, and for odd length we drop rev's middle digit, so we return true if either matches.

longest-common-prefix.hook: Line the words up and read down the columns until any word disagrees.
longest-common-prefix.ask: Given a list of strings, return the longest string that every one of them starts with. If they share no common start at all, return an empty string.
longest-common-prefix.exampleWhy: All three start with f, then l, but at the third letter flower has o and flight has i.

brute.idea: Try every prefix of the first word, from longest to shortest, and check whether every word starts with it.
steps: Take a prefix of the first word
Check every word starts with it
First prefix that passes is the answer
brute.whySlow: Each candidate prefix re-checks every word from scratch, so long shared words repeat the same comparisons m times over.

optimal.insight: Scan column by column. Each character position is checked once across all words, and the first mismatch or short word ends the answer.
steps: Use the first word as the reference
For each position i, read its character
Any word too short or different? Stop
Return the first i characters

codeNotes.match: if i == len(s) or s[i] != ch:

codeNotes.note: Prefix is everything before column i

pitfalls: Check the length before indexing, or a short word crashes the loop.
An empty string in the list makes the answer empty immediately.

say.intro: Okay, Longest Common Prefix. We get a list of words. We want the longest beginning they all share. Flower, flow, and flight. They all start with f. Then l. But at the third letter? Flower has o, and flight has i. So the answer is f l.
say.brute: The brute force tries every prefix of the first word. Start with the whole word, then keep trimming it shorter. For each candidate, check whether every word starts with it. The first one that passes wins. It works. But every candidate re checks every word from the very start. So long shared words get compared over and over.
say.insight: Think about it this way. Read the words like a table, one column at a time. Position zero in every word. Then position one. And so on. Each character gets compared exactly once. The moment a word runs out, or shows a different letter, we stop. That's exactly where the shared prefix ends.
say.anim: We start with first set to flower, our reference word for comparison. At index zero, character f is checked against flow and flight, both matching. At index one, character l is compared, and both flow and flight still match. At index two, character o is checked, but flight has i there instead. That mismatch triggers an early return, slicing first up to index two. The final answer, the longest common prefix among all words, is fl.
say.code: Let's walk the code. We go one column at a time. For each index i, we grab the first word's character as the reference. Then we check every other word. Has that word already ended? Or does its letter differ? Either way, we return the first i characters. That's everything before column i. And if we never hit a mismatch? Then the whole first word is shared.
say.outro: Linear in the total number of characters. The pattern is arrays and strings. Scan vertically, and stop at the first disagreement.

longest-common-prefix.title: Longest Common Prefix
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, the standard wrapper for this problem's method.
This method takes a list of strings and returns the longest prefix shared by all of them.
We take the first word as our reference, since any common prefix must be a prefix of it.
We walk through each character position of the first word, scanning column by column.
At each position we remember the first word's character there, which every other word must match.
We loop over all the remaining words to compare each one against that character.
If a word is too short at this position or has a different character, the shared prefix has ended.
We return the first word up to but not including this position, which is the longest common prefix.
If we never hit a mismatch, the entire first word is shared by everyone, so we return it.

count-commas-in-range-ii.hook: Do not count number by number. Ask how many numbers cross each thousand line.
count-commas-in-range-ii.ask: Count the total number of commas used when writing every integer from 1 to n in standard format, where a comma separates each group of three digits from the right.
count-commas-in-range-ii.exampleWhy: Only 1,000 and 1,001 and 1,002 reach four digits, and each has exactly one comma.

brute.idea: Walk every number from 1 to n, count its digits, and add how many commas that many digits need.
steps: For each i from 1 to n
Digits d = len(str(i))
Add (d - 1) // 3 commas
brute.whySlow: n can be 10 to the 15th; looping over a quadrillion numbers would take years.

optimal.insight: Every number at least one thousand has a first comma, every number at least a million a second. Sum n minus each threshold plus one.
steps: Start the threshold at 1,000
While threshold ≤ n, add n - threshold + 1
Multiply the threshold by 1,000
Return the running total

codeNotes.note: Next comma starts at a million

pitfalls: Off by one: from threshold to n inclusive is n - threshold + 1 numbers.
Use 64-bit integers in other languages; the total exceeds 32 bits.

say.intro: Okay, Count Commas in Range. We write every number from one up to n. How many commas do we use? A comma goes after each group of three digits, counting from the right. Take n equal to one thousand and two. Only the last three numbers have a comma, one each. So the answer is three.
say.brute: The brute force walks every number from one to n. For each one, count its digits. Subtract one, divide by three, and round down. That's its comma count. Add them all up. It's correct. So what's the catch? n can be ten to the fifteenth. Visiting a quadrillion numbers one by one would take years.
say.insight: Here's the trick. Flip the question around. Don't ask how many commas each number has. Ask how many numbers earn each comma. Every number from one thousand up gets a first comma. Every number from a million up gets a second. So the answer is a short sum over thresholds. And there are at most five of them.
say.anim: We start with n equal to one thousand two, and total set to zero. Threshold begins at one thousand, marking where the first comma appears. Since threshold one thousand is less than or equal to n, the loop runs. Total becomes three, counting numbers from one thousand up to n that get a comma. Threshold multiplies by one thousand, now becoming one million, for the next comma check. Threshold one million exceeds n, so the loop stops here. The function reaches the return statement with total still equal to three. The final answer returned is three, matching the expected comma count.
say.code: Let's walk the code. The threshold starts at one thousand. That's the smallest number with a comma. We loop while the threshold is at most n. Why is that cheap? Because there are at most five thresholds below ten to the fifteenth. Each round, we add n minus the threshold, plus one. That's how many numbers earn this comma. Then we multiply the threshold by a thousand. The next comma starts at a million.
say.outro: Logarithmic time, constant space. The pattern is math. Count contributions per threshold, instead of simulating every number.

count-commas-in-range-ii.title: Count Commas in Range II
lineNotes: We define a class named Solution, which is the container the judge expects for this method.
The method countCommas takes the integer n and returns the total number of commas as an integer.
We start total at zero to accumulate the commas written across all numbers.
We set threshold to one thousand, the smallest number that needs its first comma.
We loop as long as threshold is at most n, since only then do some numbers reach that comma level.
Every number from threshold up to n has one comma at this level, so we add n minus threshold plus one.
We multiply threshold by one thousand to move to the next comma level, such as a million.
Once the threshold exceeds n, we return the total, which counts every comma across all numbers.

merge-sorted-array.hook: Fill nums1 from the back, and the empty slots protect every value you still need.
merge-sorted-array.ask: Two sorted arrays: nums1 holds m real values followed by n empty slots, nums2 holds n values. Merge them into nums1 in sorted order, in place, without returning anything.
merge-sorted-array.exampleWhy: Merging 1, 2, 3 with 2, 5, 6 in sorted order gives 1, 2, 2, 3, 5, 6 inside nums1.

brute.idea: Copy nums2 into the empty tail of nums1, then sort the whole array.
steps: Copy nums2 into nums1 from index m
Sort nums1 in place
brute.whySlow: Sorting throws away the fact that both halves were already sorted, paying a log factor for nothing.

optimal.insight: Merge from the largest end. Writing into nums1 from the back never overwrites a value we have not read yet.
steps: Pointers i and j at the last real values
Write pointer k at the very end
Place the larger of nums1[i] and nums2[j] at k
Stop when nums2 is used up

codeNotes.note: Two read pointers, one write pointer
Leftover nums1 values are already placed
Bigger value goes to the back
Take from nums2 on ties too

pitfalls: Merging from the front overwrites unread nums1 values.
Loop on j, not i: leftover nums1 values are already in place.

say.intro: Okay, Merge Sorted Array. We have two sorted arrays. The first one has empty slots at the end, exactly enough for the second. We need to merge them into the first array, in place, still sorted. So one, two, three, merged with two, five, six, becomes one, two, two, three, five, six.
say.brute: The quick fix is easy. Copy the second array into the empty slots. Then sort everything. It works, and it uses no extra space. But sorting costs n log n. And think about what we're ignoring. Both halves were already sorted. We're paying for work that was handed to us for free.
say.insight: Here's the trick. Merge from the back. The biggest value overall belongs in the last slot. And it's either the last real value of nums one, or the last value of nums two. Why go backwards? Because the back is empty. We only ever overwrite empty slots, or values we've already moved. Nothing gets lost.
say.anim: We start with pointers i at 2, j at 2, and k at 5, the last slots. Nums1 at i is 3, smaller than nums2 at j which is 6, so we place 6. Nums1 becomes 1,2,3,0,0,6 and j moves down to 1, k to 4. Now nums1 at i is still 3, less than nums2 at j which is 5. We place 5 into position, giving 1,2,3,0,5,6, j drops to 0. This time nums1 at i, which is 3, beats nums2 at j, which is 2. So we copy 3 from nums1 itself, array becomes 1,2,3,3,5,6, i decreases to 1. Nums2 at j is 2, now larger, so we write 2 next, finishing the merge. J falls below zero, loop ends, giving the final sorted array 1,2,2,3,5,6.
say.code: Let's walk the code. We set up two read pointers and one write pointer. i sits on the last real value of nums one, j on the end of nums two, k on the last slot. We loop while nums two has values left. Leftover nums one values are already in place. The bigger value goes to the back. On a tie, we take from nums two. Then we move the write slot left.
say.outro: Linear time, constant space. The pattern is two pointers, run backwards so the output never tramples unread input.

merge-sorted-array.title: Merge Sorted Array
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container the problem expects for our merge method.
The merge method takes nums1 with m real values, nums2 with n values, and modifies nums1 in place.
We set i to the last real value in nums1, j to the last of nums2, and k to the final slot.
We loop while nums2 still has unplaced values, since leftover nums1 values are already in the correct spots.
If nums1 still has values and its current one is larger than nums2's current one, we take nums1's.
We copy that larger nums1 value into the slot at k, the back of the merged region.
We move i one step left, since that nums1 value has now been placed.
Otherwise nums2's current value is larger or equal, or nums1 is exhausted, so we take from nums2.
We copy the nums2 value into the slot at k, filling the largest remaining position.
We move j one step left, since that nums2 value has now been placed.
Either way we move k one slot left, ready to fill the next largest position.

remove-duplicates-from-sorted-array.hook: A slow writer and a fast reader compact a sorted array in a single pass.
remove-duplicates-from-sorted-array.ask: Given a sorted array, remove duplicates in place so each value appears once, keeping order. Put the k unique values at the front and return k.
remove-duplicates-from-sorted-array.exampleWhy: The distinct values are 0, 1, 2, 3 and 4, so five unique values move to the front.

brute.idea: Collect the distinct values with a set, sort them, and copy them back over the front of the array.
steps: Build a set of the values
Sort the distinct values
Write them to the front, return the count
brute.whySlow: It ignores that the input is already sorted: pays for sorting and for a whole extra set.

optimal.insight: In a sorted array duplicates sit next to each other. A value is new exactly when it differs from the last value we kept.
steps: Writer k starts at 1
Reader i scans from index 1
If nums[i] differs from nums[k - 1], write it at k
Return k

pitfalls: Compare with the last kept value, not just the previous index.
Return the count; the judge only checks the first k slots.

say.intro: Okay, Remove Duplicates from Sorted Array. We get a sorted array. We need to squeeze out the repeats in place. Each distinct value should appear once, at the front, in order. Then return how many there are. Zero, zero, one, one, one, two, two, three, three, four. That's five distinct values.
say.brute: A brute force tosses every value into a set. Then it sorts the set, and copies it back over the front of the array. It works. But here's the problem. It wastes the best clue we were given. The array is already sorted! We pay n log n to sort again, plus a whole extra set in memory.
say.insight: Now, notice something. The array is sorted, so equal values are always neighbours. That means a value is new exactly when it differs from the last one we kept. So we use two pointers. A fast reader visits every element. A slow writer marks where the next unique value belongs.
say.anim: We start with k at 1, marking the next spot for a unique value. At i equals 1, nums at i matches the last kept value, so nothing changes. At i equals 2, value 1 differs from kept value 0, so we write it at index k. K becomes 2, and the array now starts with 0, 1 in order. At i equals 5, value 2 is new, so it gets placed at index k, making k 3. At i equals 7, value 3 is new, placed at index k, advancing k to 4. At i equals 9, value 4 is new, placed at index k, advancing k to 5. The loop ends and the function returns 5, the count of unique elements.
say.code: Let's walk the code. The writer k starts at one. Why? Because the first value is always kept. The fast reader i walks from index one to the end. At each step, we compare the new value with the last one we kept. If it's different, the slow writer stores it in slot k, and k moves forward. At the end, k is the count of unique values.
say.outro: Linear time, constant extra space. The pattern is two pointers. A fast reader and a slow writer, compacting in place.

remove-duplicates-from-sorted-array.title: Remove Duplicates from Sorted Array
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container that holds our method for this problem.
This method takes the sorted list nums and returns how many unique values it holds at the front.
We set k to one, since the first element is always unique and already sits in place.
We loop with i from one up to the end of nums, scanning every element after the first.
We compare the current number to the last kept value at position k minus one, since a difference means a new value.
When the value is new, we copy it into position k, extending the unique section at the front.
We then increase k by one so the next unique value goes in the following slot.
After the loop ends, we return k, which is the count of unique values now at the front.

pascals-triangle.hook: Every row is built from the row above it. Keep the last row and the triangle writes itself.
pascals-triangle.ask: Given numRows, return the first numRows rows of Pascal's triangle, where each row starts and ends with 1 and every inner number is the sum of the two numbers above it.
pascals-triangle.exampleWhy: Row four is 1, then 1 + 3, 3 + 3, 3 + 1, then 1, which is 1, 4, 6, 4, 1.

brute.idea: Compute every entry independently with the recursive rule C(r, c) = C(r-1, c-1) + C(r-1, c), with no memory.
steps: For each row r and column c
Edges return 1
Otherwise recurse on the two parents
brute.whySlow: Each entry recomputes the whole sub-triangle above it; row 30 alone needs hundreds of millions of calls.

optimal.insight: The row above already holds both parents of every entry. Build each row from the previous one instead of recomputing.
steps: Start with row [1]
New row begins with 1
Each inner value sums two neighbours above
End the row with 1 and append

codeNotes.note: Parents live in the last row
Becomes the parent of the next

pitfalls: Row r has r + 1 entries; inner columns run from 1 to r - 1.

say.intro: Okay, Pascal's Triangle. We're given a number of rows, and we build that many rows of the triangle. Every row starts and ends with one. Each number inside is the sum of the two numbers right above it. For five rows, the last row is one, four, six, four, one.
say.brute: The brute force computes every entry on its own, with the recursive rule. An entry is the sum of its two parents. Edges are one. But there's no memory. So each call rebuilds the whole little triangle above it. The work roughly doubles every row. Thirty rows would need hundreds of millions of calls.
say.insight: Here's the key. Where do the parents of every entry live? In the row we just built! So keep the previous row around. Then each new value is a single addition. That's dynamic programming in its simplest form. Reuse yesterday's answers, instead of recomputing them.
say.anim: We start with rows containing just the first row, which is one. For row one, we grab the previous row and start a new row with a leading one. For row two, previous row is one, one, and we build a new row by adding neighbors. We add prev of zero and prev of one to get two, placed in the middle. For row three, using previous row one, two, one, we compute three and three as sums of neighbors. For row four, previous row one, three, three, one gives sums four, six, four between the edges. Each new row is appended, built entirely from the row above it, avoiding recomputation. The final triangle returned is one, then one one, then one two one, one three three one, and one four six four one.
say.code: Let's walk the code. We start with the tip of the triangle, a single row holding one. For each new row, we grab the last row. That's where the parents live. We start with one. Then each inner value is the sum of the two above it. Every row ends with one, too. We append the row, and it becomes the parent of the next.
say.outro: Quadratic time, which matches the output size. The pattern is one dimensional dynamic programming. Each row depends only on the row before it.

pascals-triangle.title: Pascal's Triangle
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container the interview platform expects for our method.
The generate method takes numRows and returns the triangle as a list of rows, each row a list of integers.
We start the triangle with the first row already in place, a single row containing just one.
We loop over row indexes from one up to numRows minus one, building each new row in turn.
We grab the previous row, the last one in rows, because it holds both parents of every new entry.
We start the new row with a one, since every row begins with one.
We loop over the inner positions of the row, from one up to just before the last index r.
Each inner entry is the sum of the two numbers above it, at positions c minus one and c in the previous row.
We finish the row by appending a one, since every row also ends with one.
We add the completed row to rows so the next iteration can build on it.
After all rows are built, we return the full triangle.

check-divisibility-by-digit-sum-and-prod.hook: Peel the digits once, keep a running sum and product, then one modulo answers it.
check-divisibility-by-digit-sum-and-prod.ask: Given a positive integer n, add its digit sum to its digit product. Return true if n is divisible by that total, and false otherwise.
check-divisibility-by-digit-sum-and-prod.exampleWhy: Digits 1, 2, 3, 6 sum to 12 and multiply to 36. 1236 divided by 48 leaves a remainder.

brute.idea: Turn n into a string, build a list of digits, then compute the sum and the product in two separate passes.
steps: Split n into a digit list
Sum the list
Multiply the list
Check the remainder
brute.whySlow: Not asymptotically slower: both are O(d). It builds a string and a list and walks the digits twice.

optimal.insight: One loop of mod ten and divide by ten yields every digit, so sum and product can be accumulated together with no extra storage.
steps: Copy n into x
Take the last digit with x % 10
Add it to the sum, multiply into the product
Check n % (sum + product)

codeNotes.note: Product starts at one, not zero
A zero digit zeroes the product
Sum is at least 1, safe to divide

pitfalls: Starting the product at zero makes it zero forever.
Keep the original n for the final check; x is consumed.

say.intro: Okay, Check Divisibility by Digit Sum and Product. Take a positive number. Add up its digits. Multiply its digits. Add those two results together. Is the number divisible by that total? Take one thousand two hundred thirty six. The sum is twelve, the product thirty six. Forty eight doesn't divide it. So, false.
say.brute: The straightforward way turns the number into a string. Then it builds a list of digits. It sums the list, and multiplies through it in a second pass. That's correct, and linear in the digits. So it isn't really slower. The cost is the extra string, the extra list, and walking the digits twice.
say.insight: Here's the thing. Arithmetic hands us the digits directly. Mod ten gives the last digit. Dividing by ten removes it. So one loop can grow the sum and the product at the same time. Just three small variables. No strings at all.
say.anim: We start with n equal to 1236, sum zero, product one, and x equal to n. Each loop extracts the last digit, here six, then adds it to sum and multiplies into product. Next digit three gives sum nine and product eighteen, as x shrinks to twelve. Digit two updates sum to eleven and product to thirty six, with x now one. Final digit one makes sum twelve and product thirty six, then x becomes zero, ending the loop. Now we check if n, 1236, divides evenly by sum plus product, forty eight. Since 1236 isn't divisible by forty eight, the function returns false.
say.code: Let's walk the code. The sum starts at zero, and the product starts at one. Not zero! Otherwise everything multiplies to nothing. While x is nonzero, we take its last digit. We add it to the sum, and multiply it into the product. A zero digit just zeroes the product, which is fine. At the end, the sum is at least one. So dividing is safe, and we check the remainder.
say.outro: Linear in the number of digits, constant space. The pattern is math. Extract digits with mod and divide.

check-divisibility-by-digit-sum-and-prod.title: Check Divisibility by Digit Sum and Product
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container the checking method lives in.
The method takes the integer n and returns a boolean saying whether n is divisible by its digit sum plus product.
We start the sum at zero, the product at one, and copy n into x so n stays intact.
We loop while x is nonzero, meaning there are still digits left to peel off.
We take x mod ten to get the current last digit and store it in d.
We add that digit to the running digit sum.
We multiply the running digit product by that digit.
We divide x by ten with integer division, dropping the last digit so the next one is exposed.
Finally we check whether the original n divides evenly by the sum plus product and return that result.

find-the-index-of-the-first-occurrence-i.hook: When a match fails halfway, KMP already knows how much of the needle still lines up.
find-the-index-of-the-first-occurrence-i.ask: Given two strings, haystack and needle, return the index where needle first appears inside haystack, or -1 if it never appears.
find-the-index-of-the-first-occurrence-i.exampleWhy: Starting at index 4, haystack reads aabaaac, exactly the needle. Earlier starts break before the end.

brute.idea: Try every start position in haystack and compare the next len(needle) characters with the needle.
steps: For each start i
Compare haystack[i:i+m] with needle
Match? return i
brute.whySlow: Each failed attempt restarts from scratch; text like aaaaab against aaab re-reads characters m times.

optimal.insight: Precompute, for each needle prefix, its longest proper prefix that is also a suffix. On a mismatch, jump there instead of restarting.
steps: Build lps for the needle
Scan haystack with needle pointer j
Match: advance j; full match returns the index
Mismatch: fall back j = lps[j - 1]

codeNotes.note: Longest prefix that is also suffix
Reuse matched part, never move back

pitfalls: Saying the brute force first is fine; most interviewers then ask for KMP.
lps[0] is always 0: a prefix cannot be its own proper border.

say.intro: Okay, Find the Index of the First Occurrence in a String. We search for a needle inside a haystack. Where does it first start? If it's not there, return minus one. Our haystack is a a b a a a b a a a c. The needle, a a b a a a c, first shows up at index four.
say.brute: The brute force tries every start position. At each one, compare the next few characters with the needle. Return the first start that fully matches. Simple, right? But a near miss throws everything away, and restarts one step later. Text full of repeated letters can force n times m comparisons.
say.insight: Here's the Knuth Morris Pratt idea. When a match fails partway, what did we just match? A piece of the needle itself! So precompute, for each prefix, its longest border. That's a piece that's both a prefix and a suffix. On a mismatch, slide the needle back to that border. The haystack pointer never moves backwards.
say.anim: We start with haystack aabaaabaaac and needle aabaaac, building a prefix table first. The lps array tracks longest matching prefix-suffix lengths for each needle position, starting all zeros. As i advances, k tracks matches, filling lps with values like one, zero, one, two, two, zero. Now we scan haystack, using j to track how much of needle currently matches. At i equals five, j reaches six, meaning six characters of needle have matched so far. At i equals six the next character mismatches, so j jumps back to two using lps instead of restarting. Matching resumes, with j climbing back up through three, four, five, and six as characters align again. At i equals ten, j equals seven means full match found, returning answer four.
say.code: Let's walk the code. The first loop builds the table. For each prefix, it stores the longest border that's also a suffix. On a mismatch, we shrink to the next shorter border. The second loop walks the haystack. We reuse whatever part already matched, and never move back. Once the whole needle has matched, we return the start index of the match.
say.outro: Linear time in both lengths. The pattern is two pointers with a failure table. Never re read a character of the text.

find-the-index-of-the-first-occurrence-i.title: Find the Index of the First Occurrence in a String
lineNotes: We define a class named Solution, as the problem platform expects for this method.
The strStr method takes haystack and needle and returns the first index where needle appears, or negative one.
We store the length of the needle in m, since we use it repeatedly.
We create the lps table of m zeros, holding the longest prefix that is also a suffix for each prefix.
We set k to zero, tracking the length of the current matched prefix-suffix as we build the table.
We loop i from one to the end of the needle, since a single character has no proper border.
While k is positive and the characters differ, we need to fall back to a shorter border.
We set k to the table entry just before k, jumping to the next shorter prefix that could still match.
If the current needle character equals the character at position k, the border can be extended.
We increase k by one, because the matching prefix and suffix are now one character longer.
We record k in the table at position i as the border length for that prefix.
We set j to zero, counting how many needle characters are currently matched in the haystack.
We scan the haystack once, getting each index i and character ch.
While some match exists and ch differs from the next needle character, we must shorten the match.
We set j to the table entry before j, reusing the overlap instead of restarting the comparison.
If ch matches the needle character at j, we can extend the current match.
We advance j by one, since one more needle character has been matched.
If j now equals m, the entire needle has been matched ending at this position.
We return i minus m plus one, which is the starting index of that full match.
If the scan finishes without a full match, we return negative one.

split-array-largest-sum.hook: Guess the answer, check it greedily, and binary search the guess.
split-array-largest-sum.ask: Split an array of non-negative numbers into k non-empty contiguous pieces so that the biggest piece sum is as small as possible. Return that smallest possible biggest sum.
split-array-largest-sum.exampleWhy: Splitting into 7, 2, 5 and 10, 8 gives sums 14 and 18; no split keeps both under 18.

brute.idea: Recursively try every place to cut off the first piece, then solve the rest with one fewer piece.
steps: Choose where the first piece ends
Recurse on the rest with k - 1
Take the max, minimise over choices
brute.whySlow: Every cut position branches again; with 1,000 numbers and 50 pieces the choices explode beyond counting.

optimal.insight: If a cap works, any bigger cap works too. So binary search the cap, and test each cap with a greedy left-to-right pass.
steps: Range from max(nums) to sum(nums)
Greedy: count pieces needed under cap mid
Pieces ≤ k? cap fits, search lower
Too many pieces? search higher

codeNotes.note: Would overflow: start a new piece
Answer always lies in this range

pitfalls: Low bound is max(nums), not 0: one number cannot be split.
Fewer than k pieces is fine; big pieces can always be split further.

say.intro: Okay, Split Array Largest Sum. We cut an array into k contiguous pieces. We want the biggest piece sum to be as small as possible. Seven, two, five, ten, eight, into two pieces. The best split is seven, two, five, and then ten, eight. Sums of fourteen and eighteen. So the answer is eighteen.
say.brute: The brute force tries every spot for the first cut. Then it recursively splits the rest into k minus one pieces. For each choice, take the larger of the first piece and the best for the rest. Keep the minimum. It's correct. But the branching explodes, roughly n to the power k.
say.insight: Let's flip the question. Given a cap, can we split into at most k pieces, all under it? A greedy pass answers that. Just pack numbers until the next one would overflow. And here's the key. If a cap works, every bigger cap works too. So we binary search for the smallest cap that works.
say.anim: We start the search with left as ten, the largest number, and right as thirty two, the total sum. We try a cap of twenty one, greedily grouping numbers without exceeding this sum per piece. Ten plus ten would exceed twenty one, so a new piece starts, giving two pieces total. Two pieces fits within k equals two, so this cap works and right shrinks to twenty one. Testing cap fifteen now needs three pieces, too many, so left moves up to sixteen. Testing cap eighteen again yields two pieces, which works, so right shrinks down to eighteen. Testing cap seventeen needs three pieces, too many, so left becomes eighteen, closing the search. Left now equals right at eighteen, so the smallest valid largest sum is eighteen.
say.code: Let's walk the code. The helper counts pieces for a given cap. If adding the next number would overflow, we start a new piece. Now, the search range. The answer always lies between the biggest number and the total sum. If the middle cap is feasible, we try a smaller cap, so high comes down. If the cap's too tight, low moves above it.
say.outro: Linear times log of the sum. The pattern is binary search on the answer, with a greedy feasibility check.

split-array-largest-sum.title: Split Array Largest Sum
lineNotes: We define a solution class that holds the method for this problem.
The splitArray method takes the list of numbers and the number of pieces k, and returns the smallest possible largest sum.
We define a helper called count_pieces that tests whether a given cap is workable by counting needed pieces.
This comment says the helper greedily counts the pieces required when no piece sum may exceed the cap.
We start with one piece, since even the whole array needs at least one piece.
The running sum of the current piece begins at zero.
We walk through each number in the array from left to right.
If adding this number would push the current piece over the cap, we must close that piece.
So we count one more piece because a new piece is starting here.
We reset the current sum to zero so the new piece starts empty.
We add the number to the current piece, whether it is in the old piece or the freshly started one.
After the loop we return how many pieces the greedy pass needed for this cap.
This comment explains that the answer lies between the largest single element and the total sum.
The left bound starts at the maximum of nums, since every number must fit inside some piece.
The right bound starts at the sum of nums, which is the cap when everything is one piece.
This comment says we now binary search over possible cap values.
We keep searching while the left and right bounds have not met.
We pick the middle cap as the average of left and right, rounded down.
We run the greedy check to see how many pieces this middle cap requires.
This comment says that when the cap works, we should look for a smaller one.
If the needed pieces is at most k, the cap works, since extra pieces can always be split further.
So we move right down to mid, keeping mid as a possible answer.
This comment says that otherwise the cap is too small and we need a bigger one.
The else branch handles the case where too many pieces were needed.
We move left up to mid plus one, since mid and anything smaller cannot work.
When the bounds meet, left is the smallest workable cap, so we return it.

majority-element.hook: A value holding over half the votes survives every pairwise cancellation.
majority-element.ask: Given an array of n numbers, return the value that appears more than n / 2 times. Such a value is guaranteed to exist.
majority-element.exampleWhy: 2 appears four times out of seven, which is more than half.

brute.idea: For each element, count how many times it appears in the whole array. Return the first one whose count exceeds half.
steps: Pick each value
Count it across the array
Count > n / 2? return it
brute.whySlow: Every candidate rescans the whole array; 50,000 numbers can mean over a billion comparisons.

optimal.insight: Boyer-Moore voting: pair each majority vote with a different vote and cancel them. The majority has too many votes to be cancelled out.
steps: Keep a candidate and a count
Count zero? adopt the current value
Same value adds one, different subtracts one
The final candidate is the majority

pitfalls: Without the guarantee, verify the candidate with a second counting pass.
A hash map count is O(n) too, but uses O(n) space.

say.intro: Okay, Majority Element. We get an array, and we need the value that shows up more than half the time. One is guaranteed to exist. In two, two, one, one, one, two, two, the value two shows up four times out of seven. So the answer is two.
say.brute: The brute force takes each value and counts how often it appears in the whole array. The first one with more than half the votes wins. It's correct. But every count rescans the array. That's quadratic. Over a billion steps for fifty thousand numbers.
say.insight: Think about it as an election. Opposing votes cancel out in pairs. We keep one candidate and a counter. A matching vote adds one. A different vote takes one away. When the counter hits zero, we pick a new candidate. Why does the majority win? Because it has more votes than everyone else combined. It's always the last one standing.
say.anim: We start with candidate unset and count at zero, scanning the array for a majority. Count is zero, so candidate becomes two, and count rises to one. Next element is also two, matching candidate, so count climbs to two. Now we see a one, which differs from candidate, so count drops to one. Another one appears, count falls back to zero, canceling candidate two completely. With count zero, candidate switches to one, and count resets to one. A two shows up, mismatching candidate one, so count drops back to zero. Count hits zero again, so candidate switches to two, finishing with count one, returning two.
say.code: Let's walk the code. We start with no candidate, and a count of zero. For each number, is the count zero? That means all previous votes cancelled out. So we start a fresh candidate. Then the vote. A match supports the candidate, and anything else cancels one vote. After the loop, we return the candidate. The majority is guaranteed to survive.
say.outro: Linear time, constant space. The pattern is arrays and counting, with Boyer Moore voting replacing a hash map.

majority-element.title: Majority Element
lineNotes: We define a Solution class that holds the method for solving the majority element problem.
The majorityElement method takes a list of integers called nums and returns the majority value as an integer.
We start with no candidate and a vote count of zero, ready to track the current leading value.
We loop through every number x in nums, treating each one as a single vote.
When the count is zero, all earlier votes have cancelled out, so we reconsider who leads.
In that case we make the current number x the new candidate.
If x matches the candidate we add one vote, otherwise we subtract one, cancelling a pair of different votes.
Since the majority has more than half the votes, it survives the cancelling, so we return the candidate.

construct-uniform-parity-array-i.hook: Odd minus even is odd. That one fact makes the answer always yes.
construct-uniform-parity-array-i.ask: For each number, either keep it or replace it with itself minus some other number in the array. Can every resulting number share the same parity, all odd or all even?
construct-uniform-parity-array-i.exampleWhy: Keep the odd 3 and 5; turn 2 into 2 - 3 = -1 and 8 into 8 - 3 = 5.

brute.idea: Try both target parities. For each number, check whether keeping it or subtracting some other number gives that parity.
steps: Try target parity even, then odd
For each i, test keep or every j
All fixable? return True
brute.whySlow: It checks every pair of numbers to rediscover a fact that parity arithmetic proves instantly.

optimal.insight: If any odd number exists, every even number minus it is odd. If none exists, every number is already even. Either way: true.
steps: Case one: some odd value exists
Keep odds, subtract that odd from each even
Case two: no odd values
Keep everything, already all even

codeNotes.match: # An odd value turns every even one odd;
# with no odd value, all are already even.

pitfalls: Prove the claim out loud; just returning True looks like a guess.

say.intro: Okay, Construct Uniform Parity Array, part one. For each number, we can keep it, or replace it with itself minus any other number. Can we make everything odd? Or everything even? Take two, three, eight, five. Keep three and five. Subtract three from two and from eight. Now everything's odd.
say.brute: The brute force tries both goals. All even, then all odd. It walks each number. If the parity's already right, fine. If not, it tries subtracting every other number to see whether one fixes it. That's quadratic work. And it's just rediscovering a fact that simple parity rules give us for free.
say.insight: Here's the thing. Even minus odd is always odd. So if there's even one odd number, keep all the odds. Subtract that odd from every even. Now everything's odd. And if there are no odd numbers at all? Then everything's already even. Either way, the answer is always yes.
say.anim: We start with the array 2, 3, 8, 5, checking if parity can always be unified. The function simply returns true, since odd and even numbers can always be matched to equal parity.
say.code: Let's walk the code. It's really just a proof. Case one, there's an odd number. Even minus odd is odd, so every even can be fixed. Case two, there are no odds. Then we keep every number unchanged, and they're all even. Both cases always succeed. So the whole function returns true. In the interview, say both cases out loud.
say.outro: Constant time, constant space. The pattern is math. Reason about parity first, and the code just disappears.

construct-uniform-parity-array-i.title: Construct Uniform Parity Array I
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container the judge expects for our method.
The uniformArray method takes the list nums1 and returns a boolean saying whether a uniform parity result is possible.
This comment explains that any odd value can be subtracted from an even one, which turns that even number odd.
It adds that if no odd value exists, every number is already even, so nothing needs to change.
Because both cases always succeed, we simply return true without even looking at the input.

roman-to-integer.hook: A smaller numeral before a bigger one means subtract. One glance ahead handles every case.
roman-to-integer.ask: Convert a valid Roman numeral string into its integer value, remembering that a smaller symbol placed before a larger one is subtracted, as in IV for 4.
roman-to-integer.exampleWhy: M is 1000, CM is 900, XC is 90 and IV is 4, which add up to 1994.

brute.idea: Rewrite the six subtractive pairs as plain repeats, like IV to IIII, then add every symbol's value.
steps: Replace each subtractive pair with repeats
Look up and add every symbol
brute.whySlow: Still linear, but six replace passes build six new strings; CM becomes DCCCC, inflating the text.

optimal.insight: Look one symbol ahead. If the next symbol is bigger, this one is subtracted; otherwise it is added.
steps: Map each symbol to its value
Walk the string left to right
Smaller than next? subtract it
Otherwise add it

codeNotes.match: if i + 1 < len(s) and val[s[i]] < val[s[i + 1]]:

pitfalls: Guard i + 1 < len(s) before peeking ahead.

say.intro: Okay, Roman to Integer. We turn a Roman numeral into a number. Usually the symbols go from big to small, and they just add up. But a smaller symbol before a bigger one gets subtracted. So M C M X C I V is a thousand, plus nine hundred, plus ninety, plus four. Nineteen ninety four.
say.brute: One brute force rewrites the six subtractive pairs as plain repeats. I V becomes four I's. C M becomes D and then four C's. And so on. After that, every symbol just adds. It's still linear, so not really slower. But it makes six passes, builds six new strings, and bloats the text along the way.
say.insight: Here's the thing. We never need to rewrite anything. When is a symbol subtracted? Exactly when the very next symbol is bigger. So one glance ahead decides the sign. Then a single left to right pass adds or subtracts as it goes.
say.anim: We start with the roman numeral mapping and a running total of zero. At index 0, M is followed by C, which is smaller, so we add one thousand. At index 1, C is followed by M, a bigger value, so one hundred is subtracted. At index 2, M is followed by X, smaller, so one thousand is added, total now nineteen hundred. At index 3, X precedes a bigger C, so ten is subtracted, giving eighteen ninety. At index 4, C precedes smaller I, so one hundred is added, reaching nineteen ninety. At index 5, I precedes bigger V, so one is subtracted, landing on nineteen eighty nine. Finally V has no next symbol, so five is added, and the function returns 1994.
say.code: Let's walk the code. First, a dictionary of the seven symbol values. Then we walk every index. Does a bigger symbol follow this one? Then it's subtractive, like C before M, so we subtract it. Otherwise, it's the normal case, and we add it. At the end, return the total.
say.outro: Linear time, constant space. The pattern is arrays and hashing. A lookup table, plus a one step look ahead.

roman-to-integer.title: Roman to Integer
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container for the method that the problem asks us to write.
The method romanToInt takes the Roman numeral string s and returns its value as an integer.
We build a dictionary mapping each Roman symbol to its number, so lookups are instant.
We start total at zero, and it will collect the running value as we scan.
We loop over every index of the string, so we can peek at the symbol after the current one.
If a next symbol exists and the current value is smaller than the next value, this symbol must be subtracted.
In that case we subtract the current symbol's value from total, as the I in IV does.
Otherwise the current symbol is not followed by a larger one, so the normal additive case applies.
We add the current symbol's value to total.
After the loop finishes, we return total as the integer value of the numeral.

concatenation-of-array.hook: Allocate the answer once, and every value lands in its two slots in one pass.
concatenation-of-array.ask: Given an array nums of length n, return an array of length 2n that is nums followed by another copy of nums.
concatenation-of-array.exampleWhy: ans[i] and ans[i + 4] both equal nums[i], giving 1, 3, 2, 1 twice.

brute.idea: Build the answer by creating a brand new list each time a value is appended, going through nums twice.
steps: Repeat twice over nums
ans = ans + [x], a fresh copy each time
brute.whySlow: Each ans + [x] copies the whole list so far; 2,000 appends copy about two million elements.

optimal.insight: The final size is known up front. Allocate 2n slots once, then write nums[i] to positions i and i + n.
steps: Allocate ans of length 2n
For each i, write nums[i] at i
Also write nums[i] at i + n

pitfalls: In Python, nums + nums is also linear and fine to mention.

say.intro: Okay, Concatenation of Array. We get an array of length n. We return an array of length two n. That's the original, followed by a second copy. So one, three, two, one becomes one, three, two, one, one, three, two, one.
say.brute: A careless version grows the answer by building a brand new list every time it adds a value. Answer equals answer plus one more item. It's correct. But each step copies everything built so far. Over two n appends, that's quadratic work. About two million element copies for just a thousand numbers.
say.insight: Here's the thing. We know the final size before we even start. So allocate all two n slots at once. Now every value has exactly two homes. Position i, and position i plus n. One pass fills both halves, with no copying at all.
say.anim: We start with nums equal to one, three, two, one, and compute n as four. An empty array of eight zeros is created to hold the final result. At i equals zero, we place one at position zero and position four. At i equals one, three goes into position one and position five. At i equals two, two is written to position two and position six. At i equals three, one fills position three and position seven, completing the loop. The function returns the finished array, duplicating nums right after itself. The final answer is one, three, two, one, one, three, two, one.
say.code: Let's walk the code. We make one allocation, at the final size. Two n zeros. Then we loop over each index i. First, we write the value into slot i. That's the first copy. Then we write it again into slot i plus n. That's the second copy, offset by n. Once the loop ends, both halves are filled, and we return the answer.
say.outro: Linear time, plus the output space we have to return anyway. The pattern is arrays. Allocate once, and write by index.

concatenation-of-array.title: Concatenation of Array
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container the problem expects for our method.
We define getConcatenation, which takes the list nums and will return the doubled list.
We store the length of nums in n, since the output size and offset both depend on it.
We allocate an answer list of zeros with two times n slots, so we never need to resize it.
We loop with i going from zero up to n minus one, visiting each element of nums once.
We copy the current element of nums into position i of ans, filling the first half.
We copy the same element into position i plus n, which fills the second half as the repeated copy.
We return ans, which now holds nums followed by another copy of nums.

add-two-integers.hook: The smallest problem on LeetCode, and a reminder to match the tool to the job.
add-two-integers.ask: Given two integers num1 and num2, return their sum.

brute.idea: Start from num1 and step by one, num2 times, upward or downward depending on the sign of num2.
steps: Pick direction from the sign of num2
Step by one, abs(num2) times
brute.whySlow: Counting one at a time takes |num2| steps; the hardware adds in a single instruction.

optimal.insight: Addition is one constant-time operation. Use the plus operator directly.
steps: Add the two numbers
Return the result

pitfalls: Without plus, a bit trick works: XOR for sum, AND shifted for carry.

say.intro: Okay, Add Two Integers. We get two numbers, and we return their sum. Twelve plus five is seventeen. They can be negative too. Minus ten plus four is minus six. Sounds trivial, right? It is. But it's a nice place to compare a counting approach with a direct one.
say.brute: A brute force treats addition as counting. Start at the first number. Take steps of one, as many times as the second number. Go up for a positive, down for a negative. You get the right answer. But it takes as many steps as the size of the second number. That's wasteful.
say.insight: Here's the thing. Addition is already a single operation. The processor adds two integers in one instruction, no matter how big they are within range. So there's nothing to simulate. Just use plus. Negatives work with no special handling. The real skill is noticing when you don't need an algorithm.
say.anim: We start with num1 equal to 12 and num2 equal to 5, ready to add. The plus operator computes total instantly, storing 17 without any loops. The function returns 17, which is the final answer.
say.code: Let's walk the code. One line does one machine addition. Total is num one plus num two. Negatives are handled automatically. Then we return it. Now, what if an interviewer bans the plus sign? Mention the bitwise version. Exclusive or gives the sum without carries. And shifted left gives the carries.
say.outro: Constant time, constant space. The pattern is math. Use the direct operation, instead of simulating it one step at a time.

add-two-integers.title: Add Two Integers
lineNotes: We define a class named Solution, which is the container the judge expects for our method.
This method named sum takes two integers, num1 and num2, and promises to give back an integer.
We add num1 and num2 with the plus operator and store the result in total, a single constant-time step.
We return total, which is the sum of the two input integers, and that finishes the solution.

next-greater-element-i.hook: A decreasing stack waits for each number's bigger neighbour, then answers all at once.
next-greater-element-i.ask: nums1 is a subset of nums2. For each value in nums1, find the first bigger value to its right in nums2, or -1 if none exists.
next-greater-element-i.exampleWhy: In nums2, 1 is followed by 3. Nothing to the right of 4 or of 2 is bigger.

brute.idea: For each value of nums1, find it in nums2, then scan to the right for the first bigger value.
steps: Locate x in nums2
Scan right for a bigger value
Record it, or -1
brute.whySlow: Every query rescans nums2; 1,000 queries over 1,000 numbers is a million comparisons.

optimal.insight: Walk nums2 with a decreasing stack. When a bigger value arrives, it is the next greater element for everything it pops.
steps: Scan nums2 left to right
Pop while the top is smaller than x
Record x as their next greater
Push x; answer nums1 from the map

codeNotes.note: x is bigger than waiting values
x waits for its own answer

pitfalls: Values are unique, so keying the map by value is safe.
Leftover stack values never found a bigger one: default -1.

say.intro: Okay, Next Greater Element, part one. Every value in the first array also appears in the second. For each one, find the first bigger value to its right, in the second array. If none, minus one. Four, one, two, against one, three, four, two. Only one has a bigger neighbour, three. So, minus one, three, minus one.
say.brute: The brute force handles each query on its own. Find the value in the second array. Then scan right until something bigger shows up. It works. But each query rescans the array. A thousand queries over a thousand numbers is about a million comparisons.
say.insight: Here's the trick. Answer every value of the second array in one pass, with a stack. Values on the stack are still waiting for something bigger. So the stack stays decreasing. When a new value arrives, it's the answer for every smaller value on top. Pop them, and record it. Then just look up the queries in a map.
say.anim: We start with nums1 four one two, nums2 one three four two, and an empty map. We scan nums2 using a stack to track values waiting for a bigger number. One has nothing bigger yet, so it gets pushed onto the empty stack. Three arrives, beats one on the stack, so next greater of one becomes three. Four arrives, beats three on the stack, so next greater of three becomes four. Two is smaller than four, so it just gets pushed alongside it. Now we look up each nums1 value, four, one, and two, in our map. Four and two have no greater value, one maps to three, giving minus one, three, minus one.
say.code: Let's walk the code. We keep a map from each value to its next greater, plus a stack. For each value x in the second array, is x bigger than the values waiting on top? Then we resolve them with x, popping each one. After that, x waits for its own answer, so we push it. Finally, we map each query. Anything still waiting means minus one.
say.outro: Linear time overall. The pattern is a monotonic stack. Values wait on it until something bigger resolves them.

next-greater-element-i.title: Next Greater Element I
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which holds the method that solves the next greater element problem.
The method takes nums1, the queries, and nums2, the array we scan, and returns a list of answers.
We create an empty dictionary called nxt that will map each value to its next greater element.
We start with an empty stack that will hold values still waiting for a bigger value, in decreasing order.
We walk through every value x in nums2 from left to right.
While the stack has items and its top is smaller than x, x is the next greater for that top.
We pop the top value and record x as its next greater element in the dictionary.
After popping smaller values, we push x onto the stack so it can wait for its own greater value.
For each value in nums1 we look up its next greater in the dictionary, using negative one when missing.

create-hello-world-function.hook: A function that returns a function: the gentlest introduction to closures.
create-hello-world-function.ask: Write createHelloWorld, which returns a new function. That function must return the string Hello World no matter what arguments it is called with. We trace calling it with args.
create-hello-world-function.exampleWhy: The arguments are an object, null and 42, but they are ignored, so the result is Hello World.

brute.idea: Return an inner function that rebuilds the greeting from its two words every single time it is called.
steps: Store the words Hello and World
Inner function joins them on each call
brute.whySlow: Not asymptotically slower; it just rebuilds the same string on every call instead of returning a constant.

optimal.insight: The returned function ignores its arguments entirely. Accept anything with a rest parameter and return the constant string.
steps: Define an inner function taking any arguments
Ignore them and return Hello World
Return the inner function, here called with args

codeNotes.note: Call the made function with args

pitfalls: In JavaScript, return the function itself: return function(...args) { return "Hello World"; }.

say.intro: Okay, Create Hello World Function. This one's a JavaScript problem about functions that return functions. We write create hello world, and it hands back a new function. No matter what arguments that function gets, it always returns hello world. Call it with an empty object, null, and forty two? Still hello world.
say.brute: A roundabout version stores the two words, hello and world. Then the inner function joins them on every call. That's correct, and still constant time. So it isn't really slower. It just repeats a little work each call that a fixed string avoids. And it adds moving parts for no benefit.
say.insight: Here's the point of the problem. A function can create and return another function. The inner function takes any number of arguments, with a rest parameter. It ignores all of them. Then it returns the fixed string. Nothing about the inputs ever changes the output.
say.anim: We start by calling f with the args list containing an empty object, null, and 42. Inside f, the rest parameter a collects all three arguments into a tuple, unused. Since the function ignores its inputs, it simply returns the fixed string Hello World. The outer call also returns Hello World, confirming the function always gives this constant answer.
say.code: Let's walk the code. It's in Python, to match the player. Inside, we define f. It accepts any number of arguments. And the arguments are ignored. It just returns hello world. To show it working, we call the made function with the args. In JavaScript, you'd simply return a function that returns the string.
say.outro: Constant time. This is a warm up on closures and higher order functions, rather than a classic algorithm pattern.

create-hello-world-function.title: Create Hello World Function
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which holds the method that builds our hello world function.
The method createHelloWorld takes self and a list of arguments, which we will use to trace a call.
Inside it we define a helper function f that accepts any number of arguments through a rest parameter.
The function f ignores whatever it receives and simply returns the constant string Hello World.
Finally we call f with the unpacked args and return its result, showing that any arguments still give Hello World.

max-consecutive-ones.hook: One running counter that resets on every zero is all this needs.
max-consecutive-ones.ask: Given an array of zeros and ones, return the length of the longest run of consecutive ones.
max-consecutive-ones.exampleWhy: The runs of ones have lengths 2, 3 and 1, and the longest is 3.

brute.idea: From every start index, count how many ones follow in a row, and keep the longest count.
steps: Pick a start index
Count ones until a zero
Keep the best count
brute.whySlow: A long run of ones is recounted from each of its starting points; 100,000 ones means billions of steps.

optimal.insight: The current run only depends on the previous element. Extend it on a one, reset it on a zero, and track the best seen.
steps: Keep cur and best at zero
A one extends cur and updates best
A zero resets cur

pitfalls: Update best inside the loop, or a run that ends the array is missed.

say.intro: Okay, Max Consecutive Ones. We get an array of zeros and ones. What's the longest unbroken run of ones? In one, one, zero, one, one, one, zero, one, the runs have lengths two, three, and one. The longest is three.
say.brute: The brute force starts at every index. It counts how many ones follow in a row, stopping at the first zero. It keeps the best count. That works. But a long run of ones gets recounted from every starting point inside it. So an array of all ones costs quadratic time.
say.insight: Think about it this way. The current run only depends on what we just saw. Is the number a one? The run grows by one. Is it a zero? The run resets to nothing. So one counter, plus the best so far, gets us through in a single pass.
say.anim: We start with best and cur both at zero, ready to scan the array. The first two elements are ones, so cur climbs to two and best matches it. A zero appears, breaking the streak, so cur resets back to zero. Three ones in a row push cur up to three, making best three too. Another zero resets cur to zero, ending that longer streak. One final one brings cur to one, but best stays at three. The loop finishes and the function returns the best value found, three.
say.code: Let's walk the code. We track the current run and the best run, both starting at zero. For each number, if it's a one, we extend the run. Then, if current beats best, we record a new longest. Why update inside the loop? Because the longest run might end the array. And if it's a zero, that breaks the run, so current goes back to zero.
say.outro: Linear time, constant space. The pattern is arrays. One running count that resets on a break, the seed of every sliding window.

max-consecutive-ones.title: Max Consecutive Ones
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container the interview platform expects for our method.
This method takes the list of zeros and ones called nums and returns the longest run of ones as an integer.
We start both best and cur at zero, where cur is the current run and best is the longest so far.
We walk through each number x in nums one at a time, from left to right.
We check whether the current number is a one, since only ones can extend a run.
On a one, we extend the current run by adding one to cur.
We update best to the larger of itself and cur, so the longest run is always remembered.
Otherwise the number is a zero, which breaks any run of ones we were building.
We reset cur to zero so the next run of ones starts counting fresh.
After the loop finishes, we return best, which holds the longest run of consecutive ones.

path-with-minimum-effort.hook: Dijkstra works for any cost that only grows along a path, including the maximum step.
path-with-minimum-effort.ask: On a grid of heights, walk from the top-left to the bottom-right moving up, down, left or right. A path's effort is its biggest height jump. Return the smallest possible effort.
path-with-minimum-effort.exampleWhy: Path 1, 3, 5, 3, 5 never jumps more than 2. Every route through 2s needs a jump of 3.

brute.idea: Try every possible effort limit from smallest to largest, and BFS to check whether the corner is reachable under it.
steps: Collect all neighbour height differences
Try limits in increasing order
BFS using only steps within the limit
First reachable limit is the answer
brute.whySlow: Up to 2·R·C distinct limits, each needing a full grid BFS: about 400 million steps on 100 by 100.

optimal.insight: Run Dijkstra where a path's cost is its largest jump. The cost never decreases along a path, so the first time we pop the target it is optimal.
steps: Heap of (effort, r, c), starting at (0, 0, 0)
Pop the cell with the smallest effort
Reached the corner? return its effort
Relax neighbours with max(effort, jump)

codeNotes.note: First pop of target is optimal
Path cost is its biggest jump

pitfalls: Combine with max, not plus: effort is the largest step, not the total.
Binary search on effort plus BFS is a valid O(RC log H) alternative.

say.intro: Okay, Path With Minimum Effort. We walk across a grid of heights, from the top left to the bottom right. A route's effort is its single biggest height jump. We want the easiest route. Here, the path one, three, five, three, five never jumps more than two. So the answer is two.
say.brute: A brute force tries every possible effort limit, from small to big. For each limit, it runs a breadth first search, only taking steps within that limit. The first limit that reaches the corner wins. It's correct. But each of up to twenty thousand limits needs its own full grid search.
say.insight: Here's the thing. This is a shortest path problem, just with a different cost. Instead of adding step costs, a path costs its biggest step. And that cost never shrinks as the path grows. That's exactly what Dijkstra needs. Always expand the cell we can reach with the least effort. The first time we pop the target, we're done.
say.anim: We start with a three by three height grid and run Dijkstra to minimize the largest jump. From cell zero zero, we explore neighbors and record efforts of two and one into best. We pop effort one at cell zero one, pushing new efforts like six and one for neighbors. We keep popping smallest efforts first, updating best values like three and five as we expand. At cell two zero with effort two, we relax neighbors, improving effort two for cell two one. We continue expanding, reaching cell two two with effort two, better than the old six. The heap pops effort two for the bottom right target cell, matching our best record. The algorithm returns two, the minimum possible effort path through the grid.
say.code: Let's walk the code. The start corner costs zero effort, so we seed the heap with it. Each round, we pop the cheapest frontier cell. If it's the target, that first pop is optimal, so we return. Stale heap entries get skipped. For each neighbour, the path cost is its biggest jump so far. If we found an easier way there, we record it and push.
say.outro: R times C, times log of R times C. The pattern is advanced graphs. Dijkstra, with a max instead of a sum.

path-with-minimum-effort.title: Path With Minimum Effort
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, as the problem platform expects, to hold our method.
The method takes the grid of heights and returns the smallest possible effort as an integer.
We read the number of rows into R and the number of columns into C from the grid.
We build a grid called best, holding the lowest known effort to reach each cell, starting at infinity.
The starting cell needs no effort to reach, so we set its best value to zero.
We seed the priority queue with effort zero at row zero and column zero, our starting position.
We loop while the heap still has candidate cells to explore, always taking the cheapest effort first.
We pop the entry with the smallest effort so far, along with its row and column.
We check whether this popped cell is the bottom-right target.
Since the cost never decreases along a path, the first time we pop the target its effort is optimal, so we return it.
If this entry's effort is worse than the best we recorded, it is stale, so we check for that.
We skip stale entries because a better route to this cell was already processed.
We loop over the four neighbors: down, up, right and left of the current cell.
We only continue if the neighbor lies inside the grid boundaries.
The effort to step there is the larger of our current effort and the height difference, since a path costs its biggest jump.
We check whether this route to the neighbor beats the best effort we have recorded for it.
If so, we update the neighbor's best effort to this smaller value.
We push the neighbor with its new effort onto the heap so it gets explored in order.
This final return is a fallback that is never reached, because the target is always popped and returned earlier.

construct-uniform-parity-array-ii.hook: Now differences must stay positive, so everything hinges on the smallest odd number.
construct-uniform-parity-array-ii.ask: For each number, keep it or replace it with itself minus a smaller number from the array, so the result is at least 1. Can every result share one parity?
construct-uniform-parity-array-ii.exampleWhy: The smallest odd is 3, but 2 is smaller, so 2 cannot become odd; and odd 3 cannot become even.

brute.idea: Try both target parities. For each number, check whether keeping it or subtracting some smaller number gives that parity.
steps: Try target even, then odd
For each i, keep or test every smaller j
All fixable? return True
brute.whySlow: Checks every pair; with 100,000 numbers that is ten billion pair checks.

optimal.insight: All even fails if any odd exists, since the smallest odd cannot change. All odd works if every even is bigger than the smallest odd.
steps: No odd numbers? already all even: true
Find the smallest odd and smallest even
True if no evens or min even > min odd

codeNotes.note: Every even can subtract min odd

pitfalls: Even minus even stays even, so evens need a smaller odd specifically.
Values are distinct, so min_even never equals min_odd.

say.intro: Okay, Construct Uniform Parity Array, part two. Same idea as before. But now we can only subtract a smaller number, so results stay positive. Can everything become odd? Or everything even? With six, three, eight, nine, two, the answer is false.
say.brute: The brute force tries both goals. For each number with the wrong parity, it searches every other number. It wants a smaller one whose difference has the right parity. That's quadratic. With a hundred thousand numbers, about ten billion pair checks. Correct, but way too slow.
say.insight: Think about the smallest odd number. To make it even, we'd subtract a smaller odd. But none exists! So all even only works when there are no odds at all. What about all odd? Each even must subtract a smaller odd. The smallest odd is the best choice. So every even must be bigger than the smallest odd.
say.anim: We start with the array six, three, eight, nine, two, tracking smallest odd and even. Six is even, so min even updates to six. Three is odd, so min odd updates to three. Eight is even but larger, so min even stays six. Nine is odd but larger, so min odd stays three. Two is even and smaller, so min even drops to two. Since an odd value exists, we check if min even beats min odd. Min even two is not greater than min odd three, so the function returns false.
say.code: Let's walk the code. In one pass, we track the two minimums, smallest odd and smallest even. Now, if no odd was seen, everything's already even. So we return true. Otherwise, the smallest odd is what fixes the evens. Every even can subtract the min odd, as long as the smallest even is bigger. That check also covers the case with no evens.
say.outro: Linear time, constant space. The pattern is math. Parity rules shrink the whole problem down to two minimums.

construct-uniform-parity-array-ii.title: Construct Uniform Parity Array II
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container the problem expects for our method.
The method uniformArray takes the list nums1 and returns true or false depending on whether a uniform parity result is possible.
We start the smallest odd and smallest even values at infinity, meaning none has been seen yet.
We loop through every number x in the list to find the smallest odd and smallest even.
If x leaves a remainder when divided by two, then x is odd.
For an odd x, we update min_odd to the smaller of its current value and x.
Otherwise the number is even, so we handle it in the else branch.
For an even x, we update min_even to the smaller of its current value and x.
If min_odd is still infinity, there are no odd numbers in the array at all.
With no odds, every number is already even, so the array is uniform and we return true.
Otherwise we return whether every even exceeds the smallest odd, so each even can subtract that odd to become odd.

distinct-subsequences-ii.hook: Track distinct subsequences by their last letter, and duplicates cancel themselves.
distinct-subsequences-ii.ask: Given a string, count its distinct non-empty subsequences, where a subsequence keeps some characters in their original order. Return the count modulo 10^9 + 7.
distinct-subsequences-ii.exampleWhy: a, b, aa, ab, ba, bb, aab, aba, abb, bab and abab are the 11 distinct ones.

brute.idea: Generate every subsequence by choosing to keep or skip each character, and put them in a set.
steps: Start with a set holding the empty string
For each char, extend every existing string
Count the set minus the empty string
brute.whySlow: A 2,000 letter string has up to 2^2000 subsequences; even 40 letters is a trillion.

optimal.insight: ends[c] counts distinct subsequences ending in c. Appending c to every distinct subsequence, plus c alone, gives the new ends[c] with no duplicates.
steps: ends holds 26 counters
For each char c: ends[c] = sum(ends) + 1
Overwrite, so old c-endings are not double counted
Answer is sum(ends)

codeNotes.note: Extend all, plus the letter alone

pitfalls: Overwrite ends[c], never add to it: older c-endings are rebuilt inside the new count.

say.intro: Okay, Distinct Subsequences, part two. We count the different non empty subsequences of a string. A subsequence keeps some letters, in order. Repeats only count once. For a b a b, there are eleven distinct ones. From single letters, all the way up to a b a b itself.
say.brute: The brute force builds every subsequence. Keep a set. For each letter, add a copy of every string in the set, with that letter on the end. The set removes duplicates for us. Correct, right? But the count can double with every letter. Forty letters already means about a trillion strings.
say.insight: Here's the trick. Group subsequences by their last letter. Say we read a c. Every distinct subsequence so far, extended by c, plus c alone, gives exactly the ones ending in c. And the old ones ending in c? They're all rebuilt inside that set. So we overwrite c's count, instead of adding to it. No duplicates sneak in.
say.anim: We start with the string abab and an ends array of all zeros, one slot per letter. First character is a, so we update ends for a, giving it value 1. Next character is b, updating ends for b to 2, counting subsequences ending there. Another a arrives, so ends for a becomes 4, combining prior counts plus one. The final b updates ends for b to 7, summing all current distinct subsequences. Now we sum the whole ends array to get the total distinct subsequences. The final answer shown is 11, matching the expected distinct subsequence count.
say.code: Let's walk the code. We keep twenty six counters, the distinct subsequences per last letter. For each character, we find the index of this letter. Then we set its counter to the sum of all counters, plus one. That's extend all, plus the letter alone. We take it modulo a billion and seven. At the end, every subsequence ends somewhere, so we return the sum.
say.outro: Linear time, constant space. The pattern is one dimensional dynamic programming, keyed by the last character.

distinct-subsequences-ii.title: Distinct Subsequences II
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container the problem expects for our method.
The method distinctSubseqII takes the string s and will return the count of distinct non-empty subsequences.
We set MOD to ten to the ninth plus seven, so we can keep numbers small as required.
We create ends as a list of twenty-six zeros, tracking distinct subsequences ending in each letter.
We loop through each character ch of the string in order, processing one new character at a time.
We convert ch into an index from zero to twenty-five by subtracting the code of the letter a.
We set ends at that index to the sum of all ends plus one, meaning every existing subsequence extended by ch, plus ch alone, taken modulo MOD.
Finally we return the total of all ends modulo MOD, since every distinct subsequence ends in exactly one letter.
