subarray-sum-equals-k.hook: A subarray sum is a difference of two prefix sums, and a hash map finds the partner.
subarray-sum-equals-k.ask: Given an array of integers, possibly negative, and a target k, count how many contiguous subarrays add up to exactly k.
subarray-sum-equals-k.exampleWhy: 3+4, 7, 7+2-3+1 and 1+4+2 each sum to 7, giving four subarrays.

brute.idea: Fix every start index, extend the end one step at a time with a running sum, and count sums equal to k.
steps: Pick a start i
Extend end j, adding nums[j]
Running sum equals k? count it
brute.whySlow: 20,000 numbers give about 200 million start and end pairs.

optimal.insight: A subarray ending here sums to k when some earlier prefix sum equals current prefix minus k. Count earlier prefixes in a hash map.
steps: Map starts with prefix 0 seen once
Add each number to the prefix sum
Add count of prefix - k to the answer
Record the current prefix

codeNotes.note: Empty prefix, for subarrays from index 0
Each partner prefix is one subarray

pitfalls: Negatives break sliding window here; prefix sums handle them.
Forgetting {0: 1} misses subarrays starting at index 0.

say.intro: Okay, Subarray Sum Equals K. We get an array, possibly with negatives. How many contiguous subarrays add up to exactly k? Here's our array. Three, four, seven, two, minus three, one, four, two. And k is seven. Four subarrays work. Like three plus four, or just the seven alone.
say.brute: The brute force fixes each start position. Then it stretches the end one step at a time, keeping a running sum. Every time the sum hits k, count it. Simple and correct. But it checks every pair of start and end. That's quadratic. Twenty thousand numbers means about two hundred million pairs.
say.insight: Here's the key. Any subarray sum is the difference of two prefix sums. So when does a subarray ending here sum to k? When some earlier prefix equals the current prefix, minus k. So keep a hash map counting every prefix sum we've seen. One lookup tells us how many subarrays end right here.
say.anim: We start with a map holding prefix sum zero seen once, and count at zero. Adding three gives prefix sum three, which minus seven isn't in the map yet. Adding four makes prefix sum seven, matching prefix minus k, so count becomes one. Adding seven, two, and negative three builds prefix sums fourteen, sixteen, and thirteen into the map. Adding one brings prefix sum to fourteen, matching an earlier prefix, raising count to three. Adding four gives eighteen, no match, so it's just recorded in the map. Adding two makes prefix sum twenty, matching prefix minus k again, count reaches four. The loop ends and the function returns four as the final answer.
say.code: Let's walk the code. The map starts with the empty prefix, zero, seen once. That covers subarrays starting at index zero. For each number, we update the sum of everything so far. Then each partner prefix, current minus k, is one subarray. So we add its count. Only after counting do we record the current prefix.
say.outro: Linear time, linear space. The pattern is arrays and hashing. Prefix sums, with a hash map of counts.

subarray-sum-equals-k.title: Subarray Sum Equals K
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container the interview platform expects for our method.
The method subarraySum takes the list nums and the target k, and returns how many subarrays sum to k.
First, we note the map must start with a prefix sum of zero already seen once.
We create prefix counts with zero mapped to one, so subarrays starting at the very beginning get counted.
We set prefix sum to zero, which will hold the running total of numbers so far.
We set count to zero, which will hold the number of matching subarrays found.
We loop over each number in nums, moving left to right through the array.
Next, we add each number into the running prefix sum.
We update prefix sum by adding the current num to it.
Now we look for earlier prefixes that equal the current prefix minus k.
We check whether the prefix sum minus k has been seen before in the map.
If it has, we add how many times it appeared, since each one gives a valid subarray ending here.
Then we record the current prefix sum for use by later positions.
If the current prefix sum is already in the map, we branch to increase its tally.
We add one to its stored count, since we have seen this prefix sum once more.
Otherwise, this prefix sum is new to the map.
We store it with a count of one, marking its first appearance.
After the loop ends, we return count as the total number of subarrays summing to k.

search-insert-position.hook: Binary search that stops at the first slot not less than the target.
search-insert-position.ask: Given a sorted array of distinct numbers and a target, return the target's index if present, otherwise the index where it would be inserted to keep the order. Must be logarithmic.
search-insert-position.exampleWhy: 7 is missing. It belongs after 6 and before 8, which is index 4.

brute.idea: Scan from the left and return the first index whose value is at least the target.
steps: Walk each index
Value ≥ target? return index
Fell off the end? return n
brute.whySlow: Linear: 10,000 elements may take 10,000 checks, and the problem demands logarithmic time.

optimal.insight: Find the first index whose value is at least the target. That is both the found position and the insert position.
steps: lo = 0, hi = n
mid value smaller than target? lo = mid + 1
Otherwise hi = mid
lo is the answer when they meet

codeNotes.note: hi = n allows inserting at the end

pitfalls: hi must start at len(nums), not len(nums) - 1, for targets past the end.

say.intro: Okay, Search Insert Position. We have a sorted array and a target. If the target's there, return its index. If not, return where it would go to keep things sorted. Is seven in one, three, five, six, eight, ten, twelve? Nope. It belongs between six and eight. That's index four.
say.brute: The brute force scans from the left. It returns the first index whose value is at least the target. If nothing qualifies, it returns the length. Correct, but linear. And the problem explicitly asks for logarithmic time. So a scan just won't cut it.
say.insight: Here's the thing. Both questions have the same answer. The first position whose value is at least the target. If the target exists, that's where it sits. If not, that's where it would go. Everything before that spot is smaller. So binary search can find it, halving the range every step.
say.anim: We start with lo at 0 and hi at 7, searching the sorted array for target 7. Mid becomes 3, pointing to value 6, which is less than target 7. Since nums at mid is too small, lo moves up to 4. Now lo is 4 and hi is 7, so mid becomes 5, pointing to value 10. Value 10 is at least target, so hi shrinks down to 5. With lo 4 and hi 5, mid becomes 4, pointing to value 8. Value 8 is at least target, so hi shrinks down to 4. Now lo equals hi at 4, so the loop ends and we return 4.
say.code: Let's walk the code. Low starts at zero. High starts at n, not n minus one. Why? That allows inserting at the very end. While low is below high, we halve the search range. If the middle is smaller than the target, the answer is to the right. Otherwise, mid could be the answer, so high moves to it. At the end, low is the first value at least the target.
say.outro: Logarithmic time, constant space. The pattern is binary search for the lower bound. A template worth memorising.

search-insert-position.title: Search Insert Position
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container that holds our search method for this problem.
The searchInsert method takes a sorted list of numbers and a target, and returns the index where the target belongs.
We set lo to zero and hi to the length of nums, so the search range includes the position just past the end.
We loop while lo is less than hi, meaning the range still holds candidate positions to check.
We compute mid as the average of lo and hi, rounded down, to probe the middle of the range.
If the value at mid is less than the target, then mid and everything before it are too small.
So we move lo up to mid plus one, discarding the left half including mid.
Otherwise the value at mid is at least the target, so mid could be the answer.
We set hi to mid, keeping mid as a candidate while discarding everything to its right.
When lo meets hi, it points to the first value at least the target, so we return lo.

sqrtx.hook: Squares only grow, so binary search the largest number whose square still fits.
sqrtx.ask: Given a non-negative integer x, return the square root of x rounded down, without using any built-in power or square root function.
sqrtx.exampleWhy: 7 squared is 49, which fits under 50; 8 squared is 64, which is too big.

brute.idea: Count upward from zero while the next number squared is still at most x.
steps: Start r at 0
While (r + 1)² ≤ x, increase r
Return r
brute.whySlow: For x near 2 billion that is about 46,000 steps instead of 31.

optimal.insight: m squared grows with m, so the answer is the last m whose square is at most x. Binary search over 0 to x finds it.
steps: lo = 0, hi = x
Pick the upper middle m
m² ≤ x? lo = m
Otherwise hi = m - 1

codeNotes.note: Upper middle avoids an infinite loop

pitfalls: With lo = mid, round mid up, or the loop never ends.
In fixed-width languages mid * mid can overflow; compare mid with x // mid.

say.intro: Okay, Square root of x. We get a non negative integer. We return its square root, rounded down. And no power or square root functions allowed. Take fifty. Seven squared is forty nine, which fits. Eight squared is sixty four, which is too big. So the answer is seven.
say.brute: The brute force counts upward. Start at zero. While the next number squared still fits under x, step up by one. Correct, but it takes about square root of x steps. For two billion, that's around forty six thousand steps. Binary search needs only about thirty one.
say.insight: Here's the thing. Squares only grow as the number grows. So there's a clean boundary. Every number up to the answer has a square that fits. Every number after it doesn't. That kind of boundary is exactly what binary search finds. About thirty steps, even for the biggest input.
say.anim: We start searching for the square root of 50, with lo at 0 and hi at 50. Mid becomes 25, but twenty five squared is too big, so hi shrinks to 24. Mid becomes 12, still too large when squared, so hi drops to 11. Mid becomes 6, and six squared fits within 50, so lo moves up to 6. Mid becomes 9, too big squared, so hi shrinks down to 8. Mid becomes 7, seven squared is 49, within 50, so lo updates to 7. Mid becomes 8, too big squared, so hi shrinks to 7, matching lo. The loop ends since lo equals hi, and the function returns 7.
say.code: Let's walk the code. The answer lies between zero and x. While low and high differ, we take the upper middle. Why upper? Rounding up avoids an infinite loop. If mid squared still fits, it could be the answer, so low moves up to it. If mid is too big, high drops below it. At the end, low is the largest square root that fits under x.
say.outro: Logarithmic time, constant space. The pattern is binary search on the answer, over a monotonic condition.

sqrtx.title: Sqrt(x)
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container this problem's method lives in.
The method mySqrt takes a non-negative integer x and returns its square root rounded down as an integer.
We set lo to zero and hi to x, so the search range covers every possible answer.
We keep looping while lo is less than hi, stopping when the range narrows to one candidate.
We pick mid as the upper middle of the range, rounding up so that the loop always makes progress.
If mid squared is at most x, then mid is a valid answer and maybe a larger one exists.
So we move lo up to mid, keeping mid as the best valid answer so far.
Otherwise mid squared is too large, so mid and everything above it can be ruled out.
We set hi to mid minus one, discarding mid and all larger values from the search.
When the loop ends, lo is the largest number whose square is at most x, so we return it.

3sum-closest.hook: Sort once, fix one number, and let two pointers steer the sum toward the target.
3sum-closest.ask: Given an array of integers and a target, pick three numbers at different positions whose sum is as close as possible to the target, and return that sum.
3sum-closest.exampleWhy: -4 + 2 + 3 = 1 hits the target exactly, so no other triple can be closer.

brute.idea: Try every triple of indices and keep the sum closest to the target.
steps: Loop i < j < k
Compute the triple sum
Keep it if closer to target
brute.whySlow: 500 numbers give about 20 million triples, each checked separately.

optimal.insight: After sorting, fix one number and move two pointers inward: too small moves left up, too big moves right down.
steps: Sort the array
Fix i, set l = i + 1, r = end
Update best with the current sum
Sum below target? l += 1; above? r -= 1
Equal to target? return immediately

codeNotes.note: Closer than any seen so far

pitfalls: Initialise best with a real triple, not infinity, to avoid overflow in other languages.

say.intro: Okay, Three Sum Closest. We pick three numbers from different positions. We want their sum as close as possible to a target, and we return that sum. Minus one, two, one, minus four, three, with a target of one. Minus four, plus two, plus three, is exactly one. So the answer is one.
say.brute: The brute force tries every triple of positions. It computes the sum, and keeps whichever is closest. That's correct. But it's cubic. Five hundred numbers means about twenty million triples.
say.insight: Here's the trick. Sort first. Then fix the smallest number of the triple. Put one pointer right after it, and one at the end. Sum too small? The only way to grow it is to move the left pointer right. Too big? Move the right pointer left. Each fixed number needs just one linear sweep.
say.anim: The array gets sorted into negative four, negative one, one, two, three. Best starts as the sum of the first three numbers, negative four. Fixing index zero, pointers l and r start at one and four. Sum is negative two, closer to target one, so best updates to negative two. Since sum is too small, left pointer moves up to find a bigger sum. Now sum is zero, still closer, so best becomes zero and left moves again. Sum reaches one, exactly matching the target, so best becomes one. Since the sum equals target exactly, the function returns one immediately.
say.code: Let's walk the code. Sorting makes pointer moves meaningful. For each i, we set pointers around the fixed number, left after it, right at the end. We compute the sum. Is it closer than any seen so far? Then we save it. Too small, and we grow the sum by moving left. Too big, and we shrink it by moving right. An exact hit can't be beaten, so we return right away.
say.outro: Quadratic time, constant extra space. The pattern is two pointers on a sorted array, steering a sum toward a target.

3sum-closest.title: 3Sum Closest
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container the problem expects for our method.
The method threeSumClosest takes the list of numbers and a target, and returns the closest achievable sum.
We sort the numbers first so the two pointer movement can reliably raise or lower the sum.
We start best as the sum of the first three numbers, giving us a valid initial candidate.
We loop the fixed index i over every position that still leaves room for two more numbers.
We place left just after i and right at the last element, spanning the remaining range.
We keep moving the pointers inward while left is still strictly before right.
We compute the current three number sum from the fixed number and both pointer values.
If this sum is nearer to the target than our best so far, it deserves to replace it.
We then record this sum as the new best answer.
If the sum is below the target, we need something larger.
So we move left up one step to pick a bigger number.
If instead the sum is above the target, we need something smaller.
So we move right down one step to pick a smaller number.
Otherwise the sum equals the target exactly, which cannot be beaten.
We return that sum immediately as the perfect answer.
After all fixed numbers and pointer sweeps finish, we return the closest sum we found.

power-of-two.hook: One bit set, nothing else. A single AND decides it in constant time.
power-of-two.ask: Given an integer n, return true if n equals two raised to some whole power, like 1, 2, 4, 8 or 16. Zero and negative numbers are never powers of two.
power-of-two.exampleWhy: 16 is 2 to the 4th, so it is a power of two. Its binary form is 10000: exactly one bit set.

brute.idea: Keep dividing by two while the number is even. A power of two shrinks all the way down to exactly 1.
steps: Reject n ≤ 0
While n is even, halve it
Return whether n reached 1
brute.whySlow: Not slow in practice, but it loops up to 31 times where one bit trick answers instantly.

optimal.insight: A power of two has exactly one 1-bit. Subtracting 1 flips that bit and all zeros below it, so n & (n-1) is 0.
steps: Powers of two are positive: require n > 0
Compute n & (n - 1): it clears the lowest set bit
Result 0 means only one bit was set

pitfalls: Forgetting n ≤ 0: zero passes the AND test and would wrongly return true.
Operator precedence: in many languages wrap n & (n - 1) in parentheses before comparing.

say.intro: Okay, Power of Two. We get an integer. Is it two multiplied by itself some number of times? Like one, two, four, eight, or sixteen. Our example is sixteen. That's two to the fourth, so the answer is true. And zero or negatives? Never powers of two.
say.brute: The brute force idea is to keep halving. Zero or negative? Return false. Otherwise, while the number is even, divide it by two. A real power of two shrinks cleanly down to one. Anything else gets stuck on an odd number bigger than one. That's logarithmic, about thirty one loops at most. Fast! But there's a neater answer.
say.insight: Look at the binary form. A power of two has exactly one bit set. A one, followed by zeros. Now subtract one. What happens? That bit flips off, and every zero below it becomes a one. So the number and the number minus one share no bits at all. Their bitwise and is zero. And that only happens for powers of two.
say.anim: We start with n equal to sixteen, which is positive, so we continue. Now we compute n and n minus one together using bitwise and. The result, lowest cleared, comes out to zero, meaning only one bit was set. Since lowest cleared equals zero, the function returns true, confirming sixteen is a power of two.
say.code: Let's walk the code. First, zero and negatives never qualify. So we return false right away. Then we compute n and n minus one. That clears the lowest set bit. Finally, is anything left? If nothing's left, there was exactly one bit. So we return whether that result is zero.
say.outro: Constant time, constant space. The pattern is bit manipulation. N and n minus one clears the lowest set bit. That trick is worth memorizing.

power-of-two.title: Power of Two
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container the judge expects for our method.
This method takes an integer n and returns a boolean saying whether n is a power of two.
First we check whether n is zero or negative, since those can never be powers of two.
In that case we return false right away, which also protects the bit trick from invalid inputs.
We compute n bitwise and n minus one, which clears the lowest set bit of n.
We return true only if that result is zero, meaning n had exactly one set bit.

move-zeroes.hook: Push the zeros back without breaking the order of everything else, in place.
move-zeroes.ask: Given an array, move every zero to the end while keeping the non-zero numbers in their original relative order. You must change the array itself, not build a copy.
move-zeroes.exampleWhy: The non-zeros 1, 3, 12 keep their order at the front; the two zeros end up at the back.

brute.idea: Collect the non-zero numbers into a new list, pad with zeros, and copy everything back into the array.
steps: Gather non-zeros into a new list
Append the right number of zeros
Copy the list back into nums
brute.whySlow: Time is fine, but it needs a full extra copy of the array, which the problem forbids.

optimal.insight: Keep a write pointer for the next non-zero slot. Each non-zero swaps into it, so zeros drift back automatically.
steps: l marks where the next non-zero belongs
Scan with r across the whole array
Non-zero at r: swap it into l, advance l
Zeros end up behind l

pitfalls: Overwriting then zero-filling also works, but writes more often than swapping.
Do not remove and append zeros: list removal is O(n) each time.

say.intro: Okay, Move Zeroes. We get an array, and we push every zero to the end. The other numbers keep their original order. And we do it in place. So zero, one, zero, three, twelve becomes one, three, twelve, followed by two zeros.
say.brute: The simple approach makes a copy. Walk the array and collect every non zero number into a new list. Pad it with zeros to the right length, and copy it back. That's linear time, which is fine. But it uses a whole extra array. And the problem explicitly asks us to work in place.
say.insight: Here's the trick. Use two pointers. The left pointer marks where the next non zero number should go. The right pointer scans everything. When right finds a non zero, swap it into the left slot, and move left forward. Why does this work? Non zeros land in order at the front. And the zeros get pushed behind them for free.
say.anim: We start with l at zero, tracking where the next non-zero value should go. At r equals zero, nums is zero, so nothing happens and we move on. At r equals one, nums is one, a non-zero value, so we swap it into position l. After swapping, the array becomes one, zero, zero, three, twelve, and l becomes one. At r equals two we see zero again, so we skip it and keep scanning. At r equals three, value three is non-zero, so it swaps into position l, giving one, three, zero, zero, twelve. At r equals four, twelve is non-zero, swapping it forward to position l. The loop ends, leaving the final array as one, three, twelve, zero, zero.
say.code: Let's walk the code. l marks the next slot for a non zero, starting at zero. Then r scans every element. When the value at r isn't zero, we swap it. The non zero moves forward, and the zero goes back. Then l steps forward, because that slot is now filled. That's it. The array changes in place, so we return nothing.
say.outro: Linear time, constant space. The pattern is two pointers. A slow writer and a fast reader, the standard way to compact an array in place.

move-zeroes.title: Move Zeroes
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container that holds the method for this problem.
The moveZeroes method takes the list nums and returns nothing, since it must change the list in place.
We set l to zero, so it marks the next slot where a non-zero number should go.
We loop r across every index of nums, scanning each element once from left to right.
We check whether the number at r is not zero, because only non-zero values need to move forward.
We swap the values at l and r, placing the non-zero number at the write slot and pushing the other value back.
We then move l forward by one, so the next non-zero number goes into the following slot.

stone-game.hook: Two perfect players, piles at both ends. Who wins? Track the score margin per range.
stone-game.ask: Piles of stones sit in a row. Alice and Bob alternate, each taking the whole pile from either end. Both play perfectly. Return true if Alice, who moves first, ends with more stones.
stone-game.exampleWhy: Alice takes a 5; whatever Bob does, she can finish with 9 or 10 of the 17 stones.

brute.idea: Recursively try both ends at every turn. The best margin for the mover is pile taken minus the opponent's best margin after.
steps: margin(i, j) for piles i..j
Take left: piles[i] - margin(i+1, j)
Take right: piles[j] - margin(i, j-1)
Keep the larger option
brute.whySlow: Every call branches twice and the same ranges are recomputed again and again: 500 piles is hopeless.

optimal.insight: The best margin on piles i..j depends only on two smaller ranges. Fill a table from short ranges to long ones.
steps: dp[i][j] = mover's best margin on piles i..j
Single pile: dp[i][i] = piles[i]
Grow length: max of the two end choices
Alice wins if dp[0][n-1] > 0

pitfalls: With an even count and odd total, Alice always wins: return True works. Mention it.
Store the score margin, not raw totals, so one table serves both players.

say.intro: Okay, Stone Game. Piles of stones sit in a row. Alice and Bob take turns grabbing a whole pile from either end. Both play perfectly. Does Alice, who goes first, finish with more stones? With five, three, four, five, Alice can always win.
say.brute: The brute force is a recursive game search. For any range of piles, define the margin. That's how far ahead the current player can finish. The player takes the left pile, minus the opponent's best margin on what's left. Or the same on the right. Keep the better one. But every call branches twice. So this is exponential.
say.insight: Here's the key. A range's margin depends only on two slightly smaller ranges. So why recompute them? Store them. Build a table where each cell holds the best margin on piles i through j. Start with single piles. Then lengths two, three, and so on. Each cell is just the better of two subtractions. That's quadratic time.
say.anim: We start with piles five, three, four, five, building a table of best score margins. The diagonal fills first, each single pile equals its own value in the table. Now we grow ranges of length two, comparing taking the left or right pile. For piles zero and one, the best margin becomes two, favoring the first player. Next we handle ranges of length three, combining smaller results already computed. Finally the full range of length four gives a margin of one, still positive. Since dp zero three is one, greater than zero, the first player wins, returning true.
say.code: Let's walk the code. We make a margin table for every range. With one pile, you just take it, so each pile goes on the diagonal. Then we fill short ranges before long ones. That way, every smaller range is ready when we need it. For each cell, we take an end and subtract the reply. Keep the better end. A positive margin on the full range means Alice wins.
say.outro: Quadratic time instead of exponential. The pattern is two dimensional dynamic programming over intervals. The classic shape for take from either end games.

stone-game.title: Stone Game
lineNotes: This line defines the Solution class that holds our stoneGame method, as the problem format requires.
The method takes the list of piles and returns true if Alice ends up with more stones.
We store the number of piles in n so we can size the table and loop bounds.
We build an n by n table where each entry will hold the best margin for the current player on that range.
We loop over every index to fill in the simplest ranges, those holding a single pile.
With one pile, the player to move takes it, so the margin on that range equals that pile.
We now grow range lengths from two up to n, so smaller ranges are always solved before larger ones.
For each length, we slide the start index i across every position where a range of that length fits.
We compute the end index j from the start and length, giving the inclusive range i to j.
The mover takes either end pile and subtracts the opponent's best margin on what remains, keeping whichever choice gives the larger margin.
Alice wins if her best margin over the whole row is positive, so we return whether that value exceeds zero.

subarray-product-less-than-k.hook: Count every subarray with a small product in one pass, by sliding a window.
subarray-product-less-than-k.ask: Given an array of positive integers and a number k, count how many contiguous subarrays have a product strictly less than k.
subarray-product-less-than-k.exampleWhy: Four singles, plus [10,5], [5,2], [2,6], [5,2,6]. [10,5,2] has product exactly 100, so it fails.

brute.idea: Start a subarray at every index and extend it right, multiplying as we go, until the product reaches k.
steps: Fix a start index i
Extend j, multiplying nums[j] in
Product ≥ k: stop this start
Otherwise count one subarray
brute.whySlow: With k large and many ones, each start extends almost to the end: 30,000 squared is 900 million steps.

optimal.insight: All numbers are positive, so shrinking the window only lowers the product. Every valid window ending at r adds r - l + 1 subarrays.
steps: Grow the window: multiply nums[r] in
Product too big: divide out nums[l], move l
Every start from l to r now works
Add r - l + 1 to the count

codeNotes.note: Grow the window to the right
Too big: shrink from the left

pitfalls: Without the k ≤ 1 guard, l runs past r and the loop breaks.
Counting r - l + 1 per step is the trick; do not list subarrays.

say.intro: Okay, Subarray Product Less Than K. We get positive integers and a number k. How many contiguous subarrays have a product strictly below k? Ten, five, two, six, with k of one hundred. There are eight. Ten, five, two doesn't count. Its product is exactly one hundred.
say.brute: The brute force fixes every start index. Then it extends right, multiplying in one number at a time. Once the product reaches k, that start is done. The numbers are positive, so the product only grows. Otherwise, each extension counts one subarray. With lots of ones, that's quadratic in the worst case.
say.insight: Here's the thing. Every number is positive, so a window behaves predictably. Adding on the right can only raise the product. Dropping on the left can only lower it. So we slide a window. Too big? Shrink from the left. Once it fits, every subarray ending at r, starting inside the window, is valid. That's the window length, all at once.
say.anim: K is 100, greater than one, so we start sliding a window across the array. At r equals zero, product becomes 10, under 100, so count increases to 1. At r equals one, product becomes 50, still valid, count jumps to 3. At r equals two, product hits 100, too big, so we shrink from the left. We divide out nums at l, product drops to 10, and l becomes 1, fixing the window. Window from l to r is valid now, adding two more subarrays, count becomes 5. At r equals three, product becomes 60, valid, adding three more, count reaches 8. Loop ends and the function returns 8, the total subarrays with product under 100.
say.code: Let's walk the code. If k is at most one, return zero. No positive product is below one. Then, for each right index, we grow the window to the right by multiplying in its number. Too big? We shrink from the left. We divide the leftmost number out, and move left forward. Finally, we add the window length. That's all the subarrays ending at r.
say.outro: Linear time, constant space. The pattern is a sliding window. Positive numbers keep it monotonic, and each step counts subarrays in bulk.

subarray-product-less-than-k.title: Subarray Product Less Than K
lineNotes: We define a Solution class that holds the method for solving this problem.
The method takes the list of positive integers nums and the threshold k, and returns a count.
If k is at most one, no product of positive integers can be strictly below it.
So we return zero right away, which also keeps the shrinking loop from running past the window.
We start the running product of the window at one, the neutral value for multiplication.
We set left to zero, so the window starts at the first element.
We set count to zero to total up all valid subarrays as we go.
We move the right edge of the window across every index of nums.
We multiply the new element at right into the running product to include it in the window.
While the product is too large, we must shrink the window from the left.
We divide the product by the element at left, removing its contribution exactly since the numbers are positive integers.
We advance left by one, which drops that element from the window.
Every valid subarray ending at right starts between left and right, so we add right minus left plus one.
After processing all positions, we return the total count of subarrays with product below k.

fruit-into-baskets.hook: Two baskets, one fruit type each. Find the longest stretch with at most two types.
fruit-into-baskets.ask: Trees stand in a row, each giving one fruit type. Starting anywhere and walking right, pick one fruit per tree, but you may only hold two types. Return the most fruit you can pick.
fruit-into-baskets.exampleWhy: Start at the second tree: 2, 3, 2, 2 uses only types 2 and 3, giving 4 fruits.

brute.idea: Try every starting tree, walk right collecting types in a set, and stop when a third type appears.
steps: Pick a start tree i
Walk right, adding types to a set
Third type: stop and record length
brute.whySlow: Each start rescans trees the previous start already saw: 100,000 trees is billions of steps.

optimal.insight: This is the longest subarray with at most two distinct values. Slide a window and keep counts of each type inside it.
steps: Add fruits[r] to the window counts
More than two types: drop fruits[l], move l
Remove a type once its count hits 0
Record the window length

fruit-into-baskets.optimalCode:
class Solution:
    def totalFruit(self, fruits: List[int]) -> int:
        basket_count = collections.defaultdict(int)
        left = 0
        best = 0
        # 1. Expand the window by adding the fruit at right
        for right in range(len(fruits)):
            basket_count[fruits[right]] += 1
            # 2. If more than two types, shrink from the left
            while len(basket_count) > 2:
                left_fruit = fruits[left]
                basket_count[left_fruit] -= 1
                # 3. Remove a type once its count hits 0
                if basket_count[left_fruit] == 0:
                    del basket_count[left_fruit]
                left += 1
            # 4. Record the window length
            window_length = right - left + 1
            if window_length > best:
                best = window_length
        return best

codeNotes.note: Fruit type to count in window

pitfalls: Forgetting to delete zero-count keys keeps len(count) wrong forever.
Space is O(1) because the map never holds more than three keys.

say.intro: Okay, Fruit Into Baskets. Trees stand in a row, each with one fruit type. You start anywhere and walk right, picking one fruit per tree. But your two baskets hold only two types. What's the most fruit you can pick? For one, two, three, two, two, it's four. Start at the second tree.
say.brute: The brute force tries every starting tree. From each start, walk right, adding fruit types to a set. When a third type shows up, stop and record how far you got. It's correct. But each start rescans trees that earlier starts already covered. So it's quadratic.
say.insight: Here's the thing. Strip away the story. This is the longest subarray with at most two distinct values. So we use a sliding window, with a count for each type inside it. Grow on the right. When a third type shows up, shrink from the left until one type is completely gone. Every tree enters and leaves at most once.
say.anim: We start with an empty basket and two pointers, left and best, both zero. Right moves to index zero, adding fruit one, giving a window length of one. Right advances to index one, adding fruit two, now best grows to two. Adding fruit three creates three distinct types, so we must shrink from the left. Fruit one is removed from the basket, and left moves forward to index one. Right moves to index three, adding another fruit two, best becomes three. Right reaches index four, adding fruit two again, best updates to four. The loop ends and the function returns four, the longest valid basket length.
say.code: Let's walk the code. We keep a map from fruit type to its count in the window. For each right index, we take the fruit at r. Now, three types? We shrink from the left, dropping one count at a time. When a type is fully gone from the window, we delete it. Once the window is valid again, we record its length.
say.outro: Linear time, constant space. The pattern is a sliding window with a frequency map. The template for longest subarray with at most k distinct values.

fruit-into-baskets.title: Fruit Into Baskets
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container the problem expects for our method.
The method totalFruit takes the list of fruits and returns the largest number of fruits we can pick.
We create a default dictionary called basket_count to track how many of each fruit type sit inside the window.
We set left to zero, marking the start of our sliding window.
We set best to zero, which will hold the longest valid window found so far.
This comment says the first step is growing the window by taking in the fruit at the right end.
We loop right across every index of the fruits list, so each tree gets added once as the window's right edge.
We add one to the count of the fruit at right, since it now belongs to the window.
This comment explains that when the window holds more than two fruit types, we must shrink it from the left.
While the basket holds more than two distinct types, we keep shrinking the window because it is invalid.
We look up which fruit type sits at the left edge, since that is the one we will drop.
We subtract one from that fruit's count because it is leaving the window.
This comment notes that a type must be fully removed once none of it remains in the window.
If the count of that left fruit has fallen to zero, then the type is no longer in the window.
We delete that type from the dictionary so the number of keys reflects the true count of distinct types.
We move left forward by one, actually shrinking the window past the dropped fruit.
This comment says that after the window is valid, we measure its length.
The window length is right minus left plus one, counting both endpoints.
We check whether this window is longer than the best we have recorded.
If it is longer, we update best to the new window length.
After processing every tree, we return best as the maximum number of fruits we can pick.

ransom-note.hook: Cut letters from a magazine to spell a note. Count once, then spend the counts.
ransom-note.ask: Given a note and a magazine, return true if the note can be spelled using letters cut from the magazine, where each magazine letter can be used only once.
ransom-note.exampleWhy: The magazine has two a's and one b, enough to supply both a's in the note.

brute.idea: For each note letter, search the remaining magazine letters for a match and cross it out.
steps: Copy the magazine into a list
Find each note letter in the list
Missing? return False
Found? remove that copy
brute.whySlow: Each search and removal scans the list: 100,000 letters each side is about 10 billion steps.

optimal.insight: Only letter counts matter. Count the magazine once, then each note letter just spends one from its count.
steps: Count every magazine letter
Walk the note letter by letter
Count already zero? Not enough letters
Otherwise spend one

pitfalls: Quick reject: a note longer than the magazine can never be built.
Space is O(1): at most 26 lowercase keys.

say.intro: Okay, Ransom Note. We get a note and a magazine. Can we spell the note by cutting letters out of the magazine? Each magazine letter can be used only once. The note is a a, and the magazine is a a b. The answer's true. The magazine has two a's to give.
say.brute: The brute force crosses letters off by hand. Copy the magazine into a list. For each note letter, search the list. Missing? Return false. Found? Remove that one copy and move on. But every search and removal scans the list. So the cost is the note length times the magazine length.
say.insight: Here's the thing. Positions in the magazine don't matter. Only how many of each letter. So count the magazine once into a table. Then walk the note. Each letter spends one from its count. If a count is already zero when we need it, we've run out. And each lookup is constant time.
say.anim: We start with ransomNote 'aa' and magazine 'aab' to compare. Counting magazine letters gives two a's and one b stored in count. We check the first letter, c equals a, against the counted magazine. Since count of a is not zero, we subtract one, leaving one a. Moving to the second letter, count now shows one a and one b. We subtract again from a, bringing its count down to zero. All ransom note letters are satisfied, with b left untouched at one. The function returns true, confirming the note can be constructed.
say.code: Let's walk the code. First, we build a counter from the magazine. That's our supply of each letter. Then we loop over the note. If a letter's count is zero, we ran out of this letter, so we return false right away. Otherwise, we spend one copy. If the loop finishes, every letter was covered. Return true.
say.outro: Linear time, constant space for lowercase letters. The pattern is arrays and hashing. When only quantities matter, count them instead of searching.

ransom-note.title: Ransom Note
lineNotes: We define a Solution class that holds the method we need to write for this problem.
The method canConstruct takes the ransom note and the magazine and returns true or false.
We build a counter of the magazine so we know how many of each letter we can cut out.
We walk through every character of the ransom note, one letter at a time.
If the counter shows zero copies of this letter left, the magazine cannot supply it.
In that case we return false right away, since the note can't be spelled.
Otherwise we spend one copy of that letter by lowering its count by one, so it can't be reused.
If we get through every letter without running out, we return true because the note can be built.

cinema-seat-allocation.hook: A billion rows, a few thousand bookings. Only the touched rows need any thought.
cinema-seat-allocation.ask: A cinema has n rows of ten seats. Some seats are reserved. A family of four needs seats 2-5, 4-7 or 6-9 in one row. Return the most families you can seat.
cinema-seat-allocation.exampleWhy: Row 1 fits only 4-7, row 2 fits only 2-5, row 3 is open inside so it takes 2-5 and 6-9.

brute.idea: Go through every row, gather its reserved seats by scanning the whole list, and check the three blocks.
steps: For each of the n rows
Scan all reservations for that row
Seat 2 if left and right free, else 1 if any block free
brute.whySlow: n can be a billion rows: even one pass over the rows, let alone rescanning bookings, is far too slow.

optimal.insight: Untouched rows always hold two families. Only rows with bookings need checking, each as a 10-bit mask.
steps: Group bookings by row as a bitmask
Ignore seats 1 and 10: they block nothing
Untouched rows give 2 each
Touched rows: 2 if left and right free, else 1 if any

codeNotes.note: Mark the seat bit in its row
Otherwise one block may still fit

pitfalls: Looping over all n rows times out: n can be 10^9.
Counting rows with only seats 1 or 10 as touched loses families.

say.intro: Okay, Cinema Seat Allocation. A cinema has n rows of ten seats, and some are booked. A family of four must sit together, in seats two to five, four to seven, or six to nine. How many families fit? In our example, with three rows, four families fit.
say.brute: The brute force walks every row. For each row, it scans the booking list to find its taken seats. Then it checks the three blocks. Left and right both free? Two families. Any block free? One. So what's the catch? n can be a billion rows. Even one pass over the rows is way too slow.
say.insight: Here's the thing. A row with no bookings always seats two families. So we count all those rows with one multiplication. Only rows with bookings need checking. And there are at most ten thousand. Store each as a bitmask of taken seats. Skip seats one and ten, since they block nothing. Then each row is a few bit tests.
say.anim: We start building a map of reserved seats per row, ignoring aisle seats outside columns two through nine. Row one gets seats two, three, and eight marked, forming bitmask 268 for that row. Row two gets seat six marked, giving it a bitmask of 64. Row three's seats one and ten are outside the two to nine range, so they're skipped. We define left, mid, and right masks, then total starts at 2 since one untouched row holds two families. Row one's mask 268 blocks all three regions, so only one family fits there, total becomes 3. Row two's mask 64 blocks the mid region, so only one family fits, total becomes 4. The loop finishes and the function returns the final answer, four families seated total.
say.code: Let's walk the code. First, aisle seats one and ten never matter, so we skip them. For every other booking, we mark the seat bit in its row. Then we set up three masks, for the left, middle, and right blocks. Free rows seat two families, so they're counted in bulk. For each booked row, two if left and right are clear. Otherwise, one block may still fit.
say.outro: Time and space depend only on bookings, not on n. The pattern is greedy counting with bitmasks. Handle the common case in bulk.

cinema-seat-allocation.title: Cinema Seat Allocation
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, as the problem platform expects.
This method takes the number of rows and the reserved seat list, and returns the maximum number of families.
We create a dictionary that maps each row with relevant reservations to a bitmask, defaulting to zero.
We loop over every reserved seat, unpacking its row number and seat number.
Only seats two through nine matter, since seats one and ten never belong to any family block.
We set the bit for that seat in the row's mask, marking it as taken.
We define three masks for the family blocks: seats two to five, four to seven, and six to nine.
Rows without relevant reservations fit two families each, so we start the total with two times the untouched rows.
We now go through the mask of each row that has at least one relevant reservation.
If both the left and right blocks are completely free, this row fits two families.
Otherwise, if any one of the left, middle or right blocks is free, we can still fit one family.
In that case we add one family to the total.
A row where all three blocks are blocked adds nothing, so we simply move on.
Finally we return the total number of families we managed to seat.

combinations.hook: Choose k numbers from 1 to n. Grow a pick list, record it, then undo and try the next.
combinations.ask: Given n and k, return every possible group of k different numbers chosen from 1 to n. Order inside a group does not matter, and the groups can be returned in any order.
combinations.exampleWhy: There are 4 choose 2 = 6 ways to pick two numbers from 1 to 4.

brute.idea: Decide in or out for every number from 1 to n, building all subsets, and keep the ones of size k.
steps: At number i, branch: include it or skip it
Past n: keep the subset if it has k items
brute.whySlow: It explores all 2^n subsets even though only n choose k are wanted, wasting most branches.

optimal.insight: Only extend a pick list that can still reach size k. Choose the next number from start onward, stopping early when too few remain.
steps: Start with an empty pick list
Size k: record a copy
Try each next number that leaves enough room
Recurse, then pop to undo

codeNotes.note: Store a copy, not the live list

codeNotes.match: for i in range(start, n - need + 2):
codeNotes.note: Stop when too few numbers remain
Only larger numbers next: no repeats
Undo the choice, try the next

pitfalls: Appending comb itself, not a copy, leaves res full of empty lists.
Starting the next loop at i + 1 prevents [2,1] duplicating [1,2].

say.intro: Okay, Combinations. We get n and k. We list every group of k different numbers from one to n. Order inside a group doesn't matter. With n of four and k of two, there are six groups. One two, one three, one four, two three, two four, and three four.
say.brute: The brute force builds every subset. For each number from one to n, branch twice. Include it, or skip it. When we run past n, keep the subset only if it has exactly k numbers. It's correct. But it explores two to the n subsets. Most have the wrong size. That's wasted work.
say.insight: Here's the idea. Only build lists that can still succeed. We keep a current pick list. The next number always comes from a start point upward. So numbers only increase, and no group repeats. And if there aren't enough numbers left to reach k? Stop early. When the list is full, record a copy. Then pop, and try the next option.
say.anim: We start with n equal 4 and k equal 2, building combinations from scratch. We pick 1 first, appending it so comb becomes just 1. Adding 2 completes a pair, so comb 1 and 2 gets saved to results. Backtracking pops 2, then tries 3 and 4, saving pairs 1 3 and 1 4. Starting fresh from 2, we again extend forward, saving pairs 2 3 and 2 4. Finally starting from 3, we extend to 4, saving the last pair 3 and 4. All start points are exhausted, so the backtracking finishes completely. The final answer lists all six pairs from 1 2 up to 3 4.
say.code: Let's walk the code. If the combination has k numbers, a full combination is ready. We store a copy, not the live list. Why? Because the live list keeps changing. Otherwise, we loop, but we stop when too few numbers remain. We push a number and recurse with only larger numbers next. That's what prevents repeats. Then we undo the choice, and try the next.
say.outro: Work proportional to the output size. The pattern is backtracking. Choose, explore, undo, with pruning so dead branches never get entered.

combinations.title: Combinations
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the standard wrapper for this problem's method.
The combine method takes n and k and returns a list of lists of integers, one per combination.
We create res as an empty list that will collect every finished combination.
We create comb as an empty list that holds the numbers picked so far in the current path.
We define a recursive helper called backtrack that takes start, the smallest number we are allowed to pick next.
If the length of comb equals k, then we have a complete group of the right size.
We append a copy of comb to res, since comb keeps changing and we need to save this snapshot.
We return right away, because there is nothing more to add to a full group.
We compute need as how many more numbers are still required to reach size k.
We loop i from start up to n minus need plus one, which stops early when too few numbers remain to finish.
We choose the number i by appending it to comb.
We recurse with start set to i plus one, so later picks are larger and never repeat numbers or orderings.
We undo the choice by popping i off comb, so the next loop value begins from a clean state.
We kick off the search by calling backtrack with start at one, the smallest available number.
After all branches are explored, we return res holding every combination.

single-number-ii.hook: Everything appears three times except one number. Count bits modulo three to find it.
single-number-ii.ask: Every number in the array appears exactly three times, except one that appears once. Return that single number, using linear time and constant extra space.
single-number-ii.exampleWhy: 0 and 1 each appear three times; 99 appears only once.

brute.idea: For each number, count how many times it appears in the whole array. The one with count 1 is the answer.
steps: Pick each number x
Count x across the whole array
Count is 1? return x
brute.whySlow: Every count rescans the array: 30,000 numbers means close to a billion comparisons.

optimal.insight: Track each bit's count modulo 3 with two masks: ones holds bits seen once, twos bits seen twice. Triples cancel to zero.
steps: ones: bits seen 1 time (mod 3)
twos: bits seen 2 times (mod 3)
Fold in x: update ones, then twos
Third sighting clears a bit from both
Leftover ones is the single number

codeNotes.note: Bits seen once so far, mod 3
Bits seen twice so far, mod 3
Toggle into ones unless already twice
Move to twos; third time clears

pitfalls: A hash map count is O(n) space: correct but fails the constant-space rule.
Alternative: sum each of 32 bits mod 3; handle the sign bit in Python.

say.intro: Okay, Single Number Two. Every number appears exactly three times, except one, which appears once. Find it, in linear time, with constant extra space. In zero, one, zero, one, zero, one, ninety nine, the zeros and ones come in threes. So the answer is ninety nine.
say.brute: The brute force takes each number and counts it by scanning the whole array again. Whichever number has a count of one wins. No extra memory, which is nice. But every count is a full scan. That's quadratic. Too slow for thirty thousand numbers.
say.insight: Think about one bit position at a time. Across the triples, each bit is set a multiple of three times. Only the single number adds an extra one. So count each bit modulo three. Two masks are enough. Ones holds bits seen once. Twos holds bits seen twice. On the third sighting, a bit clears from both. The triples just vanish.
say.anim: We start with both ones and twos set to zero, tracking bit counts modulo three. Processing the first zero, the masks update but ones and twos stay at zero. Now x is one, so ones becomes one, capturing this bit seen once. Another zero arrives, leaving ones and twos unchanged at one and zero. A second one appears, moving that bit from ones into twos since it's seen twice. More zeros and ones cycle through, with twos toggling back to zero after three occurrences. Finally x is ninety nine, and ones updates to capture this unique value. The loop ends, and the function returns ones, giving the final answer ninety nine.
say.code: Let's walk the code. Ones tracks bits seen once so far, modulo three. Twos tracks bits seen twice. For each number, we toggle it into ones, unless the bit's already in twos. Then we move it to twos. And on the third time, it clears from both. At the end, only the single number remains, sitting in ones.
say.outro: Linear time, constant space. The pattern is bit manipulation. Two masks act as a tiny counter, running on every bit at once.

single-number-ii.title: Single Number II
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container the problem expects for our method.
The method singleNumber takes the list of numbers and returns the one value that appears only once.
We start ones at zero, so no bit has yet been seen exactly once.
We start twos at zero as well, so no bit has yet been seen exactly twice.
We loop through every number x in the array, updating our two masks as we go.
We toggle the bits of x into ones, but only keep those bits that are not already in twos.
We toggle the bits of x into twos, but clear those bits that just landed in ones.
After all triples cancel out to zero, ones holds only the bits of the single number, so we return it.

longest-valid-parentheses.hook: Find the longest well-formed run of brackets. A stack of indices measures it as you go.
longest-valid-parentheses.ask: Given a string of open and close parentheses, return the length of the longest substring that is a valid, properly matched sequence of brackets.
longest-valid-parentheses.exampleWhy: The substring "()()" in the middle is valid and has length 4; no longer valid run exists.

brute.idea: Start at every index and extend right, tracking the open-minus-close balance. Balance zero means a valid run.
steps: Fix a start index i
Extend j, updating the balance
Balance negative: stop this start
Balance zero: record j - i + 1
brute.whySlow: Every start rescans the rest of the string: 30,000 characters is about 450 million steps.

optimal.insight: Keep a stack of indices with a base marker below. After a match, the index on top marks where the current valid run began.
steps: Push -1 as the starting base
Open bracket: push its index
Close bracket: pop
Stack empty: this close is the new base
Otherwise run length is i - stack top

pitfalls: Counting matched pairs overall gives wrong answers for "()(()": runs must be contiguous.
A two-pass left/right counter also works in O(1) space.

say.intro: Okay, Longest Valid Parentheses. We get a string of open and close brackets. What's the longest stretch where every bracket is properly matched? For close, open, close, open, close, close, the answer is four. That's the open close open close in the middle.
say.brute: The brute force starts at every index and extends right, tracking a balance. Plus one for open, minus one for close. If the balance goes negative, that start is dead. When it hits zero, we've got a valid run, so record its length. But each start rescans the string. That's quadratic.
say.insight: Here's the trick. Use a stack of indices, not characters. Seed it with minus one, as a base. Push every open bracket's index. On a close, pop. Is the stack now empty? Then this close bracket is unmatched. It becomes the new base. Otherwise, the top is the barrier right before our valid run. So the length is i minus that index.
say.anim: We start with a stack holding just a base marker, negative one, and best at zero. At index zero we see a closing bracket, so we pop, the stack empties, and we push zero as a new base. At index one we hit an opening bracket, pushing its index, so the stack becomes zero and one. At index two a closing bracket pops the stack back to zero, and best updates to two. Index three opens again, pushing three, giving stack zero and three. Index four closes, popping to zero, and best jumps up to four. Index five closes with an empty stack, so we push five as a fresh base marker. The loop ends and the function returns four as the longest valid parentheses length.
say.code: Let's walk the code. We start the stack with minus one. That's the base index, before the string. For an open bracket, we push its index. For a close, we pop to match it. If that left the stack empty, it was an unmatched close. So we reset the base to this index. Otherwise, the length since the last barrier is a candidate for best.
say.outro: Linear time, linear space. The pattern is a stack of indices. The top always marks the last barrier.

longest-valid-parentheses.title: Longest Valid Parentheses
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container for the method the problem asks us to write.
This method takes the string s of parentheses and returns the length of the longest valid substring as an integer.
We start the stack with negative one, a base marker meaning the position just before the string begins.
We set best to zero, which tracks the longest valid length found so far.
We loop through the string, getting each index i and its character c together.
If the character is an open parenthesis, we need to remember it for a later match.
We push its index onto the stack so a future close parenthesis can pair with it.
Otherwise the character is a close parenthesis, so we try to match it against the stack.
We pop the top of the stack, which removes either a matching open index or the old base marker.
If the stack is now empty, the close parenthesis had nothing to match and the popped item was the base.
We push the current index as the new base marker, since no valid run can cross this position.
Otherwise the pop removed a real open parenthesis, so we have a valid match.
The valid run extends from just after the new stack top to i, so we update best with that length if larger.
After scanning everything, we return best as the longest valid parentheses length.

online-stock-span.hook: Each day, how many days back was the price no higher? Fold old days into a monotonic stack.
online-stock-span.ask: Design a class that receives one stock price per day and returns its span: the number of consecutive days, ending today, whose price was at most today's price.
online-stock-span.exampleWhy: 75 covers 60, 70, 60 and itself: span 4. Then 85 covers everything back to after 100: span 6.

brute.idea: Store every price. On each call, walk backward from today while prices are at most today's price.
steps: Append today's price to the history
Walk back while prices are ≤ today
Return how far we walked
brute.whySlow: A rising market makes every call walk the whole history: 10,000 calls is 50 million steps.

optimal.insight: A day beaten by today can never matter again. Keep a decreasing stack of (price, span) and absorb smaller days.
steps: Start today's span at 1
Pop days with price ≤ today
Add each popped span to today's
Push (price, span) and return span

codeNotes.note: Pairs of price and span, decreasing
Smaller or equal days get absorbed

pitfalls: Use ≤, not <: equal prices count toward the span.
Each price is pushed and popped once, so total work is linear.

say.intro: Okay, Online Stock Span. We design a class that gets one stock price per day. It returns the span. How many days in a row, ending today, had a price at most today's? For one hundred, eighty, sixty, seventy, sixty, seventy five, eighty five, the spans are one, one, one, two, one, four, six.
say.brute: The brute force keeps the full price history. Each day, it appends the new price. Then it walks backward while earlier prices are at most today's, counting days. Sounds fine. But in a steadily rising market, every call walks the whole history. So each call can take linear time.
say.insight: Here's the thing. Once today beats an earlier day, that earlier day can never stop a future walk. Why? Anything that beats today beats it too. So fold it in. Keep a stack of price and span pairs, with prices decreasing. Pop every pair today beats, and add its span to today's. Each day is pushed and popped once.
say.anim: We start with an empty stack, ready to track prices and their spans. Price 100 arrives, span starts at 1, and since the stack is empty it just gets pushed. Price 80 is smaller than 100, so no popping happens and span stays 1. Price 60 is also smaller than the top, so it gets pushed with span 1 too. Price 70 beats 60, so we pop it, adding its span to get span 2, then push. Price 60 again is smaller than the top, so it pushes directly with span 1. Price 75 beats both 60 and 70, popping them and accumulating span up to 4. Finally price 85 beats everything remaining, popping down to span 6, the final answer.
say.code: Let's walk the code. The stack holds pairs of price and span, decreasing. In next, the span starts at one, because today always counts. Then, smaller or equal days get absorbed. We pop each one. And we inherit the days they covered, by adding their span. Finally, today becomes a summary entry. We push it, and return the span.
say.outro: Amortized constant time per call. The pattern is a monotonic stack. Keep only days that still matter, and let each new day absorb the rest.

online-stock-span.title: Online Stock Span
lineNotes: We define a class called StockSpanner that will receive one stock price per day and report its span.
The constructor runs once when the spanner is created, setting up the state we need to remember past days.
We start with an empty stack that will hold pairs of price and span, kept in decreasing order of price.
The next method takes today's price and returns today's span, being called once for each new day.
We start today's span at one, since today always counts itself as a day at most today's price.
While the stack has entries and the top price is at most today's price, those days are beaten and can be absorbed.
We pop the top entry and add its span to ours, because all the days it covered also count for today.
Now we push today's price with its span onto the stack, so future days can absorb it if they beat it.
We return today's span, which is the count of consecutive days ending today with price at most today's.

remove-element.hook: Delete a value from an array in place. A write pointer keeps only what stays.
remove-element.ask: Remove every occurrence of val from the array in place. Return k, the number of remaining elements, with those elements placed in the first k slots in any order.
remove-element.exampleWhy: Five values are not 2: 0, 1, 3, 0, 4. They fill the first five slots.

brute.idea: Repeatedly find an occurrence of val and delete it from the list, shifting everything after it left.
steps: Search the list for val
Delete it, shifting later items left
Repeat until none remain
brute.whySlow: Each delete shifts the tail: an array full of val costs about n squared over two moves.

optimal.insight: We never need to delete. Copy each kept value forward to a write pointer; whatever lies past it is ignored.
steps: k is the next write slot
Scan every element x
x is not val: write it at k, advance k
Return k

codeNotes.note: Next slot for a kept value

pitfalls: Deleting from a list while iterating it skips elements.
The judge ignores everything after index k; do not bother clearing it.

say.intro: Okay, Remove Element. We get an array and a value. We remove every copy of that value, in place. Then return how many elements remain, sitting in the first slots. Zero, one, two, two, three, zero, four, two. Remove the twos, and five numbers are left. Zero, one, three, zero, four.
say.brute: The brute force deletes as it goes. Walk the list. When the current element equals the value, delete it. That shifts everything after it one step left. It works. But every deletion moves the whole tail. So an array full of the value costs quadratic time.
say.insight: Here's the thing. We never actually need to delete anything. The judge only reads the first k slots. So keep a write pointer. Scan every element. When it isn't the value, copy it to the write spot, and move the pointer forward. Each element gets read once, and written at most once.
say.anim: We start with k at zero, our write pointer into the array. As x is 0, not equal to val, we copy it forward and bump k to 1. Next x is 1, kept again, copied in place, and k becomes 2. Now x is 2, matching val, so it's skipped and k stays put. We keep skipping value 2 entries, then copy 3, 0, and 4 forward in turn. Each kept value overwrites the next slot, pushing k up to 5. The last element is 2 again, so it's ignored, leaving k unchanged. The loop ends and the function returns k, giving the final answer 5.
say.code: Let's walk the code. k marks the next slot for a kept value, starting at zero. We loop over every number. We keep everything except the value. When we keep one, we copy it forward into place at slot k, then bump k. When the loop ends, k is the count of kept values. So we return it.
say.outro: Linear time, constant space. The pattern is two pointers. A reader scans everything, and a writer only advances for keepers.

remove-element.title: Remove Element
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container the judge expects for our method.
The removeElement method takes the list nums and the value val to remove, and returns how many elements remain.
We set k to zero, and it serves as the write pointer marking where the next kept value goes.
We loop over every value x in nums, reading each element once from left to right.
We check whether x differs from val, because only values we want to keep should be copied forward.
We copy x into the slot at position k, overwriting an older value that is no longer needed.
We advance k by one so the next kept value lands in the following slot.
We return k, the count of kept elements, which now fill the first k slots of nums.

smallest-stable-index-i.hook: Prefix max on the left, suffix min on the right. Precompute one, sweep with the other.
smallest-stable-index-i.ask: For each index i, the instability is the largest value up to i minus the smallest value from i onward. Return the first index whose instability is at most k, or -1 if none is.
smallest-stable-index-i.exampleWhy: At index 3 the prefix max is 5 and the suffix min is 4, so instability is 1 ≤ 3. Earlier ones are 5, 5, 4.

brute.idea: For every index, compute the prefix max and the suffix min from scratch and test the difference.
steps: For each index i
Scan nums[0..i] for the max
Scan nums[i..n-1] for the min
Difference ≤ k? return i
brute.whySlow: Each index rescans the whole array: twice the work of the answer, times n.

optimal.insight: Suffix minimums can be precomputed right to left. Then a left-to-right sweep keeps a running prefix max.
steps: Build suf[i] = min of nums[i..n-1]
Sweep left to right with a running max
max - suf[i] ≤ k? return i
No index found: return -1

codeNotes.note: Min from i to the end

pitfalls: Both ranges include index i itself; do not exclude it from either side.

say.intro: Okay, Smallest Stable Index. For each index, take the biggest value from the start up to it. Subtract the smallest value from it to the end. That's the instability. What's the first index where it's at most k? For five, zero, one, four, with k of three, the answer is index three.
say.brute: The brute force handles each index on its own. Scan the left part for its max. Scan the right part for its min. Test the difference. The first index that passes wins. But each index rescans the whole array. So it's quadratic.
say.insight: Here's the thing. Both pieces are running values. The prefix max only grows as we move right. So one variable can carry it. The suffix min is easiest from the other end. So precompute every suffix min in one right to left pass. Then sweep left to right, updating the running max. Each index is a constant time check.
say.anim: We start with the array five, zero, one, four, and k equal to three. We build a suffix minimum array by scanning right to left. The suffix minimum array ends up as zero, zero, one, four. Now best starts at five, the first element, for our prefix maximum. At each index we update best and check if best minus suffix min fits within k. At indices one and two the gap stays too large, so we keep scanning. At index three best stays five and suffix min is four, giving a gap of one. Since one is within k, we return index three as the smallest stable index.
say.code: Let's walk the code. First, we build the suffix minimum array. Each entry is the min from i to the end, filled from the right. Then we sweep, keeping a running prefix maximum. At each index, we compare that max with the suffix min. If the difference is at most k, the first stable index wins. We return it right away.
say.outro: Linear time, linear space. The pattern is prefix and suffix arrays. Precompute one direction, sweep the other.

smallest-stable-index-i.title: Smallest Stable Index I
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container the judge expects for our method.
The method takes the list of numbers and the threshold k, and returns the first stable index or negative one.
We store the length of nums in n so we can loop over it cleanly.
We copy nums into suf, so the last entry is already correct as its own suffix minimum.
We loop i from the second to last index down to zero, moving right to left.
Each suffix minimum becomes the smaller of the current number and the suffix minimum just to its right.
We start the running prefix maximum, called best, at the first number in the list.
Now we sweep every index from left to right, checking instability as we go.
We update best to the larger of itself and the current number, keeping the prefix maximum through index i.
Instability is best minus the suffix minimum at i, and we check whether it is at most k.
If the check passes, this is the first stable index, so we return i immediately.
If the loop finishes without finding any stable index, we return negative one.

running-sum-of-1d-array.hook: Each running total is just the previous total plus one number. Never add from scratch.
running-sum-of-1d-array.ask: Given an array, return a new array where position i holds the sum of all numbers from the start up to and including position i.

brute.idea: For each position, add up every number from the start to that position from scratch.
steps: For each index i
Sum nums[0..i] from scratch
Append the total
brute.whySlow: Each total re-adds numbers already summed: n positions times up to n additions.

optimal.insight: The running sum at i is the running sum at i - 1 plus nums[i]. Build it in place, left to right.
steps: Leave nums[0] as it is
Add the previous total into each next slot
Return the updated array

pitfalls: Modifying in place destroys the input; copy first if the caller needs it.

say.intro: Okay, Running Sum of a One D Array. We get an array of numbers. We return an array where each spot holds the total of everything up to that point. For three, one, two, ten, one, the running sums are three, four, six, sixteen, and seventeen.
say.brute: The brute force computes every total from scratch. For each position, start a sum at zero. Add every number from the beginning up to there. Append it to the result. It's correct. But we keep re adding the same numbers over and over. That's quadratic.
say.insight: Here's the thing. Each running total is just the previous total, plus one new number. Sixteen is six plus ten. Seventeen is sixteen plus one. So we never need to start over. Walk the array once, left to right. Add the previous slot into the current one. The array becomes its own running sum. No extra memory.
say.anim: We start with the array 3, 1, 2, 10, 1, ready to build running sums. At index 1, we add the previous value, turning 1 into 4. At index 2, we add nums at index 1, making 2 become 6. At index 3, adding the prior sum turns 10 into 16. At index 4, we add 16 to 1, giving us 17. The loop finishes since every element now holds its cumulative sum. The function returns the final running sum array: 3, 4, 6, 16, 17.
say.code: Let's walk the code. The first total is just the first number, so it stays put. Then we loop from index one to the end. Each slot becomes the previous total plus this number. Why does that work? Because the previous slot already holds its running total. At the end, the array holds prefix sums, and we return it.
say.outro: Linear time, constant extra space. The pattern is the prefix sum. The building block behind range queries and lots of subarray problems.

running-sum-of-1d-array.title: Running Sum of 1d Array
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container that the interview platform expects for our answer.
This method takes the list of numbers and will return a list of the same length holding running sums.
We loop with i starting at one, because the first element is already its own running sum.
We add the previous element, which already holds the running sum so far, into the current element, updating it in place.
We return the same list, which now contains the running sum at every position.

is-subsequence.hook: Can s be found inside t, in order, skipping letters? Walk both strings with two pointers.
is-subsequence.ask: Given strings s and t, return true if s can be formed by deleting some letters from t without changing the order of the remaining letters.
is-subsequence.exampleWhy: a, b and c appear in t in that order: a at 0, b at 2, c at 5.

brute.idea: Compute the longest common subsequence of s and t with a DP table. s is a subsequence exactly when that equals len(s).
steps: Table cell = LCS of s prefix and t prefix
Match: diagonal plus one
No match: best of up or left
Compare the final cell to len(s)
brute.whySlow: It fills a full table of 100 by 10,000 cells, when one pass over t is enough.

optimal.insight: Matching the next letter of s as early as possible in t is never worse. So greedily scan t once.
steps: i points into s, j into t
Letters equal: advance i
Always advance j
i reached the end of s? true

codeNotes.match: while i < len(s) and j < len(t):

pitfalls: Follow-up with many s: precompute next positions of each letter in t, then binary search.

say.intro: Okay, Is Subsequence. We get two strings, s and t. Can we make s by deleting some letters from t, keeping the rest in order? Take a b c inside a h b g d c. The answer's true. The a, the b, and the c show up in t in that order.
say.brute: One heavy approach builds the longest common subsequence table. Each cell holds the answer for a prefix of s and a prefix of t. If the final value equals the length of s, it's a subsequence. That works. But it costs the product of the two lengths, in both time and memory.
say.insight: Here's the thing. We don't need the whole table. Matching the next letter of s at its earliest spot in t is never a mistake. Why? It leaves the most of t for the remaining letters. So walk both strings with two pointers. When letters match, advance in s. Always advance in t.
say.anim: We start with s equal abc and t equal ahbgdc, pointers i and j both at zero. At position zero, s of i is a and t of j is a, they match, so i moves forward. Next, t has h which does not match b, so only j advances, skipping it. Now t has b, matching s of i, so i increments to two while scanning continues. Letters g and d in t do not match c, so j keeps moving past them. Finally t reaches c, matching s of i, so i increments to three, completing s. The loop ends since i now equals the length of s, meaning all letters matched. The function returns true, confirming abc is indeed a subsequence of ahbgdc.
say.code: Let's walk the code. Both pointers start at zero. We stop when either string ends. At each step, we compare the current letters. If they match, we're greedy. We take the earliest match, and move forward in s. Either way, t always moves forward. At the end, did i reach the length of s? Then all of s was matched.
say.outro: Linear in the length of t, constant space. The pattern is two pointers with a greedy match. The go to move for subsequence checks.

is-subsequence.title: Is Subsequence
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the wrapper this problem's starter code expects for the method below.
This method takes the pattern string s and the larger string t, and returns a true or false answer.
We set i to zero, so it points at the next letter of s we still need to match.
We set j to zero, so it points at the current letter of t we are scanning.
We loop while both strings have letters left, stopping once s is fully matched or t runs out.
We compare the current letter of s with the current letter of t to see if they match.
On a match, we advance i, since matching this letter early is never worse and we now need the next one.
Whether or not we matched, we advance j so we scan t exactly once from left to right.
Finally we return true only if i reached the length of s, meaning every letter of s was matched in order.

path-sum-ii.hook: Every root-to-leaf path that hits the target. Walk the tree with one shared path list.
path-sum-ii.ask: Given a binary tree and a target sum, return every path from the root down to a leaf whose node values add up exactly to the target, as lists of values.
path-sum-ii.exampleWhy: 5+4+11+2 = 22 and 5+8+4+5 = 22. Every other root-to-leaf path misses 22.

brute.idea: Collect every root-to-leaf path as a brand-new list, then keep the ones whose sum equals the target.
steps: DFS, copying the path at every node
At a leaf, save the full path
Afterwards, keep paths with the target sum
brute.whySlow: It copies the path at every node and stores every leaf path, even the ones that miss the target.

optimal.insight: Carry the remaining sum down the tree and share one path list: push on the way down, pop on the way back up.
steps: Push node value, subtract it from remaining
Leaf with remaining 0: save a copy
