Recurse left and right
Pop the value before returning

codeNotes.note: What the rest must add up to
Leaf that hits the target exactly
Save a copy of the path

pitfalls: Check for a leaf: stopping at remain 0 on an inner node is wrong.
Values can be negative, so you cannot prune when remain goes below zero.

say.intro: Okay, Path Sum Two. We get a binary tree and a target. We return every root to leaf path whose values add up to the target. With a target of twenty two, there are two. Five, four, eleven, two. And five, eight, four, five.
say.brute: The brute force collects everything first. Walk the tree, copying the path at every node. At each leaf, save the whole path. Then keep only paths summing to twenty two. It works. But it copies at every step, and stores every leaf path, even all the ones that miss.
say.insight: Here's the trick. Do the checking on the way down. Carry the amount still needed, subtracting each node as we go. And share one path list for the whole search. Push a value when we enter a node. Pop it when we leave. Only when a leaf brings the remainder to exactly zero do we copy the path.
say.anim: We start at root five, with target sum twenty two and an empty path. We push four and eleven onto the path, remaining sum drops to thirteen. At leaf seven, remaining sum is negative five, so this path fails. We push two, remaining sum hits zero, so path five four eleven two is saved. We pop back up, trying the right subtree from eight with remaining sum nine. Pushing four then leaf five, remaining sum reaches zero, saving five eight four five. We try leaf one instead, but remaining sum four isn't zero, so it fails. Final answer returned is five four eleven two, and five eight four five.
say.code: Let's walk the code. When we step down to a node, we extend the path with its value. Then we subtract it. That's what the rest must add up to. Is this a leaf that hits the target exactly? Then we save a copy of the path. Not the live list, a copy. We recurse into both children. Finally, we step back up and undo, popping the value.
say.outro: Linear extra space for the path, with copies only for real answers. The pattern is tree depth first search with backtracking. Push, explore, pop.

path-sum-ii.title: Path Sum II
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container the problem expects for our method.
The pathSum method takes the tree root and a target sum, and returns a list of paths.
We create res as an empty list that will collect every valid root to leaf path.
We create path as one shared list that tracks the values on the current route from the root.
We define a helper called dfs that visits a node while carrying the remaining sum still needed.
If the node is empty, we have fallen off the tree and there is nothing to process.
So we return immediately, ending this branch of the recursion.
We push the current node's value onto the path because we are stepping onto this node.
We subtract the node's value from remain so it reflects what is still needed below.
If the node is a leaf and remain is exactly zero, this path adds up to the target.
We append a copy of path to res, since path will keep changing as we backtrack.
We recurse into the left child, passing along the updated remaining sum.
We recurse into the right child the same way, exploring the other subtree.
We pop the node's value off path to backtrack, restoring the path for the caller.
We start the search at the root with the full target sum as the remaining amount.
Finally we return res, which holds all the valid root to leaf paths.

rotate-array.hook: Rotate right by k in place, with no extra array. Three reversals do it.
rotate-array.ask: Given an array and a number k, shift every element k places to the right, wrapping the ones that fall off the end around to the front. Change the array in place.
rotate-array.exampleWhy: The last three numbers, 5, 6, 7, wrap around to the front; the rest shift right by three.

brute.idea: Rotate by one step, k times: save the last element, shift everything right by one, put it at the front.
steps: Reduce k modulo n
Save the last element
Shift all others right by one
Put it at index 0; repeat k times
brute.whySlow: Each single step moves the whole array: n and k near 100,000 means 10 billion moves.

optimal.insight: Reversing the whole array puts the last k at the front, but backwards. Reverse each part again to fix their order.
steps: k = k mod n
Reverse the whole array
Reverse the first k elements
Reverse the remaining n - k

codeNotes.note: Last k move to the front
Fix the order of the front
Fix the order of the back

pitfalls: Forgetting k %= n breaks when k is larger than the array.
A copy with nums[:] = nums[-k:] + nums[:-k] is O(n) extra space.

say.intro: Okay, Rotate Array. We shift every element k places to the right. Elements that fall off the end wrap around to the front. And we do it in place. For one through seven, with k of three, we get five, six, seven, one, two, three, four.
say.brute: The brute force rotates one step at a time. Save the last element. Shift everything else one place right. Put the saved element at the front. Repeat k times. No extra memory, which is good. But each step moves the whole array. So the cost is n times k.
say.insight: Here's a neat trick. Reverse the whole array. Now the last k elements are at the front, just backwards. The rest are at the back, also backwards. So reverse each of those two parts once more. Both come out in the right order! Three reversals, each a simple two pointer swap.
say.anim: We start with the array one through seven, and k is three. First we reverse the entire array, swapping outer elements inward. After the full reversal completes, the array becomes seven six five four three two one. Now we reverse just the first three elements to fix their order. That gives us five six seven at the front, restoring their original sequence. Next we reverse the remaining four elements to fix their order too. The final array is five six seven one two three four, the rotated result.
say.code: Let's walk the code. First, we take k modulo the length. Full rotations change nothing. The reverse helper swaps the two ends, and walks them inward. We reverse the whole array, so the last k move to the front. Then we reverse the first k, to fix the order of the front. And finally the rest, to fix the order of the back.
say.outro: Linear time, constant space. The pattern is two pointers, used as an in place reversal. The same trick rotates strings and words.

rotate-array.title: Rotate Array
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which holds the method that rotates the array.
The rotate method takes the list and the shift amount k, and changes the list in place.
We store the length of nums in n so we can reuse it for bounds.
We reduce k to its remainder after dividing by n, since rotating a full length changes nothing.
We define a helper called reverse that flips the section of nums between positions l and r.
We keep swapping while the left pointer is still before the right pointer, so each pair is swapped once.
We swap the elements at the left and right positions, which moves them to each other's places.
We move the left pointer one step to the right, toward the middle.
We move the right pointer one step to the left, also toward the middle.
First we reverse the entire array, which puts the last k elements at the front but in backward order.
Next we reverse the first k elements to restore their original order.
Finally we reverse the remaining elements from k to the end, restoring their order and completing the rotation.

sort-an-array.hook: Sort without the built-in, in n log n. Split in half, sort each half, merge them.
sort-an-array.ask: Sort an array of integers in ascending order without using any built-in sort, in O(n log n) time.
sort-an-array.exampleWhy: The same four numbers, rearranged from smallest to largest.

brute.idea: Insertion sort: take each element and slide it left past every larger element until it sits in order.
steps: Take the next element
Shift larger elements one place right
Drop it into the gap
brute.whySlow: Reverse-sorted input shifts every element past all earlier ones: 50,000 numbers is over a billion moves.

optimal.insight: Two sorted halves merge into one sorted list in linear time. Split recursively: log n levels, each costing n.
steps: Length 0 or 1 is already sorted
Split in half and sort each recursively
Merge: repeatedly take the smaller front
Append whatever remains

codeNotes.note: Take the smaller front; ≤ keeps it stable

pitfalls: Quicksort with a fixed pivot hits O(n²) on sorted or all-equal input.
Heap sort gives O(1) extra space if the interviewer pushes on memory.

say.intro: Okay, Sort an Array. We sort a list of integers from smallest to largest. No built in sort allowed. And it has to run in n log n time. For five, two, three, one, the answer is one, two, three, five.
say.brute: The simple approach is insertion sort. Take each element, and slide it left past every bigger element until it's in order. No extra memory. Fast on nearly sorted data, too. So what's the catch? On reversed input, every element travels past all the earlier ones. That's quadratic.
say.insight: Here's the thing. Merging two sorted lists is easy, and linear. Compare their fronts, and take the smaller one each time. So split the array in half. Sort each half the same way. Then merge. The halving goes about log n levels deep. Each level does linear work. That's n log n, guaranteed, on any input.
say.anim: We start with the array five, two, three, one, ready to be split in half recursively. The left half five, two splits further into single elements five and two. Merging five and two compares them and builds the sorted pair two, five. Now the right half three, one splits and merges into sorted pair one, three. The two sorted halves two, five and one, three are merged by comparing front elements. One, then two, then three get appended in order as pointers advance. The remaining five is appended since the right side is exhausted. Final merged result is one, two, three, five, the fully sorted array.
say.code: Let's walk the code. The base case is a list of length zero or one. It's already sorted, so we return it. Otherwise, we split at the middle, and sort each half recursively. Then we merge. Two pointers take the smaller front each time. On a tie, we take from the left, which keeps it stable. When one half runs out, the leftovers are already sorted, so we append them.
say.outro: N log n time, linear extra space. The pattern is divide and conquer. Split, solve the halves, and combine in linear time.

sort-an-array.title: Sort an Array
lineNotes: We define a Solution class that holds the sorting method for this problem.
The sortArray method takes a list of integers and will return it sorted in ascending order.
We define a helper function called merge sort that recursively sorts whatever list it receives.
The base case checks whether the list has one or zero items, since such a list is already sorted.
In that case we simply return the list unchanged, which stops the recursion.
We compute mid as the length of the array divided by two, rounded down, to split it into halves.
We recursively sort the left half, which is everything before mid, and call the result left.
We recursively sort the right half, from mid onward, and call the result right.
We create an empty list called merged to build the combined sorted result.
We set both pointers i and j to zero, pointing at the front of left and right.
We loop while both halves still have unmerged elements, so we can compare their current front values.
We check whether the current left element is less than or equal to the current right element.
If so, we append the left element to merged, since it is the smaller one.
Then we advance i so it points to the next element in left.
Otherwise the right element is strictly smaller, so we handle that case here.
We append the right element to merged because it is the smaller of the two fronts.
Then we advance j so it points to the next element in right.
After the loop, we append any leftover elements from left, which are already sorted and larger than everything merged.
We likewise append any leftover elements from right, though only one of these two leftovers will be nonempty.
We return merged, which now holds all elements of this sublist in sorted order, built in linear time.
Finally we call merge sort on the input nums and return the fully sorted list.

integer-to-roman.hook: Turn a number into Roman numerals by always taking the biggest symbol that fits.
integer-to-roman.ask: Convert an integer from 1 to 3999 into a Roman numeral string, using the subtractive forms like IV, IX, XL, XC, CD and CM where the rules require them.

brute.idea: Write the number additively with only the seven basic symbols, then patch fours and nines with string replacements.
steps: Emit M, D, C, L, X, V, I additively
Replace DCCCC, CCCC, LXXXX, XXXX
Replace VIIII and IIII last
brute.whySlow: Not slower asymptotically, but it needs extra passes and breaks if the replacements run in the wrong order.

optimal.insight: Treat the six subtractive pairs as symbols of their own. Then greedily taking the largest value that fits is always right.
steps: List 13 values from 1000 down to 1
Include 900, 400, 90, 40, 9, 4 as symbols
While the value fits, append and subtract
Move to the next smaller value

codeNotes.note: Subtractive pairs as their own symbols
Pay off that much of the number

pitfalls: Leaving out 900, 400, 90, 40, 9 and 4 produces invalid forms like IIII.

say.intro: Okay, Integer to Roman. We turn a number, from one to three thousand nine hundred ninety nine, into Roman numerals. Fours and nines use subtractive forms. Like I V for four, and C M for nine hundred. For fifty eight, the answer is L V I I I. Fifty, five, and three ones.
say.brute: One approach writes the number using only the seven basic symbols. So four comes out as four I's. Then it patches the result with string replacements. I I I I becomes I V, and so on. It works. But it needs extra passes. And the replacements break if they run in the wrong order.
say.insight: Here's the trick. Treat the six subtractive pairs as symbols of their own. Nine hundred, four hundred, ninety, forty, nine, and four. Now we've got thirteen values, sorted largest first. And a greedy rule just works. Take the biggest value that fits. Append its symbol. Subtract. Repeat. No patching needed.
say.anim: We start converting the number 58 into roman numerals using value symbol pairs. The loop checks each pair from largest to smallest, starting with one thousand. Values like one hundred and ninety are skipped since fifty eight is smaller. Fifty fits, so we append the symbol L and subtract fifty, leaving eight. Five fits next, appending V and reducing the number down to three. Ones get added one at a time, appending I three times until zero. All symbols join together into the final roman numeral string, LVIII.
say.code: Let's walk the code. The list holds subtractive pairs as their own symbols, thirteen pairs from a thousand down to one. For each pair, we're greedy. While the biggest value still fits, we append its symbol. Then we pay off that much of the number, by subtracting it. At the end, we join the symbols in order, and return the string.
say.outro: Constant time, since the number is bounded. The pattern is greedy. With the right coins, always taking the largest that fits is correct.

integer-to-roman.title: Integer to Roman
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container the interview platform expects for our method.
The method intToRoman takes an integer called num and will return its Roman numeral as a string.
We build a list of value and symbol pairs, starting with the largest values, M for one thousand and CM for nine hundred.
The list continues with D, CD, C, XC, L and XL, so subtractive pairs sit in descending order among normal symbols.
It ends with X, IX, V, IV and I, completing all thirteen symbols needed so greedy choice always works.
We start with an empty list called res to collect the Roman symbols we pick.
We loop through each value and symbol pair, moving from the largest value down to the smallest.
While num is at least the current value, that symbol still fits and we keep using it.
We append the current symbol to res because it represents a chunk of the number.
We subtract that value from num so we track what remains to be converted.
Finally we join all collected symbols into one string and return it as the Roman numeral.

reverse-string.hook: Reverse a character array in place. Swap the ends and walk inward.
reverse-string.ask: Given a list of characters, reverse it in place, changing the original list and using only constant extra memory.

brute.idea: Build a reversed copy by reading from the back, then write the copy into the original list.
steps: Read characters from last to first into a copy
Write the copy back over s
brute.whySlow: Time is fine, but it uses a full extra copy where the problem demands constant memory.

optimal.insight: The first and last characters trade places, then the second and second to last. Two pointers meeting in the middle do it.
steps: l at the start, r at the end
Swap s[l] and s[r]
Move both inward
Stop when they meet

codeNotes.note: Right pointer at the last character

pitfalls: s = s[::-1] rebinds a local name and leaves the caller's list unchanged.

say.intro: Okay, Reverse String. We get a word as a list of characters. We reverse it in place, using only constant extra memory. For h e l l o, the result is o l l e h. That's hello, read backwards.
say.brute: The easy approach builds a reversed copy. Read the characters from last to first into a new list. Then write that list back over the original. Linear time, which is fine. But it uses a whole extra copy of the string. And the problem asks for constant memory.
say.insight: Think about it this way. Reversing just means each character trades places with its mirror. The first swaps with the last. The second with the second to last. And so on. So put a pointer at each end. Swap, and step both inward. When they meet, we're done. The middle character, if there is one, is already in place.
say.anim: We start with the array h, e, l, l, o, and set pointer l to index 0. Pointer r is set to index 4, the last position in the array. Since l is less than r, we enter the loop to swap characters. The characters at l and r swap, turning h and o into o and h. L moves to 1 and r moves to 3, closing in toward the middle. Now the e and l at positions 1 and 3 swap places. L and r both reach index 2, so the loop stops since l is not less than r. The final reversed array is o, l, l, e, h.
say.code: Let's walk the code. The left pointer starts at zero, and the right pointer starts at the last character. We loop while left is less than right. When they meet, the middle element stays put. Each round, we swap the outer pair. Then left steps forward, and we close in from the right. The list changes in place, so we return nothing.
say.outro: Linear time, constant space. The pattern is two pointers moving toward each other. The same move behind palindrome checks.

reverse-string.title: Reverse String
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container the judge expects for our reverse string method.
The method takes the list of characters s and returns nothing, since we change the list in place.
We set l, the left pointer, to zero so it starts at the first character.
We set r, the right pointer, to the last index, which is the length of s minus one.
We loop only while l is less than r, so the pointers stop once they meet in the middle.
We swap the characters at l and r in one step, putting each into the other's position without extra memory.
We move the left pointer one step to the right, toward the middle.
We move the right pointer one step to the left, so the next pair of characters gets swapped.

longest-non-decreasing-subarray-after-re.hook: One replacement can bridge two sorted runs. Precompute runs from both sides, then try every spot.
longest-non-decreasing-subarray-after-re.ask: You may change at most one element to any value. Return the length of the longest contiguous stretch that is non-decreasing, meaning each element is at least the one before it.
longest-non-decreasing-subarray-after-re.exampleWhy: Change the second 1 to 3: [1,2,3,3] is non-decreasing, length 4.

brute.idea: For each index, try replacing it with a neighbor's value, then measure the longest non-decreasing run of the new array.
steps: Try no change, then each index i
Replace nums[i] by nums[i-1] or nums[i+1]
Scan the array for the longest run
brute.whySlow: Every candidate rescans the whole array: 100,000 elements means about 20 billion steps.

optimal.insight: Replacing nums[i] joins the run ending at i-1 with the run starting at i+1, if nums[i-1] ≤ nums[i+1].
steps: left[i]: run length ending at i
right[i]: run length starting at i
Changing i extends one side by 1
If nums[i-1] ≤ nums[i+1], join both sides

codeNotes.note: Change i to extend the left run

codeNotes.match: if 0 < i < n - 1 and nums[i - 1] <= nums[i + 1]:

pitfalls: Bridging needs nums[i-1] ≤ nums[i+1]; otherwise only one side can be extended.

say.intro: Okay, Longest Non Decreasing Subarray After Replacing at Most One Element. We can change one element to anything we like. What's the longest stretch where each number is at least the one before? For one, two, three, one, two, change the second one to three. One, two, three, three. Length four.
say.brute: The brute force tries every possible change. For each index, replace it with its left or right neighbour. Those are the most useful choices. Then scan the whole new array for its longest non decreasing run. That's about two n candidates, each with a full scan. So it's quadratic.
say.insight: Here's the key. One change at index i can do three things. It can extend the run ending right before i. It can extend the run starting right after i. Or, if the left neighbour is at most the right neighbour, it can bridge both runs into one. So precompute run lengths ending at each index, and starting at each index.
say.anim: We start with the array one, two, three, one, two, and build two helper arrays. Left tracks increasing runs ending at each index, growing to one, two, three as values rise. Right tracks increasing runs starting at each index, computed backward across the array. Best starts at three, the longest run found directly in the left array. At index one, we check if removing it joins runs, trying left plus one and right plus one. Since nums before and after index one can merge, best becomes four by joining both runs. Checking the remaining indices confirms four stays the best possible merged length. The function returns four, the longest subarray achievable by replacing one element.
say.code: Let's walk the code. In the left array, the run ending at i grows when the order holds. In the right array, built from the back, the run starting at i grows the same way. Then, for each index, we try three options. Change i to extend the left run. Or to extend the right run. And if the neighbours fit, bridge both runs.
say.outro: Linear time, linear space. The pattern is one dimensional dynamic programming. Runs from both directions, combined around each index.

longest-non-decreasing-subarray-after-re.title: Longest Non-Decreasing Subarray After Replacing at Most One Element
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container the problem expects for our method.
The method longestSubarray takes the list nums and returns the length of the best stretch we can build.
We store the length of nums in n so we can reuse it throughout.
If there are at most two elements, we can always fix the array with one change.
So we simply return n, since the whole array can be made non-decreasing.
We create a left array of ones, where left at i will hold the run length ending at i.
We create a right array of ones, where right at i will hold the run length starting at i.
We scan left to right from index one to fill in the left run lengths.
If the previous element is at most the current one, the run continues without a break.
In that case left at i becomes left at the previous index plus one.
We scan right to left, starting at the second to last index, to fill in the right run lengths.
If the current element is at most the next one, the run starting here continues rightward.
Then right at i becomes right at the next index plus one.
We start best as the longest natural run, which needs no replacement at all.
Now we try replacing each index i, looping over every position in the array.
If i has a left neighbor, we can consider extending the run ending before it.
We replace nums at i to extend the left run by one, updating best if larger.
If i has a right neighbor, we can consider extending the run starting after it.
We replace nums at i to prepend one element to the right run, updating best if larger.
For an interior index where the left neighbor is at most the right neighbor, we can bridge both runs.
Then the replaced element joins both runs, giving left run plus one plus right run, and we update best.
Finally we return best as the longest achievable non-decreasing subarray length.

making-a-large-island.hook: Flip one water cell to land. Label each island once, then each flip is just a lookup.
making-a-large-island.ask: Given a square grid of 1s (land) and 0s (water), you may change at most one 0 into a 1. Return the size of the largest island possible, where islands connect up, down, left and right.
making-a-large-island.exampleWhy: Flipping the top-right 0 joins the top island (2 cells) and the right island (2 cells): 2 + 2 + 1 = 5.

brute.idea: Try flipping every water cell, then flood fill the whole grid to measure the largest island.
steps: Measure the largest island as is
For each 0, set it to 1
Flood fill to find the biggest island
Set it back to 0
brute.whySlow: Every flip re-floods the whole grid: a 500 by 500 grid means about 60 billion cell visits.

optimal.insight: Label every island with an id and record its size once. A flipped cell then joins its distinct neighboring ids.
steps: DFS each island, painting it with id 2, 3, ...
Record size per id
For each 0, collect distinct neighbor ids
1 + their sizes is a candidate

codeNotes.note: Paint the cell with its island id
Covers a grid with no water

codeNotes.match: best = max(best, 1 + sum(size[i] for i in ids))

pitfalls: Use a set of ids: two sides touching the same island must count it once.
Recursive DFS can hit Python's recursion limit on 500 by 500; use a stack.

say.intro: Okay, Making a Large Island. We have a square grid of land and water. We can turn one water cell into land. What's the biggest island we can get? Land connects up, down, left, and right. In our three by three grid, flipping the top right corner joins two islands of two. That makes five.
say.brute: The brute force tries every flip. For each water cell, turn it into land. Flood fill the whole grid to find the biggest island. Then turn it back. But each flood fill touches every cell. And there can be a quarter of a million water cells. The work explodes.
say.insight: Here's the thing. The islands don't change between flips. So measure them just once. Paint each island with its own id, two, three, four, and so on. Record each id's size. Now a flipped water cell simply joins the islands touching it. Look at its four neighbours, gather their distinct ids, and add one plus their sizes.
say.anim: We start with the grid, ready to scan each cell for land we haven't labeled yet. At row zero, col zero, we find land and begin painting this island with label two. The first island finishes, sized two, so island_size now maps label two to size two. Next unlabeled land is found, and painting begins again using the new label three. A third tiny island appears, getting label four with size one, completing the labeling pass. We scan all island sizes, tracking the best single island size, which starts at two. Now we check each water cell, collecting distinct neighboring island ids to try flipping it. Flipping this water cell joins islands three and two, giving a total of five, our new best. After checking all water cells, the largest possible island size is five, the final answer.
say.code: Let's walk the code. The paint function paints the cell with its island id, and spreads to its neighbours. That way we measure each island once, and store its size. We also start best at the biggest island. That covers a grid with no water. Then, for each water cell, we collect neighbour ids in a set, to count each island once. The flipped cell joins its neighbours, so best is one plus their sizes.
say.outro: Linear in the number of cells. The pattern is graphs. Label connected components once, then answer each question by lookup.

making-a-large-island.title: Making A Large Island
lineNotes: We define the Solution class that holds the method for solving the problem.
The method largestIsland takes the grid and returns the size of the largest island possible after one flip.
We store n, the side length of the square grid.
We create an empty dictionary that will map each island label to its size.
This comment says step one is to flood fill each island, give it a unique label, and record its size.
We define a helper called paint that floods an island from a cell and returns the cells it covered.
If the cell is outside the grid bounds, we stop the search from going further.
Out of bounds cells contribute zero land, so we return zero.
If the cell is not unpainted land, meaning water or already labeled, we should not count it.
Such a cell adds nothing, so we return zero.
We paint the current land cell with the island label so it is never visited again.
We start the count at one for this cell.
We recurse downward and add the number of cells found there.
We recurse upward and add the cells found there.
We recurse to the right and add the cells found there.
We recurse to the left and add the cells found there.
We return the total number of cells in this island reached from here.
We start labels at two so they never collide with zero for water or one for unpainted land.
We loop over every row of the grid.
We loop over every column in that row.
When we find unpainted land, we have discovered a new island.
We paint the island and record its size in the dictionary under the current label.
We increase the label so the next island gets a different id.
This comment says we track the best answer so far, which matters if the grid is all land.
We start best at zero.
We loop through every recorded island size.
If this island is larger than best, we update it.
We set best to that larger size, covering the case with no water cell to flip.
This comment says that for each water cell we gather the distinct neighboring island ids.
We loop over every row again.
We loop over every column again.
We only consider water cells because those are the ones we could flip.
We create an empty set so each neighboring island is counted only once.
We list the four neighboring positions below, above, right and left of this cell.
We iterate over each neighbor position.
We check the neighbor is inside the grid and holds a label greater than one, meaning it is part of an island.
We add that label to the set so duplicate neighbors of the same island collapse into one.
This comment says the candidate size is one for the flipped cell plus the sizes of distinct neighboring islands.
We start the total at one for the flipped cell itself.
We loop over each distinct neighboring island id.
We add that island's recorded size to the total.
If this total beats the best so far, we should keep it.
We update best to this larger total.
We return the largest island size found.

kids-with-the-greatest-number-of-candies.hook: Give one kid all the extra candy. Can they top everyone? Compare against the max once.
kids-with-the-greatest-number-of-candies.ask: Each kid has some candies. For each kid, return true if giving them all the extra candies would make their total at least as large as every other kid's.
kids-with-the-greatest-number-of-candies.exampleWhy: The most anyone has is 5. Every kid except the one with 1 reaches at least 5 after adding 3.

brute.idea: For each kid, add the extras and compare against every other kid one by one.
steps: Give kid i the extra candies
Compare with every other kid
Anyone has more? false, else true
brute.whySlow: Every kid rescans every other kid, even though the comparison target is always the same maximum.

optimal.insight: Beating everyone just means reaching the current maximum. Find it once, then each kid is a single comparison.
steps: Find the largest pile once
For each kid, add the extras
Compare with the largest pile

codeNotes.note: The bar every kid must reach

pitfalls: Use ≥, not >: equal to the maximum still counts as greatest.

say.intro: Okay, Kids With the Greatest Number of Candies. Each kid has some candies, and we have a pile of extras. For each kid, if we gave them all the extras, would they have the most? Ties count. With two, three, five, one, three, and three extras, everyone except the kid with one can reach the top.
say.brute: The brute force checks each kid against every other kid. Add the extras to this kid's pile. Then look at all the other piles. Anyone still have more? Then false. Otherwise true. That's correct. But it compares every pair of kids. So it's quadratic.
say.insight: Here's the thing. To have the most, a kid only needs to reach the current maximum. Nobody else changes, since the extras go to one kid at a time. So find the biggest pile once, before the loop. Then each kid needs just one comparison. Their candies plus the extras, against that maximum.
say.anim: We start with candies two, three, five, one, three, and three extra candies to give out. The maximum candy count is found once, and it's five. First kid has two candies, plus three is five, which meets the max, so true. Second kid has three, plus three is six, beating five, so true. Third kid already has five, the max itself, so true. Fourth kid has one, plus three is four, short of five, so false. Fifth kid has three, plus three equals six, meeting the max, so true. Final answer: true, true, true, false, true.
say.code: Let's walk the code. First, we find the largest pile. That's the bar every kid must reach. Then there's one check per kid. Their candies plus the extras, compared with the bar. And we use at least, not strictly more. Why? Because ties count as greatest. We collect the answers and return the list.
say.outro: Linear time, constant extra space. The pattern is arrays. Precompute the one value every query needs, instead of recomputing it.

kids-with-the-greatest-number-of-candies.title: Kids With the Greatest Number of Candies
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container the judge expects for our method.
This method takes the candies list and the extra candies amount, and returns a list of true or false answers.
We find the largest candy count once, since reaching that maximum is all a kid needs to tie for greatest.
We start an empty result list that will collect one answer for each kid in order.
We loop over each kid's candy count, one kid at a time, keeping the original order.
For each kid we check whether their candies plus the extras reach the maximum, and append that true or false answer.
After checking every kid, we return the list of answers.

remove-linked-list-elements.hook: Remove every node with a given value. A dummy head means even the first node is easy.
remove-linked-list-elements.ask: Given the head of a linked list and a value, remove every node holding that value and return the head of the resulting list.
remove-linked-list-elements.exampleWhy: Both 6 nodes are unlinked; the other nodes stay in their original order.

brute.idea: Copy the values you keep into a Python list, then build a brand-new linked list from them.
steps: Walk the list, keeping values not equal to val
Build new nodes from the kept values
Return the new head
brute.whySlow: Time is fine, but it allocates a full new list and array instead of relinking existing nodes.

optimal.insight: Put a dummy node before the head. Then every removal, including the head, is the same move: skip cur.next.
steps: Dummy node points at the head
Look at the node after cur
Match: link cur past it
No match: step cur forward

codeNotes.note: No special case for the head
Check the next node, not cur
Unlink it; stay put for repeats

pitfalls: Advancing cur after a removal skips back-to-back matches like 7, 7.

say.intro: Okay, Remove Linked List Elements. We get a linked list and a value. We remove every node holding that value, and return the new head. For one, two, six, three, four, five, six, with value six, we get one, two, three, four, five.
say.brute: The simple approach copies what we keep. Walk the list, and put every value that isn't six into a Python list. Then build a fresh linked list from those values. That's linear time. But it allocates a whole new list of nodes, plus an array. We could just relink the nodes we already have.
say.insight: Here's the thing. Removing a node means pointing the node before it past it. So what about the head? It has nothing before it. A dummy node fixes that. Put it in front of the head, and now every node has a predecessor. Then one rule handles everything. Next node matches? Skip it. Otherwise, step forward.
say.anim: We create a dummy node pointing to the head, so removing the first element works like any other. Cur starts at dummy, and we walk forward since node 1 does not equal 6. Cur moves to node 1, then to node 2, since neither value matches six. Cur points to node 2, and its next node 6 matches the target, so we skip it. The six is removed, cur next now jumps straight to node 3. Cur advances through nodes 3 and 4, since their values aren't six. Cur sits at node 5, and its next node 6 matches, so we skip it again. We return dummy next, giving the final list one two three four five.
say.code: Let's walk the code. We create a dummy in front of the head, so there's no special case for the head. We check the next node, not cur itself. Why? Because we need the node before to unlink it. If it matches, we unlink it, and stay put, in case of repeats. Otherwise, cur moves on. At the end, the head may have changed, so we return the node after the dummy.
say.outro: Linear time, constant space. The pattern is linked lists with a dummy head. It removes every special case at the front.

remove-linked-list-elements.title: Remove Linked List Elements
lineNotes: We define a Solution class that holds the method for this problem.
The method takes the head of a linked list and a target value to remove.
We create a dummy node pointing to head, so removing the original head works like any other removal.
We set cur to the dummy node, so cur always sits just before the node we inspect.
We loop as long as the node after cur exists, meaning there is still something to check.
We check whether the next node holds the value we want to remove.
If so, we skip that node by linking cur to the node after it, without moving cur.
Otherwise the next node is a keeper, so we handle that case in this branch.
We advance cur to the next node, since that node is safe and we move on.
We return the node after dummy, which is the true head of the cleaned list.

valid-palindrome-ii.hook: One delete allowed. The trick is knowing exactly which two characters deserve a second chance.
valid-palindrome-ii.ask: Given a lowercase string, return true if it is a palindrome already, or can become one by deleting at most one character.
valid-palindrome-ii.exampleWhy: The ends match until c meets d. Deleting that d leaves abccba, which reads the same both ways.

brute.idea: Try every possible deletion. Remove each character in turn and check whether what is left is a palindrome.
steps: Already a palindrome? return True
For each i, build s without s[i]
Reversed copy equal? return True
brute.whySlow: Each of n deletions copies and reverses the string: 100,000 letters means ten billion character operations.

optimal.insight: Matching ends never need deleting. At the first mismatch, the only candidates are the left or right character, so check just those two.
steps: Two pointers start at both ends
Matching characters: move both inward
First mismatch: skip left or skip right
Check the remaining middle is a palindrome

codeNotes.match: return is_pal(l + 1, r) or is_pal(l, r - 1)

pitfalls: After the one delete, do not allow a second mismatch: use a strict check.
You must try both skips; checking only one fails cases like cuppucu.

say.intro: Okay, Valid Palindrome Two. You get a string, and you're allowed to delete at most one character. Can it read the same both ways? Take a b c c d b a. The outer letters match, then c bumps into d. Delete that d, and you get a b c c b a. So the answer is true.
say.brute: The obvious move is to try every deletion. First, check if the string is already a palindrome. If not, remove each character in turn. Build the shorter copy and compare it with its reverse. Any copy works? Return true. So what's the catch? That's n copies, and each one costs n work. For a hundred thousand letters, that's ten billion character operations.
say.insight: Here's the thing. If the two ends match, deleting either one can never help. So we just step inward. Now, the first time the ends disagree, one of those two characters has to go. Why? Because everything outside them already matches. So we're down to just two options. Skip the left one, or skip the right one, and check the middle.
say.anim: We start with the string abccdba, pointers l at 0 and r at 6. Characters a and a match, so both pointers move inward, l becomes 1 and r becomes 5. Next, b and b also match, so l moves to 2 and r moves to 4. Now l is 2 and r is 4, and the characters c and d differ, a mismatch. Since we can't fix both sides, we try skipping either the left or right character. Skipping the left character checks index 3 against 4, but d and c don't match, so this fails. Skipping the right character instead checks index 2 against 3, c and c match, so it succeeds. Since one of the two options worked, the function returns true, confirming it's a valid palindrome.
say.code: First, a small helper. It checks whether the slice from i to j is a plain palindrome. Then we put l at the front and r at the back. While they haven't crossed, we compare the two characters. If they differ, that's our one delete. We return whether dropping the left or dropping the right gives a palindrome. Otherwise, the ends matched, so both pointers squeeze inward.
say.outro: Linear time, constant space. Two pointers squeezing from both ends. And you spend your one second chance only at the first disagreement.

valid-palindrome-ii.title: Valid Palindrome II
lineNotes: We define a class named Solution, which holds the method that LeetCode will call for this problem.
The validPalindrome method takes the string s and returns true if it is a palindrome after deleting at most one character.
Inside it we define a helper called is_pal that checks whether the substring between indices i and j is a palindrome.
The helper loops while i is still less than j, comparing characters moving inward from both ends.
If the characters at i and j differ, this substring is not a palindrome.
So the helper immediately returns false when it finds that mismatch.
When the characters match, we move i one step to the right.
We also move j one step to the left, shrinking the window toward the middle.
If the loop finishes without any mismatch, the helper returns true because the substring is a palindrome.
Back in the main method, we set l to zero and r to the last index of s.
We loop while l is less than r, comparing the outer characters first.
If the characters at l and r differ, we have found the first mismatch and must use our one deletion.
We return true if skipping the left character or skipping the right character leaves a palindrome, since only those two deletions can help.
When the ends match, we move l one step to the right, since matching ends never need deleting.
We also move r one step to the left to compare the next pair.
If we never hit a mismatch, the string is already a palindrome, so we return true.

maximal-square.hook: The biggest square ending at a cell is limited by its three neighbours. That one rule solves it.
maximal-square.ask: Given a grid of zero and one characters, find the largest square made entirely of ones and return its area.
maximal-square.exampleWhy: The top-left 2 by 2 block is all ones. No 3 by 3 square of ones exists, so the area is 4.

brute.idea: Treat every cell as a top-left corner and grow a square from it until some cell inside is a zero.
steps: Pick each cell as a corner
Grow size k while the whole square is ones
Keep the largest size seen
brute.whySlow: Every growth step rechecks the whole square. On a 300 by 300 grid of ones that is trillions of cell checks.

optimal.insight: Let dp be the side of the largest square whose bottom-right corner is this cell. It equals one plus the minimum of top, left and top-left.
steps: Pad a dp grid with an extra zero row and column
Zero cell: dp stays 0
One cell: 1 + min(top, left, diagonal)
Track the largest side; return its square

pitfalls: Cells are the strings "1" and "0", not integers.
Return the area, side times side, not the side.

say.intro: Okay, Maximal Square. You get a grid of zeros and ones. Find the biggest square that's all ones. In our three by three grid, the top left two by two block is all ones. But no three by three square works. So the answer is the area. Four.
say.brute: The brute force treats every cell as a top left corner. From there, it grows a square one size at a time. At each size, it rechecks every cell inside. Hit a zero? Stop and record the size. So what's the problem? On a big grid full of ones, every corner grows a long way. And every step rescans the whole square. The work explodes.
say.insight: Think about it this way. Instead of the top left corner, look at the bottom right one. How big can a square ending here be? It's limited by its top, left and diagonal neighbours. If any of them is small, there's a hole nearby. So the side here is one plus the smallest of those three. And each cell is computed just once.
say.anim: We start with a three by three grid of ones and zeros, and a padded dp table of zeros. At row zero, column zero, the cell is one, so dp becomes one, giving best equal to one. Moving right, column one is also one, so dp becomes one again, keeping best at one. On row one, column zero is one, so dp there becomes one from its left neighbor. At row one, column one, all three neighbors are one, so dp jumps to two, updating best. Row one column two sees mismatched neighbors, so dp settles at one, a smaller square. On row two, column one becomes one since its top neighbor was one before it. Row two, column two takes the minimum of its neighbors two, one, and one, becoming two. Best squared gives the final answer four, the largest square area found.
say.code: We make a table with one extra row and column of zeros. That padding means edges need no special cases. Then we loop over every cell. A zero ends every square, so it stays zero. For a one, we take one plus the smallest of top, left and diagonal. The weakest neighbour sets the limit. We track the largest side so far. And at the end we return side times side, because they want area.
say.outro: Linear in the number of cells. That's two dimensional dynamic programming. Each answer is built from three neighbours you already know.

maximal-square.title: Maximal Square
lineNotes: We define the Solution class that holds our method for the maximal square problem.
The method takes the grid of character digits and returns the area of the largest all-ones square.
We read the number of rows and columns from the matrix so we know the grid size.
We build a table of zeros with one extra row and column, so border lookups need no special cases.
We start best, the largest side length found so far, at zero.
We loop over every row of the original matrix by index.
Inside each row, we loop over every column by index.
We only extend a square when the current cell holds the character one.
The side here is one plus the smallest of the top, left, and top-left neighbors, shifted by one for padding.
We update best if this cell's square side is larger than any seen before.
Finally we return best times best, converting the largest side length into the area.

nth-digit.hook: Skip whole blocks of numbers at once instead of writing the sequence out digit by digit.
nth-digit.ask: Write 1, 2, 3, 4 and so on as one endless string of digits. Return the digit sitting at position n, counting from one.
nth-digit.exampleWhy: Digits 1 to 189 cover 1 through 99. Six more digits reach 100 and 101, landing on the last 1 of 101.

brute.idea: Write numbers one after another into a growing string until it has at least n digits, then read position n.
steps: Append str(i) for i = 1, 2, 3, ...
Stop once the length reaches n
Return digit n - 1 of the string
brute.whySlow: n can be two billion: that is hundreds of millions of numbers written out and gigabytes of memory.

optimal.insight: Numbers with the same digit count form blocks: 9 one-digit, 90 two-digit, 900 three-digit. Subtract whole blocks, then divide.
steps: Block of d-digit numbers holds 9 · 10^(d-1) · d digits
While n exceeds the block, subtract it and grow d
Number = start + (n - 1) // d
Digit index inside it = (n - 1) % d

pitfalls: Use n - 1 for zero-based division, or you land one number too far.

say.intro: Okay, Nth Digit. Imagine writing one, two, three, and so on, forever, as one long string of digits. Which digit sits at position n? Say n is one hundred ninety five. The answer is one. It's the last digit of one hundred and one.
say.brute: The simple way is to just write it all out. Append each number, keep a running length, and stop once you have n digits. Then read position n. So what's wrong? It's linear time and linear memory. And n can be two billion. That means writing hundreds of millions of numbers, and gigabytes of memory.
say.insight: Here's the thing. Numbers with the same length come in blocks. Nine one digit numbers. Ninety two digit numbers. Nine hundred three digit numbers. Each block holds count times length digits. So we can skip a whole block at once. Once n lands inside a block, one division tells us the number. And the remainder tells us which digit.
say.anim: We start with n equal to 195, checking single digit numbers first. Length is 1 and count is 9, but 195 exceeds this block, so we subtract. We subtract 9 from n, leaving 186, and move to two digit numbers. Now length is 2 and count is 90, but 186 still exceeds this block, so we subtract again. After subtracting 180, n becomes 6, and we move to three digit numbers. Now length is 3 and count is 900, and 6 fits within this block, so the loop stops. We compute num as 101, the three digit number containing our target digit. Extracting the correct digit from 101 gives the final answer, 1.
say.code: We start with the first block. Length one, count nine, starting at one. While n lies past this block, we skip the whole block. Subtract its digits, add one to the length, and multiply count and start by ten. Then, which number holds the digit? Start, plus n minus one, divided by length. And which digit inside it? n minus one, mod length.
say.outro: Logarithmic time, constant space. That's the math pattern. Count in blocks, and use division instead of simulation.

nth-digit.title: Nth Digit
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container the problem expects for our method.
The method findNthDigit takes n, the one-based position in the endless digit string, and returns that digit.
We start with numbers of length one, nine of them, beginning at one.
While n is larger than the total digits in the current block, the answer lies in a later block.
We subtract the whole block's digit total from n, skipping past all those digits.
We increase length by one because the next block has numbers with one more digit.
The count of numbers in the next block grows tenfold, like nine, ninety, nine hundred.
The first number of the next block also grows tenfold, like one, ten, one hundred.
Now n falls inside this block, so we find which number holds it by dividing the zero-based offset by length.
We turn that number into text, pick the digit at the remainder position, and return it as an integer.

length-of-last-word.hook: The answer lives at the end of the string, so start there and ignore everything else.
length-of-last-word.ask: Given a sentence of words and spaces, possibly with extra spaces anywhere, return how many letters the final word has.
length-of-last-word.exampleWhy: Skipping the two trailing spaces, the last word is moon, which has 4 letters.

brute.idea: Split the whole sentence into words, then return the length of the last one.
steps: Split on whitespace into a list
Take the last word
Return its length
brute.whySlow: Same linear time, but it reads every character and copies every word just to look at the last one.

optimal.insight: Only the tail matters. Walk backwards past trailing spaces, then count letters until the next space or the start.
steps: Start i at the last index
Skip trailing spaces
Count letters moving left
Stop at a space or the front

pitfalls: Guard i >= 0 when the sentence is a single word with no leading space.

say.intro: Okay, Length of Last Word. You get a sentence with spaces, and there can be extra spaces anywhere, even at the end. Return the length of the last word. In fly me to the moon, with two trailing spaces, the last word is moon. So the answer is four.
say.brute: The quick approach is to split the sentence into words and take the last one. And honestly, that's linear time. It's not slow. So what's the catch? It reads every character and copies every word into memory. All that, just to look at one word at the very end. That's linear extra space for no good reason.
say.insight: Here's the thing. The answer only lives at the tail of the string. So why start at the front? Start at the end instead. First, walk left past any trailing spaces. Then count letters as you keep walking left. Stop at a space, or when you fall off the front. We never touch the earlier words. And we only need two numbers.
say.anim: We start at index nineteen, the last character of the string, which is a space. The pointer moves backward, skipping trailing spaces until it lands on index seventeen, the letter n. Length starts at zero as we begin counting letters in the last word. Each loop step counts a letter and moves left, length growing to one, two, three, four. At index thirteen we hit a space, so the counting loop stops. The function returns length, giving a final answer of four.
say.code: We begin at the very last index. While that character is a space, we step left. That skips the trailing spaces. Now we're inside the last word. We set length to zero. While we're still in range and not on a space, we count one letter and step left. When that loop ends, length holds exactly the letters in the final word.
say.outro: Linear time in the worst case, constant space. A simple string scan. The lesson? Start where the answer lives.

length-of-last-word.title: Length of Last Word
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container the problem expects for our method.
This method takes the string s and returns an integer, the length of its last word.
We set i to the last index of the string so we can walk backwards from the end.
While the character at i is a space, we keep looping to skip any trailing spaces.
Each time we see a trailing space, we move i one step to the left.
We set length to zero, ready to count the letters of the last word.
We loop while i is still valid and the current character is not a space, staying inside the last word.
Each letter we pass adds one to length, counting the final word's letters.
We move i one step left to examine the previous character in the word.
We return length, which now holds the number of letters in the last word.

find-peak-element.hook: No sorted array, yet binary search still works. Just follow the uphill slope.
find-peak-element.ask: Given an array where neighbours always differ, return the index of any element larger than both neighbours. Treat positions beyond the ends as minus infinity. Aim for logarithmic time.
find-peak-element.exampleWhy: 6 at index 5 is bigger than 5 on its left and 4 on its right, so it is a peak.

brute.idea: The global maximum is always a peak. Scan the whole array and return the index of the largest value.
steps: Track the best index so far
Larger value? update best
Return best after the scan
brute.whySlow: It reads every element. The problem demands logarithmic time, and a million elements means a million reads instead of twenty.

optimal.insight: If nums[m] < nums[m+1], we are on an upward slope, so a peak must exist to the right. Otherwise one exists at m or to its left.
steps: Search between l and r
Look at mid and its right neighbour
Rising: peak lies right, l = m + 1
Falling: peak at m or left, r = m

codeNotes.note: m itself might be the peak

pitfalls: Falling side: set r = m, never m - 1, since m may be the peak.

say.intro: Okay, Find Peak Element. A peak is bigger than both its neighbours, and the edges count as minus infinity. Return the index of any peak, in logarithmic time. In one, two, one, three, five, six, four, the six at index five is a peak. So we return five.
say.brute: Here's an easy way. The largest value is always a peak, because nothing beats it. So scan the array and return where the maximum is. It's correct. So what's the problem? It's linear time. And the problem asks for logarithmic time. A million elements means a million reads, instead of about twenty.
say.insight: Look at the middle and its right neighbour. Is the neighbour bigger? Then we're walking uphill. Keep climbing right, and we must hit a peak. Why? Because the far edge is minus infinity, so the hill has to come down. If the middle is bigger instead, a peak sits at the middle or to its left. Either way, we throw away half.
say.anim: We start searching for a peak with left at 0 and right at 6. Middle index m is 3, where nums[3] is 3, less than nums[4] which is 5. Since it's increasing here, the peak must be to the right, so left moves to 4. Now m is 5, nums[5] is 6, greater than nums[6] which is 4. That means a peak could be at m or earlier, so right becomes 5. Next m is 4, nums[4] is 5, less than nums[5] which is 6, so left moves to 5. Now left equals right at 5, so the loop ends. The function returns index 5, confirming the peak value 6.
say.code: We set l to zero and r to the last index. We stop when just one index remains, so we loop while l is less than r. Take the middle. Notice that middle plus one always stays in range. If the middle is less than the next value, we're going uphill. The peak must lie right, so l becomes middle plus one. Otherwise r becomes the middle, because the middle itself might be the peak.
say.outro: Logarithmic time, constant space. That's binary search on a condition, not on sorted values. Just follow the slope uphill.

find-peak-element.title: Find Peak Element
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container the problem expects for our method.
This method takes the list of numbers and returns the index of any peak element.
We set left to zero and right to the last index, so the search covers the whole array.
We keep looping while left is less than right, stopping when only one candidate index remains.
We compute the middle index by averaging left and right and rounding down.
We compare the middle value with its right neighbour to see whether we are climbing upward.
Since the slope rises, a peak must lie to the right, so we move left to one past the middle.
Otherwise the middle is not lower than its right neighbour, so a peak exists at the middle or to its left.
We shrink the range by setting right to the middle, keeping the middle as a possible peak.
When left meets right, that single index is a peak, so we return it.

greatest-common-divisor-of-strings.hook: Strings can have a greatest common divisor too, and Euclid finds it.
greatest-common-divisor-of-strings.ask: A string t divides s if s is t repeated some number of times. Return the longest string that divides both inputs, or an empty string if none does.
greatest-common-divisor-of-strings.exampleWhy: Both are AB repeated, four times and three times. Their lengths 8 and 6 have gcd 2, giving AB.

brute.idea: Try every prefix length from longest to shortest, and return the first prefix that builds both strings by repetition.
steps: Try k from min length down to 1
Skip k unless it divides both lengths
Repeat the prefix and compare to both
First match is the answer
brute.whySlow: Each candidate rebuilds both strings. With lengths near 1,000 and many divisors, that repeats thousands of characters of work per try.

optimal.insight: A common divisor exists only if str1 + str2 equals str2 + str1. When it does, the answer is the prefix of length gcd of the lengths.
steps: Compare str1 + str2 with str2 + str1
Different? No divisor, return empty
Run Euclid on the two lengths
Return the prefix of that length

pitfalls: Without the concatenation test, the gcd prefix may not divide either string.

say.intro: Okay, Greatest Common Divisor of Strings. A string divides another if repeating it builds the other exactly. We want the longest string that divides both. A B four times, and A B three times? The answer is A B. And if nothing works, return the empty string.
say.brute: The brute force tries every candidate length, longest first. A length only makes sense if it divides both string lengths. For each one, take that prefix and repeat it to rebuild both strings. Then compare. First match wins. So what's the catch? Every try costs the full length of both strings. And there can be lots of tries.
say.insight: Here's the aha. If both strings are built from the same block, then gluing them in either order gives the same thing. Think about it. It's just the block, repeated, either way. So if the two orders differ, there's no answer. And if they match? The longest block has length equal to the gcd of the two lengths. Just like with numbers.
say.anim: We check if str1 plus str2 equals str2 plus str1, confirming a common divisor exists. We set a to eight and b to six, the lengths of str1 and str2. The loop runs since b is six, computing the greatest common divisor using Euclid's algorithm. Now a becomes six and b becomes two, the remainder of eight divided by six. The loop continues since b is two, updating a and b again. Now a becomes two and b becomes zero, ending the loop since b is falsy. With b now zero, the loop stops and a holds the gcd value two. The function returns the first two characters of str1, giving the final answer 'AB'.
say.code: First, the same building block test. We compare string one plus string two, against string two plus string one. If they differ, no common divisor exists, so we return the empty string. Otherwise, we run Euclid on the two lengths. Each step replaces the pair with the second value and the remainder. When the remainder hits zero, we have the gcd. We return the prefix of that length.
say.outro: Linear time for the comparison, plus a tiny gcd. That's the math pattern. Borrow Euclid from number theory, and apply it to strings.

greatest-common-divisor-of-strings.title: Greatest Common Divisor of Strings
lineNotes: We define a class called Solution, which holds the method that solves this problem.
This method takes two strings, str1 and str2, and returns the longest string that divides both of them.
If joining the strings in both orders gives different results, they share no repeating base piece.
In that case we return an empty string, since no common divisor string exists.
We store the lengths of str1 and str2 in a and b, to compute their greatest common divisor.
We loop with the Euclidean algorithm, continuing until b becomes zero.
Each pass replaces a with b and b with the remainder of a divided by b, shrinking the pair.
When the loop ends, a holds the gcd of the lengths, so we return that prefix of str1.

string-compression.hook: Compress the array into itself. A read pointer runs ahead while a write pointer follows behind.
string-compression.ask: Given an array of characters, replace each run of repeats with the character followed by its count, if the count exceeds one. Write it in place and return the new length.
string-compression.exampleWhy: aaa becomes a3, bb becomes b2, and a lone c stays c. That is a, 3, b, 2, c: five characters.

brute.idea: Build the compressed result in a separate list, then copy it back into the front of the input.
steps: Find each run with an inner pointer
Append the character, plus count if over 1
Copy the new list into chars
Return its length
brute.whySlow: Time is already linear, but it needs a second list as large as the input; the problem asks for constant extra space.

optimal.insight: The compressed form is never longer than what we have read. So a write pointer can safely overwrite cells the read pointer already passed.
steps: Read pointer measures each run
Write the character at the write pointer
If run > 1, write each digit of the count
Return the write pointer

codeNotes.match: while read < len(chars) and chars[read] == ch:

pitfalls: A count of 12 must be written as two characters, 1 and 2.
Runs of length one get no count at all.

say.intro: Okay, String Compression. You get an array of characters. Each run of the same character becomes that character, then the run length. Unless the run is just one. You have to do it in place and return the new length. Three a, two b, one c becomes a three b two c. That's five cells.
say.brute: The straightforward way builds the answer in a fresh list. Find each run, append the character, and append the count's digits if it's more than one. Then copy the list back over the input. It's linear time, which is fine. So what's the catch? Memory. That second list is as big as the input. And the problem wants constant space.
say.insight: Here's the thing. A compressed run is never longer than the run itself. A run of one writes one cell. A run of two writes two. A run of twelve writes three. So a write pointer can trail behind the read pointer. It only overwrites cells we've already read. We never destroy data we still need.
say.anim: We start with the array a, a, a, b, b, c, and both pointers at zero. The inner loop scans matching characters, counting a run of three a's. We write a at position zero, then write the digit 3 for its count. Now read moves to b, and we count a run of two b's. We write b, then write the digit 2 since the run exceeds one. Finally c appears alone, so we write just c with no count digit. The write pointer now equals five, giving the final compressed length. The function returns 5, matching the expected compressed size.
say.code: Both pointers start at zero, and the writer never passes the reader. For each run, we remember the character and measure the run by advancing read. Then we write the character once and step forward. If the run is longer than one, we write its count, one digit per cell. Notice that counts like twelve take two cells. At the end, write is the length of the compressed prefix.
say.outro: Linear time, constant extra space. Two pointers. A fast reader and a slow writer, sharing one array.

string-compression.title: String Compression
lineNotes: We define a solution class that holds the method for compressing the character array.
The compress method takes the list of characters and will modify it in place, returning the new length.
We start both the write pointer and the read pointer at zero, the front of the array.
We loop as long as the read pointer has not gone past the end of the array.
We remember the character at the read pointer, which begins the current run of repeats.
We reset the run counter to zero before counting this new group of characters.
This inner loop keeps going while we are inside the array and the current character equals the run character.
We advance the read pointer to move on to the next character in the run.
We increase the run count because we just consumed another copy of the character.
We write the run character at the write position, which is safe since write never passes read.
We move the write pointer forward one cell after storing the character.
We only add a count when the run is longer than one, as the problem requires.
We turn the run number into a string so we can handle each digit as its own character.
We store the current digit at the write position, since counts above nine take several cells.
We advance the write pointer after each digit so the next one lands in the following cell.
We return the write pointer, which equals the length of the compressed array.

shortest-path-in-binary-matrix.hook: Shortest path with equal step costs means one thing: breadth first search, eight directions at a time.
shortest-path-in-binary-matrix.ask: In an n by n grid of zeros and ones, find the fewest cells on a path of zeros from the top-left to the bottom-right, moving in eight directions. Return -1 if impossible.
shortest-path-in-binary-matrix.exampleWhy: The route goes right, right, down, down along the top and right edge: four cells, counting both ends.

brute.idea: Explore every simple path with depth first search, tracking visited cells, and keep the shortest length that reaches the corner.
steps: DFS from the top-left in 8 directions
Never revisit a cell on the current path
At the corner, record the length
Backtrack and try other branches
brute.whySlow: The number of simple paths grows exponentially. Even a 10 by 10 open grid has astronomically many.

optimal.insight: Every move costs the same, so BFS reaches each cell first by a shortest path. The first time we pop the corner, its distance is the answer.
steps: Blocked start or end? return -1
Queue the start with distance 1
Pop a cell; corner? return its distance
Push unvisited open neighbours, marking them now

codeNotes.match: if r == n - 1 and c == n - 1:

pitfalls: Mark cells when pushing, not popping, or the queue fills with duplicates.
Length counts cells, so the start alone is 1.

say.intro: Okay, Shortest Path in Binary Matrix. You get a square grid of zeros and ones. You can step onto zeros in any of eight directions. How many cells are on the shortest path from top left to bottom right? If there's no path, return minus one. In our example, the path hugs the top and right edges. Four cells.
say.brute: The brute force tries every route with depth first search. From the start, step in all eight directions, never reusing a cell on this path. Reach the corner? Record the length, back up, and keep exploring. It does find the answer. So what's the problem? The number of paths grows exponentially. Even a modest open grid never finishes.
say.insight: Here's the key. Every step costs exactly one. And when every step costs the same, breadth first search explores cells in order of distance. So the first time we reach a cell, we got there the shortest way. Why bother visiting it again? We don't. Each cell is visited once, and when the corner comes off the queue, we're done.
say.anim: We start at the top left corner, marking it visited with distance one. The algorithm checks all eight neighbors, skipping blocked or out of bounds cells. Cell zero one gets queued with distance two, since it is open. Now exploring from zero one, cell zero two is discovered at distance three. Both one two and zero two are in the queue, each at distance three. Processing one two, its neighbor two two is found open at distance four. The queue pops two two, which is exactly the bottom right corner. The function returns four, the shortest path length through the grid.
say.code: First, if the start or the end is blocked, there's no path. Return minus one. The path length counts cells, so the start goes in the queue with distance one. We pop cells in order. The first arrival is shortest, so if it's the corner, we return its distance. Otherwise we check all eight neighbours, diagonals included. We mark each one visited when we enqueue it, so nothing gets added twice.
say.outro: Each cell once, so linear in the grid. That's the graphs pattern. Unweighted shortest path? Reach for breadth first search.

shortest-path-in-binary-matrix.title: Shortest Path in Binary Matrix
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, as the problem platform expects, to hold our method.
This method takes the grid and returns the number of cells on the shortest clear path.
We store the grid's side length in n, since the grid is square.
If the start or the end cell is blocked by a one, no path can exist.
So we return negative one right away in that blocked case.
We create a queue seeded with the start cell and a path length of one, since the start counts.
We mark the start as visited by setting it to one, so we never revisit it.
We loop as long as the queue still has cells to explore.
We pop the oldest cell from the front, getting its row, column, and distance so far.
We check whether this cell is the bottom-right corner.
Since BFS reaches cells in order of distance, the first arrival at the corner gives the shortest length, so we return d.

For each row offset we try each column offset of negative one, zero, or one, covering all eight directions.
We compute the neighbor's row and column by adding the offsets to the current position.
We only continue if the neighbor is inside the grid and is an unvisited open cell holding zero.
We mark that neighbor as visited right away, so no other cell can enqueue it again.
We push the neighbor onto the queue with its distance one larger than the current cell.
If the queue empties without reaching the corner, no path exists, so we return negative one.

can-make-arithmetic-progression-from-seq.hook: You do not need to sort. Minimum, maximum and a hash set pin down the only possible progression.
can-make-arithmetic-progression-from-seq.ask: Given an array of numbers, decide whether its elements can be rearranged so that every pair of neighbours has the same difference.
can-make-arithmetic-progression-from-seq.exampleWhy: Rearranged as 1, 4, 7, 10, every step is plus 3, so it forms an arithmetic progression.

brute.idea: Sort the numbers, then check that every consecutive difference equals the first one.
steps: Sort the array
Take the first difference
Any different gap? return False
brute.whySlow: Sorting costs n log n. Fine for small inputs, but we only need membership checks, which hashing does in linear time.

optimal.insight: The progression must run from min to max in n - 1 equal steps. So the step is fixed; just check every value lands on a distinct slot.
steps: Find min, max; step = (max - min) / (n - 1)
Not a whole number? return False
Step 0 means all equal: True
Values must be distinct and on the grid

codeNotes.match: lo, hi, n = min(arr), max(arr), len(arr)

codeNotes.note: Step must be a whole number
A repeat means a missing slot

codeNotes.match: return all((x - lo) % step == 0 for x in seen)
codeNotes.note: Every value sits on a slot

pitfalls: A zero step needs its own case, or the modulo divides by zero.

say.intro: Okay, Can Make Arithmetic Progression from Sequence. You get some numbers. Can you rearrange them so neighbours always differ by the same amount? Seven, one, ten, four can become one, four, seven, ten. Each step is three. So the answer is true.
say.brute: The natural move is to sort. After sorting, any progression would be in order. Take the first gap, and check that every later pair has the same gap. Short and correct. So what's the cost? The sort. That's n log n time. Not terrible. But we can do better, because we really just need to check membership.
say.insight: Think about it this way. If a progression exists, it starts at the minimum and ends at the maximum. And there are n minus one equal steps between them. So the step is forced. Maximum minus minimum, divided by n minus one. Now every value has to land on one of the n slots. Distinct values, all on the grid? Then they fill every slot.
say.anim: We start with array 7, 1, 10, 4, finding its min, max, and length. Low is 1, high is 10, and n is 4; we check if the range divides evenly. The range divides evenly, so we compute the fixed step size between values. Step equals 3, which is nonzero, so we continue checking the sequence. We build a set of all array values to check for duplicates. The set has four unique values, matching the array length, so no duplicates. Now we verify each value lands exactly on a step from the minimum. All values align perfectly, so the function returns true, confirming an arithmetic progression.
say.code: We grab the minimum and maximum, the ends of the progression. The step must be a whole number, so if the range doesn't divide evenly, return false. If the step is zero, all values are equal. That's trivially true. Next we build a set. A repeat means some slot is missing, so fewer than n values means false. Finally, we check that every value sits on a slot.
say.outro: Linear time with a hash set. Once the shape is forced, check membership instead of sorting.

can-make-arithmetic-progression-from-seq.title: Can Make Arithmetic Progression From Sequence
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container that the judge expects for this problem.
This method takes the array and returns true if it can be rearranged into an arithmetic progression.
We find the smallest value, the largest value, and the count of elements, since the progression must span from smallest to largest.
If the range between largest and smallest does not divide evenly into n minus one steps, no equal step can exist.
In that uneven case we return false right away.
Otherwise we compute the step as the range divided by the number of gaps, n minus one.
A step of zero means every element is identical, which is trivially a valid progression.
So in that all-equal case we return true immediately.
We build a set of the values to check for duplicates and to test each value's position.
If the set has fewer items than n, some value repeats, which a nonzero step cannot allow.
In that case we return false because duplicates cannot fit distinct slots.
Finally we check that every value sits exactly on a step boundary starting from the minimum, returning true only if all do.

minimum-moves-to-clean-the-classroom.hook: Your position alone is not enough. The state is where you are, what you collected, and your energy left.
minimum-moves-to-clean-the-classroom.ask: A student starts at S with limited energy; each move costs one. Reset cells refill energy. Avoid obstacles. Return the fewest moves to collect every litter cell, or -1.
minimum-moves-to-clean-the-classroom.exampleWhy: Grab the left litter, step down onto the reset cell, then step right onto the last litter: three moves.

brute.idea: Run BFS over full states (row, column, collected mask, energy), keeping a visited set of every exact state.
steps: State = cell, litter mask, energy left
Pop a state; all litter collected? done
Move to open neighbours, spend 1 energy
Skip exact states already seen
brute.whySlow: Same worst case, but it treats each energy level as new. Arriving with less energy than before is useless, yet still explored.
