optimal.insight: BFS over (cell, litter mask), but for each pair only keep a new arrival if it has more energy than any earlier one. Less energy is dominated.
steps: Number each litter cell for a bitmask
BFS from S with full energy
Moving costs 1; R refills; L sets its bit
Keep a state only if it beats the best energy
Return steps when the mask is full

codeNotes.match: ne = energy if classroom[nr][nc] == "R" else e - 1

pitfalls: Visiting by cell alone is wrong: the same cell matters with a different mask.
Litter on the final move still counts even when energy hits zero.

say.intro: Okay, Minimum Moves to Clean the Classroom. A student starts at S with some energy. Each move costs one energy. Reset cells refill it, and obstacles block the way. What's the fewest moves to collect all the litter? In our two by two room, we grab the left litter, refill on the reset cell, then grab the last. Three moves.
say.brute: Every move costs one, so breadth first search is the right tool. But here's the thing. The cell alone isn't enough state. We also need which litter we've collected, as a bitmask, and how much energy is left. The simple version remembers every exact state. It works. So what's wrong? It re explores the same cell and mask at every lower energy level.
say.insight: Now, notice something. Say we reach a cell with the same litter collected, but with less energy than an earlier visit. Can that ever help? No. The earlier visit took no more moves, and it can do everything this one can. So for each cell and mask, we remember the best energy seen. A new state only survives if it beats that.
say.anim: We start with a two by two classroom, student at top right, litter at bottom left and bottom right. The student begins at position zero one with full energy four and zero litter collected. Moving down to one one collects the second litter, dropping energy to three, and gets queued. Moving left to zero zero collects the first litter too, energy three, another valid new state. From one one, moving up to one zero resets energy to four since it's a refill tile. Exploring further, the cell one one with mask two now arrives with less energy, so it's skipped as dominated. Eventually a path reaches one one with both litters collected, mask three, after three steps. The search finishes and returns three, the minimum moves needed to clean the whole classroom.
say.code: First, we give each litter cell its own bit. All bits set means the room is clean, so we return the step count. We pop states in move order. Out of energy? Then we're stuck here. Otherwise, for each open neighbour, we update the mask and energy. Landing on a reset cell refills energy. Finally, we prune. We only push an arrival if it has more energy than the best stored.
say.outro: Breadth first search over a bigger state, with pruning. When the map alone isn't enough, add what matters to the state.

minimum-moves-to-clean-the-classroom.title: Minimum Moves to Clean the Classroom
lineNotes: We define the Solution class that holds our method for this problem.
The method takes the classroom grid and the starting energy, and returns the fewest moves or negative one.
We record the number of rows and columns of the grid as m and n.
We create a dictionary that will map each litter cell to its own bit index.
We loop over every row of the grid to scan for special cells.
Inside each row we loop over every column to look at each cell.
If the cell is the letter S, we have found the starting position.
We save that cell's row and column as the start.
Otherwise, if the cell holds litter, we handle it in the next line.
We assign this litter cell the next free bit index, using the current size of the dictionary.
The full mask has one bit set per litter piece, so matching it means everything is collected.
We record the best energy seen for the start state, which has no litter collected and full energy.
We start the queue with the start cell, empty mask, full energy, and zero steps.
We run the breadth first search until no states remain, so the first success is the shortest.
We take the oldest state off the queue and unpack its position, mask, energy, and steps.
If the mask shows all litter collected, this state is the answer.
We return the step count, which is minimal because breadth first search explores by increasing steps.
If energy is zero, the student cannot move any further from here.
So we skip this state and move on to the next one in the queue.
We try moving down, up, right, and left from the current cell.
We only proceed if the neighbor is inside the grid and is not an obstacle.
If the neighbor holds litter, we turn on its bit in the mask, otherwise the mask stays the same.
Stepping onto a reset cell refills energy to full, and any other cell costs one energy.
We only continue if this arrival has more energy than any earlier arrival at the same cell and mask.
We record the new higher energy as the best for this cell and mask combination.
We push the new state with one more step so it gets explored later.
If the queue empties without collecting all litter, the task is impossible, so we return negative one.

dungeon-game.hook: Plan backwards from the princess. The health you need here depends only on what lies ahead.
dungeon-game.ask: A knight walks from the top-left to the bottom-right of a grid, moving only right or down. Cells add or remove health, which must stay at least 1. Return the minimum starting health.
dungeon-game.exampleWhy: Going right, right, down, down costs at most 6 health along the way, so starting with 7 keeps him alive.

brute.idea: Recursively try both moves from every cell and take whichever path needs less health, with no memory of earlier answers.
steps: At the princess: need max(1, 1 - cell)
Else ask right and down for their need
Need here = max(1, min(those) - cell)
brute.whySlow: The same cells are recomputed along every path that reaches them. A 200 by 200 dungeon has more paths than atoms.

optimal.insight: Forward DP fails because health and score conflict. Backwards, each cell needs only max(1, cheaper next need - its value), filled once.
steps: Pad the grid with infinity, 1 beside the goal
Fill from bottom-right to top-left
need = max(1, min(down, right) - cell)
Answer is need at the top-left

pitfalls: A forward DP on max health collected gives wrong answers.
Clamp to 1: big potions cannot let health dip to 0 earlier.

say.intro: Okay, Dungeon Game. A knight starts at the top left and must reach the princess at the bottom right. He can only move right or down. Each cell adds or drains health, and health can never drop below one. What's the smallest starting health? In our example, the best route needs seven.
say.brute: The brute force asks, from each cell, how much health do I need to finish? At the goal, just enough to survive that cell. Anywhere else, ask the cell to the right and the cell below. Take the cheaper one, and adjust for this cell. So what's the catch? With no memory, the same cells get solved again and again. That's exponential.
say.insight: Here's the trick. Going forward fails. Why? A path can collect lots of health later, but dip dangerously low early on. So go backwards. The health you need at a cell only depends on the cells ahead. It's the cheaper next need, minus this cell's value. But never less than one. Fill that table once, from the princess back to the start.
say.anim: We start with the dungeon grid and set up a need table filled with infinity. We seed the bottom right edges with health need of one, our base case. Working backwards from row two, we compute each cell's minimum health needed to survive. Moving to row one, needs rise sharply, like eleven at column one, due to harsh penalties. Finally row zero fills in, combining neighbors and cell values to get final needs. Need at zero zero becomes seven, meaning the knight needs seven starting health. The function returns seven, confirming seven is the minimum initial health required.
say.code: We make a need table one bigger in each direction. Outside the grid is unreachable, so the border is infinity. The two cells just past the goal are one, because we leave the goal with one health. Then we work backwards from the princess. Each cell takes the cheaper path ahead, subtracts its own value, and never goes below one. The top left is the starting health required.
say.outro: Each cell once, so linear in the grid. Two dimensional dynamic programming, solved backwards from the goal.

dungeon-game.title: Dungeon Game
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container the interview platform expects for our method.
The method calculateMinimumHP takes the dungeon grid and returns the smallest starting health that keeps the knight alive.
We read the number of rows as m and the number of columns as n from the dungeon grid.
We build a need table one row and column larger than the grid, filled with infinity so out of bounds moves are never chosen.
We set the two cells next to the princess's cell to one, so the last cell requires only enough health to end at one.
We loop over rows from the bottom up to the top, because each cell depends on cells below it.
Inside each row we loop over columns from right to left, so the right neighbor is already computed.
Each cell needs the cheaper of the down or right requirement minus its own value, but never less than one.
We return the need at the top-left cell, which is the minimum starting health for the whole trip.

top-k-frequent-words.hook: Count, then let a heap order by frequency and alphabet at the same time.
top-k-frequent-words.ask: Given a list of words and k, return the k most frequent words, highest count first. Ties are broken alphabetically.
top-k-frequent-words.exampleWhy: the appears 4 times, is 3, sunny 2, day 1. Exactly four distinct words, ordered by count.

brute.idea: Count every word, sort all distinct words by count descending then alphabetically, and take the first k.
steps: Count each word in a dictionary
Sort by (-count, word)
Return the first k
brute.whySlow: It fully sorts every distinct word even when k is tiny, paying n log n where only k pops are needed.

optimal.insight: Store (-count, word) pairs. Python compares tuples left to right, so one min-heap orders by frequency, then alphabetically, for free.
steps: Count each word with a hash map
Build (-count, word) pairs
Heapify in linear time
Pop k times

pitfalls: A size-k min-heap needs reversed alphabet order for ties; easy to get wrong.

say.intro: Okay, Top K Frequent Words. You get a list of words and a number k. Return the k most common words, most frequent first. Ties go alphabetically. In our example, the shows up four times, is three times, sunny twice, and day once. With k equal to four, that's the whole ranking.
say.brute: The simple approach counts every word. Then it sorts all the distinct words by count, highest first, using the word to break ties. Then it takes the first k. Correct, and pretty clean. So what's the catch? It sorts everything. That's n log n, even when you only want the top two or three.
say.insight: Here's the thing. Put a pair into a min heap. Negative count, then the word. Pairs compare left to right. So the smallest pair has the biggest count. And among equal counts, it has the alphabetically first word. The heap does the ranking for us. Building it takes linear time. Then we only pop k times.
say.anim: We start with an empty count dictionary to track word frequencies. We loop through each word, building counts: the, day, is, and sunny appear once. As more words repeat, the count for the climbs to four, is to three, sunny to two. Each word becomes a pair of negative count and word, so smallest negative means most frequent. Heapify arranges these pairs into a min-heap, ordering by frequency then alphabetically. Popping the heap four times pulls out words in order of highest frequency first. The final answer is the, is, sunny, and day, the top four frequent words.
say.code: First, we tally each word in a dictionary. Next, we build pairs of negative count and word. Negating the count puts the biggest first. Then heapify turns that list into a heap in linear time. Finally, we pop the k best words, keeping just the word from each pair. They come out in exactly the order we need.
say.outro: A linear build, plus k log n pops. That's the heap pattern. Encode the ranking in a pair, and let the heap sort it.

top-k-frequent-words.title: Top K Frequent Words
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container the interview platform expects for our method.
The method takes a list of words and a number k, and returns the k most frequent words.
We start with an empty dictionary called count to track how many times each word appears.
We loop through every word in the input list, one at a time.
For each word we add one to its stored count, using zero as the default when it is new.
We build a list of pairs holding the negative frequency and the word, so higher counts sort first.
We heapify the list in place, turning it into a min-heap in linear time.
We pop the heap k times, keeping only the word from each pair, which gives frequency order with alphabetical ties.

smallest-stable-index-ii.hook: Each index needs a max to its left and a min to its right. Precompute one, stream the other.
smallest-stable-index-ii.ask: For each index i, take the largest value from the start up to i, minus the smallest value from i to the end. Return the first index where that is at most k, or -1.
smallest-stable-index-ii.exampleWhy: At index 3, the max so far is 5 and the min from there on is 4. 5 minus 4 is 1, within 3.

brute.idea: For every index, rescan the prefix for its maximum and the suffix for its minimum, then test the difference.
steps: For each i, max of nums[0..i]
Min of nums[i..n-1]
Difference ≤ k? return i
brute.whySlow: Each index rescans the whole array. 100,000 numbers means ten billion reads.

optimal.insight: Suffix minimums can be precomputed right to left in one pass. Prefix maximum just grows as we scan left to right.
steps: Fill suf[i] = min(nums[i], suf[i + 1])
Scan left to right with a running max
Score = running max - suf[i]
First score ≤ k wins

codeNotes.note: Min of everything to the right

pitfalls: Both ranges include index i itself.

say.intro: Okay, Smallest Stable Index Two. For each index, take the biggest value up to it. Subtract the smallest value from it to the end. Return the first index where that score is at most k. Take five, zero, one, four, with k three. Index three scores five minus four. That's one, so the answer is three.
say.brute: The brute force follows the definition exactly. For each index, scan the prefix to find its maximum. Scan the suffix to find its minimum. Subtract, and compare with k. So what's the catch? Every index rescans up to the whole array. That's n squared. With a hundred thousand numbers, it's billions of reads.
say.insight: Here's the thing. Neighbouring indexes share almost all their work. The minimum from i onward is just the smaller of the value at i, and the minimum from i plus one onward. So one pass from the right builds every suffix minimum. And the prefix maximum? It only ever grows. So we just carry it along as we scan from the left.
say.anim: We start with nums 5, 0, 1, 4 and k equal to 3. We build the suffix minimum array from right to left, starting with 4. At index 2, suffix min becomes 1, since nums is 1. At index 1, suffix min stays 0, matching nums value there. At index 0, suffix min is 0, giving suf array 0, 0, 1, 4. Now we scan left to right, tracking the running prefix maximum, starting at 5. At index 0, run max minus suf is 5, which exceeds k, so we continue. We keep updating run max through indices 1 and 2, still too large. At index 3, run max is 5 and suffix min is 4, giving difference 1, within k, so we return 3.
say.code: We build a suffix minimum array. The last suffix is one element, so its cell is just the last number. Walking right to left, each cell holds the min of everything to the right. Then we walk left to right, streaming the prefix max. At each index, if max minus suffix min is at most k, it's stable. The first one wins, so we return it. Otherwise, minus one.
say.outro: Linear time, linear space. Precompute the suffix, stream the prefix, and never rescan.

smallest-stable-index-ii.title: Smallest Stable Index II
lineNotes: We define the Solution class that holds the method for this problem.
This method takes the list nums and the threshold k, and returns the first stable index or negative one.
We store the length of nums in n so we can reuse it for sizing and looping.
We create a list called suf of n zeros to hold the suffix minimums.
The last suffix minimum is just the last number, since nothing lies to its right.
We walk from the second to last index back to zero, building suffix minimums right to left.
Each suffix minimum is the smaller of the current number and the suffix minimum just after it.
We start run max at the first element, which is the prefix maximum before scanning.
Now we scan every index from left to right to test stability.
We update run max with the current number so it always holds the largest value from the start through i.
If the prefix maximum minus the suffix minimum at i is at most k, this index is stable.
Because we scan in order, the first stable index is returned immediately as the answer.
If no index satisfied the condition, we return negative one.

best-sightseeing-pair.hook: Split the score into a left part and a right part, and the pair search collapses into one pass.
best-sightseeing-pair.ask: Each spot has a value. A pair i < j scores values[i] + values[j] + i - j. Return the highest score of any pair.
best-sightseeing-pair.exampleWhy: Pair index 0 and 2: 8 plus 5 minus the distance 2 gives 11, the best of all pairs.

brute.idea: Try every pair i < j, compute its score, and keep the maximum.
steps: Pick i
Try every j after i
Keep the best score
brute.whySlow: With 50,000 spots there are over a billion pairs to score.

optimal.insight: The score is (values[i] + i) + (values[j] - j). For each j, we only need the best values[i] + i seen before it.
steps: Keep best_i = max of values[i] + i so far
At j, score = best_i + values[j] - j
Update the answer
Then fold j into best_i

codeNotes.note: Best left part: value plus index
Each j is a right end
Pair j with the best left
j can be a future left

pitfalls: Update the answer before best_i, so j never pairs with itself.

say.intro: Okay, Best Sightseeing Pair. Each spot has a value. A pair scores both values, minus the distance between them. Find the best pair. In eight, one, five, two, six, take eight and five. That's thirteen minus two, which is eleven. And nothing beats it.
say.brute: The brute force tries every pair. For each first spot, loop over every later spot. Compute the score and keep the best. Simple and correct. So what's the problem? It's n squared. With fifty thousand spots, that's over a billion pairs.
say.insight: Here's the trick. Split the score into two pieces. The left spot's value plus its index. And the right spot's value minus its index. Notice that each piece depends on only one spot. So for any right spot, who's the best partner? Simply the earlier spot with the biggest value plus index. And we can keep that as one number while we scan.
say.anim: We start with values 8, 1, 5, 2, 6, and best_i set to 8, the first value. Ans starts at 0, tracking the best sightseeing pair score found so far. At j equals 1, we compute ans using best_i plus value minus index, staying 8. Best_i updates by comparing to value plus index, but 8 still remains the best. At j equals 2, ans becomes 11, combining best_i 8 with value 5 minus 2. At j equals 3, the new pair score doesn't beat 11, so ans stays the same. At j equals 4, best_i is now 10, but the resulting score still can't beat 11. The function returns ans, giving the final best sightseeing pair score of 11.
say.code: We start the best left part at the first value plus its index, which is zero. Then each j, from one onward, is a right end. We pair j with the best left so far, and update the answer. Now, notice the order. Only after scoring, j can become a future left. We compare its value plus j with the best. At the end, return the answer.
say.outro: Linear time, constant space. One dimensional dynamic programming. Carry the best prefix value forward, and pair each new spot with it.

best-sightseeing-pair.title: Best Sightseeing Pair
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container the judge expects for the method that solves this problem.
This method takes the list of values and returns the highest score of any sightseeing pair as an integer.
We start best_i as the first value, which equals values at index zero plus zero, the best left spot so far.
We set the answer to zero as a starting point, since any real pair score will be compared against it.
We loop j from one to the end, treating each position as the right spot of a pair.
We update the answer using the best left term plus values at j minus j, keeping whichever score is larger.
Now we update best_i with values at j plus j, so later right spots can use this position as a left spot.
Finally we return the answer, which holds the highest pair score found during the single pass.

binary-tree-inorder-traversal.hook: Recursion makes this a three-liner. The interview question is doing it with your own stack.
binary-tree-inorder-traversal.ask: Given the root of a binary tree, return its node values in inorder: left subtree, then the node, then the right subtree.
binary-tree-inorder-traversal.exampleWhy: This is a search tree, so visiting left, node, right lists the values in sorted order, 1 through 7.

brute.idea: Recurse: traverse the left subtree, record the node, then traverse the right subtree.
steps: Empty node: return
Recurse left
Record the value
Recurse right
brute.whySlow: Same complexity, but it leans on the call stack; a skewed tree of 100,000 nodes overflows Python recursion.

optimal.insight: Simulate the call stack. Push nodes while going left; when you cannot go further, pop, record it, and turn right.
steps: Push nodes while sliding left
Pop: that node is next in order
Record it, then move to its right child
Stop when stack and pointer are empty

codeNotes.note: Defer node until left is done

pitfalls: Loop while cur or stack: checking only the stack stops early.

say.intro: Okay, Binary Tree Inorder Traversal. You get a binary tree. List its values in order. Everything in the left subtree, then the node, then everything in the right subtree. Our example is a search tree with four at the root. So inorder gives one through seven, sorted.
say.brute: The textbook answer is recursion. Walk left, record the node, walk right. Linear time, three lines. So what's the catch? It's not slower. But it leans on the call stack. A very lopsided tree is as deep as it is long, and that overflows recursion. And interviewers almost always ask for the iterative version next.
say.insight: Here's the thing. Recursion is just a stack the language manages for you. So let's manage it ourselves. Slide left from the current node, pushing every node you pass. Why push them? Because each one has to wait until its left side is done. When you can't go left any more, pop the top. That's the next node in order. Record it, then go right.
say.anim: We start at root node 4, with an empty result list and empty stack. We push nodes while going left: 4, then 2, then 1, reaching the leftmost node. Node 1 has no left child, so we pop it, record it, and move right to none. We pop node 2, append it, then move right into node 3, pushing it onto the stack. Node 3 is popped and recorded, giving result one two three, then we return to node 4. Node 4 pops next, appended to result, and we move right into node 6's subtree. We traverse left to 5, pop it, then pop 6 itself, then explore its right child 7. Finally node 7 pops and is appended, giving the final answer one through seven.
say.code: We start with an empty result, an empty stack, and a pointer at the root. We keep going while work remains somewhere, in the pointer or on the stack. We push each node and move left, deferring it until its left side is done. When we hit the leftmost unvisited node, we pop it. Its left side is finished, so we record its value. Then we handle the right subtree.
say.outro: Linear time, space equal to the tree height. The tree pattern here is simple. An explicit stack replaces recursion.

binary-tree-inorder-traversal.title: Binary Tree Inorder Traversal
lineNotes: We define a Solution class that holds the method for this problem.
The inorderTraversal method takes the root of a binary tree and returns a list of node values.
We create an empty result list and an empty stack that will simulate the recursion call stack.
We set cur to the root so it acts as our pointer for walking through the tree.
We keep looping as long as there is a current node to explore or saved nodes waiting on the stack.
This inner loop keeps descending as long as the current node exists, heading toward the leftmost node.
Before moving left, we push the current node onto the stack so we can return to it later.
We move cur to its left child, going as deep left as possible.
With no more left children, we pop the most recent node, which is the next one to visit in inorder.
We record the popped node's value in the result, since its left subtree is fully handled.
We turn to the right child so its subtree gets traversed next, or cur becomes empty if there is none.
Once the loop finishes, we return the list of values in inorder.

largest-number.hook: Sort the numbers, but not by size. Compare which concatenation order wins.
largest-number.ask: Given non-negative integers, arrange them so that writing them side by side forms the largest possible number. Return it as a string.
largest-number.exampleWhy: 5 then 34 then 3 then 30 gives 534330. Placing 3 before 30 wins, because 330 beats 303.

brute.idea: Try every ordering of the numbers, join each one, and keep the largest string.
steps: Generate every permutation
Join it into one string
Keep the biggest
Strip leading zeros
brute.whySlow: Just 12 numbers have 479 million orderings; 100 numbers would never finish.

optimal.insight: a should come before b exactly when a + b > b + a as strings. This rule is consistent, so sorting with it is optimal.
steps: Turn every number into a string
Sort with a + b versus b + a
All zeros? return "0"
Join the sorted strings

codeNotes.note: a first makes a bigger number

pitfalls: Plain string sort puts 30 before 3, which is wrong.
Input of all zeros must return "0", not "000".

say.intro: Okay, Largest Number. You get some non negative integers. Order them so that, written side by side, they make the biggest number possible. For three, thirty, thirty four and five, the best order is five, thirty four, three, thirty. That gives five three four three three zero.
say.brute: The brute force tries every ordering. For each one, join the strings and keep the largest. Strip leading zeros at the end. It's guaranteed correct. So what's the catch? There are n factorial orderings. Just twelve numbers gives almost half a billion. Hopeless for real inputs.
say.insight: Here's the trick. To decide between two numbers, glue them both ways. Does a then b beat b then a? Then a goes first. Take three and thirty. Three thirty versus thirty three. Three thirty wins. Now, this rule is consistent across every pair. So we can just sort with it. And then every neighbour sits in its best order.
say.anim: We start by converting each number into a string, like turning five into the string five. Now we sort these strings using a custom comparison to decide their best order. Comparing thirty and three, combining them differently shows three should come first. Comparing thirty four and thirty, thirty four wins because it forms a larger combined number. The comparisons continue, repeatedly placing five and thirty four ahead of smaller combinations. After sorting, strs becomes five, thirty four, three, thirty, the optimal order found. Finally we join these strings together into one single result string. The function returns five three four three three zero as the largest possible number.
say.code: First, we turn every number into a string. We compare as text, not values. Our compare says a goes first when a then b makes the bigger string. We sort with that pair rule. Now, one edge case. If the first string is zero, everything is zero, so it all collapses to a single zero. Otherwise, we glue the strings in winning order.
say.outro: n log n comparisons, each as long as the numbers. That's greedy. Find a pairwise rule, check it's consistent, then sort by it.

largest-number.title: Largest Number
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container the problem expects for our method.
The method largestNumber takes a list of non-negative integers and returns the biggest possible concatenation as a string.
We convert every number to a string so we can compare and join them by their digits.
We define a helper compare function that decides which of two strings should come first in the final answer.
If putting a before b gives a larger combined string than b before a, then a should come first.
We return negative one to tell the sort that a belongs ahead of b.
If putting b before a gives a larger combined string, then b should come first.
We return one to tell the sort that b belongs ahead of a.
If both orders give the same combined string, we return zero because their order does not matter.
We sort the strings using this custom comparison, converted into a key so Python's sort can use it.
After sorting, if the first string is zero, then every number must be zero, since zero would be the largest leader.
In that case we return a single zero instead of a string like several zeros in a row.
Otherwise we join the sorted strings with no separator to build the largest number.

count-commas-in-range.hook: Do not format a hundred thousand numbers. Count how many numbers cross each comma threshold.
count-commas-in-range.ask: Write every integer from 1 to n with commas every three digits from the right. Return the total number of commas used.
count-commas-in-range.exampleWhy: Only 1,000, 1,001 and 1,002 have four digits, and each has one comma: 3 in total.

brute.idea: Loop over every number from 1 to n and add its comma count, which is (digits - 1) // 3.
steps: For i from 1 to n
Count digits of i
Add (digits - 1) // 3
brute.whySlow: It touches every number. Fine for 100,000, but the same task for 10^15 would take forever.

optimal.insight: Every number at or above 1,000 has a first comma; at or above 1,000,000 a second. Each threshold t adds n - t + 1 commas.
steps: Start with threshold 1000
While threshold ≤ n, add n - threshold + 1
Multiply threshold by 1000
Return the total

codeNotes.note: Next comma starts at a million

pitfalls: Off by one: threshold to n inclusive is n - threshold + 1 numbers.

say.intro: Okay, Count Commas in Range. Write every number from one to n, with a comma every three digits from the right. How many commas do you write? Say n is one thousand and two. Only one thousand, one thousand and one, and one thousand and two have commas. One each. So the answer is three.
say.brute: The brute force loops over every number from one to n. It counts the digits, takes digits minus one, and divides by three, rounding down. That's that number's commas. And for a hundred thousand, it's fast enough. So what's the catch? It touches every single number. That doesn't scale if n gets much bigger.
say.insight: Here's the thing. Flip the question. Don't ask how many commas each number has. Ask how many numbers have a given comma. Every number from one thousand up has a first comma. Every number from a million up has a second. So the first comma appears n minus nine hundred ninety nine times. And every later threshold works the same way.
say.anim: We start with n equal to 1002 and total set to 0. Threshold is set to 1000, our first comma boundary. The while loop checks if threshold 1000 is at most 1002, which is true. Total becomes 3, since numbers from 1000 to 1002 each have one comma. Threshold multiplies by 1000, now reaching one million. The loop checks again, but one million exceeds 1002, so it stops. The function returns total, which holds the final comma count. The final answer is 3 commas for numbers up to 1002.
say.code: The threshold starts at one thousand, the smallest number with a comma. While the threshold is at most n, this comma appears at all. So we add the numbers from threshold to n. That's n minus threshold plus one. Then we multiply the threshold by a thousand. The next comma starts at a million. Finally, we return the total.
say.outro: Logarithmic time, constant space. That's the math pattern. Count by contribution, not by listing everything.

count-commas-in-range.title: Count Commas in Range
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container the judge expects for the method that follows.
This method takes n and returns the total count of commas used when writing every number from one to n.
We start total at zero, since no commas have been counted yet.
We set threshold to one thousand, the smallest number that needs a comma.
We loop as long as threshold is at most n, meaning at least one number reaches that comma level.
Every number from threshold up to n has this comma, so we add n minus threshold plus one to total.
We multiply threshold by one thousand to move to the next comma level, such as one million.
Once the thresholds exceed n, we return total as the final comma count.

path-existence-queries-in-a-graph-i.hook: The nodes are sorted, so every connected component is just a contiguous block. One pass labels them all.
path-existence-queries-in-a-graph-i.ask: Nodes have sorted values; two nodes share an edge if their values differ by at most maxDiff. For each query pair, report whether a path connects them.
path-existence-queries-in-a-graph-i.exampleWhy: The gap from 2 to 5 exceeds 2, splitting off node 0. Nodes 1, 2, 3 chain together through 5, 6, 8.

brute.idea: Build every edge by checking all pairs, then answer each query with a fresh depth first search.
steps: Check all pairs to build edges
For each query, DFS from u
Answer: was v reached?
brute.whySlow: With 100,000 nodes, building edges alone is ten billion pair checks, before running any searches.

optimal.insight: In sorted order, if any jump is too wide, nothing can cross it. Components are runs between big gaps, so label them in one sweep.
steps: Node 0 gets component 0
Gap to previous > maxDiff? start new component
Otherwise share the previous label
Query: same label means connected

codeNotes.note: Big gap starts a new block

pitfalls: Only neighbouring gaps matter; no edge can jump over a too-wide gap.

say.intro: Okay, Path Existence Queries in a Graph One. Each node has a value, and the values are sorted. Two nodes are joined when their values differ by at most max diff. For each query, is there a path? With values two, five, six, eight and max diff two, node zero is cut off. Nodes one, two and three link up.
say.brute: The brute force builds the graph literally. Check every pair, and add an edge when the values are close enough. Then, for each query, search from the first node and see if it reaches the second. So what's the problem? Building the edges alone is n squared. And every query repeats a full search.
say.insight: Here's the thing. The values are sorted. So if two neighbours differ by more than max diff, can anything on the left reach the right? No. Everything further away is even further apart. And if every neighbouring gap is small, the whole run chains together. So components are just contiguous blocks. They split at the big gaps.
say.anim: We start with four sorted values and initialize all component labels to zero. At index one, the gap from two to five is three, exceeding maxDiff, so a new component starts. At index two, six minus five is only one, so it joins the same component as before. At index three, eight minus six is two, within maxDiff, so it stays in that component. Now comp is zero, one, one, one, marking two separate components in the sequence. For each query, we just compare the component labels of the two indices. The final answer is false, false, true, true, matching components across valid gaps.
say.code: We give each node a component label, starting at zero. Then one sweep in sorted order, from the second node on. Each node copies the previous label. But a big gap starts a new block, so we add one. Then every query is easy. Same block means a path.
say.outro: Linear time for the labels, constant per query. Find the structure in the components, instead of searching.

path-existence-queries-in-a-graph-i.title: Path Existence Queries in a Graph I
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container the judge expects for this problem's method.
The method takes the node count, the sorted values, the maximum allowed difference, and the list of query pairs.
We create a component label list of size n, starting every node at label zero.
We sweep through nodes from index one onward, comparing each node with the one just before it.
Each node copies the previous label, adding one when the gap between neighbors exceeds maxDiff, since that gap starts a new component.
For each query pair we return whether both nodes share the same label, meaning a path connects them.

zigzag-conversion.hook: You never need the zigzag picture. Just know which row each character lands in.
zigzag-conversion.ask: Write a string down and up across numRows rows in a zigzag, then read the rows left to right, top to bottom. Return that string.
zigzag-conversion.exampleWhy: Rows read PAHN, then APLSIIG, then YIR. Glued together they give PAHNAPLSIIGYIR.

brute.idea: Draw the zigzag literally in a 2-D grid, one column per character, then read the grid row by row.
steps: Allocate numRows by n empty grid
Place character i in column i
Bounce the row at top and bottom
Read every cell, row by row
brute.whySlow: The grid is mostly empty: 1,000 rows by 1,000 characters is a million cells for a thousand letters.

optimal.insight: Only row order matters. Keep one string per row, and bounce a row pointer down and up as you walk the input.
steps: One empty string per row
Append the character to the current row
Flip direction at the top or bottom
Join all rows

pitfalls: numRows of 1 would bounce forever between rows 0 and 0; return early.

say.intro: Okay, Zigzag Conversion. Write a string in a zigzag across some rows. Straight down, then diagonally back up, and repeat. Then read each row left to right. Paypal is hiring, on three rows, reads P A H N on top. Then A P L S I I G in the middle. And Y I R at the bottom.
say.brute: The literal approach draws the picture. Make a grid with one row per zigzag row, and one column per character. Place each character in its row, bouncing at the top and bottom. Then read every cell, row by row. It's correct. So what's wrong? The grid is mostly empty. It wastes rows times length, in both time and space.
say.insight: Here's the thing. The columns don't matter at all. Inside each row, characters already show up in the order we meet them. So all we need is one growing string per row. Plus a row pointer. It moves down, bounces at the bottom, moves up, and bounces again at the top. Every character is handled exactly once.
say.anim: We check if numRows is one or too big, which isn't the case here, so we proceed. Three empty row strings are created, and we start at row zero moving downward with step one. Each character is appended to its current row, bouncing the pointer down then up in a zigzag. At row two, the bottom, the step flips to negative one so the pointer starts moving upward. At row two again with character I, step flips back to negative one to bounce upward once more. At row zero with character H, step resets to one, sending the pointer back downward. Characters keep filling rows N, G, and R as the zigzag pattern continues to the end. Finally the three rows are joined together, giving the final answer PAHNAPLSIIGYIR.
say.code: First, if there's one row, or more rows than characters, no zigzag is possible. Return the string as is. Next, we make one bucket per row. We start at row zero, heading down. Each character drops into its current row. At the top, we turn down. When we hit the bottom, we head back up. Then we move the row. Finally, we read the rows top to bottom and join them.
say.outro: Linear time, linear space. A simple simulation. Track the row, not the picture.

zigzag-conversion.title: Zigzag Conversion
lineNotes: We define the Solution class that holds the method for this problem.
The convert method takes the input string and the number of rows, and returns the zigzag reading.
If there is only one row or at least as many rows as characters, the zigzag changes nothing.
In that case we simply return the original string unchanged.
We create a list with one empty string for each row to collect characters.
We start at row zero and set step to one so we first move downward.
We loop over every character in the input string in its original order.
We append the current character to the string belonging to the current row.
When we are at the top row, we must start heading downward.
So we set step to one to move down.
Otherwise, if we are at the bottom row, we must turn around and head upward.
So we set step to negative one to move up.
We add step to row, moving the pointer to the row for the next character.
Finally we join all row strings from top to bottom into one result and return it.

shuffle-the-array.hook: Two halves, one pass. Index arithmetic tells you exactly where each element belongs.
shuffle-the-array.ask: The array holds x1 to xn followed by y1 to yn. Return them interleaved as x1, y1, x2, y2, and so on.
shuffle-the-array.exampleWhy: The x half is 2, 5, 1 and the y half is 3, 4, 7. Alternating them gives 2, 3, 5, 4, 1, 7.

brute.idea: Start with the x half, then insert each y value into its slot in the middle of the list.
steps: Copy the first half
Insert y_i at position 2i + 1
Return the list
brute.whySlow: Each middle insert shifts every later element. 500 pairs means about 125,000 shifts instead of 1,000 writes.

optimal.insight: x_i sits at index i and y_i at index n + i. Walk i once and append the pair; no shifting needed.
steps: Loop i from 0 to n - 1
Append nums[i]
Append nums[n + i]

pitfalls: n is half the length, not the full length.

say.intro: Okay, Shuffle the Array. The array holds two halves. The x values, then the y values, each of length n. Interleave them. X one, y one, x two, y two, and so on. With two, five, one, then three, four, seven, you get two, three, five, four, one, seven.
say.brute: One way is to copy the x half, then insert each y value into its gap. Y one goes after x one. Y two after x two. And so on. It gives the right answer. So what's the catch? Inserting into the middle of a list shifts everything after it. Do that n times, and you've got n squared work, for what should be a simple copy.
say.insight: Here's the thing. We don't need to move anything around. We already know where every value lives. X i sits at index i. And y i sits at index n plus i. So we walk i from zero up to n minus one, and append those two values in turn. Every value gets written once, straight into its final spot.
say.anim: We start with nums holding six values and n equal to three, result list empty. At i equals zero, we grab nums at index zero, the value two, into result. Then we append nums at index three, value three, pairing x with its matching y. Next i equals one, we add nums at index one, value five, to result. We pair it with nums at index four, value four, growing result further. At i equals two, value one gets appended, then paired with value seven. The loop finishes after walking through all three pairs without any shifting. Final answer returned is two, three, five, four, one, seven.
say.code: We build the answer in order, starting with an empty list. Then we loop i over the first half. That's one step per pair. First, we append x i, from the first half, at index i. Then we append y i, from the second half, at index n plus i. When the loop finishes, every pair is in place. We return the list.
say.outro: Linear time and space. Use index arithmetic to find each value, instead of shifting things around.

shuffle-the-array.title: Shuffle the Array
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container this problem expects for our method.
The shuffle method takes the array nums and the number n, which is half the length of nums.
We start with an empty list called res that will hold the interleaved result.
We loop i from zero up to n minus one, visiting each pair exactly once.
We append the x value at index i, which is the next first-half element in the output.
Then we append the y value at index n plus i, its partner from the second half.
Finally we return res, which now holds x1, y1, x2, y2 and so on in order.

number-of-visible-people-in-a-queue.hook: Scan from the right with a decreasing stack. Everyone you pop is someone you can see.
number-of-visible-people-in-a-queue.ask: People with distinct heights stand in a line facing right. Someone can see a person to the right if everyone between is shorter than both. Count visible people for each.
number-of-visible-people-in-a-queue.exampleWhy: Height 10 sees 6, then 8 over 6, then 11 over everyone. 5 and 9 are hidden, so the count is 3.

brute.idea: For each person, walk right tracking the tallest so far. Anyone taller than that is visible; stop at someone at least as tall.
steps: For each i, scan j to the right
Taller than everyone between? count them
Stop once heights[j] ≥ heights[i]
brute.whySlow: A strictly decreasing line makes every person scan to the end: 100,000 people means five billion checks.

optimal.insight: Going right to left, keep a decreasing stack of who is still visible. A new person sees everyone shorter they pop, plus the next taller one.
steps: Scan from the right
Pop shorter people; each pop is seen
Stack not empty? see one taller person
Push the current person

codeNotes.note: Shorter people are seen, then hidden
Popped person is seen, then hidden

pitfalls: Forgetting the one taller person left on the stack undercounts by one.

say.intro: Okay, Number of Visible People in a Queue. People stand in a line, all looking right, with different heights. You can see someone if everyone between you is shorter than both of you. How many people does each person see? In ten, six, eight, five, eleven, nine, the first person sees six, eight and eleven. So three.
say.brute: The brute force has each person look right. Track the tallest person seen so far. Anyone taller than that is visible. Reach someone at least as tall as you? They block everything after, so stop. It's correct. So what's the catch? If heights only go down, everyone scans to the end. That's n squared.
say.insight: Here's the trick. Scan from the right, and keep a stack of people still visible from the left. When a new person arrives, everyone shorter on the stack is visible to them. But now they're hidden from everyone further left. Forever. So pop them and count them. And if someone taller is still on the stack? The new person sees them too.
say.anim: We start with heights 10, 6, 8, 5, 11, 9, and an empty answer array and stack. Scanning right to left, person at index 5 with height 9 sees nobody, stack becomes 9. At index 4, height 11 pops the shorter 9 off the stack, giving one visible person. At index 3, height 5 is shorter than 11, so it just sees that one taller person. At index 2, height 8 pops the shorter 5, then sees taller 11, totaling two visible. At index 1, height 6 is shorter than 8, so it sees one person and stops. At index 0, height 10 pops 6 and 8, then sees 11, giving three visible people. The final answer array is 3, 1, 2, 1, 1, 0.
say.code: We make the answer array and an empty stack. We process from the right, last person first. While the top of the stack is shorter, it's seen, then hidden. So we pop it and add one. Each popped person is seen, then hidden. Then, if anyone is left on the stack, that's the first taller person. Add one more. Finally, we push this person. Now they block those behind.
say.outro: Each person is pushed and popped once, so linear time. That's the monotonic stack pattern.

number-of-visible-people-in-a-queue.title: Number of Visible People in a Queue
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container LeetCode expects for the method we are about to write.
This method takes the list of heights and returns how many people each person can see to their right.
We store the number of people in the queue in n, so we can size our answer and loop correctly.
We create the answer list filled with zeros, one slot for each person in the queue.
We start with an empty stack that will hold heights of people still visible, shrinking toward the top.
We loop from the last person back to the first, since each person only cares about people on their right.
While the top of the stack is shorter than the current person, that shorter person is visible and blocked from anyone further left.
We pop that shorter person off the stack because the current person will block them from everyone to the left.
Each popped person is someone the current person can see, so we add one to the answer for this position.
After popping, if the stack still has someone, that person is taller and the current person can see them too.
We add one more to the answer for that first taller person, since they are visible but block everything behind them.
We push the current height onto the stack so people to the left can consider them.
Finally we return the answer list holding the visible counts for every person.

single-element-in-a-sorted-array.hook: Pairs start on even indexes until the single element breaks the rhythm. Binary search finds the break.
single-element-in-a-sorted-array.ask: In a sorted array, every value appears exactly twice except one, which appears once. Find that value in logarithmic time and constant space.
single-element-in-a-sorted-array.exampleWhy: Every other value appears twice. Only 2 has no partner beside it.

brute.idea: Walk the array in steps of two. The first position where a pair does not match holds the single element.
steps: Check nums[i] and nums[i + 1] for even i
Mismatch? nums[i] is the single
Reached the end? it is the last
brute.whySlow: It reads half of the array. The problem demands logarithmic time: 100,000 numbers means 50,000 checks instead of 17.

optimal.insight: Left of the single, each pair starts at an even index. Right of it, pairs start at odd ones. Test an even mid against its right neighbour.
steps: Binary search over l and r
Snap mid to an even index
Pair intact? single is right: l = m + 2
Pair broken? single at m or left: r = m

codeNotes.note: Make m the start of a pair
Single is m or to its left

pitfalls: Without snapping mid to even, the pair test checks the wrong neighbour.

say.intro: Okay, Single Element in a Sorted Array. The array is sorted. Every number appears exactly twice, except one, which appears once. Find it, in logarithmic time. In one one, two, three three, four four, eight eight, the loner is two.
say.brute: The simple approach walks the array two at a time and checks each pair. The first pair that doesn't match starts with the single. If every pair matches, it's the last value. It uses constant space. So what's the problem? It's linear time. And the problem asks for logarithmic.
say.insight: Here's the thing. Before the single, every pair starts on an even index. Zero and one. Two and three. And so on. Now, the single shifts everything after it by one. So later pairs start on odd indexes. Pick an even middle. Does it match its right neighbour? Then the rhythm is intact, and the single is further right. Otherwise, it's here or to the left.
say.anim: We start with left at 0 and right at 8, spanning the whole array. Mid is calculated as 4, which is even, so no adjustment is needed. Nums at 4 and 5 are 3 and 4, not equal, so we move right to 4. Now mid becomes 2, still even, comparing nums at 2 and 3. Nums at 2 and 3 are 2 and 3, different, so right shrinks to 2. Mid is 1, odd, so we decrease it to 0 to check a proper pair. Nums at 0 and 1 are both 1, equal, so left jumps to 2. Left now equals right at index 2, and the single element is 2.
say.code: We set l and r to the ends, and narrow until one index remains. We take the middle. If it's odd, we step back by one, to make it the start of a pair. If the value there equals the next one, the rhythm is intact so far. The single lies further right, so l jumps to middle plus two. Otherwise, the single is the middle or left of it, so r moves there.
say.outro: Logarithmic time, constant space. Binary search on a property. Here, it's the parity of where pairs begin.

single-element-in-a-sorted-array.title: Single Element in a Sorted Array
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container the problem expects for our method.
The method takes the sorted list nums and returns the one value that appears only once.
We set left to zero and right to the last index, so the search covers the whole array.
We loop while left is less than right, narrowing the window until one candidate index remains.
We compute mid as the average of left and right, rounded down.
We check whether mid is odd, because we want to compare pairs starting at even positions.
If mid is odd, we move it back by one so it lands on an even index.
We compare the value at mid with its right neighbour to see if the pair is intact.
If they match, the single lies to the right, so left jumps past this pair to mid plus two.
Otherwise the pairing has already broken at or before mid, so the single is not to the right.
We set right to mid, keeping mid since it could itself be the single element.
When left meets right, that index holds the single element, so we return its value.

first-unique-character-in-a-string.hook: Two passes beat one clever pass. Count everything first, then find the first count of one.
first-unique-character-in-a-string.ask: Given a string, return the index of the first character that appears exactly once. If none exists, return -1.
first-unique-character-in-a-string.exampleWhy: l, o and e all repeat later. v at index 2 appears only once, so the answer is 2.

brute.idea: For each character, count how many times it appears in the whole string. The first one with count one wins.
steps: For each index i
Count s[i] across the whole string
Count is 1? return i
brute.whySlow: Every index rescans the full string: 100,000 letters means up to ten billion comparisons.

optimal.insight: Counting is separate from ordering. One pass builds a frequency map; a second pass in original order finds the first count of one.
steps: Count every character
Walk the string again in order
First count of 1? return its index
None? return -1

pitfalls: Scan the string, not the map, in the second pass to keep order.

say.intro: Okay, First Unique Character in a String. Return the index of the first character that appears only once. If every character repeats, return minus one. In love leet code, l, o and e all show up again later. But the v at index two appears just once. So the answer is two.
say.brute: The brute force takes each character and counts how often it appears in the whole string. The first one with a count of one wins. Short and simple. So what's the catch? Every index rescans the entire string. For a hundred thousand letters, that can be ten billion comparisons.
say.insight: Here's the thing. Counting and ordering are two separate questions. So answer them separately. First pass, count every letter with a hash map. Second pass, walk the string again from the start. Return the first index whose letter has a count of one. Both passes are linear. And there are at most twenty six letters to store.
say.anim: We start with the string loveleetcode and an empty count map. The first loop scans every character, building up counts as it goes. Notice letters like l and e climb to two and three as repeats appear. After the full pass, e appears four times, while v, t, c, d appear once. Now a second loop walks the string in order checking each count. Index zero is l with count two, so it is skipped. Index one is o with count two, also skipped, not unique. Index two is v with count one, so we return index two as the answer.
say.code: We start with a dictionary from letter to frequency. In the first pass, we tally every character. Then a second pass walks the string again, with indexes. Why a second pass? Because it keeps the original order. The first character with a count of exactly one is unique, and the earliest one wins. So we return its index. If nothing qualifies, minus one.
say.outro: Linear time, constant space for lowercase letters. Count first, then scan in order.

first-unique-character-in-a-string.title: First Unique Character in a String
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container the interview platform expects for our method.
The method firstUniqChar takes a string s and returns an integer index of the first unique character.
We start with an empty dictionary called count that will hold how many times each character appears.
The first pass walks through every character in the string, one at a time, to build the counts.
For each character we look up its current count, defaulting to zero, then add one and store it back.
The second pass walks the string again in original order, tracking both the index and the character.
We check whether this character's total count equals one, meaning it appears exactly once in the whole string.
Because we scan in original order, the first such character gives the answer, so we return its index immediately.
If the loop finishes without finding any character with count one, we return negative one to signal none exists.

unique-3-digit-even-numbers.hook: Choose distinct digits, not positions, and the duplicates take care of themselves.
unique-3-digit-even-numbers.ask: Given a list of digits, count how many distinct three-digit even numbers can be formed, using each copy at most once and no leading zero.
unique-3-digit-even-numbers.exampleWhy: The numbers are 202, 220, 250, 252, 502, 520 and 522: seven distinct even values.

brute.idea: Try every ordered triple of positions, build the number, and collect valid ones in a set to remove duplicates.
steps: Loop over three distinct positions i, j, k
Skip a leading zero or odd last digit
Add the number to a set
Return the set size
brute.whySlow: Repeated digits build the same number many times; the set has to throw those copies away afterwards.

optimal.insight: Count each digit. Then pick hundreds, tens and units from distinct digit values, borrowing from the counts, so each number appears once.
steps: Count copies of each digit
Pick a nonzero hundreds digit, take one copy
Pick a tens digit still in stock
Count even units digits still in stock

pitfalls: Choosing positions instead of values counts 202 twice when 2 repeats.

say.intro: Okay, Unique Three Digit Even Numbers. You get some digits. Count the distinct three digit even numbers you can build. Each copy of a digit is used once at most, and there's no leading zero. With zero, two, two and five, we can make seven numbers. From two oh two, up to five two two.
say.brute: The brute force tries every ordered triple of positions. It skips triples with a leading zero or an odd last digit. It builds the number and drops it into a set. Why the set? Duplicate digits build the same number several times. So what's the catch? It's cubic in the number of digits. And the set is doing cleanup work.
say.insight: Here's the thing. Think in digit values, not positions. Count how many copies of each digit you have. Pick the hundreds digit from the distinct values, and borrow a copy. Pick the tens digit from what's left. Then just count the even units digits still in stock. Every number shows up exactly once. So we don't need a set.
say.anim: We start with digits zero, two, two, five, counted as two twos, one zero, one five. We loop over hundreds digit a, skipping zero since it cannot lead a three digit number. With a as two, we try tens digit b as zero, then count valid even units digits c. Units digit two works, giving total one, then five fails since it is odd. Next with b as two, units zero and two both work, pushing total up to four. Now b is five, units two and five give two more, total reaches four then five. Switching hundreds digit a to five, we repeat with b as zero and two, adding more valid combos. After trying all hundreds, tens, and units combinations, total climbs to seven. The function returns seven, the total count of unique three digit even numbers.
say.code: First we count the copies available per digit. For the hundreds, we skip zero, because there's no leading zero. We use one copy for hundreds. Then we try each tens digit still available, and borrow that too. Next, we count every even units digit in stock. After each choice, we put the copy back. That way, later choices see the full stock.
say.outro: At most ten values per position, so constant work after counting. Count the values, then enumerate them.

unique-3-digit-even-numbers.title: Unique 3-Digit Even Numbers
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container the interview platform expects for our method.
The method totalNumbers takes a list of digits and returns how many distinct three-digit even numbers can be built.
We count how many copies of each digit we have, so each copy can be used at most once.
We start the answer total at zero before trying any number combinations.
We loop over each distinct digit value a as a candidate for the hundreds place.
If a is zero, it would be a leading zero, which is not allowed for a three-digit number.
So we skip this value and move on to the next hundreds candidate.
We borrow one copy of a from the counts, since the hundreds place now uses it.
We loop over each distinct digit value b as a candidate for the tens place.
If no copies of b remain, we cannot place it in the tens spot.
So we skip this b and try the next one.
We borrow one copy of b for the tens place, reducing its remaining count.
We loop over each distinct digit value c as a candidate for the units place.
If c still has a copy left and is even, the number is valid, so we count it.
Because each distinct digit triple is visited once, we add one to the total without double counting.
We return the borrowed copy of b so other tens choices see the original counts.
We return the borrowed copy of a so the next hundreds choice starts from the original counts.
After trying every hundreds, tens and units combination, we return the total count of distinct even numbers.

add-binary.hook: Grade-school column addition, but every column only holds a zero or a one.
add-binary.ask: Given two strings made of zeros and ones, each a binary number, return their sum as a binary string.
add-binary.exampleWhy: 1011 is eleven and 111 is seven. Eleven plus seven is eighteen, which is 10010 in binary.

brute.idea: Turn each string into a number by doubling and adding bits, add the numbers, then peel bits back off.
steps: Build value of a: double, add each bit
Build value of b the same way
Add the two values
Repeatedly take remainder by 2 for the bits
brute.whySlow: With 10,000 bits the numbers are huge; each doubling costs O(n), and fixed-width languages simply overflow.

optimal.insight: Never build the numbers. Add column by column from the right, carrying a one exactly like decimal addition by hand.
steps: Point i and j at the last bits of a and b
Column total = carry plus whichever bits remain
Write total mod 2, carry total div 2
Stop when both strings and the carry are used up
Reverse the collected bits

codeNotes.match: while i >= 0 or j >= 0 or carry:
codeNotes.note: Keep going while anything is left

pitfalls: Forgetting the final carry: 1 plus 1 must give 10, not 0.
Prepending to a string each step is quadratic; append, then reverse.

say.intro: Okay, Add Binary. You get two binary strings. Return their sum, also in binary. Our example adds one zero one one, which is eleven, to one one one, which is seven. Eighteen in binary is one zero zero one zero. So that's the answer.
say.brute: The brute force turns both strings into real numbers. Walk each string, doubling the value and adding the next bit. Add the two numbers. Then keep taking the remainder by two to read the bits back out. It works. So what's the catch? With ten thousand bits, those numbers are huge. Every doubling touches the whole number, so it's n squared. And in most languages, it just overflows.
say.insight: Here's the thing. We never need the numbers at all. Binary addition is the same column addition you learned at school. Line the strings up on the right. Add one column at a time. Write down the last bit, and carry the rest left. And each column is at most one plus one plus a carry. So the total never goes above three.
say.anim: We start with a equal to 1011 and b equal to 111, building result digit by digit. Pointers i and j start at the last digits, three and two, with carry zero. We add a's digit and b's digit plus carry, getting total two, appending zero and carrying one. Next column adds one, one and carry one, total three, so we append one and carry one. With b exhausted, we add a's digit plus carry, total two, append zero, carry one. Now both strings are exhausted but carry one remains, so we append zero then one more one. The loop ends since i, j and carry are all finished, leaving digits built in reverse. Reversing the collected digits gives the final answer, the string 10010.
say.code: We start at the rightmost bits, with a carry of zero. We keep going while anything is left, bits in either string or a carry. Each pass adds the carry plus whatever bits are there. The total mod two is this column's output bit. And the total divided by two is the overflow, which moves one column left. The bits were built backwards, so we reverse at the end.
say.outro: Linear time in the longer string. That's bit manipulation. Simulate the hardware adder, one column at a time.

add-binary.title: Add Binary
lineNotes: We define a class called Solution, which is the container the interview platform expects for our method.
The addBinary method takes two binary strings, a and b, and returns their sum as a binary string.
We start with an empty list called res to collect the result digits, which will come out in reverse order.
We set i and j to the last indexes of a and b, and carry to zero.
We keep looping while either string has digits left or a carry remains, so a final carry still gets written.
We start this column's total with the carry from the previous column.
If a still has an unread digit at position i, we need to include it.
We convert that character of a to a number and add it to the total.
We move i one step left to prepare for the next column.
If b still has an unread digit at position j, we include it too.
We convert that character of b to a number and add it to the total.
We move j one step left for the next column.
The digit to write for this column is the total modulo two, which we append as a string.
The new carry is the total divided by two, rounded down, which is one when the total is two or three.
Digits were collected from least significant first, so we reverse them and join them into the final binary string.

maximum-score-of-non-overlapping-interva.hook: Weighted interval scheduling with a twist: at most four picks, and ties broken by smallest indices.
maximum-score-of-non-overlapping-interva.ask: Each interval has a start, end and weight. Pick at most four that share no points, maximizing total weight. Among best choices, return the lexicographically smallest sorted list of indices.
maximum-score-of-non-overlapping-interva.exampleWhy: Interval 2 weighs 5 and interval 3 weighs 3; they do not touch, and no other choice beats a total of 8.

brute.idea: Try every set of one to four intervals, keep only sets with no overlaps, and remember the best score with the smallest index list.
steps: Enumerate all index combinations of size 1 to 4
Reject any pair that shares a point
Keep the highest score, smallest list on ties
brute.whySlow: With 50,000 intervals there are about 10^17 four-way combinations, hopeless.

optimal.insight: Sort by start. For each interval, either skip it or take it and jump, by binary search, to the first interval starting after it ends.
steps: Sort indices by start; keep the sorted starts for bisect
State: position i in sorted order, picks left k
Take: weight plus best from first start after its end, with k minus 1
Skip: best from i plus 1 with same k
Prefer higher score, then lexicographically smaller index list

codeNotes.note: Best (score, indices) per picks and position
First interval starting strictly after r
Take it: add weight and index

codeNotes.match: if take[0] > skip[0] or (take[0] == skip[0] and take[1] < skip[1]):
codeNotes.note: Higher score wins, else smaller list
Up to four picks from everything

pitfalls: Touching endpoints overlap here, so bisect_right on the end, not bisect_left.
Ties need the index list compared, not just the score.

say.intro: Okay, Maximum Score of Non overlapping Intervals. Each interval has a start, an end and a weight. Pick at most four that never share a point. Maximize the total weight, and break ties with the smallest list of indices. Here, interval two, weight five, plus interval three, weight three, gives eight. That's the best.
say.brute: The brute force tries every group of one, two, three or four intervals. Sort each group. If any neighbours touch, throw it away. Otherwise sum the weights and keep the best, with the smaller index list winning ties. So what's the catch? That's about n to the fourth groups. With fifty thousand intervals, it never finishes.
say.insight: Think about it this way. It's weighted interval scheduling, with a budget of four. Sort by start. At each interval, we have two choices. Skip it. Or take it, and jump straight to the first interval starting after it ends. Binary search finds that jump. Then we have one fewer pick left. Each state keeps its best score, and its smallest index list.
say.anim: We start with six intervals, and sort their indices by start time for processing. With k equal to one, we scan backward, deciding to take or skip each interval. Interval five offers a take score of one versus a skip score of zero, so we take it. After the first pass, taking interval two alone gives the best single score of five. With k equal to three, combining intervals two and three yields a higher score of eight. Adding interval zero actually lowers the total, so skipping stays better at eight. In the final pass with four picks allowed, score eight using intervals two and three still wins. The algorithm returns the optimal non overlapping intervals, giving indices two and three.
say.code: First, we sort indices by start point. The table stores the best score and index list, per number of picks and position. For each interval, binary search finds the first interval starting strictly after its end. If we take it, we add its weight and its index. If we skip, we copy the next cell. Higher score wins. On a tie, the smaller list wins. The answer is up to four picks from everything.
say.outro: Sorting plus binary search, so n log n. Two dimensional dynamic programming. Position by picks left, with a take or skip choice.

maximum-score-of-non-overlapping-interva.title: Maximum Score of Non-overlapping Intervals
lineNotes: We define a class named Solution, which is the container the judge expects for the method.
The method takes the list of intervals and returns the best list of indices, so we start by defining it.
We store the number of intervals in n for use in the loops and table sizes.
We build order, the interval indices sorted by start, so we can scan in start order and binary search.
We collect the start values in that sorted order into starts, which gives bisect a sorted list to search.
We create a table for zero to four picks, each position holding a score of zero and an empty list of indices.
We loop over k from one to four, the number of intervals we are still allowed to pick.
We walk the sorted positions from last to first so later subproblems are already solved.
We look up idx, the original index of the interval at this sorted position.
We unpack that interval into its start, end and weight, naming them l, r and w.
We binary search for j, the first sorted position whose start is strictly greater than this end, so there is no overlap.
We fetch the best score and picks achievable from position j using one fewer interval.
We build the take option by adding the weight and inserting idx into the picks, kept sorted for comparison.
We build the skip option as the best answer from the next position using the same k.
We prefer take if it scores higher, or ties on score with a lexicographically smaller index list.
In that case we store take as the best answer for this position and k.
Otherwise skipping is at least as good, so we handle that branch.
We store skip as the answer for this position and k.
We return the index list from the full problem: position zero with up to four intervals.

isomorphic-strings.hook: Two words with the same shape: can one be relabeled, letter for letter, into the other?
isomorphic-strings.ask: Given strings s and t of equal length, decide whether a one-to-one character replacement turns s into t. Every occurrence of a character must map the same way, and no two characters may share a target.
isomorphic-strings.exampleWhy: p maps to t, a to i, e to l, r to e. Every mapping is consistent and no two letters share a target.

brute.idea: Two positions must agree in s exactly when they agree in t. Compare every pair of positions in both strings.
steps: For each position i
Check every earlier position j
s[i]==s[j] must equal t[i]==t[j]
brute.whySlow: 50,000 characters means over a billion pair checks.

optimal.insight: Keep two dictionaries: s to t and t to s. One pass checks every pair is consistent in both directions.
steps: Walk both strings together
If a is mapped, it must map to b
If b is mapped back, it must map to a
Otherwise record both directions

codeNotes.match: for a, b in zip(s, t):
if s_to_t.get(a, b) != b or t_to_s.get(b, a) != a:

pitfalls: One map is not enough: s = ab, t = aa passes forward but fails backward.

say.intro: Okay, Isomorphic Strings. You get two strings of the same length. Can you relabel the letters of the first to get the second, with a consistent one to one mapping? Paper and title work. P becomes t, a becomes i, e becomes l, and r becomes e. So the answer is true.
say.brute: The brute force uses a neat fact. Two positions share a letter in the first string exactly when they share a letter in the second. So compare every pair of positions, in both strings, and fail on any disagreement. It's correct. So what's the catch? It's n squared. Fifty thousand characters means over a billion comparisons.
say.insight: Here's the better idea. Build the mapping as we go. One dictionary maps letters of the first string to the second. A second dictionary maps back. At each position, if either letter is already mapped somewhere else, we fail. Now, why do we need the second one? Because it stops two different letters from landing on the same target.
say.anim: We start with two empty maps tracking letter pairings between paper and title. Comparing p and t, neither map has a conflict, so we record p maps to t. Next, a and i are checked, pass consistently, and get added to both maps. P and t appear again, matching the earlier mapping, so no conflict occurs. E and l are new, checked for consistency, then stored in both dictionaries. Finally r and e are paired up, completing consistent mappings for every letter. All character pairs matched consistently, so the function returns true, confirming isomorphism.
say.code: We keep a mapping in both directions, two empty dictionaries. Then we pair up characters by position. If the forward map sends a somewhere else, or the reverse map sends b somewhere else, that's a conflict. Conflict in either direction fails, so we return false. Otherwise, we record the forward mapping, and then the reverse mapping. If the loop finishes cleanly, return true.
say.outro: Linear time, constant space for a fixed alphabet. Two maps together enforce a true one to one match.

isomorphic-strings.title: Isomorphic Strings
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container for the method that solves the isomorphic strings problem.
The method isIsomorphic takes strings s and t and returns a boolean saying whether one can be turned into the other.
We create two empty dictionaries, one mapping characters from s to t and another mapping characters from t back to s.
We walk through both strings together, getting the paired characters a from s and b from t at each position.
We look up each mapping with a default, and if either existing mapping disagrees with the current pair, the replacement is inconsistent.
When a conflict is found, we immediately return false because no valid one-to-one mapping can exist.
Otherwise we record that character a in s maps to character b in t.
We also record the reverse, that b maps back to a, so two characters can never share one target.
If the loop finishes without any conflict, every pair was consistent in both directions, so we return true.

richest-customer-wealth.hook: A warm-up in reading a grid: sum each row, keep the biggest.
richest-customer-wealth.ask: Each row of a grid is one customer and each cell is money in one bank. A customer's wealth is their row sum. Return the largest wealth.
richest-customer-wealth.exampleWhy: Row sums are 17, 11 and 15. The first customer is richest with 17.

brute.idea: Compute every customer's wealth into a list, sort it, and take the last value.
steps: Sum each row into a list
Sort the list of wealths
Return the largest
brute.whySlow: Same scan of every cell, but it stores all sums and sorts them just to read one maximum.

optimal.insight: We only ever need the largest sum, so keep a single running best instead of a list.
steps: Start best at zero
Sum one customer's row
Update best if this sum is larger
Return best after the last row

codeNotes.note: Running maximum, all money is positive

pitfalls: Do not sum columns: rows are customers, columns are banks.

say.intro: Okay, Richest Customer Wealth. You get a grid. Each row is a customer, and each cell is the money they keep in one bank. A customer's wealth is their row sum. Return the largest. Our rows sum to seventeen, eleven and fifteen. So the answer is seventeen.
say.brute: A first attempt computes every customer's wealth and stores them all in a list. Then it sorts the list and takes the last value. That's correct. And it reads each cell once, just like the best solution. So what's wasted? Memory for every sum. And a whole sort, just to find one maximum.
say.insight: Here's the thing. There's no clever trick hiding here. And that's the lesson. Every cell has to be read at least once. So the grid size is the floor. The only improvement is to stop storing what we don't need. Keep one running best. Compare each row sum against it, as soon as you compute it.
