say.anim: We start with best set to zero, ready to track the richest customer. The first row, two eight seven, sums to a wealth of seventeen. Seventeen beats zero, so best updates to seventeen. Next row, seven one three, sums to eleven, which is less than best. The last row, one nine five, sums to fifteen, still below seventeen. No more rows remain, so the loop finishes without changing best. The function returns seventeen, the richest customer's total wealth.
say.code: We keep a running maximum, starting at zero. That's safe, because all money is positive. Then we loop over the rows, one customer per row. We sum the row to get the total across all their banks. Is this a new richest customer? If so, it replaces best. After the last row, we return the largest wealth seen.
say.outro: Time is the size of the grid, and extra space is constant. Sometimes the best answer is just one clean scan with a running maximum.

richest-customer-wealth.title: Richest Customer Wealth
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container this problem's method lives in.
The method maximumWealth takes the grid of accounts, where each row is one customer, and returns an integer.
We start best at zero, a single running maximum so we never need to store every customer's total.
We loop over each row in accounts, so each pass looks at one customer's bank balances.
We add up the money in the current row to get that customer's total wealth.
We check whether this customer's wealth beats the best total we have seen so far.
If it does, we replace best with this wealth so best always holds the largest sum.
After every customer is checked, we return best as the richest customer's wealth.

first-missing-positive.hook: Find the smallest missing positive in linear time, with no extra memory. The array becomes the hash table.
first-missing-positive.ask: Given an unsorted list of integers, return the smallest positive integer that does not appear in it. You must use linear time and constant extra space.
first-missing-positive.exampleWhy: 1, 2, 3 and 4 are all present, but 5 is not, so 5 is the smallest missing positive.

brute.idea: Try 1, then 2, then 3, scanning the whole array each time, until a value is not found.
steps: Start with x equal to 1
Scan the array for x
Found? Try x plus 1
Not found? Return x
brute.whySlow: If the array holds 1 to 100,000, that is 100,000 full scans, about ten billion checks.

optimal.insight: The answer is between 1 and n plus 1. So put each value v in 1..n at index v minus 1; the first misplaced slot reveals it.
steps: For each slot, swap its value toward its home index
Ignore values that are not in 1 to n
Stop swapping when the home already holds that value
First index i whose value is not i plus 1 gives i plus 1

codeNotes.match: while 1 <= nums[i] <= n and nums[nums[i] - 1] != nums[i]:
codeNotes.note: In range and not already home
Send it home, examine what returns

pitfalls: Without the duplicate check the swap loop never ends on inputs like [1,1].
Compute j before swapping; nums[i] changes during the swap.

say.intro: Okay, First Missing Positive. You get an unsorted list. Return the smallest positive integer that's missing. Here's the catch. Linear time, and constant extra space. In four, one, minus one, three, six, two, we have one, two, three and four. But no five. So the answer is five.
say.brute: The simplest idea is to try one, then two, then three. For each one, scan the whole array to see if it's there. Return the first one you can't find. It uses no extra memory. So what's the problem? If the array holds every number up to a hundred thousand, that's a hundred thousand full scans.
say.insight: Here's the key. With n numbers, the answer has to be between one and n plus one. So the array itself can be our hash table. Put each value v in its home, at index v minus one, by swapping. Ignore negatives, zeros, and anything too big. Afterwards, the first slot not holding its own number gives the answer.
say.anim: We start with the array four, one, negative one, three, six, two, length six. At index zero, value four belongs at index three, so we swap them. Now value three sits at index zero, but it belongs at index two, swap again. Index zero now holds negative one, which is invalid, so we move on. At index one, value one belongs at index zero, so we swap it there. At index four, value six belongs at index five, swap it into place. Then value two at index four belongs at index one, swap it there too. Scanning the fixed array, every slot matches except index four holding negative one, giving answer five.
say.code: For each index, we check its value. Is it in range, and not already home? Then we find the home index for this value. We send it home with a swap, and examine whatever comes back. Each swap places one value for good, so the total work is linear. Then we scan again for the first slot missing its value. If one through n are all present, we return n plus one.
say.outro: Linear time, constant space. The array's own indices become the hash table. That's often called cyclic sort.

first-missing-positive.title: First Missing Positive

range-module.hook: Track a set of half-open ranges that merge, split and answer coverage queries.
range-module.ask: Design a structure that adds a half-open range, removes one, and answers whether a whole range is currently tracked. Ranges can overlap, merge and split.
range-module.exampleWhy: Adds merge into 10 to 25; removing 14 to 16 splits it. 13 to 15 crosses the hole, the others do not.

brute.idea: Treat the ranges as unit cells. Keep a set of every integer x whose cell [x, x+1) is tracked.
steps: Add: insert every integer in the range
Remove: discard every integer in the range
Query: check every integer is present
brute.whySlow: Ranges reach a billion; adding [1, 10^9) means a billion set inserts.

optimal.insight: Store sorted boundaries only. Even positions start ranges, odd positions end them; parity of a bisect position says inside or outside.
steps: track is a sorted list of alternating starts and ends
Bisect both ends to find the affected slice
Even index means outside, odd means inside a range
Replace the slice with the needed boundary points

range-module.optimalCode:
import bisect

class RangeModule:
    def __init__(self):
        # track holds sorted boundary points, alternating start, end, start, end...
        self.track = []

    def addRange(self, left: int, right: int) -> None:
        # 1. Find where left and right fit among the boundaries
        start_index = bisect.bisect_left(self.track, left)
        end_index = bisect.bisect_right(self.track, right)
        # 2. Even index means this point is outside any range, so it needs to be added
        new_boundaries = []
        if start_index % 2 == 0:
            new_boundaries.append(left)
        if end_index % 2 == 0:
            new_boundaries.append(right)
        # 3. Replace the old boundaries in between with the new merged ones
        self.track[start_index:end_index] = new_boundaries

    def queryRange(self, left: int, right: int) -> bool:
        # 1. Find where left and right fit among the boundaries
        start_index = bisect.bisect_right(self.track, left)
        end_index = bisect.bisect_left(self.track, right)
        # 2. Both points must fall in the same odd-indexed (inside) segment
        return start_index == end_index and start_index % 2 == 1

    def removeRange(self, left: int, right: int) -> None:
        # 1. Find where left and right fit among the boundaries
        start_index = bisect.bisect_left(self.track, left)
        end_index = bisect.bisect_right(self.track, right)
        # 2. Odd index means this point is inside a range, so it needs to stay as a boundary
        new_boundaries = []
        if start_index % 2 == 1:
            new_boundaries.append(left)
        if end_index % 2 == 1:
            new_boundaries.append(right)
        # 3. Replace the old boundaries in between with the new split ones
        self.track[start_index:end_index] = new_boundaries

codeNotes.note: Sorted boundaries: start, end, start, end

codeNotes.match: def addRange(self, left: int, right: int) -> None:
codeNotes.note: Add: swallow boundaries between left and right
No boundary inside, and we are inside
Left lands inside: cut it there

pitfalls: Mixing bisect_left and bisect_right breaks touching ranges like [10,20) and [20,30).
Ranges are half-open: right itself is never tracked.

say.intro: Okay, Range Module. We design a structure that tracks half open ranges of numbers. It can add a range, remove a range, and check if a whole range is covered. In our run, ten to twenty and eighteen to twenty five merge. Then removing fourteen to sixteen punches a hole. Queries that avoid the hole return true.
say.brute: The brute force treats the number line as unit cells. It keeps a set of every covered cell. Adding or removing touches every integer in the range, and a query checks them all. Simple. So what's the catch? Ranges can stretch to a billion. One call could mean a billion set operations.
say.insight: Here's the thing. Only the edges matter. Keep a sorted list of boundaries, alternating start, end, start, end. Binary search tells you where a number falls. And the position's parity tells you if it's inside a range. Even means outside, odd means inside. An update just replaces the boundaries between left and right, with at most two new points.
say.anim: We start with an empty track list, ready to store range boundaries. Adding range ten to twenty finds both indices at zero, outside any range, so both boundaries get inserted. Adding eighteen to twenty five finds start index one, inside, but end index two, outside, so only twenty five is added, merging ranges. Removing fourteen to sixteen finds both indices odd, inside the range, so fourteen and sixteen become new split boundaries. Querying ten to fourteen gives matching odd index one, meaning it's fully inside, so the result is true. Querying thirteen to fifteen gives different indices one and two, spanning a gap, so the result is false. Querying sixteen to twenty four gives matching odd index three, inside a merged range, so it returns true.
say.code: We keep sorted boundaries, start, end, start, end. To add, we binary search for left and right, and swallow every boundary between them. If left lands outside, at an even spot, it becomes a new start. Right works the same way. For a query, there must be no boundary inside, and we must be inside. Removal mirrors add. If left lands inside a range, we cut it there.
say.outro: Queries take log time, and updates are bounded by the boundaries they erase. Intervals, stored as a sorted boundary list.

text-justification.hook: The word processor classic: pack lines greedily, then spread the spaces fairly.
text-justification.ask: Given words and a width, lay them out in lines of exactly that width. Pack as many words per line as fit, spread extra spaces evenly with the left gaps getting more, and left-justify the last line.
text-justification.exampleWhy: Three words fit the first line with 8 spare spaces, split 4 and 4. The last line is left-justified and padded.

brute.idea: Grow each line by rebuilding the joined string to test fit, then drip spaces in one at a time into the narrowest gap.
steps: Try appending a word, rebuild the line, measure it
Too long? Close the line
Add one space at a time to the leftmost narrowest gap
brute.whySlow: Rebuilding the trial line for every word and placing spaces one by one repeats work; correct but wasteful.

optimal.insight: Track letters on the line. A word fits if letters plus single gaps plus the word fit. Then divmod splits the spare spaces in one step.
steps: Add words while letters plus gaps stay within width
On overflow, spare = width minus letters
divmod spare by gaps: base size, and extras for left gaps
Single word lines and the last line are left-justified

text-justification.optimalCode:
class Solution:
    def fullJustify(self, words: List[str], maxWidth: int) -> List[str]:
        result = []
        current_line = []
        letters_count = 0
        # 1. Pack words onto a line while letters plus gaps still fit
        for word in words:
            if letters_count + len(current_line) + len(word) > maxWidth:
                # 2. Line is full: distribute the spare spaces across the gaps
                if len(current_line) == 1:
                    line = current_line[0] + " " * (maxWidth - letters_count)
                else:
                    gaps = len(current_line) - 1
                    spare = maxWidth - letters_count
                    base_spaces = spare // gaps
                    extra_spaces = spare % gaps
                    line = ""
                    for index, w in enumerate(current_line[:-1]):
                        line += w
                        spaces = base_spaces
                        if index < extra_spaces:
                            spaces += 1
                        line += " " * spaces
                    line += current_line[-1]
                result.append(line)
                current_line = []
                letters_count = 0
            current_line.append(word)
            letters_count += len(word)
        # 3. Last line is left-justified with single spaces and padding
        last_line = " ".join(current_line)
        last_line += " " * (maxWidth - len(last_line))
        result.append(last_line)
        return result

Lone word: pad on the right

codeNotes.match: row += word + " " * (q + (1 if k < r else 0))
codeNotes.note: First r gaps get one extra

say.intro: Okay, Text Justification. You get a list of words and a line width. Every line must be exactly that wide. Pack as many words as fit. Spread the extra spaces evenly, with left gaps getting more. And left justify the last line. Here, this is an fills the first line, with eight spare spaces. Four in each gap.
say.brute: A clumsy version rebuilds the joined line every time it tries one more word, just to measure it. Then it adds spaces one at a time, to whichever gap is narrowest. It gets the right answer. So what's wrong? It keeps redoing work. Rebuilding strings and dripping in spaces is wasted effort. This problem is really just arithmetic.
say.insight: Here's the thing. Keep a running count of letters on the current line. Does a new word fit? Check letters, plus one space per gap, plus the word. If that's over the width, close the line. The spare space is width minus letters. Divide it by the number of gaps. Everyone gets the quotient. The remainder gives the leftmost gaps one extra.
say.anim: We start packing words into the first line, tracking total letters so far. Adding example would exceed sixteen characters, so the line breaks here with three words. Two gaps share eight spare spaces evenly, four each, since there's no remainder. The finished line reads This, four spaces, is, four spaces, an, filling sixteen characters. Adding justification would overflow again, so example, of, and text form the next line. Three spare spaces over two gaps give one extra space to the first gap. This produces example, two spaces, of, one space, text, exactly sixteen characters wide. The last line, justification, is left justified with trailing spaces, giving our final three lines.
say.code: For each word, we count letters, one space per gap, and the new word. If that overflows, we close the line. A lone word just gets padded on the right. Otherwise, division gives each gap its even share, plus leftovers. The first few gaps, one per leftover, get one extra space. Then we start a fresh line. Finally, the last line is left justified, with single spaces and padding.
say.outro: Linear in the total text. That's greedy. Pack each line full, then share out the slack with simple division.

wildcard-matching.hook: A star can swallow any number of characters. The trick is not trying every split twice.
wildcard-matching.ask: Given a string and a pattern with question marks, matching one character, and stars, matching any sequence including empty, decide whether the pattern matches the entire string.
wildcard-matching.exampleWhy: The first star matches nothing, a matches a, the second star swallows dce, and b matches b.

brute.idea: Recurse on positions in string and pattern. A star tries matching nothing, or one character and staying on the star.
steps: Pattern used up: string must be too
Star: skip it, or eat one character
Otherwise characters must match, then advance both
brute.whySlow: Each star branches two ways and the same positions get re-solved again and again; many stars explode exponentially.

optimal.insight: There are only m times n distinct position pairs. Fill a table from the ends backward so each pair is solved exactly once.
steps: dp[i][j]: does s from i match p from j
Both ends reached: True
Star: dp[i][j+1] or dp[i+1][j]
Else: characters match and dp[i+1][j+1]

codeNotes.note: Suffix of s against suffix of p

codeNotes.match: dp[i][j] = dp[i][j + 1] or (i < m and dp[i + 1][j])
codeNotes.note: Star: match empty, or eat one

codeNotes.match: dp[i][j] = i < m and p[j] in (s[i], "?") and dp[i + 1][j + 1]

pitfalls: Row i equals m still matters: trailing stars can match an empty suffix.
Do not confuse with regex: here star stands alone, not after a character.

say.intro: Okay, Wildcard Matching. You get a string and a pattern. A question mark matches any one character. A star matches any sequence, even an empty one. The pattern has to match the whole string. Star a star b matches a d c e b. The first star takes nothing. The second star swallows d c e.
say.brute: The brute force recurses on a position in the string and a position in the pattern. At a star, it branches. Either the star matches nothing, or it eats one character and stays put. Otherwise, the characters must match. So what's the catch? It branches at every star. And it solves the same positions again and again. That's exponential.
say.insight: Here's the thing. The recursion only ever asks about a pair of positions. And there are just m times n pairs. So store each answer in a table, and compute it once. Work backward from the ends. Every cell only depends on cells to its right or below. And those are already filled by the time we get there.
say.anim: We start with string adceb and pattern star a star b, building a table of match possibilities. The base case dp at five four is true, meaning both strings are empty and matched. Row by row, filling backward, we compare each pattern character to decide if a star can match freely. At row three, a direct letter match succeeds and star positions propagate true values leftward. At row one, matching letter b lets true values spread through the star cells in that row. By row zero, the star at the start lets earlier true values flow all the way to position zero. The final row shows dp at zero zero is true, confirming a full match. The function returns true, meaning wildcard pattern star a star b matches adceb.
say.code: Each cell answers one question. Does this suffix of the string match this suffix of the pattern? Empty matches empty, so the bottom right corner is true. For a star, there are two options. Match empty by skipping the star, or eat one character and stay. Otherwise, the single character must match, and the diagonal cell must be true. The top left cell is the whole string against the whole pattern.
say.outro: Time and space are m times n. Two dimensional dynamic programming. One index into each string, and every state solved once.

basic-calculator.hook: Evaluate plus, minus and nested parentheses in one pass, no eval allowed.
basic-calculator.ask: Given a valid expression string with non-negative integers, plus, minus, parentheses and spaces, return its value. Minus may be unary, as in minus open parenthesis.
basic-calculator.exampleWhy: Innermost first: 1 plus 3 is 4, 5 minus 4 is 1, and 2 minus 1 is 1.

brute.idea: Repeatedly find an innermost pair of parentheses, evaluate the flat expression inside, and splice the number back into the string.
steps: Find the first closing parenthesis
Its matching opener is the last one before it
Evaluate the flat inside, splice the value in
No parentheses left: evaluate the flat string
brute.whySlow: Each splice rebuilds the whole string; deeply nested input of 300,000 characters means billions of copied characters.

optimal.insight: Only plus and minus exist, so a parenthesis just scales its contents by a sign. Push the running result and sign when entering one.
steps: Build multi-digit numbers as digits arrive
On plus or minus, fold the number in and set the sign
On open, push result and sign, then restart
On close, finish, multiply by saved sign, add saved result

basic-calculator.optimalCode:
class Solution:
    def calculate(self, s: str) -> int:
        stack = []
        result = 0
        number = 0
        sign = 1

        for char in s:
            if char.isdigit():
                # 1. Build multi-digit numbers as digits arrive
                number = number * 10 + int(char)
            elif char == "+" or char == "-":
                # 2. On plus or minus, fold the number in and set the sign
                result += sign * number
                number = 0
                if char == "+":
                    sign = 1
                else:
                    sign = -1
            elif char == "(":
                # 3. On open, push result and sign, then restart
                stack.append(result)
                stack.append(sign)
                result = 0
                sign = 1
            elif char == ")":
                # 4. On close, finish, multiply by saved sign, add saved result
                result += sign * number
                number = 0
                previous_sign = stack.pop()
                previous_result = stack.pop()
                result = previous_result + previous_sign * result

        return result + sign * number

codeNotes.note: Fold the number in, record the new sign
Apply the sign before the parenthesis
Last number may still be pending

pitfalls: Unary minus like -(2+3) works because res starts at 0.
Forgetting the trailing number: 1 + 1 ends without an operator.

say.intro: Okay, Basic Calculator. You get an expression with numbers, plus, minus, parentheses and spaces. Evaluate it, without using eval. Our example is two minus, open, five minus, open, one plus three. Inside out, one plus three is four. Five minus four is one. And two minus one gives one.
say.brute: The brute force does what we'd do on paper. Find an innermost pair of parentheses. Evaluate the flat expression inside, and paste the number back into the string. Repeat until no parentheses are left. It works. So what's the catch? Every paste rebuilds the whole string. With deep nesting, that's n squared.
say.insight: Here's the thing. With only plus and minus, a parenthesis does just one job. It multiplies everything inside by the sign in front of it. So when we enter one, we push the result so far, and that sign, onto a stack. Then start fresh. When we leave, multiply by the saved sign, and add the saved result back.
say.anim: We start with an empty stack, result zero, number zero, and sign one. The digit two is read, building number up to two. At the minus sign, result folds in number two, becoming two, then sign flips to negative one. At the open parenthesis, we push result two and sign negative one onto the stack, then reset. Inside, digit five builds number five, then the minus sign folds it into result five and sign becomes negative one. Another open parenthesis pushes result five and sign negative one, resetting result and sign again. Digits one and three combine with a plus to make result four inside the innermost parentheses. At each closing parenthesis, we pop the saved sign and result to rebuild the outer expression, finally returning one.
say.code: Numbers can have many digits, so digits build up num. On a plus or minus, we fold the number into the result, and record the new sign. On an open parenthesis, we save the outside result and sign, then reset. On a close, we fold in the last number, apply the sign from before the parenthesis, and rejoin the outside result. At the end, the last number may still be pending, so we add it.
say.outro: One pass, linear time, and stack depth equals nesting depth. Save the outer context when you go deeper. Restore it on the way out.

longest-continuous-subarray-with-absolut.hook: A sliding window that must know its own max and min at every moment.
longest-continuous-subarray-with-absolut.ask: Given numbers and a limit, return the length of the longest contiguous block where the largest and smallest values differ by at most the limit.
longest-continuous-subarray-with-absolut.exampleWhy: In 2, 4, 7, 2 the max is 7 and the min is 2, a gap of exactly 5. No longer block fits.

brute.idea: Start a block at every index and extend it right, tracking max and min, until the gap exceeds the limit.
steps: For each start i
Extend j, updating running max and min
Gap too big? Stop extending
Record the longest valid length
brute.whySlow: With 100,000 numbers and a large limit, nearly every start extends to the end: about five billion steps.

optimal.insight: Slide a window, and keep two monotonic deques: decreasing for the max, increasing for the min. Their fronts are the window's extremes.
steps: Add the new number to both deques, popping weaker tails
While front max minus front min exceeds limit, shrink left
Drop a front if it is the element leaving
Record the window length

codeNotes.note: Smaller values can never be max again
Larger values can never be min again

pitfalls: Pop with strict comparisons so duplicates stay; otherwise a leaving duplicate removes the wrong copy.

say.intro: Okay, Longest Continuous Subarray With Absolute Difference Within a Limit. We want the longest block of neighbours whose max and min differ by at most the limit. With ten, one, two, four, seven, two, and a limit of five, take two, four, seven, two. Seven minus two is five. So the answer is four.
say.brute: The brute force tries every start, and extends right with a running max and min. As soon as the gap passes the limit, it stops. Simple. So what's the catch? With a generous limit, almost every start runs to the end. That's n squared. A hundred thousand numbers means billions of steps.
say.insight: Here's the thing. Shrinking a block never makes it worse. So a sliding window works. But how do we know the window's max and min as it slides? Two monotonic deques. One keeps values in decreasing order, so its front is the max. The other keeps increasing order, so its front is the min.
say.anim: We start with empty max and min deques, left at zero, scanning nums with limit five. At index zero, value ten enters both deques as the current window's max and min. At index one, value one is added, keeping deques ten and one for max, one for min. Max minus min is nine, too big, so we shrink the window, dropping ten and moving left to one. Index two brings value two, window max and min update to two and one, best becomes two. Values four then seven extend the window, max updates to seven, best grows to three. Difference hits six, exceeding limit, so we pop one from minq and advance left to two. Finally index five adds two, window from index two to five fits within limit five, best becomes four. The function returns four, the longest subarray length with difference within the limit.
say.code: For each new number, we clean up the deques first. Smaller values can never be max again, so we pop them from the max deque. Larger values can never be min again, so we pop them from the min deque. Then we append. If the window is too spread, we shrink it. If the leaving element was the max or min, we drop that front. Finally, it's a valid window, so we record its length.
say.outro: Each number enters and leaves each deque once, so linear time. Sliding window, powered by monotonic deques.

longest-continuous-subarray-with-absolut.title: Longest Continuous Subarray With Absolute Diff Less Than or Equal to Limit
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container the interview platform expects for our method.
The method takes the list of numbers and the limit, and returns the length of the longest valid block.
We create two empty deques, one to track the window's maximum and one to track its minimum.
We set both the left edge of the window and the best length found so far to zero.
We loop over the array, with right as the current index and x as the new value entering the window.
Before adding x, we check whether the back of the max deque holds a smaller value.
Any smaller value at the back can never be the maximum again, so we pop it off.
We then append x to the max deque, which keeps it in decreasing order from front to back.
Similarly, we check whether the back of the min deque holds a larger value than x.
Those larger values can never be the minimum again, so we pop them off.
We append x to the min deque, keeping it in increasing order from front to back.
While the front of the max deque minus the front of the min deque exceeds the limit, the window is invalid and must shrink.
If the current max at the front is the value leaving at left, we must remove it from the deque.
We pop the front of the max deque because that value is no longer inside the window.
If the current min at the front is also the value leaving at left, we must remove it too.
We pop the front of the min deque so it only holds values still in the window.
We move the left edge one step right, officially dropping that element from the window.
Now the window is valid, so we update best with the larger of its old value and the current window length.
After scanning all numbers, we return the longest valid window length we found.

minimum-number-of-days-to-make-m-bouquet.hook: If you can finish by day d, you can finish by any later day. That is a binary search.
minimum-number-of-days-to-make-m-bouquet.ask: Each flower blooms on a given day. A bouquet needs k adjacent bloomed flowers, each used once. Return the earliest day you can make m bouquets, or minus one if impossible.
minimum-number-of-days-to-make-m-bouquet.exampleWhy: By day 3, flowers 0, 2 and 4 have bloomed, giving three one-flower bouquets. Day 2 gives only two.

brute.idea: Try each distinct bloom day in increasing order, and simulate how many bouquets are possible on that day.
steps: Sort the distinct bloom days
For each day, count runs of k bloomed flowers
First day reaching m bouquets is the answer
brute.whySlow: Up to 100,000 distinct days, each needing a full pass over 100,000 flowers.

optimal.insight: Feasibility is monotonic in the day. So binary search the day between the earliest and latest bloom, testing each guess in one pass.
steps: Need more than n flowers? Return minus one
Search days from min bloom to max bloom
can(day): greedily count runs of k bloomed flowers
Feasible? Search left. Not? Search right

codeNotes.match: run = run + 1 if b <= day else 0

pitfalls: Check m times k against n first; otherwise the search returns a wrong day.
Flowers must be adjacent: reset the run on any unbloomed flower.

say.intro: Okay, Minimum Number of Days to Make m Bouquets. Each flower blooms on a certain day. A bouquet needs k neighbouring bloomed flowers. What's the earliest day you can make m bouquets? With bloom days one, ten, three, ten, two, and three bouquets of one flower, day three works. So the answer is three.
say.brute: The brute force tries each bloom day, in increasing order. For each day, walk the garden and count runs of bloomed flowers. Cut a bouquet whenever a run reaches k. The first day that makes m bouquets wins. So what's the catch? That's a full pass per candidate day. In the worst case, n squared.
say.insight: Here's the key. If you can make enough bouquets by some day, can you make them on a later day? Yes. Flowers never unbloom. So the answer flips from no to yes exactly once. That means we can binary search on the day itself. Each guess costs one linear pass. And we only need a logarithmic number of guesses.
say.anim: We need three bouquets of one flower each from bloom days one, ten, three, ten, two. Binary search starts with low at one and high at ten, the earliest and latest bloom days. Testing day five, we scan flowers, counting consecutive ready blooms to form bouquets. Flowers one, three, and two are ready by day five, giving us three bouquets, enough for m. Since day five works, we shrink high to five and try a smaller midpoint, three. At day three, flowers one, three, and two again bloom in time, forming three bouquets. Day three still works, so high shrinks to three and we test day two next. At day two only flowers one and two qualify, giving just two bouquets, not enough. Now low equals high at three, ending the search with the minimum day of three.
say.code: First, if there aren't enough flowers in total, return minus one. The helper walks the garden and counts adjacent bloomed flowers. When a run hits k, it completes a bouquet greedily, and starts over. Then we binary search. The answer lies between the earliest and latest bloom days. If the middle day works, we try an earlier day. Otherwise, we move later.
say.outro: n times log of the day range. Binary search on the answer. When feasibility flips just once, search the answers directly.

minimum-number-of-days-to-make-m-bouquet.title: Minimum Number of Days to Make m Bouquets
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container the judge expects for our method.
The minDays method takes the bloom days, the bouquet count m, and the flowers per bouquet k.
If m times k exceeds the number of flowers, there simply are not enough flowers to ever succeed.
In that impossible case we return minus one right away.
We define a helper called can that checks whether m bouquets are possible by a given day.
We start the bouquet count and the current run of adjacent bloomed flowers both at zero.
We walk through every flower's bloom day in order, keeping adjacency by position.
If this flower has bloomed by the day we extend the run, otherwise the run resets to zero.
Once the run reaches k we have enough adjacent flowers for one bouquet.
We count that bouquet.
We reset the run to zero because those flowers cannot be reused.
After the pass, we return whether we made at least m bouquets.
We set the search range from the earliest bloom day to the latest bloom day.
We keep searching while the range still contains more than one candidate day.
We pick the middle day of the current range to test.
If the middle day works, the answer could be this day or earlier.
So we shrink the upper bound down to mid, keeping it as a candidate.
Otherwise the middle day is too early to succeed.
So we move the lower bound past mid, to mid plus one.
When the range collapses, lo is the earliest feasible day, and we return it.

next-permutation.hook: The next arrangement in dictionary order, found in place with one scan from the right.
next-permutation.ask: Rearrange the list in place into the next larger arrangement in lexicographic order. If it is already the largest, wrap around to the smallest, which is sorted ascending.
next-permutation.exampleWhy: The suffix 5, 4, 2 is already maxed out. Bump 3 to the next larger value, 4, then sort what follows.

brute.idea: Generate every distinct permutation in sorted order, find the current one, and copy in the one after it.
steps: Generate and sort all distinct permutations
Find the current arrangement
Copy the next one, wrapping to the first
brute.whySlow: Twelve numbers already have 479 million permutations; a hundred is unthinkable.

optimal.insight: The longest decreasing suffix cannot grow. Increase the digit just before it by the smallest possible amount, then make the suffix as small as possible.
steps: From the right, find i with nums[i] < nums[i+1]
From the right, find first j with nums[j] > nums[i]
Swap them; the suffix stays decreasing
Reverse the suffix to make it ascending

codeNotes.note: Smallest suffix value bigger than nums[i]
Suffix bounds; whole array if no pivot

pitfalls: Use >= and <= so duplicates like [1,1,5] work.
No pivot means largest arrangement: reverse everything.

say.intro: Okay, Next Permutation. Rearrange a list, in place, into the next larger arrangement in dictionary order. If it's already the largest, wrap around to the smallest. For one, three, five, four, two, the next one is one, four, two, three, five.
say.brute: The brute force lists every distinct arrangement and sorts them. It finds where the current one sits, and copies in the next one. Obviously correct. So what's the catch? There are n factorial arrangements. Twelve numbers already give nearly half a billion. Hopeless beyond tiny inputs.
say.insight: Here's the trick. Look from the right. The longest decreasing tail is already as big as it can get. So the change has to happen just before it, at the pivot. Swap the pivot with the smallest tail value that's bigger than it. Now, notice the tail is still decreasing. So reversing it gives the smallest possible tail.
say.anim: We start with the array one, three, five, four, two, scanning from the right. Index i moves left while each element is not smaller than the next, finding the decreasing suffix. At i equals one, nums at one is three, which is less than five, so we stop. Now j starts from the end, searching for the smallest value bigger than nums at i. J lands on index three, value four, the first number greater than three. We swap nums at i and j, turning the array into one, four, five, three, two. Next we reverse the suffix after i to make it as small as possible. The final next permutation is one, four, two, three, five.
say.code: First, we skip the decreasing suffix. i starts second from the end and moves left while values aren't increasing. If there's a pivot, j walks in from the end. It finds the smallest suffix value bigger than the pivot. We swap them, bumping the pivot up minimally. Then we set the suffix bounds. If there's no pivot, that's the whole array. Finally, we reverse, and descending becomes ascending.
say.outro: Linear time, constant space. One scan to find the pivot, then a two pointer reversal to reset the tail.

next-permutation.title: Next Permutation
lineNotes: We define a class named Solution that holds the method for this problem.
The method takes the list nums and modifies it in place, so it returns nothing.
We start index i at the second to last position, to compare each element with its right neighbor.
We scan leftward while the current element is not smaller than its neighbor, which skips the decreasing suffix.
Each time the pair is still non increasing, we move i one step to the left.
If i is still valid, we found a pivot that can be increased; otherwise the whole list is decreasing.
We set j to the last index to search the suffix from its right end.
We move j left until nums at j is strictly greater than the pivot, giving the smallest larger value.
We decrement j to keep looking for that slightly larger element in the suffix.
We swap the pivot with that element, which bumps the prefix up by the smallest possible amount.
We set l just after the pivot and r at the end, to reverse the suffix.
We loop while the two pointers have not met in the middle.
We swap the values at l and r, turning the decreasing suffix toward ascending order.
We move l one step right.
We move r one step left, and when no pivot existed this reversal wraps the list to sorted order.

odd-even-jump.hook: Alternating jumps to the next-higher and next-lower value. Precompute the targets, then solve backwards.
odd-even-jump.ask: From a start index, odd jumps go right to the smallest value at least as big; even jumps go to the largest value at most as big, ties to the nearest. Count starts that reach the last index.
odd-even-jump.exampleWhy: Starting at index 1, 3 or 4 reaches the end. From 0 and 2 the jump sequence gets stuck.

brute.idea: From every start, simulate the jumps, scanning everything to the right to find each landing spot.
steps: For each start, alternate odd and even jumps
Scan rightward for the best legal target
No target? Stuck. Reached the end? Count it
brute.whySlow: Up to n starts, each with up to n jumps, each scanning up to n values: trillions for 20,000 elements.

optimal.insight: Each index has fixed odd and even targets. Find them all with a monotonic stack over sorted indices, then DP backwards: odd[i] = even[up[i]].
steps: Sort indices by value; a stack yields each next-higher target
Sort by negative value for each next-lower target
Last index is good for both parities
odd[i] = even[up[i]], even[i] = odd[down[i]]
Count indices where odd is true

codeNotes.note: Odd jumps: smallest value at least as big
Even jumps: largest value at most as big
After an odd jump, next is even
Every start begins with an odd jump

pitfalls: Ties go to the smallest index, so sort by (value, index) in both orders.
Starts begin with an odd jump: count odd, not even.

say.intro: Okay, Odd Even Jump. From any start, odd jumps go right, to the smallest value at least as big. Even jumps go to the largest value at most as big. Ties go to the nearest. How many starts reach the end? In two, three, one, one, four, three starts succeed.
say.brute: The brute force simulates every start. For each jump, it scans everything to the right to find the legal target. Then it flips between odd and even. So what's the catch? A start can make many jumps. And each scan is linear. In the worst case, that's cubic.
say.insight: Two observations. First, the target of a jump from an index never changes. So compute every target once. Visit indices in sorted value order with a monotonic stack, and you get them all. Second, after an odd jump comes an even one. So a start is good on an odd jump exactly when its target is good on an even jump. Solve that from right to left.
say.anim: We start with array two, three, one, one, four, computing odd jump targets using a stack. The stack tracks indices, popping smaller values when a bigger one arrives, linking nearest larger values. After processing, the odd jump array up becomes one, four, three, four, none. Now we repeat the process sorted by descending value to build down jumps for even steps. Down jumps end up as two, two, three, none, none, completed using the same stack idea. Working backwards, we fill odd and even arrays, starting with index four marked true for both. Each index checks its up and down jump to decide if it reaches the end on odd or even turns. After finishing the backward pass, three indices can reach the end, giving the final answer three.
say.code: A helper with a stack lets each earlier index find its target. Sorting by value gives the odd jumps, smallest value at least as big. Sorting by negative value gives the even jumps, largest value at most as big. Going backwards, after an odd jump the next is even, so odd copies even of its target. Every start begins with an odd jump, so we count odd.
say.outro: Sorting dominates, so n log n. One dimensional dynamic programming, fed by a monotonic stack that finds every jump target.

odd-even-jump.title: Odd Even Jump
lineNotes: We define the solution class that holds the method for this problem.
The method takes the array and returns how many starting indices can reach the last index.
We store the array length in n for use throughout.
We define a helper that, given indices in a chosen sorted order, finds each index's next jump target.
We create a result list nxt of size n, starting with no target for every index.
We create an empty stack that will hold indices still waiting for a larger index to their right.
We walk through the indices in the given sorted order, visiting values in the order a jump would prefer.
While the top of the stack is an index smaller than the current one, the current index is its jump target.
We pop that waiting index and record the current index as its target.
We push the current index onto the stack so it waits for a later, larger index.
We return the list of targets for every index.
For odd jumps we sort indices by value then index, and the helper finds each index's next-higher-or-equal target.
For even jumps we sort by negative value then index, so the helper finds the next-lower-or-equal target with ties going to the nearest.
We create two boolean lists, odd and even, saying whether each index can reach the end starting with that jump type.
The last index trivially reaches itself, so both odd and even are true there.
We go backward from the second-to-last index so that targets to the right are already computed.
If an odd jump from index i has a target, we can use it.
After an odd jump we must make an even jump, so odd at i equals even at the target.
If an even jump from index i has a target, we can use it.
After an even jump the next one is odd, so even at i equals odd at the target.
Every good starting index begins with an odd jump, so we count the true values in odd.

russian-doll-envelopes.hook: Nest envelopes in two dimensions by turning it into a one-dimensional longest increasing subsequence.
russian-doll-envelopes.ask: Each envelope has a width and height. One fits inside another only if both are strictly smaller. Return the largest number of envelopes that can be nested inside one another.
russian-doll-envelopes.exampleWhy: 2 by 3 fits in 5 by 4, which fits in 6 by 7, which fits in 7 by 8: four envelopes.

brute.idea: Sort by width, then classic quadratic DP: each envelope's best chain extends the best chain of any envelope that fits inside it.
steps: Sort envelopes by width
dp[i] starts at 1
For each smaller j that fits, dp[i] = dp[j] + 1
Answer is the max dp
brute.whySlow: 100,000 envelopes means about five billion pair checks.

optimal.insight: Sort by width ascending and height descending. Equal widths can then never chain, so the answer is the LIS of heights, solvable with binary search.
steps: Sort by width up, height down
tails[k] = smallest tail height of a chain of length k+1
Binary search each height in tails
Append if largest, else replace the first tail at least as big

codeNotes.note: Same width: taller first, so no chaining

pitfalls: Sorting heights ascending for equal widths wrongly lets 6 by 4 nest in 6 by 7.
tails is not an actual chain, only its length is meaningful.

say.intro: Okay, Russian Doll Envelopes. Each envelope has a width and a height. One fits inside another only if both are strictly smaller. How many can we nest? Here, two by three goes into five by four. Then six by seven. Then seven by eight. So the answer is four.
say.brute: The brute force sorts by width and runs the classic dynamic program. For each envelope, look at every earlier one that fits inside it, and extend the best chain from there. It's correct. So what's the catch? It compares every pair. That's n squared. A hundred thousand envelopes means billions of checks.
say.insight: Here's the clever sort. Width ascending, but for equal widths, height descending. Why? Now two envelopes with the same width can never both show up in an increasing run of heights. So the whole problem becomes the longest strictly increasing subsequence of heights. And that has a well known n log n solution, with binary search.
say.anim: The envelopes get sorted by width ascending, with equal widths sorted by height descending. We start with an empty tails list to track the longest increasing height sequence. Height 3 is checked against tails, found empty, so it gets appended, giving tails of 3. Height 4 is bigger than 3, so it extends tails to 3 and 4. Height 7 extends the sequence again, making tails 3, 4, and 7. Height 4 replaces the 7 since it fits earlier, keeping tails as 3, 4, 7. Height 8 extends tails one more time, reaching 3, 4, 7, 8. The final tails length is 4, meaning the longest chain of envelopes is 4.
say.code: We sort with same width, taller first, so equal widths can't chain. Tails holds the smallest ending height for each chain length. For each height, binary search finds the first tail at least that big. If it's past the end, the longest chain grows by one. Otherwise, same length but a smaller tail is better, so we replace it. Finally, the length of tails is the length of the longest chain.
say.outro: n log n time. Longest increasing subsequence with binary search, after one clever sort.

russian-doll-envelopes.title: Russian Doll Envelopes
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container for the method that solves the envelope nesting problem.
The method maxEnvelopes takes a list of envelopes, each with a width and height, and returns the longest nesting chain length.
We sort by width ascending and height descending, so envelopes with equal widths can never form an increasing height sequence.
We create an empty list called tails, where each slot holds the smallest possible ending height for a chain of that length.
We loop through the sorted envelopes, ignoring the width since the sort handled it, and look only at each height.
We binary search for the first position in tails where the value is at least this height.
If that position is the end of tails, this height is larger than every tail so far.
In that case we append the height, which extends the longest chain found so far by one.
Otherwise there is an existing tail that is at least as large as this height.
We replace that tail with the smaller height, keeping chain endings as small as possible for future extensions.
The length of tails equals the longest strictly increasing height chain, which is the maximum number of nested envelopes.

4sum.hook: 3Sum with one more loop. Sorting turns the inner pair into a two-pointer squeeze.
4sum.ask: Given numbers and a target, return every unique set of four values, at four distinct positions, that sums to the target. The order of the result does not matter.
4sum.exampleWhy: Sorted: -2, -1, 0, 0, 1, 2. Exactly three distinct value sets of four add up to zero.

brute.idea: Sort, then try every combination of four positions, keeping matches in a set to remove duplicates.
steps: Sort the numbers
Four nested loops over positions
Sum matches? Add the tuple to a set
brute.whySlow: With 200 numbers that is about 65 million quadruples, far slower than needed.

optimal.insight: After sorting, fix the first two values; the last two come from a two-pointer squeeze that moves toward the target in linear time.
steps: Sort the numbers
Loop i, then j, skipping repeated values
lo and hi squeeze the rest toward the target
On a match, record it and skip duplicates

codeNotes.note: Too small: raise the low end

codeNotes.match: while lo < hi and nums[lo] == nums[lo - 1]:
codeNotes.note: Skip duplicates of the third value

pitfalls: Skip duplicates at every level, or the same quadruplet appears twice.
In fixed-width languages the sum can overflow 32 bits; use 64.

say.intro: Okay, Four Sum. You get some numbers and a target. Return every unique group of four values, from four different positions, that adds up to the target. For one, zero, minus one, zero, minus two, two, and a target of zero, there are exactly three groups.
say.brute: The brute force sorts the numbers, then tries every combination of four positions. Matches go into a set, so duplicates collapse. It's correct. So what's the catch? It's n to the fourth. With two hundred numbers, that's around sixty five million combinations. Way more work than we need.
say.insight: Here's the thing. Once the list is sorted, the last two values don't need two loops. Fix the first two values. Then put one pointer just after them, and another at the end. Sum too small? Move the low pointer up. Too big? Move the high pointer down. That squeeze is linear. So the whole thing is cubic.
say.anim: The array is sorted into negative two, negative one, zero, zero, one, two. With i at zero, j starts at one, and pointers lo and hi scan from the ends. Total is negative one, too small, so lo moves right to increase the sum. Total hits zero, so negative two, negative one, one, two is saved as a match. Next with j at two, lo and hi squeeze again and find zero, zero summing correctly, adding another quadruplet. Moving i to one, duplicates are skipped and pointers find negative one, zero, zero, one as a valid sum. With i at two, remaining pairs only overshoot the target, so no more matches appear. The final answer returned is three unique quadruplets summing to zero.
say.code: We sort first, because sorted order enables the squeeze. The outer loop fixes i, and skips a repeated first value. The second loop does the same for j. Then two pointers run over the rest. If the total is too small, we raise the low end. Too big, we lower the high end. When we've found a quadruplet, we record it. Then we skip duplicates of the third value, and step inward.
say.outro: Cubic time, no extra space beyond the output. Sort, fix the outer values, and squeeze the inner pair.

4sum.title: 4Sum
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container the judge expects for our method.
The fourSum method takes a list of numbers and a target, and returns a list of quadruplets.
We sort the numbers first so duplicates sit together and two pointers can move by comparing sums.
We store the length as n and start an empty result list to collect answers.
The outer loop picks the first value, stopping early enough to leave room for three more values.
If this first value equals the previous one, we have already handled it, so we check for that duplicate.
We skip this repeated first value to avoid producing duplicate quadruplets.
The second loop picks the second value after the first, leaving room for two pointers at the end.
If this second value matches the one before it, within the same first value, it is a repeat.
We skip that repeated second value to keep the results unique.
We place the low pointer just after the second value and the high pointer at the last element.
We squeeze the pointers inward as long as they have not crossed.
We add the four chosen values into one running total to compare with the target.
If the total is too small, we need something bigger.
So we move the low pointer right to a larger value.
If instead the total is too large, we need something smaller.
So we move the high pointer left to a smaller value.
Otherwise the total equals the target, so we have found a valid quadruplet.
We record the four values as a new list in the result.
We advance the low pointer past the value we just used.
While the new low value repeats the previous one, we keep checking so we do not duplicate.
We keep moving low right until it lands on a fresh value or meets high.
We also move the high pointer left, since the old high value cannot pair again with a new low.
After all loops finish, we return the collected unique quadruplets.

accounts-merge.hook: Accounts sharing any email are the same person. That is connected components in disguise.
accounts-merge.ask: Each account is a name followed by emails. Accounts sharing any email belong to the same person. Merge them and return each person's name followed by their emails in sorted order, accounts in any order.
accounts-merge.exampleWhy: The first two Johns share johnsmith, so they merge. The third John shares nothing and stays separate.

brute.idea: Keep merging any two accounts whose email sets intersect, restarting after each merge, until nothing changes.
steps: Turn each account into an email set
Find any two sets that overlap
Merge them and start the scan again
No overlaps left: sort and output
brute.whySlow: Each merge restarts a full pairwise scan; 1,000 accounts can mean a billion set intersections.

optimal.insight: Treat accounts as nodes; a shared email is an edge. Union-find joins an account to the first owner of each email in near-constant time.
steps: Map each email to the first account that had it
Seen before? Union this account with that owner
Group emails by their owner's root
Output name plus sorted emails per group

codeNotes.match: return [[accounts[r][0]] + sorted(es) for r, es in groups.items()]

pitfalls: Never merge by name: two different Johns can exist.
N is the total number of emails; sorting them dominates.

say.intro: Okay, Accounts Merge. Each account is a name followed by emails. If two accounts share any email, they're the same person, and we merge them. Return each person with their emails sorted. Here, the first two Johns share john smith, so they merge. The other John and Mary stay separate.
say.brute: The brute force keeps hunting for any two accounts whose emails overlap. When it finds a pair, it merges them and starts the whole scan over. Eventually nothing overlaps. It's correct. So what's the catch? Every merge triggers another full scan of all pairs. With lots of accounts, the work grows roughly cubically.
say.insight: Think about it this way. Each account is a node in a graph. Two accounts share an edge when they share an email. A merged person? That's just a connected component. And union find builds components fast. Remember the first account that owned each email. When an email shows up again, union the new account with that owner.
say.anim: We start with four accounts and a parent array mapping each account to itself. Account 0's emails are scanned, and johnsmith and john_newyork both get owner set to 0. Account 1 shares johnsmith with account 0, so we union account 1 into account 0's group. Union sets parent of root 1 to root 0, merging these two John accounts together. Account 2, Mary, and account 3, Johnny Bravo, have unique emails, so no unions happen. Now we group emails by find root, placing johnsmith, john_newyork, and john00 all under root 0. Mary's email groups under root 2, and Johnny Bravo's email groups separately under root 3. Finally we build results: John's merged emails, Mary's account, and Johnny Bravo's account as final answer.
say.code: Every account starts as its own root. Find uses path halving, which keeps the trees flat. Next, we map each email to the first account seen with it. If an email is shared, we union the accounts. Then we collect emails under each root. Finally, for each root, we output the name first, then the sorted emails.
say.outro: Near linear unions, with sorting as the main cost. Connected components, found with union find.

accounts-merge.title: Accounts Merge
lineNotes: We define the Solution class that holds the method for this problem.
The method accountsMerge takes the list of accounts and returns the merged accounts with sorted emails.
Each account starts as its own parent, so every account is initially its own separate group.
We define find to locate the root representative of an account's group.
We loop while x is not its own parent, meaning we have not yet reached the root.
We apply path compression by pointing x to its grandparent, which flattens the tree and speeds later lookups.
Then we move x up to its parent and continue climbing.
Once x is its own parent, we return it as the root.
We define union to merge the groups containing two accounts.
We find the root of the first account.
We find the root of the second account.
Only if the roots differ do we need to merge, since equal roots are already joined.
We attach the first root under the second root, merging the two groups into one.
This comment says we will record which account first owned each email.
The owner dictionary starts empty and maps each email to its first account index.
We loop over every account by its index.
We take the emails of this account by skipping the name at position zero.
We go through each email in the current account.
We check whether this email has already been claimed by an earlier account.
This comment explains that a repeated email means the two accounts belong to the same person.
We union the current account with the email's first owner, linking the two groups.
Otherwise the email is new to us.
We record the current account as the owner of this email.
This comment says we now gather emails by the root of their owner's group.
The groups dictionary maps each root to a list of its emails, creating lists automatically.
We iterate over every email we recorded in owner.
We look up the account index that first owned this email.
We find the final root of that account, which identifies the merged person.
We append the email to the list for that root.
This comment says we will build the output with the name and sorted emails.
The result list will hold the final merged accounts.

The name comes from the root account, since all merged accounts share the same name.

We put the name first, followed by the sorted emails, and add that to the result.
We return the list of merged accounts.

asteroid-collision.hook: Rocks flying left and right: only a left-mover meeting a right-mover ever collides.
asteroid-collision.ask: Each number is an asteroid: size is the absolute value, sign is direction. Moving at equal speed, colliding asteroids destroy the smaller one, or both if equal. Return what survives.
asteroid-collision.exampleWhy: -6 destroys 5 and then 3 as it flies left. 2 destroys -1. 2 and 4 both move right and never meet.

brute.idea: Repeatedly scan for a right-mover directly followed by a left-mover, resolve that one collision, and restart the scan.
steps: Scan for a positive followed by a negative
Remove the smaller, or both if equal
Restart until no such pair exists
brute.whySlow: Each collision restarts the scan and deleting from a list shifts elements; 10,000 asteroids means millions of steps.

optimal.insight: Survivors so far sit on a stack. A new left-mover only fights right-movers on top of the stack, nearest first.
steps: Walk asteroids left to right
Left-mover meets positive top: compare sizes
Smaller top explodes; keep fighting the next top
Equal: both explode. Bigger top: newcomer explodes
Survivors get pushed

codeNotes.match: while alive and a < 0 and stack and stack[-1] > 0:

pitfalls: A left-mover followed by a right-mover never collides: check the order, not just signs.

say.intro: Okay, Asteroid Collision. Each number is an asteroid. Its size is the absolute value, and its sign is its direction. Positive moves right. When two meet, the smaller one explodes. If they're equal, both do. For three, five, minus six, two, minus one, four, the survivors are minus six, two and four.
say.brute: The brute force simulates one crash at a time. Scan for a right mover followed right away by a left mover. Resolve that crash, then start the scan over. Stop when no such pair is left. So what's the catch? Every crash restarts the scan. And deleting from the middle of a list shifts everything after it. That's n squared.
say.insight: Here's the thing. A crash only happens when a left mover meets right movers before it. And which one does it hit first? The nearest one. That's exactly a stack. Keep the survivors so far on a stack. When a left mover arrives, it fights the top while the top moves right. It pops every one it beats.
say.anim: We start with an empty stack and the asteroid list to process one by one. Three and five are positive, moving right, so they simply get pushed onto the stack. Negative six moves left and collides, destroying five then three since both are smaller. Stack is empty now, so negative six survives and gets pushed alone. Two is positive, no collision possible, so it joins the stack peacefully. Negative one meets two, they're equal size, so both destroy each other instantly. Four is positive again, no clash occurs, so it gets appended safely. Final surviving stack returned is negative six, two, and four.
say.code: For each asteroid, we assume it survives. Only right then left can collide, so we fight while it moves left and the top moves right. If the top is smaller, it explodes. We pop it and keep fighting. Same size? Both explode. If the top is bigger, the newcomer dies. Each survivor joins the stack. And at the end, the stack holds the final state.
say.outro: Each asteroid is pushed and popped at most once, so linear time. The most recent survivor is always the next to collide. That's a stack.

asteroid-collision.title: Asteroid Collision
lineNotes: This defines the Solution class that holds our method for the asteroid collision problem.
The method takes a list of asteroid values and returns the list of survivors after all collisions.
We start with an empty stack that will hold the asteroids that have survived so far.
We process each asteroid in order, calling the current one a.
We assume the current asteroid survives until a collision proves otherwise.
We keep fighting while a is alive, moving left, and the stack top is a right-mover, since only that pair collides.
If the top asteroid is smaller than the size of a, the top is destroyed.
So we pop the smaller right-mover off the stack and keep checking the next one.
If the sizes are equal, both asteroids are destroyed, starting with removing the top.
We pop the top from the stack for the tie.
We also mark a as dead, since both explode and nothing more should happen.
Otherwise the top asteroid is bigger than a, so a loses the fight.
We mark a as not alive, which ends the loop and keeps the top on the stack.
After the collisions, we check whether a survived them all.
If it survived, we push it onto the stack as the newest survivor.
Once every asteroid is processed, the stack holds the final survivors and we return it.

bus-routes.hook: Count buses, not stops. Breadth-first search where each level is one more bus ride.
bus-routes.ask: Each bus loops forever along its list of stops. Starting at a source stop, return the fewest buses needed to reach the target stop, or minus one if impossible.
bus-routes.exampleWhy: Bus 0 takes us from 1 to 7, bus 1 from 7 to 6, and bus 2 from 6 to 9: three buses.

brute.idea: Track every stop reachable with k buses. Each round, scan all routes; any route touching a reachable stop adds all its stops.
steps: Start with only the source reachable
Each round, scan every route for a reachable stop
Add that route's stops; target reached? return rounds
No growth? Return minus one
brute.whySlow: Every round rescans all routes, even ones already used: up to 500 rounds over 100,000 stops.

optimal.insight: BFS by number of rides, and board each bus at most once. A map from stop to buses finds boardable buses instantly.
steps: Map each stop to the buses that serve it
BFS from the source, storing rides taken
At a stop, board each unused bus
Visit all its stops; target means rides plus one

codeNotes.note: Which buses can I board here?
Each bus is ridden at most once

pitfalls: Marking only stops, not buses, rescans long routes repeatedly and times out.
Source equals target needs zero buses.

say.intro: Okay, Bus Routes. Each bus loops forever around its list of stops. Starting at a source stop, what's the fewest buses you need to reach the target? Here, the first bus takes us from one to seven. The second from seven to six. And the third from six to nine. So the answer is three.
say.brute: The brute force tracks every stop reachable with k buses. Each round, it scans every route. Any route touching a reachable stop adds all its stops. When the target shows up, the round number is the answer. It's correct. So what's the catch? Every round rescans every route. Even the ones we've already used up.
say.insight: Here's the thing. We're counting buses, not stops. So it's breadth first search, where each level is one more ride. And the key detail? Mark buses as used. Once you've boarded a bus, all its stops are reachable at that level. Riding it again later can never help. And a map from stop to buses makes boarding instant.
say.anim: Source is 1 and target is 9, so we build a map from stops to buses first. We scan each route, recording which buses stop at each number. Now stop one is seen, and we start breadth first search with zero rides. At stop 1 we board bus 0, marking it seen and exploring stops 2 and 7. Next we process stop 2, finding no new buses, then move to stop 7. At stop 7 bus 1 gets boarded, adding stops 3 and 6 with two rides. From stop 6 we board bus 2, checking its stops 6 and 9. Stop 9 matches the target, so the function returns three rides as the answer.
say.code: If source equals target, we return zero. Then we build a map from each stop to its buses. That answers which buses can I board here. We run breadth first search by number of rides. At each stop, we board every unused bus and mark it, so each bus is ridden at most once. If the target is on this bus, we return rides plus one. Otherwise, new stops are reached with one more bus.
say.outro: Each bus and stop is handled once, so linear in total route length. Breadth first search over buses, not stops.

bus-routes.title: Bus Routes
lineNotes: We define the Solution class that holds the method for this problem.
The method takes the bus routes, a source stop and a target stop, and returns the fewest buses needed.
If the source already equals the target, no ride is needed at all.
So we return zero immediately in that trivial case.
We build a map from each stop to the list of buses that visit it.
We loop over every bus with its index and its route of stops.
For each stop on that route, we look at the stop itself.
We record this bus under that stop so boardable buses can be found instantly later.
We create sets for buses already boarded and stops already visited, starting with the source stop.
The queue starts with the source stop and zero rides taken, setting up a breadth first search by rides.
We keep searching while there are still stops waiting to be explored.
We take the oldest stop from the queue along with how many rides it took to reach it.
For this stop, we try every bus that passes through it.
If we already boarded this bus before, it cannot help us any faster.
So we skip it and move to the next bus.
Otherwise we mark this bus as boarded so we never ride it twice.
We walk through every stop that this bus can reach on its loop.
If one of those stops is the target, we have found our destination.
Boarding this bus costs one more ride, so we return rides plus one, which is the minimum thanks to breadth first order.
If the stop is not the target, we check whether we have visited it before.
We mark that new stop as visited to avoid queuing it again.
We add it to the queue with one more ride than the current count.
If the queue empties without reaching the target, the destination is unreachable, so we return minus one.

candy.hook: Neighbors with higher ratings need more candy. Two sweeps, one from each side, settle it.
candy.ask: Children stand in a line with ratings. Each gets at least one candy, and any child rated higher than a neighbor must get more than that neighbor. Return the minimum total candies.
candy.exampleWhy: Candies 2, 1, 2, 3, 1 satisfy every neighbor rule, and no smaller total does.

brute.idea: Give everyone one candy, then keep sweeping the line fixing any violated neighbor rule until nothing changes.
steps: Everyone starts with one
Higher than a neighbor but not more candy? Bump it
Repeat full sweeps until stable
brute.whySlow: A long decreasing slope needs one sweep per child; 50,000 children means billions of checks.

optimal.insight: Split the rule in two. A left-to-right pass satisfies left neighbors, a right-to-left pass satisfies right ones; taking the max satisfies both minimally.
steps: Start everyone at one candy
Left pass: higher than left neighbor means left plus one
Right pass: higher than right neighbor means at least right plus one
Sum the candies

pitfalls: Equal ratings impose nothing: a child equal to a neighbor may get fewer.
Overwriting instead of taking the max breaks the left-pass guarantee.

say.intro: Okay, Candy. Children stand in a line, each with a rating. Every child gets at least one candy. And a child rated higher than a neighbour must get more than that neighbour. What's the fewest candies in total? For ratings one, zero, two, three, one, we hand out two, one, two, three, one. That's nine.
say.brute: The brute force starts everyone at one and sweeps the line. Whenever a child outranks a neighbour but doesn't have more candy, bump them up. Repeat full sweeps until nothing changes. It gets the right answer. So what's the catch? A long downhill slope needs one sweep per child. That's n squared.
say.insight: Here's the thing. Each child has two separate rules. One about the left neighbour, and one about the right. A left to right pass handles every left rule. Why? Each child only needs to beat the value just set before it. A right to left pass handles the right rules. Take the larger of the two, and both rules hold, with the fewest candies.
say.anim: We start with ratings one, zero, two, three, one, and everyone gets one candy. Scanning left to right, we only raise candies when a rating beats its left neighbor. At index two rating two beats rating zero, so candies becomes two there. At index three rating three beats rating two, so candies climbs to three. Index four rating one isn't bigger than three, so it stays at one candy. Now scanning right to left, we fix right neighbor violations using a max comparison. Index three's rating beats index four's, but three candies already exceeds two, so nothing changes. Index zero's rating one beats index one's rating zero, raising candies there to two. Summing all candies, one plus one plus two plus three plus one, gives the final answer nine.
say.code: Everyone gets at least one candy to start. In the left pass, a child rated above their left neighbour beats the left neighbour by one. Now we sweep from the right. A child rated above their right neighbour must beat right without breaking left. So they take the larger of their current count, and the right neighbour plus one. The sum is the minimum total.
say.outro: Two linear passes. That's greedy. Split a two sided rule into two one sided sweeps, and keep the maximum.

candy.title: Candy
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container that the interview platform expects for our method.
The candy method takes the list of ratings and returns the minimum total number of candies as an integer.
We store the number of children in n, since we will loop over the line several times.
We give every child one candy to start, which satisfies the rule that each child gets at least one.
The first pass goes left to right, starting at the second child so each child has a left neighbor.
We check whether this child is rated higher than the child on the left, which would require more candy.
If so, we give this child one more candy than the left neighbor, which is the smallest amount that satisfies the left rule.
The second pass goes right to left, starting at the second to last child so each child has a right neighbor.
We check whether this child is rated higher than the child on the right, which would require more candy.
We set this child to the larger of the current count and the right neighbor's count plus one, so the left pass result is preserved.
Finally we add up all the candies, which gives the minimum total satisfying both neighbor rules.

check-if-a-parentheses-string-can-be-val.hook: Some brackets are locked, some are wildcards. Two balance sweeps decide it without trying any choices.
check-if-a-parentheses-string-can-be-val.ask: Given a bracket string and a lock mask, unlocked positions may become either bracket. Return true if some choice makes the whole string a valid balanced bracket sequence.
check-if-a-parentheses-string-can-be-val.exampleWhy: Positions 1 and 3 are locked. Changing positions 0 and 4 to open brackets gives ()()(), which is valid.

brute.idea: Try every assignment of open or close to the unlocked positions, and check each resulting string for balance.
steps: List the unlocked positions
Try all 2^k assignments
Balance never negative and ends at zero? True
brute.whySlow: With 100,000 unlocked positions there are 2^100000 assignments.

optimal.insight: Odd length always fails. Otherwise, from the left, treat wildcards as opens: closes must never win. From the right, treat them as closes: opens never win.
steps: Odd length: impossible
Left sweep: count opens and wildcards against locked closes
Right sweep: count closes and wildcards against locked opens
Neither count went negative: valid

codeNotes.match: open_ += 1 if c == "(" or l == "0" else -1

codeNotes.note: Too many locked closes so far

codeNotes.match: close += 1 if c == ")" or l == "0" else -1
codeNotes.note: From the right, wildcards act as closers

pitfalls: One sweep is not enough: (( with locks 11 passes left-to-right but fails.
Remember the odd length check; the sweeps alone miss it.

say.intro: Okay, Check if a Parentheses String Can Be Valid. You get a bracket string and a lock mask. Locked brackets stay as they are. Unlocked ones can become either kind. Can we balance the string? Here, two closing brackets are locked. Flip two free ones into openers, and it's valid. So the answer is true.
say.brute: The brute force tries every way to fill the unlocked spots, two choices each. Then it checks if the result balances. Definitely correct. So what's the catch? With k free spots, there are two to the k choices. A hundred thousand free spots? Beyond astronomical.
say.insight: Here's the thing. First, an odd length can never balance. Then sweep left to right, and treat every free bracket as an opener. If locked closers ever outnumber everything else, nothing can fix it. Now sweep right to left the same way. This time, free brackets act as closers, against locked openers. Pass both sweeps, and a valid choice is guaranteed.
say.anim: The string has six characters, so the length check passes immediately. We scan left to right, treating unlocked characters as flexible open brackets. Open count climbs to one even though the character is a closing bracket, since it's unlocked. Processing more characters, open_ stays nonnegative, reaching values like one and zero safely. By the end of the left pass, open_ reaches two, confirming closes never outnumber opens. Now scanning right to left, treating unlocked characters as flexible close brackets. Close count steadily rises through one, two, three, four, five, and six without going negative. Both passes succeed, so the function returns true, meaning the string can be made valid.
say.code: First, an odd length can never balance, so we return false. In the left sweep, wildcards help as openers. We add one for an opener or a free spot, and subtract one for a locked close. Too many locked closes so far? The count goes negative, and we fail. From the right, wildcards act as closers, against locked openers. If both directions are satisfiable, we return true.
say.outro: Two linear passes, constant space. Let every wildcard help whichever side is in danger, and check from both ends.

check-if-a-parentheses-string-can-be-val.title: Check if a Parentheses String Can Be Valid
lineNotes: We define the Solution class that holds the method for this problem.
The method takes the bracket string and the lock mask, and returns whether some valid arrangement exists.
If the length of the string is odd, no balanced sequence is possible, so we check that first.
In that odd case we return false immediately.
We start a counter called open underscore at zero to track how many opens we could have pending.
We walk through the string and mask together, one character and its lock flag at a time.
A open bracket or an unlocked spot counts as an open and adds one, while a locked close subtracts one.
If the counter drops below zero, even the best choice leaves too many closes at this point.
So we return false because a prefix can never be repaired by later characters.
Now we reset a counter called close to zero for the right to left pass.
