We walk both strings in reverse, so we examine characters from the end toward the start.
A close bracket or an unlocked spot adds one, while a locked open bracket subtracts one.
If this counter goes negative, there are too many opens in a suffix even with wildcards as closes.
In that case we return false since the suffix cannot be balanced.
If the length is even and both passes survive, a valid arrangement exists, so we return true.

check-if-array-is-sorted-and-rotated.hook: A sorted array, rotated, has at most one place where the values step down.
check-if-array-is-sorted-and-rotated.ask: Return true if the array could be a non-decreasing sorted array that was rotated by some number of positions, including zero. Duplicates are allowed.
check-if-array-is-sorted-and-rotated.exampleWhy: Rotating 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 left by two positions gives 3, 4, 5, 1, 2.

brute.idea: Try every rotation of the array and check whether any of them is sorted.
steps: For each rotation offset x
Build the rotated copy
Sorted? Return true
brute.whySlow: Each of n rotations copies and scans the array, so work is quadratic instead of a single pass.

optimal.insight: Walk the array circularly and count drops, where a value is bigger than the next. A rotated sorted array has at most one.
steps: Compare each value with the next, wrapping at the end
Count positions where the value drops
At most one drop means sorted and rotated

codeNotes.note: Only the rotation seam may drop

pitfalls: Without the wrap-around, 2, 1, 3, 4 looks fine with a single drop.
Equal neighbors are not drops; use strict greater-than.

say.intro: Okay, Check if Array Is Sorted and Rotated. Could this array be a sorted list, in non decreasing order, that was rotated some number of places? Three, four, five, one, two is one through five, rotated. So the answer is true.
say.brute: The brute force tries every rotation. For each offset, build the rotated copy and check if it's sorted. If any rotation is sorted, return true. It works. So what's the catch? Each of the n rotations copies and scans the whole array. That's n squared, for a question that needs one pass.
say.insight: Think about it this way. Picture the array as a circle. A sorted array, read around the circle, steps down exactly once. That's at the seam, where the end wraps back to the start. Or never, if all values are equal. And rotation? It just moves the seam. So count the places where a value is bigger than the next one, wrapping around. At most one is allowed.
say.anim: We start with the array three four five one two, and set n to five. Drops starts at zero as we begin looping through each index. At index zero, three is less than four, so no drop here. At index one, four is less than five, still no drop. At index two, five is greater than one, so that counts as a drop. Drops is now one, and the remaining comparisons find no more drops. With drops at one, which is at most one, the array qualifies. The function returns true, confirming the array is sorted and rotated.
say.code: We count descents around the circle, starting at zero. For each index, we compare the value with the next one. At the wrap, the last compares with the first. That's what the modulo does. Each time we've found a step down, we add one. Finally, only the rotation seam may drop. So we return whether drops is at most one.
say.outro: Linear time, constant space. A single circular scan, counting the one feature that matters.

check-if-array-is-sorted-and-rotated.title: Check if Array Is Sorted and Rotated
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which holds the method that answers the sorted and rotated question.
The check method takes the list nums and returns true or false depending on whether it is a rotated sorted array.
We store the length of nums in n so we can use it for looping and wrapping around.
We start a counter called drops at zero to track how many times a value is larger than the next.
We loop through every index i from zero up to n minus one, covering each adjacent pair.
We compare the current value to the next one, using modulo n so the last element wraps around to the first.
Whenever the current value is bigger than the next, we add one to drops, since that marks a break in order.
We return true if there is at most one drop, because a rotated sorted array has no more than one circular drop.

check-if-grid-can-be-cut-into-sections.hook: Project every rectangle onto one axis, merge the intervals, and count the clean gaps.
check-if-grid-can-be-cut-into-sections.ask: Non-overlapping rectangles sit on an n by n grid. Can two horizontal cuts, or two vertical cuts, split the grid into three sections that each contain at least one rectangle, with no rectangle cut?
check-if-grid-can-be-cut-into-sections.exampleWhy: Horizontal cuts at y equal 2 and y equal 4 avoid every rectangle and leave rectangles in all three sections.

brute.idea: For each axis, try every pair of candidate cut lines at rectangle edges, and check every rectangle against them.
steps: Collect edge coordinates on one axis
Try every pair of cuts a below b
Each rectangle wholly in one section, none empty? True
brute.whySlow: With 100,000 rectangles there are billions of cut pairs, each checking every rectangle.

optimal.insight: Each rectangle is an interval on the chosen axis. A legal cut is a gap between merged intervals; two gaps give three sections.
steps: Project rectangles to x intervals, and to y intervals
Sort intervals by start
Sweep: a start at or past the reach is a gap
Two gaps on either axis means true

codeNotes.note: Nothing crosses here: a cut fits

pitfalls: Touching edges are fine to cut between: use >=, not >.
Gaps beyond two are fine; any two of them work.

say.intro: Okay, Check if Grid can be Cut into Sections. Rectangles sit on a square grid without overlapping. Can we make two horizontal cuts, or two vertical cuts, so no rectangle gets sliced? And each of the three sections has to hold at least one rectangle. Here, horizontal cuts at two and four work. So the answer is true.
say.brute: The brute force tries every pair of cut lines at rectangle edges, on each axis. For each pair, it checks every rectangle sits fully in one section, and no section is empty. So what's the catch? That's edges squared, times rectangles. Roughly cubic. Far too slow for a hundred thousand rectangles.
say.insight: Here's the thing. Look at one axis at a time. Each rectangle becomes an interval, from its low edge to its high edge. Where can a cut go? Exactly where no interval crosses it. That's a gap between merged intervals. So sort the intervals, sweep, and count the gaps. Two gaps give three sections. And each section automatically holds a rectangle.
say.anim: We extract x-intervals and y-intervals from each rectangle to check both axes for valid cuts. First we sort the x-intervals and merge overlapping ones, tracking how far coverage reaches. Each interval's start is compared to the current reach to detect a gap, but none appear. With zero gaps found, the x-axis cannot be split into three sections, so it returns false. Now we sort the y-intervals and repeat, merging intervals and watching for gaps between them. Start two meets reach two, so a gap is counted, making gaps equal to one. Another gap appears when start four meets reach four, bringing gaps up to two. Two gaps on the y-axis mean three sections exist, so the final answer is true.
say.code: The helper sorts the intervals, and sweeps them left to right. If an interval starts at or past our reach, nothing crosses here. A cut fits, so we count a gap. Then we update reach, the furthest edge covered so far. Two cuts make three sections, so two gaps means success. Finally, we try both vertical cuts and horizontal cuts.
say.outro: Sorting makes it m log m. That's intervals. Project, sort, merge, and count the gaps.

check-if-grid-can-be-cut-into-sections.title: Check if Grid can be Cut into Sections
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container the judge expects for our method.
The main method takes the grid size and the list of rectangles, and returns whether two valid cuts exist.
We define a helper called can_cut that checks one axis, given a list of start and end spans.
Sorting the spans by start puts them in order so we can sweep across the axis from left to right.
We start with zero gaps and set reach to the end of the first span, the farthest point covered so far.
We loop over every remaining span, unpacking its start and end values.
If this span starts at or beyond reach, there is a clean gap where a cut can safely go.
So we count one more gap, since a cut here slices no rectangle.
We then extend reach to the larger of the old reach and this span's end, merging overlapping spans.
Two or more gaps mean two cuts and three sections, each holding at least one rectangle, so we return that result.
We build the horizontal spans for the x axis, using each rectangle's left and right coordinates.
We build the spans for the y axis the same way, using each rectangle's bottom and top coordinates.
A valid answer exists if either the x axis or the y axis allows two cuts, so we return the or of both checks.

count-special-subsequences.hook: Turn a four-index product equation into two matching ratios, then count with a hash map.
count-special-subsequences.ask: Count index quadruples p, q, r, s, each at least two apart in order, where nums[p] times nums[r] equals nums[q] times nums[s].
count-special-subsequences.exampleWhy: Index sets 0,2,4,6 and 1,3,5,7 and 0,2,5,7 satisfy the equation with the required spacing.

brute.idea: Try every valid index quadruple with gaps of at least two, and test the product equation directly.
steps: Loop p, then q from p plus 2
Then r from q plus 2, s from r plus 2
Products equal? Count it
brute.whySlow: With 1,000 numbers that is around forty billion quadruples.

optimal.insight: Rewrite as nums[p] over nums[q] equals nums[s] over nums[r]. Sweep r; keep a count of reduced left ratios, then look up right ratios.
steps: Move r from index 4 rightward
Add all ratios p over q with q = r minus 2
Reduce each fraction by its gcd
For each s at least r plus 2, add matching count

codeNotes.note: Left pairs keyed by reduced fraction
Newest q now allowed for this r
Store p over q in lowest terms

pitfalls: Floating-point ratios can collide or miss; use gcd-reduced integer pairs.
Add only q equal to r minus 2 each step, or pairs get double counted.

say.intro: Okay, Count Special Subsequences. We count groups of four indices, p, q, r, s, each at least two apart. The rule? The value at p times the value at r equals the value at q times the value at s. In three, four, three, four, three, four, three, four, exactly three groups work. So the answer is three.
say.brute: The brute force loops over all four indices, keeping the gaps, and checks the products. Straightforward. So what's the catch? It's n to the fourth. A thousand numbers means tens of billions of groups. Way too slow.
say.insight: Here's the trick. Divide both sides. Now the rule says p over q equals s over r. See what happened? The left pair and the right pair are separate. So we sweep r forward. Each step unlocks one new q. We add its ratios with every earlier p to a counter. Then each s to the right just looks up its matching ratio.
say.anim: We start with the array three four three four three four three four, length eight. The outer loop sets r to four, fixing the right side of our ratio comparison. We scan p from zero, building reduced ratios of nums p over nums q, here one over one. Now s sweeps forward, reducing nums s over nums r and looking up matches in our ratio counter. At s equals six we find a matching ratio, adding one to total. At s equals seven another match appears, bumping total to two matches found so far. R advances to five, q becomes three, and we add new ratios like three over four. More s values match these ratios, pushing total up to three by the end. The loop finishes and the function returns the final answer, three special subsequences.
say.code: We keep a counter of left pairs, keyed by reduced fraction. For each r, the newest q is now allowed, at r minus two. For every p at least two before q, we store p over q in lowest terms, using the gcd. Then the right pairs keep the gap. For every s at least two after r, we reduce s over r. Matching ratios give special subsequences, so we add the count.
say.outro: n squared instead of n to the fourth. Split the equation into two halves, and match them with a counter.

count-special-subsequences.title: Count Special Subsequences
lineNotes: This line declares the Solution class that holds our method for the problem.
We define the method that takes the list nums and returns the count of special subsequences.
We store the length of nums in n so we can use it for loop bounds.
We create a counter to track how often each reduced ratio of left values has appeared.
We start the running answer total at zero.
We sweep r from four up to n minus three, since r needs two indices before q and two after it.
We set q to r minus two, the newest index allowed to sit two positions before r.
For this new q, we loop over every p that is at least two positions before q.
We compute the greatest common divisor of nums at p and nums at q to reduce the ratio.
We add one to the counter for the reduced pair of nums at p over nums at q, recording that left ratio.
Now we loop over every s that is at least two positions after r.
We compute the greatest common divisor of nums at s and nums at r to reduce this right ratio.
We add to total the count of stored left ratios matching nums at s over nums at r, since equal ratios mean equal cross products.
After all sweeps, we return the total number of special subsequences.

count-ways-to-build-good-strings.hook: Climbing stairs in disguise: each step appends a block of zeros or a block of ones.
count-ways-to-build-good-strings.ask: Build strings by repeatedly appending either zero copies of 0 or one copies of 1. Count distinct strings whose length is between low and high, modulo 10^9 + 7.
count-ways-to-build-good-strings.exampleWhy: Blocks have length 1 and 2. There are 3, 5 and 8 ways to reach lengths 3, 4 and 5: 16 total.

brute.idea: Recursively explore every sequence of appends, counting each string whose length lands in range.
steps: From length L, count it if within range
Recurse on L plus zero and L plus one
Stop when L exceeds high
brute.whySlow: The recursion tree doubles every step; high up to 100,000 is hopeless.

optimal.insight: Different append sequences always produce different strings. So the count for length L is the count for L minus zero plus L minus one.
steps: dp[0] = 1, the empty string
dp[L] = dp[L - zero] + dp[L - one]
Take everything modulo 10^9 + 7
Sum dp from low to high

codeNotes.note: One way to build the empty string

pitfalls: Sum lengths low through high, not only dp[high].
Apply the modulo inside the loop, not just at the end.

say.intro: Okay, Count Ways To Build Good Strings. Start from empty. Each step, append a block of zeros of a fixed length, or a block of ones of a fixed length. How many strings have a length between low and high? With blocks of length one and two, and lengths three to five, there are sixteen.
say.brute: The brute force explores every sequence of appends, recursively. At each length, count it if it's in range. Then branch. Add a zero block, or add a one block. Stop past high. So what's the catch? The tree doubles at every level. The work is exponential.
say.insight: Here's the thing. Every string ends with either a zero block or a one block. And different append sequences always give different strings. So how many ways build length L? The ways for L minus the zero length, plus the ways for L minus the one length. That's just climbing stairs. We solve it bottom up, in one pass.
say.anim: We start with low three, high five, zero length one, one length two. The dp array begins as one followed by zeros, counting ways to build each length. At length one, we add dp of zero since zero equals one, giving dp one equals one. At length two, both zero and one appends apply, combining to make dp two equal two. Length three sums dp two and dp one, since different sequences never repeat, giving three. Length four combines dp three and dp two, reaching five good strings. Length five adds dp four and dp three, making dp five equal eight. Summing dp from low three to high five gives the final answer, sixteen.
say.code: The table starts with one way to build the empty string. Then for each length up to high, we add two counts. One where the last block was zeros, from one zero block back. And one where the last block was ones, from one one block back. We take the modulo to keep numbers small. Finally, every length in range counts, so we sum low through high.
say.outro: Linear in high. One dimensional dynamic programming. Each length depends on the lengths one block shorter.

count-ways-to-build-good-strings.title: Count Ways To Build Good Strings
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, as the problem setup expects for this method.
This method takes low, high, zero and one, and returns the count of good strings.
We set MOD to ten to the ninth plus seven so counts stay small.
We make dp with one way to build length zero, the empty string, and zeros for lengths up to high.
We loop over each length from one up to high, filling in ways to build that length.
If length is at least zero, we can end by appending a block of zeros.
We add the ways to build length minus zero, since appending that block reaches the current length.
If length is at least one, we can end by appending a block of ones.
We add the ways to build length minus one, covering strings whose last block is ones.
We reduce this length's count modulo MOD so numbers never grow too large.
We sum the counts from low through high, take the result modulo MOD, and return it.

delete-nodes-and-return-forest.hook: Delete a few nodes from a tree and the pieces left behind become a forest. Collect every root.
delete-nodes-and-return-forest.ask: Given a binary tree with distinct values and a list of values to delete, remove those nodes. Return the roots of all the separate trees that remain, in any order.
delete-nodes-and-return-forest.exampleWhy: Removing 3 frees its children 6 and 7 as new roots; removing 5 just trims it from under 2.

brute.idea: Handle one deleted value at a time: search every current tree for it, cut it from its parent, and add its children as new trees.
steps: For each value to delete
Search every tree in the forest
Cut the node out, adopt its children
brute.whySlow: Each deletion re-searches the whole forest: a thousand nodes and a thousand deletions is a million node visits.

optimal.insight: One post-order pass decides everything: a node starts a new tree exactly when it survives and its parent was deleted or absent.
steps: Put the deletion values in a set
DFS passing whether the parent was deleted
Survivor with no parent? It is a new root
Return None upward for deleted nodes to cut links

codeNotes.note: Children of a deleted node become roots

codeNotes.match: return None if deleted else node
codeNotes.note: Parent drops the link to deleted child

pitfalls: Cut the parent's pointer to a deleted child, or the old subtree stays attached.
Use a set for to_delete; scanning the list each time is quadratic.

say.intro: Okay, so we have a binary tree and a list of values to delete. Every deletion snaps the tree into pieces. We return the root of every piece. Delete three and five from this seven node tree, and three trees are left. One is rooted at one. Six and seven stand alone.
say.brute: The obvious way handles one deletion at a time. Search every tree in the forest for the value. Cut the node from its parent. Then add its children as new trees. Is it correct? Yes. But every deletion searches everything again. So the cost is nodes times deletions.
say.insight: Think about it this way. When does a node start a new tree? Exactly when it survives and its parent is gone. Or when it had no parent at all. So one depth first pass can decide everything. We pass a flag down saying whether the parent was deleted. And on the way back up, a deleted node returns nothing. That cuts its parent's link.
say.anim: We start with root node 1, and the delete set contains nodes 3 and 5. Node 1 is not deleted and is a root, so it becomes the first tree in the forest. We descend to node 2, then node 4, neither deleted, so they stay attached as children. Node 5 is checked and found in the delete set, so it gets removed, becoming null. Back at node 1, we process its right side, where node 3 is also deleted. Node 6, a child of deleted node 3, survives and becomes its own new tree root. Similarly, node 7 survives after node 3 is deleted, so it also becomes a new root. The final forest holds three trees, rooted at nodes 1, 6, and 7.
say.code: Here's the code. First, the delete values go in a set, for instant lookups. The helper takes a node and a flag saying its parent is gone. If the node survives and that flag is set, it starts a new tree. A deleted node makes its children roots, so we pass that down. Finally, a deleted child returns nothing, and the parent drops the link.
say.outro: Linear time and space. The pattern is trees. Pass context down, clean up on the way back. One post order pass does it all.

delete-nodes-and-return-forest.title: Delete Nodes And Return Forest
lineNotes: We define a Solution class that holds the method for solving this problem.
The delNodes method takes the tree root and the list of values that must be deleted.
We turn the delete list into a set so checking whether a value is removed is fast.
We create an empty list called forest to collect the roots of the remaining trees.
We define a helper dfs that visits a node and knows whether this node is a possible new root.
If the node is empty, there is nothing to process here.
So we return nothing, which also lets a parent link to nothing.
We record whether this node's value is in the remove set, meaning it must be deleted.
If the node is a root candidate and survives, it begins a new tree in the forest.
We add that surviving root node to the forest list.
We recurse into the left child, passing deleted so the child knows if its parent vanished, and reattach the result.
We do the same for the right child, updating the right link with whatever the recursion returns.
A deleted node returns nothing so its parent drops it, while a surviving node returns itself.
We start the traversal at the root, which counts as a root candidate because it has no parent.
Finally we return the forest list holding all the roots of the remaining trees.

design-task-manager.hook: Tasks get added, re-prioritised and cancelled. Always run the top one fast with a lazy heap.
design-task-manager.ask: Build a task manager. Each task has a user, an id and a priority. Support adding, editing priority, removing, and executing the highest priority task, breaking ties by higher task id, returning its user or minus one.
design-task-manager.exampleWhy: Task 102 drops to 8, so 103 at 15 runs first for user 3; later 105 at 15 beats the rest.

brute.idea: Keep a dictionary of task id to user and priority. To execute, scan every task for the highest priority, then highest id.
steps: Store tasks in a dictionary
Edit and remove update it directly
execTop scans all tasks for the max
brute.whySlow: Every execTop scans every task: a hundred thousand tasks and calls means ten billion comparisons.

optimal.insight: Never delete from the heap. Push fresh entries on edit, and when popping, skip any entry that no longer matches the live dictionary.
steps: Dictionary holds each live task's user and priority
Heap holds (-priority, -taskId) entries
Edit pushes a new entry; remove only touches the dictionary
execTop pops until an entry matches the dictionary

codeNotes.note: Negate: max priority, then max id
Old entry becomes stale, not removed

codeNotes.match: if taskId in self.info and self.info[taskId][1] == -negP:

pitfalls: Check the priority too, not just the id: an edited task leaves a stale entry behind.
Ties go to the higher taskId, so negate the id as well.

say.intro: Okay, so we're designing a task manager. Each task belongs to a user and has a priority. We add tasks, edit priorities, remove tasks, and execute the top one. Top means highest priority, and ties go to the bigger task id. Executing returns that task's user, or minus one if nothing is left.
say.brute: The simple design is just a dictionary. Task id maps to user and priority. Add, edit and remove are instant. So what's the catch? Execute top has to scan every task to find the best one. With a hundred thousand tasks and a hundred thousand calls, that's billions of comparisons.
say.insight: Here's the trick. Use a heap, but never delete from it. An edit just pushes a fresh entry. A removal only touches the dictionary. So the heap fills up with stale entries. Is that a problem? Not really. When we pop, we check each entry against the dictionary. If it doesn't match, we quietly throw it away.
say.anim: We initialize empty info and heap, then add three tasks for users 1, 2, and 3. Add inserts task 104 for user 4 with priority 5 into the heap. Edit updates task 102's priority to 8 by pushing a fresh heap entry, keeping the old one stale. ExecTop pops the stale entry for task 102, but its priority no longer matches, so it's skipped. The next popped entry, task 103 with priority 15, matches info, so it executes and returns user 3. Rmv deletes task 101 from info, leaving its heap entry invalid for future pops. Add inserts task 105 for user 5 with priority 15 into the heap. ExecTop pops task 105, finds a valid match, and returns user 5 as the final answer.
say.code: Now the code. The heap stores negated priority and negated id. That way the smallest entry is the best task. On an edit, the old entry just becomes stale. We never dig it out. Remove deletes from the dictionary only. Execute pops and skips anything stale or removed. When it finds a live entry, it removes that task and returns its user.
say.outro: Logarithmic time per operation, amortised. The pattern is a heap with lazy deletion. Don't clean up early. Clean up when you pop.

design-task-manager.title: Design Task Manager
lineNotes: We define a TaskManager class that tracks live tasks in a dictionary and orders them with a heap.
The constructor takes the starting list of tasks, each with a user, task id and priority.
We create an info dictionary mapping each task id to its current user and priority.
We create an empty heap that will hold priority and task id entries for finding the top task.
We loop over every starting task, unpacking its user id, task id and priority.
Each starting task is inserted by calling the add method, so setup shares the same logic.
The add method registers a new task given its user, id and priority.
We record the task in the info dictionary, overwriting any older version of that task id.
We push negative priority and negative task id, so the min heap yields highest priority, then highest id.
The edit method changes the priority of an existing task.
We look up the task's user from the dictionary, ignoring its old priority.
We call add with the new priority, which updates the dictionary and pushes a fresh heap entry.
The rmv method removes a task from the manager.
We delete it only from the dictionary and leave the heap alone, so its old entries become stale.
The execTop method runs and removes the best task, returning its user or minus one.
We keep looping while the heap still has entries to examine.
We pop the top entry and unpack its negated priority and negated task id.
We flip the negated task id back to the real task id.
We accept the entry only if the task still exists and its live priority matches this entry.
A valid entry means we remove the task from the dictionary and return its user id.
If the heap empties without finding a valid entry, no task remains, so we return minus one.

fibonacci-number.hook: The textbook recursion is exponential. Two variables make it linear.
fibonacci-number.ask: The Fibonacci sequence starts zero, one, and every later number is the sum of the two before it. Given n, return the n-th Fibonacci number.
fibonacci-number.exampleWhy: The sequence runs 0, 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, so position 6 holds 8.

brute.idea: Translate the definition directly: fib of n calls fib of n minus one and fib of n minus two.
steps: Base cases: n below 2 returns n
Otherwise recurse on n-1 and n-2
Add the two results
brute.whySlow: The same values are recomputed again and again: fib of 30 makes over a million calls.

optimal.insight: Each number only needs the previous two. Build upward from the bottom, keeping just those two values.
steps: Start with a = 0 and b = 1
Repeat n times: slide the pair forward
a now holds fib of n

pitfalls: Plain recursion without memo is exponential; mention memoization as the middle step.

say.intro: Okay, Fibonacci. The sequence starts with zero and one. Every later number is the sum of the two before it. Given n, we return the number at position n. For six, it goes zero, one, one, two, three, five, eight. So the answer is eight.
say.brute: The brute force just copies the definition. Fib of n calls fib of n minus one and fib of n minus two. It reads beautifully. So what's wrong? It recomputes the same values over and over. The call tree doubles at every level. Fib of thirty already needs over a million calls.
say.insight: Now, notice something. Each number only needs the previous two. Nothing else. So why start at the top and branch? Start at the bottom instead. Keep two variables, the last two numbers. Slide them forward one step at a time. That's dynamic programming, with the table shrunk to two cells.
say.anim: We start with a set to zero and b set to one, since n is six. The loop begins, updating a and b together using the previous two values. Now a becomes one, as the first Fibonacci step completes. After more iterations, a is two and b is three, building upward steadily. Now a reaches three and b reaches five, continuing the pattern. Next, a becomes five and b becomes eight, nearing the final value. After six loops, a holds eight and b holds thirteen. The function returns a, giving the final answer eight.
say.code: Here's the code. We start a at zero and b at one. Those are fib zero and fib one. Then we loop n times, advancing one position each time. Each step slides the window: a takes the old b, and b takes the old sum. It all happens in one simultaneous assignment. After the loop, a is fib of n, so we return it.
say.outro: Linear time and constant space. The pattern is one dimensional dynamic programming. Build up from the base cases, and keep only what you need.

fibonacci-number.title: Fibonacci Number
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container the problem expects for our method.
The fib method takes n and returns the n-th Fibonacci number as an integer.
We start a at zero and b at one, the first two Fibonacci numbers.
We loop n times, using an underscore because we never need the loop counter itself.
Each pass slides the window forward: a becomes b, and b becomes the old a plus the old b.
After n steps a holds the n-th Fibonacci number, so we return it.

find-all-duplicates-in-an-array.hook: Find every repeated number without any extra memory, by using the array itself as a checklist.
find-all-duplicates-in-an-array.ask: An array of length n holds numbers from 1 to n, each appearing once or twice. Return every number that appears twice, in linear time and constant extra space.
find-all-duplicates-in-an-array.exampleWhy: The numbers 2 and 3 each appear twice; every other value appears once.

brute.idea: Remember every number in a hash set. If a number is already in the set, it is a duplicate.
steps: Walk the array once
Seen before? Record it as a duplicate
Otherwise add it to the set
brute.whySlow: Time is fine, but the set uses linear extra memory, breaking the constant-space requirement.

optimal.insight: Values are 1 to n, so each value names an index. Flip that slot negative to mark it seen; finding it already negative means a repeat.
steps: For each value, compute index abs(value) - 1
Slot already negative? Value is a duplicate
Otherwise negate the slot to mark it

codeNotes.note: abs: slot may already be flipped

pitfalls: Always use abs(n): an earlier step may already have made n negative.
This mutates the input; restore signs afterwards if the caller needs it.

say.intro: Okay, so we get n numbers, all between one and n. Each one appears once or twice. We return the ones that show up twice. In four, three, two, seven, eight, two, three, one, the repeats are two and three.
say.brute: The natural first answer is a hash set. Walk the array. If a number is already in the set, it's a duplicate. Otherwise, add it. That's linear time, which is great. So what's the catch? The set can grow as big as the array. And the problem wants constant extra space.
say.insight: Here's the thing. Every value from one to n names a position in the array. So the array can be its own checklist. When we see a value, we flip the number at its position to negative. Later, if we land on a slot that's already negative, we've seen this value before. That's a duplicate.
say.anim: We start with the array and an empty results list to collect duplicates. For value four, we compute index three and flip that slot negative to mark it seen. Next value two points to index one, which is still positive, so we negate it. Values seven and eight mark indices six and seven negative, showing them as visited. Now value two again points to index one, already negative, revealing a duplicate. Similarly, value three finds index two already negative, so three joins the duplicates. The last value one simply marks index zero negative, nothing new found. The function returns the final list of duplicates, two and three.
say.code: Now the code. For each number, we take its absolute value minus one as the index. Why absolute? Because an earlier flip may have made it negative. If the number at that index is already negative, we've seen it before. That's the second sighting, so we record it. Otherwise it's the first sighting, and we mark it by negating.
say.outro: Linear time and constant extra space. The pattern is index marking. When values fit the index range, the array is your hash set.

find-all-duplicates-in-an-array.title: Find All Duplicates in an Array
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container the problem expects for our method.
The method findDuplicates takes the list nums and will return a list of numbers that appear twice.
We start with an empty result list called res to collect the duplicates we discover.
We loop through every number n in nums, visiting each element exactly once for linear time.
Since values run from one to n, we take the absolute value of n minus one as its index, ignoring any earlier sign flip.
We check whether the slot at that index is already negative, which would mean this value was seen before.
If it is negative, this value is a repeat, so we append its absolute value to res.
Otherwise this is the first time we see the value, so we handle it in the else branch.
We flip the slot at idx to negative, marking the value as seen without using any extra space.
After the loop finishes, we return res holding every number that appeared twice.

find-first-and-last-position-of-element-.hook: Binary search finds a target. A tiny tweak makes it find the very first and very last copy.
find-first-and-last-position-of-element-.ask: Given a sorted array and a target, return the first and last index where the target appears, or minus one, minus one if it is absent. It must run in logarithmic time.
find-first-and-last-position-of-element-.exampleWhy: The 7s occupy indices 2 through 5, so the range is from 2 to 5.

brute.idea: Scan from left to right. Record the first index holding the target and keep updating the last one.
steps: Walk every index
First match sets the start
Every match updates the end
brute.whySlow: Linear scan ignores sorting: a million copies of the target means a million steps, not twenty.

optimal.insight: Run binary search twice. On a match, record it but keep going: left to find the first copy, right to find the last.
steps: Standard binary search loop
On a match, record the index
Left-biased: keep searching left half
Right-biased: keep searching right half

codeNotes.note: Keep shrinking toward the wanted edge

pitfalls: Finding one match and expanding outward is O(n) when the target repeats many times.

say.intro: Okay, so we get a sorted array and a target. We return the first and last index of that target. If it's missing, we return minus one twice. Here the sevens sit at indices two through five. So the answer is two and five.
say.brute: The simple way scans left to right. The first time we see the target, we record the start. Every time we see it, we update the end. It's correct, and it's easy. But it's linear. And it completely ignores the fact that the array is sorted. That's the whole point of the problem.
say.insight: So here's the idea. Run binary search twice, with one small twist. Normally we stop when we hit the target. Instead, we record the index and keep going. Why? Because there might be another copy further out. To find the first copy, keep searching left. To find the last copy, keep searching right. Each search is logarithmic.
say.anim: We search for target seven, first running binary search biased to find the leftmost match. Lo is zero, hi is seven, mid becomes three, where nums holds seven, so idx updates to three. Since we want the leftmost copy, hi shrinks to two and search continues left. Mid becomes one, value five is too small, so lo moves up to two. Mid is two, another seven found, idx updates to two, then hi shrinks further. Loop ends, so the left bound function returns two as the first position. Now we search again, this time biased right, tracking idx as seven keeps appearing at three, five. Mid six holds nine, too big, hi shrinks and loop ends, returning five as last position. Combining both searches gives the final answer: positions two and five.
say.code: Here's the code. One helper does both searches, with a flag saying which way to lean. It probes the middle each time. On a match, it remembers that index. Then it keeps shrinking the range toward the wanted edge, left or right. We call it once for the first copy, then once for the last copy.
say.outro: Logarithmic time, constant space. The pattern is binary search on a boundary. On a match, don't stop. Keep narrowing toward the edge you need.

find-first-and-last-position-of-element-.title: Find First and Last Position of Element in Sorted Array
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, as the platform expects, to hold our method.
The searchRange method takes the sorted array and a target, and returns the first and last positions.
We define a helper called bound that runs one binary search, leaning left or right depending on leftBias.
We set lo to zero, hi to the last index, and idx to minus one as the not found default.
We loop while the search window between lo and hi still contains at least one index.
We compute mid as the average of lo and hi, rounded down, to probe the middle.
If the middle value is smaller than the target, the target must lie to the right.
So we move lo to just past mid, discarding the left half.
Otherwise, if the middle value is larger than the target, the target must lie to the left.
So we move hi to just before mid, discarding the right half.
Otherwise the middle value equals the target, so we have found a match.
We record mid in idx as the best answer so far, but we keep searching.
If we are hunting for the first occurrence, we check the leftBias flag.
Then we shrink hi to before mid, looking for an earlier copy on the left.
Otherwise we are hunting for the last occurrence, so we go the other way.
We move lo to after mid, looking for a later copy on the right.
When the window is empty, we return idx, which holds the furthest match found or minus one.
We call bound twice, left biased for the first index and right biased for the last, and return both.

find-the-difference.hook: One extra letter hides in a shuffled string. XOR makes every matching pair cancel out.
find-the-difference.ask: String t is string s shuffled, with exactly one extra letter inserted somewhere. Return that extra letter.
find-the-difference.exampleWhy: Both strings contain a, b, c and d once; only t has an e.

brute.idea: Sort both strings, then walk them side by side. The first position where they differ holds the extra letter.
steps: Sort s and t
Compare position by position
First mismatch, or t's last letter, wins
brute.whySlow: Sorting costs n log n time and copies of both strings, when one linear pass is enough.

optimal.insight: XOR of a value with itself is zero. XOR every character code from both strings: pairs cancel, leaving only the extra letter.
steps: Start with x = 0
XOR in every character of s and t
Convert the leftover code back to a letter

pitfalls: Summing codes of t minus s also works in O(n); XOR avoids any overflow worry.

say.intro: Okay, so string t is string s, shuffled, with one extra letter added somewhere. We have to find that letter. Here s is a b c d, and t is d b e a c. Every letter of s shows up in t. The one left over is e.
say.brute: A first attempt sorts both strings. Once sorted, the letters line up. So we walk them side by side. The first position where they differ holds the extra letter. And if they never differ, it's the last letter of t. That works, but it costs n log n time, plus copies of both strings.
say.insight: Here's a neat trick with exclusive or. Any value XORed with itself gives zero. And the order doesn't matter. So what if we XOR every character code from both strings together? Each letter of s meets its twin in t. They cancel out. The only thing left standing is the extra letter.
say.anim: We start with x at zero, combining strings abcd and dbeac to compare. Each letter's code gets XORed into x, one character at a time. After a, b, c, and d, matching letters start canceling each other out. By frame nine x is four, since a, b, c, d from both strings partly cancel. Continuing through d, b, and a again, those duplicates cancel back to zero effect. Now e, the extra letter, gets XORed in, pushing x up to one hundred three. The final c cancels too, leaving x equal to one hundred one. Converting one hundred one back to a character gives the final answer, e.
say.code: Here's the code. We start x at zero, because zero is XOR's identity. Then we loop over every letter, first from s, then from t. Each character code gets XORed into x. Matching pairs cancel to zero. So at the end, only the extra letter survives. We turn x back into a character and return it.
say.outro: Linear time and constant space. The pattern is bit manipulation. XOR cancels pairs, so whatever is unpaired is left standing.

find-the-difference.title: Find the Difference
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container this problem's method lives in.
The method takes the original string s and the shuffled string t, and returns the single extra letter.
We start x at zero, because XOR with zero leaves any value unchanged, making it a neutral starting point.
We loop over every character in s joined with t, so each letter from both strings gets visited.
We XOR the character code of c into x, so letters appearing twice cancel out to zero.
Only the extra letter's code remains in x, so we convert it back to a character and return it.

find-the-minimum-cost-array-permutation.hook: Fourteen numbers, billions of orderings. Bitmask DP shrinks it to a few hundred thousand states.
find-the-minimum-cost-array-permutation.ask: Given a permutation nums of 0 to n-1, find the cyclic permutation perm minimising the sum of |perm[i] - nums[perm[i+1]]|, wrapping around. Return the lexicographically smallest one with that minimum score.
find-the-minimum-cost-array-permutation.exampleWhy: Score is |0-0| + |1-2| + |2-1| = 2, the minimum, and 0, 1, 2 is the smallest such order.

brute.idea: Try every permutation in lexicographic order, compute its score, and keep the first one that achieves the lowest score.
steps: Generate permutations in sorted order
Score each one around the cycle
Keep the first strictly better score
brute.whySlow: For n = 14 there are 87 billion permutations: hopeless.

optimal.insight: The score is a cycle, so rotating never changes it: start at 0. Then only the used set and last element matter.
steps: Fix perm[0] = 0
dp(mask, last) = cheapest way to finish
Close the cycle with |last - nums[0]|
Rebuild greedily: smallest next that keeps the optimum

codeNotes.match: best = min(best, abs(last - nums[nxt]) + dp(mask | 1 << nxt, nxt))

pitfalls: Without fixing perm[0] = 0 the state must also track the start, multiplying work by n.
Rebuild the path from dp values; storing whole paths per state costs too much memory.

say.intro: Okay, this one's a puzzle. We order the numbers zero to n minus one. Each neighbouring pair has a cost, and the order wraps around at the end. We want the cheapest order. Among ties, we want the lexicographically smallest one. For one, zero, two, the answer is zero, one, two, with cost two.
say.brute: The brute force tries every permutation in sorted order. It scores each one around the cycle, and keeps the first that's strictly cheapest. Going in sorted order handles ties for free. So what's the problem? N can be fourteen. Fourteen factorial is about eighty seven billion orderings. Way too many.
say.insight: Two ideas save us. First, the score is a cycle. Rotating a permutation never changes it. So the best answer can always start with zero. Second, once we know which elements are used and which came last, the past doesn't matter. That's a bitmask state, with n times two to the n entries.
say.anim: We start with nums one, zero, two, and set full mask to seven covering all elements. Permutation begins at zero, since rotating a cycle never changes its total score. We explore next elements from zero, trying each unused index to extend the path. Recursive calls compute costs for different masks and last values, caching results for reuse. For mask one and last zero, best cost after trying all options comes out to two. Index one gives the matching cost, so we append it, making perm zero, one. Now exploring from last equals one, index two matches the optimal cost and gets appended. All elements are used, giving the final minimum cost permutation zero, one, two.
say.code: Here's the code. The dp state is the set of used elements and the last one placed. When everything is used, we close the cycle back to zero. Otherwise, we try each unused next element and keep the cheapest. To rebuild, we always start at zero, the rotation trick. Then we keep picking the smallest choice that stays optimal.
say.outro: Exponential in n, but tiny for fourteen. The pattern is dynamic programming over a bitmask and the last element.

find-the-minimum-cost-array-permutation.title: Find the Minimum Cost Array Permutation
lineNotes: This line declares the Solution class that holds our method.
We define findPermutation, which takes nums and returns the cheapest permutation as a list.
We store the length of nums in n, the number of elements to arrange.
We build full as a bitmask with all n bits set, meaning every index has been used.
We memoize the helper with cache so each state of used set and last element is solved only once.
The function dp takes a mask of used indices and the last placed element, and returns the minimum remaining cost.
If the mask is full, every element is placed, so we handle the wrap-around step.
We return the closing cost, the absolute difference between last and nums at index zero, since the cycle starts at zero.
We start best at infinity so any real candidate cost will replace it.
We loop over every candidate next element from zero to n minus one.
We only consider candidates whose bit is not yet set in the mask, meaning unused so far.
We take the minimum of the step cost to this candidate plus the best cost of the rest after adding it.
After trying all candidates, we return the minimum cost found.
We begin the answer with zero fixed at the front, and the mask marks only zero as used.
We keep building until the mask shows every element has been placed.
We read the last placed element from the end of perm.
We try candidates in increasing order so the first optimal one gives the lexicographically smallest answer.
We accept an unused candidate only if its step cost plus the remaining optimum equals the optimum from the current state.
We append that candidate to the permutation.
We mark the candidate as used by setting its bit in the mask.
We break immediately, because the smallest valid candidate is already chosen for this position.
Once all elements are placed, we return the completed permutation.

find-the-string-with-lcp.hook: Rebuild a hidden word from a table of common-prefix lengths, or prove that no word fits.
find-the-string-with-lcp.ask: An n by n matrix claims lcp[i][j] is the longest common prefix of the suffixes starting at i and j. Return the alphabetically smallest lowercase word matching it, or an empty string if none exists.
find-the-string-with-lcp.exampleWhy: Positions 0 and 2 share a prefix, as do 1 and 3, so two alternating letters: abab is smallest.

brute.idea: Assign letters the same greedy way, then check every pair by actually comparing suffixes character by character.
steps: Greedy: same letter where lcp is positive
For every pair, measure the real common prefix
Any mismatch with the table? Return empty
brute.whySlow: Measuring each of n squared pairs takes up to n steps: a billion operations for n = 1000.

optimal.insight: lcp > 0 means same first letter, so letters are forced greedily. Then lcp[i][j] must equal 1 + lcp[i+1][j+1] or 0: check bottom-up.
steps: Scan left to right, giving each unlabeled slot the next letter
Copy that letter to every j with lcp[i][j] > 0
More than 26 letters? Impossible
Verify each cell from the bottom-right corner

codeNotes.note: Already forced by an earlier letter
Positive lcp forces the same letter

codeNotes.match: expect = 1 + nxt if word[i] == word[j] else 0
codeNotes.note: LCP recurrence from the next diagonal

pitfalls: Building the word is not enough: the table may be impossible, so always verify every cell.
Diagonal must be n - i; the recurrence check catches bad diagonals too.

say.intro: Okay, so we're handed a table. For every pair of positions, it claims how long the suffixes starting there agree. We have to rebuild the alphabetically smallest word that fits. If no word could produce this table, we return empty. This table describes alternating letters. So the answer is a b a b.
say.brute: The brute force builds a candidate word, then checks it the honest way. For every pair of positions, it walks both suffixes letter by letter. It measures their real common prefix and compares with the table. It's correct. But there are n squared pairs, and each one can take n steps. That's cubic.
say.insight: Two ideas. First, a positive entry means two positions start with the same letter. So scanning left to right, each new position gets the next unused letter. That's forced, and it's the smallest. Second, the table follows a rule. Equal letters give one plus the entry diagonally below. Otherwise zero. Checking that from the bottom corner is quadratic.
say.anim: We start with the lcp matrix and an empty word array of length four. Since position zero is unassigned, we scan row zero, finding positive lcp values at zero and two, assigning letter a. Position one is still empty, so we assign the next letter, b, to indices one and three. Now word is fully built as a, b, a, b, with two distinct letters used. We now verify from the end backward, checking each lcp entry matches the expected value from matching letters. Row by row, each computed expect value matches the actual lcp entry, confirming consistency. Continuing upward, the first row checks also align perfectly with the given lcp matrix. All checks pass, so the final reconstructed string returned is abab.
say.code: Here's the code. We walk the positions, skipping any already forced by an earlier letter. If we've used all twenty six letters, we're out, so it's impossible. Otherwise, every later position with a positive entry gets the same letter. Then the check. Each cell should equal one plus the next diagonal cell. Any mismatch means the table is invalid.
say.outro: Quadratic time. The pattern is greedy construction, then verification. Build the smallest candidate, then prove it fits.

find-the-string-with-lcp.title: Find the String with LCP
lineNotes: We define a class named Solution, as the problem platform expects.
The method takes the lcp matrix and returns the smallest valid string, or an empty string if none exists.
We store n as the size of the matrix, which is also the length of the word.
We create a word list of n empty slots, to be filled with letters.
We set c to zero, the index of the next unused letter in the alphabet.
We scan each position from left to right, assigning letters greedily to get the smallest word.
If this position already has a letter, an earlier position claimed it.
So we skip it and move to the next position.
If all twenty six letters are used and a new one is needed, no valid word exists.
So we return an empty string.
We look at every position j from i onward, since those might share a first letter with i.
A positive lcp between i and j means their first letters must be equal.
We give position j the letter at offset c from a, so all linked positions share it.
We advance c so the next new group gets the next letter.
Now we validate the matrix, walking i from the last index down to zero so later entries are known.
For each i we also walk j from the end down to zero, covering every pair.
We read the lcp of the next positions, using zero when i plus one or j plus one is out of range.
If the letters match, the expected lcp is one plus the next value; otherwise it must be zero.
If the given lcp entry differs from what we expect, the matrix is inconsistent.
So we return an empty string.
All checks passed, so we join the letters into one string and return it.

first-bad-version.hook: Every version after the bug is broken. Find the first bad one in about thirty checks.
first-bad-version.ask: Versions 1 to n are good up to some point, then bad from there on. Using as few calls to isBadVersion as possible, return the first bad version.
first-bad-version.exampleWhy: Versions 1 to 6 pass, 7 onward fail, so 7 is the first bad version.

brute.idea: Test the versions one by one from the start, and return the first one the checker says is bad.
steps: Start at version 1
Ask isBadVersion for each version in turn
Return the first bad one
brute.whySlow: n can be two billion: a linear scan could make two billion API calls instead of thirty-one.

optimal.insight: Good then bad is a sorted yes-no sequence. Binary search for the boundary: a bad middle means the answer is at or before it.
steps: Search the range 1 to n
Middle bad? Answer is mid or earlier
Middle good? Answer is after mid
Stop when the range is one version

codeNotes.note: Bad: mid could be the first

pitfalls: Use hi = mid, not mid - 1, or you may skip the first bad version.
On LeetCode, firstBadVersion takes only n; isBadVersion is predefined.

say.intro: Okay, so versions are numbered one to n. At some point a bug slipped in. Every version from then on is bad. We have a checker that says whether a version is bad. Our job? Find the first bad one, using as few checks as possible. With ten versions, the bug arrives at seven.
say.brute: The obvious way tests versions one at a time from the start. Return the first bad one. It's correct. But n can be over two billion. In the worst case, that's two billion calls to the checker. And the problem specifically asks us to keep those calls low.
say.insight: Here's the thing. The answers form a sorted pattern. Good, good, good, then bad, bad, bad. Finding where it flips is binary search. If the middle is bad, the first bad version is the middle or earlier. If it's good, the first bad is strictly later. Every check cuts the range in half.
say.anim: We have ten versions, and version seven onward are bad, we need the first bad one. Lo starts at one and hi at ten, our search range for the boundary. Mid becomes five, and since version five is not bad, we move lo to six. Now lo is six, hi stays ten, mid becomes eight, which is bad, so hi becomes eight. With hi now eight, mid becomes seven, which is bad, so hi shrinks to seven. Now lo six, hi seven, mid is six, not bad, so lo moves to seven. Lo and hi are both seven now, so the loop ends and we return lo. The first bad version is found to be seven, matching the expected answer.
say.code: Here's the code. The checker is simulated here, since LeetCode provides the real one. We loop while low is below high, and stop when one candidate remains. If the middle is bad, it could be the first, so high moves to the middle. If it's good, the first bad is later, so low moves past it. When they meet, that's the boundary.
say.outro: Logarithmic time and constant space. The pattern is binary search on a boundary. Find where a yes or no answer flips.

first-bad-version.title: First Bad Version
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container the judge expects for our method.
The method takes the number of versions n and a bad value, and returns the first bad version.
We build a small stand-in for the judge's check, which says a version is bad when it reaches the bad value.
We set lo to one and hi to n, so the search window covers every version.
We keep looping while lo is less than hi, meaning more than one candidate remains.
We pick mid as the whole-number average of lo and hi, probing the middle of the window.
We ask whether the middle version is bad, since that tells us which half holds the boundary.
If mid is bad, the first bad version is at or before it, so we move hi down to mid.
Otherwise the middle version is good, which means the boundary must lie somewhere after it.
So we move lo up to mid plus one, discarding mid and everything before it.
When lo and hi meet, that single remaining version is the first bad one, so we return lo.

max-consecutive-ones-iii.hook: Flip at most k zeros for the longest run of ones: keep a window holding at most k zeros.
max-consecutive-ones-iii.ask: Given an array of zeros and ones and a number k, return the length of the longest stretch of consecutive ones you can make by flipping at most k zeros into ones.
max-consecutive-ones-iii.exampleWhy: Flip the zeros at indices 4 and 5: indices 4 to 9 become six ones in a row.

brute.idea: Try every start index and extend to the right, counting zeros, until a third zero would be needed.
steps: Pick a start index
Extend right, counting zeros
Stop past k zeros; record the length
brute.whySlow: Every start rescans to the right: a hundred thousand elements means up to five billion steps.

optimal.insight: The question is really: longest window containing at most k zeros. Grow the right edge, and shrink the left only when there are too many zeros.
steps: Move the right edge one step
Count zeros entering the window
Too many zeros? Advance the left edge
Record the window length

pitfalls: Do not actually flip anything; just count zeros inside the window.

say.intro: Okay, so we have an array of zeros and ones. We're allowed to flip up to k zeros into ones. What's the longest run of ones we can make? Here k is two. Flip the zeros at indices four and five, and they join four ones. That's a run of six.
say.brute: The brute force tries every starting index. From each start, it extends right, counting zeros. It stops the moment it would need a third flip. The longest stretch wins. It works. But every start rescans the array, so the time is quadratic.
say.insight: Here's the reframe. Forget flipping. We're really asking: what's the longest window with at most k zeros? That's a sliding window. Push the right edge forward every step. If the window holds too many zeros, pull the left edge forward until it's valid again. Both edges only move forward. So it's linear.
say.anim: We start with left pointer, zero count, and best length all set to zero. The right pointer scans through the ones, growing the window with best reaching five. At index five we hit a third zero, so zero count becomes three, exceeding k. The left pointer shifts right twice, shrinking the window until a zero is removed, zeros drops to two. Window now spans from left four to right six, giving best length five again. At index ten another zero pushes zeros to three, so left pointer moves again to shrink. After adjusting left to five, best length updates to six, the largest window found. The function returns six, the longest run of ones allowing at most two zeros.
say.code: Here's the code. The right edge grows every step. If the new cell is zero, a zero entered the window, so we count it. Now, if that needs too many flips, we shrink. The left edge only moves forward, dropping zeros from the count as it goes. Once the window is valid again, we record its size.
say.outro: Linear time, constant space. The pattern is sliding window. Grow on the right, shrink on the left whenever a limit breaks.

max-consecutive-ones-iii.title: Max Consecutive Ones III
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container the problem expects for our method.
The method longestOnes takes the array nums and the flip limit k, and returns the longest window length.
We start the left edge, the zero count, and the best length all at zero.
We loop the right edge r across every position in nums, growing the window one element at a time.
We check whether the new element at the right edge is a zero.
If it is a zero, we add one to the count of zeros inside the window.
While the window holds more zeros than k allows, we must shrink it from the left.
We check whether the element leaving at the left edge is a zero.
If so, we reduce the zero count because that zero is leaving the window.
We move the left edge one step right, shrinking the window.
Now the window is valid, so we update best with the larger of best and the current window length.
After scanning everything, we return best as the longest valid window found.

maximum-number-of-distinct-elements-afte.hook: Nudge each number by at most k to make as many values distinct as possible. Sort, then place greedily.
maximum-number-of-distinct-elements-afte.ask: Each number may be shifted once by any amount between minus k and plus k. Return the largest possible count of distinct values in the array afterwards.
maximum-number-of-distinct-elements-afte.exampleWhy: The 4s can become 3, 4 and 5; the fourth 4 has no free slot, and 5 moves to 6.

brute.idea: Sort, then for each number try every value from x minus k to x plus k and take the first one not already used.
steps: Sort the numbers
Try x-k, x-k+1, and so on
Take the first unused value
brute.whySlow: k can be a billion: scanning candidate values one at a time is hopeless.

optimal.insight: After sorting, every used value is at most the last one placed. So jump straight to max(prev + 1, x - k), the lowest free slot.
steps: Sort the numbers
Candidate = max(prev + 1, x - k)
Within x + k? Count it, prev = candidate
Otherwise this number must collide

codeNotes.note: Smallest numbers claim low slots first

pitfalls: Place each number as low as possible; placing high wastes room for later numbers.

say.intro: Okay, so each number may move up or down by at most k, once. We want as many different values as possible. Here we have four fours and a five, with k equal to one. We can make three, four, five and six. That's four distinct values.
say.brute: A first attempt sorts the numbers. Then for each one, it tries every value from x minus k up to x plus k. It takes the first value nobody has used yet. Sorted order makes that fair, so it's correct. So what's the catch? K can be a billion. Trying values one at a time is far too slow.
say.insight: Now, notice something. After sorting, every value we've already used is at most the last one we placed. So the lowest free slot is easy. It's the larger of previous plus one, and x minus k. If that's within reach, take it. If not, this number has to duplicate. Placing low always leaves the most room for later numbers.
say.anim: We sort the array into 4,4,4,4,5 and set k to 1. We start with count zero and prev at negative infinity, then begin looping. For the first 4, candidate becomes max of prev plus one and 3, giving 3. Since 3 fits within range, count becomes 1 and prev updates to 3. Next 4 gives candidate 4, which fits, raising count to 2 and prev to 4. Another 4 yields candidate 5, still valid, pushing count to 3 and prev to 5. The fourth 4 gives candidate 6, but that's too far from x, so it's skipped. Finally, the 5 produces candidate 6, which works, making count 4 and prev 6. The loop ends and the function returns the final answer, 4.
say.code: Here's the code. First we sort, so the smallest numbers claim low slots first. The previous slot starts at minus infinity, because nothing's placed yet. For each number, the candidate is the lowest value still free. If the candidate is within x plus k, it's reachable. So we place it, count it, and remember it as previous.
say.outro: Sorting dominates, so n log n time. The pattern is greedy. Go in sorted order, and always take the lowest slot available.

maximum-number-of-distinct-elements-afte.title: Maximum Number of Distinct Elements After Operations
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container for the method that solves this problem.
This method takes the list nums and the shift limit k, and returns the maximum number of distinct values.
We sort nums so we can process values from smallest to largest and greedily assign the lowest free slots.
We start count at zero and set prev, the last value we placed, to negative infinity so the first element is unconstrained.
We loop over each value x in the sorted list, deciding where it can land.
The candidate is the larger of one above prev and x minus k, giving the lowest free value x can reach.
If the candidate does not exceed x plus k, then x can be shifted there legally.
Since the placement works, we add one to count because we gained a new distinct value.
We record the candidate as prev, so later elements must land strictly above it.
Finally we return count, the largest number of distinct values we managed to create.

maximum-points-you-can-obtain-from-cards.hook: Take k cards from either end. Every choice is just a split between left and right.
maximum-points-you-can-obtain-from-cards.ask: Cards sit in a row with point values. You take exactly k cards, each from the left end or the right end. Return the largest total score you can get.
maximum-points-you-can-obtain-from-cards.exampleWhy: Take 3, 1 and 9 from the left and 8 from the right: 3 + 1 + 9 + 8 = 21.

brute.idea: Any valid pick is i cards from the left and k minus i from the right. Sum each split from scratch.
steps: Try i from 0 to k
Sum the first i cards
Add the last k - i cards
brute.whySlow: Each split re-adds up to k cards: k of a hundred thousand means about ten billion additions.

optimal.insight: Neighbouring splits differ by one card: swap the innermost left card for the next card from the right. Update the total in O(1).
steps: Start with all k cards from the left
Swap one left card for one right card
Update the running total
Track the best total

codeNotes.note: Start: all k from the left
Move i cards to the right side
Gain a right card, lose a left

pitfalls: Greedy picking the bigger end card fails; a small card can guard a big one.
Equivalent view: minimise the middle window of n - k cards.

say.intro: Okay, so cards sit in a row. We must take exactly k of them, each from the left end or the right end. We want the biggest total. Here k is four. Take three, one and nine from the left, plus eight from the right. That scores twenty one.
say.brute: Here's the key observation. Any sequence of picks is just some cards from the left and the rest from the right. So the brute force tries every split, from zero left cards up to k. It sums each side from scratch. That's k plus one splits, each costing up to k additions. Quadratic in k.
say.insight: Now think about neighbouring splits. How are they different? By exactly one card. Going from i left cards to i minus one drops the innermost left card. And it adds the next card from the right end. So keep a running total. Fix it with one subtraction and one addition. It's a sliding window that wraps around the ends.
say.anim: We start by summing the first four cards, giving a total of fifteen. Best is initialized to fifteen, our starting score from the left side. At i equals one, we swap one left card for one right card, total becomes twenty one. That beats fifteen, so best updates to twenty one. At i equals two, swapping another card drops total down to thirteen, worse than best. At i equals three, total rises to sixteen, still less than twenty one. At i equals four, all left cards are swapped, total reaches twenty, still below best. The loop ends and the function returns the best score found, twenty one.
say.code: Here's the code. We start with all k cards from the left. That's our total and our best so far. Then we move i cards to the right side, one at a time. Each step gains a card from the right and loses one from the left. After each swap, we keep the best split. Finally we return it.
say.outro: Linear in k, constant space. The pattern is sliding window. When options differ by one element, update instead of recomputing.

maximum-points-you-can-obtain-from-cards.title: Maximum Points You Can Obtain from Cards
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container the problem expects for our method.
The maxScore method takes the list of card points and the number of cards k, and returns the best score.
We start by taking all k cards from the left end and store their sum as total.
We record that all-left sum as best, since it is our first candidate answer.
We loop i from one to k, where i is how many cards we now take from the right.
Each step swaps out the innermost left card for the next right card, adjusting total in constant time.
After each swap we compare the new total with best and keep whichever is larger.
Once every split from all-left to all-right has been checked, we return best as the maximum score.

maximum-product-of-three-numbers.hook: The biggest product of three is not always the three biggest numbers. Two negatives can win.
maximum-product-of-three-numbers.ask: Given an array of integers, possibly negative, pick three of them so their product is as large as possible, and return that product.
maximum-product-of-three-numbers.exampleWhy: The top three give 3 · 2 · 1 = 6, but -10 · -8 · 3 = 240 is bigger.

brute.idea: Try every triple of distinct positions, multiply, and keep the largest product.
steps: Pick i < j < l
Multiply the three values
Keep the maximum
brute.whySlow: Ten thousand numbers give about 170 billion triples.

optimal.insight: The winner is either the three largest, or the largest times the two most negative. Track those five values in one pass.
steps: Track the top three values
Track the two smallest values
Compare max1·max2·max3 with max1·min1·min2

codeNotes.match: max1, max2, max3 = n, max1, max2
codeNotes.note: New leader shifts the others down

codeNotes.match: return max(max1 * max2 * max3, max1 * min1 * min2)

pitfalls: Forgetting the two-negatives case gives 6 instead of 240 here.
Sorting gives the same answer in O(n log n); fine to mention first.

say.intro: Okay, so we pick three numbers to make the biggest product. The input is minus ten, minus eight, one, three and two. The three biggest give only six. But minus ten times minus eight times three? That's two hundred forty. Two negatives make a positive.
say.brute: The brute force tries every triple of positions. It multiplies them and keeps the largest. Negatives take care of themselves, since it checks everything. But the number of triples grows with the cube of n. Ten thousand numbers means about a hundred seventy billion products.
say.insight: Here's the thing. Only two triples can ever win. Either the three largest numbers. Or the largest number times the two most negative ones, whose product is positive. So we only need five values. The top three, and the bottom two. We can find all five in one pass, without sorting.
say.anim: We initialize the three max trackers to negative infinity and the two min trackers to infinity. Processing negative ten, it becomes max1, and also updates min1 since it's the smallest so far. Negative eight becomes the new max1, pushing negative ten down, and also becomes the new min2. Value one beats all current maxes, so max1, max2, max3 shift to one, negative eight, negative ten. Three is bigger still, becoming max1, pushing one and negative eight into max2 and max3. Two isn't bigger than max1 three, but it beats max2 one, so max2 and max3 update to two and one. Now we compare the product of the three largest against the largest times the two smallest negatives. The final answer returned is two hundred forty, from three times negative ten times negative eight.
say.code: Here's the code. We track the three largest values seen so far. When a new leader arrives, it shifts the others down. Separately, we track the two most negative values. At the end, only two candidates can win. The top three multiplied, or the top one times the bottom two. We return the larger.
say.outro: Linear time, constant space. The pattern is math. Reason about signs, and the candidates shrink to just two.

maximum-product-of-three-numbers.title: Maximum Product of Three Numbers
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container for the method that solves this problem.
The method maximumProduct takes a list of integers called nums and returns the best product of three of them.
We start max one, max two and max three at negative infinity so any real number will beat them.
We start min one and min two at positive infinity so any real number will be smaller.
We loop through each number n in nums once, updating our tracked values as we go.
If n beats the current largest, it becomes the new first place candidate.
We shift the old largest down to second and the old second down to third, then put n in first.
Otherwise, if n beats the second largest, it belongs in second place.
We push the old second down to third and place n as the new second largest.
Otherwise, if n only beats the third largest, it takes third place.
We simply set max three to n, since nothing else needs to shift.
Separately, if n is smaller than the smallest so far, it is the most negative value seen.
We move the old smallest to second smallest and store n as the new smallest.
Otherwise, if n is smaller than the second smallest, it takes that second spot.
We set min two to n, keeping the two most negative numbers tracked.
We return the larger of the three biggest multiplied, or the biggest times the two most negative, since two negatives make a positive.

maximum-sum-of-3-non-overlapping-subarra.hook: Pick three non-overlapping windows with the biggest total. Fix the middle one; the sides are precomputed.
maximum-sum-of-3-non-overlapping-subarra.ask: Given an array and a length k, choose three non-overlapping subarrays of length k with the largest total sum. Return their starting indices, choosing the lexicographically smallest answer on ties.
maximum-sum-of-3-non-overlapping-subarra.exampleWhy: Windows [1,2], [2,6] and [7,5] total 23; starting at 1 instead of 0 ties but is lexicographically larger.

brute.idea: Try every valid triple of start positions in order, sum the three windows, and keep the first strictly best total.
steps: Loop starts a, b, c, each k apart
Sum all three windows
Keep the first strictly larger total
brute.whySlow: Twenty thousand elements give about a trillion triples, each summing windows.

optimal.insight: Fix the middle window. The best left window ending before it and the best right window after it are prefix and suffix maxima, precomputed.
steps: Window sums W with a sliding sum
left[i]: best window start at or before i
right[i]: best window start at or after i
For each middle j, combine left[j-k], j, right[j+k]

codeNotes.match: left[i] = i if W[i] > W[left[i - 1]] else left[i - 1]
right[i] = i if W[i] >= W[right[i + 1]] else right[i + 1]
codeNotes.note: >= from the right: earliest on ties

codeNotes.match: for j in range(k, m - k):
codeNotes.note: Middle window leaves room both sides

pitfalls: Tie-breaking direction matters: > on the left scan, >= on the right scan.

say.intro: Okay, so we pick three separate windows, each of length k. We want the biggest total, and we return their starting indices. On ties, we want the earliest answer. Here k is two. Windows starting at zero, three and five give the biggest total, twenty three.
say.brute: The brute force tries every triple of starting positions that don't overlap, in order. It sums all three windows. It keeps the first strictly better total, which also handles ties. But that's cubic in the array length, times the window cost. With twenty thousand elements, it explodes.
say.insight: Here's the trick. Fix the middle window. Now what's the best left window? Just the best one that ends before it. And the best right window is the best one starting after it. Those are prefix and suffix maximums over the window sums. Precompute them once. Then each middle position costs constant time.
say.anim: We start building window sums of size two from the array one, two, one, two, six, seven, five, one. The window sums fill in as we slide, reaching values like thirteen and twelve for the strongest windows. Final window sums are three, three, three, eight, thirteen, twelve, six across all seven positions. Now we scan left to right, tracking the best window index seen so far, landing on three then four. Scanning right to left, we track the best window from the end, settling on index four for several spots. We test middle windows starting at index two, pairing with left window zero and right window four. At middle index three we find a better combination, pairing left zero with right window five. The best triple found is indices zero, three, and five, giving the final answer zero three five.
say.code: Here's the code. First, sliding window sums. Then the left best array. It replaces only on strictly greater, so ties keep the earliest. The right best array scans backwards, replacing on greater or equal. Again, earliest wins. Each middle window leaves room on both sides. And only a strictly better total replaces our answer.
say.outro: Linear time and space. The pattern is dynamic programming with precomputed best on the left and right.

maximum-sum-of-3-non-overlapping-subarra.title: Maximum Sum of 3 Non-Overlapping Subarrays
lineNotes: We define a class named Solution, as the problem platform expects for this method.
The method takes the array nums and the window length k, and returns the three starting indices.
We start the window sums list with the sum of the first k numbers.
We loop over every remaining index so we can slide the window one step at a time.
Each new window sum adds the entering number and subtracts the number that just left the window.
