We store m as the number of windows, which is the length of the window sums list.
We create left, which will hold the best window start at or before each position, initially all zero.
We scan forward from index one to fill in left using earlier results.
We switch to index i only if its sum is strictly larger, so ties keep the earlier, lexicographically smaller start.
We create right, which holds the best window start at or after each position, initially pointing to the last window.
We scan backward from the second last window so each entry can reuse the answer on its right.
We switch to i when its sum is at least as large, so ties favor the smaller index.
We set best to none, meaning no triple has been chosen yet.
We try every middle window start j that leaves room for a full window on each side.
We look up the best left start ending at least k before j, and the best right start at least k after j.
If this is the first triple or its total beats the best total so far, we want to record it.
We save the triple of left, middle and right starts as the new best answer.
We return the best triple of starting indices.

merge-strings-alternately.hook: Zip two words together letter by letter, then tack on whatever is left over.
merge-strings-alternately.ask: Given two strings, build a new string by taking letters alternately, starting with the first string. When one runs out, append the rest of the other.
merge-strings-alternately.exampleWhy: a, p, b, q alternate; then word1 is used up, so r and s are appended.

brute.idea: Loop over positions up to the longer length, appending each word's letter at that position to a growing string.
steps: Loop i up to the longer length
Append word1[i] if it exists
Append word2[i] if it exists
brute.whySlow: Strings are immutable; each += may copy the whole result, so it can be quadratic. Same answer, riskier cost.

optimal.insight: Use one pointer per word and collect letters in a list, joining once at the end: each letter is copied exactly once.
steps: Pointers i and j at the start
Take word1[i] if available
Take word2[j] if available
Join the list once

codeNotes.note: List of letters, not a string

codeNotes.match: while i < len(word1) or j < len(word2):
codeNotes.note: Run until both are used up
One linear join at the end

pitfalls: Use or, not and, in the loop condition, or the leftover tail is lost.

say.intro: Okay, so we have two words. We build a new one by taking letters in turn, starting with the first word. When one word runs out, the rest of the other goes on the end. With a b and p q r s, we get a, p, b, q, then the leftover r s.
say.brute: A quick version loops over positions up to the longer length. At each position, it adds each word's letter if it exists, with string plus equals. The answer is right. But here's the catch. Strings can't change in place. So each addition can copy everything built so far. Worst case, that's quadratic.
say.insight: The fix is simple. Give each word its own pointer, and collect letters in a list. Appending to a list is cheap. Then we join once at the end, which copies each letter exactly once. And the loop keeps going while either word has letters left. So the leftover tail comes along for free.
say.anim: We start with word1 ab and word2 pqrs, and an empty result list. Pointer i is zero, so we grab word1's a and append it to res. Pointer j is zero, so we grab word2's p, appending each letter only once. Now i moves to one, adding b, then j adds q, building res step by step. Word1 is exhausted, so only word2's letters r and s get appended now. J reaches three, appending the final s since word1 has nothing left. The loop ends since both pointers reached their word lengths. We join the list into a string, giving the final answer apbqrs.
say.code: Here's the code. We collect a list of letters, not a string. The loop runs until both words are used up. Each round, word one always goes first, if it has a letter left. Then word two adds its next letter. Both pointers move forward. Finally, one linear join turns the list into the answer.
say.outro: Linear time. The pattern is two pointers, one per input, each moving on its own until both are done.

merge-strings-alternately.title: Merge Strings Alternately
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the wrapper this problem's solution method lives in.
This method takes two words and returns a single merged string built by alternating their letters.
We start with an empty list called res to collect letters, since appending to a list is cheap.
We set both pointers i and j to zero, one for each word's current position.
We loop as long as either word still has unused letters, so leftovers from the longer word get handled.
If the first word still has a letter at position i, we take it on this turn.
We append that letter from the first word to the result list.
We advance the first pointer i so the next round uses the next letter.
Then if the second word still has a letter at position j, we take it too.
We append that letter from the second word to the result list.
We advance the second pointer j so we never copy the same letter twice.
Finally we join all collected letters into one string in a single step and return it.

minimum-cost-for-tickets.hook: Day pass, week pass or month pass? Work backwards from your last trip and every choice becomes easy.
minimum-cost-for-tickets.ask: You travel on given days of the year. Passes cover 1, 7 or 30 consecutive days at given prices. Return the minimum total cost to cover every travel day.
minimum-cost-for-tickets.exampleWhy: Day pass on day 1, a 7-day pass covering days 4 to 8, and a day pass on day 20: 2 + 7 + 2.

brute.idea: At the first uncovered travel day, try buying each pass, skip the days it covers, and recurse on the rest.
steps: At travel day i, try all three passes
Skip the days that pass covers
Recurse and keep the cheapest total
brute.whySlow: The same suffix of days is solved again and again: 365 travel days means an astronomical number of branches.

optimal.insight: The cheapest way to cover days from index i onward depends only on i. Fill dp from the last travel day backwards.
steps: dp[n] = 0: nothing left to cover
For each day i from the end
For each pass, find the first day it misses
dp[i] = min of cost + dp[that day]

codeNotes.match: while j < n and days[j] < days[i] + span:

codeNotes.note: Buy here, then best for the rest

pitfalls: A longer pass is not always cheaper per day; always compare all three.
Index by travel days, not all 365 calendar days, for O(n).

say.intro: Okay, so we travel on certain days of the year. We can buy passes lasting one, seven or thirty days, each with its own price. What's the cheapest way to cover every trip? Here, a day pass on day one, a week pass for days four to eight, and a day pass on day twenty. Total cost, eleven.
say.brute: The brute force stands at the first uncovered travel day. It tries all three passes. Each pass covers some days, so we skip those and recurse on the rest. Keep the cheapest. It's correct. But it branches three ways every step, and solves the same leftover days again and again. That's exponential.
say.insight: Now, notice something. The best cost from travel day i onward depends only on i. Nothing before it matters. So fill a table from the last travel day backwards. At each day, try each pass. Jump to the first travel day it doesn't cover. Then add the cost we already know from there.
say.anim: We start with days one, four, six, seven, eight, twenty, and three ticket costs. We build a dp array backwards, so dp of six, the base case, stays zero. At day twenty, index five, the cheapest pass costs two, giving dp of five equal two. At index four, day eight, buying a one day pass plus dp five gives dp four equal four. At index three, day seven, costs combine to make dp three equal six. At index two, day six, trying all spans gives the minimum dp two equal eight. At index one, day four, comparing options yields dp one equal nine. Finally at index zero, day one, dp zero becomes eleven, the minimum total cost.
say.code: Here's the code. The table has one extra slot past the last trip, holding zero. We fill from the end backwards. For each pass, a pointer skips the days this pass covers. Then we buy here, and add the best cost for the rest. Keep the cheapest of the three. The answer is the first entry.
say.outro: Linear in the number of travel days. The pattern is dynamic programming over what's left of the input.

minimum-cost-for-tickets.title: Minimum Cost For Tickets
lineNotes: We define the solution class that holds the method for this problem.
The method takes the travel days and the three pass prices, and returns the minimum total cost.
We store n as the number of travel days we need to cover.
We create dp with n plus one zeros, where dp at n means no days remain and costs nothing.
We loop i from the last travel day backwards to the first, so later answers are ready when needed.
We start dp at i as infinity so any real pass cost will replace it.
We set j to i, the pointer for the first day not covered by the current pass.
We try each pass, pairing its cost with its span of one, seven or thirty days.
We move j forward while the day at j still falls inside the pass starting on day i.
Each step advances j past a travel day that this pass already covers.
We price this pass as its cost plus dp at j, and keep the cheaper option for dp at i.
Finally we return dp at zero, the minimum cost to cover all travel days.

minimum-height-trees.hook: Which root makes this tree shortest? Peel off leaves layer by layer until only the center is left.
minimum-height-trees.ask: Given an undirected tree with n nodes, any node can be chosen as the root. Return every node that, as root, gives the smallest possible height.
minimum-height-trees.exampleWhy: Rooting at 3 or 4 gives height 2; every other root gives height 3.

brute.idea: Root the tree at every node in turn, measure its height with a BFS, and keep the nodes with the smallest height.
steps: For each node, BFS outward
Count levels to get the height
Return all nodes with the minimum
brute.whySlow: One full BFS per node: twenty thousand nodes means four hundred million edge visits.

optimal.insight: The best roots sit at the middle of the longest path. Trimming all leaves at once, repeatedly, closes in on that middle from every side.
steps: Build adjacency sets
Collect all current leaves
Remove them; neighbours left with one edge become leaves
Stop when two or fewer nodes remain

codeNotes.note: One or two nodes: all are centers

codeNotes.match: leaves = [i for i in range(n) if len(adj[i]) == 1]

codeNotes.note: Peel the leaf off its neighbour

pitfalls: Handle n = 1 (no edges) separately; there are no leaves to start from.
There are never more than two answers.

say.intro: Okay, so we have a tree with n nodes. Any node can be the root. Some roots make it tall. Others make it short. We return every root giving the smallest height. Here node three connects to zero, one, two and four. Four connects to five. Rooting at three or four gives height two.
say.brute: The brute force tries every node as the root. It measures the height with a breadth first search, counting levels. Then it returns the nodes with the smallest height. Each search is linear. But we run one per node. So the total is quadratic.
say.insight: Think about it this way. The best roots sit at the middle of the longest path. Leaves are the worst roots you could pick. So peel off every leaf at once. Their neighbours may become new leaves. So peel again. Like an onion, we close in on the center from every side. The last one or two nodes standing are the answer.
say.anim: We have six nodes and five edges, building an adjacency list to represent the tree. Edges are added both ways, so node three connects to zero, one, two, and four. Now every node's neighbors are set, with node five linked only to node four. Leaves zero, one, two, and five have just one neighbor, so we start trimming them. Each leaf is removed from its neighbor's set, shrinking the tree toward the center. After trimming, node three becomes a new leaf since only node four remains attached. Node four also becomes a leaf once node five is removed, leaving just two nodes. Only nodes three and four remain, so they are the minimum height tree roots.
say.code: Here's the code. With one or two nodes, they're all centers, so return them. Otherwise, collect the outermost layer, the leaves. At most two centers can survive, so we loop while more remain. For each leaf, peel it off its neighbour. If that neighbour is now a leaf, it joins the next layer.
say.outro: Linear time and space. The pattern is graphs, trimming leaves inward, layer by layer.

minimum-height-trees.title: Minimum Height Trees
lineNotes: We define the Solution class that holds our method for finding the roots of minimum height trees.
The method takes the node count n and the edge list, and returns the list of best root nodes.
If the tree has two nodes or fewer, every node is already a valid answer.
So we return all node labels from zero up to n minus one.
We build an adjacency list where each node gets a set holding its neighbors.
We loop over each edge, reading its two endpoints a and b.
We add b to the neighbor set of a.
We add a to the neighbor set of b, since the tree is undirected.
The first leaves are all nodes with exactly one neighbor, collected into a list.
We track remaining as the count of nodes still in the tree, starting at n.
We keep trimming while more than two nodes remain, because the middle is one or two nodes.
We subtract the current leaf count from remaining, since all of those leaves are about to be removed.
We prepare an empty list to collect the leaves that appear after this round of trimming.
We go through each current leaf to detach it from the tree.
We pop the leaf's only neighbor out of its set, giving us the node it hangs from.
We remove the leaf from that neighbor's set, cutting the connection on both sides.
If the neighbor now has just one connection, it has become a leaf itself.
We add that neighbor to the new leaves list for the next round.
We replace the leaves with the new leaves, moving one layer inward.
When one or two nodes remain, those leftover leaves are the centers, so we return them.

minimum-number-of-arrows-to-burst-balloo.hook: Each arrow pops every balloon it crosses. Shoot at the earliest ending balloon and count the arrows.
minimum-number-of-arrows-to-burst-balloo.ask: Balloons are horizontal intervals from start to end. A vertical arrow at x bursts every balloon whose interval contains x. Return the minimum number of arrows needed to burst them all.
minimum-number-of-arrows-to-burst-balloo.exampleWhy: An arrow at 6 bursts [1,6] and [2,8]; an arrow at 12 bursts [7,12] and [10,16].

brute.idea: Repeatedly shoot at the smallest end among the remaining balloons, removing every balloon that arrow bursts.
steps: Find the smallest end left
Shoot there; drop balloons it hits
Repeat until none remain
brute.whySlow: Each arrow rescans all remaining balloons: disjoint balloons need n arrows and n squared work.

optimal.insight: Some arrow must hit the earliest-ending balloon; shooting at its end hits the most others. Sort by end and sweep once.
steps: Sort balloons by end
Start beyond the last arrow? Shoot at its end
Otherwise it is already burst

codeNotes.note: Shoot as far right as allowed

pitfalls: Use start > arrowX, not >=: touching endpoints share an arrow.
Avoid end - start comparisons; coordinates near 2^31 can overflow in other languages.

say.intro: Okay, so each balloon covers a stretch of the x axis. An arrow shot straight up at x bursts every balloon covering x. What's the fewest arrows to pop them all? Here, one arrow at six pops two balloons. One at twelve pops the other two.
say.brute: A correct but slow way repeats one step. Find the smallest end among the balloons left. Shoot there. Remove everything that arrow hits. Shooting at the smallest end is safe. But each round rescans everything that's left. If every balloon is separate, that's quadratic.
say.insight: Here's the thing. Whichever balloon ends first must be hit by some arrow. Where should that arrow go? At its end. Anything further right would miss it, and anything further left hits fewer balloons. So sort by end once, and sweep. If a balloon starts after the last arrow, fire a new arrow at its end.
say.anim: The balloons get sorted by their end points, giving this new order. Arrows start at zero and arrowX starts at negative infinity, meaning no arrow yet. First balloon starts at one, past arrowX, so we shoot an arrow here. Arrows becomes one and arrowX moves to six, that arrow's position. Next balloon starts at two, not past six, so this arrow already bursts it. Balloon starting at seven is past arrowX, so a new arrow is needed. Arrows becomes two and arrowX updates to twelve for this new shot. Last balloon starts at ten, already covered by arrowX twelve, no new arrow; answer is two.
say.code: Here's the code. We sort by end, so the earliest end comes first. The last arrow starts at minus infinity, since no arrow's been fired yet. For each balloon, we ask: does the last arrow miss it? If it does, we fire a new one, as far right as allowed, at this balloon's end. Then we return the count.
say.outro: Sorting dominates, so n log n time. The pattern is intervals. Sort by end, and greedily cover as much as you can.

minimum-number-of-arrows-to-burst-balloo.title: Minimum Number of Arrows to Burst Balloons
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container the problem expects for our method.
The method takes the list of balloon intervals and returns the minimum number of arrows as an integer.
We sort the balloons by their end coordinate so the earliest-ending balloon always comes first in the sweep.
We start the arrow count at zero because no arrows have been shot yet.
We set arrowX to negative infinity so the first balloon is never considered already burst.
We loop through each balloon, reading its start and end in sorted order.
If the balloon starts after the last arrow position, that arrow cannot reach it and we need a new one.
So we count one more arrow for this balloon.
We place that new arrow at this balloon's end, which lets it burst as many following overlapping balloons as possible.
After the sweep, we return the total number of arrows used.

minimum-path-sum.hook: Down or right through a grid of costs. Each cell only needs the best way into it.
minimum-path-sum.ask: Given a grid of non-negative numbers, find a path from the top left to the bottom right, moving only down or right, that has the smallest sum. Return that sum.
minimum-path-sum.exampleWhy: The path 1, 3, 1, 1, 1 along the top then down the right side sums to 7.

brute.idea: From each cell, try going down and going right recursively, and keep the cheaper of the two paths.
steps: At the target, return its value
Otherwise recurse down and right
Add this cell to the cheaper result
brute.whySlow: The same cells are re-solved along every path that reaches them: a 20 by 20 grid has billions of paths.

optimal.insight: The cheapest path into a cell comes from above or from the left. Keep one row of best costs and update it in place.
steps: dp holds best costs for the current row
First column: only from above
Other cells: cell + min(above, left)
Answer is the last entry

codeNotes.note: dp[c] is above, dp[c-1] is left

pitfalls: Greedy picking the cheaper neighbour fails; a cheap step can lead into expensive cells.

say.intro: Okay, so we have a grid of costs. We walk from the top left to the bottom right, moving only down or right. We want the smallest total. In this three by three grid, the best path goes along the top, then down the right side. That totals seven.
say.brute: The brute force stands on a cell and tries both moves, down and right. It returns the cheaper path plus the current cell. It's correct. But paths overlap a lot. Every cell gets solved again for each route that reaches it. So the work grows exponentially with the grid.
say.insight: Here's the key. How can you enter a cell? Only from directly above, or directly from the left. So the cheapest way in is the cheaper of those two, plus this cell. We go row by row with one array of best costs. Before an update, a slot holds the value from above. And its left neighbour is already updated.
say.anim: We start with a three by three grid and prepare a row of infinite costs. The first cell is set to zero, since that's where we begin. Row zero fills in: costs become one, four, and five across the columns. Moving to row one, each cost adds the cell value to the cheaper neighbor. Row one gives two, seven, six, carrying forward the best path so far. In the final row, dp updates to six, eight, then seven using the same rule. The last value in dp holds the answer after processing every row. The function returns seven, the minimum path sum through the grid.
say.code: Here's the code. We start with a row of infinities, the row above the grid, which is unreachable. One slot holds zero, so we start just before the top left cell. In the first column, a cell can only come from above. Everywhere else, the slot holds above, and the slot before it holds left. Take the cheaper, plus this cell.
say.outro: Time proportional to the grid, space to one row. The pattern is grid dynamic programming, squeezed down to a single row.

minimum-path-sum.title: Minimum Path Sum
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container the judge expects for our method.
The minPathSum method takes the grid and returns the smallest sum of any down-and-right path.
We read the number of rows and columns from the grid so we know how far to loop.
We make a single row of best costs, filled with infinity so unreached cells never win a minimum.
We set the first entry to zero so adding the starting cell's value later gives the right cost.
We walk through the grid one row at a time, updating our single row of costs as we go.
The first column can only be reached from above, so we add this row's first cell to its running cost.
For the rest of the columns in this row, we move left to right so the left neighbor is already updated.
Each cell's best cost is its own value plus the smaller of the cost from above or from the left.
After all rows are processed, the last entry holds the cheapest cost to reach the bottom right corner, which we return.

minimum-weighted-subgraph-with-the-requi.hook: Two sources must both reach one destination. Find where their paths merge with three Dijkstras.
minimum-weighted-subgraph-with-the-requi.ask: In a weighted directed graph, choose edges of minimum total weight so that both src1 and src2 can reach dest. Return that weight, or minus one if impossible.
minimum-weighted-subgraph-with-the-requi.exampleWhy: Paths 0→2 and 1→2 meet at node 2, then share 2→4: weights 2 + 3 + 1 = 6.

brute.idea: Compute all-pairs shortest paths with Floyd-Warshall, then try every node as the meeting point.
steps: Floyd-Warshall over every middle node
For each meeting node v, add three distances
Return the smallest, or -1
brute.whySlow: A hundred thousand nodes means 10^15 relaxations and ten billion matrix cells.

optimal.insight: The optimal subgraph is a Y shape: both paths meet at some node v, then share v to dest. Three single-source Dijkstras give every term.
steps: Dijkstra from src1 and from src2
Dijkstra from dest on reversed edges
For every v, sum the three distances
Take the minimum, or -1 if infinite

codeNotes.match: a, b, c = dijkstra(src1, fwd), dijkstra(src2, fwd), dijkstra(dest, rev)
best = min(a[v] + b[v] + c[v] for v in range(n))
return best if best < math.inf else -1

pitfalls: Adding the two separate shortest paths double counts shared edges; the meeting point fixes that.
Distance to dest needs the reversed graph, not a forward run.

say.intro: Okay, so we have a directed, weighted graph. We keep a set of edges so that two sources can both reach a destination. We want the lightest set. Here, both sources reach node two, then share the edge from two to four. That totals six.
say.brute: The brute force computes shortest distances between every pair of nodes with Floyd Warshall. Then it tries every node as the place the two routes meet. It's correct. But Floyd Warshall is cubic and needs a full distance matrix. With a hundred thousand nodes, that's hopeless.
say.insight: Here's the thing. The best subgraph looks like a Y. Both sources travel to some meeting node. Then they share one path to the destination. So we need three distance arrays. From source one. From source two. And into the destination. How do we get that last one? Run Dijkstra from the destination on reversed edges.
say.anim: We build forward and reverse adjacency lists from the edges for later Dijkstra runs. First Dijkstra starts at source one, node zero, computing shortest distances using forward edges. Distances update as we relax edges, finding node two at two and node three at four. Node four finishes at distance three, completing the first shortest path array from zero. Second Dijkstra starts at source two, node one, exploring forward edges to find distances. After relaxing edges, node four settles at distance four from source two. Third Dijkstra runs on reverse edges from destination node four to reach all nodes. Combining all three distance arrays at each node, the minimum total weight found is six.
say.code: Here's the code. We build a reversed graph too, so we can get distances into the destination. The Dijkstra helper uses a min heap and skips stale entries. We do three single source runs. Then we try every meeting point, summing its three distances. If the best is still infinite, there's no valid subgraph, so return minus one.
say.outro: Three Dijkstras, so roughly edges times log n. The pattern is shortest paths from several sources, joined at a meeting point.

minimum-weighted-subgraph-with-the-requi.title: Minimum Weighted Subgraph With the Required Paths
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, as the problem platform expects.
The minimumWeight method takes the node count, the edge list, the two sources, and the destination.
We build fwd, an adjacency list with one empty list per node, for following edges forward.
We build rev, a second adjacency list, for the reversed graph so we can measure distances into the destination.
We loop over every edge, unpacking its start node, end node, and weight.
In fwd we record that the start node reaches the end node with this weight.
In rev we record the opposite direction, from end node back to start node, with the same weight.
We define a Dijkstra helper that takes a source node and an adjacency list.
We start every distance at infinity, since nothing is known to be reachable yet.
The source is at distance zero from itself.
The heap starts holding just the source with distance zero, so we always expand the closest node first.
We keep running while the heap still has candidate nodes to process.
We pop the node with the smallest known distance along with that distance.
If the popped distance is larger than the recorded one, this entry is stale.
So we skip it and move on to the next heap entry.
We look at every neighbor of the current node along with the edge weight.
If going through the current node gives a shorter path to the neighbor, we take it.
We update the neighbor's best distance to this shorter value.
We push the neighbor with its new distance so it gets expanded later.
We return the full list of shortest distances from the source.
We run Dijkstra from src1 and src2 on the forward graph, and from dest on the reversed graph.
For each possible meeting node, we add the two distances in and the distance out to dest, then take the minimum.
If best is still infinity, no meeting node works, so we return minus one; otherwise we return best.

n-th-tribonacci-number.hook: Like Fibonacci, but each term sums the previous three. Keep three variables and roll forward.
n-th-tribonacci-number.ask: The Tribonacci sequence starts 0, 1, 1, and each later term is the sum of the three before it. Given n, return the n-th term.
n-th-tribonacci-number.exampleWhy: The sequence runs 0, 1, 1, 2, 4, 7, 13, so position 6 holds 13.

brute.idea: Follow the definition directly: recurse on n-1, n-2 and n-3, and add the results.
steps: Base cases for 0, 1 and 2
Recurse on the three previous terms
Add them up
brute.whySlow: Three-way branching recomputes the same terms constantly: n of 37 means tens of billions of calls.

optimal.insight: Each term needs only the previous three, so build upward keeping a sliding window of three values.
steps: Start with 0, 1, 1
Repeat n times: shift the window forward
The first value is the answer

codeNotes.match: a, b, c = b, c, a + b + c

pitfalls: Plain recursion without memo is exponential; memoization or iteration fixes it.

say.intro: Okay, Tribonacci. It's Fibonacci with one more term. The sequence starts zero, one, one. Every later number is the sum of the three before it. For six, we get zero, one, one, two, four, seven, thirteen. So the answer is thirteen.
say.brute: The brute force follows the definition. Handle the first three terms directly. Otherwise, recurse on the three previous positions and add them up. It's short and obviously right. But every call spawns three more, and the same terms get computed again and again. That's exponential.
say.insight: Now, notice something. Each term only needs the three before it. So build the sequence from the bottom up, with just three variables. Each step shifts them forward. The oldest value drops out, and the sum of all three comes in. That's dynamic programming with a table of size three.
say.anim: We start with a, b, c set to 0, 1, and 1. The loop will run six times, sliding the window each time. First update: a becomes 1, b becomes 2, c becomes 1 plus the sum. Now b is 2 and c is 4, as values keep shifting forward. After three iterations, a is 2, b is 4, and c is 7. Now a is 4, b is 7, and c reaches 13. Values keep climbing: a is 7, b is 13, c is 24. After six loops, the function returns a, giving the answer 13.
say.code: Here's the code. We start a, b and c at the first three terms, zero, one and one. Then we loop n times, advancing one position each time. Each step shifts the window of three. A takes b, b takes c, and c becomes the sum of all three. After the loop, a is the nth term.
say.outro: Linear time, constant space. The pattern is one dimensional dynamic programming. Keep only the last few states you need.

n-th-tribonacci-number.title: N-th Tribonacci Number
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container the judge expects for our tribonacci method.
The tribonacci method takes n and returns the n-th term of the sequence as an integer.
We start a sliding window of three values: a is term zero, b is term one, and c is term two.
We loop n times, because each pass moves the window forward by exactly one term.
Each pass shifts the window, so a becomes b, b becomes c, and c becomes the sum of all three.
After n shifts, a holds the n-th term, so we return it.

number-of-ways-to-form-a-target-string-g.hook: Spell a target using columns of a word list, moving strictly rightward. Count letters per column, then DP.
number-of-ways-to-form-a-target-string-g.ask: Words all have the same length. Build target left to right, taking each letter from some word at column k, after which columns up to k are unusable. Count the ways, modulo 10^9 + 7.
number-of-ways-to-form-a-target-string-g.exampleWhy: a from column 0 or 1, b from column 1 or 2, a from column 3, with several words offering each letter: 6 ways.

brute.idea: Recursively, at column k for target letter i, either skip the column or use it with any word that has the letter there.
steps: Skip column k
Or use it: count words with target[i] there
Multiply and recurse on the next letter
brute.whySlow: Without memo the skip-or-use choices branch exponentially in the word length L: L = 1000 is impossible.

optimal.insight: Which word a letter comes from only multiplies the count. Precompute letter counts per column, then dp[i] = ways to form target prefix of length i.
steps: freq[k][ch]: words with ch at column k
dp[0] = 1: empty prefix
Each column: dp[i+1] += dp[i] · freq
Update i backwards so each column is used once

codeNotes.note: Backwards: column used once per path
Extend prefix i using column k

pitfalls: Looping i forwards lets one column supply two target letters.
Take the modulo at every step.

say.intro: Okay, so all the words have the same length. We spell the target one letter at a time. Each letter comes from some column and any word with that letter there. And every pick has to be strictly right of the last one. With these three words, there are six ways to spell a b a.
say.brute: The brute force recursion stands at a target letter and a column. It can skip the column. Or it can use it, multiplying by how many words match there. Both branches recurse. Without memoisation, those skip or use choices branch exponentially with the word length.
say.insight: Two ideas. First, which word supplies a letter only multiplies the count. So precompute how many words have each letter in each column. Second, a one row table. Entry i counts the ways to form the first i target letters, using columns seen so far. Each new column can extend prefix i to i plus one.
say.anim: We want ways to build target aba from words acca, bbbb, caca. We scan each word, counting letter occurrences at each column index. For bbbb, every column simply adds one to the letter b's count. For caca, columns record counts for letters c and a respectively. Dp starts as one, zero, zero, zero, representing ways to match prefixes. At column zero, dp updates using freq of a, giving dp one, one, zero, zero. At column two, matching c's and a's pushes dp to one, two, three, zero. After the last column, dp becomes one, four, five, six, finishing the computation. The function returns six, the total number of ways to form target aba.
say.code: Here's the code. First, letter counts per column. The table starts with one way to form nothing. Then we take columns strictly left to right. Inside each column, we walk the target backwards. Why backwards? So a column is used once per path. We extend prefix i using column k, modulo the big prime.
say.outro: Columns times target length, plus the counting pass. The pattern is dynamic programming, squeezed to one row.

number-of-ways-to-form-a-target-string-g.title: Number of Ways to Form a Target String Given a Dictionary
lineNotes: We define the Solution class that holds the method for this problem.
The numWays method takes the list of words and the target string, and returns the number of ways.
We set MOD to one billion seven, since the answer must be reported modulo that prime.
We store the target length as m and the shared word length as L.
We build a table freq with one row per column, each holding twenty-six zero counts for the letters.
We loop over every word so we can tally its letters into the column counts.
For each word we walk through its letters, getting both the column index k and the letter.
We add one to freq at column k for that letter, counting how many words have it there.
We start dp with one way to build the empty prefix, and zero ways for every longer prefix.
We process the columns one at a time from left to right, so each column is used at most once.
We go through target positions backward so updating a longer prefix does not reuse the current column twice.
We add to dp of i plus one the ways for prefix i times the number of words offering that target letter at column k, modulo MOD.
We return dp at m, the number of ways to form the whole target.

palindrome-linked-list.hook: Is a singly linked list a palindrome? Reverse half of it in place and compare.
palindrome-linked-list.ask: Given the head of a singly linked list, return true if its values read the same forwards and backwards. Ideally use linear time and constant extra space.
palindrome-linked-list.exampleWhy: Reading 1, 2, 3, 2, 1 backwards gives the same sequence.

brute.idea: Copy the values into an array, then check whether the array equals its reverse.
steps: Walk the list into an array
Compare with the reversed array
brute.whySlow: Time is optimal, but copying every value costs linear extra memory; the follow-up asks for constant.

optimal.insight: Find the middle with slow and fast pointers, reverse the second half in place, then walk both halves together.
steps: Fast moves two, slow moves one: slow lands mid
Reverse the list from slow onward
Compare head half with reversed half

codeNotes.note: Twice the speed: slow ends mid
Reverse the second half in place

pitfalls: Loop on right, the reversed half: it is never longer than the front half.
The list is modified; reverse it back if the caller needs it intact.

say.intro: Okay, so we get a singly linked list. Do its values read the same both ways? One, two, three, two, one does. So the answer is true. What's the catch? We can only walk forwards.
say.brute: The easy answer copies every value into an array. Then it checks if the array equals its reverse. That's linear time and totally correct. The cost is memory. We're storing a copy of the whole list. And the follow up wants constant extra space. So we have to work inside the list itself.
say.insight: Here's the trick. We combine two linked list moves. First, a slow pointer takes one step while a fast pointer takes two. When fast runs out, slow is at the middle. Second, we reverse the second half in place. Now we can walk it from the tail. Then two pointers compare values pair by pair.
say.anim: We start with the list one, two, three, two, one, and two pointers at the head. Slow and fast pointers race ahead, slow moving one step, fast moving two steps. Fast reaches the end, so slow now sits right at the middle, node three. Now we reverse the second half in place, flipping links from three onward. Reversal finishes, giving us one, two, three as the new second half, reversed. Left starts at the original head, right starts at the reversed half's head. We compare values one and one, two and two, three and three, all matching. Both pointers reach the end with no mismatches, so the function returns true.
say.code: Here's the code. Fast moves at twice the speed, so slow ends at the middle. Then we reverse the second half in place. When that's done, prev is the old tail. Now we walk from the head and from prev together. A mirror mismatch means it's not a palindrome. If all mirrored pairs match, we return true.
say.outro: Linear time and constant space. The pattern is linked lists. Fast and slow pointers, plus reversing in place.

palindrome-linked-list.title: Palindrome Linked List
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container the interview platform expects for our method.
The isPalindrome method takes the head of a linked list and returns true or false.
We start both slow and fast at the head so we can find the middle.
We loop while fast and the node after fast both exist, so fast can safely jump two steps.
Each time through, slow moves forward one node, so it advances at half the speed of fast.
Fast moves two nodes ahead, so when it reaches the end, slow sits at the middle.
We set prev to nothing, since the reversed second half will start with no node behind it.
We loop through the second half starting at slow, reversing it until slow runs off the end.
We save the node after slow in nxt so we do not lose the rest of the list.
We point slow's next link backward at prev, which reverses one link.
We move prev forward to slow, so prev always holds the head of the reversed part.
We move slow forward to the saved nxt node, continuing down the original list.
We set left to the original head and right to prev, the head of the reversed second half.
We loop while right has nodes, since the second half is the same length or shorter than the first.
We compare the values at left and right, checking whether they differ.
If any pair differs, the list cannot be a palindrome, so we return false immediately.
We advance both left and right one node, so we compare the next matching pair.
If every pair matched, the list reads the same both ways, so we return true.

palindrome-partitioning-ii.hook: Cut a string into palindromes with as few cuts as possible. Greedy longest pieces can fail.
palindrome-partitioning-ii.ask: Given a string, split it into pieces so that every piece reads the same forwards and backwards. Return the smallest number of cuts needed to do that.
palindrome-partitioning-ii.exampleWhy: Cut once: a | baab. Both pieces are palindromes. Taking aba first would force two cuts.

brute.idea: Try every palindrome prefix as the first piece, then recursively solve the rest. Keep the smallest total.
steps: Start at index i
Try every palindrome s[i:j]
Recurse on the rest from j
Keep the minimum cuts
brute.whySlow: Without memory the same suffix is solved again and again; a string of all a's explodes exponentially.

optimal.insight: Let cuts[i] be the fewest cuts for the first i letters. Every palindrome s[lo..hi] found by expanding a center offers cuts[lo] + 1.
steps: cuts[i] starts at i - 1, the worst case
Expand around each center, odd and even
Each palindrome lo..hi updates cuts[hi + 1]
Answer is cuts[n]

codeNotes.note: Worst case: cut between every letter

codeNotes.match: while lo >= 0 and hi < n and s[lo] == s[hi]:

codeNotes.note: Prefix before lo, plus one cut

pitfalls: cuts[0] = -1 is the trick: a whole-string palindrome then costs zero cuts.
Precomputing an n by n palindrome table also works but costs n squared memory.

say.intro: Palindrome Partitioning Two. We chop a string into pieces, and every piece must be a palindrome. What's the fewest cuts we can get away with? Take a, b, a, a, b. One cut does it: a, then b a a b. And here's the trap. Grab the long a b a first, and you're stuck paying two cuts.
say.brute: Okay, so the obvious way. Stand at the current position. Try every palindrome that starts there as the first piece. Then recursively solve whatever is left, and keep the smallest total. It's correct. So what's the catch? Nothing is remembered. The same suffix gets solved again and again. On a long run of identical letters, the number of splits grows exponentially.
say.insight: Here's the thing. Think in prefixes instead. Let cuts of i be the fewest cuts for the first i letters. Now, say the letters from lo to hi form a palindrome. Then the prefix ending at hi can reuse the best answer before lo, plus one cut. How do we find every palindrome? Expand around each center. That's quadratic work in total.
say.anim: We start with string abaab and initialize cuts as negative one, zero, one, two, three, four. At center zero, single letter a is a palindrome, so cuts at index one stays zero. At center one, expanding around b finds aba is a palindrome, setting cuts at index three to zero. At center two, expanding around a finds baab, updating cuts at index four to two, then index five to one. Center three checks letter a alone, keeping cuts at index four at one. Center four checks the final b, leaving cuts unchanged since no longer palindrome extends further. The function returns cuts at index five, giving the minimum cuts needed as one.
say.code: Let's walk the code. First, fill cuts with i minus one. That's the worst case, a cut between every letter. Next, for each center, try both an odd and an even length palindrome. While both ends match, we grow outward. Each palindrome updates the cell just past hi, using the cell at lo plus one. Finally, return the last cell.
say.outro: Quadratic time, linear space. The pattern is one dimensional dynamic programming over prefixes. Expand around center feeds it every palindrome.

palindrome-partitioning-ii.title: Palindrome Partitioning II
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container the interview platform expects for our method.
The method minCut takes the string s and returns the smallest number of cuts needed for palindrome pieces.
We store the length of s in n so we can use it for bounds and array sizing.
We set cuts at index i to i minus one, the worst case of cutting between every letter, with the empty prefix at negative one.
We loop over every possible center position in the string, and expand a palindrome around each one.
For each center we try two shapes, using odd as zero for even length and one for odd length, covering both kinds of palindromes.
We start the left and right pointers at the center, with right shifted by odd so we begin with an even pair or a single letter.
We keep expanding while both pointers stay inside the string and the two letters match, which means the current slice is a palindrome.
Since s from lo to hi is a palindrome, the first hi plus one letters need at most the cuts for the first lo letters plus one.
We move the left pointer one step outward to test a longer palindrome.
We move the right pointer one step outward as well, keeping the palindrome centered.
After all centers are processed, cuts at n holds the minimum cuts for the whole string, which we return.

peak-index-in-a-mountain-array.hook: The array climbs then falls. One comparison tells you which side of the summit you are on.
peak-index-in-a-mountain-array.ask: You get an array that strictly increases up to one peak and then strictly decreases. Return the index of that peak, using logarithmic time.
peak-index-in-a-mountain-array.exampleWhy: Values rise to 12 at index 6, then every value after it is smaller.

brute.idea: Walk from the left until the next value is smaller. That position is the peak.
steps: Scan i from 0 upward
Stop when arr[i] > arr[i + 1]
Return i
brute.whySlow: A peak near the end of 100,000 values means 100,000 comparisons, and the problem demands log time.

optimal.insight: Compare arr[mid] with arr[mid + 1]. Rising means the peak is to the right; falling means mid or something left of it is the peak.
steps: Search lo = 0, hi = n - 1
Look at mid and its right neighbor
Rising: peak is right, lo = mid + 1
Falling: peak at mid or left, hi = mid
Stop when lo == hi

pitfalls: Pair lo < hi with hi = mid; using lo <= hi there loops forever.

say.intro: Peak Index in a Mountain Array. The values climb to one summit, then fall. We return the summit's index. And there's a twist. We have to do it in logarithmic time. In our array, values rise to twelve at index six. After that, every step goes down.
say.brute: The obvious move? Walk from the left. Stop at the first spot where the next value is smaller. That's the peak. Simple, and correct. But it's linear. If the summit sits near the end of a hundred thousand values, we touch almost all of them. And the problem explicitly asks for better.
say.insight: Here's the thing. Any single position tells you which slope you're on. Compare mid with its right neighbor. Is mid smaller? Then we're still climbing, so the peak is strictly to the right. Otherwise we're heading down. So the peak is mid itself, or somewhere to its left. Either way, each check throws away half the array.
say.anim: We start searching the mountain array with lo at 0 and hi at 11. Mid is 5, and since arr at mid is less than the next value, we move lo right. Now lo is 6, and mid becomes 8; arr at mid is greater, so hi shrinks to 8. Mid is now 7, still falling, so hi moves down to 7. Mid becomes 6, again descending, so hi shrinks to 6, matching lo. With lo equal to hi at 6, the loop ends, pinpointing the peak. The function returns 6, the index of the mountain’s peak value.
say.code: Let's walk the code. Lo starts at zero, hi at the last index. The peak is somewhere in there. We loop until they meet, taking mid each time. Is mid smaller than the next value? Then we're still climbing. So the peak is strictly right, and lo becomes mid plus one. Otherwise, hi becomes mid, because mid might be the peak.
say.outro: Logarithmic time, constant space. The pattern is binary search on a condition. The question we keep asking: which slope am I on?

peak-index-in-a-mountain-array.title: Peak Index in a Mountain Array
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the wrapper the judge expects for this problem.
This method takes the mountain array and returns the index of its single peak.
We set lo to zero and hi to the last index, so the search covers the whole array.
We loop while lo is less than hi, stopping once the window shrinks to one candidate.
We compute mid as the average of lo and hi, rounded down, to probe the middle of the window.
If the value at mid is less than its right neighbor, we are still climbing uphill.
Since we are climbing, the peak must be right of mid, so we move lo to mid plus one.
Otherwise the array is falling at mid, which means the peak is at mid or to its left.
So we set hi to mid, keeping mid as a possible peak while discarding everything to its right.
When lo and hi meet, that single index is the peak, so we return lo.

put-marbles-in-bags.hook: It looks like a partition DP, but every split just adds one pair sum.
put-marbles-in-bags.ask: Split a row of marble weights into k contiguous bags. A bag costs its first plus last weight. Return the largest total cost minus the smallest total cost over all ways to split.
put-marbles-in-bags.exampleWhy: Pair sums are 4, 8, 6, 5, 6. Two biggest give 14, two smallest give 9, so 14 - 9 = 5.

brute.idea: Try every choice of k - 1 cut positions, compute each score, and track the largest and smallest.
steps: Pick k - 1 cut points
Score = ends + both sides of each cut
Track max and min score
brute.whySlow: With 100,000 marbles and k around 50,000 the number of cut sets is astronomically large.

optimal.insight: The two ends are always counted. A cut after index i adds weights[i] + weights[i + 1]. So pick the k - 1 largest and smallest pair sums.
steps: Build pair sums of neighbors
Sort them
Max score uses the k - 1 largest
Min score uses the k - 1 smallest
Return the difference

codeNotes.note: Each possible cut costs one pair sum

pitfalls: When k is 1, cuts is 0; slicing pairs[len:] keeps it empty, not the whole list.
Selecting with two heaps is fine too, still n log n.

say.intro: Put Marbles in Bags. We split a row of weights into k bags, each one a contiguous run. A bag costs its first weight plus its last weight. We want the best total minus the worst total. For one, three, five, one, four, two, with three bags, the answer is five.
say.brute: Okay, so the brute force. Try every way to place k minus one cuts. For each choice, add up the bag costs. Track the largest and smallest totals. It's correct. So what's the problem? The number of cut sets is a binomial coefficient. With a hundred thousand marbles, that's far beyond anything we could list.
say.insight: Think about what one cut actually does. Cut between neighbors i and i plus one. One bag ends, another starts. That adds exactly those two weights. Now, notice the very first and last weights are always counted. So they cancel in the difference. The whole problem becomes this. Pick k minus one pair sums, largest versus smallest.
say.anim: We start with weights one three five one four two, and k equals three. We build pairs by summing each adjacent pair of weights, representing possible cut points. At index zero, four is added, since one plus three equals four. More adjacent sums get added, giving pairs four, eight, six, five, and six. The pairs list is sorted to find the largest and smallest sums easily. With cuts equal two, the two largest pairs sum to fourteen for big. The two smallest pairs sum to nine, stored as small. Subtracting small from big gives the final answer, five.
say.code: Let's walk the code. Each possible cut costs one pair sum, so we build that list. Then we sort it, cheapest cuts first. Three bags need two cuts, so we take k minus one. The big total uses the most expensive cuts at the end. The small total uses the cheapest ones at the front. Return big minus small. The row's ends never show up, because they cancel.
say.outro: Sorting makes it n log n time. The pattern is greedy. Turn a partition into independent choices, then just take the extremes.

put-marbles-in-bags.title: Put Marbles in Bags
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container the problem expects for our method.
The method putMarbles takes the list of weights and the number of bags k, and returns an integer.
We start with an empty list called pairs to hold the cost of every possible cut.
We loop over every index that has a right neighbor, so each adjacent position is considered once.
For each index, we add the sum of that weight and the next one, since cutting there adds both to the total.
We sort the pair sums so the smallest are at the front and the largest at the end.
We need exactly k minus 1 cuts to make k bags, so we store that count in cuts.
The maximum score uses the largest cuts, so we sum the last cuts values of the sorted pairs.
The minimum score uses the smallest cuts, so we sum the first cuts values of the sorted pairs.
The fixed end weights cancel out, so the answer is just the big sum minus the small sum.

random-pick-with-weight.hook: Weighted dice in log time: lay the weights end to end and throw a dart.
random-pick-with-weight.ask: Build an object from positive weights. Each call to pickIndex returns a random index, where index i is chosen with probability w[i] divided by the total weight.
random-pick-with-weight.exampleWhy: One seeded run. Index 1 owns half the total weight, so it shows up most often.

brute.idea: Pick a random number from 1 to the total, then walk the weights subtracting until it runs out.
steps: Draw target in 1..total
Walk weights, adding a running sum
First index where sum ≥ target
brute.whySlow: Ten thousand picks over ten thousand weights is a hundred million steps; each pick rescans the list.

optimal.insight: Prefix sums turn the weights into consecutive segments on a line. A random dart lands in segment i with exactly the right probability, and binary search finds it.
steps: Build prefix sums once
Draw target in 1..total
Binary search first prefix ≥ target
That index owns the dart

codeNotes.note: Seeded so a demo run replays
Segment end points on a line
Index i covers up to here

pitfalls: Target in 1..total pairs with bisect_left; a 0-based target needs bisect_right.
Expanding each index w[i] times wastes memory when weights are large.

say.intro: Random Pick with Weight. We get some weights. Each pick returns a random index, chosen in proportion to its weight. With weights two, five and three, index one should come up half the time. Index two gets thirty percent. Index zero gets twenty.
say.brute: Here's the simple way. Draw a random number from one to the total. Then walk the weights, keeping a running sum. Return the first index where the sum reaches the target. Correct? Yes. The catch is that every pick rescans the whole list. Ten thousand picks over ten thousand weights is a hundred million steps.
say.insight: Think about it this way. Lay the weights end to end on a number line. Index zero covers one to two. Index one covers three to seven. Index two covers eight to ten. Now throw a random dart. It lands in each segment with exactly the right probability. And since the running sums are sorted, binary search finds the segment fast.
say.anim: We start with weights two, five, and three, building prefix sums as segments. Looping through the weights, total grows to two, then seven, then ten, forming prefix array two, seven, ten. Total weight is ten, meaning darts thrown will range from one to ten. A random target of six lands inside segment one, so bisect returns index one. Next target three also falls in segment one, giving another index one result. Target seven lands exactly at the boundary, still mapping to index one. Finally target one falls in the first segment, so bisect returns index zero. The four pick calls return one, one, one, and zero, matching the expected output.
say.code: Let's walk the code. We seed the random generator, so a demo run replays the same way. The constructor builds the segment end points on a line. Each running total marks where index i ends. To pick, we throw the dart: a random integer from one to the total. Then bisect left finds the first segment reaching the dart.
say.outro: Linear setup, logarithmic picks. The pattern is binary search over prefix sums. It's the classic way to sample from weights.

random-pick-with-weight.title: Random Pick with Weight
lineNotes: We import the random module so we can generate random numbers for picking indices.
We define a Solution class that holds the weights and supports weighted random picking.
The constructor receives the list of positive weights w, which we will convert into prefix sums.
We create a seeded random generator with seed seven so the picks are reproducible.
We start an empty prefix list that will hold the running totals of the weights.
We set total to zero to accumulate the sum of weights as we walk through them.
We loop over each weight x in the input list, in order.
We add the current weight to total, extending the end of the current segment on the line.
We append the running total to the prefix list, marking where this index's segment ends.
We save the final total so pickIndex knows the full range for the random dart.
The pickIndex method returns one random index, weighted by each original weight.
We draw a random integer between one and the total, inclusive, as our dart position on the line.
We binary search for the first prefix value at least the target, which gives the segment index the dart landed in.

range-sum-query-immutable.hook: Answer any range sum in constant time by paying once, up front.
range-sum-query-immutable.ask: Build an object from an integer array. Then answer many queries asking for the sum of the elements between indices left and right, inclusive.

brute.idea: Store the array and, for every query, add up the elements from left to right.
steps: Keep nums as given
Loop left to right per query
Return the total
brute.whySlow: Ten thousand queries over ten thousand elements means a hundred million additions, repeating the same work.

optimal.insight: Store prefix[i] = sum of the first i elements. Any range sum is a difference of two prefixes: prefix[right + 1] - prefix[left].
steps: prefix starts with a single 0
Append running sums once
Query: subtract two prefix values

codeNotes.note: Everything to right, minus before left

pitfalls: The leading zero avoids a special case when left is 0.
Off by one: use right + 1, since prefix is shifted by one.

say.intro: Range Sum Query, Immutable. We get an array once. Then come many questions: what's the sum between two indices? The array never changes. For three, minus one, four, one, minus five, nine, zero to two sums to six. Two to five sums to nine.
say.brute: The direct way? Keep the array. For every query, loop from left to right, adding as we go. Each answer is right. But each query can cost the whole array length. Ten thousand queries on ten thousand numbers is a hundred million additions. And most of them repeat sums we already did.
say.insight: Here's the thing. The array never changes. So let's precompute running totals, just once. Prefix of i is the sum of the first i numbers, starting with zero. Now, what's the sum from left to right? Everything up to right, minus everything before left. One subtraction. So every query becomes constant time.
say.anim: We start with the array and an initial prefix list containing just zero. We loop through each number, adding it to the running total to build prefix sums. After processing all six numbers, the prefix list holds cumulative sums ending at nine. For sumRange zero to two, we subtract prefix zero from prefix three, giving six. For sumRange one to four, prefix one subtracted from prefix five gives negative one. For sumRange two to five, prefix two subtracted from prefix six gives nine. The final outputs are null, six, negative one, and nine, matching the expected result.
say.code: Let's walk the code. Prefix starts with a single zero, the sum of zero elements. Then for each number, we append the running total so far. To answer a query, we take prefix at right plus one, minus prefix at left. Notice the leading zero. It means a range starting at index zero needs no special case.
say.outro: Linear setup, constant time per query. The pattern is prefix sums. Precompute once, then answer any range by subtraction.

range-sum-query-immutable.title: Range Sum Query - Immutable
lineNotes: We define a class called NumArray that will hold precomputed sums so many range queries can be answered quickly.
The constructor takes the integer array nums and sets up the data we need for later queries.
We start the prefix list with a single zero, representing the sum of the first zero elements.
We loop over each number x in nums, building the prefix sums one element at a time.
We append the last prefix value plus x, so each entry holds the running total of elements so far.
The sumRange method takes left and right indices and will answer each query without looping over the array.
We return prefix at right plus one minus prefix at left, which leaves exactly the sum from left through right inclusive.

remove-k-digits.hook: Smallest number after deleting k digits: a big digit before a smaller one must go.
remove-k-digits.ask: Given a number as a string and an integer k, delete exactly k digits so the remaining number is as small as possible. Return it without leading zeros, or 0 if nothing is left.
remove-k-digits.exampleWhy: Deleting 4, 3 and one 2 leaves 1219; no other three deletions give a smaller number.

brute.idea: Repeat k times: try deleting each single digit and keep the smallest resulting number.
steps: Try removing each position
Keep the smallest candidate
Repeat k times
Strip leading zeros
brute.whySlow: Each round builds n strings of length n; with 100,000 digits that is billions of character copies.

optimal.insight: Higher places matter most. Whenever a digit is bigger than the digit after it, removing it shrinks the number, so keep an increasing stack.
steps: Scan digits left to right
Pop while top > current and k > 0
Push the current digit
Trim leftover k from the end
Strip leading zeros

codeNotes.match: while k and stack and stack[-1] > d:
codeNotes.note: Bigger digit before smaller: remove it
Still increasing: drop from the end

pitfalls: Forgetting leftover k on an increasing input like 12345.
Empty result must become 0, not an empty string.

say.intro: Remove K Digits. We get a number as a string. We must delete exactly k digits to make it as small as possible. For one four three two two one nine, with three deletions, the best is one two one nine. Leading zeros get dropped. And if nothing's left, the answer is zero.
say.brute: Okay, so the brute force deletes one digit per round. Each round, try removing every position, and keep the smallest result. Do that k times. It works. But every round builds n new strings of length n. With a hundred thousand digits, that's billions of character copies.
say.insight: Here's the thing. The leftmost digits matter most. Say a digit is bigger than the one right after it. Delete it, and a smaller digit slides into a higher place. That always helps. So we keep a stack of digits that stays increasing. A bigger digit on top gets popped, as long as we still have deletions.
say.anim: We start with the number 1432219 and need to remove three digits. Digits 1 and 4 are pushed since the stack keeps increasing so far. Digit 3 is smaller than 4, so we pop 4 to shrink the number, k drops to 2. Digit 2 is smaller than 3, so we pop 3 too, k becomes 1. Digit 2 gets pushed, matching the previous 2 in the stack. Digit 1 is smaller, so we pop the last 2, using up our final removal, k is now 0. With no removals left, digits 2, 1, and 9 are simply appended. After trimming leading zeros, the final answer shown is 1219.
say.code: Let's walk the code. For each digit, check the top of the stack. Bigger digit before a smaller one? Pop it. That spends one deletion. Then push the digit. Now, what if deletions remain? The stack is increasing, so we drop them from the end. Then strip the leading zeros. And if everything got removed, we return zero.
say.outro: Linear time and space. The pattern is a monotonic stack. Greedily remove any bigger value that sits before a smaller one.

remove-k-digits.title: Remove K Digits
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the wrapper this problem's submission format expects.
The method removeKdigits takes the number as a string and k, the count of digits we must delete.
We start with an empty stack that will hold the digits we keep, in increasing order.
We walk through each digit of the number from left to right, since higher places matter most.
While we still have removals left and the stack top is bigger than the current digit, we want to drop that top.
We pop the larger digit off the stack, because removing it makes the number smaller.
We decrease k by one to record that one removal has been used.
We push the current digit onto the stack, keeping the stack in nondecreasing order.
If removals remain after the loop, the stack is already increasing, so the largest digits sit at the end.
We cut the last k digits from the stack to use up the remaining removals.
We join the stack into a string and strip leading zeros so the result has no extra zeros in front.
If the result is empty we return the string zero, otherwise we return the cleaned number.

reverse-pairs.hook: Counting pairs where one number beats double another, faster than checking every pair.
reverse-pairs.ask: Count the pairs of indices i before j where nums[i] is strictly greater than twice nums[j].
reverse-pairs.exampleWhy: Only the two 3s beat twice the final 1, giving pairs (1, 4) and (3, 4).

brute.idea: Check every pair i < j directly and count those where nums[i] > 2 · nums[j].
steps: Pick i
Scan every j after i
Count when nums[i] > 2 · nums[j]
brute.whySlow: 50,000 numbers means about 1.25 billion pair checks.

optimal.insight: Merge sort: once both halves are sorted, one sweeping pointer counts all left-right pairs in linear time.
steps: Split the range in half, recurse
Both halves now sorted
For each left value, advance j while it beats 2 · nums[j]
Add j - mid to the count
Merge the halves

codeNotes.match: while j < hi and nums[i] > 2 * nums[j]:

codeNotes.note: Right values below half of nums[i]

pitfalls: Count before merging; after merging the left-right split is gone.
In other languages 2 · nums[j] overflows 32 bits; use 64-bit.

say.intro: Reverse Pairs. We count pairs where an earlier number is more than twice a later number. Take one, three, two, three, one. Both threes are more than twice that final one. So there are exactly two pairs.
say.brute: The brute force checks every pair. For each index, scan every later index. Count when the earlier value beats twice the later one. It's correct. But it's quadratic. With fifty thousand numbers, that's more than a billion comparisons.
say.insight: Here's the trick. Use merge sort. Any pair either sits in the left half, sits in the right half, or crosses the middle. Recursion counts the first two. Now, what about crossing pairs? Both halves are already sorted. So as the left value grows, the pointer into the right half only moves forward. One linear sweep counts them all.
say.anim: We start with the array one, three, two, three, one, and begin merge sorting it. The array splits at mid equals two, sorting the left and right halves separately. In the smallest left split, index zero and one are compared but no pair counts yet. Comparing index three against the right half, j reaches five, adding one reverse pair. Merging indices two through four finds another match, keeping count at one so far. Now the full left and right halves merge, sweeping pointer j counts cross pairs. Index one needs j to move to three, adding one more pair, count becomes two. The final sorted array is one one two three three, giving two reverse pairs total.
say.code: Let's walk the code. A helper sorts a range and returns its count. First, recurse on both halves to count the pairs inside each one. Then start j at mid. Here's the key. J never moves backwards. For each left value, slide j over the right values below half of it. Add j minus mid. Finally, a linear merge keeps the halves sorted.
say.outro: n log n time, linear space. The pattern is two pointers over sorted halves, powered by merge sort's divide and conquer.

reverse-pairs.title: Reverse Pairs
lineNotes: We define the Solution class that holds the method for this problem.
The reversePairs method takes the list of numbers and returns how many reverse pairs it contains.
We define a helper called sort that counts pairs and sorts the slice from lo up to hi.
If the slice has at most one element, there is nothing to pair or sort.
In that base case we return zero, since a single element forms no pairs.
We compute mid as the midpoint so the slice splits into a left and right half.
We recursively sort both halves and start count with the pairs found entirely inside each half.
We start pointer j at mid, the beginning of the right half.
We walk each index i through the left half, which is already sorted.
While nums at j is less than half of nums at i, we advance j through the right half.
Each advance of j means another right element forms a valid pair with the current i.
We add the number of right elements passed, j minus mid, to count; j never moves back because the left is ascending.
We merge the two sorted halves back into the slice so the parent call sees sorted data.
We return the total count of pairs for this slice.
We start the whole process on the full range and return its count.

reverse-vowels-of-a-string.hook: Reverse only the vowels and leave every other character exactly where it is.
reverse-vowels-of-a-string.ask: Given a string, reverse the order of its vowels, lowercase or uppercase, while every other character keeps its position. Return the new string.
reverse-vowels-of-a-string.exampleWhy: Vowels I, e, e, A become A, e, e, I in the same slots.

brute.idea: Collect all vowels in a list, then rebuild the string, filling vowel slots from the end of that list.
steps: First pass: collect vowels
Second pass: copy characters
Vowel slot? take the last vowel
brute.whySlow: Not slower asymptotically. It makes two passes and keeps an extra vowel list; two pointers do one in-place sweep.

optimal.insight: The first vowel swaps with the last vowel, the second with the second last. Two pointers moving inward pair them up directly.
steps: l at start, r at end
Move l past consonants
Move r past consonants
Both vowels: swap, move both

pitfalls: Forgetting uppercase vowels.
Building the string with += in a loop is quadratic in many languages.

say.intro: Reverse Vowels of a String. We flip the order of the vowels only. Everything else stays put. In ice cream, written with a few capitals, the vowels are capital I, e, e, and capital A. Reversed, they become capital A, e, e, capital I.
say.brute: Here's a straightforward way. First pass: collect every vowel into a list. Second pass: rebuild the string, and fill each vowel slot from the end of that list. Is it slow? Honestly, no. It's already linear time. What it costs is an extra list and a second pass.
say.insight: Think about what reversing means. The first vowel trades places with the last. The second trades with the second to last. And so on. So put one pointer at each end. Move each one inward until both sit on vowels. Swap them, and keep going. Every character gets looked at once, in a single sweep.
say.anim: We start with the string IceCreAm, split into characters, and set up two pointers. Pointer l is at zero and r is at seven, scanning from both ends inward. The character at r is not a vowel, so r moves inward to six. Both chars l and r are vowels, I and A, so they swap places. Pointers keep moving, skipping consonants like c and r until vowels are found again. The vowels e and e swap, though identical, keeping the inward pointer logic consistent. Now l equals four and r equals four, so the loop stops. The final reversed vowel string is AceCreIm.
say.code: Let's walk the code. Make a vowel set with both cases, since both count. Turn the string into a list, because Python strings are immutable. Now loop while l is left of r. Consonant on the left? Move l right. Consonant on the right? Move r left. Otherwise, we have a pair of vowels. Swap them and move both.
say.outro: Linear time, one pass. The pattern is two pointers from both ends. It's the natural fit for any reverse in place problem.

reverse-vowels-of-a-string.title: Reverse Vowels of a String
lineNotes: We define a class called Solution, which is the container the judge expects for this problem.
This method takes the string s and returns a new string with its vowels in reversed order.
We build a set of all ten vowels, both cases, so each membership check is fast.
Strings cannot be changed in place, so we copy the characters into a list we can modify.
We set left to zero and right to the last index, so two pointers start at both ends.
We loop while left is still less than right, so every vowel pair is handled once.
If the character at left is not a vowel, it must stay put, so we skip past it.
We move left one step forward to look at the next character.
Otherwise, if the character at right is not a vowel, we should skip over it as well.
We move right one step backward to look at the previous character.
Otherwise both pointers sit on vowels, so they are ready to be swapped.
We swap the two vowels, which puts the first vowel at the end and the last at the front.
After swapping, we move left forward so it searches for the next vowel.
We also move right backward so it searches for the next vowel from the other end.
Finally we join the list back into one string and return it as the answer.

rotate-list.hook: Rotating a list a billion times is just one cut, once you know its length.
rotate-list.ask: Given the head of a linked list and a number k, rotate the list to the right by k places: the last k nodes move to the front, in order.
rotate-list.exampleWhy: Seven rotations on five nodes equals two rotations, so 4 and 5 move to the front.

brute.idea: Rotate by one, k times: detach the last node and put it at the front each time.
steps: Walk to the last node
Detach it
Link it before head
Repeat k times
brute.whySlow: k can be two billion; even on a tiny list that is billions of full walks.

optimal.insight: Rotating n times changes nothing, so use k mod n. Then close the list into a ring and cut it n - k nodes from the head.
steps: Find length n and the tail
k = k mod n; zero means done
Link tail to head, making a ring
Walk n - k - 1 steps to the new tail
Break the ring there

pitfalls: Skipping k mod n turns a huge k into a timeout.
Empty or single-node lists must return immediately.

say.intro: Rotate List. We rotate a linked list to the right by k places. So the last k nodes move to the front. With one through five and k equal to seven, we get four, five, one, two, three. Why? Seven rotations of five nodes is the same as two.
say.brute: Okay, so the brute force rotates one step at a time. Walk to the last node. Detach it. Hook it in front of the head. Do that k times. What's the catch? Each step is a full walk of the list. And k can be two billion. Even a tiny list would take billions of walks.
say.insight: Here's the thing. Rotating by the full length lands you right back where you started. So only k mod n matters. Now, notice something else. A rotation is just a different place to cut a ring. So link the tail back to the head. Walk to the node that should be the new tail. Then break the ring right after it.
say.anim: We start with list one through five, and k equals seven rotations. The loop walks the list counting nodes, ending with n equal to five. K mod n reduces seven to two, since five rotations change nothing. The tail connects back to head, forming a ring of the five nodes. New tail starts at head, then advances two steps to node three. New head becomes node four, right after the new tail's position. The ring is cut by setting new tail's next to none. Final answer returned is the rotated list four, five, one, two, three.
say.code: Let's walk the code. Empty and single node lists return right away. Then walk to the tail, counting nodes as we go. Reduce k mod n, since full turns do nothing. If it's zero, return the head. Next, link the tail to the head, closing the ring. Walk n minus k minus one steps to the new tail. Its next is the new head. Break the ring there.
say.outro: Linear time, constant space. The pattern is linked list pointer surgery. Measure the length, make a ring, cut once.

rotate-list.title: Rotate List
lineNotes: We define the Solution class that holds our rotate right method for the linked list problem.
The method takes the head of the list and a rotation count k, and returns the new head.
If the list is empty or has only one node, rotating cannot change anything.
So we simply return the head as it is in that trivial case.
We start counting the length n at one and place tail at the head node.
We walk forward until tail reaches the last node, the one with no next.
Each step moves tail one node further along the list.
We add one to n for every node we step onto, so n ends as the full length.
We reduce k modulo n, since rotating by the full length returns the original list.
If k is now zero, the rotation would leave the list unchanged.
So we return the original head right away without touching any links.
We link the tail back to the head, turning the list into a closed ring.
We start new tail at the head and will walk it to the cutting point.
We loop n minus k minus one times to land on the node just before the new head.
Each iteration advances new tail by one node around the ring.
The node after new tail is the new head, since the last k nodes begin there.
We cut the ring by setting the next of new tail to none, ending the list.
We return the new head, which is the start of the rotated list.

row-with-maximum-ones.hook: Find the row with the most ones; ties go to the earliest row.
row-with-maximum-ones.ask: Given a binary matrix, return the index of the row with the most ones and how many ones it has. If several rows tie, choose the smallest index.
row-with-maximum-ones.exampleWhy: Rows 1 and 3 both have three ones; row 1 comes first, so the answer is [1, 3].

brute.idea: Count each row with a nested loop into a list of counts, then scan that list for the first maximum.
steps: Count ones in every row
Store all counts
Find the max count
Return its first index
brute.whySlow: Not slower asymptotically. It stores every count and makes extra passes; one pass with a running best is enough.

optimal.insight: Keep a running best. Replace it only on a strictly larger count, so ties automatically keep the earlier row.
steps: Best starts at row 0, count -1
Count ones in each row
Strictly larger? update best
Return [row, count]

codeNotes.note: Strictly greater keeps earliest on ties

pitfalls: Using >= would pick the last tied row, not the first.

say.intro: Row With Maximum Ones. We have a matrix of zeros and ones. Which row has the most ones? We return its index and its count. Ties go to the earliest row. Here, rows one and three both have three ones. So the answer is row one, with three.
