say.brute: A first attempt counts every row with a nested loop. It stores all the counts in a list. Then it finds the maximum and looks up the first index holding it. Is that slow? Honestly, no. The time is already optimal. What it wastes is an extra list, plus a couple of extra passes over it.
say.insight: We have to read every cell once anyway. So the real goal is one clean pass with constant memory. Keep a running best row and best count. Replace them only when a row has strictly more ones. Why strictly? Because then ties never replace. The earliest row with the top count wins automatically.
say.anim: We start with best_row at 0 and best_count at negative one, before checking any rows. Row 0 is 0,1,1, summing to a count of 2, which beats negative one. So best_row becomes 0 and best_count updates to 2. Row 1 is 1,1,1, giving count 3, which is strictly greater than 2. Best_row updates to 1 and best_count updates to 3. Row 2 sums to 2, which is not greater than 3, so nothing changes. Row 3 sums to 3, tying the current best, so it does not replace it. The final answer returned is row 1 with a maximum count of 3.
say.code: Let's walk the code. Best count starts at minus one, so any row beats it. For each row, we just sum it. The values are zero or one, so the sum counts the ones. Is that sum strictly greater than the best? Then update both. Strictly greater keeps the earliest row on ties. Finally, return the index and its count.
say.outro: Linear in the matrix size, constant space. The pattern is a single scan with a running best.

row-with-maximum-ones.title: Row With Maximum Ones
lineNotes: We define a Solution class that holds the method for solving this problem.
The method takes the binary matrix and returns a list containing the best row index and its count of ones.
We start with best row at zero and best count at negative one so the first row always replaces it.
We loop through the matrix, getting each row along with its index so we can report the position.
Since entries are zero or one, summing the row gives the number of ones in it.
We only update when this count is strictly greater than the best, so ties keep the earlier row.
When a row wins, we record its index and its count as the new best pair.
After checking every row, we return the best row index together with its number of ones.

simplify-path.hook: Turn a messy Unix path into its canonical form, one folder at a time.
simplify-path.ask: Given an absolute Unix path, return its simplest form: single slashes, no dot folders, double dot goes up one level, no trailing slash. Other dot names are ordinary folders.
simplify-path.exampleWhy: The double slash and dot vanish, and .. cancels docs, leaving home, user, pics.

brute.idea: Split into names, then repeatedly find the first .., delete it with the name before it, and rescan.
steps: Split on slashes, drop empties and dots
Find the first ..
Delete it and its parent
Rescan until none left
brute.whySlow: Each .. restarts the scan and deleting from a list shifts elements; thousands of .. parts cost quadratic work.

optimal.insight: A path is a stack of folders. A name pushes, .. pops, and empty parts or dots do nothing.
steps: Split the path on slashes
Name: push it
..: pop if not empty
Empty or dot: skip
Join with slashes

pitfalls: Three dots is a valid folder name, not a parent.
Popping an empty stack at the root must do nothing.

say.intro: Simplify Path. We get an absolute Unix path, and we return its clean form. Repeated slashes collapse. Single dots disappear. Double dot goes up one folder. And no trailing slash. So slash home, double slash, user, dot, docs, dot dot, pics becomes slash home slash user slash pics.
say.brute: Here's a brute force. Split the path into names, dropping empty pieces and dots. Then scan for the first double dot. Delete it, along with the name before it. Then start scanning again. It works. So what's wrong? Every double dot restarts the scan and shifts the list. Long paths take quadratic time.
say.insight: Think about it this way. A path is really a stack of folders. Read left to right. A folder name pushes onto the stack. Double dot pops the most recent folder, if there is one. Empty pieces and single dots change nothing. One pass, and whatever's left on the stack is the answer.
say.anim: We start with an empty stack, ready to process each slash separated part of the path. The part home is not empty or a dot, so it gets pushed onto the stack. Next, user is pushed too, making the stack hold home and user. A single dot part is ignored since it means staying in place. Docs is pushed, giving us home, user, docs on the stack. Seeing double dot pops docs, moving back up one folder level. Pics is pushed next, leaving home, user, pics as the final stack. Joining the stack with slashes gives the simplified path home user pics.
say.code: Let's walk the code. Split on slashes. Notice double slashes just become empty parts. For each piece, is it double dot? Then go up one level by popping. But only if the stack isn't empty, since root has no parent. Otherwise, skip empty pieces and single dots. Everything else is a real name, even three dots, so push it. Finally, rebuild the path with slashes.
say.outro: Linear time and space. The pattern is a stack. Whenever an input can cancel the most recent item, push and pop.

simplify-path.title: Simplify Path
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container for the method that simplifies a Unix path.
The method simplifyPath takes an absolute path string and will return its simplified canonical form.
We start with an empty stack that will hold the folder names of the simplified path in order.
We split the path on slashes and loop over each part, which may be a name, a dot, or empty.
If the part is a double dot, we need to move up one folder level.
We only go up if the stack has something in it, since the root has no parent.
Popping the stack removes the most recent folder, which is exactly what going up one level means.
Otherwise, if the part is not empty and not a single dot, it is a real folder name.
We push that folder name onto the stack, treating names like triple dots as ordinary folders.
We join the stack with slashes and put a slash in front, giving a clean path with no trailing slash.

snapshot-array.hook: Take thousands of snapshots without copying the array even once.
snapshot-array.ask: Design an array of a given length, initially zeros, supporting set(index, val), snap() which returns a snapshot id, and get(index, snap_id) which returns the value at that index when that snapshot was taken.
snapshot-array.exampleWhy: Index 0 was 5 at snap 0 and 6 at snap 1; index 1 was still 0 at snap 0.

brute.idea: Keep the live array and append a full copy of it on every snap. Get reads the copy directly.
steps: set writes the live array
snap copies the whole array
get indexes the saved copy
brute.whySlow: 50,000 snaps of a 50,000-length array means 2.5 billion copied cells, mostly unchanged.

optimal.insight: Store changes, not copies. Each index keeps a sorted history of (snap_id, value); get binary searches for the last change at or before snap_id.
steps: Each index starts with (-1, 0)
set appends or overwrites for current snap
snap just increments a counter
get: binary search the history
optimal.time: O(1) set and snap, O(log s) get

codeNotes.note: Same snap: overwrite, do not grow
Last change at or before snap_id

pitfalls: Several sets between snaps must not pile up duplicate entries.
Search for (snap_id, inf) so equal snap ids are included.

say.intro: Snapshot Array. We design an array that starts as all zeros. It supports set, snap, and get. And get can read any index as it was at any past snapshot. In our run, index zero is five at snapshot zero, and six at snapshot one. Index one is still zero at snapshot zero.
say.brute: The simple design keeps a live array. On every snap, it appends a full copy. Reading an old value is then just indexing into a saved copy. It works. But what does each snap cost? The whole length. Fifty thousand snaps of fifty thousand cells copies billions of cells. And almost all of them are unchanged.
say.insight: Here's the thing. Most cells never change between snapshots. So store changes, not copies. Each index keeps a list of pairs: the snap id when it changed, and the new value. Snap ids only grow, so that list stays sorted. That means get can binary search for the last change at or before the snapshot we want.
say.anim: We create three indices, each starting with default history entry negative one, zero. Setting index zero to five appends a new entry since the snapshot id changed. Snap returns zero as the current snapshot id, then increments it to one. Setting index zero to six and index one to four appends new history entries at snapshot one. Another snap call returns one, then increments the snapshot id to two. Getting index zero at snapshot zero binary searches history and returns five. Getting index zero at snapshot one finds position two, returning value six. Getting index one at snapshot zero finds position zero, returning the default value zero.
say.code: Let's walk the code. Every index starts with the pair minus one, zero. That means zero, from the beginning. Set checks the last pair. Same snap? Overwrite it, so the list doesn't grow. Otherwise append. Snap copies nothing. It just bumps the counter and returns the old id. Get uses bisect right to find the last change at or before that snap id.
say.outro: Constant time set and snap, logarithmic get. The pattern is binary search over a per index version history.

snapshot-array.title: Snapshot Array
lineNotes: We import the bisect module so we can binary search each index's sorted change history later.
We define the SnapshotArray class that stores only changes rather than full copies of the array.
The constructor takes the length of the array we need to support.
This comment says every index begins with a single placeholder history entry meaning value zero before any snapshot.
We create an empty list called history that will hold one change list per index.
We loop once for each index from zero up to the length.
For each index we append a list holding the pair negative one and zero, so lookups always find a default zero.
We set the current snapshot id to zero, since the first snapshot taken will return zero.
The set method takes an index and a value to store at that index.
This comment says we overwrite the entry if this index already changed in the current snapshot, otherwise we add one.
We read the most recent snapshot id and value recorded for this index from the end of its history.
We check whether that last change happened during the current snapshot period.
If so, we replace the last entry with the new value so the history stays one entry per snapshot.
Otherwise the last change belongs to an earlier snapshot, so we need a new entry.
We append a pair of the current snapshot id and the new value to this index's history.
The snap method takes a snapshot and returns its id.
This comment says we return the current id first and then increment it for the next snapshot.
We save the current snapshot id in result so we can return it after incrementing.
We increase the current snapshot id by one, so later sets belong to the next snapshot.
We return the saved id as the id of the snapshot just taken.
The get method takes an index and a snapshot id to look up.
This comment says we binary search for the last change made at or before the given snapshot id.
We grab the history list for this index to search through.
Using bisect right with the pair of snap id and infinity, then subtracting one, gives the last entry whose snap id is at most the target.
We return the value from that entry, which is the value the index held when that snapshot was taken.

sort-colors.hook: Three colors, one pass, no extra memory: the Dutch national flag problem.
sort-colors.ask: An array holds only 0, 1 and 2, meaning red, white and blue. Sort it in place so all 0s come first, then 1s, then 2s, without using a library sort.
sort-colors.exampleWhy: Two of each color, grouped in the order 0, 1, 2.

brute.idea: Bubble sort: keep swapping neighbors that are out of order until a pass makes no swaps.
steps: Sweep left to right
Swap neighbors out of order
Repeat until nothing swaps
brute.whySlow: It ignores that there are only three values; a reversed array needs about n squared over two swaps.

optimal.insight: Keep three regions: 0s before low, 2s after high, unknown between mid and high. Each look at nums[mid] shrinks the unknown region.
steps: low = mid = 0, high = n - 1
0: swap to low, advance low and mid
1: just advance mid
2: swap to high, shrink high only

codeNotes.note: Do not advance mid: unseen value

pitfalls: After swapping with high, recheck nums[mid]; it is a value we have not seen.
Counting 0s, 1s and 2s then rewriting is also linear, but two passes.

say.intro: Sort Colors. The array holds only zeros, ones and twos, meaning red, white and blue. We sort it in place, without a library sort. Two, zero, two, one, one, zero becomes zero, zero, one, one, two, two. And the follow up? One pass, constant extra space.
say.brute: A brute force just sorts by hand. Say, bubble sort. Swap neighbors that are out of order, until a full sweep makes no swaps. It's correct, and it uses no memory. But it's quadratic. And here's the real problem. It completely ignores that there are only three possible values.
say.insight: So let's use that. Keep three regions. Everything before low is zero. Everything after high is two. Between mid and high is still unknown. Now look at the value at mid. A zero swaps down to low. A one just stays. A two swaps up to high. Every step shrinks the unknown region by one.
say.anim: We start with low, mid, and high pointers at zero, zero, and five on this array. Nums at mid is two, so we swap it with high and shrink high to four. Now nums at mid is zero, so we swap with low, advancing both low and mid. Another zero at mid triggers the same swap, moving low to two and mid to two. Nums at mid is now two again, so we swap with high, shrinking high to three. Nums at mid is one, meaning it's already correctly placed, so mid just advances. Another one at mid simply advances mid again, since ones stay in the middle. Mid now exceeds high, loop ends, giving sorted output zero zero one one two two.
say.code: Let's walk the code. Low and mid start at zero, high at the last index. Those are our three region boundaries. We loop while the unknown region isn't empty. A zero gets sent to the front, and low and mid both advance. A one just moves mid. A two gets sent to the back, and high shrinks. But mid stays put. Why? The value we swapped in is unseen.
say.outro: One pass, constant space. The pattern is two pointers, here really three, partitioning an array in place.

sort-colors.title: Sort Colors
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container the interview platform expects for our method.
The sortColors method takes the list nums and sorts it in place, so it returns nothing.
We set low and mid to zero and high to the last index, creating three regions with everything unknown at first.
We loop while mid has not passed high, because the entries from mid through high are still unexamined.
If the value at mid is zero, it belongs in the front region, so we handle that case.
We swap the entries at low and mid, which puts the zero in the front region.
We move low forward by one because the zero region has grown by one slot.
We also move mid forward, since the value swapped in from low is known to be a one.
If the value at mid is one, it already sits in the correct middle region.
We simply advance mid by one, shrinking the unknown region without any swap.
Otherwise the value at mid is two, which must go to the back region.
We swap the entries at mid and high, sending the two to the end of the array.
We move high down by one, and keep mid in place because the swapped-in value is still unchecked.

substring-with-concatenation-of-all-word.hook: Find every spot where all the words appear back to back, in any order.
substring-with-concatenation-of-all-word.ask: Given a string s and a list of words that all share one length, return every starting index where some ordering of all the words, each used once, appears concatenated in s.
substring-with-concatenation-of-all-word.exampleWhy: catdog starts at 0 and dogcat at 3; catcat at 6 lacks dog.

brute.idea: At every start index, chop the next m words and compare their counts with the word counts.
steps: Try every start i
Slice m chunks of length w
Compare chunk counts to word counts
brute.whySlow: Neighboring starts share almost all their chunks, yet each one recounts all m words from scratch.

optimal.insight: Run w separate windows, one per offset, that step a whole word at a time. Each word enters and leaves a window once, like a counting sliding window.
steps: For each offset 0..w - 1
Add the next word to the window
Unknown word: reset the window
Too many copies: shrink from the left
m words inside: record left

substring-with-concatenation-of-all-word.optimalCode:
class Solution:
    def findSubstring(self, s: str, words: List[str]) -> List[int]:
        wlen, total = len(words[0]), len(words)
        need = Counter(words)
        res = []
        for offset in range(wlen):
            left, count = offset, 0
            seen = Counter()
            for right in range(offset, len(s) - wlen + 1, wlen):
                word = s[right:right + wlen]
                if word not in need:
                    seen.clear()
                    count = 0
                    left = right + wlen
                    continue
                seen[word] += 1
                count += 1
                while seen[word] > need[word]:
                    seen[s[left:left + wlen]] -= 1
                    count -= 1
                    left += wlen
                if count == total:
                    res.append(left)
                    seen[s[left:left + wlen]] -= 1
                    count -= 1
                    left += wlen
        return res

codeNotes.note: Foreign word: start over after it

pitfalls: Words can repeat, so compare counts, not sets.
Matches can start at any offset, not only multiples of the word length.

say.intro: Substring with Concatenation of All Words. All the words share one length. We return every index where the words appear back to back, in any order, each used once. In cat dog cat cat, with words cat and dog, matches start at zero and at three.
say.brute: Okay, so the brute force tries every start. It slices the next chunks, one per word, counts them, and compares with the word counts. It's correct. So what's the waste? Neighboring starts share almost all their chunks. Yet each one recounts every word from scratch.
say.insight: Here's the key. Any match lines up with one of w offsets, where w is the word length. So for each offset, slide a window that moves a whole word at a time. Keep a counter of words inside. Add a word on the right. Too many copies of it? Drop words from the left. And an unknown word resets everything.
say.anim: We start with string catdogcatcat and words cat and dog, each length three. Offset zero begins a window at left zero, scanning whole words at a time. At right zero we read cat, it matches, so count becomes one. At right three we read dog, count reaches two, equal to total words needed. A full match is found, so left zero gets added to the results. Sliding forward, cat then dog again forms another valid match at left three. Offset one and two scan different starting points but find invalid fragments like atd and tdo. After all offsets finish, the final answer returned is indices zero and three.
say.code: Let's walk the code. First, count the words. Then run one window per word alignment. Step right one word at a time. Is it a foreign word? Clear the window and start over after it. Otherwise count it. Too many copies? Shrink from the left. When all the words are present, we have a match. Record the start, then slide on by one word.
say.outro: Linear in the string, times the word length. The pattern is a sliding window with counts, stepping in whole words.

substring-with-concatenation-of-all-word.title: Substring with Concatenation of All Words
lineNotes: We define a Solution class that holds the method for this problem.
The method takes the string s and the list of words, and returns a list of starting indices.
We record the shared word length and the total number of words, since every window is built from these.
We count how many times each word appears in the list, which is the target we must match.
We create an empty result list to collect every valid starting index.
We loop over each offset from zero up to the word length, so every possible alignment gets its own window.
For this offset, we start left at the offset and set the count of words in the window to zero.
We create a fresh counter to track how many times each word appears in the current window.
The right pointer jumps one whole word at a time, stopping when no full word fits.
We cut out the word of length wlen that starts at right.
If this word is not in the required list, no window containing it can be valid.
So we clear the window counts completely.
We also reset the word count to zero because the window is now empty.
We move left past this bad word, to the next word position.
We continue to the next word, skipping the rest of this loop body.
The word is useful, so we add one to its count in the window.
We increase the window word count by one as well.
If this word appears more often than allowed, we need to shrink the window from the left.
We remove the leftmost word from the window counts, since it must leave.
We decrease the word count to match that removal.
We advance left by one word length to the new window start.
When the window holds exactly the total number of words, with no excess, it is a valid match.
We record left as a valid starting index in the result.
To keep sliding, we remove the leftmost word from the counts.
We lower the word count by one for that removed word.
We move left forward one word so the window can look for the next match.
After all offsets are processed, we return the collected starting indices.

sudoku-solver.hook: Fill a Sudoku by guessing, checking instantly, and undoing guesses that lead nowhere.
sudoku-solver.ask: Given a 9 by 9 Sudoku with empty cells marked by dots, fill it in place so every row, column and 3 by 3 box contains digits 1 to 9 exactly once.
sudoku-solver.exampleWhy: Five cells are empty; each has exactly one digit that fits its row, column and box.

brute.idea: Backtrack cell by cell, but check each guess by rescanning the whole row, column and box on the board.
steps: Find the next empty cell
Try digits 1 to 9
Scan row, column and box to check
Recurse; undo on failure
brute.whySlow: Same search, but every guess rescans 27 cells, and finding the next blank rescans the board from the top.

optimal.insight: Track which digits each row, column and box already holds in sets. A guess is then checked in constant time, and undone just as fast.
steps: Record digits per row, column, box
List the empty cells once
Try each digit not in any of the three sets
Recurse to the next empty cell
Dead end: remove the digit, try another

sudoku-solver.optimalCode:
class Solution:
    def solveSudoku(self, board: List[List[str]]) -> None:
        rows = [set(row) for row in board]
        cols = [set(col) for col in zip(*board)]
        boxes = [{board[r][c] for r in range(9) for c in range(9) if r // 3 * 3 + c // 3 == b} for b in range(9)]
        empty = [(r, c) for r in range(9) for c in range(9) if board[r][c] == "."]

        def solve(i):
            if i == len(empty):
                return True
            r, c = empty[i]
            b = r // 3 * 3 + c // 3
            for d in "123456789":
                if d in rows[r] or d in cols[c] or d in boxes[b]:
                    continue
                board[r][c] = d
                rows[r].add(d)
                cols[c].add(d)
                boxes[b].add(d)
                if solve(i + 1):
                    return True
                rows[r].remove(d)
                cols[c].remove(d)
                boxes[b].remove(d)
            board[r][c] = "."
            return False

        solve(0)

codeNotes.match: if d in rows[r] or d in cols[c] or d in boxes[b]:

pitfalls: Forgetting to undo the sets when a guess fails.
Picking the cell with fewest options first speeds up hard puzzles a lot.

say.intro: Sudoku Solver. We get a nine by nine board with some empty cells. We fill it in place, so every row, column, and three by three box has the digits one to nine exactly once. In our board, five cells are empty. And each has only one digit that fits.
say.brute: A plain backtracking solver scans for the next empty cell. It tries digits one to nine. To check each guess, it rescans the whole row, column, and box. Then it recurses, and undoes on failure. The search is fine. So what's slow? Every guess costs twenty seven reads. And the board gets rescanned from the top each time.
say.insight: Here's the fix. Keep a set of used digits for every row, every column, and every box. Now checking a guess is three constant time lookups. Placing or undoing a digit is three quick adds or removes. And we list the empty cells once, up front. So the recursion just walks that list.
say.anim: We build row, column, and box sets tracking which digits already exist nearby. Only five empty cells remain, starting with row zero, column two. Trying digit one, three, it conflicts, but four fits, so it's placed there. Moving to row zero column three, digits one through five fail until six works. At row one column one, digits fail until seven satisfies row, column, and box. Row four column four skips one, then places five since four conflicts first. Finally row eight column eight tries digits, settling on nine as the valid choice. All five empty cells are filled successfully, completing the solved sudoku board.
say.code: Let's walk the code. We build digit sets for each row, column, and three by three box. Then we list the blanks, so we visit only those. For each blank, try every digit. The conflict check is constant time. If it fits, commit it and go deeper. If that fails, undo it. That's the backtrack. And if no digit fits, reset the cell.
say.outro: Exponential in the empty cells, but fast in practice. The pattern is backtracking. Choose, explore, undo.

sudoku-solver.title: Sudoku Solver
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the wrapper the problem expects for our solver method.
The solveSudoku method takes the board and fills it in place, so it returns nothing.
We build one set per row holding every character already present in that row.
We build one set per column by transposing the board with zip, collecting each column's characters.
We build nine box sets, where box index is row over three times three plus column over three, collecting each box's characters.
We list the coordinates of every empty cell, so the search just walks through this list in order.
We define a recursive helper solve that tries to fill the empty cell at position i in that list.
If i equals the number of empty cells, every blank is filled and we have a solution.
So we return True to signal success all the way up the recursion.
We read the row and column of the current empty cell from the list.
We compute which box this cell belongs to using the same index formula as before.
We try each digit from one to nine as a candidate for this cell.
If the digit already appears in this row, column, or box, it would break the rules.
So we skip that digit and move on to the next candidate.
Otherwise we tentatively write the digit into the board at this cell.
We record the digit in the row set so later cells see it as used.
We record the digit in the column set as well.
We record the digit in the box set too, keeping all three trackers consistent.
We recurse to fill the next empty cell, checking whether this choice leads to a full solution.
If the deeper search succeeded, we return True immediately and keep the board as filled.
Otherwise we backtrack by removing the digit from the row set, undoing our guess in constant time.
We remove the digit from the column set as well.
We remove it from the box set, fully restoring the earlier state before trying the next digit.
If no digit worked, we reset this cell to a dot so the board is left clean.
We return False to tell the previous call its choice was wrong and it must try another.
We start the search at the first empty cell, and the board fills in place.

sum-of-square-numbers.hook: Is c a sum of two squares? Squeeze two pointers from both ends.
sum-of-square-numbers.ask: Given a non-negative integer c, decide whether there are two integers a and b with a squared plus b squared equal to c.
sum-of-square-numbers.exampleWhy: 4 squared is 16 and 5 squared is 25, and 16 + 25 = 41.

brute.idea: Try every pair a, b from 0 up to the square root of c and check a² + b².
steps: For each a up to sqrt(c)
For each b up to sqrt(c)
Check a² + b² == c
brute.whySlow: For c near two billion, both loops run about 46,000 times: over two billion checks.

optimal.insight: Squares are sorted. Start a at 0 and b at sqrt(c): too small, raise a; too big, lower b. Like Two Sum on a sorted list.
steps: a = 0, b = isqrt(c)
Sum too small: a += 1
Sum too big: b -= 1
Equal: return True
Pointers cross: False

pitfalls: Use integer square root; float sqrt can be off for big c.
Zero counts: c = 0 and c = 4 are true.

say.intro: Sum of Square Numbers. Given a number c, can two whole numbers squared add up to it? For forty one, yes. Four squared is sixteen. Five squared is twenty five. Together, forty one.
say.brute: The brute force tries every pair. Both numbers are at most the square root of c. So loop a and b over that range, and check each sum. It's correct. But how many checks is that? About c in total. For c near two billion, that's over two billion checks.
say.insight: Here's the thing. The squares form a sorted list. So this is really Two Sum on sorted values. Start a at zero, and b at the square root of c. Sum too small? The only fix is a bigger a. Sum too big? We need a smaller b. Notice each step rules out one candidate forever.
say.anim: We start with c equal to 41, setting a to 0 and b to 6. With a 0 and b 6, total is 36, too small, so a increases to 1. Now a is 1 and b is 6, total becomes 37, still too small, a becomes 2. With a 2, total is 40, still less than 41, so a increases to 3. Now a is 3, total is 45, too big, so b decreases to 5. With a 3 and b 5, total is 34, too small, so a increases to 4. Now a is 4 and b is 5, total equals 41, matching c exactly. The function returns true, confirming 41 is a sum of two squares.
say.code: Let's walk the code. A starts at zero and b at the integer square root. Those are the smallest and largest candidates. We loop while a hasn't passed b. Why let them be equal? Because one plus one is a valid answer. Compute the sum. Equal to c? Return true. Need bigger? Raise a. Too big? Lower b. If they cross, return false.
say.outro: Square root of c time, constant space. The pattern is two pointers closing in on a sorted range.

sum-of-square-numbers.title: Sum of Square Numbers
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container this problem's method lives in.
The method judgeSquareSum takes the integer c and returns true or false depending on whether c is a sum of two squares.
We set a to zero and b to the integer square root of c, giving the widest possible range.
We loop while a is no greater than b, so each pair is checked only once.
We compute total as a squared plus b squared, the value of the current pair.
We check whether total equals c, which would mean we found a valid pair.
In that case we return true immediately because the answer is confirmed.
If total is less than c, the sum is too small and we need something larger.
So we raise a by one, which increases the sum.
Otherwise total is greater than c, meaning the sum is too big.
So we lower b by one, which decreases the sum.
If the pointers cross without a match, we return false since no pair exists.

summary-ranges.hook: Compress a sorted list into runs of consecutive numbers.
summary-ranges.ask: Given a sorted list of unique integers, describe it with the fewest ranges. Write a range as a->b, or just a when it holds one number.
summary-ranges.exampleWhy: Runs are 0 to 2, 4 to 5, 7 alone, and 9 to 10.

brute.idea: Walk every integer from the smallest to the largest value, opening and closing ranges by set membership.
steps: Put all numbers in a set
Walk every value from min to max + 1
Present: open a range
Missing: close the open range
brute.whySlow: Two numbers like -2^31 and 2^31 - 1 force about four billion steps, though the list has two items.

optimal.insight: Only the list matters, not the gaps. Mark where a run starts, extend while the next number is exactly one more, then emit it.
steps: Mark start at nums[i]
Extend i while next is one more
Emit a or a->b
Continue after the run

codeNotes.match: while i + 1 < len(nums) and nums[i + 1] == nums[i] + 1:

pitfalls: Empty input returns an empty list.
Check i + 1 bounds before reading nums[i + 1].

say.intro: Summary Ranges. We get a sorted list of unique numbers. We describe it with as few ranges as possible. Zero, one, two, four, five, seven, nine, ten becomes zero to two, four to five, seven on its own, and nine to ten.
say.brute: Here's a tempting approach. Walk every integer from the smallest value to the largest. Check each one against a set. Open a range when a number is present, close it when one is missing. It's correct. So what's wrong? The cost depends on the value span, not the list. Two numbers far apart could mean four billion steps.
say.insight: Here's the thing. We never need to look at the gaps. Only neighbors in the list matter. A run keeps going exactly while the next number is one more than the current one. So remember where the run starts. Push forward while the numbers stay consecutive. Then write the run out, and start the next one.
say.anim: We start with nums 0,1,2,4,5,7,9,10 and an empty result list. Start marks the beginning of a run, here 0, and we extend while numbers increase by one. i reaches 2, the run stops since 4 is not 3, so we record 0 to 2. A new run begins at 4, extends to 5, then breaks, so we append 4 to 5. Start becomes 7, but 9 isn't 8, so this single number run just appends 7. Start is 9, extends to 10 since they're consecutive, giving us 9 to 10. Index 8 exceeds the list length, so the loop ends and we return the result. The final answer is 0 to 2, 4 to 5, 7, and 9 to 10.
say.code: Let's walk the code. A new run begins, so record start as the current number. Then extend i while the next number is exactly one more. Now, did the run hold just one number? Append it alone. Otherwise it's a multi number run. Append start, an arrow, and the current number. Then step past the run.
say.outro: Linear time, one pass. The pattern is two pointers marking the start and end of each consecutive run.

summary-ranges.title: Summary Ranges
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container the interview platform expects for our method.
The method summaryRanges takes the sorted list of unique integers and returns a list of range strings.
We create an empty list called res to collect the finished range strings.
We set i to zero so we begin scanning at the first number.
The outer loop keeps running while i is still inside the list, handling one range per pass.
We remember the number at position i as start, the beginning of a new run.
The inner loop checks whether a next number exists and equals the current one plus one.
If the run continues, we advance i so it ends up on the last number of the run.
Now we check whether the run's last number equals start, meaning the run holds just one number.
In that case we append start as a plain string, since a single number needs no arrow.
Otherwise the run covers several numbers, so we take the other branch.
We append a string showing start, an arrow, and the last number of the run.
We move i one past the run's end so the next pass begins a fresh run.
Once every number is covered, we return the list of range strings.

trapping-rain-water-ii.hook: Rain on a 3D landscape: water escapes through the lowest point of the wall around it.
trapping-rain-water-ii.ask: Given a grid of heights, return the total volume of rain water the landscape can hold, where water can escape off any edge of the grid.
trapping-rain-water-ii.exampleWhy: The wall is height 3 all around, so the inner cells fill to 3: 2 units plus 1 unit.

brute.idea: Guess each inner water level as infinity, then repeatedly lower it to the lowest neighbor level until nothing changes.
steps: Border levels = their heights
Inner levels start at infinity
Level = max(height, lowest neighbor level)
Repeat until stable, sum the differences
brute.whySlow: A long winding path can need m · n full sweeps; on a 200 by 200 grid that is over a billion cell updates.

optimal.insight: Water level is set by the lowest point of the surrounding wall. Grow inward from the border, always from the lowest wall cell, using a min-heap.
steps: Push all border cells into a min-heap
Pop the lowest wall cell
Each unseen neighbor below it holds the difference
Push neighbor with height max(wall, its own)
Repeat until the heap is empty

codeNotes.match: if r in (0, m - 1) or c in (0, n - 1):
codeNotes.note: The border is the first wall
Fill up to the wall height

pitfalls: Push max(wall, height), not the raw height, or water levels drop wrongly.
The 1-D two-pointer trick does not work in 2-D.

say.intro: Trapping Rain Water Two. Now the landscape is a grid of heights. Water can escape off any edge. How much water does it hold? In our grid, a wall of height three surrounds two inner cells, heights one and two. They hold two units and one unit. Three in total.
say.brute: Okay, so a brute force. Set each border level to its height, and every inner level to infinity. Then sweep the grid. Lower each inner level to the larger of its own height and its lowest neighbor's level. Repeat until nothing changes. It does converge. But a winding path can need a full sweep per cell. That's quadratic in the grid size.
say.insight: Here's the thing. Water in a basin only rises to the lowest point of the wall around it. Anything higher leaks out there. So treat the border as the wall. Always grow inward from its lowest cell, using a min heap. A neighbor below that wall holds the difference. Then it joins the wall, at the wall's height.
say.anim: We start with a three by four height map, mostly walls of height three with a dip inside. All border cells get pushed into the min-heap and marked seen, since they can't trap water. We pop the smallest border height, three, and check its unseen inner neighbor. Cell one one has height one, so water rises to fill it up to three, adding two units. Next we examine cell one two, height two, adding one more unit of trapped water. The heap keeps popping the lowest wall so far, expanding inward one cell at a time. Eventually every inner cell is visited and the heap empties out completely. The function returns water equal to three, the total trapped rainwater.
say.code: Let's walk the code. Push every border cell into a min heap. The border is the first wall. Then pop the lowest cell, because the lowest wall point leaks first. Look at each unseen neighbor inside the grid. Fill it up to the wall height, adding the difference if it's positive. Then the neighbor joins the wall, pushed with the larger of the two heights.
say.outro: m n log of m n time. The pattern is a min heap growing inward from the boundary. Think of it as a Dijkstra style flood.

trapping-rain-water-ii.title: Trapping Rain Water II
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container the problem expects for our method.
The method takes the grid of heights and returns the total trapped water as an integer.
We read the number of rows as m and the number of columns as n.
We build a grid of false flags called seen to track which cells have already been queued.
We start with an empty heap that will hold wall cells ordered by their effective height.
We loop over every row of the grid to find border cells.
Inside each row we loop over every column, so we visit every cell once.
A cell is on the border if its row or column is the first or last.
We push each border cell onto the min-heap with its height and position, since water escapes from there.
We mark that border cell as seen so we never add it again.
We start the water total at zero before expanding inward.
We keep going while the heap still has wall cells to process.
We pop the lowest wall cell, whose height h is the lowest current barrier around the unexplored area.
We look at the four neighbors of this cell: down, up, right and left.
For each neighbor that is inside the grid and not yet seen, we continue processing it.
We mark the neighbor as seen so it is handled only once.
Water above the neighbor rises to h, the lowest wall, so we add h minus its height if positive.
We push the neighbor with its effective height, the larger of h and its own height, as the new wall level.
After the heap empties, we return the total water collected.

unique-length-3-palindromic-subsequences.hook: Count distinct three-letter palindromes hiding in a string, without checking every triple.
unique-length-3-palindromic-subsequences.ask: Given a string, count how many different length three palindromes, like aba, can be formed as subsequences. Each distinct palindrome counts once, however many ways it appears.
unique-length-3-palindromic-subsequences.exampleWhy: bbb, bcb, bab and aba can all be picked in order from bbcbaba.

brute.idea: Try every index triple i < j < k with matching ends, and add the three letters to a set.
steps: Pick i < j < k
Ends equal? s[i] == s[k]
Add s[i] s[j] s[k] to a set
Return the set size
brute.whySlow: 100,000 letters means about 10^14 triples, hopelessly slow.

optimal.insight: A palindrome x?x is possible exactly when some letter sits between the first and last x. Use the outermost pair: distinct letters between them.
steps: For each letter in the string
Find its first and last index
Count distinct letters strictly between
Add that to the answer

codeNotes.note: Need room for a middle letter
Each distinct middle is one palindrome

pitfalls: Count distinct palindromes, not ways to pick them.
The middle letter may equal the ends, as in bbb.

say.intro: Unique Length Three Palindromic Subsequences. We count the different three letter palindromes we can pick, in order, from a string. Each one counts once, however many ways it shows up. In b b c b a b a there are four. B b b, b c b, b a b, and a b a.
say.brute: The brute force tries every triple of positions, in order. When the first and last letters match, it adds that three letter string to a set. At the end, it returns the set's size. Correct? Yes. But it's cubic. A hundred thousand letters means about ten to the fourteen triples.
say.insight: Think about what a three letter palindrome is. An outer letter, any middle letter, then the outer letter again. Now fix the outer letter. Which pair should we use? The widest one, its first and last occurrence. That leaves the most room. Every distinct letter between them gives exactly one palindrome. There are at most twenty six outer letters.
say.anim: We start with count zero and the string bbcbaba, looping through its distinct letters in order. For letter a, first occurs at index four and last at index six. Since the gap is more than one, we count distinct letters between them, adding one, making count one. For letter b, first is at index zero and last at index five. Letters between them give three distinct values, raising count to four. For letter c, first and last are both at index two, so no middle characters exist. The loop ends and the function returns the final count. The answer is four unique palindromic subsequences found in bbcbaba.
say.code: Let's walk the code. Loop over each distinct letter. There are at most twenty six. Find its first and last positions, the widest pair. Is there room for a middle letter between them? Then count the distinct letters in that slice. Each distinct middle is one palindrome. Add it to the total, and return.
say.outro: Twenty six passes over the string, so linear time. The pattern is hashing. Fix the outer letter, and count distinct middles with a set.

unique-length-3-palindromic-subsequences.title: Unique Length-3 Palindromic Subsequences
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container the problem expects for our method.
This method takes the string s and returns an integer, the number of unique length three palindromic subsequences.
We start count at zero to accumulate the total number of distinct palindromes found.
We loop over each distinct letter in s, treating it as the outer letter of a palindrome; sorting only gives a stable order.
For this letter we find its first and last positions in the string, giving the widest possible outer pair.
We only continue if the last position is at least two past the first, so something sits between them.
We add the number of distinct letters strictly between those positions, since each one gives a different palindrome with this outer letter.
Finally we return count, the total of unique palindromes across all outer letters.

vertical-order-traversal-of-a-binary-tre.hook: Read a tree column by column, top to bottom, breaking ties by value.
vertical-order-traversal-of-a-binary-tre.ask: Give each node a row and column: the root is at (0, 0), a left child goes down and left, a right child down and right. Return the values column by column, sorted by row, then by value.
vertical-order-traversal-of-a-binary-tre.exampleWhy: 5 and 6 share row 2, column 0, so they appear in value order after the root 1.

brute.idea: Find the column range, then for each column walk the whole tree collecting nodes in that column and sort them.
steps: One walk to find all columns
For each column, walk the whole tree
Sort that column by row, value
brute.whySlow: A tree leaning one way has n columns, so n full walks: a thousand nodes means a million visits.

optimal.insight: Record every node once as a tuple (col, row, value). One sort puts them in exactly the required order; then group by column.
steps: DFS records (col, row, val)
Sort all tuples once
Start a new list when col changes
Append values in order

codeNotes.note: New column starts a new list

pitfalls: Same row and column ties sort by value, so plain BFS order is not enough.
Sort by row before value, or a deep small value jumps ahead.

say.intro: Vertical Order Traversal of a Binary Tree. Every node gets a row and a column. Left children step one column left. Right children step one column right. We list columns left to right, each one top to bottom, and ties go by value. For one through seven, five and six share a spot. So they come in value order.
say.brute: Okay, so a brute force first walks the tree to learn which columns exist. Then, for each column, it walks the entire tree again. It collects the nodes in that column and sorts them. It works. But what if the tree leans to one side? Then there are as many columns as nodes. That's n full walks, quadratic.
say.insight: Here's the thing. Visit every node once, and write down a tuple: column, row, value. Now look at the order we need. Column first, then row, then value. That's exactly plain tuple order. So one sort does all the work. Then walk the sorted list, and start a new group whenever the column changes.
say.anim: We start a depth first search from root value one at row zero, column zero. Moving left to node two, row one, column negative one, then further left to node four. Back up, we visit node five at row two, column zero, recording its position. Now exploring the right side, visiting node three, then its children six and seven. All nodes are collected as column, row, value tuples, then sorted by column first. We walk the sorted list, starting a new group whenever the column changes. Column zero gathers values one, five, and six, ordered correctly by row. The final vertical order traversal is four, two, one five six, three, seven.
say.code: Let's walk the code. The search appends column first, because column sorts first. Then row, then value. A left child goes down and left, to column minus one. A right child goes down and right. Then sort the list, so it's column, then row, then value. Finally walk it. A new column starts a new list, and each value is appended.
say.outro: n log n time, linear space. The pattern is trees. Traverse once with coordinates, then let a sort do the ordering.

vertical-order-traversal-of-a-binary-tre.title: Vertical Order Traversal of a Binary Tree
lineNotes: We define a Solution class that holds the method for solving the vertical order traversal problem.
The verticalTraversal method takes the root of a binary tree and returns a list of column lists.
We start with an empty list called nodes to collect a tuple for every node in the tree.
We define a helper function dfs that walks the tree while tracking each node's row and column.
If the current node is empty, we have reached past a leaf and there is nothing to record.
So we return immediately, which stops the recursion along this path.
We append a tuple of column, row, and value, putting column first so sorting groups by column.
We recurse into the left child, moving one row down and one column to the left.
We recurse into the right child, moving one row down and one column to the right.
We start the traversal at the root, which sits at row zero and column zero.
One sort orders tuples by column, then row, then value, which matches the required tie-breaking exactly.
We create an empty result list that will hold one inner list per column.
We set prev_col to none so the first node always starts a new column group.
We loop through the sorted tuples, unpacking each into column, row, and value.
When the column differs from the previous one, we have reached a new column group.
We append a fresh empty list to the result to hold values for this new column.
We update prev_col to the current column so following nodes in it join the same group.
We add the node's value to the last list in the result, which is the current column.
Finally we return the result, with columns ordered left to right and values properly sorted.

132-pattern.hook: Small, big, middle: find that shape in an array with one backward pass.
132-pattern.ask: Return true if there are indices i < j < k with nums[i] < nums[k] < nums[j]: a small number, then a big one, then one in between.

brute.idea: For each middle j, keep the smallest value to its left, then scan right for a value strictly between.
steps: Track the minimum before j
Scan every k after j
Check min < nums[k] < nums[j]
brute.whySlow: 200,000 numbers means about 20 billion pair checks in the worst case.

optimal.insight: Scan from the right with a decreasing stack. Anything popped by a bigger value is a valid 2; keep the largest as third. A value below third finishes it.
steps: Walk from right to left
Value below third? found a 1
Pop smaller values; each becomes third
Push the current value

codeNotes.note: Popped value has a bigger 3 before it

pitfalls: Comparisons are strict: equal values do not form a pattern.
Scanning left to right with a plain stack misses cases; go right to left.

say.intro: One Three Two Pattern. We look for three positions in order. The first is the smallest. The second is the largest. The third sits strictly in between. In three, five, zero, three, four, the values three, five, four make that shape. So the answer is true.
say.brute: A brute force fixes the middle element, the big one. It keeps the smallest value to its left. Then it scans everything to the right for a number strictly between. The running minimum already saves a loop. But it's still quadratic. Two hundred thousand numbers means billions of checks.
say.insight: Here's the trick. Walk from the right. Keep a stack that decreases from bottom to top. Now, when a bigger value arrives, it pops smaller ones. Why does that matter? Every popped value has a bigger number before it. So it's a valid middle value, the two. Keep the largest one as third. Any later number below third completes the pattern.
say.anim: We start with an empty stack and third set to negative infinity. Scanning from the right, we push four, then three, then zero onto the stack. Now x is five, bigger than everything on the stack, so popping begins. We pop zero, three, and four, each becoming the new third value in turn. After popping, third is four and the stack is empty, so we push five. Next x is three, which is less than third, which is four. This satisfies the one three two pattern, so the function returns true.
say.code: Let's walk the code. Third holds the best two seen so far, starting at minus infinity. We scan from the right. Is the current value below third? Then it's the one, and the pattern is complete. Otherwise, pop every smaller value. Each popped value has a bigger three before it, so save it as third. Then push the current value, a candidate three.
say.outro: Linear time and space. The pattern is a monotonic stack, scanning backwards to remember the best middle value.

132-pattern.title: 132 Pattern
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container the problem expects for our method.
The method find132pattern takes the list nums and returns true if a one three two pattern exists.
We start with an empty stack that will hold candidate big values while scanning from the right.
We set third to negative infinity, meaning no valid middle value, the two, has been found yet.
We loop over nums in reverse, so each x acts as a possible smallest value, the one.
If x is less than third, we have a small number before a big one and a middle one.
So we return true immediately, since the one three two pattern has been confirmed.
While the stack top is smaller than x, that top can be a valid two beneath the bigger x.
We pop that smaller value and store it in third, so the last popped is the largest such two.
We push x onto the stack, keeping the stack decreasing from bottom to top as a candidate three.
If the loop finishes without finding any x below third, we return false because no pattern exists.

apply-operations-to-maximize-score.hook: Each element wins some subarrays. Count them, then spend k picks on the biggest winners.
apply-operations-to-maximize-score.ask: Start with score 1. Up to k times, pick a new subarray and multiply the score by its element with the most distinct prime factors, leftmost on ties. Return the best score modulo 10^9 + 7.
apply-operations-to-maximize-score.exampleWhy: 9 wins [9], [9, 3] and [9, 3, 8]. Spending both operations on it gives 9 · 9 = 81.

brute.idea: List every subarray, find its winning element by scanning, then multiply the k largest winners.
steps: Compute prime scores
For every subarray, scan for its winner
Sort winners, largest first
Multiply the top k
brute.whySlow: With 100,000 numbers there are five billion subarrays before even scanning them.

optimal.insight: Element i wins every subarray between the previous score ≥ its own and the next strictly greater score. Monotonic stacks find both bounds; then spend k on the largest values.
steps: Prime score of every number
Monotonic stack: left and right bounds
Wins = (i - left) · (right - i)
Largest values first, take min(k, wins)
Fast power modulo 10^9 + 7

codeNotes.note: Leftover x is one more prime
Strictly bigger score ends its reign
Score at least as big blocks left

codeNotes.match: res = res * pow(nums[i], take, MOD) % MOD

pitfalls: Ties go left: block with >= on the left, > on the right.
take can be huge; use pow with a modulus, not a loop.

say.intro: Apply Operations to Maximize Score. Each operation picks a new subarray. We multiply our score by its element with the most distinct prime factors, leftmost on ties. With eight, three, nine, three, eight and two operations, the best is nine times nine. Eighty one.
say.brute: The brute force lists every subarray. It scans each one to find the winner. Then it sorts all the winners, largest first, and multiplies the top k. It's correct. But there are quadratically many subarrays, and each scan is linear. That's cubic. A hundred thousand numbers is hopeless.
say.insight: Let's flip the question. How many subarrays does each element win? Element i wins while the subarray stays between two walls. On the left, the previous element whose prime score is at least as big. On the right, the next one with a strictly bigger score. A monotonic stack finds both walls in one pass. Then spend k greedily, largest values first.
say.anim: We start with nums 8, 3, 9, 3, 8 and k equals 2, computing prime scores for each. For 8, we factor out 2 twice, giving it a prime score of 1. Similarly, 3 and 9 each reduce to a prime score of 1. All scores equal 1, so left and right boundary arrays start as defaults before the stack scan. Since no score is strictly greater than another, every index just gets pushed without popping. Final left bounds are negative one, 0, 1, 2, 3 with right bounds all staying at 5. Sorting by value descending, index 2 holding 9 is processed first, taking both available operations. Multiplying 9 squared gives 81, using up all of k and ending the loop. The function returns 81 as the final maximized score.
say.code: Let's walk the code. Prime score uses trial division. Notice any leftover x above one is one more prime. Next, the stack. A strictly bigger score ends an element's reign, setting its right bound. Whatever's left on the stack has a score at least as big. That blocks the left. Wins are left distance times right distance. Finally, fast modular power multiplies in each value.
say.outro: The pattern is a monotonic stack counting each element's reach. Then a greedy choice of the biggest values finishes it.

apply-operations-to-maximize-score.title: Apply Operations to Maximize Score
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, as required by the problem's submission format.
The maximumScore method takes the list nums and the number of allowed operations k, and returns the best score.
We set MOD to ten to the ninth plus seven, since the final answer must be reported modulo that prime.
We store the length of nums in n for use in the array setup and loops.
We define a helper that computes the number of distinct prime factors of a number.
We start the count at zero and begin trial division with the smallest prime candidate, two.
We loop while p squared is at most x, because any remaining factor beyond that must be a single prime.
If p divides x evenly, then p is a new distinct prime factor.
So we increase the score by one for this prime.
We then keep dividing out p so it is counted only once.
Each division reduces x by one factor of p.
We move on to the next candidate divisor.
If x is still above one, what remains is a leftover prime, so we add one for it and return.
We compute the prime score for every element of nums and store them in scores.
We set left to negative one and right to n for every index, meaning no bound found yet.
We create an empty stack that will hold indices with non-increasing prime scores.
We scan each index from left to right.
While the stack top has a strictly smaller score than the current index, the current one is its next strictly greater element.
We pop that index and record the current index as its right boundary.
If the stack still has something, its top has a score at least as large as ours.
That top index becomes our left boundary, since ties go to the leftmost element.
We push the current index onto the stack to continue the scan.
We start the result at one, the initial score.
We visit indices in order of decreasing value of nums, so the biggest multipliers get used first.
The number of subarrays where this element wins is the left span times the right span, capped by the remaining k.
We multiply the result by the element raised to take, using modular exponentiation to keep numbers small.
We subtract the operations we just used from k.
If no operations remain, we can stop early.
We break out of the loop since nothing more can be applied.
We return the final score modulo ten to the ninth plus seven.

array-reduce-transformation.hook: Write reduce yourself: fold an array into one value, step by step.
array-reduce-transformation.ask: Given numbers, a reducer function fn, and a starting value init, apply val = fn(val, x) to each number in order, starting from init. Return the final val, or init for an empty array.

brute.idea: Recursive version: reduce the rest of the array, starting from fn(init, first element).
steps: Empty array? return init
Apply fn to init and nums[0]
Recurse on nums[1:]
brute.whySlow: Each call copies the remaining slice, and recursion depth n overflows the stack on long arrays.

optimal.insight: A reduce is just an accumulator. Start it at init and feed it every element in order; one loop, no copies, no recursion.
steps: val = init
For each x: val = fn(val, x)
Return val

codeNotes.note: Test harness passes JavaScript source text

pitfalls: Do not skip init or seed with nums[0]; empty arrays must return init.

say.intro: Array Reduce Transformation. We rebuild reduce by hand. We get numbers, a reducer function, and a starting value. Each number gets fed into the function, along with the running value. With one through five, a reducer that adds each square, and a start of zero, we get fifty five.
say.brute: Here's a recursive version. Empty array? Return the starting value. Otherwise, apply the function to the start and the first number. Then recurse on the rest. It's correct. So what's the problem? Each call copies the remaining slice. That's quadratic. And a long array overflows the call stack.
say.insight: Here's the thing. Reduce is just an accumulator. Start it at the initial value. Then walk the array once. Each step, replace the accumulator with the function applied to it and the current element. No copies. No recursion. And notice, an empty array naturally returns the initial value.
say.anim: We start with the array one through five and the string function sum, init is zero. The code parses the string, extracting arguments accum and curr, then the return body. It builds a real lambda from that text, so fn now squares curr and adds it to accum. Val starts at init, zero, before looping through every number in the array. With x equal to one, val updates from zero to one, accumulating the squared term. Next x is two, so val jumps from one to five, adding two squared. X becomes three, pushing val from five to fourteen as the pattern continues. After processing all elements, val reaches fifty five, which is the final returned answer.
say.code: Let's walk the code. Our test harness hands the reducer over as JavaScript source text. So the first lines turn it into a small Python function. Then the accumulator starts at init. For each number, we fold it in. Val becomes the function applied to val and that number. Return val. With an empty array, that's just init.
say.outro: Linear time, constant space. The pattern is the simplest one there is. A single left to right pass with an accumulator.

array-reduce-transformation.title: Array Reduce Transformation
lineNotes: We define a Solution class that holds the reduce method for this problem.
The reduce method takes the numbers, a reducer function fn, and an initial value init, returning an integer.
If fn arrives as a string of source code instead of a callable, we need to convert it first.
We pull out the parameter list by slicing the text between the opening and closing parentheses.
We extract the function body by slicing the text after the word return up to the final semicolon.
We build a lambda from those arguments and body using eval, and replace fn with that callable.
We set val, our accumulator, to the starting value init.
We loop through each number x in nums, in the given order.
We update val by calling fn with the current val and x, folding each element into the accumulator.
We return val, which is the final result, or simply init when nums is empty.

battleships-in-a-board.hook: Count ships on a grid in one pass, without marking anything.
battleships-in-a-board.ask: A grid holds X for ship cells and dots for water. Ships are straight horizontal or vertical lines and never touch each other. Return how many ships there are.
battleships-in-a-board.exampleWhy: One single-cell ship top left, one vertical ship on the right, one horizontal ship bottom left.

brute.idea: Treat ships as islands: for each unvisited X, flood fill its whole ship and count one.
steps: Scan every cell
Unvisited X: count a ship
Flood fill to mark its cells
brute.whySlow: Same time, but it needs a visited set and a stack as large as the grid; the follow-up wants constant space.

optimal.insight: Every ship has exactly one top-left cell: an X with no X above it and no X to its left. Count those heads.
steps: Scan cells row by row
Skip water
Skip X with X above
Skip X with X to the left
Count the rest

codeNotes.note: Part of a vertical ship above
Part of a horizontal ship left

pitfalls: This only works because ships never touch; general islands need a flood fill.

say.intro: Battleships in a Board. The grid has X for ship cells and dots for water. Ships are straight lines, and no two ships touch. How many ships are there? In our board, three. A single cell top left, a vertical ship on the right, and a horizontal ship along the bottom.
say.brute: The general approach treats each ship as an island. Scan the grid. When we hit an unvisited X, count a ship and flood fill all its cells. Is that slow? Honestly, no. It's already linear time. What it costs is memory. A visited set and a stack as big as the grid. And the follow up wants constant space.
say.insight: Here's the thing. Ships are straight and never touch. So each ship has exactly one head, its top left cell. When is a cell a head? It's an X, the cell above isn't an X, and the cell to its left isn't an X. So we just count heads. No marking, no extra memory.
say.anim: We start with count at zero and scan the board row by row for ship cells. At row 0, column 0 we find an X with nothing above or left, so it counts as a new ship. Columns 1 and 2 in row 0 are empty, so we skip them and keep scanning. At row 0, column 3 we find another X with no X to its left, counting as a second ship. Row 1 cells are mostly dots or have an X directly above, so none are counted. In row 2, column 0 is an X with nothing above or left, giving a third ship. Column 1 is an X but has a left neighbor X, so it is skipped as part of the same ship. The loop finishes and the function returns the final count of three battleships.
say.code: Let's walk the code. Loop over every cell. Water? Nothing to count, skip it. X above? Then it's part of a vertical ship, so skip. X to the left? Part of a horizontal ship, skip. Anything that survives is the head of a new ship. Add one, and return the count.
say.outro: Linear time, constant space. The pattern is a grid problem solved by counting one representative per ship.

battleships-in-a-board.title: Battleships in a Board
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container the interview platform expects for our method.
The method countBattleships takes the board, a grid of X and dot characters, and returns the number of ships.
We start count at zero, and it will track how many ship heads we find.
We loop over every row index of the board, going from top to bottom.
Inside each row we loop over every column index, so we visit every cell in the grid.
If the current cell is not an X, it is water and cannot be a ship head.
So we continue straight to the next cell without doing any more checks.
If the row is not the first and the cell above is an X, this cell continues a vertical ship.
In that case we skip it, since the ship's head was already counted higher up.
If the column is not the first and the cell to the left is an X, this cell continues a horizontal ship.
We skip it too, because the head of that ship sits further left and was counted already.
Reaching here means an X with no X above or left, so it is a new ship's top-left head and we add one.
After scanning the whole grid, we return count as the total number of ships.

best-time-to-buy-and-sell-stock-ii.hook: Unlimited trades sounds hard to plan. It is actually the easiest stock problem of all.
best-time-to-buy-and-sell-stock-ii.ask: You get daily stock prices. You may buy and sell as often as you like, holding at most one share at a time. Return the largest total profit you can make.
best-time-to-buy-and-sell-stock-ii.exampleWhy: Buy at 1, sell at 5 for 4. Buy at 3, sell at 6 for 3. Total profit 7.

brute.idea: Try every plan: from each day, either skip it or buy and sell on some later day, then recurse on the rest.
steps: Start at day i with no share
Skip day i, or buy at i and sell at j
Recurse from day j
Keep the best total
brute.whySlow: The number of buy and sell plans doubles with each day; thirty days is already about a billion plans.

optimal.insight: Any profitable rise from a low to a high equals the sum of its daily up-steps. So just collect every positive day-to-day gain.
steps: Walk days 1 to n-1
If today beats yesterday, add the difference
Ignore every drop
Return the running total

pitfalls: Selling and rebuying the same day is allowed, so splitting long climbs costs nothing.
Do not hunt for valleys and peaks with nested loops; the one-day sum is identical.

say.intro: Okay, so we get daily stock prices. We can trade as many times as we like, but we hold at most one share. With seven, one, five, three, six, four, we buy at one and sell at five. Then buy at three and sell at six. That's a total of seven.
say.brute: The brute force explores every trading plan. From some day, we either skip it, or buy there and sell on a later, higher day. Then we repeat from the sell day and keep the best total. It's correct. But the number of plans roughly doubles with every extra day. That's exponential.
say.insight: Here's the trick. Any climb from a low to a high is just the sum of its small daily rises. Buying at one and selling at five earns the same as four tiny one day trades along the way. So we never need to plan. We just collect every day the price went up from yesterday.
say.anim: We start with prices seven, one, five, three, six, four, and profit at zero. At i equals one, price drops from seven to one, so no profit added. At i equals two, price rises from one to five, a gain of four. Profit becomes four after adding that rise, then we check i equals three. Price falls from five to three, so this day contributes nothing. At i equals four, price climbs from three to six, adding three more. Profit updates to seven, summing every upward step along the way. Final day drops from six to four, so loop ends and we return seven.
say.code: Here's the code. Profit starts at zero. It's the total of all gains we collect. We loop from the second day, comparing each day with yesterday. Only rising days matter. So whenever today is higher, we bank the one day gain. Drops are simply ignored. At the end, we return profit.
say.outro: Linear time, constant space. The pattern is greedy. Take every small gain, because together they add up to the best total.

best-time-to-buy-and-sell-stock-ii.title: Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock II
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the standard wrapper this problem expects for the answer.
The method maxProfit takes the list of daily prices and returns the largest total profit as an integer.
We start profit at zero, since with no gains collected yet we have made nothing.
We loop from the second day to the last, so each day can be compared with the day before.
We check whether today's price is higher than yesterday's, meaning there is an up-step worth collecting.
When price rose, we add that day's gain to profit, which is the same as buying yesterday and selling today.
After visiting every day, we return profit, which holds the sum of all positive daily gains.

best-time-to-buy-and-sell-stock-iii.hook: Two trades at most. Four running numbers track every possible state in one pass.
best-time-to-buy-and-sell-stock-iii.ask: Given daily stock prices, make at most two buy-then-sell transactions, never holding more than one share at once. Return the maximum total profit.
best-time-to-buy-and-sell-stock-iii.exampleWhy: Buy at 0, sell at 3 for 3. Then buy at 1, sell at 4 for 3 more. Total 6.

brute.idea: Pick a split day. The best single trade on the left plus the best single trade on the right. Try every split.
steps: For each split day k
Best one-trade profit in prices before k
Best one-trade profit from k onward
Keep the largest sum
brute.whySlow: Every split rescans the whole array; 100,000 days means about 10 billion price checks.

optimal.insight: Track four best balances: after first buy, first sell, second buy, second sell. Each day updates each from the one before it.
steps: buy1: best balance after first buy
sell1: best after selling it
buy2: buy again using sell1 money
sell2: final profit after second sale
Update all four every day

codeNotes.note: Holding is impossible before day one
Reinvest first profit into second buy
Best with up to two trades

pitfalls: sell2 already covers one trade only, since buy2 can rebuy on the same day.
Update order matters little here, but each state must read the previous state.

say.intro: Okay, now we're allowed at most two trades. Each time, we buy before we sell. With prices three, three, five, zero, zero, three, one, four, we buy at zero and sell at three. Then buy at one and sell at four. That earns six.
say.brute: Two trades never overlap, so some day splits them. The brute force tries every split. On the left, it finds the best single trade. On the right, the best single trade. Then it adds them. Each split rescans the prices. That's quadratic, around ten billion checks for a hundred thousand days.
say.insight: Here's a better way to think about it. We're always in one of four stages. Holding the first share. Done with the first sale. Holding the second share. Done with the second sale. For each stage, we track the best money balance so far. Each day, a stage either stays put, or advances from the one before it.
say.anim: We start with buy1 and buy2 at negative infinity, and both sells at zero. At price 3, buy1 becomes negative three, tracking the best first purchase cost. At price 5, sell1 updates to 2, our best profit from one transaction. At price 0, buy1 resets to 0, and buy2 climbs to 2 using sell1. At price 3, sell1 rises to 3, and sell2 jumps to 5 using buy2. At price 4, sell1 reaches 4, pushing sell2 up to 6 overall. The function returns sell2, the best possible profit from two transactions. The final answer shown is six, matching the expected output.
say.code: Here's the code. The buy values start at minus infinity, since holding is impossible before day one. Each day, buy one tracks the cheapest first purchase so far. Sell one is the best single completed trade. Buy two reinvests that first profit into a second buy. And sell two is the best with up to two trades.
say.outro: Linear time and constant space. The pattern is dynamic programming, with trade stages squeezed into four rolling values.

best-time-to-buy-and-sell-stock-iii.title: Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock III
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container the interview platform expects for our method.
The maxProfit method takes the list of daily prices and returns the best total profit from at most two transactions.
We start both buy balances at negative infinity, since no share has been bought yet and any real purchase beats that.
We start both sell balances at zero, because doing nothing yields zero profit and that is the baseline.
We loop over each day's price, calling it p, and update all four balances in order.
The first buy balance keeps the better of its old value or spending p today, which is negative p.
The first sell balance keeps the better of its old value or selling today at p on top of the best first buy.
The second buy balance keeps the better of its old value or using first sell profit to buy again at p.
The second sell balance keeps the better of its old value or selling today at p on top of the second buy.
We return the second sell balance, which already covers the cases of one transaction, two transactions, or none.

binary-tree-zigzag-level-order-traversal.hook: Level order, but every other row reads right to left. One flag flips the direction.
binary-tree-zigzag-level-order-traversal.ask: Given a binary tree, return its values level by level. The first level reads left to right, the next right to left, and the direction keeps alternating.
binary-tree-zigzag-level-order-traversal.exampleWhy: Level one is 1. Level two reversed is 3, 2. Level three reads left to right again.

brute.idea: For each depth, walk the whole tree collecting nodes at that depth, then reverse odd depths.
steps: Find the tree height
For each depth d, DFS the whole tree
Collect values exactly at depth d
Reverse the list when d is odd
brute.whySlow: Every level restarts from the root; a skewed tree of 2,000 nodes means about 4 million visits.

optimal.insight: A normal BFS already produces each level in order. Just reverse the row before saving it on every other level.
steps: Queue starts with the root
Pop exactly one level's worth of nodes
Push their children for the next level
Reverse the row when the flag says so
Flip the flag

codeNotes.note: Exactly the nodes of this level

pitfalls: Do not reverse the order children are queued; that scrambles deeper levels.
Freeze len(q) before the inner loop, or you will read into the next level.

say.intro: Okay, so we read the tree one level at a time. But we alternate direction. Left to right, then right to left, and so on. For the full tree one to seven, we get one. Then three and two. Then four, five, six, seven.
say.brute: A brute force approach handles one depth at a time. For depth zero, walk the whole tree and keep nodes at that depth. Then do it again for depth one, and so on. Reverse every odd row. It works. But every level restarts from the root. A tall, skinny tree costs about n times its height.
say.insight: Here's the thing. Breadth first search already visits the tree level by level, left to right. If we handle exactly one level per round, each row comes out in normal order. So zigzag is just a presentation detail. Reverse the row before saving it, on every other level. One true or false flag tracks the direction.
say.anim: We start with root node one, and the queue holds just that node. Node one is dequeued, added to the row, and its children two and three enqueued. Level one is left to right, so row one is saved as is. Now left_to_right flips to false, so this level will be reversed before saving. Nodes two and three are processed, appending their children four, five, six to the queue. Row two was two then three, but it gets reversed to three, two before saving. Left_to_right flips back to true, so nodes four through seven build row four, five, six, seven normally. Final zigzag result is one, then three two, then four five six seven.
