say.code: Here's the code. An empty tree gives an empty list. Otherwise, the queue starts with the root. Each round, we pop exactly the nodes of this level. First in, first out keeps the levels in order. We save the row, reversing every other one. Then we flip the direction for the next level.
say.outro: Linear time and linear space. The pattern is trees. Level order traversal, plus a direction flag.

binary-tree-zigzag-level-order-traversal.title: Binary Tree Zigzag Level Order Traversal
lineNotes: We define the Solution class that holds our zigzag level order traversal method.
The method takes the root of a binary tree and returns a list of lists of values.
First we check whether the tree is empty, since there would be nothing to traverse.
For an empty tree we simply return an empty list.
We set up the result list, a queue holding the root, and a flag saying the first level goes left to right.
We keep looping as long as the queue still has nodes waiting to be processed.
At the start of each level we create an empty row to collect that level's values.
We loop exactly as many times as nodes currently in the queue, which is the size of this level.
We remove the node at the front of the queue so we can process it.
We add that node's value to the current row.
If the node has a left child, we check for it here.
We put the left child on the queue so it gets processed in the next level.
If the node has a right child, we check for it here.
We enqueue the right child as well, keeping normal left to right order in the queue.
We save the row as is when going left to right, or reversed otherwise, into the result.
We flip the direction flag so the next level is read the opposite way.
Once the queue is empty, every level has been handled and we return the result.

bitwise-xor-of-all-pairings.hook: Millions of pairs, but XOR cancels in twos. Only parity of the lengths matters.
bitwise-xor-of-all-pairings.ask: XOR every number in nums1 with every number in nums2, giving one value per pair. Return the XOR of all those pair values.
bitwise-xor-of-all-pairings.exampleWhy: nums2 has even length, so nums1 cancels out. nums1 has odd length, so XOR of nums2 remains: 13.

brute.idea: Literally build every pair, XOR the two numbers, and fold all results into one running XOR.
steps: For each a in nums1
For each b in nums2
result ^= a ^ b
brute.whySlow: Both arrays can hold 100,000 numbers, so that is 10 billion pairs.

optimal.insight: Each nums1 value appears len(nums2) times. XORing a value with itself an even number of times gives zero.
steps: If len(nums2) is odd, XOR in all of nums1
If len(nums1) is odd, XOR in all of nums2
Otherwise that side cancels to zero

codeNotes.note: Each nums1 value used len(nums2) times

pitfalls: Mixing up which length controls which array: nums1 survives when nums2 is odd.

say.intro: Okay, so we pair every number in the first list with every number in the second. We XOR each pair. Then we XOR all those results together. For two, one, three against ten, two, five, zero, the answer is thirteen.
say.brute: The brute force does exactly what the statement says. Two nested loops visit every pair. It XORs the two numbers and folds the result into a running total. Short and correct. But with a hundred thousand numbers on each side, that's ten billion pairs. Far too slow.
say.insight: Two facts about XOR help. Order doesn't matter. And anything XORed with itself vanishes. Now, how often does each first list number show up? Once per element of the second list. If that count is even, it cancels completely. If it's odd, it survives exactly once. The same logic works the other way round.
say.anim: We start with nums1 as 2, 1, 3 and nums2 as 10, 2, 5, 0, result set to zero. Nums2 has even length, so we skip xoring nums1, since those pairings cancel out. Nums1 has odd length, three elements, so we do need to xor all of nums2. We loop through nums2, starting with b equal to ten, updating result each time. Result becomes ten after xoring with ten, then eight after xoring with two. Next b is five, making result thirteen, the running xor of nums2 values. Xoring with zero changes nothing, so result stays thirteen after the final step. The function returns result, giving the final answer of thirteen.
say.code: Here's the code. Each first list value is used once per second list element. So if the second list has odd length, that value survives, and we XOR it in. Then the symmetric check. If the first list has odd length, every second list value survives. Everything with an even count cancelled to zero.
say.outro: Linear time and constant space. The pattern is bit manipulation. XOR pairs cancel, so only odd counts matter.

bitwise-xor-of-all-pairings.title: Bitwise XOR of All Pairings
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container this problem's method lives in.
The method xorAllNums takes two lists of integers and returns a single integer, the combined XOR of all pairings.
We start result at zero, since XORing with zero leaves any value unchanged.
If the length of nums2 is odd, each value in nums1 appears an odd number of times, so it counts.
We loop over every value a in nums1, because each of them survives the cancellation.
We XOR each a into result, building up the XOR of all nums1 values.
If the length of nums1 is odd, each value in nums2 appears an odd number of times in the pairings.
We loop over every value b in nums2, since these values survive when nums1 has odd length.
We XOR each b into result, adding the contribution of nums2 to the answer.
We return result, which holds the XOR of all pair values without ever building the pairs.

check-if-n-and-its-double-exist.hook: Is some number exactly twice another? A set checks both directions as you walk.
check-if-n-and-its-double-exist.ask: Given an array, return true if there are two different positions i and j where arr[i] equals two times arr[j].
check-if-n-and-its-double-exist.exampleWhy: 14 is exactly double 7, and they sit at different positions.

brute.idea: Check every ordered pair of different positions and ask whether one value is double the other.
steps: Pick index i
Scan every index j not equal to i
arr[i] == 2 * arr[j]? return True
brute.whySlow: Every element is compared against every other one; 10,000 numbers means 100 million checks.

optimal.insight: When we reach x, its partner is either 2x or x/2. A set of earlier values answers both instantly.
steps: Walk the array once
Is 2x already seen? Found
Is x even and x/2 seen? Found
Otherwise add x to the set

codeNotes.note: Partner is double, or half if even
Add after checking, so x never pairs itself

pitfalls: Zero is its own double; checking before adding means it needs two zeros.
Only look for x/2 when x is even, or 7 would match 3.

say.intro: Okay, so we want two different positions where one value is exactly twice the other. In seven, one, fourteen, eleven, fourteen is double seven. So the answer is true.
say.brute: The brute force compares every pair of positions. For each index, it scans all the others and asks whether one is twice the other. It's simple and correct. But it's quadratic. Ten thousand numbers means a hundred million comparisons, mostly on pairs that could never match.
say.insight: Here's the thing. When we stand on a number, only two partners could work. Its double. Or its half, if it's even. So why search the array at all? A hash set of numbers we've already seen answers both questions instantly. And checking before adding means a number never pairs with itself.
say.anim: We start with an empty set called seen and the array of numbers. X is 7, but neither 14 nor its half are in the empty set, so we add it. Now seen holds 7, and x becomes 1, still no match found. Seen now holds 1 and 7, and x moves to 14. Checking 14, double is 28, but half is 7, which is already in seen. Since 7 is in seen, the condition is true, so we return true immediately. The final answer returned is true, confirming a valid double pair exists.
say.code: Here's the code. The seen set holds values we've met so far. For each number, the partner is its double, or its half if it's even. If either is in the set, we return true. Otherwise we add the number. Adding after checking means x never pairs itself. If the loop ends, no pair was found.
say.outro: Linear time with a hash set, and linear space. The pattern is arrays and hashing. When you know exactly what partner you need, look it up, instead of searching for it.

check-if-n-and-its-double-exist.title: Check If N and Its Double Exist
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which holds the method that solves the problem of finding a number and its double.
The method checkIfExist takes the array arr and returns a boolean telling us whether such a pair exists.
We start with an empty set called seen to remember every value we have already passed.
We loop through the array, handling each value x one at a time from left to right.
We check whether double x is already seen, or whether x is even and its half is already seen.
If either partner was seen earlier, we immediately return true because a valid pair of different positions exists.
Otherwise we add x to seen so later numbers can match against it, and only after checking so x never pairs with itself.
If the loop finishes without finding any pair, we return false.

construct-binary-tree-from-inorder-and-p.hook: The last postorder value is the root. Inorder tells you which nodes go left.
construct-binary-tree-from-inorder-and-p.ask: You get the inorder and postorder traversals of a binary tree with distinct values. Rebuild the tree and return its root.
construct-binary-tree-from-inorder-and-p.exampleWhy: Postorder ends with 3, the root. In inorder, 9 sits left of 3 and 15, 20, 7 sit right.

brute.idea: Take the root from the end of postorder, find it in inorder by linear search, split both lists, recurse.
steps: Root is postorder[-1]
Scan inorder to find the root
Slice left and right parts of both lists
Recurse on each part
brute.whySlow: Each node does a linear search and copies slices; a skewed 3,000-node tree costs millions of operations.

optimal.insight: Read postorder backwards: root, then right subtree, then left. A hash map gives each root's inorder position in O(1).
steps: Map each value to its inorder index
Pop roots from the end of postorder
Build the right subtree before the left
Inorder bounds say when a subtree is empty

codeNotes.match: idx = {v: i for i, v in enumerate(inorder)}

codeNotes.note: Right first: postorder reversed is root-right-left

pitfalls: Building left before right consumes the wrong postorder values.
pop() mutates postorder; copy it if the caller needs it intact.

say.intro: Okay, so we get two traversals of the same tree, inorder and postorder. We have to rebuild the tree. Postorder ends in three, so three is the root. In inorder, nine sits to its left. Fifteen, twenty and seven sit to its right.
say.brute: The brute force follows that idea directly. Take the last postorder value as the root. Scan inorder to find it. Slice both lists into left and right parts, and recurse. It's correct. But every node pays for a linear search and fresh slices. On a skewed tree, that's quadratic.
say.insight: Now, notice something. Read postorder from the back. It lists the root, then the whole right subtree, then the left. So if we pop from the end and always build right before left, each pop is exactly the next root we need. And a hash map from value to inorder index tells us instantly where each root splits its range.
say.anim: We build a hash map giving each inorder value its index, like 9 at 0 and 3 at 1. Popping the last postorder value, 3 becomes the root since postorder's end is always the root. Next we pop 20, making it root of the right subtree between indices 2 and 4. Popping 7, we find its inorder index 4, so it has no right children, only possibly left. Since lo exceeds hi on both sides, 7 becomes a leaf node returned upward. Back at 20, we build its left side, popping 15 as root for indices 2 to 2. With lo greater than hi both ways, 15 also becomes a leaf, completing 20's subtree. Finally we build the left side of root 3, popping 9 as a leaf with no children. The recursion completes, returning the tree rooted at 3 with children 9 and 20, and 20 having 15 and 7.
say.code: Here's the code. First, a map from value to inorder index, for instant root lookup. The helper takes an inorder range. An empty range means no subtree. Otherwise, the next root comes from postorder's end. We build the right side first, because reversed postorder is root, right, left. Then the left subtree.
say.outro: Linear time and space. The pattern is trees. Rebuild from traversals, with a hash map replacing the search.

construct-binary-tree-from-inorder-and-p.title: Construct Binary Tree from Inorder and Postorder Traversal
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container the interview platform expects for our method.
The buildTree method takes the inorder and postorder lists and returns the root of the rebuilt tree.
We build a hash map from each value to its inorder position so root lookups take constant time.
We define a helper called build that rebuilds the subtree covering inorder positions from lo to hi.
If lo is greater than hi, the range is empty, so there is no subtree to build.
In that empty case we return None, which becomes a missing child.
We pop the last postorder value, which is the root of the current subtree, and make a node from it.
We look up the root's inorder position as mid, which splits the range into left and right parts.
We build the right subtree first from mid plus one to hi, because postorder reversed gives root, then right.
Then we build the left subtree from lo to mid minus one, using the remaining postorder values.
We return the finished root node for this subtree to the caller.
We start the recursion over the full inorder range and return the root of the whole tree.

construct-k-palindrome-strings.hook: Each palindrome can hide at most one odd letter. Count odd letters and you are done.
construct-k-palindrome-strings.ask: Using every character of s exactly once, can you build exactly k non-empty palindromes? Return true or false.
construct-k-palindrome-strings.exampleWhy: Only b has an odd count, so we need at least 1 palindrome; 9 letters allow up to 9.

brute.idea: For every character, count its occurrences by rescanning the string, then count how many letters are odd.
steps: For each distinct letter c
Count c by scanning all of s
Tally letters with odd counts
Check odd ≤ k ≤ len(s)
brute.whySlow: Rescanning s for every letter costs up to 100,000 scans of 100,000 characters.

optimal.insight: A palindrome holds at most one odd-count letter, in its middle. So we need at least odd-count palindromes and at most len(s).
steps: Too few letters for k? False
Count each letter once
Count letters with odd frequency
Possible exactly when odd ≤ k

codeNotes.note: Odd letters need their own middle
Enough palindromes to host every odd letter

pitfalls: Forgetting k > len(s): you cannot make more non-empty strings than letters.

say.intro: Okay, so we must use every letter of a string to build exactly k palindromes. Can we do it? For annabelle with k equal to two, yes. For example, anna and elble.
say.brute: A brute force way to get letter counts takes each distinct letter, and rescans the whole string to count it. Then it tallies how many letters have odd counts. The final check is right. But rescanning the string for every new letter is quadratic in the worst case.
say.insight: Think about how a palindrome is built. Letters pair up across the middle. Only the single middle spot can hold an unpaired letter. So every letter with an odd count needs its own palindrome. If there are at most k odd letters, we can always split the pairs to reach exactly k. As long as k isn't bigger than the length.
say.anim: We start with s equal to annabelle and k equal to two, checking string length first. Counts are built for each letter: a and n and e and l appear twice, b appears once. We loop through these counts, checking each for an odd number of occurrences. Letter b has count one, an odd count, so odd increases to one. The remaining letters all have even counts, so odd stays at one. Finally we compare odd, which is one, against k, which is two. Since one is less than or equal to two, the function returns true.
say.code: Here's the code. First, each palindrome needs at least one letter. So if k is bigger than the length, return false. Next, count the frequency of every letter. Each odd letter needs its own middle, so we count those. Finally, we need enough palindromes to host every odd letter. Return whether odd is at most k.
say.outro: Linear time, constant space for lowercase letters. Odd letters set the minimum. The length sets the maximum.

construct-k-palindrome-strings.title: Construct K Palindrome Strings
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container the problem expects for our method.
The method canConstruct takes the string s and the number k, and returns true or false.
If k is larger than the length of s, we cannot make that many non-empty palindromes.
In that case we immediately return false, since every palindrome needs at least one character.
We count how many times each letter appears in s using a Counter.
We start a tally called odd at zero to track letters with odd counts.
We loop over each letter's count in the counter.
We check whether this count is odd, meaning it leaves a remainder of one when divided by two.
Each odd count adds one to odd, since that letter needs its own palindrome middle.
We return true only if odd is at most k, because each odd letter needs a separate palindrome.

contains-duplicate-ii.hook: Equal values close together. Keep only the last k numbers in a set.
contains-duplicate-ii.ask: Return true if two different positions i and j hold the same value and are at most k apart.
contains-duplicate-ii.exampleWhy: Each repeat is exactly 3 positions after its twin, which is more than k = 2.

brute.idea: For each index, look ahead at the next k positions for an equal value.
steps: Pick index i
Check i+1 up to i+k
Equal? return True
brute.whySlow: With 100,000 numbers and k near 100,000, that is billions of comparisons.

optimal.insight: Only the last k values can be a valid partner. A set holding exactly that window answers in O(1).
steps: Window set holds the previous k values
Current value already in window? True
Add it to the window
Evict the value that slid out

codeNotes.note: Values from the last k positions
Drop the value now too far back

pitfalls: Evict nums[i - k], not nums[i - k - 1]; off by one breaks the limit.
A map of last index works too: check i - last[x] ≤ k.

say.intro: Okay, so we need two equal values whose positions are at most k apart. In one, two, three, one, two, three with k equal to two, every repeat is three steps from its twin. That's too far. So the answer is false.
say.brute: The brute force takes each index and looks ahead at the next k positions for a match. The moment it finds one, it returns true. That's correct. But every number may do k comparisons. With a large k and a large input, that's billions of checks.
say.insight: Here's the thing. A partner only counts if it's within the last k positions. So keep a set holding exactly those last k values. That's a sliding window. Each new number asks the set, are you in here? Then it joins the window. And the value that's fallen too far behind leaves.
say.anim: We start with an empty window set and k equal to two. At index zero, value one isn't in the window, so we add it. At index one, value two is new too, giving window one and two. At index two, value three is added, but now window exceeds size k. We remove the oldest value, one, keeping only the last two elements. At index three, value one isn't in the current window, so it's added again. This pattern repeats for values two and three, always trimming the window to size two. No duplicates ever appear within the window, so the function returns false.
say.code: Here's the code. The window set holds values from the last k positions. For each number, if it's already in the window, we've found a close enough duplicate. Return true. Otherwise, x joins the window. If the window's too big now, we drop the value that's too far back.
say.outro: Linear time, with space bounded by k. The pattern is a fixed size sliding window backed by a hash set.

contains-duplicate-ii.title: Contains Duplicate II
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container this problem's method lives in.
The method takes a list of numbers and a distance k, and returns true or false.
We start with an empty set called window that will hold only the most recent values.
We loop through the numbers, getting both the position i and the value x at each step.
If x is already in the window, then an equal value appeared within the last k positions.
In that case we immediately return true, since we found a valid nearby duplicate pair.
Otherwise we add x to the window so later values can be compared against it.
If the window now holds more than k values, it has grown too large and must shrink.
We remove the value at position i minus k, the oldest one, so only the last k remain.
If the loop finishes without finding any close duplicate, we return false.

count-non-decreasing-subarrays-after-k-o.hook: Raising each element up to the running max is the cheapest fix. Slide from the right.
count-non-decreasing-subarrays-after-k-o.ask: For each subarray you may add 1 to elements, at most k times total. Count the subarrays that can be made non-decreasing this way.
count-non-decreasing-subarrays-after-k-o.exampleWhy: Of 21 subarrays, only the four starting [6, 3, 1] need more than 7 raises. 21 minus 4 is 17.

brute.idea: Fix each start. Extend right, raising each element to the running max, and stop once the cost passes k.
steps: For each start i
Extend j, tracking the running max
Cost grows by max - nums[j]
Count until cost exceeds k
brute.whySlow: For 100,000 numbers and huge k, that is about 5 billion window extensions.

optimal.insight: Cost only grows as a window widens, so walk the left edge leftward with a shrinking right edge. Group elements by their governing prefix max.
steps: Move left edge i from right to left
nums[i] absorbs smaller groups; cost rises
Groups are (max value, count) in a deque
While cost > k, drop the rightmost element
Add window length j - i + 1

codeNotes.note: Whole group now raised to nums[i]
Every end from i to j works

pitfalls: Use the prefix max of the subarray, not of the whole array.
The answer can exceed 32 bits; Python is fine, other languages need long.

say.intro: Okay, so each subarray may get up to k single increments. How many subarrays can become non decreasing? With six, three, one, two, four, four and k equal to seven, only four subarrays are too costly. They all start with six, three, one. That leaves seventeen.
say.brute: The cheapest fix raises each element to the largest value before it. So the brute force fixes a start and extends right. It keeps a running max, and adds the max minus each element to the cost. It stops once the cost passes k. That's quadratic. Billions of steps for big inputs.
say.insight: Here's the key. Widening a window never lowers its cost. So if the left edge moves left, the furthest valid right edge can only move left too. That's two pointers. To update the cost fast, group elements under the prefix max that governs them. A new left value swallows every smaller group, paying the gap times the group size.
say.anim: We start with cost, res zero, and j at the last index of the array. At i equals five, value four forms its own group, and res becomes one. At i equals four, value four merges with the existing group, keeping cost at zero and res at three. At i equals three, value two starts a new group, pushing res up to six. At i equals two, value one adds another group, growing res to ten. At i equals one, value three merges groups one and two into a group of three, raising cost to three and res to fifteen. At i equals zero, value six merges all groups into one of size six, pushing cost to sixteen, over the limit. The right edge j shrinks step by step, trimming the group until cost drops back to three, leaving res at seventeen, the final answer.
say.code: Here's the code. The new left edge moves leftward. Every group it swallows gets raised to its value, and we add that cost. Then we push one merged group, led by this value. While the cost is over k, we remove the rightmost element's raise and pull the right edge in. Every end from here to there works, so we add them.
say.outro: Linear time, thanks to amortised merging. The pattern is sliding window, paired with a monotonic deque of groups.

count-non-decreasing-subarrays-after-k-o.title: Count Non-Decreasing Subarrays After K Operations
lineNotes: We define the Solution class that holds the method for this problem.
This method takes the array nums and the budget k, and returns the count of valid subarrays.
We start with result zero, cost zero, and set j to the last index, the right edge of the window.
We create a double-ended queue to hold groups of values, each with a count of elements it governs.
We loop the left edge i from the last index down to zero, widening the window leftward.
We start a new group for nums at i, with a count of one for itself.
While the front group has a value no larger than nums at i, that group is now governed by this new element.
We pop that front group, reading its value v and its element count c.
Raising those c elements up to nums at i adds the difference times c to the cost.
We merge the popped group's count into the new group's count.
We push the new group with value nums at i and its merged count onto the front.
While the cost exceeds k, the window is too wide, so we must shrink the right edge.
Removing the element at j lowers the cost by the gap between its group's value and its own value.
We reduce the count of the last group by one since that element leaves the window.
If the last group has no elements left, we need to discard it.
We pop the empty group from the back of the queue.
We move j one step left to shrink the window.
Every right end from i through j gives a valid subarray starting at i, so we add j minus i plus one.
After processing all left edges, we return the total count.

count-primes.hook: Do not test numbers one by one. Cross out multiples and let the primes survive.
count-primes.ask: Given n, return how many prime numbers are strictly less than n.
count-primes.exampleWhy: Below 30 the primes are 2, 3, 5, 7, 11, 13, 17, 19, 23 and 29: ten of them.

brute.idea: For every number below n, try dividing by everything up to its square root. No divisor means prime.
steps: For each x from 2 to n-1
Try divisors 2 up to sqrt(x)
No divisor found? count it
brute.whySlow: For n = 5 million that is roughly 10 billion trial divisions.

optimal.insight: Sieve of Eratosthenes: each prime p crosses out its multiples, starting at p squared. Whatever is never crossed out is prime.
steps: Mark every number as prime
For p up to sqrt(n), if p is still prime
Cross out p², p² + p, ...
Count what remains marked

codeNotes.note: Primes past sqrt(n) cross nothing new

codeNotes.match: for m in range(p * p, n, p):

pitfalls: Strictly less than n: n itself is never counted.
Starting at 2p instead of p² is still correct, just slower.

say.intro: Okay, so given n, how many primes are strictly smaller than it? For thirty, the primes are two, three, five, seven, eleven, thirteen, seventeen, nineteen, twenty three and twenty nine. That's ten.
say.brute: The brute force checks each number on its own. For every value below n, it tries dividing by everything up to its square root. If nothing divides it, it's prime. That's correct. But for five million numbers, it adds up to around ten billion divisions.
say.insight: Let's flip the question. Instead of asking if each number has a divisor, let every prime cross out its own multiples. Start with everything marked prime. Each prime p crosses out p squared, then every pth number after. Why start at p squared? Smaller multiples were already crossed out by smaller primes. Whatever survives is prime.
say.anim: We start with n equal to thirty, and since it's at least three, we build a sieve. An is_prime array of thirty trues is created, with zero and one marked false immediately. P equals two, a prime, so we start crossing out its multiples from four onward. Four, six, eight, ten, and onward up to twenty eight get marked false as multiples of two. Now p equals three, still prime, so we cross out nine, twelve, fifteen, up through twenty seven. P equals four is skipped since it's already false, then p equals five crosses out twenty five. Finally we sum all the remaining true entries in the sieve to count primes. The function returns ten, confirming there are ten primes below thirty.
say.code: Here's the code. There are no primes below two, so tiny inputs return zero. Every number is assumed prime until crossed out. We only loop p up to the square root, because primes past that cross nothing new. Each prime starts at p squared, since smaller multiples are already crossed. The survivors are the primes, so we count them.
say.outro: Nearly linear time, n log log n, with one flag per number. The pattern is math: the sieve of Eratosthenes. Cross out composites, and the primes are what is left.

count-primes.title: Count Primes
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container for the method that LeetCode will call.
The method countPrimes takes n and returns how many primes are strictly less than n.
If n is less than three, there are no primes below it, so we handle that edge case first.
In that case we return zero right away, since zero and one are not prime and two is excluded.
We build a list of n entries, all true, assuming every number starts out as a possible prime.
We mark zero and one as false, because neither of them is a prime number.
We loop p from two up to the integer square root of n minus one, since larger factors are unnecessary.
We only act when p is still marked prime, because multiples of composites were already crossed out by smaller primes.
For each such p, we walk through its multiples starting at p squared, stepping by p, up to below n.
We mark each of those multiples as false, since each one has p as a factor and is composite.
Finally we sum the list, counting each true entry, which gives the number of primes below n.

count-the-number-of-powerful-integers.hook: The suffix is fixed. Only the prefix varies, so count prefixes digit by digit.
count-the-number-of-powerful-integers.ask: Count integers between start and finish that end with the digit string s and whose every digit is at most limit.
count-the-number-of-powerful-integers.exampleWhy: The prefix before 21 can be 0 to 33 using digits 0 to 3: 16 choices, all at most 3500.

brute.idea: Enumerate every number ending in s: prefix times 10^len(s) plus s. Check range and digits.
steps: For each prefix p up to finish / 10^L
Build x = p · 10^L + s
In range and all digits ≤ limit? count
brute.whySlow: finish can be 10^15 with a one-digit s: about 10^14 candidates.

optimal.insight: Count powerful numbers up to x by walking x's prefix digits: each smaller allowed digit frees all later positions, giving (limit+1)^rest options.
steps: Answer = count(finish) - count(start - 1)
Walk prefix digits of x left to right
Smaller digit d: add d · (limit+1)^remaining
Digit over limit: add (limit+1)^remaining, stop
All prefix digits kept: add 1 if x's tail ≥ s

codeNotes.note: Every allowed digit here is smaller
Range as difference of prefix counts

pitfalls: Count leading zero prefixes: s by itself is a valid number.
Compare the tail as equal-length strings, not as different-length numbers.

say.intro: Okay, so a number is powerful if it ends with a given digit string, and no digit goes over a limit. Our range is one to thirty five hundred, the limit is three, and the suffix is twenty one. The part before twenty one can be zero up to thirty three, using small digits. That's sixteen numbers.
say.brute: The brute force lists every number ending in the suffix. It tries each possible prefix and glues the suffix on. Then it checks the range and the digits. Fine for small ranges. But with a finish near ten to the fifteen and a short suffix, that's about a hundred trillion candidates.
say.insight: Here's the plan. Count powerful numbers up to x, then subtract the count below start. To count up to x, walk its prefix digits. Picking a smaller allowed digit at some position frees every later one. That gives limit plus one choices per free position. And a digit above the limit ends the walk.
say.anim: We want powerful integers between 1 and 3500, using suffix 21 and digit limit 3. We count powerful numbers up to 3500 by converting it to the string 3500. With two extra digits beyond the suffix length, we start scanning each prefix digit. At position 0, digit is 3, which is within the limit, so we add 12 to res. At position 1, digit is 5, which exceeds the limit of 3. Since this digit is too big, remaining positions are free, giving 16 total up to 3500. Now we count powerful numbers up to 0, which trivially returns 0. Subtracting gives 16 minus 0, so the final answer is 16.
say.code: Here's the code. We count the free prefix positions before the suffix. If a digit is above the limit, every allowed digit here is smaller, so we add all free choices and stop. Otherwise, we choose a smaller digit and leave the rest free. On an exact prefix match, the tail decides. The range is a difference of prefix counts.
say.outro: Logarithmic time in the range. The pattern is digit counting, a lightweight cousin of digit dynamic programming.

count-the-number-of-powerful-integers.title: Count the Number of Powerful Integers
lineNotes: We define the Solution class that holds the method for this problem.
The method takes start, finish, limit and the suffix string s, and returns the count of powerful integers.
We define a helper called count that returns how many powerful integers are at most x.
We convert x to a string t so we can walk through its digits one at a time.
If t is shorter than s, no number up to x can end with s.
So in that case we return zero immediately.
We set m to the number of prefix digits in t, which is its length minus the length of s.
We start the running result res at zero.
We loop over each prefix position of x from left to right.
We read the current digit d of x at this position.
If d is bigger than limit, we cannot match x here, so every allowed digit at this spot is smaller.
We then return res plus limit plus one raised to the remaining prefix positions, counting all free choices, and stop.
Otherwise each allowed digit smaller than d frees later positions, adding d times limit plus one to the power of the positions after this one.
After the loop, x's prefix is fully allowed, so we compare x's own last digits with s.
If that tail is at least s, then x itself with its prefix is powerful, so we add one.
We return the total count of powerful integers up to x.
The answer is the count up to finish minus the count up to start minus one, leaving only the range.

count-triplets-that-can-form-two-arrays-.hook: a equals b means the whole span XORs to zero. Then every middle split works.
count-triplets-that-can-form-two-arrays-.ask: Count triplets i < j ≤ k where the XOR of arr[i..j-1] equals the XOR of arr[j..k].
count-triplets-that-can-form-two-arrays-.exampleWhy: Spans 2,3,1 and 1,6,7 each XOR to zero, and each has 2 split points. Total 4.

brute.idea: Try every i, j, k, computing both XORs with running values as k grows.
steps: Pick i and j
Compute a = XOR of arr[i..j-1]
Grow k, keeping b = XOR of arr[j..k]
Count every a == b
brute.whySlow: With 300 numbers that is about 4.5 million triplets, far more than needed.

optimal.insight: a == b exactly when prefix[i] == prefix[k+1]. Each such pair gives k - i triplets, so track count and index sum per prefix.
steps: Keep a running prefix XOR
Per prefix value: how often, and index sum
Add count · k - indexSum for this k
Record the new prefix with index k+1

codeNotes.note: Sum of k - i over matches
This prefix ends at index k+1

pitfalls: Each zero-XOR span i..k gives k - i triplets, not one.
The O(n²) prefix pair scan is also accepted; mention it first.

say.intro: Okay, so we pick a span and split it at some point into a left part and a right part. We want their XORs to be equal. How many triplets work? In two, three, one, six, seven, there are four.
say.brute: The brute force tries every start, every split and every end. It keeps the left XOR as the split moves, and the right XOR as the end grows. Every match adds one. That's cubic. Millions of triplets for just a few hundred numbers.
say.insight: Here's the thing. Two values are equal exactly when their XOR is zero. So the left equals the right when the whole span XORs to zero. And then it doesn't matter where the split goes. Any of the k minus i splits works. A span XORs to zero when the prefix XOR before it equals the prefix XOR after it.
say.anim: We start with prefix zero and dictionaries tracking counts and index totals for each prefix value. At k equals zero, prefix becomes two, no match yet, so result stays zero. At k equals one, prefix becomes one, still no repeated prefix, result unchanged. At k equals two, prefix returns to zero, matching the initial prefix, adding two triplets. At k equals three, prefix becomes six, a new value, so result stays at two. At k equals four, prefix becomes one again, matching an earlier prefix, adding two more triplets. The loop finishes and the function returns the final result. The total count of valid triplets is four.
say.code: Here's the code. We seed the maps with the empty prefix at index zero. For each position k, we update the prefix XOR, covering everything up to k. Then we add the sum of k minus i over all matches, using the count and index sum stored for this prefix. Finally, this prefix gets recorded as ending at index k plus one.
say.outro: Linear time and space. The pattern is prefix XOR, the XOR twin of prefix sums.

count-triplets-that-can-form-two-arrays-.title: Count Triplets That Can Form Two Arrays of Equal XOR
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, as the problem platform expects for this function.
The method countTriplets takes the array arr and returns the number of valid triplets as an integer.
We make two dictionaries: count of how often each prefix XOR appeared, and total of their index sums, both seeded with prefix zero at index zero.
We start the running prefix XOR and the result both at zero.
We loop over the array, getting each index k and value x, treating k as the right end of the triplet.
We fold x into the prefix, so prefix now equals the XOR of everything up to index k.
For earlier equal prefixes at positions i, each adds k minus i triplets, so we add count times k minus the index sum.
We record that this prefix value has now been seen one more time.
We add k plus one to the index sum for this prefix, since the current prefix sits at position k plus one.
After the loop, we return the accumulated number of triplets.

counting-words-with-a-given-prefix.hook: One query, many words. Just check each word's start, nothing fancier needed.
counting-words-with-a-given-prefix.ask: Given a list of words and a string pref, return how many words begin with pref.
counting-words-with-a-given-prefix.exampleWhy: attention and attend begin with at; pay and practice do not.

brute.idea: For each word, generate every prefix into a set, then check whether pref is in it.
steps: For each word
Generate every prefix of the word
Is pref among them? count it
brute.whySlow: Same big O, but it builds every prefix of every word, doing up to L times more copying.

optimal.insight: A word starts with pref when its first len(pref) characters equal pref. Compare only that much.
steps: For each word
Compare its first len(pref) characters
Match? add one to the count

codeNotes.note: Stops after at most len(pref) chars

pitfalls: Use startswith, not in: the prefix must sit at the start.
A trie only pays off for many different prefix queries.

say.intro: Okay, a quick one. We get a list of words and a prefix. How many words start with that prefix? For pay, attention, practice and attend, with prefix a t, two words match. Attention and attend.
say.brute: A wasteful approach builds every prefix of every word and puts them in a set. Then it checks whether our prefix is there. The count comes out right. But for a long word, it creates and stores every prefix. Only one prefix length could ever matter. The rest is pure waste.
say.insight: Here's the thing. Only one length matters, the length of the given prefix. So for each word, compare just its first few characters with the prefix, and stop. For a single query, that's the least work possible. What about a trie? It only pays off when many different prefixes are asked against the same words.
say.anim: We start with count at zero and prefix set to at. First word pay is checked, but it doesn't start with at. Next word attention starts with at, so count becomes one. Practice is checked next, but it fails the prefix test. Attend also starts with at, so count increases to two. All words have been checked, so the loop ends here. The function returns two, matching the expected output.
say.code: Here's the code. The count holds matching words so far. We check every word once. The starts with check stops after at most the prefix length, and it bails out on the first mismatch. When it passes, count goes up by one. At the end, we return the total words with this prefix.
say.outro: Time is the number of words times the prefix length, with constant extra space. For a single query, a plain linear scan beats any fancy structure.

counting-words-with-a-given-prefix.title: Counting Words With a Given Prefix
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container this problem's method lives in.
This method takes the list of words and the prefix string, and returns an integer count.
We start a counter called count at zero, since no matching words have been found yet.
We loop over every word in the list, looking at one word at a time.
We check whether the current word starts with pref, which compares only the first few characters.
When the word matches, we add one to count to record another word with that prefix.
After checking every word, we return count as the total number of words beginning with pref.

cousins-in-binary-tree-ii.hook: Cousin sum equals level sum minus your own family. BFS gives both.
cousins-in-binary-tree-ii.ask: Replace every node's value with the sum of its cousins: nodes on the same depth with a different parent. Return the modified root.
cousins-in-binary-tree-ii.exampleWhy: Level three sums to 18. Siblings 1 and 10 sum 11, so they get 7. Node 7 gets 11.

brute.idea: Record each node's depth, parent and value. For each node, scan all nodes for same depth, different parent.
steps: DFS records depth, parent, value
For each node, scan every node
Same depth, other parent? add value
Write the sums back
brute.whySlow: A complete tree of 100,000 nodes has a level of 50,000; scanning it per node is billions of checks.

optimal.insight: Cousin sum = next level's total minus the sum of your siblings. A parent knows both its children, so it writes their values.
steps: Process the tree level by level
Sum all children of this level
Each parent adds its own children
Child value = level sum - family sum

codeNotes.note: Total of the whole next level
Everything on the level except siblings

pitfalls: Compute family before overwriting either child, or the second child sees a changed value.
Siblings are not cousins, and neither is the node itself.

say.intro: Okay, so we replace each node with the sum of its cousins. Cousins are nodes on the same level with a different parent. Here the bottom level is one, ten and seven. One and ten share a parent, so each gets seven. Seven gets one plus ten, eleven.
say.brute: The brute force records every node's depth, parent and value. Then for each node, it scans the whole list. It adds values at the same depth with a different parent. It works. But every node rescans everything. A level of fifty thousand nodes means billions of checks.
say.insight: Think about it this way. A node's cousins are everyone on its level, minus itself and its sibling. So the cousin sum is the level total, minus the family total. No searching needed. And if we go level by level, a parent can see both its children. So it computes their family sum and writes the answer straight into each child.
say.anim: The root value five becomes zero, since the root has no cousins. We scan root's children, four and nine, summing them to get next level total thirteen. Each child's new value is next level sum minus its own sibling pair, so four and nine both become zero. Now we sum the grandchildren, one, ten, and seven, giving next sum eighteen. Node four's children one and ten become seven each, since family sum was eleven. Node nine's single child seven becomes eleven, since its family sum was just seven. The last level has no children, so no further sums are computed. The final tree values are zero, zero, zero, seven, seven, and eleven, matching the expected output.
say.code: Here's the code. The root has no cousins, so it becomes zero. For each level, we first add up the total of the whole next level. Then, for each parent, siblings share this parent, so we sum its children. Each child becomes everything on the level except siblings. Then the children become the next level.
say.outro: Linear time and linear space. The pattern is level order traversal. Level total, minus family.

cousins-in-binary-tree-ii.title: Cousins in Binary Tree II
lineNotes: We define the Solution class that holds the method for this problem.
The method takes the root of the tree and returns the modified root.
The root has no cousins, so we set its value to zero right away.
We start a level list holding just the root, to process the tree one depth at a time.
We loop while the current level has nodes, moving down one depth each pass.
We reset next_sum to zero, to total the original values of the next level.
We walk through every node on the current level to collect its children's values.
For each node we look at both its left and right child.
We only handle a child if it actually exists.
We add that child's original value into next_sum, the total for the next level.
We prepare an empty list to hold the nodes of the next level.
We walk the current level again, this time to overwrite the children's values.
We compute family, the combined original value of this node's children, which are siblings of each other, treating missing children as zero.
We loop over this node's two children again to update them.
We skip any child that does not exist.
Each child's new value is the next level total minus its family sum, which equals its cousins' sum.
We add the updated child to next_level so we can process its children on the next pass.
We move down by making next_level the current level.
Once all levels are done, we return the root of the modified tree.

critical-connections-in-a-network.hook: An edge is critical if no back edge loops around it. Tarjan finds them all in one DFS.
critical-connections-in-a-network.ask: Servers are linked by undirected connections. Return every connection whose removal would leave some servers unable to reach others.
critical-connections-in-a-network.exampleWhy: 0, 1, 2 form a cycle, so any one link is spare. Server 3 hangs only on link 1-3.

brute.idea: Remove each connection in turn and BFS from server 0. If anyone becomes unreachable, that connection is critical.
steps: For each edge e
Build the graph without e
BFS from node 0
Not all reached? e is critical
brute.whySlow: 100,000 edges each trigger a full BFS: around 10 billion steps.

optimal.insight: In a DFS, low[v] is the earliest discovery time v's subtree can reach by a back edge. If low[v] > disc[u], edge u-v is a bridge.
steps: DFS, stamping discovery times
low[u] = min over children's low and back edges
Skip the edge back to the parent
low[child] > disc[u] means bridge

codeNotes.note: Do not count the edge we came by
Child cannot climb above u: bridge

pitfalls: Recursion depth can hit 100,000; raise the limit or use an iterative DFS.
With parallel edges, skip the parent edge by id, not by node.

say.intro: Okay, so some links are the only path between parts of a network. We have to find all of them. Here there are four servers. Zero, one and two form a cycle. Server three hangs off server one by a single link. So the link from one to three is critical.
say.brute: The brute force removes each link in turn and runs a breadth first search from server zero. If someone becomes unreachable, that link was critical. It's easy to trust. But every edge triggers a full search. With a hundred thousand edges, that's billions of steps.
say.insight: Here's Tarjan's idea. Do one depth first search. Each node gets a discovery time, and a low value. Low is the earliest time its subtree can reach through a back edge. Now, what if a child's low is still later than its parent's discovery time? Then that subtree has no other way up. The edge between them is a bridge.
say.anim: We build an adjacency list from the connections, linking nodes zero through three together. DFS starts at node zero, setting its discovery and low time to zero. Moving to node one, then node two, each gets increasing discovery and low values. Node two sees node zero already visited, so it updates its low value using discovery time, finding a cycle back. Node three is visited next from node one, getting discovery and low time three. Node three's low value stays three, higher than node one's discovery time, flagging a bridge. The edge between one and three is recorded as critical since no back edge covers it. The final answer is the single critical connection between nodes one and three.
say.code: Here's the code. First, we stamp each node's discovery time. For each neighbour, we skip the edge we came by. An unvisited child gets explored, and we inherit the child's best reach. If the child can't climb above us, that edge is a bridge. A visited neighbour is a back edge to an ancestor, so it can lower our low.
say.outro: Linear time in nodes plus edges. The pattern is graphs: Tarjan's bridge finding.

critical-connections-in-a-network.title: Critical Connections in a Network
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, the standard wrapper for this problem's method.
The method takes the server count n and the connection list, and returns the list of critical connections.
We build an adjacency list with one empty neighbor list for each server.
We loop over each connection, unpacking its two endpoints u and v.
Since links are undirected, we add v to the neighbor list of u.
We also add u to the neighbor list of v so both directions exist.
We set disc to negative one for unvisited, low to zero, and start an empty result list.
We start a discovery clock called time at zero, to stamp each server as it is visited.
We define a recursive dfs taking the current server u and the server we came from, parent.
We declare time as nonlocal so the nested function can increment the shared clock.
We stamp u with the current time as both its discovery time and its initial low value.
We advance the clock so the next discovered server gets a later stamp.
We loop over every neighbor v of the current server u.
We check whether v is just the parent we came from.
We skip the parent so the edge we arrived on is not mistaken for a back edge.
If v has never been discovered, it becomes a tree child of u.
We recurse into v, passing u as its parent, to explore its whole subtree.
After returning, we lower low of u to low of v if the subtree reaches earlier.
If low of v is greater than disc of u, the subtree cannot bypass this edge, so it is a bridge.
We record the edge u to v as a critical connection in the result.
Otherwise v was already visited, meaning the edge u to v is a back edge.
We lower low of u to the discovery time of v, since u can reach that earlier server.
We start the depth first search from server zero with no parent, as the graph is connected.
We return the list of all bridges found.

decode-string.hook: Nested brackets mean nested work. Push your progress on a stack, pop it at the close.
decode-string.ask: Decode a string where k[text] means text repeated k times. Brackets can nest. Return the fully expanded string.
decode-string.exampleWhy: Inside first: 2[c] is cc, so a2[c] is acc. Repeat that 3 times: accaccacc.

brute.idea: Repeatedly find an innermost k[letters] with a pattern, replace it with its expansion, until no brackets remain.
steps: Search for digits[letters] with no inner bracket
Replace it by letters repeated
Repeat until no [ remains
brute.whySlow: Each pass rescans and rebuilds the whole growing string; deep nesting means many full rewrites.

optimal.insight: When [ opens, save the text so far and the repeat count. When ] closes, pop them and attach the repeated inner text.
steps: Digits build the count
[ pushes (text so far, count) and resets
Letters extend current text
] pops: prev + current · count

codeNotes.note: Save outer text and its count

pitfalls: Multi-digit counts like 12[a]: accumulate digits, do not read one.
L here is the output length, which can be far larger than s.

say.intro: Okay, so a number followed by text in brackets means repeat that text that many times. And these can nest. For three, then a, then two of c, the inside becomes c c. So we get a c c, and three copies of that. A c c, a c c, a c c.
say.brute: The brute force finds an innermost bracket, a number followed by plain letters. It replaces it with the expansion. Then it searches again, and again, until no brackets remain. It works. But each pass rescans and rebuilds the whole string. Deep nesting means many full rewrites.
say.insight: Here's the thing. Nesting is a stack. When a bracket opens, we pause the outer work. We push the text so far and the repeat count, then start fresh. When a bracket closes, we pop them back. Repeat the inner text, and glue it on. One pass, left to right, does it all.
say.anim: We start with an empty stack, empty current text, and number zero. The digit three is read, building num up to three. An open bracket pushes empty text and three onto the stack, then resets cur and num. Letter a is appended, making cur equal a. Digit two is parsed, then another bracket pushes a and two onto the stack. Letter c is appended, making cur equal c. Closing bracket pops a and two, building cur as a plus c repeated twice, giving acc. Final closing bracket pops empty and three, repeating acc three times to get accaccacc, the answer.
say.code: Here's the code. Digits extend the current number, since counts can have several digits. An opening bracket saves the outer text and its count on the stack. Then we start fresh inside the bracket. A closing bracket pops the saved pair, repeats the inner text, and reattaches it. Letters just get appended.
say.outro: Linear in the output length. The pattern is a stack that saves outer context for nested structure.

decode-string.title: Decode String
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container the interview platform expects for our method.
The decodeString method takes the encoded string s and will return the fully expanded string.
We start with an empty stack, an empty current string, and a repeat count of zero.
We walk through the input one character at a time.
If the character is a digit, we are reading part of a repeat count.
We shift the existing number one place left and add this digit, so multi-digit counts like twelve work.
When we hit an open bracket, a new nested section begins.
We push the text built so far and the pending repeat count onto the stack to resume later.
Then we reset the current text to empty and the number to zero for the new section.
When we hit a closing bracket, the current section is complete and ready to be repeated.
We pop the saved outer text and its repeat count k from the stack.
We repeat the inner text k times and attach it to the saved outer text, forming the new current string.
Any other character must be a letter, so we handle it in this final branch.
We simply append that letter to the current string being built.
After processing every character, the current string holds the fully decoded result, which we return.

defanging-an-ip-address.hook: Swap every dot for bracket-dot-bracket. The lesson is how you build the new string.
defanging-an-ip-address.ask: Given a valid IPv4 address, return a copy where every period is replaced by [.] so the address cannot be clicked.
defanging-an-ip-address.exampleWhy: Each of the three dots becomes [.], and all digits stay as they are.

brute.idea: Walk the characters and glue each piece onto a growing result string with plus.
steps: Start with an empty string
For each character, pick it or [.]
result = result + piece
brute.whySlow: Strings are immutable, so each plus may copy the whole result; harmless at 15 characters, quadratic in general.

optimal.insight: Collect the pieces in a list and join once at the end, so every character is copied exactly once.
steps: Walk the address once
Dot? append [.]
Otherwise append the character
Join the list into one string

codeNotes.note: One final copy builds the string

pitfalls: address.replace('.', '[.]') is the idiomatic one-liner; mention it.

say.intro: Okay, an easy warm up. We take an address like two fifty five dot one hundred dot fifty dot zero. Every period gets wrapped in square brackets. The digits stay exactly as they are. So we end up with three bracketed dots.
say.brute: The most direct approach walks the characters and glues each piece onto a result string with plus. For a short address, that's totally fine. So what's the catch? Strings can't change in place. Each plus may build a brand new copy of everything so far. On long text, that turns quadratic.
say.insight: The better habit is simple. Collect the pieces in a list, then join them once at the very end. Appending to a list is cheap. And the final join copies each character exactly once. It's the same idea as a string builder in other languages. In Python, the built in replace does this for you.
say.anim: We start with the address 255.100.50.0 and an empty parts list. Each character is checked, and regular digits like 2, 5, 5 get appended as is. When a dot is found, we append the string bracket dot bracket instead. The loop continues, copying digits one hundred into parts normally. Another dot triggers appending bracket dot bracket again before fifty. The final dot is replaced the same way before the last zero. Finally all parts are joined into one string in a single pass. The result is 255 bracket dot bracket 100 bracket dot bracket 50 bracket dot bracket 0.
say.code: Here's the code. The parts list holds pieces of the answer. We loop over each character. Only periods change. A period gets the defanged dot, wrapped in brackets. Anything else goes in as it is. Then one final join builds the whole string in a single copy.
say.outro: Linear time and space. The pattern is simple string building. Build with a list, then join once.

defanging-an-ip-address.title: Defanging an IP Address
lineNotes: We define a class named Solution, which is the container the judge expects for our solution method.
This method takes the address string and returns a new string with every period replaced by the bracketed version.
We start with an empty list called parts to collect the output pieces without repeatedly rebuilding a string.
We loop over the address one character at a time so every character gets examined exactly once.
We check whether the current character is a period, since only periods need to be defanged.
When it is a period, we add the three character bracketed period to parts in its place.
Otherwise we fall into this branch, meaning the character is a digit that should stay unchanged.
We append the original character to parts as is, preserving the digits in their original order.
Finally we join all the pieces into one string in a single pass and return the defanged address.

design-a-stack-with-increment-operation.hook: Increment the bottom k elements in O(1)? Leave a note and settle it when popping.
design-a-stack-with-increment-operation.ask: Design a stack with a maximum size. push ignores overflow, pop returns -1 when empty, and increment(k, val) adds val to the bottom k elements.
design-a-stack-with-increment-operation.exampleWhy: Stack 1,2,3 gets +100 on all, then +100 on bottom two: pops give 103, 202, 201, then -1.

brute.idea: Store values in a list and make increment loop over the bottom k elements, adding val to each.
steps: push: append if room
pop: remove the top or return -1
increment: loop over min(k, size) values
brute.whySlow: 1,000 increments on a full 1,000-element stack touch a million values.

optimal.insight: Record val at index k-1 only. Popping index i adds inc[i] and hands it down to i-1, since it covers everything below.
steps: inc[i] is pending for elements 0..i
increment: add val at min(k, size) - 1
pop: return top + inc[top]
Pass inc[top] down to the new top

codeNotes.note: New element has no pending increment

pitfalls: k may exceed the current size: clamp with min.
Forgetting to pass the increment down loses it for lower elements.

say.intro: Okay, so we build a stack with a size limit, plus one extra move. Add a value to the bottom k elements. Here we push one, two, three. Then add one hundred to all, and one hundred to the bottom two. Pops give one oh three, two oh two, two oh one. Then minus one.
say.brute: The simple design keeps a list. Push appends if there's room. Pop removes the top, or returns minus one. Increment loops over the bottom k elements and adds the value to each. That's correct. But every increment can touch the whole stack. With many calls, that adds up fast.
say.insight: Here's the thing. Nobody looks at a value until it's popped. So increment just leaves a note at the highest affected index. The note means: everything from here down owes this much. When we pop the top, we add its note to its value. Then we pass the note down to the new top, since it covered that one too.
say.anim: We create a custom stack with max size three, starting empty. We push one then two, each stored with an increment of zero. Popping with no increments below returns two, the top value unchanged. We push two, three, then try four, but the stack is full. Increment adds one hundred to index four, capped at the top slot. Increment two adds one hundred more, but only to the second slot. Popping now applies stored increments downward, returning one hundred three first. Further pops return two hundred two, then two hundred one, then negative one for empty.
say.code: Here's the code. On push, the new element has no pending increment, so its note is zero. On pop, we take the pending amount for the top. That note also covers everything below, so we add it to the next note down. Then we return value plus note. Increment is lazy. It marks only the boundary.
say.outro: Constant time per operation. The pattern is a stack with lazy propagation. Leave a note, settle up on pop.

design-a-stack-with-increment-operation.title: Design a Stack With Increment Operation
lineNotes: We define a class called CustomStack that wraps a stack with a size limit and lazy increments.
The constructor takes maxSize, the largest number of elements the stack may ever hold.
We store maxSize in self max so push can check capacity later.
We create an empty list called stack to hold the actual pushed values.
We create a parallel empty list called inc to hold pending increments for each stack position.
The push method takes a value x to place on top of the stack.
We only push when the current stack length is still less than the maximum size, so overflow is ignored.
We append x to the top of the stack.
We append a zero to inc, since the new element has no pending increment yet.
The pop method removes and returns the top value with any pending increments applied.
We check whether the stack is empty.
If it is empty, we return negative one as the problem requires.
We pop the top pending increment into add, since it must be applied to this element.
If elements remain below, we need to pass that increment down to them.
We add the popped increment to the new top of inc, because it also covers everything beneath.
We return the popped stack value plus its increment, giving the correct final value.
The increment method adds val to the bottom k elements of the stack.
We only do work if the stack is not empty, to avoid indexing an empty list.
We add val at index k capped by stack size, minus one, recording it lazily and letting pop spread it downward.

divide-nodes-into-the-maximum-number-of-.hook: Groups are BFS layers. Try every start, and odd cycles make it impossible.
divide-nodes-into-the-maximum-number-of-.ask: Put nodes into numbered groups so every edge joins groups whose numbers differ by exactly one. Return the most groups possible, or -1 if impossible.
divide-nodes-into-the-maximum-number-of-.exampleWhy: The square 1-2-3-4 splits into 3 layers from any corner. Lonely node 5 adds 1 group. Total 4.

brute.idea: Compute all-pairs distances with Floyd-Warshall. Reject odd cycles, then each component's best is its largest distance plus one.
steps: Floyd-Warshall all-pairs shortest paths
Edge with equal distances from a node? -1
Component answer = longest distance + 1
Sum over components
brute.whySlow: 500 nodes means 125 million relaxations, mostly between nodes that are far from any edge.

optimal.insight: Starting BFS from node s, layer number is a valid group. The best start gives the deepest layering. Components add independently.
steps: BFS from every node
Edge inside one layer? odd cycle, return -1
Layers reached = groups for that start
Keep the max per component, then sum

pitfalls: The graph may be disconnected: sum per component, never take one global max.
Starting BFS at only one node per component misses the deepest layering.

say.intro: Okay, so every edge must join two groups whose numbers differ by exactly one. We want as many groups as possible. Here we have a square of nodes one to four, plus a lonely node five. The square gives three groups. Node five adds one more. That's four.
say.brute: A brute force computes every pairwise distance with Floyd Warshall. If some edge has both ends at the same distance from a node, there's an odd cycle. Then the answer is minus one. Otherwise each component gives its longest distance plus one. Correct, but cubic in the number of nodes.
say.insight: Here's the idea. A breadth first search splits a component into layers. Edges join neighbouring layers, or the same layer. Same layer means an odd cycle, so it's impossible. Otherwise, layer numbers are a valid grouping. Try every starting node, keep the deepest layering per component. Separate components just add up.
say.anim: We build an adjacency graph from the five nodes and four edges given. Starting BFS from node 1, we assign layer zero and explore neighbors two and four at layer one. Node three gets layer two, completing the cycle without any same layer conflicts. This BFS from node 1 found three groups, so best for this component becomes three. Trying BFS from node 3 also produces three layers, matching the previous best. BFS from node 4 similarly reaches three layers across the same connected component. Node 5 is isolated, forming its own component with just one group. Summing the best groups per component, three plus one gives the final answer four.
say.code: Here's the code. In the search, layer number equals group number. An edge inside one layer means an odd cycle, so we fail. Otherwise the helper returns the number of groups, plus a component id. We keep the best start per component. Then components stack their groups, so we add them up.
say.outro: Quadratic time, fine for five hundred nodes. The pattern is graph layering plus a bipartite check.

divide-nodes-into-the-maximum-number-of-.title: Divide Nodes Into the Maximum Number of Groups
lineNotes: We define the Solution class that holds the method for this problem.
The method takes the node count and edge list and returns the maximum number of groups or negative one.
We build an adjacency list with an empty neighbor list for each node from one to n.
We loop over every edge, reading its two endpoints a and b.
Since edges are undirected, we add b to the neighbor list of a.
We also add a to the neighbor list of b.
We define a helper that runs a breadth first search from a given source node.
We start a distance map with the source at zero and a queue holding just the source.
We keep processing nodes while the queue still has nodes waiting.
We pop the next node u from the front of the queue.
We look at every neighbor v of the current node u.
If v has not been reached yet, we haven't assigned it a layer.
We give v a layer one greater than u, since it is one step further out.
We add v to the queue so its own neighbors get explored later.
Otherwise if v already has the same layer as u, an odd cycle exists, so grouping is impossible.
We return negative one with a dummy component id to signal failure.
We return the layer count, which is the deepest distance plus one, along with the smallest node label as component id.
We create a map that tracks the best group count for each component.
We try every node as a starting point for the search.
We run the search from s and receive the group count and component id.
If the search reported failure, the graph is not bipartite in that component.
Then we immediately return negative one for the whole problem.
We record for this component the larger of its previous best and this start's group count.
Components are independent, so we sum each component's best group count as the answer.

divide-two-integers.hook: No division allowed. Subtract the biggest shifted divisor that fits, like long division in binary.
divide-two-integers.ask: Divide two integers without using multiplication, division or mod. Truncate toward zero, and clamp the result to the 32-bit signed range.
divide-two-integers.exampleWhy: 43 divided by 5 is 8.6, truncated to 8. Signs differ, so the answer is -8.

brute.idea: Work with absolute values and subtract the divisor again and again, counting how many times it fits.
steps: Take absolute values
Subtract divisor while it fits
Count each subtraction
Apply the sign and clamp
brute.whySlow: 2,147,483,647 divided by 1 means two billion subtractions.

optimal.insight: Build the quotient bit by bit: from bit 31 down, if divisor shifted left by i still fits, subtract it and set bit i.
steps: Handle the one overflow case first
Work with absolute values
For i from 31 down to 0
If a >> i ≥ b, subtract b << i, add 1 << i
Restore the sign

codeNotes.note: Set bit i of the quotient

pitfalls: Testing a >> i ≥ b avoids shifting b past 32 bits in fixed-width languages.
Python's // floors negatives; that is why we divide absolute values.

say.intro: Okay, so we divide two integers without using multiply, divide or mod. And we round toward zero. Forty three divided by minus five is minus eight point six. Rounded toward zero, that's minus eight.
say.brute: The brute force uses absolute values and keeps subtracting the divisor while it fits. It counts each subtraction. Then it applies the sign and clamps to the thirty two bit range. Correct. But dividing two billion by one means two billion subtractions.
say.insight: Think of long division, but in binary. Why subtract five one at a time? Subtract the biggest power of two multiple of five that still fits. Go from bit thirty one down to bit zero. Whenever the divisor, shifted left by i, fits in what's left, subtract it and set bit i of the answer. Just thirty two steps.
say.anim: Dividend is 43 and divisor is negative 5, not the overflow edge case. Signs differ, so the result will be negative, and we take absolute values a 43, b 5. We start scanning bits from 31 down to 0, building the quotient bit by bit. For high bits like 31 down to 25, shifting a right is still smaller than b, so nothing happens. We keep checking lower bits, from 24 down to 13, still no match yet. Continuing down through bits 12 to 7, the shifted value still stays below b. At bit 3, a shifted right equals b, so we subtract and set that bit, making q equal 8. No more bits fit, so the final answer returned is negative 8.
say.code: Here's the code. There's only one result that overflows, so we handle it first. The sign is negative when exactly one input is negative. Then, for each bit, we ask: does the divisor times two to the i fit in a? If it does, we remove that chunk, and set bit i of the quotient. Finally, restore the sign.
say.outro: Thirty two steps, logarithmic time. The pattern is bit manipulation. Binary long division with shifts.

divide-two-integers.title: Divide Two Integers
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container for the divide method that LeetCode expects.
The divide method takes a dividend and a divisor and returns their integer quotient truncated toward zero.
We check the one overflow case, where the smallest 32-bit integer is divided by negative one.
In that case the true answer is too big, so we return the largest 32-bit signed integer.
We decide the result is negative when exactly one of the two inputs is negative.
We work with absolute values of both numbers so the bit logic only deals with nonnegative values.
We start the quotient q at zero and will build it up bit by bit.
We loop the bit position i from thirty-one down to zero, trying the largest shifts first.
We check whether the divisor shifted left by i fits into a, by testing whether a shifted right by i is at least b.
If it fits, we subtract the divisor shifted left by i from a, removing that chunk.
We then add one shifted left by i to the quotient, setting bit i of the answer.
Finally we return the quotient with its sign restored, negating it if the signs differed.

evaluate-boolean-binary-tree.hook: Leaves are true or false, inner nodes are OR and AND. Just evaluate bottom up.
evaluate-boolean-binary-tree.ask: In a full binary tree, leaves are 0 (False) or 1 (True). Inner nodes are 2 (OR) or 3 (AND). Return the value of the root.
evaluate-boolean-binary-tree.exampleWhy: Left: 0 OR 1 is True. Right leaf is True. Root AND gives True.

brute.idea: Compute a value for every node in postorder with an explicit stack and a dictionary, then read the root.
steps: Push nodes for a postorder walk
Leaf: store its value
Inner: combine both stored children
Return the root's stored value
brute.whySlow: Same O(n) time, but it stores every node's result and never short-circuits, even when one side decides.

optimal.insight: A node's value depends only on its children, so recursion evaluates it directly. OR and AND can skip the right side.
steps: Leaf: return val == 1
Evaluate the left child
OR node: left True decides
AND node: left False decides
Otherwise evaluate the right child

codeNotes.note: Full tree: no left means leaf

pitfalls: Return a boolean, not the raw 0 or 1 value.
Short-circuit is safe here; it only skips work, never changes the answer.

say.intro: Okay, so leaves hold zero for false or one for true. Inner nodes hold two for OR, or three for AND. Here the root is AND. Its left child is zero OR one, which is true. Its right child is true. So the result is true.
say.brute: A heavier approach walks the tree in postorder with an explicit stack. It stores a result for every node in a dictionary. Each inner node waits until both children are stored, then combines them. Still linear time. But it keeps every value in memory, and always evaluates both sides.
say.insight: Here's the thing. A node's value depends only on its two children. So plain recursion mirrors the definition exactly. A leaf returns whether it's one. An inner node evaluates its left child first. For OR, a true left side already decides it. For AND, a false left side does. Only otherwise do we visit the right.
say.anim: We start at the root node, value 3, which has children, so we recurse left. Now at node value 2, an OR node, it also has children, so we recurse left. We reach a leaf node with value 0, which evaluates directly to false. Back at the OR node, left is false, so we must check the right child too. That right child is a leaf with value 1, which evaluates to true. False or true is true, so the OR node at value 2 returns true. Back at the root, an AND node, left is true, so we evaluate the right leaf, value 1, which is true. True and true gives true, so the whole tree evaluates to true.
say.code: Here's the code. It's a full tree, so no left child means a leaf. A leaf returns true for one, false for zero. Otherwise, we evaluate the left side. Two means OR, so we return left or the right subtree. Three means AND, which short circuits the same way.
say.outro: Linear time, space equal to the height. The pattern is trees. Postorder recursion that combines child results.

evaluate-boolean-binary-tree.title: Evaluate Boolean Binary Tree
lineNotes: We define a Solution class that holds the method for evaluating the boolean tree.
The evaluateTree method takes the root node and returns the boolean value of the whole tree.
Since the tree is full, a node with no left child is a leaf and needs no recursion.
For a leaf we return true when its value is one, and false when it is zero.
For an inner node we first recursively evaluate the left subtree and store the result in left.
We check whether the node value is two, which means this inner node is an OR operation.
For OR we return left or the right result, so the right side is skipped when left is true.
Otherwise the node is AND, so we return left and the right result, skipping the right side when left is false.

find-all-possible-recipes-from-given-sup.hook: Recipes need other recipes. Topological sort cooks each one the moment it becomes possible.
find-all-possible-recipes-from-given-sup.ask: Each recipe lists ingredients, which may be supplies or other recipes. Supplies are unlimited. Return every recipe you can eventually make.
find-all-possible-recipes-from-given-sup.exampleWhy: Bread uses only supplies. Sandwich then has bread and meat. Burger then has sandwich, meat and bread.

brute.idea: Sweep all recipes repeatedly, making any whose ingredients are all available, until a sweep makes nothing new.
steps: Available = supplies
Sweep recipes: all ingredients available? make it
Add made recipes to available
Stop when a sweep adds nothing
brute.whySlow: A chain of 100 recipes listed backwards needs 100 sweeps, each rechecking every ingredient.

optimal.insight: Treat it as a dependency graph. Count each recipe's missing ingredients; when the count hits zero, it is cookable and unlocks others.
steps: missing[r] = ingredients not in supplies
Link each missing ingredient to recipes needing it
Queue recipes with zero missing
Cooking r decrements recipes waiting on r

codeNotes.note: In-degree: one more thing to wait for
Edge from ingredient x to recipe r

codeNotes.match: q = deque(r for r in recipes if missing[r] == 0)

codeNotes.note: r is now available to nxt

pitfalls: Recipes in a cycle never reach zero, so they are correctly excluded.
Unknown ingredients keep the count above zero forever; that is intended.
