say.intro: Okay, so each recipe needs ingredients, and some ingredients are recipes themselves. Supplies never run out. With yeast, flour and meat, we can make bread. Bread plus meat makes a sandwich. Then sandwich, meat and bread make a burger. So all three are possible.
say.brute: The brute force sweeps the recipe list again and again. In each sweep, any recipe whose ingredients are all available gets made. Then it becomes available too. We stop when a sweep makes nothing new. It works. But a long chain listed in the wrong order needs one full sweep per recipe.
say.insight: Here's the thing. This is a dependency graph, so use topological sort. For each recipe, count how many ingredients aren't plain supplies. Link each such ingredient to the recipes waiting on it. Recipes with a count of zero can be cooked right now. Cooking one lowers the count for everything waiting on it. That may unlock more.
say.anim: We start with supplies yeast, flour, and meat already available. For bread, both yeast and flour are already supplied, so nothing is missing. For sandwich, bread is not yet available, so its missing count becomes one. For burger, both sandwich and bread are missing, giving it a missing count of two. Only bread has zero missing ingredients, so it starts in the queue. Cooking bread unlocks sandwich, dropping its missing count to zero and queuing it. Cooking sandwich then unlocks burger, whose missing count also reaches zero. All recipes get cooked, giving the final answer bread, sandwich, burger.
say.code: Here's the code. For every ingredient that isn't a supply, the recipe has one more thing to wait for. We record an edge from that ingredient to the recipe. Recipes cookable from supplies alone go in the queue. When we cook one, it's now available to every recipe waiting on it. Once every ingredient is ready, that recipe gets cooked.
say.outro: Linear in the total input size. The pattern is graphs, using Kahn's topological sort.

find-all-possible-recipes-from-given-sup.title: Find All Possible Recipes from Given Supplies
lineNotes: We import deque for the queue and defaultdict for the waiting lists.
We import List so the type hints in the method signature are valid.
We define the Solution class that holds the method.
The method takes recipes, their ingredient lists, and the starting supplies, and returns the recipes we can make.
The first step is to track which supplies we already have.
We put the supplies into a set so checking whether we have an item is fast.
The second step is to count how many ingredients each recipe is still missing.
We create a dictionary that maps each recipe to its missing ingredient count.
We create a map from each ingredient to the list of recipes waiting on it, defaulting to an empty list.
We loop over every recipe by its index so we can pair names with ingredient lists.
We grab the current recipe name from the recipes list.
We grab the list of ingredients that this recipe needs.
We start this recipe's missing count at zero before examining its ingredients.
We go through each ingredient this recipe needs.
If the ingredient is not already in our supplies, it counts as missing.
We increase the recipe's missing count by one for this absent ingredient.
We record that this recipe is waiting on that ingredient, so we can unlock it later.
The third step is to start with recipes that have nothing missing.
We create an empty queue to hold recipes that are ready to cook.
We loop through all the recipes to find the ones ready right away.
If a recipe has zero missing ingredients, it can be made immediately.
We add that ready recipe to the queue.
The fourth step is to cook recipes and unlock the ones waiting on them.
We create an empty result list to collect every recipe we can make.
We keep processing while the queue still has recipes ready to cook.
We take the next ready recipe from the front of the queue.
We add it to the result since we can make it.
We look at every recipe that was waiting on the one we just cooked.
We reduce that waiting recipe's missing count by one, since one ingredient is now available.
If its missing count reaches zero, that recipe has everything it needs.
We add the newly unlocked recipe to the queue so it gets cooked and may unlock others.
We return the list of all recipes we were able to make.

find-k-closest-elements.hook: The answer is one contiguous window. Binary search for where it starts.
find-k-closest-elements.ask: Given a sorted array, return the k values closest to x, in ascending order. On a distance tie, the smaller value wins.
find-k-closest-elements.exampleWhy: 7 and 9 are 1 away. 5 and 11 are both 3 away; the tie goes to the smaller, 5.

brute.idea: Sort all values by distance to x, breaking ties by value. Take the first k and sort those again.
steps: Sort by (|a - x|, a)
Take the first k
Sort them ascending
brute.whySlow: It re-sorts all 10,000 values and ignores that the array is already sorted.

optimal.insight: Compare window starts mid and mid+1: if arr[mid+k] is closer to x than arr[mid], the window should start later.
steps: Search start in [0, n - k]
Compare x - arr[mid] with arr[mid + k] - x
Left side farther? lo = mid + 1
Else hi = mid
Return arr[lo : lo + k]

codeNotes.match: if x - arr[mid] > arr[mid + k] - x:
codeNotes.note: Left end farther than next right

pitfalls: Do not use abs in the comparison; signed differences handle x outside the array.
Use strict greater-than so ties favour the left, smaller values.

say.intro: Okay, so we get a sorted array, a count k, and a target x. We return the k values closest to x, in order. Ties go to the smaller value. Here k is three and x is eight. Seven and nine are one away. Five and eleven tie at three away, so five wins. Five, seven, nine.
say.brute: The brute force sorts every value by its distance to x, breaking ties by value. It takes the first k and sorts them back into order. It's short and correct. But it spends n log n time. And it ignores the fact that the array was already sorted.
say.insight: Here's the thing. In a sorted array, the k closest values always form one unbroken window. So we only need to find where the window starts. Compare a window starting at mid with one starting at mid plus one. They differ in just two values, the left end and the next right. If the left end is farther from x, move right.
say.anim: We start with the array, k equal to three, and x equal to eight. The search window begins with lo at zero and hi at four. Mid is two, comparing arr at mid five with arr at mid plus k eleven against x. Eight minus five isn't bigger than eleven minus eight, so hi moves down to two. Now mid is one, comparing arr value three against arr value nine around x. Eight minus three is bigger than nine minus eight, so lo moves up to two. Lo now equals hi at two, so the search loop stops. Slicing from index two for three elements gives the final answer five, seven, nine.
say.code: Here's the code. Lo and hi cover the possible window starts. We take the middle. If the left end is farther than the next right value, the window should start later. So we slide the window right. On ties, we keep the smaller values by moving hi instead. The answer is an already sorted window.
say.outro: Logarithmic search, plus k to copy. The pattern is binary search on where the answer starts.

find-k-closest-elements.title: Find K Closest Elements
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container the problem expects for our method.
The method takes a sorted array, a window size k, and a target x, and returns the k closest values.
We search over possible window start positions, so lo is zero and hi is the array length minus k.
We keep narrowing the range of candidate starts until lo and hi meet at a single start.
We pick the middle candidate start, mid, and compare the window beginning there with the window beginning one later.
If x is farther from the left edge at mid than from the new right element at mid plus k, the window should shift right.
In that case the start cannot be mid, so we move lo up to mid plus one.
Otherwise the window at mid is at least as good, with ties favoring the smaller values on the left.
So we keep mid as a possible answer by setting hi to mid.
When the search ends, lo is the best start, and we return the k elements beginning there.

find-largest-value-in-each-tree-row.hook: One answer per level. BFS hands you each row; take its max.
find-largest-value-in-each-tree-row.ask: Given the root of a binary tree, return a list holding the largest value on each level, from top to bottom.
find-largest-value-in-each-tree-row.exampleWhy: Row one is 1. Row two is 3 and 2, max 3. Row three is 5, 3, 9, max 9.

brute.idea: Find the height. For each depth, walk the whole tree from the root to find that depth's maximum.
steps: Compute tree height h
For each depth d, DFS from the root
Track the max at depth d
brute.whySlow: Every level restarts from the root; a skewed tree of 10,000 nodes means 50 million visits.

optimal.insight: Level order BFS processes one row at a time, so track a running max per row in a single pass.
steps: Queue starts with the root
Pop exactly one row of nodes
Track the row's maximum
Queue children, then save the max

pitfalls: Do not start row_max at 0; node values can be negative.
DFS with depth index works too: res[depth] = max(...).

say.intro: Okay, so for every level of the tree, we report its biggest value. The top row is just one. The second row is three and two, so three. The third row is five, three and nine, so nine. The answer is one, three, nine.
say.brute: The brute force first finds the tree's height. Then for each depth, it walks down from the root to that depth and takes the largest value there. It's correct. But every level starts over from the root. A tall, skinny tree costs about n times its height.
say.insight: Here's the thing. Breadth first search already visits the tree one row at a time. If we handle exactly one row per round, we can keep a running max as we pop its nodes. When the row ends, that max is the answer for that level. Every node gets visited once.
say.anim: We start with root node 1, and the queue begins with just that node. We process level one, taking node 1, updating row max to 1, and queueing its children 3 and 2. Row max 1 is saved to results, finishing the first row. Level two begins, comparing nodes 3 and 2, updating row max to 3 as children 5 and 3 get queued. Row max 3 is appended, completing the second row. Level three processes nodes 5, 3, and 9, pushing row max up to 9. Row max 9 is appended as the final row result. The function returns the final answer, one, three, nine, the largest value per row.
say.code: Here's the code. An empty tree has no rows, so return an empty list. Each round, the row max starts at minus infinity, because values can be negative. We pop exactly this row's nodes, queueing their children. The row max tracks the best value in this row. Then we append it, one answer per level.
say.outro: Linear time. The pattern is level order traversal, with one running max per row.

find-largest-value-in-each-tree-row.title: Find Largest Value in Each Tree Row
lineNotes: We define the Solution class that holds our method for this problem.
The method largestValues takes the root of a binary tree and returns a list of the largest value per row.
First we check whether the tree is empty, since there would be nothing to process.
If the root is missing, we return an empty list because there are no rows.
We create the result list and a queue seeded with the root, which starts our level order traversal.
We loop as long as the queue still holds nodes, with each pass handling exactly one row.
We reset the row maximum to negative infinity so any real node value will beat it.
We loop over the number of nodes currently in the queue, which is exactly the size of this row.
We pop the next node from the front of the queue to process it.
We update the row maximum by keeping the larger of the current maximum and this node's value.
If the node has a left child, we check it so it can join the next row.
We add the left child to the queue for the next level.
If the node has a right child, we check it as well.
We add the right child to the queue for the next level.
After finishing the row, we append its maximum to the result list in top to bottom order.
Once the queue is empty, we return the list of row maximums.

find-missing-and-repeated-values.hook: One number sneaks in twice, another vanishes. A set and one sum catch both.
find-missing-and-repeated-values.ask: An n by n grid should hold every number from 1 to n² exactly once, but one number appears twice and another is missing. Return the repeated number and the missing number.
find-missing-and-repeated-values.exampleWhy: 9 appears in two cells and 5 appears nowhere, so the answer is [9,5].

brute.idea: For every value from 1 to n², scan the whole grid and count how often it appears. Count 2 is repeated, count 0 is missing.
steps: Loop x from 1 to n²
Scan every cell, counting matches
Count 2: repeated; count 0: missing
brute.whySlow: Each of the n² values rescans all n² cells. A 50 by 50 grid means over six million checks.

optimal.insight: A set spots the repeat the moment we see it twice. Then the sum 1 + ... + n² tells us exactly which number is missing.
steps: Walk every cell once, keeping a set and a running sum
Already in the set? That is the repeated value
Expected sum minus (actual sum minus repeat) is the missing value

codeNotes.note: Drop the duplicate, the gap is missing

pitfalls: Subtract the repeat from the actual sum first, or the difference is off by it.
Values run to n², not n: size the sum formula on n squared.

say.intro: Okay, so here's the setup. An n by n grid should hold every number from one to n squared, exactly once. But one number sneaked in twice. And another one vanished. In our grid, nine shows up in two cells. Five is nowhere. So we return nine and five.
say.brute: What's the obvious first try? Take every number from one to n squared. For each one, scan the whole grid and count it. Count two means repeated. Count zero means missing. Simple, right? But here's the catch. Every value rescans every cell. That's n to the fourth work. A fifty by fifty grid is over six million checks.
say.insight: Here's the thing. We can get both answers in one walk. A set catches the repeat. The moment we see a value that's already in the set, that's our duplicate. And the missing one? Pure arithmetic. We know exactly what one plus two up to n squared adds to. Our grid sum is that, plus the repeat, minus the missing number. So rearrange, and the missing number just falls out.
say.anim: We start with a three by three grid and an empty set to track seen numbers. We scan each row, adding numbers to seen and summing them into total. At nine, we find it already in seen, so repeated becomes nine. We keep scanning the remaining rows, adding new numbers and updating total each time. After the loop, total reaches forty nine, and seen holds all distinct values found. Expected sum for numbers one through nine is calculated as forty five. Missing is computed as five, since expected minus total minus repeated gives that value. The final answer returned is nine repeated and five missing.
say.code: Let's walk the code. We start with an empty set. Then we loop over every cell. Already in the set? That's the repeat, so we save it. Either way, we add the value to the running total. After the loop, the Gauss formula gives the expected sum. Finally, take out the duplicate, and the gap is the missing number.
say.outro: Linear in the number of cells. One set, one sum. That's arrays and hashing at its simplest.

find-missing-and-repeated-values.title: Find Missing and Repeated Values
lineNotes: We define a class named Solution, which is the container the judge expects for this problem.
This method takes the grid and returns a list holding the repeated number and the missing number.
We store the grid size n, the number of rows, which also equals the number of columns.
We create an empty set called seen to remember every number we have already encountered.
We start repeated at zero, and it will hold the duplicate once we find it.
We start total at zero to accumulate the sum of every value in the grid.
We loop over each row of the grid so we can visit every cell.
Inside each row we loop over each number x, visiting every cell one at a time.
We check whether x is already in seen, which would mean this number appears a second time.
If so, we record x as the repeated value, since only one number is duplicated.
We add x to the seen set so any later copy will be detected.
We add x to the running total, which will include the duplicate twice and skip the missing number.
We compute the expected sum of one through n squared using the formula n squared times n squared plus one, divided by two.
Removing the duplicate once from the total leaves the sum without the missing number, so expected minus that gives the missing value.
We return the repeated number first and the missing number second, as the problem requires.

find-pivot-index.hook: Balance the array on one index. A running left sum does it in a single pass.
find-pivot-index.ask: Return the leftmost index where the sum of everything strictly to its left equals the sum of everything strictly to its right. If no index balances, return -1.
find-pivot-index.exampleWhy: Left of index 3 sums to 1 + 7 + 3 = 11, and right of it sums to 5 + 6 = 11.

brute.idea: Try every index. Add up everything to its left and everything to its right from scratch, and compare.
steps: Pick index i
Sum nums[:i] and nums[i + 1:] from scratch
Equal? return i
brute.whySlow: Every index re-adds the whole array, so 10,000 numbers means about 100 million additions.

optimal.insight: Once we know the total, the right sum is just total minus left minus the current number. Only the left sum needs tracking.
steps: Compute the total once
Walk left to right with a running left sum
Right sum is total - left - nums[i]
Equal? return i, else add nums[i] to left

codeNotes.note: One pass for the grand total
Move x into the left side

pitfalls: Exclude nums[i] from both sides; it belongs to neither.
Negatives are allowed, so never stop early when left exceeds right.

say.intro: Okay, so we want a balance point. Find the leftmost index where everything on its left adds up to everything on its right. The pivot itself counts on neither side. In one, seven, three, six, five, six, index three works. Eleven on the left. Eleven on the right.
say.brute: The obvious way? Try every index. Add up the left side from scratch. Add up the right side from scratch. Compare. It's correct. But each index rescans the whole array. That's n squared. With ten thousand numbers, you're doing about a hundred million additions.
say.insight: Here's the thing. The two sides aren't independent. Think about it this way. If you know the total, and you know the left sum, then the right sum is just the total, minus the left, minus the current number. No need to add it up. So we compute the total once. Then we carry one running left sum as we walk.
say.anim: We start with the array, and compute total sum equal to 28. Left sum starts at zero before we scan through the numbers. At index 0, value 1, right sum is 27, not equal to left. Left becomes 1, then at index 1, value 7, right sum is 20. Left becomes 8, then at index 2, value 3, right sum is 17. Left becomes 11, then at index 3, value 6, right sum equals 11. Left and right both equal 11, so this index is the pivot. The function returns 3, confirming index 3 as the pivot index.
say.code: Let's walk the code. First, one pass gets the grand total. Then for each index, we derive the right side instead of summing it. If left equals right, we return right away. Why right away? Because that guarantees the leftmost answer. Otherwise, we move the value into the left side and keep going.
say.outro: Linear time, constant space. Don't recompute the other side. Derive it. That's the prefix sum trick.

find-pivot-index.title: Find Pivot Index
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container the interview platform expects for our method.
This method takes the list of numbers and returns the leftmost pivot index as an integer.
We compute the total sum of the list once up front so right sums come cheaply later.
We start left at zero because nothing sits to the left of the first index.
We loop through each index and value together, so we know both the position and the number there.
The right sum is the total minus the left sum minus the current number, which avoids re-summing.
We check whether the left sum equals the right sum, which is exactly the pivot condition.
If they match, we return the current index immediately, which guarantees we get the leftmost pivot.
Otherwise we add the current number to left, so it counts as left side for the next index.
If the loop finishes without finding a balance, we return negative one to signal no pivot exists.

find-the-occurrence-of-first-almost-equa.hook: Allow one typo when matching. Two Z-arrays, one forward and one backward, find it in linear time.
find-the-occurrence-of-first-almost-equa.ask: Find the smallest index where a substring of s, the same length as pattern, differs from pattern in at most one character. Return -1 if no such substring exists.
find-the-occurrence-of-first-almost-equa.exampleWhy: s[1..3] is "bcb", which matches "bcc" after changing one letter; index 0 "abc" needs three changes.

brute.idea: Slide a window of pattern length over s and compare letter by letter, giving up once two letters differ.
steps: Try each start i
Compare s[i + j] with pattern[j]
Second mismatch: stop this window
At most one mismatch? return i
brute.whySlow: With s and pattern both near 100,000 long, each window may scan thousands of letters before failing.

optimal.insight: One mismatch splits the window into a matching prefix and a matching suffix. Z-arrays give longest prefix and suffix matches at every start, in linear time.
steps: Z-array of pattern + s: prefix match length at each start
Z-array of both reversed: suffix match length at each end
Window at i is fine if prefix + suffix ≥ m - 1
Return the first such i

codeNotes.note: Reuse a match inside the Z-box
Extend the match letter by letter
Prefix match length at each start

codeNotes.match: if pre[m + i] + suf[n - i] >= m - 1:

pitfalls: Index the reversed Z-array carefully: window i ends at reversed position n - i.
Prefix plus suffix can overlap; that only means an exact match, still valid.

say.intro: Okay, so we slide a pattern along a string. We want the first spot where it matches with at most one wrong letter. Here s is a b c b c d, and the pattern is b c c. At index one we see b c b. Change one letter and it matches. So the answer is one.
say.brute: First idea? Try every starting index. Compare the window to the pattern letter by letter. Give up after a second mismatch. Easy to write. But what's the cost? Length of s times length of the pattern. If both are near a hundred thousand, nearly matching windows push that into the billions.
say.insight: Here's the aha. A window with one bad letter looks like this. A matching prefix, then the bad letter, then a matching suffix. So what do we really need? For every start, how far the pattern's prefix matches. For every end, how far its suffix matches. The Z algorithm gives all the prefix matches in linear time. Run it again on both strings reversed, and you get the suffixes.
say.anim: We start with string abcbcd and pattern bcc, looking for an almost equal match. First we build the z array for pattern plus string, tracking prefix matches at each position. After processing, the prefix z array ends up as 0,0,0,0,2,0,2,0,0. Next we build the z array for the reversed pattern plus reversed string for suffix matches. That suffix z array comes out as 0,1,0,0,1,0,1,0,0. At index 0, prefix plus suffix matches don't reach the needed mismatch tolerance, so we continue. At index 1, the combined matches satisfy the condition, so we return 1 as the answer.
say.code: Let's walk the code. Inside the Z box, we reuse a match we already know. Then we extend it letter by letter. When we pass the box, we slide it right. One Z array gives the prefix match at each start. A second, on reversed strings, gives the suffix match. If together they cover all but one letter, we return that start.
say.outro: Linear time. The Z box is a two pointer window that reuses earlier work. Remember that shape for string matching.

find-the-occurrence-of-first-almost-equa.title: Find the Occurrence of First Almost Equal Substring
lineNotes: We define a Solution class that holds the method for this problem.
The method minStartingIndex takes the text s and the pattern and returns the smallest almost matching start index.
We define a helper that computes the Z-array, where each entry is the longest prefix match starting at that position.
We create the Z-array z filled with zeros, one slot per character of the input string t.
We set left and right to zero, tracking the rightmost matching box found so far.
We loop over every position i from one to the end, since position zero is trivially the whole string.
If i lies inside the current box, we can reuse earlier work instead of starting from scratch.
We seed z at i with the smaller of the remaining box width and the mirrored Z value, which is safe.
We keep extending the match while characters at the prefix and at position i continue to agree.
Each successful comparison increases z at i by one.
If the match at i reaches farther right than before, we update the box.
We set left to i and right to the end of this new match.
We return the finished Z-array.
We store the pattern length as m and the text length as n.
We run Z on pattern followed by s, so pre tells how long a prefix of pattern matches at each spot in s.
We run Z on the reversed pattern plus reversed s, so suf tells how long a suffix of pattern matches ending at each spot.
We try each possible window start i from zero up to n minus m, in increasing order.
If the matching prefix plus matching suffix covers at least m minus one characters, at most one mismatch exists.
We return this index immediately, since scanning in order makes it the smallest valid start.
If no window qualifies, we return negative one.

finding-3-digit-even-numbers.hook: Do not permute the input. Count the digits, then build numbers in sorted order.
finding-3-digit-even-numbers.ask: Using three digits from the array, each at most as often as it appears, list every distinct three-digit even number with no leading zero, sorted ascending.
finding-3-digit-even-numbers.exampleWhy: Only 2s and 8s exist; 888 needs three 8s but there are only two, so it is excluded.

brute.idea: Try every ordered triple of distinct indices, keep numbers that are even with no leading zero, then dedupe and sort.
steps: Loop over three distinct indices i, j, k
Skip leading zero or odd last digit
Add the number to a set
Return the sorted set
brute.whySlow: 100 digits give nearly a million index triples, though at most 450 distinct answers exist.

optimal.insight: Only the count of each digit matters. Choose digit values, not positions: at most 9 × 10 × 5 tries, and they come out sorted.
steps: Count how many of each digit 0 to 9 we have
Pick hundreds 1 to 9, tens 0 to 9, units even
Borrow a digit from the count while it is in use
Append in loop order, already sorted

codeNotes.note: Borrow it while we use it

pitfalls: Forgetting to borrow lets 888 through with only two 8s.
Equivalently loop 100 to 998 step 2 and check counts; also constant work.

say.intro: Okay, so we pick three digits from the array. Each digit can be used only as often as it appears. We list every distinct even number they make, with no leading zero. From two, two, eight, eight, two, we get seven numbers. Notice eight eight eight is missing. Why? We only own two eights.
say.brute: The obvious way? Try every ordered triple of positions. Skip it if it starts with zero or ends odd. Otherwise, throw the number in a set, then sort. That's cubic. A hundred digits means almost a million triples. And there are at most four hundred and fifty possible answers.
say.insight: Here's the thing. Positions don't matter. Only how many of each digit we have. So count the digits first. Then pick digit values, not indices. Hundreds from one to nine. Tens from zero to nine. Units from the even digits. While a digit is in use, we borrow it from the count. And since we loop values in order, the output comes out sorted and unique for free.
say.anim: We start by counting digits: three twos and two eights appear in our input. We pick hundreds digit a equals 2, since twos are available. With b equals 2, c equals 2 works, giving us the number 222. Still with a and b at 2, c equals 8 works too, adding 228 to results. Now b becomes 8, pairing with c equals 2 and c equals 8 to make 282 and 288. Digits 4 through 6 have zero count, so those hundreds choices are skipped entirely. Now a equals 8, combining with b equals 2 and b equals 8 to build 822, 828, and 882. All combinations tried, the final sorted even numbers are 222, 228, 282, 288, 822, 828, and 882.
say.code: Let's walk the code. First, a count of each digit. The hundreds loop starts at one, so never zero. We borrow that digit while we use it. The units loop only visits even digits. Looping in order keeps the list ascending, with no duplicates. And after each loop, we give the digit back.
say.outro: Count once, then the work is a constant. Count values, don't enumerate positions. That's arrays and hashing.

finding-3-digit-even-numbers.title: Finding 3-Digit Even Numbers
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container this problem's method lives in.
The method findEvenNumbers takes the list of digits and returns a sorted list of valid even numbers.
We create a count array of ten zeros, one slot for each possible digit value.
We loop over every digit in the input list to tally how often each appears.
Each digit increments its slot in count, so we know how many copies we have.
We start an empty result list to collect the valid numbers as we build them.
We try every hundreds digit a from one to nine, which rules out a leading zero.
If no copies of a remain, this hundreds digit is unavailable.
So we skip to the next candidate for a.
We use one copy of a by decreasing its count, so it cannot be reused unfairly.
We try every tens digit b from zero to nine, since zero is fine in the middle.
If no copies of b are left, we cannot use it as the tens digit.
So we skip to the next candidate for b.
We use one copy of b by decreasing its count.
We try only even ones digits c, stepping by two from zero to eight, to guarantee evenness.
If at least one copy of c remains after using a and b, the number is buildable.
We append the number a times one hundred plus b times ten plus c, and the loop order keeps results ascending.
We restore the copy of b so the next tens choice sees the correct counts.
We restore the copy of a so the next hundreds choice starts with correct counts.
We return the result, already distinct and sorted because we iterated over digit values in order.

finding-mk-average.hook: Trim the extremes from a sliding window, live. A Fenwick tree finds the k-th smallest sums in log time.
finding-mk-average.ask: Stream integers in. On request, take the last m numbers, drop the k smallest and k largest, and return the floor of the average of the rest, or -1 if fewer than m have arrived.
finding-mk-average.exampleWhy: With m = 3, 64 falls out of the window, leaving [16,96,48]. Dropping 16 and 96 leaves 48.

brute.idea: Keep the last m numbers in a queue. On every average request, sort the window, slice off k from each end, and average the middle.
steps: addElement: append, pop the oldest beyond m
calculate: copy and sort the window
Average the middle m - 2k values
brute.whySlow: With m = 100,000 and 100,000 calls, every average re-sorts the whole window: about 10¹¹ operations.

optimal.insight: Values are at most 100,000. A Fenwick tree over values keeps counts and sums, so the sum of the t smallest is a log-time descent.
steps: Queue holds the last m values in arrival order
Fenwick trees hold count and sum per value
Sum of t smallest: binary-lift down the tree
Middle = smallest(m - k) - smallest(k)

codeNotes.note: How many copies of each value

codeNotes.match: if nxt <= self.size and self.cnt[nxt] < t:
codeNotes.note: Whole block fits below the t-th

pitfalls: Ties: the t-th smallest may sit among duplicates, so add the leftover count times that value.
Three balanced sorted multisets also give O(log m); say it if you know SortedList.

say.intro: Okay, so numbers stream in. When asked, we take the last m numbers. Throw away the k smallest and the k largest. Average the rest, rounding down. Here m is three and k is one. After sixty four, sixteen, ninety six, forty eight, the window is the last three. Drop sixteen and ninety six. Forty eight is left.
say.brute: The simple way? Keep the last m numbers in a queue. Adding is cheap. But every average request copies the window, sorts it, slices off both ends, and averages the middle. So what's the problem? Windows of a hundred thousand, and a hundred thousand calls. Sorting every single time is far too slow.
say.insight: Here's the thing. The values are small, at most a hundred thousand. So index a Fenwick tree by value. It stores how many copies of each value are in the window, and their total. Now the sum of the t smallest values is one walk down the tree, in log time. And the middle sum? The m minus k smallest, minus the k smallest.
say.anim: We start MKAverage with m equal to three and k equal to one, setting up our tracking trees. Adding sixty-four updates the Fenwick trees, climbing indexes sixty-four, one hundred twenty-eight, and beyond. Next we add sixteen and ninety-six, each updating counts and sums at their respective tree positions. Then forty-eight is added, and since the window exceeds size three, sixty-four is removed again. Now we descend the tree to sum the smallest two values, tracking position and remaining count. Position lands on thirty-two, then forty, giving a total sum of sixteen so far. We repeat the descent for the smallest one value, walking down through tree indexes again. The middle sum comes out to forty-eight, giving a final MK average result of forty-eight.
say.code: Let's walk the code. One tree counts copies of each value. Another holds their total, for fast sums. To find the smallest t, we swallow whole blocks that fit below t. The remaining copies all share one value, so we add those too. When the window is full, the oldest value leaves. Finally, the middle sum is two prefix sums subtracted.
say.outro: Log time per call. When you need order statistics on a sliding window, keep it in a tree indexed by value.

finding-mk-average.title: Finding MK Average
lineNotes: We define the MKAverage class, which will track a stream of numbers and answer middle average queries.
The constructor takes m, the window size, and k, the number of values trimmed from each end.
This comment says we first store the parameters and build Fenwick trees covering the whole value range.
We save m so we know how many recent numbers form the window.
We save k so we know how many smallest and largest values to discard.
We set the maximum possible value to one hundred thousand, which sizes our trees.
The count tree starts at zero and records how many window values fall in each Fenwick range.
The sum tree starts at zero and records the total of window values in each Fenwick range.
A deque holds the window in arrival order so we can remove the oldest value quickly.
This helper updates both Fenwick trees when a value enters or leaves the window.
This comment says we add delta copies of the value into both trees.
We start the walk at the index equal to the value itself.
We keep climbing while the index stays within the maximum value.
At each node we adjust the count by delta.
At each node we adjust the sum by delta times the value.
We jump to the next responsible node by adding the lowest set bit of the index.
This helper returns the sum of the smallest target_count values in the window.
This comment says we descend the Fenwick tree by binary lifting to find that sum.
Position tracks the largest index whose prefix holds fewer values than we need, starting at zero.
Total sum accumulates the sum of all values skipped over, starting at zero.
Remaining is how many more smallest values we still need to account for.
Step begins at one and will grow to the highest power of two within range.
We loop while doubling step would still fit within the maximum value.
We double step to find that largest power of two.
Now we descend, trying each power of two from largest down to one.
We compute the candidate position reached by taking this step.
If the candidate is in range and its count is less than remaining, we can safely take the whole block.
We move our position forward to the candidate.
We subtract that block's count from remaining since those values are now fully taken.
We add that block's sum into the running total.
We halve the step to try the next smaller power of two.
The values at the next index all equal position plus one, so we add remaining copies of it to the total.
This method handles a new number arriving in the stream.
This comment says the queue must keep only the last m values.
We append the new number to the back of the window.
We add the new number into the Fenwick trees with a count of one.
If the window now holds more than m values, the oldest must go.
We pop the oldest value from the front of the deque.
We remove that oldest value from the Fenwick trees by updating with minus one.
This method answers a query for the MK average.
If fewer than m numbers have arrived, the average is undefined.
So we return negative one in that case.
This comment says the middle sum equals the smallest m minus k sum minus the smallest k sum.
We compute that difference, which leaves out the k smallest and k largest values.
We return the floor of the middle sum divided by the m minus two k values it contains.

house-robber-iii.hook: House Robber, but the street is a binary tree. Each node returns two answers.
house-robber-iii.ask: Houses form a binary tree. Robbing a house and its direct parent or child on the same night triggers the alarm. Return the most money you can steal.
house-robber-iii.exampleWhy: Rob 4 and 5, the root's two children: 9. Taking the root forces skipping both, giving only 3 + 1 + 3 + 1 = 8.

brute.idea: At each node, either rob it and jump to its grandchildren, or skip it and recurse on its children. Take the better.
steps: Rob: node value plus best of the four grandchildren
Skip: best of left plus best of right
Return the max
brute.whySlow: Grandchildren get solved again from their grandparents, so the same subtrees are recomputed exponentially many times.

optimal.insight: Let every node report a pair: best if it is robbed, best if it is not. A parent combines its children's pairs in constant time.
steps: Post-order DFS returns (with node, without node)
With node: value + both children's without
Without node: max of each child's pair, summed
Answer is the larger of the root's pair

codeNotes.note: Best of the root's two options

pitfalls: Skipping a node does not force robbing its children; take each child's max.
A memo dict on nodes also works, but the pair return needs no extra map.

say.intro: Okay, so this time the houses form a binary tree. Rob a house and its parent or child on the same night, and the alarm goes off. In our tree, robbing the two children, four and five, gives nine. Robbing the root only gives eight.
say.brute: The direct way follows the rules. At each node, either rob it, and jump to its four grandchildren. Or skip it, and recurse into its two children. Take the better one. Correct, but here's the catch. Each grandchild gets solved from its grandparent, and again from its parent. Those repeats pile up. The work can grow exponentially.
say.insight: So how do we stop the repeats? Have each node return two numbers instead of one. The best total if this node is robbed. And the best total if it isn't. Now a parent decides in constant time. Robbed? Then both children must be skipped. Skipped? Then each child just picks its own better option.
say.anim: We start at the root node 3, about to explore its left subtree first. Leaf node 1 has no children, so both its rob and skip values are zero. Node 4 explores its child, leaf 3, which also returns zero for both options. Node 4 combines results: robbing it gives 4, skipping gives 4 too. Now we move right to node 5, exploring its children 1 and leaf nodes. Node 5 computes robbing as 5, and skipping as 1 from its children. At root 3, robbing gives 8, skipping gives 9, since skipping allows both subtrees fully. The final maximum value returned is 9, the best possible robbery amount.
say.code: Let's walk the code. An empty subtree gives zero either way. We visit children first, so it's post order. If we rob this node, the children must be skipped. If we skip it, the children choose freely. At the end, return the best of the root's two options.
say.outro: Linear time, one visit per house. Return a pair from each node. That's dynamic programming on trees.

house-robber-iii.title: House Robber III
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container the interview platform expects for our answer.
The rob method takes the root of the house tree and returns the maximum money we can steal.
Inside it we define a helper called dfs that returns a pair of best values for one node.
If the current node is empty, there is nothing to rob, so we handle this base case first.
An empty node returns zero for both robbed and not robbed, giving the recursion a clean stopping point.
We recursively solve the left child, getting its pair of robbed and not robbed totals.
We do the same for the right child, so both subtrees are fully solved before we combine them.
If we rob this node, we add its value to the not robbed totals of both children, since they must be skipped.
If we skip this node, each child is free, so we add the better option from the left and from the right.
We return the pair of robbed total and not robbed total so the parent can use them.
Finally we run dfs from the root and return the larger of its two values as the answer.

house-robber-iv.hook: Minimise the biggest single heist. Guess a cap, then a greedy check says yes or no.
house-robber-iv.ask: Rob at least k non-adjacent houses. Your capability is the largest amount taken from one house. Return the smallest capability that still lets you rob k houses.
house-robber-iv.exampleWhy: Rob houses 0 and 4, worth 2 and 1. The biggest single take is 2, and no plan with two houses does better.

brute.idea: The answer is one of the house values. Try them from smallest up, greedily checking whether k houses fit under each cap.
steps: Sort the distinct values
For each cap, greedily rob houses ≤ cap, skipping neighbours
First cap reaching k houses wins
brute.whySlow: Up to 100,000 candidate caps, each with a full greedy pass: ten billion steps.

optimal.insight: Feasibility is monotonic: if a cap works, any bigger cap works. So binary search the cap, and check each guess greedily.
steps: Search cap between min and max house value
Greedy: take any house ≤ cap, then skip its neighbour
At least k taken? Try a smaller cap
Otherwise raise the cap

pitfalls: Taking the earliest affordable house is always safe; it never blocks a better plan.
Search on values, not indices; do not sort nums.

say.intro: Okay, so we must rob at least k houses, never two neighbours. Our capability is the most we take from any one house. We want it as small as possible. In two, seven, nine, three, one with k equal to two, rob the first and last houses. The biggest take is just two.
say.brute: The answer must be one of the house values, right? So sort the values and try them from smallest up. For each cap, walk the street greedily. Take any house at or below the cap, and skip its neighbour. The first cap that reaches k wins. But that's quadratic. A hundred thousand caps, each needing a full pass.
say.insight: Now, notice something. If a cap lets us rob k houses, any bigger cap works too. The answer is monotonic. And what loves a monotonic yes or no question? Binary search. So instead of trying every cap, we halve the range each time. The greedy walk is our check. One pass per halving.
say.anim: We start with houses 2,7,9,3,1 and need to rob at least 2, searching capability range 1 to 9. Mid guess is 5; we scan houses, robbing nonadjacent ones with value at most 5. House 2 and house 3 both qualify, giving a count of 2, meeting our target. Since count reached 2, hi shrinks to 5, and we try a smaller mid of 3. Scanning again, houses 2 and 3 still qualify, count hits 2, so hi becomes 3. Next mid is 2; only house 2 and house 1 qualify, count reaches 2 again. Hi shrinks to 2, then mid drops to 1, but only house 1 qualifies now, count just 1. Since count falls short, lo rises to 2, loop ends, and the answer returned is 2.
say.code: Let's walk the code. The answer lies between the smallest and largest values. For each middle cap, we walk the houses. An affordable house? Take it. Then skip the neighbour. If we reach k, the cap is feasible, so try smaller. If not, we need a bigger cap.
say.outro: n times log of the value range. Binary search on the answer, with a greedy check inside. A classic pairing.

house-robber-iv.title: House Robber IV
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container the judge expects for our method.
The method minCapability takes the list of house values and k, the number of houses we must rob.
We set the search range for the capability between the smallest and the largest house value.
We keep searching while the low end is below the high end, so the range still holds several candidates.
We pick the middle value of the range as the capability we want to test.
We start a greedy check with a count of zero robbed houses and an index at the first house.
We walk through every house from left to right until we run past the end.
If this house's value fits within the guessed capability, we are able to rob it.
We count this robbed house toward our total.
We jump ahead two houses, because we cannot rob the adjacent neighbor.
Otherwise this house is too valuable for the guessed capability and must be skipped.
We move forward just one house to consider the next one.
If we robbed at least k houses, this capability works, so a smaller one might also work.
We shrink the upper bound down to mid, keeping mid as a possible answer.
Otherwise the capability was too small to rob k houses.
We raise the lower bound to just above mid, since mid and anything lower fails.
When the range collapses to one value, that is the smallest feasible capability, so we return it.

insert-delete-getrandom-o1.hook: Constant-time insert, delete and random pick. The trick: delete by swapping with the last element.
insert-delete-getrandom-o1.ask: Design a set of integers that supports insert, remove and getRandom, where getRandom returns each current element with equal probability. Every operation must run in average constant time.
insert-delete-getrandom-o1.exampleWhy: Removing 10 moves 30 into its slot. 20 is already present, so inserting it fails. After removing 30, only 20 remains to pick.

brute.idea: Keep the values in a plain list. Check membership by scanning, remove by searching, and pick a random index.
steps: insert: scan for val, append if missing
remove: scan for val, delete it, shifting the rest
getRandom: random index into the list
brute.whySlow: Membership checks and middle deletions scan or shift the list: 200,000 calls on a large set is billions of moves.

optimal.insight: A list gives O(1) random access; a map from value to index gives O(1) lookup. Delete by moving the last element into the hole.
steps: List holds values; map holds each value's index
Insert: append and record the index
Remove: copy the last value into the hole, pop the end
getRandom: pick a random list slot

codeNotes.note: Value to its position in vals
New value goes at the end
Uniform pick over a dense list

pitfalls: Update the moved element's index before deleting val; order matters when val is last.
A set alone cannot pick a random element in O(1).

say.intro: Okay, so we design a set with three moves. Insert, remove, and pick a random element. Each one in constant time on average. In our run we insert ten, twenty and thirty. Remove ten. Fail to insert twenty again. Remove thirty. So the random pick has to be twenty.
say.brute: The simple way? Keep a plain list. Insert scans it to avoid duplicates. Remove searches for the value and deletes it, shifting everything after it. Random is easy, just pick an index. But the scans and shifts are linear. A big set with lots of calls means billions of operations.
say.insight: Here's the thing. We need two strengths at once. A list gives random access, so the random pick is trivial. A map from value to index gives instant lookup. So what's the hard part? Deleting from the middle of the list. The trick: copy the last element into the hole, fix its index, then pop the end. Popping the end is constant time.
say.anim: We start with an empty list and an empty map to track values and their positions. Inserting 10, 20, and 30 appends each to the list and records its index in the map, returning true each time. Removing 10 finds its index 0, moves last value 30 into that spot, and updates the map. The list shrinks and 10 is deleted from the map, so remove returns true. Trying to insert 20 again fails since it is already in the map, so insert returns false. Removing 30 finds index 0, moves last value 20 into that spot, and updates the map. The list shrinks again and 30 is deleted from the map, so remove returns true. Finally getRandom picks randomly from the remaining list, returning the only value left, 20.
say.code: Let's walk the code. The map sends each value to its position in the list. A new value goes at the end. To remove, the last element fills the hole. Then we update the moved value's index. Pop the end, constant time. And random just picks from the dense list.
say.outro: Constant average time for everything. List plus index map, and swap with the last to delete. Remember that one.

insert-delete-getrandom-o1.title: Insert Delete GetRandom O(1)
lineNotes: We import the random module so we can pick a uniformly random element later.
We define a class called RandomizedSet that bundles the list and the map together.
The constructor sets up the empty starting state for a new set.
We create a list called vals that stores the elements and gives constant time random access.
We create a dictionary called index that maps each value to its position in vals.
The insert method adds a value and reports whether it was actually new.
We check whether the value is already a key in the index map.
If it already exists, we return False because sets do not allow duplicates.
We record the value's future position, which is the current length of vals, in the index map.
We append the value to the end of the list, which takes constant time.
We return True to signal that the insertion succeeded.
The remove method deletes a value and reports whether it was present.
We check whether the value is missing from the index map.
If it is missing, we return False since there is nothing to remove.
We look up the position of the value to remove and store it as i.
We grab the last element of the list, which will fill the hole.
We overwrite the slot at position i with the last element, covering the removed value.
We update the index map so the moved last element now points to position i.
We pop the final list entry, which is now a duplicate, keeping removal constant time.
We delete the removed value's key from the index map to finish cleanup.
We return True to signal that the removal succeeded.
The getRandom method returns one current element with equal probability.
We use random choice on the list, which picks uniformly because the list holds exactly the current elements.

intersection-of-two-arrays.hook: Which values do two arrays share? Put one in a set and walk the other.
intersection-of-two-arrays.ask: Given two integer arrays, return every value that appears in both, listing each shared value once. Any order is fine.
intersection-of-two-arrays.exampleWhy: 4 and 9 appear in both arrays. 5 and 8 appear in only one, and repeats are listed once.

brute.idea: For each value in the first array, scan the second array looking for it, and skip values already reported.
steps: Take x from nums1
Already in result? skip
Scan nums2 for x; found means shared
brute.whySlow: Each value rescans the whole second array: 1,000 by 1,000 is a million comparisons for a tiny answer.

optimal.insight: A set of the first array answers is x shared in constant time. Removing a value after reporting it prevents duplicates.
steps: Build a set from nums1
Walk nums2
In the set? report it and remove it

pitfalls: Without removing from the set, 9 in nums2 twice would be reported twice.
set(nums1) & set(nums2) is a fine one-liner; explain it is the same idea.

say.intro: Okay, so we get two lists of numbers. Return the values they share, each one once, in any order. With four, nine, five and nine, four, nine, eight, four, the shared values are nine and four. Five and eight only live on one side.
say.brute: The obvious way? Take each value from the first array. Scan the whole second array looking for it. Found it, and not already reported? Add it. It's correct. But every lookup is a full scan. A thousand numbers on each side means a million comparisons. All for a handful of results.
say.insight: Here's the thing. We keep asking one question. Does this value exist on the other side? And a hash set answers that instantly. So put the first array into a set. Walk the second array once. When a value is in the set, report it. Then remove it from the set. Why remove it? So a later repeat isn't reported twice.
say.anim: We start by turning nums1 into a set called seen, holding nine, four, and five. We loop through nums2, checking each value against the seen set for fast lookups. X is nine, which is in seen, so we append it to result and remove it. Next x is four, also found in seen, so it joins result too, then gets removed. Now x is nine again, but it was already removed, so it's skipped as a duplicate. X is eight, not in seen at all, so nothing happens this round. X is four again, already removed earlier, so it's ignored to avoid duplicates. The loop ends and the function returns the final intersection, nine and four.
say.code: Let's walk the code. First, a set of the distinct values in the first array. Then for each value in the second, an instant check. Is it shared? If so, report it. Then remove it, so we never report it twice.
say.outro: Linear time. When you keep asking whether something exists, turn one side into a set.

intersection-of-two-arrays.title: Intersection of Two Arrays
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container the interview platform expects for our method.
The intersection method takes two integer lists and will return a list of values found in both.
We build a set called seen from the first array, giving constant time membership checks and dropping its duplicates.
We start an empty list called result to collect the shared values we find.
We loop through each value x in the second array, checking one value at a time.
If x is in seen, then it appears in both arrays and qualifies as shared.
We add x to result because it is a confirmed shared value.
We remove x from seen so a repeat of x in the second array is not reported again.
After checking every value in the second array, we return result holding each shared value exactly once.

interval-list-intersections.hook: Two sorted interval lists, one zipper. Overlap is max of starts to min of ends.
interval-list-intersections.ask: Given two lists of disjoint, sorted, closed intervals, return all the intervals where they overlap, in sorted order.
interval-list-intersections.exampleWhy: [0,2] meets [1,5] on [1,2]; [5,10] touches [1,5] at 5 and meets [8,12] on [8,10]; and so on.

brute.idea: Compare every interval of the first list with every interval of the second, keeping any non-empty overlap.
steps: Pick an interval from each list
Overlap is max of starts to min of ends
Non-empty? keep it
brute.whySlow: Most pairs are far apart, yet all are checked: 1,000 intervals each means a million pairs.

optimal.insight: Both lists are sorted. The interval that ends first cannot overlap anything later, so discard it and advance that pointer only.
steps: One pointer per list
Overlap = [max of starts, min of ends] if non-empty
Advance whichever interval ends first
Stop when either list runs out

pitfalls: Use lo <= hi, not <: closed intervals touching at a point overlap.
Advance by end time, not start time.

say.intro: Okay, so we get two lists of closed intervals. Each list is sorted, with no overlaps inside it. We return every stretch where an interval from one meets an interval from the other. For example, zero to two meets one to five on one to two. And five to ten touches one to five at just the point five.
say.brute: The obvious way? Compare every interval in the first list with every one in the second. Each overlap runs from the later start to the earlier end. Keep it if it isn't empty. It even comes out in order. But it checks every pair. A thousand intervals per list is a million comparisons.
say.insight: Here's the thing. The lists are sorted, so let's use that. Keep one pointer in each list. Look only at the current pair. Record their overlap. Then ask, which one ends first? That one can't overlap anything further along. Why? Everything later starts later. So drop it, and advance only that pointer. One interval gone per step. That's linear.
say.anim: We start with pointers i and j both at zero, and an empty result list. Comparing the first intervals, the overlap is lo one, hi two, so we add one, two. Since firstList's interval ended first, we advance i to one and discard it. Now comparing intervals at i one and j zero, overlap lo five hi five is added. SecondList's interval ended first this time, so j advances to one. Next overlap is eight to ten, added, then i advances since its interval ended first. Intervals thirteen,twenty three and eight,twelve don't overlap, so j moves forward again. Overlaps fifteen,twenty three and twenty four,twenty four and twenty five,twenty five get added as pointers advance. Final result is one two, five five, eight ten, fifteen twenty three, twenty four twenty four, twenty five twenty five.
say.code: Let's walk the code. The overlap starts at the later start. It ends at the earlier end. These are closed intervals, so touching counts. We keep it if low is at most high. Then we drop whichever interval ends first.
say.outro: Linear time. Overlap is max start to min end. Then discard whichever ends first. That's the intervals zipper.

interval-list-intersections.title: Interval List Intersections
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, as the problem platform expects, to hold our method.
This method takes the two sorted interval lists and returns the list of their intersections.
We start two pointers, i and j, at zero so each walks through its own list.
We create an empty result list to collect every overlapping interval we find.
We keep looping while both pointers are still inside their lists, since an overlap needs one interval from each.
The overlap starts at the larger of the two start points, so lo takes the maximum of the starts.
The overlap ends at the smaller of the two end points, so hi takes the minimum of the ends.
If lo is less than or equal to hi, the two intervals truly overlap, and touching endpoints count because they are closed.
In that case we append the interval from lo to hi to the result.
Now we compare end points, because the interval that ends first cannot overlap anything further in the other list.
If the first list's interval ends earlier, we discard it by moving i forward.
Otherwise the second list's interval ends first or at the same time as the first's.
So we advance j to move past the second list's interval.
Once either list runs out, no more overlaps are possible, so we return the collected result.

majority-element-ii.hook: At most two values can beat a third of the vote. Keep two candidates and cancel the rest.
majority-element-ii.ask: Given an integer array of length n, return every value that appears more than n / 3 times, rounded down. Ideally use linear time and constant extra space.
majority-element-ii.exampleWhy: n = 8, so we need more than 2 copies. 1 and 2 each appear 3 times; 3 and 4 appear once.

brute.idea: For each value, count its occurrences by scanning the whole array, and keep it if the count exceeds n / 3.
steps: Take each value x
Already reported? skip
Count x by scanning; above n / 3? keep
brute.whySlow: Each value triggers a full count scan: 50,000 numbers means up to 2.5 billion comparisons.

optimal.insight: Three distinct values cancel each other out without hurting any true winner. Since at most two can exceed n / 3, two candidate slots suffice.
steps: Keep two candidates with vote counts
Match a candidate? add a vote
Empty slot? claim it
Otherwise remove one vote from both
Verify both candidates with a real count

codeNotes.match: cand1, cand2, cnt1, cnt2 = None, None, 0, 0

pitfalls: Always verify: surviving candidates are only possible winners.
Test matches against both candidates before claiming an empty slot, or one value fills both.

say.intro: Okay, so we return every value that shows up more than a third of the time. In one, two, three, one, two, one, two, four there are eight numbers. So a winner needs at least three copies. One has three. Two has three. The answer is one and two.
say.brute: The obvious way? Take each value and count it by scanning the whole array. Above a third, and not reported yet? Keep it. No extra memory. But every count is a full scan. Fifty thousand numbers can mean billions of comparisons.
say.insight: Here's the thing. How many values can each hold more than a third? At most two. So keep two candidates, each with a vote count. When a third, different value shows up, take one vote from both. That cancels three distinct values at once. And a true winner can't be wiped out that way. At the end, count the survivors to confirm.
say.anim: We start with two empty candidate slots and their counters both at zero. First value one has no candidate yet, so it becomes candidate one with count one. Next value two fills the empty second slot, becoming candidate two with count one. Value three matches neither candidate, so both counts get decremented, dropping candidate one's count to zero. Value one reclaims the empty slot, becoming candidate one again with count one. More twos and ones arrive, incrementing their matching counters up to two each. Value four matches neither, so both counts are decremented again, showing cancellation at work. Checking true counts confirms one and two both exceed a third of the array, giving the final answer one two.
say.code: Let's walk the code. Two slots, two vote counts. We check for a match before looking for an empty slot. If a slot is empty, we claim it. Otherwise three distinct values cancel. Finally, a second pass confirms the real winners.
say.outro: Linear time, constant space. Boyer Moore voting, stretched to two candidates. No frequency map needed.

majority-element-ii.title: Majority Element II
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container the interview platform expects for our method.
The method takes a list of integers and returns a list of every value appearing more than a third of the time.
We start with two empty candidate slots and two counters at zero, since at most two values can win.
We loop over each number x in the array exactly once, which keeps the whole algorithm linear.
If x matches the first candidate, we are looking at a vote for that candidate.
So we increase the first counter by one to strengthen that candidate.
Otherwise, if x matches the second candidate, it is a vote for that one.
So we increase the second counter by one.
If neither candidate matches and the first counter is zero, that first slot is free to be taken.
We make x the first candidate and set its counter to one.
Otherwise, if the second counter is zero, the second slot is free.
We make x the second candidate and set its counter to one.
If x matches neither candidate and both slots are occupied, three distinct values are present and they cancel out.
We decrease the first counter by one to account for that cancellation.
We decrease the second counter by one as well, so each of the three values loses a vote.
Since the candidates are only possible winners, we verify each by counting it in nums and keep those exceeding the length divided by three, rounded down.

make-the-string-great.hook: Letters cancel with their opposite case neighbour. A stack does all the chain reactions in one pass.
make-the-string-great.ask: Repeatedly delete any adjacent pair that is the same letter in opposite cases, like aA or Bb, until none remain. Return the final string, which may be empty.
make-the-string-great.exampleWhy: bB cancels, which brings a next to A, which cancels too. Finally cC cancels, leaving nothing.

brute.idea: Scan for any bad adjacent pair, cut it out, and start scanning again from the beginning until a full scan finds nothing.
steps: Scan for an opposite case pair
Found? cut it out and rescan
No pair? return the string
brute.whySlow: Each removal restarts the scan and rebuilds the string, so nested pairs cost quadratic time.

optimal.insight: After a pair cancels, the only new neighbours are the stack top and the next letter. So compare each letter with the stack top.
steps: Walk the string left to right
Top is the same letter, opposite case? pop
Otherwise push the letter
Join the stack

codeNotes.match: if stack and stack[-1] != c and stack[-1].lower() == c.lower():

pitfalls: aa is not bad: require different characters with equal lowercase.
abs(ord(a) - ord(b)) == 32 is an equivalent check.

say.intro: Okay, so a pair of neighbouring letters is bad if it's the same letter in opposite cases. Like lower b next to capital B. We keep deleting bad pairs until none are left. With a, b, capital B, capital A, c, capital C, everything cancels. We return the empty string.
say.brute: The obvious way? Scan for any bad pair. Cut it out. Then start scanning again from the beginning. Stop when a full scan finds nothing. It's correct. But each removal restarts the scan and rebuilds the string. Deeply nested pairs make that quadratic.
say.insight: Now, notice where a new bad pair can appear. After a pair cancels, who become neighbours? Only the letter just before it, and the letter just after. And that's exactly what a stack holds. The survivors so far, with the latest one on top. So compare each new letter with the top. They cancel? Pop. Otherwise, push.
say.anim: We start with an empty stack and the string abBAcC to clean up. Letters a and b get pushed since the stack top never matches the next letter. Now c is capital B, which matches lowercase b on top, so we pop it. Next c is A, matching the remaining a, so that also gets popped. Stack is empty again, then c gets pushed as a fresh letter. Finally capital C matches lowercase c on top, so it pops too. The stack ends up empty after all these cancelling pairs. Joining the empty stack gives the final answer, an empty string.
say.code: Let's walk the code. The stack holds the letters that survived so far. For each new letter, we check the top. Same letter, different case? Then we cancel the pair by popping. Otherwise, the letter survives, for now. At the end, we join the stack into a string.
say.outro: Linear time. When removals expose new neighbours, let a stack track the survivors.

make-the-string-great.title: Make The String Great
lineNotes: We define a class named Solution, which is the wrapper this problem expects for the method.
The makeGood method takes the string s and returns the final string after all bad adjacent pairs are removed.
We start with an empty stack that will hold the letters that survive so far.
We walk through the string one character at a time, calling the current letter c.
If the stack has a top that is a different character but the same letter ignoring case, the two form a bad pair.
In that case we pop the top off the stack, which cancels the pair.
Otherwise the new letter does not cancel with the top, so we take the else branch.
We push c onto the stack because it is safe next to the current top.
Finally we join the stack letters into one string and return it, which is empty if everything canceled.

manhattan-distances-of-all-arrangements-.hook: Sum distances over every arrangement without listing any. Count each cell pair once, then multiply.
manhattan-distances-of-all-arrangements-.ask: Place k identical pieces on an m by n grid, one per cell. Over every possible arrangement, add up the Manhattan distance between every pair of pieces. Return the total modulo 10⁹ + 7.
manhattan-distances-of-all-arrangements-.exampleWhy: All cell pairs on a 2 by 3 grid sum to 25, and each pair appears in 4 arrangements, so 100.

brute.idea: Enumerate every way to choose k cells, and for each arrangement sum the distances over all pairs of chosen cells.
steps: List all cells
Try every k-subset of cells
Add the distance of every pair inside it
brute.whySlow: The number of arrangements explodes: a 10 by 10 grid with 5 pieces already has 75 million.

optimal.insight: Flip the sum. Each pair of cells appears in exactly C(mn - 2, k - 2) arrangements. So total = (sum over cell pairs) × that count.
steps: Row gap d occurs (m - d) times, times n² column choices
Column gap d occurs (n - d) times, times m² row choices
Add both for the all-pairs distance sum
Multiply by C(mn - 2, k - 2)

codeNotes.note: Row pairs at vertical gap d
Column pairs at horizontal gap d

codeNotes.match: pair_sum = rows * n * n + cols * m * m

pitfalls: Outside Python, compute the binomial with factorials and modular inverses.
x and y distances are independent; never loop over pairs of cells.

say.intro: Okay, so we place k identical pieces on an m by n grid, at most one per cell. For every possible arrangement, we add up the Manhattan distance between every pair of pieces. Then we return the grand total. On a two by three grid with three pieces, that total is one hundred.
say.brute: The obvious way? List every way to choose k cells. For each arrangement, loop over every pair of pieces and add their distance. It's a faithful reading of the problem. But the number of arrangements explodes. A ten by ten grid with five pieces already has seventy five million.
say.insight: Here's the thing. Flip the sum around. Forget arrangements. Think about one pair of cells. How many arrangements contain that pair? Every way to place the other k minus two pieces elsewhere. That's one binomial count, the same for every pair. So the answer is the sum of all pair distances, times that count. And rows and columns can be counted separately.
say.anim: We start with a grid of 2 rows, 3 columns, and k equals 3 pieces. Rows sums the row distance contributions, giving rows equals 1 after the loop. Now cols accumulates column distance contributions across column gaps of 1 and 2. After the loop, cols ends up equal to 4. Pair sum combines row and column totals weighted by grid dimensions, giving 25. Ways counts arrangements of remaining pieces using combinations, giving 4. Multiplying pair sum by ways and taking mod gives the final answer, 100.
say.code: Let's walk the code. For each vertical gap d, we count the row pairs that far apart. We do the same for columns, with horizontal gaps. Adding both gives every cell pair's distance, summed. Then we multiply by the arrangements containing a given pair. That's the contribution technique.
say.outro: Near linear time. Count how often each pair contributes, instead of enumerating everything. That's the trick.

manhattan-distances-of-all-arrangements-.title: Manhattan Distances of All Arrangements of Pieces
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container the problem expects for our method.
The method distanceSum takes the grid height m, width n, and the number of pieces k.
We set the modulus to ten to the ninth plus seven, since the answer can be enormous.
We start rows at zero to accumulate the total vertical distance across all row pairs.
We loop d over every possible row gap from one up to m minus one.
A gap of d has m minus d row pairs, so we add d times that count to rows.
We start cols at zero to accumulate the total horizontal distance across all column pairs.
We loop d over every possible column gap from one up to n minus one.
A gap of d has n minus d column pairs, so we add d times that count to cols.
Each row pair is matched with n choices of column for both cells, giving n squared, and similarly for columns, so pair_sum totals every cell pair's distance.
Fixing two cells for a pair, the other k minus two pieces fill the remaining cells, so ways is the combination of m times n minus two choose k minus two.
We multiply pair_sum by ways to count each pair in every arrangement, then take the result modulo the large prime.

maximize-subarray-sum-after-removing-all.hook: Delete every copy of one value, then run Kadane. A segment tree makes each deletion cheap.
maximize-subarray-sum-after-removing-all.ask: You may delete all copies of one chosen value, as long as something remains, or delete nothing. Return the largest possible sum of a non-empty contiguous subarray afterwards.
maximize-subarray-sum-after-removing-all.exampleWhy: Deleting every -2 leaves [-1,3,4], whose best subarray 3 + 4 = 7 beats the untouched best of 5.

brute.idea: Try every distinct value: build the array without it, and run Kadane's algorithm on what remains. Also try deleting nothing.
steps: Kadane on the original array
For each distinct value, filter it out
Kadane on the filtered array
Keep the best
brute.whySlow: With up to 100,000 distinct values, each needs a full Kadane pass: about ten billion steps.

optimal.insight: Kadane merges: each segment keeps sum, best prefix, best suffix, best inside. Blank out one value's positions, read the root, restore.
steps: Segment tree over nums with Kadane summaries
Answer starts as the root's best
For each value, blank its positions and read the root
Restore those positions; total updates are n

codeNotes.note: Best crosses the middle via suffix + prefix

pitfalls: Empty slots need -inf prefix and best, or an empty subarray would score 0.
Skip a value that fills the whole array; the result must stay non-empty.

say.intro: Okay, so we may pick one value and delete every copy of it. Or delete nothing. Then we want the best contiguous sum. In minus one, three, minus two, four, minus two, delete both minus twos. Now three and four join up. That's seven.
say.brute: The obvious way? Try every distinct value. Build the array without it. Run Kadane's algorithm for the best subarray sum. Also try deleting nothing. It's correct. But every distinct value costs a full pass. A hundred thousand distinct values is around ten billion steps.
say.insight: Here's the thing. Kadane's answer can be merged from two halves. Give each segment four numbers. Its total, best prefix, best suffix, and best inside. Two neighbours combine in constant time. So put those in a segment tree. To delete a value, blank out its positions, in log time each. Read the root. Then put them back. Every position gets touched just twice.
say.anim: We start with the array negative one, three, negative two, four, negative two, building a segment tree. Each leaf stores a value as its sum, best prefix, best suffix, and best inside subarray. After building, the tree root shows a best subarray sum of five across the whole array. Now we try removing each distinct value in turn, blanking its positions to empty segments. Removing negative one and restoring it keeps the best sum at five, no improvement yet. Removing both negative two positions merges three and four together, raising best up to seven. Removing the single four instead doesn't help, so best stays locked at seven. The function returns seven, the maximum subarray sum after removing one value's occurrences.
say.code: Let's walk the code. A deleted slot contributes nothing. When merging, the best can cross the middle, using a suffix plus a prefix. A point update rebuilds one ancestor at a time. For each value, we delete every copy. The root holds the whole array answer. Then we put the copies back.
say.outro: n log n time. Kadane's state, made mergeable, inside a segment tree. That's dynamic programming meeting a data structure.

maximize-subarray-sum-after-removing-all.title: Maximize Subarray Sum After Removing All Occurrences of One Element
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, as the problem platform expects.
The method takes the list nums and returns the best subarray sum after at most one value is removed.
NEG is negative infinity, used as a safe stand-in for no valid choice.
EMPTY is a blank segment with sum zero and negative infinity for prefix, suffix and best, so it contributes nothing.
The leaf helper builds the node for a single element.
A leaf has its sum, best prefix, best suffix and best inside all equal to that value.
The merge helper combines a left segment a and a right segment b into one segment.
The merged sum is the two sums added, and the best prefix is either a's prefix or all of a plus b's prefix.
The best suffix is either b's suffix or all of b plus a's suffix, and the best inside is the max of a's, b's, or a's suffix joined to b's prefix.
We start size at one to find a power of two that fits all the numbers.
We loop while size is smaller than the length of nums.
Each pass doubles size, so the tree has a perfect shape.
The tree array holds twice size nodes, all initially EMPTY so padding leaves are harmless.
We walk through nums with each index and value.
Each value is placed as a leaf at its slot in the bottom level.
We build internal nodes from the bottom up, going from size minus one down to one.
Each parent is the merge of its left and right children.
The update helper sets one position to a new node and refreshes ancestors.
We shift the index to its leaf position in the tree.
We store the new node at that leaf.
We climb until we reach the root.
Moving to the parent is done by halving the index.
We recompute that parent by merging its two children.
The positions dictionary will map each value to the list of indices where it appears.
We scan nums again to fill that map.
Each index is appended to the list for its value.
The initial best is the root's best inside, which is the answer when nothing is deleted.
We try deleting each distinct value x, along with its list of indices.
If x fills the whole array, deleting it would leave nothing, so we check that by length.
In that case we skip this value.
Otherwise we go through every index where x occurs.
We blank each of those positions by setting it to EMPTY.
We read the root's best inside for the array without x and keep the larger best.
Now we loop over the same indices to restore the array.
Each position gets its original leaf back so the next value starts from the full array.
We return the best sum found across all choices.
