maximum-absolute-sum-of-any-subarray.hook: Biggest positive or most negative subarray? It is just the highest prefix sum minus the lowest.
maximum-absolute-sum-of-any-subarray.ask: Return the largest absolute value of the sum of any contiguous subarray. The empty subarray counts, with sum 0.
maximum-absolute-sum-of-any-subarray.exampleWhy: The subarray [-5,1,-4] sums to -8, whose absolute value 8 is the largest possible.

brute.idea: Try every start, extend the end one step at a time with a running sum, and track the largest absolute value.
steps: Fix a start index
Extend the end, adding one value at a time
Track the max of abs(sum)
brute.whySlow: There are n² / 2 subarrays: 100,000 numbers means five billion sums.

optimal.insight: Any subarray sum is a difference of two prefix sums. The largest absolute difference is simply max prefix minus min prefix.
steps: Walk once, keeping the prefix sum
Track the highest and lowest prefix, starting at 0
Answer is highest minus lowest

pitfalls: Order does not matter: the absolute value lets lo come after hi.
Running Kadane for max and for min, then taking the larger, is the equivalent DP.

say.intro: Okay, so we look at every contiguous subarray and take its sum. We want the largest absolute value. A big negative counts just as much as a big positive. In two, minus five, one, minus four, three, minus two, the stretch minus five, one, minus four sums to minus eight. So the answer is eight.
say.brute: The obvious way? Fix each start. Extend the end one step at a time, keeping a running sum. Track the biggest absolute value. No wasted re-adding. But there are still about n squared over two subarrays. A hundred thousand numbers? Five billion sums.
say.insight: Here's the thing. Every subarray sum is a difference of two prefix sums. The prefix at its end, minus the prefix before its start. And since we take the absolute value, order doesn't matter. So what's the biggest absolute sum? The highest prefix minus the lowest prefix. Count the empty prefix of zero too. One pass finds both.
say.anim: We start with prefix sum, running max, and running min all set to zero. Adding 2 makes prefix 2, so hi updates to 2 while lo stays at 0. Adding negative 5 drops prefix to negative 3, pushing lo down to negative 3. Adding 1 brings prefix to negative 2, but hi and lo remain unchanged. Adding negative 4 sends prefix to negative 6, a new lowest low point. Adding 3 raises prefix to negative 3, still within existing bounds. Adding negative 2 lowers prefix to negative 5, not a new extreme. Finally hi minus lo, 2 minus negative 6, gives the maximum absolute sum 8.
say.code: Let's walk the code. The empty prefix counts too, so we start everything at zero. Each step, the prefix grows by the next number. We track the highest prefix so far. And the lowest prefix so far. The answer is the widest gap between them.
say.outro: Linear time, constant space. A subarray sum is just a gap between two prefixes.

maximum-absolute-sum-of-any-subarray.title: Maximum Absolute Sum of Any Subarray
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container the problem expects for our method.
The method maxAbsoluteSum takes a list of integers called nums and returns the largest absolute subarray sum.
We start prefix, hi, and lo all at zero, since the empty prefix has sum zero and counts.
We loop through each number x in nums, building the running prefix sums one at a time.
We add x to prefix so it holds the sum of all elements seen so far.
We update hi to the larger of itself and prefix, tracking the maximum prefix sum seen.
We update lo to the smaller of itself and prefix, tracking the minimum prefix sum seen.
We return hi minus lo, because the biggest difference between any two prefix sums equals the best absolute subarray sum.

maximum-candies-allocated-to-k-children.hook: Guess a share size, count how many children it feeds, and binary search the guess.
maximum-candies-allocated-to-k-children.ask: Split candy piles into smaller piles, never merging two. Give k children one pile each, all the same size. Return the largest size every child can get, or 0.
maximum-candies-allocated-to-k-children.exampleWhy: Size 5 gives one share from each pile: three shares. Size 6 gives only two, from 8 and 6.

brute.idea: Try every share size from the biggest pile downward. The first size that feeds k children is the answer.
steps: Try size c from max pile down to 1
Shares = sum of pile // c
At least k? return c
None work? return 0
brute.whySlow: Piles reach ten million, so we may test ten million sizes, each scanning 100,000 piles.

optimal.insight: Bigger shares feed fewer children. That monotonic yes-or-no means we can binary search the share size.
steps: Search sizes between 0 and the largest pile
Count shares: sum of pile // mid
Enough? keep mid and go higher
Not enough? go lower

codeNotes.note: Round up: avoids an endless loop

codeNotes.match: if sum(c // mid for c in candies) >= k:
codeNotes.note: How many children does mid feed?

pitfalls: With lo = mid, round mid up or the loop can stall.
Start lo at 0 so mid is never zero and the answer can be 0.

say.intro: Okay, so we have piles of candy. We can split a pile, but never merge two. Each of k children gets one pile, all the same size. How big can that size be? With five, eight and six for three children, every child gets five.
say.brute: The obvious way? Try every share size, counting down from the biggest pile. For each size, count how many shares each pile can make. The first size that feeds k children wins. But piles can hold ten million candies. That's millions of sizes, each scanning every pile.
say.insight: Now, notice something. If a share size feeds k children, any smaller size does too. And if a size fails, every bigger size fails. So the answer is monotonic. That's binary search on the share size. Each guess costs one pass over the piles, dividing each one by the guess. And ten million only needs about twenty four guesses. That's the whole speedup.
say.anim: We start with candies five, eight, six, needing shares for three children, searching sizes zero to eight. Mid is four, giving enough candies for at least three children, so low moves up to four. Mid becomes six, but that share is too big, satisfying fewer than three children, so high drops to five. Now low is four and high is five, narrowing the search range further. Mid is five, which still allocates enough candies, so low updates to five. Low now equals high at five, ending the binary search loop. The function returns five, the maximum candies each of the three children can get.
say.code: Let's walk the code. Zero is always feasible, so low starts there. We round mid up. Why? Rounding down could loop forever. Then we count how many children mid can feed, pile by pile. Feasible? Keep it, and try bigger. Too big? Shrink the range below mid.
say.outro: n times log of the biggest pile. Binary search on the answer, with a simple counting check.

maximum-candies-allocated-to-k-children.title: Maximum Candies Allocated to K Children
lineNotes: We define the Solution class, which holds the method that solves the candy allocation problem.
This method takes the candy piles and the number of children, and returns the largest equal share size.
We set lo to zero as the safe answer and hi to the biggest pile, the maximum possible share.
We keep searching while lo is less than hi, meaning the answer is not yet pinned down.
We pick mid as the upper middle, rounding up so that setting lo to mid always makes progress.
We count how many children each pile can feed at size mid, and check whether the total reaches k.
Enough children can be fed, so mid works and we move lo up to mid to try bigger shares.
Otherwise the share size is too big to serve everyone, so we handle the failing case here.
Since mid fails, we lower hi to just below mid, discarding all larger sizes.
When lo meets hi, we return lo as the largest share size that still feeds k children.

maximum-number-of-points-from-grid-queri.hook: Answer every flood fill at once. Sort the queries and grow one frontier with a min-heap.
maximum-number-of-points-from-grid-queri.ask: For each query, start at the top-left cell and move through cells whose value is strictly less than the query. Count how many distinct cells you can reach. Return the counts in query order.
maximum-number-of-points-from-grid-queri.exampleWhy: Below 5 we reach the five cells valued 1 to 3 at the top and left. Below 6 the 5s open, reaching eight cells. Below 2 only the start.

brute.idea: For each query separately, flood fill from the top-left through cells smaller than the query and count them.
steps: For each query q
BFS from (0, 0) through cells < q
Record how many cells were visited
brute.whySlow: 10,000 queries times 100,000 cells is a billion cell visits, mostly repeating the same regions.

optimal.insight: A bigger query reaches everything a smaller one does. Sort queries and keep one frontier in a min-heap, always expanding the cheapest cell.
steps: Sort query indices by value
Min-heap frontier starts at the top-left cell
Pop cells smaller than q, count them, push neighbours
Record the count for that query
optimal.time: O(mn log mn + k log k)

pitfalls: Mark cells seen when pushed, not when popped, or they enter the heap twice.
Return answers in the original query order, not the sorted one.

say.intro: Okay, so for each query, we start at the top left cell. We can walk through any cell whose value is strictly smaller than the query. How many cells can we reach? In our grid, query five reaches five cells. Query six reaches eight. Query two reaches only the start.
say.brute: The obvious way? Handle each query on its own. Start cell too big? Zero. Otherwise, breadth first search through cells below the query, and count. It's correct. But every query floods the same regions again and again. Ten thousand queries on a hundred thousand cells is a billion visits.
say.insight: Here's the thing. A bigger query reaches everything a smaller one does, and more. So sort the queries, and grow one region. Keep the region's border in a min heap, keyed by cell value. For each query, pop the cheapest border cell while it's below the query. Count it. Push its neighbours. And the count carries straight into the next query.
say.anim: We start with the grid and queries, sorting query indices so we process smallest first, here order two, zero, one. The heap begins with just the top left cell, value one, since that is our starting point. Query two equals two, so we pop value one, count becomes one, and push neighbors two and two into the heap. Query index zero, value five, keeps expanding, popping twos then five, pushing new cells like three and seven. Count climbs to five as more cells under five get absorbed, giving answer five for the first query. Now query one, value six, pops five and keeps going, pushing cell value one at row two, column two. That tiny value one gets absorbed too, count reaches eight before the heap's smallest exceeds six. Final answer array is five, eight, one, matching the expected output exactly.
say.code: Let's walk the code. We answer small queries first. The frontier is a heap keyed by cell value. While the cheapest frontier cell is below the query, we enter it. A counted cell is never uncounted for later queries. Finally, we store each answer in the original query order.
say.outro: Each cell is pushed and popped once. Sort the queries offline, and grow a single frontier.

maximum-number-of-points-from-grid-queri.title: Maximum Number of Points From Grid Queries
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, as the problem platform expects.
The maxPoints method takes the grid and the list of queries and returns a list of counts.
We record the number of rows as m and the number of columns as n.
We sort the query indexes by query value, so we can process smaller queries first while remembering original positions.
We prepare an answer list of zeros, one slot for each query, to fill in original order.
The heap starts with the top-left cell, stored with its value and coordinates so the cheapest cell pops first.
We mark the top-left cell as seen so we never push it into the heap twice.
The count starts at zero and tracks how many cells we have reached so far across queries.
We loop over query indexes in sorted order, so each larger query builds on the progress of earlier ones.
While the cheapest frontier cell is strictly less than the current query, we keep expanding the region.
We pop the cheapest cell from the heap, getting its value and its row and column.
Since this cell is reachable under the current query, we add one to the count.
We look at the four neighbors of this cell: down, up, right, and left.
We only accept neighbors that are inside the grid and have not been seen before.
We mark the neighbor as seen right away so it cannot enter the heap again.
We push the neighbor onto the heap with its value, so it becomes part of the frontier.
Once no more cells can be expanded, we store the current count as this query's answer at its original index.
After all queries are handled, we return the filled answer list in the original query order.

maximum-score-after-splitting-a-string.hook: Zeros on the left, ones on the right. Slide the cut and update both counts in constant time.
maximum-score-after-splitting-a-string.ask: Split a binary string into two non-empty parts. The score is the number of zeros in the left part plus the number of ones in the right part. Return the best score.
maximum-score-after-splitting-a-string.exampleWhy: Cut after the first character: left "0" has one zero, right "11101" has four ones, for 5.

brute.idea: Try every cut position and count zeros on the left and ones on the right from scratch.
steps: Try each cut i from 1 to n - 1
Count zeros in s[:i]
Count ones in s[i:]
Keep the best total
brute.whySlow: Every cut recounts the whole string, so n cuts cost n² character checks.

optimal.insight: Moving the cut one step right moves one character across. A 0 adds a left zero; a 1 removes a right one.
steps: Count all ones: the right side before any cut
Move each character into the left
0: zeros + 1; 1: ones - 1
Track the best zeros + ones

codeNotes.note: Ones on the right, before any cut

pitfalls: Stop one character early: the right part may not be empty.
All ones still scores n - 1, not 0.

say.intro: Okay, so we cut a string of zeros and ones into two non-empty parts. The score is zeros on the left plus ones on the right. For zero, one, one, one, zero, one, cut after the first character. One zero on the left, four ones on the right. Score five.
say.brute: The obvious way? Try every cut. For each one, count the left zeros and the right ones from scratch. Keep the best. Simple and correct. But every cut rescans the whole string. So the total work is quadratic. For a long string, that's a lot of wasted rereading.
say.insight: Here's the thing. When the cut moves one step right, exactly one character crosses over. If it's a zero, the left gains a zero. If it's a one, the right loses a one. So count all the ones once. Then slide the cut and adjust two counters. Constant time per step.
say.anim: We start by counting ones in the string, giving four ones and zero zeros. The loop begins, checking each split point before the last character. At index zero the character is zero, so zeros becomes one, score jumps to five. At index one the character is one, so ones drops to three, score stays five. At index two ones drops to two, giving a lower score of three. At index three ones drops to one, score falls further to two. At index four zeros becomes two, raising the score back to three. The loop ends and the function returns the best score found, which is five.
say.code: Let's walk the code. Before any cut, all the ones are on the right. We stop one short of the end, so both parts stay non-empty. A zero joins the left. A one leaves the right. After each step, we check the score at this cut, and keep the best one we've seen.
say.outro: Linear time, constant space. Running counts beat rescanning, every time.

maximum-score-after-splitting-a-string.title: Maximum Score After Splitting a String
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container this problem's method lives in.
The method maxScore takes a binary string s and returns the best score as an integer.
We start by counting every one in the string, since with an empty left part all ones sit on the right.
Zeros counts the zeros in the left part, which starts at zero because the left part is empty.
Best tracks the highest score seen so far, starting at zero.
We loop over each index except the last, so the right part always keeps at least one character.
At each step we check whether the character being moved to the left part is a zero.
If it is a zero, we add one to zeros because the left part gained a zero.
Otherwise the character is a one, so it leaves the right part.
We subtract one from ones, since that one is no longer counted on the right.
We compute the score for this cut as zeros plus ones and keep it if it beats best.
After checking every possible cut, we return the best score found.

maximum-twin-sum-of-a-linked-list.hook: Pair the first node with the last, second with second last. Reverse half the list to walk both ends together.
maximum-twin-sum-of-a-linked-list.ask: In a linked list of even length n, node i and node n - 1 - i are twins. Return the largest sum of a node's value and its twin's value.
maximum-twin-sum-of-a-linked-list.exampleWhy: Twin pairs are 5 + 6 = 11, 4 + 3 = 7, and 2 + 1 = 3. The largest is 11.

brute.idea: Copy the values into an array, then pair index i with index n - 1 - i using two pointers.
steps: Copy every value into an array
Pair the left and right ends
Track the biggest sum, moving both inward
brute.whySlow: Time is already linear; the cost is an extra array of n values, which the in-place reversal avoids.

optimal.insight: Find the middle with slow and fast pointers, reverse the second half, and the twins line up side by side.
steps: Slow moves 1, fast moves 2: slow stops at the middle
Reverse the list from the middle
Walk the head and reversed half together
Track the largest pair sum

maximum-twin-sum-of-a-linked-list.optimalCode:
class Solution:
    def pairSum(self, head: Optional[ListNode]) -> int:
        slow = fast = head
        while fast and fast.next:
            slow = slow.next
            fast = fast.next.next
        prev = None
        while slow:
            nxt = slow.next
            slow.next = prev
            prev = slow
            slow = nxt
        best = 0
        first, second = head, prev
        while second:
            best = max(best, first.val + second.val)
            first = first.next
            second = second.next
        return best

codeNotes.note: Twice as fast: slow ends mid
Front half and reversed back half

pitfalls: Even length means slow lands on the first node of the second half; reverse from there.
The input list is modified; restore it if the caller needs it.

say.intro: Okay, so the list has an even number of nodes. The first and last are twins. Then the second and second last, and so on. We want the biggest twin sum. In five, four, two, one, three, six, the pairs give eleven, seven and three. So the answer is eleven.
say.brute: The simple way? Copy every value into an array. Two pointers start at both ends, add the pair, and move inward. That's already linear time. So what's wrong? Memory. It stores a second copy of every value. And interviewers love to ask you to avoid that.
say.insight: Here's the problem. A singly linked list can't walk backwards. So make the back half walk forwards. Slow and fast pointers find the middle. Then reverse the second half in place. Now the head of the list and the head of the reversed half are twins. Step both forward, and you visit every pair.
say.anim: We start with the list five, four, two, one, three, six, using slow and fast pointers. Slow and fast both move, slow one step and fast two steps, to find the middle. Fast reaches the end, so slow now sits at the middle of the list. Now we reverse the second half, flipping pointers until it becomes six, three, one. First points to the original head, second points to the reversed half's head. Adding five and six gives eleven, which becomes our best twin sum so far. Next pairs, four plus three and two plus one, both equal seven, smaller than eleven. The loop ends and the function returns eleven as the maximum twin sum.
say.code: Let's walk the code. Fast moves twice as fast, so slow ends at the middle. Then we reverse, flipping one pointer at a time. Now we walk the front half and the reversed back half together. Each step adds one twin pair.
say.outro: Linear time, constant extra space. Fast and slow pointers, plus an in place reversal.

maximum-twin-sum-of-a-linked-list.title: Maximum Twin Sum of a Linked List
lineNotes: We define the Solution class that holds the method for this problem.
The pairSum method takes the head of the linked list and returns the largest twin sum as an integer.
We start both slow and fast at the head so we can find the middle of the list.
We loop while fast and the node after it exist, since fast moves two steps at a time.
Slow moves one node forward each round, so it ends up at the middle.
Fast jumps two nodes forward, so when it runs out, slow sits at the start of the second half.
We set prev to none, which will become the tail end of the reversed second half.
We loop through the second half, starting at slow, until we run out of nodes.
We save the next node in nxt before we change any link, so we do not lose the rest.
We point the current node's next back to prev, which reverses one link.
We move prev up to the current node, since it is now the head of the reversed part.
We advance slow to the saved next node to continue reversing.
We set best to zero to track the largest twin sum we find.
We place first at the original head and second at the head of the reversed half, so twins line up.
We loop while second has nodes, since both halves have equal length.
We compare best with the sum of the current twin values and keep the larger one.
We move first forward one node in the first half.
We move second forward one node in the reversed second half to reach the next twin.
We return best, the maximum twin sum across all pairs.

maximum-width-of-binary-tree.hook: Count the gaps too. Number nodes like a heap and width is last index minus first plus one.
maximum-width-of-binary-tree.ask: Return the maximum width over all levels of a binary tree. A level's width runs from its leftmost to its rightmost node, counting the missing positions in between as if the tree were complete.
maximum-width-of-binary-tree.exampleWhy: The bottom level has 6 at the far left and 7 at the far right, with five empty positions between: width 7.

brute.idea: Build each level with explicit None placeholders for missing children, trim the ends, and measure its length.
steps: Level list keeps None placeholders
Trim None from both ends; length is width
Expand every entry, None into two Nones
brute.whySlow: Placeholders double every level: two long branches 30 levels deep create a billion entries.

optimal.insight: Give each node its heap index: children of i are 2i and 2i + 1. Gaps are then implicit in the numbers.
steps: BFS level by level, storing (node, index)
Width = last index - first index + 1
Children get 2i and 2i + 1
Keep the largest width

pitfalls: In fixed-width languages, indices overflow; subtract the level's first index.
Width counts nulls between ends, not after the last real node.

say.intro: Okay, so a level's width runs from its leftmost node to its rightmost node. The empty spots in between count too, as if the tree were complete. We want the widest level. In our tree, the bottom level has six on the far left and seven on the far right. Five gaps between. Width seven.
say.brute: The obvious way? Draw the gaps for real. Each level is a list with placeholders for missing children. Trim the placeholders off both ends, and measure what's left. Then expand, so every placeholder becomes two. Correct, but placeholders double every level. A deep lopsided tree explodes.
say.insight: Here's the thing. We don't need to store the gaps. We just need to count them. So number the nodes like a heap. The root is zero. The children of index i are two i, and two i plus one. Every missing spot still owns a number. So a level's width is its last index minus its first, plus one.
say.anim: We start at the root, labeled position zero, giving it a heap index. The root's children, three and two, get positions zero and one using two times i and two times i plus one. At this level width is two, so best becomes two so far. Next level has five at position zero and nine at position three, since node two had no left child. The gap between positions zero and three makes width four, updating best to four. Now six sits at position zero and seven at position six, spreading the row wide. This gives width seven, which becomes the new best value. The loop ends with no more levels, and the final answer returned is seven.
say.code: Let's walk the code. The root sits at index zero. Each level, the gaps are counted by index, last minus first, plus one. A left child gets two i. A right child gets two i plus one. Keep the best width.
say.outro: Linear time. Breadth first search, with heap style numbering to count the gaps.

maximum-width-of-binary-tree.title: Maximum Width of Binary Tree
lineNotes: This line declares the Solution class that holds our method for the problem.
The method takes the root of the tree and returns the maximum width as an integer.
We start best at zero to track the largest width seen across all levels.
The current level begins as a list holding the root paired with heap index zero.
We loop as long as the current level contains any nodes to process.
Width is last index minus first index plus one, and we keep the larger of that and best.
We create an empty list to collect the nodes of the next level.
We walk through each node on this level along with its heap position.
If the node has a left child, we handle it here.
We add the left child with position two times pos, following heap numbering.
If the node has a right child, we handle it here.
We add the right child with position two times pos plus one, the next slot after the left.
The next level becomes the current level, so the loop moves one depth down.
After all levels are processed, we return the largest width found.

meeting-rooms-iii.hook: Simulate the booking desk with two heaps: free rooms by number, busy rooms by end time.
meeting-rooms-iii.ask: n rooms. Meetings are handled by original start time. Each takes the lowest-numbered free room; if none are free it waits for the earliest freed room, keeping its duration. Return the room that hosted the most meetings, lowest number on ties.
meeting-rooms-iii.exampleWhy: Rooms 0, 1, 2 take the first three. [4,9] waits for room 2, [6,8] for room 1. Rooms 1 and 2 tie at two; 1 is lower.

brute.idea: Track when each room frees up. For each meeting, scan rooms for the lowest free one, or else the earliest to free.
steps: Sort meetings by start
Scan rooms for the lowest one free by start
None free? earliest room, shift the meeting
Count the room
brute.whySlow: Every meeting scans all rooms: 100,000 meetings and 100 rooms is ten million checks, versus logarithmic heap work.

optimal.insight: Two heaps answer both questions instantly: lowest free room number, and which busy room frees first, ties by room number.
steps: Sort meetings; free heap holds all rooms
Release busy rooms ending by this start
Free room? take the lowest
Else pop earliest busy, delay by its end
Count; return the busiest room
optimal.time: O(m log m + m log n)

codeNotes.note: Sorted list is already a heap
Ties go to the lowest room

pitfalls: Release all finished rooms first, then take the lowest number, not the one freed earliest.
Delayed meetings keep their duration: new end is t + end - start.

say.intro: Okay, so we have n rooms and a list of meetings. Each meeting takes the lowest numbered free room. None free? It waits for the first room to open, and keeps its length. We return the room that hosted the most meetings. With three rooms and five meetings, room one wins.
say.brute: The obvious way? Track when each room frees up. For each meeting in start order, scan for the lowest free room. None free? Pick the room that frees earliest, and push the meeting later. It's a correct simulation. But every meeting scans every room.
say.insight: Here's the thing. The simulation keeps asking two questions. What's the lowest numbered free room? And which busy room frees first? A min heap answers each one. So keep a heap of free rooms, and a heap of busy rooms keyed by end time, then room number. Before each meeting, release every room that's finished.
say.anim: We sort the meetings and start with three free rooms, zero and one and two. Meeting one starts at time one, no rooms are busy, so room zero is assigned. Meeting two starts at time two, room one is free, so it takes room one. Meeting three starts at time three, room two is free, so it takes room two. Meeting four starts at time four, but all rooms are busy now. Room two frees earliest at time five, so it delays and reassigns to room two. Meeting five similarly waits, taking the next free room one at time ten. Counts end at one, two, and two, so room one is returned as most booked.
say.code: Let's walk the code. A sorted list of rooms is already a heap. Before each meeting, release rooms that have finished. If one's free, take the lowest numbered room. Otherwise, the meeting is delayed. Same duration, later start. And ties go to the lowest room.
say.outro: Log time per meeting. Two heaps, one for free rooms and one for busy rooms.

meeting-rooms-iii.title: Meeting Rooms III
lineNotes: We define the Solution class that holds the method for this problem.
The method takes the number of rooms and the meeting list, and returns the busiest room number.
We sort meetings by start time so they are handled in their original order of starting.
The free heap starts as all room numbers in order, so popping gives the lowest-numbered free room.
The busy heap starts empty and will hold pairs of end time and room number.
The count list tracks how many meetings each room has hosted, starting at zero for every room.
We loop through each meeting in order, reading its start and end times.
While the earliest-ending busy room has finished by this start time, we need to release it.
We pop that finished room from the busy heap, ignoring its end time and keeping the room number.
We push the released room onto the free heap so it can be chosen by number again.
If any room is free, this meeting can begin right at its original start time.
We pop the lowest-numbered free room from the free heap to host the meeting.
We mark that room busy until the meeting's end time by pushing end and room onto the busy heap.
Otherwise every room is occupied, so the meeting must wait for the earliest room to free up.
We pop the busy room with the earliest end time, with ties broken by smaller room number.
We push it back with a delayed end of t plus the meeting's duration, since the meeting keeps its length.
Whichever room got the meeting, we increase its meeting count by one.
Finally we return the first index holding the maximum count, which gives the lowest room number on ties.

middle-of-the-linked-list.hook: One pointer runs twice as fast. When it reaches the end, the slow one is at the middle.
middle-of-the-linked-list.ask: Given the head of a singly linked list, return its middle node. If there are two middle nodes, return the second one.
middle-of-the-linked-list.exampleWhy: Six nodes have two middles, 3 and 4. We return the second, node 4, which prints as [4,5,6].

brute.idea: Walk the list once to count its nodes, then walk again n // 2 steps from the head.
steps: First pass: count the nodes
Second pass: step n // 2 times
Return that node
brute.whySlow: Not asymptotically slower: it just walks the list one and a half times instead of once.

optimal.insight: If fast moves two steps for every one step of slow, slow has covered half the list when fast hits the end.
steps: Start slow and fast at the head
Slow moves 1, fast moves 2
Stop when fast cannot move two
Slow is the middle

codeNotes.note: Stop at the end, odd or even

pitfalls: Checking fast.next.next instead returns the first middle on even lengths.
This same loop is the first step of palindrome and reorder-list problems.

say.intro: Okay, so we return the middle node of a linked list. If the length is even, there are two middles, and we return the second. For one through six, the middles are three and four. So we return node four, which prints as four, five, six.
say.brute: The obvious way? Walk the list once to count the nodes. Then walk again from the head, halfway. That's linear time and constant space. So it's not really slow. It just takes two passes and a separate count. So, about one and a half trips over the list. Can we do better?
say.insight: Here's the trick. One pass, two pointers. Slow moves one step. Fast moves two. When fast hits the end, slow has gone exactly half as far. Think about it. That puts slow right at the middle. And the loop condition decides which middle we land on. With an even length, slow ends on the second one, which is exactly what we want.
say.anim: We start with slow and fast both pointing at node one of the list. The loop checks fast and fast's next exist, so we proceed. Slow moves one step to node two, while fast jumps two steps to node three. Fast still has room, so slow advances to node three and fast jumps to node five. Fast continues, slow moves to node four, and fast jumps past node six to none. Now fast is none, so the loop stops since fast ran out of nodes. We return slow, which has reached the middle after fast traveled twice as fast. The final answer is the sublist starting at node four, five, six.
say.code: Let's walk the code. Both pointers start together at the head. The loop stops at the end, whether the length is odd or even. Inside, slow takes one step and fast moves at double speed. When fast stops, slow is halfway. And for even lengths, that's the second middle.
say.outro: One pass, constant space. The classic tortoise and hare.

middle-of-the-linked-list.title: Middle of the Linked List
lineNotes: We define a Solution class that holds the method for solving the middle of the linked list problem.
The middleNode method takes the head of a singly linked list and returns the node in the middle.
We start both slow and fast at the head so they begin the race from the same node.
We keep looping as long as fast exists and has a next node, meaning it can still take two steps.
Each loop, slow moves forward one node, so it advances at half the speed of fast.
Fast jumps two nodes ahead each loop, so it reaches the end when slow is at the halfway point.
When the loop ends, slow sits at the middle, and for even lengths it lands on the second middle, so we return it.

minimize-the-maximum-edge-weight-of-grap.hook: The threshold is a decoy. Reverse the edges and run Dijkstra with max instead of plus.
minimize-the-maximum-edge-weight-of-grap.ask: In a directed weighted graph, delete edges so every node can reach node 0, each node keeps at most threshold outgoing edges, and the heaviest remaining edge is as light as possible. Return that weight, or -1 if impossible.
minimize-the-maximum-edge-weight-of-grap.exampleWhy: Keep 1→2, 2→3, 3→4 and 4→0. Every node reaches 0, each has one outgoing edge, and the heaviest is 2.

brute.idea: Try each distinct weight as the cap, ascending. Keep edges up to the cap and check whether everything reaches node 0.
steps: Sort the distinct edge weights
For a cap, search backwards from node 0 on light edges
All nodes reached? return the cap
No cap works? return -1
brute.whySlow: Up to 100,000 distinct weights, each needing a full graph search: about ten billion steps.

optimal.insight: A tree pointing into node 0 needs just one outgoing edge per node, so threshold never binds. Minimise the bottleneck with a heap from 0.
steps: Reverse every edge so we search outward from 0
Min-heap of (edge weight, node), start at (0, 0)
Pop lightest; answer = max weight popped so far
Every node reached? answer, else -1

codeNotes.note: Already attached by a lighter edge

codeNotes.match: return ans if len(seen) == n else -1

pitfalls: threshold ≥ 1 always suffices: each node keeps only its edge toward 0.
Search must follow reversed edges; forward edges answer reachability from 0.

say.intro: Okay, so we may delete edges from a directed graph. But every node must still reach node zero, and each node keeps at most a threshold of outgoing edges. We want the heaviest kept edge as light as possible. In our graph, a chain of edges into zero works, and its heaviest weight is two.
say.brute: The obvious way? Try every distinct weight as a cap, lightest first. Keep only edges up to the cap. Search backwards from node zero. The first cap that reaches every node wins. Correct, but it runs a full graph search per weight. That can be ten billion steps.
say.insight: Here's the aha. If every node can reach zero, each node needs just one outgoing edge, its next step toward zero. So the threshold never matters. What's left is a bottleneck problem. Reverse the edges. Grow outward from zero. Always attach the node with the lightest edge. That's Dijkstra, but with max instead of sum.
say.anim: We build a reverse graph, mapping each target node to its incoming edges with weights. Reverse edges are ready, so we start a heap from node 0 with weight 0. We pop node 0, mark it seen, and push its incoming edge, weight 1 from node 4. Node 4 is popped, ans becomes 1, and we push weight 5 from node 1 and weight 2 from node 3. Node 3 pops with weight 2, ans updates to 2, pushing node 1 at weight 3 and node 2 at weight 2. Node 2 pops cheaply at weight 2, pushing node 1 again at weight 1, the smallest option. Node 1 finally pops at weight 1 since all nodes are now seen, keeping ans at 2. All five nodes are visited, so the function returns the final answer, 2.
say.code: Let's walk the code. We reverse the edges to search away from node zero. Node zero starts free, at weight zero. Pop the lightest entry. Already attached by a lighter edge? Skip it. Otherwise, the bottleneck is the heaviest edge used so far. If someone can't reach zero, we return minus one.
say.outro: E log E time. A minimax path, found with a Dijkstra style heap.

minimize-the-maximum-edge-weight-of-grap.title: Minimize the Maximum Edge Weight of Graph
lineNotes: We define the Solution class that holds the method for this problem.
The method takes the node count, the edge list and a threshold, and returns the minimized maximum edge weight.
We build a reversed adjacency map so we can walk outward from node 0 along edges backward.
We loop over every edge, unpacking its source a, destination b and weight w.
In the reversed graph, node b stores the weight and its original source a as a neighbor.
We keep a set of nodes already reached, meaning they can reach node 0.
The heap starts with node 0 at cost zero, since it needs no edge to reach itself.
The answer starts at zero and will track the largest edge weight we are forced to use.
We keep expanding while the heap still has candidate edges to consider.
We pop the candidate with the smallest edge weight, which is the cheapest way to extend the tree.
If that node was already reached by a cheaper edge, this entry is stale.
So we skip it and move on to the next candidate.
Otherwise we mark the node as reached, since it now has a path to node 0.
We update the answer to the larger of itself and this edge weight, which is the bottleneck.
We look at every node that has an edge pointing into the current node.
We only consider those nodes that have not yet been reached.
We push the connecting edge weight and that node onto the heap as a new candidate.
If every node was reached we return the bottleneck answer, otherwise some node cannot reach zero, so we return negative one.

minimize-xor.hook: Match a bit count while staying as close to num1 as possible: greedy, from the top bit down.
minimize-xor.ask: Given num1 and num2, build the number x that has exactly as many 1 bits as num2, choosing it so that x XOR num1 is as small as possible.
minimize-xor.exampleWhy: 18 is 10010 and num2 = 7 needs three 1 bits. Copy 16 and 2, then add the lowest free bit: 10011 = 19.

brute.idea: Try every x with the right number of 1 bits, up to a safe limit, and keep the one whose XOR with num1 is smallest.
steps: Count the 1 bits of num2
Try every x below 2^bits
Keep x with the right count and smallest XOR
brute.whySlow: num1 can be a billion, so the loop tries up to about two billion candidates.

optimal.insight: XOR is small when x agrees with num1 on the high bits. Spend 1 bits on num1's highest set bits, then fill the lowest empty bits.
steps: need = number of 1 bits in num2
Scan num1 from its top bit: copy set bits while need > 0
If bits are still needed, set the lowest zero bits of x
Return x

codeNotes.note: How many 1 bits x must have
Copy num1's high set bits first
Only fill positions that are empty

pitfalls: Filling leftover bits from the top instead of the bottom makes the XOR huge.
When need is smaller than num1's bit count, drop num1's lowest set bits, not its highest.

say.intro: Okay, so we build a number x. It must have exactly as many one bits as num two. And x XOR num one should be as small as possible. Here num one is eighteen, which is one zero zero one zero in binary. Num two is seven, with three one bits. The answer is nineteen.
say.brute: The obvious way? Try every candidate. Count the one bits of num two. Then loop over every x up to just above num one. Right bit count? Compute the XOR and keep the smallest. It's correct. But num one can be a billion. That's billions of numbers to test.
say.insight: Think about what makes an XOR small. Every bit where x and num one differ costs us. And here's the thing. A high bit costs more than all the lower bits combined. So spend our one bits matching num one's highest set bits first. Bits left over? Put them in the lowest empty spots, where a mismatch is cheapest.
say.anim: We start with num1 eighteen and num2 seven, needing three bits set to match num2's ones. Scanning num1's bits from the top, bit four is set, so x grabs it, becoming sixteen. Bit three is zero, so we skip it, keeping x unchanged and need at two. Bit one is set in num1, so x adds it, updating x to eighteen with one need left. Bit zero is zero in num1, so no change, finishing the high bit pass with need one. Now we fill the lowest empty bit, setting bit zero to satisfy the last needed bit. X becomes nineteen, need drops to zero, so the loop ends and we return the final answer. The function returns nineteen, the minimized XOR result for inputs eighteen and seven.
say.code: Let's walk the code. First, count how many one bits x must have. Then we copy num one's high set bits first, from the top down. Any leftover bits go low. And we only fill positions that are empty, starting from bit zero.
say.outro: Logarithmic time, constant space. With XOR, decide the high bits first. They dominate everything below them.

minimize-xor.title: Minimize XOR
lineNotes: We define the Solution class that holds our method for this problem.
This method takes num1 and num2 and returns the number x that minimizes x XOR num1.
We count the one bits in num2, since x must have exactly that many one bits.
We start x at zero and will build it up bit by bit.
We scan the bit positions of num1 from the highest down to zero, so high bits are handled first.
If we still need ones and num1 has a one at this bit, we want to match it.
We set that same bit in x, so it cancels against num1 in the XOR.
We reduce the count of ones still needed by one.
We reset the bit position to zero to begin filling the lowest empty positions.
If any ones remain to place, we loop until the need reaches zero.
We check whether this bit in x is still empty, meaning it is not already set.
We set this empty low bit in x, which costs the least possible XOR value.
We reduce the remaining need by one after placing that bit.
We move up to the next bit position and keep searching for empty spots.
We return x, which has the right number of ones and the smallest XOR with num1.

minimum-area-rectangle.hook: A rectangle is fixed by one diagonal. Guess the diagonal, then ask a hash set for the other two corners.
minimum-area-rectangle.ask: Given distinct points on a grid, find the smallest area of any rectangle whose four corners are all in the list and whose sides are horizontal and vertical. Return 0 if none exists.
minimum-area-rectangle.exampleWhy: Corners (3,1), (3,3), (4,1), (4,3) make a rectangle 1 wide and 2 tall, area 2, smaller than the 2 by 2 square.

brute.idea: Treat every pair of points as a diagonal and search the whole list for the two missing corners.
steps: Pick two points with different x and y
Scan the list for the two other corners
Both found? Update the smallest area
brute.whySlow: Each corner check scans all n points, so 500 points means about 60 million comparisons.

optimal.insight: Store the points in a hash set. Then checking whether a corner exists costs O(1), so each diagonal is tested instantly.
steps: Put every point into a set
Try each pair as opposite corners
Skip pairs sharing an x or a y
If (x1,y2) and (x2,y1) are in the set, record the area

codeNotes.match: seen = {(x, y) for x, y in points}

codeNotes.note: Each pair is a candidate diagonal

codeNotes.match: if x1 == x2 or y1 == y2:
codeNotes.note: Same row or column is not a diagonal

codeNotes.match: if (x1, y2) in seen and (x2, y1) in seen:
return best if best < math.inf else 0

pitfalls: Lists are not hashable: store points as tuples in the set.
Remember to return 0, not infinity, when no rectangle exists.

say.intro: Okay, so we get a list of distinct points. We want the smallest rectangle, with sides parallel to the axes, whose four corners are all in the list. Here, the points at x three and four, with y one and three, make a rectangle one wide and two tall. The answer is two.
say.brute: Here's a useful fact. An axis aligned rectangle is fixed by one diagonal. So try every pair of points as a diagonal. Then scan the whole list for the two missing corners. But that scan is linear, for every pair. So it's cubic. Five hundred points means tens of millions of comparisons.
say.insight: So what's the slow part? Asking whether a point exists. And a hash set answers that instantly. So load every point into a set first. Now take each pair with different x and different y. The other two corners are forced. Two set lookups tell us right away whether the rectangle is real.
say.anim: We store all six points in a set, letting us check corners instantly. Starting with point one one, we pair it with each later point to test rectangles. Point one one and point three three form a diagonal, giving area four. Point one one and point four three also work, but area four does not beat the best. Now point one three checks against three one and four one for matching corners. Point three one pairs with point four three, finding corners that shrink best to two. Point three three and point four one confirm a valid rectangle too, area still two. After checking all pairs, the smallest rectangle area found is two.
say.code: Let's walk the code. A set gives constant time lookups for any corner. Each pair is a candidate diagonal. If they share a row or column, it's not a diagonal, so skip it. Then check: do the other two corners exist? If so, update the best area. No rectangle found means zero.
say.outro: Quadratic time, linear space. Turn an expensive search into a set lookup.

minimum-area-rectangle.title: Minimum Area Rectangle
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container the interview platform expects for our method.
The method minAreaRect takes the list of points and returns the smallest rectangle area as an integer.
We build a hash set of point pairs so that checking whether any corner exists takes constant time.
We set best to infinity so that any real rectangle area we find will be smaller.
We loop over each point with its index, treating it as one corner of a possible diagonal.
We pair it with every later point, so each diagonal is considered once without repeating pairs.
If the two points share an x or a y, they lie on a line and cannot be opposite corners.
We skip that pair and move on to the next candidate.
For a true diagonal, we check that the other two corners both exist in the set.
When all four corners exist, we compute width times height and keep the smaller area as best.
If best is still infinity no rectangle was found so we return zero, otherwise we return best.

minimum-area-rectangle-ii.hook: Rectangles can be tilted now. A right angle plus one hash lookup still pins down the fourth corner.
minimum-area-rectangle-ii.ask: Given distinct points, find the smallest area of any rectangle whose four corners are all in the list, at any angle. Return 0 if no rectangle can be formed.
minimum-area-rectangle-ii.exampleWhy: The four points form a tilted square with sides of length root 2, so the area is 2.

brute.idea: Try every group of four points and test whether some pairing of them gives two diagonals with the same midpoint and length.
steps: Choose four points
Try the three ways to pair them as diagonals
Same midpoint and same length? It is a rectangle
brute.whySlow: With 50 points there are about 230,000 groups of four, each checked three ways.

optimal.insight: Fix corner A and points B, C. If AB is perpendicular to AC, the fourth corner must be B + C - A. One lookup confirms it.
steps: Put all points in a set
For each corner A, try every pair B, C
Dot product of AB and AC is zero? Right angle
If B + C - A is in the set, record |AB| · |AC|

codeNotes.match: seen = {(x, y) for x, y in points}
codeNotes.note: Fast check for the fourth corner
Not a right angle at A, skip

codeNotes.match: if (bx + cx - ax, by + cy - ay) in seen:
area = math.hypot(bx - ax, by - ay) * math.hypot(cx - ax, cy - ay)
return best if best < math.inf else 0

pitfalls: Compare the dot product with integers, not floats, so the right angle test stays exact.
Grouping diagonals by midpoint and length also works; both are fine for n ≤ 50.

say.intro: Okay, so this time the rectangle can be tilted at any angle. Our four points form a diamond. One two, two one, one zero, and zero one. Each side is root two long. So the diamond is really a square, with area two.
say.brute: The obvious way? Try every group of four points. Four points make a rectangle when two diagonals share a midpoint and have equal length. There are three ways to pair them, so check all three. That's n to the fourth groups. Fifty points is about a quarter of a million.
say.insight: Here's the shortcut. Pick a corner A, and two other points B and C. Is the dot product of A to B and A to C zero? Then there's a right angle at A. And now the fourth corner is forced. It must sit at B plus C minus A. A hash set tells us instantly if it's there. That removes a whole loop.
say.anim: We start with four points and build a set to quickly check if a corner exists. Fixing corner A at point one, two, we begin testing pairs B and C for right angles. With B as two, one and C as one, zero, the perpendicular check passes. The missing corner B plus C minus A is found in the set, giving area two. Now trying a new corner A at two, one, we repeat the same perpendicular search. Corner A shifts to one, zero, scanning further point pairs for right angles again. Finally corner A is zero, one, completing the last round of checks without improvement. The loop ends and the smallest rectangle area found is two point zero.
say.code: Let's walk the code. A set gives a fast check for the fourth corner. For each corner A, try pairs B and C. Not a right angle at A? Skip it. Otherwise, the fourth corner completes the rectangle, if it's in the set. The area is the side lengths multiplied. And no rectangle means zero.
say.outro: Cubic time, linear space. A right angle plus some vector math lets a set find the missing corner.

minimum-area-rectangle-ii.title: Minimum Area Rectangle II
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, as required by the problem's submission format.
The method takes the list of points and returns the smallest rectangle area as a float.
We store every point as a tuple in a set so checking whether a corner exists takes constant time.
We save the number of points in n to use in our loop bounds.
We start best at infinity so any real rectangle area will replace it.
We try every point as corner A, the corner where the right angle sits.
We unpack the coordinates of corner A into ax and ay.
For this corner A, we loop over every point as candidate B.
We loop over later points as candidate C, so each pair of B and C is considered only once.
We check whether A coincides with B or C, since A must be a different point.
If so, we skip this pair and move on.
We read the coordinates of point B from the list.
We read the coordinates of point C from the list.
The dot product of vectors AB and AC being zero means they are perpendicular, so a nonzero value is rejected.
In that case the angle at A is not a right angle, so we skip this pair.
We compute the fourth corner as B plus C minus A and check whether it exists in the set.
If it does, the area is the length of AB times the length of AC.
We keep the smaller of the current best and this new area.
After all loops, we return best if a rectangle was found, otherwise zero.

minimum-difference-between-largest-and-s.hook: Three free changes only ever matter at the extremes. Sort, then compare four windows.
minimum-difference-between-largest-and-s.ask: You may change up to three numbers to any values you like. Return the smallest possible gap between the largest and smallest numbers afterwards.
minimum-difference-between-largest-and-s.exampleWhy: Sorted: 1 2 3 6 9 14 20. Change 9, 14 and 20, leaving 1 to 6, a gap of 5.

brute.idea: Changing a number is the same as deleting it. Try every set of three numbers to delete and measure the spread of what is left.
steps: Pick three positions to change
Take max minus min of the rest
Keep the smallest result
brute.whySlow: There are about n³ / 6 choices, each scanned in linear time: hopeless for 100,000 numbers.

optimal.insight: A useful move always removes an extreme value. So after sorting, we remove some of the smallest and the rest from the largest: only four splits exist.
steps: Four or fewer numbers? Answer is 0
Sort the array
Remove k smallest and 3 - k largest, for k = 0 to 3
Return the smallest remaining spread

codeNotes.note: Extremes now sit at the ends

pitfalls: Forgetting the small case: with at most four numbers the answer is always 0.
Only the 4 smallest and 4 largest matter, so partial selection gives O(n).

say.intro: Okay, so we can change up to three numbers to anything we like. We want the largest and smallest values to end up as close as possible. Sorted, our numbers are one, two, three, six, nine, fourteen, twenty. The best we can do is a gap of five.
say.brute: First, a trick. Changing a number is really the same as deleting it. Why? We can just copy a value that stays. So the brute force tries every set of three numbers to delete. Then it measures what's left. That's about n cubed over six choices, each with a linear scan. Far too slow.
say.insight: Here's the thing. Deleting a middle value never shrinks the gap. So every useful move removes an extreme. After sorting, we take some from the small end, and the rest from the large end. With three moves, how many splits are there? Just four. Zero and three. One and two. Two and one. Three and zero.
say.anim: We have seven numbers, more than four, so we continue instead of returning zero. The array gets sorted into 1, 2, 3, 6, 9, 14, 20. Best starts at infinity as we prepare to try four possible removal splits. With left at zero and right at three, we compare nums six minus nums one, giving five. Next, left is one and right is four, comparing nine minus two, which is worse, best stays five. With left two and right five, fourteen minus three is nine, still not better. Finally left three and right six, twenty minus six is fourteen, so five remains best. The loop ends and the function returns five, the minimum possible difference.
say.code: Let's walk the code. Four numbers or fewer? Three changes can make them all equal, so return zero. Otherwise, sort, so the extremes sit at the ends. For each split, drop that many smallest values. Then drop the rest of the three from the largest end. The answer is the smallest spread of what remains.
say.outro: n log n for the sort, constant extra space. Only the extremes are worth changing. That's the greedy insight.

minimum-difference-between-largest-and-s.title: Minimum Difference Between Largest and Smallest Value in Three Moves
lineNotes: We define the Solution class that holds the method for this problem.
The method minDifference takes a list of numbers and returns the smallest possible gap after at most three changes.
If there are four numbers or fewer, we can make them all equal, so the gap can be zero.
In that case we return zero right away.
We sort the numbers so the smallest values sit at the front and the largest at the back.
We start best at infinity so any real gap we find will replace it.
We loop left over zero to three, which is how many of the three moves remove the smallest values.
The right index is the matching spot from the end, since the remaining moves remove the largest values.
We compare the gap between the numbers at right and left with best, and keep the smaller one.
After trying all four splits, we return the smallest gap found.

minimum-falling-path-sum.hook: Each cell only cares about the best of three cells above it. One row of memory solves the grid.
minimum-falling-path-sum.ask: Start anywhere in the top row of a square grid and move down one row at a time, straight or one step diagonally. Return the smallest possible sum of the cells visited.
minimum-falling-path-sum.exampleWhy: Path 1 → 5 → 7 sums to 13, as does 1 → 4 → 8. No falling path is cheaper.

brute.idea: From every top cell, recursively try all three moves down and keep the cheapest total.
steps: Start from each cell in the top row
Recurse into the three cells below
Return this cell plus the cheapest child
brute.whySlow: Paths branch three ways per row: a 100 row grid has about 3^100 paths.

optimal.insight: The cheapest way to reach a cell only depends on the cheapest ways to reach the three cells above it. Compute row by row.
steps: Copy the first row as the best costs so far
For each next row, each cell adds the min of its three parents
Replace the previous row with the new one
Return the smallest value in the last row

codeNotes.note: Best cost to reach each top cell
Fill one row at a time
Cheapest of up to three parents
Path can end in any column

pitfalls: Edge columns have only two parents: clamp the slice instead of indexing out of range.
Return the minimum of the last row, not its first or last cell.

say.intro: Okay, so we start in any cell of the top row. We fall down one row at a time, straight down or one step diagonally. We want the smallest total. In our grid, one, then five, then seven gives thirteen. Nothing is cheaper.
say.brute: The obvious way? Try every path. From each top cell, recurse into the three cells below. Each of those branches three more ways. So the number of paths grows like three to the n. A hundred row grid? Completely out of reach.
say.insight: Now, notice something. The cheapest way to reach a cell only depends on the cheapest ways to reach the three cells right above it. That's a dynamic programming recurrence. So fill the grid one row at a time. And since each row only needs the row above, one array of size n is all the memory we need.
say.anim: We start with the matrix, and prev is set to the first row, two one three. For row one, we build a new cur array to hold updated path sums. At column zero, the best cost above is one, so cur becomes seven. At column one, best is one again, giving cur six, then column two gives five. Prev updates to seven six five, then row two begins with a fresh cur array. Column zero picks best six, making cur thirteen; column one also gives thirteen. Column two adds nine to best five, making fourteen, finishing prev as thirteen thirteen fourteen. Finally we return the minimum of prev, giving the answer thirteen.
say.code: Let's walk the code. We start with the best cost to reach each top cell, which is just the top row. Then we fill one row at a time. For each cell, take the cheapest of up to three parents. Add this cell's own value. At the end, the path can end in any column, so we take the minimum.
say.outro: Quadratic time, linear space. Each cell builds on a few neighbours from the row before. Classic grid dynamic programming.

minimum-falling-path-sum.title: Minimum Falling Path Sum
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container the problem expects for our method.
The method minFallingPathSum takes the square grid called matrix and returns the smallest falling path sum as an integer.
We store the grid's side length in n, since the grid is square and rows equal columns.
We copy the top row into prev, because the cheapest cost to reach any top cell is just its own value.
We loop over rows from one to the last, building each row's costs from the row above.
We create cur as a fresh row of n zeros to hold the cheapest costs for this row.
We loop over every column c in the current row to compute its cheapest arrival cost.
We take the minimum of prev over columns c minus one to c plus one, clamping the left edge at zero.
The cheapest cost to reach this cell is its own value plus the best of the cells above it.
We make cur the new prev, so the next row looks back at these freshly computed costs.
After the last row, the answer is the smallest value in prev, since a path may end in any column.

minimum-number-of-operations-to-move-all.hook: Every ball's cost grows by one per step. Sweep left, then right, carrying a running total.
minimum-number-of-operations-to-move-all.ask: Each box holds zero or one ball. For every box, return how many single steps it would take to move all balls into that box.
minimum-number-of-operations-to-move-all.exampleWhy: Balls sit at boxes 2, 4 and 5. Box 0 needs 2 + 4 + 5 = 11 moves; box 4 needs 3.

brute.idea: For each target box, add up the distance from every ball to that box.
steps: Pick a target box i
Add |i - j| for every ball at j
Store the total
brute.whySlow: Every box rescans every other box: 2,000 boxes means 4 million distance sums.

optimal.insight: Moving one box right adds one step for every ball already behind you. Track balls seen and their total cost in one sweep each way.
steps: Sweep left to right: add the running cost, then update it
Running cost grows by the number of balls passed
Repeat right to left and add both sweeps

minimum-number-of-operations-to-move-all.optimalCode:
class Solution:
    def minOperations(self, boxes: str) -> List[int]:
        n = len(boxes)
        ans = [0] * n
        balls = moves = 0
        for i in range(n):
            ans[i] += moves
            balls += boxes[i] == "1"
            moves += balls
        balls = moves = 0
        for i in range(n - 1, -1, -1):
            ans[i] += moves
            balls += boxes[i] == "1"
            moves += balls
        return ans

codeNotes.note: Left sweep: cost of balls on the left
Right sweep: cost of balls on the right
Left cost plus right cost per box

pitfalls: Add the running cost before counting the current box's own ball.
Both sweeps add into the same answer array; do not overwrite.

say.intro: Okay, so each box holds zero or one ball. One move shifts a ball to a neighbouring box. For every box, we want the total moves to gather all the balls there. With boxes zero, zero, one, zero, one, one, the answer is eleven, eight, five, four, three, four.
say.brute: The obvious way? Treat each box as a target on its own. Loop over every box with a ball, and add up the distances. It's correct. But every target scans every box. That's quadratic. Two thousand boxes means four million steps.
say.insight: Here's the thing. When the target moves one box right, every ball on its left gets one step further away. So if we know how many balls we've passed, the left side cost grows by exactly that count. One sweep from the left covers every ball on the left. A second sweep from the right covers the rest.
say.anim: We start with boxes string zero zero one zero one one, and an answer array of six zeros. Sweeping left to right, we track balls seen so far and moves accumulated behind each box. At index two we spot a ball, balls becomes one, adding no moves yet since none accumulated. By index three balls equals one, so ans at three gets one move added. Continuing right, moves grow to two then four as more balls pile up behind later boxes. Now we sweep right to left, resetting balls and moves to add leftover moves from the right side. Index four gains one move, then index three jumps to four after combining both sweeps. Finishing the backward sweep, the final answer array becomes eleven, eight, five, four, three, four.
say.code: Let's walk the code. Both sweeps add into one answer array. The left sweep adds the cost of balls on the left, then counts this box's ball. The right sweep does the same for balls on the right. So each box ends up with left cost plus right cost.
say.outro: Linear time, constant extra space. Carry a running total instead of recomputing it.

minimum-number-of-operations-to-move-all.title: Minimum Number of Operations to Move All Balls to Each Box
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container the judge expects for this problem.
The method minOperations takes the boxes string and returns a list of step counts, one per box.
We store n as the number of boxes so we can reuse it for sizing and looping.
We create the answer list of n zeros, which will accumulate the cost from both directions.
We start balls and moves at zero, since nothing has been seen yet on the left side.
We sweep left to right, visiting every box index from zero up to n minus one.
Before counting this box, we add moves to its answer, which is the cost of pulling all left balls here.
If this box holds a ball, we increase the balls count by one for later boxes.
We add balls to moves, because stepping one box right costs one extra step per ball seen so far.
We reset balls and moves to zero to prepare for the sweep from the right side.
We now sweep right to left, from the last index down to zero.
We add the current moves to this box's answer, covering the cost of balls coming from the right.
If this box contains a ball, we increment balls so boxes further left account for it.
We add balls to moves, since each step left adds one more step for every ball on the right.
We return the answer list, where each entry combines left and right costs for that box.

minimum-size-subarray-sum.hook: All numbers are positive, so a window that is big enough can only shrink from the left.
minimum-size-subarray-sum.ask: Given positive numbers and a target, find the length of the shortest contiguous run whose sum is at least the target. Return 0 if no run reaches it.
minimum-size-subarray-sum.exampleWhy: 4 + 3 = 7 reaches the target with just two numbers. No single number is 7 or more.

brute.idea: Start a run at every index and extend it until the sum reaches the target. Keep the shortest length found.
steps: Pick a start index
Extend right, adding numbers
Stop when sum ≥ target and record the length
brute.whySlow: Each start may scan to the end: 100,000 numbers means billions of additions.

optimal.insight: Positive numbers mean growing a window raises its sum and shrinking lowers it. So both ends only ever move right.
steps: Grow the window by adding nums[right]
While the sum reaches the target, record the length
Then drop nums[left] and move left forward
Return the shortest length, or 0

codeNotes.note: Grow the window on the right

codeNotes.match: return 0 if best == math.inf else best

pitfalls: Use while, not if, when shrinking: one new number may allow several shrinks.
The two pointer trick needs positive numbers; negatives break it.

say.intro: Okay, so we get positive numbers and a target. We want the shortest contiguous run whose sum is at least the target. With target seven and two, three, one, two, four, three, the run four and three works. Just two numbers. So the answer is two.
say.brute: The obvious way? Start a run at every index. Keep adding numbers to the right until the sum reaches the target. Record the length, move to the next start. But every start may scan to the end. That's quadratic. A hundred thousand numbers is far too slow. So what can we reuse?
say.insight: Here's the key. Every number is positive. So adding a number always raises the sum, and removing one always lowers it. Once a window hits the target, what's the only useful move? Shrink it from the left, and see how short it gets. Neither pointer ever goes backwards. That's one linear pass.
say.anim: We start with left and total at zero, target seven, scanning the array for subarrays. As right moves through the array, total accumulates values like two, five, then six. At right equals three, total reaches eight, meeting target, so window size four becomes best. The window shrinks from the left since sum still exceeds target, raising left to one. Adding four makes total ten, triggering shrinking again until best improves to three. Adding the last value three brings total to nine, still above target, so shrinking continues. Left moves to four, shrinking total to seven, and best shrinks further to two. After the loop ends, the function returns two, the minimum subarray length found.
say.code: Let's walk the code. We grow the window on the right. While the window is valid, we try shrinking. First, record this window's length, if it beats the best. Then drop the leftmost number, and move left forward. And if we never reached the target at all, return zero.
say.outro: Linear time, constant space. Grow on the right, shrink on the left while it stays valid. That's the sliding window.

minimum-size-subarray-sum.title: Minimum Size Subarray Sum
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container the problem expects for our method.
The method takes a target sum and a list of positive numbers, and returns the shortest qualifying length.
We start the left edge of the window at zero and the running total of the window at zero.
We set best to infinity so any real window length we find will replace it.
We move the right edge across the list, reading each position and its value one at a time.
We add the new value to the total, growing the window to include the right edge.
While the window sum reaches the target, we keep trying to shrink it from the left.
We record the smaller of the current best and the present window length, which is right minus left plus one.
We subtract the leftmost value from the total, since that element is leaving the window.
We advance left by one, which is safe because positive numbers mean shrinking only lowers the sum.
If best never changed we return zero, otherwise we return the shortest window length found.

move-pieces-to-obtain-a-string.hook: Pieces can never pass each other. So match them in order and check each one moved the legal way.
move-pieces-to-obtain-a-string.ask: Strings hold L pieces, R pieces and blanks. L can slide left and R can slide right through blanks. Decide whether start can be turned into target.
move-pieces-to-obtain-a-string.exampleWhy: The L slides one step left to index 0, and the R slides two steps right to index 5.

brute.idea: Search every reachable arrangement with breadth first search, sliding one piece one step at a time, until target appears.
steps: Queue the start string
Try every legal one step slide
Queue each new string not seen before
Found target? Return True
brute.whySlow: The number of reachable strings explodes with length; 100,000 characters is impossible.

optimal.insight: Pieces never jump over each other, so the k-th piece of start must become the k-th piece of target, same letter, moved the allowed direction.
steps: Skip blanks in both strings with pointers i and j
Both finished? Success. Only one finished? Fail
Letters differ? Fail
L must not move right; R must not move left

codeNotes.note: Jump to the next piece in start

codeNotes.match: return i == n and j == n

pitfalls: Checking only piece counts is not enough: order and direction both matter.
Pieces cannot pass through each other, so relative order is fixed.

say.intro: Okay, so we have L pieces, R pieces and blanks. An L can slide left into a blank. An R can slide right into a blank. Can we turn start into target? Here the L slides one step left, and the R slides two steps right. So yes, true.
say.brute: The obvious way? Simulate everything. Breadth first search from the start string. Try every legal one step slide. Queue each new arrangement. If target ever shows up, the answer is true. It works on tiny inputs. But the number of arrangements explodes as the string grows.
say.insight: Here's the key. Pieces can never jump over each other. So the first piece in start must become the first piece in target. The second becomes the second, and so on. Each matched pair must be the same letter. And an L can only end up further left, or in place. An R, only further right, or in place.
say.anim: We start with start equal underscore L underscore R underscore underscore, target L underscore underscore underscore underscore R. Pointer i skips underscores and lands on index one, finding letter L in start. Target j is already at zero with letter L, matching start, and L at i equals j is fine. Both pointers advance, now i is two and j is one, continuing the scan. Pointer i skips ahead to index three, landing on letter R in start. Pointer j skips four underscores in target, reaching index five where letter R sits. Letters match as R, and since i three is less than j five, the right move direction holds. Pointers finish together at the string end, so the function returns true, confirming the transformation works.
say.code: Let's walk the code. Each round, we jump to the next piece in both strings. Both must run out together. Piece order can never change, so the letters must match. An L can't move right. An R can't move left. Otherwise, step past the matched pair.
say.outro: Linear time, constant space. Walk both strings in step, and match the pieces in order.

move-pieces-to-obtain-a-string.title: Move Pieces to Obtain a String
lineNotes: We define a class named Solution, as the problem platform expects.
The method canChange takes the start and target strings and returns whether start can become target.
We store the common length of the strings in n.
We set both pointers i and j to zero, one for start and one for target.
We loop forever, handling one pair of matching pieces per pass until a return happens.
While i is inside the string and start has a blank at i, we keep skipping.
Each blank in start is skipped by moving i one step right.
Likewise, while j is inside the string and target has a blank at j, we keep skipping.
Each blank in target is skipped by moving j one step right.
If either pointer has reached the end, no more pieces remain in that string.
We return true only if both pointers hit the end together, meaning both have the same number of pieces.
If the next pieces have different letters, the order of pieces cannot match, so we return false.
So we return false for that letter mismatch.
A piece L can only move left, so if its start position i is left of target position j, it fails.
We return false because that L would need to move right.
A piece R can only move right, so if its start position i is right of target position j, it fails.
We return false because that R would need to move left.
This pair is valid, so we advance i to look for the next piece in start.
We advance j likewise to the next piece in target and repeat the loop.

next-greater-element-ii.hook: A circular array is just the array twice. A monotonic stack answers every next-greater question in one sweep.
next-greater-element-ii.ask: The array wraps around, so after the last element comes the first. For each number, return the first larger number found walking forward, or -1 if none exists.
next-greater-element-ii.exampleWhy: Each of 1, 2, 3 is beaten by its neighbour. 4 is the maximum, so -1. The last 3 wraps around to find 4.

brute.idea: For each index, walk forward around the circle until a larger number appears, or until we come all the way back.
steps: Pick index i
Check the next n - 1 positions, wrapping with modulo
First larger value is the answer
brute.whySlow: In a descending array every scan runs the full circle: 10,000 numbers means 100 million checks.

optimal.insight: Keep a stack of indices still waiting for a larger number. Each new value settles every smaller waiter. Walking the array twice handles the wrap.
steps: Loop i from 0 to 2n - 1, value nums[i mod n]
Pop every waiting index with a smaller value; this value is its answer
Push i only during the first pass
Indices left waiting keep -1

codeNotes.note: x is the answer for smaller waiters

pitfalls: Store indices, not values, on the stack, since duplicates need separate answers.
Push only in the first lap, or indices get answered twice.

say.intro: Okay, so the array is circular. After the last number, we wrap back to the first. For each number, we want the first larger number walking forward. For one, two, three, four, three, the answer is two, three, four, minus one, four. See the last three? It wraps around to find the four.
say.brute: The obvious way? Handle each index on its own. Walk forward, wrapping around, until you find something larger, or come all the way back. Now picture a descending array. Every walk covers the whole circle. So the total work is quadratic.
say.insight: Here's the trick. Keep a stack of indices still waiting for a larger number. Their values always decrease from bottom to top. Why does that help? When a new value arrives, it's the answer for every smaller waiter on top. So we pop them all. And the wrap? We just walk the array twice.
say.anim: We start with array one two three four three, all answers set to negative one. Index zero holds value one, pushed onto the empty stack as a waiter. At index one, value two beats one, so index zero gets answer two. Value three now beats two, settling index one with answer three, stack empties again. Value four beats three, giving index two answer four, then four is pushed. Value three can't beat four, so it just gets pushed to wait its turn. Wrapping around past the end, we revisit early values to help leftover waiters. Second pass through, value four finally beats three, giving index four answer four. Final answers are two three four negative one four, the completed result.
say.code: Let's walk the code. The default is minus one, for when nothing larger exists. We loop twice, and the second lap simulates the wrap. While the top is smaller, x is the answer for that waiter. We settle that index and pop it. And we only push on the first lap, so each index waits just once.
