say.outro: Linear time. Each index is pushed and popped at most once. A monotonic stack, plus a second lap for the wrap.

next-greater-element-ii.title: Next Greater Element II
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container the problem expects for our method.
This method takes the list nums and returns a list holding each element's next greater value.
We store the length of nums in n, since we will use it for sizing and wrapping.
We create the answer list of length n filled with negative one, the default when no greater value exists.
We start an empty stack that will hold indices still waiting for a larger number.
We loop over twice the length of nums so every element gets a chance to see values after the wrap.
We read the current value x using the index modulo n, which wraps back to the start on the second pass.
While the stack has waiting indices and the value at the top is smaller than x, we keep settling them.
We pop that waiting index and record x as its next greater element in the answer.
We only push new indices during the first pass, so each index enters the stack exactly once.
We push the current index onto the stack so it can wait for a larger value later.
Finally we return the answer list, where unresolved indices still hold negative one.

number-of-digit-one.hook: Do not count numbers. Count, for each digit position, how often it shows a 1.
number-of-digit-one.ask: Given n, count how many times the digit 1 is written in total when you write out every number from 0 up to n.
number-of-digit-one.exampleWhy: From 0 to 121, the ones place shows 1 thirteen times, the tens place 20 times, and the hundreds place 22 times.

brute.idea: Write out every number from 1 to n and count the ones in each.
steps: Loop x from 1 to n
Count the 1 digits in x
Add them to the total
brute.whySlow: n can be a billion, so we would convert a billion numbers to text.

optimal.insight: At each position, split n into high digits, the current digit and low digits. The current digit alone decides how many full and partial cycles of 1s occur.
steps: For each place value p = 1, 10, 100 ...
high = digits above, cur = digit at p, low = digits below
cur 0: high · p. cur 1: high · p + low + 1
cur ≥ 2: (high + 1) · p

codeNotes.match: high, cur, low = n // (p * 10), n // p % 10, n % p

codeNotes.note: Current digit passed 1: full extra cycle

pitfalls: The cur = 1 case is the tricky one: add low + 1, not p.
Brute force is fine for small n, but times out near a billion.

say.intro: Okay, so given n, we write out every number from zero to n. How many times do we write the digit one? For n equal to one hundred twenty one, the answer is fifty five.
say.brute: The obvious way? Write out every number from one to n. Count the ones in each. Add them up. Simple and correct. But n can be a billion. That's a billion numbers, each with several digits. Way too slow.
say.insight: Here's the thing. Flip the question. Don't ask how many ones each number has. Ask how often each digit position shows a one. Fix a position. Split n into the high digits above it, the current digit, and the low digits below. Every full cycle of the high part gives one block of ones. Then the current digit decides the rest. Nothing, part of a block, or one more full block.
say.anim: We start with n equal to 121, count at zero, and p at one. At the ones place, high is 12, current digit is 1, and low is 0. Since current digit is 1, count becomes high times p plus low plus one, giving 13. Now p is 10, high is 1, current digit is 2, and low is 1. Current digit above 1 means we add high plus one times p, making count 33. Now p is 100, high is 0, current digit is 1, and low is 21. Current digit 1 again adds high times p plus low plus one, count reaches 55. Since p now exceeds n, the loop ends and the function returns 55.
say.code: Let's walk the code. We do one round per digit position. First, split n around this position. If the current digit is one, there's a partial cycle, so we add low plus one extra ones. If it's past one, we add a full extra cycle. Then we move to the next position.
say.outro: Logarithmic time, constant space. Count by position, not by number. The digits of n tell you everything.

number-of-digit-one.title: Number of Digit One
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container the problem expects for our method.
The method countDigitOne takes the number n and returns the total count of digit one written from zero to n.
We start count at zero to accumulate the number of ones across all digit positions.
We set p to one, meaning we begin by examining the ones place.
We loop while p is at most n, so we cover every digit position that n actually has.
We split n into the high digits above this position, the current digit, and the low digits below it.
If the current digit is zero, only complete cycles of the higher digits contribute ones at this position.
In that case we add high times p, since each full cycle gives p numbers with a one here.
If the current digit is one, we also get a partial cycle, so we handle that case separately.
We add high times p for full cycles, plus low plus one for the numbers where the prefix matches n exactly.
Otherwise the current digit is above one, so the current cycle at this position is completed in full.
We add high plus one times p, counting every full cycle including the current one.
We multiply p by ten to move to the next digit position on the left.
After all positions are processed, we return the accumulated count of ones.

number-of-sub-arrays-with-odd-sum.hook: A subarray sum is odd exactly when its two prefix sums have different parity. Just count parities.
number-of-sub-arrays-with-odd-sum.ask: Count how many contiguous subarrays have an odd sum. Return the count modulo one billion and seven.
number-of-sub-arrays-with-odd-sum.exampleWhy: Of the 28 subarrays of 1..7, exactly 16 have odd sums, for example [1], [1,2] and [2,3].

brute.idea: Start at every index, extend to the right with a running sum, and count each time the sum is odd.
steps: Pick a start i
Extend j to the right, adding arr[j]
Count when the running sum is odd
brute.whySlow: There are about n² / 2 subarrays: 100,000 numbers gives 5 billion sums.

optimal.insight: Sum of a subarray = prefix(j) - prefix(i). It is odd exactly when one prefix is odd and the other even, so count prefix parities.
steps: Start with one even prefix: the empty one
Update the running parity with each number
Odd prefix: add the number of even prefixes so far
Even prefix: add the number of odd prefixes so far

pitfalls: Forgetting the empty prefix misses every subarray that starts at index 0.
Apply the modulo; the count can exceed two billion.

say.intro: Okay, so we count the contiguous subarrays whose sum is odd. For one through seven, there are twenty eight subarrays in total. Sixteen of them have an odd sum. So the answer is sixteen.
say.brute: The obvious way? Try every start index. Extend to the right with a running sum. Count each time the sum is odd. Every subarray gets checked once. But there are about n squared over two of them. A hundred thousand numbers means billions of steps.
say.insight: Here's the thing. Every subarray sum is a difference of two prefix sums. And when is a difference odd? Exactly when one side is odd and the other is even. So as we scan, we only need two counts. How many earlier prefixes were odd, and how many were even. An odd prefix pairs with every even one before it. And the other way around.
say.anim: We start with odd and even prefix counts at zero and one, and ans at zero. Processing one, parity flips to one, so we add even's count and bump odd to one. Processing two, parity stays one, we add even again and odd becomes two, ans is now two. Processing three, parity turns even, so we add odd's count instead, ans jumps to four. Processing four stays even, adding odd again, pushing ans up to six. Processing five flips parity odd, adding even's count, ans climbs to nine, odd now three. Processing six keeps parity odd, adding even again, ans rises to twelve, odd becomes four. Processing seven flips parity even, adding odd's count four, giving final ans sixteen, the answer.
say.code: Let's walk the code. The empty prefix counts as even, so even starts at one. For the running sum, only the last bit matters. If the prefix is odd, odd minus even is odd, so add the even count. If it's even, even minus odd is odd, so add the odd count. And since the answer can be huge, we take it modulo a billion and seven.
say.outro: Linear time, constant space. Count earlier prefixes, instead of listing subarrays.

number-of-sub-arrays-with-odd-sum.title: Number of Sub-arrays With Odd Sum
lineNotes: We define a class named Solution, which is the container the problem expects for our method.
The method numOfSubarrays takes the array arr and will return the number of subarrays with an odd sum.
We set MOD to one billion and seven, the modulus the answer must be reported under.
We start odd at zero and even at one, because the empty prefix has sum zero, which is even.
We set both the running parity and the answer to zero before scanning the array.
We loop over each number x in arr, extending the prefix by one element at a time.
We flip the running parity only when x is odd, by combining it with the lowest bit of x.
If the current prefix parity is odd, we handle the case where earlier even prefixes pair with it.
Each earlier even prefix gives an odd difference, so we add the even count to the answer.
We then record this new odd prefix by increasing the odd count by one.
Otherwise the current prefix parity is even, so we need earlier odd prefixes to get an odd sum.
Each earlier odd prefix gives an odd difference, so we add the odd count to the answer.
We then record this new even prefix by increasing the even count by one.
After the loop we return the answer modulo MOD, keeping the large count within the required range.

number-of-substrings-containing-all-thre.hook: Fix where a substring ends. Then every start up to the oldest of the last a, b and c works.
number-of-substrings-containing-all-thre.ask: The string uses only a, b and c. Count the substrings that contain at least one of each letter.
number-of-substrings-containing-all-thre.exampleWhy: Ending at index 2 gives 1 substring, at 3 gives 2, at 4 gives 3, and at 5 gives 4: 10 total.

brute.idea: Check every substring of length three or more and count the ones whose letter set is exactly a, b and c.
steps: Pick a start i
Try every end j
Count if the set of letters is a, b, c
brute.whySlow: Every substring is rebuilt and turned into a set: hopeless for 50,000 characters.

optimal.insight: For a substring ending at i, it is valid exactly when it reaches back past the oldest of the latest a, b and c. That gives min(last) + 1 starts.
steps: Remember the last index of a, b and c
At each i, update the last index of s[i]
Every start from 0 to min(last) is valid
Add min(last) + 1 to the count

codeNotes.note: All starts up to the oldest letter

pitfalls: Before all three letters appear, min is -1 and adds 0, which is correct.
Count substrings by their end; counting by start needs a shrinking window instead.

say.intro: Okay, so the string only has the letters a, b and c. We count the substrings that contain at least one of each. For a, b, c, a, b, c, there are ten of them. So the answer is ten.
say.brute: The obvious way? Look at every substring. Build it, turn it into a set of letters, and check if all three are there. There are about n squared over two substrings. And each check copies text. So it's cubic. That won't survive fifty thousand characters.
say.insight: Here's the trick. Count substrings by where they end. Say a substring ends at index i. When does it contain all three letters? When it starts at or before the oldest of the latest a, b and c. So remember the last position of each letter. Every start from zero up to the smallest one works. That's the minimum, plus one, substrings.
say.anim: We start with last seen positions of a, b, c all set to negative one. At index 0, character a updates last to 0, but b and c are still missing, so count stays 0. At index 1, b updates last to 1, still missing c, so count remains 0. At index 2, c updates last to 2, now all three seen, adding min plus one gives count 1. At index 3, a updates to 3, the oldest is b at 1, adding 2 makes count 3. At index 4, b updates to 4, oldest is c at 2, adding 3 makes count 6. At index 5, c updates to 5, oldest is a at 3, adding 4 makes count 10. The loop finishes and the function returns the final count, which is 10.
say.code: Let's walk the code. Minus one means a letter hasn't been seen yet. At each index, we record the latest position of this letter. Then we add all the starts up to the oldest letter. That's the smallest position, plus one. Before all three appear, the minimum is minus one, so we add zero.
say.outro: Linear time, constant space. Count valid windows by their right end. That's the sliding window idea.

number-of-substrings-containing-all-thre.title: Number of Substrings Containing All Three Characters
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container the problem expects for our method.
This method takes the string s and returns an integer count of substrings containing all three letters.
We record the latest index of each letter, starting each at negative one to mean not yet seen.
We start the running total of valid substrings at zero.
We walk through the string, getting each index i and its character together.
We update the latest seen position of the current character to the current index.
The smallest latest index tells how many starting points work, so we add that plus one to the count; unseen letters add zero.
After scanning every ending position, we return the total count of valid substrings.

partition-array-into-two-arrays-to-minim.hook: 2^30 subsets is too many, but 2^15 per half is easy. Meet in the middle, then binary search.
partition-array-into-two-arrays-to-minim.ask: The array has 2n numbers. Split them into two groups of exactly n numbers each so that the difference between the two group sums is as small as possible. Return that difference.
partition-array-into-two-arrays-to-minim.exampleWhy: Total is 22. Groups [3,9] and [7,3] sum to 12 and 10, a difference of 2. No split reaches 11 and 11.

brute.idea: Try every way to choose n of the 2n numbers for the first group, and measure how far its sum is from half the total.
steps: Loop over every bitmask of 2n bits
Keep masks with exactly n bits set
Difference is |total - 2 · chosen sum|
brute.whySlow: With n = 15 there are 2^30, about a billion, masks to test.

optimal.insight: Split the array into halves. If k numbers come from the left half, exactly n - k come from the right. Pair them with binary search on sorted sums.
steps: List subset sums of each half, grouped by how many numbers were used
Sort each right-half group
For each left sum using k numbers, search right sums using n - k
Check the neighbours of total / 2 - a

codeNotes.note: Sizes must add up to n
Find sums closest to the target

pitfalls: Group sums by count; mixing sizes would allow groups that are not exactly n long.
Check both neighbours around the insertion point, not just one.

say.intro: Okay, so we have two n numbers. Split them into two groups of exactly n each, and make the sums as close as possible. For three, nine, seven, three, the total is twenty two. The best split gives twelve and ten. So the answer is two.
say.brute: The obvious way? Try every way to choose n numbers for the first group. A bitmask over all positions does it, keeping only masks with exactly n bits. Then the difference is the total minus twice the chosen sum. But with n equal to fifteen, that's about a billion masks.
say.insight: Here's the trick. Meet in the middle. Split the array into a left half and a right half. If the first group takes k from the left, it must take n minus k from the right. So list every subset sum of each half, grouped by size. Sort the right groups. Now, for each left sum, binary search for the right sum that lands closest to half the total.
say.anim: We split the array into two halves, each of size two, to search efficiently. For the left half three and nine, we compute sums for every subset by size. Left gives sums grouped by count: zero, three and nine, or twelve. Now we do the same for the right half, seven and three, building its subset sums. Right sums sorted are zero, three and seven, or ten, ready for binary search. For each left sum, we binary search the matching right group to balance totals. Checking sum zero paired with ten, we get a difference of two, our best so far. After trying every split combination, the minimum possible difference found is two.
say.code: Let's walk the code. A helper groups subset sums by size. We run it on two halves, with two to the n subsets each. For each size k, the sizes must add up to n. Binary search finds the sums closest to the target. Then we take the difference of the two groups, and keep the smallest.
say.outro: Two to the n times n, instead of four to the n. That's meet in the middle, with binary search.

partition-array-into-two-arrays-to-minim.title: Partition Array Into Two Arrays to Minimize Sum Difference
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container the judge expects for this problem.
The method takes the list of numbers and returns the smallest possible difference between the two group sums.
We set n to half the length of nums, since each group must hold exactly n numbers.
We compute the total of all numbers so any chosen subset sum tells us the other group's sum too.
We define a helper that lists every subset sum of one half, organized by how many elements were picked.
We create n plus one empty lists, one for each possible subset size from zero to n.
We loop over every bitmask from zero up to two to the n, representing every subset of the half.
For each mask we add up the elements whose bit is set, giving that subset's sum.
We count the set bits to get the subset size and file this sum under that size.
We return the sums grouped by subset size.
We build the grouped subset sums for the left half and the right half separately.
We go through each size group in the right half so we can prepare it for searching.
We sort each group, which is required for binary search to work.
We start best at infinity so any real difference will replace it.
We try every count k of numbers taken from the left half into the first group.
The first group needs n minus k from the right, so we grab that sorted list of options.
For each left subset sum a with k elements, we look for the best right partner.
We binary search for the right sum closest to half the total minus a, which balances the two groups.
The best partner is either just below or at the search position, so we check both neighbors.
We make sure the neighbor index is actually inside the options list.
We compute the difference between the groups as total minus twice the first group sum, and keep the smaller value.
After checking every combination, we return the smallest difference found.

perfect-squares.hook: Greedy takes 9 and fails. Build the answer for every smaller number instead.
perfect-squares.ask: Given n, return the fewest perfect squares, like 1, 4, 9 and 16, that add up to exactly n. The same square may be used more than once.
perfect-squares.exampleWhy: 12 = 4 + 4 + 4 uses three squares. Greedy 9 + 1 + 1 + 1 needs four.

brute.idea: Try every square as the first piece, and solve what remains recursively. Keep the fewest pieces.
steps: For each square j² ≤ n
Solve n - j² recursively
Answer is 1 + the best remainder
brute.whySlow: The same remainders are solved again and again; even n = 100 makes millions of calls.

optimal.insight: The best answer for n is 1 plus the best answer for n - j², for some square j². Compute every value from 1 up to n once.
steps: dp[0] = 0, everything else infinity
For each i from 1 to n
Try every square j² ≤ i
dp[i] = min(dp[i], dp[i - j²] + 1)

codeNotes.note: Use j², reuse the solved remainder

pitfalls: Greedy largest-square-first is wrong: 12 gives 9 + 1 + 1 + 1.
BFS over remainders also works and is often faster in practice.

say.intro: Okay, so given n, we want the fewest perfect squares that add up to exactly n. Squares can repeat. For twelve, the answer is three. Four plus four plus four. Now, notice the greedy trap. Take nine first, and you're left with three ones. That's four squares.
say.brute: The obvious way? Try every square as the first piece. Solve the leftover recursively. Keep the smallest count. It's correct. But the same leftovers get solved again and again. Twelve minus four, and twelve minus one minus one minus one, both lead to eight. The calls explode.
say.insight: So what do we do when the same subproblems keep coming back? Solve each one once. The best answer for i is one plus the best answer for i minus some square. So fill an array from zero up to n. Each entry looks back at every square that fits, and takes the cheapest remainder.
say.anim: We start with n equal twelve, initializing dp array to infinity except dp of zero. For small i values one, two, and three, only j equals one works, giving dp values one, two, three. At i equals four, trying j equals two gives four minus four, so dp becomes one, better than four. At i equals eight, j equals two gives dp eight equals two, using two squares of two and four. At i equals nine, j equals three gives dp nine equals one, since nine is itself a perfect square. Finally at i equals twelve, comparing options with j one, two, three gives dp twelve equals three. The function returns three, meaning twelve is the sum of three perfect squares like four, four, four.
say.code: Let's walk the code. Zero needs no squares. We solve every smaller total first. For each one, we try each square that fits. Use j squared, then reuse the solved remainder, plus one. At the end, the last entry holds the fewest squares for n.
say.outro: n times root n time, linear space. Build each answer from smaller ones you've already solved.

perfect-squares.title: Perfect Squares
lineNotes: We define a solution class that holds the method for solving the perfect squares problem.
The method numSquares takes the target number n and returns the fewest perfect squares that sum to it.
We build a table where zero needs zero squares and every other value starts at infinity as an unknown best.
We loop through every value i from one up to n so each answer is computed once.
For each i we start trying squares with j equal to one.
We keep trying values of j as long as j squared does not exceed i.
We update the best for i by comparing it with one plus the best for i minus j squared.
We increase j by one to try the next perfect square.
Finally we return the table entry for n, which holds the fewest squares needed.

permutation-sequence.hook: Do not list permutations. Factorials tell you each digit directly.
permutation-sequence.ask: Write all orderings of the digits 1 to n in sorted order. Return the k-th one as a string, without generating the whole list.
permutation-sequence.exampleWhy: With 4 digits, each first digit leads a block of 6. Position 9 is in the second block, so it starts with 2.

brute.idea: Generate permutations in sorted order and stop at the k-th one.
steps: Generate permutations in order
Count each one
Return the k-th
brute.whySlow: k can be 9! = 362,880, so we may build hundreds of thousands of permutations.

optimal.insight: After fixing the first digit, the rest has (n - 1)! orderings. So k divided by (n - 1)! picks the first digit directly.
steps: Make k zero-based
Block size is (size - 1)!
idx = k // block picks the next digit
Remove it and continue with k % block

codeNotes.note: Orderings per choice of next digit
Which block, and position inside it
Use that digit and remove it

pitfalls: Forgetting k -= 1 shifts every answer by one block at boundaries.
Remove each used digit so later indices refer to remaining digits.

say.intro: Okay, so list every ordering of the digits one to n, in sorted order. Which one sits at position k? For n equal to four and k equal to nine, the answer is two, three, one, four.
say.brute: The obvious way? Generate the permutations in order, counting as you go. Stop at the k th one. It works. But k can be as big as nine factorial. That's about three hundred sixty thousand orderings. Building them all just to throw them away? Wasteful.
say.insight: Here's the thing. The list has structure. Once the first digit is fixed, the rest can be arranged in n minus one factorial ways. So the list is made of equal blocks, one per first digit. Divide k by the block size, and you know which digit comes first. The remainder tells you where you are inside that block. Then repeat with one fewer digit.
say.anim: We start with digits one through four and k equals nine, then decrement k to eight. With size four, block is six, the factorial of three, giving groups of six permutations. Dividing eight by six gives index one and remainder two, so we pick digit two. Remaining digits are one, three, four; block becomes two, index one picks digit three. Remaining digits one and four; block is one, k stays zero, picking digit one. Only digit four remains, so it gets appended automatically to complete the sequence. All digits are used up, leaving the final answer ready to join together. The function returns the string two three one four as the ninth permutation.
say.code: Let's walk the code. We subtract one from k, because zero based makes division clean. At each size, the block is the orderings per choice of next digit. Divmod tells us which block, and our position inside it. Then we use that digit and remove it from the list.
say.outro: Quadratic in n, and n is at most nine. The factorial number system turns counting into division.

permutation-sequence.title: Permutation Sequence
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container the problem expects for our method.
The method getPermutation takes n and k and returns the k-th permutation as a string.
We build a list of digit strings from one up to n, which we will pick from and remove.
We subtract one from k so it becomes a zero-based index into the sorted list of permutations.
We start an empty list called out to collect the chosen digits in order.
We loop with size counting down from n to one, since each step fixes one digit with fewer remaining.
Block is the factorial of size minus one, the number of permutations that share each choice of leading digit.
Dividing k by block gives idx, the digit position to pick, and the remainder becomes the new k within that block.
We remove the digit at position idx from the remaining digits and append it to out.
After all digits are placed, we join them into one string and return it.

print-binary-tree.hook: Height fixes the grid size. Then every child sits a halving gap to the left or right of its parent.
print-binary-tree.ask: Draw a binary tree in a grid of strings. The grid has height + 1 rows and 2^(height+1) - 1 columns. The root sits in the middle of the top row, and each child is offset by a halving gap.
print-binary-tree.exampleWhy: Height 2 gives 3 rows and 7 columns. 1 sits at column 3, its children at 1 and 5, and 4 at column 2.

brute.idea: Find the height by walking level by level, then place nodes with a queue that pops from the front of a list.
steps: Count levels with a level-by-level walk
Create the empty grid
Pop each node from the queue and place it
Queue children with the halved gap
brute.whySlow: Same grid cost, but list.pop(0) shifts the queue each time, so placement is quadratic in nodes.

optimal.insight: Once the height is known, a node at row r has children exactly 2^(h - r - 1) columns away. One recursive pass places everything.
steps: Compute the height recursively
Build a grid of empty strings
Place the root in the middle column
Recurse: children go gap columns left and right, gap halving each row

codeNotes.match: return -1 if not node else 1 + max(height(node.left), height(node.right))

pitfalls: Height here counts edges: a single node has height 0 and one row.
The empty grid cells dominate the cost, not the nodes.

say.intro: Okay, so we draw a tree into a grid of strings. The rows are the height plus one. The width is two to the height plus one, minus one. Our tree has one at the root, two and three below, and four under two. That's three rows and seven columns.
say.brute: A simple version counts the levels with a level by level walk. Then it places nodes using a queue that pops from the front of a list. That's correct. But popping from the front shifts the whole list every time. Honestly, the grid costs the same either way. The real difference is the extra shifting, and longer code.
say.insight: Here's the thing. The layout is fixed by the height alone. Once we know it, the root goes in the middle column. Each child sits a fixed gap left or right of its parent. And that gap halves on every level. So one recursive pass places every node.
say.anim: We start by computing the tree height recursively, diving down through node 1 and its children. The deepest node, 4, returns height 0, and the recursion builds back up to a total height of 2. With height 2, we calculate 7 columns and build a 3 by 7 grid of empty strings. Placing starts at row 0, column 3, writing 1 into the middle of the grid. The gap is 2, so node 2 goes to row 1, column 1, left of center. Node 2 has no left child, but its right child, 4, is placed at row 2, column 2. Back at the root, node 3 is placed on the right at row 1, column 5, using the same gap logic. The final grid shows 1 centered on top, 2 and 3 below, and 4 beneath 2, matching the expected output.
say.code: Let's walk the code. Height counts edges, so an empty tree is minus one. The width doubles with every level. When we place a node, the offset to its children halves at each row. And we start with the root in the middle.
say.outro: Time and space match the size of the grid. Compute a global property first, then lay out the nodes recursively.

print-binary-tree.title: Print Binary Tree
lineNotes: We define a Solution class that holds the method for printing the tree.
The printTree method takes the root of the tree and returns a grid of strings.
We define a helper function called height that measures how deep the tree goes below a node.
An empty node has height negative one, otherwise it is one plus the taller of its two subtrees.
We call height on the root to get h, the number of levels below the root.
The grid needs two to the power of h plus one, minus one columns, so every level has room.
We build h plus one rows, each filled with cols empty strings, as the blank grid.
We define place, a recursive helper that writes a node's value at row r and column c.
If the node is missing, there is nothing to write.
So we simply return and leave those cells empty.
We write the node's value as a string into its cell in the grid.
Only nodes above the last row can have children to place, so we check r against h.
The gap to each child is two to the power of h minus r minus one, halving at each level.
We place the left child one row down and gap columns to the left.
We place the right child one row down and gap columns to the right.
We start at the top row, in the middle column, which is cols minus one divided by two.
After the recursion fills every node, we return the finished grid.

recover-a-tree-from-preorder-traversal.hook: Dashes give depth, preorder gives order. A stack of the current path rebuilds the tree in one pass.
recover-a-tree-from-preorder-traversal.ask: A preorder walk wrote each node as dashes for its depth followed by its value. Rebuild the binary tree. A node with one child always has it on the left.
recover-a-tree-from-preorder-traversal.exampleWhy: 1 is the root. 2 and 5 have one dash, so they are its children; 3, 4 and 6, 7 have two dashes.

brute.idea: Parse the string into (depth, value) tokens, then recursively build: the left child follows the root, and the right child is the next token at depth + 1.
steps: Parse into (depth, value) tokens
Root is the first token in a range
Scan for the next token one level deeper
Recurse into the left and right ranges
brute.whySlow: Each level rescans its range to find the right child; a deep, skewed tree makes this quadratic.

optimal.insight: In preorder, a node at depth d hangs off the most recent node at depth d - 1. A stack holding the current root-to-node path finds it instantly.
steps: Count dashes to get the depth, then read the number
Pop the stack until its size equals the depth
Attach the node as left child if free, else right
Push the node

codeNotes.note: Each dash is one level deeper
Climb back up to the parent

codeNotes.match: if stack and stack[-1].left is None:

codeNotes.note: Bottom of the stack is the root

pitfalls: Values can be multi-digit; do not read one character per node.
Pop until the stack size equals the depth, not depth minus one.

say.intro: Okay, so a preorder walk wrote each node as some dashes, one per level, then its value. We have to rebuild the tree. In our string, one is the root. Two and five have one dash. Three, four, six and seven have two. So two and five are the root's children.
say.brute: The obvious way? First parse the string into depth and value pairs. Then build recursively. In any range, the first token is the root, and the next is its left child. To find the right child, scan forward for the next token one level deeper. But that rescanning makes skewed trees quadratic.
say.insight: Here's the thing. In preorder, a node at depth d always belongs to the most recent node at depth d minus one. So keep a stack holding the current path from the root. When a node arrives at depth d, pop until the stack has exactly d nodes. Now the top is its parent. No left child yet? Go left. Otherwise, go right.
say.anim: We start with an empty stack, reading the string to rebuild the tree using dashes as depth markers. Node 1 is created at depth zero and pushed, becoming the root of our tree. Node 2 has one dash, so depth is 1, and it becomes node 1's left child. Node 3 has two dashes, depth 2, attaching as node 2's left child. Node 4 also has depth 2, so after popping node 3, it becomes node 2's right child. Node 5 has depth 1, popping back to node 1, becoming its right child. Node 6 at depth 2 attaches as node 5's left child after matching the stack size. Node 7, also depth 2, becomes node 5's right child, completing the tree as 1,2,5,3,4,6,7.
say.code: Let's walk the code. Each dash is one level deeper, so we count them. Values can have several digits, so we read them all. Then we climb back up to the parent by popping. The left child is filled first, then the right. At the end, the bottom of the stack is the root.
say.outro: Linear time, stack space equal to the height. Preorder plus depth tells you exactly where each node goes.

recover-a-tree-from-preorder-traversal.title: Recover a Tree From Preorder Traversal
lineNotes: We define the Solution class that holds the method for rebuilding the tree.
The method takes the traversal string and returns the root of the recovered binary tree.
We start with an empty stack that will hold the current path from root to the latest node.
We set i to zero as our reading position and n to the length of the traversal string.
We loop until the reading position has consumed the entire string, handling one node per pass.
For each node we reset depth to zero before counting its leading dashes.
While the current character is a dash, we keep counting, since dashes encode the node's depth.
Each dash found increases depth by one.
We advance the reading position past that dash.
We reset val to zero before reading the digits of this node's value.
We keep reading while characters remain and are digits, since values can have several digits.
We shift val one decimal place and add the new digit to build the number.
We advance the reading position past the digit we just consumed.
We create a new tree node holding the parsed value.
We pop the stack until its size equals depth, leaving the parent of this node on top.
Each pop discards a finished node that cannot be an ancestor of the new node.
If a parent exists and its left child is empty, the new node goes on the left.
We attach the new node as the left child of the parent on top.
Otherwise, if a parent exists, its left is taken so the new node becomes the right child.
We attach the new node as the right child of the parent on top.
We push the new node so it becomes part of the current path for later nodes.
At the end, the bottom of the stack is the root, so we return it.

remove-duplicates-from-sorted-array-ii.hook: Allow each value twice. Just compare with the element two places back in the kept part.
remove-duplicates-from-sorted-array-ii.ask: The array is sorted. Remove extra copies in place so each value appears at most twice, keep the order, and return how many elements remain at the front.
remove-duplicates-from-sorted-array-ii.exampleWhy: The four 1s shrink to two, so the front becomes 0, 0, 1, 1, 2, 3, 3: seven elements.

brute.idea: Walk the array and delete any element equal to the one two places before it.
steps: Start at index 2
Equal to nums[i - 2]? Delete it with pop
Otherwise move forward
brute.whySlow: Each pop shifts every later element left; many duplicates make this quadratic.

optimal.insight: The kept prefix is sorted. A new value is allowed unless it equals the value two slots back in the kept prefix.
steps: k counts the kept elements
Keep x if k < 2 or x != nums[k - 2]
Write x at nums[k] and grow k
Return k

codeNotes.note: Third copy would match two back
First k slots are the answer

pitfalls: Compare with the kept prefix nums[k - 2], not the original nums[i - 2].
The same idea works for at most m copies: compare with nums[k - m].

say.intro: Okay, so the array is sorted, and each value may stay at most twice. We compact it in place, and return how many we kept. For zero, zero, one, one, one, one, two, three, three, the extra ones go. Seven elements are left.
say.brute: The obvious way? Walk the array and delete any element equal to the one two places back. That gives the right array. But here's the catch. Each delete shifts every later element left. An array full of duplicates costs quadratic time. Can we avoid shifting at all?
say.insight: Here's the thing. Don't delete. Write. Keep a write pointer k, marking the end of the kept prefix. Since the array is sorted, when is a value a third copy? Exactly when it equals the value two slots back in the kept part. If not, copy it to position k, and move k forward. Nothing ever shifts.
say.anim: We start with k at zero, scanning the sorted array for duplicates beyond two. The first two zeros and the first two ones get kept, since k is still under two. K reaches four, keeping two ones so far in the result. The next two ones match nums at k minus two, so they're skipped entirely. Value two differs from the kept pair, so it's written in, growing k to five. Value three is new too, so it's added, pushing k to six. The second three also differs from two slots back, so it's kept, making k seven. Final answer is seven, the length of the cleaned array with at most two duplicates.
say.code: Let's walk the code. We track a write position, which is also the kept count. For each value, a third copy would match two back, so we skip it. Otherwise, we overwrite in place and move forward. At the end, the first k slots are the answer.
say.outro: Linear time, constant space. A fast reader and a slow writer, compacting in place. Classic two pointers.

remove-duplicates-from-sorted-array-ii.title: Remove Duplicates from Sorted Array II
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container for the method that solves this problem.
The method removeDuplicates takes the sorted list nums and will return the count of elements kept.
We set k to zero, which is both the size of the kept prefix and the next write position.
We loop over each value x in nums, reading values in order while we write kept ones at the front.
We keep x if fewer than two are kept, or if x differs from the value two slots back.
Since the check passed, we write x into position k of nums, extending the kept prefix in place.
We increase k by one so the prefix grows and the next write goes to the following slot.
After the loop we return k, the number of elements kept with each value appearing at most twice.

remove-duplicates-from-sorted-list.hook: Sorted means duplicates sit side by side. Just unlink the next node whenever it repeats.
remove-duplicates-from-sorted-list.ask: Given the head of a sorted linked list, delete nodes so that every value appears only once, and return the list.
remove-duplicates-from-sorted-list.exampleWhy: One extra 1 and two extra 3s are unlinked, leaving 1, 2, 3, 4.

brute.idea: Copy the distinct values into a Python list, then build a brand new linked list from them.
steps: Walk the list, saving each new value
Build fresh nodes from the saved values
Return the new head
brute.whySlow: Same linear time, but it allocates a new list and new nodes instead of fixing links in place.

optimal.insight: Because the list is sorted, every duplicate is right next to its original. Skip it by pointing cur.next past it.
steps: Start cur at the head
If cur.next has the same value, unlink it
Otherwise move cur forward
Return the head

codeNotes.note: Need a next node to compare
Unlink it; stay put for more

pitfalls: Do not advance cur after unlinking; a third copy may follow.
An empty list must return None without crashing.

say.intro: Okay, so we get the head of a sorted linked list. We delete repeated nodes, so each value appears once. For one, one, two, three, three, three, four, we unlink one extra one and two extra threes. The answer is one, two, three, four.
say.brute: A simple approach copies the distinct values into a list as it walks. Then it builds a brand new linked list from them. To be fair, that's also linear time. So what's wrong with it? Memory. It allocates a second list and fresh nodes, when we could just fix the original in place.
say.insight: Here's the thing. The list is sorted. So every duplicate sits right next to its original. Stand on a node and look at the next one. Same value? Skip it, by pointing our next pointer past it. Different? Step forward. That's it. No extra memory at all.
say.anim: We start with cur at head, pointing to the first node, value one. Cur next also equals one, a duplicate, so we skip it by relinking cur next. Now the list shows one, two, three, three, three, four, duplicate removed. Cur next is two, different from one, so cur simply moves forward. Cur now sits at the first three, which matches the next three, so we skip it. After skipping, list is one, two, three, three, four, another duplicate remains. Still equal threes detected, so we skip again, shrinking the duplicates further. Cur reaches four, the last node, loop ends, returning one, two, three, four.
say.code: Let's walk the code. We need a next node to compare, so we loop while there is one. If the duplicate sits right after cur, we unlink it. And we stay put, in case more copies follow. If it's a new value, we advance. At the end, we return the original head.
say.outro: Linear time, constant space. Change the links in place, instead of rebuilding.

remove-duplicates-from-sorted-list.title: Remove Duplicates from Sorted List
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which holds the method that LeetCode will call to solve this problem.
This method takes the head of a sorted linked list and returns the head of the list after duplicates are removed.
We start a pointer called cur at the head so we can walk along the list.
We loop while cur and the node after it both exist, since we always compare neighbors.
We check whether the next node holds the same value as cur, which means it is a duplicate.
If so, we point cur's next past the duplicate, which removes it, and we stay on cur to check the new neighbor.
Otherwise, the next value is different, so no duplicate sits right after cur.
In that case we advance cur to the next node and continue comparing.
Finally we return head, which is still the first node since the first occurrence of any value is always kept.

reorganize-string.hook: Always place the most common letter you are allowed to. A max-heap makes that choice instant.
reorganize-string.ask: Rearrange the letters of s so that no two neighbours are the same letter. Return any valid arrangement, or an empty string if it is impossible.
reorganize-string.exampleWhy: Three a's need two separators between them; b, b and c provide them, giving ababac.

brute.idea: Backtrack: build the string letter by letter, trying each remaining letter that differs from the last one, and undo on dead ends.
steps: Try each available letter different from the last
Recurse on the shorter remainder
Dead end? Undo and try the next letter
brute.whySlow: Impossible inputs force the search through huge numbers of partial strings before giving up.

optimal.insight: The most frequent letter is the hardest to place, so place it as early as possible. Hold back the letter just used for one turn.
steps: Count letters and push (-count, letter) into a heap
Pop the most frequent letter and append it
Push back the letter held from last turn
Hold this letter if it has copies left
Too short at the end? Return empty

reorganize-string.optimalCode:
class Solution:
    def reorganizeString(self, s: str) -> str:
        heap = [(-cnt, ch) for ch, cnt in collections.Counter(s).items()]
        heapq.heapify(heap)
        out = []
        prev = None
        while heap:
            cnt, ch = heapq.heappop(heap)
            out.append(ch)
            if prev:
                heapq.heappush(heap, prev)
            cnt += 1
            prev = (cnt, ch) if cnt < 0 else None
        return "".join(out) if len(out) == len(s) else ""

codeNotes.match: heap = [(-cnt, ch) for ch, cnt in collections.Counter(s).items()]

codeNotes.note: Last turn's letter is allowed again

codeNotes.match: prev = (cnt, ch) if cnt < 0 else None
codeNotes.note: Cool down the letter just used

pitfalls: Quick impossibility check: any letter more than (n + 1) / 2 times cannot work.
Push the held letter back only after popping the next one.

say.intro: Okay, so we rearrange the letters so no two neighbours match. If that's impossible, we return an empty string. For a, a, a, b, b, c, the three a's need separators. The b's and the c supply them. One answer is a, b, a, b, a, c.
say.brute: The obvious way? Backtracking. Build the answer one letter at a time, trying every letter that differs from the last one. Stuck? Undo and try another. It finds an answer. But in the worst case, especially when no answer exists, it explores an exponential number of partial strings.
say.insight: Here's the thing. Which letter is the hardest to fit? The most frequent one. So spend it as early as we can. A max heap always hands us the most frequent letter. There's just one rule. We can't reuse the letter we just placed. So we hold it out for one turn, and push it back after the next pop.
say.anim: We build a heap counting letters, so a appears three times, b twice, c once. We pop the most frequent letter, a, and place it first in the output. We hold a back one turn, then pop b and add it, giving ababac so far as ab. We push b back, pop a again since it is still most frequent, output becomes aba. We alternate again, pushing a back and popping b, extending output to abab. With no letter left waiting, we pop a once more, making output ababa. Finally c is popped and appended, filling the last slot of the string. All characters placed with no repeats, so the final answer is ababac.
say.code: Let's walk the code. Negative counts turn the heap into a max heap. Each round, we pop the most frequent allowed letter. Then last turn's letter is allowed again, so it goes back in. We cool down the letter just used. And if we get stuck early, it's impossible.
say.outro: n log k time, where k is the alphabet size. Serve the most demanding item first, with a one turn cooldown.

reorganize-string.title: Reorganize String
lineNotes: We define the Solution class that holds the method for this problem.
The method reorganizeString takes the string s and returns a rearranged string or an empty one.
We count each letter and build a heap list of negative counts with letters, so the most frequent comes first.
We turn that list into a min heap, which acts as a max heap on counts because of the negatives.
We create an empty list called out to collect the letters of our arrangement.
We set prev to none, since no letter is being held back at the start.
We loop as long as the heap still has letters available to place.
We pop the letter with the largest remaining count, since the most frequent letter is hardest to place.
We append that letter to out, placing it at the next position.
If a letter was held back from the previous turn, we handle it now.
We push the held back letter into the heap so it becomes available again, now that a different letter sits between.
We add one to the negative count, which means one copy of this letter has been used.
If copies remain, we hold this letter back for one turn in prev, otherwise prev becomes none.
If out has every letter we return the joined string, otherwise it was impossible so we return an empty string.

reverse-words-in-a-string.hook: Read the string backwards, one word at a time, and the spaces take care of themselves.
reverse-words-in-a-string.ask: Reverse the order of the words in s. The result must have single spaces between words and no leading or trailing spaces, even if s had extra spaces.
reverse-words-in-a-string.exampleWhy: The four words come out last to first, and the doubled and edge spaces disappear.

brute.idea: Split into words, then build the answer by putting each new word in front of everything built so far.
steps: Split s into words
Prepend each word to the result
Return the result
brute.whySlow: Each prepend copies the whole result string, so many short words make it quadratic.

optimal.insight: Scanning from the right meets the words already in reversed order. Two pointers mark each word's end and start.
steps: Start i at the last character
Skip spaces moving left
Mark the word's end, then move left past its letters
Collect the slice, then join with single spaces

pitfalls: s.split() with no argument already drops extra spaces; split(" ") does not.
Check i < 0 after skipping spaces, or trailing spaces add an empty word.

say.intro: Okay, so we reverse the order of the words. Exactly one space between them, and none at the edges. Our input has extra spaces at the start, in the middle, and at the end. The answer is blue is sky the.
say.brute: The obvious way? Split the string into words. Then build the answer by putting each new word in front of everything so far. The result is right. But strings can't be changed in place. So every prepend copies the whole result again. With many short words, that adds up to quadratic work.
say.insight: Here's the thing. Read the string from right to left. Now the words show up already reversed. So use two pointers. One skips spaces moving left. When it lands on a letter, mark that as the end of a word. Keep moving left until a space. The slice between them is the next word.
say.anim: We start scanning the string from the right, with index i at eighteen. Trailing spaces get skipped until i lands on a letter at position seventeen. End marks the word's end, then i walks left through letters of blue. The word blue is captured, and scanning continues leftward for the next word. Spaces are skipped again, then end and i trace out the word is. Words now holds blue and is, so the loop moves further left. Similarly, sky gets extracted by marking its end and scanning past its letters. Finally the word the is found near the start, completing the word list. Joining the words gives the final reversed string: blue is sky the.
say.code: Let's walk the code. We start from the right end. First, skip any run of spaces. Then mark the last letter of this word. Move left to its start, and slice out one word. Finally, join them with single spaces, so there's nothing at the edges.
say.outro: Linear time, linear space for the output. Scan from the end, and slice out each word.

reverse-words-in-a-string.title: Reverse Words in a String
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container this problem's method lives in.
The method reverseWords takes the string s and returns the words reversed with clean single spacing.
We start with an empty list called words to collect each word as we find it.
We set i to the last index of s so we scan from the right.
The outer loop keeps running as long as i has not moved past the start of the string.
This inner loop skips over any spaces, moving i leftward until it lands on a letter or runs out.
Each step in that skip loop decrements i by one to move left past a space.
If i fell below zero, only spaces remained, so there is no further word to collect.
We break out of the outer loop because the scan is finished.
We record end as the index of the last character of the current word.
This loop moves i left through the word's letters until it hits a space or the string's start.
Each step decrements i by one, so i ends up just before the word's first character.
We slice from i plus one through end and append that word, which naturally arrives in reversed order.
We join the collected words with single spaces, giving the result with no leading or trailing spaces.

separate-squares-i.hook: Area below a line only grows as the line rises. That monotonic curve is begging for binary search.
separate-squares-i.ask: Squares are given by bottom-left corner and side length, and may overlap. Find the lowest horizontal line with equal total square area above and below it.
separate-squares-i.exampleWhy: Total area is 5. At y = 7/6, the big square has 7/3 below and the small one 1/6: exactly 2.5.

brute.idea: Area below grows linearly between square edges. Check each gap between consecutive edges and interpolate inside the one where half the area is reached.
steps: Collect all bottom and top edges, sorted
For each gap, compute area below both ends
First gap reaching half: interpolate inside it
brute.whySlow: There are up to 2n edges, and each needs an O(n) area sum: 50,000 squares means billions of operations.

optimal.insight: Area below the line never decreases as the line rises. So binary search on y for the lowest line where below reaches half.
steps: lo = lowest bottom, hi = highest top
below(y) sums l · min(l, max(0, y - bottom))
If twice below(mid) ≥ total, move hi down; else move lo up
Stop when the gap is under 1e-6

codeNotes.match: total = sum(l * l for _, _, l in squares)
codeNotes.note: Overlaps count twice, so just add

codeNotes.match: return sum(l * min(l, max(0, line - y)) for _, y, l in squares)
codeNotes.note: Each square's slice under the line
Half reached: answer is at or below mid
Lowest line that balances the area

pitfalls: Use ≥, not >, so the search finds the lowest balancing line.
Sorting edge events and sweeping gives an exact O(n log n) answer too.

say.intro: Okay, so each square is given by its bottom left corner and side length. Overlaps count twice. We want the lowest horizontal line with equal area above and below. With a two by two square and a one by one square, the answer is seven sixths. About one point one seven.
say.brute: Between square edges, the area below the line grows in a straight line. So sort all the bottom and top edges. For each gap, compute the area below both ends. The first gap that reaches half the total? Interpolate inside it. Correct, but each edge needs a full sum over the squares. That's quadratic.
say.insight: Here's the thing. As the line rises, the area below it can only grow. That's monotonic. And monotonic means binary search. Search on y, from the lowest bottom to the highest top. Area below the middle is at least half? The answer is at or below it, so move the top down. Otherwise, move the bottom up.
say.anim: We total the squared side lengths of both squares, giving a total area of five. The search starts between lo zero and hi two, bracketing the possible line height. At mid one point five, the area below the line is three point five, more than half. Since that's too much area, hi shrinks down to one point five. The loop keeps narrowing lo and hi, checking if double the below area meets the total. Mid values hover near one point one six seven, with below area closing in on two point five. Lo and hi squeeze together tightly around one point one six six six six seven. Once the gap is tiny, the loop stops, returning the final answer one point one six six six seven.
say.code: Let's walk the code. Overlaps count twice, so the total is just a sum. For any line, we add each square's slice under the line. We keep halving to shrink to the needed precision. If half is reached, the answer is at or below mid. And we return the lowest line that balances the area.
say.outro: n times the log of the range over the precision. Binary search on the answer, driven by a monotonic area.

separate-squares-i.title: Separate Squares I
lineNotes: We define the Solution class that holds the method for this problem.
The method takes the list of squares and returns the lowest y coordinate of a line splitting the area equally.
We compute the total area by summing each square's side length times itself, ignoring overlap since areas simply add.
The lowest possible line sits at the smallest bottom edge among all squares, so we set lo to that.
The highest useful line is the largest top edge, bottom y plus side length, so we set hi to that.
We define a helper called below that computes the total area lying under a given horizontal line.
For each square, the covered height under the line is clamped between zero and its side, then multiplied by the side to get area.
We keep halving the search interval until its width is smaller than a tiny tolerance of one millionth.
We take mid as the midpoint of the current low and high bounds.
If twice the area below mid is at least the total, then below has reached half, so mid is a valid candidate.
Since mid works, we pull hi down to mid to look for an even lower line.
Otherwise the area below is less than half, so the answer must lie higher.
In that case we raise lo up to mid, discarding the lower half.
After the loop ends, hi is within tolerance of the lowest valid line, so we return it.

shortest-common-supersequence.hook: The shortest string containing both is both strings minus their longest common subsequence.
shortest-common-supersequence.ask: Return the shortest string that contains both str1 and str2 as subsequences, meaning you can delete characters from it to get either one. Any shortest answer is accepted.
shortest-common-supersequence.exampleWhy: Deleting the first c leaves abac; deleting the final ac leaves cab. Five letters is the minimum.

brute.idea: Recursively merge from the front: shared letters are taken once; otherwise try taking from either string and keep the shorter result.
steps: Equal first letters? Take it once
Else try each string's letter first
Keep the shorter merged result
brute.whySlow: Each mismatch branches two ways with no memory: strings of length 1,000 are hopeless.

optimal.insight: Shared letters should be written once, so share as many as possible: the longest common subsequence. Build its table, then walk it to merge.
steps: Fill lcs[i][j] for the suffixes str1[i:] and str2[j:]
Walk from the front: equal letters are written once
Otherwise write the letter whose skip keeps the longer LCS
Append whatever remains of either string

codeNotes.note: Skip a letter from one string
Skipping str1[i] keeps the best LCS

pitfalls: The LCS length alone is not enough; walk the table to build the string.
Do not forget the leftover tail of whichever string is not finished.

say.intro: Okay, so we want the shortest string containing both inputs as subsequences. For a, b, a, c and c, a, b, one answer is c, a, b, a, c. Delete its first c, and you get a, b, a, c. Delete its last two letters, and you get c, a, b.
say.brute: The obvious way? Merge the strings from the front. Same first letter? Write it once and move on in both. Otherwise, try writing each string's letter first, recurse, and keep the shorter result. But there's no memory of earlier work. Every mismatch doubles the calls. That's exponential.
say.insight: Here's the thing. Every letter of both strings must show up. But a letter they share can be written just once. So the shortest answer shares as many letters as possible. And that's exactly the longest common subsequence. Fill the classic LCS table. Then walk it. Matching letters are written once. On a mismatch, write the letter whose skip keeps the bigger LCS.
say.anim: We start with abac and cab, building a table to find their longest shared pattern. The lcs table starts filled with zeros, sized for every position in both strings. Comparing characters backward, matching letters add one plus the diagonal value in the table. The table fills in, recording how many shared letters remain from each position onward. Once complete, the full table shows two shared letters overall between the two strings. Now we walk forward, comparing characters and picking whichever path keeps more matches ahead. Since str1 and str2 differ at c, we take c first, then match a and b together. After appending remaining letters, the shortest common supersequence built is cabac.
say.code: Let's walk the code. A shared letter extends the LCS by one. Otherwise, we skip a letter from one string, taking the better option. During the walk, if skipping the first string's letter keeps the best LCS, we write that letter. At the end, we append the leftover tail.
say.outro: m times n time and space. Build the LCS table, then walk it to rebuild the answer.

shortest-common-supersequence.title: Shortest Common Supersequence
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, as the problem platform expects.
This method takes two strings and returns the shortest string that has both as subsequences.
We store the lengths of str1 and str2 in m and n for later use.
We build a table of zeros with one extra row and column, holding suffix longest common subsequence lengths.
We loop i backward from the end of str1, so shorter suffixes are solved first.
Inside that, we loop j backward through str2 the same way.
If the current characters of both strings match, we can extend a common subsequence.
On a match, the table value is one plus the value for both suffixes after these characters.
Otherwise the characters differ, so we must skip one of them.
We take the larger of skipping a character from str1 or from str2.
We create an empty list called out to collect the characters of the answer.
We set both pointers i and j to zero to start merging from the front.
We keep merging while both strings still have unused characters.
If the current characters match, they are shared and should be written only once.
We append that shared character to out.
We advance i past the shared character in str1.
We advance j past it in str2 as well.
If skipping str1's character keeps the common subsequence at least as long, we choose to write str1's character.
We append the current character of str1 since it is not shared yet.
We move i forward in str1.
Otherwise skipping str2's character preserves more shared letters, so we handle str2 instead.
We append the current character of str2 to out.
We move j forward in str2.
We join the collected characters and add whatever remains of str1 and str2, giving the shortest supersequence.

shortest-palindrome.hook: Find the longest palindrome at the start of s. KMP finds it in one linear pass.
shortest-palindrome.ask: You may only add characters to the front of s. Return the shortest palindrome you can make this way.
shortest-palindrome.exampleWhy: aacecaa is already a palindrome prefix. Only the last a is left over, so we add one a in front.

brute.idea: Try prefixes from longest to shortest. The first palindromic prefix tells us what is left over to mirror in front.
steps: For end from n down to 0
Is s[:end] a palindrome?
Yes: prepend the reverse of s[end:]
brute.whySlow: Strings like aaaa...ab fail almost every check after a long comparison: 50,000 letters is billions of steps.

optimal.insight: The longest palindromic prefix of s is the longest prefix of s that is also a suffix of reversed s. KMP's prefix function computes exactly that.
steps: Build t = s + # + reverse(s)
Compute the KMP prefix function of t
Its last value is the palindromic prefix length
Prepend the reverse of the rest

codeNotes.note: Fall back to a shorter border

pitfalls: Without the separator, the match can run past s and overcount.
The empty string is already a palindrome: return it unchanged.

say.intro: Okay, so we can only add characters to the front of the string. We want the shortest palindrome we can build. For a, a, c, e, c, a, a, a, the first seven letters are already a palindrome. Only the final a is left over. So we add one a in front.
say.brute: The obvious way? Find the longest prefix that's already a palindrome. Try prefixes from longest to shortest, reversing each one to compare. The first match tells us which tail to mirror. But each check can take linear time. A bad input fails almost every check. That's quadratic.
say.insight: Here's the thing. A prefix of s is a palindrome exactly when it also shows up as a suffix of s reversed. And finding the longest prefix that's also a suffix? That's what the KMP prefix function does. So glue s, a separator, and s reversed together. Run KMP once. The last value is the length of the longest palindromic prefix.
say.anim: We build a combined string, s plus a separator plus s reversed, to compare them. We start computing the prefix function array lps, tracking matches between prefix and suffix. As i grows, lps stays mostly zero since characters don't match yet, like at index two. Around index six, matches start building, growing lps values to two, showing overlap length increasing. The algorithm keeps comparing characters, sometimes falling back using previous lps values when mismatches occur. From index fourteen onward, lps grows steadily to five, six, then seven, meaning long matching overlap. The final lps value seven tells us the longest palindromic prefix length, giving the shortest palindrome 'aaacecaaa'.
say.code: Let's walk the code. The separator stops matches from crossing over. At each position, while the letters differ, we fall back to a shorter border. When they match, the border grows by one. Finally, we mirror only the unmatched tail onto the front.
say.outro: Linear time and space. Turn a palindrome question into a prefix equals suffix question.

shortest-palindrome.title: Shortest Palindrome
lineNotes: We define a class named Solution, which is the container the judge expects for our method.
The method shortestPalindrome takes the string s and returns the shortest palindrome built by adding characters only to its front.
We build t by joining s, a separator hash, and the reverse of s, so matches cannot run past the separator.
We create the lps array of zeros, one slot per character of t, to hold prefix function values.
We loop i from one through the end of t, since the first position always has a value of zero.
We start k as the previous lps value, the length of the border we are currently trying to extend.
While k is nonzero and the current character fails to match the one at position k, we need to fall back.
We fall back by setting k to the lps value just before k, which is the next shorter border.
If the current character now matches the character at position k, the border can be extended.
So we increase k by one to record the longer matching prefix.
We store k into lps at position i as the longest border ending there.
The last lps value is the length of the longest palindromic prefix, so we reverse s, take the leftover characters, and put them in front of s.

shortest-unsorted-continuous-subarray.hook: Sorting the whole array tells you the answer, but two linear sweeps tell you faster.
shortest-unsorted-continuous-subarray.ask: Find the shortest contiguous slice of the array that, once sorted on its own, leaves the entire array sorted. Return that slice's length, or zero if the array is already sorted.
shortest-unsorted-continuous-subarray.exampleWhy: Sorting 6, 4, 8, 10, 9 gives 4, 6, 8, 9, 10, and then the whole array is in order.

brute.idea: Every pair that is out of order must sit inside the slice. Check all pairs and stretch the bounds to cover each inversion.
steps: For each pair i < j
If nums[j] < nums[i], they must be sorted
Widen left to i and right to j
Length is right - left + 1
brute.whySlow: Ten thousand numbers means about fifty million pair checks just to find two indices.

optimal.insight: A position is out of place on the right if something bigger came before it, and on the left if something smaller comes after it.
steps: Sweep left to right keeping the running max
Any value below that max marks the end
Sweep right to left keeping the running min
Any value above that min marks the start
Answer is end - start + 1

codeNotes.note: Largest value seen from the left
Smallest value seen from the right

pitfalls: The slice is not just the first and last inversion; values inside can push bounds outward.
Start and end must default so a sorted array returns zero.

say.intro: Okay, so this one's Shortest Unsorted Continuous Subarray. We want the smallest window that, once sorted, makes the whole array sorted. Take two, six, four, eight, ten, nine, fifteen. The mess runs from six to nine. Sort just those five numbers and everything lines up. So the answer is five.
say.brute: The first idea is to check every pair. If a later number is smaller than an earlier one, that pair is out of order. Both of them have to live inside the window. So we stretch the left bound and the right bound to cover them. It's correct. But what's the catch? Every pair means quadratic work, about fifty million checks for ten thousand numbers.
say.insight: Here's the thing. When is a number out of place? When something bigger shows up before it, or something smaller shows up after it. So sweep from the left with a running maximum. The last number that falls below it marks the right end. Then sweep from the right with a running minimum. The last number above it marks the left end.
say.anim: We start with the array two, six, four, eight, ten, nine, fifteen, tracking start and end. At index one hi becomes six, and from the right lo is nine at index five, nothing flagged yet. At index two four is less than hi six, so end updates to two, marking a misplaced value. Scanning from the right, nine exceeds lo four, so start updates to four. Hi grows to ten at index four, while lo drops to four from the right side. At index five nine is less than hi ten, pushing end forward to five. On the right, six exceeds lo two, so start moves back to one, widening the unsorted range. Finally end minus start plus one gives five, the length of the shortest unsorted subarray.
say.code: Start is zero and end is minus one. Why? So an already sorted array gives zero. One loop does both sweeps. Index i walks forward, updating the max. If a value is smaller than that max, it's misplaced, so mark end. Index j mirrors it from the back, tracking the min. Anything bigger than that min marks start. Return end minus start plus one.
say.outro: Linear time, constant space. The pattern is two pointers. Sweep in from both ends, and let each side remember the best value it's seen.

shortest-unsorted-continuous-subarray.title: Shortest Unsorted Continuous Subarray
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container LeetCode expects for the method that follows.
This method takes the list nums and returns an integer, the length of the shortest slice that must be sorted.
We store the length of nums in n so we can use it for the loop and for indexing from the right.
We set start to zero and end to negative one, so that an already sorted array gives a length of zero.
We set hi to the first element as the running maximum from the left, and lo to the last element as the running minimum from the right.
We loop i from zero to n minus one, scanning from the left and from the right at the same time.
We update hi to the largest value seen so far from the left, including the current element.
If the current element is smaller than hi, something bigger came before it, so it is out of place.
In that case we move end to i, since the last such position marks the right edge of the slice.
We compute j as the mirror position of i, walking from the right end toward the left.
We update lo to the smallest value seen so far from the right, including the element at j.
If the element at j is bigger than lo, something smaller comes after it, so it is out of place.
Then we move start to j, since the leftmost such position marks the left edge of the slice.
We return end minus start plus one, which is the slice length, or zero when nothing was out of place.

smallest-string-starting-from-leaf.hook: Picking the smaller child at every step looks right, and is wrong. Try every leaf instead.
smallest-string-starting-from-leaf.ask: Each tree node holds a letter, zero for a up to twenty five for z. Read each path from a leaf up to the root as a word, and return the alphabetically smallest such word.
smallest-string-starting-from-leaf.exampleWhy: The leaf a climbs to d then z, giving adz, which beats bbz, dbz and cdz.

brute.idea: Collect every leaf-to-root string into a list, then take the minimum of the list.
steps: DFS, pushing each letter on a path
At a leaf, store the reversed path
Pop on the way back
Return the smallest stored string
brute.whySlow: Same time, but it keeps every candidate string alive at once: thousands of leaves times the height in memory.

optimal.insight: Build each word from the leaf end by prepending letters on the way down, and keep only the best word seen so far.
steps: DFS from the root carrying the current word
Prepend this node's letter
At a leaf, compare with the best so far
Recurse into both children

codeNotes.note: Prepend: word reads leaf to root

codeNotes.match: if not node.left and not node.right:
if best is None or word < best:
codeNotes.note: Keep the smallest word so far

pitfalls: Choosing the smaller child greedily fails: the suffix above can change which word wins.
Only leaves count; a node with one child is not an end point.

say.intro: Okay, so this is Smallest String Starting From Leaf. Every node holds a letter. Read upward from any leaf to the root, and you get a word. We want the alphabetically smallest one. In our tree, the root is z. The leaf a climbs through d to z, spelling a d z. That beats every other leaf.
say.brute: The simple approach just collects everything. Walk the tree depth first, pushing letters onto a path. At each leaf, reverse the path and save the word. When the walk ends, return the smallest one. It works. But think about the memory. We're holding every candidate word at once, roughly the number of leaves times the height.
say.insight: Here's the thing. We never need more than the current best word. So build the word as we go down, putting each new letter in front. That way it already reads from leaf to root. At a leaf, compare it with the best and keep the smaller. Now, why not just pick the smaller child greedily? Because letters higher up can flip the comparison.
say.anim: We start at the root with value twenty five, which becomes letter z, and best is still empty. Going left into node one, word becomes bz, then down again to another one, making bbz. This is a leaf, so bbz becomes our first best candidate since none exists yet. Backtracking up, we explore the right child three, forming leaf word dbz, which is not smaller than bbz. Now we try the root's right branch, going through three to get dz, then down to zero giving adz. Adz is smaller than bbz, so best updates to adz. Checking the last leaf two gives cdz, which is bigger than adz, so best stays unchanged. After exploring all paths, the function returns adz as the smallest string from any leaf.
say.code: Best starts empty, since we haven't seen a leaf word yet. The helper takes a node and the word so far. A missing node just returns. Otherwise, we put this node's letter in front, so the word reads leaf to root. Only a leaf ends a word. There, we keep the word if it beats best. If it's not a leaf, we explore both subtrees. Finally, return best.
say.outro: Time is n times the height, from building strings, with height-sized extra space. The pattern is trees. Depth first search, carrying state down each path.

smallest-string-starting-from-leaf.title: Smallest String Starting From Leaf
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container for the method that solves this problem.
The method smallestFromLeaf takes the root of the tree and returns the smallest leaf to root word as a string.
We start best as none, meaning no complete word has been found yet.
We define a helper function dfs that walks the tree carrying the word built so far.
We declare best as nonlocal so the helper can update the outer variable instead of making a new one.
If the current node is empty, there is nothing to process on this branch.
So we simply return and let the caller continue with other branches.
We convert the node value to a letter and put it in front of word, so the word reads leaf to root.
A node with no left and no right child is a leaf, so word is now a complete path.
If no best exists yet or this word is alphabetically smaller, it becomes a new candidate.
We then record this word as the new best.
We return because a leaf has no children to explore.
For an internal node, we recurse into the left child, passing the word built so far.
We do the same for the right child, so every root to leaf path gets checked.
We start the search from the root with an empty word.
Finally we return best, which holds the smallest word found among all leaves.

sort-list.hook: No random access means no quicksort tricks. Merge sort was born for linked lists.
sort-list.ask: Given the head of a singly linked list, return the list sorted in ascending order, ideally in n log n time.
sort-list.exampleWhy: Relinking the five nodes by value gives minus one, zero, three, four, five.

brute.idea: Insertion sort: take nodes one by one and walk a sorted list to find where each belongs.
steps: Keep a dummy head for the sorted list
Detach the next node from the input
Walk sorted list to its spot
Splice it in
brute.whySlow: Each insert may walk the whole sorted part: fifty thousand nodes means over a billion steps.

optimal.insight: Splitting at the middle and merging two sorted lists both need only sequential access, so merge sort fits lists perfectly.
steps: Find the middle with slow and fast pointers
Cut the list in two
Sort each half recursively
Merge the halves by relinking nodes

codeNotes.match: if not head or not head.next:
codeNotes.note: Zero or one node is sorted
Fast starts ahead: slow stops left of middle

pitfalls: Starting fast at head on two nodes never splits, causing infinite recursion.
Recursion uses log n stack; bottom-up merge sort reaches true O(1) space.
