say.intro: Okay, so this is Sort List. We get the head of a linked list, and we need to return it sorted. Our list is minus one, five, three, four, zero. After sorting, the nodes get relinked as minus one, zero, three, four, five. Notice we're moving nodes, not just swapping values.
say.brute: The natural first try is insertion sort. Keep a sorted list behind a dummy head. Take each node from the input. Walk the sorted list until you hit the first bigger value, and splice the node in there. It uses no extra memory, which is nice. But each insertion might walk the whole sorted part. So it's n squared.
say.insight: Here's the thing. Linked lists have no random access. So quicksort and heapsort get awkward. But merge sort only needs two things. Splitting at the middle, which slow and fast pointers handle. And merging two sorted lists, which is one simple walk. Both are sequential. So we get n log n time without any arrays.
say.anim: We start with the list negative one, five, three, four, zero, finding its middle to split it. Each half keeps splitting recursively until lists shrink down to single nodes like five and three. Single node lists are already sorted, so they return immediately as base cases. Now we merge small sorted pieces back together, comparing values like negative one and five. Merging continues upward, combining negative one, three, five into one sorted sublist. On the other branch, zero and four merge into the sorted pair zero, four. The two sorted halves merge together, comparing values step by step to build the final order. The fully sorted list is negative one, zero, three, four, five, our final answer.
say.code: Zero or one node? Already sorted, so return it. Next, slow starts at head and fast starts one step ahead. Why? So slow stops just left of the middle. We cut the list after slow. Then we sort each half recursively. To merge, we use a dummy and a tail, always taking the smaller head. Finally, we attach whatever run is left over.
say.outro: N log n time, with only the recursion stack for space. The pattern is linked lists. Find the middle with slow and fast pointers, then merge.

sort-list.title: Sort List
lineNotes: We define the Solution class that holds our sorting method for the linked list problem.
The sortList method takes the head of a linked list and returns the head of the sorted list.
Base case: if the list is empty or has only one node, it is already sorted.
So we simply return head unchanged, which stops the recursion.
We start slow at head and fast one step ahead, so the middle search lands on the first half's end.
We loop while fast and the node after it exist, so fast can safely jump two nodes.
Each pass moves slow one step and fast two steps, so slow ends at the middle when fast finishes.
We save the second half's start as mid, then cut the list by setting slow's next to nothing.
We recursively sort both halves, getting sorted lists called left and right.
We create a dummy node and a tail pointer to build the merged list without special-casing the head.
We loop merging as long as both left and right still have nodes.
We compare the current values, taking the smaller from left when left is strictly smaller.
We attach the left node to tail and advance left to its next node.
Otherwise the right value is smaller or equal, so we take from right.
We attach the right node to tail and advance right to its next node.
After attaching either node, we move tail forward to the newly appended node.
One list ran out, so we attach whichever remainder is left, since it is already sorted.
We return the node after dummy, which is the head of the fully merged sorted list.

squares-of-a-sorted-array.hook: Negative numbers scramble the order after squaring, but the biggest square always sits at an end.
squares-of-a-sorted-array.ask: Given a sorted array that may contain negatives, return the squares of every number, also in sorted order.

brute.idea: Square every number, then sort the result.
steps: Square each value
Sort the squared list
Return it
brute.whySlow: Sorting throws away the fact that the input is already sorted, paying an extra log n factor.

optimal.insight: The largest square comes from whichever end has the larger absolute value, so fill the answer from the back.
steps: Pointers at both ends
Compare absolute values
Write the bigger square at the back
Move that pointer inward

pitfalls: Filling from the front fails: the smallest square hides in the middle.
Compare absolute values, not raw values.

say.intro: Okay, so this is Squares of a Sorted Array. The input is sorted, but it can have negatives. And squaring negatives breaks the order. Minus four, minus one, zero, three, ten become sixteen, one, zero, nine, one hundred. We need them sorted: zero, one, nine, sixteen, one hundred.
say.brute: The obvious move is to square everything and then sort. It's short, it's correct, and lots of people stop there. So what's wrong with it? Sorting costs n log n. And it ignores the most useful fact we were handed. The input was already sorted. The follow up even asks for linear time.
say.insight: Think about it this way. Where can the biggest square come from? Either the most negative number on the left end, or the largest number on the right end. Nothing in the middle can beat both ends. So put a pointer on each end. Take whichever has the bigger absolute value. Write its square into the last open slot.
say.anim: We start with the array negative four, negative one, zero, three, ten, and an empty result. Pointers l and r begin at the two ends, comparing absolute values to find the largest square. Ten has the bigger absolute value, so its square, one hundred, fills the last slot. Now negative four beats three, so sixteen fills the next spot from the right. Comparing negative one and zero, zero wins, placing nine in the middle position. Negative one is now largest, so one fills the next slot from the right. Only zero remains, so its square, zero, fills the first position. The function returns the fully sorted squares: zero, one, nine, sixteen, and one hundred.
say.code: We make a result array of the same length, and fill it from the back. Left starts at zero, right at the end. Those are the two extremes. We loop i from the last index down. If the left value has the bigger magnitude, its square wins this slot, and left moves in. Otherwise the right square wins, and right moves in. Return the result.
say.outro: Linear time, with only the output array. The pattern is two pointers. When the extremes hold the answer, squeeze in from both ends.

squares-of-a-sorted-array.title: Squares of a Sorted Array
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container the problem expects for our method.
The method sortedSquares takes the sorted list nums and will return a sorted list of squares.
We store the length of nums in n so we can reuse it for sizing and looping.
We create a result list of n zeros, to be filled in from the back.
We set left to zero and right to the last index, so two pointers start at both ends.
We loop i from the last index down to zero, filling the largest remaining square first.
If the absolute value at left beats the one at right, the left end holds the biggest square.
We square the left value and place it at position i in the result.
We move the left pointer one step inward, since that value has been used.
Otherwise the right end has an absolute value at least as large, so it supplies the square.
We square the right value and place it at position i in the result.
We move the right pointer one step inward, since that value has been used.
After every slot is filled, we return the result, which is sorted in ascending order.

string-matching-in-an-array.hook: Glue every word into one long string, and substrings reveal themselves by showing up twice.
string-matching-in-an-array.ask: Given a list of distinct lowercase words, return every word that appears inside some other word in the list. Any order is fine.
string-matching-in-an-array.exampleWhy: as sits inside mass, and hero sits inside superhero. The other two words are not inside anything.

brute.idea: For each word, check it against every other word with a substring search.
steps: Pick word i
Search inside every other word j
Found? record it and stop
brute.whySlow: Every ordered pair gets its own search: 100 words is 9,900 separate scans that restart from scratch.

optimal.insight: Join all words with a separator. A word is inside another exactly when it occurs at least twice in the joined text.
steps: Join words with a space
For each word, find its first occurrence
Find its last occurrence
Different positions means it is a substring

codeNotes.note: Two occurrences: it lives elsewhere too

pitfalls: Without a separator, a match could span two neighbouring words.
Words are distinct, so a second occurrence must be inside another word.

say.intro: Okay, so this is String Matching in an Array. We get a list of different words. We return every word that shows up inside another one. With mass, as, hero and superhero, the word as hides in mass. And hero hides in superhero. So we return as and hero.
say.brute: The straightforward way checks every ordered pair. For each word, search for it inside every other word. If it turns up, record it and move on. That's correct. But each pair is its own separate search. With a hundred words, that's nearly ten thousand scans.
say.insight: Here's a neat trick. Join all the words into one long text, with a space between each. Every word shows up in that text at least once, as itself. When does it show up twice? Only if it also lives inside another word. So compare the first and last spots where it appears. If they differ, it's a substring.
say.anim: We start with the words mass, as, hero, and superhero. All words are joined into one text string separated by spaces. For mass, its first and last positions match, so it is not a substring. For as, the first and last find positions differ, meaning it appears twice. So as gets added to the result list. For hero, it also appears twice inside superhero, so it is added too. For superhero, it only appears once, so it is skipped. The final answer returned is as and hero.
say.code: First, we join the words with spaces. Why the space? It stops a match from crossing two words. Then we do one search per word. We compare text dot find, the first position, with text dot r find, the last. If they're different, the word occurs twice, so it lives somewhere else too. Append it. Then return the list.
say.outro: Roughly n searches over a text of total length T. The pattern is arrays and hashing with strings. Reshape the input so one simple check answers the question.

string-matching-in-an-array.title: String Matching in an Array
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container the judge expects for our method.
This method takes the list of words and returns the list of words found inside other words.
We join all the words into one text, separated by spaces so matches cannot span two words.
We start an empty result list to collect the words that qualify.
We loop over each word in the original list to test it one at a time.
If the first and last positions of the word in the text differ, it occurs at least twice.
Since a word appears once as itself, a second occurrence means it sits inside another word, so we add it.
Finally we return the collected list of words that are substrings of other words.

string-to-integer-atoi.hook: Not hard, just full of traps: spaces, signs, junk characters and overflow, all in one pass.
string-to-integer-atoi.ask: Convert a string to a 32-bit signed integer: skip leading spaces, read an optional sign, read digits until a non-digit, and clamp the result to the 32-bit range.
string-to-integer-atoi.exampleWhy: Minus 91,283,472,332 is far below the smallest 32-bit value, so it clamps to minus 2,147,483,648.

brute.idea: Strip spaces, read the sign, collect all digits into a string, convert at the end and clamp.
steps: Strip leading spaces
Read optional sign
Collect the digit run
Convert, then clamp
brute.whySlow: Not asymptotically slower: it copies the digits and needs big integers, and in fixed-width languages it overflows.

optimal.insight: Walk one index forward and build the number digit by digit, clamping the moment it leaves the 32-bit range.
steps: Skip spaces
Read the sign
Append digits with num times ten plus d
Clamp as soon as it overflows

codeNotes.match: if i < n and s[i] in "+-":

codeNotes.note: Stopped at a non-digit or the end

pitfalls: A sign after digits, like 0-1, ends parsing: the answer is 0.
Check overflow inside the loop, not after, in fixed-width languages.

say.intro: Okay, so this is String to Integer, or a to i. We turn text into a thirty two bit number. Skip spaces, read an optional sign, then read digits. And clamp to the thirty two bit range. Our input is about minus ninety one billion. Way too small. So we return the minimum, about minus two point one billion.
say.brute: A simple version strips spaces, reads the sign, and gathers all the digits into a separate string. Then it converts at the end and clamps. Honestly, that's still linear time. So what's the problem? It copies the digits, and it leans on huge integers. Most languages don't have those. The overflow would already have happened.
say.insight: Here's the thing. We can do it all in one forward walk with a single index. Build the number one digit at a time. Multiply by ten, add the new digit. After each digit, check if the signed value has left the thirty two bit range. The moment it does, return the limit. We never hold a huge number.
say.anim: We start with the string and set INT_MAX and INT_MIN as our clamp bounds. The index skips leading spaces, moving from index zero to index two. A minus sign is found, setting sign to negative one and advancing the index. Digit parsing begins, building num one digit at a time starting from zero. Num grows steadily, becoming ninety one, then nine twelve, then nine thousand one twenty eight. Num keeps climbing through nine million range values as each digit is appended. Num reaches 9128347233, and sign times num drops below INT_MIN, triggering a clamp. The function returns INT_MIN, giving the final clamped answer of negative 2147483648.
say.code: We set the two limits first. Then we skip leading spaces, and only spaces. Next, we allow at most one sign. If we see plus or minus, record it and step past. Then, while we see digits, multiply by ten and append the digit. The moment sign times num overflows, we clamp and return the limit. When we hit a non-digit or the end, return sign times num.
say.outro: Linear time, constant space. The pattern is math. Parse a number digit by digit, and guard against overflow as you go.

string-to-integer-atoi.title: String to Integer (atoi)
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container that the interview platform expects for our method.
The method myAtoi takes the input string s and returns a plain integer.
We store the 32-bit limits, the maximum as two to the 31 minus one and the minimum as negative two to the 31.
We set the index i to zero and record n as the length of the string.
This loop keeps going while we are inside the string and the current character is a space.
Each time we see a space, we move the index forward to skip it.
We default the sign to positive one, in case no sign character appears.
If a character remains and it is a plus or minus, we know a sign was given.
We set sign to negative one for a minus and positive one for a plus.
We advance the index past the sign character so the next step starts at the digits.
We start the running number at zero before reading any digits.
We loop while characters remain and the current one is a digit, stopping at the first non-digit.
We shift the number left one decimal place and add the new digit.
If the signed value exceeds the maximum, we immediately return the maximum to clamp the overflow.
Returning early here means we never keep building a huge number.
If the signed value drops below the minimum, we immediately return the minimum instead.
Again we stop right away, because any further digits could only push it further out of range.
If the value is still in range, we move to the next character.
When the digits end, we return the number multiplied by its sign as the final answer.

swap-adjacent-in-lr-string.hook: L can only drift left, R only right, and they can never pass each other. That is the whole problem.
swap-adjacent-in-lr-string.ask: A move replaces XL with LX, or RX with XR. Given strings start and result made of L, R and X, decide whether some sequence of moves turns start into result.
swap-adjacent-in-lr-string.exampleWhy: Ignoring X, both read R L R. The first R slides right, L slides left, the last R slides right.

brute.idea: Treat every string as a state and breadth-first search over all legal moves until we reach result.
steps: Start a queue with start
Apply every XL or RX swap
Enqueue unseen strings
Reached result? true
brute.whySlow: The number of reachable strings explodes; a length 10,000 string has astronomically many arrangements.

optimal.insight: X is empty space. Letters keep their relative order, each L can only move left, each R only right.
steps: Skip X in both strings
Next letters must match
An L must not be left of its target
An R must not be right of its target
Both must run out together

codeNotes.note: Both must run out of letters together
Letters can never pass each other

pitfalls: Matching letter order alone is not enough; direction of movement matters too.
Check that both strings run out of letters at the same time.

say.intro: So, Swap Adjacent in L R String. One move turns X L into L X, or R X into X R. So L slides left and R slides right. Can moves turn start into result? From R X X L R X to X R L X X R, yes. Each R slides right, and the L slides left.
say.brute: The brute force treats each string as a state. Run breadth first search from start, try every legal swap, and remember strings we've already seen. If result ever comes out of the queue, return true. It's honest and correct. But here's the catch. The number of reachable strings grows exponentially with the length.
say.insight: Think of X as empty space. An L only moves left. An R only moves right. And since they only swap with X, letters can never jump over each other. So drop the Xs, and the letter sequences must match exactly. Then check each matching pair. An L can't end up to the right. An R can't end up to the left.
say.anim: We start comparing start RXXLRX and result XRLXXR, skipping X placeholders as we go. Result's leading X is skipped, landing j at 1, pointing to R, matching start's R at 0. Since it's an R and i isn't greater than j, we advance both pointers together. Start skips its X characters, moving i to 3 where an L sits. Result's L at position 2 matches, and since i equals j, the L move is valid. Start's R at index 4 compares against result, skipping more X's until j reaches 5. Both show R, and i is less than j, so the right move is allowed. Both pointers reach the end at position 6, so the function returns true, confirming transformation.
say.code: We keep i in start and j in result. Each round, skip Xs on both sides, since X is just empty space. If either string ran out, both must run out together, so return that check. If the letters differ, they'd have to pass each other, so return false. An L with i less than j would move right. An R with i greater than j would move left. Both mean false. Otherwise, advance both.
say.outro: Linear time, constant space. The pattern is two pointers. Walk two sequences in step, and compare only the pieces that matter.

swap-adjacent-in-lr-string.title: Swap Adjacent in LR String
lineNotes: We define a Solution class that holds the method for this problem.
The method canTransform takes the start and result strings and returns whether start can become result.
We store the common length of the strings in n, since both must have equal length.
We set both pointers i and j to zero, one for start and one for result.
We loop while either pointer still has characters left to examine.
We move i forward past every X in start, since X is just empty space.
Each step of this inner loop advances i by one over an X.
We likewise move j forward past every X in result to find its next letter.
Each step here advances j by one over an X in result.
If either pointer has run off the end, we need to check whether both did.
We return true only if both ran out together, meaning the letter counts matched.
If the next letters differ, the order of letters cannot match, so the answer is false.
We return false because letters can never pass through each other.
An L can only move left, so if its position in start is left of its target, it fails.
We return false because that L would need to move right, which is impossible.
An R can only move right, so if its start position is right of its target, it fails.
We return false because that R would need to move left, which is impossible.
This pair of letters is valid, so we advance i to look at the next letter in start.
We advance j as well to compare the next letter in result.
If every letter pair checked out, we return true since the transformation is possible.

swap-nodes-in-pairs.hook: Three pointer moves per pair, plus a dummy node, and the head case disappears.
swap-nodes-in-pairs.ask: Swap every two adjacent nodes in a linked list and return the new head. Change the links, not the values. A final odd node stays in place.
swap-nodes-in-pairs.exampleWhy: Pairs 1,2 and 3,4 swap; 5 has no partner and stays at the end.

brute.idea: Copy every node into an array, swap neighbours in the array, then relink the nodes in array order.
steps: Collect nodes into a list
Swap entries 0 and 1, 2 and 3
Relink nodes in order
End the last node
brute.whySlow: Same linear time, but it spends an extra array of n references that pointer rewiring avoids.

optimal.insight: A dummy before the head makes every pair look the same: prev, a, b. Three link changes swap them.
steps: Put a dummy before head
Name the pair a and b after prev
a points past b; b points to a
prev points to b, then prev becomes a

swap-nodes-in-pairs.optimalCode:
class Solution:
    def swapPairs(self, head: Optional[ListNode]) -> Optional[ListNode]:
        dummy = ListNode(0, head)
        prev = dummy
        while prev.next and prev.next.next:
            a, b = prev.next, prev.next.next
            a.next = b.next
            b.next = a
            prev.next = b
            prev = a
        return dummy.next

codeNotes.note: Head pair handled like any other
Stop when fewer than two remain
First node skips to next pair
a is now the pair's tail

pitfalls: Order matters: set a.next before b.next, or you lose the rest of the list.
Return dummy.next, not head; head has moved to second place.

say.intro: Okay, so this is Swap Nodes in Pairs. We walk a linked list and swap each two neighbours. And we move nodes, not values. One, two, three, four, five becomes two, one, four, three, five. Five has no partner, so it just stays at the end.
say.brute: A simple approach copies every node into an array. Swap entries zero and one, two and three, and so on. Then relink the nodes in array order, and cut the last link. It's linear time. So what's wrong? It spends a whole extra array. Careful pointer rewiring doesn't need one.
say.insight: Here's the trick. Put a dummy node in front of the head. Now every pair looks the same. A previous node, then a, then b. Three link changes do the swap. A points past b. B points back to a. And previous points to b. Now a is second, so it becomes the previous node for the next pair.
say.anim: We start with the list one through five, and add a dummy node before the head. Prev begins at dummy, checking that two more nodes exist ahead for swapping. A is node one and b is node two, the first pair to swap. A's next jumps to b's next, pointing one ahead to node three. B's next is set to a, so two now points back to one. Prev's next becomes b, linking dummy's chain through two then one. Prev moves to a, now pointing at one, ready for the next pair, three and four. After swapping three and four similarly, the final list reads two one four three five.
say.code: We make a dummy pointing at head, so the head pair is handled like any other. Previous starts at the dummy. We stop when fewer than two nodes remain. Otherwise, call them a and b. First, a skips ahead to the next pair. Then b points back to a, and previous points to b. So b now leads. A is now the pair's tail, so previous moves to a. Return the dummy's next.
say.outro: Linear time, constant space. The pattern is linked lists. A dummy head plus careful pointer order turns edge cases into the normal case.

swap-nodes-in-pairs.title: Swap Nodes in Pairs
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which holds the method that the problem asks us to write.
The swapPairs method takes the head of a linked list and returns the head of the list after swapping pairs.
We create a dummy node with value zero pointing at head, so the first pair needs no special handling.
We set prev to the dummy, so prev always sits just before the next pair to swap.
We loop only while two nodes remain after prev, so a final odd node is left alone.
We name the pair: a is the first node after prev, and b is the one right after it.
We point a to whatever follows b, so the rest of the list stays attached after the swap.
We point b back to a, which puts the two nodes in swapped order.
We point prev to b, so the previous part of the list now connects to the swapped pair.
We move prev to a, which is now the tail of the swapped pair, ready for the next pair.
We return the dummy's next node, which is the true head of the list after all swaps.

symmetric-tree.hook: A tree is symmetric when its left side is the mirror image of its right side.
symmetric-tree.ask: Given the root of a binary tree, return true if the tree is a mirror image of itself around its centre line, and false otherwise.
symmetric-tree.exampleWhy: Both children are 2; the outer grandchildren are 3 and 3, the inner ones 4 and 4.

brute.idea: Go level by level. Write down every level's values, including gaps, and check that each level reads the same backwards.
steps: Start with the root level
Record values, None for gaps
Not a palindrome? false
Build the next level
brute.whySlow: Same linear time, but it stores entire levels, up to half the tree, where recursion needs only the height.

optimal.insight: Two subtrees are mirrors when their roots match, left of one mirrors right of the other, and right mirrors left.
steps: Compare the root's left and right children
Both empty: mirror
One empty or values differ: not a mirror
Recurse outer pair and inner pair

codeNotes.match: if not a and not b:
if not a or not b or a.val != b.val:
return mirror(a.left, b.right) and mirror(a.right, b.left)

pitfalls: Comparing a.left with b.left checks equality, not mirroring.
Values alone are not enough; gaps must be mirrored too.

say.intro: Okay, so this is Symmetric Tree. Is a binary tree a mirror image of itself? In our tree, the root is one, with two and two below it. The outer grandchildren are three and three. The inner ones are four and four. Fold it down the middle and everything lines up. So the answer is true.
say.brute: One approach goes level by level. Write down every value on a level, including empty spots. Then check that the list reads the same forwards and backwards. Build the next level and repeat. That's linear time. But what does it cost in memory? A whole level at once. In a wide tree, that's half of all the nodes.
say.insight: Here's the thing. Mirroring is a relationship between two subtrees. When are two trees mirrors? When their roots match. And the left child of one mirrors the right child of the other. And the right of one mirrors the left of the other. So write a helper that takes two nodes at once, pairing outer with outer and inner with inner.
say.anim: We start comparing the tree's left and right subtrees, rooted at value one. Nodes two and two match, so we recurse deeper to check their children mirror correctly. Now comparing three and three, values match, so we dive into their children next. Both children are empty here, so this branch returns true immediately. The three and three branch confirms symmetry, returning true back up the call chain. Next we compare four and four, matching values, then check their empty children too. Four and four mirror successfully, confirming that whole branch is symmetric. All branches matched perfectly, so the tree is symmetric, and the final answer is true.
say.code: The helper, mirror, takes nodes a and b. If both are empty, two gaps mirror each other, so that's a match. If only one is empty, or the values differ, it's a shape or value mismatch. Return false. Otherwise, check the outer pair, a's left with b's right. Then the inner pair, a's right with b's left. Finally, compare the root's two halves.
say.outro: Linear time, height-sized stack space. The pattern is trees. When the question compares two subtrees, recurse on two nodes at once.

symmetric-tree.title: Symmetric Tree
lineNotes: We define a Solution class that holds the method for checking whether a binary tree is symmetric.
The isSymmetric method takes the root of the tree and returns true or false.
We define a helper called mirror that checks whether two subtrees, a and b, are mirror images of each other.
If both a and b are empty, there is nothing to compare, so the two sides match.
In that case we return true, since two missing nodes are trivially mirrors of each other.
If only one is empty, or the values differ, the two subtrees cannot be mirrors.
So we return false right away, because the shape or value mismatch breaks the symmetry.
Otherwise we recurse, pairing the outer children together and the inner children together, and both pairs must be mirrors.
We start by comparing the left subtree of the root against the right subtree of the root.

unique-number-of-occurrences.hook: Count the values, then check that no two counts collide. Two hash structures, one pass each.
unique-number-of-occurrences.ask: Given an array of integers, return true if every distinct value appears a different number of times, and false if two values share the same count.
unique-number-of-occurrences.exampleWhy: 1 appears three times, 2 twice and 3 once. The counts 3, 2 and 1 are all different.

brute.idea: For each distinct value, count it by scanning the array, then compare every pair of counts.
steps: Skip values seen earlier
Count the value with a full scan
Compare every pair of counts
Equal pair? false
brute.whySlow: Each count rescans the array: a thousand distinct values means a million element checks.

optimal.insight: A hash map counts every value in one pass, and a hash set spots a repeated count instantly.
steps: Count each value in a map
Walk the counts
Count already in the set? false
Otherwise add it

pitfalls: Compare counts, not values; the values are already distinct as map keys.
A one-liner works too: len(set(counts)) == len(counts).

say.intro: Okay, so this is Unique Number of Occurrences. We count how often each value appears. Then we return true only if no two values share a count. In one, two, two, one, one, three, one shows up three times. Two shows up twice. Three just once. All different, so true.
say.brute: The brute force counts each distinct value by rescanning the whole array. Then it compares every pair of counts, looking for a match. It's correct. But every count is another full scan. So with lots of distinct values, it grows quadratically. Around a million checks for a thousand values.
say.insight: Here's the thing. Two hash structures do it in linear time. A hash map counts every value in one pass. After that, we only care about the counts themselves. So walk them, and keep a set of counts we've seen. Hit a count that's already in the set? Then two values collide, and the answer is false.
say.anim: We start with the array one, two, two, one, one, three and an empty count map. We loop through each number, building up counts of how many times it appears. After processing, counts show one appears three times and two appears twice. Final counts are one maps to three, two maps to two, three maps to one. Now we check each count value against a seen set to catch duplicates. Count three is new, so we add it to seen, which becomes three. Count two is also new, so seen grows to two and three. Count one is unique too, so seen becomes one, two, three, and we return true.
say.code: We start with an empty dictionary and tally each value. Then we look only at the counts. We make an empty set and loop over the dictionary's values. If a count is already in the set, two values share it. Return false. Otherwise, add it. If the loop finishes, every count was unique. Return true.
say.outro: Linear time and space. The pattern is arrays and hashing. Count with a map, then catch duplicates with a set.

unique-number-of-occurrences.title: Unique Number of Occurrences
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container the problem expects for our method.
This method takes the array and returns true or false depending on whether all occurrence counts are different.
We start with an empty dictionary called count that will map each value to how many times it appears.
We loop through every number x in the array so each element gets counted exactly once.
For each x we read its current count, defaulting to zero, add one, and store it back.
We create an empty set called seen to remember which occurrence counts we have already encountered.
Now we loop over the counts themselves, one for each distinct value in the array.
We check whether this count is already in seen, since that would mean two values share a count.
If the count was already seen, we return false immediately because the occurrences are not unique.
Otherwise we add this count to seen so any later duplicate count will be caught.
If the loop finishes without finding a repeated count, we return true because all counts are distinct.

zero-array-transformation-i.hook: Every query can hit each index at most once, so all that matters is how many queries cover it.
zero-array-transformation-i.ask: Each query lets you subtract one from any chosen indices in a range. After all queries, can every number reach zero? That works exactly when each index is covered at least as many times as its value.
zero-array-transformation-i.exampleWhy: Coverage is 1, 2, 3, 2, which meets or beats every value 1, 2, 3, 1.

brute.idea: For each query, walk its range and add one to a coverage counter at every index. Then compare with nums.
steps: Coverage array of zeros
For each query, add 1 across its range
Any value above its coverage? false
brute.whySlow: A hundred thousand full-length queries means ten billion increments.

optimal.insight: A difference array adds one to a whole range in constant time: plus one at the start, minus one after the end.
steps: diff[l] += 1, diff[r + 1] -= 1
Running sum of diff is coverage
Value above coverage? false
Otherwise true

pitfalls: Size the difference array n + 1 so r + 1 never overflows.
Each query decrements an index at most once, so coverage, not order, decides.

say.intro: Okay, so this is Zero Array Transformation One. Each query picks a range, and we can subtract one from any indices inside it. So an index can drop by at most the number of queries covering it. Here, coverage is one, two, three, two. That's enough for one, two, three, one. So true.
say.brute: The brute force builds coverage directly. Start a counter array of zeros. For every query, walk from its left end to its right end, adding one at each index. Then check every value against its coverage. Simple, right? But with a hundred thousand long queries, that's billions of increments.
say.insight: Here's the thing. Adding one across a whole range can take constant time with a difference array. Put plus one at the left end. Put minus one just past the right end. Later, a running sum turns those markers back into the true coverage of every index. All in one pass.
say.anim: We start with nums one two three one and three range queries to apply. A difference array of zeros is created, one longer than nums, to track range updates. For query zero to three, we add one at index zero and subtract one after index three. For query one to two, we add one at index one and subtract one after index two. For query two to three, we add one at index two and subtract one after index three. Now we sweep through, accumulating cover and comparing it against each value in nums. At each index, cover climbs to one, two, three, then two, always meeting or exceeding nums. Since no value ever exceeds its cover, the function returns true as expected.
say.code: We make a difference array one slot longer than nums. Why one extra? So r plus one always has a home. For each query, coverage starts at l, so add one there. It stops after r, so subtract one at r plus one. Then we keep a running sum, which gives the coverage. If a number is bigger than its coverage, not enough queries reach it. Return false. Otherwise, true.
say.outro: Linear in the array plus the queries. The pattern is prefix sums. A difference array applies lots of range updates cheaply.

zero-array-transformation-i.title: Zero Array Transformation I
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container the problem expects for our method.
The method isZeroArray takes the list nums and the list of queries, and returns whether everything can reach zero.
We store the length of nums in n so we can size our helper array and loop bounds.
We build a difference array of zeros with one extra slot, so the end marker never goes out of range.
We loop over each query, unpacking its left and right ends into l and r.
At the left end we add one to diff, marking where this query's coverage begins.
Just after the right end we subtract one, marking where this query's coverage stops.
We start a running cover count at zero, which will track how many queries cover the current index.
We walk through every index of nums from left to right.
We add the diff value at this index to cover, giving the number of queries covering it.
If the value at this index is larger than its cover, we cannot subtract enough times to reach zero.
In that case we immediately return False, since one failing index makes the whole array impossible.
If every index had enough coverage, we return True.

01-matrix.hook: Do not search outward from every 1. Flood outward from every 0 at the same time.
01-matrix.ask: Given a grid of zeros and ones, return a grid where each cell holds the number of up, down, left or right steps to its nearest zero.
01-matrix.exampleWhy: The bottom middle 1 needs two steps to reach a 0; every other 1 touches a 0 directly.

brute.idea: With no walls, distance is Manhattan distance. For every 1, measure it against every 0 and keep the smallest.
steps: List all zero cells
For each 1, try every zero
Keep the smallest Manhattan distance
brute.whySlow: A grid of ten thousand cells can mean fifty million cell pairs compared.

optimal.insight: Multi-source BFS: start the queue with every zero. Each cell is reached first by its nearest zero.
steps: Mark zeros as distance 0 and enqueue them
Pop a cell, look at four neighbours
Unvisited neighbour gets distance plus one
Enqueue it; each cell is set once

codeNotes.note: Minus one means not reached yet
Every zero is a starting source

pitfalls: BFS from each 1 separately is quadratic; start from all zeros together.
Mark distance when enqueueing, not when popping, to avoid duplicates.

say.intro: Okay, so this is Zero One Matrix. For every cell in a grid of zeros and ones, we want the number of steps to the nearest zero. Moves go up, down, left or right. In our grid, most ones touch a zero. The bottom middle one is two steps away. So it becomes two.
say.brute: Here's a fun fact. With no walls, the distance between two cells is just the row gap plus the column gap. So the brute force lists every zero. Then, for each one, it measures against every zero and keeps the smallest. That's quadratic in the number of cells. Tens of millions of pairs for a big grid.
say.insight: So let's flip the direction. Instead of each one hunting for a zero, let every zero spread outward at the same time. Put all zeros in a breadth first search queue at distance zero. Why does that work? The queue hands out cells in order of distance. So the first time we reach a cell, it's from its nearest zero.
say.anim: We start with the grid, and build a distance matrix filled with minus one everywhere. Scanning every cell, each zero in the input gets distance zero and joins the queue immediately. After scanning, the queue holds all five zero cells, ready to expand outward together. Popping position zero zero, we check its neighbor at row one column zero, already zero. Expanding from row zero column one, the cell below it gets distance one, since it's unvisited. Expanding from row one column zero, cell row two column zero becomes distance one. Finally cell row two column one gets distance two, reached through two neighboring ones. The queue empties and we return the final matrix, with the farthest cell valued two.
say.code: We make a distance grid filled with minus one, meaning not reached yet. Every zero is a starting source. It gets distance zero and joins the queue. Then we pop cells one by one, so nearest cells come out first. For each neighbour inside the grid that's still minus one, set its distance one higher and push it. First visit is the shortest. Return the grid.
say.outro: Linear in the number of cells. The pattern is graphs. Multi-source breadth first search, starting from every target at once.

01-matrix.title: 01 Matrix
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, as the problem platform expects, to hold the method that solves the problem.
The method updateMatrix takes the grid mat and returns a grid of distances to the nearest zero.
We read the number of rows and columns from the grid so we can loop and check bounds later.
We build a distance grid filled with negative one, meaning every cell is not yet visited or reached.
We create an empty double-ended queue that will drive the breadth-first search outward from all zeros.
We loop over every row index in the grid to scan for zeros.
Inside each row we loop over every column index to look at each cell.
We check whether the current cell holds a zero, since zeros are our starting sources.
A zero cell has distance zero to itself, so we record that in the distance grid.
We push that zero cell onto the queue so the search will expand outward from it.
We keep processing while the queue has cells, which spreads distances level by level.
We take the oldest cell off the front of the queue, so closer cells are handled before farther ones.
We try the four neighbors: down, up, right, and left, using row and column offsets.
We compute the neighbor's row and column by adding the offset to the current position.
We only continue if the neighbor is inside the grid and has not been given a distance yet.
The neighbor is one step farther than the current cell, and since we reach it first from the nearest zero, this is final.
We add the neighbor to the queue so its own neighbors get explored later.
Once the queue empties every cell has its shortest distance, so we return the distance grid.

add-strings.hook: Grade-school addition, right to left with a carry. The trick is doing it without converting to int.
add-strings.ask: Given two non-negative integers written as strings, return their sum as a string, without converting the whole strings to numbers or using big-integer libraries.
add-strings.exampleWhy: 6 plus 7 is 13: write 3, carry 1. 5 plus 7 plus 1 is 13 again. 4 plus 1 is 5.

brute.idea: Same column addition, but build the answer by gluing each new digit onto the front of a string.
steps: Walk both strings from the right
Add digits and carry
Prepend the digit to the answer string
brute.whySlow: Prepending copies the whole answer each time: ten thousand digits means fifty million character copies.
brute.code:
class Solution:
    def addStrings(self, num1: str, num2: str) -> str:
        i, j = len(num1) - 1, len(num2) - 1
        carry = 0
        res = ""
        while i >= 0 or j >= 0 or carry:
            d1 = ord(num1[i]) - ord('0') if i >= 0 else 0
            d2 = ord(num2[j]) - ord('0') if j >= 0 else 0
            carry, digit = divmod(d1 + d2 + carry, 10)
            res = str(digit) + res
            i -= 1
            j -= 1
        return res

optimal.insight: Add column by column from the right with a carry, append digits to a list, and reverse once at the end.
steps: Pointers at the last digit of each string
Missing digit counts as zero
Sum, carry, and append the digit
Reverse and join once

codeNotes.match: while i >= 0 or j >= 0 or carry:
codeNotes.note: Keep going for a final carry

codeNotes.match: d1 = ord(num1[i]) - ord('0') if i >= 0 else 0

pitfalls: Forgetting the final carry turns 99 plus 1 into 00.
int(num1) breaks the rules; convert one character at a time.

say.intro: Okay, so this is Add Strings. Two numbers show up as text. We return their sum as text, without turning the whole strings into integers. Four five six plus seven seven is five three three. We'll do it exactly the way you learned at school.
say.brute: A natural first version walks both strings from the right. Add the two digits and the carry, then glue the new digit onto the front of the answer. The arithmetic is right. So what's the catch? Strings can't grow at the front cheaply. Every prepend copies the whole answer. So the total work becomes n squared.
say.insight: Here's the fix. Keep the column addition, but collect digits in a list, backwards. Appending to a list is constant time. If one number is shorter, its missing digits just count as zero. And the loop keeps going while there's still a carry. At the end, reverse the list once and join it.
say.anim: We start with num1 456 and num2 77, setting pointers i and j to their last digits. At the first column, digits 6 and 7 add together, giving carry 1 and digit 3, appended to res. Next column adds 5 and 7 plus carry 1, producing digit 3 again, res now holds 3 and 3. Now num2 is exhausted, so only digit 4 plus carry 1 is added, giving digit 5 with no carry. The loop ends since both indices are negative and carry is zero. Finally the list of digits gets reversed and joined into the final answer, 533.
say.code: Set i and j to the last index of each string, carry to zero, and an empty list. We keep looping while either pointer is valid, or a final carry remains. Each digit comes from its character code, or zero if that string is used up. Divide the total by ten. The tens become the carry. We append the digit, not prepend. The digits were built backwards, so reverse and join.
say.outro: Linear in the longer number. The pattern is math. Simulate grade school addition with two pointers and a carry.

add-strings.title: Add Strings
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container the problem expects for our method.
The addStrings method takes two digit strings and returns their sum as a string.
We set i and j to the last index of each string so we start at the ones column.
The carry starts at zero because nothing has overflowed from a previous column yet.
We create an empty list res to collect result digits, which is cheaper than building a string repeatedly.
We loop while either string has digits left or a carry remains, so a final carry still produces a digit.
For the first number, we convert the current character to its digit value, or use zero if that string is exhausted.
We do the same for the second number, treating missing digits as zero so unequal lengths work naturally.
We add both digits and the carry, then divmod by ten gives the new carry and the digit to keep.
We convert the digit to a string and append it to res, building the answer from least significant digit.
We move i one position left to reach the next column of the first number.
We move j one position left likewise for the second number.
Since digits were added in reverse order, we reverse res once and join it into the final string.

all-nodes-distance-k-in-binary-tree.hook: Trees only point down, but distance goes up too. Add parent links and it becomes plain BFS.
all-nodes-distance-k-in-binary-tree.ask: Given a binary tree, a target node's value and a number k, return the values of all nodes exactly k edges away from the target, in any order.
all-nodes-distance-k-in-binary-tree.exampleWhy: From 5, two steps down reach 7 and 4; one step up to 3 then down reaches 1.

brute.idea: For every node, compute its distance to the target through their lowest common ancestor using root paths.
steps: Find the root-to-target path
For each node, find its root path
Distance = both lengths minus twice the shared prefix
Keep nodes at distance k
brute.whySlow: Every node triggers a fresh search from the root: 500 nodes means about 250,000 visits.

optimal.insight: Record each node's parent. Then the tree is an undirected graph, and BFS from the target for k levels finds the answer.
steps: DFS once to map every node to its parent
Start BFS at the target
Expand left, right and parent, k times
Whatever is in the queue is the answer

pitfalls: Without a seen set, BFS walks back to where it came from.
Here target arrives as a value; on LeetCode it is the node itself.

say.intro: So, All Nodes Distance K in Binary Tree. Given a target node and a number k, return every node exactly k edges away. Moves up count too. From five, with k of two, we reach seven and four below. And one, by going up to three and back down. So the answer is seven, four, one.
say.brute: The brute force measures each node separately. Find the path from the root to the target. Then, for every node, find its own root path. The shared start is their common ancestors. So the distance is both lengths minus twice that shared part. It works. But each node needs a fresh search, which is n squared.
say.insight: Here's the real problem. Tree edges only point down. So what if every node also knew its parent? Then the tree is just an ordinary undirected graph, with up to three neighbours per node. Now run breadth first search from the target, expanding exactly k rings. A seen set stops us from walking backwards.
say.anim: We start building a parent map by traversing the whole tree with a stack, tracking target five. As we pop each node, we record its parent, linking children back to nodes three, one, and eight. We find node five equals our target, so we save it as the starting node. We continue traversing, recording parents for nodes two, four, and seven as the stack empties. Parent map is complete, so we start breadth first search from node five, marking it seen. From five we explore neighbors six, two, and three, adding each unseen one to the queue. This finishes level one, now we expand level two from nodes six, two, and three. We discover seven, four, and one as new neighbors, giving the final answer seven, four, one.
say.code: First, an iterative depth first search records each node's parent. That adds the missing upward edge. It also remembers the target node. Then a queue starts there, with a seen set. We expand exactly k rings. Each ring, we pop every node and push its unseen neighbours. That's three of them: down left, down right, and up. Whatever's left in the queue is the k-th ring.
say.outro: Linear time and space. The pattern is graphs. Give the tree parent pointers, and it becomes a graph for breadth first search.

all-nodes-distance-k-in-binary-tree.title: All Nodes Distance K in Binary Tree
lineNotes: We define the Solution class that holds the method for this problem.
The method distanceK takes the tree root, the target value, and the distance k.
We create an empty dictionary called parent to map each node to its parent node.
We set start to none; it will hold the target node once we find it.
We seed a stack with the root and no parent, to traverse the tree iteratively.
We loop until the stack is empty, visiting every node in the tree.
We pop a node and its parent from the stack for processing.
If the popped node is empty, meaning a missing child,
we skip it and move on to the next stack entry.
We record this node's parent in the dictionary, which lets us walk upward later.
We check whether this node's value equals the target value.
If so, we remember this node as start, our BFS starting point.
We push the left child along with the current node as its parent.
We push the right child the same way, with the current node as its parent.
We create a queue holding just the start node to begin breadth first search.
We create a seen set with start so we never walk back onto visited nodes.
We repeat the expansion k times, once for each edge of distance.
For each level, we process exactly the nodes currently in the queue.
We take the next node off the front of the queue.
We look at its three neighbors: left child, right child, and parent.
We only consider neighbors that exist and have not been visited yet.
We mark that neighbor as seen so it will not be revisited.
We add the neighbor to the queue, so it forms the next distance level.
After k levels, the queue holds exactly the nodes at distance k, and we return their values.

alternating-groups-ii.hook: Do not recheck every window. Track how long the current alternating run is.
alternating-groups-ii.ask: Tiles in a circle are red or blue. Count the windows of k consecutive tiles, wrapping around, in which every neighbouring pair has different colours.
alternating-groups-ii.exampleWhy: From tile 3, colours alternate for seven tiles around the circle, which holds exactly two windows of six.

brute.idea: For each of the n starting tiles, check the next k minus 1 neighbouring pairs for a repeat colour.
steps: Pick a start tile
Check k - 1 neighbour pairs, wrapping
No repeat? count it
brute.whySlow: With a hundred thousand tiles and large k, that is up to ten billion pair checks.

optimal.insight: A window ending at tile i is alternating exactly when the alternating run ending at i is at least k long.
steps: Walk i past the end by k - 1, wrapping
Colour differs from previous? run grows
Same colour? run resets to 1
run ≥ k? count one window

codeNotes.match: for i in range(1, n + k - 1):

pitfalls: Forgetting the wrap-around misses windows that cross the end.
Walking too far double counts; stop at n + k - 2.

say.intro: Okay, so this is Alternating Groups Two. Tiles sit in a circle, each red or blue. We count windows of k neighbouring tiles where the colours keep alternating, wrapping around the end. With zero, one, zero, zero, one, zero, one, and k of six, the run wraps around. That gives two windows.
say.brute: The brute force tries every starting tile. From each start, it checks the next k minus one neighbour pairs, wrapping with modulo. If no two neighbours match, the window counts. Simple and correct. But it's n times k work. That's up to ten billion checks at the limits.
say.insight: Here's the thing. Windows overlap almost completely. So why recheck them? Instead, walk once and track how long the current alternating run is. If a tile differs from the one before, the run grows. If it matches, the run resets to one. Whenever the run reaches k, the window ending here works. Walk k minus one extra tiles to handle the wrap.
say.anim: We start with the color array and k equal to six, checking runs around the circle. At i equals one colors differ, so the alternating run grows to two. The run keeps extending to three as colors keep alternating through i equals two. At i equals three two same colors break the streak, so run resets to one. The run builds back up again as alternation continues through i equals six. By i equals eight the run reaches six, meeting k, so count becomes one. At i equals nine the run hits seven, still valid, so count becomes two. After one more break and final checks, the loop ends and returns count as two.
say.code: Count starts at zero, and run starts at one. We extend the loop by k minus two extra tiles, using modulo to wrap. If this tile differs from the one before, it's still alternating, so run goes up. If the colour repeats, that breaks the run, so reset to one. Whenever run is at least k, the window ending here qualifies. Add one to count.
say.outro: Linear time, constant space. The pattern is sliding window. Track one running length instead of rechecking every window.

alternating-groups-ii.title: Alternating Groups II
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container this problem's method lives in.
The method takes the circle of tile colors and the window size k, and returns how many alternating windows exist.
We store the number of tiles as n so we can wrap indexes around the circle.
We start the answer count at zero and the current alternating run length at one, since the first tile alone is a run.
We loop from index one up to n plus k minus two, which extends past the end so windows wrapping around are covered.
We compare the current tile with the previous one, using modulo n so indexes wrap back to the start.
If the two colors differ, the alternating pattern continues, so we grow the run by one.
Otherwise the pattern breaks at this tile.
So we reset the run length to one, starting a fresh run at the current tile.
If the run is at least k long, the window of k tiles ending at this tile is fully alternating.
In that case we add one to the count of valid windows.
After scanning every ending position, we return the total count of alternating windows.

angle-between-hands-of-a-clock.hook: No simulation needed: each hand's angle is a one-line formula.
angle-between-hands-of-a-clock.ask: Given an hour and a minute, return the smaller angle, in degrees, between the hour hand and the minute hand of an analog clock.
angle-between-hands-of-a-clock.exampleWhy: The minute hand is at 90 degrees. The hour hand is a quarter past 3, at 97.5. They differ by 7.5.

brute.idea: Start both hands at twelve and tick forward one minute at a time until the given time.
steps: Both hands at 0 degrees
Each minute: minute hand +6, hour hand +0.5
Take the gap and its complement
brute.whySlow: Up to 719 loop iterations where two multiplications give the same angles directly.

optimal.insight: Minute hand moves 6 degrees per minute; hour hand moves 30 per hour plus half a degree per minute.
steps: Minute angle = minutes * 6
Hour angle = (hour mod 12) * 30 + minutes * 0.5
Gap = absolute difference
Answer = min(gap, 360 - gap)

codeNotes.note: Hour hand creeps with the minutes

pitfalls: Forgetting the hour hand moves during the hour gives 0 for 3:15.
Use hour % 12 so 12 o'clock is 0 degrees.

say.intro: So, Angle Between Hands of a Clock. Given an hour and minutes, return the smaller angle between the hands. At a quarter past three, the minute hand points at the three. But the hour hand has crept a quarter of the way toward four. So the gap is seven and a half degrees, not zero.
say.brute: A simulation starts both hands at twelve and ticks forward one minute at a time. Each tick moves the minute hand six degrees, and the hour hand half a degree. At the end, take the gap between them. It's right. But it loops up to seven hundred times. And a simple formula answers it directly.
say.insight: Think about it this way. Each hand's position is just a rate. The minute hand covers three hundred sixty degrees in sixty minutes. That's six degrees a minute. The hour hand covers thirty degrees an hour, plus half a degree for every minute past. Subtract the two. There are two ways around the clock, so take the smaller one.
say.anim: We start with hour three and minutes fifteen, ready to compute the minute angle. Minute angle becomes ninety, since minutes times six gives that result. Hour angle becomes ninety seven point five, combining hour position and minute offset. Diff is calculated as seven point five, the absolute difference between the two angles. The function returns the smaller angle, giving a final answer of seven point five.
say.code: Minute angle is minutes times six, since it's three sixty over sixty minutes. Hour angle is hour modulo twelve, times thirty. Plus minutes times one half, because the hour hand creeps with the minutes. The modulo makes twelve o'clock count as zero. Take the absolute difference. Then take the smaller way round: that, or three sixty minus that.
say.outro: Constant time and space. The pattern is math and geometry. Turn each moving part into a rate, then compare angles directly.

angle-between-hands-of-a-clock.title: Angle Between Hands of a Clock
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container for the method that solves the clock angle problem.
The method angleClock takes the hour and the minutes and returns the smaller angle between the two hands.
The minute hand moves six degrees per minute, so we multiply minutes by six to get its angle.
The hour hand sits at thirty degrees per hour, using hour mod twelve so twelve becomes zero, plus half a degree per minute.
We take the absolute difference between the two angles, which gives one of the two possible angles between the hands.
The other angle is three hundred sixty minus that difference, so we return whichever of the two is smaller.

apply-operations-to-an-array.hook: Merge equal neighbours and push zeros back, both in one pass with a write pointer.
apply-operations-to-an-array.ask: Walk left to right: whenever nums[i] equals nums[i + 1], double nums[i] and zero nums[i + 1]. Then move every zero to the end, keeping the order of the rest.
apply-operations-to-an-array.exampleWhy: 2,2 merge into 4 and 0; then 1,1 merge into 2 and 0. Shifting zeros back gives 1, 4, 2.

brute.idea: Do the operations exactly as written, then shift zeros by removing each one and appending it at the end.
steps: Apply each merge left to right
Count the zeros
Remove a zero, append it, repeat
brute.whySlow: Each remove shifts the rest of the list: two thousand elements with many zeros means millions of moves.

optimal.insight: Merges only touch i and i + 1, so the value at i is final once processed. Swap it to a write pointer right away.
steps: Write pointer starts at 0
Apply the merge at i
nums[i] nonzero? swap it to write
Advance write

codeNotes.match: if i + 1 < n and nums[i] == nums[i + 1]:

pitfalls: Operations are sequential: a zero created at i + 1 can merge with another zero.
Shifting zeros before merging gives a different, wrong answer.

say.intro: Okay, so this is Apply Operations to an Array. Walk left to right. When a number equals its right neighbour, double it, and set the neighbour to zero. Then push every zero to the back. In one, two, two, one, one, zero, the twos merge into four. The ones merge into two. We get one, four, two, then zeros.
say.brute: The literal approach does the merges in one pass, then fixes the zeros. For each zero, remove it from the list and append it at the end. That's easy to trust. But what does each removal cost? It shifts every element after it. So with lots of zeros, the work turns quadratic.
say.insight: Here's the thing. A merge at index i only touches i and i plus one. So once we've passed index i, its value is final. That means we can shift zeros in the same pass. Keep a write pointer for the next nonzero slot. Swap each final nonzero value into it right away.
say.anim: We start with the array one two two one one zero, and write pointer at zero. At index zero, one and two differ, so nothing merges and one stays, moving to write position zero. At index one, nums one and two both equal two, so they merge into four and the next becomes zero. Since four is nonzero, it swaps into write position one, advancing the write pointer. Index two is now zero after merging, so it gets skipped and write stays put. At index three, values one and one match, merging into two with the next slot zeroed out. That two swaps into write position two, giving array one four two zero zero zero. The loop finishes and the final answer is one four two zero zero zero.
say.code: Write points at the next slot for a nonzero. We loop i over every index. If the next element equals the current one, we merge equal neighbours. Double the current, and the partner becomes a zero. Then, if the current value isn't zero, it's final. So swap it into write and move write forward. Return the array.
say.outro: Linear time, constant space. The pattern is two pointers. A reader and a writer compact values in place.

apply-operations-to-an-array.title: Apply Operations to an Array
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the wrapper this problem's solution method lives in.
This method takes the list nums, applies the merge operations, and returns the rearranged list.
We store the length of nums in n so we can check bounds cleanly.
We set write to zero; it marks where the next nonzero value should be placed.
We loop through every index i from left to right, processing the array in order as the problem requires.
If a next element exists and equals the current one, we have a pair that must be merged.
We double the current value, since merging two equal numbers gives twice that number at position i.
We set the next element to zero, which also keeps it from merging again with its own neighbor.
After any merge, if the value at i is nonzero, it is final and ready to be moved forward.
We swap the values at write and i, placing the nonzero value at the front and sending a zero or filler back.
We advance write by one so the next nonzero value lands right after this one, keeping order.
We return nums, which now has all merged values in order followed by the zeros.

apply-transform-over-each-element-in-arr.hook: Rebuild map from scratch: call a function on every element and its index, into a fresh array.
apply-transform-over-each-element-in-arr.ask: Given an array and a function fn, return a new array where position i holds fn applied to the element at i and to i itself, without using a built-in map.
apply-transform-over-each-element-in-arr.input:
function plusI(n, i) { return n + i; }
[10,20,30,40]
apply-transform-over-each-element-in-arr.exampleWhy: plusI adds each index to its element: 10 plus 0, 20 plus 1, 30 plus 2, 40 plus 3.

brute.idea: Loop over the array and grow the answer by concatenating a one-element list each time.
steps: Start with an empty list
Call fn on element and index
Concatenate a new list with the value
brute.whySlow: Each concatenation copies the whole list so far: a thousand elements means half a million copies.

optimal.insight: The output length is known up front, so allocate it once and fill each slot with fn(arr[i], i).
steps: Turn fn into a callable
Allocate a result of length n
Fill slot i with fn(arr[i], i)
Return the new array

codeNotes.note: The JS function text becomes callable
Pass both the value and index
Extra arguments are ignored, like JS

pitfalls: fn takes the index as a second argument; passing only the value breaks plusI.
Never mutate arr; return a new array.

say.intro: Okay, so this is Apply Transform Over Each Element in Array. It's a JavaScript problem, where we rebuild the built in map. Each output slot gets the function applied to the element and its index. With plus i on ten, twenty, thirty, forty, we add each index. That gives ten, twenty one, thirty two, forty three.
say.brute: A first attempt loops over the array and grows the answer by concatenating a one element list each time. The values come out right. So what's wrong? Concatenation builds a brand new list and copies everything so far. A thousand elements means about half a million copies. That's quadratic for a linear job.
say.insight: Here's the thing. We know the output length before we even start. So allocate the result once, the same length as the input. Then fill slot i with the function called on the element and on i. Why pass the index? Because functions like plus i use it. Others just ignore the extra argument.
say.anim: We start by compiling the function string plusI into a real callable. The parser extracts parameters n and i from the function signature. Now we have a working lambda that adds n and i together. A result array of four zeros is allocated upfront, matching the input length. At index zero, we compute ten plus zero, storing ten in the result. At index one, twenty plus one gives twenty one, filling the next slot. Continuing, thirty plus two becomes thirty two at index two. Finally forty plus three gives forty three, completing the output as ten, twenty one, thirty two, forty three.
say.code: Our Python version gets the function as text. So a small helper turns that JavaScript text into something callable. Next, we allocate the output once, the same length as the array. Then a loop fills each slot, passing both the value and the index. Extra arguments are ignored, just like in JavaScript. Then we return the new array.
say.outro: Linear time and space. The pattern is arrays. Preallocate the output, fill it in one pass, and never touch the input.

apply-transform-over-each-element-in-arr.title: Apply Transform Over Each Element in Array
lineNotes: We define a Solution class that holds both the mapping method and a helper that turns function text into something callable.
The map method takes the function as a string plus the input array, and returns the transformed list of integers.
We call compile on the function string to get a real Python callable, which we store as f.
Since the output length equals the input length, we preallocate a result list of zeros that size.
We loop over every index i from zero up to the length of arr, avoiding any built-in map.
At each index we call f with the element and its index, and store the answer in the same slot of res.
After the loop fills every slot, we return the finished result list.
The compile helper converts a JavaScript style function string into a Python lambda so we can run it.
We use a regular expression to capture the parameter list and the returned expression from inside the braces of the function text.
We split the captured parameter text on commas, strip whitespace from each name, and drop empty entries, giving a clean parameter list.
We build a lambda with those parameters plus a catch-all for extras, using eval so the returned expression becomes executable code.

assign-cookies.hook: Give each child the smallest cookie that satisfies them. Sorting makes that a single sweep.
assign-cookies.ask: Each child needs a cookie at least as big as their greed factor, and gets at most one cookie. Given greed factors and cookie sizes, return the most children you can satisfy.
assign-cookies.exampleWhy: Cookies 1, 2 and 3 satisfy the children with greed 1, 2 and 3. Child 4 cannot be satisfied.

brute.idea: Take children from least greedy up; for each, scan every cookie for the smallest unused one that fits.
steps: Sort children by greed
For each child, scan all cookies
Pick the smallest unused fitting cookie
Count successful matches
brute.whySlow: Every child rescans every cookie: thirty thousand of each means nearly a billion checks.

optimal.insight: Sort both lists. Walk cookies from small to large; each cookie goes to the least greedy unsatisfied child if it fits.
steps: Sort greed factors and cookie sizes
Child pointer starts at the least greedy
Cookie fits? that child is content, advance
Too small? skip the cookie
optimal.time: O(n log n + m log m)

codeNotes.match: if child < len(g) and size >= g[child]:

pitfalls: Giving a big cookie to an easy child wastes it; match smallest to smallest.
Cookies can be an empty list; the loop simply does nothing.

say.intro: So, Assign Cookies. A child is happy only with a cookie at least as big as their greed. And each child gets at most one. We want the most happy kids. The children want one, two, three and four. Cookies are one, three, two and one. Three kids can be happy, but not the one who wants four.
say.brute: The brute force sorts the children by greed. Then, for each child, it scans every cookie for the smallest unused one that still fits. It makes the right choices. But every child rescans the whole cookie list. That's quadratic, nearly a billion checks at the limits.
say.insight: Here's the greedy idea. Never waste a big cookie on an easy child. Sort both lists. Then walk the cookies from smallest to largest. Each cookie goes to the least greedy child still waiting, if it's big enough. And if it's too small for that child? Then it's too small for everyone left. So skip it.
say.anim: We start with children's greed values and cookie sizes before sorting. Both arrays get sorted, giving cookies one, one, two, three in order. Child pointer starts at zero as we scan cookies from smallest to largest. First cookie size one matches child zero's requirement, satisfying that child. Next cookie size one is too small for child one, who needs two. Cookie size two satisfies child one, so child pointer moves to two. Cookie size three satisfies child two, advancing child pointer to three. Loop ends and the function returns three satisfied children as the answer.
say.code: Sort both lists, so the smallest cookies come first. Child starts at zero, pointing at the least greedy child still unsatisfied. We loop over each cookie. If a child is waiting and the cookie fits their greed, feed this child, and move child forward. At the end, child is exactly how many kids we fed.
say.outro: Sorting dominates, so n log n time. The pattern is greedy. Match the smallest resource that works to the smallest need.

assign-cookies.title: Assign Cookies
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container the problem expects for our method.
The method takes the greed factors in g and the cookie sizes in s, and returns the count of satisfied children.
We sort the greed factors so the least greedy children come first.
We sort the cookie sizes so we can try the smallest cookies first and waste nothing.
We set child to zero, which is the index of the least greedy child still unsatisfied and also our running count.
We loop over each cookie size from smallest to largest, offering each cookie once.
If children remain and this cookie is at least as big as the current child's greed, it satisfies them.
We move to the next child, since this one is satisfied and the count of happy children grows by one.
We return child, which equals the total number of children we managed to satisfy.

backspace-string-compare.hook: Backspaces only erase what came before, so read both strings backwards and skip.
backspace-string-compare.ask: Two strings are typed into empty editors, where a hash sign means backspace. Return true if both editors end up showing the same text.
backspace-string-compare.exampleWhy: In ab#c the b is erased, and in ad#c the d is erased. Both editors show ac.

brute.idea: Simulate both editors with a stack: push letters, pop on backspace, then compare the results.
steps: Push each letter onto a stack
On # pop if not empty
Compare the two final stacks
brute.whySlow: Already linear time, but it builds two full copies of the text; the follow-up asks for O(1) space.

optimal.insight: Read from the end: count pending backspaces and skip that many letters. The surviving characters appear in reverse order.
steps: Pointers at the end of both strings
Move each to its next surviving letter
Letters differ? false
Both exhausted together? true

codeNotes.match: if i < 0 or j < 0 or s[i] != t[j]:
codeNotes.note: One ran out, or letters differ
A backspace erases one earlier letter

pitfalls: Reading forwards fails: a later # can erase what you already compared.
Backspace on an empty editor does nothing; skip just stays unused.

say.intro: Okay, so this is Backspace String Compare. Each string is typed into an editor, and the hash sign is a backspace. Do both editors end up the same? A b hash c loses the b. A d hash c loses the d. Both show a c, so the answer is true.
say.brute: The straightforward way simulates each editor with a stack. Push letters. Pop one whenever we see a backspace, if there's anything to pop. Then compare the two stacks. Honestly, that's already linear time. So what's the issue? Space. It copies both texts, and the follow up wants constant memory.
say.insight: Here's the thing. A backspace only affects letters before it. So read each string from the end. Keep a count of pending backspaces. Each hash adds one. Each letter we meet while the count is positive gets erased instead. The first letter we can't erase is the next visible one. Then compare those pairs one at a time.
say.anim: We start comparing from the ends of both strings, s is ab hash c and t is ad hash c. Scanning s from index three, there's no backspace, so nextChar returns index three, the letter c. Scanning t from index three similarly finds no hash, returning index three, also the letter c. Both characters are c, they match, so we move inward to compare the next pair. In s, index two is a hash, so skip becomes one and we skip the b at index one. In t, index two is also a hash, skipping index one, landing on a at index zero. Both remaining characters are a, they match, and both pointers now go negative. With both strings fully consumed and matching, the function returns true.
say.code: We start i and j from the ends. Each round, a helper moves each pointer to its next surviving letter. If one ran out, or the letters differ, we decide right there. Both out means true. Otherwise false. Inside the helper, a backspace erases one earlier letter, so it bumps skip. A letter while skip is positive is erased. It returns the index of the next surviving letter.
say.outro: Linear time, constant space. The pattern is two pointers. Scan from the back, so you already know about future edits.

backspace-string-compare.title: Backspace String Compare
lineNotes: We define a class named Solution, as the problem platform expects.
The method backspaceCompare takes strings s and t and returns whether they match after backspaces are applied.
We start two pointers, i and j, at the last positions of s and t.
We loop as long as either string still has characters left to examine.
We move i backward to the next surviving character in s, skipping letters erased by backspaces.
We do the same for j in t, finding its next surviving character.
If both pointers ran out, every character matched, so the editors show the same text.
This return True ends the comparison early because nothing remains in either string.
If only one string ran out, or the surviving characters differ, the texts cannot be equal.
So we return False for that mismatch.
The characters matched, so we step i one position further left.
We likewise step j one position left to compare the next pair.
If the loop finishes with no mismatch, the final texts are equal, so we return True.
The helper nextChar finds the index of the next character that survives, scanning leftward from a given index.
We start a skip counter at zero to track pending backspaces.
We keep scanning while the index is still inside the string.
If the current character is a hash, it is a backspace.
So we increase skip by one to erase another letter later.
Otherwise, if skip is positive, this letter is erased by a backspace.
We use up one pending backspace by decreasing skip.
Otherwise the letter is not erased and is a real surviving character.
So we break out of the loop and keep this index.
After handling a hash or erased letter, we move one position left.
We return the index of the surviving character, or negative one if none remains.
