basic-calculator-ii.hook: Multiply and divide right away, postpone plus and minus on a stack, then sum.
basic-calculator-ii.ask: Evaluate a string expression with non-negative integers, plus, minus, times and divide, and spaces. Respect precedence, and truncate division toward zero. No eval.
basic-calculator-ii.exampleWhy: Times and divide first: 2*2 is 4 and 8/4 is 2. Then 3 plus 4 minus 2 is 5.

brute.idea: Tokenize, then repeatedly collapse the first times or divide in the token list, and finally add and subtract left to right.
steps: Split into numbers and operators
Collapse each * or / in place
Fold the remaining + and - left to right
brute.whySlow: Each collapse splices the list and shifts everything after it: long expressions cost quadratic time.

optimal.insight: Push each term onto a stack: plus and minus push signed numbers, times and divide combine with the top immediately.
steps: Build the current number digit by digit
At an operator or the end, apply the previous operator
+ or - pushes, * or / updates the top
Answer is the sum of the stack

codeNotes.note: Pretend a plus before the first number

codeNotes.match: if ch in "+-*/" or i == len(s) - 1:

pitfalls: Python's // floors; -3 // 2 is -2, so use int(a / b).
Handle the last number: the string may end with a digit or a space.

say.intro: Okay, so this is Basic Calculator Two. We evaluate an expression with plus, minus, times and divide. Precedence matters, and no eval allowed. Take three plus two times two minus eight divided by four. Times and divide go first, giving four and two. Then three plus four minus two is five.
say.brute: A direct approach splits the text into numbers and operators. Then it scans the list, and every time it finds a times or divide, it swaps those three tokens for the result. Finally it adds and subtracts left to right. It's correct. But each replacement shifts the rest of the list. So long inputs cost quadratic time.
say.insight: Think of the expression as a sum of terms. Plus and minus start new terms. Times and divide only change the current term. So keep a stack of terms. When a number ends, look at the operator before it. Plus pushes it. Minus pushes its negative. Times or divide combine it with the top right away. The answer is the sum.
say.anim: We start with an empty stack and parse the expression using a running number and operator. The digit three is read, building num equal to three before the plus sign appears. Since the operator is plus, three is pushed onto the stack, which now holds three. Next we read two, then see a multiply sign, pushing two onto the stack making it three, two. We read another two, then hit minus, so op multiplies: top of stack becomes four. Eight is parsed, then division appears, so minus pushes negative eight, giving stack three, four, negative eight. Finally four is read, and division combines negative eight divided by four into negative two. Summing the stack three plus four minus two gives the final answer five.
say.code: We pretend there's a plus before the first number, so op starts as plus. A digit extends num. When a number just ended, we apply the previous op. Plus pushes num. Minus becomes a negative term. Times multiplies the top. Divide truncates toward zero. Then remember this operator and reset num. Only additions remain, so return the sum of the stack.
say.outro: Linear time, with a stack. The pattern is stack. Handle high precedence right away, and let the low ones wait.

basic-calculator-ii.title: Basic Calculator II
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, as expected for this problem's submission format.
The calculate method takes the expression string and returns the final integer result.
We create an empty stack that will hold each signed term to be summed at the end.
We start with the current number at zero and the previous operator as plus, so the first term is simply added.
We loop over every character in the string along with its index, so we can detect the last position.
If the character is a digit, we handle it as part of the number being built.
We shift the current number one decimal place left and add this digit, building multi-digit numbers.
When we hit an operator or reach the last character, the current number is complete and must be applied.
If the previous operator was plus, we apply it by pushing the number as is.
We push the positive number onto the stack as its own term.
If the previous operator was minus, we push the negated number so the final sum subtracts it.
We push the negative of the number onto the stack as its own term.
If the previous operator was times, we must combine with the most recent term right away for precedence.
We pop the top term, multiply it by the number, and push the product back.
Otherwise the previous operator was divide, which also binds tighter than plus and minus.
We pop the top, divide by the number, and convert to int to truncate toward zero before pushing.
We remember the current character as the next operator and reset the number to zero for the next term.
Finally we sum every term on the stack, which gives the value of the whole expression.

best-time-to-buy-and-sell-stock-iv.hook: Generalise one transaction to k with two small arrays: best cash after each buy, and each sell.
best-time-to-buy-and-sell-stock-iv.ask: Given daily stock prices and a limit k, find the maximum profit using at most k buy-then-sell transactions, never holding more than one share at once.
best-time-to-buy-and-sell-stock-iv.exampleWhy: Buy at 2, sell at 6 for 4. Buy at 0, sell at 3 for 3. Total 7.

brute.idea: On each day, either do nothing, or buy if empty-handed, or sell if holding. Recurse on every choice.
steps: State: day, transactions left, holding
Option 1: skip the day
Option 2: buy or sell
Return the better of the two
brute.whySlow: Two choices per day for a thousand days is 2 to the 1000 paths, with huge repeated work.

optimal.insight: buy[t] is the best cash while holding the t-th share; sell[t] the best after t sales. Each day relaxes them in order.
steps: buy all minus infinity, sell all zero
For each price and each t from 1 to k
buy[t] = max(buy[t], sell[t-1] - price)
sell[t] = max(sell[t], buy[t] + price)
Answer is sell[k]

codeNotes.note: Buy using profit from t-1 trades
Best with at most k trades

pitfalls: If k ≥ n/2 the limit never binds; sum every rise to avoid huge tables.
Buying and selling the same day is harmless: it adds zero profit.

say.intro: Okay, so this is Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock Four. We get daily prices and can make at most k trades. Each trade is a buy, then a sell. With k of two and prices two, six, five, zero, three, buy at two, sell at six. Then buy at zero, sell at three. That's seven.
say.brute: The brute force tries every choice on every day. Holding nothing? Buy or wait. Holding a share? Sell or wait. Selling uses up one transaction. Recursing on both options is correct. But it explores two to the n paths. And it recomputes the same states again and again.
say.insight: Here's the thing. Only a few numbers really matter. For each trade count t, keep two values. Buy of t is the most cash while holding the t-th share. Sell of t is the most cash after t completed sales. Each new price can improve buy of t from sell of t minus one. Then it improves sell of t from buy of t.
say.anim: We start with k equals two, tracking buy and sell arrays for up to two trades. Price two arrives, buying the first share costs negative two, since selling nothing gives zero. Price six arrives, selling share one at this price gives sell of four. The second buy uses sell one minus price, then sells give sell two equal four. Price zero lets buy one improve to zero, since holding cash costs nothing now. Buy two improves to four, meaning two shares bought cheaply at two and zero. Price three arrives, selling the second share yields sell two equal seven, the best so far. The function returns sell of k, giving a final maximum profit of seven.
say.code: Buy starts at minus infinity, because we can't hold before buying. Sell starts at zero, since no trades means no profit. For each price, we loop t from one to k. Buy of t takes the better of staying put, or buying using the profit from t minus one trades. Sell of t takes the better of staying put, or selling the t-th share today. Return sell of k.
say.outro: N times k time, k space. The pattern is two dimensional dynamic programming, over days and trade counts.

best-time-to-buy-and-sell-stock-iv.title: Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock IV
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container the problem expects for our answer.
The maxProfit method takes the transaction limit k and the list of daily prices, and returns the best profit.
We create a buy list of size k plus one, starting at negative infinity because no share has been bought yet.
We create a sell list of size k plus one, starting at zero because doing nothing earns zero profit.
We loop over each day's price, processing days in order so each decision uses only earlier information.
For each day we loop over transaction numbers from one up to k, updating every transaction level.
Holding the t-th share is best of keeping the old state or buying today using cash after t minus one sales.
Cash after t sales is best of the old value or selling today the share held for transaction t.
After all days, the best profit with at most k sales is stored in sell at index k.

binary-tree-cameras.hook: Never put a camera on a leaf. Put it on the leaf's parent, and work upward.
binary-tree-cameras.ask: A camera on a node watches itself, its parent and its children. Return the minimum number of cameras needed so that every node in the binary tree is watched.
binary-tree-cameras.exampleWhy: In this five-node chain, cameras on the second and fourth nodes cover everyone; one camera reaches at most three.

brute.idea: Try every set of nodes, smallest sets first, and return the size of the first set that watches every node.
steps: Collect nodes and their parents
Try all sets of size 1, 2, 3...
Mark each camera's node, parent, children
All covered? return the size
brute.whySlow: A thousand nodes has 2 to the 1000 subsets; even 40 nodes is a trillion.

optimal.insight: Post-order greedy with three states: needs cover, has camera, covered. A child needing cover forces a camera on its parent.
steps: Empty child counts as covered
Any child uncovered? place a camera here
Any child has a camera? this node is covered
Otherwise this node needs cover
Root still needs cover? add one

codeNotes.note: A child is unwatched: camera here
Root has no parent to help

pitfalls: Empty children must count as covered, or leaves get cameras.
Remember the root: it may still need cover after the DFS.

say.intro: Okay, so this is Binary Tree Cameras. A camera on a node watches the node, its parent and its children. We want the fewest cameras that watch the whole tree. Our tree is a chain of five nodes. One camera covers at most three in a row. So we need two, on the second and fourth nodes.
say.brute: The brute force tries sets of nodes, smallest first. For each set, mark every camera's node, its parent and its children as watched. The first set that covers everything is the answer. It's correct. But how many sets are there? Two to the n. Hopeless past a few dozen nodes.
say.insight: Here's the key. A camera on a leaf is wasteful. Its parent would watch that same leaf, plus more. So decide from the bottom up. Each node reports one of three states. Needs cover, has a camera, or covered. If any child needs cover, put a camera here. If a child has a camera, we're covered. Otherwise, ask the parent for help.
say.anim: We start at the root node, camera count initialized to zero before the traversal begins. The algorithm dives deep first, recursing down through nodes 2 and 3 before evaluating anything. Leaf node 4's children are null, so each null returns state 2, meaning already covered. Node 5 has both children covered, so it returns 0, meaning it still needs coverage. Node 4 sees a child needing coverage, so it places a camera, cameras becomes 1. Node 3 sees a camera below it, so it just returns covered, state 2, no new camera. Node 2 has both children covered already, so it returns 0, still needing coverage itself. Root sees a child needing coverage, places the second camera, final answer is 2.
say.code: A missing child returns two, meaning covered. We go post order, so the children decide first. If a child is unwatched, put a camera here and return one. If a child's camera watches us, return two. Otherwise return zero, which means we need cover. Finally, the root has no parent to help. So if it still needs cover, add one more camera.
say.outro: Linear time, height-sized stack. The pattern is trees. Greedy in post order, where children report and parents decide.

binary-tree-cameras.title: Binary Tree Cameras
lineNotes: We define the Solution class that holds our method for solving the camera coverage problem.
The method minCameraCover takes the root of the binary tree and returns the minimum number of cameras needed.
We start a counter called cameras at zero to track how many cameras we place.
We define a helper dfs that walks the tree in post-order and returns a state for each node.
Declaring cameras as nonlocal lets the helper update the outer counter instead of making a new local variable.
If the node is empty, there is nothing to watch, so we handle the base case here.
We return two, meaning covered, so that missing children never force a camera onto their parent.
We recurse on the left and right children first, so we know their states before deciding about this node.
If either child returns zero, meaning it needs cover, this node must hold a camera to watch that child.
We increase the camera count by one since we place a camera on the current node.
We return one, signaling that this node has a camera.
If either child has a camera, this node is already watched by it, so no camera is needed here.
We return two, meaning this node is covered but has no camera itself.
Otherwise both children are covered without cameras, so this node is unwatched and returns zero to ask its parent for cover.
After the traversal, we check whether the root itself ended up needing cover, since it has no parent to help.
If the root needs cover, we add one extra camera on the root.
We return the total number of cameras placed.

boats-to-save-people.hook: The heaviest person needs a boat no matter what. The only question is who rides along.
boats-to-save-people.ask: Each boat carries at most two people with total weight at most limit. Given everyone's weight, return the minimum number of boats needed to carry all of them.
boats-to-save-people.exampleWhy: Sorted 1 to 5: pair 1 with 5, 2 with 4, and 3 goes alone. Three boats.

brute.idea: Sort, then repeatedly pop the heaviest and pull the lightest off the front of the list if they fit.
steps: Sort the weights
Pop the heaviest into a boat
Lightest fits too? pop it from the front
Count the boat
brute.whySlow: Same greedy, but popping the front shifts the whole list: fifty thousand people means over a billion moves.

optimal.insight: Pair the heaviest with the lightest. If even the lightest cannot join, nobody can, so the heaviest rides alone.
steps: Sort weights
Pointers at lightest and heaviest
Fit together? move the light pointer too
Heavy pointer always moves; add a boat

pitfalls: Use l <= r so the last single person still gets a boat.
Pairing heavy with heavy first can waste space and cost extra boats.

say.intro: Okay, so this is Boats to Save People. Each boat holds at most two people, under a weight limit. We want the fewest boats for everyone. With weights five, one, four, two, three and a limit of six, one rides with five. Two rides with four. And three goes alone. That's three boats.
say.brute: A first version sorts the weights, then keeps popping the heaviest person. Can the lightest squeeze in too? If so, remove them from the front of the list. The choices are right. But here's the catch. Removing from the front shifts the whole list every time. So it turns quadratic.
say.insight: Think about the heaviest person. They need a boat no matter what. Who's the best partner to try? The lightest person. If even they don't fit, nobody does. So sort once. Put one pointer on the lightest, one on the heaviest. Each boat takes the heaviest, plus the lightest when the sum fits.
say.anim: We start with people weights five, one, four, two, three and a boat limit of six. After sorting, people become one, two, three, four, five, with pointers at both ends. Lightest one plus heaviest five equals six, fitting the limit, so they pair up. Both pointers move inward, and boats increases to one for this pair. Now two plus four equals six, so they also share a boat together. Only person weighing three remains, needing a boat alone since no partner is left. Boats count reaches three after this final solo rider is counted. The loop ends and the function returns three, the minimum boats needed.
say.code: We sort, then put the lightest on the left and the heaviest on the right. We loop while left hasn't passed right. When they're equal, it means one person is left. If the lightest plus the heaviest fits, the lightest can share the boat, so left moves forward. Either way, the heaviest always leaves. So right moves back and we add a boat.
say.outro: Sorting gives n log n time. The pattern is greedy with two pointers. Pair the extremes, and the heaviest always leaves.

boats-to-save-people.title: Boats to Save People
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container the problem expects for our method.
The method takes the list of people weights and the boat limit, and returns the minimum number of boats.
We sort the weights so the lightest person is at the front and the heaviest at the back.
We place the left pointer on the lightest person and the right pointer on the heaviest person.
We start the boat count at zero before handing out any boats.
We loop while the pointers have not crossed, meaning someone still needs a boat, including when both point at one person.
We check whether the lightest and heaviest remaining people together fit within the limit.
If they fit, the lightest person shares the boat, so we move the left pointer forward.
The heaviest person always boards this boat, either alone or with a partner, so we move the right pointer back.
We count one boat for this trip since each loop pass sends off exactly one boat.
After everyone is assigned, we return the total number of boats used.

build-array-from-permutation.hook: A one-liner problem with a sneaky follow-up: do it in place, with no extra array.
build-array-from-permutation.ask: Given a permutation of 0 to n minus 1, build ans where ans[i] = nums[nums[i]]. The follow-up asks for O(1) extra space.
build-array-from-permutation.exampleWhy: Index 3 holds 5, and nums[5] is 4, so ans[3] is 4. Every slot follows one hop.

brute.idea: Make a fresh answer array and fill each slot with nums[nums[i]] by direct lookup.
steps: Create an empty answer list
For each i, append nums[nums[i]]
Return the new list
brute.whySlow: Time is already linear. The only cost is a second n-sized array; the follow-up forbids that extra memory.

optimal.insight: Every value is below n, so one slot can hold two numbers: old value plus n times new value.
steps: Pass 1: add n · (nums[nums[i]] % n) to nums[i]
% n always recovers the original value
Pass 2: divide every slot by n
What remains is the new value

codeNotes.note: Pack new value above the old one
Read the original, even if packed

pitfalls: Reading nums[nums[i]] without % n picks up already-packed values and breaks.
Encoding works because values are below n; say that assumption aloud.

say.intro: Okay, so this is Build Array from Permutation. We get a permutation of zero to n minus one. For each index, we follow one hop. The answer at i is nums of nums of i. With zero, two, one, five, three, four, index three holds five. And nums of five is four. So slot three becomes four.
say.brute: The brute force is the obvious one. Make a new list, walk every index, and append nums of nums of i. It's linear time and totally correct. So what's the problem? Memory. It builds a second array the same size as the input. And the follow up asks us to rebuild in place, with constant extra space.
say.insight: Here's the trick. Every value is smaller than n. So one slot can hold two numbers at once. Keep the old value as the remainder, and add n times the new value on top. Why is that safe? Because the slot modulo n always gives back the original, even after packing. Then a second pass divides by n, leaving only the new value.
say.anim: We start with nums holding zero, two, one, five, three, four, and n equals six. For each index, we encode both old and new values into a single number using n. After processing index one, nums becomes zero, eight, one, five, three, four, packing two values together. By index three, nums holds zero, eight, thirteen, twenty nine, three, four, still encoded. After the first loop finishes, all values are combined, ending as zero, eight, thirteen, twenty nine, thirty three, twenty two. Now the second loop divides each entry by n to unpack the real answer values. Dividing step by step restores clean numbers like one, two, four, five, and three. The final decoded array is zero, one, two, four, five, three, the correct permutation result.
say.code: First, n is the length, and every value is below it. The first loop packs the new value above the old one. It adds n times nums of nums of i, modulo n. Now, notice that modulo. It reads the original, even if that slot is already packed. The second loop divides each slot by n, keeping only the new value. Same array, rebuilt in place.
say.outro: Linear time, constant extra space. The pattern is arrays and hashing, with the classic trick of packing two values into one slot.

build-array-from-permutation.title: Build Array from Permutation
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container the interview platform expects for our method.
The buildArray method takes the list nums and returns a new arrangement, which we will build in place.
We store the length of nums as n, since every value is below n and n works as our encoding base.
We loop over every index i from zero up to n minus one, visiting each slot once.
We add n times the old value of the slot nums at nums of i, recovered with modulo n, packing old and new together.
A second loop over every index lets us strip away the old values now that all new values are stored.
Dividing each slot by n with integer division drops the old value and leaves only the new value, nums of nums of i.
We return nums itself, which now holds the answer, so we used constant extra space.

bulls-and-cows.hook: A guessing game with duplicate digits. One pass and ten counters settle it.
bulls-and-cows.ask: Compare a secret and a guess of equal length. Bulls are right digit, right place. Cows are right digit, wrong place, without double counting. Return xAyB.
bulls-and-cows.exampleWhy: 8 is in the right place: one bull. 1, 7 and 0 appear in the secret elsewhere: three cows.

brute.idea: Count bulls first. Then for each non-bull guess digit, search the secret for an unused matching digit.
steps: Mark matching positions as bulls
For each other guess digit, scan the secret
Take the first unused match as a cow
brute.whySlow: Each guess digit rescans the whole secret: a 1,000-digit guess means about a million checks.

optimal.insight: Keep one balance per digit: secret adds one, guess subtracts one. A sign flip means an earlier unmatched partner exists.
steps: Same digit at same index: a bull
Otherwise secret digit meets a waiting guess digit if count < 0
Guess digit meets a waiting secret digit if count > 0
Then update both counts

codeNotes.note: Secret pushes up, guess pushes down

pitfalls: Never let a bull digit also count as a cow; skip bull positions entirely.
Duplicates: a cow needs an unmatched partner, not just any occurrence.

say.intro: So, Bulls and Cows. We compare a secret with a guess. A bull is a digit in exactly the right place. A cow is in the secret, but somewhere else. For one eight zero seven against seven eight one zero, eight is a bull. The other three are cows. So the hint is one A three B.
say.brute: The brute force takes two sweeps. First, mark every position where the digits match as a bull. Then, for each leftover guess digit, scan the secret for an unused match, and claim it as a cow. It works. But each guess digit can rescan the whole secret. So it's quadratic.
say.insight: Here's the thing. Cows only depend on counts, not positions. So keep a balance for each of the ten digits. A secret digit pushes its balance up. A guess digit pushes it down. Now, say a secret digit shows up while its balance is negative. That means a guess digit was waiting for it. That's a cow. The mirror rule handles guess digits.
say.anim: We start comparing secret 1807 against guess 7810, tracking bulls and cows. First digits 1 and 7 differ, so we update the balance count instead of bulls. Digits 8 and 8 match exactly, so bulls increases to 1. Digits 0 and 1 differ, but guess's 1 was already seen, giving a cow. Digits 7 and 0 differ; both counts show earlier unmatched partners, adding two cows. Loop finishes with bulls equal to 1 and cows equal to 3. The final answer returned is 1A3B.
say.code: Bulls and cows start at zero, with one balance per digit. We walk the two strings side by side. An exact match is a bull. Otherwise, check the balances. A negative secret balance means a guess digit was waiting. That's a cow. A positive guess balance means a secret digit was waiting. Another cow. Then the secret pushes its balance up, and the guess pushes down.
say.outro: One pass, constant space. The pattern is arrays and hashing. When position doesn't matter, keep counts, and let the sign say who's waiting.

bulls-and-cows.title: Bulls and Cows
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container the interview platform expects for this method.
The getHint method takes the secret and the guess and will return the hint string.
We start both the bulls counter and the cows counter at zero.
We make a list of ten zeros, one running balance for each digit from zero to nine.
We walk through secret and guess together, looking at the digit pair at each position.
If the two digits at this position are equal, we have an exact match.
In that case we add one to bulls, and we leave the balances untouched.
Otherwise the digits differ, so both might still pair up with digits from other positions.
If the balance for the secret digit is negative, an earlier guess digit was waiting for it, so that is a cow.
We add one to cows because this secret digit matches an earlier unmatched guess digit.
If the balance for the guess digit is positive, an earlier secret digit was waiting for it, so that is a cow.
We add one to cows because this guess digit matches an earlier unmatched secret digit.
We raise the balance for the secret digit, recording one unmatched secret copy that later guesses can use.
We lower the balance for the guess digit, recording one unmatched guess copy that later secrets can use.
Finally we return the bulls and cows formatted as a string like xAyB.

can-place-flowers.hook: Plant as early as you can. Here, being greedy is provably never wrong.
can-place-flowers.ask: A flowerbed has planted plots (1) and empty plots (0). Flowers cannot be adjacent. Can n more flowers be planted?
can-place-flowers.exampleWhy: Plot 2 has empty neighbours, and so does the last plot. That is two new flowers.

brute.idea: Try every subset of empty plots: for each valid plot, either plant there or skip it, and keep the best total.
steps: At plot i, try skipping it
If its neighbours are empty, also try planting
Return the larger count
brute.whySlow: Two choices per plot doubles the work each time: 40 plots already means about a trillion branches.

optimal.insight: Planting at the first free spot never hurts: it only blocks a plot to its right, which a later flower could not beat.
steps: Walk the bed left to right
Empty plot with empty neighbours? Plant it
Count it, stop early once count reaches n
Ends of the bed count as empty neighbours

codeNotes.note: Plant now so the next plot sees it
Stop as soon as we have enough

pitfalls: Forgetting the boundaries: the first and last plots have only one neighbour.
Not marking the plot planted lets the next plot plant right beside it.

say.intro: Okay, so this is Can Place Flowers. A flowerbed is a row of plots. Ones are planted, zeros are empty, and no two flowers can touch. Can we add n more? In one, zero, zero, zero, one, zero, zero, we plant in the middle of the first gap, and at the very end. Two flowers fit, so true.
say.brute: The brute force tries every choice. At each plot, we either skip it, or plant there if both neighbours are empty. We keep the best total and compare it with n. It's correct. But every plot can double the branches. That's exponential. Forty plots already means about a trillion paths.
say.insight: Here's the thing. Planting as early as you can is never a mistake. Why? A flower at the first legal spot only blocks plots to its right. And any plan that planted further right could slide that flower left without losing anything. So one greedy sweep gives the maximum.
say.anim: We start with the flowerbed one zero zero zero one zero zero, needing to plant two flowers. At index one the plot is empty, but its left neighbor is occupied, so left is false. At index two both neighbors are empty, so we plant a flower and count becomes one. At index three the plot is empty but the right neighbor is occupied, so we skip it. At index five both sides are free, satisfying the greedy rule for planting. At index six both neighbors are empty, so we plant another flower, raising count to two. Count now meets the required two flowers, so the function returns true.
say.code: We keep a count. For each empty plot, check both sides. The left edge counts as empty, and so does the right edge. If both sides are clear, we plant now, setting the plot to one. That way, the next plot sees it. Add one to the count. We stop as soon as we have enough. Otherwise, return whether count reached n. That also handles n equal to zero.
say.outro: Linear time, constant space. The pattern is greedy. Take the earliest safe choice, because it never blocks a better answer.

can-place-flowers.title: Can Place Flowers
lineNotes: This defines the Solution class that holds our method for the problem.
The method takes the flowerbed list and the number n of new flowers we need to plant, returning a boolean.
We start a counter called count at zero to track how many flowers we have planted so far.
We store the length of the flowerbed in size so we can check the boundaries easily.
We loop through every plot index in the flowerbed from left to right, planting greedily at the first free spot.
We only consider this plot if it is currently empty, since planted plots cannot be used again.
The left side is fine if we are at the first plot or the plot before this one is empty.
The right side is fine if we are at the last plot or the plot after this one is empty.
If both neighbors are free, this plot is a legal place to plant a flower.
We plant a flower here by setting this plot to one, which blocks the next plot from being used.
We increase count by one because we just placed another flower.
We check whether we have already planted at least n flowers, so we can stop early.
If we have enough flowers, we return true immediately without scanning the rest of the bed.
After the loop ends, we return whether our count reached n, which covers the case where n is zero or we finished scanning.

capacity-to-ship-packages-within-d-days.hook: We cannot search the packages, so we binary search the answer itself.
capacity-to-ship-packages-within-d-days.ask: Packages ship in order, filling the ship each day up to its capacity. Find the smallest capacity that ships everything within the given number of days.
capacity-to-ship-packages-within-d-days.exampleWhy: With capacity 6 the days are 3+2, 2+4, 1+4. Capacity 5 would need four days.

brute.idea: Try every capacity from the heaviest package upward and return the first one that ships in time.
steps: Start at the heaviest package weight
Simulate loading day by day
Fits within the days? Return it
Otherwise try one more
brute.whySlow: S is the total weight. With 50,000 packages of weight 500, that is up to 25 million capacities to test.

optimal.insight: Feasibility is monotonic: if capacity c works, every bigger capacity works. So binary search between max weight and total.
steps: lo = heaviest package, hi = total weight
Try mid with a greedy day count
Fits? Search left half, keep mid
Too many days? Search right of mid

codeNotes.note: Answer must lie in this range
Ship is full: start a new day

pitfalls: The lower bound is max(weights), not 1: a heavier package could never be loaded.
Use lo < hi with hi = mid, or you can loop forever.

say.intro: Okay, so this is Capacity to Ship Packages. A conveyor belt holds packages in a fixed order. Each day, the ship takes as many as fit under its capacity. We want the smallest capacity that finishes in time. For three, two, two, four, one, four in three days, six works. Five would need four days.
say.brute: The brute force tries capacities one by one. It starts at the heaviest package, since anything smaller can't carry it. For each capacity, simulate the days greedily, and stop at the first one that fits. Each simulation is linear. But how many capacities are there? Up to the total weight. That can be tens of millions.
say.insight: Here's the key. Feasibility is monotonic. If a capacity works, any bigger one works too. So the answers look like no, no, no, then yes forever. And we can binary search for that boundary. The search runs from the heaviest package to the total weight. Each probe is the same greedy day count.
say.anim: We start binary search with capacity between four, the heaviest package, and sixteen, the total weight. Testing capacity ten, we simulate loading packages day by day to count ships needed. Load exceeds ten, so we start a new day, needing two shipments so far. Only two days needed for capacity ten, well under three, so we shrink the upper bound to ten. Now testing capacity seven, again tracking load and counting days as weights accumulate. This time three days are needed for capacity seven, still within the limit, so hi shrinks to seven. Testing a smaller capacity five quickly needs four days, which is too many, so lo increases to six. Finally capacity six works in exactly three days, so hi becomes six and lo meets hi at six.
say.code: The answer must lie between the heaviest package and the total. So that's lo and hi. While they differ, mid is the candidate capacity. We count days. When the ship is full, start a new day. If it works, try smaller, so hi becomes mid. If it's too slow, we need more capacity, so lo becomes mid plus one. When they meet, that's the answer.
say.outro: N log S time, constant space. The pattern is binary search on the answer. When a yes or no check is monotonic, search the value.

capacity-to-ship-packages-within-d-days.title: Capacity To Ship Packages Within D Days
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, as the platform expects, to hold the method that solves the shipping problem.
The method takes the package weights in order and the allowed number of days, and returns the smallest workable capacity.
We set low to the heaviest package and high to the total weight, since the answer must lie between them.
We keep searching while low is less than high, narrowing the range until one candidate capacity remains.
We pick the middle capacity of the range as the candidate to test for feasibility.
We start with one day needed and an empty load, then simulate shipping with this candidate capacity.
We go through each package weight in order, since packages must ship in the given sequence.
If adding this package would exceed the candidate capacity, the current day is full and we must start another.
We count one more day as needed because the package will go on a new ship day.
We reset the load to zero so the new day starts empty before adding the package.
We add the current package weight to the day's load, whether on the old day or the new one.
If the days needed fit within the allowed days, this capacity works and a smaller one might also work.
So we move high down to mid, keeping mid as a possible answer.
Otherwise the capacity is too small and fails to ship everything in time.
So we move low up to mid plus one, discarding mid and every smaller capacity.
When low meets high, that value is the smallest feasible capacity, so we return it.

car-pooling.hook: Pick-ups and drop-offs along one road. Record only the changes, then sweep once.
car-pooling.ask: Each trip is passengers, start and end kilometre, on a car driving one way. Riders get off at end before new ones board. Can the car always stay within capacity?
car-pooling.exampleWhy: Between km 3 and 5 both trips ride together: 2 + 3 = 5 passengers, exactly the capacity.

brute.idea: For every kilometre on the route, add up the passengers of every trip that covers it.
steps: Loop over each kilometre
Sum trips where start ≤ km < end
Over capacity? Return False
brute.whySlow: L is the route length. 1,000 trips over 1,000 km means a million trip checks, mostly wasted.

optimal.insight: The load only changes at pick-ups and drop-offs. Mark +num at start and -num at end, then a running sum gives the load.
steps: Make a change array over the route
Add riders at start, subtract at end
Sweep, keeping a running load
Load above capacity? Return False

codeNotes.note: Running sum is the current load

pitfalls: Drop-offs happen before pick-ups: the end is exclusive, so subtract at stop.
If locations are huge, sort the events instead: O(n log n).

say.intro: Okay, so this is Car Pooling. A car drives east. Each trip says how many passengers, where they get on, and where they get off. Can we carry everyone without going over capacity? With capacity five, two riders go from one to five, and three from three to seven. They overlap at exactly five. So true.
say.brute: The brute force checks every kilometre separately. For each point on the road, loop over every trip and add the passengers riding through it. If any point goes over capacity, we fail. It works. But it's trips times road length. And most of those checks see nothing change.
say.insight: Here's the thing. The load only changes at pick up and drop off points. So just record those changes. Plus the passengers at the start, minus them at the end. Then one sweep with a running total rebuilds the load everywhere. That's a difference array. It's the go-to trick for lots of overlapping intervals.
say.anim: We have two trips and a car capacity of five seats. The end time is seven, so we build a change array of eight zeros. For the first trip, two passengers join at stop one and leave at stop five. For the second trip, three passengers join at stop three and leave at stop seven. Now we sweep through, adding each change to a running load value. Load rises to two, then jumps to five after the second pickup, still within capacity. Load drops back to three, then to zero as passengers exit. Load never exceeds five, so the function returns true.
say.code: We make a change array, one slot per kilometre. For each trip, riders board at the start, so add them there. Riders leave at the stop, so subtract them there. Then we walk the array. The running sum is the current load. We check after each stop. If the load ever tops capacity, return false. If the sweep finishes, return true.
say.outro: Time is trips plus road length. The pattern is intervals. Mark where ranges start and end, then sweep once.

car-pooling.title: Car Pooling
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container for the method that answers the car pooling question.
The method takes the list of trips and the car's capacity, and returns whether every trip can be served without overloading.
We find the farthest drop-off kilometre across all trips, so we know how long our timeline array must be.
We build a change array of zeros, one slot per kilometre from zero up to that farthest point.
We loop over each trip, unpacking the passenger count, the start kilometre, and the stop kilometre.
At the start kilometre we add the passengers, since they board there and the load goes up.
At the stop kilometre we subtract the passengers, since they get off there and the load goes down.
We set a running load to zero, representing the number of passengers currently in the car.
We walk through the change array in kilometre order, looking at each net change in passengers.
We add each delta to the load, so the load always reflects who is in the car at that kilometre.
If the load ever exceeds the capacity, the car is overfull at that point.
In that case we return false immediately, because one overload is enough to make the plan impossible.
If we finish the whole route without exceeding capacity, we return true.

check-if-number-is-a-sum-of-powers-of-th.hook: Distinct powers of three? That is just base three with no digit 2.
check-if-number-is-a-sum-of-powers-of-th.ask: Return true if n can be written as a sum of distinct powers of three, like 1, 3, 9, 27, each used at most once.
check-if-number-is-a-sum-of-powers-of-th.exampleWhy: 91 = 81 + 9 + 1, three different powers of three, so the answer is true.

brute.idea: Try every subset of the powers of three up to n and check whether any subset sums exactly to n.
steps: List powers of three up to n
For each power: take it or skip it
Remainder hits zero? Return True
brute.whySlow: Subsets grow as 2 to the number of powers: about n to the 0.63, versus a handful of divisions.

optimal.insight: Using each power at most once means every base-three digit of n must be 0 or 1. A digit 2 is impossible.
steps: Take n % 3 for the lowest base-three digit
A digit of 2 means False
Divide n by 3 and repeat
Reach 0 with no 2? True

pitfalls: Greedy subtracting the largest power also works, but the base-three view explains why.

say.intro: Okay, so this is Check if Number is a Sum of Powers of Three. Can we write n as a sum of different powers of three? Like one, three, nine, twenty seven, each used at most once. Ninety one works. Eighty one plus nine plus one. Twenty one doesn't, because it would need some power twice.
say.brute: The brute force lists every power of three up to n, then searches subsets. For each power, take it or skip it. We succeed if the remainder ever hits exactly zero. That's correct. But the number of subsets doubles with every extra power. So the work grows exponentially.
say.insight: Here's the aha moment. Writing n as a sum of powers of three is just writing n in base three. Each power used at most once? That means every base three digit must be zero or one. So read the digits, lowest first, using modulo three and division. If we ever see a two, the answer is false.
say.anim: We start with n equal to ninety one, checking its base three digits one by one. The first digit is one, which is fine, so we divide n down to thirty. Now the digit is zero, still allowed, and n becomes ten. Next digit is one again, safe, reducing n to three. This digit is zero, passing the check, leaving n as one. The last digit is one, no twos found, and n finally reaches zero. Since no digit was ever two, the loop ends successfully. The function returns true, confirming ninety one is a sum of distinct powers of three.
say.code: We loop while n is above zero, peeling off base three digits. The digit is n modulo three, the lowest digit in base three. If it's a two, we'd need a power twice. So return false. Otherwise, divide n by three to shift to the next digit. When n hits zero with no twos, return true.
say.outro: Logarithmic time, constant space. The pattern is math. When you see distinct powers of b, think base b.

check-if-number-is-a-sum-of-powers-of-th.title: Check if Number is a Sum of Powers of Three
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container the judge expects for our method.
The method checkPowersOfThree takes the integer n and returns a boolean telling us whether n is a sum of distinct powers of three.
We loop while n is greater than zero, peeling off one base three digit of n each pass.
We compute digit as n mod three, which gives the current lowest base three digit of n.
We check whether that digit equals two, since a two would mean some power of three is needed twice.
If the digit is two, we return false immediately because n cannot be built from distinct powers.
We divide n by three using integer division, which drops the lowest digit and moves to the next one.
If the loop finishes, every base three digit was zero or one, so we return true.

cherry-pickup.hook: Two trips look independent, but greedy fails. Send two walkers at once instead.
cherry-pickup.ask: In an n by n grid of cherries, empty cells and thorns, go from top-left to bottom-right moving right or down, then back. Maximise the cherries picked, each counted once.
cherry-pickup.exampleWhy: Go down, down, right, right for 4 cherries, then come back through the top for the last 1.

brute.idea: Enumerate every right-or-down path, try every pair of paths, and count the cherries on their union of cells.
steps: List all monotone paths avoiding thorns
Try every pair as there and back
Count cherries on the union of cells
Keep the maximum
brute.whySlow: The path count grows like 4 to the n: a 15 by 15 grid has millions of paths, squared.

optimal.insight: The return trip is just a second forward walk. Move both walkers together: after k steps, r1 + c1 = r2 + c2, so three numbers define the state.
steps: State (r1, c1, r2); c2 is implied
Collect both cells, once if they coincide
Try the four combined moves, memoised
Thorn or off-grid is minus infinity

pitfalls: Greedy best first trip, then best second trip, is wrong; the trips must be planned together.
If both walkers share a cell, add its cherry only once.

say.intro: Okay, so this is Cherry Pickup. We cross an n by n grid from top left to bottom right, moving only right or down. Then we come back, moving left or up. Thorns block us, and each cherry counts once. Here, the best plan grabs four cherries going down the left side. Then one more on the way home. Five.
say.brute: The brute force lists every right or down path that dodges thorns. Then it tries every pair. One is the trip out, and the other, reversed, is the trip back. For each pair, count the cherries on the combined cells. It's correct. But the number of paths explodes exponentially, and we're squaring it.
say.insight: Two ideas here. First, the trip back is just another forward path. So imagine two walkers starting together. Second, move them in lockstep. After the same number of steps, row plus column is equal for both. So the state is just r one, c one and r two. Each state tries four combined moves. Memoization makes it cubic.
say.anim: We start with a three by three grid, including a thorny cell worth negative one. Two walkers begin together at row zero, column zero, tracked by r1, c1, and r2. The walkers advance step by step, checking grid values to avoid thorns and invalid cells. Some paths hit the edge or a thorn, returning negative infinity to be ignored. Deeper recursive calls return small totals like two and three as cherries get collected. Combining results upward, got builds up to four cherries along one promising path. Finally the two walkers finish together, both reaching the last cell successfully. The recursion returns five, the maximum cherries collected, confirming the final answer is five.
say.code: Dp takes r one, c one and r two. The same step count fixes c two. Off the grid or on a thorn, that state is dead, so return minus infinity. At the bottom right, return its cherry. Otherwise take both cells, but if they're the same cell, count the cherry once. Then add the best of the four combined moves. Finally, no path means zero.
say.outro: Cubic time and space. The pattern is two dimensional dynamic programming, with two walkers in lockstep so their states merge.

cherry-pickup.title: Cherry Pickup
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container LeetCode expects for the cherry pickup answer.
The cherryPickup method takes the grid and returns the largest number of cherries both trips can collect.
We store the grid size as n, since the grid is square.
We cache results so each state of the two walkers is only computed once.
The helper dp takes the first walker's row and column and the second walker's row, describing the whole state.
Both walkers have taken the same number of steps, so the second walker's column equals the first's row plus column minus its own row.
If either walker has stepped off the grid at the bottom or right edge, the state is invalid.
We return negative infinity there so this path is never chosen over a valid one.
If either walker stands on a thorn, that path is blocked.
Again we return negative infinity to rule out the blocked path.
If the first walker has reached the bottom-right corner, the second has too, since they move in lockstep.
We return that corner's value, because there is nothing further to collect.
We start by collecting the cherries on the first walker's current cell.
If the walkers are on different cells, we can pick the second walker's cell too.
Only when the cells differ do we add the second walker's cherries, so a shared cell is never counted twice.
We try all four moves, each walker going down or right, and take the best result.
The four combinations are covered by these remaining calls, with the second line finishing the options for the second walker.
We return the cherries collected here plus the best future total.
The answer is the start state's result, clamped to zero when no valid path exists.

circular-array-loop.hook: A circular array is a hidden linked list. Floyd's slow and fast pointers find the loop.
circular-array-loop.ask: Each value says how far to jump, forward or backward, around a circular array. Is there a cycle longer than one whose jumps all go the same direction?
circular-array-loop.exampleWhy: Index 0 jumps to 2, then 3, then back to 0. All jumps are forward, length 3.

brute.idea: From every start, follow jumps while the direction stays the same, remembering visited indices; a revisit means a valid cycle.
steps: For each start, walk the jumps
Stop on a direction change or self-loop
Revisit an index? Cycle found
brute.whySlow: Each start may walk the whole array again: 5,000 indices means up to 25 million jumps.

optimal.insight: Each index points to exactly one next index, like a linked list. Use slow and fast pointers, and zero out paths proven dead.
steps: From each live index, run slow and fast
Stop if fast meets a sign change
slow meets fast: cycle, unless a self-loop
No cycle: zero out that whole path

codeNotes.note: Same direction for the fast steps

pitfalls: A self-loop (jump lands on itself) has length 1 and must be rejected.
In other languages, fix negative modulo with ((x % n) + n) % n.

say.intro: Okay, so this is Circular Array Loop. Each number says how far to jump. Forward if positive, backward if negative, wrapping around. We need a cycle longer than one, all in the same direction. In two, minus one, one, two, two, index zero goes to two, then three, then back to zero. All forward. So true.
say.brute: The brute force starts a walk from every index. It follows the jumps and remembers where it's been. It stops if the direction flips, or an index jumps to itself. Landing on a visited index means a valid cycle. But each start can rewalk most of the array. So it's quadratic.
say.insight: Here's the thing. Every index has exactly one next index. So the array is really a linked list in disguise. That means slow and fast pointers can find a loop in constant space. And when a walk fails, every index on that path is dead. So we zero it out and never walk it again. Now the total work is linear.
say.anim: We start with the array two, negative one, one, two, two, and compute its length. At index zero, value two is nonzero, so we set slow and fast pointers moving forward. Slow sits at zero while fast jumps ahead to index two, both following same sign moves. Slow and fast aren't equal yet, so slow advances to two and fast advances to three. Now slow is two and fast is zero, still matching signs, so the loop keeps going. They aren't equal again, so slow moves to three and fast moves back to three. Slow and fast both land on index three, meeting inside a real cycle. Since index three doesn't point to itself, this confirms a true cycle, returning true.
say.code: A helper computes the next index, and Python's modulo wraps negatives correctly. For each live index, slow starts there, fast one jump ahead. We keep going while fast's next steps stay the same direction. If they meet, that's a loop, unless it's length one. That doesn't count. Otherwise, slow moves once and fast moves two jumps. After a failure, mark the dead path with zeros.
say.outro: Linear time, constant space. The pattern is linked lists. When each element points to one next, slow and fast pointers find the cycle.

circular-array-loop.title: Circular Array Loop
lineNotes: We define a Solution class that holds the method for this problem.
The method takes the array of jumps and returns true if a valid circular loop exists.
We store the length of nums as n, which we need for wrapping around the circle.
We define a helper that gives the next index reached from index i.
It adds the jump at i to i and wraps with modulo n, which also handles negative jumps.
We try every index as a possible starting point for a loop.
If the value here is zero, this index was already proven to be a dead end.
So we skip it and move on to the next starting index.
We start slow at i and fast one step ahead, ready for the tortoise and hare walk.
We keep going only while the starting direction matches both fast steps, so the path never changes direction.
If slow meets fast, we have found a cycle and must check its length.
If the next step from slow is slow itself, the cycle has length one, which is not allowed.
So we break out of the loop for this start without accepting it.
Otherwise the cycle is longer than one and all one direction, so we return true.
Slow moves forward by one step along the path.
Fast moves forward by two steps along the path.
After the walk fails, we remember the direction of the starting value as sign.
We begin a cleanup walk at the starting index j.
We continue while the current value still points in the same direction as sign.
We save the next index first, since we are about to erase the current value.
We set this value to zero to mark it as a proven dead end.
We move to the saved next index and keep clearing the path.
If no start index produced a valid loop, we return false.

concatenate-non-zero-digits-and-multiply.hook: Squeeze out the zeros, then multiply by the digit sum. Pure arithmetic does it.
concatenate-non-zero-digits-and-multiply.ask: Drop every zero digit from n and read what is left as a number x. Return x times the sum of its digits.
concatenate-non-zero-digits-and-multiply.exampleWhy: Non-zero digits give x = 1234, their sum is 10, and 1234 · 10 = 12340.

brute.idea: Convert n to a string, filter out the zeros, join the rest back into a number, and sum the digits separately.
steps: Turn n into a string
Keep the non-zero characters
Join them into x, sum them
Return x times the sum
brute.whySlow: Same linear time in the digit count d; it just builds temporary strings and lists that arithmetic avoids.

optimal.insight: Peel digits off with % 10. Each non-zero digit goes into the next place of x: 1s, then 10s, then 100s.
steps: Take the last digit with n % 10
Non-zero? Add it at the current place
Raise the place by 10, add to the sum
Drop the digit with n // 10

codeNotes.note: Next slot in x: ones first

pitfalls: Only advance place for non-zero digits, or zeros sneak back into x.
n = 0 gives x = 0 and sum 0, so the answer is 0.

say.intro: So, Concatenate Non-Zero Digits and Multiply by Sum. Drop every zero digit of n, and read what's left as x. Then return x times its digit sum. For one zero two zero three zero zero four, x is one thousand two hundred thirty four. The digit sum is ten. So the answer is twelve thousand three hundred forty.
say.brute: The quick approach uses strings. Turn n into text, keep the non-zero characters, and join them back into a number. Separately, add them up. That's linear in the number of digits, and honestly fine. The only downside? It builds temporary strings and lists. Plain arithmetic needs none of that.
say.insight: Here's the thing. We can do it all with arithmetic. Peel off the last digit with modulo ten. If it's not zero, drop it into the next free place of x. Ones first, then tens, then hundreds. And add it to a running sum. Zeros just get skipped. So the place value only grows when we keep a digit.
say.anim: We start with n as 10203004, and x and digit sum both set to zero. The last digit, 4, is nonzero, so it gets added into x at the ones place. X becomes 4, digit sum becomes 4, and place moves up to ten. The next digit is zero, so it gets skipped entirely, no update happens. Digit 3 is nonzero, added at the hundreds place, making x 34 and sum 7. Digit 2 is nonzero too, placed at the next slot, giving x 234 and sum 9. Finally digit 1 is added, making x 1234 and digit sum 10 total. Multiplying x 1234 by digit sum 10 gives the final answer, 12340.
say.code: X and the sum start at zero. Place starts at one, the next slot in x, ones first. While n is positive, d is the last digit of n. If d isn't zero, we place it, adding d times place to x. Zeros are skipped. Place only grows on non-zero digits, so it's multiplied by ten there. Either way, divide n by ten to drop the digit. Return x times the sum.
say.outro: Linear in the digits, constant space. The pattern is math. Peel digits with modulo and division, no strings needed.

concatenate-non-zero-digits-and-multiply.title: Concatenate Non-Zero Digits and Multiply by Sum I
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container the problem expects for our method.
The method sumAndMultiply takes the integer n and will return the product of the compacted number and its digit sum.
We start x at zero, and it will hold the number built from the non-zero digits.
We start digit_sum at zero to accumulate the sum of the non-zero digits as we see them.
We set place to one, meaning the next kept digit goes into the ones position of x.
We loop while n is greater than zero, so we process every digit from right to left.
We take n modulo ten to peel off the current last digit and call it d.
We check whether d is nonzero, since zero digits must be skipped entirely.
We add d times place into x, putting this digit in the next open position.
We multiply place by ten so the next kept digit lands one position further left.
We add d to digit_sum, since this nonzero digit counts toward the total.
We divide n by ten with integer division to drop the last digit and move on.
Finally we return x times digit_sum, which is the required product.

concatenated-words.hook: Word Break, run once per word, with the dictionary being the list itself.
concatenated-words.ask: Given unique words, return every word that can be built by joining at least two shorter words from the same list.
concatenated-words.exampleWhy: catdog splits into cat and dog, both in the list. cat and dog cannot be split.

brute.idea: For each word, recursively try every prefix found in the set, then split the rest, counting the pieces.
steps: Try each prefix of the word
Prefix in the set? Recurse on the rest
Empty rest with 2+ pieces: success
brute.whySlow: No memo: a word like aaaa...ab with 30 letters retries the same suffixes about a billion times.

optimal.insight: This is Word Break per word: dp[i] is true if the first i letters split into words. Just forbid the whole word itself.
steps: Put every word in a hash set
For each word, dp[0] = True
dp[i] true if dp[j] and word[j:i] is a word
Skip the piece that is the entire word
dp[n] true? It is concatenated

codeNotes.note: First i letters split into words

pitfalls: Forgetting to exclude the word itself makes every word count as concatenated.
L³ counts slicing and hashing substrings; a trie can cut that down.

say.intro: Okay, so this is Concatenated Words. We get a list of unique words. Return the ones made by gluing together at least two shorter words from the same list. With cat, dog and catdog, only catdog counts. It splits into cat and dog. The short ones can't be split at all.
say.brute: The brute force treats each word as a puzzle. Try every prefix. If the prefix is in the list, split the rest recursively, counting pieces. Reach the end with at least two pieces, and it's a hit. But without memory, the same suffixes get retried over and over. That's exponential in the word length.
say.insight: Here's the thing. This is just Word Break, once per word. Let dp of i mean the first i letters can be split into words. Dp of i is true if some earlier dp of j is true, and the slice from j to i is a word. Just one twist. A word can't match itself as a single piece.
say.anim: We start with three words, building a set for fast lookups. Checking cat first, we set up a dp array tracking valid splits of its letters. We scan every split point, but none form cat from smaller dictionary words. Dp at the end stays false, so cat alone isn't a concatenation. Dog gets the same treatment, and it also fails to split into smaller words. Now catdog gets its own dp array of size seven to test splits. Dp becomes true at index three, meaning cat matches the first part. Dp at index six becomes true, since dog completes the match after cat. Catdog gets appended, and the final answer returned is catdog.
say.code: All the words go into a set, so lookups are instant. For each word, dp has one slot per prefix length. The empty prefix is always splittable, so it starts true. For each end i, we try each start j. A word can't use itself as one piece. If dp of j is true and the slice is a word, the first i letters split into words. If the whole word splits, keep it.
say.outro: Polynomial per word, not exponential. The pattern is one dimensional dynamic programming. Word Break, run on each word against the list.

concatenated-words.title: Concatenated Words
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container LeetCode expects for our method.
This method takes the list of words and returns the list of words that are concatenations of other words.
We put all words into a set so checking whether a piece is a word is fast.
We start an empty result list to collect the words that qualify as concatenated.
We loop over each word in the list and test it separately with word break logic.
We store the length of the current word as n for use in the table.
We create a table dp of size n plus one, all false, where dp at i means the first i letters can be split.
We set dp at zero to true, since an empty prefix is trivially splittable and gives us a starting point.
We loop i over each prefix end position from one up to n.
We loop j over every possible split point before i, so the piece runs from j to i.
A split works if the prefix up to j is splittable, the piece is a word, and it is not the whole word itself.
When such a split is found, we mark dp at i as true.
We break out early, since one valid split is enough for this prefix.
After filling the table, we check whether the full word can be split into smaller words.
If so, we add the word to our result list.
Finally we return the list of all concatenated words.

construct-binary-tree-from-preorder-and-.hook: Preorder tells you the root. Postorder tells you where the left subtree ends.
construct-binary-tree-from-preorder-and-.ask: Given preorder and postorder traversals of a binary tree with distinct values, rebuild any tree that matches both.
construct-binary-tree-from-preorder-and-.exampleWhy: 1 is the root, 2 starts the left subtree, and 2 sits at index 2 in postorder: left size 3.

brute.idea: Recurse on sliced copies: find the left child's position in postorder with a linear search, then split both arrays.
steps: Root is preorder[0]
Search postorder for preorder[1]
Slice both arrays, recurse left and right
brute.whySlow: Every call scans and copies its arrays: a skewed tree of 3,000 nodes means millions of copied values.

optimal.insight: The node after the root in preorder is the left child, and in postorder it closes the left subtree. Its index gives the size.
steps: Map each value to its postorder index
Root = preorder[pre_lo]
Left size = index of preorder[pre_lo + 1] - post_lo + 1
Recurse with index ranges, no slicing

codeNotes.match: post_idx = {v: i for i, v in enumerate(postorder)}

codeNotes.note: Left child ends the left subtree

codeNotes.match: root.right = build(pre_lo + left_size + 1, pre_hi, post_lo + left_size)

pitfalls: A one-child node is ambiguous; any valid tree is accepted, so treat it as left.
Check pre_lo == pre_hi before reading preorder[pre_lo + 1].

say.intro: So, Construct Binary Tree from Preorder and Postorder Traversal. We get both traversals of a tree with distinct values, and rebuild a tree that fits. Preorder is one, two, four, five, three, six, seven. Postorder is four, five, two, six, seven, three, one. The result is a perfect tree, one on top, two and three below.
say.brute: The brute force recurses on copies. The root is the first preorder value. The next preorder value is the left child. So find it in postorder, and its position gives the left subtree's size. Then slice both arrays and recurse. Every call searches and copies. So a lopsided tree costs quadratic time.
say.insight: Here's the thing. All we need is the left subtree's size, and a hash map gives it instantly. Preorder lists the left child right after the root. And postorder finishes the left subtree exactly at that child. So the child's postorder index tells us where the left subtree ends. Then recurse with index ranges, not copies.
say.anim: We build a lookup mapping each postorder value to its index, for fast size checks. We start building the whole tree, root 1, spanning preorder indices 0 through 6. Left size comes out to 3, telling us how many nodes form the left subtree. Recursing, we build node 2 as root, then find its own left subtree is just size 1. Node 4 has no children, so it becomes a leaf and returns immediately. Node 2 then builds its right side, giving node 5 as its only child. Back at the top, we now build the right subtree of root 1, starting with node 3. Nodes 6 and 7 are built as leaves under node 3, completing its children. The recursion finishes, reconstructing the tree as 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7.
say.code: A hash map maps each value to its postorder position, so lookups are instant. Build takes a preorder range and a postorder start. Preorder starts with the root. A single node is a leaf. Otherwise, the left child's postorder index tells us where the left subtree ends. So we build the left part. And the rest is the right subtree.
say.outro: Linear time and space. The pattern is trees. One traversal gives the root, the other measures the subtrees.

construct-binary-tree-from-preorder-and-.title: Construct Binary Tree from Preorder and Postorder Traversal
lineNotes: We define a Solution class that holds the method for rebuilding the tree.
The method takes the preorder and postorder lists and returns the root of the rebuilt tree.
We map each value to its index in postorder so we can look up positions in constant time.
We define a recursive helper build that takes a preorder range and the starting postorder index of the same subtree.
If the preorder low index passes the high index, the subtree is empty.
In that empty case we return nothing, which becomes a missing child.
The first preorder value in the range is the subtree root, so we create a node for it.
If the range holds just one element, the node is a leaf.
We return that leaf node right away since it has no children.
The next preorder value is the left child, and its postorder index minus the start plus one gives the left subtree size.
We build the left subtree from the preorder elements right after the root, using the computed left size and the same postorder start.
We build the right subtree from the remaining preorder elements, with the postorder start shifted past the left subtree.
We return the finished root node for this subtree.
We start the recursion over the whole preorder range with postorder starting at zero, and return the full tree.

contiguous-array.hook: Turn zeros into minus ones, and equal counts become a zero-sum subarray.
contiguous-array.ask: Given an array of 0s and 1s, return the length of the longest contiguous subarray with as many 0s as 1s.
contiguous-array.exampleWhy: The last six values, three 1s then three 0s, balance out. No longer window balances.

brute.idea: Check every start and end, keeping running counts of 0s and 1s, and record the longest balanced window.
steps: Fix a start index
Extend the end, updating the counts
Counts equal? Update the best length
brute.whySlow: Every start rescans to the end: 100,000 bits means about 5 billion window checks.

optimal.insight: Keep a balance: +1 for a 1, -1 for a 0. Two equal balances mean the stretch between them is balanced.
steps: Running balance starts at 0, seen at index -1
Add +1 or -1 for each value
Seen this balance before? Window from there
Otherwise record its first index

pitfalls: Store only the first index of each balance; overwriting it shrinks the windows.
Seeding balance 0 at index -1 handles windows that start at index 0.

say.intro: Okay, so this is Contiguous Array. We get zeros and ones. We want the longest stretch with as many zeros as ones. In zero, one, one, one, one, one, zero, zero, zero, the last six values balance perfectly. Three ones, then three zeros. So the answer is six.
say.brute: The brute force tries every window. Fix a start, then extend the end one step at a time. Keep a running difference. Plus one for a one, minus one for a zero. Whenever it's zero, the window is balanced, so record its length. It's correct. But every start rescans everything after it. That's quadratic.
say.insight: Here's the trick. Treat zeros as minus one, and keep a running balance. When is a window balanced? Exactly when the balance at its end matches the balance just before its start. So remember the first index where each balance showed up. Whenever a balance repeats, the stretch since its first sighting is balanced, and as long as possible.
say.anim: We start with balance zero and a map recording balance negative one at index negative one. At index zero we see a zero, so balance drops to negative one, already seen, nothing new stored. At index one we see a one, balance returns to zero, matching the start, giving length two. Balance keeps rising through index four as ones push it up to four, storing each new balance. Now zeros arrive, balance drops back to three, matching an earlier balance, giving best length four. Balance drops to two, matching index three's balance, stretching best length to six. Balance drops to one, matching index two's balance, but length six still stands as best. The function returns six, the longest contiguous subarray with equal zeros and ones.
say.code: The map starts with balance zero at index minus one, before any element. For each value, ones push the balance up and zeros push it down. Have we seen this balance earlier? Then the stretch between them is balanced. So update best. If not, record this index. We keep only the earliest index, because that gives the longest window.
say.outro: Linear time and space. The pattern is arrays and hashing. Prefix sums plus first sightings find the longest balanced stretch.

contiguous-array.title: Contiguous Array
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, as the problem platform expects, to hold our method.
The method findMaxLength takes a list of zeros and ones and returns the longest balanced stretch length.
We create a map of first positions, seeding balance zero at index negative one so stretches starting at the beginning count.
We start both the running balance and the best length at zero.
We loop through the array, getting each index i and its value x.
We add one to the balance for a one and subtract one for a zero.
If we have seen this balance before, the stretch since then has equal zeros and ones.
We compare the current best with the distance from that first occurrence to now, keeping the larger.
Otherwise, this balance is brand new, so we handle it in the following line.
We record the current index as the first place this balance appeared, since earliest positions give the longest stretches.
After scanning everything, we return the best length found, which is zero if no balanced stretch exists.

convert-sorted-array-to-binary-search-tr.hook: Sorted array in, balanced tree out. The middle element is always the root.
convert-sorted-array-to-binary-search-tr.ask: Given a strictly increasing array, build a height-balanced binary search tree containing all its values.
convert-sorted-array-to-binary-search-tr.exampleWhy: 0 is the middle, so it is the root. -10 and -3 go left, 5 and 9 go right.

brute.idea: Recurse on sliced copies: pick the middle value as the root, then slice the left and right halves into new lists.
steps: Pick the middle as root
Slice the left half into a new list
Slice the right half, recurse on both
brute.whySlow: Correct and balanced, but every level copies all n values again: about n log n wasted copying.

optimal.insight: The middle splits the values into two halves whose sizes differ by at most one, so the tree stays balanced. Pass indices, not copies.
steps: helper(lo, hi) builds from nums[lo..hi]
Empty range returns None
Root is the middle value
Left from lo..mid-1, right from mid+1..hi

pitfalls: Either middle works for even lengths; both give a balanced tree.
Slicing looks clean but quietly copies the array at every level.

say.intro: So, Convert Sorted Array to Binary Search Tree. We turn a sorted array into a height balanced search tree. That means the two sides of every node differ in height by at most one. For minus ten, minus three, zero, five, nine, zero becomes the root. The two smaller values go left, the two larger go right.
say.brute: The simplest version recurses on copies. Take the middle value as the root. Slice the left half into a new list, slice the right half, and recurse on each. The tree comes out correct and balanced. So what's the catch? The slicing. Every level copies all n values again. That's n log n instead of linear.
say.insight: Here's the thing. The middle element is always the right root. It splits what's left into two halves whose sizes differ by at most one. So recursing on each half keeps every subtree balanced. And the array never changes. So we can pass a low and high index instead of copying. Each value gets touched once.
say.anim: We start building a balanced tree from the sorted array negative ten, negative three, zero, five, nine. The middle index two picks value zero as the root, splitting the array evenly. For the left half, mid becomes one, making negative three the next node. Going further left, mid is zero, so negative ten becomes a leaf with no children. Back at negative three, its right side is empty, so that subtree is complete. Now the right half starting at index three builds around nine as its local root. Within that, mid three gives five, which sits as nine's left child with no right side. All subtrees combine into the final balanced tree, rooted at zero as expected.
say.code: Build takes a low and a high index. If low passes high, the range is empty, so there's no node. Otherwise, the middle value becomes the root. Smaller values go on the left, so the left child is built from low to mid minus one. Larger values go on the right, built from mid plus one to high. We start with the whole array.
say.outro: Linear time, logarithmic stack space. The pattern is trees. Divide and conquer on a sorted range, and always pick the middle.

convert-sorted-array-to-binary-search-tr.title: Convert Sorted Array to Binary Search Tree
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container the interview platform expects for our method.
The method sortedArrayToBST takes the sorted list nums and returns the root of a balanced binary search tree.
We define a helper called build that constructs a subtree from the slice of nums between indices lo and hi.
If lo has moved past hi, the slice is empty, so there is nothing to build here.
In that empty case we return None, which becomes a missing child in the tree.
We pick mid as the upper middle index, so the two halves differ in size by at most one.
We create a new tree node holding the middle value, which becomes the root of this subtree.
We recursively build the left subtree from the indices before mid, since those values are smaller.
We recursively build the right subtree from the indices after mid, since those values are larger.
We return this root so the caller can attach it as a child or use it as the final tree.
We start the recursion over the whole array, from index zero to the last index, and return the finished tree.

convert-sorted-list-to-binary-search-tre.hook: No random access in a list, so build the tree in order and walk the list once.
convert-sorted-list-to-binary-search-tre.ask: Given the head of a sorted singly linked list, build a height-balanced binary search tree containing its values.
convert-sorted-list-to-binary-search-tre.exampleWhy: 0 is the middle node, so it becomes the root, with smaller values left and larger right.

brute.idea: Find the middle with slow and fast pointers, cut the list there, make it the root, and recurse on both halves.
steps: Slow and fast find the middle node
Cut the list before the middle
Middle is root, recurse on each half
brute.whySlow: Each level walks every node again to find the middles: 20,000 nodes means about 300,000 hops.

optimal.insight: An in-order traversal visits values in sorted order, exactly the list order. Build the left subtree first, then take the current list node.
steps: Count the nodes
build(lo, hi) first builds the left half
The current list node becomes the root
Advance the list, then build the right half

codeNotes.note: Next list value is this root

pitfalls: Copying the list into an array is O(n) time too, but costs O(n) extra space.
The left subtree must be built before reading the current list node.

say.intro: So, Convert Sorted List to Binary Search Tree. This time the sorted values come in a singly linked list. We still need a height balanced search tree. For minus ten, minus three, zero, five, nine, the middle node, zero, becomes the root. Minus three and minus ten go left. Nine and five go right.
say.brute: The brute force finds the middle every time. Slow and fast pointers walk the list. The middle becomes the root, and we cut the list just before it. Then recurse on each half. It works. But each level walks every node again just to find its middle. So it costs n log n.
say.insight: Here's the thing. An in order walk of a search tree visits values in sorted order. That's exactly the list order. So build the tree in order.
