First, build the whole left subtree, which uses up the smaller values. Then the current list node becomes the root. Then build the right subtree. The list pointer only moves forward, once per node.
say.anim: We start with the sorted list negative ten, negative three, zero, five, nine. The code first walks the whole list, counting nodes until size reaches five. Now recursion builds the tree, always finishing the left half before using the current node. With lo zero and hi four, mid becomes two, so it recurses left first. Negative ten becomes a leaf, since its range has no room on either side. Negative three gets built next, with negative ten attached as its left child. Zero becomes the root, taking negative three's subtree as its left branch. After building the right side similarly, the final balanced tree root is zero.
say.code: We count the nodes once, up front. A shared pointer, cur, starts at the head. Build takes an index range, and an empty range returns nothing. We pick the middle. The left subtree goes first, consuming the smaller values. Then the next list value is this root. Each node is consumed exactly once, so we advance cur. The right subtree takes what remains.
say.outro: Linear time, logarithmic stack. The pattern is trees. An in order build lets a sorted list fill the tree, no random access needed.

convert-sorted-list-to-binary-search-tre.title: Convert Sorted List to Binary Search Tree
lineNotes: We define a Solution class that holds the method for this problem.
The method takes the head of a sorted linked list and returns the root of a balanced binary search tree.
We start a counter called size at zero to count the list nodes.
We set node to head so we can walk the list without losing the head.
We loop as long as node points to a real list node.
Each time through, we add one to size to count this node.
We move node to the next node in the list.
We store a shared pointer cur at the head, which tracks the next list value to consume.
We define a helper build that constructs a balanced tree from the index range lo to hi.
If lo is greater than hi, the range is empty, so there is nothing to build.
In that empty case we return None to mark a missing child.
We pick mid as the upper middle index, which keeps the tree height balanced.
We recursively build the left subtree first, which consumes list nodes in sorted order up to the middle.
Now cur sits at the middle value, so we create the root tree node from it.
We advance cur to the next list node, since that value is now used.
We attach the already built left subtree to the root's left side.
We build the right subtree from the remaining indices and attach it as the root's right child.
We return the finished root of this subtree to the caller.
We start the whole process by building a tree over indices zero through size minus one.

count-and-say.hook: Read the previous term out loud. That is literally the whole rule.
count-and-say.ask: Start from "1". Each next term describes the previous one: for each run of equal digits, write the run length then the digit. Return the nth term.
count-and-say.exampleWhy: 1, 11, 21, 1211, then 1211 reads as one 1, one 2, two 1s: 111221.

brute.idea: Recurse down to term one, then describe each returned string by appending run counts with string concatenation.
steps: Get term n - 1 recursively
Scan it for runs of equal digits
Append count then digit to a string
brute.whySlow: Same work as the loop, but the recursion uses n stack frames and repeated string += can copy.

optimal.insight: Each term is a run-length encoding of the last. Iterate n - 1 times, scanning runs with two pointers and joining a list.
steps: Start with "1"
Scan runs with a start and an end pointer
Append count and digit to a parts list
Join and repeat n - 1 times

codeNotes.match: while j < len(s) and s[j] == s[i]:

pitfalls: Count before digit: 21 means one 2, one 1, not two 1s.
L is the final length; terms grow about 30 percent each step.

say.intro: Okay, so this is Count and Say. The sequence starts with one. Each next term describes the one before, out loud. One is one one. That's two ones, so two one. Then one two, one one. Read that aloud and you get one one, one two, two ones. So term five is one one one two two one.
say.brute: The direct approach is recursive. Ask for the previous term. Scan it for runs of equal digits. For each run, append its length and its digit to an output string. It's correct, and the work matches any method. So what's wrong? A stack of n recursive calls. And repeated string concatenation, which can copy the string again and again.
say.insight: Here's the thing. Each term is just the run length encoding of the term before. So let's iterate instead. Start from one, and repeat n minus one times. Scan the current string with two pointers. The left one marks where a run starts. The right one walks to its end. Collect each count and digit in a list, then join once.
say.anim: We start with the string one, the seed for counting and saying. Scanning the run of ones, we find two of them, giving the part two one. Joining parts makes the new string two one, representing two ones. Now scanning two one, we count one two then one one, building parts two one, one one. The next pass turns that into one two one one, describing the previous run lengths. Scanning one two one one finds runs of two ones, one two, and one one. These parts join into the string one one one two two one. After four iterations, the final answer returned is one one one two two one.
say.code: S starts as term one. We describe the term n minus one times. Parts collects the pieces. For each start i, j walks forward to extend the current run while the digit matches. Then we say the count, then the digit, and jump i to j. We join once per term, giving the next term. Finally, return s.
say.outro: Linear in the total length produced. The pattern is arrays and hashing, with two pointers doing run length encoding.

count-and-say.title: Count and Say
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container the problem expects for our method.
The method countAndSay takes n and returns the nth term of the sequence as a string.
We start with s as the string one, which is the first term.
We repeat the encoding step n minus one times, since the first term is already built.
For each round we create an empty list called parts to collect the run descriptions.
We set i to zero so our scan begins at the first character of the current term.
We loop while i is still inside the string, so every run gets processed.
We set j equal to i so j can advance to find the end of this run.
We keep moving j forward while it stays in range and the digit matches the one at i.
Each matching digit pushes j one step to the right, extending the run.
We append the run length, j minus i, followed by the digit, to describe this run.
We jump i to j, so the next run starts right after the one just handled.
We join all the parts into one string, which becomes the next term.
After all rounds finish, we return s as the nth term.

count-complete-tree-nodes.hook: Count a complete tree faster than visiting every node, using perfect subtrees.
count-complete-tree-nodes.ask: Given the root of a complete binary tree, return how many nodes it has, in less than linear time.
count-complete-tree-nodes.exampleWhy: Levels hold 1, 2 and 4 nodes, and the last level has 3 more: 10 in total.

brute.idea: Ignore completeness and visit every node with a recursive traversal, adding one per node.
steps: Empty tree counts 0
Count left subtree and right subtree
Add one for the root
brute.whySlow: It visits all n nodes. The problem explicitly asks for better than O(n).

optimal.insight: If the leftmost and rightmost depths match, the subtree is perfect: 2^h - 1 nodes, no traversal needed. At least one child is always perfect.
steps: Measure depth along the left edge
Measure depth along the right edge
Equal? Return 2^h - 1
Otherwise 1 + count(left) + count(right)

codeNotes.note: One side is perfect, so cheap

pitfalls: Say why it is log squared: log n levels of recursion, each measuring log n depth.
A binary search on the last level also gives O(log² n).

say.intro: Okay, so this is Count Complete Tree Nodes. In a complete binary tree, every level is full except maybe the last, which fills from the left. We need to count nodes faster than visiting each one. For values one to ten, the top three levels hold seven nodes. The last level adds three. That's ten.
say.brute: The brute force ignores the shape. Count the left subtree, count the right subtree, add one for the root. It's short and correct, and it works for any binary tree. But it visits every node. That's linear. And the problem explicitly asks for better than linear.
say.insight: Here's the aha. Walk down the leftmost edge and the rightmost edge. If the depths match, the subtree is perfect. A perfect tree of height h has two to the h, minus one, nodes. So return that instantly. If they differ, recurse. Now, notice this. In a complete tree, at least one child is always perfect. So each level costs just one more depth walk.
say.anim: We start at the root node 1, checking if the tree is empty before measuring depths. Walking left from node 1, left height reaches 4 down through nodes 2, 4, and 8. Walking right from node 1, right height only reaches 3, so this subtree isn't perfect. Recursing into node 2, its left height is 3 but right height is only 2, again unequal. At node 4, left and right heights both equal 2, meaning this subtree is perfect. At node 5, left height is 2 but right height is only 1, so we recurse further. Node 10 is a single leaf, a perfect tree of height 1, giving one node. Combining all subtree counts, the algorithm returns the final total of 10 nodes.
say.code: An empty tree has zero nodes. We walk the left edge, following left children, to get one height. Then we walk the right edge. If the edges match, it's a perfect subtree. So two to the h, minus one, nodes, instantly. Otherwise, return one plus both subtree counts. One side is always perfect, so that call is cheap.
say.outro: Log squared time, logarithmic space. The pattern is trees. Use the shape, and count perfect subtrees with a formula.

count-complete-tree-nodes.title: Count Complete Tree Nodes
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which holds the method that counts nodes in a complete binary tree.
The countNodes method takes the root of the tree and returns the total number of nodes as an integer.
First we check whether the root is empty, since an empty tree needs special handling.
If there is no root, we return zero because an empty tree has no nodes.
We start left height at zero and set node to the root to begin walking down the left edge.
We loop as long as node exists, stepping down the leftmost path of the tree.
Each step down the left side adds one to the left height.
We move node to its left child, continuing toward the bottom of the leftmost path.
Now we reset right height to zero and set node back to the root for the right edge walk.
We loop again while node exists, this time following the rightmost path.
Each step along the right side adds one to the right height.
We move node to its right child, continuing down the rightmost path.
If the left and right heights match, the tree is perfect, so we can skip traversing it.
A perfect tree of that height has two to the height minus one nodes, computed quickly with a bit shift.
Otherwise we count the root plus both subtrees recursively, and one of them is perfect so it resolves immediately.

count-elements-with-maximum-frequency.hook: Count everything once, and keep the running answer as the leader changes.
count-elements-with-maximum-frequency.ask: Find the highest frequency of any value in nums, then return the total number of elements whose value has that frequency.
count-elements-with-maximum-frequency.exampleWhy: 1 and 2 each appear twice, the maximum. Together they make up 4 elements.

brute.idea: For each element, scan the whole array to count its frequency, then sum the elements that hit the maximum.
steps: For each element, count matches by scanning
Track the highest count
Second pass: add elements with that count
brute.whySlow: Each element rescans the array: 100,000 values means about 10 billion comparisons.

optimal.insight: Update a hash map as you go. A new record resets the total; tying the record adds that frequency again.
steps: Increment the count of x
Beats the max? Max and total become f
Ties the max? Add f to total
Return the total

pitfalls: The answer counts elements, not distinct values: multiply by the frequency.
A two-pass Counter version is also O(n) and fine to mention.

say.intro: Okay, so this is Count Elements With Maximum Frequency. We look at how often each value appears. Find the highest frequency. Then return how many elements belong to values with that frequency. In one, two, two, three, one, four, both one and two appear twice. That's the max. Together, that's four elements.
say.brute: The brute force counts each element's frequency by scanning the whole array. Then it finds the biggest count, and adds up every element that matches it. Easy to trust. But it compares every element with every other one. That's quadratic. For big inputs, billions of comparisons.
say.insight: Here's the thing. Count with a hash map, and keep the answer updated as you go. When a value's count beats the max, the max becomes that count. So does the total, since only this value qualifies. And when a count ties the max? Another value just joined the leaders. So add that count to the total.
say.anim: We start with nums 1, 2, 2, 3, 1, 4 and empty tracking variables. Processing 1, its frequency becomes 1, a new record, so max and total both become 1. Processing 2, its frequency becomes 1, tying the record, so total adds 1, becoming 2. Processing the second 2, frequency hits 2, a new record, resetting max and total to 2. Processing 3, frequency is 1, below the record, so nothing changes. Processing the second 1, frequency becomes 2, tying the record, so total grows to 4. Processing 4, frequency is 1, still below the record, so total stays unchanged. The loop ends and the function returns total, giving the final answer 4.
say.code: Freq is our hash map, and max f and total start at zero. For each value, we count it, and read the new count f. Is it a new record frequency? Then max f and total both become f, because only this value counts now. If another value ties the record, add f to total. After the loop, total is the answer.
say.outro: One pass, linear time and space. The pattern is arrays and hashing. Count with a map, and keep a running answer as counts change.

count-elements-with-maximum-frequency.title: Count Elements With Maximum Frequency
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container for the method that solves this problem.
The method takes the list nums and returns an integer count of elements with maximum frequency.
We start with an empty hash map called freq to track how many times each value appears.
We set both max_f, the highest frequency seen, and total, the running answer, to zero.
We loop through each value x in nums, processing the numbers one at a time.
We increase the count of x in freq by one, treating a missing value as zero.
We store the updated count of x in f so we can compare it with the record.
If f beats the current record max_f, we have a new maximum frequency.
We set max_f to f and reset total to f, since only this value currently holds the record.
Otherwise, if f ties the record, another value has reached the maximum frequency.
We add f to total, because all occurrences of this tying value now count toward the answer.
After the loop, we return total, the count of elements whose value has the maximum frequency.

count-good-numbers.hook: Count with multiplication, then raise to a quadrillion power with fast exponentiation.
count-good-numbers.ask: A digit string is good if even indices hold even digits and odd indices hold primes 2, 3, 5 or 7. Count good strings of length n, modulo 10^9 + 7.
count-good-numbers.exampleWhy: Five even slots with 5 choices, five odd slots with 4: 5^5 · 4^5 = 3,200,000.

brute.idea: Multiply choice by choice: loop over all n positions, multiplying by 5 or 4 depending on the index parity.
steps: Start with 1
Even index: multiply by 5
Odd index: multiply by 4
Take mod each time
brute.whySlow: n can be 10^15: even a billion multiplications a second would take about 12 days.

optimal.insight: The answer is 5^ceil(n/2) · 4^floor(n/2). Fast exponentiation squares the base and halves the exponent, so it needs only log n steps.
steps: Even slots: (n + 1) // 2, odd slots: n // 2
power: square base, halve exponent
Multiply in the base when the exponent bit is 1
Combine both powers modulo 10^9 + 7

codeNotes.note: This bit of the exponent is set
Index 0 is even, so round up

codeNotes.match: return power(5, evens) * power(4, odds) % MOD

pitfalls: Python's pow(5, e, MOD) does this built in; know how to write it anyway.
In fixed-width languages, multiply in 64-bit before taking the modulus.

say.intro: Okay, so this is Count Good Numbers. A digit string is good when even indexes hold even digits, and odd indexes hold primes. Two, three, five or seven. Count good strings of length n, modulo a big prime. At length ten, five even slots with five choices, five odd slots with four. That's three million two hundred thousand.
say.brute: The direct count walks every position. Start at one. Multiply by five for each even index, and four for each odd one, taking the modulus as we go. It's linear and correct. So what's the problem? N can reach ten to the fifteenth. Even at a billion steps a second, that runs for days.
say.insight: Here's the thing. The answer is a product of two powers. Five to the number of even slots, times four to the number of odd slots. And powers can be computed by repeated squaring. Square the base, halve the exponent. Whenever the exponent's lowest bit is one, multiply the base into the result. About fifty steps total.
say.anim: We start with n equal to ten, setting up the modulus for our calculation. Evens becomes five and odds becomes five, splitting digit positions for the formula. First call computes five to the power five using fast exponentiation, squaring base each loop. Exponent shrinks to two then one, base grows to six twenty five then multiplies into result. Loop ends, returning three thousand one twenty five as five raised to the fifth power. Second call computes four to the power five the same way, squaring base repeatedly. After the final multiplication, result reaches one thousand twenty four for four to the fifth. Multiplying both results modulo the prime gives the final answer, three million two hundred thousand.
say.code: Power keeps a result, starting at one. While the exponent is positive, check its low bit. If this bit is set, multiply the base in. Then square the base to get the next power of two, and halve the exponent. Index zero is even, so the even count rounds up. Five even choices, four primes. Multiply both powers modulo the prime.
say.outro: Logarithmic time, constant space. The pattern is math. Multiply independent choices, then use fast exponentiation.

count-good-numbers.title: Count Good Numbers
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the wrapper this problem's solution lives in.
This method takes the length n and returns how many good digit strings of that length exist.
We set MOD to one billion seven so every product stays small and the final answer fits the required modulus.
We define a helper called power that computes a base raised to an exponent under the modulus using fast exponentiation.
We start result at one, which is the neutral value for multiplication and the answer when the exponent is zero.
We loop while the exponent is still positive, handling one binary digit of the exponent each time.
If the lowest bit of the exponent is one, the current base contributes to the answer.
In that case we multiply result by the current base and reduce by the modulus to keep numbers bounded.
We square the base and reduce by the modulus, so it represents the next power of two in the exponent.
We shift the exponent right by one bit, which halves it and discards the bit we just handled.
Once the exponent reaches zero, we return result as the modular power, having used only about log of the exponent steps.
Even indices count is n plus one divided by two rounded down, which is the ceiling of n over two.
Odd indices count is n divided by two rounded down, since the remaining positions are the odd ones.
Each even index has five choices and each odd index has four, so we multiply the two powers and take the modulus.

count-good-triplets-in-an-array.hook: Fix the middle element, count partners on each side, and a Fenwick tree does the counting.
count-good-triplets-in-an-array.ask: Two permutations of 0 to n - 1. Count triplets of values that appear in increasing position order in both arrays.
count-good-triplets-in-an-array.exampleWhy: The good triplets are (4,0,2), (4,0,3), (4,1,2) and (4,1,3): in order in both arrays.

brute.idea: Map each value to its position in nums2, then try every triple of indices in nums1 and check their nums2 positions increase.
steps: Record each value's position in nums2
Loop over all i < j < k in nums1
Positions increasing in nums2? Count it
brute.whySlow: With 100,000 elements that is about 1.7 · 10^14 triples, hopelessly slow.

optimal.insight: Rewrite nums1 as positions in nums2. A good triplet is an increasing triple. For each middle, multiply smaller-before by larger-after.
steps: Translate each nums1 value to its nums2 position
Sweep nums1, querying a Fenwick tree
left = seen positions smaller than p
right = (n - 1 - p) - (i - left)
Add left · right, then insert p

count-good-triplets-in-an-array.optimalCode:
class Solution:
    def goodTriplets(self, nums1: List[int], nums2: List[int]) -> int:
        n = len(nums1)
        pos2 = [0] * n
        for i, v in enumerate(nums2):
            pos2[v] = i
        tree = [0] * (n + 1)
        res = 0
        for i, v in enumerate(nums1):
            p = pos2[v]
            left = 0
            j = p
            while j > 0:
                left += tree[j]
                j -= j & -j
            right = (n - 1 - p) - (i - left)
            res += left * right
            j = p + 1
            while j <= n:
                tree[j] += 1
                j += j & -j
        return res

codeNotes.note: Where each value sits in nums2

pitfalls: Counting right needs no second tree: larger positions minus those already seen.
Fenwick indices start at 1, so store position p at index p + 1.

say.intro: Okay, so this is Count Good Triplets in an Array. We get two permutations of the same values. A good triplet is three values in the same relative order in both arrays. Here there are four. For example, four, zero, two is in order in both lists. We need to count them all.
say.brute: The brute force first records where each value sits in the second array. Then it tries every triple of indices in the first array. Do their positions in the second array also increase? That's three nested loops. Cubic time. With a hundred thousand elements, there's no way it finishes.
say.insight: Here's the trick. Rewrite the first array as positions in the second array. Now a good triplet is just an increasing triple. So fix the middle element. For each middle, multiply the smaller values before it by the larger values after it. A Fenwick tree tracks which positions we've seen. So smaller before is just a prefix sum.
say.anim: We start with nums1 and nums2, mapping each value to its position in nums2. Pos2 fills in as we scan nums2, recording where each value sits. Now we process nums1, starting with value four at position zero in nums2. Left counts smaller values seen before, right counts larger values after, giving zero good triplets here. The fenwick tree updates to mark this position as seen, for future counting. Next, value zero at position two finds one smaller value before it and two larger after, adding two. Value one at position one again finds one smaller before and two larger after, adding two more, total four. Values three and two contribute nothing more, and the final count of good triplets is four.
say.code: First, we record where each value sits in nums two. Then we walk nums one, and p is the current position. A prefix sum on the tree counts earlier values with smaller positions. Later and larger positions come by subtraction. The pairs around this middle are left times right, so add that. Finally, insert this position into the tree.
say.outro: N log n time, linear space. The pattern is trees, here a Fenwick tree. Fix the middle, count each side, and multiply.

count-good-triplets-in-an-array.title: Count Good Triplets in an Array
lineNotes: We define a class named Solution, as the problem platform expects.
The method goodTriplets takes both permutations and returns the count of good triplets as an integer.
We store n as the length of nums1, which equals the length of nums2.
We create pos2, an array of zeros, to hold each value's position in nums2.
We loop over nums2 with index and value, so we can record where each value sits.
We set the position of value v in pos2 to index i.
We build a Fenwick tree of size n plus one, one-indexed, to count positions already seen.
We initialize the result counter res to zero.
We walk through nums1 in order, so the index i tells how many values came before.
We look up p, the position in nums2 of the current value, which makes it our middle candidate.
We start left at zero, to count earlier values with smaller position in nums2.
We set j to p, so the query covers positions strictly less than p.
We loop while j is positive, climbing down the Fenwick tree for a prefix sum.
We add the tree entry at j into left, accumulating the prefix count.
We remove the lowest set bit of j, jumping to the next range to sum.
Right counts later values with larger position: all larger positions, minus those larger positions already seen earlier in nums1.
We add left times right to res, counting every triplet that uses this value as the middle.
We set j to p plus one, the one-indexed slot for this position, before inserting it.
We loop while j is within the tree size, to update every range covering this position.
We increment the tree entry at j, recording that this position has now been seen.
We add the lowest set bit to j, moving to the next range that contains this position.
After processing all values, we return res as the total number of good triplets.

count-number-of-nice-subarrays.hook: Count odd numbers as a prefix sum, and the problem becomes subarray sum equals k.
count-number-of-nice-subarrays.ask: Count the contiguous subarrays of nums that contain exactly k odd numbers.
count-number-of-nice-subarrays.exampleWhy: Any window holding both 1s works: 4 choices of start times 4 choices of end = 16.

brute.idea: Try every start, extend the end, count odd numbers as you go, and count windows with exactly k odds.
steps: Fix a start index
Extend the end, counting odds
Exactly k odds? Count the window
More than k? Stop extending
brute.whySlow: Each start rescans forward: 50,000 numbers means over a billion window checks.

optimal.insight: Let odds be the running count of odd numbers. A window ending here is nice if an earlier prefix had odds - k. A map counts those.
steps: count[0] = 1 for the empty prefix
Add 1 to odds on each odd number
Add count[odds - k] to the answer
Record this prefix in count

codeNotes.note: Starts that leave exactly k odds

pitfalls: Look up before you record, or a window could start after it ends.
Also solvable with sliding windows: atMost(k) - atMost(k - 1).

say.intro: Okay, so this is Count Number of Nice Subarrays. A subarray is nice if it has exactly k odd numbers. Our input is three twos, a one, two twos, a one, then three twos. K is two. So every window must include both ones. Four ways to pick the start, four to pick the end. Sixteen.
say.brute: The brute force fixes each start, then extends the end one step at a time, counting odds. Every time the count equals k, that window is nice. Once the count passes k, we stop. Even with that early exit, a long run of even numbers keeps it quadratic.
say.insight: Here's the thing. Turn odd numbers into ones, and even numbers into zeros. Now we want subarrays that sum to exactly k. That's the classic prefix sum problem. Keep a running count of odds. A window ending here is nice when an earlier prefix had k fewer odds. And a hash map tells us how many prefixes like that exist.
say.anim: We start with count tracking zero odds seen once, odds and res both at zero. As we scan even numbers, odds stays at zero and count for zero keeps growing. At the first odd number, odds becomes one, giving us a new prefix count entry. Hitting the second odd number makes odds two, matching k, so res jumps to four. More even numbers keep odds at two, each adding matching prefixes, res rises to eight. Continuing through evens, res climbs to twelve as matching prefixes accumulate steadily. The final even numbers push res up to sixteen before the loop finishes. The function returns res, giving the final answer of sixteen nice subarrays.
say.code: Count maps an odd total to how many prefixes had it. The empty prefix has zero odds, so zero starts with one. For each number, update the running odd count. Then add how many earlier prefixes had odds minus k. Those are the starts that leave exactly k odds. Finally, record this prefix in the map.
say.outro: Linear time and space. The pattern is arrays and hashing. Prefix sums plus a hash map count subarrays with an exact total.

count-number-of-nice-subarrays.title: Count Number of Nice Subarrays
lineNotes: We define a class named Solution, which is the wrapper this problem expects for our method.
The method numberOfSubarrays takes the list nums and the target number k of odd values, and returns an integer.
We start a map where zero odd numbers has been seen once, representing the empty prefix before any element.
We set both odds, the running odd count, and res, the answer total, to zero.
We loop through each number x in nums, treating each position as the end of a possible subarray.
We add the remainder of x divided by two to odds, so odd numbers raise the count by one.
We add how many earlier prefixes had odds minus k odd numbers, since each gives a subarray with exactly k odds.
We record the current odds value in the map, increasing its count by one for future positions.
After the loop finishes, we return res as the total number of nice subarrays.

count-of-smaller-numbers-after-self.hook: Walk right to left and ask a Fenwick tree how many smaller values it has seen.
count-of-smaller-numbers-after-self.ask: For each element of nums, count how many elements to its right are strictly smaller. Return those counts.
count-of-smaller-numbers-after-self.exampleWhy: Right of 5 are 2, 1 and 3, all smaller: 3. Right of 6 only 1 and 3: 2.

brute.idea: For each index, scan everything to its right and count the values smaller than it.
steps: Pick index i
Scan all j > i
Count nums[j] < nums[i]
brute.whySlow: 100,000 numbers means about 5 billion comparisons.

optimal.insight: Process from the right so everything seen is to the right. Rank the values, then a Fenwick tree counts seen ranks below this one.
steps: Rank values 1..m by sorted order
Walk from the right end
Query the tree for ranks below this rank
Insert this rank into the tree

codeNotes.match: ranks = {v: i + 1 for i, v in enumerate(sorted(set(nums)))}

pitfalls: Query rank r - 1, not r, so equal values are not counted.
Merge sort counting is the other O(n log n) answer interviewers accept.

say.intro: Okay, so this is Count of Smaller Numbers After Self. For every element, count how many elements to its right are strictly smaller. For five, two, six, one, three, the answer is three, one, two, zero, zero. Five has two, one and three after it. All smaller. Six has one and three after it.
say.brute: The brute force does exactly what the problem says. For each index, scan everything to its right and count the smaller ones. Simple and correct. But each element rescans the rest of the array. That's quadratic. For a hundred thousand numbers, billions of comparisons.
say.insight: Here's the thing. Walk from right to left. Now everything we've already seen lies to the right. So we need a structure that answers, how many seen values are smaller than this one? And it has to accept inserts. First, rank the values from one to m. Then a Fenwick tree over those ranks does both in logarithmic time.
say.anim: We assign ranks to each unique number, so 1,2,3,5,6 become ranks 1 through 5. Processing from the right, we start with value 6 at index 4, rank 3. The tree is empty, so the count of smaller values seen so far is zero. Next we handle value 1 at index 3, rank 1, again finding zero smaller numbers seen. At index 2, value 6 has rank 5, and the tree reports two smaller values already seen. Value 2 at index 1 has rank 2, and we find one smaller number seen so far. Finally value 5 at index 0 has rank 4, and the tree counts three smaller values. The final result array is three, one, two, zero, zero, matching the expected output.
say.code: First, we compress the values to ranks, one through m. Then we walk right to left. Strictly smaller means ranks below r. So we sum the tree over those ranks, stepping down by the lowest set bit. That counts smaller values already seen, and it's the answer for this index. Then we insert this rank, stepping up by the lowest set bit.
say.outro: N log n time, linear space. The pattern is trees, a Fenwick tree. Sweep one way, and count what you've seen with prefix sums.

count-of-smaller-numbers-after-self.title: Count of Smaller Numbers After Self
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container the problem expects for our method.
The method countSmaller takes the list nums and returns a list of counts, one per element.
We sort the distinct values and give each a rank starting at one, so values compress into a small range.
We store m, the number of distinct values, which is the size of the rank range.
We create the Fenwick tree as an array of zeros with m plus one slots, since it is one indexed.
We create the result list res, filled with zeros, with one slot for each number in nums.
We loop from the last index down to zero so every number already processed lies to the right.
We look up the rank of the current number and call it r.
We set j to r minus one so the query covers only ranks strictly smaller than this one.
We reset total to zero before accumulating the count of smaller numbers seen so far.
While j is positive, we keep walking down the Fenwick tree to gather prefix sums.
We add the tree value at j to total, since that node covers a block of ranks.
We drop the lowest set bit of j to jump to the next block still needing a count.
We store total in res at index i as the count of smaller numbers to its right.
We set j to r to start inserting the current number's rank into the tree.
While j is within the rank range m, we keep updating the tree nodes that cover this rank.
We add one to the tree at j, recording that one more number with this rank has been seen.
We add the lowest set bit to j to move up to the next node responsible for this rank.
After all elements are processed, we return the list of counts.

count-palindromic-subsequences.hook: Length five palindromes look like ab x ba. Fix the middle, count pairs on each side.
count-palindromic-subsequences.ask: Given a string of digits, count its subsequences of length 5 that are palindromes, modulo 10^9 + 7.
count-palindromic-subsequences.exampleWhy: Choosing indices 0,1,2 or 0,1,3, then 4 and 5, both spell 10301: two subsequences.

brute.idea: Try every choice of five indices, build the subsequence, and count the ones that read the same backwards.
steps: Choose every set of five indices
Build the five-character string
Palindrome? Count it
brute.whySlow: C(10,000, 5) is about 8 · 10^17 subsequences. Not feasible.

optimal.insight: A length-5 palindrome is a, b, middle, b, a. Track pair counts left of the middle and right of it: answer adds left[a][b] · right[b][a].
steps: Build right-side counts of singles and pairs
Move each index from the right side to middle
Add left[a][b] · right[b][a] over digit pairs
Then add the index to the left counts

codeNotes.note: d starts new pairs with later x
Remove pairs that began with d

pitfalls: Only 10 digits, so 100 pair types: the constant factor is the whole trick.
Loop only over digits present to keep the work small.

say.intro: Okay, so this is Count Palindromic Subsequences. Given a string of digits, count length five subsequences that read the same both ways. For one zero three three zero one, pick one, zero, either three, zero, one. Both spell one zero three zero one. So the answer is two.
say.brute: The brute force picks every set of five indices. It builds the five character string, and checks if it equals its reverse. That's correct. But the number of index sets grows like n to the fifth. For ten thousand digits, that's close to a billion billion subsequences.
say.insight: Here's the thing. Look at the shape. A, b, middle, b, a. So fix the middle. Then we need pairs a then b on the left, times pairs b then a on the right. There are only ten digits, so just a hundred pair types. Keep pair counts for both sides, and update them as the middle slides right. That makes it linear.
say.anim: We start with the string one zero three three zero one, scanning it to count pair patterns. Scanning from the right, right2 builds counts of digit pairs appearing after each position. By the time we finish the reverse scan, right2 holds pair counts like one and two for various digits. Now moving left to right, at digit one we remove it from right1 and right2 before checking pairs. With left2 still empty, no palindrome pairs exist yet, so ans stays zero. At the next digit zero, left2 updates to record a pair of one and zero seen so far. Now ans increases to one, since a left pair one zero matches a right pair zero one. At digit three, matching left and right pairs raise ans to two. After processing all digits, the final count of five length palindromic subsequences is two.
say.code: First, we build the right side counts, walking backwards. Each digit d starts new pairs with every later digit x. Then, for each middle d, it leaves the right side. So we remove it, and remove the pairs that began with d. Next, we add the mirror pairs around this middle, left a b times right b a. Finally, d joins the left side.
say.outro: Linear time, with a factor of a hundred. The pattern is dynamic programming over counts. Fix the center, and combine pair tables.

count-palindromic-subsequences.title: Count Palindromic Subsequences
lineNotes: We define a class named Solution, as the problem platform expects.
The method takes the digit string s and returns the count of palindromic subsequences of length five.
We set MOD to ten to the ninth plus seven, the modulus for the final answer.
We convert each character of s into an integer so digits can index our count tables.
We collect the distinct digits present, sorted, so later loops only visit digits that actually occur.
We create left1 and right1, arrays of ten counters for single digits on each side of the middle.
left2 is a ten by ten table counting ordered digit pairs among positions left of the middle.
right2 is the same kind of table, for pairs among positions right of the middle.
We first scan the string from the end, building right-side counts for every suffix.
For each digit d, we loop over every digit x that could be the later partner in a pair.
We add the count of x already seen on the right to right2 for pair d then x, since d comes first.
Then we record d in right1 as one more occurrence on the right.
We initialize the answer accumulator to zero.
Now we sweep left to right, treating each digit d as the middle of a palindrome.
We remove the middle digit from right1 so the right side holds only positions after it.
We loop over digits x to undo pairs that started with the middle digit.
We subtract right1 of x from right2 for d then x, removing pairs that used the middle position.
We loop over the outer digit a of the palindrome.
We loop over the inner digit b of the palindrome.
We add left pairs a then b times right pairs b then a, forming a, b, middle, b, a.
After counting, we begin updating the left side to include the current digit as a later partner.
We add left1 of x to left2 for pair x then d, since x came earlier than d.
We increment left1 for d, so the current digit counts as left for future middles.
We return the total reduced modulo MOD, keeping the big count within bounds.

count-square-submatrices-with-all-ones.hook: Each cell tells you the biggest square ending there, and that number is also its count.
count-square-submatrices-with-all-ones.ask: Given a grid of 0s and 1s, count every square submatrix, of any size, made entirely of 1s.
count-square-submatrices-with-all-ones.exampleWhy: Six single 1s, plus one 2 by 2 square in the bottom-left corner: 7 squares.

brute.idea: For every top-left cell and every size, check whether the whole square is ones.
steps: Pick a top-left cell
Try sizes 1, 2, 3, ...
Check every cell in the square
All ones? Count it
brute.whySlow: k is min(m, n). For a 300 by 300 grid that is far beyond a trillion cell checks.

optimal.insight: The largest all-ones square with bottom-right corner here is 1 + min(up, left, up-left). A size-k corner contributes k squares.
steps: Walk the grid row by row
Cell is 1 and not on the top or left edge?
Set it to 1 + min of three neighbours
Add the cell value to the total

codeNotes.match: if matrix[r][c] and r > 0 and c > 0:
codeNotes.note: Edges and zeros stay as they are
Size k means k squares end here

pitfalls: Modifying the input saves space; ask first, or copy it.
Add the cell value, not one: a 3 means three squares end here.

say.intro: Okay, so this is Count Square Submatrices with All Ones. Given a grid of zeros and ones, count every square of every size that's all ones. In this three by three grid, there are six single ones. And the bottom left corner forms one two by two square. So the answer is seven.
say.brute: The brute force tries every top left corner and every size, checking every cell in each square. Once a size fails, bigger ones from that corner fail too, so we stop. But a square of side k touches k squared cells. With lots of corners and sizes, a big grid explodes.
say.insight: Here's the key. In each cell, store the side of the biggest all ones square whose bottom right corner sits there. It's one plus the smallest of the cells above, to the left, and diagonally up left. Why? Because the square is only as big as its weakest neighbour allows. And a value of k means exactly k squares end here, one of each size.
say.anim: We start with total at zero and our three by three matrix of ones and zeros. Row zero can't form squares since there's no row above, so each cell just adds its own value. On row one, cell zero adds one, making total three. At row one, column one, both neighbors are one, so this cell becomes two, adding two squares. Row two starts, and column zero contributes one, bringing total to five. At row two, column one, the minimum of neighbors is one, so this cell becomes two, adding two more. The last cell is zero, so it contributes nothing, leaving total at seven. The function returns seven, the total count of all-ones square submatrices.
say.code: Total starts at zero, and we visit each cell in row order. Edges and zeros stay as they are. Otherwise, a one grows the smallest neighbouring square. So it becomes one plus the minimum of its three neighbours. Either way, add the cell's value to the total. A size of k means k squares end here.
say.outro: Linear in the grid, constant extra space. The pattern is two dimensional dynamic programming. Build each cell from up, left and diagonal.

count-square-submatrices-with-all-ones.title: Count Square Submatrices with All Ones
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container the problem expects for our method.
The countSquares method takes the grid of zeros and ones and returns the total number of all-ones squares.
We start total at zero to accumulate the count of squares as we visit each cell.
We loop over every row index of the matrix, moving from top to bottom.
Inside each row we loop over every column index, so we visit each cell in order.
If the cell is a one and not in the first row or column, it might extend a larger square.
We overwrite the cell with one plus the minimum of its upper, left, and upper-left neighbors, giving the largest square ending here.
We add the cell's value to total, since a corner with size k contributes exactly k squares.
After visiting every cell, we return total as the count of all square submatrices of ones.

count-subarrays-with-majority-element-i.hook: Turn every element into plus one or minus one, and majority becomes a prefix sum comparison.
count-subarrays-with-majority-element-i.ask: Given an array and a target value, count the subarrays in which target appears strictly more than half of the time.
count-subarrays-with-majority-element-i.exampleWhy: [2], [2], [2,2], [1,2,2] and [2,2,3] each have more 2s than other values. No other subarray does.

brute.idea: Try every start index, extend the end one step at a time, and keep a running count of target.
steps: Pick a start index i
Extend j, counting target hits
Hits more than half the length? count it
brute.whySlow: Every one of the n squared over two subarrays is checked; 100,000 elements means billions of checks.

optimal.insight: Map target to +1 and everything else to -1. A subarray is a majority exactly when its sum is positive: prefix[j] > prefix[i].
steps: Keep a running prefix sum, shifted to stay non-negative
Count how many times each prefix value occurred
Track how many earlier prefixes sit strictly below the current one
Each step adds that count to the answer

count-subarrays-with-majority-element-i.optimalCode:
class Solution:
    def countMajoritySubarrays(self, nums: List[int], target: int) -> int:
        n = len(nums)
        count = [0] * (2 * n + 2)
        cur = n
        count[cur] = 1
        less = 0
        ans = 0
        for x in nums:
            if x == target:
                less += count[cur]
                cur += 1
            else:
                cur -= 1
                less -= count[cur]
            ans += less
            count[cur] += 1
        return ans

codeNotes.note: How often each prefix value appeared
Offset so prefix sums stay non-negative
Old equals now sit below us
Equals to new value no longer below
Every lower earlier prefix is a valid start

pitfalls: Strictly more than half: a tie is not a majority, so compare with strict less.
Prefix sums go negative; offset by n or use a hash map.

say.intro: Count Subarrays With Majority Element. We get an array and a target. We count the subarrays where the target shows up strictly more than half the time. For one, two, two, three, with target two, five subarrays qualify. Two two is one. One two two is another.
say.brute: Okay, so the brute force. Pick a start index. Extend the end one step at a time, counting how often the target appears. Are the hits more than half the length? Count that subarray. It's simple, and correct. But it checks every subarray. That's quadratic. For big arrays, billions of checks.
say.insight: Here's the trick. Turn the target into plus one, and everything else into minus one. Now a subarray has a majority exactly when its sum is positive. With prefix sums, that means the prefix at the end beats the prefix before the start. And notice, each step moves the prefix by exactly one. So we can keep a running count of earlier prefixes below us.
say.anim: We start with nums one two two three and target two, mapping matches to plus one. Cur begins at four, the middle offset, marking a balanced prefix sum of zero. First element one isn't target, so cur decreases to three and less drops to zero. Element two matches target, so less increases using count at cur, becoming one, cur moves to four, adding one to ans. Second two also matches, less jumps to three, cur becomes five, ans grows to four. Element three isn't target, cur drops back to four, less becomes one, ans reaches five. The loop ends and the function returns the final answer, five majority subarrays.
say.code: Let's walk the code. The count array records how often each prefix value appeared. We start at offset n, so prefixes never go negative. Now, on the target, earlier prefixes equal to us are about to sit below us. So add them to less, then step up. Otherwise, step down, and those equal to the new value no longer count. Each step, every lower earlier prefix is a valid start.
say.outro: Linear time and space. The pattern is prefix sums. Turn a majority condition into a positive sum.

count-subarrays-with-majority-element-i.title: Count Subarrays With Majority Element I
lineNotes: We define the Solution class that holds the method for this problem.
The method takes the array nums and the target value, and returns the number of majority subarrays.
We store the length of nums in n to size our counting array and set the starting offset.
We make a count array of size two n plus two, indexed by prefix sum shifted by n to avoid negatives.
We set cur, the current prefix sum position, to n, which represents a prefix sum of zero.
We record that the empty prefix with sum zero has been seen once.
The variable less tracks how many earlier prefixes have a sum strictly smaller than the current one.
The variable ans accumulates the total number of subarrays with a positive sum.
We walk through each element x in nums, updating the running prefix sum one step at a time.
If x equals target, the prefix sum will go up by one.
Moving up, every prefix that had the old sum now becomes smaller, so we add its count to less.
We then increase cur by one to reflect the new prefix sum.
Otherwise the element is not the target and the prefix sum will go down by one.
We first decrease cur by one to move to the lower prefix sum.
Prefixes at this new sum are no longer strictly smaller, so we subtract their count from less.
Each earlier prefix with a smaller sum gives a majority subarray ending here, so we add less to ans.
We record the current prefix sum as seen, so later positions can compare against it.
After processing everything, we return the total count of majority subarrays.

count-the-number-of-complete-components.hook: A component is complete when its edge count hits the maximum possible. Count, do not compare pairs.
count-the-number-of-complete-components.ask: Given n vertices and a list of undirected edges, count the connected components in which every pair of vertices is directly joined by an edge.
count-the-number-of-complete-components.exampleWhy: The triangle 0,1,2 is complete, the pair 3,4 is complete, and lone vertex 5 is trivially complete.

brute.idea: From every vertex, flood fill its whole component, then check that each member's neighbours are all the other members.
steps: Flood fill from every vertex u
Count it only when u is the smallest member
Check every member links to all others
brute.whySlow: It repeats the same flood fill once per vertex, and compares neighbour sets for every member.

optimal.insight: A component with k vertices is complete exactly when it has k times k minus one over two edges. Sum the degrees during one traversal.
steps: Build an adjacency list
Traverse each unvisited component once
Count its vertices and total degree
Complete if degree sum equals k times k minus one

codeNotes.note: Degree sum is twice the edge count

pitfalls: Degree sum counts each edge twice: compare with k times k minus one, not half.
Isolated vertices are complete components too.

say.intro: Count the Number of Complete Components. We get a graph with n vertices and some edges. We count the components where every pair of vertices is directly connected. With six vertices, the triangle zero one two counts. The pair three four counts. And lonely vertex five counts too. So, three.
say.brute: The brute force floods out from every single vertex to find its component. It only counts the component from its smallest member. Then it checks that each member's neighbours, plus itself, make up the whole component. What's the waste? The same flood fill repeats once per vertex. That's n times the size of the graph.
say.insight: Here's the thing. A complete component with k vertices has the most edges possible. That's k times k minus one over two. So we never check pairs. In one traversal, count the vertices and add up their degrees. Why degrees? Each edge gets counted twice. So the component is complete when the degree sum equals k times k minus one.
say.anim: We build an adjacency list from the edges, connecting each pair of vertices both ways. Starting from vertex 0, we traverse its component using a stack, marking nodes as seen. We visit vertices 0, 2, and 1, summing their degrees as we explore the stack. Nodes reach 3 and degree reaches 6, matching 3 times 2, so this component is complete. Next we explore vertices 3 and 4, finding 2 nodes and degree 2, another complete component. Finally vertex 5 is isolated, with 1 node and 0 degree, still satisfying the complete condition. Each of the three components turns out complete, so the final answer is 3.
say.code: Let's walk the code. First, build an adjacency list for the graph. Then loop over start vertices, skipping ones already seen. That way each component is explored once. Pop a vertex, count it, and add its degree. Remember, the degree sum is twice the edge count. When the stack empties, compare with nodes times nodes minus one. Maximum edges means complete.
say.outro: Linear in vertices plus edges. The pattern is graphs. Traverse each component once, and judge it by simple counts.

count-the-number-of-complete-components.title: Count the Number of Complete Components
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container for the method the problem asks us to write.
This method takes the vertex count n and the edge list, and returns how many connected components are complete.
We build an adjacency list with one empty neighbor list for every vertex from zero to n minus one.
We loop over every edge, unpacking its two endpoints a and b.
Since the graph is undirected, we add b to the neighbor list of a.
We also add a to the neighbor list of b so the connection goes both ways.
We create a seen array of false values so each vertex is visited only once across all traversals.
We start the count of complete components at zero.
We try every vertex as a possible starting point of a new component.
If this vertex was already visited, it belongs to a component we have already handled.
So we skip it and move on to the next starting vertex.
We mark the start as seen, since we are about to explore its component.
We initialize a stack with the start vertex to run an iterative depth first search.
We reset the node counter and the degree sum to zero for this new component.
We keep exploring while the stack still has vertices waiting to be processed.
We pop a vertex u from the stack to process it now.
We count u as one more vertex in the current component.
We add the degree of u, meaning its number of neighbors, to the running degree total.
We look at each neighbor v of u to continue the traversal.
If v has not been seen yet, it is a new vertex of this component.
We mark v as seen right away so it is never pushed onto the stack twice.
We push v onto the stack so its neighbors get explored later.
The degree sum counts each edge twice, so a complete component needs exactly nodes times nodes minus one in total degree.
When that condition holds, every pair is joined, so we increase the count of complete components.
After all starting vertices are processed, we return the number of complete components.

count-the-number-of-consistent-strings.hook: Turn the allowed letters into a set once, and every membership check becomes instant.
count-the-number-of-consistent-strings.ask: Given a string of allowed letters and a list of words, count how many words use only allowed letters.
count-the-number-of-consistent-strings.exampleWhy: aaab and baa use only a and b. The other three words contain d, which is not allowed.

brute.idea: For every letter of every word, scan the allowed string to see if the letter is in it.
steps: Take each word
For each letter, scan allowed
Any letter missing? the word fails
brute.whySlow: Each letter rescans allowed, up to 26 characters, so every letter costs up to 26 comparisons.

optimal.insight: Build a set of allowed letters once. Then each letter check is constant time, and a word is consistent if all its letters are in the set.
steps: Put allowed letters into a set
For each word, check every letter in the set
Count the words that pass

codeNotes.match: if all(c in ok for c in w):

pitfalls: A 26 bit mask works too: word mask OR allowed mask must equal allowed mask.

say.intro: Count the Number of Consistent Strings. We get a string of allowed letters and a list of words. A word is consistent if every letter in it is allowed. With allowed letters a and b, only a a a b and b a a pass. The rest contain a d. So the answer is two.
say.brute: The brute force checks each letter of each word by scanning the allowed string from the start. If some letter never matches, the word fails. It works. So what's wasteful? Every single letter can cost up to twenty six comparisons. And we repeat the same scans again and again.
say.insight: Here's the thing. The allowed string never changes. So prepare it once. Put its letters into a set. Now every membership question is a constant time lookup. A word is consistent exactly when all its letters are in that set. The total work? One look at every letter of every word.
say.anim: We build a set of allowed letters, just a and b, from the allowed string. Count starts at zero as we begin looping through each word in the list. The word ad has a d, which is not allowed, so it is skipped. The word bd also contains d, so it fails the check too. The word aaab only has a and b, so count increases to one. The word baa also only uses allowed letters, so count becomes two. The word badab contains d, so it does not count as consistent. The loop ends and the function returns the final count, which is two.
say.code: Let's walk the code. Build a set of allowed letters for constant time lookup. Start a counter at zero. For each word, ask whether every letter is allowed. Notice the all check stops at the first bad letter. So failing words get rejected early. If a consistent word is found, add one. Return the counter.
say.outro: Linear in the total number of letters. The pattern is hashing. Build a set once, then answer membership instantly.

count-the-number-of-consistent-strings.title: Count the Number of Consistent Strings
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container for the method that solves this problem.
This method takes the allowed letters and the list of words, and returns how many words are consistent.
We build a set from the allowed string once, so each later letter lookup takes constant time.
We start our count of consistent words at zero before looking at any word.
We loop over every word in the list, one at a time.
We check whether every letter in the current word is in the allowed set, which makes the word consistent.
When the word passes that check, we add one to our running count.
After all words are checked, we return the final count of consistent words.

count-valid-sequences.hook: Count everything, subtract the bad ones. Even product just means not all odd.
count-valid-sequences.ask: Count sequences of k positive integers that sum to n and whose product is even. Order matters. Return the count modulo one billion and seven.
count-valid-sequences.exampleWhy: Six ordered ways split 5 into 3 parts. Only 1+1+3, 1+3+1 and 3+1+1 are all odd, leaving three valid.

brute.idea: Recursively choose each part from 1 upward, tracking the remaining sum and whether any part was even.
steps: Choose the next part x
Recurse on what is left of n
Count when all k parts sum to n with an even part
brute.whySlow: It visits every composition one by one; there are exponentially many when n and k are large.

optimal.insight: Stars and bars: all sequences number C(n-1, k-1). All-odd sequences write each part as 2a+1, giving C((n-k)/2 + k-1, k-1). Subtract.
steps: Precompute factorials modulo the prime
Total = C(n-1, k-1)
If n-k is odd, no all-odd sequence exists
Otherwise subtract C((n-k)/2 + k-1, k-1)

codeNotes.match: pow(fact[b] * fact[a - b] % MOD, MOD - 2, MOD)

pitfalls: Subtracting under a modulus can go negative; take the result modulo again.
k odd parts sum to n only when n and k share parity.

say.intro: Count Valid Sequences. We count ordered sequences of k positive numbers that add up to n, and have an even product. For n equal to five and k equal to three, there are six ordered splits. But three of them use only odd numbers. So the answer is three.
say.brute: The brute force builds sequences part by part. Pick the next number, recurse on what's left, and remember whether we've seen an even number. At the end, count the ones with an even part. It's correct. But it lists every single sequence. And how many are there? Exponentially many.
say.insight: Here's the thing. A product is even unless every part is odd. So count everything, then subtract the all odd ones. Stars and bars gives the total, n minus one choose k minus one. Now, the odd ones. Write each part as two a plus one. The a values are free, and sum to half of n minus k. That's another binomial.
say.anim: We start with n equal 5 and k equal 3, setting up our modulus. A factorial table builds step by step, filling fact with growing products up to 120. Now we compute total, the count of all sequences, using comb of 4 and 2. That combination evaluates to 6, representing every possible sequence arrangement. Since n minus k is even, we must subtract sequences made entirely of odd parts. We compute odd using comb of 3 and 2, which evaluates to 3. Finally we subtract odd from total, giving 6 minus 3. The final answer returned is 3, matching the expected valid sequence count.
say.code: Let's walk the code. First, build factorials modulo the prime. To divide, comb uses a Fermat inverse. Then stars and bars counts all sequences. Now, what if n minus k is odd? Then no all odd sequence exists, so return the total. Otherwise, subtract the odd product ones, and take the result modulo the prime again.
say.outro: Linear time for the factorials. The pattern is combinatorics. Count everything, then subtract the complement.

count-valid-sequences.title: Count Valid Sequences
lineNotes: We define a Solution class that holds the method for this problem.
The method takes n as the required sum and k as the number of parts, and returns a count.
We set MOD to one billion and seven, the modulus used for the final answer.
We create a factorial table of size n plus one, starting with every entry set to one.
We loop i from one up to n to fill in each factorial in turn.
Each factorial equals the previous one times i, reduced by the modulus to keep numbers small.
We define a helper comb that computes a binomial coefficient using the factorial table.
If b is negative or larger than a, there are no ways to choose, so we handle that case first.
In that invalid case the helper returns zero.
Otherwise we compute a factorial divided by b factorial and a minus b factorial, using a modular inverse through Fermat's little theorem.
The total count of all sequences by stars and bars is choose n minus one, k minus one.
If n minus k is odd, an all-odd sequence is impossible, so we check that parity.
In that case every sequence has an even product, so we return the total directly.
Otherwise we count all-odd sequences by writing each part as two a plus one, giving choose of half of n minus k plus k minus one, k minus one.
We subtract the all-odd count from the total and take the modulus so the result stays nonnegative.

count-vowels-permutation.hook: Five vowels, five counters. Each new letter just reshuffles who can follow whom.
count-vowels-permutation.ask: Count strings of length n made of vowels where a is followed only by e, e by a or i, i by anything but i, o by i or u, and u by a. Modulo one billion and seven.
count-vowels-permutation.exampleWhy: Extending valid strings letter by letter, the counts grow 5, then 10, then 19, then 35 strings of length four.

brute.idea: Build every valid string letter by letter with depth first search, following the allowed transitions, and count the finished ones.
steps: Start from each vowel
Recurse into each allowed next vowel
Count when the length reaches n
brute.whySlow: The number of valid strings grows exponentially; n of 20,000 is hopeless.

optimal.insight: Only the last letter matters. Keep five counts of strings ending in each vowel, and update all five per length.
steps: Start with one string ending in each vowel
a can come after e, i or u
e after a or i; i after e or o
o after i; u after i or o
Sum the five counts

codeNotes.note: Length one: one string per vowel
Grow the strings one letter at a time

codeNotes.match: return (a + e + i + o + u) % MOD

pitfalls: Flip the rules: count by what may come before each vowel, not after.
Update all five at once, or use temporaries.

say.intro: Count Vowels Permutation. We count strings of length n made from the five vowels. But each vowel restricts what can follow it. For example, a can only be followed by e. U only by a. For length four, there are thirty five valid strings. And the counts get huge fast.
say.brute: The brute force builds every valid string with depth first search. Start from each vowel. Recurse into every vowel allowed next. Count a string when it reaches length n. It's correct. So what's the catch? The number of valid strings grows exponentially. For long lengths, it never finishes.
say.insight: Here's the key. Can we add a letter? That depends only on the last letter. So we keep just five numbers, how many strings end in each vowel. Now flip the rules around. To end in a, the letter before must be e, i, or u. Do that for every vowel. Each new length is a simple combination of the five old counts.
say.anim: We start with n equal to four and set the modulus value. All five counts, a, e, i, o, u, begin at one for length one. The loop begins, updating each count based on which letters can precede it. After one update, counts become a three, e two, i two, o one, u two. After another update, counts are a six, e five, i three, o two, u three. After the final update, counts reach a eleven, e nine, i seven, o three, u five. Now we sum all five counts together modulo the given number. The final answer, the total number of valid strings, is thirty five.
say.code: Let's walk the code. At length one, there's one string per vowel. So all five counts start at one. Then we grow the strings one letter at a time, n minus one times. Who may precede a? E, i, or u, so new a is their sum. The others follow the same idea. Tuple assignment updates all five at once. Finally, return all endings together.
say.outro: Linear time, constant space. The pattern is one dimensional dynamic programming. Keep only the state that matters, the last letter.

count-vowels-permutation.title: Count Vowels Permutation
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container the problem expects for our method.
The method countVowelPermutation takes the string length n and returns how many valid vowel strings exist.
We set MOD to one billion and seven so every count stays small and matches the required answer.
For length one, each vowel alone is a valid string, so all five counts start at one.
We loop n minus one times, extending strings by one letter each pass, and ignore the loop variable itself.
We update all five counts at once: a follows e, i or u; e follows a or i; i follows e or o; o follows only i; u follows i or o.
Finally we add the five counts together, take the modulo, and return the total number of valid strings of length n.

counter.hook: A tiny closure that remembers a number between calls. The classic intro to captured state.
counter.ask: Given n, build a counter function that returns n on its first call, then one more than before on every later call. Report what each call returns.
counter.exampleWhy: The first call returns 10, and each later call returns one more: 11, 12, 13.

brute.idea: Keep no state. For the i-th call, start again from n and add one i times.
steps: For call number i
Start from n
Add one, i times
brute.whySlow: Each call recounts from scratch, so k calls cost about k squared over two additions.

optimal.insight: A closure can capture n and update it. Return the current value, then bump it, so each call is constant time.
steps: Define an inner function that sees n
Return the current n and increase it
Call it once per requested call

codeNotes.note: Rebind the captured n, not a local
Hand back the value before bumping

pitfalls: Without nonlocal, n += 1 raises UnboundLocalError in Python.
In JavaScript, return n++ returns the old value then increments.

say.intro: Counter. This is a warm up about closures. Given a starting number n, we return a counter function. Its first call returns n. Each later call returns one more. Starting at ten, four calls give ten, eleven, twelve and thirteen.
say.brute: A stateless brute force rebuilds the answer for every call. For the i th call, start again from n, and add one, i times. The numbers come out right. But each call does more work than the last. So k calls cost about k squared over two additions. And it misses the whole point.
say.insight: So what is the point? A function can remember things. An inner function closes over n from the outer scope. Every call sees the same n, not a fresh copy. So it can hand back the current value, then bump n by one. It's ready for the next call. Constant time, every time.
say.anim: We start with n equal to ten and four call requests to process. The closure bumps n to eleven, but returns the previous value, ten. Next call runs, incrementing n to twelve while returning the prior value, eleven. Third call increments n to thirteen, returning twelve, since counter returns before incrementing visibly. Fourth call bumps n to fourteen, returning thirteen as the captured value. All calls finish, giving the final answer: ten, eleven, twelve, thirteen.
say.code: Let's walk the code. Inside, we define counter. The nonlocal line rebinds the captured n, not a new local. Then we add one, to remember the next value. And we return n minus one, the value before the bump. In JavaScript, that's just n plus plus. The last line makes one call per request.
say.outro: Constant time per call. The key idea is closures. A function carries its own private state between calls.

counter.title: Counter
lineNotes: We define a Solution class that holds the method answering the counter problem.
The createCounter method takes the starting number n and a list of calls, and returns the results of each call.
Inside it we define a counter function, a closure that remembers n from the enclosing method.
The nonlocal statement lets counter change the captured n instead of creating a new local variable.
We bump n by one so the next call will see a value one larger than before.
We return n minus one, which is the value before the bump, so the first call gives the original n.
We call counter once for each entry in calls and collect the returned values into a list, each taking constant time.

delete-node-in-a-linked-list.hook: You cannot reach the node before it. So do not delete this node; become the next one.
delete-node-in-a-linked-list.ask: You are handed a node in a singly linked list, not the head, and it is never the tail. Remove its value from the list, keeping all other values in order.
delete-node-in-a-linked-list.exampleWhy: Node 9 copies 7 from its successor and skips over it, so the list reads 4, 5, 1, 7, 3.

brute.idea: Shift every value after the node one place left, then cut off the last node.
steps: Copy each next value into the current node
Walk forward until the second to last node
Cut the tail
brute.whySlow: It walks and rewrites every node after the target, when only one copy is needed.

optimal.insight: Copy the next node's value into this node, then unlink the next node. The value disappears in constant time.
steps: Reach the given node
Copy the next node's value into it
Point it past the next node

codeNotes.note: Test harness only: find the given node
Take on the next node's value

pitfalls: On LeetCode you receive the node itself: the two lines are the whole answer.
This trick fails for the tail, which is why the problem forbids it.

say.intro: Delete Node in a Linked List. We're handed a node in the middle of a singly linked list. Not the head. So we can't reach the node before it. Yet we have to make its value vanish. With four, five, one, nine, seven, three, and node nine, we get four, five, one, seven, three.
say.brute: Here's one honest approach. Shift values. Starting at our node, copy each next value back one place, walking forward. Then cut off the last node. Everything after the target slides left by one. It works. But it touches every node after the target. That's linear work for something we can do instantly.
say.insight: Normally, deleting needs the previous node. We don't have it. So let's change the question. Do we really have to remove this exact node? No. Only its value. So copy the next node's value into this node. Now it's a duplicate of its successor. Then unlink the successor. Two assignments. Constant time.
say.anim: We start at the head node, value four, searching for the node holding nine. Target's value four isn't nine, so we move forward to value five. Still not nine, we keep walking the list, now checking value one. Value one isn't nine either, so target advances again, now pointing at nine. Target's value equals nine, so the loop stops right here. We copy the next node's value, seven, into target, overwriting nine. Then we skip over the old seven node, linking target directly to the next seven. Nine is gone, leaving the list as four, five, one, seven, three.
say.code: Let's walk the code. Our test harness passes the head and a value, so the first loop just finds the node. On LeetCode, you're given it directly. Then the real answer is two lines. This node takes on the next node's value. Then it skips the now duplicate next node, pointing past it.
say.outro: Constant time and space. The pattern is linked lists. When you can't reach the previous node, copy forward and skip.

delete-node-in-a-linked-list.title: Delete Node in a Linked List
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which holds the method that removes the requested value from the linked list.
The deleteNode method receives the head of the list and the value to remove, and it changes the list in place.
We start a pointer called target at the head so we can walk the list looking for the value.
We keep looping as long as the value at target is not the value we want to delete.
Inside the loop we move target forward to the next node, bringing us closer to the match.
Once found, we copy the next node's value into target, so the old value is overwritten and disappears.
We then point target's next to the node after its next, unlinking the duplicate node and finishing the deletion.

delete-the-middle-node-of-a-linked-list.hook: Fast pointer moves two, slow moves one. When fast falls off, slow is right before the middle.
delete-the-middle-node-of-a-linked-list.ask: Given the head of a linked list, delete the middle node, the one at index n over two rounded down, and return the head.
delete-the-middle-node-of-a-linked-list.exampleWhy: Seven nodes, so the middle is index three, the value 7. Removing it leaves 1, 3, 4, 1, 2, 6.

brute.idea: Count the nodes in one pass, then walk again to the node just before index n over two and unlink.
steps: Walk the list to count n
Walk n over two minus one steps
Skip the next node
brute.whySlow: Same big O, but it needs two full traversals; the one-pass version halves the pointer walking.

optimal.insight: Start fast two nodes ahead of slow. When fast reaches the end, slow stops just before the middle, ready to unlink it.
steps: One node? Return empty
Slow at head, fast at head.next.next
Advance slow by one, fast by two
Unlink slow.next

codeNotes.note: Head start makes slow stop one early
Stop when fast runs off the end

pitfalls: Starting both at head lands slow on the middle, not before it.
Handle the single node list separately.

say.intro: Delete the Middle Node of a Linked List. We remove the node at index n over two, rounded down, and return the head. Our list has seven nodes. So the middle is index three, the seven. Removing it leaves one, three, four, one, two, six.
say.brute: The straightforward way counts first. Walk the whole list to learn its length. Then walk again, stopping just before the middle, and point past it. Is that slow? Not really. It's linear time and constant space. It just takes two passes, when one is enough.
say.insight: Here's the trick. Fast and slow pointers. Fast moves two steps for every one of slow. So when fast hits the end, slow is halfway. But wait. To delete, we need the node before the middle. So give fast a head start of two nodes. Now slow stops exactly one node early, ready to unlink.
say.anim: We start with the list one, three, four, seven, one, two, six, checking it has more than one node. Slow starts at node one, fast jumps ahead two nodes to node four. The loop checks fast and its next exist, so we keep moving both pointers. Slow advances to node three, fast jumps forward to node one at position five. Fast still has a next node, so the loop continues advancing both pointers. Slow moves to node four, fast jumps ahead to node six, the last node. Now fast has no next node, so the loop stops with slow just before the middle. Slow's next pointer skips over seven, unlinking the middle node from the list. The final list returned is one, three, four, one, two, six, with seven removed.
say.code: Let's walk the code. A single node? The list becomes empty, so return nothing. Then slow starts at the head, and fast two nodes ahead. That head start makes slow stop one early. Keep moving until fast runs off the end. Then unlink the middle node by pointing slow past it. Return the head.
say.outro: One pass, constant space. The pattern is fast and slow pointers to find the middle of a linked list.

delete-the-middle-node-of-a-linked-list.title: Delete the Middle Node of a Linked List
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which holds the method that solves the problem.
The deleteMiddle method takes the head of a linked list and returns the head of the modified list.
If the head has no next node, the list has one node, so the middle is the head itself.
In that single node case we return nothing, since deleting the only node leaves an empty list.
We set slow to the head and fast to two nodes ahead, giving slow the head start it needs to stop before the middle.
We keep looping while fast exists and has a next node, meaning fast can still jump two steps.
Each loop, slow moves forward one node, so it advances at half the speed of fast.
Fast moves forward two nodes, so when it runs out of list, slow sits just before the middle.
