We point slow's next to the node after the middle, which unlinks the middle node from the list.
We return the head, which is still the start of the list after the deletion.

design-hashmap.hook: Build the data structure you use every day: buckets plus chaining.
design-hashmap.ask: Implement a hash map with put, get and remove for integer keys and values, without using any built-in hash table. get returns -1 for a missing key.
design-hashmap.exampleWhy: Key 1 maps to 1, key 3 is missing, key 2 is updated to 1, then removed, so its last get returns -1.

brute.idea: Keep one flat list of key value pairs and scan it for every operation.
steps: put: scan for the key, update or append
get: scan for the key
remove: scan and delete the pair
brute.whySlow: Every call scans all stored pairs; 10,000 keys means 10,000 comparisons per call.

optimal.insight: Hash the key to one of many buckets. Each bucket holds only a few pairs, so every operation scans a tiny list.
steps: Allocate a fixed array of buckets
Bucket index is key modulo the size
Search only that bucket's short chain
Update, append, or remove inside it

codeNotes.match: for k, v in self.buckets[key % self.size]:

pitfalls: put on an existing key must update, not add a second pair.
Too few buckets makes chains long; resize when the load gets high.

say.intro: Design HashMap. We build our own hash map, with put, get and remove. And no built in hash table allowed. In the example, we store keys one and two. We read key one, and miss on key three. We update key two, then remove it. So the last get returns minus one.
say.brute: The simplest design keeps one flat list of key value pairs. Put scans the list, then updates or appends. Get scans for the key. Remove filters it out. Everything is correct. So what's the problem? Every call scans every stored pair. With ten thousand keys, that's ten thousand comparisons per call.
say.insight: Here's the thing. Split the pairs into lots of small lists, called buckets. A hash function tells us which bucket a key must live in. Here it's just the key modulo the number of buckets. Now we only search that one bucket. With a thousand buckets and spread out keys, each chain stays tiny. So each operation is constant time on average.
say.anim: We start by creating one thousand empty buckets to store our key value pairs. Putting key one with value one finds an empty bucket and appends the pair. Putting key two with value two does the same, landing in its own bucket. Getting key one scans its bucket, finds a match, and returns value one. Getting key three finds no matching pair, so it returns negative one. Putting key two again finds the existing pair and updates its value to one. Removing key two locates the pair at index zero and pops it from the bucket. Getting key two now finds an empty bucket, returning negative one as the final answer.
say.code: Let's walk the code. The constructor makes a thousand buckets, one chain per bucket. Put hashes to a bucket. Existing key? Overwrite its value. New key? Add it to the chain. Get uses the same hash, key modulo the bucket count. It returns minus one if the key isn't there. Remove deletes the pair from that short chain.
say.outro: Constant time on average. The pattern is hashing. Hash into buckets, and chain the collisions.

design-hashmap.title: Design HashMap
lineNotes: We define a class called MyHashMap that will store integer keys and values using our own bucket structure.
The constructor sets up the empty map before any put, get or remove calls happen.
We fix the number of buckets at one thousand and store it in size.
We build buckets as a list of one thousand empty lists, each ready to hold key value pairs.
The put method takes a key and a value and stores or updates that pair.
We hash the key by taking it modulo size, and grab the bucket that key belongs to.
We walk through every pair in that bucket to see whether the key is already stored.
If a pair's first item equals the key, we have found an existing entry for it.
We overwrite that pair's value with the new one so the key is updated rather than duplicated.
We return right away since the update is finished and no new pair is needed.
If the loop finds nothing, we append a fresh pair of key and value to the bucket.
The get method takes a key and returns its value, or negative one if missing.
We scan the pairs in the key's bucket, unpacking each into k and v.
We check whether the stored key k matches the key we are looking for.
On a match we return the stored value v immediately.
If the scan ends without a match, the key is absent, so we return negative one.
The remove method takes a key and deletes its pair if it exists.
We find the key's bucket by taking the key modulo size, just like in put.
We loop over the bucket with enumerate so we know both the index and the pair.
We test whether this pair's key equals the key we want to remove.
We pop the pair at index i out of the bucket, deleting that entry.
We return right away, since we must not keep iterating after changing the list.

design-parking-system.hook: Three counters, indexed by car type. Sometimes the best design is the smallest one.
design-parking-system.ask: A lot has a fixed number of big, medium and small spaces. Each arriving car of type 1, 2 or 3 parks in its own size if a space is free; report true or false.
design-parking-system.exampleWhy: One big and one medium space fill up. No small spaces exist, and the second big car finds the big space taken.

brute.idea: Record every parked car in a list, and count matching types each time a car arrives.
steps: Store the three capacities
Count parked cars of this type
Below capacity? park it
brute.whySlow: Each arrival recounts every parked car, so k arrivals cost about k squared over two checks.

optimal.insight: We only need how many free spaces remain per type. Keep three counters and decrement on each successful park.
steps: Store free spaces in a list indexed by type
If zero free, return False
Otherwise decrement and return True

pitfalls: carType is 1, 2 or 3: subtract one before indexing.

say.intro: Design Parking System. A lot has a fixed number of big, medium and small spaces. Each car has a type, one, two or three, and can only use its own size. Does it park? We return true or false. With one big, one medium and no small spaces, we get true, true, false, false.
say.brute: A literal simulation remembers every parked car in a list. When a new car arrives, count the parked cars of that type. Compare with the capacity. It's correct. But every arrival rescans the whole list. A thousand arrivals cost about half a million checks.
say.insight: Here's the thing. Do we care which cars parked? No. We only care how many spaces of each type are still free. So keep three numbers. An arrival checks its own counter. Zero? The car is turned away. Otherwise, take one space by decrementing. Every call is one lookup and one update.
say.anim: We start with one big spot, one medium spot, and zero small spots. A car of type one arrives, checking if big spots are free, since one remains. Big spots drop to zero, and the car parks successfully, returning true. A type two car checks medium spots, which still has one free, so it parks. A type three car checks small spots, but zero are free, so it fails. Another type one car checks big spots, now zero, so it fails too. Final results show two cars parked successfully and two were rejected.
say.code: Let's walk the code. The constructor stores free spaces per car type, in a list. Now, notice the types are one based. So add car subtracts one to get the index. None left? Return false. Otherwise, take one space by decrementing the counter, and return true.
say.outro: Constant time per call, constant space. The pattern is simple. Store just the counts you need, indexed by type.

design-parking-system.title: Design Parking System
lineNotes: We define a ParkingSystem class that will track how many parking spaces remain for each car size.
The constructor takes the starting counts of big, medium and small spaces for the lot.
We store those three counts in a list called free, ordered so car type minus one is the index.
The addCar method receives a car type of one, two or three and reports whether it can park.
We look up the free count for this car type and check whether it has already hit zero.
If no space is free for that size, we return false because the car cannot park.
Otherwise we take one space by decrementing the free count for that car type.
We then return true to confirm the car successfully parked.

distribute-elements-into-two-arrays-i.hook: A pure simulation: follow the rule exactly, and remember only the two last elements.
distribute-elements-into-two-arrays-i.ask: Put the first number in arr1 and the second in arr2. Each later number goes to arr1 if arr1's last element is bigger than arr2's, otherwise to arr2. Return arr1 followed by arr2.
distribute-elements-into-two-arrays-i.exampleWhy: 5 > 4 sends 3 to arr1. Then 3 < 4 sends 8 and 1 to arr2, and 3 > 1 sends 7 to arr1.

brute.idea: Simulate, but rebuild each array by copying it plus the new element every time.
steps: Start arr1 with nums[0], arr2 with nums[1]
Compare the last elements
Rebuild the chosen array with the new element
brute.whySlow: Copying the whole array on every append makes n appends cost n squared element copies.

optimal.insight: There is no trick; the rule only looks at the two last elements. Appending in place makes each step constant time.
steps: Seed arr1 and arr2 with the first two numbers
For each next number, compare the two tails
Append to arr1 if its tail is larger, else arr2
Concatenate at the end

pitfalls: The problem is 1-indexed; in 0-indexed code, nums[0] and nums[1] seed the arrays.

say.intro: Distribute Elements Into Two Arrays. The first number goes to array one. The second goes to array two. After that, each number joins array one if its last element is bigger than array two's last element. Otherwise it joins array two. We return both, joined. Here, that's five, three, seven, four, eight, one.
say.brute: A careless simulation rebuilds an array every time it grows. It writes array one equals array one plus the new element. That makes a brand new copy each time. The answer comes out right. But the copying adds up to quadratic work. For a process this simple, that's wasteful.
say.insight: Here's the thing. There's no clever shortcut here. And that's the lesson. The rule only looks at the two last elements. So the job is to follow it exactly, while keeping each step cheap. Appending in place is amortised constant time. So the whole thing is one linear pass.
say.anim: We start by putting the first two numbers, five and four, into separate arrays. Now we check each remaining number against the last elements of both arrays. Five is greater than four, so three joins arr1, making it five and three. Now three is not greater than four, so eight goes into arr2 instead. Three is still less than eight, so one also gets added to arr2. Finally three is less than eight, wait seven compares to eight, so seven joins arr1. With all numbers placed, we combine arr1 and arr2 into one list. The final answer is five, three, seven, four, eight, one.
say.code: Let's walk the code. The first two moves are fixed. Five seeds array one, and four seeds array two. Then loop over the rest. Only the tails decide. Is array one's last element bigger? Append there. Otherwise, append to array two. Each append is amortised constant time. Finally, concatenate once, at the end.
say.outro: Linear time. The pattern is simulation. Follow the rule precisely, and keep each step constant time.

distribute-elements-into-two-arrays-i.title: Distribute Elements Into Two Arrays I
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container the judge expects for our method.
The method resultArray takes the list of numbers and returns the final combined list after distribution.
We start arr1 with the first number and arr2 with the second number, as the problem requires.
We loop over every remaining number, skipping the first two since they are already placed.
We compare the last element of arr1 with the last element of arr2 to decide where this number goes.
If arr1 has the bigger last element, we append the current number to arr1.
Otherwise, meaning arr2's last element is bigger, we take the other branch.
In that case we append the current number to arr2, and ties also land here.
Finally we return arr1 followed by arr2 joined together as one list.

duplicate-zeros.hook: Shifting right in place? Work backwards, so you never overwrite something you still need.
duplicate-zeros.ask: Duplicate every zero in a fixed length array, in place, shifting the rest right. Elements pushed past the end are dropped.
duplicate-zeros.exampleWhy: Each of the first two zeros is doubled, pushing 5 and the last 0 off the end of the array.

brute.idea: Walk forward; at each zero, insert another zero after it and drop the last element.
steps: Scan left to right
At a zero, insert a zero after it
Pop the last element and skip two
brute.whySlow: Each insert shifts every later element; many zeros means quadratic shifting.

optimal.insight: Each element moves right by the number of zeros before it. Count zeros, then fill from the back so nothing is overwritten early.
steps: Count all zeros
Walk i from the end backwards
Write arr[i] at i + zeros if it fits
At a zero, decrement zeros and write the copy

codeNotes.note: Move to its final slot, if inside

pitfalls: Writing front to back overwrites values before they are moved.
Bounds check every write: shifted slots may fall past the end.

say.intro: Duplicate Zeros. We double every zero in a fixed length array, in place. The other values shift right. Anything pushed past the end disappears. So one, zero, two, three, zero, four, five, zero becomes one, zero, zero, two, three, zero, zero, four.
say.brute: The direct approach walks forward. At each zero, insert another zero right after it. Pop the last element to keep the length. Then jump past both zeros. It's correct, and uses no extra memory. So what's the catch? Every insert shifts all the later elements. With lots of zeros, that's quadratic.
say.insight: Here's the thing. Look at where each element ends up. It moves right by exactly the number of zeros before it. So count the zeros first. Then fill the array from the back. Why the back? Because then every value is read before anything overwrites it. When we pass a zero, we write its copy too. And earlier elements shift one less.
say.anim: We start with the array one zero two three zero four five zero, length eight. Counting zeros finds three, so later elements will shift right by three spots. At index seven, shifting would go out of bounds, and the value is zero, so zeros drops to two. At index six, five is copied into position eight, but that's out of range, so nothing writes. At index five, four copies into index seven, filling the array's last slot. At index four, the zero copies forward, then zeros decreases to one and writes another zero behind it. Moving left, three and two each shift into their new positions further right. At index one, the zero duplicates itself, dropping zeros to zero and finishing the shifts. Index zero just copies one into place, and the loop ends with final array one zero zero two three zero zero four.
say.code: Let's walk the code. Count all the zeros. That's the shift for the last element. Then go back to front, so nothing gets overwritten early. Move each element to its final slot, if it's inside the array. Is it a zero? Then earlier elements shift one less, so decrement zeros. And write the duplicate zero, again only if it fits.
say.outro: Linear time, constant space. The pattern is two pointers, a read index and a write index, moving backwards.

duplicate-zeros.title: Duplicate Zeros
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container the judge expects for our method.
The method duplicateZeros takes the array and modifies it in place, so it returns nothing.
We store the length of the array in n, since the array size stays fixed.
We count how many zeros are in the array, which tells us how far the first element shifts.
We loop from the last index down to zero, going backward so we never overwrite values we still need.
We check whether the shifted position, index plus remaining zeros, still falls inside the array bounds.
If it fits, we copy the current element to its new shifted position to the right.
If the current element is zero, we need to handle its duplicate copy too.
We decrease the zero count, because elements to the left of this zero shift by one fewer.
We check that the duplicate's position, index plus the updated zero count, is still inside the array.
If it fits, we write a zero there, which creates the duplicated zero right next to the copied one.

evaluate-division.hook: Every equation is a weighted edge. A query is just a path, and the answer is the product along it.
evaluate-division.ask: Given equations like a divided by b equals 2, answer queries like a divided by c. Return -1 when the answer cannot be determined.
evaluate-division.exampleWhy: a/c = (a/b)(b/c) = 6, b/a = 1/2. e and x never appear, so those are unknown; a/a is 1.

brute.idea: Precompute every ratio between every pair of variables with Floyd-Warshall style chaining, then read answers off a table.
steps: Store direct ratios both ways
For each middle k, chain i to k to j
Look up each query in the table
brute.whySlow: It computes every pair's ratio up front, cubic in variables, even when only a few queries are asked.

optimal.insight: a/b = 2 is an edge a to b with weight 2, and b to a with weight one half. A query multiplies weights along any path.
steps: Build a weighted graph with both directions
Unknown variable? answer -1
BFS from the numerator, multiplying weights
Reach the denominator: return the product

codeNotes.match: if src not in graph or dst not in graph:

pitfalls: x/x is -1 when x is unknown, not 1.
Weighted union-find also works and answers each query in near constant time.

say.intro: Evaluate Division. We're told a divided by b is two, and b divided by c is three. Then we answer queries. A over c is six. B over a is one half. A over a is one. And anything with an unknown variable, like e or x, gets minus one.
say.brute: One approach precomputes everything. Store each ratio in both directions. Then chain them through every possible middle variable, like Floyd Warshall. Eventually the table holds every connected pair. Each query is a lookup. The catch? Building that table is cubic in the number of variables. Even if we only ask a few questions.
say.insight: Think about it this way. Each variable is a node. A over b equals two is an edge from a to b, weight two. And an edge back, weight one half. Now, what's a over c? The product of weights along any path from a to c. There are no contradictions, so any path works. A simple search answers each query.
say.anim: We build a graph where each equation becomes two weighted edges, forward and reciprocal. Edge a to b gets weight 2, and b to a gets weight one half. Edge b to c gets weight 3, and c to b gets weight one third. For query a over c, breadth first search starts at a with product 1. It moves to b with product 2, then from b reaches c multiplying by 3, giving 6. For query b over a, search starts at b and reaches a directly with product 0.5. Query a over e fails since e is missing, and a over a trivially returns 1. Query x over x fails too, giving the final answers six, half, negative one, one, negative one.
say.code: Let's walk the code. Each equation adds an edge both ways. The reverse edge carries the reciprocal. The search first checks for unknown variables. Can't answer? Return minus one. Then start at the numerator, with product one. Pop a node. Reached the denominator? Return the product. Otherwise, push unvisited neighbours, multiplying ratios along the path.
say.outro: Linear in the graph, per query. The pattern is graphs. Model ratios as weighted edges, and multiply along a path.

evaluate-division.title: Evaluate Division
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container this problem's method lives in.
The calcEquation method takes the equations, their values, and the queries, and returns a list of answers.
We create a graph as a dictionary where each variable maps to a list of neighbors with weights.
We loop over each equation paired with its value, unpacking the two variables a and b.
We add an edge from a to b with weight v, since a divided by b equals v.
We add the reverse edge from b to a with weight one over v.
We define a helper bfs that finds the product of weights along a path from source to destination.
If either variable never appeared in any equation, the answer is unknowable.
So we return negative one in that case.
We start a queue holding the source with a running product of one, since a variable divided by itself is one.
We keep a seen set starting with the source so we never revisit nodes or loop forever.
We keep exploring while the queue still has nodes waiting.
We pop the next node along with the product accumulated from the source to it.
We check whether this node is the destination we are looking for.
If so, the accumulated product is the answer to the query, so we return it.
Otherwise we look at every neighbor of this node together with the edge weight.
We only consider neighbors we have not already visited.
We mark that neighbor as seen so it is queued at most once.
We enqueue the neighbor with the product multiplied by the edge weight, extending the path ratio.
If the queue empties without reaching the destination, they are not connected, so we return negative one.
We answer every query by running bfs on each pair and collect the results in a list.

excel-sheet-column-number.hook: Excel columns are just base 26 numbers whose digits run from 1 to 26 instead of 0 to 25.
excel-sheet-column-number.ask: Given an Excel column title like A, Z, AA or AB, return its column number, where A is 1, Z is 26 and AA is 27.
excel-sheet-column-number.exampleWhy: A is worth 1 times 26, and B adds 2, so AB is column 28.

brute.idea: Count upward from column 1, converting each number to its title, until the title matches.
steps: Increment the column number
Convert it to a title
Stop when the title matches
brute.whySlow: FXSHRXW is column 2,147,483,647: billions of conversions just to count up to it.

optimal.insight: Read the title like a base 26 number, left to right: multiply the running total by 26 and add the letter's value, 1 to 26.
steps: Start the result at zero
For each letter, shift left: multiply by 26
Add the letter's value, A as 1

pitfalls: Digits are 1 to 26, not 0 to 25: forgetting the +1 breaks everything.

say.intro: Excel Sheet Column Number. Spreadsheet columns go A to Z, then A A, A B, and so on. Given a title, we return its column number. A is one. Z is twenty six. And A B is twenty eight. Why? A counts one full alphabet, and B adds two.
say.brute: The brute force just counts. Start at column one. Convert each number to its title. Keep going until the title matches. It's guaranteed to be right. But the work equals the answer itself. The biggest title is about two billion. That's a lot of counting.
say.insight: Here's the thing. A column title is just a number in base twenty six. There's one twist. The digits run from one to twenty six, not zero to twenty five. So we read it like any number, left to right. Each new letter shifts the total one place, multiplying by twenty six. Then we add that letter's value.
say.anim: We start with the title AB and result set to zero. The first letter A converts to digit value one. Result becomes zero times twenty six plus one, giving one. Next letter B converts to digit value two. Result becomes one times twenty six plus two, giving twenty eight. The loop ends since all letters have been processed. The function returns twenty eight as the final column number.
say.code: Let's walk the code. Start the result at zero. For each letter, find its value. A is one, Z is twenty six. Then shift one base twenty six place, and add. That's the result times twenty six, plus the digit. After the last letter, the result is our column number.
say.outro: Linear in the title length. The pattern is math. Spot a positional number system, then evaluate it left to right.

excel-sheet-column-number.title: Excel Sheet Column Number
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container the interview platform expects for our method.
The method titleToNumber takes the column title string and returns its column number as an integer.
We start result at zero, since an empty title contributes nothing before we read any letters.
We loop over each letter of the title from left to right, just like reading digits of a number.
We turn the letter into its value by subtracting the code of A and adding one, so A is one and Z is twenty six.
We shift the running total one place by multiplying by twenty six, then add this letter's value.
After all letters are processed, we return result as the final column number.

expression-add-operators.hook: Try plus, minus and times between digits. The trick is undoing the last operand when you multiply.
expression-add-operators.ask: Given a string of digits and a target, insert plus, minus or times between digits so the expression equals the target. Return every such expression; numbers may not have leading zeros.
expression-add-operators.exampleWhy: 2*3+2 is 6 + 2 = 8, and 2+3*2 is 2 + 6 = 8. Nothing else reaches 8.

brute.idea: Generate every way to place times, plus, minus or nothing between digits, then evaluate each full string.
steps: Choose an operator or nothing per gap
Skip operands with leading zeros
Evaluate the full expression; keep matches
brute.whySlow: Every expression is re-parsed from scratch at the end, multiplying the exponential count by n.

optimal.insight: Track the running value and the last operand. Multiplying undoes the last operand and adds last times x, so precedence costs constant time.
steps: Pick the next operand num[i..j]
Stop extending at a leading zero
Plus: value + x, last = x
Minus: value - x, last = -x
Times: value - last + last·x, last = last·x

codeNotes.note: Value so far, plus the last operand
No multi-digit numbers starting with zero
First operand: no operator before it

codeNotes.match: value - last + last * x, last * x

pitfalls: Store last as negative after minus, or later multiplications go wrong.
0 alone is a valid operand; 05 is not.

say.intro: Expression Add Operators. We get a string of digits and a target. We insert plus, minus, or times between digits, and return every expression that hits the target. Numbers can span several digits, but no leading zeros. For two three two with target eight, we find two times three plus two, and two plus three times two.
say.brute: The brute force tries every choice in every gap. Times, plus, minus, or nothing at all. That builds every possible expression string. At the end, it throws out leading zeros and evaluates each string from scratch. The count is exponential. And re parsing every one adds even more work.
say.insight: So what's the hard part? Precedence. Times binds tighter than plus. Here's the fix. Remember the last operand we added. When we multiply by x, take that last operand back out. Then add last times x instead. Now the value is always correct as we go. We never parse a full string.
say.anim: We start with the digit string two three two and a target of eight. First digit two becomes the initial value, with last set to two. Multiplying by three gives path two times three, value six, last six. Adding the final two makes value twelve, which misses the target. Trying addition instead gives path two times three plus two, value eight, a match. Backtracking, path two plus three plus two then multiplying gives value eight again. The search continues exploring bigger chunks like three two and twenty three with pluses, minuses, and multiplies. After exploring all combinations, the two valid expressions found are two times three plus two and two plus three times two.
say.code: Let's walk the code. The helper carries the value so far, plus the last operand. Try every next operand, but stop at a leading zero. No multi digit numbers starting with zero. The first operand has no operator before it. After that, times undoes last and applies the product first. Plus just adds. And minus remembers the negative operand as last.
say.outro: Still exponential, but no re parsing. The pattern is backtracking. Carry just enough state to handle precedence as you go.

expression-add-operators.title: Expression Add Operators
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, as the problem platform expects.
The addOperators method takes the digit string and the target value, and returns all expressions that hit the target.
We start with an empty list called res to collect every valid expression.
We define a recursive helper dfs that tracks the index, the expression so far, the running value, and the last operand.
If the index reaches the end of the digit string, we have used every digit and can check the result.
We compare the running value to the target to see if this expression is valid.
When it matches, we add the built expression string to the results.
We return here either way, since there are no more digits to place.
We try every possible next operand by letting j extend the number from index i to each later digit.
If the number has more than one digit and starts with zero, it would have a leading zero.
So we break out of the loop, because longer numbers starting at this zero are all invalid too.
We slice out the substring from i through j as the current operand text.
We convert that substring to an integer so we can do arithmetic with it.
At the very first position there is no operator to place before the number.
So we start the expression with just this number, setting both the value and the last operand to it.
Otherwise we must choose an operator to place before the number.
For times, we undo the last operand from the value and add last times x, which respects precedence in constant time.
For plus, we add x to the value and record x as the new last operand.
For minus, we subtract x from the value and record negative x as the last operand so a later times works correctly.
We kick off the search at index zero with an empty path and zero value and last.
Finally we return the collected list of expressions.

factorial-trailing-zeroes.hook: Every trailing zero is a 10, which is a 2 times a 5. Twos are plentiful, so count the fives.
factorial-trailing-zeroes.ask: Given n, return how many zeros appear at the end of n factorial, without computing the factorial.
factorial-trailing-zeroes.exampleWhy: 1 to 100 holds 20 multiples of 5 and 4 multiples of 25: 20 + 4 = 24 fives.

brute.idea: For every number from 1 to n, divide out factors of five and add them up.
steps: Loop i from 1 to n
While i divisible by 5, divide and count
Return the total count
brute.whySlow: It visits all n numbers, though only every fifth one contributes anything.

optimal.insight: Multiples of 5 give one five each, multiples of 25 one more, 125 one more. Sum n over 5, n over 25, and so on.
steps: Divide n by 5 and add the quotient
Repeat with the quotient
Stop when it reaches zero

codeNotes.note: Until no higher power of five fits
Multiples of the next power of five

pitfalls: Computing the factorial itself overflows fast in most languages.
Multiples of 25 contribute two fives, not one.

say.intro: Factorial Trailing Zeroes. Given n, how many zeros sit at the end of n factorial? Every trailing zero comes from a ten. And ten is two times five. Twos are everywhere, so the fives decide. For one hundred, the answer is twenty four.
say.brute: The brute force looks at every number from one to n. It divides out each factor of five and adds it to a counter. We never build the giant factorial, and it's correct. But it walks through all n numbers. And only every fifth one has a five at all.
say.insight: Here's the thing. Count fives in groups. Every multiple of five gives one five. Every multiple of twenty five gives a second. Every multiple of a hundred twenty five gives a third. So the answer is n over five, plus n over twenty five, plus n over a hundred twenty five, and so on. Each one rounded down.
say.anim: We start with n equal to 100 and count initialized to zero. The loop checks n is nonzero, so we continue dividing by five. Dividing 100 by five gives 20, counting multiples of five up to 100. Count becomes 20, adding those twenty multiples of five found so far. Dividing 20 by five gives 4, capturing extra fives from multiples of 25. Count becomes 24, adding four more fives from numbers like 25 and 50. Dividing 4 by five gives zero, since no more multiples of 125 remain. The loop ends and the function returns 24 as the final answer.
say.code: Let's walk the code. Start the count at zero. Loop until no higher power of five fits, meaning n hits zero. Each round, divide n by five. That gives the multiples of the next power of five. Each of those contributes one more five, so add n to the count. Return the count.
say.outro: Logarithmic time. The pattern is math. Count prime factors instead of building the giant number.

factorial-trailing-zeroes.title: Factorial Trailing Zeroes
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container for the method that solves the trailing zeroes problem.
The method trailingZeroes takes the integer n and returns how many zeros end n factorial, without computing it.
We start count at zero, which will accumulate the total number of factors of five found.
We loop as long as n is not zero, since once it reaches zero no more fives remain.
We divide n by five using integer division, giving how many multiples of the current power of five exist up to n.
We add that quotient to count, since each such multiple contributes one more factor of five.
Finally we return count, which equals the number of trailing zeros because each zero needs one five paired with a two.

find-a-safe-walk-through-a-grid.hook: Edges cost zero or one. A deque turns Dijkstra into a plain linear BFS.
find-a-safe-walk-through-a-grid.ask: Walk from the top left to the bottom right of a binary grid. Each cell with 1 costs one health. Can you arrive with at least 1 health left?
find-a-safe-walk-through-a-grid.exampleWhy: Going down the left column and along the bottom row avoids both 1 cells, so health stays at 1.

brute.idea: Depth first search over every simple path, subtracting health on unsafe cells and backtracking when health drops below one.
steps: Step into a cell, pay its cost
Health below one? back out
Reach the corner? return True
Try all four neighbours
brute.whySlow: The number of simple paths explodes; a 50 by 50 grid is far beyond reach.

optimal.insight: Find the minimum damage path. With weights 0 or 1, push free moves to the front of a deque and costly ones to the back.
steps: dist holds least damage to each cell
Pop from the front of the deque
Relax each neighbour with its cell cost
Cost 0 goes front, cost 1 goes back
Safe if health minus damage is at least one

codeNotes.note: The start cell can hurt too
Cost one: back of the deque
Cost zero: front of the deque
Need at least one health left

pitfalls: Count the start cell's cost too.
Plain BFS by steps is wrong; minimise damage, not distance.

say.intro: Find a Safe Walk Through a Grid. We start in the top left corner and want the bottom right. Cells marked one are unsafe, and cost one health each. We start with one health. The middle column has two unsafe cells. But going down and along the bottom avoids them. So the answer is true.
say.brute: The brute force tries every simple path with depth first search. Step into a cell and pay its cost. Health below one? Back out. Reach the corner? Success. Otherwise, try all four neighbours, and backtrack. So what's wrong? The number of paths explodes exponentially. Big grids are hopeless.
say.insight: Here's the thing. We only need the path with the least damage. That's a shortest path problem, where each step costs zero or one. Dijkstra would work. But with just two weights, there's a simpler trick. Use a deque. Free moves go to the front. Costly moves go to the back. So cells come out in order of damage.
say.anim: We start at cell zero zero, with grid values zero one zero, zero one zero, zero zero zero, and health one. The deque pops zero zero, exploring neighbors to find the cheapest damage path using zero one weights. Free moves with weight zero get pushed to the front, like reaching row two column zero with distance zero. Costly moves with weight one, like cell zero one, get pushed to the back of the deque instead. The algorithm keeps expanding, updating distances like cell two two reaching zero and cell one two reaching zero. Further exploration updates farther cells, like row one nc three with distance one, always favoring low cost moves. Eventually the deque empties after all reachable cells have their minimum damage distances calculated. The final distance to the bottom right corner is zero, so health minus distance meets the safety threshold, returning true.
say.code: Let's walk the code. Damage starts at infinity everywhere. Notice the start cell can hurt too, so it begins at its own cost. Pop from the front. For each neighbour, compute the damage via this cell. Better? Record it. Cost one goes to the back of the deque. Cost zero goes to the front. Finally, we need at least one health left.
say.outro: Linear in the grid size. The pattern is zero one BFS. A deque does the job of a heap.

find-a-safe-walk-through-a-grid.title: Find a Safe Walk Through a Grid
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container the judge expects for our method.
The method takes the grid and starting health, and returns true if we can reach the end safely.
We read the number of rows as m and columns as n from the grid.
We build a distance table of the same size, filled with infinity to mean not yet reached.
The start cell's distance is its own damage, since stepping on a one there already costs health.
We create a deque holding just the starting cell, ready for zero-one breadth first search.
We keep looping as long as the deque still has cells to process.
We take a cell from the front, which always has the smallest known damage.
We look at the four neighbors: down, up, right, and left of the current cell.
We only continue if the neighbor lies inside the grid bounds.
The new damage is the current cell's damage plus the neighbor's own cost.
We only act if this route reaches the neighbor with less damage than before.
We record the improved damage for that neighbor.
If the neighbor costs health, it is a weight one edge.
So we push it to the back of the deque to be processed later.
Otherwise the neighbor is free, a weight zero edge.
So we push it to the front, so it is processed immediately with the same damage.
Finally we return whether health minus the damage at the bottom right corner leaves at least one.

find-all-anagrams-in-a-string.hook: A fixed size window slides across s. Add one letter, drop one letter, compare counts.
find-all-anagrams-in-a-string.ask: Given strings s and p, return every start index in s where a substring is an anagram of p, a rearrangement of the same letters.
find-all-anagrams-in-a-string.exampleWhy: cba at index 0 and bac at index 6 both use one a, one b and one c.

brute.idea: For every window of length p, count its letters from scratch and compare with p's counts.
steps: Count p's letters once
For each start i, count s[i:i+len(p)]
Equal counts? record i
brute.whySlow: Each window is recounted from scratch: 30,000 by 30,000 is far too much work.

optimal.insight: Neighbouring windows share all but two letters. Slide the window: add the new letter, remove the one that fell off, compare 26 counts.
steps: Count p into need
Add s[i] to the window counts
Once longer than p, remove s[i - len(p)]
Counts equal? record the window start

pitfalls: Record i - len(p) + 1, the window start, not i.
If p is longer than s, the answer is empty.

say.intro: Find All Anagrams in a String. Given a text s and a pattern p, we return every position in s where a substring is a rearrangement of p. In c b a e b a b a c d, with pattern a b c, two windows match. C b a at index zero, and b a c at index six.
say.brute: The brute force looks at every window as long as p. It counts the window's letters from scratch. Counts match p's counts? Record the start. It's correct. But each window costs the length of p. That's n times m. Far too slow for strings of thirty thousand letters.
say.insight: Here's the thing. Neighbouring windows overlap almost completely. When the window slides one step, one letter enters on the right. One leaves on the left. That's it. So keep a count array for the window, and update just those two letters. Comparing twenty six counts is constant time. So every step is constant time.
say.anim: We build a need array counting letters a, b, c once each from the pattern. Sliding through s, we add each new letter into the have array as we go. At index two, have matches need exactly, so index zero is recorded as a match. As the window slides past length three, the oldest letter is removed from have. The window keeps sliding, adding new letters and subtracting the ones that fall off. At index eight, have equals need again, so index six is appended to res. The function returns res, giving the final answer zero and six.
say.code: Let's walk the code. Need holds the letter counts of p. Then walk s. Each new letter enters the window, so add it to have. Once the window gets longer than p, the oldest letter leaves. Subtract it. Now compare. Comparing twenty six counts is constant time. If have equals need, record the window start index.
say.outro: Linear time, constant space. The pattern is a fixed size sliding window with incremental counts.

find-all-anagrams-in-a-string.title: Find All Anagrams in a String
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container the problem expects for our method.
The method findAnagrams takes strings s and p and returns a list of starting indexes where anagrams of p begin.
We create two arrays of 26 zeros, need for the letter counts of p and have for the current window.
We loop over each letter c in p to build up the target counts.
For each letter we add one to its slot, found by subtracting 97 from its character code.
We start an empty result list to collect the starting indexes of matching windows.
We walk through s with index i and letter c, treating i as the right edge of the window.
We add the new letter at the right edge to the window counts.
Once i reaches the length of p, the window has grown too big and its leftmost letter must leave.
We subtract one from the count of the letter that just fell off the left, at position i minus the length of p.
If the window counts equal the needed counts, the current window is an anagram of p.
We record the window's start index, which is i minus the length of p plus one.
After scanning the whole string, we return the list of all starting indexes.

find-all-lonely-numbers-in-the-array.hook: Lonely means seen once and no neighbours. One count map answers all three questions.
find-all-lonely-numbers-in-the-array.ask: A number x is lonely if it appears exactly once and neither x minus 1 nor x plus 1 is in the array. Return all lonely numbers in any order.
find-all-lonely-numbers-in-the-array.exampleWhy: 6 and 5 are neighbours of each other. 10, 8, 1 and 3 appear once with no neighbours present.

brute.idea: For each number, scan the whole array to count copies of itself and look for its neighbours.
steps: Pick x
Scan everything: count x, look for x - 1, x + 1
Exactly one copy and no neighbour? keep x
brute.whySlow: Every number rescans the full array: 100,000 numbers means 10 billion comparisons.

optimal.insight: Count every number once in a hash map. Then each lonely test is three constant time lookups: x itself, x minus 1, x plus 1.
steps: Count all numbers in a map
For each x, check its count is one
Check x - 1 and x + 1 are absent

codeNotes.match: if count[x] == 1 and x - 1 not in count and x + 1 not in count:

pitfalls: A duplicated value is never lonely, even with no neighbours.
Indexing a Counter with a missing key adds nothing, but use in for clarity.

say.intro: Find All Lonely Numbers in the Array. A number is lonely when it appears exactly once. And neither one less nor one more appears anywhere. In ten, six, five, eight, one, three, six and five are neighbours. So the lonely ones are ten, eight, one and three.
say.brute: The brute force checks each number by scanning the whole array. While scanning, it counts copies of the number, and watches for a neighbour that differs by one. One copy and no neighbour? It's lonely. It's correct. But every number triggers a full scan. That's quadratic.
say.insight: Here's the thing. All three questions are membership questions. How many times does x appear? Is x minus one present? Is x plus one present? A hash map of counts answers each one in constant time. So count everything once. Then walk the array again, and test each number with three quick lookups.
say.anim: We build a count map from the array, each number appearing exactly once here. Checking ten, it has no neighbors nine or eleven, so it's lonely. Checking six, its neighbor five exists, so six is not lonely. Checking five, its neighbor six exists, so five is skipped too. Checking eight, no seven or nine present, so eight joins the result. Checking one, no zero or two in the map, so one qualifies. Checking three, no two or four present, so three is added too. The loop finishes and returns ten, eight, one, three as lonely numbers.
say.code: Let's walk the code. First, a counter holds the frequency of every value. Then loop over the array. For each number, check two things. Is it unique, with count exactly one? And does it have no neighbours, meaning neither one less nor one more is a key? If so, it's a lonely number. Add it to the result.
say.outro: Linear time and space. The pattern is hashing. Count once, then answer each question with a constant time lookup.

find-all-lonely-numbers-in-the-array.title: Find All Lonely Numbers in the Array
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container that the problem's required method lives inside.
This method takes the list nums and returns a list of every lonely number found in it.
We build a counter that records how many times each number appears in nums, giving constant time lookups.
We start an empty result list that will collect each lonely number we discover.
We walk through every number x in nums, checking each one for loneliness.
A number is lonely if it appears exactly once and neither its predecessor nor its successor appears in the counter.
When all three checks pass, we add x to the result list.
After checking every number, we return the result list holding all the lonely numbers.

find-all-numbers-disappeared-in-an-array.hook: Values are 1 to n, so the array can be its own hash set. Use the sign as the mark.
find-all-numbers-disappeared-in-an-array.ask: An array of n numbers holds values from 1 to n, some repeated. Return every value in 1 to n that never appears.
find-all-numbers-disappeared-in-an-array.exampleWhy: Eight slots, values 1 to 8. The 2 and 3 repeat, crowding out 5 and 6.

brute.idea: For each value from 1 to n, scan the array to see whether it appears.
steps: Loop v from 1 to n
Scan the array for v
Not found? add v
brute.whySlow: Each of the n values scans all n numbers: 100,000 squared is 10 billion checks.

optimal.insight: Each value v points at index v - 1. Flip that slot negative to mark v as seen. Slots still positive belong to missing values.
steps: For each x, take index abs(x) - 1
Make that slot negative
Positive slots i mean i + 1 is missing

codeNotes.note: abs: x may already be flipped

codeNotes.match: return [i + 1 for i in range(len(nums)) if nums[i] > 0]
codeNotes.note: Unmarked slots are the missing values

pitfalls: Use abs(x): earlier marks may have made x negative.
This mutates the input; mention it, or restore signs afterwards.

say.intro: Find All Numbers Disappeared in an Array. We have n numbers, each between one and n, with some repeats. Which values in that range never show up? With eight numbers, the twos and threes repeat. So five and six are missing.
say.brute: The brute force checks each value from one to n. It scans the whole array for it. Not found? Add it to the answer. It uses no extra memory. But every check is a full scan, so the total is n squared. For a hundred thousand numbers, that's ten billion checks.
say.insight: Here's the thing. The values run from one to n, exactly like the indices. So the array can be its own set. When we see value v, we mark index v minus one by making it negative. The sign carries the mark. The absolute value keeps the data. After one pass, any slot still positive was never marked. Its value is missing.
say.anim: We start with the array four, three, two, seven, eight, two, three, one. For value four, we compute index three and flip that slot negative, marking four seen. Value three points to index two, which also turns negative, marking three seen. Value two points to index one, flipping it negative, marking two seen. Negative seven still means seven, so index six flips negative too. Eight points to index seven, flipping it negative as well. The remaining values two, three, and one point to already negative slots, so nothing changes. Slots four and five stay positive, meaning five and six were never marked, giving answer five, six.
say.code: Let's walk the code. For each number, take the absolute value first. Why? It may already be flipped. Subtract one to get the index. Only flip it if it's still positive, so duplicates don't flip it back. Negative means value i plus one was seen. Finally, the unmarked slots are the missing values. Return those indices plus one.
say.outro: Linear time, no extra space. The pattern is using the array itself as a hash set, with signs as marks.

find-all-numbers-disappeared-in-an-array.title: Find All Numbers Disappeared in an Array
lineNotes: We define a Solution class that holds the method for solving this problem.
The method takes the list nums and returns a list of the values from one to n that are missing.
We loop over every value x in nums, so each present number gets a chance to mark its slot.
We take the absolute value of x, since earlier marking may have flipped it, and subtract one to get its index.
We check whether the slot at that index is still positive, meaning this value has not been marked yet.
We flip that slot to negative, which records that the value index plus one has been seen, without flipping it twice.
We collect index plus one for every slot that is still positive, since those values never appeared in the array.

find-greatest-common-divisor-of-array.hook: Find the smallest and largest, then let Euclid do the rest in a handful of steps.
find-greatest-common-divisor-of-array.ask: Return the greatest common divisor of the smallest and largest numbers in the array.
find-greatest-common-divisor-of-array.exampleWhy: The smallest is 12 and the largest is 40. The largest number dividing both is 4.

brute.idea: Take the min and max, then try every divisor from the min downwards until one divides both.
steps: Find min and max
Try d from min down to 1
First d dividing both is the answer
brute.whySlow: Trial division may test every number up to the minimum; Euclid needs only logarithmic steps.

optimal.insight: gcd(a, b) equals gcd(b, a mod b). Replacing the pair with its remainder shrinks numbers fast until one hits zero.
steps: Find the min and max in one pass
Replace (a, b) with (b, a mod b)
When b is zero, a is the gcd

codeNotes.note: Stop when the remainder is zero

pitfalls: It is the gcd of min and max only, not of the whole array.
math.gcd exists; know Euclid anyway in case you are asked.

say.intro: Find Greatest Common Divisor of Array. We take the smallest and largest numbers in the array. Then we return their greatest common divisor, the biggest number dividing both. Here the smallest is twelve, and the largest is forty. Their answer is four.
say.brute: The brute force finds the minimum and maximum. Then it tries every divisor, starting at the minimum and counting down. The first one dividing both numbers wins. It works. But in the worst case, it tries almost every number up to the minimum. With big numbers, that's slow.
say.insight: Here's what Euclid noticed. Any number dividing both a and b also divides the remainder of a divided by b. So the answer for a and b equals the answer for b and that remainder. Each swap shrinks the numbers fast. When the remainder hits zero, the other number is our answer.
say.anim: We start with the array, finding its max, 40, and min, 12. The loop checks if b, 12, is nonzero, so we continue. We update a and b using the remainder trick, giving a as 12 and b as 4. Again b, now 4, is nonzero, so the loop keeps going. Applying the remainder step again sets a to 4 and b to 0. Now b is 0, so the loop ends since gcd stabilizes. The function returns the current value of a, which is 4. The final greatest common divisor of the array is 4.
say.code: Let's walk the code. Only the extremes matter, so a is the maximum, and b is the minimum. Loop until the remainder is zero. Each step, replace the pair with b, and a mod b. That's Euclid. Same answer, smaller numbers. Tuple assignment updates both at once. When b hits zero, return a.
say.outro: Linear to scan, logarithmic for Euclid. The pattern is math. Specifically, the Euclidean algorithm for greatest common divisors.

find-greatest-common-divisor-of-array.title: Find Greatest Common Divisor of Array
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container the problem expects for our method.
The findGCD method takes a list of integers called nums and returns their greatest common divisor as an integer.
We set a to the largest number in nums and b to the smallest, since those are the two values we need.
We loop for as long as b is not zero, because a zero remainder means the answer is found.
We replace a with b and b with the remainder of a divided by b, shrinking the pair while keeping the same gcd.
When b reaches zero, a holds the greatest common divisor, so we return it.

find-in-mountain-array.hook: One peak, two sorted halves. Three binary searches find the target within about fifty reads.
find-in-mountain-array.ask: An array rises strictly to a single peak, then falls strictly. Return the smallest index holding target, or -1, using at most 100 reads of the array.
find-in-mountain-array.exampleWhy: 3 appears at index 2 on the way up and index 5 on the way down; the smaller index wins.

brute.idea: Read the array from left to right and return the first index equal to target.
steps: Read index 0, 1, 2 and so on
Equal to target? return it
End reached: return -1
brute.whySlow: Up to 10,000 reads, but the judge allows only 100: a linear scan is rejected.

optimal.insight: Binary search for the peak by comparing mid with mid + 1. Then each side is sorted, so binary search the rising side first.
steps: Find the peak: rising at mid means peak is right
Binary search the ascending left part
Found? that is the smallest index
Else binary search the descending right part

codeNotes.note: Still climbing: peak is to the right
lo and hi met at the summit
Bigger means target lies further right

pitfalls: On LeetCode, read with mountainArr.get(i) and mountainArr.length().
Search the left side first, or you may return the larger index.

say.intro: Find in Mountain Array. The array climbs strictly to one peak, then falls strictly. We return the smallest index holding the target, or minus one. And here's the catch. We can read at most one hundred values. In our array, three appears at index two and index five. So the answer is two.
say.brute: The brute force reads left to right and returns the first match. The first match is the smallest index, so it's correct. But the array can hold ten thousand values. And the judge allows only one hundred reads. So a linear scan gets rejected outright.
say.insight: Here's the thing. A mountain is two sorted arrays glued at the peak. So first, binary search for the peak. Is mid smaller than the next value? Still climbing, so the peak is to the right. Now each side is sorted. Search the rising side first. Why? It holds the smaller indices. Only then try the falling side.
say.anim: We start with the mountain array and target value three, searching for the peak first. Low and high begin at zero and six, binary searching for the mountain's peak. At mid three, four is less than five, so we move low up to four. At mid five, three is less than one is false, so high shrinks to five. At mid four, five is less than three is false, so high becomes four, matching low. The peak is found at index four, where the value five sits highest. Now we binary search the rising left side, from zero to four, for target three. At mid two, the value three equals target, so we return index two as the answer.
say.code: Let's walk the code. First loop: still climbing means the peak is to the right. Lo and hi meet at the summit. Second loop searches the ascending side first, for the smaller index. Third loop searches the descending side. There, the comparisons flip. A bigger value means the target lies further right. Neither found it? Return minus one.
say.outro: Logarithmic reads, well under one hundred. The pattern is binary search. Find the turning point, then search each sorted half.

find-in-mountain-array.title: Find in Mountain Array

meta.name: findInMountainArray

lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container the judge expects for the method.
The method takes the mountain array and a target value, and returns the smallest index holding the target or negative one.
We store the array length in n so we can set search boundaries.
We start the peak search with lo at the first index and hi at the last index.
We keep narrowing the range while lo is still less than hi, stopping when they meet at the peak.
We compute mid as the middle index between lo and hi.
If the value at mid is smaller than the next value, we are on the rising slope.
So the peak must be to the right, and we move lo to mid plus one.
Otherwise we are on the peak or the falling slope.
So the peak is at mid or to its left, and we set hi to mid.
When the loop ends, lo and hi agree, and we record that index as the peak.
Now we reset the search range to the rising side, from the first index up to the peak.
We run a standard binary search on the ascending part while the range is not empty.
We pick the middle index of the current range.
We read the value at mid once and store it in v to save array reads.
If v equals the target, we have found it on the rising side.
We return mid immediately, which is the smallest index because the rising side is searched first.
If v is smaller than the target, the target must lie further right.
So we move lo to mid plus one.
Otherwise v is larger than the target, so the target lies to the left.
We move hi to mid minus one.
If the rising side had no match, we set the range to just after the peak through the last index.
We binary search the descending part while the range is not empty.
We choose the middle index of this range.
We read the value at mid once and keep it in v.
If v equals the target, we found it on the falling side.
We return mid as the answer.
Because this side is descending, a larger v means the target lies further right.
So we move lo to mid plus one.
Otherwise v is smaller than the target, so the target lies to the left in the descending part.
We move hi to mid minus one.
If neither side contained the target, we return negative one.

find-minimum-in-rotated-sorted-array-ii.hook: Duplicates break the usual binary search tie. When unsure, shrink by one and keep going.
find-minimum-in-rotated-sorted-array-ii.ask: A sorted array, possibly with duplicates, was rotated. Find its minimum while doing as little work as possible.
find-minimum-in-rotated-sorted-array-ii.exampleWhy: The array was sorted as 0,1,2,2,4,4,5,6,6,7 and rotated; the drop from 7 to 0 marks the minimum.

brute.idea: Scan every element and keep the smallest one seen.
steps: Start with the first element
Compare each element with the best so far
Return the smallest
brute.whySlow: Always reads all n elements, even when binary search could finish in log n steps.

optimal.insight: Compare mid with the right end. Bigger: minimum is right of mid. Smaller: it is at mid or left. Equal: drop hi safely.
steps: lo at the start, hi at the end
nums[mid] > nums[hi]: move lo past mid
nums[mid] < nums[hi]: move hi to mid
Equal: hi minus one, still safe

codeNotes.note: The drop is right of mid
mid to hi is sorted: keep mid
Tie: nums[hi] has a copy at mid
lo and hi meet at the minimum

pitfalls: Compare with nums[hi], not nums[lo]; the left comparison is ambiguous.
All duplicates, like 2,2,2,2, forces linear time; no algorithm avoids that.

say.intro: Find Minimum in Rotated Sorted Array Two. A sorted array, maybe with duplicates, got rotated. We find its smallest value, doing as little work as we can. In four, five, six, six, seven, zero, one, two, two, four, the minimum is zero. It sits right after the drop from seven.
say.brute: The brute force scans every element and keeps the smallest. Easy, and correct. But it always reads all n elements. And the array is mostly sorted. Usually binary search can find the drop with only a logarithmic number of reads.
say.insight: Here's the trick. Compare the middle with the right end. Middle bigger? The drop is right of mid. Middle smaller? Then mid through the end is sorted. So the minimum is at mid or to its left. Now, what if they're equal? We can't tell. But the right end has a copy at mid. So dropping it is safe.
say.anim: We start with lo at 0 and hi at 9 for this rotated array. Mid is 4, and nums at mid is greater than nums at hi, so minimum lies right. Lo jumps to mid plus one, now lo is 5. Mid becomes 7, nums at mid is less than nums at hi, so hi moves to mid. Hi shrinks to 7, mid recalculates to 6, still shrinking the search leftward. Mid is 5 now, nums at mid less than nums at hi, hi becomes 5. Lo and hi meet at 5, ending the loop. The function returns nums at lo, giving the minimum value 0.
say.code: Let's walk the code. Middle bigger than the right end? The drop is right of mid, so lo moves past it. Middle smaller? Mid to hi is sorted, so keep mid by setting hi to mid. A tie? The value at hi has a copy at mid, so shrink hi by one. Eventually lo and hi meet at the minimum.
say.outro: Logarithmic on average, linear in the worst case. The pattern is binary search on a rotated array, comparing with the right end.

find-minimum-in-rotated-sorted-array-ii.title: Find Minimum in Rotated Sorted Array II
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container the problem expects for our method.
The findMin method takes the rotated array nums and returns its smallest value as an integer.
We set lo to zero and hi to the last index, so the search window covers the whole array.
We keep looping while lo is less than hi, stopping once the window shrinks to a single element.
We compute mid as the average of lo and hi, rounded down, to probe the middle of the window.
If the middle value is bigger than the value at hi, the drop point must lie to the right of mid.
So we move lo to one past mid, since mid itself cannot be the minimum.
If the middle value is smaller than the value at hi, the minimum is at mid or somewhere to its left.
So we set hi to mid, keeping mid as a possible answer while discarding everything right of it.
Otherwise the middle and hi values are equal, so we cannot tell which side holds the minimum.
We shrink hi by one, which is safe because another equal value remains at mid, so the minimum is not lost.
When the window collapses, lo points at the minimum, so we return the value at lo.

find-missing-elements.hook: The range is pinned by the min and max. A set tells you which values in between are gone.
find-missing-elements.ask: Unique integers originally covered a full range, but some went missing. The smallest and largest remain. Return the missing integers in sorted order.
find-missing-elements.exampleWhy: The range is 3 to 8. Values 3, 4, 5 and 8 are present, so 6 and 7 are missing.

brute.idea: For every value between min and max, scan the array to check whether it is there.
steps: Find min and max
For each v in between, scan nums
Not found? add v
brute.whySlow: Each value in the range rescans the whole array, multiplying range by n.

optimal.insight: Put the numbers in a set. Then walk the range from min to max in order and keep values the set does not contain.
steps: Build a set of nums
Walk v from min to max
Missing from the set? add v

codeNotes.note: Walking in order keeps output sorted

pitfalls: Include max: the range end needs + 1.
No sorting needed: walking the range is already in order.

say.intro: Find Missing Elements. We get unique numbers that once filled a whole range. Some went missing. But the smallest and largest are still there. We return the missing ones, sorted. With three, eight, five and four, the range is three to eight. So six and seven are missing.
say.brute: The brute force walks every value from the minimum to the maximum. For each one, it scans the whole array. Not there? It's missing. That works. But every value costs a full scan. So the total is the size of the range, times n.
say.insight: Here's the thing. The minimum and maximum fix the range. For each value, there's only one question. Is it present? A set answers that in constant time. And notice something nice. We walk the range from low to high. So the missing values come out already sorted. No sorting needed.
say.anim: We start with the list three, eight, five, four, which gets turned into a set. We prepare an empty results list, then loop v from three up to eight. V is three, four, five, and eight, all found in the seen set, so nothing happens. V is six, which is missing from the set, so we append it to results. V is seven, also missing, so it gets appended too, giving results six, seven. V is eight, which is in the set, so the loop finishes without adding it. The function returns the final answer, the missing elements six and seven.
say.code: Let's walk the code. Build a set from the numbers, for constant time membership. Then walk v from the minimum up to the maximum, including it. Walking in order keeps the output sorted. Is v missing from the set? That's a gap in the range. Append it. Return the result.
say.outro: Linear in n plus the range. The pattern is hashing. A set turns every presence check into constant time.

find-missing-elements.title: Find Missing Elements
lineNotes: We define a Solution class that holds the method for solving the missing elements problem.
This method takes the list of numbers and returns a list of the integers missing from the range.
We put all the numbers into a set called seen so membership checks take constant time.
We start an empty list called res that will collect the missing values in sorted order.
We loop through every integer from the smallest number up to the largest, inclusive, in increasing order.
For each value, we check whether it is absent from the seen set.
If the value is absent, we append it to res because it is a missing integer.
After the loop finishes, we return res, which is already sorted since we walked the range in order.

find-numbers-with-even-number-of-digits.hook: Counting digits sounds like arithmetic, but the string length already knows the answer.
find-numbers-with-even-number-of-digits.ask: Given a list of positive integers, return how many of them have an even number of digits.
find-numbers-with-even-number-of-digits.exampleWhy: 12 has two digits and 7896 has four; 345, 2 and 6 have an odd count.

brute.idea: For each number, count its digits by dividing by ten until it reaches zero, then check the count's parity.
steps: Take the next number
Divide by 10 until zero, counting steps
Even count? add one to the answer
brute.whySlow: Not asymptotically slower: same O(n·d). It is just a hand-written inner loop where a built-in does the job.

optimal.insight: The number of digits is just the length of the number written as text. One check per number: is that length even?
steps: Walk the list once
Turn each number into its decimal string
Even length? count it
Return the count

codeNotes.note: Numbers with an even digit count

pitfalls: Negative numbers would add a minus sign to the string; constraints keep values positive.

say.intro: Okay, so here's a quick one. We get a list of positive numbers. How many of them have an even number of digits? Take twelve, three forty five, two, six, and seven eight nine six. Twelve has two digits. Seven eight nine six has four. The rest are odd. So the answer is two.
say.brute: The hands-on way is pure arithmetic. Take a number and keep dividing by ten until it hits zero. Count the divisions. That count is the number of digits. If it's even, bump the answer. Here's the thing, though. This isn't slow. It's already linear in the total digits. It's just more code than we need.
say.insight: So what's the shortcut? Think about how a number looks when you write it down. The digit count is just the length of its text. So turn each number into a string and check if the length is even. Same work under the hood. But now it's one short line that's really hard to get wrong.
say.anim: We start with count at zero and our list of five numbers. First number is 12, which has two digits, an even count. Count increases to one since 12 qualifies. 345 has three digits, odd, so it's skipped. 2 and 6 each have one digit, both odd, both skipped. 7896 has four digits, even, so count increases again. After checking all numbers, count ends up at two. The function returns 2, matching the expected output.
say.code: We start a counter at zero. Then we loop over the numbers, looking at each one once. For each number, we take the length of its string form. If that length is even, we add one. At the end, we return the counter. That's the total of even-digit numbers.
say.outro: Linear in the total digits, constant extra space. Pattern: math and geometry. Remember this one. When a question is about digits, the string form often just answers it.

find-numbers-with-even-number-of-digits.title: Find Numbers with Even Number of Digits
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container the judge expects for our method.
The method findNumbers takes the list of numbers called nums and returns an integer count.
We start count at zero, since so far we have not seen any number with an even digit count.
We loop over every number x in nums so each one gets checked exactly once.
We turn x into text, take its length as the digit count, and test whether that length is even.
When the digit count is even, we add one to count to record this number.
After the loop finishes, we return count as the total of numbers with an even number of digits.

find-original-array-from-doubled-array.hook: Every number has a twin twice its size. Start from the smallest and the pairing becomes forced.
find-original-array-from-doubled-array.ask: An array was made by taking some original list, appending double every element, and shuffling. Given the shuffled result, return the original list, or an empty list if no original could produce it.
find-original-array-from-doubled-array.exampleWhy: Pair 1 with 2, 3 with 6 and 4 with 8. The smaller halves, 1, 3 and 4, form the original.

brute.idea: Sort, then repeatedly take the smallest remaining number and search the list for its double, deleting both.
steps: Sort the numbers
Pop the smallest remaining value x
Search for 2x; missing means fail
Remove 2x and record x
brute.whySlow: Popping the front and searching for each double scans the list every time: 100,000 numbers means billions of moves.

optimal.insight: The smallest unmatched number cannot be anyone's double, so it must be an original. Walk in sorted order and use a count map to claim its double instantly.
steps: Sort and count every value
Skip values whose count is already used up
Claim one copy of x and one copy of 2x
No 2x left? return empty

codeNotes.note: Smallest first: it must be an original
How many copies remain of each value
x is part of the original

pitfalls: Zero is its own double: decrement x before checking 2x so one zero cannot pair with itself.
Processing in unsorted order can pair x with 2x when x should pair with x/2.

say.intro: Someone took a list, added the double of every element, and shuffled it all. We get the result. Can we recover the original? If not, return empty. Take one, three, four, two, six, eight. One pairs with two. Three with six. Four with eight. So the original is one, three, four.
say.brute: The obvious approach? Sort the numbers. Then pop the smallest one and search the rest of the list for its double. Missing? We fail. Found? Delete it and record the small number. Repeat. The catch is that every pop and every search walks the list. So it's n squared.
say.insight: Here's the key question. Can the smallest unmatched number be somebody's double? No. Its half would be even smaller, and nothing smaller is left. So the smallest number must be an original. Its partner is forced. Now, if we walk in sorted order with a count map, claiming a double is just a constant time lookup.
say.anim: The array gets sorted to 1,2,3,4,6,8, then we build a count map of each value. Starting with x equals 1, its count is nonzero, so we claim it as an original. We check for its double, 2, find it available, and decrement its count too. One gets appended to the result, since it paired successfully with its double. Next x is 2, but its count is already zero, so we skip it as already used. X equals 3 is unmatched, so we claim it and consume its double, 6. X equals 4 works the same way, pairing with its double, 8, and getting added. Values 6 and 8 are skipped since they were already used as doubles, giving final answer 1,3,4.
say.code: First, sort the array, so the smallest comes first. It has to be an original. Then build a counter of how many copies remain of each value. Walk the sorted values. If this count is zero, it was already used as a double, so skip. If its double has no copies left, it's impossible, return empty. Otherwise, use both copies and append the value.
say.outro: Sorting dominates, so n log n time and linear space. The pattern is greedy. When the smallest item has only one possible role, commit to it.

find-original-array-from-doubled-array.title: Find Original Array From Doubled Array
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container the problem expects for our method.
The method takes the shuffled changed list and returns the original list, or an empty list if impossible.
We sort changed so the smallest remaining number always comes first and must be an original, never a double.
We build a counter that records how many times each value appears, letting us claim doubles instantly.
We start an empty result list that will hold the original numbers we confirm.
We walk through every number in sorted order, treating each as a candidate original.
If its count is already zero, this number was used earlier as someone's double.
So we skip it and move on to the next number.
Otherwise we claim this number as an original by decrementing its count.
We check whether any copy of its double remains available to pair with it.
If no double remains, the array cannot be valid, so we return an empty list.
Otherwise we consume one copy of the double by decrementing its count.
We record this number as part of the original array.
After every number is paired successfully, we return the collected original array.

find-players-with-zero-or-one-losses.hook: Only losses matter here. Count them once and both answer lists fall out.
find-players-with-zero-or-one-losses.ask: Each match lists a winner and a loser. Return two sorted lists: players who never lost, and players who lost exactly once. Only count players who played at least one match.
find-players-with-zero-or-one-losses.exampleWhy: 1, 2 and 10 never lose. 4, 5, 7 and 8 each lose once. 3, 6 and 9 lose twice.

brute.idea: Collect every player, then for each player scan all matches to count how many times they appear as the loser.
steps: Gather every player who played
For each player, scan every match
Count matches where they lost
Bucket by zero or one loss
brute.whySlow: Each player rescans every match: 100,000 matches and 100,000 players is ten billion checks.

optimal.insight: One pass over the matches can tally every player's losses in a hash map. Winners get an entry with zero so they are not forgotten.
steps: Make a map from player to losses
Winner: ensure an entry with zero
Loser: add one to their count
Sort players with zero and with one

codeNotes.note: Winners exist even with no loss

pitfalls: Use setdefault for winners: plain assignment to zero would erase earlier losses.

say.intro: Each match gives us a winner and a loser. We want two sorted lists. Who never lost? And who lost exactly once? In this example, one, two and ten are undefeated. And four, five, seven and eight each lost exactly one match.
say.brute: The brute force first collects every player. Then, for each player, it scans every single match and counts how often they lost. Zero losses goes in list one. One loss goes in list two. So what's the problem? That's players times matches. With a hundred thousand of each, that's ten billion checks.
say.insight: Think about it this way. Why look at a match more than once? One pass can tally everyone's losses in a hash map. But here's the trap. Undefeated players never show up as a loser. So they'd never get an entry. The fix is to give each winner a zero, without wiping out losses we already counted.
say.anim: We start with an empty losses map and begin scanning each match pair. Player one wins, so they get zero losses, while player three now has one loss. As matches continue, player three's losses climb to two while new winners appear with zero. Player four wins against five, giving four zero losses and five its first loss. Player ten beats four, but four later loses to nine, bumping four's loss count up. After the loop, losses map holds final counts for every player involved. We filter players with zero losses into one list and one loss into another. The final answer returns players with zero losses as one, two, ten and one loss as four, five, seven, eight.
say.code: We start with an empty map from player to losses. For each match, we call set default on the winner. That way winners exist even with no loss. Then we add one to the loser's tally. After the loop, we sort the players with zero losses. Then we sort the players with exactly one. Return both.
say.outro: One pass to count, then sorting the output. Pattern: arrays and hashing. Tally once in a map, then filter. Just don't forget the people who never lose.

find-players-with-zero-or-one-losses.title: Find Players With Zero or One Losses
lineNotes: We define a class named Solution, which is the standard wrapper for this problem's solution method.
The method findWinners takes the list of matches and returns two lists of player numbers.
We create an empty dictionary called losses that will map each player to their number of losses.
We loop over every match, unpacking each one into the winner w and the loser l.
