For the winner, setdefault adds an entry of zero only if missing, so existing loss counts are never overwritten.
For the loser, we read the current count, defaulting to zero, then add one and store it back.
We collect every player with zero losses and sort them, since the answer must be in increasing order.
We collect every player with exactly one loss and sort them the same way.
We return both sorted lists together, the never-lost players first and the lost-once players second.

find-the-count-of-good-integers.hook: Don't test every number. Build the few palindromes, then count how many numbers share their digits.
find-the-count-of-good-integers.ask: A number is good if its digits can be rearranged into a palindrome divisible by k, with no leading zeros. Count the good integers that have exactly n digits.
find-the-count-of-good-integers.exampleWhy: Two-digit palindromes divisible by 4 are 44 and 88. Each digit set has one arrangement, so 2.

brute.idea: Scan every number with n digits for k-palindromes and record their digit sets, then scan again counting numbers whose sorted digits match.
steps: Scan all n-digit numbers
Palindrome and divisible by k? record sorted digits
Scan all n-digit numbers again
Count those whose sorted digits were recorded
brute.whySlow: For n = 10 that is nine billion numbers per scan, while only about 90,000 palindromes exist.

optimal.insight: A palindrome is fixed by its left half, so only about 10 to the n over 2 exist. Collect their digit multisets, then count arrangements with combinatorics.
steps: Enumerate every left half
Mirror it into a full palindrome
Divisible by k? store its sorted digits
For each digit multiset, count arrangements without a leading zero

codeNotes.note: Mirror; odd n shares the middle

pitfalls: Deduplicate by sorted digits first, or the same multiset is counted many times.
Arrangements starting with zero are not n-digit numbers; exclude them.

say.intro: This one has a twist. A number is good if you can shuffle its digits into a palindrome that k divides, with no leading zero. We count good numbers with exactly n digits. With two digits and k equal to four, only forty four and eighty eight work. So the answer is two.
say.brute: The brute force scans every n digit number. It keeps the palindromes that k divides and records their sorted digits. Then it scans every n digit number again, counting ones whose sorted digits were recorded. Sounds fine? With ten digits, that's nine billion numbers per scan. Hopeless.
say.insight: Here's the thing. A palindrome is completely decided by its left half. So we don't need ten to the n candidates. We only build about ten to the n over two. For each palindrome k divides, store its digit multiset. Then count the arrangements with factorials. And remove the ones that would start with zero.
say.anim: We need two digit good integers divisible by four, starting with an empty seen set. We loop left digits one through nine, building each palindrome by mirroring the digit. For left equals one, palindrome eleven is checked but it fails divisibility by four. Left equals four gives palindrome forty four, which divides evenly by four, so it's saved. Left equals eight gives palindrome eighty eight, also divisible by four, added to seen. After the loop, seen holds forty four and eighty eight; now count arrangements for each. For forty four, counting permutations of its digits gives exactly one valid arrangement. Similarly eighty eight contributes one more valid arrangement, bringing total to two. The function returns two, the count of good integers for n equals two, k equals four.
say.code: First, the half length. The left half decides the palindrome. For each left half, we mirror it. When n is odd, the middle digit is shared. If k divides it, we store its sorted digits once in a set. Then for each stored multiset, we pick a nonzero first digit and arrange the rest freely. Finally, divide out the repeated digits.
say.outro: Roughly the square root of the search space instead of all of it. Pattern: math and geometry. Enumerate a smaller structure, then count with combinatorics.

find-the-count-of-good-integers.title: Find the Count of Good Integers
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, as the problem setup expects.
The method takes the digit count n and divisor k, and returns how many good integers exist.
We create an empty set called seen to store each distinct digit multiset that forms a valid palindrome.
We compute half as the length of the left half, rounding up so the middle digit is included for odd n.
We loop over every possible left half, starting at a power of ten so there are no leading zeros.
We convert the current left half into a string so we can mirror it.
We build the palindrome by appending the reversed left half, dropping the middle digit when n is odd.
If the palindrome is divisible by k, it qualifies, so we handle it next.
We sort its digits into a string key and add it to seen, so equal multisets are counted once.
We precompute factorials from zero up to n for use in counting arrangements.
We initialize total to zero to accumulate the count of good integers.
We loop over each distinct digit multiset that produced a valid palindrome.
We count how many times each digit appears in this multiset using a Counter.
We place a nonzero digit first, giving n minus the zero count choices, times the factorial of n minus one for the rest.
We loop over each digit's frequency to correct for repeated digits.
We divide by the factorial of each frequency, removing duplicate orderings of identical digits.
We add this multiset's number of valid arrangements into the running total.
We return the total count of good integers with exactly n digits.

find-the-highest-altitude.hook: Altitude is just a running sum. Track its peak as you go.
find-the-highest-altitude.ask: A biker starts at altitude zero. Each value in gain is the change in altitude to the next point. Return the highest altitude reached at any point, including the start.
find-the-highest-altitude.exampleWhy: Altitudes are 0, -5, -4, 1, 1, -6. The highest of them is 1.

brute.idea: For every point, recompute its altitude from scratch by summing all gains before it, and keep the largest.
steps: For each point i
Sum gain[0] through gain[i-1]
Keep the largest sum seen
brute.whySlow: Each point re-adds every earlier gain, repeating work the previous point already did.

optimal.insight: Each altitude is the previous altitude plus one gain. Keep a single running sum and its maximum.
steps: Start at altitude zero, best zero
Add each gain to the altitude
Update best when altitude is higher

codeNotes.note: Start point counts as altitude zero

pitfalls: Starting best at the first altitude misses the start point at zero when all gains are negative.

say.intro: A biker starts at altitude zero. Each number says how much the altitude changes to the next point. What's the highest altitude ever reached? With minus five, one, five, zero, minus seven, the altitudes go zero, minus five, minus four, one, one, minus six. The peak is one.
say.brute: The brute force recomputes every altitude from scratch. For each point, it adds up all the gains before it, and keeps the biggest total. That's correct. But notice the waste. Point number i re-adds i gains. Every point repeats work the previous point already did. So it's n squared.
say.insight: So what do we actually need? Each altitude is just the previous altitude plus one more gain. There's no reason to restart the sum. Keep one running total. That's a prefix sum. And remember the largest value it ever takes. One small detail. The starting point counts too, and that's zero.
say.anim: We start with altitude and best both set to zero, and gains listed. First gain is negative five, so altitude drops to negative five. Best stays zero since negative five is lower than the current best. Adding gain one brings altitude up to negative four, still below best. Adding gain five raises altitude to one, which becomes the new best. Gain zero keeps altitude at one, so best remains unchanged at one. Final gain negative seven drops altitude to negative six, below the best. The loop ends and the function returns the highest altitude reached, one.
say.code: We set altitude and best to zero. That covers the starting point. For each gain, we add it to the altitude. That's our running prefix sum. Then best becomes the larger of best and altitude, so we remember the highest point. Because best starts at zero, a ride that only goes downhill still reports the start.
say.outro: Linear time, constant space. The pattern is arrays and hashing, specifically a prefix sum. Carry the total forward instead of recomputing it.

find-the-highest-altitude.title: Find the Highest Altitude
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container the problem expects for our method.
The method largestAltitude takes the list gain of altitude changes and returns the highest altitude as an integer.
We set both the current altitude and the best altitude to zero, since the biker starts at zero.
We loop through each gain value in order, visiting each next point along the trip.
We add the current gain to the running altitude, giving the altitude at the new point.
We update best to the larger of itself and the current altitude, tracking the maximum seen so far.
After the loop finishes, we return best, which holds the highest altitude including the starting point.

find-the-largest-almost-missing-integer.hook: Sliding every window is a trap. Only the two ends of the array can appear in just one window.
find-the-largest-almost-missing-integer.ask: A value is almost missing if it appears in exactly one contiguous window of length k. Return the largest almost missing value, or minus one if none exists.
find-the-largest-almost-missing-integer.exampleWhy: Only 3 and 7 sit in a single window of size 3. The larger one is 7.

brute.idea: Slide every window of size k, count how many windows contain each value, and return the largest value with count one.
steps: For each window start
Collect the distinct values inside
Add one to each value's window count
Largest value with count one wins
brute.whySlow: Every window is rebuilt from scratch, so each element is touched up to k times.

optimal.insight: If 1 < k < n, every interior position lies in at least two windows. Only nums[0] or nums[-1], appearing once overall, can qualify.
steps: k equals n: one window, return the max
k equals 1: largest value appearing once
Otherwise check only the first and last values
They qualify only if they appear once

codeNotes.match: once = [x for x in nums if count[x] == 1]

codeNotes.note: Only the ends sit in one window

pitfalls: An end value that reappears in the middle lands in more windows; check its total count.

say.intro: A value is almost missing if it shows up in exactly one window of length k. We want the largest such value, or minus one. Take three, nine, two, one, seven with k equal to three. Only three and seven sit in a single window. So the answer is seven.
say.brute: The brute force slides every window of length k. It collects the distinct values inside and adds one to each value's window count. At the end it returns the largest value with a count of one. The catch? Every window gets rebuilt from scratch. So that's n times k.
say.insight: Let's ask a better question. Which positions can be in only one window? When k is strictly between one and n, every interior position is covered at least twice. Only the very first and very last elements are covered once. And only if they don't appear anywhere else. Then there are two edge cases. k equals n, and k equals one.
say.anim: We start with nums 3, 9, 2, 1, 7 and k equal to 3. A counter tracks how many times each number appears, all exactly once here. Since k is neither n nor 1, only the first and last elements can qualify. Checking x equals 3, the first element, which appears only once. Best updates to 3 since it passed the uniqueness check. Now x equals 7, the last element, also appearing only once. Best updates again, becoming 7 since it is larger. The function returns best, giving the final answer 7.
say.code: First, count every value. If k equals n, there's a single window holding everything, so return the max. If k equals one, every window is a single element. Return the largest value that appears once. Otherwise, only the two ends sit in one window. For each, check that its count is one, so it doesn't reappear. Keep the larger.
say.outro: Linear time, by thinking about coverage instead of sliding. Pattern: arrays and hashing. And a careful look at the edge cases.

find-the-largest-almost-missing-integer.title: Find the Largest Almost Missing Integer
lineNotes: We define the Solution class that holds the method for this problem.
The method takes the list nums and the window length k, and returns the largest almost missing integer.
We store the length of nums in n so we can compare it with k.
We build a counter of how many times each value appears in nums.
If k equals n, there is only one window, so every value qualifies.
In that case we return the maximum of nums, since all its values appear in exactly that one window.
If k equals one, each window is a single element, so a value qualifies when it appears exactly once.
We collect every value whose count is exactly one into the list called once.
We return the largest of those values, or minus one if the list is empty.
For the middle cases we start best at minus one, meaning no answer found yet.
Only the first and last elements can sit in a single window, so we check just those two.
A candidate qualifies only if it appears exactly once in the whole array, otherwise another window would contain it.
We update best to the larger of its current value and this candidate.
We return best, which is the largest qualifying endpoint or minus one if neither qualified.

find-the-length-of-the-longest-common-pr.hook: Comparing every pair is slow. Store every prefix of one side, then probe from the other.
find-the-length-of-the-longest-common-pr.ask: Given two arrays of positive integers, find the longest digit prefix shared by some number from the first array and some number from the second. Return its length, or zero if none.
find-the-length-of-the-longest-common-pr.exampleWhy: 123 is a prefix of 1234, giving length 3. 456 only shares 45, and 9 shares nothing.

brute.idea: Compare every number in the first array with every number in the second, character by character.
steps: Pick x from arr1 and y from arr2
Walk their digit strings while they match
Keep the longest match length
brute.whySlow: 50,000 by 50,000 pairs is 2.5 billion comparisons before even looking at digits.

optimal.insight: A numeric prefix is just the number with trailing digits chopped off. Put every prefix of arr1 in a hash set, then shorten each arr2 value until it hits the set.
steps: For each x in arr1, add x, x//10, x//100 to a set
For each y in arr2, chop digits until y is in the set
Record the digit length of that hit
Return the longest

codeNotes.note: Every prefix of every arr1 number

codeNotes.match: while x and x not in prefixes:
codeNotes.note: Stop early: shorter ones already stored

codeNotes.match: while y and y not in prefixes:

pitfalls: Common prefixes within the same array do not count; only cross-array pairs matter.

say.intro: We have two arrays of positive numbers. Pick one number from each side. What's the longest run of leading digits they share? Here, one twenty three is a prefix of one two three four. That's three digits. So the answer is three.
say.brute: The brute force compares every pair. Take each left number and each right number, turn both into strings, and walk forward while the digits match. Keep the longest run. So what's the catch? Fifty thousand numbers per side is two and a half billion pairs. Way too slow.
say.insight: Here's the trick. What is a prefix of a number? It's the number with digits chopped off the end. And chopping a digit is just integer division by ten. So put every prefix of every left number into a hash set. Then shrink each right number, digit by digit, until it lands in the set. No pairs at all.
say.anim: We start with arr1 and arr2, building a set of all prefixes from arr1. Taking twelve, we add it, then chop it down to one, adding that too. Next, one twenty three gets added, then shrinks to twelve, already in the set. Forty five is added, then shrinks to four, which also gets added. Now we check arr2: twelve thirty four shrinks to one twenty three, found in prefixes, giving best length three. Four fifty six shrinks to forty five, matching a prefix, best stays three. Nine shrinks to zero, no match found, so it contributes nothing. The loop ends and the function returns the final answer, three.
say.code: We start with an empty set for every prefix of the left numbers. For each left number, we loop, stopping early if that prefix is already stored. Shorter ones are there too. Each step drops the last digit. Then each right number shrinks until it's zero or in the set. If something's left, its digit length is a candidate for best.
say.outro: Linear in the total digits, not quadratic in pairs. Pattern: arrays and hashing. A hash set of prefixes is basically a cheap trie.

find-the-length-of-the-longest-common-pr.title: Find the Length of the Longest Common Prefix
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the wrapper this problem's method lives in.
This method takes two lists of positive integers and returns the length of the longest shared digit prefix.
We start with an empty set called prefixes to hold every prefix of every number in the first array.
We loop over each number x in the first array to record all of its prefixes.
We keep going while x is nonzero and not already in the set, since a seen prefix means its shorter ones are seen too.
We add the current x to the prefixes set, recording this prefix.
We divide x by ten with integer division, chopping off the last digit to get the next shorter prefix.
We set best to zero, which is the answer if no prefix is shared.
We loop over each number y in the second array to look for a matching prefix.
While y is nonzero and not in the set, we keep trimming, looking for the longest prefix of y that matches.
We chop the last digit off y by integer dividing by ten, trying a shorter prefix.
If y is still nonzero after the loop, we found a prefix that exists in the set.
We update best with the larger of its current value and the number of digits in y.
We return best, the length of the longest common prefix found, or zero if none.

find-the-lexicographically-smallest-vali.hook: Grab the earliest index every time, but only spend your one mismatch when the rest still fits.
find-the-lexicographically-smallest-vali.ask: Pick increasing indices from word1, one per letter of word2, so the picked letters match word2 with at most one mismatch. Return the lexicographically smallest such index list, or empty.
find-the-lexicographically-smallest-vali.exampleWhy: Index 1 is a, index 2 is c used as the one change for b, then index 4 is c.

brute.idea: Try every choice of which letter of word2 is the mismatch, match greedily for each, and keep the smallest result.
steps: Choose a wildcard position, or none
Greedily match earliest indices
Wildcard position takes the next index
Keep the smallest complete sequence
brute.whySlow: Each of the m wildcard choices rescans word1: 300,000 by 300,000 is far too slow.

optimal.insight: Precompute, for each suffix of word1, how much of word2's tail it matches exactly. Then a left-to-right greedy knows when spending the mismatch is safe.
steps: Right to left: last[i] = earliest word2 index whose tail fits in word1[i:]
Left to right: take i if letters match
Else, if unused and last[i+1] ≤ j+1, take i as the change
Return the sequence only if all of word2 matched

codeNotes.match: elif not used and last[i + 1] <= j + 1:
codeNotes.note: Spend the change only if rest fits

codeNotes.match: return res if j == m else []

pitfalls: Spending the change at the first mismatch without the suffix check can strand the rest of word2.
Lexicographic order is on indices, not on the resulting letters.

say.intro: We pick increasing positions in word one, one for each letter of word two. The picked letters can differ from word two in at most one place. We want the smallest list of positions. For b a c d c and a b c, the answer is one, two, four.
say.brute: The brute force tries every choice of which letter in word two gets the mismatch. Plus the choice of no mismatch at all. For each choice, it matches greedily, taking the earliest position every time. Then it keeps the smallest result. But that rescans word one for every letter of word two. Quadratic.
say.insight: Greedy is right here. The real question is when it's safe to spend our one change. So first, sweep from the right. For every suffix of word one, record how much of the end of word two it matches exactly. Now sweep left to right. At a mismatch, spend the change only if the remaining suffix can cover the rest.
say.anim: We start with word one bacdc and word two abc, lengths five and three. We build the last array backward, tracking how much of word two still matches each suffix. After the backward pass, last becomes one two two two two three, showing match progress. Now we scan forward, matching characters or spending one allowed mismatch to stay valid. At index one, letters match directly, so we append it and res becomes one. At index two, we use our one allowed mismatch, appending two and setting used true. At index four, c matches again, appending four to complete the match. All of word two is matched, giving the final answer one, two, four.
say.code: First we build the suffix match table, greedily matching from the right. Then we walk word one with pointer j. If the letters match, it's a free match, so we always take it. Otherwise, if the change is unused and the rest still fits, we spend it. At the end, if j didn't reach the end, it was impossible. Return empty.
say.outro: Two linear sweeps. Pattern: greedy, backed by a suffix table. The table tells us when a greedy move is still safe.

find-the-lexicographically-smallest-vali.title: Find the Lexicographically Smallest Valid Sequence
lineNotes: This is the start of the Solution class that holds our method.
The method takes word1 and word2 and returns a list of chosen indices.
We store the lengths of word1 and word2 as n and m.
We build a last array of size n plus one, filled with m, meaning nothing matched yet at the end.
We set j to m, the count of word2 letters still unmatched while scanning from the right.
We loop i backward from the last index of word1 down to zero to process each suffix.
If letters remain and word1 at i equals the word2 letter just before j, we can match greedily from the back.
Matching that letter means the unmatched prefix of word2 shrinks, so we decrease j by one.
We record in last at i the smallest word2 prefix length that the suffix starting at i leaves unmatched.
We start an empty result list to hold the chosen indices.
The used flag tracks whether we have spent our single allowed mismatch yet.
We reset j to zero as the next word2 position we need to fill going forward.
We scan word1 from left to right, trying to pick each index in turn.
If we have already matched all of word2, there is nothing left to pick.
So we stop the loop early.
If the current letter equals the needed word2 letter, taking it is the smallest choice and costs nothing.
We append this index to the result.
We advance j to the next word2 letter.
Otherwise, if the mismatch is unspent and the suffix after i can still match the remaining tail of word2 exactly, we can afford a mismatch here.
We append this index, using it as the mismatched pick.
We mark the mismatch as used so it cannot be spent again.
We advance j since this position now covers the current word2 letter.
If every letter of word2 got placed we return the indices, otherwise we return an empty list.

find-the-maximum-number-of-elements-in-s.hook: Squares grow so fast that every chain is tiny. Just follow it with a count map.
find-the-maximum-number-of-elements-in-s.ask: Choose numbers that can be laid out as x, x squared, x to the fourth, up to a peak, then back down symmetrically. Return the largest number of elements such a subset can have.
find-the-maximum-number-of-elements-in-s.exampleWhy: Two 2s and two 4s plus one 16 form 2, 4, 16, 4, 2: five elements.

brute.idea: For each value, climb the chain x, x squared, and so on, counting copies with a full list scan at every step.
steps: Start a chain at each value x
Count copies of x by scanning the list
Two or more? add 2 and square x
Finish with the peak, or give one back
brute.whySlow: Every count is a full scan, so 100,000 numbers cost about ten billion checks.

optimal.insight: Every level below the peak needs two copies, the peak needs one. Squaring explodes, so each chain is a handful of O(1) hash lookups.
steps: Count values; handle 1s separately (odd count)
From each x, while count ≥ 2: add 2, square
Peak present? add 1, else drop back by 1
Keep the longest chain

codeNotes.match: best = ones if ones % 2 else ones - 1

codeNotes.note: Peak, or reuse last pair's one

pitfalls: 1s loop forever when squared; count them apart and keep an odd number.
Use get, not indexing, so lookups do not insert keys mid-iteration.

say.intro: We pick numbers that form x, x squared, x to the fourth, up to a peak, and then mirror back down. What's the biggest such subset? From two, four, sixteen, four, two, five and twenty five, we build two, four, sixteen, four, two. That's five elements.
say.brute: The brute force starts a chain at every value. At each level, it scans the whole list to count copies. Two or more? Add two to the length and square the value. Sounds reasonable. But every count is a full scan. With a hundred thousand numbers, that's about ten billion checks.
say.insight: Look at the shape. Every level below the peak needs two copies, one for each side. The peak needs just one. And here's the nice part. Squaring grows so fast that any chain passes a billion in a few levels. With a count map, each level is an instant lookup. Just watch out for one. One squared is still one.
say.anim: We count each number's frequency, getting counts like two for 2, two for 4, one for 16. There are no ones in this list, so ones is zero and best starts at one. We start chasing a chain from 2, squaring repeatedly while duplicates exist. Two squares to four, then four squares to sixteen, each step adding two to length. Sixteen only appears once, so we add one more, giving a chain length of five. Trying the chain starting at four gives length three, smaller than our current best. The remaining chains, from sixteen, five, and twenty five, each only reach length one. After checking all chains, the best answer returned is five.
say.code: First, pull the ones out, since one squared is one. The pattern length must be odd, so keep the largest odd count of ones. For every other value, while it has a pair for both sides, add two. Then climb to the next square. At the end, if that value exists, it's the peak. Otherwise, give one back.
say.outro: Near linear time, because chains are tiny. Pattern: arrays and hashing. A count map turns repeated searches into instant lookups.

find-the-maximum-number-of-elements-in-s.title: Find the Maximum Number of Elements in Subset
lineNotes: We define the Solution class that holds the method for this problem.
The method takes a list of integers called nums and returns the largest valid subset size.
We count how many times each number appears using a Counter, since only frequencies matter here.
We remove the number one from the counts and save how many ones there were, because one squared stays one.
We start best at one, since any single number alone forms a valid pattern.
We only handle ones specially if at least one copy exists.
Ones can form a symmetric pattern of odd length, so we use all ones if odd, otherwise one fewer.
We loop over each distinct number other than one as a possible starting value of a chain.
For each start we reset length to zero before climbing its chain.
While the current value has at least two copies, it can sit on both sides of the pattern.
We add two to the length for that pair of matching elements.
We square x to move up to the next level of the chain.
At the top, if the value exists we add one for the peak, otherwise subtract one because the last pair's peak is missing.
We update best if this chain gives a longer valid pattern.
We return the best length found.

find-the-minimum-and-maximum-number-of-n.hook: The max gap is first-to-last. The min gap is always between neighbours. One pass gets both.
find-the-minimum-and-maximum-number-of-n.ask: In a linked list, a critical point is a node strictly above or strictly below both neighbours. Return the smallest and largest distance between any two critical points, or minus one twice if fewer than two exist.
find-the-minimum-and-maximum-number-of-n.exampleWhy: Critical points sit at positions 2, 4 and 5. Closest pair is 4 and 5; farthest is 2 and 5.

brute.idea: Walk the list to collect every critical position, then compare every pair of positions for min and max distance.
steps: Walk the list with prev, cur, next
Record each critical position
Compare every pair of positions
Keep smallest and largest gap
brute.whySlow: With 100,000 alternating values almost every node is critical, so the pair check is billions of comparisons.

optimal.insight: Positions arrive in increasing order. The largest gap is last minus first, and the smallest gap must be between consecutive critical points.
steps: Walk with prev and cur, tracking the index
On a critical point, remember the first one
Update min gap with distance to the previous one
Answer is min gap and last minus first

codeNotes.match: prev, cur, i = cur, nxt, i + 1

pitfalls: Equal neighbours are not critical: comparisons must be strict.
Fewer than two critical points must return minus one for both values.

say.intro: A critical point in a linked list is a node strictly higher, or strictly lower, than both neighbours. We want the closest and farthest distances between critical points. In five, three, one, two, five, one, two, they sit at positions two, four and five. So the answer is one and three.
say.brute: The brute force walks the list once and collects every critical position into an array. Then it compares every pair of positions for the smallest and largest gap. Fine for a few points. But what if nearly every node is critical? Then that pair loop is quadratic. Billions of comparisons.
say.insight: Here's the thing. We discover critical points in order, left to right. So the farthest pair? It's just the first and the last. And the closest pair? It must be two neighbouring critical points. Anything in between would be closer. So all we need is the first position, the previous one, and a running minimum.
say.anim: We start with first and last set to negative one, and best set to infinity. We walk the list with prev, cur, and next pointers, checking each node for a critical point. At index two, value one is a local minimum, so first and last both become two. At index four, value five is a local maximum, so best updates to two and last becomes four. At index five, value one is another local minimum, giving a smaller gap of one, so best becomes one and last becomes five. The loop ends since no more nodes remain to compare. The function returns best as one and last minus first as three, giving the final answer one, three.
say.code: We start with first and last at minus one. No critical point yet. For each node, we check if it's a local max or a local min. If it is, best becomes the smaller of best and the gap from last. Then we slide the three node window forward. At the end, return best and last minus first.
say.outro: One pass, constant space. Pattern: linked list. Slide a small window of neighbours, and only remember what you need.

find-the-minimum-and-maximum-number-of-n.title: Find the Minimum and Maximum Number of Nodes Between Critical Points
lineNotes: We define the Solution class that holds the method for this problem.
The method takes the head of a linked list and returns a list holding the minimum and maximum distances.
We set first and last to minus one, meaning no critical point has been found yet.
We set best, the smallest gap so far, to infinity so any real gap will replace it.
We start with prev at head, cur at the second node, and index i at one.
We loop while cur and its next both exist, since a critical point needs two neighbours.
We save the node after cur as nxt so we can compare all three values.
We check whether cur is a local maximum or a local minimum compared with prev and nxt.
If this is the first critical point found, which we detect by first still being minus one.
We record the current index as the position of the first critical point.
Otherwise this is a later critical point, so we handle the gap to the previous one.
We update best with the distance from the previous critical point, since consecutive points give the smallest gap.
We update last to the current index so the next gap is measured from here.
We slide the window forward by moving prev to cur, cur to nxt, and incrementing i.
After the loop, if best is still infinity, fewer than two critical points were found.
In that case we return minus one and minus one as required.
Otherwise we return the smallest gap best and the largest gap, which is last minus first.

find-the-number-of-subsequences-with-equ.hook: Three choices per number and only 200 possible GCDs. Track the pair of GCDs, not the subsets.
find-the-number-of-subsequences-with-equ.ask: Count ordered pairs of non-empty, disjoint subsequences whose elements have the same GCD. Return the count modulo one billion and seven.
find-the-number-of-subsequences-with-equ.exampleWhy: Only {10} with {20,30}, and the reverse, both have GCD 10.

brute.idea: Assign each number to the first subsequence, the second, or neither, and test every assignment's two GCDs.
steps: Enumerate all 3^n assignments
Compute each side's GCD
Both non-empty and equal? count it
brute.whySlow: With 200 numbers, 3 to the 200 assignments is astronomically more than anyone can enumerate.

optimal.insight: Only the two running GCDs matter, never which elements were used. State (g1, g2), with 0 meaning empty, has at most 201² values.
steps: dp maps (g1, g2) to ways; start with (0, 0)
Each number: skip it, add to side one, or side two
Fold it into that side's GCD
Sum ways where g1 equals g2 and is positive

codeNotes.match: for key in ((a, b), (math.gcd(a, x), b), (a, math.gcd(b, x))):
codeNotes.note: Skip, side one, or side two

pitfalls: gcd(0, x) is x, so 0 cleanly means empty; exclude a == b == 0 at the end.
Pairs are ordered: (A, B) and (B, A) both count.

say.intro: We count ordered pairs of non-empty subsequences that share no index and have the same greatest common divisor. For ten, twenty, thirty, only ten paired with twenty and thirty works. It counts in both orders. So the answer is two.
say.brute: The brute force gives every number three options. Side one, side two, or neither. That's three to the n assignments. For each, compute both GCDs and count it if they're equal and non-empty. So how bad is that? With two hundred numbers, it will never finish.
say.insight: Now, here's the key. Do we care which numbers went where? Not really. For the future, all that matters is each side's current GCD. Values are at most two hundred, so there are only about forty thousand GCD pairs. So we run dynamic programming over that pair. Zero means empty. That counts every assignment at once.
say.anim: We start with nums ten, twenty, thirty and one empty state tracking two gcds, both zero. Processing ten, each state branches three ways: skip, add to first gcd, or add to second gcd. After ten, dp holds three states, representing skip, include in group one, or group two. Processing twenty expands these into combinations like ten and twenty, tracking both running gcds together. After twenty, dp has grown with pairs like ten and twenty appearing as a matched state. Now processing thirty, every existing state again branches three ways, updating gcds with thirty included. We see state ten comma ten appear twice, meaning both subsequences reached equal gcd ten. Summing all states where the two gcds match and are positive gives the final answer, two.
say.code: We start with one way where both sides are empty, GCD zero. For each number, we look at every reachable GCD pair. Each has three moves. Skip the number, fold it into side one, or into side two. We add the ways, modulo a billion and seven. Finally, we sum the states where both GCDs are equal and positive.
say.outro: Polynomial instead of exponential. Pattern: two dimensional dynamic programming. The state is just the pair of running GCDs.

find-the-number-of-subsequences-with-equ.title: Find the Number of Subsequences With Equal GCD
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container that the judge expects for this problem.
This method takes the list of numbers and returns how many valid pairs of disjoint subsequences exist.
We set the modulus to one billion and seven so that all counts stay small.
Our state map starts with both running GCDs at zero, meaning both subsequences are empty, with one way.
We process each number in the input one at a time, deciding where it goes.
We create a fresh counting map for the next step, defaulting missing states to zero ways.
We loop over every current state, unpacking the two GCDs and the number of ways to reach them.
For each state we try three choices: skip the number, add it to the first subsequence, or add it to the second.
We add the current ways to the resulting state's count, taking the modulus to keep numbers bounded.
After handling this number, the new map becomes our current state map for the next number.
Finally we sum ways over states where both GCDs match and are nonzero, meaning both subsequences are non-empty, modulo the prime.

find-the-prefix-common-array-of-two-arra.hook: A number becomes common the exact moment its second copy shows up.
find-the-prefix-common-array-of-two-arra.ask: Given two permutations A and B of 1 to n, return an array where entry i counts the numbers seen in both A up to i and B up to i.
find-the-prefix-common-array-of-two-arra.exampleWhy: After index 0 nothing is shared; after index 1 both 1 and 3 are; then 2, then 4.

brute.idea: For every index, build sets of both prefixes and count the size of their intersection.
steps: For each index i
Take sets of A[0..i] and B[0..i]
Record the intersection size
brute.whySlow: Each prefix is rebuilt from scratch, so the work grows with the square of n.

optimal.insight: Each value appears once in A and once in B. Count sightings; when a value's count hits two, it just became common.
steps: Keep a seen-count per value
At index i, bump counts for A[i] and B[i]
Each count reaching 2 adds one to common
Append common

pitfalls: When A[i] equals B[i], the same value is counted twice in one step; that is correct.

say.intro: We get two permutations of one to n. At each index, how many numbers have appeared in both prefixes so far? For one, three, two, four and three, one, two, four, the answer is zero, two, three, four.
say.brute: The brute force rebuilds everything at each index. Turn both prefixes into sets, then count the overlap. Each prefix costs up to n work, and there are n of them. So it's n squared. It works. But it keeps redoing the same counting.
say.insight: Here's the thing. Each array is a permutation. So every value shows up exactly once in A, and once in B. When does a value become common? At the exact moment we see it the second time. So keep a sighting count per value. Whenever a count hits two, bump a running total. That total is the answer.
say.anim: We start with arrays A and B, a seen counter array, and common set to zero. At the first pair, one and three, each gets counted once, so neither is common yet. Result so far is zero, since nothing has appeared in both arrays. Now three and one are seen again, each count hits two, so common jumps to two. Next pair is two and two, seen twice immediately, making common three. Finally four and four both arrive, pushing common up to four. The result array fills in as zero, two, three, four. The function returns the prefix common array zero, two, three, four.
say.code: We make a sighting count array, one slot per value. At each index, we process both new elements. For each, add one to its count. If that count is now two, it's the second sighting. The value is in both, so common goes up. Then we append the running count. That's the answer for this index.
say.outro: Linear time and space. Pattern: arrays and hashing. Catch the moment a condition becomes true, instead of recomputing it.

find-the-prefix-common-array-of-two-arra.title: Find the Prefix Common Array of Two Arrays
lineNotes: We define a class named Solution, which is the container the judge expects for the method.
This method takes the two permutations A and B and returns the prefix common array as a list.
We make a seen list of zeros, sized one more than the length of A, so values index directly.
We start the running count of common numbers, called common, at zero.
We create an empty result list called res to collect the answer for each position.
We walk through A and B together, taking one value from each at every index.
For each of the two values at this index, we loop over them one at a time.
We add one to the sighting count for that value in the seen list.
If the value's count reaches two, it has now appeared in both arrays.
In that case we increase common by one, since a new shared number just appeared.
After handling both values, we append the current common count to res as this prefix's answer.
Finally we return res, which holds the common count for every prefix.

find-the-safest-path-in-a-grid.hook: First flood distances out from every thief, then find the path whose worst cell is best.
find-the-safest-path-in-a-grid.ask: In a square grid with thieves, a path's safeness is its smallest Manhattan distance to any thief. Return the largest safeness of any path from the top-left to the bottom-right.
find-the-safest-path-in-a-grid.exampleWhy: Going down the left column then along the bottom keeps every cell at least 2 from the thief.

brute.idea: Compute each cell's distance by checking every thief, then try safeness values from high to low with a BFS each time.
steps: Distance per cell: min over all thieves
For s from high to low
BFS using only cells with distance ≥ s
First s that reaches the end wins
brute.whySlow: Checking every thief per cell is n to the fourth, and each threshold repeats a full BFS.

optimal.insight: Multi-source BFS from all thieves gives every cell's distance in one sweep. Then a max-heap Dijkstra always extends the path with the safest frontier cell.
steps: Seed a queue with every thief at distance 0
BFS outward to label every cell
Max-heap from (0,0) keyed by the path's minimum distance
Pop the safest; reaching the corner returns its value

codeNotes.note: Every thief is a BFS source
First arrival is the best bottleneck
Path safety is its minimum cell

pitfalls: Running a BFS from each thief separately is quadratic in thieves; seed them all at once.
Start and end cells count too: a thief there makes the answer zero.

say.intro: Some grid cells hold thieves. A path's safeness is the closest it ever gets to a thief, in grid steps. We want the safest path from top left to bottom right. With one thief in the top right of a three by three grid, the best path stays two steps away.
say.brute: The brute force measures each cell's distance by checking every thief. That alone is n to the fourth. Then it tries every safeness value from high to low. For each, it runs a fresh search using only cells that are far enough away. The first value that reaches the corner wins. Lots of repeated work.
say.insight: Two ideas fix this. First, run one breadth first search from all thieves at once. It labels every cell with its distance in one sweep. Second, notice a path is only as safe as its worst cell. So use a max heap and always extend the safest frontier. Why does that work? The first time we pop the corner, it's optimal.
say.anim: We start with a three by three grid, with a single thief marked at position zero, two. We run a multi-source breadth-first search from the thief cell, initializing its distance to zero. The search spreads outward layer by layer, filling in distance values for neighboring cells. By the end of the sweep, every cell now holds its distance from the nearest thief. Now we run a max-heap Dijkstra, starting at the top-left cell with safety value two. The heap always expands the frontier cell with the highest safety factor, tracking visited cells. We keep popping the safest reachable cell, pushing new neighbors with updated minimum safety values. We reach the bottom-right corner, and the maximum safeness factor returned is two.
say.code: First, every thief goes in the queue as a source. The search fills in each cell's distance to the nearest thief. Then we push the start into a heap, negated so it acts like a max heap. When we pop the corner, we return. That first arrival is the best bottleneck. Each neighbour gets pushed with the path's minimum cell.
say.outro: n squared log n overall. Pattern: advanced graphs. A multi source breadth first search, then a max min version of Dijkstra.

find-the-safest-path-in-a-grid.title: Find the Safest Path in a Grid
lineNotes: We define the Solution class that holds the method for this problem.
The method takes the grid of thieves and returns the largest safeness of any path.
We store the grid size as n since the grid is square.
We build a distance grid of the same size, filled with negative one to mean unvisited.
We create a queue that will drive the breadth first search from every thief at once.
We loop over every row of the grid to find thieves.
We loop over every column in the current row.
If the cell holds a thief, we handle it as a starting source.
A thief cell has distance zero to itself, so we record that in the distance grid.
We push the thief cell into the queue so the search spreads outward from it.
We keep running the search while the queue still has cells to process.
We take the oldest cell off the queue so cells are handled in order of distance.
We look at the four neighbors of this cell: down, up, right, and left.
If the neighbor is inside the grid and not yet given a distance, we continue.
Its distance is one more than the current cell, which is the shortest distance to any thief.
We add the neighbor to the queue so its own neighbors get processed later.
We start the heap with the top-left cell, negating its distance so the smallest value means the safest.
We mark the starting cell as seen so we never push it again.
We loop while the heap still holds frontier cells to explore.
We pop the cell with the best safeness so far, which is the most negative stored value.
If this cell is the bottom-right corner, we have reached the goal along the safest route.
We return the negated value to convert back to the real safeness.
We examine the four neighbors of the current cell.
If the neighbor is inside the grid and unseen, we will consider it.
We mark the neighbor as seen so it is added to the heap only once.
We push it with the worse of the path's safeness and the neighbor's own, since a path is only as safe as its weakest cell.
If the heap empties without reaching the goal, we return zero as a fallback.

find-the-shortest-superstring.hook: This is travelling salesman in disguise: maximise total overlap with a bitmask DP.
find-the-shortest-superstring.ask: Given up to 12 words, none inside another, return the shortest string that contains every word as a substring.
find-the-shortest-superstring.exampleWhy: ab overlaps bc on b to give abc, which overlaps ca on c to give abca, four letters.

brute.idea: Try every order of the words, merge each neighbour pair with its largest overlap, and keep the shortest result.
steps: Generate every permutation
Merge left to right using maximum overlap
Keep the shortest merged string
brute.whySlow: Twelve words have 479 million orders; each merge then costs more work on top.

optimal.insight: Length is total letters minus overlaps between neighbours. dp[mask][i] = best overlap for an order of the words in mask starting at i: Held-Karp.
steps: Precompute overlap for every ordered pair
dp over subsets: start i, then the best next word
Pick the start with the largest total overlap
Rebuild the string by following stored choices

codeNotes.note: Largest suffix of a = prefix of b
Words still to place after i
Overlap gained by choosing j next

pitfalls: Greedy merging of the largest overlap first is not always optimal.
Store the chosen next word, or rebuilding the string is painful.

say.intro: Given up to twelve words, none inside another, we build the shortest string that contains all of them. For a b, b c and c a, overlap a b with b c to get a b c. Then overlap c a to get a b c a. Just four letters.
say.brute: The brute force tries every order of the words. For each order, it merges neighbours using their largest overlap. Then it keeps the shortest. So how many orders are there? Twelve words have almost five hundred million. That's factorial time. Way too slow.
say.insight: Here's the reframe. The final length is the total letters minus the overlaps between neighbours. So we want the order with the most total overlap. That's the travelling salesman problem on twelve nodes. And we know how to beat factorial. Held Karp dynamic programming over subsets. For each set and starting word, store the best overlap.
say.anim: We start with three words: ab, bc, and ca, ready to merge them. The code compares each pair of words, checking how much their ends and starts overlap. It finds ab overlaps bc by one letter, and bc overlaps ca by one letter too. Now ca overlaps ab by one letter, filling in the overlap table completely. The algorithm builds dp over subsets, tracking the best overlap ending at each word. For mask three, starting after ab then bc, it accumulates overlap one so far. It keeps extending subsets, always choosing the next word with the biggest overlap gain. Tracing back from the full mask rebuilds the order, giving the final answer abca.
say.code: First, for every ordered pair, find the largest suffix of one that's a prefix of the other. Then, for each subset and start word, look at the words still to place. Choosing word j next gains their overlap plus the best for the rest. At the end, pick the best starting word. Then follow the choices, appending only each word's non-overlapping tail.
say.outro: Still exponential, but two to the n instead of n factorial. Pattern: advanced graphs. Bitmask dynamic programming for a travelling salesman path.

find-the-shortest-superstring.title: Find the Shortest Superstring
lineNotes: We define the Solution class that holds the method for this problem.
The method takes a list of words and returns the shortest string containing all of them.
We store n as the number of words.
We build an n by n table ov, starting at zero, for overlaps between word pairs.
We loop over each word a as the left word, keeping its index i.
We loop over each word b as the right word, keeping its index j.
We skip pairs where both indices point to the same word.
We try overlap sizes from the longest possible down to one, so the first match is the largest.
If the end of a matches the first k letters of b, we have an overlap of size k.
We record that overlap length in ov for the pair i and j.
We stop searching since the largest overlap has already been found.
The full mask has every word bit set, representing all words used.
The dp table holds the best total overlap for each subset and starting word.
The nxt table remembers which word follows, with minus one meaning none chosen yet.
We process every nonempty subset of words as a mask, building from smaller subsets.
For each mask we try every word i as the first word of the ordering.
The rest mask is the subset with word i removed.
We skip words not in the mask, and masks where nothing remains after removing i.
We continue because there is nothing to compute for these cases.
We try each word j as the one placed right after i.
If j is in the rest and gives a better overlap, or nothing is set yet, we take it as a candidate.
We update dp with the overlap of i and j plus the best overlap of the rest starting at j.
We record j as the next word after i for this mask.
We pick the starting word whose full-set ordering has the largest total overlap.
We begin the result with that word and set mask to all words.
We keep following the next pointers until no next word exists.
We read the next word j after the current word i.
We append only the part of word j that does not overlap with word i.
We remove word i from the mask since it is now placed.
We move on so word j becomes the current word.
We return the assembled shortest superstring.

find-the-xor-of-numbers-which-appear-twi.hook: Remember what you have seen. The second sighting gets folded into the XOR.
find-the-xor-of-numbers-which-appear-twi.ask: Every number appears once or twice. Return the XOR of all numbers that appear twice, or zero if none do.
find-the-xor-of-numbers-which-appear-twi.exampleWhy: 4 and 2 each appear twice. 4 XOR 2 is 6.

brute.idea: For each distinct number, count its occurrences by scanning the whole list; XOR it in if the count is two.
steps: Take each distinct value
Count it with a full scan
Count is 2? XOR it into the answer
brute.whySlow: Each count rescans the entire list; a set replaces those scans with a single lookup.

optimal.insight: A number is a duplicate exactly when we meet it again. Keep a seen set and XOR a number in on its second sighting.
steps: Start with answer zero and an empty set
Seen before? XOR it into the answer
Otherwise add it to the set

codeNotes.note: Second sighting: it is a duplicate
Fold the duplicate into the XOR

pitfalls: XOR of the whole array cancels duplicates instead of keeping them; that solves the opposite problem.

say.intro: Every number shows up once or twice. We XOR together the ones that show up twice. If there are none, return zero. In four, one, two, four, three, two, the duplicates are four and two. Four XOR two is six.
say.brute: The brute force takes each distinct value and counts it by scanning the whole list. If the count is two, XOR it in. Simple enough. But every count is a full scan. So the total work is n squared. Can we avoid the rescans?
say.insight: Yes. Think about when a number becomes a duplicate. It's exactly when we bump into it a second time. So keep a set of numbers we've already seen. If the current number is already in the set, it's a duplicate. Fold it into the running XOR right away. One pass is enough.
say.anim: We start with an empty seen set and answer zero, ready to scan the array. Four is new, so it gets added to seen, then one and two are added the same way. Now x is four again, already in seen, so we xor it into ans, making ans four. Three is new, so it joins the seen set without changing ans. Two appears again, already seen, so we xor it in, updating ans to six. The loop finishes and the function returns the final answer. The duplicate numbers four and two xor together to give the final answer six.
say.code: We keep a set of numbers we've met once so far. For each number, we check whether it's already in the set. If it is, that's the second sighting. It's a duplicate, so we fold it into the XOR. Otherwise, it's the first sighting, and we remember it. If nothing repeats, the answer just stays zero.
say.outro: Linear time and space. Pattern: bit manipulation, paired with a hash set to catch the second sighting.

find-the-xor-of-numbers-which-appear-twi.title: Find the XOR of Numbers Which Appear Twice
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container for the method that solves this problem.
This method takes the list of numbers and returns one integer, the XOR of every number that appears twice.
We create an empty set called seen to remember which numbers we have already encountered.
We start the answer at zero, which is the identity for XOR and also the correct result when no duplicates exist.
We loop through each number x in the list, looking at them one at a time.
We check whether x is already in seen, which means this is its second appearance.
Since this is a second sighting, we XOR x into the answer, and each duplicate only counts once.
Otherwise this is the first time we have met x, so we handle it in this branch.
We add x to the seen set so a later repeat will be recognized as a duplicate.
After the loop ends, we return the answer, which is zero if nothing repeated.

find-words-containing-character.hook: A straight scan with a membership test. The interview point is saying why nothing beats linear.
find-words-containing-character.ask: Given a list of words and a letter, return the indices of the words that contain that letter, in any order.
find-words-containing-character.exampleWhy: Only abc at index 0 and aaaa at index 2 contain the letter a.

brute.idea: For every word, compare the letter against each character by hand, flagging the word on a match.
steps: Take the next word
Compare x with each character in turn
Match found? record the index and stop
brute.whySlow: Not asymptotically slower: every letter may need checking either way. It is just more code than a membership test.

optimal.insight: Any correct answer must read every letter in the worst case, so one pass with a built-in membership test is already optimal.
steps: Enumerate words with their indices
Check whether x is in the word
Collect matching indices

pitfalls: Return indices, not the words themselves.

say.intro: We get a list of words and one letter. Which words contain that letter? We return their positions. For a b c, b c d, four a's, and c b c, looking for a, the answer is positions zero and two.
say.brute: The hands-on version loops over every word, then over every character, comparing it with the target. On a match, it records the index and stops early. Now, is this slow? Not really. It's already linear in the total letters. It's just longer than it needs to be.
say.insight: Here's a useful way to think about it. Could any solution skip reading letters? No. If no word contains the target, we must read every letter. So linear is the best possible. A built in membership test does that character loop for us. It stops at the first match too. Same optimal bound, one readable line.
say.anim: We start with an empty result list and the letter a as our target. At index 0, word abc contains a, so we add 0 to the result. At index 1, word bcd does not contain a, so it's skipped. At index 2, word aaaa contains a, so index 2 is added too. At index 3, word cbc has no a, so it's left out. The loop finishes after checking every word once, keeping it efficient. The function returns the final answer, indices 0 and 2.
say.code: We loop over the words, getting each index and word together. Then we ask if the letter is in the word. That check stops at the first match. If it's there, we record the word's index. Return the list. That's the whole solution, and the indices come out in order naturally.
say.outro: Linear in total letters, which is optimal. Pattern: arrays and hashing. One pass, with a fast membership check doing the heavy lifting.

find-words-containing-character.title: Find Words Containing Character
lineNotes: We define a Solution class that holds the method for solving this problem.
The method takes a list of words and a letter x, and returns a list of indices.
We start with an empty result list that will collect the indices of matching words.
We loop through the words with enumerate, getting each word's index and the word itself in one pass.
We use the built-in membership test to check whether the letter x appears anywhere in the current word.
When the letter is found, we append the current index to the result list.
After checking every word, we return the result list of indices.

fizz-buzz.hook: The famous screening question. The trick is testing fifteen first, or building the word from parts.
fizz-buzz.ask: For every number from 1 to n, output Fizz if divisible by 3, Buzz if divisible by 5, FizzBuzz if by both, and otherwise the number itself as text.
fizz-buzz.exampleWhy: 3, 6, 9, 12 give Fizz; 5 and 10 give Buzz; 15 is divisible by both, so FizzBuzz.

brute.idea: Chain the four cases with if and elif, checking divisibility by both 3 and 5 first.
steps: Loop i from 1 to n
Divisible by 15? FizzBuzz
Else by 3? Fizz; else by 5? Buzz
Else the number as text
brute.whySlow: Same O(n). The weakness is fragility: every new rule multiplies the combined cases you must order correctly.

optimal.insight: Build the word from parts: add Fizz if 3 divides, add Buzz if 5 divides. Empty means use the number. Combined cases come for free.
steps: Loop i from 1 to n
Start with an empty word
Append Fizz for 3, Buzz for 5
Empty word? use the number instead

pitfalls: Checking 3 before 15 in an if-elif chain prints Fizz for 15.
Numbers must be strings in the output list.

say.intro: Okay, the classic. For each number from one to n, output Fizz if three divides it. Buzz if five divides it. Fizz Buzz if both do. Otherwise, the number itself as text. With n equal to fifteen, the list ends with fourteen, then Fizz Buzz.
say.brute: Most people start with an if and else chain. Check three and five together first. Then three alone, then five alone, then the number. It's linear and correct. So what's wrong with it? It's fragile. Put the checks in the wrong order and fifteen prints just Fizz. Add a third rule, and the combinations multiply.
say.insight: Here's a better way to think about it. Don't list every combination. Build the word from independent parts. Start empty. If three divides the number, append Fizz. If five divides it, append Buzz. Fifteen gets both, for free. If nothing was appended, use the number. A new rule is just one more line.
say.anim: We start with an empty result list and n equal to fifteen. For i equal to one, word starts empty since neither three nor five divides it, so we append one. At i equal to three, three divides evenly, so word becomes Fizz and gets appended. At i equal to five, five divides evenly, so word becomes Buzz and gets appended. At i equal to six, three divides again, giving Fizz, showing the pattern repeating. At i equal to fifteen, both three and five divide, so word becomes FizzBuzz. The function returns the final list, correctly mixing numbers, Fizz, Buzz, and FizzBuzz.
say.code: We loop from one to n, inclusive, because the answer is one indexed. Start an empty word. If three divides i, we add Fizz. If five divides i, we add Buzz, so fifteen gets both. Then we append the word. If no rule fired, we append the number as text instead.
say.outro: Linear time. Pattern: math and geometry, with a bit of modular arithmetic. Compose independent rules instead of listing their combinations.

fizz-buzz.title: Fizz Buzz
lineNotes: We define a Solution class that holds the method for solving the Fizz Buzz problem.
The fizzBuzz method takes the number n and returns a list of strings for each number up to n.
We start with an empty list called res to collect the answer for each number.
We loop the variable i through every number from one up to and including n.
For each number we begin with an empty string called word that will be built from parts.
We check whether i divides evenly by three, meaning the remainder is zero.
If it does, we add the text Fizz onto word.
Separately we check whether i divides evenly by five, using a plain if rather than else.
If so, we add Buzz onto word, so numbers divisible by both naturally become FizzBuzz.
We append word to res, or the number as text if word is empty, since an empty string counts as false.
After the loop finishes, we return the completed list of results.

flipping-an-image.hook: Reverse and invert in a single sweep: two pointers swap and flip at the same time.
flipping-an-image.ask: Given a square grid of zeros and ones, reverse every row, then flip every bit, and return the result.
flipping-an-image.exampleWhy: Row 1,1,0 reverses to 0,1,1 and inverts to 1,0,0. The other rows follow the same steps.

brute.idea: Build a reversed copy of every row, then build another copy with each bit inverted.
steps: Reverse each row into a new list
Invert each bit into another new list
Return the new grid
brute.whySlow: Same time, but it allocates two extra n by n grids and passes over the data twice.

optimal.insight: Reversing swaps row[l] with row[r]; inverting flips each. Do both in one move: swap and XOR with 1, meeting in the middle.
steps: For each row, put l at the start and r at the end
Swap row[l] and row[r], each XOR 1
Move inward until l passes r
The middle cell gets flipped once

pitfalls: Using l < r skips the middle element of odd rows, leaving it uninverted.

say.intro: We get a square grid of zeros and ones. Reverse every row. Then invert every bit, so zeros become ones and ones become zeros. Take the first row, one, one, zero. Reversed, it's zero, one, one. Inverted, it's one, zero, zero.
say.brute: The straightforward version makes a reversed copy of every row. Then it makes another copy with every bit flipped. Time is fine, since each cell gets touched a constant number of times. But it builds two extra grids and walks the data twice. That's wasteful.
say.insight: So can we do both at once? Think about what reversing is. Swap the cell at the left pointer with the one at the right, and move inward. And inverting is just XOR with one. So in one assignment, we swap the two cells and flip both. Here's the subtle part. Let the pointers meet, so the middle cell flips exactly once.
say.anim: We start with the image, and the first row is 1, 1, 0. Pointers l and r sit at opposite ends, swapping and flipping bits at once. After swapping and inverting, the row becomes 1, 0, 0, saving an extra pass. Moving to row two, 1, 0, 1, we repeat the same meet-in-the-middle swap and flip. That row finishes as 0, 1, 0 after both positions update together. The last row, 0, 0, 0, gets swapped and flipped into 1, 1, 1. All rows are now reversed and inverted in a single combined pass. The final flipped and inverted image is 1,0,0 then 0,1,0 then 1,1,1.
say.code: For each row, we put pointers at both ends. We loop while left is at most right. That includes the middle cell. In one tuple assignment, we swap the two cells and invert them together. Then both pointers move inward. At the end, we return the same grid. It was modified in place.
say.outro: n squared time, constant extra space. Pattern: two pointers. Fold two transformations into one inward sweep.

flipping-an-image.title: Flipping an Image
lineNotes: We define a Solution class that holds the method for solving the flipping an image problem.
The method takes a square grid of zeros and ones called image and returns the transformed grid.
We loop over each row of the image so every row gets reversed and inverted in place.
We set left to zero and right to the last index of the row, preparing two pointers.
We loop while left is not past right, so the pointers meet in the middle and handle a center element.
We swap the two end values while XORing each with one, which reverses and flips the bits together.
We move the left pointer one step to the right toward the middle.
We move the right pointer one step to the left toward the middle.
After processing every row, we return the modified image as the final answer.

frequency-of-the-most-frequent-element.hook: Sort, then grow a window whose elements can all be raised to its largest value within budget.
frequency-of-the-most-frequent-element.ask: You may increase any elements by one, at most k times in total. Return the largest number of equal elements you can create.
frequency-of-the-most-frequent-element.exampleWhy: Raise 1 by three and 2 by two to make 4, 4, 4, using exactly five increments.

brute.idea: Sort. For each element as the target, walk left adding the cost to raise each neighbour until the budget runs out.
steps: Sort the numbers
Pick each index as the target
Walk left, adding target minus value
Stop when cost exceeds k; record the count
brute.whySlow: Every target restarts its leftward walk, so 100,000 numbers can mean five billion steps.

optimal.insight: After sorting, the best group is a contiguous window ending at its target. Its cost is target times width minus window sum, so a sliding window works.
steps: Sort the numbers
Extend r and add nums[r] to the window sum
While nums[r] · width - sum > k, shrink from the left
Track the largest width

codeNotes.note: Cost to raise all to nums[r]

pitfalls: Only increments are allowed, so the target must be the window's largest value.
Recomputing the window cost each time makes it quadratic; keep a running sum.

say.intro: We may add one to any element, at most k times in total. What's the largest group of equal values we can make? With one, two, four, seven and k equal to five, we raise one and two up to four. That costs exactly five. So the answer is three.
say.brute: The brute force sorts the numbers, then treats each one as the target. It walks left, adding the cost to raise each neighbour up to the target. It stops when the budget runs out. So what's slow? Every target restarts its walk. That's n squared.
say.insight: Here's the thing. After sorting, the cheapest values to raise are the ones just below the target. So the best group is always a window ending at the target. What does that window cost? The target times the width, minus the window's sum. That changes smoothly as the window moves. So a sliding window with a running sum does it.
say.anim: We start with the sorted array one, two, four, seven, and budget k equals five. The window expands to include each number, adding it to the running total. At r equals two, total is seven, cost fits within budget, so best becomes three. Now r equals three, total jumps to fourteen, cost exceeds k, so we shrink the window. We remove nums at left twice, shrinking the window until the cost condition is satisfied. With l now two, the window covers four and seven, cost fits, best stays three. The loop finishes checking all elements using this sliding window technique. The function returns three, the maximum frequency achievable within budget five.
say.code: First, sort, so the closest values become neighbours. For each right index, we add its value to a running sum. While the cost to raise everything up to the right value exceeds k, we shrink. We drop the left value from the total and move left forward. Then we record the widest affordable window.
say.outro: n log n for the sort, then linear. Pattern: sliding window. The cost grows with the window, so shrink from the left.

frequency-of-the-most-frequent-element.title: Frequency of the Most Frequent Element
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container the problem expects for our method.
The method maxFrequency takes the list nums and the budget k, and returns the largest achievable frequency.
We sort nums so that the best group of elements to raise becomes a contiguous window.
We start left, total and best all at zero, tracking the window start, its sum, and the best width.
We move the right edge across every index, treating the element at right as the target value.
We add the new right element into total so total is the sum of the current window.
While raising the whole window to the target costs more than k, the window is too expensive and must shrink.
We subtract the leftmost element from total because it is leaving the window.
We move left forward by one, dropping that element and lowering the cost of the window.
We record the larger of best and the current window width as the best frequency so far.
After checking every right edge, we return best as the maximum frequency achievable.

frog-jump.hook: The state is not just which stone, but which stone and how you arrived there.
frog-jump.ask: Stones sit at increasing positions. A frog starts on the first stone with a first jump of one. After a jump of k it can jump k minus one, k, or k plus one. Can it reach the last stone?
frog-jump.exampleWhy: Jumps of 1, 2, 2, 3, 4 and 5 land on stones 1, 3, 5, 8, 12 and 17.

brute.idea: Recursively try all three next jumps from every position, with no memory of states already explored.
steps: From position p with last jump k
Try jumps k-1, k and k+1
Recurse whenever a stone is there
True if any branch reaches the end
brute.whySlow: The same stone and jump pair is re-explored along many paths, so branches multiply exponentially.

optimal.insight: Record, for each stone, the set of jump sizes that can land there. Process stones in order and push each size's three successors forward.
steps: Map each stone to an empty set of jump sizes
First stone gets jump 0
For each stone and size k, try k-1, k, k+1
Answer: the last stone's set is non-empty

codeNotes.match: jumps = {s: set() for s in stones}
codeNotes.note: Stone to jump sizes that land there
Any way to land on the last stone

pitfalls: Jumps of zero must be skipped, or the frog stays put forever.
Tracking only reachable stones loses the jump size; the state needs both.

say.intro: Stones sit at increasing positions across a river. The frog starts on the first stone, and its first jump is one unit. If its last jump was k, the next must be k minus one, k, or k plus one. Can it reach the last stone? Here, yes. Jumps of one, two, two, three, four, five.
say.brute: The brute force is plain recursion. From each position and last jump size, try all three next jumps. Recurse whenever a stone is there. So what's the catch? There's no memory. The same stone and jump size get explored again and again, along different paths. The work blows up exponentially.
say.insight: Here's the key. The state isn't just the stone. It's the stone plus the jump that landed there. So for each stone, keep a set of jump sizes that can reach it. Walk the stones left to right. Push each size's three successors forward. Each stone holds at most n sizes, so it's n squared overall.
say.anim: We start by giving each stone an empty set to track possible jump sizes landing there. Stone zero begins with jump size zero, so we try steps of negative one, zero, and one. Jump size one reaches stone one, recording that a jump of one landed there. From stone one, jump size two reaches stone three, adding two to its jump set. From stone three, jumps of two and three reach stones five and six respectively. These jumps keep propagating forward, filling stones six and eight with possible jump sizes. Eventually jump size four reaches stone twelve, keeping the frog moving forward successfully. Jump size five finally lands on stone seventeen, so the function returns true.
say.code: We map every stone to a set of jump sizes that land there. We seed the first stone with zero, so the next jump must be one. For each stone and each size, we try three next jumps. If a step lands on a stone, we add it to that stone's set. At the end, is the last stone's set non-empty?
say.outro: n squared time and space. Pattern: two dimensional dynamic programming, over the stone and the last jump size.

frog-jump.title: Frog Jump
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container the problem expects for our method.
The canCross method takes the list of stone positions and returns whether the frog can reach the last stone.
We build a dictionary mapping each stone position to an empty set that will hold jump sizes able to land there.
We seed the first stone with a jump size of zero, so the first real jump naturally becomes one.
We loop over every stone in increasing order, so all jumps landing on a stone are recorded before we use it.
For each jump size that reached this stone, we consider what the frog can do next.
The next jump can be one less, the same, or one more than the jump that brought us here.
We only accept positive steps that land exactly on an existing stone, ignoring jumps into water or backward.
We record that this step size can land on the target stone, pushing the information forward.
If the last stone has any recorded jump size, the frog reached it, so we return true, otherwise false.

fruits-into-baskets-iii.hook: Find the leftmost basket big enough, fast: a max segment tree lets you descend straight to it.
fruits-into-baskets-iii.ask: Place fruits left to right. Each goes into the leftmost unused basket with capacity at least its quantity; if none exists it stays unplaced. Return how many fruit types remain unplaced.
fruits-into-baskets-iii.exampleWhy: 4 goes in the basket of 5, 2 in the basket of 3, and 5 does not fit the remaining 4.

brute.idea: For each fruit, scan baskets from the left until one is unused and big enough, then mark it used.
steps: Take the next fruit
Scan baskets from the left
First unused basket that fits takes it
No basket? count it unplaced
brute.whySlow: Each fruit may rescan every basket: 100,000 of each is up to ten billion checks.

optimal.insight: A segment tree storing the maximum capacity per range lets us descend left whenever the left half can fit, finding the leftmost fit in log n.
steps: Build a max segment tree over baskets
Root max too small? fruit is unplaced
Else descend: left child if it fits, else right
Set that leaf to 0 and update ancestors

codeNotes.note: Even the biggest basket is too small

codeNotes.match: i = 2 * i if tree[2 * i] >= f else 2 * i + 1

codeNotes.note: Repair maxima on the way up

pitfalls: Sorting baskets breaks the leftmost rule; positions matter.
Mark used baskets as capacity 0 so they never match again.

say.intro: We place fruits from left to right. Each fruit goes into the leftmost unused basket with enough capacity. If none fits, it stays unplaced. With fruits four, two, five and baskets three, five, four, the five finds nothing left that fits. So one fruit is unplaced.
say.brute: The brute force scans baskets from the left for every fruit. It takes the first unused one that's big enough and marks it used. Easy. But in the worst case, each fruit walks past every basket. A hundred thousand of each is ten billion checks.
say.insight: So what do we really need? The leftmost position with capacity at least some value. And positions get removed over time. A segment tree of range maximums handles that. Start at the root. If the left half's maximum fits, go left. Otherwise go right. Why does that work? Preferring left always finds the leftmost fit, in log n steps.
say.anim: We start with fruits 4, 2, 5 and baskets 3, 5, 4, building a segment tree over baskets. The tree fills in with leaf values 3, 5, 4, then combines upward to track max capacity per range. For fruit 4, the root max is 5, so we descend, finding basket index 5 with capacity 5 fits. That basket is zeroed out and we update ancestors upward, keeping the tree accurate. For fruit 2, we descend again and place it at index 4, using the basket with capacity 3. We clear that leaf and refresh the tree values up to the root. For fruit 5, the root max is now only 4, too small, so it stays unplaced. The function returns 1, meaning only one fruit could not be placed in any basket.
say.code: First, we put the basket capacities in the leaves. For each fruit, if even the biggest basket at the root is too small, we count it. Otherwise we descend, preferring left whenever it fits.
