That gives the leftmost fit. We zero that leaf, since the basket's used. Then we repair the maxima on the way up.
say.outro: n log n overall. Pattern: trees. Here a segment tree is basically a binary search for the leftmost fit.

fruits-into-baskets-iii.title: Fruits Into Baskets III
lineNotes: We define the Solution class that holds the method for this problem.
The method takes the fruit quantities and basket capacities and returns the count of fruits left unplaced.
We record n as the number of baskets.
We start size at one to find a power of two that fits all baskets.
We keep doubling while size is still smaller than the number of baskets.
Each pass doubles size, so the leaf level becomes a power of two.
We create the tree array of zeros with room for internal nodes and leaves, so padding leaves hold zero capacity.
We copy the basket capacities into the leaf positions starting at index size.
We build the internal nodes from the bottom up, walking indices from size minus one down to one.
Each internal node stores the larger capacity of its two children, giving the range maximum.
We initialize the unplaced counter to zero.
We process each fruit in order from left to right.
If the root maximum is smaller than the fruit, no basket anywhere can hold it.
So we count this fruit as unplaced.
We skip to the next fruit since nothing needs updating.
Otherwise we start at the root to search for the leftmost fitting basket.
We descend while we are still on an internal node rather than a leaf.
We go left if the left child can fit the fruit, otherwise right, which guarantees the leftmost fit.
At the leaf we set its capacity to zero, marking that basket as used.
We move up to the parent to begin refreshing the maximums.
We continue upward until we pass the root.
Each ancestor is recomputed as the max of its two children to reflect the removed basket.
We step to the next parent up the tree.
Finally we return the total number of unplaced fruits.

gcd-of-odd-and-even-sums.hook: Both sums have closed forms, and consecutive integers never share a factor. The answer is n.
gcd-of-odd-and-even-sums.ask: Add up the first n odd numbers and the first n even numbers. Return the greatest common divisor of the two sums.
gcd-of-odd-and-even-sums.exampleWhy: Odd sum 1+3+5+7 is 16, even sum 2+4+6+8 is 20, and gcd(16, 20) is 4.

brute.idea: Add the odd and even numbers with a loop, then run Euclid's algorithm on the two totals.
steps: Loop i from 1 to n
Add 2i-1 to the odd sum, 2i to the even sum
Run Euclid on the two sums
brute.whySlow: Linear work for an answer that is a closed form; it hides the math the interviewer wants to see.

optimal.insight: The odd sum is n squared and the even sum is n times n plus one. Since n and n plus one are coprime, the GCD is exactly n.
steps: Odd sum = n²
Even sum = n(n + 1)
gcd(n², n(n+1)) = n · gcd(n, n+1) = n

codeNotes.note: First n odd numbers sum to n²

pitfalls: Say the proof out loud: factor out n, then gcd(n, n + 1) is 1.

say.intro: Add up the first n odd numbers. Add up the first n even numbers. What's the greatest common divisor of the two totals? For n equal to four, the odd sum is sixteen and the even sum is twenty. Their greatest common divisor is four.
say.brute: The direct approach just loops from one to n. Each odd number goes into one total, each even number into the other. Then it runs Euclid's algorithm on the two totals. It's linear and perfectly correct. But here's the thing. It hides a closed form the interviewer wants you to spot.
say.insight: So let's look at the math. The first n odd numbers always sum to n squared. The first n even numbers sum to n times n plus one. Both share a factor of n. So the answer is n times the GCD of n and n plus one. Do consecutive numbers share a factor? Never. So the answer is just n.
say.anim: n is 4, so sum_odd becomes 4 times 4, which is 16. Next sum_even is computed as 4 times 5, giving 20. Since n and n plus one share no common factors, their gcd reduces to just n. The function returns 4, the final GCD of the odd and even sums.
say.code: First, the odd sum is n times n. The first n odd numbers always add up to that. The even sum is n times n plus one. That's twice the triangle number. These lines just document the reasoning. Then we return n, because consecutive integers are coprime.
say.outro: Constant time, from a two line proof. Pattern: math and geometry. Find the closed form, then remember that neighbours are coprime.

gcd-of-odd-and-even-sums.title: GCD of Odd and Even Sums
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container the problem expects for our method.
This method takes n, the count of odd and even numbers to add, and returns their greatest common divisor.
The sum of the first n odd numbers is n squared, so we store that as sum odd.
The sum of the first n even numbers is n times n plus one, so we store that as sum even.
This comment shows the math: factoring out n leaves the gcd of n and n plus one, which is one, so the answer is n.
Because consecutive numbers share no common factor, we skip computing any gcd and simply return n.

get-the-maximum-score.hook: Common values split both arrays into segments. At each junction, keep whichever side's segment was bigger.
get-the-maximum-score.ask: Two sorted arrays of distinct numbers. Walk one from the start, and at any value present in both you may switch arrays. Return the largest possible sum of values on the path, modulo one billion and seven.
get-the-maximum-score.exampleWhy: Path 2, 4, 6, 8, 10 switches at 4 and at 8, totalling 30.

brute.idea: Recursively explore both choices at every shared value, trying every possible sequence of switches.
steps: Start on either array
Walk forward adding values
At a shared value, try staying and switching
Return the best total
brute.whySlow: Every shared value doubles the paths: 40 shared values already means a trillion paths.

optimal.insight: Shared values are junctions every path passes. Between junctions, take the larger segment sum. Two pointers compute both segment sums in one merge.
steps: Merge both arrays with pointers i and j
Smaller value adds to its side's running sum
Equal value: both sums become max(a, b) plus it
Answer: max(a, b) at the end, modulo

codeNotes.note: Best sums ending on each array
Take the modulo only at the end

pitfalls: Taking the modulo mid-way corrupts the max comparisons; Python ints let you wait.
A shared value is counted once, not once per array.

say.intro: We have two sorted arrays. We walk one of them from the start. Whenever we hit a value that's in both, we may switch to the other array. We want the biggest sum along the way. Here, two, four, six, eight, ten switches at four and eight. It scores thirty.
say.brute: The brute force explores every option. At each shared value, it tries both staying and switching, then keeps walking. Sounds fine at first. But every shared value doubles the number of paths. Forty shared values is already about a trillion paths.
say.insight: Here's the key. Shared values are junctions. Every path passes through them, on one side or the other. Between two junctions, each array offers one segment. And those segments don't affect each other. So at every junction, just keep the bigger segment sum. A two pointer merge tracks both running sums in one pass.
say.anim: We start with two pointers and two running sums, a and b, both at zero. Nums1's value 2 is smaller, so it adds to a, making a equal 2. At value 4, both arrays match, a junction, so a and b merge to 6. Nums1 continues alone, adding 5 to a, bringing a up to 11. Now nums2 is smaller, adding 6 into b, making b equal 12. Another shared value, 8, merges the paths again, setting a and b to 20. Nums2's remaining value 9 adds into b, raising b to 29. Finally nums1's last value 10 adds to a, giving a a total of 30, the maximum path sum.
say.code: We keep the best sum ending on each array, both starting at zero. If a value is only in the first array, we add it to the first sum. If it's only in the second, we add it there. At a junction, both sums become the better one plus the value. We take the modulo only at the end.
say.outro: Linear time, constant space. Pattern: two pointers. Merge the sorted arrays, and pick the best segment at each junction.

get-the-maximum-score.title: Get the Maximum Score
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the wrapper this problem expects for the method.
The method maxSum takes two sorted arrays of distinct numbers and returns the best path score.
We start two pointers, i and j, at the beginning of the first and second arrays.
We also set two running sums, a for the path on the first array and b for the second.
We loop until both arrays are fully consumed, so no value is left out of the merge.
If the second array is exhausted or the current first value is smaller, the first array's value comes next.
We add that smaller value from the first array into its running sum a.
Then we advance the first pointer i to the next element.
Otherwise, if the first array is exhausted or its value is larger, the second array's value comes next.
We add that value from the second array into its running sum b.
Then we advance the second pointer j to the next element.
Otherwise the two current values are equal, meaning we have reached a junction where we may switch.
At the junction both sums become the larger of a and b plus the shared value, keeping the best path.
We advance the first pointer past the shared value.
We advance the second pointer past it too.
At the end we return the larger sum, taken modulo one billion and seven, as the problem requires.

guess-number-higher-or-lower.hook: Every answer halves the range. Thirty-one guesses cover two billion numbers.
guess-number-higher-or-lower.ask: A number was picked between 1 and n. Calling guess tells you whether your guess is too high, too low, or correct. Find the picked number.
guess-number-higher-or-lower.exampleWhy: Guess 5 is too low, guess 8 is too high, guess 6 is correct.

brute.idea: Guess 1, then 2, then 3, and so on, until the API says the guess is correct.
steps: Start at 1
Call guess on the current number
Correct? return it; otherwise try the next
brute.whySlow: Ignores the higher or lower hint: n can be two billion, so up to two billion calls.

optimal.insight: The hint says which half contains the pick. Guess the middle of the remaining range and discard the wrong half every time.
steps: Range is 1 to n
Guess the midpoint
Too high: move hi below mid; too low: move lo above
Stop when guess returns 0

codeNotes.note: Local stand-in for the judge's API
Too high: drop the upper half
Too low: drop the lower half

pitfalls: guess returns -1 when your number is too HIGH; the sign is easy to flip.
In fixed-width languages, lo + (hi - lo) / 2 avoids overflow.

say.intro: Someone picked a number from one to n. Every time we guess, an API tells us if we're too high, too low, or right. Our job is to find the number. With n equal to ten and the pick being six, we find it in three guesses.
say.brute: The brute force guesses one, then two, then three, and keeps going until the API says correct. See the problem? It totally ignores the higher or lower hint. And n can be over two billion. That's up to two billion calls.
say.insight: So let's use the hint. It tells us which half of the range holds the pick. So always guess the middle. Too high? Throw away the top half. Too low? Throw away the bottom half. Every guess halves the range. That's why about thirty one guesses cover two billion numbers.
say.anim: We start searching between lo equals 1 and hi equals 10 for the pick. Mid is calculated as 5, and guessing 5 returns 1, meaning pick is higher. So lo moves up to 6, narrowing the range to 6 through 10. Mid becomes 8, and guessing 8 returns negative one, meaning pick is lower. So hi shrinks to 7, narrowing the range to 6 through 7. Mid is now 6, and guessing 6 returns zero, a match found. The function returns mid, giving the final answer of 6.
say.code: First, a small local function stands in for the judge's API. Then we set low to one and high to n. The pick is somewhere in there. Each round, we guess the midpoint, halving the range. If the guess is too high, we drop the upper half. If it's too low, we drop the lower half.
say.outro: Logarithmic time, constant space. Pattern: binary search. Use each hint to throw away half of what's left.

guess-number-higher-or-lower.title: Guess Number Higher or Lower

meta.name: guessNumber

lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container the guessNumber method lives in.
The guessNumber method takes the upper bound n and the hidden pick, and returns the picked number.
We define a small helper called guess that stands in for the real API the problem provides.
It returns zero if the guess matches the pick, negative one if too high, and one if too low.
We set lo to one and hi to n, so the search range covers every possible pick.
We loop as long as lo has not passed hi, meaning at least one candidate remains.
We compute mid as the average of lo and hi, rounded down, to probe the center of the range.
We call guess on mid and store the hint in res.
If res is zero, we have found the picked number.
So we return mid immediately as the answer.
If res is negative, our guess was too high, so the pick lies below mid.
We move hi down to just below mid, discarding the upper half.
Otherwise the guess was too low, so the pick lies above mid.
We move lo up to just above mid, discarding the lower half.
If the loop ends without a match, we return negative one, though a valid pick means this never happens.

guess-the-word.hook: Each guess only tells you how many letters line up. Make every guess split the field.
guess-the-word.ask: One six-letter word from a list is secret. Each guess returns how many positions match exactly. Find the secret within the allowed number of guesses.
guess-the-word.exampleWhy: Guessing ccbazz scores 3; only acckzz also matches ccbazz in exactly 3 places, so the second guess wins.

brute.idea: Guess the words one by one in list order until a guess scores six matches.
steps: Take the next word in the list
Ask the master for its score
Six matches? Stop
brute.whySlow: It ignores every score. With 100 words and 10 guesses it fails most secrets outright.

optimal.insight: A score of s means the secret matches our guess in exactly s places. Keep only such words, and guess the word whose worst-case group is smallest.
steps: For each candidate, group the others by match count
Pick the word whose largest group is smallest
Guess it and read the score
Keep only candidates with that same score against it

codeNotes.note: Every word could still be the secret
Biggest group this guess might leave

pitfalls: Guessing randomly from the filtered list usually works but can exceed the limit on adversarial tests.
The secret matches the guess exactly score times: filter with equality, not at least.

say.intro: Okay, this one's a game. One word from a list of six letter words is the secret. Each guess only tells us how many positions match exactly. And guesses are limited. Here the secret is a c c k z z. Our first guess scores three, only one word fits, and the second guess wins.
say.brute: The brute force just guesses the words in list order until one scores six. Will it eventually hit the secret? Sure. But it throws away every score it hears. With a hundred words and only ten guesses, it fails most of the time.
say.insight: Here's the thing. A score is a filter. If our guess scores three, the secret matches it in exactly three places. Every word that doesn't is gone. So which guess shrinks the field fastest? The one whose worst case leaves the fewest survivors. That's minimax. Group the others by match count, and pick the smallest largest group.
say.anim: We start with six candidate words and up to ten guesses allowed. For each word we compute match counts against every other candidate, searching for the safest guess. Guessing ccbazz gives a worst case group size of two, the best so far. Eiowzz looks worse, its worst case group size jumps to four. Ccbazz remains best, so we guess it and get a score of three matches. We filter candidates down to those matching ccbazz with score three, leaving just acckzz. Now acckzz is the only candidate, so it becomes our next guess. Guessing acckzz scores six, a perfect match, so the secret word is acckzz.
say.code: At first, every word could still be the secret. Each round, for each candidate, we count how its scores would split the list. That's the biggest group this guess might leave. We keep the guess with the smallest worst group. Then we score it against the secret. Finally, we keep only words that score the same.
say.outro: n squared work per guess, but very few guesses. Pattern: greedy minimax. Always make the move with the smallest worst case.

guess-the-word.title: Guess the Word

meta.name: findSecretWord

lineNotes: We define the Solution class that holds our method for solving the guessing problem.
The method receives the secret, the word list, and the number of guesses we are allowed to make.
We define a helper called match that counts how many positions agree between two words.
It adds up one for every position where the paired letters from both words are equal.
We start with candidates as a copy of the full word list, since any word could be secret.
We loop once per allowed guess, using an underscore because the loop number itself is never needed.
We set the best guess to the first candidate and the best worst-case size to something larger than any possible group.
We try every candidate word as a possible guess to see which one splits the candidates best.
For this word, we group all candidates by their match score and take the size of the largest group, the worst case.
If this worst case is smaller than the best one seen so far, this word is a better guess.
We then remember this word as the best guess and record its smaller worst-case size.
We make the guess with the best word and get its score, here by comparing against the secret.
If the score equals the word length, every letter matches, so we found the secret.
In that case we return immediately because the problem is solved.
Otherwise we keep only candidates whose match with our guess equals the score, since only those could be the secret.

h-index.hook: A researcher's impact in one number, found without sorting.
h-index.ask: Given how many times each paper was cited, return the largest h such that at least h papers each have at least h citations.
h-index.exampleWhy: Three papers have at least 3 citations (3, 6, 5), but only two have at least 4.

brute.idea: Try every h from n down to zero, counting papers with at least h citations each time.
steps: Try h = n, n-1, ... 0
Count papers with citations ≥ h
First h with count ≥ h wins
brute.whySlow: Each candidate h rescans every paper: 5,000 papers means up to 25 million checks.

optimal.insight: The answer is at most n, so any citation count above n acts like n. Bucket papers by capped citations, then sum buckets from the top.
steps: Make n + 1 buckets
Drop each paper into bucket min(c, n)
Walk h from n down, adding bucket sizes
Stop at the first h with papers ≥ h

codeNotes.note: Papers with at least h citations
First h from the top wins

pitfalls: Sorting descending and finding the last i with citations[i] > i is O(n log n): mention it first.
Forgetting to cap at n overflows the bucket array.

say.intro: Each number is how many citations one paper got. We want the largest h where at least h papers have h or more citations. For three, zero, six, one, five, three papers have at least three. But only two have at least four. So the answer is three.
say.brute: The brute force tries every h from n down to zero. For each one, it scans all the papers and counts how many have at least h citations. The first h where the count reaches h wins. It works. But every guess rescans the whole list. That's n squared.
say.insight: Here's a neat observation. Can h ever be bigger than the number of papers? No. So a paper with a thousand citations counts the same as one with n. That means we can bucket papers by citation count, capped at n. Then walk h downward, adding up bucket sizes. That's how many papers have at least h.
say.anim: We start with citations three, zero, six, one, five, and n equals five. We create six buckets to count papers by capped citation values. We loop through each citation, placing it into its bucket, capping at n. After filling, buckets show counts for citation values zero through five. Now we scan buckets from the top, accumulating papers seen so far. At h equals five, papers reach two, which is less than five. At h equals four, papers stay at two, still less than four. At h equals three, papers become three, matching h, so we return three.
say.code: We make one bucket per possible h. For each citation count, we cap huge counts at n and drop it in its bucket. Then we walk h from the top, adding that bucket to a running total. That's the papers with at least h citations. The first h where the total reaches h wins.
say.outro: Linear time with a counting array. Pattern: arrays and hashing. When values are bounded by n, bucket them instead of sorting.

h-index.title: H-Index
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the standard wrapper for this problem's solution method.
The hIndex method takes the list of citation counts and returns the largest valid h as an integer.
We store the number of papers in n, since the h-index can never exceed that.
We create a bucket list of zeros with n plus one slots, one for each possible capped citation count.
We loop over each citation count in the input list, one paper at a time.
We cap each count at n and add one to that bucket, since higher counts behave the same as n.
We start a running total of papers at zero, which will count papers with at least h citations.
We try h from n down to zero, so the first valid h we find is the largest.
We add the bucket for h to the running total, so it counts papers with at least h citations.
We check whether at least h papers have h or more citations, which is exactly the h-index condition.
When the condition holds, we return h immediately, because we are scanning from the largest candidate downward.
As a fallback we return zero, though the loop always returns by h equals zero, so this is just a safety net.

how-many-numbers-are-smaller-than-the-cu.hook: For every number, how many others are smaller? A running count answers all at once.
how-many-numbers-are-smaller-than-the-cu.ask: For each number in the array, count how many other numbers in the array are strictly smaller than it, and return those counts in the same order.
how-many-numbers-are-smaller-than-the-cu.exampleWhy: Four numbers are below 8, none below 1, one below each 2, and three below 3.

brute.idea: For each number, scan the whole array and count values that are smaller.
steps: Pick nums[i]
Scan every nums[j]
Count nums[j] < nums[i]
brute.whySlow: Every element rescans the entire array; the same comparisons repeat for equal values.

optimal.insight: Values are small. Count each value, then take prefix sums: the count of numbers smaller than v is the sum of counts below v.
steps: Count occurrences, shifted by one slot
Prefix-sum the counts
count[x] now holds numbers below x
Read the answer for each number

codeNotes.note: One slot per value, plus one
Shift so prefix excludes x itself

pitfalls: Without the plus-one shift you count equal values as smaller.
Sorting plus a first-index map also works in O(n log n).

say.intro: For each number, how many numbers in the array are strictly smaller? Take eight, one, two, two, three. Four numbers are below eight. None are below one. One is below each two. And three are below three.
say.brute: The brute force takes each number and scans the whole array, counting smaller values. Simple and correct. But it's n squared. And notice the two twos. They repeat exactly the same work. Can we share it?
say.insight: Here's the thing. The values are small, at most one hundred. So why compare pairs? Just count how often each value appears. How many values are smaller than v? It's the total count of every value below v. That's a prefix sum. Shift each count up one slot. Then after the prefix sum, slot x is the answer for x. No comparisons at all.
say.anim: We build a count array sized for the largest value, all zeros to start. For each number, we bump the slot one position after its value, tallying occurrences. Notice two appears twice, so index three gets incremented twice, becoming two. After counting, the array holds shifted frequencies for values one through eight. Now we sweep forward, adding each previous count to build running totals. These prefix sums now represent how many numbers are smaller than each value. The final count array is zero,zero,one,three,four,four,four,four,four,five. Mapping each original number through this array gives the answer four,zero,one,one,three.
say.code: We make a count array with one slot per value, plus one. For each number, we add one at x plus one. That shift means the prefix excludes x itself. Then we sweep, adding each slot into the next. That's a running total of smaller values. Finally, we just look up each answer.
say.outro: Linear in the input plus the value range. Pattern: arrays and hashing. Counting and prefix sums replace pairwise comparisons.

how-many-numbers-are-smaller-than-the-cu.title: How Many Numbers Are Smaller Than the Current Number
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container the problem expects for our method.
The method takes the list nums and returns a list of counts, one per number, in the original order.
We make a count array of zeros, sized to the largest value plus two, so shifting each index by one still fits.
We loop through every number x in nums to tally how often each value appears.
We add one at position x plus one, so each tally sits just after its value, ready for prefix sums.
We then walk through the count array from index one to the end to build running totals.
Each position adds the total before it, so count at v becomes how many numbers are strictly less than v.
We return, for each x in nums, the count at x, giving its number of strictly smaller values in the original order.

implement-queue-using-stacks.hook: Two last-in-first-out stacks make one first-in-first-out queue. Pour one into the other.
implement-queue-using-stacks.ask: Build a queue with push, pop, peek and empty, using only stack operations: push to top, pop from top, peek top, size and is empty.
implement-queue-using-stacks.exampleWhy: Items leave in arrival order: 1, 2, 3, then 4, and the queue ends empty.

brute.idea: Keep one stack with the oldest item on top. On every push, unstack everything, put the new item down, restack.
steps: Move all items to a temp stack
Push the new item
Move everything back on top
brute.whySlow: Every single push moves every stored item twice; n pushes cost n squared moves.

optimal.insight: Pouring a stack into another reverses it, so the oldest item lands on top. Only pour when the out-stack is empty; each item moves once.
steps: Push onto the inbox stack
Pop or peek from the outbox stack
Outbox empty? Pour the whole inbox into it
Each item is moved at most once

codeNotes.note: Pour only when outbox is empty

codeNotes.match: return not self.inbox and not self.outbox

pitfalls: Pouring while the outbox still has items breaks the order.
A single pop can cost O(n); the amortized bound is per operation over a sequence.

say.intro: We need a queue, first in, first out. But we can only use stacks, which are last in, first out. We push one, two, three. Peek and pop give one. Push four. Then pops give two, three, four, and the queue is empty.
say.brute: The brute force keeps one stack with the oldest item on top. To push, it unstacks everything, puts the new item at the bottom, and stacks it all back. Pops are instant. But what does a push cost? Every stored item moves twice. A long run of pushes gets n squared.
say.insight: Here's the trick. Pour one stack into another, and the order flips. Flip last in first out, and you get first in first out. So use two stacks. New items go into an inbox. Pops come from an outbox. Only when the outbox is empty do we pour the inbox across. Each item moves at most once. So it's constant time on average.
say.anim: We start with empty inbox and outbox stacks for our queue. Pushing one, two, and three just appends them onto the inbox stack. For peek, since outbox is empty, we pour inbox into outbox, reversing the order. Now outbox holds three, two, one, so the top value one is returned. Popping removes that top element, returning one as the oldest queued item. After pushing four, peek pops two, then three, since outbox still has those left. Outbox is now empty, so four pours over from inbox before peeking returns four. Finally both stacks are empty, so empty returns true, confirming the queue is clear.
say.code: Push always appends to the inbox. Pop first calls peek, to make sure the outbox is filled. Inside peek, we only pour when the outbox is empty. Each item popped from the inbox goes onto the outbox. That reversal puts the oldest on top. And empty is true only if both stacks are empty.
say.outro: Amortized constant time per operation. Pattern: stacks. Two reversals cancel out, turning last in first out into first in first out.

implement-queue-using-stacks.title: Implement Queue using Stacks
lineNotes: We define a class called MyQueue that will behave like a queue while using only stacks inside.
The constructor sets up the two stacks we will rely on.
We create two empty lists, an inbox for newly pushed items and an outbox for items ready to leave.
The push method adds a new value to the queue.
We simply append the value to the inbox, which takes constant time.
The pop method removes and returns the oldest item in the queue.
We call peek first so that the outbox is guaranteed to hold the oldest item on top.
Then we pop from the outbox and return that front item.
The peek method returns the front item without removing it.
We only refill when the outbox is empty, so the existing order stays correct.
While the inbox still has items, we keep pouring them over.
Each pop from the inbox is appended to the outbox, reversing the order so the oldest ends up on top.
The top of the outbox is now the front of the queue, so we return it.
The empty method reports whether the queue holds any items at all.
The queue is empty only when both the inbox and the outbox have nothing in them.

implement-stack-using-queues.hook: A queue only serves its oldest item. Rotate it so the newest comes first.
implement-stack-using-queues.ask: Build a stack with push, pop, top and empty, using only queue operations: add to back, remove from front, peek front, size and is empty.
implement-stack-using-queues.exampleWhy: The newest item always leaves first: 3, then 4, then 2, leaving 1 inside.

brute.idea: Use two queues. To pop, move all but the last item into the other queue, take the last, then swap roles.
steps: Push: add to the back of q1
Pop: move n-1 items into q2
Take the last one, swap the queues
Top: pop, then push it back
brute.whySlow: Not asymptotically worse; it moves n items on every pop and top, needs two queues, and top is pop plus push.

optimal.insight: Pay once at push time: add the new item, then rotate every older item behind it. The front of the queue is then always the stack top.
steps: Append the new item to the back
Rotate the older n-1 items behind it
Pop and top read the front
Empty checks the single queue

codeNotes.note: Front item goes to the back

pitfalls: Rotating len(q) times instead of len(q) - 1 puts the new item back at the end.
Use deque.popleft; list.pop(0) is itself O(n).

say.intro: Now the flip side. We need a stack, last in, first out. But we only have a queue, which serves its oldest item first. Push one, two, three. Top and pop both give three. Push four. Then pops give four, then two. The stack still isn't empty.
say.brute: The brute force uses two queues. Push just appends. To pop, it moves every item except the last into the other queue, takes that last one, and swaps the queues. Top does the same dance. Honestly? Not asymptotically worse. It just pays linear time on every pop and top, instead of once per push.
say.insight: Here's the thing. A queue can rotate. Take the front item and add it to the back. The order shifts by one. So when we push, we append the new item, then rotate all the older items behind it. Now the newest item is at the front. That's exactly where a stack's top belongs. One queue, and reads are instant.
say.anim: We start with an empty queue that will secretly act as our stack. Pushing one just appends it, so the queue becomes one. Pushing two appends it, then rotates once, making the queue two then one. Pushing three appends it, then rotates twice so three ends up in front. Calling top reads the front of the queue, correctly returning three. Popping removes the front element, returning three as the last pushed value. Pushing four appends and rotates twice, placing four back at the front. Two more pops return four then two, following proper stack order. Finally empty checks the queue, and since one remains, it returns false.
say.code: One queue is enough. On push, we append x, then loop over every older item. Each time, the front item goes to the back. After that, the newest item is at the front. So pop just takes from the front. Top reads the front without removing it.
say.outro: Linear push, constant pop and top. Pattern: stacks, built by rotating a queue so the newest item is always in front.

implement-stack-using-queues.title: Implement Stack using Queues
lineNotes: We define a class called MyStack that will behave like a stack while using only a queue inside.
The constructor runs when a new stack is created and sets up its starting state.
We create one empty double ended queue named q, which is the only storage we use.
The push method takes an integer x and adds it as the new top of the stack.
We first append x to the back of the queue, where it temporarily sits behind all older items.
We loop one time for each older item, which is the length of the queue minus one.
Each pass removes the front item and appends it to the back, so older items rotate behind the new one.
The pop method removes and returns the top of the stack.
Because the newest item is always at the front, removing from the front gives the stack's top in constant time.
The top method returns the current top element without removing it.
We simply peek at the front of the queue, which is the most recently pushed item.
The empty method reports whether the stack holds any items.
The stack is empty exactly when the queue is empty, so we return the negation of the queue's truthiness.

insert-delete-getrandom-o1-duplicates-al.hook: Constant-time random picks need an array; constant-time deletes need a map. Use both.
insert-delete-getrandom-o1-duplicates-al.ask: Build a multiset supporting insert, remove one copy, and getRandom, where each element is returned with probability proportional to its copies, all in average constant time.
insert-delete-getrandom-o1-duplicates-al.exampleWhy: Insert is true only for a new value; both 4s are removed; 9 never existed; only 7s remain to pick.

brute.idea: Store everything in a plain list. Insert appends, remove searches the list, getRandom picks a random index.
steps: Insert: check membership, then append
Remove: list.remove scans for the value
getRandom: random.choice on the list
brute.whySlow: Membership checks and removals scan the list: 200,000 operations on a big list is billions of steps.

optimal.insight: Delete from the middle of an array in O(1) by overwriting the slot with the last element and popping the end. A map of value → set of indices finds the slots.
steps: Array holds every copy for random picks
Map each value to the set of its indices
Remove: take any index of val, move last element there
Fix the moved element's index set, pop the end

codeNotes.note: True only for a new value
Fill the hole with the last item
Add before discard: handles i == end

pitfalls: Discarding before adding breaks when the removed slot is the last one.
Index lists instead of sets make removal O(k) for many duplicates.

say.intro: We keep a bag of numbers, duplicates allowed. Insert says whether the value is new. Remove deletes one copy. Get random returns a value, weighted by its copies. In our run, two fours and a seven go in. Both fours come out. Removing nine fails. Only sevens remain.
say.brute: The brute force keeps a plain list. Get random is easy. Just pick a random index. But insert must scan the list to see if the value is new. And remove must search the list and shift everything after the hole. Both are linear. So a long run of operations gets slow.
say.insight: Random picks need an array. So can an array lose any element in constant time? Yes, if we cheat a little. Copy the last element into the hole, then pop the end. To find a hole fast, keep a map from each value to the set of its indices. After the swap, just fix the moved value's index set.
say.anim: We start with an empty list called nums and an empty index map. We insert four, adding it at index zero and returning true since it's new. We insert four again, now duplicated in nums, so insert returns false. We insert seven, a new value, growing nums and returning true. Removing four pops an index, swaps in the last element seven, and shrinks nums, returning true. Removing four again swaps in the last four, shrinks nums, and returns true. Removing nine fails since nine was never inserted, so it returns false. We insert seven again, then getRandom picks from nums and returns seven.
say.code: We map each value to all its positions. Insert appends, and returns true only for a new value, when its set has one entry. To remove, we fill the hole with the last item. We add the hole to the last item's set before discarding the old end. That handles the case where they're the same. Get random picks a copy uniformly.
say.outro: Average constant time for all three. Pattern: arrays and hashing. An array for random access, a hash map for locations.

insert-delete-getrandom-o1-duplicates-al.title: Insert Delete GetRandom O(1) - Duplicates allowed
lineNotes: We import the random module so we can pick a random element later in getRandom.
We define the RandomizedCollection class, which will behave like a multiset with constant time operations.
The constructor sets up the two structures we need to store values and find them quickly.
We create nums, an array holding every copy of every value, which makes random picking easy.
We create idx, a map from each value to the set of positions where it sits in nums.
The insert method adds one copy of a value and reports whether the value was new.
We record the upcoming position, which is the current length of nums, in the set of indices for this value.
We append the value to the end of nums so the array and index map stay in sync.
We return true only when the value now has exactly one index, meaning it was not present before.
The remove method deletes one copy of a value and reports whether anything was removed.
If the value has no indices, it is not in the collection.
So we return false because there is nothing to remove.
We pop an arbitrary index of this value, giving us the slot we will free up.
We read the last element of nums, which will fill the hole left by the removed copy.
We overwrite the slot at index i with the last element, effectively deleting the old value there.
We add index i to the last value's set because that value now lives in this slot too.
We discard the old last position from that set, since the array is about to shrink past it.
We pop the end of nums, dropping the duplicate in the final slot in constant time.
We return true to confirm one copy was removed.
The getRandom method returns a random element, with probability proportional to how many copies exist.
Since nums holds every copy, a uniform random choice from it gives each value the right weighted probability.

integer-break.hook: Split a number into parts with the biggest product. The answer is almost all threes.
integer-break.ask: Break the integer n into at least two positive integers that sum to n, and return the largest possible product of those parts.

brute.idea: Dynamic programming: best[i] is the max product for i, trying every first part j.
steps: For each i from 2 to n
Try every first part j
Keep j·(i-j) or j·best[i-j]
brute.whySlow: Correct, but it tries every split of every smaller number when a simple rule gives the answer.

optimal.insight: Any part of 5 or more gains by splitting off a 3, since 3·(p-3) > p. So use 3s, but end with 4 = 2·2, never 3 + 1.
steps: n ≤ 3: must split, answer n - 1
While n > 4, take a 3
Multiply the leftover 2, 3 or 4 in

pitfalls: Never leave a 1: 3 + 1 → split as 2 + 2 instead, which is why we stop at 4.
n = 2 and 3 are special because at least two parts are required.

say.intro: Split a number into at least two positive parts. Make their product as big as possible. For thirteen, the best split is three, three, three and four. Those multiply to one hundred and eight.
say.brute: The standard first approach is dynamic programming. For each number up to n, try every first part. Either keep the rest whole, or use the best product already found for it. It's correct and pretty clean. But it's n squared, trying every split of every smaller number.
say.insight: So let's think about one part, p. If p is five or more, splitting off a three gives three times p minus three. That's bigger than p. So big parts always get split. Ones are wasteful too. That leaves twos and threes. And three threes beat two twos twice over. So take threes. But when four is left, keep it as two times two.
say.anim: We start with n equal to thirteen, which is greater than three, so we continue. Product is initialized to one before the loop begins breaking n into threes. While n stays above four, we keep peeling off threes to maximize the product. Product becomes three and n drops to ten after the first split. Product grows to nine and n shrinks to seven after another split off. Product reaches twenty seven and n becomes four, stopping the loop since four is not above four. Now we multiply the product by the remaining four instead of splitting further. The final answer returned is one hundred eight, the maximum product for breaking thirteen.
say.code: First, small inputs. If n is three or less, the split is forced. Two gives one times one, three gives one times two. Otherwise, while n is above four, we peel off a three. Each three multiplies into the product. When the loop ends, the leftover is two, three or four. Multiply it in and return.
say.outro: Linear time, constant space, no table at all. Pattern: math. Prove which parts are optimal, then apply that rule greedily.

integer-break.title: Integer Break
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container the problem expects for our method.
The method integerBreak takes the integer n and returns the largest product from splitting it into at least two parts.
For n of three or less, we handle the small cases separately because splitting into threes does not help there.
In those cases the best split is one and n minus one, so the product is n minus one.
We start product at one, which will accumulate the factors of three we peel off.
We keep looping while n is greater than four, since any part of five or more gains by splitting off a three.
Each pass multiplies product by three, locking in one part of size three.
We subtract three from n, leaving the remaining amount still to be split.
Finally we return product times the leftover n, which is two, three, or four, so we never end with a bad one.

ipo.hook: Limited cash, limited projects. Always grab the most profitable one you can afford right now.
ipo.ask: You start with w capital and may finish at most k projects. Each needs some minimum capital and adds its profit to your capital. Maximise your final capital.
ipo.exampleWhy: Do the free project for 1, then the profit-3 project, reaching 4, then the profit-5 one: 9.

brute.idea: Each round, scan every unused project and pick the most profitable one you can afford.
steps: Repeat k times
Scan all unused affordable projects
Take the max profit, add to capital
brute.whySlow: Every round rescans all projects: k and n of 100,000 means ten billion checks.

optimal.insight: Capital only grows, so projects only ever become affordable. Sort by capital, push newly affordable ones into a max-heap of profits, pop the best.
steps: Sort projects by required capital
Push every affordable project's profit to a max-heap
Pop the largest profit, add it to capital
Repeat k times or until the heap is empty

codeNotes.match: while i < len(projects) and projects[i][0] <= w:

pitfalls: Popping the heap without the empty check crashes when nothing is affordable.
Greedy is safe only because profits are non-negative, so capital never drops.

say.intro: We start with some capital, and we can finish at most k projects. Each project needs a minimum capital to start, then adds its profit. Here we start with zero and can do three. The free one earns one. Then we afford the profit three project. Then profit five. We end with nine.
say.brute: The brute force repeats k times. Scan every unused project, pick the most profitable one we can afford, take it, add the profit. The greedy choice is right. So what's wrong? Every round rescans every project. That's k times n. Far too slow at the limits.
say.insight: Here's the key. Capital never goes down. So once a project is affordable, it stays affordable. Sort projects by required capital. Then, as capital grows, sweep a pointer forward and push each newly unlocked profit into a max heap. Each round, pop the biggest profit. Every project gets pushed and popped at most once.
say.anim: We start with capital zero and four projects sorted by required capital. Only the project needing zero capital is affordable, so profit one enters the heap. We pop that profit, adding one to capital, which becomes one. Now two more projects become affordable, pushing profits two and three into the heap. The best available profit, three, is popped, growing capital to four. The last project, needing three capital, becomes affordable, adding profit five to the heap. We pop the largest profit five, boosting capital to nine. After three projects chosen, the final maximized capital returned is nine.
say.code: First, sort the projects, cheapest first. Each round, we unlock everything we can now afford. Each profit gets pushed negated, so the heap acts like a max heap. If nothing is ready, we stop early. Otherwise we pop and subtract. Minus a negative adds the profit.
say.outro: Sorting plus heap work, n log n overall. Pattern: heap. Pair it with a sweep that unlocks options as your resources grow.

ipo.title: IPO
lineNotes: We define the Solution class that holds the method for this problem.
The method takes the project limit k, starting capital w, and the lists of profits and capital requirements.
We pair each project's capital with its profit and sort, so projects are ordered by the capital they require.
We create an empty list called ready that will act as a heap of affordable project profits.
We set i to zero, a pointer marking the next project in sorted order not yet considered.
We loop up to k times, because each pass picks exactly one project to complete.
While the next project's required capital is within our current capital, we keep unlocking projects.
We push that project's profit onto the heap as a negative number, since Python's heap is a min-heap and we want the max.
We advance the pointer i to look at the next project in the sorted list.
If no affordable project is waiting in the heap, then nothing more can be done.
So we break out of the loop early, since our capital cannot grow any further.
We pop the largest profit from the heap and subtract its negative value, which adds that profit to our capital.
After finishing at most k projects, we return the final capital we have accumulated.

island-perimeter.hook: Every land cell brings four edges. Every shared border hides two of them.
island-perimeter.ask: Given a grid of land and water containing exactly one island with no lakes, return the length of the island's coastline.
island-perimeter.exampleWhy: 7 land cells give 28 edges; 6 shared borders each remove 2, leaving 16.

brute.idea: For every land cell, look in all four directions and count sides touching water or the grid edge.
steps: Visit every cell
Land? Check up, down, left, right
Water or outside: add one
brute.whySlow: Same big O; it does four neighbour checks per land cell instead of two, plus bounds checks each time.

optimal.insight: Count four per land cell, then subtract two for every land-land border. Checking only up and left counts each border exactly once.
steps: Scan cells row by row
Land adds 4
Land above? Subtract 2
Land to the left? Subtract 2

codeNotes.note: A lone square has four sides
Shared border with the cell above
Shared border with the cell left
Edges that face water or outside

pitfalls: Checking all four neighbours and subtracting 2 double-counts each border.
A DFS works too but is unnecessary: no lakes means simple counting suffices.

say.intro: A grid holds one island of land cells, connected side by side, with no lakes inside. How long is its coastline? Our island has seven land cells and a perimeter of sixteen.
say.brute: The direct approach visits every land cell and looks in all four directions. Each side facing water, or falling off the grid, adds one. Honestly? This is already linear in the grid size. It just does four neighbour checks, with bounds tests, for every land cell.
say.insight: Here's a cleaner way. Think in edges. Every land cell brings four edges. Now, when two land cells touch, that border isn't coastline. It removes two edges, one from each cell. And if we only look up and left while scanning, each shared border gets counted once. So it's four per land cell, minus two per shared border.
say.anim: We start with a grid of land and water, scanning row by row for land cells. At row zero column one we find land, adding four to the perimeter, now four. Moving to row one column zero, another land cell adds four, perimeter becomes eight. At row one column one, land above and left both subtract two each, perimeter drops to eight. Row one column two has land above, subtracting two, leaving perimeter at ten. Row two column one adds four then subtracts two for land above, perimeter now twelve. Row three column zero finds land above, subtracting two, perimeter climbing to sixteen. Row three column one has land above and left, subtracting four total, perimeter settles at sixteen. After scanning the whole grid, the final perimeter returned is sixteen.
say.code: We loop over every cell. For land, we add four. A lone square has four sides. If there's land above, that's a shared border, so we subtract two. If there's land to the left, same thing, subtract two. At the end, we return the total. Those are exactly the edges that face water or the outside.
say.outro: Linear in the grid, constant space. Pattern: graphs on a grid. Sometimes counting edges beats a full traversal.

island-perimeter.title: Island Perimeter
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container the problem expects for our method.
The method islandPerimeter takes the grid of zeros and ones and returns the coastline length as an integer.
We read the number of rows and columns from the grid so we can loop over every cell.
We start perim at zero, and it will accumulate the total coastline length.
The outer loop walks through each row index of the grid.
The inner loop walks through each column index within the current row.
We only act when the current cell is land, meaning its value is one.
Each land cell starts with four sides exposed, so we add four to perim.
If there is a row above and that cell is land, we have a shared border with the cell above.
A shared border hides one side on each of the two cells, so we subtract two.
If there is a column to the left and that cell is land, we have a shared border with the left neighbor.
Again that border hides two sides in total, so we subtract two from perim.
After visiting every cell, we return perim as the island's total perimeter.

k-items-with-the-maximum-sum.hook: A bag of ones, zeros and minus ones. Pick k. Take the best first.
k-items-with-the-maximum-sum.ask: A bag holds numOnes ones, numZeros zeros and numNegOnes minus ones. Pick exactly k items and return the largest possible sum.
k-items-with-the-maximum-sum.exampleWhy: Take 3 ones and 2 zeros; the last 2 picks must be minus ones, so 3 - 2 = 1.

brute.idea: Build the whole bag, sort it from largest to smallest, and add the first k items.
steps: Build the list of all items
Sort it descending
Sum the first k
brute.whySlow: Builds and sorts up to 150 items when three comparisons give the answer directly.

optimal.insight: Ones help, zeros are free, minus ones hurt. Take ones first, then zeros, and only then the minus ones you are forced to take.
steps: Take as many ones as possible
Fill remaining picks with zeros
Any picks left must be minus ones

k-items-with-the-maximum-sum.optimalCode:
class Solution:
    def kItemsWithMaximumSum(self, numOnes: int, numZeros: int, numNegOnes: int, k: int) -> int:
        take = min(k, numOnes)
        total = take
        k -= take
        k -= min(k, numZeros)
        total -= min(k, numNegOnes)
        return total
pitfalls: Forgetting to cap by k when k is smaller than numOnes.

say.intro: A bag holds some ones, some zeros, and some minus ones. We must pick exactly k items to make the biggest sum. With three ones, two zeros, four minus ones, and seven picks, the best sum is one.
say.brute: The brute force builds the whole bag as a list, sorts it from biggest to smallest, and adds the first k. That's correct. The largest k items give the largest sum. But think about it. We're building and sorting a list, just to count things we already know.
say.insight: Here's the thing. There are only three kinds of item, and their order is obvious. Ones help. Zeros are neutral. Minus ones hurt. So greedily take as many ones as we can. Then fill with zeros. Only when both run out are we forced into minus ones. Three tiny calculations replace the whole list. No sorting needed.
say.anim: We start with three ones, two zeros, four negative ones, and k equals seven. We take all three ones first since ones boost the sum most, giving total three. K drops by three, now four remaining picks left to make. Zeros are free, so we take both, reducing k to two remaining picks. Forced to pick two negative ones now, subtracting two from total. Total becomes one after subtracting the forced negative ones. The function returns one, matching the expected maximum sum.
say.code: First, take ones, since each adds one. That's the smaller of k and the number of ones. Then zeros cost nothing, so we reduce k by as many zeros as fit. Whatever picks are left are forced minus ones. We subtract those and return the total.
say.outro: Constant time and space. Pattern: greedy. When the item values are fixed, always grab the best remaining kind first.

k-items-with-the-maximum-sum.title: K Items With the Maximum Sum
lineNotes: We define a Solution class that holds the method for solving this problem.
This method takes the counts of ones, zeros and minus ones, plus k, the number of items to pick.
We take as many ones as we can, which is the smaller of k and numOnes.
Each one adds one to the sum, so total starts equal to the number of ones taken.
We subtract the ones taken from k, leaving the number of items we still must pick.
Next we use up zeros, which add nothing, reducing k by the smaller of k and numZeros.
Any picks still left must be minus ones, so we subtract that count from total, capped by numNegOnes.
Finally we return total, the largest sum achievable with exactly k items.

keys-and-rooms.hook: Each room hides keys to other rooms. Can you open them all?
keys-and-rooms.ask: Rooms are numbered from 0, and only room 0 starts unlocked. Each room holds keys to other rooms. Return true if you can eventually enter every room.
keys-and-rooms.exampleWhy: Room 0 opens 1 and 3, room 3 opens 4, room 1 opens 2: all five rooms.

brute.idea: Repeatedly sweep all rooms; any opened room's keys open new rooms. Stop when a sweep changes nothing.
steps: Mark room 0 open
Sweep every open room's keys
Repeat until nothing new opens
Check every room is open
brute.whySlow: A chain of rooms can open only one new room per sweep, so n sweeps over all keys.

optimal.insight: Rooms are nodes and keys are edges. The question is just whether every node is reachable from room 0: one DFS.
steps: Start with room 0 seen and on the stack
Pop a room, read its keys
Unseen key? Mark it and push it
All rooms seen?

pitfalls: Mark rooms seen when pushed, not when popped, or rooms are pushed many times.

say.intro: Rooms are numbered from zero, and only room zero is unlocked. Each room holds keys to other rooms. Can we get into every room? Room zero opens one and three. Three opens four. One opens two. So the answer is true.
say.brute: The brute force keeps sweeping. Mark room zero open. Then go through every open room and use its keys. If anything new opened, sweep again. Stop when a sweep changes nothing. What's the problem? A long chain of rooms opens only one room per sweep. That can be n squared.
say.insight: Here's the thing. This is a graph in disguise. Each room is a node. Each key is a directed edge to another room. So can we open every room? That's just asking if every node is reachable from node zero. One depth first search answers it, touching each room and key exactly once.
say.anim: We start with room 0 seen, and a stack holding just room 0. Popping room 0, we look at its keys, 1 and 3, adding both as new rooms. Next we pop room 3, finding key 0 already seen but key 4 is new. Popping room 4, it has no keys, so nothing new gets added. Popping room 1 reveals key 2, which gets added to seen and stack. Room 2 has no keys, so the stack finally empties out completely. We compare seen, now five rooms, against all five total rooms. Since every room was visited, the function returns true.
say.code: We start with room zero unlocked and seen. While the stack has rooms, we pop one and enter it. For each key, we check if it's new. Only new rooms get marked and pushed. When the stack empties, we check whether we reached every room.
say.outro: Linear in rooms plus keys. Pattern: graphs. Reachability from a start node, with a depth first search.

keys-and-rooms.title: Keys and Rooms
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container this problem's method lives in.
This method takes the list of rooms, where each room lists the keys inside it, and returns true or false.
We start a seen set containing only room zero, since that room is unlocked from the beginning.
We create a stack holding room zero, so our depth first search begins from the starting room.
We keep looping as long as the stack still has rooms whose keys we have not examined.
We pop the most recently added room off the stack, so we explore deeply before backtracking.
We look at every key found inside this room, since each key is an edge to another room.
We check whether this key opens a room we have not already reached.
We mark that room as seen right away, so no other path will push it again.
We push the newly found room onto the stack so we later explore the keys inside it.
Finally we return true only if the number of seen rooms equals the total number of rooms.

kth-ancestor-of-a-tree-node.hook: Climbing one parent at a time is slow. Store jumps of 1, 2, 4, 8 instead.
kth-ancestor-of-a-tree-node.ask: Given a tree as a parent array, answer many queries: what is the k-th ancestor of a node? Return -1 if it does not exist.
kth-ancestor-of-a-tree-node.exampleWhy: 3's parent is 1; 5's grandparent is 0; 6 has only two ancestors, so the third is -1.

brute.idea: Store the parent array and follow it k times for each query.
steps: Start at node
Step to the parent, k times
Fell off the root? -1
brute.whySlow: A 50,000-node chain with 50,000 deep queries is 2.5 billion parent steps.

optimal.insight: Binary lifting: precompute each node's 2^j-th ancestor. Any k is a sum of powers of two, so answer with one jump per set bit.
steps: up[0] is the parent array
For each set bit j of k, jump up[j]
Hit -1? Return -1
optimal.time: O(n log n) build, O(log n) query

codeNotes.note: Enough levels for any k ≤ n

pitfalls: Too few levels: LOG must cover the largest k, which can be n.
Check for -1 before indexing up[j] again.

say.intro: A tree is given as a parent array. We answer lots of queries asking for a node's k-th ancestor, or minus one if there isn't one. In our tree, three's parent is one. Five's grandparent is zero. And six has no third ancestor.
say.brute: The brute force just climbs. For each query, step to the parent k times. Simple. But each query costs k steps. On a long chain with many deep queries, that's billions of steps.
say.insight: The trick is called binary lifting. For every node, precompute its ancestor one step up, two up, four, eight, and so on. Why is that cheap? A jump of two to the j is two jumps of half that. So each level builds from the one before. Then any k is a sum of powers of two. One jump per set bit.
say.anim: We build the tree with seven nodes and their immediate parents, computing a bit length of three. For each power of two, we precompute ancestors two steps up, like node one's grandparent is minus one. To find node three's first ancestor, we check bit zero of k, which is one, jumping to node one. Higher bits are zero, so we stop and return one as the answer. For node five with k equals two, bit one is set, jumping up to node zero, the final answer. For node six with k equals three, we jump by bit zero to node two, then bit one gives minus one, meaning no such ancestor. For node six with k equals two, jumping by bit one lands on node zero, our answer. Finally for node four with k equals one, bit zero jumps to node one, the last answer shown.
say.code: First, we set enough levels for any k up to n. Level zero is just the parent array, a jump of one step. Each next level takes two half jumps from the level below. To answer a query, we walk the bits of k. If bit j is set, we jump by two to the j. If we climbed past the root, return minus one.
say.outro: Log n per query, after an n log n build. Pattern: trees. Binary lifting is a doubling table for fast ancestor jumps.

kth-ancestor-of-a-tree-node.title: Kth Ancestor of a Tree Node
lineNotes: We define a class called TreeAncestor that preprocesses the tree so many ancestor queries can be answered quickly.
The constructor receives the number of nodes n and the parent array, where the root has parent negative one.
We set LOG to the bit length of n, at least one, since no jump needs more bits than that.
We start the table up with a copy of parent, which holds every node's first ancestor at level zero.
We loop j from one up to LOG, building the table of two to the j step ancestors level by level.
We grab prev, the most recently built level, which holds ancestors at two to the j minus one steps.
For each node we jump twice using prev, keeping negative one when the first jump already falls off the tree.
The query method takes a node and k, and returns that node's k-th ancestor or negative one.
We loop over bit positions j from zero up to LOG, covering each possible bit of k.
If bit j of k is set, we need to jump exactly two to the j steps.
We make that jump by replacing node with its two to the j step ancestor from the table.
After jumping, we check whether we landed on negative one, meaning we went past the root.
In that case the ancestor does not exist, so we return negative one right away.
When all set bits are processed, node is the k-th ancestor, so we return it.

kth-missing-positive-number.hook: How many numbers are missing before index i? Arithmetic tells you, so binary search it.
kth-missing-positive-number.ask: Given a strictly increasing array of positive integers and k, return the k-th positive integer that does not appear in the array.
kth-missing-positive-number.exampleWhy: Missing numbers are 1, 5, 6, 8, 9, 10...; the fifth one is 9.

brute.idea: Count up from 1, skipping numbers present in the array, until k numbers have been skipped over.
steps: Put arr in a set
Count x = 1, 2, 3...
x missing? Decrease k
k hits 0: return x
brute.whySlow: It walks every integer up to the answer, which can be about n + k steps.

optimal.insight: Before index i, arr[i] - i - 1 numbers are missing. That count only grows, so binary search for the first index with at least k missing.
steps: missing(i) = arr[i] - i - 1
Binary search the first i with missing(i) ≥ k
Answer is lo + k

codeNotes.note: Answer may be past the end

pitfalls: hi must start at len(arr), not len(arr) - 1, for answers beyond the last element.

say.intro: We get a strictly increasing list of positive numbers. What's the k-th positive number that's missing from it? For two, three, four, seven, eleven, the missing numbers are one, five, six, eight, nine, and so on. The fifth is nine.
say.brute: The brute force counts up from one. Every number not in the list uses up one of our k. When k hits zero, that's the answer. It works. But it walks every integer up to the answer. So it's linear in n plus k.
say.insight: Here's the key. If nothing were missing, the value at index i would be i plus one. So how many are missing before index i? The value, minus i, minus one. And that count never goes down. So we can binary search for the first index with at least k missing. If lo list numbers come before the answer, the answer is lo plus k.
say.anim: We start with the array, k equal to five, lo at zero, and hi at five. Mid becomes two, where arr of mid minus mid minus one is less than five, so lo moves to three. Mid becomes four, missing count there is six, which meets k, so hi shrinks to four. Mid becomes three, missing count is three, still below five, so lo moves up to four. Now lo equals hi at four, so the binary search ends. We return lo plus k, four plus five, giving nine as the answer.
say.code: We set lo to zero and hi to the length, since the answer may be past the end. Each round, we check the middle. If too few are missing before mid, the answer is further right, so lo moves past mid. Otherwise mid might be the boundary, so hi comes down to mid. Finally, lo list numbers come before it. Return lo plus k.
say.outro: Logarithmic time, constant space. Pattern: binary search, on a derived quantity that only goes up. Here, the missing count.

kth-missing-positive-number.title: Kth Missing Positive Number
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container the judge expects for our method.
The method takes the sorted array and k, and returns the k-th positive integer that is missing from the array.
We set lo to zero and hi to the length of arr, so the search covers every possible answer position.
We loop while lo is less than hi, narrowing the range until it holds a single candidate index.
We compute mid as the average of lo and hi, rounded down, to test the middle of the range.
We check whether the count of missing numbers before mid, which is arr at mid minus mid minus one, is still less than k.
If fewer than k are missing there, the answer lies further right, so we move lo to mid plus one.
Otherwise the answer is at or before mid, so we handle that case in this branch.
We set hi to mid, keeping mid as a possible first index with at least k missing.
At the end lo counts the array elements below the answer, so adding k gives the k-th missing number.

kth-smallest-element-in-a-sorted-matrix.hook: Rows and columns are sorted. Search the answer's value, not its position.
kth-smallest-element-in-a-sorted-matrix.ask: Given an n by n matrix whose rows and columns are sorted ascending, return the k-th smallest element overall, counting duplicates.

brute.idea: Flatten every element into one list, sort it, and take index k - 1.
steps: Collect all n² values
Sort them
Return the (k-1)-th
brute.whySlow: Ignores the sorted structure entirely and stores all n² values: 90,000 for n = 300.

optimal.insight: For a guess mid, count elements ≤ mid in O(n) by walking a staircase from the top-right. Binary search the smallest value with count ≥ k.
steps: Search values from top-left to bottom-right
Count elements ≤ mid with a staircase walk
Count < k? Go higher, else lower
lo ends on a real matrix value

pitfalls: Use lo < hi and hi = mid so lo lands on an actual element.
A min-heap of row heads also works in O(k log n).

say.intro: Every row and every column is sorted. We want the k-th smallest value overall, duplicates included. Our three by three matrix sorts to one, five, nine, ten, eleven, twelve, thirteen, thirteen, fifteen. So the eighth is thirteen.
say.brute: The brute force pours every value into one list, sorts it, and takes position k minus one. Correct. But it totally ignores the sorted rows and columns. It uses n squared memory, and pays for a sort on top.
say.insight: Here's the reframe. Search over values, not positions. Pick a guess, mid. How many elements are at most mid? We can count that in linear time. Start at the top right. In each row, slide left past values that are too big. The column never moves right again. It's a staircase. Count below k? The answer is bigger. Otherwise, it's mid or smaller.
say.anim: We start with lo at 1 and hi at 15, searching for the eighth smallest value. Mid is guessed as 8, and we walk each row counting elements not greater than mid. After scanning all rows, count equals 6, which is less than 8, so mid is too small. We raise lo to 9 and try mid equals 12, counting again row by row. This time count reaches 6 still less than 8, so lo becomes 13. Trying mid 14, the staircase count reaches 8, meeting our target, so hi shrinks to 14. Now testing mid 13, counting gives exactly 8, so hi tightens down to 13. Lo and hi converge at 13, and the function returns 13 as the answer.
say.code: First, lo and hi are the smallest and largest values. For each mid, we walk the staircase. The column only moves left, past values bigger than mid. Then each row adds column plus one elements that are at most mid. If the count is too small, the answer is bigger, so lo moves up. Otherwise hi comes down.
say.outro: n times log of the value range, constant space. Pattern: binary search on the answer, using a count that only goes up.

kth-smallest-element-in-a-sorted-matrix.title: Kth Smallest Element in a Sorted Matrix
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which wraps the method that LeetCode expects for this problem.
The method kthSmallest takes the sorted matrix and k, and returns the k-th smallest value overall.
We store the matrix size in n, since the matrix has n rows and n columns.
We set lo to the top-left value and hi to the bottom-right, the smallest and largest values.
We binary search on values while lo is less than hi, narrowing toward the answer.
We pick mid as the average of lo and hi, using integer division, as our guess value.
We reset count to zero and start col at the last column, the top-right corner of the staircase.
We walk down through each row from top to bottom, reusing the column position between rows.
While the current value exceeds mid, we need to step left, since larger values cannot be counted.
We move col one step left, skipping an entry that is greater than mid.
Every entry at or left of col in this row is at most mid, so we add col plus one.
If fewer than k elements are at most mid, the answer must be larger than mid.
So we raise lo to mid plus one, discarding mid and everything below it.
Otherwise at least k elements are at most mid, so mid could be the answer or too big.
So we set hi to mid, keeping mid as a candidate while shrinking the upper bound.
When lo meets hi, that value is the smallest one with count at least k, so we return it.

largest-divisible-subset.hook: Sort first, and divisibility becomes a chain. Then it is longest increasing subsequence.
largest-divisible-subset.ask: Given distinct positive integers, return the largest subset where, for every pair, the bigger number is divisible by the smaller one.
largest-divisible-subset.exampleWhy: 2 divides 4 and 8, and 4 divides 8. No four of these numbers form a chain.

brute.idea: Try subsets from largest size down, checking every pair for divisibility, and return the first that works.
steps: Sort the numbers
For each size from n down to 1
Try every combination of that size
All pairs divide? Return it
brute.whySlow: Exponential: 1,000 numbers have 2^1000 subsets.

optimal.insight: After sorting, if b divides c and a divides b, then a divides c. So a valid subset is a chain, and we extend chains like LIS.
steps: Sort ascending
size[i] = longest chain ending at nums[i]
Extend from any j < i where nums[j] divides nums[i]
Follow prev links back from the best end

codeNotes.note: Order turns pairs into a chain

codeNotes.match: if nums[i] % nums[j] == 0 and size[j] + 1 > size[i]:
codeNotes.note: Extend the chain ending at j

pitfalls: Without sorting, divisibility is not transitive along your scan order.
Store back-links: lengths alone cannot rebuild the subset.

say.intro: From a set of distinct positive numbers, find the biggest subset where, in every pair, the larger number divides by the smaller. For nine, three, eight, four and two, the answer is two, four and eight.
say.brute: The brute force tries subsets from the largest size downward. It checks every pair and returns the first one that works. On five numbers? Fine. But the number of subsets doubles with every number added. That's exponential. Thirty numbers is already a billion subsets.
say.insight: Here's the trick. Sort first. Now divisibility chains. If a divides b, and b divides c, then a divides c. So a valid subset is just a chain where each number divides the next. We only need to check neighbours. Sound familiar? It's longest increasing subsequence, with divides in place of less than.
say.anim: We start with nums unsorted, then sort it into 2, 3, 4, 8, 9 for chain building. Each number begins with size one, meaning every element is its own chain of length one. At index 2, value 4, since 4 divides evenly by 2, its chain size grows to two. At index 3, value 8 extends the chain from 4, giving size three, the best so far. At index 4, value 9 checks divisibility but never beats the existing best chain size three. We walk backward from index 3 using prev pointers, collecting 8, then 4, then 2. Reversing that collected list gives the final largest divisible subset, 2, 4, 8.
say.code: First we sort. That order turns pairs into a chain. Each index starts with chain length one and no back link. For each i, we check every earlier j. If j's value divides i's and gives a longer chain, we extend the chain ending at j. At the end, we walk the chain backwards from the best ending, and reverse.
say.outro: n squared time, linear space. Pattern: one dimensional dynamic programming. A longest chain, with back pointers to rebuild it.

largest-divisible-subset.title: Largest Divisible Subset
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container the problem expects for our method.
The method takes a list of distinct positive integers and returns the largest subset in which every pair divides evenly.
We sort the numbers so any divisor comes before its multiples, letting us build chains from left to right.
We store the length of the list as n for use in the arrays and loops.
We make size, set to one for every number since each alone is a chain, and prev, set to negative one meaning no predecessor.
We set best to zero, tracking the index where the longest chain found so far ends.
We loop over each index i, treating nums at i as the possible end of a chain.
For each i we loop over every earlier index j, which holds a smaller number we might extend from.
If nums at i is divisible by nums at j and extending j gives a longer chain than i has, we take it.
We then update size at i to the extended length and record j as its predecessor so we can rebuild the chain.
After checking all j, we test whether the chain ending at i beats the best chain so far.
If it does, we update best to i so it points at the end of the longest chain.
We create an empty list called subset to collect the answer numbers.
We walk backward through the chain until best becomes negative one, meaning no predecessor remains.
At each step we append the current number to subset.
We then jump to the predecessor of the current index, moving one step back along the chain.
We reverse the collected list so numbers appear in increasing order, then return it as the largest divisible subset.

largest-number-at-least-twice-of-others.hook: Is the biggest number at least double everything else? Only the runner-up matters.
largest-number-at-least-twice-of-others.ask: The largest number in the array is unique. Return its index if it is at least twice every other number, otherwise return -1.
largest-number-at-least-twice-of-others.exampleWhy: 8 is the largest and the runner-up is 4; 8 ≥ 2 · 4, so return index 1.

brute.idea: For each index, check whether its value is at least twice every other value.
steps: Pick candidate i
Compare against every other j
All pass? Return i
brute.whySlow: Every candidate rescans the whole array, though only the maximum can possibly win.

optimal.insight: If the max is at least twice the second largest, it is at least twice everything. Track the top two in one pass.
steps: Walk the array once
New max? Old max becomes second
Else maybe update second
Compare max with twice second

codeNotes.match: second, best, idx = best, x, i
return idx if best >= 2 * second else -1

pitfalls: Forgetting to demote the old max to second when a new max appears.

say.intro: The array has one unique largest number. Is it at least twice every other number? If so, return its index. Otherwise, minus one. For one, eight, three, two, four, eight is at least twice four, the next biggest. So we return index one.
say.brute: The brute force tries every index as a candidate and compares it to every other number. If a candidate survives, return it. It works, but it's n squared. And think about it. Only the maximum could ever win. So most of that work is wasted.
say.insight: Here's the thing. If the largest is at least twice the second largest, is it twice everything else too? Yes, automatically. Everything else is even smaller. So we only need the top two values. One pass tracks them. When a new maximum shows up, the old maximum becomes the runner up.
say.anim: We start with best and second both set to negative one, and index zero. At index zero, value one beats best, so best becomes one and idx becomes zero. At index one, value eight beats best, so second becomes one and best becomes eight. At index two, value three is not bigger than best but beats second, updating second to three. At index three, value two fails both checks, so nothing changes. At index four, value four beats second, updating second to four, best stays eight. Now we check if best, eight, is at least twice second, which is four. Eight is exactly twice four, so the function returns index one as the answer.
