say.code: We start best and second at minus one, below any value. For each value, if it beats best, the old max gets demoted to second. We record the new best and its index. Otherwise, if it beats second, it's the new runner up. At the end, only the runner up matters. Is best at least twice second?
say.outro: Linear time, constant space. Pattern: arrays. Track the top two in a single pass, instead of comparing every pair.

largest-number-at-least-twice-of-others.title: Largest Number At Least Twice of Others
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container for the method that solves this problem.
The method dominantIndex takes the list nums and returns an integer index, either of the dominant element or negative one.
We start both best and second at negative one so any real number in the array will beat them.
We set idx to zero, which will remember the position of the current largest value.
We loop through nums, getting each position i along with its value x, so we only need one pass.
If x is bigger than best, we have found a new largest number.
We shift best down into second, store x as the new best, and record its position i in idx.
Otherwise, if x is bigger than second, it is not the max but is the new runner up.
We update second to x so it always holds the second largest value seen so far.
Finally we return idx if best is at least twice second, since that covers every other number, otherwise negative one.

lemonade-change.hook: Give change from a cash drawer. Spend the tens first and keep fives for later.
lemonade-change.ask: Lemonade costs 5. Customers pay with 5, 10 or 20 bills in order, and you start with no money. Return true if you can give every customer correct change.
lemonade-change.exampleWhy: The first 20 gets a 10 and a 5; the second gets three 5s. Every customer receives change.

brute.idea: Keep the actual bills in a list, and search it for change notes each time someone pays more than 5.
steps: Add the paid bill to the drawer list
Search for a 10, then 5s, to cover change
Cannot cover it? Return False
brute.whySlow: Every search and removal scans the drawer list, which can hold up to n bills.

optimal.insight: Only counts of 5s and 10s matter; 20s are never given back. For 15 change, a 10 + 5 beats three 5s, since 5s are more flexible.
steps: 5: keep it
10: give back one 5
20: prefer a 10 and a 5
Otherwise three 5s, else fail

pitfalls: Paying 15 with three 5s when a 10 is available can fail a later 10 customer.

say.intro: Lemonade costs five. Customers pay in order with a five, ten or twenty, and our drawer starts empty. Can we give everyone correct change? In our line, the first twenty gets a ten and a five. The second gets three fives. So the answer is true.
say.brute: The brute force keeps the actual bills in a list. When someone overpays, it searches for a ten, then for fives, removing each note it hands over. Correct, sure. But every search and removal scans the list. That's n squared.
say.insight: Here's the thing. We only need counts. And twenties are never useful as change, so track just fives and tens. A ten needs a five back. A twenty needs fifteen. Either a ten and a five, or three fives. Which do we prefer? The ten. A five helps everyone. A ten only helps twenties. So spend the less flexible note first.
say.anim: We start with zero five dollar bills and zero ten dollar bills in hand. Two customers pay with fives, so our five count rises to two. A ten dollar bill arrives, so we give back one five as change. Another five comes in, giving us two fives and one ten on hand. A twenty arrives, so we break it using a ten and a five, the flexible choice. Two more five dollar payments bring our five count up to three. The final twenty arrives, and with no tens left we use three fives instead. All bills are processed successfully, so the function returns true.
say.code: We count only fives and tens, since twenties never go back. A five just adds to fives. A ten comes in and a five goes out, if we have one. For a twenty, we're greedy. Spend a ten and a five first. If we can't, fall back to three fives. Otherwise, fail.
say.outro: Linear time, constant space. Pattern: greedy. Always spend the least flexible resource first.

lemonade-change.title: Lemonade Change
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container the problem expects for our method.
The method lemonadeChange takes the list of bills in order and returns true or false.
We start with zero five dollar bills and zero ten dollar bills, since we begin with no money.
We loop over each bill b, handling customers in the order they arrive.
If the customer pays with a five, no change is needed.
We simply add one to our count of fives.
Otherwise, if the customer pays with a ten, we must give back five dollars.
If we have no five to give back, we cannot make change, so we fail.
Here we return false immediately because this customer cannot be served.
We hand over one five and keep the ten, so five goes down by one and ten goes up by one.
For a twenty, we first prefer giving change of one ten and one five, if we have both.
We use up one ten and one five, since tens are only useful for this case and fives are more flexible.
If that is not possible, we try giving three fives as change for the twenty.
We subtract three from our count of fives.
If neither combination of change is available, we reach this fallback case.
We return false because we cannot give fifteen dollars in change.
If we get through every customer without failing, we return true.

length-of-longest-fibonacci-subsequence.hook: Two numbers fix the whole Fibonacci chain. So index your DP by the last pair.
length-of-longest-fibonacci-subsequence.ask: Given a strictly increasing array, return the length of the longest subsequence where every element is the sum of the previous two, or 0 if none has length 3.
length-of-longest-fibonacci-subsequence.exampleWhy: 1, 2, 3, 5, 8: each number is the sum of the two before it.

brute.idea: Try every starting pair and keep extending with a set lookup for the next sum.
steps: Pick a pair (a, b)
While a + b is in the set, step forward
Track the longest chain
brute.whySlow: Each of n² pairs re-walks its chain from scratch; chains grow like log of the max value.

optimal.insight: A chain ending in (arr[j], arr[k]) must come from a chain ending in (arr[i], arr[j]) where arr[i] = arr[k] - arr[j]. Reuse that length.
steps: Map each value to its index
For each pair j < k, find i with arr[i] = arr[k] - arr[j]
If i < j, dp[j,k] = dp[i,j] + 1 (default 2)
Track the max

codeNotes.match: index = {x: i for i, x in enumerate(arr)}
if i is not None and i < j:

codeNotes.note: Extend the chain ending at i, j

pitfalls: Without i < j you would reuse an element or go backwards.
Return 0, not 2, when no chain of length 3 exists.

say.intro: In a strictly increasing array, find the longest subsequence where each number is the sum of the two before it. For one through eight, the chain one, two, three, five, eight has length five.
say.brute: Here's a useful fact. Any two numbers decide the rest of the chain. So the brute force tries every starting pair, then keeps checking a set for the next sum. Correct. But each of the n squared pairs rebuilds its chain from scratch. That's extra work on top.
say.insight: So let's name each chain by its last two numbers. A chain ending in the pair j and k must come from a chain ending in i and j. And what's i? The value at k minus the value at j. A hash map finds it instantly. So the length for j and k is the length for i and j, plus one. Every pair is computed once.
say.anim: First we build an index mapping each value to its position in the array. For k equals 1 and j equals 0, we look for an index i where arr of i equals arr of k minus arr of j. When i is less than j, we extend the chain, setting dp at j,k to three. The pattern repeats, building longer chains like dp at 2,4 reaching four. Best updates to four as we find a fibonacci-like run ending at index four. We keep scanning pairs, extending valid chains and tracking the best length found so far. Best climbs to five once a five-term fibonacci subsequence is confirmed. The function returns five, the length of the longest fibonacci-like subsequence.
say.code: First, we map each value to its position. For every pair j before k, we look up the number that would come before the pair. It must sit strictly before j. If it does, we extend the chain ending at i and j by one. A new chain starts at length two. We keep the best.
say.outro: n squared time and space. Pattern: two dimensional dynamic programming, keyed by the last two elements of the sequence.

length-of-longest-fibonacci-subsequence.title: Length of Longest Fibonacci Subsequence
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container the problem expects for our method.
The method takes a strictly increasing array and returns the length of the longest Fibonacci-like subsequence.
We build a lookup from each value to its position so we can find any needed earlier number instantly.
We create an empty dictionary dp that will store chain lengths keyed by the pair of last two indices.
We start best at zero, which is the answer if no chain of length three exists.
We loop k over every index, treating arr at k as the last element of a possible chain.
For each k we loop j over earlier indices, treating arr at j as the second to last element.
We look up the index of arr at k minus arr at j, which is the value that must come before arr at j.
We only continue if that value exists and its index i is smaller than j, keeping the order valid.
We set the chain length for the pair j and k to the length for i and j plus one, defaulting to two.
We update best with the larger of its current value and this new chain length.
After checking all pairs, we return best, which is zero when no valid chain was found.

length-of-longest-subarray-with-at-most-.hook: Grow the window right, and shrink it left the moment any number appears too often.
length-of-longest-subarray-with-at-most-.ask: Return the length of the longest contiguous subarray in which every value appears at most k times.
length-of-longest-subarray-with-at-most-.exampleWhy: [1,2,3,1,2,3] has each value twice; adding either neighbour makes some value appear three times.

brute.idea: For every start, extend right with a fresh count map until some value exceeds k.
steps: Pick start i
Extend j, counting nums[j]
Count > k? Stop this start
Record j - i + 1
brute.whySlow: Each start rebuilds counts for nearly the same window: 100,000 numbers means billions of updates.

optimal.insight: Only the number just added can break the rule. So when it exceeds k, slide the left edge until that number is back to k.
steps: Add nums[right] to the counts
While its count > k, drop nums[left]
Window is valid: record its length

codeNotes.note: Only x can be over k

pitfalls: Checking every key of the map each step turns this back into O(n · distinct).

say.intro: We want the longest contiguous stretch where no value appears more than k times. With k equal to two, one two three one two three works. That's length six. But extend it either way, and something shows up three times.
say.brute: The brute force tries every start, then extends right with a fresh count map. It stops as soon as some value appears more than k times, recording valid lengths along the way. The problem? Each start rebuilds nearly the same counts. That's n squared.
say.insight: Here's the key. The window was valid before we added the newest number. So which number can be over the limit now? Only that one. When it is, slide the left edge right, decrementing counts, until it's back down to k. Each index enters and leaves the window at most once. So the whole scan is linear.
say.anim: We track counts of each number using a sliding window with left and right pointers. Right moves through the array, adding each number to the count map as it goes. By index three, number one appears twice, still within the limit of two. At right equals five, all three numbers now have count two, window size six. Adding another one makes its count three, exceeding k, so we shrink from the left. Left moves forward, decrementing counts, until number one's count drops back to two. Similarly at index seven, adding two pushes its count too high, so left advances again. The loop finishes and the function returns best, giving a final answer of six.
say.code: For each right index, we take in the new number and bump its count. Then, while that number is over k, we shrink. Only x can be over k. We drop the left edge's number from the counts and move left forward. Now the window is valid, so we update best with its length.
say.outro: Linear time with a hash map of counts. Pattern: sliding window. Shrink only when the newest element breaks the rule.

length-of-longest-subarray-with-at-most-.title: Length of Longest Subarray With at Most K Frequency
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the wrapper this problem expects for our method.
The method takes the list nums and the limit k, and returns the length of the longest valid subarray.
We create a counting dictionary that defaults to zero, tracking how often each value appears in the current window.
We start both the left edge of the window and the best length at zero.
We loop over nums, with right as the window's right edge and x as the value being added.
We add the new value x to the window by increasing its count by one.
Only x can break the rule, so while its count exceeds k we must shrink the window.
We remove the value at the left edge from the counts, since it is leaving the window.
We move the left edge one step right, making the window smaller.
Now the window is valid, so we update best with the larger of its old value and the current window length.
After scanning every position, we return best as the longest valid subarray length.

letter-case-permutation.hook: Every letter is a two-way switch. Flip each one and branch.
letter-case-permutation.ask: Given a string of letters and digits, return every string you can make by changing letters to lowercase or uppercase. Digits stay as they are. Any order.
letter-case-permutation.exampleWhy: Two letters, each with two cases, gives four strings; the digits never change.

brute.idea: Treat every character as a switch, try all 2^n masks, and remove duplicates caused by digits.
steps: For every bitmask over all positions
Swap case where the bit is set
Skip strings already produced
brute.whySlow: Digits double the masks for nothing: a12 tries 8 masks for 2 distinct strings.

optimal.insight: Branch only on letters. At each letter, explore keeping its case, then flip it, explore, and flip it back.
steps: Walk positions left to right
Recurse with the character unchanged
If it is a letter, swap case and recurse
Undo the swap on the way back

pitfalls: Forgetting to undo the swap leaks a flipped letter into sibling branches.

say.intro: We get a string of letters and digits. Return every version you can make by switching letters between lower and upper case. Digits stay fixed. For a one b two, there are two letters with two cases each. So four strings.
say.brute: The brute force treats every character as a switch. It tries every bitmask over the whole string, flipping case where a bit is set. But wait. Flipping a digit does nothing. So many masks make duplicates, filtered with a set. Each digit doubles the work for zero new strings.
say.insight: Here's the thing. Only letters create choices. So walk the string one position at a time. At each spot, first explore keeping the character as it is. If it's a letter, flip its case and explore again. Then flip it back. That's a binary tree with one level per letter. Every leaf is a distinct answer. No duplicates.
say.anim: We start with the string a1b2, splitting it into characters for easy swapping. Backtracking walks forward keeping each character as is, since digits never branch. At index four we have built a1b2, so it gets added to the results. Backtracking back to index two, since b is a letter, we flip it to uppercase B. Now chars form a1B2, reaching the end again and appending this new permutation. After undoing flips, we move to index zero and flip a to uppercase A. With A1b2 formed, recursion repeats, eventually flipping b too to make A1B2. All branches finish, giving the final answer: a1b2, a1B2, A1b2, and A1B2.
say.code: When the full string is built, we join it and record it. Otherwise, branch one is to keep this character and recurse on the next position. Then we check if it's a letter. Digits don't branch. If it is, we flip its case for branch two, recurse again, and flip it back.
say.outro: Two to the number of letters results, each of length n. Pattern: backtracking. Branch on each real choice, and undo it on the way back.

letter-case-permutation.title: Letter Case Permutation
lineNotes: We define a Solution class that holds the method for solving the problem.
The method takes the string s and returns a list of every possible case permutation.
We start with an empty list called res to collect all the finished strings.
We turn s into a list of characters called chars so we can change letters in place.
We define a recursive helper called backtrack that decides the case of the character at index i.
If i equals the length of chars, we have made a choice for every position.
In that case we join the characters into one string and add it to res.
Then we return to stop going deeper and let the earlier calls try their other options.
First we recurse to the next index with the current character left unchanged, covering the keep-case branch.
We only branch further if the current character is a letter, since digits have just one form.
We flip the letter's case with swapcase to set up the second branch.
We recurse to the next index again, now exploring all strings that use the flipped letter.
We flip the letter back to its original case so the backtracking leaves chars as we found it.
We kick off the search by calling backtrack at index zero.
Finally we return res, which holds every case permutation of the input.

lfu-cache.hook: Evict the least-used key, ties broken by least recent. All in constant time.
lfu-cache.ask: Design a cache with fixed capacity. get returns a value or -1; put inserts or updates. When full, evict the least frequently used key, breaking ties by least recently used.
lfu-cache.exampleWhy: Key 2 is evicted first (used once vs key 1's twice); later 1 and 3 tie and 1 is older.

brute.idea: Store value, use count and last-used time per key. On eviction, scan every key for the smallest (count, time).
steps: get: bump count and timestamp
put: update or insert
Full? Scan all keys for the minimum
Evict that key
brute.whySlow: Every eviction scans the entire cache: 10,000 keys and 200,000 calls is billions of comparisons.

optimal.insight: Group keys by frequency, each group an ordered list by recency. Track the minimum frequency; the victim is the oldest key in that group.
steps: vals and freq maps per key
groups[f]: keys with frequency f, oldest first
Touch: move key from group f to f + 1
Evict the oldest key of groups[minFreq]
New key: frequency 1, minFreq = 1

codeNotes.match: if not self.groups[f] and self.minFreq == f:

codeNotes.note: A new key is least used

pitfalls: Capacity 0: put must do nothing.
Updating an existing key also counts as a use.

say.intro: We build a cache with fixed capacity. When it's full, evict the least frequently used key. Ties go to the least recently used. With capacity two, key one gets read, so when three arrives, two is evicted. Later, one and three tie on uses. One is older, so it goes.
say.brute: The brute force stores a value, a use count and a last used time for every key. When the cache is full, it scans every key for the smallest count, breaking ties by oldest time. So what's the cost? Every eviction is a full scan. That's linear in the capacity.
say.insight: Here's the idea. Group keys by how many times they've been used. Inside each group, keep keys in recency order, oldest first. And track the smallest frequency that has keys. Using a key moves it up one group. Evicting? Just remove the oldest key from the minimum group. Every step is constant time.
say.anim: We create an LFU cache with capacity two, ready to track keys by frequency. We put key one with value one, giving it frequency one and setting minFreq to one. We put key two with value two, also starting at frequency one. Getting key one touches it, bumping its frequency from one to two, and returns value one. Putting key three evicts the least frequent key, which is key two, then inserts three at frequency one. Getting key two returns negative one since it was just evicted. Getting key three bumps its frequency to two and returns its value three. Putting key four evicts key one since it has the lowest frequency, inserting four at frequency one. Getting key one returns negative one, key three bumps to frequency three returning three, then key four returns four.
say.code: We map each frequency to an ordered group of keys, oldest first. Touching a key moves it out of its group. If that emptied the minimum group, the minimum goes up. The key becomes newest in the next group. At capacity, we pop the oldest key at the minimum frequency. A new key is least used, so the minimum resets to one.
say.outro: Constant time get and put. Pattern: linked lists with hashing. Ordered buckets per frequency. Think of it as L R U's bigger sibling.

lfu-cache.title: LFU Cache
lineNotes: We import defaultdict and OrderedDict, which give us automatic frequency groups and ordered recency tracking.
We define the LFUCache class that implements the least frequently used eviction policy.
The constructor takes the capacity, the maximum number of keys the cache may hold.
We store the capacity so later puts know when the cache is full.
The values dictionary maps each key to its stored value.
The frequencies dictionary maps each key to how many times it has been used.
The groups map each frequency to an ordered dictionary of keys, oldest first, to break ties by recency.
We start the minimum frequency at zero because the cache is empty.
The touch helper records one more use of a key by moving it up a frequency group.
This comment says touch moves the key from its current frequency group to the next one.
We look up the key's current frequency before changing anything.
We remove the key from its old frequency group.
If that group is now empty and it was the minimum frequency group, the minimum must change.
In that case we raise the minimum frequency by one, since the key lands exactly there.
The new frequency is the old frequency plus one.
We record the new frequency for the key.
We append the key to the newer group, making it the most recently used there.
The get method returns the value for a key, or negative one if absent.
We first check whether the key is missing from the values dictionary.
If it is missing, we return negative one.
Otherwise we touch the key, since reading counts as a use.
We then return the stored value.
The put method inserts a new key or updates an existing one.
A cache with zero capacity can store nothing, so we check for that case.
We return immediately without doing anything in that case.
This comment says an existing key just gets a new value and a frequency bump.
We check whether the key is already in the cache.
We overwrite its stored value with the new one.
We touch the key to increase its frequency and refresh its recency.
We return because the update is complete and no eviction is needed.
This comment says that when the cache is full we evict the oldest key in the minimum frequency group.
We check whether the cache has reached its capacity.
We pop the first item from the minimum frequency group, which is the least recently used among the least frequent.
We delete the evicted key from the values dictionary.
We also delete the evicted key from the frequencies dictionary.
This comment says the new key will be inserted with frequency one.
We store the new key's value.
We set its frequency to one.
We add the key to the frequency one group as its newest entry.
We reset the minimum frequency to one, because a brand new key is now the least used.

linked-list-cycle-ii.hook: Floyd's tortoise and hare don't just detect a cycle. They find where it starts.
linked-list-cycle-ii.ask: Given the head of a linked list, return the node where a cycle begins, or nothing if there is no cycle. Do not modify the list.
linked-list-cycle-ii.exampleWhy: The tail 5 links back to index 2, so the cycle starts at the node with value 0.

brute.idea: Walk the list, remembering every node in a hash set. The first node seen twice is the cycle start.
steps: Walk node by node
Already in the set? That node starts the cycle
Otherwise add it and continue
brute.whySlow: Same time, but it stores every node: O(n) extra memory when O(1) is possible.

optimal.insight: When slow and fast meet, the distance from head to the cycle start equals the distance from the meeting point forward to it. Restart one pointer at head.
steps: slow moves 1, fast moves 2
Fast reaches the end? No cycle
They meet: move slow back to head
Step both by 1; they meet at the start

codeNotes.note: Reaching the end means no cycle
Fast gains one step per move
Same speed: meet at cycle start

pitfalls: In phase two both pointers move one step; moving fast by two breaks the math.

say.intro: We get a linked list that might loop back on itself. Where does the cycle begin? If there's no cycle, return nothing. Here the tail, five, links back to index two. So the cycle starts at the node holding zero.
say.brute: The simple approach walks the list and puts every node in a hash set. The first node already in the set is where the cycle starts. That's linear time, and perfectly correct. So what's the catch? It stores every node. That's linear extra memory.
say.insight: Use a slow pointer and a fast one that moves twice as fast. If there's a cycle, they meet inside it. Now here's the aha. The distance from the head to the cycle start equals the distance from the meeting point to the start, modulo the loop. So reset one pointer to the head. Step both one at a time. They meet at the start.
say.anim: Both slow and fast pointers start together at the head node, value three. Slow moves one step to two, fast jumps two steps to zero, no meeting yet. Slow advances to zero while fast speeds ahead to seven, still not matching. Slow reaches negative four, fast wraps around back to zero, still searching for a meeting. Now slow and fast both land on seven, confirming a cycle exists. Slow resets to head while fast stays put, both will now move one step at a time. Slow and fast step forward together, approaching the cycle's starting node. They meet at node zero, which is exactly where the cycle begins, the final answer.
say.code: We loop while fast and its next exist. Reaching the end means no cycle. Each move, slow takes one step and fast takes two, so fast gains one step per move. Once they meet, we restart slow at the head. Then both move at the same speed. Where they meet is the cycle start.
say.outro: Linear time, constant space. Pattern: linked lists with fast and slow pointers. This is Floyd's cycle detection.

linked-list-cycle-ii.title: Linked List Cycle II
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which holds the method that finds where a cycle begins in a linked list.
The detectCycle method takes the head of the list and returns the node where the cycle starts, or nothing.
We start both slow and fast at the head, so they begin the chase from the same place.
We loop while fast and the node after it exist, since reaching the end of the list means no cycle.
Each step moves slow forward by one node and fast forward by two nodes.
If slow and fast are the very same node, they have met inside the cycle.
We send slow back to the head, setting up the equal distance trick from the key idea.
We keep looping until slow and fast land on the same node.
Now both pointers move one node at a time, so they meet exactly where the cycle begins.
We return that meeting node, which is the start of the cycle.
If the loop ends because fast ran out of nodes, there is no cycle, so we return None.

long-pressed-name.hook: A sticky keyboard can repeat letters, but never invent new ones.
long-pressed-name.ask: Your friend typed their name, but some keys may have been held down, repeating a letter. Return true if typed could be name with some letters long-pressed.
long-pressed-name.exampleWhy: a, e and x were held longer; every letter of alex appears in order with nothing new.

brute.idea: Compress both strings into runs of letter and count, then compare run by run.
steps: Build runs for name and typed
Same number of runs?
Each run: same letter, typed count ≥ name count
brute.whySlow: Same time, but it builds two full run lists first: extra memory and an extra pass.

optimal.insight: Walk typed once. Each character either matches the next letter of name, or must repeat the previous typed character. Anything else is a typo.
steps: Pointer i into name
typed[j] matches name[i]? Advance i
Else it must equal typed[j-1]
End: all of name matched?

codeNotes.match: if i < len(name) and name[i] == ch:
codeNotes.note: Matches the next letter of name
Not a repeat: a real typo
Did we type the whole name?

pitfalls: Forgetting the final check misses typed strings that stop early, like alex vs aal.

say.intro: Your friend typed their name, but sometimes held a key too long, so a letter repeated. Given the name and the typed text, could it be the name with long presses? Alex typed as a a l e e x x is fine. Only repeats were added.
say.brute: One approach compresses both strings into runs. Like a twice, l once. Then the runs must have the same letters in the same order. And every typed run must be at least as long as the name's. Linear time, honestly. But it builds two extra lists before comparing anything.
say.insight: Here's the thing. We can check as we go, with two pointers. Walk the typed text once, with a pointer into the name. Is the typed character the next letter of the name? Advance the name pointer. If not, there's only one excuse. A long press. So it must equal the previous typed character. Anything else is a real typo.
say.anim: We start matching name alex against typed aaleexx, with index i at zero. The first a matches name's a, so i moves forward to one. The second a doesn't match name's next letter l, but it repeats the previous typed character, so it's fine. L and e each match the next letters of name, advancing i to three. The extra e repeats the previous typed character, so it's accepted as a long press. X matches the final letter of name, advancing i to four, completing the name. The last x also repeats the previous character, so it's allowed too. I equals the length of name, so the function returns true.
say.code: We walk the typed text with its index. If the character matches the next letter of name, we advance the name pointer. Otherwise, is it a repeat of the previous typed character? If it's the first character, or it's different, that's a real typo. Return false. At the end, did we type the whole name?
say.outro: Linear time, constant space. Pattern: two pointers, moving through two strings at different speeds.

long-pressed-name.title: Long Pressed Name
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container this problem's method lives in.
The method takes the intended name and the typed string, and returns whether typed could come from name.
We set i to zero, so it points at the next letter of name we still need to match.
We walk through typed once, tracking each position j and its character ch.
If name still has letters left and the current one equals ch, this typed character is a match.
On a match we advance i, moving on to the next letter we need from name.
Otherwise ch must be a long press, so if it is the first character or differs from the previous typed one, it is a typo.
In that case we return false immediately, since the character is neither the next letter nor a repeat.
After the loop we return true only if i reached the end of name, meaning every letter was matched.

longest-arithmetic-subsequence-of-given-.hook: The difference is fixed, so every number knows exactly what came before it.
longest-arithmetic-subsequence-of-given-.ask: Given an array and a fixed difference, return the length of the longest subsequence where each element minus the previous one equals that difference.
longest-arithmetic-subsequence-of-given-.exampleWhy: 7, 5, 3, 1 appears in order, each step subtracting 2.

brute.idea: From every start, scan forward and greedily take each next value that continues the sequence.
steps: Pick start i
want = arr[i] + difference
Scan right: found want? Extend and update want
Keep the longest
brute.whySlow: Every start rescans the rest of the array: 100,000 numbers means about 5 billion checks.

optimal.insight: The only possible predecessor of x is x - difference. A hash map of best length ending at each value extends it in O(1).
steps: Walk the array once
dp[x] = dp[x - difference] + 1
Missing predecessor counts as 0
Answer is the largest dp value

codeNotes.note: Best length ending at each value

pitfalls: Key by value, not index: later copies of a value should overwrite earlier ones.

say.intro: We want the longest subsequence where each number is exactly the difference more than the one before. With a difference of minus two, the array has seven, five, three, one, in order. So the answer is four.
say.brute: The brute force tries every starting index. From there it scans right, taking each number that continues the sequence. Taking the earliest match is always safe, so it's correct. But every start rescans the rest of the array. That's n squared.
say.insight: Here's the key. The difference is fixed. So how many values can come right before x? Exactly one. X minus the difference. So keep a hash map from each value to the longest chain ending there. When we see x, its chain is one longer than the chain ending at x minus the difference. One pass, constant work per number.
say.anim: We start with an empty map tracking the best chain length ending at each value. For value 1, there's no predecessor three higher, so its chain length becomes 1. At the second 5, we check value 7 already in the map, extending its chain to length 2. At value 3, predecessor 5 has length 2, so 3 now reaches chain length 3. At value 2, predecessor 4 has length 1, giving 2 a chain length of 2. At the final 1, predecessor 3 has length 3, extending 1 to chain length 4. We scan all chain lengths in the map to find the maximum value. The longest arithmetic subsequence with difference negative two has length 4.
say.code: We start with an empty map, the best length ending at each value. For each number x, we extend the only possible predecessor. Look up x minus the difference, default zero, and add one. A later copy of a value just overwrites. Why is that fine? It's never shorter. Finally, return the longest chain ending anywhere.
say.outro: Linear time and space. Pattern: one dimensional dynamic programming, with a hash map keyed by value.

longest-arithmetic-subsequence-of-given-.title: Longest Arithmetic Subsequence of Given Difference
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container the problem expects for our method.
The method takes the array and the fixed difference, and returns the length of the longest valid subsequence.
We start with an empty dictionary dp that will record the best subsequence length ending at each value.
We walk through the array in order, so every element can only extend subsequences built from earlier elements.
For each x, we look up the length ending at x minus difference, defaulting to zero, add one, and store it for x.
Finally we return the largest length stored in dp, which is the longest arithmetic subsequence overall.

longest-continuous-increasing-subsequenc.hook: Find the longest uphill stretch in an array, without ever looking back.
longest-continuous-increasing-subsequenc.ask: Given an array of integers, return the length of the longest contiguous run where every element is strictly bigger than the one before it.
longest-continuous-increasing-subsequenc.exampleWhy: 4, 7, 8, 9 climbs four times in a row; 1, 3, 5 breaks at 4 and only reaches three.

brute.idea: Start a run at every index and extend it to the right while each next number is bigger. Keep the longest run seen.
steps: Pick a start index i
Extend j while nums[j] > nums[j - 1]
Record the run length j - i
brute.whySlow: On a fully increasing array of 10,000 numbers, every start rescans to the end: about 50 million checks.

optimal.insight: A run only ever breaks at a drop. So carry the current run length forward: grow it on a rise, reset it to one on a drop.
steps: Start with a current run of 1
Rise from the previous number? Extend the run
Otherwise restart the run at 1
Track the best run seen

codeNotes.note: A single element is a run of one
Strictly bigger keeps the run alive
Drop or tie: start a new run here
Remember the longest run so far

pitfalls: Equal neighbours break the run: the comparison must be strictly greater.

say.intro: Okay, so this is Longest Continuous Increasing Subsequence. We want the longest stretch of neighbours that keeps going strictly up. Take one, three, five, four, seven, eight, nine, two. One, three, five climbs, then four breaks it. Four, seven, eight, nine climbs for four numbers. So the answer is four.
say.brute: The obvious way? Try every starting point. From each index, walk right while the next number is bigger. Then record how far you got. That's correct, but it repeats a lot of work. Think about an array that only goes up. Every start walks all the way to the end. That's n squared time.
say.insight: Here's the thing. A run can only end at a drop or a tie. Everything before that point is already counted. So why restart from scratch? We just carry one number, the current run length. Next value bigger? Add one. Not bigger? Reset to one. One pass, and the best length we ever saw is the answer.
say.anim: We start with best and cur both set to one, tracking the current run. At index one, three is greater than one, so cur grows to two. At index two, five beats three, cur rises to three, matching best. At index three, four is less than five, a drop, so cur resets to one. Values rise again through indices four to six, cur climbing to two, three, then four. Best updates to four, the longest increasing run found so far. At index seven, two is less than nine, another drop resets cur to one. The loop ends and the function returns best, giving the final answer four.
say.code: Now the code. We set best and current to one, because a single number is already a run. We loop from the second index. If this number beats the previous one, current grows by one. Otherwise it's a drop or a tie, so current goes back to one. After each step, best takes the larger of the two. Then we return best.
say.outro: Linear time, constant space. It's a sliding window that resets. Grow while the rule holds, restart the moment it breaks.

longest-continuous-increasing-subsequenc.title: Longest Continuous Increasing Subsequence
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container the interview platform expects for our method.
The method takes the list nums and returns the length of the longest strictly increasing contiguous run.
We start both best and cur at one, since any single element is already a run of length one.
We loop the index i from one to the end, comparing each element with the one before it.
We check whether the current number is strictly bigger than the previous one, meaning the run continues.
On a rise, we extend the current run by adding one to cur.
Otherwise the run has broken, so we fall into this branch to handle a drop or an equal value.
On a drop or tie, we reset cur to one because a new run starts at this element.
After updating cur, we keep best as the larger of itself and cur, recording the longest run seen.
Finally we return best, which holds the length of the longest increasing run in the array.

longest-increasing-subsequence-ii.hook: Classic LIS with a twist: each step up can be at most k. Binary search no longer works.
longest-increasing-subsequence-ii.ask: Given an array and a number k, return the length of the longest strictly increasing subsequence where each consecutive pair differs by at most k.
longest-increasing-subsequence-ii.exampleWhy: 1, 3, 4, 5, 8 rises every time by at most 3. Reaching 15 would need a jump of 7.

brute.idea: Classic LIS dynamic programming: for each element, look back at every earlier element that is smaller and within k, and extend its best chain.
steps: dp[i] starts at 1
Scan earlier j that are smaller by at most k
dp[i] = max(dp[i], dp[j] + 1)
brute.whySlow: With 100,000 numbers, looking back over every earlier element costs about 5 billion comparisons.

optimal.insight: Index the dp by value, not position. The best chain ending at v extends the best chain ending at values v - k to v - 1: a range maximum.
steps: Segment tree over values 0 to max(nums)
For value v, query the max over [v - k, v - 1]
Store that max plus one at leaf v
Answer is the max over the whole tree

codeNotes.note: Leaves are values; internal nodes hold maxima

codeNotes.match: lo, hi = max(0, v - k) + size, v + size
codeNotes.note: Half-open value range v - k to v
Chain ending at v: best before plus one
Refresh ancestors up to the root

pitfalls: The patience-sorting binary search trick fails here: it ignores the at-most-k gap.
Query must exclude v itself, or equal values would chain.

say.intro: This is Longest Increasing Subsequence two. We pick numbers in order, each strictly bigger than the last. But here's the twist. Every jump can be at most k. With k equal to three, one, three, four, five, eight works. Every rise is three or less. Fifteen would need a jump of seven. So the answer is five.
say.brute: The first idea is the textbook dynamic program. For each number, look back at every earlier number. Keep the ones that are smaller and within k. Take the best chain among them, plus one. That's correct. So what's the catch? Each element scans everything before it. That's n squared. A hundred thousand numbers means billions of comparisons.
say.insight: Here's the trick. Flip the table around. Don't store answers by position, store them by value. The best chain ending at value v is one plus the best chain ending anywhere from v minus k to v minus one. That's just a range maximum over values. A segment tree answers that in log time. Then one point update, also log time.
say.anim: We build a segment tree sized for values up to the max, all zeros to start, tracking best chains by value. Processing four, we query the range for values one through three, finding best equals zero so far. Processing value two, no smaller values qualify, so its chain length becomes one in the tree. Back at value four, the query now finds best equals one, extending the chain to length two. Value three queries values zero through two, finds best two, giving it chain length three. Value four is revisited, now the range query returns best three, updating its chain to four. Value five queries values two through four, finds best three, giving chain length four at five. Values eight and fifteen extend further, reaching chain lengths five, the tree root now holds five, the final answer.
say.code: Let's walk the code. We build a flat segment tree. Leaves are values, and internal nodes hold maxima. For each number v, we query the half open range from v minus k up to v. The query climbs bottom up from both ends. The chain ending at v is that best plus one. We write it in, then refresh every ancestor up to the root. The root holds the overall answer.
say.outro: From n squared down to n log of the maximum value. It's one dimensional dynamic programming, with a segment tree making each step a range maximum.

longest-increasing-subsequence-ii.title: Longest Increasing Subsequence II
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container the problem expects for our method.
The method takes the numbers and the limit k, and returns the length of the longest valid increasing subsequence.
We size the value axis as the maximum number plus one, so every value in nums gets its own slot.
We build an iterative segment tree array of zeros, with leaves at size onward holding the best chain length ending at each value.
We process each number v in order, since a subsequence must respect the original positions.
We set the query range to values from v minus k, floored at zero, up to v, shifted into leaf positions; the right end is exclusive so v itself is not included.
We start best at zero, meaning no earlier chain can be extended yet.
We loop while the left boundary is still left of the right boundary, climbing the tree level by level.
If lo is a right child, its node is wholly inside the range, so we handle it.
We take the larger of best and that node's stored maximum.
Then we move lo one step right, so it no longer includes the node we just used.
If hi is odd, the node just before it belongs to the range, so we handle that case.
We step hi left to that node, since the right end is exclusive.
We fold that node's value into best, keeping the maximum chain length found.
We move lo up to its parent level to continue narrowing the range.
We move hi up to its parent level as well.
Now we locate the leaf for value v, where we will record the chain ending at v.
We set that leaf to the larger of its old value and best plus one, extending the best earlier chain by v.
We move to the parent of the leaf so we can refresh the maximums above it.
We keep climbing until we pass the root at index one.
Each ancestor is recomputed as the maximum of its two children, keeping range queries correct.
We step up to the next ancestor.
The root holds the maximum over all values, which is the length of the longest valid subsequence.

longest-nice-subarray.hook: No two numbers may share a set bit. One integer can remember the whole window.
longest-nice-subarray.ask: Given positive integers, return the length of the longest contiguous subarray in which every pair of different elements has bitwise AND equal to zero, meaning no two share a set bit.
longest-nice-subarray.exampleWhy: 3, 8 and 48 use bits {0,1}, {3} and {4,5}: no overlap. Adding 1 or 10 creates a shared bit.

brute.idea: From every start, extend right while OR-ing numbers into a mask. Stop when the next number shares a bit with the mask.
steps: Pick a start i, empty mask
Extend j while mask & nums[j] == 0
OR nums[j] in and record the length
brute.whySlow: A nice window holds at most 30 numbers, so this is linear, but every start rescans up to 30 elements again.

optimal.insight: Because bits in a nice window never overlap, their OR works like a reversible set: XOR removes the leftmost number exactly. So slide the window instead of restarting.
steps: Keep used = OR of the window
While x shares a bit with used, drop the left number
Add x to used
Window length is a candidate answer

codeNotes.note: Bits owned by numbers in the window
Conflict: x shares a bit with someone
Disjoint bits, so XOR removes it exactly
Window is nice: record its length

pitfalls: Removing with XOR only works because window bits are disjoint; never XOR an overlapping value.

say.intro: Okay, Longest Nice Subarray. A subarray is nice when no two of its numbers share a set bit. Take one, three, eight, forty eight, ten. Three, eight and forty eight use completely separate bits. One overlaps with three. Ten overlaps with eight. So the longest nice subarray has length three.
say.brute: The simple approach starts at every index. It keeps merging numbers into a mask of bits. As soon as the next number shares a bit with the mask, that start is done. Now, a nice window holds at most thirty numbers. So it isn't truly n squared. But every start throws its work away and rescans the same elements.
say.insight: Here's the key observation. In a nice window, the bits never overlap. So the window's mask is just a set of owned bits. Want to remove the leftmost number? One XOR takes its bits out exactly. That means we can slide. When a new number conflicts, drop numbers from the left until it fits. Then add it. Each number enters once and leaves once.
say.anim: We start with used, left, and best all set to zero, tracking our nice subarray bits. At right equals zero, x is 1, no overlap with used, so we or it in, best becomes 1. At right equals one, x is 3 overlaps used, so we xor out nums at left and move left forward. Now used is 3, no overlap, window grows to size two, best updates to 2. At right equals two and three, x values 8 and 48 fit cleanly, best grows to 3. At right equals four, x is 10 overlaps, so we shrink the window twice, removing bits 1 and 8. After shrinking, used becomes 58 with no overlap, but window size stays three. The loop ends and the function returns best, giving a final answer of 3.
say.code: Now the code. We keep a mask of bits owned by numbers in the window, plus a left pointer and the best length. For each new number, we check for a conflict. Does it share a bit with someone? While it does, we XOR out the leftmost number and move left forward. Disjoint bits make that removal exact. Then we claim the new number's bits. The window is nice, so we record its length.
say.outro: Linear time, constant space. It's a sliding window, with a bitmask standing in for a hash set. That works because the bits never overlap.

longest-nice-subarray.title: Longest Nice Subarray
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, as the problem platform expects for this function.
This method takes the list of numbers and returns the length of the longest nice subarray.
We start with used as zero, meaning no bits are currently taken by the window.
We set both left and best to zero, so the window starts empty and the best length is zero.
We loop over the array, with right as the window's end index and x as the new number.
While the new number shares any bit with used, the window is not nice and must shrink.
We remove the leftmost number from used using exclusive or, which cleanly clears exactly its bits.
We move left forward by one, dropping that number from the window.
Once no bits overlap, we add the new number's bits into used with or.
We update best with the larger of its current value and the current window length.
After scanning everything, we return the longest nice window length we found.

longest-palindrome.hook: You may rearrange the letters freely. Only the counts matter, and pairs are the currency.
longest-palindrome.ask: Given a string of upper and lowercase letters, return the length of the longest palindrome you can build by rearranging some or all of its letters. Case matters.
longest-palindrome.exampleWhy: Use cccc and dd as mirrored pairs, plus one leftover letter in the middle: dccaccd has length 7.

brute.idea: For each distinct letter, scan the whole string to count it. Take its even part, and allow one odd letter in the centre.
steps: For each distinct letter, count it with a full scan
Add the largest even amount
If any letter was odd, add one
brute.whySlow: Each of up to 52 letters rescans the whole string: 52 passes where one counting pass would do.

optimal.insight: A palindrome is mirrored pairs plus at most one middle letter. Greedily use every pair you have; if any letter is left over, it becomes the centre.
steps: Count every letter in one pass
Add each count rounded down to even
If letters remain unused, add one for the centre

codeNotes.note: One pass to count every letter
Use all pairs of this letter
Something left over can sit in the middle

pitfalls: Add only one centre letter, not one per odd count.
Case matters: A and a are different letters.

say.intro: This is Longest Palindrome. Careful, we're not searching inside the string. We can rearrange the letters however we like. So how long a palindrome can we build? From one a, one b, four c's and two d's, we can make d, c, c, a, c, c, d. That's length seven.
say.brute: A slow approach handles each distinct letter separately. For every letter, scan the whole string to count it. Add the largest even amount. And remember whether any letter had an odd count. It works. But with up to fifty two different letters, that's fifty two full passes. One pass is enough.
say.insight: Think about what a palindrome looks like. The left half mirrors the right half. So letters come in pairs. Plus at most one letter, alone in the middle. So we greedily take every pair of every letter. Is anything left over after that? Then one leftover letter goes in the centre, for one extra.
say.anim: We start with the string abccccdd and count each letter's frequency. Counts show c appears four times, d twice, a and b once each. For a with count one, we add zero pairs, since one letter can't pair up. For b, also count one, length stays at zero after adding zero pairs. For c, count four gives two full pairs, adding four to length, now four. For d, count two gives one pair, adding two more, length becomes six. Since length six is less than the string length eight, we add one for a center letter. The final answer returned is seven, the longest possible palindrome length.
say.code: Let's read the code. First, one pass counts every letter. Then for each count, we use all pairs of that letter. That's the count rounded down to even. Now, is the total still shorter than the string? Then something is left over, and it can sit in the middle. So we add exactly one, since only one centre letter is allowed. Then we return the length.
say.outro: Linear time, constant space. It's greedy counting. Use every pair, then spend one leftover letter in the middle.

longest-palindrome.title: Longest Palindrome
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container the problem expects for our method.
The method longestPalindrome takes the string s and returns the length of the longest palindrome we can build.
We count how many times each character appears in s, keeping uppercase and lowercase letters separate since case matters.
We start the palindrome length at zero before adding any mirrored pairs.
We loop over each character's count, ignoring which letter it is, since only the counts matter.
We add the largest even number not exceeding the count, because each pair can sit symmetrically on both sides.
If our length is still less than the string length, some letter had an odd leftover that we skipped.
In that case we add one, because a single leftover letter can serve as the palindrome's middle.
We return the final length as the longest palindrome we can build.

longest-palindromic-subsequence.hook: Delete letters, keep order, end with a palindrome. Interval DP makes it quadratic.
longest-palindromic-subsequence.ask: Given a string, return the length of the longest subsequence that reads the same forwards and backwards. A subsequence keeps the original order but may skip letters.
longest-palindromic-subsequence.exampleWhy: Skip the a and keep bbbb, which is a palindrome of length 4.

brute.idea: Recurse on the ends of the range. Matching ends add two and shrink both sides; otherwise try dropping either end and keep the better.
steps: Range i..j; empty gives 0, one letter gives 1
Ends equal: 2 + solve(i + 1, j - 1)
Else max(solve(i + 1, j), solve(i, j - 1))
brute.whySlow: The same ranges are recomputed again and again; with 1,000 letters the branching explodes far past any time limit.

optimal.insight: There are only n² distinct ranges. Store each answer in dp[i][j], filling shorter ranges first by walking i from the end.
steps: dp[i][i] = 1 for single letters
Walk i from right to left, j from i + 1 rightwards
Equal ends: dp[i + 1][j - 1] + 2
Otherwise the better of dropping either end

codeNotes.note: Bottom-up so row i + 1 is ready
A single letter is a palindrome
Matching ends wrap the inner answer
Drop one end, keep the better

pitfalls: Fill order matters: i must go downwards so dp[i + 1] is already computed.
Subsequence, not substring: letters may be skipped.

say.intro: Okay, Longest Palindromic Subsequence. We may delete letters, but the rest must stay in order. We want the longest result that reads the same both ways. Take b, b, b, a, b. Delete the a, and four b's are left. That's a palindrome. So the answer is four.
say.brute: The natural recursion looks at the two ends of a range. Do they match? Then they wrap a palindrome, so add two and solve the inside. Don't match? One of them has to go. So try dropping the left end, try dropping the right end, and keep the better. That's correct. But it recomputes the same ranges again and again. That's exponential.
say.insight: Here's the thing. Every call is defined by just two numbers, the left end and the right end. So there are only n squared different ranges. Store each answer in a table. Now we just need smaller ranges ready before bigger ones. Going from the last row upward, left to right in each row, does exactly that.
say.anim: We start with the string bbbab and build a table of zeros to store subsequence lengths. Starting from the end, each single letter gets a palindrome length of one on the diagonal. At i equals three, j equals four, letters a and b differ, so we take the max of neighbors. At i equals two, matching b's let us add two to the inner value, giving three. At i equals one, matching b's again extend diagonally, building up values like two and three. At i equals zero, matching b's keep extending, filling the top row with three and three. Finally s of zero and s of four both equal b, so dp zero four becomes four. The function returns dp zero four, giving the final answer four.
say.code: Now the code. The cell at i, j holds the best answer inside that range. We loop i from the end backward, so row i plus one is ready. A single letter is a palindrome, so the diagonal gets one. Then j moves right. Matching ends wrap the inner answer, plus two. Otherwise, drop one end and keep the better cell. Finally, return the whole string's range, the top right corner.
say.outro: Quadratic time and space, instead of exponential. It's two dimensional dynamic programming over intervals. Answer small ranges first, then build outward.

longest-palindromic-subsequence.title: Longest Palindromic Subsequence
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container that the problem's required method lives in.
The method takes the string s and returns an integer, the length of its longest palindromic subsequence.
We store the length of s in n so we can size the table and bound the loops.
We build an n by n table of zeros, where dp at i and j will hold the answer for the range from i to j.
We walk i from the last index down to zero, so shorter ranges starting later are already solved.
A single letter is a palindrome of length one, so we set dp at i and i to one.
For each i, we walk j from just after i to the end, covering every range starting at i.
We compare the letters at both ends of the range to see whether they can match.
If the ends match, both join the palindrome, so we add two to the inner range's answer at i plus one and j minus one.
Otherwise the ends cannot both be used, so we handle that case in this branch.
We take the better of dropping the left letter or dropping the right letter, using the two neighboring ranges.
The full string is the range from zero to n minus one, so we return that table entry.

longest-subsequence-with-non-zero-bitwis.hook: Looks like a subset search. It is really three cases and one XOR pass.
longest-subsequence-with-non-zero-bitwis.ask: Given an array of non-negative integers, return the length of the longest subsequence whose XOR is not zero, or 0 if no such subsequence exists.
longest-subsequence-with-non-zero-bitwis.exampleWhy: 6 XOR 3 XOR 4 XOR 1 is 0, so all four fails. Dropping the 1 leaves XOR 1, which is non-zero.

brute.idea: Try every non-empty subset, compute its XOR, and keep the largest subset size whose XOR is non-zero.
steps: Loop over every bitmask of the n elements
XOR the chosen elements and count them
Non-zero XOR? Update the best size
brute.whySlow: Just 40 numbers already give a trillion subsets; with 100,000 numbers this never finishes.

optimal.insight: If the total XOR is non-zero, take everything. If it is zero, removing any one non-zero element leaves a non-zero XOR. Only an all-zero array gives zero.
steps: XOR all the numbers together
Non-zero total: answer is n
All elements zero: answer is 0
Otherwise drop one non-zero element: n - 1

codeNotes.note: All zeros: every subsequence XORs to 0
Remove one non-zero element; XOR becomes it

pitfalls: Removing a zero does not help; you must remove a non-zero element.

say.intro: This is Longest Subsequence With Non Zero Bitwise XOR. We pick elements, keeping their order. We want the most elements whose XOR isn't zero. Take six, three, four, one. All four XOR to zero, so taking everything fails. Drop the one, and the rest XOR to one. So the answer is three.
say.brute: The brute force tries every subset. For each one, XOR the chosen numbers together and count them. Keep the biggest count with a non zero result. Sounds fine? It isn't. There are two to the n subsets. Even forty numbers means about a trillion. For a hundred thousand numbers, it's hopeless.
say.insight: So think about the total XOR instead. If it's already non zero, just take all n elements. Done. If it's zero, remove any single non zero element x. Why does that work? Because XOR undoes itself. The rest now XORs to exactly x, which isn't zero. That gives n minus one. And the only way to get nothing? Every element is zero.
say.anim: We start with nums 6, 3, 4, 1 and total set to zero. We loop through each number, XORing it into total to combine all bits. After XORing 6 and 3, total becomes 5. After XORing in 4, total drops to 1. After XORing in the last value 1, total becomes zero. Since total is zero, we check if the array has any nonzero numbers. Max of nums is 6, not zero, so removing one element fixes it. We return length minus one, giving the final answer 3.
say.code: Let's look at the code. We XOR the whole array into a total. Already non zero? Keep every element, and return the length. Next, if the largest number is zero, it's all zeros. Every subsequence XORs to zero, so return zero. Otherwise, remove one non zero element. The XOR becomes that element. So return the length minus one.
say.outro: Linear time, constant space. It's bit manipulation. XOR is its own inverse, so removing one element changes the total predictably.

longest-subsequence-with-non-zero-bitwis.title: Longest Subsequence With Non-Zero Bitwise XOR
lineNotes: We define a class named Solution, which is the container the interview platform expects for our method.
The method longestSubsequence takes a list of integers called nums and returns the length of the longest subsequence with non-zero XOR.
We start total at zero, since zero is the identity value for XOR and won't change anything.
We loop through every number x in the array so we can fold each one into the total.
We XOR x into total, so after the loop total holds the XOR of the entire array.
We check whether the total XOR is not zero, meaning the whole array already qualifies.
In that case we return the length of nums, because taking every element gives the longest possible subsequence.
Now the total is zero, so we check whether the largest element is zero, which means every element is zero.
If every element is zero, any subsequence XORs to zero, so we return zero.
Otherwise some element is non-zero, and removing it makes the XOR non-zero, so we return the length of nums minus one.

longest-substring-of-one-repeating-chara.hook: Point updates, then the longest same-letter run, again and again. A segment tree merges runs.
longest-substring-of-one-repeating-chara.ask: Given a string and a list of updates, each setting one position to a new letter, return after every update the length of the longest block of one repeated letter.
longest-substring-of-one-repeating-chara.exampleWhy: bbbacc has run bbb (3); bbbccc has bbb and ccc (3); bbbbcc has bbbb (4).

brute.idea: Apply each update to a character list, then rescan the whole string to find the longest run of equal letters.
steps: Write the new letter into position i
Scan left to right, counting the current run
Record the longest run for this query
brute.whySlow: 100,000 updates, each rescanning 100,000 letters, is 10 billion steps.

optimal.insight: A segment holds three facts: its prefix run, suffix run and best run. Two halves merge in O(1) by joining the left suffix with the right prefix.
steps: Each node stores prefix, suffix and best run lengths
Merge: if middle letters match, join suffix and prefix
An update rewrites one leaf and remerges its ancestors
The root's best is the answer

codeNotes.note: Per node: prefix, suffix, best run
Halves touch with the same letter
Left half is one run: prefix spills right
Index -1 visits every leaf: the build
Root's best run after this update

pitfalls: Prefix extends past the middle only if the whole left half is one run.
Size arrays 4n for a recursive segment tree.

say.intro: Okay, Longest Substring of One Repeating Character. We get a string and a list of updates. Each update changes one letter. After each one, we report the longest block of a single repeated letter. For b, a, b, a, c, c, the three updates give three, three, and finally four b's in a row.
say.brute: The obvious approach applies each update, then scans the whole string. Count the current run, and remember the longest. That's one full pass per query. Is that a problem? With a hundred thousand letters and a hundred thousand updates, it's about ten billion steps. Way too slow.
say.insight: Here's the idea. Split the string into halves, recursively. For each piece, keep three numbers. The run at its start, the run at its end, and its best run. Two neighbours merge in constant time. The best either stays inside one half, or crosses the middle. Crossing means the left suffix joins the right prefix. And an update only touches one path to the root.
say.anim: We start with string babacc, building a segment tree of prefix, suffix and best runs. Each leaf stores a run of one, since single characters always match themselves. Merging nodes joins matching boundary characters, letting runs like bb and bb combine into four. After the initial build, best at the root is three, our first answer. Now index three changes to c, updating chars to babacc's variant bbcbcc, rebuilding affected nodes. Merges propagate upward, combining suffix and prefix runs across the updated segment. Next index three changes to b, giving bbbbcc, merging four b's into one long run. The final answers are three, three, and four, matching the longest repeating runs after each update.
say.code: Now the code. Three arrays hold each node's prefix, suffix and best run. The pull step merges two children. First, do the halves touch with the same letter? If the left half is one whole run, its prefix spills right. And the run crossing the middle competes for best. Update recurses down to one leaf. Passing minus one visits every leaf, which is the build. After each query, we record the root's best run.
say.outro: Log time per update, instead of linear. It's a segment tree whose nodes store just enough to merge in constant time.

longest-substring-of-one-repeating-chara.title: Longest Substring of One Repeating Character
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, as the problem platform expects.
The method takes the string, the replacement letters, and the positions, and returns the longest run after each update.
We copy the string into a mutable list of characters and record its length as n.
We allocate three arrays of size four times n for each segment tree node's prefix run, suffix run, and best run.
The pull helper recomputes one node's three facts by merging its two children.
We find the midpoint of the node's range, which is where the left and right halves split.
We compute the indices of the left child and right child in the tree arrays.
The node's prefix starts as the left child's prefix and its suffix starts as the right child's suffix.
The node's best starts as the larger of the two children's best runs.
Only if the characters at the midpoint and just after it match can runs join across the split.
If the left child is one single run covering its whole range, the prefix can extend into the right child.
So we add the right child's prefix to the node's prefix.
If the right child is one single run covering its whole range, the suffix can extend into the left child.
So we add the left child's suffix to the node's suffix.
The joined run across the middle, left suffix plus right prefix, may beat the current best, so we take the max.
The update helper walks down to a leaf and rebuilds the facts on the way back up.
When the range shrinks to a single position, we have reached a leaf.
A leaf is a run of length one, so prefix, suffix, and best are all set to one.
We return so the leaf needs no further work.
We compute the midpoint to decide which child contains the index.
If the index is negative, meaning build everything, or it falls in the left half, we recurse left.
That recursion handles the left child with its range from lo to mid.
If the index is negative, or it falls in the right half, we recurse right.
That recursion handles the right child with its range from mid plus one to hi.
After the children are correct, we pull to recompute this node from them.
We call update with a negative index to build the whole tree once from the initial string.
We create an empty list to collect the answers.
We loop over each query pairing the new character with its position.
We write the new character into the character list so merges see the change.
We update the tree along the path to that position, fixing only the affected nodes.
The root's best value is the longest run now, so we append it to the output.
After all queries, we return the list of answers.

lowest-common-ancestor-of-a-binary-tree.hook: No ordering to guide you this time. Let each subtree report what it found.
lowest-common-ancestor-of-a-binary-tree.ask: Given a binary tree and two of its nodes p and q, return their lowest common ancestor: the deepest node that has both p and q in its subtree. A node counts as its own descendant.
lowest-common-ancestor-of-a-binary-tree.exampleWhy: 6 is in 5's left subtree and 4 is in 5's right subtree, so 5 is the deepest node above both.

brute.idea: Start at the root. If p and q are both in the left subtree, move left; both in the right, move right; otherwise the current node splits them.
steps: At node: is it p or q? Return it
Search the left subtree for p and for q
Both left: go left. Neither: go right
Split: this node is the answer
brute.whySlow: Every level searches its whole subtree again; on a skewed tree of 100,000 nodes that is billions of visits.

optimal.insight: One post-order pass: each subtree returns p or q if it contains one. The first node receiving answers from both sides is the LCA.
steps: Empty, p or q: return this node
Recurse into left and right
Both sides non-empty: this node is the LCA
Otherwise pass up whichever side found something

codeNotes.match: if root is None or root is p or root is q:
codeNotes.note: Found a target, or fell off the tree
What does the left subtree contain?
Bubble up the side that found something

pitfalls: When p is an ancestor of q, returning p early is still correct.
Compare nodes by identity, not just by value.

say.intro: This is Lowest Common Ancestor of a Binary Tree. Given two nodes, find the deepest node with both of them below it. A node counts as below itself. In our tree, six hangs under five on the left. Four sits under two, on five's right. So five is the lowest node above both.
say.brute: A straightforward approach walks down from the root. At each node, search the left subtree for p and for q. Both on the left? Go left. Neither? Go right. Split? We've found it. So what's wrong with that? Every level searches its subtree from scratch. On a long skewed tree, that's n squared time.
say.insight: Turn it around. Let information flow upward instead. Each subtree reports back whether it contains p or q. It returns that node, or nothing. Now, a node that hears a hit from both left and right? That's exactly where the paths split. Otherwise, it just passes the single hit up. One visit per node.
say.anim: We start at root node 3, searching its subtrees for nodes 6 and 4. Node 6 matches our target p, so it immediately returns itself up the call stack. The search dives into node 2's subtree, checking nodes 7, 0, and 8, but finds neither target there. Node 2 finds q is not in either child, so right stays None and left stays None. Back at node 5, left holds node 6 and right is None, so one side found a match. Node 5 returns itself as root since left found node 6, making it a candidate ancestor. Meanwhile node 1's subtree, containing 0 and 8, finds neither p nor q at all. Back at root 3, left carries node 5 up while right is empty, so node 5 is the final lowest common ancestor.
say.code: Let's walk the code. If we found a target, or fell off the tree, return the node. Otherwise, recurse left. What does the left subtree contain? Then recurse right. If both sides returned something, p and q split here. So this node is the answer. Otherwise, bubble up whichever side found something.
say.outro: Linear time, and space equal to the tree's height. It's a post order traversal, where children report their findings up to the parent.

lowest-common-ancestor-of-a-binary-tree.title: Lowest Common Ancestor of a Binary Tree
lineNotes: We define a Solution class that holds the method for finding the lowest common ancestor.
This method takes the tree root plus the two target nodes p and q and returns their lowest common ancestor.
This comment introduces the base case: stop when the node is empty or is one of the targets.
If root is empty, or is p, or is q, we have reached a stopping point in the search.
We return root itself, which is none for an empty spot or the target node we just found.
This comment says we now search both the left and right subtrees for p and q.
We recurse into the left child and store whatever target or ancestor that subtree reports in left.
We do the same on the right child and store the result in right.
This comment explains that finding something on both sides means the current node is the answer.
If left and right are both not none, p and q sit in different subtrees of this node.
So this node is the lowest common ancestor, and we return root.
This comment says that otherwise we simply pass up whichever side found something.
If the left side found a node, then either it is one target or the answer already found there.
We return left, bubbling that result up toward the parent.
Otherwise we return right, which is either the found node or none if neither side found anything.

magnetic-force-between-two-balls.hook: Maximise the minimum gap. Do not search placements; binary search the answer itself.
magnetic-force-between-two-balls.ask: Given basket positions and m balls, place the balls in distinct baskets so that the smallest distance between any two balls is as large as possible. Return that largest possible minimum distance.
magnetic-force-between-two-balls.exampleWhy: Balls at 1, 4 and 8 have gaps 3 and 4, so the minimum is 3. No placement keeps every gap at 4.

brute.idea: Try every candidate gap from the largest possible downwards. For each, greedily place balls left to right; the first gap that fits all m balls wins.
steps: Sort the positions
Try gaps from the even-spread bound down to 1
Greedy placement fits m balls? Return gap
brute.time: O(n log n + n·D), D = gap range
brute.whySlow: The gap range can reach a billion, and each candidate costs a full greedy pass over the baskets.

optimal.insight: Feasibility is monotonic: if gap g fits m balls, every smaller gap fits too. So binary search for the largest feasible gap, checking each with one greedy pass.
steps: Sort the positions
canPlace(gap): greedily drop a ball whenever the gap allows
Binary search gap between 1 and the even-spread upper bound
Feasible? Move lo up. Not feasible? Move hi down
optimal.time: O(n log n + n log D)

codeNotes.note: Far enough from the last ball: place one
Gap cannot beat an even spread
Round up so lo = mid always progresses

pitfalls: With lo = mid, round mid up or the loop never ends.
Greedy placement only works after sorting.

say.intro: Okay, Magnetic Force Between Two Balls. We have baskets at fixed positions, and m balls. We want the closest pair of balls as far apart as possible. Baskets sit at one, two, four, eight and nine, with three balls. Use one, four and eight. Every gap is at least three.
say.brute: The brute force tries gaps from the largest possible value downward. For each gap, put the first ball in the leftmost basket. Then drop each next ball in the first basket far enough away. The first gap that fits all m balls wins. The problem? The gap range can be a billion values. Each one needs a full pass.
say.insight: Now notice something. Feasibility only flips once. If a gap of g works, any smaller gap works too. If g fails, anything larger fails. So the answers look like yes, yes, yes, no, no. That shape is exactly what binary search needs. So we binary search on the answer, and check each guess greedily in linear time.
say.anim: We sort the positions to get 1, 2, 4, 8, and 9, with m equal to 3. The search range for the gap starts at lo equals 1 and hi equals 4. We test mid equals 3, greedily placing balls to see if this gap fits three balls. Balls land at 1, 4, and 8, since each jump is at least 3 apart, giving count 3. Gap 3 works, so lo moves up to 3 and we try mid equals 4 next. With gap 4, only two balls fit, at positions 1 and 8, so it fails. Since gap 4 fails, hi shrinks to 3, closing the search range. The loop ends and the function returns 3, the maximum minimum distance.
say.code: Here's the code. First we sort, because greedy placement needs left to right order. The helper places a ball whenever a basket is far enough from the last one. The search runs from one up to an even spread, since no gap can beat that. We take the middle rounded up, so lo always makes progress. If it's feasible, we try a larger gap. Otherwise, hi drops below mid. Return lo.
say.outro: From scanning every gap to a logarithmic number of greedy checks. That's binary search on the answer, whenever feasibility is monotonic.

magnetic-force-between-two-balls.title: Magnetic Force Between Two Balls
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container the judge expects for our method.
The method takes the basket positions and the number of balls m, and returns the largest possible minimum gap.
We sort the positions first so that a greedy left to right pass can reason about neighboring balls.
We define a helper called canPlace that checks whether m balls fit with every gap at least the given size.
We place the first ball in the leftmost basket, so count starts at one and last holds that position.
We scan every remaining basket in sorted order, considering each as a spot for the next ball.
If this basket is at least gap away from the last placed ball, it is a valid spot.
We place a ball there, so we increase the count by one.
We update last to this basket, so later distances are measured from the newest ball.
We return whether we managed to place at least m balls using this gap.
