We search gaps from one up to the largest conceivable gap, which is the total span divided evenly among m minus one spaces.
We keep searching while the low and high bounds have not met.
We pick the upper middle value so that the search always makes progress when we move low up.
If mid works as a gap, then the answer is at least mid, so we try larger ones.
We move low up to mid, keeping this feasible gap as our best candidate.
Otherwise the gap is too large to fit all the balls.
So we shrink high to just below mid, discarding all gaps that are too big.
When the bounds meet, low holds the largest feasible minimum gap, and we return it.

matrix-diagonal-sum.hook: Two diagonals, one shared centre. Touch only the cells you need.
matrix-diagonal-sum.ask: Given a square matrix, return the sum of the primary diagonal plus the secondary diagonal, counting the centre cell only once when the size is odd.
matrix-diagonal-sum.exampleWhy: Primary 1 + 5 + 9 and secondary 3 + 5 + 7; the shared 5 counts once: 25.

brute.idea: Visit every cell of the matrix and add it if it lies on either diagonal.
steps: Loop over every row i and column j
Add the cell if it lies on either diagonal
brute.whySlow: It checks all n² cells to use only about 2n of them; most of the work is skipped cells.

optimal.insight: Row i meets the primary diagonal at column i and the secondary at column n - 1 - i. Read those two cells directly, then undo the double-counted centre.
steps: For each row i, add mat[i][i]
Also add mat[i][n - 1 - i]
If n is odd, subtract the centre once

codeNotes.note: Primary diagonal cell in row i
Odd size: both diagonals share the centre

pitfalls: Forgetting the odd-size centre counts it twice; even sizes have no shared cell.

say.intro: This is Matrix Diagonal Sum. We add up both diagonals of a square matrix. Top left to bottom right, and top right to bottom left. In the three by three grid of one to nine, that's one, five, nine. Plus three and seven. The shared five counts once. So we get twenty five.
say.brute: The brute force visits every cell. Is the row equal to the column? Add it. Do row plus column equal n minus one? Add it. That's correct, and it counts the centre once naturally. But think about the cost. It checks n squared cells. Only about two n of them ever matter.
say.insight: Here's the thing. Each row touches each diagonal in exactly one known place. In row i, the primary diagonal is at column i. The secondary is at column n minus one minus i. So why search? Just read those two cells directly. The only catch is an odd size. Both diagonals pass through the centre, so subtract it once.
say.anim: We start with a 3 by 3 matrix, and n is set to 3. At i equals 0, we add mat[0][0], which is 1, giving total 1. Then we add mat[0][2], which is 3, bringing total to 4. At i equals 1, we add the center value 5 twice, reaching total 14. At i equals 2, we add mat[2][2] and mat[2][0], reaching total 30. Since n is odd, we subtract the double counted center value 5. The final total becomes 25, which is the correct diagonal sum.
say.code: Now the code. For each row i, we add the primary diagonal cell, at column i. Then the secondary diagonal, at the mirrored column. After the loop, we check the size. An odd size means both diagonals share the centre. So we remove the double count by subtracting the centre once. Then we return the total.
say.outro: Linear in the side length, constant space. It's math and geometry. Compute the positions directly, instead of searching for them.

matrix-diagonal-sum.title: Matrix Diagonal Sum
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the wrapper the judge expects for this problem.
The method diagonalSum takes the square matrix mat and will return the combined diagonal sum as an integer.
We store the size of the matrix in n, which is both its row count and column count.
We start total at zero to accumulate every diagonal cell we visit.
We loop over each row index i from zero up to n minus one.
We add the primary diagonal cell in this row, which sits at column i.
We add the secondary diagonal cell, which sits at column n minus one minus i in the same row.
If n is odd, both diagonals cross at one centre cell that we counted twice.
We subtract the centre cell, found at row and column n divided by two rounded down, to count it once.
We return total as the final diagonal sum.

max-points-on-a-line.hook: Fix one point, and every line through it is just a slope. Count slopes in a hash map.
max-points-on-a-line.ask: Given distinct points on a plane, return the maximum number of them that lie on one straight line.
max-points-on-a-line.exampleWhy: (1,4), (2,3), (3,2) and (4,1) all lie on the line x + y = 5.

brute.idea: Every line is defined by two points. For each pair, count how many points are collinear with it using a cross product.
steps: Pick a pair of points i, j
For every point k, test the cross product is 0
Track the largest count
brute.whySlow: 300 points give 45,000 pairs, each scanning 300 points: about 13 million checks, cubic growth.

optimal.insight: Anchor one point. Every other point defines a direction from it; points on the same line share a direction. Reduce each direction exactly and count duplicates.
steps: Pick an anchor point
For each later point, take dx and dy
Divide by their gcd and fix the sign
Count each direction; best count plus the anchor

codeNotes.note: Reduce so equal slopes get equal keys
Normalise the sign of the direction
One more point on this line
Plus one for the anchor itself

pitfalls: Floating-point slopes can collide or split; use reduced integer pairs.
Vertical lines have dx = 0: no division.

say.intro: Okay, Max Points on a Line. Given points on a plane, find the largest group on one straight line. Look at our six points. One four, two three, three two and four one all sit on the same falling diagonal. No line hits five of them. So the answer is four.
say.brute: Any two points define a line. So the brute force tries every pair. For each pair, it checks every other point with a cross product. Is it on that line? That's correct, and it avoids fractions. But it's cubic. Three hundred points already means millions of checks.
say.insight: Here's the trick. Fix one anchor point. Any line through it is defined by its direction. So for every other point, take the step from the anchor. Divide both parts by their greatest common divisor, and fix the sign. Why? So points on the same line give the identical key. Then a hash map just counts them.
say.anim: We start with best equal to one, anchoring on each point in turn. Anchored at point one one, we check direction to point three two, normalized to two one. Point five three gives the same reduced direction two one, so best grows to three. Other points give different directions like one zero and one two, tracked separately in slopes. Now anchored at three two, point four one gives direction one negative one, appearing three times, pushing best to four. Anchoring continues on remaining points, but no direction beats three matches again. Finally the function returns four, the most points found lying on one line.
say.code: Let's walk the code. For each anchor, we start a fresh map of direction counts. For each later point, take the differences in x and y. Reduce them by their gcd, so equal slopes get equal keys. Then normalise the sign of the direction. That's one more point on this line, so bump its count. The best is that count plus one, for the anchor itself.
say.outro: n squared time instead of cubic. It's math and geometry with hashing. Turn a geometric property into an exact key, then count matches.

max-points-on-a-line.title: Max Points on a Line
lineNotes: This defines the Solution class that holds our method for the problem.
The method maxPoints takes a list of points and returns the largest count of points sharing one line.
We start best at one, since any single point trivially lies on a line.
We loop over each point as the anchor, naming its coordinates x one and y one.
We create a fresh counting dictionary for this anchor, mapping each reduced direction to how many points share it.
We pair the anchor only with later points, since earlier pairs were already handled from the other side.
We compute the difference in x and in y from the anchor to the other point.
We take the greatest common divisor of the two differences so equal directions reduce to the same pair.
We divide both differences by that divisor, giving an exact direction without any floating point error.
If the direction points left, or straight down, we need to normalize its sign so opposite directions match.
We flip both signs, so a direction and its opposite become the same key.
We increment the count for this direction, since another point lies on that line through the anchor.
We update best with this direction's count plus one for the anchor itself.
After checking all anchors, we return the largest line size found.

maximal-rectangle.hook: A 2-D grid problem that is secretly the histogram problem, solved once per row.
maximal-rectangle.ask: Given a grid of 0 and 1 characters, return the area of the largest rectangle made entirely of 1s.
maximal-rectangle.exampleWhy: Rows 2 and 3, columns 3 to 5, are all 1s: a 2 by 3 rectangle of area 6.

brute.idea: Build column heights of consecutive 1s ending at each row. For every cell, extend left while tracking the minimum height and the area it allows.
steps: Update heights for this row
For each column j, walk left to k
Area = min height on k..j times width
brute.whySlow: Each cell walks left across the whole row: 200 by 200 means 8 million steps, versus 40 thousand.

optimal.insight: Each row turns the grid above it into a histogram of 1-heights. Largest rectangle in a histogram is a monotonic stack problem, linear per row.
steps: Grow heights: plus one on 1, reset to 0 on 0
Keep a stack of increasing heights
A lower bar pops taller bars and measures their width
Zero sentinel at the end flushes the stack

codeNotes.note: Extra zero bar flushes the stack
Histogram of 1s ending at this row
Lower bar: taller bars cannot extend

pitfalls: Heights reset to 0 on a 0 cell; they do not just stop growing.
Cells are the strings 0 and 1, not integers.

say.intro: This is Maximal Rectangle. We have a grid of zeros and ones. We want the largest rectangle filled entirely with ones. In our four by five grid, rows two and three share ones in the last three columns. That's a two by three block, area six. Nothing bigger fits.
say.brute: A slower approach still builds column heights. That's the count of consecutive ones ending at each row. Then, for every cell, walk left, track the smallest height so far, and try each width. That beats checking every rectangle. But each cell scans its whole row. So it costs rows times columns squared.
say.insight: Look at the grid one row at a time. Each column's run of ones above that row forms a histogram. So the best rectangle sitting on this row? It's the largest rectangle in that histogram. And a monotonic stack finds that in one pass. Do it for every row, and keep the maximum.
say.anim: We start with a grid of zeros and ones, tracking column heights as we scan each row. For the first row, heights become one, zero, one, zero, zero, building a small histogram. A monotonic stack scans these heights, popping taller bars to compute rectangle areas, giving best equal to one. Row two updates heights to two, zero, two, one, one, and the stack finds best equal to three. Row three makes heights three, one, three, two, two, a tall uniform histogram across most columns. The stack pops through these bars, and best jumps up to six, the biggest rectangle so far. The last row drops some heights to zero, so the stack trims areas but best stays six. The function returns six, the maximal rectangle area found in the binary matrix.
say.code: Now the code. Heights gets one extra zero bar at the end, to flush the stack. For each row, we update the histogram of ones ending here. Add one on a one, reset on a zero. Then the stack scan. An index of minus one reads that zero sentinel. When a lower bar arrives, taller bars can't extend past it, so we pop. The width spans between the neighbours. Return the best area.
say.outro: Linear in the grid size. It's a monotonic stack, reusing largest rectangle in histogram once per row.

maximal-rectangle.title: Maximal Rectangle
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container the problem expects for our method.
The method takes the grid of character digits and returns the area of the largest all-ones rectangle.
We read the number of columns from the first row of the matrix.
We make a heights list with one extra slot at the end, which stays zero as a sentinel to flush the stack.
We start the best area at zero, since no rectangle has been found yet.
We process the grid one row at a time, treating each row as the base of a histogram.
For each column in this row, we update that column's bar height.
If the cell is one we extend the bar by one, otherwise we reset its height to zero.
We create a fresh stack holding negative one as a left boundary marker for each row.
We sweep every column including the sentinel column, so all remaining bars get popped at the end.
While the current bar is shorter than the bar on top of the stack, that taller bar cannot extend further right.
We pop the top bar and take its height as the height of a candidate rectangle.
The width runs between the new stack top and the current column, and we keep the largest area seen.
We push the current column index so the stack keeps bar heights in increasing order.
After all rows are processed, we return the best area found.

maximize-active-section-with-trade-i.hook: Sacrifice one block of 1s to merge the zeros around it. Only neighbouring zero blocks matter.
maximize-active-section-with-trade-i.ask: Given a binary string, you may once turn a block of 1s that has 0s on both sides into 0s, then turn a 0 block bordered by 1s into 1s. Return the most 1s possible.
maximize-active-section-with-trade-i.exampleWhy: Zero blocks 000 and 0 surround the middle 1. Clearing it and filling gives 4 + 3 + 1 + 1 = 9 ones.

brute.idea: Pad with 1 on both ends. Try clearing every 1-block surrounded by 0s, then fill the longest 0-block, and keep the best total.
steps: Pad t = 1 + s + 1
For each 1-block with 0s on both sides
Clear it and find the longest 0-block
Ones minus block plus that 0-block length
brute.whySlow: Each candidate block rebuilds the string and rescans it: 50,000 blocks over 100,000 letters is billions of steps.

optimal.insight: Clearing a 1-block merges it with its two neighbouring 0-blocks; filling that merged block nets their two lengths. So the gain is the best sum of adjacent 0-blocks.
steps: Count all ones
Walk the string block by block
At each 0-block, add the previous 0-block length
Answer: ones plus the best such pair

codeNotes.match: while j < n and s[j] == s[i]:
codeNotes.note: Find the end of this block
Gain: both zero blocks become ones

pitfalls: A 1-block touching the string's end is not surrounded by 0s; it cannot be traded.

say.intro: Okay, Maximize Active Section With Trade one. In a binary string, we may trade once. Clear a block of ones with zeros on both sides. Then fill a block of zeros bordered by ones. For one, zero zero, one, zero zero zero, one, zero, one, the best trade gives nine ones out of ten.
say.brute: The brute force tries every block of ones that has zeros on both sides. For each one, build the new string with that block cleared. Find the longest run of zeros, and compute the total. It's correct. But every candidate rebuilds and rescans the whole string. That's n squared.
say.insight: Here's the thing. When you clear a block of ones, it fuses with the zero blocks on either side. Filling that fused block gives back the ones you cleared. Plus both zero blocks. So what's the net gain? Just the sum of two neighbouring zero blocks. Scan the blocks once, and keep the best adjacent pair.
say.anim: We start with the string one zero zero one zero zero zero one zero one, counting four ones. The scanner finds the first zero block from index one to three, giving a length of two. Next it finds a bigger zero block from index four to seven, length three, merging with prev two for best five. Another zero block from index seven to eight, length one, becomes the new prev. Then a zero block from index eight to nine, length one, combines with prev for a sum of two, less than best. The last block at index nine is a single one, so prev resets to one and scanning ends. Adding the best gain of five to the four original ones gives the final answer nine.
say.code: Let's read the code. First we count the ones we already have. Then we walk the string, finding the end of each block. If this is a zero block and there was a previous one, a block of ones sits between them. Their combined size is a possible gain, since both zero blocks become ones. Then we remember this zero block for the next. Return the ones plus the best gain.
say.outro: Linear time, constant space. It's greedy. Reduce the trade to its net effect, the sum of two adjacent zero blocks.

maximize-active-section-with-trade-i.title: Maximize Active Section with Trade I
lineNotes: We define the Solution class that holds the method for this problem.
The method takes the binary string s and returns the maximum count of ones after at most one trade.
We count the ones already in the string, since they stay active and form our baseline answer.
We start best, the largest gain so far, and prev, the length of the last zero block, both at zero.
We set i to zero as our scan position and n to the length of s.
We loop while i is still inside the string, processing one block of equal characters per pass.
We set j to i so it can scan forward to find the end of the current block.
We advance j while it stays in range and matches the character at i, marking the block's end.
Each step of that scan moves j one position to the right.
If the block we just measured is made of zeros, we handle it as a possible trade partner.
If prev is nonzero, a zero block came before with only a block of ones between, so they are adjacent zero blocks.
We update best to the larger of itself and prev plus this block's length, the gain from merging both zero blocks.
We record this zero block's length as prev, ready to pair with the next zero block.
We jump i to j so the next pass begins at the start of the following block.
We return the original ones plus the best gain, which is zero if no valid trade exists.

maximize-active-section-with-trade-ii.hook: The same trade, now on many substrings. Precompute pair sums, then answer with binary search and a sparse table.
maximize-active-section-with-trade-ii.ask: Given a binary string and queries l, r, apply the best single trade to the substring s[l..r] only, and return the total number of 1s in the whole string for each query.
maximize-active-section-with-trade-ii.exampleWhy: s has 2 ones. In 00010, merging 000 and 0 gains 4 (6). In 1000100 the gain is 5. In 10001, no trade.

brute.idea: For every query, scan the substring block by block like the single-trade version, and take the best sum of adjacent 0-blocks.
steps: Cut s[l..r]
Scan its blocks, pairing neighbouring 0-blocks
Answer: total ones plus the best pair
brute.whySlow: 100,000 queries each scanning up to 100,000 characters is 10 billion steps.

optimal.insight: Inside a query only the two end 0-blocks get clipped. Every other adjacent pair is fixed, so precompute pair sums and range-max them with a sparse table.
steps: List the 0-blocks; pair[k] = size[k] + size[k + 1]
Build a sparse table for range max over pairs
Binary search the first and last 0-block touching l..r
Clip end blocks; combine edge pairs with the inner range max

maximize-active-section-with-trade-ii.optimalCode:
class Solution:
    def maxActiveSectionsAfterTrade(self, s: str, queries: List[List[int]]) -> List[int]:
        ones, n = s.count("1"), len(s)
        starts, ends = [], []
        i = 0
        while i < n:
            j = i
            while j < n and s[j] == s[i]:
                j += 1
            if s[i] == "0":
                starts.append(i)
                ends.append(j - 1)
            i = j
        size = [e - b + 1 for b, e in zip(starts, ends)]
        table = [[size[k] + size[k + 1] for k in range(len(size) - 1)]]
        step = 1
        while 2 * step <= len(table[0]):
            last = table[-1]
            table.append([max(last[k], last[k + step]) for k in range(len(last) - step)])
            step *= 2
        out = []
        for l, r in queries:
            a = bisect.bisect_left(ends, l)
            b = bisect.bisect_right(starts, r) - 1
            gain = 0
            if b > a:
                first = ends[a] - max(starts[a], l) + 1
                last = min(ends[b], r) - starts[b] + 1
                if b == a + 1:
                    gain = first + last
                else:
                    gain = max(first + size[a + 1], size[b - 1] + last)
                    if b - a >= 3:
                        p = (b - 2 - a).bit_length() - 1
                        gain = max(gain, table[p][a + 1], table[p][b - 1 - (1 << p)])
            out.append(ones + gain)
        return out

codeNotes.match: table = [[size[k] + size[k + 1] for k in range(len(size) - 1)]]
codeNotes.note: Gain of trading between blocks k and k + 1

codeNotes.match: table.append([max(last[k], last[k + step]) for k in range(len(last) - step)])
codeNotes.note: Sparse table: max over doubling windows
End blocks are clipped by l and r
O(1) max over fully inside pairs

pitfalls: The answer counts ones in the whole string, not just the substring.
Only the two end blocks are clipped; inner pairs use precomputed sums.

say.intro: This is Maximize Active Section With Trade two. Same trade as before, with a twist. Each query picks a substring, and the trade happens only inside it. But we report the ones in the whole string. For one, zero zero zero, one, zero zero, the queries give six, seven, and two, when no trade fits.
say.brute: The brute force reruns the single trade solution for every query. Cut out the substring, walk its blocks, and take the best sum of two neighbouring zero blocks. That's linear per query. Sounds okay? With a hundred thousand queries over a hundred thousand characters, it's ten billion steps.
say.insight: Here's the key. Inside any query, the zero blocks are the same as in the full string. Except the first and last, which the query edges may clip. So precompute the sum of every adjacent pair of zero blocks. Then build a sparse table for range maximum. Each query needs two binary searches, plus constant work.
say.anim: We start with string 1000100, which has two ones, so ones equals two. Scanning the string finds the first zero block from index one to three, size three. A second zero block is found from index five to six, size two. We precompute pair sums and build a sparse table for fast range max queries. For query one to five, only the first block is clipped, giving gain four, total six. For query zero to six, both blocks fully fit, gain five, total seven. For query zero to four, only the first block overlaps, giving gain zero, total two. The final answer returned is six, seven, and two.
say.code: Now the code. We record each zero block's start and end. The gain of trading between neighbouring blocks is their combined size. The sparse table stores the max over doubling windows. For a query, binary search finds the first zero block reaching into it, and the last. The end blocks get clipped by the query edges. Then the table gives the max over fully inside pairs, in constant time.
say.outro: Log time per query instead of linear. It's binary search plus a sparse table. Precompute everything the queries don't change.

maximize-active-section-with-trade-ii.title: Maximize Active Section with Trade II
lineNotes: We define the solution method, which takes the binary string and a list of query ranges.
We count the ones in the whole string and store the string length.
We prepare two lists to hold the start and end positions of every block of zeros.
We set a scanning index i to zero to walk through the string.
We loop while the index is still inside the string.
We set j to i so we can extend a run of equal characters.
We advance j while it stays in bounds and the character matches the one at i.
Each step moves j forward, so j ends just past the current run.
We check whether this run is made of zeros, since only zero blocks matter.
We record the start index of that zero block.
We record the end index of the block, which is j minus one.
We jump i to j so the next run begins right after this one.
We compute the size of each zero block from its start and end.
We build the base sparse table level holding the sum of sizes of each adjacent pair of zero blocks.
We set step to one, the span of the next table level.
We keep building levels while a doubled span still fits in the base row.
We take the most recent level to combine into the next one.
We append a level where each entry is the larger of two overlapping earlier entries, doubling the covered range.
We double step to prepare for the next level.
We create the output list for query answers.
We loop over each query with its left and right bounds.
We binary search for a, the first zero block that ends at or after l.
We binary search for b, the last zero block that starts at or before r.
We start with a gain of zero in case no trade is possible.
A trade needs at least two zero blocks touching the range, so we check b exceeds a.
We compute the first block's size clipped to the left bound l.
We compute the last block's size clipped to the right bound r.
We check whether the two blocks are adjacent in the block list.
With only two blocks, the gain is simply the sum of both clipped sizes.
Otherwise there are blocks in the middle, so we handle that case.
We take the best pair involving a clipped end block with its unclipped neighbor.
If there are at least two fully inside middle blocks, we also need a range maximum over their pair sums.
We find p, the largest power of two exponent fitting the number of middle pairs, using the bit length.
We update the gain with two overlapping sparse table lookups covering all middle pairs.
We add the ones in the string to the gain and store the result for this query.
We finish the loop having processed every query.
We return the list of answers.

maximum-average-subarray-i.hook: A fixed-size window sliding along the array: add one in, take one out.
maximum-average-subarray-i.ask: Given an array and a length k, find the contiguous subarray of exactly k elements with the largest average, and return that average.
maximum-average-subarray-i.exampleWhy: 12, -5, -6, 50 sums to 51, the best of any four in a row, and 51 / 4 = 12.75.

brute.idea: For every starting index, add up the next k numbers from scratch and keep the largest sum. Divide by k at the end.
steps: Pick a start i
Sum nums[i] to nums[i + k - 1]
Keep the largest sum; divide by k
brute.whySlow: Neighbouring windows share k - 1 numbers, yet each is re-added: up to 2.5 billion additions for n = 100,000.

optimal.insight: Sliding the window one step changes only two numbers: one enters on the right, one leaves on the left. Update the sum in O(1).
steps: Sum the first k numbers
Slide: add nums[i], subtract nums[i - k]
Track the largest window sum
Divide the best sum by k once

codeNotes.note: One in on the right, one out left

pitfalls: Start best at the first window, not 0: all numbers may be negative.

say.intro: Okay, Maximum Average Subarray one. We slide a window of exactly k numbers along the array. Which window has the highest average? With k equal to four, twelve, minus five, minus six, fifty sums to fifty one. That's the largest of any four in a row. So the answer is twelve point seven five.
say.brute: The brute force tries every starting index. It adds up the next k numbers from scratch, keeps the biggest sum, and divides by k at the end. But think about it. Neighbouring windows share all but one number. We re-add them every time. So the cost is n times k.
say.insight: Two observations. First, every window has the same length. So the biggest average is simply the biggest sum. Second, when the window moves one step, only two numbers change. One enters, one leaves. So keep a running sum. Add the new number, subtract the old one, and compare. Each step is constant work.
say.anim: We start by summing the first four numbers, giving window a value of two. Best is initialized to two, matching the first window's sum. At i equals four, fifty enters and one leaves, making window fifty-one. Fifty-one beats two, so best updates to fifty-one. At i equals five, three enters and twelve leaves, dropping window to forty-two. At i equals six, negative two enters and negative five leaves, window becomes forty-five. At i equals seven, negative four enters and negative six leaves, window becomes forty-seven. Best stays fifty-one, so dividing by four gives the final answer twelve point seven five.
say.code: Here's the code. We sum the first window, and call it the best. Then for each next index, one number comes in on the right, and one goes out on the left. We compare sums, not averages, so there's no division yet. Only at the very end do we divide once, by k, and return it.
say.outro: Linear time, constant space. It's a fixed size sliding window. Update the running total instead of recomputing it.

maximum-average-subarray-i.title: Maximum Average Subarray I
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container the problem expects for our method.
The method findMaxAverage takes the list nums and the window length k, and returns the best average as a float.
We start by adding up the first k numbers to get the sum of the initial window.
We record that first window sum as the best sum seen so far.
We loop index i from k to the end, so each step slides the window one position right.
We add the new number at i and subtract the number that just left, updating the sum in constant time.
We keep the larger of the best sum so far and the current window sum.
Finally we divide the best sum by k, since comparing sums is equivalent to comparing averages for equal lengths.

maximum-element-after-decreasing-and-rea.hook: Build the tallest staircase that starts at 1 and climbs at most one per step.
maximum-element-after-decreasing-and-rea.ask: Given positive integers, you may lower any value and reorder freely. The array must start at 1 and adjacent values may differ by at most 1. Return the largest value achievable.
maximum-element-after-decreasing-and-rea.exampleWhy: Sorted: 1, 2, 2, 3, 7, 9. Lower to 1, 2, 2, 3, 4, 5: each step rises at most one, ending at 5.

brute.idea: Build the staircase by repeatedly removing the smallest remaining value, and set each step to the smaller of that value and previous plus one.
steps: Find and remove the smallest remaining value
Step = min(value, previous step + 1)
Repeat until empty
brute.whySlow: Finding the minimum by scanning each time is selection sort: 100,000 values means about 5 billion comparisons.

optimal.insight: Values may only go down, so use small values early and big values late. After sorting, each element becomes min(itself, previous + 1).
steps: Sort ascending
Start the staircase at 0
Each value becomes min(value, previous + 1)
The last step is the answer

codeNotes.note: Small values first, big values last
So the first step becomes exactly 1
Climb by one, unless this value is too small

pitfalls: Values can be lowered but never raised: the cap is min, not max.
Counting sort gives O(n): values above n can be capped at n.

say.intro: This is Maximum Element After Decreasing and Rearranging. We can lower numbers and reorder them. The array must start at one. Neighbours can differ by at most one. How high can it climb? From seven, two, two, nine, three, one, we can build one, two, two, three, four, five. So the answer is five.
say.brute: A slow version builds the staircase step by step. Repeatedly find the smallest remaining number, and remove it. The next step is the smaller of that number and the previous step plus one. The logic is right. But finding the minimum by scanning every time? That's selection sort. n squared.
say.insight: Here's the thing. Numbers can only go down. So a big number is wasted early, and a small number blocks the climb late. That tells us to sort ascending. Then walk the sorted list. Each step wants to be previous plus one, but can't exceed its own value. Take the minimum of those two, every step. That builds the tallest staircase.
say.anim: We start with the array seven, two, two, nine, three, one, then sort it ascending. Current starts at zero, and we walk through each sorted value one by one. At value one, current becomes the smaller of one plus zero and one, so one. At value two, current increases to two, matching the rule of rising by at most one. At the second two, current stays capped at three instead of jumping higher. At value seven, current can only climb to four, since it must increase gradually. At value nine, current rises one more step to five, its final limit. The function returns five, the maximum possible value after rearranging and decreasing.
say.code: Now the code. We sort, so small values come first and big values last. Current starts at zero, so the first step becomes exactly one. For each number, current climbs by one, unless this value is too small. Then it's capped at the value. After the loop, current is the top of the staircase. Return it.
say.outro: n log n for the sort, then one pass. It's greedy. Sort, then make the locally best choice at every step.

maximum-element-after-decreasing-and-rea.title: Maximum Element After Decreasing and Rearranging
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container that the problem's required method lives in.
This method takes the array of positive integers and returns the largest possible maximum value after decreasing and rearranging.
We sort the array in ascending order so small values come first and large values come later.
We set cur to zero, representing the value before the first element, so the first element must become one.
We loop over each value x in the sorted array, processing them from smallest to largest.
We set cur to the smaller of cur plus one and x, since we can only lower values and steps are at most one.
After the loop, cur holds the final element's value, which is the largest achievable maximum, so we return it.

maximum-good-subarray-sum.hook: Subarray sums are prefix differences. Remember the cheapest prefix before each value.
maximum-good-subarray-sum.ask: Given an array and k, a subarray is good when its first and last elements differ by exactly k. Return the largest sum of a good subarray, or 0 if none exists.
maximum-good-subarray-sum.exampleWhy: 2, 4, 5 starts at 2 and ends at 5, a difference of 3, and sums to 11.

brute.idea: Try every start i, extend the end j while keeping a running sum, and record the sum whenever the endpoints differ by exactly k.
steps: Pick a start i, running sum 0
Extend j, adding nums[j]
abs(nums[i] - nums[j]) == k? Record the sum
brute.whySlow: 100,000 numbers give about 5 billion start and end pairs to check.

optimal.insight: Sum of i..j is a prefix difference. For end value x, pick a start valued x - k or x + k, with the smallest prefix before it.
steps: Walk left to right with a running prefix sum
Look up stored prefixes for values x - k and x + k
Candidate sum: prefix through x minus that prefix
Store this x with the prefix before it, if smaller

codeNotes.note: Value -> smallest prefix sum before it

codeNotes.match: for target in (x - k, x + k):
codeNotes.note: A good start differs from x by k
Sum from that start through x

codeNotes.match: if x not in minPrefix or prefix < minPrefix[x]:
codeNotes.note: Keep only the cheapest start for x

pitfalls: Sums can be negative: start best at minus infinity, not 0.
Store x after querying, so a start never pairs with itself.

say.intro: Okay, Maximum Good Subarray Sum. A subarray is good when its first and last numbers differ by exactly k. We want the good one with the biggest sum. With k equal to three, take two, four, five. It starts at two and ends at five, a difference of three. It sums to eleven, the best possible.
say.brute: The brute force picks every start, then extends the end one step at a time. It keeps a running sum. Whenever the two ends differ by exactly k, it records the sum. Simple and correct. But it checks every pair of start and end. That's n squared, about five billion pairs for a hundred thousand numbers.
say.insight: Here's the idea. A subarray sum is a difference of two prefix sums. If the end value is x, the start value must be x minus k or x plus k. Want a big sum? Then we want the start whose prefix before it is as small as possible. So a hash map stores, for every value, the smallest prefix seen before it.
say.anim: We start with an empty prefix map, prefix sum zero, and best set to negative infinity. At x equals negative one, we check targets negative four and two, neither found, so we store prefix zero for value negative one. At x equals three, targets zero and six are missing too, so we record prefix negative one for value three. At x equals two, target negative one matches, giving best equals four using prefix plus x minus stored prefix. At x equals four, targets one and seven are absent, so we save prefix four for value four. At x equals five, target two matches value two's stored prefix, updating best to eleven. The loop ends with final prefix thirteen, and the function returns the best value found. The maximum good subarray sum is eleven.
say.code: Let's walk the code. The map goes from each value to the smallest prefix sum before it. For each number x, a good start differs from x by k. So we check both partner values in the map. The sum from that start through x is prefix plus x, minus the stored prefix. Then we store x, keeping only the cheapest start. If no good subarray exists, we return zero.
say.outro: Linear time and space. It's arrays and hashing, with prefix sums. Every subarray sum becomes one lookup.

maximum-good-subarray-sum.title: Maximum Good Subarray Sum
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container this problem's method lives in.
The method takes the list nums and the integer k, and returns the largest good subarray sum.
We create an empty dictionary minPrefix that maps each value to the smallest prefix sum seen before any occurrence of it.
We start prefix at zero, representing the running sum of all elements before the current one.
We set best to negative infinity so any real subarray sum will beat it, and so we can detect no match.
We walk through each number x in nums, treating it as a possible last element of a good subarray.
For the current x, we try both possible start values, x minus k and x plus k, since the difference can go either way.
We check whether a start value matching that target has already appeared earlier in the array.
If so, the sum from that start to x is prefix plus x minus the stored smallest prefix, and we keep the maximum.
We then see whether x is new or has a smaller prefix than stored, since a smaller prefix gives a larger future sum.
In that case we record the current prefix as the best starting prefix for value x.
We add x to prefix so it now includes the current element for the next iteration.
Finally we return best, or zero if it never changed from negative infinity, meaning no good subarray exists.

maximum-length-substring-with-two-occurr.hook: Keep a window where no letter appears more than twice, and shrink only when one does.
maximum-length-substring-with-two-occurr.ask: Given a string, return the length of the longest substring in which every character appears at most two times.
maximum-length-substring-with-two-occurr.exampleWhy: bcba has two b's, one c and one a. Any five-letter window holds at least three b's.

brute.idea: From every start, extend right while counting letters; stop when some letter reaches three, and record the length.
steps: Pick a start i, fresh counts
Extend j, count s[j]
Count hits 3? Stop; else record length
brute.whySlow: A valid window holds at most 52 letters, but every start recounts up to 52 letters again.

optimal.insight: When a letter hits three, every longer window starting here is also invalid. So just move the left edge forward until that letter is back to two.
steps: Add s[right] to the counts
While its count exceeds 2, drop s[left]
Window length is a candidate
Each letter enters and leaves once

codeNotes.note: New letter enters on the right
Only the new letter can break the rule

pitfalls: Shrink with while, not if: you may need several steps to drop a repeat.

say.intro: This is Maximum Length Substring With Two Occurrences. We want the longest stretch where no letter shows up more than twice. Take b, c, b, b, b, c, b, a. The ending b, c, b, a has two b's, one c and one a. Every longer stretch has three b's. So the answer is four.
say.brute: The brute force starts at each index with fresh counts. It extends right, and stops as soon as some letter appears a third time. It records the longest valid stretch. Valid windows are short here, so it's not truly n squared. But each start recounts letters the previous start already counted.
say.insight: So here's the thing. Say adding a letter pushes its count to three. Any window still starting at the current left edge is broken. So move the left edge forward, removing letters, until that count drops back to two. Now the window is valid again. Both edges only move right. So each letter is handled at most twice.
say.anim: We start scanning the string bcbbbcba with empty counts, left and best both zero. As we add letters b and c, their counts stay at one or two, so best grows to three. At index three, count of b hits three, becoming invalid for this window. We shrink from the left, dropping letters until b's count falls back to two. Another b at index four pushes count to three again, so we shrink left further. Index six brings another b overflow, so left slides forward once more to fix it. Adding the final letter a keeps all counts valid, but best stays at four. The loop ends and the function returns four as the maximum valid length.
say.code: Now the code. At each position, the new letter enters on the right, and its count goes up. Only that new letter can break the rule. So while its count is above two, we shrink from the left. Decrease the leftmost letter's count, and move left forward. Now the window is valid, so we record its size. Return the best.
say.outro: Linear time, space bounded by the alphabet. It's a sliding window with a counter. Grow on the right, shrink on the left only when the rule breaks.

maximum-length-substring-with-two-occurr.title: Maximum Length Substring With Two Occurrences
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container the problem expects for our method.
The method takes the string s and returns the length of the longest substring where each character appears at most twice.
We make a default dictionary called count to track how many times each character appears in the current window.
We set both left, the window's start, and best, the longest valid length so far, to zero.
We loop over the string, with right as the window's end index and c as the character there.
We add one to the count for the new character c, since it just entered the window.
If c now appears more than twice, the window is invalid, so we keep shrinking it from the left.
We reduce the count of the character at the left edge, because that character is leaving the window.
We move left forward by one, and repeat until c is back down to two occurrences.
Now the window is valid, so we update best with the larger of its old value and the current window length.
After scanning the whole string, we return best as the longest valid substring length.

maximum-number-of-events-that-can-be-att.hook: One event per day. Each day, attend the open event that expires soonest.
maximum-number-of-events-that-can-be-att.ask: Given events with start and end days, you can attend one event per day on any day within its range. Return the maximum number of events you can attend.
maximum-number-of-events-that-can-be-att.exampleWhy: Day 1: [1,1]. Day 2: [2,2]. Day 3: [1,4]. Day 4: [3,4]. Event [1,2] has no day left.

brute.idea: Same greedy, no heap: walk every day and scan all events for the unattended open one that ends earliest.
steps: For each day from first start to last end
Scan all events open today and not attended
Attend the one with the earliest end
brute.whySlow: 100,000 days times 100,000 events is 10 billion scans; most events checked each day are not even open.

optimal.insight: Among events open today, the one ending soonest is the most urgent; the others can wait. A min-heap of end days gives it instantly.
steps: Sort events by start day
Push the end days of events starting by today
Pop the earliest end and attend it
Next day: discard events already over
Jump ahead when no event is open

codeNotes.note: Process events in order of start day
Nothing open: skip to the next start
Open event: remember its end day

pitfalls: Sorting by end day alone fails; you need the heap to pick among open events.
Skip empty gaps instead of looping day by day.

say.intro: Okay, Maximum Number of Events That Can Be Attended. Each event runs over a range of days, and we attend one event per day. Our events are one to four, day one, day two, one to two, and three to four. We can attend four. The one to two event loses out, because days one and two are taken.
say.brute: The brute force uses the right greedy rule, but no clever structure. For every day, scan all events. Find the open, unattended one that ends soonest, and attend it. The catch? It rescans every event on every day. That's days times events, about ten billion steps at full size.
say.insight: Here's the rule. On any day, attend the open event that ends soonest. Why? Anything ending later has more chances. Now, how do we find it fast? Sort events by start. Once an event opens, push its end day into a min heap. Pop the smallest to attend. And before each new day, throw away events that already ended.
say.anim: Events are sorted by start day, giving us this ordered list to process. On day one, we push all events starting today, ending days one, two, and four, into the heap. We pop the soonest ending event, end day one, attending it and moving to day two. On day two, event ending day two joins the heap, then we pop the smallest, attending it. Day three brings another event ending day four, and we pop the earliest remaining one. On day four, no new events start, so we just pop the last event ending day four. The heap is now empty and all events have been processed successfully. The function returns four, the maximum number of events we could attend.
say.code: Let's walk the code. We process events in order of start day. If nothing is open, we skip ahead to the next start. Each event that has started pushes its end day onto the heap. We pop the earliest ending one and count it. That's today's event. Then we move to the next day, and drop events that already ended. Return the count.
say.outro: n log n time, for sorting and heap work. It's a heap driving an earliest deadline first greedy.

maximum-number-of-events-that-can-be-att.title: Maximum Number of Events That Can Be Attended
lineNotes: We define the Solution class that holds the method for this problem.
The maxEvents method takes a list of events, each with a start day and an end day.
We sort events by start day so we can add them to consideration in chronological order.
We create an empty heap that will hold end days of events currently open for attending.
We set i to zero as our event pointer, n to the event count, and attended to zero.
We start the current day at zero and will move it forward as we attend events.
We keep looping while there are unseen events or open events still waiting in the heap.
If no events are open right now, we have nothing to attend and must jump ahead.
We jump day forward to the next event's start day, never moving backward.
While events have started by today, we keep pulling them in from the sorted list.
We push each newly opened event's end day onto the heap so the earliest deadline surfaces first.
We advance the pointer i to move on to the next unseen event.
We pop the smallest end day, attending the most urgent open event today.
We increase the attended count because we used today on one event.
We move to the next day since only one event can be attended per day.
Now we clean up expired events whose end day is before the new day.
We pop those expired end days since they can no longer be attended.
After the loop finishes, we return the total number of events attended.

maximum-number-of-vowels-in-a-substring-.hook: Count vowels in every window of length k without ever recounting.
maximum-number-of-vowels-in-a-substring-.ask: Given a lowercase string and a length k, return the largest number of vowels found in any substring of exactly k characters.
maximum-number-of-vowels-in-a-substring-.exampleWhy: lee, eet and ode each contain two vowels. No three-letter window has three.

brute.idea: For every start, count the vowels in the next k characters from scratch and keep the largest count.
steps: Pick a start i
Count vowels in s[i : i + k]
Keep the largest count
brute.whySlow: Neighbouring windows share k - 1 letters, yet each is recounted: billions of checks for long strings and large k.

optimal.insight: Moving the window one step adds one letter and removes one. Adjust the vowel count by those two letters only.
steps: Add the entering letter if it is a vowel
Once past k, remove the leaving letter if a vowel
Track the largest count

codeNotes.match: if i >= k and s[i - k] in vowels:

pitfalls: Only subtract once the window is full, when i reaches k.

say.intro: This is Maximum Number of Vowels in a Substring of Given Length. We look at every window of exactly k letters. Which one has the most vowels? In leetcode, with k equal to three, lee, eet and ode each have two vowels. None has three. So the answer is two.
say.brute: The brute force tries every starting point. It counts vowels in the next k letters from scratch, and keeps the largest count. That works. But neighbouring windows share all but one letter. We recount them every time. For long strings with a large k, that's n times k work.
say.insight: Here's the thing. When the window slides one step right, exactly one letter enters. One letter leaves. Everything in between is unchanged. So why recount? Keep a running vowel count. Add one if the entering letter is a vowel. Subtract one if the leaving letter was. Each step is constant work.
say.anim: We start with the string leetcode, window size three, and counters at zero. At index zero, letter l isn't a vowel, so count stays zero and best stays zero. At index one, e is a vowel, count becomes one, best updates to one. At index two, e again, count rises to two, best becomes two, the first window. Index three is t, not a vowel, no window removal yet, best stays two. At index four, c enters, the leftmost letter l leaves but wasn't a vowel, count drops to one. At index five, o adds a vowel making count two, then e leaves, dropping count back to one. Finally at index seven, e adds back to count two, and the function returns best as two.
say.code: Now the code. A set of vowels gives us a constant time check. We walk each index. If the entering letter is a vowel, add one. If the window is already full, look k places back. Was the leaving letter a vowel? Then subtract one. After that, update the best window so far. Return the best.
say.outro: Linear time, constant space. It's a fixed size sliding window. One letter in, one letter out, update the count.

maximum-number-of-vowels-in-a-substring-.title: Maximum Number of Vowels in a Substring of Given Length
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container the problem expects for our method.
The method maxVowels takes the string s and the window length k, and returns an integer answer.
We build a set of the five vowels so checking whether a letter is a vowel is fast.
We start both the current vowel count and the best count seen so far at zero.
We walk through the string one character at a time, tracking both the index i and the character c.
If the new character entering the window is a vowel, we check it for counting.
In that case we add one to the vowel count for the current window.
Once the index reaches k, the window is too long, and we check the letter that just fell off the left side.
If that departing letter was a vowel, we subtract one from the count so the window stays accurate.
After updating, we keep the larger of the best so far and the current window's vowel count.
Finally we return the best count, which is the most vowels found in any window of size k.

maximum-product-of-two-digits.hook: The biggest product of two digits always comes from the two biggest digits.
maximum-product-of-two-digits.ask: Given a positive integer n, return the largest product of any two of its digits. The same digit may be used twice only if it appears twice in n.
maximum-product-of-two-digits.exampleWhy: The digits are 2, 9, 4 and 7. The two largest, 9 and 7, multiply to 63.

brute.idea: List the digits and try the product of every pair of positions, keeping the largest.
steps: Split n into a list of digits
Multiply every pair i < j
Keep the largest product
brute.whySlow: With at most 10 digits this is tiny, but it checks every pair when only the top two matter.

optimal.insight: Digits are non-negative, so the product grows with each factor. Track only the largest and second largest digit in one pass.
steps: Peel off digits with mod 10
New largest? Old largest becomes second
Else maybe update second
Return largest times second

codeNotes.note: New maximum pushes the old one down

pitfalls: A repeated digit must fill second too; use elif d > second, not skip ties.

say.intro: Okay, Maximum Product of Two Digits. Take the digits of a number, and pick two to multiply. We want the largest product. For two thousand nine hundred forty seven, the digits are two, nine, four and seven. The best pair is nine and seven. That gives sixty three.
say.brute: The brute force lists the digits and multiplies every pair, keeping the largest. Honestly, with at most ten digits, that's fast. About forty five pairs. Its weakness is that it does far more work than needed. And it ignores the simple structure of the problem.
say.insight: So what's that structure? Digits are never negative. A bigger factor always gives a bigger or equal product. That means the answer is just the largest digit times the second largest. And we can track both in one pass, without storing the digits at all.
say.anim: We start with n equal to 2947, and first and second both set to zero. We extract the last digit, 7, and n becomes 294. Since 7 beats first, first becomes 7 and second stays 0. Next digit is 4, n becomes 29, but 4 is not bigger than first, 7. Since 4 beats second, second updates to 4. Next digit is 9, n becomes 2; since 9 beats first, first becomes 9 and second becomes 7. Final digit is 2, n becomes 0, too small to update first or second. Loop ends, and multiplying first times second gives the final answer, 63.
say.code: Let's read the code. First and second start at zero. While n has digits, we take the last one with n mod ten, then divide n by ten. If the digit beats first, it's a new maximum. The old one gets pushed down to second. Otherwise, if it beats second, it lands there. Ties land here too, so twenty two gives four. Return first times second.
say.outro: Linear in the number of digits, constant space. It's simple math. Track the top two values in a single pass.

maximum-product-of-two-digits.title: Maximum Product of Two Digits
lineNotes: We define a class named Solution, which holds the method that solves this problem.
The method maxProduct takes the integer n and returns the largest product of two of its digits.
We start both first and second at zero, since digits are never negative and these will hold the two biggest digits.
We loop while n is nonzero, peeling off one digit at a time until none remain.
We take n modulo ten to get the last digit and call it d.
We divide n by ten, dropping the last digit so the next pass sees the next one.
If d beats the current largest digit, it becomes a new champion and we must update both trackers.
We move the old first down into second and store d as the new first.
Otherwise, if d only beats second, it is the new runner-up while first stays unchanged.
We set second to d, which keeps second as the best digit that is not larger than first.
Finally we return first times second, the product of the two largest digits, which is the maximum possible.

maximum-product-of-two-elements-in-an-ar.hook: Maximise (a - 1) times (b - 1). Just find the two largest numbers in one pass.
maximum-product-of-two-elements-in-an-ar.ask: Given an array of positive integers, choose two different indices i and j and return the largest value of (nums[i] - 1) * (nums[j] - 1).
maximum-product-of-two-elements-in-an-ar.exampleWhy: The two largest values are 7 and 6, so (7 - 1) * (6 - 1) = 6 * 5 = 30.

brute.idea: Try every pair of different indices and compute the product of each value minus one. Keep the largest.
steps: Pick i and j with i < j
Compute (nums[i] - 1) * (nums[j] - 1)
Keep the largest
brute.whySlow: It checks every pair, about 125,000 for 500 numbers, when only the two largest values can win.

optimal.insight: All values are at least 1, so both factors are non-negative and grow with the value. The two largest numbers always win.
steps: Track the largest and second largest
Bigger than largest? Shift largest down
Else bigger than second? Replace second
Return (largest - 1) * (second - 1)

codeNotes.note: Largest and second largest so far
New maximum; old one becomes second
Apply the minus one at the end

pitfalls: Equal maximums count twice: [5,5] uses both, so ties must update second.

say.intro: This is Maximum Product of Two Elements in an Array. Pick two different positions. Subtract one from each value, and multiply. We want the largest result. In three, seven, one, five, six, two, the best choice is seven and six. That gives six times five, thirty.
say.brute: The brute force tries every pair of positions. It computes the product of each value minus one, and keeps the largest. Correct, but n squared. Five hundred numbers is over a hundred thousand pairs. And the answer only ever depends on two values. The largest, and the runner up.
say.insight: Here's why. Every value is at least one. So each factor, value minus one, is never negative. And it grows with the value. A bigger number can only help. So the answer always uses the largest and second largest numbers. And we can find both in a single pass.
say.anim: We start tracking the two largest values, first and second, both set to zero. X is 3, bigger than first, so first becomes 3 and second stays 0. X is 7, bigger than first, so first becomes 7 and second becomes 3. X is 1, too small for either slot, so nothing changes. X is 5, bigger than second, so second updates from 3 to 5. X is 6, again bigger than second, so second updates to 6. X is 2, not large enough to beat first or second, loop ends. Multiplying first minus one and second minus one gives the final answer, 30.
say.code: Now the code. We track the largest and second largest so far, starting at zero. For each number, is it a new maximum? Then the old first becomes second, and it takes first. Otherwise, if it fits between them, it's the new second. At the end, we apply the minus one to both, and multiply.
say.outro: Linear time, constant space. Track the top two values in one pass, instead of comparing every pair.

maximum-product-of-two-elements-in-an-ar.title: Maximum Product of Two Elements in an Array
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container the problem expects for our method.
The method maxProduct takes a list of positive integers called nums and returns the best product as an integer.
We start both first and second at zero, since they will track the two largest values seen so far.
We loop through every number x in nums, examining each one exactly once.
If x beats the current largest, it deserves to become the new first place.
We set first to x and push the old first down into second, keeping the top two ordered.
Otherwise, if x only beats second, it is the new runner up even though it is not the largest.
We update second to x, since it is bigger than the old second but not bigger than first.
Finally we subtract one from each of the two largest values and return their product, which is the maximum possible.

maximum-sum-circular-subarray.hook: Kadane, plus one twist: a wrapping subarray is the total minus the worst middle.
maximum-sum-circular-subarray.ask: Given a circular array, where the end connects back to the start, return the largest sum of a non-empty subarray that uses each element at most once.
maximum-sum-circular-subarray.exampleWhy: Wrap around: 4, 3, -4, 2, -1, 5 sums to 9, skipping only the -6.

brute.idea: Try every start and every length up to n, walking around the circle with a running sum, and keep the largest.
steps: Pick a start i
Extend up to n elements, wrapping with mod n
Keep the largest running sum
brute.whySlow: 30,000 numbers give about 900 million start and length pairs.

optimal.insight: A wrapping subarray is everything except one middle chunk. So its best sum is the total minus the minimum subarray, found with a second Kadane.
steps: Kadane for the maximum subarray
Kadane for the minimum subarray
Wrapping best = total - minimum
All negative? Return the maximum alone

codeNotes.note: Kadane: extend or restart, for maximum
All negative: removing everything is not allowed

pitfalls: All negative: total - minimum is 0, an empty subarray. Return the maximum instead.

say.intro: Okay, Maximum Sum Circular Subarray. The array is a circle, so a subarray can wrap past the end. We want the biggest sum. Take three, minus four, two, minus one, five, minus six, four. Start at the last four, wrap around to three, and keep going up to five. Only minus six is skipped. That sums to nine.
say.brute: The brute force tries every starting point and every length up to n. It walks around the circle, keeping a running sum. It never misses a candidate. But that's n squared. With thirty thousand numbers, it's close to a billion steps.
say.insight: Here's the trick. There are two cases. A normal subarray is plain Kadane. A wrapping one takes everything except one chunk in the middle. So its sum is the total minus that chunk. To maximise it, remove the minimum subarray. That's Kadane again, run for minimums. One catch. If every number is negative, return the plain maximum.
say.anim: We start Kadane style tracking, initializing current max and min sums to zero. Best max and best min both start at three, the first array value, and total resets to zero. Processing three, current max becomes three, current min becomes three, total grows to three. At negative four, current max drops to negative one, current min falls to negative four, updating bestMin. With two, current max rises to two while current min stays low around negative two. At five, current max jumps to six, giving a new best max of six so far. At negative six, current min bottoms out at negative six, our new best min, since wrap subtracts this chunk. Bestmax six stays nonnegative, so final answer compares it to total minus bestmin, giving nine.
say.code: Let's walk the code. Kadane for the maximum: extend the running sum, or restart it. Same idea for the minimum. And each number goes into the total. After the loop, we check for all negatives. Removing everything isn't allowed, so if the best maximum is negative, return it. Otherwise, take the larger of the normal case and the wrap around case, total minus the minimum.
say.outro: Linear time, constant space. It's Kadane's algorithm run twice, using the complement to handle the wrap.

maximum-sum-circular-subarray.title: Maximum Sum Circular Subarray
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, as the problem platform expects for this method.
The method takes the list nums and returns the largest sum of a circular subarray.
We start the running maximum and running minimum subarray sums at zero before scanning.
We seed the best maximum and best minimum with the first element so the subarray is never empty.
We set total to zero so we can add up every element for the wrapping case.
We loop over each number x in nums, updating all our running values in one pass.
The current max either extends the previous run with x or restarts at x, whichever is larger.
The current min either extends the previous run with x or restarts at x, whichever is smaller.
We update the best maximum if the current max run beats it, which handles the non-wrapping case.
We update the best minimum if the current min run beats it, giving the chunk to cut out.
We add x to total so we know the whole array sum.
If the best maximum is negative, every element is negative, so removing the minimum chunk would leave nothing.
In that case we return the best maximum, which is the single largest element.
Otherwise we return the larger of the plain best and the wrapping best, which is total minus the best minimum.

maximum-sum-of-distinct-subarrays-with-l.hook: A fixed window of length k, but only windows with no repeats count.
maximum-sum-of-distinct-subarrays-with-l.ask: Given an array and k, return the largest sum among subarrays of length exactly k whose elements are all distinct. Return 0 if no such subarray exists.
maximum-sum-of-distinct-subarrays-with-l.exampleWhy: 4, 2, 9 has no repeats and sums to 15. Windows with two 9s do not qualify.

brute.idea: For every start, take the next k elements, check they are distinct with a set, and if so compare their sum.
steps: Pick a start i
Window = nums[i : i + k]
All distinct? Compare its sum
brute.whySlow: Each window rebuilds its set and sum from scratch: k = 50,000 and n = 100,000 means billions of steps.

optimal.insight: Slide the window and keep a count map plus a running sum. The window is all distinct exactly when the map has k keys.
steps: Add the entering number to the counts and sum
Past k, remove the leaving number
Delete keys whose count hits 0
k distinct keys? Compare the sum

codeNotes.note: Keep keys equal to distinct values
k keys in k slots: no repeats

pitfalls: Delete zero-count keys, or the distinct check over-counts.

say.intro: This is Maximum Sum of Distinct Subarrays With Length K. We look at every window of exactly k numbers. Only windows with no repeats count. We want the biggest sum. In one, five, four, two, nine, nine, nine, with k equal to three, four, two, nine sums to fifteen. The later windows repeat nine.
say.brute: The brute force takes every window. It builds a set to check that all values differ, and sums the window if so. Simple and correct. But each window rebuilds its set and its sum from scratch. That's n times k. For large k, that's billions of steps.
say.insight: So slide the window instead. Keep a running sum, and a count of each value inside. When a number enters, add it. When one leaves, subtract it, and delete its key once its count hits zero. Now here's the neat part. The window has no repeats exactly when the number of keys equals k.
say.anim: We start with the array and k equal to three, sliding a window to find distinct sums. By index two, the window holds one, five, four, summing to ten, a new best. At index three, value one repeats, so it's removed as the window slides forward. Index four adds nine, but five drops out, giving window sum fifteen, our new best. At index five, nine repeats so the window isn't distinct, no update happens here. Finally at index six, two leaves and three nines remain, so count stays below three. The loop ends and the function returns fifteen as the maximum distinct subarray sum.
say.code: Now the code. The entering number joins the window, in the map and in the sum. Once we're past k, the number leaving on the left comes out. If its count hits zero, we delete its key, so keys always match distinct values. Then the check. k keys in k slots means no repeats, so we compare the sum with the best. Return the best.
say.outro: Linear time, space up to k. It's a sliding window with a hash map tracking which values are inside.

maximum-sum-of-distinct-subarrays-with-l.title: Maximum Sum of Distinct Subarrays With Length K
lineNotes: We define the Solution class that holds the method for this problem.
The method takes the array nums and window length k, and returns the best distinct window sum as an integer.
We create a count map defaulting to zero to track how many times each value appears in the current window.
We start both the running window sum and the best answer at zero, which also covers the no valid subarray case.
We loop through the array with index i and value x, treating each element as the new right edge of the window.
We add one to the count of x since it just entered the window.
We add x to the running window sum to keep the total current.
Once i reaches k, the window has grown too large, so we must drop the leftmost element.
We find the outgoing element, which sits k positions behind the current index.
We decrease the count of that old value because it is leaving the window.
We subtract the old value from the window sum so it covers only the last k elements.
If the old value's count dropped to zero, it no longer appears in the window.
We delete that key so the number of keys reflects only values truly present.
If the map has exactly k keys, all k window elements are distinct, so the window is valid.
We update best to the larger of itself and the current window sum.
After processing every element, we return the largest valid sum found, or zero if none existed.

maximum-xor-of-two-numbers-in-an-array.hook: Checking every pair is quadratic. Greedily claiming one bit at a time is linear.
maximum-xor-of-two-numbers-in-an-array.ask: Given a list of non-negative integers, find the largest value you can get by XOR-ing any two of them together.
maximum-xor-of-two-numbers-in-an-array.exampleWhy: 5 is 00101 and 25 is 11001. They differ in the top three bits, giving 11100, which is 28.

brute.idea: Try every pair of numbers, XOR them, and keep the largest result seen.
steps: Pick nums[i]
XOR it with every nums[j] after it
Keep the maximum
brute.whySlow: With 200,000 numbers that is about 20 billion XORs, far beyond any time limit.

optimal.insight: A high bit beats all lower bits combined. Decide bits from the top: keep a 1 if two prefixes can XOR to it.
steps: Go from the highest bit down to bit 0
Collect every number's prefix down to this bit
Guess the answer gets a 1 at this bit
If two prefixes XOR to the guess, keep it

codeNotes.note: Make room for the next bit

codeNotes.match: prefixes = {num >> bit for num in nums}
codeNotes.note: Every number cut to this length

codeNotes.match: if any(want ^ p in prefixes for p in prefixes):
codeNotes.note: a ^ b = want means b = a ^ want

pitfalls: A bitwise trie gives the same O(n · 32) bound; either is accepted.
Prefixes must be compared, not whole numbers: lower bits are still undecided.

say.intro: Okay, Maximum XOR of Two Numbers in an Array. We get a list of non negative integers. We want the biggest XOR of any two of them. Take three, ten, five, twenty five, two, eight. The winner is five with twenty five. They disagree in the top three bits, so the XOR is twenty eight.
say.brute: The brute force tries every pair. For each number, XOR it with every number after it, and keep the largest result. Simple and correct. But it's n squared. With two hundred thousand numbers, that's around twenty billion pairs. Hopeless.
say.insight: Here's the key fact. One high bit is worth more than all the lower bits together. So we build the answer greedily, from the top bit down. At each bit, we guess the answer can have a one there. Can any two numbers, cut to that many leading bits, XOR to our guess? Then the guess holds. A hash set checks that in one pass.
say.anim: We start with ans at zero and scan bits from the highest down, building the answer greedily. At bit four, prefixes are just zero and one, so trying want equals one succeeds, ans becomes one. At bit three, prefixes include zero, one, and three, so want equals three works, ans becomes three. At bit two, prefixes are zero, one, two, six, want equals seven succeeds, ans becomes seven. At bit one, prefixes come from deeper shifts, but want equals fifteen fails, so ans stays fourteen. At bit zero, prefixes are full numbers, want equals twenty nine fails, ans stays at twenty eight. The loop finishes after checking every bit from high to low. The function returns twenty eight, the maximum XOR of any two numbers in the array.
say.code: Let's walk the code. The answer starts at zero, and we loop from the highest bit first. We shift the answer left to make room for the next bit. Every number gets cut to this length, into a set. Then we optimistically guess a one here. Now, if a XOR b equals our guess, then b equals a XOR the guess. So we look that up in the set. Found it? Keep the guess.
say.outro: The number of values times the bit width. It's bit manipulation. Decide bits greedily, from the top down.

maximum-xor-of-two-numbers-in-an-array.title: Maximum XOR of Two Numbers in an Array
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container the interview platform expects for our method.
The method findMaximumXOR takes a list of non-negative integers and returns the largest XOR of any two of them.
We start the answer at zero and will build it one bit at a time from the top.
We loop over bit positions from the highest bit in the largest number down to bit zero.
We shift the answer left by one, making room for the new lowest bit, which starts as zero.
We collect every number shifted right by this bit, giving the set of prefixes down to the current bit.
We form a candidate called want by setting the new lowest bit of the answer to one, hoping to get it.
If any prefix XORed with want is also a prefix, then two numbers can produce that candidate.
In that case we accept the candidate and keep the one bit in the answer.
After all bits are decided, we return the answer, which is the maximum XOR.

merge-two-2d-arrays-by-summing-values.hook: Two lists already sorted by id. Walk them together like the merge step of merge sort.
merge-two-2d-arrays-by-summing-values.ask: Two lists of id and value pairs are each sorted by unique id. Combine them into one id-sorted list, adding values when an id appears in both.
merge-two-2d-arrays-by-summing-values.exampleWhy: Ids 1 and 4 appear in both lists, so their values add up. Ids 2 and 3 appear once and copy over.

brute.idea: Ignore the sorted order. Add every pair into a dictionary keyed by id, then sort the keys.
steps: Sum values per id in a dictionary
Sort the ids
Emit id and total pairs
brute.whySlow: It re-sorts data that already arrived sorted, paying an extra log factor and a hash map for nothing.

optimal.insight: Both lists are sorted by id, so the smaller front id is always the next id of the answer.
steps: Put one pointer at the front of each list
Equal ids: emit the sum, advance both
Otherwise emit the smaller id, advance that pointer
Copy whatever is left of either list

codeNotes.match: while i < len(nums1) and j < len(nums2):

pitfalls: Advance both pointers on equal ids, or the id is emitted twice.
Do not forget the tails after the loop ends.

say.intro: This is Merge Two 2D Arrays by Summing Values. Each list holds pairs of id and value, sorted by id, with no repeats inside a list. We merge them into one sorted list. Ids one and four appear in both, so their values add to six and six. Ids two and three just copy across.
say.brute: The brute force ignores the order we were given. Pour every pair into a dictionary, adding values for the same id. Then sort the ids, and write out each id with its total. It works. But it sorts data that was already sorted. That's an extra log factor, plus a hash map.
say.insight: Here's the thing. Both lists are sorted. So the next id in the answer is always the smaller of the two front ids. Sound familiar? It's the merge step from merge sort. Keep a pointer into each list. If the front ids match, emit their sum and step both. Otherwise, emit the smaller one, and step only that list.
say.anim: We start with two sorted lists and pointers i and j both at zero. Both front ids are one, so we sum their values and add six to the result. Now id two is smaller than id three, so we take two with value three directly. Id three is smaller than id four, so we append three with value two from the second list. Both remaining ids are four, so we merge them into six and advance both pointers. Both lists are exhausted, so no leftover elements need extending. The final merged result is one six, two three, three two, and four six.
say.code: Now the code. We loop while both lists still have pairs, reading the two fronts. Same id? Add the values, append the pair, and advance both pointers. Otherwise, the smaller id goes next, and only its pointer moves. After the loop, one list may have leftovers. They're already sorted, so we just append them.
say.outro: Linear time, with no extra structure. It's two pointers, the classic merge of two sorted sequences.

merge-two-2d-arrays-by-summing-values.title: Merge Two 2D Arrays by Summing Values
lineNotes: We define a class named Solution, as the problem platform expects for this method.
The method mergeArrays takes two id and value lists, each already sorted by id, and returns the merged list.
We set both pointers, i and j, to zero so each starts at the front of its list.
We create an empty result list that will hold the merged pairs in id order.
We loop while both lists still have unread pairs, since we need a front from each to compare.
We grab the current pair from each list and name them a and b for easy comparison.
If both pairs have the same id, we must combine them into a single entry.
We append a new pair with that shared id and the sum of both values.
We move the first pointer forward because that pair has been used.
We move the second pointer forward too, since its pair was also consumed.
Otherwise, if the id in a is smaller, it must come next in the sorted answer.
We append pair a to the result because no id in the other list can match it.
We advance the first pointer to look at the next pair of the first list.
In the remaining case, the id in b is smaller, so b comes next.
We append pair b to the result since it has the smallest unused id.
We advance the second pointer to move past the pair we just added.
One list is exhausted, so we append whatever remains of the first list, already sorted and unmatched.
We likewise append any remaining pairs from the second list, which also have no partners left.
We return the merged list, sorted by id with duplicate ids summed.

minimized-maximum-of-products-distribute.hook: Do not build the distribution. Guess the maximum, and ask whether it is enough.
minimized-maximum-of-products-distribute.ask: You have n stores and several product types with quantities. Each store gets at most one type. Spread everything so the largest amount any store holds is as small as possible, and return that amount.
