minimized-maximum-of-products-distribute.exampleWhy: With cap 3, eleven needs four stores and six needs two: exactly six stores. Cap 2 would need nine.

brute.idea: Try every cap x from 1 upward. The first cap where the stores needed fit within n is the answer.
steps: Each type needs ceil(q / x) stores
Stop at the first x that fits
brute.whySlow: Quantities reach 100,000, so we may test 100,000 caps, each scanning all product types.

optimal.insight: If cap x fits, every larger cap fits too. That yes or no answer is monotonic, so binary search the cap.
steps: Search caps between 1 and the largest quantity
Stores needed: sum of ceil(q / mid)
Fits? try a smaller cap: hi = mid
Too many stores? lo = mid + 1

codeNotes.match: stores = sum((q + mid - 1) // mid for q in quantities)

codeNotes.note: Fits: this cap might be the answer
Too many stores: cap must grow

pitfalls: Start lo at 1, never 0, or the division crashes.
Use ceiling division: 11 items at cap 3 need four stores, not three.

say.intro: Okay, Minimized Maximum of Products Distributed to Any Store. We have n stores, and piles of different product types. A store may take only one type. We want the fullest store as empty as possible. With six stores, and piles of eleven and six, the best cap is three.
say.brute: The brute force tries caps one by one. For a cap x, a pile of q items needs q over x stores, rounded up. Add that over all piles. The first cap that fits within n stores is the answer. The problem? Caps can reach a hundred thousand. And every check scans every pile.
say.insight: Now notice something. If a cap works, any bigger cap works too, because bigger caps only need fewer stores. So the yes or no answer flips exactly once. Whenever feasibility is monotonic like that, binary search the answer. Each check is still one pass. But we only need about seventeen of them.
say.anim: We start with lo at 1 and hi at 11, the largest quantity to distribute. Mid becomes 6, and splitting quantities into groups of 6 needs only 3 stores. Since 3 stores fits within 6 allowed, we shrink hi down to 6. Now mid is 3, but distributing with cap 3 requires 6 stores, too many. Since 6 exceeds our limit of 6 stores isn't failing, hi tightens to 3. Mid becomes 2, needing 9 stores, far more than the allowed 6. Since 9 exceeds 6, we raise lo to mid plus one, which is 3. Loop ends since lo equals hi, and the function returns 3 as the answer.
say.code: Here's the code. The cap range to search runs from one up to the biggest pile. We take the middle cap. For each product type, ceiling division tells us how many stores it needs. Does the total fit within n? Then this cap might be the answer, so hi moves to mid. Too many stores? The cap must grow, so lo moves past mid. Return lo.
say.outro: From linear in the largest pile, down to logarithmic checks. That's binary search on the answer.

minimized-maximum-of-products-distribute.title: Minimized Maximum of Products Distributed to Any Store
lineNotes: We define the Solution class, which holds the method that solves this distribution problem.
The method takes the number of stores and the list of product quantities, and returns the smallest possible maximum load.
We set the search range for the cap from one up to the largest single quantity.
We keep searching while the low end is below the high end, narrowing toward the smallest workable cap.
We pick the middle value of the range as the candidate cap to test.
For each quantity we round up its division by the cap to count stores needed, then add them all.
If the stores needed do not exceed n, this cap works, so we check the condition.
Since the cap works, we move the high end down to mid, in case a smaller cap also works.
Otherwise the cap is too small and needs too many stores, so we handle that case here.
We discard mid and everything below it by setting low to mid plus one.
When low meets high, that value is the smallest feasible cap, so we return it.

minimum-add-to-make-parentheses-valid.hook: You do not need a real stack here. One counter of open brackets is enough.
minimum-add-to-make-parentheses-valid.ask: Given a string of only open and close parentheses, return the fewest parentheses you must insert anywhere to make it balanced.
minimum-add-to-make-parentheses-valid.exampleWhy: Two closers have no opener before them, and two openers at the end never close: two plus two insertions.

brute.idea: Keep deleting matched "()" pairs until none remain. Whatever is left must each get a partner.
steps: Find an adjacent "()" pair
Delete it and repeat
Leftover length is the answer
brute.whySlow: Each deletion rescans and rebuilds the string, so 1,000 characters can cost about half a million character steps.

optimal.insight: A stack of open brackets only ever holds "(", so its size is all that matters. Track it with one counter.
steps: open counts unmatched "(" so far
On "(": open += 1
On ")" with open > 0: match it
On ")" with open = 0: we must add a "("
Answer: added plus leftover open

pitfalls: A closer with nothing open cannot borrow from later openers: count it immediately.

say.intro: This is Minimum Add to Make Parentheses Valid. We get a string of brackets, and may insert brackets anywhere. What's the fewest insertions that balances it? In our example, two closers arrive with nothing open. And two openers at the end never get closed. That's four insertions.
say.brute: The brute force keeps deleting matched pairs. Find an opener directly followed by a closer, remove the pair, and repeat. Once no pair is left, every remaining bracket needs its own partner. So the leftover length is the answer. But each removal rebuilds the string. That's n squared.
say.insight: The usual tool is a stack of open brackets. But think about it. That stack only ever holds the same symbol. So its size is all we need. One counter tracks waiting openers. A closer either matches one of them, or it's an orphan. And an orphan forces an insertion right now.
say.anim: We start with open_count and added both at zero for the string. First character is an open paren, so open_count increases to one. Next is a close paren, and since open_count is positive, it decreases back to zero. Another close paren arrives, but open_count is zero, so added increases to one. Another close paren with nothing open means added climbs to two. The remaining two characters are open parens, pushing open_count up to two. Finally we add leftover open_count to added for the total insertions needed. The function returns four, matching the expected answer.
say.code: Let's walk the code. Open counts the unmatched openers waiting. A new opener joins the wait, so open goes up. A closer with something open matches a waiting opener, so open goes down. A closer with nothing open is an orphan. We insert an opener for it, so added goes up. At the end, leftover openers need closers. Return added plus open.
say.outro: One pass, constant space. It's a stack collapsed into a counter, the standard bracket matching trick.

minimum-add-to-make-parentheses-valid.title: Minimum Add to Make Parentheses Valid
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container the problem expects for our method.
The method takes the string s of parentheses and returns the minimum number of insertions as an integer.
We start open_count at zero, which stands in for the size of a stack of unmatched open brackets.
We start added at zero to count the open brackets we must insert for close brackets that have no partner.
We walk through the string one character at a time, handling each parenthesis in order.
If the current character is an open parenthesis, it might be matched later, so we handle it here.
We increase open_count by one because there is now one more unmatched open bracket waiting.
Otherwise the character is a close bracket, and if open_count is above zero we have an open bracket to pair it with.
We decrease open_count by one because this close bracket cancels one waiting open bracket.
If there is no waiting open bracket, this close bracket can never be matched by anything earlier.
We increase added by one, since we must insert an open bracket before this close bracket to fix it.
At the end we return added plus open_count, covering unmatched closes fixed plus unmatched opens that each need a closing bracket.

minimum-amount-of-time-to-fill-cups.hook: Two cups per second, but never two of the same type. The biggest pile sets the floor.
minimum-amount-of-time-to-fill-cups.ask: Each second you may fill two cups of different types, or one cup of any type. Given how many cold, warm and hot cups you need, return the minimum seconds.
minimum-amount-of-time-to-fill-cups.exampleWhy: Warm needs four cups and can only be filled once per second, so at least four seconds. Four is achievable.

brute.idea: Simulate. Every second, fill one cup of each of the two largest piles, then re-sort.
steps: Sort the three piles
Fill the two largest, one cup each
Count seconds until all are empty
brute.whySlow: Runs once per second of the answer. Amounts are tiny here, but a closed formula needs no loop at all.

optimal.insight: Two limits: the largest pile needs one second per cup, and every second fills at most two cups. The answer is the larger limit.
steps: Sort so c is the largest pile
If a + b ≤ c, the big pile alone decides: c
Otherwise pairs always exist: ceil(total / 2)

codeNotes.note: One cup of c per second
Two cups per second, rounded up

pitfalls: Round the total up: five cups need three seconds, not two.

say.intro: Okay, Minimum Amount of Time to Fill Cups. A dispenser makes cold, warm and hot water. Each second, we fill two cups of different types, or just one cup. With one cold, four warm and two hot, we need four seconds. Why? The warm cups alone take four.
say.brute: The brute force simulates the greedy schedule. Every second, take one cup from each of the two biggest piles. Then sort again, so the biggest stay on top. Count the seconds until everything is empty. It's correct. But it loops once for every second of the answer.
say.insight: Think about lower bounds instead. The biggest pile shrinks by at most one per second. So we need at least that many seconds. And no second fills more than two cups. So we need at least half the total, rounded up. One of these limits is always reachable. So the answer is just the larger of the two.
say.anim: We start with cups needing one, four, and two seconds of hot or cold water. After sorting, a is 1, b is 2, and c is 4, the largest pile. Since a plus b is 3, which is less than or equal to c, we just use c. The function returns 4, since filling the biggest pile alone takes the longest.
say.code: Now the code. We sort, so c is the largest pile. Can the small piles keep up? If together they're no bigger than c, they can't. They pair with c every second and still run out. So the answer is c, one cup of c per second. Otherwise, it's two cups per second. Return the total divided by two, rounded up.
say.outro: Constant time, from two simple bounds. It's greedy. Find the lower bound, then show it's achievable.

minimum-amount-of-time-to-fill-cups.title: Minimum Amount of Time to Fill Cups
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container the problem expects for our method.
The method fillCups takes the list amount holding the counts of cold, warm and hot cups needed.
We sort the three counts so a is the smallest, b the middle, and c the largest pile.
If the two smaller piles together do not exceed the largest, the largest pile is the bottleneck.
In that case we return c, since each second can fill only one cup from the biggest pile.
Otherwise we can pair cups nearly every second, so we return the total divided by two, rounded up.

minimum-cost-to-cut-a-stick.hook: The order of cuts changes the price. Choose the last cut of each piece, not the first.
minimum-cost-to-cut-a-stick.ask: A stick of length n must be cut at given positions. Each cut costs the length of the piece being cut. Pick the order of cuts that minimises the total cost.
minimum-cost-to-cut-a-stick.exampleWhy: Cutting at 3, then 5, then 1, then 4 costs 7 + 4 + 3 + 2 = 16. No order is cheaper.

brute.idea: For a piece from lo to hi, try every cut inside it as the next cut, and recurse on both halves.
steps: List the cuts strictly inside lo..hi
Try each as the first cut
Cost = hi - lo + both halves
Take the minimum
brute.whySlow: The same sub-piece is solved again and again; with 100 cuts the number of orders explodes.

optimal.insight: A piece is defined by two neighbouring cut positions. Sort cuts, add both ends, and solve every interval once, shortest first.
steps: c = [0] + sorted cuts + [n]
dp[i][j]: cheapest way to finish piece c[i]..c[j]
Try each cut k between i and j
dp[i][j] = c[j] - c[i] + min(dp[i][k] + dp[k][j])

codeNotes.note: Cut positions plus both stick ends

codeNotes.match: best = min(dp[i][k] + dp[k][j] for k in range(i + 1, j))

pitfalls: Index the DP by cut positions, not by length n: n can be a million.
Forgetting to sort cuts breaks the neighbour structure.

say.intro: This is Minimum Cost to Cut a Stick. A stick of length seven must be cut at one, three, four and five. Each cut costs the length of the piece it splits. Cut at three first, then five, one and four. That costs sixteen. No order does better.
say.brute: The brute force tries every possible first cut on a piece. That cut costs the piece length. Then we recurse on the left part and the right part, and keep the cheapest choice. Correct. But it solves the same smaller pieces over and over. So it grows exponentially.
say.insight: Here's the thing. Every piece that ever appears runs between two neighbouring positions in the sorted cuts, with zero and n added at the ends. So there are only about m squared distinct pieces. Solve each one once, from short to long. For a piece, try every cut inside it, and add the piece length.
say.anim: We build the cut array by adding stick ends zero and seven to the sorted cuts. A dp table is created to store minimum cost for every interval between two cuts. We start with intervals of length two, the smallest possible piece ranges. Each small interval costs just its length, since no cuts lie strictly inside it. Now length three intervals combine two smaller pieces, picking the cheapest split point. Length four intervals reuse previous results, like dp at zero to four becoming ten. Finally the full interval from zero to seven is solved using all smaller subresults. The function returns sixteen, the minimum total cost to make all the cuts.
say.code: Let's walk the code. The positions list holds the sorted cuts, plus both stick ends. We loop over short intervals before long ones. For each interval, we find the best first cut inside, the split with the cheapest left plus right. Then we pay this piece's length once. The answer sits in the cell for the whole stick.
say.outro: Cubic in the number of cuts, instead of exponential. It's interval dynamic programming, a two dimensional classic.

minimum-cost-to-cut-a-stick.title: Minimum Cost to Cut a Stick
lineNotes: We define a class named Solution, as required by the problem's submission format.
The minCost method takes the stick length n and the list of cut positions, and returns the minimum total cost.
We sort the cuts and add zero and n at the ends, so every piece sits between two neighbouring positions.
We store the number of positions in m, which is the number of cuts plus two.
We build an m by m table dp of zeros, where dp at i and j is the best cost for that piece.
We loop over interval length in index steps, starting at two, so shorter intervals are solved before longer ones.
For each length, we loop over every starting index i so that the end index still fits inside the array.
We set j to i plus length, giving the right end of the current piece.
We try every cut k strictly between i and j as the first cut, and keep the cheapest sum of the two sub-piece costs.
The cost of this piece is its actual length, c at j minus c at i, plus the best split cost found.
The answer is the table entry for the whole stick, from the first position to the last.

minimum-cost-walk-in-weighted-graph.hook: AND only ever turns bits off. So the cheapest walk uses every edge it can reach.
minimum-cost-walk-in-weighted-graph.ask: In a weighted undirected graph, a walk may repeat edges, and its cost is the bitwise AND of its edge weights. For each query pair, return the minimum walk cost, or -1 if unreachable.
minimum-cost-walk-in-weighted-graph.exampleWhy: 0 and 3 share a component whose weights 7, 7, 1 AND to 1. Node 4 is isolated, so -1.

brute.idea: For each query, BFS from the start to find its whole component, AND every edge weight inside, and check the end is in it.
steps: BFS from u over all edges
AND each weight met along the way
v reached? answer the AND, else -1
brute.whySlow: Every query re-explores its component: 100,000 queries on a 100,000-edge graph is 10 billion steps.

optimal.insight: Walks may repeat edges, so a walk can touch every edge of its component. ANDing more only lowers cost: answer = AND of the whole component.
steps: Union-find over the nodes
Each root stores the AND of its component edges
Merging two roots ANDs their values and the new weight
Query: same root? its AND, else -1

codeNotes.note: Fold both sides and this edge

pitfalls: Do not search for a shortest path: extra edges can only help an AND.
Start costs at -1 (all ones), not 0, or every AND collapses to 0.

say.intro: Okay, Minimum Cost Walk in Weighted Graph. A walk may reuse edges and nodes. Its cost is the bitwise AND of every weight it crosses. For each query, we want the cheapest walk between two nodes. Here, nodes zero and three cost one. Node four has no edges, so that query is minus one.
say.brute: The brute force answers each query on its own. Search from the start node, and visit its whole component. AND together every edge weight you meet. Did we reach the end node? Then that AND is the answer. Otherwise, minus one. Correct, but every query explores the graph again.
say.insight: Here's the insight. AND can only switch bits off, never on. And a walk may repeat edges. So it can detour across every edge in its component and come back. That means the cheapest walk just ANDs the whole component. Now it's a grouping problem. Union find handles that almost for free, storing one AND per group.
say.anim: We start with each node as its own parent and cost set to minus one, meaning unvisited. Processing edge zero to one with weight seven, we union their roots and set cost of root one to seven. Next edge one to three with weight seven merges their components, keeping cost seven since anding seven with seven stays seven. Edge one to two with weight one unions again, anding cost down to one for that merged group. Now all of zero, one, two, three share one root, carrying the final cost of one. Querying zero and three, both find root two, so the answer is their component cost, one. Querying three and four, their roots differ since four is isolated, so the result is negative one. The final output is one and negative one, matching the expected answer.
say.code: Now the code. Every node starts as its own parent, with cost minus one. Minus one has every bit set. Find walks to the root, and path halving keeps trees flat. For each edge, we find both roots. We fold both sides and this edge into one AND, and link them. For each query, the same component gives the stored AND. Otherwise it's unreachable, so minus one.
say.outro: Near linear time for all queries together. It's union find, carrying a summary per component.

minimum-cost-walk-in-weighted-graph.title: Minimum Cost Walk in Weighted Graph
lineNotes: We define the Solution class that holds the method for this problem.
The method takes the node count, the edge list, and the queries, and returns a list of answers.
We start a union find structure where every node is its own parent.
We store an AND value per node, starting at negative one, which has all bits set.
We define find to locate the root representative of a node's component.
We loop climbing upward while the current node is not its own parent.
We apply path compression by pointing the node to its grandparent to speed up later searches.
We then move up to that parent and continue the climb.
Once the node is its own parent, we return it as the root.
We go through every edge with its endpoints u and v and weight w.
We find the roots of both endpoints to see which components they belong to.
We fold the weight and the first component's AND into the second root's cost, since the merged component's walk can use all those edges.
We link the first root under the second so the two components become one.
We create an empty list to collect the answers.
We go through each query pair of start s and target t.
We find the roots of the start and target to check whether they are connected.
If roots match we append the component's AND cost, otherwise we append negative one for unreachable.
We return the list of answers for all queries.

minimum-genetic-mutation.hook: Fewest single-letter changes is a shortest path question. Shortest path in an unweighted graph means BFS.
minimum-genetic-mutation.ask: Genes are 8-letter strings over A, C, G and T. One mutation changes one letter, and every intermediate gene must be in the bank. Return the fewest mutations from start to end, or -1.
minimum-genetic-mutation.exampleWhy: AACCGGTT becomes AACCGGTA by changing the last letter, then AAACGGTA by changing the third letter.

brute.idea: Depth-first search every chain of single mutations through unused bank genes, and keep the shortest chain that reaches the end.
steps: From the current gene, try each one-letter neighbour
Recurse, marking genes on the current path
Record the shortest chain reaching endGene
brute.whySlow: It explores every possible chain, not just the shortest, so the work can grow factorially with the bank size.

optimal.insight: Each gene is a node and one mutation is an edge. BFS visits genes in order of distance, so the first time we reach endGene is the minimum.
steps: Queue the start gene at distance 0
Pop a gene; if it is endGene, return its distance
Push every unseen bank gene one letter away
Queue empties: unreachable, return -1

codeNotes.match: if nxt not in seen and sum(a != b for a, b in zip(gene, nxt)) == 1:
codeNotes.note: Unseen and exactly one letter apart

pitfalls: The start gene need not be in the bank, but the end gene must be.
Mark genes seen when enqueued, or the queue fills with duplicates.

say.intro: This is Minimum Genetic Mutation. A gene is an eight letter string of A, C, G and T. One mutation changes one letter. Every gene along the way must be in the bank. In our example, we change the last letter, then the third letter. So the answer is two.
say.brute: The brute force uses depth first search. From the current gene, try every bank gene one letter away. Recurse, then undo the choice. Whenever a chain reaches the end gene, record its length. It finds the minimum. But it explores every possible chain. That can grow factorially.
say.insight: Think of each gene as a node, and each single mutation as an edge. All edges cost the same. So the fewest mutations is a shortest path in an unweighted graph. That's breadth first search. It explores in rings of increasing distance. So the first time it touches the end gene, that distance is the minimum.
say.anim: We start a breadth first search from the gene AACCGGTT, with zero mutations so far. We pop AACCGGTT, it's not the end gene, so we check each bank gene for a one letter mutation. AACCGGTA differs by one letter, so it gets added to the queue at step one. Now we pop AACCGGTA at step one, still not matching, and explore its neighbors. AACCGCTA and AAACGGTA each differ by one mutation, so both join the queue at step two. We pop AACCGCTA next at step two, but it still isn't the target gene. Finally we pop AAACGGTA, which matches the end gene exactly. The function returns two, the minimum number of mutations needed.
say.code: Let's walk the code. The queue holds a gene and its distance. We pop the front. Is it the end gene? The first arrival is the shortest, so return the distance. Otherwise, scan the bank for genes that are unseen and exactly one letter apart. Mark each one on enqueue, so it's never added twice. If the queue empties, the end gene was never reached. Return minus one.
say.outro: Each gene is visited once. It's graphs. Model states as nodes, then breadth first search for the shortest path.

minimum-genetic-mutation.title: Minimum Genetic Mutation
lineNotes: This defines the Solution class that holds our method for the problem.
The method takes the start gene, the end gene and the bank, and returns the fewest mutations.
We start a queue holding the start gene paired with zero steps, which sets up breadth first search.
We create a seen set containing the start gene so we never revisit a gene.
We keep looping as long as the queue still has genes left to explore.
We pop the oldest gene from the front of the queue along with its mutation count.
We check whether the current gene already matches the end gene.
If it matches, breadth first order guarantees this step count is the minimum, so we return it.
We scan every gene in the bank as a possible next mutation from the current gene.
A candidate qualifies if it is unseen and differs from the current gene in exactly one letter position.
We mark the candidate as seen right away so no other path can queue it again.
We enqueue the candidate with one more step than the current gene.
If the queue empties without reaching the end gene, no valid mutation path exists, so we return negative one.

minimum-number-of-days-to-eat-n-oranges.hook: Eating one orange at a time is only worth it to reach a multiple of 2 or 3.
minimum-number-of-days-to-eat-n-oranges.ask: Each day you eat one orange, or half of them if the count is even, or two thirds if divisible by three. Return the fewest days to eat all n oranges.
minimum-number-of-days-to-eat-n-oranges.exampleWhy: 10 → 9 by eating one, 9 → 3 by eating two thirds, 3 → 1 by two thirds, then eat the last.

brute.idea: Fill a table for every count from 1 to n: best of eating one, halving, or taking two thirds.
steps: days[i] = days[i - 1] + 1
Even? try days[i // 2] + 1
Divisible by 3? try days[i // 3] + 1
brute.whySlow: n can be two billion, so a table with one entry per orange count is far too big and slow.

optimal.insight: Single bites are only for reaching a multiple. From k, it takes k mod 2 bites to halve, k mod 3 to cut to a third. Only n // 2 and n // 3 matter.
steps: days(k) for k ≤ 1 is k
Halve: k % 2 single days, then 1 + days(k // 2)
Third: k % 3 single days, then 1 + days(k // 3)
Memoise; only O(log² n) states appear

codeNotes.note: Eat singles down to even, then halve
Eat singles down to a multiple of 3

pitfalls: Recursing on k - 1 alone recreates the O(n) chain and overflows the stack.

say.intro: Okay, Minimum Number of Days to Eat N Oranges. Each day, we eat one orange. Or half of them, if the count is even. Or two thirds, if it divides by three. With ten oranges, eat one to reach nine. Then drop to three, then to one, then finish. Four days.
say.brute: The brute force fills a table for every count from one up to n. Each entry is one more than the previous count, improved by halving or the two thirds move when allowed. It's correct, and linear. So what's the catch? n can be two billion. The table alone is far too large.
say.insight: Here's the thing. Eating single oranges only helps to land on a multiple of two or three. From k oranges, it takes k mod two single days before we can halve. And k mod three before we can cut to a third. So each count only branches to k over two and k over three. With memoisation, just a few hundred states ever appear.
say.anim: We start with n equal to ten, and memo already holding base cases zero and one. Days for ten recurses down, computing halve and third paths for five, two, and one. For k equals two, halve costs one, third costs two, so memo stores two days. For k equals five, halve costs three, third also costs three, so memo stores four days. Now for ten, halve equals four using the five result just computed. Branching into three, halve costs two and third costs one, giving memo three equals two. Back at ten, third equals three, so minimum of four and three plus one is four. The function returns four, meaning ten oranges take four days to eat.
say.code: Now the code. The memo starts with the base cases, zero and one. For a new count, the halving route eats singles down to even, then halves. So it's the remainder plus the days for half. The third route eats singles down to a multiple of three, likewise. We store the smaller route, plus the big eating day. Then return the memo entry.
say.outro: Log squared, instead of linear. It's one dimensional dynamic programming, memoised over a sparse set of states.

minimum-number-of-days-to-eat-n-oranges.title: Minimum Number of Days to Eat N Oranges
lineNotes: We define the Solution class that holds our method for this problem.
The minDays method takes the starting orange count n and returns the fewest days needed.
We create a memo dictionary seeded with zero oranges taking zero days and one orange taking one day.
We define a helper called days that computes the minimum days to eat k oranges using recursion.
We only compute k if it is not already in memo, so each value is solved once.
For the halving route, we eat k mod 2 single oranges to reach an even count, then recurse on k divided by two.
For the thirds route, we eat k mod 3 single oranges to reach a multiple of three, then recurse on k divided by three.
We store in memo one day for the final big bite plus the cheaper of the two routes.
We return the memoized answer for k, whether it was just computed or already known.
We kick everything off by calling days with n and returning that result.

minimum-number-of-increments-on-subarray.hook: Every climb in the array needs new operations. Every descent comes for free.
minimum-number-of-increments-on-subarray.ask: Start from an all-zero array. One operation adds 1 to every element of a chosen subarray. Return the fewest operations that build the target array.
minimum-number-of-increments-on-subarray.exampleWhy: Climbing to 3 costs 3. Dropping to 1 is free. Climbing from 1 to 5 costs 4 more. Descents are free: 7.

brute.idea: Slice the target into horizontal layers. At each height h, every maximal run of elements ≥ h needs one operation.
steps: For each height h from 1 to the maximum
Count runs of elements ≥ h
Add the run counts together
brute.whySlow: Heights reach 100,000 and so does n, so scanning every layer is about 10 billion steps.

optimal.insight: An operation covering i can extend to i - 1 for free. Only the amount target[i] rises above target[i - 1] needs new operations.
steps: Pay target[0] to build the first element
Walk left to right
Rise of d over the previous element: pay d
Fall: the extra operations simply end, pay 0

pitfalls: Do not count descents: operations that stop early cost nothing extra.

say.intro: This is Minimum Number of Increments on Subarrays to Form a Target Array. We start from all zeros. One operation adds one to every element of any subarray. How few operations build the target? For three, one, five, four, two, the answer is seven.
say.brute: The brute force slices the target into horizontal layers, like a skyline. At height one, height two, and so on, count the separate runs tall enough to reach that height. Each run is one operation. It's correct. But with heights and lengths up to a hundred thousand, that's billions of steps.
say.insight: Look at neighbours instead. Any operation covering the previous element can just stretch to cover this one too. For free. So when do we pay? Only when the array climbs, by exactly the amount it climbs. When it falls, some operations simply end. So the answer is the first value, plus every rise.
say.anim: We start with target 3, 1, 5, 4, 2, and ops set to the first value, 3. At i equals 1, target drops from 3 to 1, so no new operations are needed. At i equals 2, target rises from 1 to 5, a jump of 4. We add that increase to ops, bringing the total up to 7. At i equals 3, target falls from 5 to 4, so nothing is added. At i equals 4, target falls again from 4 to 2, still no addition. With the loop finished, the function returns the final ops value. The minimum number of operations needed is 7.
say.code: Here's the code. The first element starts from zero, so ops begins at its value. Then we loop from the second element. Only rises cost anything. If this element beats the previous one, add the difference. Those are new operations starting here. Falls and flat steps add nothing, because running operations just stop. Return ops.
say.outro: One pass, constant space. It's greedy. Count only the rises, like a skyline of stacked intervals.

minimum-number-of-increments-on-subarray.title: Minimum Number of Increments on Subarrays to Form a Target Array
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container the problem expects for our method.
The method takes the target array and returns the fewest operations needed to build it from zeros.
We start ops at the first target value, since building the first element from zero needs that many operations.
We loop through every index after the first, comparing each element with the one just before it.
We check whether the current target is higher than the previous one, because only a rise needs new operations.
When it rises, we add just the difference to ops, since existing operations extend over the rest for free.
Finally we return ops as the minimum number of operations needed to form the target array.

minimum-number-of-pushes-to-type-word-i.hook: Eight keys, distinct letters. Fill every key's first slot before any key's second.
minimum-number-of-pushes-to-type-word-i.ask: You may remap letters onto phone keys 2 to 9 however you like. Typing a letter costs its position on its key. Given a word of distinct letters, return the minimum total presses.
minimum-number-of-pushes-to-type-word-i.exampleWhy: Eight letters take first slots at one press each. The other three take second slots at two presses: 8 + 6 = 14.

brute.idea: Simulate the keypad: put each letter on the key that currently holds the fewest letters, and pay its new position.
steps: Keep a letter count for 8 keys
Put each letter on the emptiest key
Pay that key's new length
brute.whySlow: Not asymptotically slower; it rescans all eight keys per letter, where a formula gives the cost directly.

optimal.insight: Letters are distinct, so order does not matter. The i-th letter placed lands in slot i // 8 + 1 of some key.
steps: Number the letters 0, 1, 2, ...
Letters 0 to 7 cost 1 press
Letters 8 to 15 cost 2, and so on
Sum i // 8 + 1

codeNotes.note: Only the count of letters matters
Every 8 letters, cost rises by one

pitfalls: There are 8 usable keys, not 9 or 10: 1, 0, * and # carry no letters.

say.intro: Okay, Minimum Number of Pushes to Type Word, part one. We can remap letters onto the eight phone keys, two to nine. Typing a letter costs its position on its key. Our word has eleven distinct letters. Eight go first on a key, and three go second. So the total is fourteen.
say.brute: The brute force simulates the keypad. For each letter, scan the eight keys, and pick the one holding the fewest letters. Add the letter there, and pay its new position. It gets the right answer. It's not even slower asymptotically. But it does needless scanning, when a formula is enough.
say.insight: Here's the thing. Every letter appears once, so all letters are equally important. Greedily, we fill the first slot on all eight keys. Then all the second slots, and so on. So the letter at position i costs i divided by eight, rounded down, plus one. Just add that up.
say.anim: We start with pushes at zero, ready to count presses for each letter of the word. For the first eight letters, index divided by eight is zero, so each costs just one push. After eight letters, pushes reaches eight, since each used the first slot on a key. Letter nine needs two pushes since it fills the second slot, bringing pushes to ten. Letter ten also needs two pushes, raising the total to twelve. The eleventh and final letter costs two more pushes, making pushes fourteen. The function returns pushes, giving the final answer fourteen.
say.code: Now the code. Only the count of letters matters. We never even look at which letters they are. We loop over positions. Every eight letters, the cost rises by one. So position i costs i integer divided by eight, plus one. Positions zero to seven cost one, and the next eight cost two. Add it all up for the total presses.
say.outro: Linear time, constant space. It's greedy. Fill the cheapest slots first.

minimum-number-of-pushes-to-type-word-i.title: Minimum Number of Pushes to Type Word I
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container the problem expects for our answer method.
The method minimumPushes takes the word and will return the smallest total number of key presses needed.
We start the running total of pushes at zero before counting any letters.
We loop over each index of the word, treating each distinct letter as the next one to place on a key.
Eight keys fill one slot at a time, so the letter at index i costs i divided by eight, rounded down, plus one.
After every letter has been added, we return the total number of pushes as the minimum.

minimum-operations-to-make-binary-array-.hook: The leftmost zero has exactly one window that can fix it. So there is no choice to make.
minimum-operations-to-make-binary-array-.ask: You may flip any three consecutive bits of a binary array. Return the fewest flips that make every element 1, or -1 if it cannot be done.
minimum-operations-to-make-binary-array-.exampleWhy: Flip indices 0 to 2, then 1 to 3, then 3 to 5. Each flip fixes the leftmost remaining zero.

brute.idea: Treat each array as a state and every 3-flip as an edge. BFS from the input until the all-ones state appears.
steps: Start BFS from the input array
Try every window of three bits
Stop when all ones is reached
brute.whySlow: There are 2^n possible arrays; for n = 30 that is already a billion states.

optimal.insight: Flip order does not matter and flipping twice cancels. The leftmost zero can only be fixed by the window starting there, so we must flip it.
steps: Scan i from 0 to n - 3
nums[i] is 0: flip i, i + 1, i + 2
Count each flip
Last two still 1? return count, else -1

codeNotes.match: return ops if nums[-1] == 1 and nums[-2] == 1 else -1

pitfalls: Check the last two elements: no window starts there to repair them.

say.intro: This is Minimum Operations to Make Binary Array Elements Equal to One, part one. One operation flips three neighbouring bits. We want all ones, with as few flips as possible. If it's impossible, return minus one. For zero, one, one, one, zero, zero, three flips do it.
say.brute: The brute force treats each possible array as a state. From any state, each window of three leads to a neighbouring state. Breadth first search from the input finds the fewest flips to all ones. It's correct. But there are two to the n states. That explodes after a few dozen bits.
say.insight: Two facts kill the search. Flipping the same window twice does nothing. And the order of flips doesn't matter. Now look at the leftmost zero. Windows starting earlier are already settled. So the only window that can fix it starts right there. The choice is forced. That's why a single left to right pass is optimal.
say.anim: We start with the array zero one one one zero zero, and zero operations. At index zero we find a zero, so we flip this window of three elements. The flip changes the array to one zero zero one zero zero, and ops becomes one. At index one there's another zero, so we flip it and the next two values. Now the array is one one one zero zero zero, with ops at two. Index two is now one, so no flip happens there, and we move on. At index three we hit a zero, so we flip that final window of three. All elements become one, giving a final answer of three operations.
say.code: Let's walk the code. We visit every window start, up to the third last index. If the bit there is zero, it's the leftmost zero, and it forces this flip. XOR with one flips a bit, so we XOR all three bits and count the flip. After the loop, the last two bits can't be touched again. If both are one, return ops. Otherwise the tail can't be fixed, so minus one.
say.outro: Linear time, constant space. It's greedy, with a forced choice at the leftmost problem position.

minimum-operations-to-make-binary-array-.title: Minimum Operations to Make Binary Array Elements Equal to One I
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container the problem expects for our method.
The minOperations method takes the binary array nums and returns the fewest flips, or negative one if impossible.
We start a counter called ops at zero to track how many three-bit flips we perform.
We scan each index that can start a window of three, stopping two short of the end.
If the current bit is zero, it must be fixed now, since only a window starting here can do it.
We flip the current bit with exclusive or one, turning that zero into a one.
We flip the next bit as well, since the window covers three consecutive positions.
We flip the third bit in the window, completing the three-bit flip.
We add one to ops because we just performed a flip operation.
At the end, we return ops if the last two bits are ones, otherwise negative one, since no window can fix them.

minimum-recolors-to-get-k-consecutive-bl.hook: Every window of length k is a candidate. Slide it and count whites in constant time.
minimum-recolors-to-get-k-consecutive-bl.ask: A row of blocks is white or black. Recolouring a white block makes it black. Return the fewest recolours needed to get k black blocks in a row.
minimum-recolors-to-get-k-consecutive-bl.exampleWhy: No three blocks in a row are all black, but BBW starting at index 1 has only one white to recolour.

brute.idea: For every starting index, count the whites in the k blocks from there. The smallest count is the answer.
steps: Try each start i
Count W in blocks[i:i + k]
Keep the minimum count
brute.whySlow: Neighbouring windows share k - 1 blocks, yet each one is recounted from scratch.

optimal.insight: Sliding the window right adds one block and drops one. Update the white count by those two blocks only.
steps: Count whites in the first k blocks
Slide: add the entering block if white
Subtract the leaving block if white
Track the smallest count

pitfalls: The block leaving the window is i - k, not i - k + 1.

say.intro: Okay, Minimum Recolors to Get K Consecutive Black Blocks. We have a row of white and black blocks. Painting a white block black costs one. We want k black blocks in a row. With k equal to three, no window is all black yet. But some windows hold just one white. So the answer is one.
say.brute: The brute force checks every window of length k. For each start, count the whites inside, and keep the smallest count. That works. But neighbouring windows overlap in all but one block. We recount them every time. That's n times k work.
say.insight: Here's the thing. When the window slides one step right, exactly one block enters, and one leaves. So the white count changes by at most those two blocks. Count the first window once. Then update in constant time per step. It's the fixed size sliding window, the simplest window there is.
say.anim: We start by counting white blocks in the first window of size three, getting one. Best is initialized to one, our current minimum white count so far. The window slides to index three, adjusting whites by adding and removing one block each side. At index four, whites rises to two as the window shifts across more white blocks. At index six, whites drops back down to one, a new best so far. Near the end, at index nine, whites climbs again to two. The loop finishes and the function returns the smallest whites value tracked. The final answer is one, the minimum recolors needed for three consecutive black blocks.
say.code: Now the code. The first window is counted once, and that's the best so far. Then we loop i from k to the end. Here, i is the entering block. In one, out one. Add one if the entering block is white. Subtract one if the block k places back, which is leaving, is white. Keep the fewest whites seen, and return it.
say.outro: Linear time, constant space. It's a fixed size sliding window with a running count.

minimum-recolors-to-get-k-consecutive-bl.title: Minimum Recolors to Get K Consecutive Black Blocks
lineNotes: We define the Solution class, which holds the method that solves this problem.
This method takes the blocks string and the target length k, and returns the fewest recolors needed.
We count the white blocks in the first window of k blocks, since each white one needs a recolor.
We start the best answer as that first window's white count, as it is our only candidate so far.
We slide the window rightward, with i as the index of the new block entering the window.
We add one if the entering block is white and subtract one if the leaving block is white, updating the count cheaply.
We keep the smaller of the best so far and the current white count, since fewer whites means fewer recolors.
After checking every window, we return the best, which is the minimum recolors required.

minimum-score-of-a-path-between-two-citi.hook: Paths may repeat roads. So any road you can reach, you can include.
minimum-score-of-a-path-between-two-citi.ask: Cities 1 to n are linked by roads with distances. A path's score is its smallest road distance, and paths may revisit roads and cities. Return the minimum score of a path from city 1 to city n.
minimum-score-of-a-path-between-two-citi.exampleWhy: Path 1 → 2 → 4 uses the road of distance 5, the smallest road reachable from city 1.

brute.idea: Try roads from shortest to longest. The first road whose endpoint is reachable from city 1 gives the answer.
steps: Sort roads by distance
For each road, search from city 1
Reachable? return its distance
brute.whySlow: Each candidate road triggers a whole new graph search: up to 100,000 searches of 100,000 roads.

optimal.insight: City n is in city 1's component, and a path can detour over any road there. The answer is the smallest road in that component.
steps: Build the adjacency list
DFS from city 1
Every road touched updates the minimum
Return the minimum road distance

pitfalls: This is not a shortest path problem: Dijkstra is unnecessary.
Check every edge out of a visited city, even to already-seen cities.

say.intro: This is Minimum Score of a Path Between Two Cities. Roads connect cities with distances. A path's score is its smallest road. And a path may repeat roads and cities. We want the lowest score from city one to city n. Here, the road of length five between two and four is reachable. So the answer is five.
say.brute: The brute force sorts roads from shortest to longest. For each road, it searches from city one, to see if that road is reachable. The first reachable road wins. Correct. But every candidate road triggers a whole new search. On big graphs, that's quadratic.
say.insight: So here's the twist. A path may repeat roads. It can wander anywhere in city one's component, cross any road, and come back. And city n is guaranteed to be in that same component. So the answer is just the smallest road anywhere in the component. One traversal finds it.
say.anim: We start building an adjacency list from the four roads given. Best is set to infinity, and we begin exploring from city one. Visiting city one's neighbors, best becomes nine, then drops to seven for city four. Exploring city four's edges updates best down to five, the smallest road seen. From city two we find city three, adding it to our visited set. Further edges keep comparing distances, but five remains the smallest value found. The stack empties, meaning every city in the component has been explored. The function returns five, the minimum score connecting cities one and four.
say.code: Let's walk the code. Roads go both ways, so the adjacency list stores each one in both directions. We explore from city one, using a stack. Pop a city. Every reachable road counts, so each road out of it can lower the best. Then we push neighbours we haven't seen, so each city is visited once. When the stack empties, return the best.
say.outro: Linear in cities plus roads. It's graphs. A plain traversal of one connected component.

minimum-score-of-a-path-between-two-citi.title: Minimum Score of a Path Between Two Cities
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, as required by the problem's submission format.
The minScore method takes the number of cities and the list of roads, and returns the smallest reachable road distance.
We build an adjacency map from each city to a list of its neighboring cities and road distances.
We loop over every road, unpacking its two endpoints and its distance.
We record the road from city a to city b along with its distance.
Roads are two-way, so we also record the road from city b back to city a.
We start best at infinity so any real road distance will replace it.
We begin a depth first search from city 1, marking it seen and placing it on the stack.
We keep exploring as long as the stack still holds cities to visit.
We pop a city from the stack to process its roads next.
We look at every neighbor of this city along with the distance of the connecting road.
Every road touching the component counts, so we update best to the smaller of itself and this distance.
If the neighbor has not been visited yet, we need to explore it later.
We mark that neighbor as seen so we never push it twice.
We push the neighbor onto the stack so its roads get examined too.
After exploring the whole component of city 1, best holds the smallest road, which is the answer.

minimum-time-to-complete-trips.hook: Given a time, counting trips is easy. So search the time, not the schedule.
minimum-time-to-complete-trips.ask: Each bus takes time[i] per trip and runs trips back to back, independently. Return the minimum time for all buses together to finish at least totalTrips trips.
minimum-time-to-complete-trips.exampleWhy: By time 3 the buses finish 3, 1 and 1 trips: five in total. At time 2 they finish only 3.

brute.idea: Try every time t = 1, 2, 3, ... and add up t // time[i]. Return the first t with enough trips.
steps: Trips at t: sum of t // time[i]
Stop at the first t that is enough
brute.whySlow: The answer can reach 10 to the 14th, so stepping one unit at a time never finishes.

optimal.insight: More time never means fewer trips. That monotonic yes or no lets us binary search the time.
steps: lo = 1, hi = fastest bus · totalTrips
Count trips at mid: sum of mid // time[i]
Enough? hi = mid
Not enough? lo = mid + 1

codeNotes.match: trips = sum(mid // t for t in time)

pitfalls: In Java or C++, the upper bound overflows 32 bits: use long.

say.intro: Okay, Minimum Time to Complete Trips. Each bus has its own trip time, and runs back to back. All buses work at once. We need at least a target number of trips. With buses taking one, two and three units, and five trips needed, time three is the earliest that works.
say.brute: The brute force tries every time, one unit at a time. At time t, each bus has finished t divided by its trip time, rounded down. Add those up. Stop at the first time that reaches the target. Correct. But the answer can be around ten to the fourteenth. It never finishes.
say.insight: Here's the thing. Waiting longer never reduces finished trips. So the question, is time t enough, flips from no to yes exactly once. That's the signal for binary search on the answer. What's a safe upper bound? The fastest bus doing every trip alone. Each check is one pass over the buses.
say.anim: We start with lo at 1 and hi at 5, the search range for the answer. We test mid equals 3, checking if 3 time units allow enough trips. Summing trips per vehicle gives 5 total trips, meeting our target of 5. Since trips is enough, we shrink hi down to 3, searching smaller times. Next we try mid equals 2, computing trips possible in that time. Only 3 trips happen, which falls short of the needed 5 trips. Since it's not enough, lo moves up to 3, narrowing the search further. Now lo equals hi equals 3, so the loop ends and we return 3.
say.code: Now the code. The fastest bus alone always suffices, so hi starts at its trip time times the total trips. We take the middle time. Then we count full trips finished by mid, summing mid divided by each bus time. Enough trips? Try less time, so hi moves to mid. Too few? We need more time, so lo moves past mid. Return lo.
say.outro: A logarithmic number of linear checks. It's binary search on the answer, with a monotonic test.

minimum-time-to-complete-trips.title: Minimum Time to Complete Trips
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container the problem expects for our method.
The method takes the list of trip times per bus and the required total number of trips, and returns a time.
We search times from one up to the fastest bus doing every trip alone, which is always enough.
We loop while the search range has more than one candidate time left.
We pick the middle time of the range as the candidate to test.
We count the trips all buses finish by this time, adding the whole trips each bus completes.
If the buses finish enough trips, this time works, so we check whether something smaller also works.
So we move the upper bound down to mid, keeping mid as a possible answer.
Otherwise the time is too short, so the answer must lie above mid.
We therefore raise the lower bound to just past mid, discarding all times that fail.
When the range collapses to one value, that is the minimum time that works, so we return it.

minimum-time-to-repair-cars.hook: Repair time grows with the square of cars. Flip it: in time t, how many cars can each mechanic fix?
minimum-time-to-repair-cars.ask: A mechanic of rank r needs r times n squared minutes to repair n cars. All mechanics work at once. Return the minimum time to repair all the cars.
minimum-time-to-repair-cars.exampleWhy: In 16 minutes the ranks 4, 2, 3, 1 fix 2, 2, 2 and 4 cars: exactly ten. At 15 minutes they fix only nine.

brute.idea: Try every time t from 1 upward. A rank r mechanic fixes floor(sqrt(t / r)) cars. Stop when the total reaches cars.
steps: Each mechanic fixes isqrt(t // r) cars
First t with enough cars wins
brute.whySlow: The answer can be 100 times a million squared, so counting minutes one by one is hopeless.

optimal.insight: More time always fixes at least as many cars, so binary search the time. Each check inverts r · n² ≤ t to n = isqrt(t / r).
steps: lo = 1, hi = best rank · cars²
At mid, each mechanic fixes isqrt(mid // r)
Enough cars? hi = mid
Too few? lo = mid + 1

codeNotes.match: fixed = sum(math.isqrt(mid // r) for r in ranks)

pitfalls: Floating sqrt can round wrongly on huge values; use an integer square root.

say.intro: This is Minimum Time to Repair Cars. A mechanic with rank r needs r times n squared minutes to repair n cars. All mechanics work in parallel. With ranks four, two, three and one, and ten cars, the best schedule takes sixteen minutes.
say.brute: The brute force tries every minute count from one upward. In t minutes, a mechanic of rank r fixes the square root of t over r cars, rounded down. Add those up, and stop at the first time that covers every car. Correct. But the answer can be in the hundreds of trillions.
say.insight: So turn the question around. Don't assign cars. Instead ask, how many cars can everyone finish within a given time? More time never fixes fewer cars. So the answer to, is t enough, flips once. Binary search the time. Each check is one integer square root per mechanic.
say.anim: We start with ranks four, two, three, one, and ten cars to fix, searching time from one to one hundred. At mid fifty, the mechanics fix nineteen cars, more than enough, so we shrink the upper bound to fifty. At mid twenty five, twelve cars get fixed, still enough, so hi drops to twenty five. At mid thirteen, only eight cars finish, too few, so lo rises to fourteen. At mid nineteen, eleven cars finish, enough, so hi becomes nineteen. At mid sixteen, exactly ten cars get fixed, meeting the goal, so hi becomes sixteen. At mid fifteen, only eight cars finish, too few, so lo becomes sixteen, closing the search. Lo now equals hi at sixteen, and the function returns sixteen as the minimum time.
say.code: Let's walk the code. The best mechanic alone always suffices, so hi starts at the best rank times cars squared. We take mid. For each mechanic, we invert r times n squared at most mid. That gives the integer square root of mid over r. Sum those up. Enough cars? Try less time, so hi moves to mid. Too few? Lo moves past mid. Return lo.
say.outro: Logarithmic checks, each one linear. It's binary search on the answer, again.

minimum-time-to-repair-cars.title: Minimum Time to Repair Cars
lineNotes: We define a solution class that holds the method for solving the repair time problem.
The method takes the list of mechanic ranks and the number of cars, and returns the minimum time.
We set the search range from one minute up to the best mechanic alone repairing every car.
We keep searching while the low bound is below the high bound, so the answer is still unsettled.
We pick the middle time between low and high as the candidate time to test.
For each rank we take the integer square root of mid divided by rank, and sum these to count cars fixed.
We check whether the mechanics can repair at least the required number of cars within this time.
If they can, this time works, so we shrink the upper bound to mid to look for something smaller.
Otherwise the time is too short, so we handle the case where we need more time.
We move the lower bound past mid, since mid and anything smaller cannot finish all the cars.
When the bounds meet, low is the smallest time that repairs all cars, so we return it.

most-stones-removed-with-same-row-or-col.hook: Stones sharing a row or column form groups. Each group can shrink to a single stone.
most-stones-removed-with-same-row-or-col.ask: Stones sit on grid points. A stone can be removed if another remaining stone shares its row or column. Return the largest number of stones you can remove.
most-stones-removed-with-same-row-or-col.exampleWhy: All six stones are linked through shared rows and columns, so one group remains as one stone: 6 - 1 = 5.

brute.idea: Compare every pair of stones to build edges, then count connected groups with DFS. Answer: stones minus groups.
steps: Pick an unvisited stone, start a new group
Scan all stones for a shared row or column
Answer = n - number of groups
brute.whySlow: Comparing every pair costs about n²: fine for 1,000 stones, wasteful when rows and columns can index the links.

optimal.insight: Remove stones from the leaves of a group inward, and each group ends with one stone. Union each stone's row with its column.
steps: Treat each row and each column as a node
A stone at (x, y) unions row x with column y
Count distinct roots among the stones
Answer = stones - groups

codeNotes.note: New row or column starts alone

pitfalls: Rows and columns must not collide in the same key space: use ~y or an offset.

say.intro: Okay, Most Stones Removed with Same Row or Column. A stone can be removed while another stone shares its row or column. How many can we remove? In our example, all six stones are linked through shared lines. So we can remove five, and keep one.
say.brute: The brute force builds the links explicitly. Pick a stone. Then repeatedly scan every other stone for a shared row or column, growing one connected group. Each finished group can lose all but one stone. So the answer is stones minus groups. But comparing every pair makes it n squared.
say.insight: Here's the key. Within a connected group, we can always remove stones from the outside in. Exactly one survives. So we only need to count groups. And think about what a stone really does. It glues its row to its column. Union find over row and column labels links them in near constant time. No pair comparisons at all.
say.anim: We start with six stones and an empty parent map to track unions. For stone zero, zero, we union row zero with column zero, encoded as negative one. Processing more stones, each row finds its column's root and merges them together. As stones link up, their roots keep pointing deeper into the same shared tree. Path compression flattens chains, so rows and columns now mostly point directly to negative three. After processing all stones, every row and column collapses into one single root. With six stones but only one group, we remove five stones, matching the expected answer.
say.code: Now the code. We keep a parent dictionary. A new row or column starts alone, as its own parent. Find uses path compression. For each stone, we union its row with its column. The column is written as tilde y, which keeps columns apart from rows. Finally, there's one survivor per group. So return the stones minus the number of distinct roots.
say.outro: Near linear time. It's union find, counting connected components.

most-stones-removed-with-same-row-or-col.title: Most Stones Removed with Same Row or Column
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container the problem expects for our method.
The method removeStones takes the list of stones and returns the maximum number of stones we can remove.
We create an empty dictionary called parent to hold the union find structure, adding nodes lazily as we meet them.
We define find, which returns the representative root of the group containing a given row or column node.
If x is not yet known, we set its parent to itself so it starts as its own group.
If x is not its own parent, it points toward a root, so we need to climb further.
We recursively find the root and store it directly as the parent of x, which is path compression.
We return the root of x, which identifies its connected group.
For each stone, we take its row x and column y as the two coordinates to connect.
We union the row x with the column y, using the bitwise not of y so column labels never collide with row labels.
We count the distinct roots among all stone rows, which gives the number of connected groups.
Each group keeps one stone, so the answer is total stones minus the number of groups.

next-greater-element-iii.hook: This is next permutation in disguise. Find the pivot, swap, and reverse the tail.
next-greater-element-iii.ask: Given a positive integer, return the smallest larger integer that uses exactly the same digits. Return -1 if none exists or it does not fit in 32 bits.
next-greater-element-iii.exampleWhy: 432 is already the largest arrangement, so 1 must grow. The next digit up is 2, and the rest go smallest first.

brute.idea: Generate every permutation of the digits, keep those larger than n that fit in 32 bits, and take the smallest.
steps: Generate all digit permutations
Keep values > n and < 2^31
Return the smallest, or -1
brute.whySlow: A 10-digit number has 3.6 million permutations, all built just to pick one.

optimal.insight: The longest non-increasing suffix is already maxed out. Bump the digit just before it by the smallest larger digit, then sort the suffix ascending.
steps: From the right, find i with d[i] < d[i + 1]
None? digits are descending: -1
From the right, find j with d[j] > d[i]; swap
Reverse the suffix after i to make it smallest

codeNotes.note: Smallest digit bigger than the pivot

pitfalls: Use >= and <= when scanning so repeated digits are handled.
The result can exceed 2^31 - 1 even when n fits: check it.

say.intro: This is Next Greater Element three. Given a number, find the smallest bigger number using exactly the same digits. If none exists, or it overflows thirty two bits, return minus one. For one thousand four hundred thirty two, the answer is two thousand one hundred thirty four.
say.brute: The brute force generates every rearrangement of the digits. It keeps those bigger than n that still fit in thirty two bits, and returns the smallest. It works. But a ten digit number has over three and a half million rearrangements. All built just to pick one.
say.insight: Read from the right. A run of digits that only goes down is already as large as it can be. Changing it alone can't help. So the digit just before that run is the pivot. Swap it with the smallest larger digit in the run. Then flip the run to ascending, its smallest arrangement. That's next permutation.
say.anim: We start with the number 1432 split into digits one, four, three, two. Scanning from the right, index two fails since three is less than two, so i decreases. At index one, four is still bigger than three, so i keeps moving left. Now i is zero, where digit one is smaller than four, so we stop here. We search from the end for the smallest digit larger than one, finding index three, digit two. Swapping positions zero and three gives two, four, three, one. Reversing everything after index zero sorts the suffix ascending into two, one, three, four. Joining the digits gives the final answer, the next greater number, two thousand one hundred thirty four.
say.code: Let's walk the code. We turn the number into digits. Then i moves left to skip the descending suffix. If i falls off, there's no bigger number, so minus one. Next, j finds the smallest digit bigger than the pivot, scanning from the end. We swap, bumping the pivot. Then the descending suffix is reversed into ascending. Finally, rebuild the number, with a thirty two bit overflow check.
say.outro: Linear in the number of digits. It's two pointers scanning from the right, the classic next permutation.

next-greater-element-iii.title: Next Greater Element III
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container LeetCode expects for the method that follows.
The method takes the integer n and returns the next greater integer with the same digits, or negative one.
We convert n to a string and split it into a list of digit characters we can rearrange.
We set i to the second to last index, to find the pivot digit scanning from the right.
We move left while the digit at i is not smaller than its right neighbor, skipping the non-increasing suffix.
Each time the pair is non-increasing, we step i one position to the left.
If i fell below zero, the whole number is non-increasing, so no larger permutation exists.
In that case we return negative one.
We set j to the last index to search the suffix for the swap partner.
We move j left until the digit at j is strictly greater than the pivot digit, giving the smallest larger digit.
Each step left shrinks the candidate toward the smallest digit that still exceeds the pivot, since the suffix is non-increasing.
We swap the pivot digit with the digit at j, which bumps the prefix to the next larger value.
We reverse the suffix after i, turning it from non-increasing into ascending order, the smallest arrangement.
We join the digits back into a string and convert to an integer called ans.
We return ans if it fits in a signed 32 bit integer, otherwise negative one.

nim-game.hook: Four stones is a trap. Every multiple of four is the same trap, repeated.
nim-game.ask: A heap has n stones. You and a friend alternate, you first, each removing 1 to 3 stones. Whoever takes the last stone wins. With perfect play, can you win?
nim-game.exampleWhy: Whatever you take from 8, your friend takes the rest of four, leaving 4. From 4 you always lose.

brute.idea: Fill a win or lose table bottom up: you win at i if some move leaves your friend at a losing count.
steps: win[0] is False: no stones, you already lost
win[i] = some k in 1..3 with not win[i - k]
Return win[n]
brute.whySlow: n reaches about two billion, so a table with one entry per stone count is far too slow and large.

optimal.insight: The table repeats True, True, True, False. On a multiple of 4, every move hands your opponent a winning count.
steps: From 1, 2 or 3 stones, take them all and win
From 4, any move leaves 1 to 3: you lose
Otherwise, take n mod 4 to leave a multiple of 4
So you win exactly when n % 4 != 0

codeNotes.note: Multiples of 4 lose; all others win

pitfalls: Spot the pattern by tabulating small n, then prove it; do not submit the O(n) table.

say.intro: Okay, Nim Game. There's a heap of stones between you and a friend. You go first. Each turn removes one, two or three stones. Whoever takes the last stone wins. Can you force a win? With eight stones, no. Whatever you take, your friend brings the heap down to four.
say.brute: The brute force builds a table of winning and losing counts. Zero stones is a loss for the player to move. A count is a win if some move leaves the opponent on a losing count. Fill the table up to n, and read the answer. Sounds reasonable? But n can be two billion.
say.insight: Write out the first few entries, and a pattern jumps out. One, two and three win, because you take everything. Four loses. Every move leaves your friend one to three. Five, six and seven win, by leaving four. Eight loses again. So you lose exactly on multiples of four.
say.anim: n is 8, and we check if it's not divisible by 4. Since 8 is a multiple of 4, the function returns false, meaning you lose.
say.code: The whole solution is one line. Multiples of four lose, and all others win. So return whether n mod four isn't zero. Why does a remainder win? Take exactly that many stones. Now your friend faces a multiple of four. Mirror their moves so each round removes four in total. And you take the last stone.
say.outro: Constant time, instead of a linear table. It's math. Tabulate small cases, spot the cycle, then prove it.

nim-game.title: Nim Game
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container that the judge expects for this problem's method.
The method canWinNim takes the stone count n and returns a boolean saying whether the first player can force a win.
We return true unless n is a multiple of four, because on those counts every move leaves your opponent a winning position.

number-of-dice-rolls-with-target-sum.hook: Each die only cares about the sum so far. Count ways per sum, one die at a time.
number-of-dice-rolls-with-target-sum.ask: You roll n dice, each with faces 1 to k. Count the ways the faces can add up to target, modulo 10^9 + 7.
number-of-dice-rolls-with-target-sum.exampleWhy: Two six-sided dice reach 7 as 1+6, 2+5, 3+4, 4+3, 5+2 and 6+1: six ways.

brute.idea: Recurse: ways(d, t) sums ways(d - 1, t - f) over every face f, memoised so each state is solved once.
steps: No dice left: 1 way if t is 0
Try every face f from 1 to k
Add ways(d - 1, t - f)
Memoise each (d, t)
brute.whySlow: Every state loops over all k faces: about 30 · 1000 · 30 additions, and a k-fold factor we can remove.

optimal.insight: new[t] sums the previous row over t - k .. t - 1: a window of k cells. Slide it, adding one cell and dropping one.
steps: dp[s]: ways for the dice so far to sum to s
Start: dp[0] = 1 with zero dice
For each die, slide a window of k cells over dp
new[t] = window sum of dp[t - k .. t - 1]

codeNotes.note: Sum t - k - 1 now needs face k + 1
Ways for this die to reach t

pitfalls: Apply the modulo as you go, not only at the end.
Without the window, the standard O(n · target · k) DP is also accepted.

say.intro: This is Number of Dice Rolls With Target Sum. We roll n dice, each with faces one to k. We count the ways the faces add up to a target, modulo a big prime. With two six sided dice and a target of seven, there are six ways. One plus six, up to six plus one.
say.brute: The brute force recursion asks a simple question. With d dice left and t still needed, try every face, and recurse with one fewer die. Plain recursion is exponential, so we memoise each pair of dice and remaining sum. That's n times target states. But each one loops over all k faces.
say.insight: Look at what one die adds. The ways to reach sum t equal the previous row, summed from t minus k up to t minus one. That's a window of k neighbouring cells. Now, as t moves up by one, a single cell enters the window, and a single cell leaves. So each cell costs constant time. The k factor disappears.
say.anim: We want two dice rolls summing to target seven, using a sliding window dp. Dp starts as one way to reach sum zero, zeros elsewhere, for zero dice. Starting first die roll, we build a new array by sliding a window of size six. At t equals one, window becomes one, so new of one is set to one. The window keeps growing, filling new with ones up through t equals seven, one way each. After one die, dp holds ones for sums one through six, zero for seven. Starting second die, we slide the window again, accumulating sums from the previous row. After two dice, dp now shows one, two, three, four, five, six ways for sums two through seven. The function returns six, the number of ways to roll two dice summing to seven.
say.code: Now the code. With zero dice, only sum zero has a way. For each die, we build a new row. At each target t, face one enters from sum t minus one. Once the window gets too wide, sum t minus k minus one drops out, since it would need face k plus one. The window is the ways for this die to reach t. Store it mod the prime. Then roll the next die.
say.outro: From n times target times k, down to n times target. It's two dimensional dynamic programming, with a sliding window sum.

number-of-dice-rolls-with-target-sum.title: Number of Dice Rolls With Target Sum
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, as the problem platform expects.
This method takes the number of dice n, faces per die k, and the target sum, and returns the count.
We set MOD to one billion seven, since answers must be reported modulo that prime.
The dp list starts with one way to make sum zero using zero dice, and zero ways for every other sum.
We loop once per die, building the table of ways for one more die each time.
We create a fresh row called new filled with zeros, covering sums from zero up to target.
The window variable holds the running sum of the previous row over the last k cells, starting at zero.
We walk through each sum t from one up to target, filling in new for that sum.
We add dp at t minus one to the window, bringing the newest cell into the range.
If t minus k minus one is still a valid index, that cell has just slid out of the window.
We subtract that old cell from the window so it only covers the last k cells.
We store the window total, reduced by the modulus, as the number of ways to reach sum t.
After finishing the row, we make it the current dp for the next die.
After all dice are used, dp at target holds the answer, which we return.

number-of-good-pairs.hook: Each new copy of a value pairs with every earlier copy. Count, do not compare.
number-of-good-pairs.ask: Given a list of numbers, count the index pairs i < j where the two values are equal.
number-of-good-pairs.exampleWhy: The three 1s make three pairs and the two 3s make one more: 3 + 1 = 4.

brute.idea: Check every pair of indices i < j and count those with equal values.
steps: Pick index i
Scan every j > i
Equal values? count the pair
brute.whySlow: Fine for n = 100, but it compares every pair, about n²/2 checks, when one pass is enough.

optimal.insight: When a value appears again, it forms a new pair with each earlier copy. Keep a count per value and add it.
steps: Walk the list once
Add the count of earlier copies of x
Then increase the count of x

codeNotes.note: Copies of each value so far

pitfalls: Add the count before incrementing, or each value pairs with itself.

say.intro: Okay, Number of Good Pairs. A good pair is two positions, the first before the second, holding the same value. In one, two, three, one, one, three, the three ones form three pairs. The two threes form one more. So the answer is four.
say.brute: The brute force checks every pair of positions. For each index, scan every later index, and count the pair when the values match. That's n squared. Fine for a hundred numbers. But it does far more comparisons than needed.
say.insight: Think about the moment a value appears again. It makes a new good pair with every earlier copy of that value. And with nothing else. So keep a running count per value. Each new copy adds the current count to the answer, then bumps the count. One pass. No pair comparisons at all.
say.anim: We start with an empty count map and zero pairs, scanning the list for identical pairs. For the first three numbers, one, two, three, counts rise to one each, no pairs yet. Now x is one again, it already appeared once, so pairs becomes one. Next x is one once more, matching two earlier ones, pairs jumps to three. X is three again, matching one earlier three, pairs increases to four. Final counts are one three times, two once, three twice, covering all numbers. The function returns four, the total number of good identical pairs found.
say.code: Here's the code. A dictionary holds the copies of each value so far. For each value, first we pair it with every earlier copy, so we add its current count. Then we record this copy, bumping the count, so the next copy pairs with it too. Why that order? Adding first means a value never pairs with itself. Return the pairs.
say.outro: Linear time, with a hash map. It's arrays and hashing. Count as you go, instead of comparing pairs.

number-of-good-pairs.title: Number of Good Pairs
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container the problem expects for our method.
The method numIdenticalPairs takes the list nums and returns an integer count of good pairs.
We create an empty dictionary called count to remember how many times each value has appeared so far.
We set pairs to zero, which will hold the running total of good pairs found.
We loop through each value x in nums, processing the numbers from left to right.
We add to pairs the number of earlier copies of x, since each one forms a new pair with this element.
We then increase the stored count for x by one, so later copies will see this occurrence too.
After the loop finishes, we return pairs as the total number of identical index pairs.

number-of-good-paths.hook: Turn on nodes from smallest value to largest. Equal values meeting in a component make good paths.
number-of-good-paths.ask: A tree has a value on every node. A good path starts and ends at equal values, and no node between them is larger. Single nodes count. Return the number of good paths.
number-of-good-paths.exampleWhy: Five single nodes, plus the path 1 → 0 → 2 → 4, whose ends are both 3 and whose middle values are smaller.

brute.idea: From each node, search only through nodes no larger than its value, counting later nodes with the same value.
steps: Start a search at each node s
Only step onto values ≤ vals[s]
Count reached nodes with equal value and index > s
Add n single-node paths
brute.whySlow: Each of up to 30,000 nodes may search most of the tree: close to a billion steps.

optimal.insight: Process values in increasing order, joining each node to neighbours no larger. When value v is added, equal-v nodes sharing a component form good paths.
steps: Group nodes by value, smallest value first
Union each node with neighbours of value ≤ v
Count group nodes per component root
A root with c such nodes adds c(c + 1)/2

codeNotes.note: Only smaller or equal neighbours are active

codeNotes.match: count = collections.Counter(find(u) for u in groups[v])

pitfalls: Count after all unions for value v, not node by node.
