c(c + 1)/2 already includes the single-node paths; do not add n again.

say.intro: This is Number of Good Paths. A tree has a value on every node. A good path starts and ends at equal values, and nothing in between is larger. A single node counts too. In our tree, the five single nodes count. Plus one longer path joining the two threes through smaller values. Six in total.
say.brute: The brute force starts a search from every node. It only walks through nodes no larger than the start value. And it counts every later node with exactly that value. Add the single nodes, and that's the answer. Correct. But each search may cover most of the tree, so it's n squared.
say.insight: Here's the trick. Switch nodes on in increasing order of value. When we reach value v, everything already on is no larger than v. Join each value v node to its active neighbours, with union find. Now, two value v nodes in the same component? They're linked only through smaller or equal values. A component with c of them adds c times c plus one over two.
say.anim: We build the adjacency list from edges, connecting nodes zero through four together. Nodes are grouped by value: value one has nodes zero and three, two has node two, three has one and four. Starting with smallest value one, we union nodes zero and three through their neighbors, since no smaller neighbors exist here. Each singleton group of value one contributes one good path, giving ans equal to two so far. For value two, node two merges with its smaller neighbors zero and three, forming one combined component. That single component for value two adds one more good path, making ans equal to three. For value three, nodes one and four end up joined into the same component through node two. Both value three nodes share one component, counter shows two, adding three paths for a final answer of six.
say.code: Let's walk the code. The smallest values join first, so we loop over values in sorted order. For each node of that value, only smaller or equal neighbours are active. So we union with just those, merging the two components. Then we count value v nodes per component, under each root. Each root adds c times c plus one over two. That's the pairs, plus the single node paths.
say.outro: Sorting, plus near linear union find. It's advanced graphs, with union find run offline in value order.

number-of-good-paths.title: Number of Good Paths
lineNotes: We define the Solution class that holds the method for this problem.
The method takes node values and edge list, and returns the count of good paths.
We store the number of nodes in n for later use.
We build an adjacency list with an empty neighbor list for every node.
We loop over each edge, reading its two endpoints a and b.
We add b to the neighbor list of a.
We add a to the neighbor list of b, since the tree is undirected.
We set up union find so each node starts as its own parent.
We define find to locate the representative root of a node's component.
We keep climbing while the node is not its own parent, meaning it is not yet a root.
We apply path compression by pointing the node to its grandparent, which speeds up later searches.
We move x up to its parent to continue the climb.
We return the root once we reach a node that is its own parent.
We create a dictionary mapping each value to the list of nodes holding it.
We loop through every node with its index and value.
We append the node index to the list for its value.
We start the answer at zero, to be built up as we process values.
We handle distinct values in increasing order so only smaller or equal nodes are connected.
For the current value v, we visit each node u that holds that value.
We look at every neighbor w of node u.
We only merge when the neighbor's value is no larger than v, so no bigger node lies on a path.
We union the components of w and u by attaching the root of w to the root of u.
We count how many nodes of value v fall into each component, keyed by the component root.
We go through each component's count of equal-valued nodes.
A component with c such nodes gives c times c plus one over two good paths, counting single nodes and pairs.
We return the total number of good paths.

number-of-paths-with-max-score.hook: Two answers at once: the best score, and how many paths reach it. Carry both in every cell.
number-of-paths-with-max-score.ask: On a square board, start at S in the bottom right and move up, left or up-left to E in the top left, avoiding X. Collect the digits. Return the best sum and how many paths achieve it.
number-of-paths-with-max-score.exampleWhy: S → 2 → 2 → 3 → E collects 2 + 2 + 3 = 7, and no other path reaches 7.

brute.idea: Explore every path from S with DFS, tracking the score, and keep the best score with its path count.
steps: From S, try up, left and up-left
Skip walls and the board edge
At E, compare the score with the best
Tie: count it; better: reset the count
brute.whySlow: The number of paths grows exponentially; a 100 by 100 board has astronomically many.

optimal.insight: The best path through a cell reuses the best path into it. Store best score and its count per cell, filled from S backwards.
steps: Fill from the bottom right towards the top left
Look at the three cells we could come from
Take the best score; add counts of all that tie
Add this cell's digit; X and unreachable stay -1

codeNotes.match: score[i][j], ways[i][j] = best + digit, cnt % MOD

pitfalls: Unreachable cells must be marked (-1), not scored 0, or they look like real paths.
Counts of tied predecessors add; they are not the maximum.

say.intro: Okay, Number of Paths with Max Score. We start at S, bottom right, and move up, left, or diagonally up left. We stop at E, top left, never stepping on an X. We collect the digits we cross. Return the best total, and how many paths reach it. Here, the best is seven, by exactly one path.
say.brute: The brute force walks every path with depth first search. At each cell, it tries all three moves, skipping walls and edges. When it reaches E, it compares the score with the best so far. A better score resets the count. A tie adds one. Correct, but the number of paths is exponential.
say.insight: Here's the thing. Any best path into a cell must use a best path into one of the three cells it came from. So each cell stores two numbers. Its best score, and how many paths achieve it. Take the best of the three neighbours. If several tie, their counts add up. Then add this cell's digit. Fill backwards from S, and each cell is done once.
say.anim: We start with the board, setting up score and ways grids filled with minus one. At the S cell, row two column two, score is zero and one way is recorded. Moving to cell two one, we check neighbors and find best score zero with one way. Cell two zero adds digit two, giving score two with one way, reusing the best path. Row one fills in, combining neighbor scores to get three, two, and five at various cells. Row zero now computes using row one results, building toward the top left cell. At cell zero zero, best neighbor score seven comes from one path, added to digit zero. The final answer is a max score of seven achieved by exactly one path.
say.code: Now the code. S gets score zero, and one way. Walls stay unreachable, with a score of minus one. For every other cell, we check the three predecessors. A strictly better score resets the count. A tie means the paths add up. If any predecessor was reachable, we collect this cell's digit, and store both values.
say.outro: Linear in the number of cells. It's two dimensional grid dynamic programming, counting optimal paths.

number-of-paths-with-max-score.title: Number of Paths with Max Score
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container LeetCode expects for this problem.
The method takes the board as a list of strings and returns the best score and the path count.
We set the modulus to one billion and seven, since path counts can grow very large.
We store n as the side length of the square board.
We build a score grid with an extra row and column of padding, filled with negative one to mean unreachable.
We build a matching ways grid, also padded, starting at zero because no paths have been counted yet.
At the start cell in the bottom right we set score to zero and ways to one, as the base case.
We loop the row index from the bottom row up to the top, since we fill backwards from the start.
Inside each row we loop the column index from right to left, so the cells below and right are already done.
If the cell is an obstacle or the start, we handle it specially and do not compute it here.
We skip to the next cell, leaving obstacles unreachable and keeping the start's base values.
We initialize the best neighbor score to negative one and the count of ways to zero.
We look at the three predecessor cells: below, right, and diagonal below-right.
If a neighbor has a strictly higher score than our best, we take it as the new best.
We also replace the count with that neighbor's ways, discarding the earlier lower-scoring paths.
If a neighbor ties the current best score, then its paths are equally good.
So we add that neighbor's ways to our running count.
Only if some neighbor was reachable, meaning best is nonnegative, do we fill in this cell.
The digit is zero for the end cell, otherwise the number written on the cell.
We store best plus digit as this cell's score, and the count reduced by the modulus as its ways.
We return score and ways at the top left, or zero and zero if no path reaches the end.

number-of-provinces.hook: A province is just a connected component. Count how many times a fresh search has to start.
number-of-provinces.ask: Given an n by n matrix where 1 means two cities are directly connected, return the number of provinces: groups of cities connected directly or through other cities.
number-of-provinces.exampleWhy: City 0 links to 1, and 1 links to 2, so cities 0, 1 and 2 form one province. City 3 stands alone.

brute.idea: Compute full reachability with Floyd-Warshall style closure, then count distinct reachability rows.
steps: Copy the matrix as reach
For each k, i, j: link i to j through k
Count distinct rows: one per province
brute.whySlow: Triple loop: 200 cities means 8 million updates, when one traversal of the matrix is enough.

optimal.insight: Each DFS from an unvisited city marks its whole province. The number of searches we start is the answer.
steps: Scan cities in order
Unvisited city: new province, start DFS
DFS marks every city reachable through 1s
Return the number of DFS starts

codeNotes.note: Direct link to a new city

pitfalls: The input is an adjacency matrix, not an edge list: scan the whole row.

say.intro: This is Number of Provinces. We get a grid where a one means two cities are directly connected. A province is a group of cities joined directly, or through others. Here, zero links to one, and one links to two. So those three form a province. City three is alone. Two provinces.
say.brute: The brute force works out full reachability. For every middle city k, and every pair i and j, if i reaches k and k reaches j, mark i as reaching j. Afterwards, cities in the same province have identical rows. Count the distinct rows. Correct, but cubic.
say.insight: Here's the thing. A province is just a connected component. Start a depth first search from any city not yet visited. It marks every city in that province. Keep scanning. The next unvisited city must belong to a new province. So the number of searches we launch is the number of provinces.
say.anim: We start with a four by four connection grid and no cities visited yet. City zero is unvisited, so we mark it seen and begin a depth first search. The search checks neighbors of city zero, finds city one connected, and marks it seen. From city one, city two is also connected, so it gets marked seen too. City two's neighbors are already seen, so this search finishes covering cities zero, one, two. Provinces becomes one, and the loop moves on since cities one and two are already visited. City three is unvisited, starts a new search, but has no connections to others. Provinces increases to two, giving the final answer of two provinces.
say.code: Let's walk the code. A seen list tracks cities already in a province. The search scans a city's row. Each direct link to a new city gets marked, and explored in turn. In the main loop, an untouched city starts a province. We run one search per province, adding one each time. Return the count.
say.outro: n squared, which is linear in the matrix size. It's graphs. Count connected components with depth first search.

number-of-provinces.title: Number of Provinces
lineNotes: We define the solution class that holds the method for counting provinces.
The method takes the connection matrix, where a one means two cities are directly linked, and returns an integer count.
We store n as the number of cities, which is the length of the matrix.
We create a seen list of n false values to track which cities have already been visited.
We define a helper function dfs that explores every city reachable from city i.
We loop over every city j to check whether it might be a neighbor of city i.
If city i is directly connected to city j and j is not yet seen, we need to visit it.
We mark city j as seen right away so no other path will visit it again.
We recurse into city j to continue exploring its neighbors, spreading across the whole province.
We start the province counter at zero before scanning the cities.
We loop over every city as a possible starting point for a new province.
If city i has not been seen, it belongs to a province we have not yet counted.
We mark city i as seen so it is not treated as a new start later.
We run dfs from city i, which marks every city in its province as seen.
We add one to the province count, since each fresh search discovers exactly one new province.
We return the total number of provinces found.

number-of-recent-calls.hook: A stream of timestamps and a fixed three second window. Old calls fall off the front.
number-of-recent-calls.ask: Design a counter. Each ping brings a new time t, always larger than before. Return how many pings, including this one, happened in the last 3000 milliseconds, from t minus 3000 up to t.
number-of-recent-calls.exampleWhy: At 6500 the window is 3500 to 6500, which holds only 6000 and 6500, so the answer is 2.

brute.idea: Keep every ping ever made. On each new ping, scan the whole history and count the times inside the window.
steps: Append t to the full history
Scan every stored time
Count times at least t - 3000
brute.whySlow: After 10,000 pings each call rescans 10,000 times, even though only recent ones can ever count again.

optimal.insight: Times only increase, so once a ping falls out of the window it is out forever. A queue lets us drop it from the front.
steps: Push the new time onto the back of a queue
Pop from the front while it is older than t - 3000
The queue length is the answer
optimal.space: O(W), W ≤ 3001 pings in a window

codeNotes.note: Queue of pings still in the window
Newest time joins at the back

pitfalls: The window is inclusive: a ping at exactly t - 3000 still counts.
Each time is pushed and popped once, so the cost is amortized constant.

say.intro: Okay, so here's Number of Recent Calls. Pings arrive with times that only go up. Each ping asks one thing. How many calls landed in the last three thousand milliseconds, counting this one? At the ping at six thousand five hundred, only six thousand and six thousand five hundred are recent. So we return two.
say.brute: The simple version keeps every ping forever. Each new ping walks the whole history and counts the times at least t minus three thousand. It's correct. So what's the catch? The history only grows. After ten thousand pings, every call rescans ten thousand old times. And most of those can never count again.
say.insight: Here's the thing. Times always increase, so the window only slides forward. Once a ping is too old, it stays too old forever. So old pings leave from the front, and new ones join at the back. What does that sound like? A queue. Each time enters once and leaves once. That's constant work per ping, on average.
say.anim: We start with an empty queue to track ping times. Ping at time 1 is added, and since nothing is too old, the count is 1. Ping at time 100 is added, still within the window, giving a count of 2. Ping at time 3001 joins the queue, all three pings remain, count is 3. At time 3002, ping 1 falls outside the three thousand window and is popped, leaving count 3. At time 6000, old pings 100 and 3001 both drop off, but count stays 3. At time 6500, two more pings fall outside the window and get removed. Only two pings remain in range, so the final returned count is 2.
say.code: The constructor makes an empty double ended queue. It holds the pings still in the window. In ping, the newest time joins at the back. Then we look at the front. Is it older than t minus three thousand? If so, we drop it forever, and keep checking. Everything left is recent, so we return the queue's length.
say.outro: Constant amortized time per ping, and memory bounded by the window. The takeaway? A sliding window over a stream lives naturally in a queue.

number-of-recent-calls.title: Number of Recent Calls
lineNotes: We define a RecentCounter class that will remember the times of recent pings and answer how many fall in the window.
The constructor runs once when the counter is created, setting up the starting state.
We create an empty double ended queue called q to hold ping times in arrival order.
The ping method receives a new time t, which is always larger than every earlier time.
We add the new time t to the back of the queue, since it is the newest ping.
While the oldest time at the front is earlier than t minus 3000, it lies outside the window.
We remove that oldest time from the front, and it never needs to come back because times only increase.
We return the queue length, which is exactly the number of pings within the last 3000 milliseconds including this one.

number-of-steps-to-reduce-a-number-to-ze.hook: Halve when even, subtract one when odd. The binary digits already tell you the count.
number-of-steps-to-reduce-a-number-to-ze.ask: Given a non-negative integer, repeatedly divide it by two if it is even, or subtract one if it is odd, until it reaches zero. Return how many steps that takes.
number-of-steps-to-reduce-a-number-to-ze.exampleWhy: 123 is 1111011 in binary: seven bits, six of them ones. Six halvings plus six subtractions make 12 steps.

brute.idea: Just simulate. While the number is not zero, apply the rule for even or odd and count one step.
steps: Even? divide by two
Odd? subtract one
Count every operation until zero
brute.whySlow: Not asymptotically slower. It loops once per operation, up to twice per bit, instead of reading each bit once.

optimal.insight: Each 0 bit costs one halving. Each 1 bit costs a subtraction then a halving, except the leading 1, which needs no final halving.
steps: Look at the lowest bit
A one costs two steps, a zero costs one
Shift right and repeat
Subtract one for the top bit's missing halving

codeNotes.note: Top bit needs no halving; zero stays zero

pitfalls: num = 0 needs zero steps; do not return minus one.
Closed form: bit_length - 1 + popcount, when num > 0.

say.intro: Number of Steps to Reduce a Number to Zero. If the number is even, we halve it. If it's odd, we subtract one. How many steps until we hit zero? For one hundred twenty three, it's twelve. And the binary form, one one one one zero one one, tells us why.
say.brute: The obvious move is to just play the game. While the number is above zero, check if it's even. If so, halve it. Otherwise, subtract one. Count a step either way. Honestly, this is already logarithmic, so it isn't slow. But it loops once per operation. Can we read the answer straight off the bits instead?
say.insight: Think in binary. Halving an even number shifts the bits right, dropping a zero. Subtracting one from an odd number turns the last one into a zero. So a zero bit costs one step. A one bit costs two: subtract, then shift. There's one exception. The leading one. Once it's gone we're at zero, so it skips the final shift.
say.anim: We start with num equal to 123 and steps at zero. Each loop checks the last bit, adding two for a one bit, one for a zero. After processing, num shrinks by halving, now sixty one, steps at two. The loop keeps halving num, through thirty, fifteen, seven, and three, accumulating steps. Now num is one, the leading bit, adding two more steps. After this halving, num becomes zero and steps reach thirteen. We subtract one since the leading bit needs no extra halving. The final answer returned is twelve steps to reduce num to zero.
say.code: We make one pass per binary digit, while the number still has bits. Check the lowest bit with a bitwise and. A one bit means subtract plus halve, so add two. A zero bit adds one. Then shift right to move to the next bit. At the end, take one off, because the top bit needs no halving. But never go below zero, so zero stays zero.
say.outro: Logarithmic time, constant space. The lesson here? Sometimes an arithmetic process can be read directly off the binary digits.

number-of-steps-to-reduce-a-number-to-ze.title: Number of Steps to Reduce a Number to Zero
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container that holds the method for this problem.
The method numberOfSteps takes a non-negative integer num and returns how many steps it takes to reach zero.
We start a counter called steps at zero to track the total operations.
We loop as long as num is nonzero, processing one bit of the number per iteration.
If the lowest bit is one we add two for subtract and halve, otherwise we add one for the halving.
We shift num right by one bit, which drops the lowest bit and moves to the next.
The leading one needs no final halving, so we subtract one from steps, and max with zero handles the case where num starts at zero.

number-of-strings-that-appear-as-substri.hook: A warm-up string check. The real lesson is knowing what your language's substring test already does.
number-of-strings-that-appear-as-substri.ask: Given a list of pattern strings and one word, count how many patterns appear somewhere inside the word as a contiguous block of characters. Duplicates in the list each count.
number-of-strings-that-appear-as-substri.exampleWhy: a, abc, bc and cab all sit inside abcab. Only d never appears, so the count is 4.

brute.idea: For each pattern, slide it across every start position in the word and compare character by character.
steps: Take one pattern
Try every start index in word
Matching slice? count it and stop
brute.whySlow: Same worst case as the built-in check, but hand-rolled slicing copies each window; the built-in search is faster and clearer.

optimal.insight: Patterns are independent, and with lengths at most 100 a direct substring search per pattern is already cheap. No fancy structure is needed.
steps: Loop over every pattern
Ask whether it occurs inside word
Add one when it does

pitfalls: Do not deduplicate patterns: three copies of a count three times.
For huge inputs, Aho-Corasick finds all patterns in one pass.

say.intro: Number of Strings That Appear as Substrings in Word. We have a list of patterns and one word. How many patterns show up inside the word? Here the word is a b c a b. Patterns a, a b c, b c and c a b all appear. Only d doesn't. So the answer is four.
say.brute: The hand rolled version slides each pattern across the word. At every start position, cut out a slice of the same length and compare. If it matches, count it and move on to the next pattern. Now, here's the thing. The worst case is the same as the built in search. It just copies a new slice at every position.
say.insight: So what's the insight? Honestly, it's restraint. Each pattern is checked on its own. And every string is at most a hundred characters. So the cleanest answer is the language's substring check, which runs a tuned search. Interviewers like seeing you notice when a simple loop is already good enough. Save the fancy structures for much bigger inputs.
say.anim: We start with count at zero, checking each pattern against the word abcab. Pattern a is checked and found inside the word, so count becomes one. Pattern abc is checked and found inside the word, raising count to two. Pattern bc is checked and found inside the word, raising count to three. Pattern d is checked but not found inside the word, so count stays three. Pattern cab is checked and found inside the word, raising count to four. All patterns are done, so the function returns the final count. The final answer shown is four matching patterns inside the word.
say.code: We start a counter for the patterns found so far. Then we check each pattern independently. Is it inside the word? Python's in operator runs that substring search for us. If yes, add one. Duplicate patterns are separate entries, so each one counts separately. When the loop ends, return the counter.
say.outro: Simple, clear, and fast enough for these limits. The pattern here is plain iteration: check each item independently, and tally.

number-of-strings-that-appear-as-substri.title: Number of Strings That Appear as Substrings in Word
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the wrapper the problem expects for our method.
The method numOfStrings takes the list of patterns and the word, and returns how many patterns appear inside the word.
We start a counter called count at zero to track how many patterns we have found so far.
We loop over every pattern in the list, treating each one independently, so duplicates are visited separately and each counts.
We check whether the current pattern appears as a contiguous block inside the word, using a direct substring search that is cheap here.
When the pattern is found, we add one to count, which is why duplicate patterns each add to the total.
After checking every pattern, we return count as the final number of patterns that are substrings of the word.

number-of-unique-xor-triplets-i.hook: Count every distinct XOR of three picks, without ever picking. The answer is a power of two.
number-of-unique-xor-triplets-i.ask: nums is a shuffle of the numbers 1 to n. Choose indices i ≤ j ≤ k, possibly repeated, and XOR the three values. Return how many different results are possible.
number-of-unique-xor-triplets-i.exampleWhy: With 1 to 5 every value from 0 to 7 is reachable, for example 1 XOR 2 XOR 3 is 0, so 8 values.

brute.idea: Try every triple of indices with i ≤ j ≤ k, XOR the three values, and collect results in a set.
steps: Loop i, then j from i, then k from j
XOR the three chosen values
Add the result to a set
Return the set size
brute.whySlow: With n = 100,000 that is about 10^14 triples, hopelessly slow.

optimal.insight: Values are exactly 1 to n. For n ≥ 3, three of them can XOR to every number below the next power of two above n.
steps: n is 1 or 2? the answer is n
Find how many bits n needs
Answer is 2 to that power

codeNotes.note: Tiny cases: only the values themselves

pitfalls: n = 1 or 2 breaks the rule: zero is not reachable, answer is n.
The order of nums is irrelevant; only n matters.

say.intro: Number of Unique XOR Triplets, part one. The array is a shuffle of one through n. We pick three positions, repeats allowed, and XOR the values. How many different results are possible? For one through five, every value from zero to seven shows up. So the answer is eight.
say.brute: The brute force tries every triple. Three nested loops pick i, then j from i, then k from j. XOR the three numbers, and drop the result into a set. The set's size is the answer. So what's the catch? That's cubic. With a hundred thousand numbers, it's around ten to the fourteen triples. Way too slow.
say.insight: Let's think about which values can exist. Pick one index three times, and you get that value back. And XOR never sets a bit above the top bit of n. So every result sits below the next power of two. Now, when n is at least three, small combinations fill every gap. Even zero, from one XOR two XOR three. So only the bit count of n matters.
say.anim: We start with nums holding five values, so n equals 5. Since n is at least 3, every XOR result below the next power of two is possible. Bits starts at 0, ready to count how many bits represent n. The loop shifts n right repeatedly, counting bits each time: n goes 5, 2, 1, 0. After three shifts, bits becomes 3, meaning n needs three bits. Finally we return 1 shifted left by bits, giving the total unique XOR values. The result is 8, matching the expected number of unique triplet XORs.
say.code: First, the tiny cases. If n is below three, return n, since only the values themselves are reachable. Otherwise, we count the bits of n. Each loop shifts n right, dropping one bit, until it hits zero. Then every value below two to that many bits is reachable. So we return one shifted left by the bit count.
say.outro: From cubic all the way down to logarithmic. The trick? Reason about which bits can ever be set, instead of enumerating.

number-of-unique-xor-triplets-i.title: Number of Unique XOR Triplets I
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which holds the method that LeetCode will call for this problem.
The method takes nums, a shuffle of one to n, and returns how many distinct triplet XOR values exist.
We set n to the length of nums, which also equals the largest value since nums is a shuffle of one to n.
If n is below three, we handle the tiny cases separately, because the full range trick needs at least three values.
For one or two elements, the number of distinct XOR results simply equals n, so we return n directly.
We set bits to zero so we can count how many binary digits n needs.
We loop while n is still nonzero, meaning there are still binary digits left to count.
Each pass adds one to bits, counting one more binary digit of the original n.
We shift n right by one position, dropping its lowest bit so the loop eventually ends.
The answer is two raised to bits, the next power of two above n, since every value from zero up to just below it is reachable.

number-of-ways-to-split-array.hook: Every split asks: left sum versus right sum. One running total answers them all.
number-of-ways-to-split-array.ask: Count the indices i, before the last element, where the sum of the first i + 1 numbers is at least the sum of the remaining numbers.
number-of-ways-to-split-array.exampleWhy: Total is 7. Only at index 2 is the left sum 5 at least the right sum 2.

brute.idea: For every split point, add up the left part and the right part from scratch and compare them.
steps: Choose split index i
Sum the left slice and the right slice
Count it if left ≥ right
brute.whySlow: Each split re-adds the whole array: 100,000 numbers means about 10 billion additions.

optimal.insight: The right sum is just total minus left sum. Keep a running left sum and each comparison costs constant time.
steps: Compute the total once
Walk the array growing the left sum
Right sum is total minus left
Count splits where left ≥ right

codeNotes.note: One pass for the full sum

pitfalls: Stop before the last index; the right side cannot be empty.
Negatives mean sums can shrink; never break early.

say.intro: Number of Ways to Split Array. A split at index i puts the first i plus one numbers on the left, and the rest on the right. It's valid when the left sum is at least the right sum. For two, minus one, four, minus six, three, five, only one split works. It's at index two.
say.brute: The straightforward way tries each split and adds both sides from scratch. Sum the left slice, sum the right slice, compare, and count. Sounds reasonable, right? But every split re-reads the whole array. That's n squared. With a hundred thousand numbers, that's around ten billion additions.
say.insight: Here's the thing. The two sides always add up to the same total. So once you know the total, the right sum is just total minus left. And as the split moves right, the left sum grows by exactly one number. Keep it as a running prefix sum. Now every split is a constant time check.
say.anim: We start by summing the whole array, giving a total of seven. Left sum and count both start at zero before we scan the array. At index zero, left becomes two, but two is less than the remaining five. At index one, left becomes one, still smaller than the right side's six. At index two, left jumps to five, now at least as big as the right side's two, so count increases. At index three, left drops to negative one, far below the remaining eight. At index four, left rises to two, still less than the remaining five. After checking all split points, the function returns a final count of one.
say.code: First, one pass for the full sum. Then we loop over every index except the last, because the right part must be non-empty. Each step, the prefix sum grows by one number. Then we get the right sum without re-adding anything. It's just total minus left. If left is at least that, count it. Finally, return the count.
say.outro: Quadratic down to linear, with constant space. The pattern is prefix sums. Derive the other side from the total, instead of recomputing it.

number-of-ways-to-split-array.title: Number of Ways to Split Array
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container this problem's method lives in.
This method takes the list of numbers and returns how many valid split positions exist.
We compute the total sum of nums once up front so the right side never needs recomputing.
We start left at zero, since no elements have been added to the left part yet.
We start count at zero to track how many valid splits we find.
We loop over indices up to but not including the last one, because the right part must be nonempty.
We add the current number to left, so left holds the sum of the first i plus one elements.
The right sum equals total minus left, so we check whether left is at least that value.
When the condition holds, this split is valid, so we increase count by one.
After checking every split position, we return count as the number of valid splits.

number-of-zigzag-arrays-i.hook: Up, down, up, down. Count every bouncing array with DP and prefix sums.
number-of-zigzag-arrays-i.ask: Count arrays of length n with values in l to r, where neighbours differ and no three in a row strictly rise or strictly fall. Return the count modulo 10^9 + 7.
number-of-zigzag-arrays-i.exampleWhy: Length 3 gives the 10 listed arrays; each extends by bouncing back, giving 16 valid arrays of length 4 using 1 to 3.

brute.idea: Build arrays one value at a time, skipping any value that repeats the previous one or continues the same direction.
steps: Start from every value
Try each next value
Skip equal or same-direction moves
Count arrays reaching length n
brute.whySlow: The number of arrays explodes exponentially; n = 2000 with 2000 values is unthinkable.

optimal.insight: Only the last value and last direction matter. Arrays ending low after a down step all feed every higher value, so prefix sums do it.
steps: up[x]: arrays ending at x after a rise
down[x]: arrays ending at x after a fall
new up[y] sums down[x] for x < y
new down[y] sums up[x] for x > y
Use running sums, one layer per length

number-of-zigzag-arrays-i.optimalCode:
class Solution:
    def zigZagArrays(self, n: int, l: int, r: int) -> int:
        MOD = 10**9 + 7
        m = r - l + 1
        up = [x for x in range(m)]
        down = [m - 1 - x for x in range(m)]
        for _ in range(n - 2):
            new_up = [0] * m
            run = 0
            for y in range(m):
                new_up[y] = run
                run = (run + down[y]) % MOD
            new_down = [0] * m
            run = 0
            for y in range(m - 1, -1, -1):
                new_down[y] = run
                run = (run + up[y]) % MOD
            up, down = new_up, new_down
        return (sum(up) + sum(down)) % MOD

codeNotes.note: Length 2 ending at x after rising

codeNotes.match: down = [m - 1 - x for x in range(m)]
codeNotes.note: Length 2 ending at x after falling
Prefix of falls, all smaller values
Suffix of rises, all larger values

pitfalls: Only m = r - l + 1 matters, not the actual values.
Summing directly over x makes it O(n · m²): use running sums.

say.intro: Number of ZigZag Arrays, part one. We count arrays of length n, using values from l to r. Neighbours must differ, and the direction must keep switching. So you never get two rises, or two falls, back to back. With length four and values one to three, there are sixteen.
say.brute: The brute force builds arrays one value at a time. From each start, try every next value. Skip it if it equals the last one, or keeps going the same direction. Count each array that reaches length n. Sounds fine, right? But the number of arrays grows exponentially. Large inputs are hopeless.
say.insight: So what do we actually need to extend an array? Just its last value, and whether the last step went up or down. That's two tables. Up of x counts arrays ending at x after a rise. Down of x, after a fall. Now, a rise into y comes from every fall ending below y. That's a prefix sum of down. And a fall into y is a suffix sum of up.
say.anim: We start with n equals 4, range from 1 to 3, giving three possible values. Up tracks arrays ending in an upward step, starting as zero, one, two. Down tracks arrays ending downward, starting as two, one, zero for each value. We build new up values using prefix sums of down, getting zero, two, three. Similarly new down values use suffix sums of up, giving three, two, zero. Second iteration repeats this, updating up to zero, three, five using prefix sums. Down becomes five, three, zero using suffix sums of the updated up array. Summing up and down arrays gives sixteen, the total zigzag arrays possible.
say.code: We fill the length two tables directly. Up of x counts arrays ending at x after rising. Down of x, after falling. For each extra length, sweep left to right with a running prefix of falls, covering all smaller values. That's the new up table. Then sweep right to left with a suffix of rises, all larger values, for the new down table. Roll forward. Return both sums, modulo a billion and seven.
say.outro: Exponential down to n times m. The pattern is two dimensional dynamic programming over length and value, sped up with prefix sums.

number-of-zigzag-arrays-i.title: Number of ZigZag Arrays I
lineNotes: We define the Solution class that holds the method for this problem.
The method takes the length n and the value range from l to r, returning the zigzag count.
We set the modulus to ten to the ninth plus seven so all counts stay small.
We shift values to start at zero, so m is the number of distinct values in the range.
Up at x counts length two arrays ending at x after a rising step, which equals x choices of smaller first value.
Down at x counts length two arrays ending at x after a falling step, which equals the number of larger first values.
We extend the array one element at a time, doing this n minus two more times.
We create a fresh up array to hold counts for the next length.
We start a running sum of down counts for values below the current one.
We walk each possible new last value y from smallest to largest.
An array ending at y by rising must previously have fallen to a smaller value, so we store the running sum.
We then add down at y into the running sum, keeping it modulo the modulus.
We create a fresh down array for the next length.
We reset the running sum to zero for the downward pass.
We walk y from largest to smallest, since falling arrays need a larger previous value.
An array ending at y by falling must previously have risen from a larger value, so we store the running sum.
We add up at y into the running sum, keeping it modulo the modulus.
We replace up and down with the new arrays, ready for the next round.
The answer sums every ending value in both directions, modulo the modulus.

number-of-zigzag-arrays-ii.hook: Same zigzag count, but n reaches a billion. Raise the DP transition to a power.
number-of-zigzag-arrays-ii.ask: Count arrays of length n, up to one billion, with values in l to r, where neighbours differ and no three in a row strictly rise or fall. Return it modulo 10^9 + 7.
number-of-zigzag-arrays-ii.exampleWhy: With only 4 and 5 available, the array must alternate: 4 5 4 5 4 or 5 4 5 4 5.

brute.idea: Run the part one DP: one layer per length, using prefix sums to move between the up and down tables.
steps: Build length 2 up and down tables
Repeat n - 2 times: prefix-sum transition
Sum both tables
brute.whySlow: n can be 10^9 layers; even 75 values per layer means about 75 billion operations.
brute.code:
class Solution:
    def zigZagArrays(self, n: int, l: int, r: int) -> int:
        MOD = 10**9 + 7
        m = r - l + 1
        up = list(range(m))
        down = [m - 1 - x for x in range(m)]
        for _ in range(n - 2):
            new_up, run = [0] * m, 0
            for y in range(m):
                new_up[y] = run
                run = (run + down[y]) % MOD
            new_down, run = [0] * m, 0
            for y in range(m - 1, -1, -1):
                new_down[y] = run
                run = (run + up[y]) % MOD
            up, down = new_up, new_down
        return (sum(up) + sum(down)) % MOD

optimal.insight: Each layer applies the same linear map to the 2m-long state. So n - 2 layers is one matrix power, found by repeated squaring.
steps: State: up and down tables stacked, length 2m
Matrix T maps the old state to the next
Apply T^(n-2) with square-and-multiply
Sum the final state

codeNotes.note: A fall ending at x can rise to y
A rise ending at x can fall to y

codeNotes.match: vec = list(range(m)) + [m - 1 - x for x in range(m)]

codeNotes.note: This power of T is needed

pitfalls: Square only while bits remain, or you waste one m³ multiply.
Matrix powers commute, so applying them to the vector in any order works.

say.intro: Number of ZigZag Arrays, part two. Same rules: values from l to r, neighbours differ, and the direction switches every step. But now the length can be a billion. With length five and only four and five available, the array must alternate. So there are exactly two.
say.brute: The baseline here is the part one solution. Keep an up table and a down table, and advance one length at a time with prefix sums. That's n times m work. It's great for lengths in the thousands. But a billion layers? Far too slow, even with only seventy five values.
say.insight: Now, notice something. Every layer does exactly the same thing. The new tables are a fixed linear mix of the old ones. So stack up and down into one vector of length two m. Then one step is just multiplying by a fixed matrix. And n minus two steps? That's the matrix to the power n minus two. Repeated squaring gets there in logarithmically many multiplications.
say.anim: We start with n equal 5, and the range l to r gives m equal 2 possible values. A transition matrix of size 4 is built to encode valid zigzag transitions between values. The matrix fills in as we compare each pair of indices, marking allowed up and down moves. The initial vector becomes 0, 1, 1, 0, representing counts for arrays of length two. Since n minus 2 equals 3, we apply the matrix once, then square it for the next power. Matrix squaring multiplies T by itself, computing new transition counts entry by entry. The squared matrix is ready, combining two layers of zigzag transitions into one. Applying it updates vec again, and since p now reaches zero, the loop ends. Summing the final vector gives the answer, two zigzag arrays total.
say.code: First we build the transition matrix. A fall ending at x can rise to any larger y. A rise ending at x can fall to any smaller y. The starting vector holds the length two counts, up then down. Then we walk the bits of n minus two. If a bit is set, this power is needed, so multiply the vector by the matrix. Then square, doubling the jump length. Return the vector's sum.
say.outro: Linear in n, down to logarithmic. The takeaway? When a DP step is linear and repeats, reach for fast matrix exponentiation.

number-of-zigzag-arrays-ii.title: Number of ZigZag Arrays II
lineNotes: We define the Solution class that holds the method for this problem.
The method takes the length n and the value range from l to r, and returns the count of zigzag arrays.
We set the modulus to one billion and seven so all counts stay small.
We compute m as the number of allowed values in the range from l to r.
The state has size twice m, one half for arrays ending in a rise and one half for ending in a fall.
We create a square transition matrix of that size, filled with zeros.
We loop over y, the value of the current last element.
We loop over x, the value of the neighbour we compare against.
If x is less than y, the previous step was a smaller value, so this state can be reached by a rise.
So we set the transition entry linking the down-state at y to the up-state at x to one.
If x is greater than y, the previous step was larger, so this state can be reached by a fall.
So we set the transition entry linking the up-state at y to the down-state at x to one.
We define a helper that multiplies two square matrices under the modulus.
We start the product matrix as all zeros.
We loop over each row of the left matrix.
We loop over the shared middle index.
We skip zero entries because the matrices are sparse and this saves work.
We loop over each column of the result.
We add the product of the two entries into the result cell, reduced by the modulus.
We return the finished product matrix.
The starting vector counts length-two arrays ending in each state: for the first half, x earlier smaller values, and for the second half, the larger ones, m minus one minus x.
We need n minus 2 more layers, so we set the exponent p to that.
We loop while the exponent still has bits left.
If the lowest bit of p is set, the current matrix power belongs in the answer.
So we apply the matrix to the vector, taking each row's dot product modulo the modulus.
We shift p right by one bit to move on to the next binary digit.
We only square the matrix if more bits remain, avoiding a wasted multiplication.
We square the matrix so it represents twice as many layers.
Finally we add all entries of the vector, modulo the modulus, to get the total number of zigzag arrays.

odd-even-linked-list.hook: Split a list into odd and even positions, in place, with two pointers and no extra memory.
odd-even-linked-list.ask: Reorder a linked list so all nodes at odd positions come first, then all nodes at even positions, keeping the original order inside each group. Use constant extra space.
odd-even-linked-list.exampleWhy: Positions 1, 3, 5, 7 hold 2, 3, 6, 7. Positions 2, 4, 6 hold 1, 5, 4. Odds first, then evens.

brute.idea: Copy the nodes into an array, take every other one for each group, then relink them in the new order.
steps: Collect all nodes into a list
Odd group is nodes[0::2], even nodes[1::2]
Relink odds then evens
brute.whySlow: Time is fine, but it stores every node in an array, breaking the required constant extra space.
brute.code:
class Solution:
    def oddEvenList(self, head: Optional[ListNode]) -> Optional[ListNode]:
        nodes = []
        cur = head
        while cur:
            nodes.append(cur)
            cur = cur.next
        dummy = ListNode(0)
        tail = dummy
        for node in nodes[0::2] + nodes[1::2]:
            tail.next = node
            tail = node
        tail.next = None
        return dummy.next

optimal.insight: Odd and even nodes alternate, so each pointer's next target is just two hops ahead. Weave two chains, then join them.
steps: odd starts at head, even at head.next
Remember where the even chain starts
Each odd skips to the next odd, each even likewise
Attach the even chain after the last odd

codeNotes.note: Keep the start of the even chain

pitfalls: Positions matter, not values: odd means first, third, fifth node.
Save even_head before relinking, or the even chain is lost.

say.intro: Odd Even Linked List. We regroup the list so nodes in positions one, three, five come first, then positions two, four, six. Order inside each group stays the same. So two, one, three, five, six, four, seven becomes two, three, six, seven, then one, five, four.
say.brute: The easy way copies every node into an array. Take every other node, starting from the first, for the odd group. The rest form the even group. Then relink them in that order. It's linear time. So what's wrong with it? It uses linear extra memory, and the problem asks for constant space.
say.insight: Here's the key. Odd and even nodes simply alternate. So from any odd node, the next odd node is just two hops ahead. Same for evens. Think of it as two pointers weaving two chains at once. Each one skips over the other's node. When we're done, we hook the even chain onto the last odd node.
say.anim: We start with the list two, one, three, five, six, four, seven. Odd points to node two, even points to node one, our two chains begin. Odd's next jumps to three, skipping one, linking odd nodes together. Even now points to node one, linked forward to five, building the even chain. The loop continues, weaving three to six and five to four similarly. Now odd links six to seven, and even moves to node four, the last even. Even becomes none, so the loop stops since no pairs remain. Odd's next attaches to even_head, joining both chains into one list. The final list returned is two, three, six, seven, one, five, four.
say.code: If the list is empty, return it. Odd starts at the head, even at the second node. We keep the start of the even chain, because we'll need it later. Then we loop, stopping when the evens run out. Each round, odd skips over an even and advances. Then even skips over an odd and advances. Finally, glue the evens after the last odd, and return the head.
say.outro: Linear time, constant space. The lesson for linked lists? Rewire pointers in place, and save any head you'll need later.

odd-even-linked-list.title: Odd Even Linked List
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container the interview platform expects for our method.
This method takes the head of a linked list and returns the head of the reordered list.
First we handle the edge case where the list is empty, since there is nothing to rearrange.
In that case we simply return head, which is already empty.
We start odd at the first node and even at the second node, the heads of our two chains.
We remember the start of the even chain, because we must attach it after the odd chain at the end.
We loop while even and its next both exist, meaning there is another odd node to pull out.
We link the current odd node to the node after even, which is the next odd node.
We advance odd to that next odd node, extending the odd chain.
We link even to the node after the new odd, which is the next even node.
We advance even to that next even node, extending the even chain.
Once the loop ends, we attach the saved even chain to the tail of the odd chain.
We return head, which is still the first node and now leads all odd nodes followed by all even nodes.

partition-array-according-to-given-pivot.hook: A stable three-way partition: smaller, equal, larger, with original order kept on both sides.
partition-array-according-to-given-pivot.ask: Rearrange the array so elements less than the pivot come first, then elements equal to it, then elements greater. The smaller and larger groups must keep their original relative order.
partition-array-according-to-given-pivot.exampleWhy: 9, 5, 3 are smaller and keep their order, the two 10s sit in the middle, then 12, 14.

brute.idea: Stable-sort the array by a key: 0 for smaller than pivot, 1 for equal, 2 for larger.
steps: Map each value to group 0, 1 or 2
Stable sort by that group
Original order survives within each group
brute.whySlow: Sorting spends n log n comparisons to arrange only three groups that a single pass can place directly.

optimal.insight: Fill smaller values from the front walking forward, larger values from the back walking backward. Whatever remains in the middle is the pivot.
steps: Start the result filled with pivot
lo pointer writes small values left to right
hi pointer writes large values right to left, scanning backward
Both groups keep order; gap is pivot

codeNotes.note: Large values fill from the right

pitfalls: Classic in-place quicksort partitioning is not stable; order would break.
Scan large values backward so they land in original order.

say.intro: Partition Array According to Given Pivot. Smaller values go first, values equal to the pivot go in the middle, and larger values go last. Within each group, the original order stays. With pivot ten, we get nine, five, three, then ten, ten, then twelve, fourteen.
say.brute: The quick fix is a stable sort. Give each number a key: zero if it's below the pivot, one if equal, two if above. Then sort by that key. Since the sort is stable, equal keys keep their order. It works. But we're paying n log n time just to arrange three groups.
say.insight: Think about it this way. We already know where every group lives. Smaller values fill from the left, in order. Larger values fill from the right. And if we scan the input backward, they land in order too. So what's left in the middle? It has to be the pivot. So we prefill the result with it, and run both scans in one loop.
say.anim: We start with the array and pivot value ten, building a result array filled entirely with tens. Two pointers, lo and hi, track where smaller and larger values will be placed, from front and back. Nine is less than ten, so it goes to position lo, and lo advances to one. Five is smaller than ten, placed at lo, while fourteen from the back is larger and placed at hi. Ten and fourteen aren't strictly smaller or larger, so the walk continues without changes. Three is smaller, filling lo, and twelve from the back is larger, filling hi, closing the gap. The final element ten matches the pivot exactly, so nothing more needs placing. The loop finishes, returning the partitioned array nine, five, three, ten, ten, twelve, fourteen.
say.code: We create a result filled with the pivot, so the middle defaults to it. Set lo to zero and hi to the last index. Each step, the forward scan places small values. If the i-th number is below the pivot, write it at lo and advance. Then the backward scan places large values. If the i-th number from the end is above the pivot, it fills from the right at hi, and hi moves left.
say.outro: A sort replaced by one linear pass. The pattern is two pointers, filling from opposite ends.

partition-array-according-to-given-pivot.title: Partition Array According to Given Pivot
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the wrapper this problem's method lives in.
This method takes the list of numbers and the pivot value, and returns the rearranged list.
We store the length of nums in n so we can use it for indexing.
We create a result list of length n filled with the pivot, so leftover middle slots are already correct.
We set lo to zero for the next smaller slot and hi to the last index for the next larger slot.
We loop i from zero to n minus one, scanning from the front and the back at once.
If the element at position i from the front is less than the pivot, it belongs in the smaller group.
We place that smaller element at position lo in the result, preserving its original relative order.
We advance lo by one so the next smaller element goes in the following slot.
We also check the element at position i from the back, asking whether it is greater than the pivot.
If so, we write that larger element into the result at position hi, filling from the end.
We move hi back by one, so scanning from the right keeps the larger elements in their original order.
We return the result, with smaller values first, pivots in the middle, and larger values last.

path-existence-queries-in-a-graph-ii.hook: Shortest paths for a hundred thousand queries. Sort, jump greedily, and double the jumps.
path-existence-queries-in-a-graph-ii.ask: Nodes are joined when their values differ by at most maxDiff. For each query pair, return the fewest edges on a path between them, or -1 if they are disconnected.
path-existence-queries-in-a-graph-ii.exampleWhy: 1 → 3 → 5 takes two hops, so query [0,2] is 2. Nothing bridges 5 and 9, so [2,3] is -1.

brute.idea: For each query, run a breadth-first search from u, checking every node pair against maxDiff as edges.
steps: Start BFS at u
Neighbours: every node within maxDiff
Record distances; answer dist[v] or -1
brute.whySlow: Each BFS scans all n² pairs; 100,000 queries on 100,000 nodes is astronomically slow.

optimal.insight: On the sorted line, the best hop always goes as far right as allowed. Precompute 2^k greedy jumps, then answer each query by binary lifting.
steps: Sort nodes by value; record positions
nxt[i]: farthest sorted index within maxDiff
up[k][i]: where 2^k greedy hops land
Query: take big jumps that stay short of the target
One more hop finishes it, or -1

codeNotes.note: Line the nodes up by value

codeNotes.match: while j + 1 < n and vals[j + 1] - vals[i] <= maxDiff:

codeNotes.note: Take the jump if still short
Final hop lands on or past b

pitfalls: Equal values at different nodes are distinct positions, at distance 1.
Query u == v is distance 0, not -1.

say.intro: Path Existence Queries in a Graph, part two. Two nodes share an edge when their values are at most max diff apart. For each query pair, we return the shortest path length, or minus one. With values five, three, one, nine, ten, and max diff two, five to one takes two hops, through three.
say.brute: The brute force runs a breadth first search for every query. From the start, any node within max diff is a neighbour. So each expansion scans all the nodes. That's n squared work per query. With a hundred thousand nodes and a hundred thousand queries? Hopeless.
say.insight: Here's the trick. Sort the values onto a line. Now neighbours form a contiguous window. And the smartest hop always goes as far right as allowed. Greedy hopping gives the shortest path. But hopping one step at a time is slow. So precompute where two, four, eight greedy hops land. Each query climbs with the biggest jumps that stay short. That's binary lifting.
say.anim: We sort the array indices by value, giving the order two, one, zero, three, four. Sorted values become one, three, five, nine, ten, ready for greedy jumps. For each index we extend j rightward while the gap stays within maxDiff of two. This builds the next array, one, two, two, four, four, the farthest reachable step. Binary lifting tables are built, doubling jumps up to four levels for fast queries. Query zero, one maps to positions one and two, needing one jump, so answer one. Query zero, two maps to positions zero and two, taking two jumps to connect. Query two, three can never reach, giving minus one, while four, three needs one jump, giving final answers one, two, minus one, one.
say.code: First, line the nodes up by value. A two pointer sweep finds the farthest reachable index from each position. Then build the jump tables, where two half size jumps make one full jump. For a query, order the two positions. If even maximal jumping never arrives, return minus one. Otherwise, take each jump if we're still short. The final hop lands on or past the target, so add one.
say.outro: From quadratic per query, down to logarithmic. The takeaway? A greedy line structure plus binary lifting handles tons of queries.

path-existence-queries-in-a-graph-ii.title: Path Existence Queries in a Graph II
lineNotes: We define the solution class that holds the method for answering the path queries.
The method takes node count, values, the maximum allowed difference, and the list of query pairs.
We sort node indices by their values, giving the order of nodes along the number line.
We create a position array to record where each original node lands in sorted order.
We loop over the sorted order, pairing each sorted position with its original node index.
We store that sorted position for the node so queries can map nodes to the line.
We build the sorted values array so we can compare neighbors by value directly.
We create nxt to hold, for each sorted position, the farthest position reachable in one hop.
We start a pointer j at zero that only moves right, giving a two pointer sweep.
We visit every sorted position i as the starting point of a hop.
While the next value is still within maxDiff of the value at i, we can reach further.
We advance j one step right to extend the reach.
We record j as the farthest position reachable from i in a single edge.
We pick the number of lifting levels so that jumps of size two to the k cover any path length.
The jump table starts with level zero, which is the single greedy hop array.
We build each higher level by doubling the previous one.
We grab the most recent level to combine with itself.
Each new level jumps twice using the previous level, so it moves two to the k hops.
We prepare a list to collect the answers.
We go through every query pair of original nodes u and v.
We convert both nodes to sorted positions and order them so a is left of b.
If both land on the same position, they are the same node or equal reach point.
The distance in that case is zero, so we add zero.
If even the maximum jump from a cannot reach b, the two are disconnected.
So we record negative one for this query.
Otherwise a path exists and we find its minimum length.
We start counting the number of hops taken at zero.
We try jump sizes from largest to smallest, as in standard binary lifting.
If jumping two to the k from a still stays left of b, that jump is safe to take.
We move a to that farther position, never overshooting b.
We add two to the k to our step count for the jump we took.
After stopping just short of b, one more hop reaches it, so we add one and record.
Finally we return the list of answers for all queries.

path-sum-iii.hook: Count downward paths with a target sum. It is subarray sum equals k, on a tree.
path-sum-iii.ask: Given a binary tree and a target, count the paths whose node values add up to the target. A path can start and end anywhere, but must go downward from parent to child.
path-sum-iii.exampleWhy: Three downward paths sum to 8: 5 → 3, 5 → 2 → 1, and -3 → 11.

brute.idea: Treat every node as a possible start, and from each one walk all downward paths, counting those that hit the target.
steps: Visit every node as a start
Walk down subtracting values
Count when the remainder hits zero
brute.time: O(n²) worst, O(n log n) balanced
brute.whySlow: On a chain-shaped tree of 1,000 nodes, every start walks the rest: about half a million steps.

optimal.insight: A path ending here sums to target exactly when some ancestor prefix equals current prefix minus target. Count prefixes on the current root path.
steps: Keep a running sum from the root
Look up how many earlier prefixes equal cur - target
Record cur, recurse into both children
Remove cur when backtracking

codeNotes.note: Empty prefix: paths starting at root
Paths ending here with the target
This prefix is now an ancestor

pitfalls: Forgetting to decrement mixes prefixes from sibling branches.
Look up before adding cur, or a zero target counts empty paths.

say.intro: Path Sum three. We count paths in a binary tree that add up to a target. A path can start and end at any node, but it must only go downward. With target eight, three paths work. Five then three. Five, two, one. And minus three then eleven.
say.brute: The brute force tries every node as a start. From each start, walk every downward path, and count each time the sum hits the target. On a balanced tree, that's n log n. But on a long chain? Every start walks nearly the whole tree again. That's n squared.
say.insight: Here's the thing. This is the subarray sum equals k trick, on the path from the root. Keep a running sum. A downward path ending here hits the target exactly when some earlier prefix equals the current sum minus the target. A hash map counts those prefixes. And when we leave a node, we remove its prefix. Why? So other branches never see it.
say.anim: We start at root value ten, tracking prefix sums seen so far starting with zero. At node ten, current sum is ten, and we check if sum minus eight was seen before. Moving to node five, current sum becomes fifteen, no match yet, so we keep going down. At node three, sum reaches eighteen, matching a stored prefix, giving us our first path found. After exploring that branch fully, we backtrack, removing eighteen from our prefix counts. Deeper at node one, sum is eighteen again, matching prefix ten, finding another valid path. Back near the top, exploring node eleven, sum eighteen matches again, adding a third path. All branches explored and backtracked, the function returns a final total of three paths.
say.code: We seed the map with the empty prefix, zero, seen once. That covers paths starting at the root. In the search, add the node's value to the running sum. Then count paths ending here with the target, by looking up sum minus target. Next, record this prefix, since it's now an ancestor. Recurse into both children. Finally, backtrack by decrementing it as we leave the branch.
say.outro: Quadratic down to linear. The pattern is a prefix sum hash map on a tree, undone as the depth first search unwinds.

path-sum-iii.title: Path Sum III
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container the problem expects for our method.
The pathSum method takes the tree root and the target sum, and returns how many downward paths hit the target.
We create a default dictionary counting how many times each prefix sum appears on the current root-to-node path.
We seed the count for prefix zero with one, so paths starting at the root are counted correctly.
We define a recursive helper dfs that visits a node while carrying the running prefix sum called cur.
If the node is missing, we have walked past a leaf and there is nothing to count.
So we return zero paths for an empty node.
We add the current node's value to the running prefix sum.
We start the result with how many earlier prefixes equal cur minus target, since each one gives a valid path ending here.
We record the current prefix sum in the dictionary so descendants can use it as a possible path start.
We recurse into the left and right children and add their path counts to our result.
On the way back up we remove this node's prefix from the dictionary, so sibling branches only see their own ancestors.
We return the total number of valid paths found at or below this node.
We kick off the search from the root with an initial prefix sum of zero and return the answer.

predict-the-winner.hook: Two perfect players pick from the ends. Track score difference, not scores.
predict-the-winner.ask: Two players alternately take a number from either end of the array. Both play optimally. Return true if player one ends with a score at least as large as player two's.
predict-the-winner.exampleWhy: Player one takes 1. Whatever player two takes, 233 becomes available, so player one wins 234 to 12.

brute.idea: Recursive minimax: the current player tries both ends and keeps whichever leaves the best score difference.
steps: diff(i, j): best lead on nums[i..j]
Take left: nums[i] - diff(i+1, j)
Take right: nums[j] - diff(i, j-1)
Keep the larger
brute.whySlow: Same subarrays are re-solved endlessly: 20 numbers already means about a million calls.

optimal.insight: Only the remaining subarray i..j matters. Store the best lead the mover can get there, and build up from short ranges to long.
steps: dp[i][i] is nums[i]
Grow range length from 2 to n
dp[i][j] = max of taking left or right, minus opponent's lead
Player one wins if dp[0][n-1] ≥ 0

codeNotes.note: My pick minus opponent's best lead

pitfalls: Greedy taking the bigger end fails, as 1, 5, 233, 7 shows.
A tie is a win for player one: use ≥ 0.

say.intro: Predict the Winner. Two players take turns grabbing a number from either end of the array. Both play perfectly. Does player one end with at least as much as player two? For one, five, two hundred thirty three, seven, yes. Player one takes one, and then two hundred thirty three always opens up.
say.brute: The brute force is plain minimax. Ask: what's the best lead the current player can get on this range? Take the left end, minus the opponent's best lead on the rest. Or take the right end the same way. Keep the larger. So what's the catch? Without memory, the same ranges get solved over and over. That's exponential.
say.insight: Here's the trick. Track the difference in scores, not the scores themselves. Then the opponent's best result is the same function on a smaller range, just subtracted. And how many ranges are there? Only about n squared. So we store the best lead for every range. Fill short ranges before long ones, and the whole game is solved in quadratic time.
say.anim: We start with nums 1, 5, 233, 7, and a 4 by 4 dp grid of zeros. The diagonal fills first, each dp cell equal to that single number's value. Now length 2 ranges get computed, comparing taking the left or right number. For i 0, j 1, dp becomes 4, meaning taking 5 beats taking 1. For i 2, j 3, dp is 226, since 233 is far better than 7. Length 3 ranges combine these results, like dp for i 1, j 3 becoming negative 221. Finally length 4 computes the whole array, giving dp of 0 to 3 equal 222. Since 222 is at least zero, the first player wins, so the answer is true.
say.code: We make an n by n table. With one number left, you just take it, so each diagonal cell is its own value. Then we loop lengths from two up, so shorter ranges are ready first. For each start, find the end. The lead is my pick minus the opponent's best lead on what's left, trying both ends. Ties count as a win, so return whether the full range is at least zero.
say.outro: Exponential down to quadratic. The pattern is interval dynamic programming, on score differences.

predict-the-winner.title: Predict the Winner
lineNotes: We define a class named Solution, which is the standard wrapper for this problem's method.
The method predictTheWinner takes the list nums and returns true if player one can at least tie.
We store n as the number of elements in nums for use in the table sizes and loops.
We build an n by n table dp, where dp of i and j will hold the best lead for the mover on range i to j.
We loop over every index i to fill in the simplest ranges, those with exactly one number.
With one number left, the mover takes it, so the best lead equals that number itself.
We now grow the range length from two up to n, so smaller ranges are always solved before larger ones.
For each length, we slide the start index i across all positions where a range of that length fits.
We compute the end index j from the start and length, so the range runs from i to j.
The mover either takes the left number or the right one, subtracting the opponent's best lead on the remaining range, and keeps the larger result.
Player one wins or ties if the best lead over the whole array is at least zero.

range-sum-of-bst.hook: Sum the values in a range, and let the BST ordering tell you which branches to skip.
range-sum-of-bst.ask: Given the root of a binary search tree and two bounds, low and high, return the sum of all node values that lie between them, inclusive.
range-sum-of-bst.exampleWhy: Only 6, 7 and 10 fall inside 6 to 10, and 6 + 7 + 10 = 23.

brute.idea: Visit every node in the tree, and add its value if it falls inside the range.
steps: Traverse the whole tree
In range? add the value
Return the total
brute.whySlow: Same worst case, but it ignores BST order and explores subtrees that cannot contain any in-range value.

optimal.insight: If a node is below low, its whole left subtree is too. If above high, its right subtree is. Skip those branches entirely.
steps: Empty node contributes zero
Value below low? search only the right
Value above high? search only the left
Otherwise add it and search both

codeNotes.note: Too small: left side is smaller still
Too big: right side is bigger still
In range: count it, explore both

pitfalls: Bounds are inclusive: values equal to low or high count.
Do not skip a node's children just because the node is out of range.

say.intro: Range Sum of B S T. We get a binary search tree and a range from low to high. We want the sum of every value inside that range. With the range six to ten, only six, seven and ten qualify. So the answer is twenty three.
say.brute: The brute force ignores the search tree property. It visits every node, adds the value if it's in range, and always recurses into both children. That's linear time. Same worst case as the better approach, actually. But it wastes effort walking whole subtrees that can't possibly contain an answer.
say.insight: So let's use the ordering. Everything on a node's left is smaller. Everything on its right is larger. So if a node is below low, can anything on its left qualify? No. We only search right. If it's above high, we only search left. Only nodes inside the range send us down both sides.
say.anim: We start at the root node 10, which falls between low 6 and high 10. Node 5 is below low 6, so its left subtree gets skipped entirely, saving work. Node 7 is within range, so we add it and explore both its children. Node 6 is in range too, contributing its value to the running total. Node 6 returns 6, and node 7 combines it to return 13 upward. Node 5's subtree sum totals 13, since only node 7 and 6 counted. Node 15 exceeds high 10, so its right subtree is skipped automatically. All branches return, and the final range sum shown is 23.
say.code: If we fell off the tree, return zero. If the value is too small, the left side is smaller still, so we only search right. If it's too big, the right side is bigger still, so we only search left. Otherwise it's in range. Count the value, and explore both subtrees, adding their sums.
say.outro: Linear in the worst case, but pruned in practice. The lesson? Let the search tree's order decide which branches to visit.

range-sum-of-bst.title: Range Sum of BST
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which holds the method that solves the range sum problem.
The method rangeSumBST takes the tree root plus the low and high bounds, and returns an integer sum.
First we check for an empty node, which is the base case when recursion walks off the tree.
An empty node contributes nothing, so we return zero.
If the current value is below low, this node and its whole left subtree are too small.
So we skip them and recurse only into the right subtree, where larger values live.
If the current value is above high, this node and its entire right subtree are too large.
So we skip them and recurse only into the left subtree, where smaller values live.
Otherwise the value is in range, so we add it to the sums from both the left and right subtrees.

range-sum-query-2d-immutable.hook: Any rectangle sum in constant time. Precompute once, then add and subtract four corners.
range-sum-query-2d-immutable.ask: Design a class that stores a matrix and answers many queries: return the sum of all cells inside the rectangle from row1, col1 to row2, col2, inclusive. Each query must be constant time.

brute.idea: Store the matrix as is. For each query, loop over every cell in the rectangle and add it up.
steps: Keep the raw matrix
Loop rows row1 to row2
Loop columns col1 to col2, adding cells
brute.whySlow: A full 200 by 200 rectangle is 40,000 additions; 10,000 queries make 400 million.

optimal.insight: Precompute sums of every top-left rectangle. Any rectangle is the big corner block minus two strips plus the doubly removed overlap.
steps: pre[r+1][c+1] = sum of cells above and left
Build it with inclusion-exclusion in one pass
Query: big block minus top strip minus left strip
Add back the corner removed twice

codeNotes.note: Extra zero row and column avoid edge checks
Cell plus above plus left minus overlap
Whole block, minus strips, plus corner

pitfalls: Forgetting to add back the overlap corner double-subtracts it.
Off-by-one: the padded table is shifted by one in both directions.

say.intro: Range Sum Query two D, Immutable. We store a matrix once. Then we answer lots of questions like, what's the sum of this rectangle? Each answer must take constant time. In our three by three grid, the top left two by two block adds up to fourteen.
say.brute: The brute force keeps the raw matrix. For each query, it loops over every cell in the rectangle and adds them up. Fine for one question. But a big rectangle has forty thousand cells. Ten thousand queries? Now we're at hundreds of millions of additions.
say.insight: Here's the idea. For every cell, precompute the sum of the whole block from the top left corner down to it. Now any rectangle is that big block, minus the strip above, minus the strip to the left. But notice, the corner where those strips overlap got removed twice. So we add it back once. Four lookups. Constant time.
say.anim: We start with the three by three matrix and build a prefix sum table one larger in each direction. Row by row, each cell adds the matrix value plus sums above and left, minus the double counted corner. By the last row, the prefix table is fully filled with cumulative sums up to each point. For region zero zero to one one, we combine four prefix corners to get fourteen. Next region one one to two two reuses the same table, returning eleven. Finally region zero one to two two is computed the same way, giving twelve. The final answers match expected output: null, fourteen, eleven, and twelve.
say.code: In the constructor, we build a table one row and one column bigger, filled with zeros. That extra zero row and column means no edge checks. Each prefix is the cell, plus the one above, plus the one to the left, minus the overlap. Then in sum region, take the whole block, subtract both strips, and add back the corner.
say.outro: From work proportional to the rectangle per query, down to constant. The pattern is prefix sums in two dimensions, with inclusion and exclusion.

range-sum-query-2d-immutable.title: Range Sum Query 2D - Immutable
lineNotes: We define a class called NumMatrix that will store precomputed data so that rectangle sum queries run fast.
The constructor receives the matrix and builds a prefix sum table once, up front.
We read the number of rows and columns from the matrix so we can size the table.
We create a table with one extra row and column of zeros, so edge cases need no special handling.
We loop over each row of the original matrix.
Inside that, we loop over each column so every cell gets visited exactly once.
Each table entry equals the cell plus the block above plus the block to the left, minus the overlap counted twice.
The sumRegion method answers a query for the rectangle between the given corners, inclusive.
We store the prefix table in a short local name p to keep the formula readable.
We take the big corner block, subtract the strip above and the strip to the left, then add back the doubly removed overlap.

rank-transform-of-an-array.hook: Replace every number by its rank. Sort the distinct values once, then look ranks up.
rank-transform-of-an-array.ask: Replace each element with its rank: 1 for the smallest value, larger values get larger ranks, equal values share a rank, and ranks are as small as possible.
rank-transform-of-an-array.exampleWhy: Distinct sorted values are 10, 20, 30, 40, so they get ranks 1 to 4; both 10s get rank 1.
