brute.idea: For each element, collect the distinct values smaller than it. Its rank is that count plus one.
steps: Take one element
Scan the array for distinct smaller values
Rank is their count plus one
brute.whySlow: Every element rescans the whole array: 100,000 elements is about 10 billion comparisons.

optimal.insight: A value's rank is its position among the sorted distinct values. Sort once, assign ranks in order, and look each element up.
steps: Deduplicate and sort the values
Assign ranks 1, 2, 3 in that order
Map every element to its rank

codeNotes.note: Next rank is one past the last

pitfalls: Sorting without deduplicating gives duplicates different ranks.
An empty array returns an empty list.

say.intro: Rank Transform of an Array. We replace each number with its rank. The smallest value gets rank one. Equal values share a rank, and there are no gaps. So forty, ten, twenty, thirty, ten becomes four, one, two, three, one.
say.brute: The direct way computes each rank from scratch. For every element, scan the whole array and collect the distinct values that are smaller. The rank is that count, plus one. It's correct. But every element rescans everything, so it's n squared. A hundred thousand numbers means about ten billion comparisons.
say.insight: Think about what a rank really is. It's just a position in sorted order, once duplicates are gone. So drop duplicates with a set, sort what's left, and hand out ranks one, two, three. Store them in a hash map. Now every element finds its rank in constant time. The sort dominates, at n log n.
say.anim: We start with the array forty, ten, twenty, thirty, ten, and an empty rank dictionary. We sort the unique values and begin assigning ranks in increasing order. Ten is the smallest value, so it gets rank one. Twenty comes next, receiving rank two in the dictionary. Thirty follows, getting rank three as the third smallest distinct value. Forty is the largest, so it receives rank four, completing the mapping. Now we build the result by looking up each original element's rank. The final output is four, one, two, three, one, matching the expected ranks.
say.code: We start with an empty dictionary, our value to rank lookup. Then we loop over the distinct values, smallest first. The next rank is one past the last, which is just the dictionary's size plus one. So there are never gaps. Finally, we build the answer with a constant time lookup per element, keeping the original order.
say.outro: n squared down to n log n. The pattern? Sort once to define the order, then use a hash map for instant lookups.

rank-transform-of-an-array.title: Rank Transform of an Array
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container the problem expects for our method.
The method arrayRankTransform takes the list arr and will return a list of ranks in the same order.
We start with an empty dictionary called rank that will map each distinct value to its rank.
We loop over the distinct values of arr in sorted order, so smaller values come first.
Each value gets a rank one more than the current size of rank, so ranks count up from one without gaps.
Finally we build the answer by looking up each original element in rank, preserving the original order and giving duplicates the same rank.

rearrange-array-elements-by-sign.hook: Alternate positive and negative while keeping order. Two write pointers, two steps apart.
rearrange-array-elements-by-sign.ask: The array has equally many positives and negatives. Rearrange it so signs alternate, starting with a positive, while numbers of the same sign keep their original order.
rearrange-array-elements-by-sign.exampleWhy: Positives 3, 1, 2 fill even slots in order; negatives -2, -5, -4 fill odd slots in order.

brute.idea: Fix positions left to right. If a slot has the wrong sign, pull the next number of the right sign forward.
steps: Even index wants positive, odd wants negative
Wrong sign? find the next correct one
Pop it and insert it here
brute.whySlow: Each insert shifts the rest of the list: 200,000 numbers can mean billions of element moves.

optimal.insight: Positives always land on even indices and negatives on odd ones, in order. Keep one write pointer for each and advance by two.
steps: pos starts at 0, neg at 1
Positive: write at pos, pos += 2
Negative: write at neg, neg += 2

codeNotes.note: Next even slot and next odd slot
Positive goes to an even index
Skip the slot reserved for a negative
Negative goes to an odd index

pitfalls: Zero never appears, so x > 0 cleanly splits the signs.
Swapping in place breaks the required relative order.

say.intro: Rearrange Array Elements by Sign. There are as many positives as negatives. We alternate signs, starting with a positive, and keep each sign's original order. So three, one, minus two, minus five, two, minus four becomes three, minus two, one, minus five, two, minus four.
say.brute: The brute force fixes positions left to right. Even slots want a positive, odd slots want a negative. If a slot has the wrong sign, search ahead for the next right one, pop it out, and insert it here. Order is preserved. So what's the problem? Every insert shifts the rest of the list. That's n squared.
say.insight: Here's the thing. We already know exactly where everything goes. The first positive lands at index zero, the second at index two, and so on. The first negative lands at one, then three. So keep two write pointers, one for even slots, one for odd. Each moves by two. One pass places every number.
say.anim: We start with an empty result array and two pointers, pos at zero and neg at one. Three is positive, so it goes to index zero, and pos jumps to two. One is also positive, placed at index two, pos advances to four. Negative two goes to index one instead, since negatives fill odd slots, neg becomes three. Negative five lands at index three, pushing neg to five. Two is positive, filling index four, pos moves to six. Negative four fills index five, completing the odd positions with neg at seven. The function returns the final array: three, negative two, one, negative five, two, negative four.
say.code: We make a result array, and track the next even slot and the next odd slot, starting at zero and one. Then loop over the numbers. A positive goes to the even index. That pointer jumps by two, skipping the slot reserved for a negative. A negative goes to the odd index, and its pointer jumps by two as well. Return the result.
say.outro: Quadratic down to linear. The pattern is two pointers, here as two write positions striding through even and odd slots.

rearrange-array-elements-by-sign.title: Rearrange Array Elements by Sign
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container the problem expects for our method.
The method rearrangeArray takes the list nums and will return a new list with signs alternating.
We create a result list of zeros with the same length as nums, ready to be filled by position.
We set the positive pointer to zero and the negative pointer to one, since positives start on even indices.
We walk through nums in its original order so that same-sign numbers keep their relative order.
We check whether the current number x is positive.
If positive, we place x into the result at the positive pointer's index.
We move the positive pointer forward by two so the next positive lands on the next even index.
Otherwise the number is negative, so we handle it in this branch.
We place the negative number x into the result at the negative pointer's index.
We advance the negative pointer by two so the next negative goes to the next odd index.
After every number is placed, we return the result list with alternating signs.

remove-all-adjacent-duplicates-in-string.hook: Remove a pair, and new pairs appear. A stack handles the chain reaction in one pass.
remove-all-adjacent-duplicates-in-string.ask: Repeatedly delete any two adjacent equal letters from the string until no such pair remains. Return the final string, which is the same whatever order you delete in.
remove-all-adjacent-duplicates-in-string.exampleWhy: Removing bb gives aaca; removing aa then gives ca, which has no adjacent equal letters.

brute.idea: Scan for the first adjacent equal pair, cut it out, and start scanning again from the beginning.
steps: Find the first pair s[i] == s[i+1]
Rebuild the string without them
Repeat until no pair is found
brute.whySlow: Each removal rebuilds the string and rescans from the start: 100,000 letters means billions of character copies.

optimal.insight: After a removal, the only new pair possible is the letter just before the gap with the letter just after. That is a stack top.
steps: Walk the string letter by letter
Top of stack equals letter? pop it
Otherwise push the letter
Join the stack

codeNotes.note: No pair: it survives for now

pitfalls: Only pairs are removed; aaa leaves a single a.
Building the result with string concatenation in a loop is quadratic.

say.intro: Remove All Adjacent Duplicates in String. Whenever two equal letters sit side by side, we delete both. And we keep going until no pairs remain. For a b b a c a, removing b b leaves a a c a. Then a a goes, leaving c a.
say.brute: The brute force does exactly what the statement says. Find the first pair of equal neighbours, cut them out, and start scanning again from the beginning. Repeat until a full scan finds nothing. But every removal copies the string and restarts. That's n squared.
say.insight: So here's the question. When a pair disappears, what new pair can form? Only the letter just before the gap meeting the letter just after. And that's a stack. Keep the surviving letters on it. Each new letter only looks at the top. Match? The pair cancels, and we pop. No match? Push it. One pass handles every chain reaction.
say.anim: We start with an empty stack and the string abbaca to process. Letter a has no match on top, so it gets pushed onto the stack. Letter b also does not match, so it joins a on the stack. Next b matches the top of the stack, so that pair cancels out by popping. Now the new top is a, matching the next a, so it pops again, revealing the hidden pair. Letter c has nothing to match, so it is pushed onto the empty stack. Final letter a does not match c, so it is pushed too, giving stack c and a. Joining the stack gives the final answer, the string ca.
say.code: We keep a list of the letters that survived so far. For each character, we ask: does it pair with the last survivor? If the stack isn't empty and the top matches, both letters vanish, so we pop. No pair? It survives for now, so we push it. At the end, join the stack into a string and return it.
say.outro: Quadratic down to linear. The lesson? With a stack, the newest survivor is the only thing a new item can touch.

remove-all-adjacent-duplicates-in-string.title: Remove All Adjacent Duplicates In String
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container the interview platform expects for our method.
The removeDuplicates method takes the string s and returns the final string after all adjacent duplicate pairs are removed.
We start with an empty stack that will hold the letters that survive so far, in order.
We walk through the string one letter at a time, calling the current letter c.
If the stack is not empty and its top letter equals c, we have found an adjacent equal pair.
In that case we pop the top letter, which deletes the pair and exposes the letter before the gap.
Otherwise, meaning there is no matching pair with the top, we fall to this branch.
We push c onto the stack because it cannot cancel anything yet and might match a later letter.
After the loop we join the remaining letters in the stack into one string and return it.

remove-all-occurrences-of-a-substring.hook: Delete a pattern, and the pieces can rejoin into the pattern again. Let a stack catch that.
remove-all-occurrences-of-a-substring.ask: Repeatedly find the leftmost occurrence of part inside s and remove it, until part no longer appears. Return what remains of s.
remove-all-occurrences-of-a-substring.exampleWhy: Removing abc three times, each removal exposing a new one, leaves dab.

brute.idea: While part still appears in s, find its leftmost occurrence and rebuild s without it.
steps: Search s for part
Cut out the leftmost match
Repeat until no match
brute.whySlow: Every removal restarts the search from the beginning and copies the whole string again.

optimal.insight: A new match can only end at the newest character. Push characters onto a stack and check whether its top spells part.
steps: Push each character onto a stack
Do the top m characters equal part?
If so, pop all m of them
Join what remains

codeNotes.note: Remove the whole match at once

pitfalls: Removals can create new matches, like ababcc becoming abc.
KMP states on the stack make the check O(1): O(n + m) total.

say.intro: Remove All Occurrences of a Substring. We keep deleting the leftmost copy of part from s, until none remain. Here's the twist. A removal can glue its neighbours into a brand new copy. For d a a b c b a a b c b c, with part a b c, three removals leave d a b.
say.brute: The brute force follows the statement. While part is still in s, find its leftmost spot and rebuild s without it. But each removal copies the string and restarts from the very beginning. Even though nothing before the cut changed. That makes it roughly n squared.
say.insight: Now, think about where a new match can appear. Walk left to right, keeping survivors on a stack. Any new match must end at the character we just added. Why? Because everything below was already checked. So after each push, compare just the top m characters with part. If they match, pop them all. That's exactly the leftmost removal the problem wants.
say.anim: We start with an empty stack and set part length to three. Characters d, a, a get pushed, but the top three never spell abc. Pushing b then c makes the top three letters abc, a match found. Those three letters are removed, shrinking the stack back to d and a. More characters get pushed until the stack again ends in a, b, c. That match gets deleted too, leaving d, a, b, a on the stack. After pushing b and c, the top three spell abc one more time. They're removed, leaving d, a, b, so the final answer is dab.
say.code: We keep a stack, with the newest character on top. Let m be the length of part. Push each character. Then ask: does the top spell part? If there are at least m characters and the last m match, remove the whole match at once. When we're done, the survivors are in original order. So we join them and return.
say.outro: No rescanning from the start. The pattern is a stack. Matches can only form at the top, so only check the top.

remove-all-occurrences-of-a-substring.title: Remove All Occurrences of a Substring
lineNotes: We define a class named Solution, which is the container the judge expects for this method.
The method removeOccurrences takes the string s and the string part we want to erase repeatedly.
We start with an empty stack that will hold the characters we have kept so far.
We store the length of part as m so we know how many characters to compare.
We walk through each character c of s from left to right, one at a time.
We push the current character onto the stack, since any new match must end at this newest character.
Once the stack has at least m characters, we join the top m and check whether they equal part.
If the top matches part, we delete those m characters from the stack, which removes that occurrence.
After processing every character, we join the stack into a string and return what remains.

remove-comments.hook: Strip C++ comments with a tiny state machine: am I inside a block comment or not?
remove-comments.ask: Given C++ source as a list of lines, delete line comments and block comments. Block comments may span lines and join text across them. Return the remaining non-empty lines.
remove-comments.exampleWhy: The line comment drops ' // set'; the block from /* to */ removes 'a' and 'b', leaving y=1;.

brute.idea: Join all lines with newlines, repeatedly cut out the earliest comment with string operations, then split and drop empty lines.
steps: Join source into one text
Find the earliest // or /*
Cut to line end, or to */
Split on newlines, drop empties
brute.whySlow: Every cut rebuilds the whole text, so many comments in a long file cost quadratic copying.

optimal.insight: Scan characters once with one flag, in_block. Only flush a line's buffer when not inside a block, so block comments merge lines.
steps: In a block: look only for */
Outside: /* opens a block, // ends the line
Otherwise copy the character to the buffer
End of line outside a block: emit buffer

codeNotes.note: Rest of the line is gone

pitfalls: Skip both characters of /* so /*/ does not close itself.
Do not reset the buffer at line end while inside a block.

say.intro: Remove Comments. We get C plus plus source as a list of lines, and we strip two kinds of comments. Line comments kill the rest of a line. Block comments can span several lines, and even join code across them. Any line that ends up empty gets dropped.
say.brute: The brute force joins all lines into one big text. It finds whichever comment marker comes first, cuts to the line end or the closing marker, and searches again. Then it splits on newlines and drops empties. It works. But every cut copies the whole text. Lots of comments makes it quadratic.
say.insight: Here's the key. We only need one piece of state. Are we inside a block comment? Inside, we ignore everything until the closing marker. Outside, slash star opens a block, double slash ends the line, and anything else is real code. Now, the subtle part. Only emit a line when we're not inside a block. That's how a block comment glues two lines together.
say.anim: We start scanning the first line, building up characters into a buffer one by one. At index seven we hit two slashes, so the rest of this line is skipped as a comment. The buffer flushes into results, giving us our first output line, int x with a space. Next line starts with slash star, setting in block true, so we stop collecting characters. Since we are inside a block comment, nothing gets appended and the buffer stays empty. On the next line we find star slash, ending the block comment and resuming normal scanning. Characters y equals one semicolon get appended since we are no longer inside a block. The final buffer flushes, giving the answer, int x with a space and y equals one semicolon.
say.code: We keep a result list, a buffer, and an in block flag. For each line, we walk the characters, peeking at two at a time. Inside a block, a closing marker ends it, and we skip both characters. Outside, an opening marker starts a block, also skipping both. A double slash means the rest of the line is gone. Anything else is real code, so we keep it. We emit only finished, non-empty lines.
say.outro: One linear pass over every character. The pattern is a string scan, driven by a tiny state machine.

remove-comments.title: Remove Comments
lineNotes: We define the Solution class that holds the method for this problem.
The method removeComments takes the list of source lines and returns the cleaned lines.
We start with an empty result list to collect the finished lines.
We keep a buffer of characters for the line currently being built, which can span source lines.
The in block flag starts false because we begin outside any block comment.
We loop over each source line in order.
We reset the index to zero to scan this line from its start.
We keep scanning while the index is still inside the current line.
We grab the two characters at the index to detect comment markers.
If we are inside a block comment, we only look for its ending marker.
When the two characters close the block, we handle the end of the comment.
We turn the in block flag off since the comment has ended.
We skip one extra character so the slash of the closing marker is not reread.
Otherwise, outside a block, we check whether a block comment starts here.
We set the in block flag on because a block comment begins.
We skip the star character so it cannot be mistaken as part of an ending marker.
If instead we see a line comment marker, we handle that case.
We break out of the loop, discarding the rest of this line.
Otherwise the character is real code, so we handle that case.
We append the current character to the buffer to keep it.
We advance the index by one to move to the next character.
After the line, we flush only if the buffer has text and we are not inside a block.
We join the buffered characters into one string and add it to the result.
We clear the buffer to start building the next output line.
We return the list of cleaned, non-empty lines.

remove-covered-intervals.hook: Sort by start, longest first, and covered intervals reveal themselves with one running maximum.
remove-covered-intervals.ask: Given distinct intervals, remove every interval that lies completely inside another one. Return how many intervals remain.
remove-covered-intervals.exampleWhy: [2,8] covers both [3,6] and [5,7], so only [1,4] and [2,8] remain.

brute.idea: For each interval, check every other interval to see whether it starts no later and ends no earlier.
steps: Pick interval a
Search for another b with b.start ≤ a.start and a.end ≤ b.end
Count a if none found
brute.whySlow: Every interval is compared with every other: a million pair checks for only 1,000 intervals.

optimal.insight: Sort by start ascending and end descending. Then an interval is covered exactly when its end is at most the largest end seen before it.
steps: Sort by start, ties by longer first
Track the maximum end so far
End beyond the maximum? it survives
Otherwise it is covered

codeNotes.note: Furthest reach of any earlier interval

pitfalls: Without the descending end tie-break, [1,2] before [1,4] is wrongly kept.
Every earlier interval starts no later, so only the end matters.

say.intro: Remove Covered Intervals. An interval is covered when another one starts at or before it, and ends at or after it. We remove covered intervals and count what's left. For one to four, three to six, two to eight, and five to seven, two to eight swallows two others. So two remain.
say.brute: The brute force checks every interval against every other one. Is there some interval that starts no later, and ends no earlier? If not, it survives. Simple enough. But that's n squared. A thousand intervals already means a million comparisons.
say.insight: So how do we get rid of one of those conditions? Sort by start. Now every earlier interval starts no later, automatically. So the current one is covered exactly when some earlier one reaches at least as far. And that's just the max end so far. There's one catch, though. Equal starts. Put the longer one first, so the shorter one is correctly seen as covered.
say.anim: Intervals get sorted by start ascending and end descending, giving this order. Count and max_end both start at zero before scanning begins. First interval ends at 4, which beats max_end zero, so it counts. Count becomes 1 and max_end updates to 4. Next interval ends at 8, beating max_end 4, so it counts too. Count becomes 2 and max_end updates to 8. Interval ending at 6 and interval ending at 7 are both covered by max_end 8. Loop finishes and the function returns the final count, which is 2.
say.code: We sort by start, and for the same start, the longer one goes first. Then we track the furthest reach of any earlier interval, starting at zero. For each interval, does its end stick out past that? Then it's not covered. It's a survivor, so add one to the count, and update the max end. Return the count.
say.outro: n squared down to n log n. For intervals, it's the classic move. Sort by start, then sweep with a running max end.

remove-covered-intervals.title: Remove Covered Intervals
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container the problem expects for our method.
This method takes the list of intervals and returns how many remain after removing covered ones.
We sort by start ascending and end descending, so an interval with the same start as a longer one comes after it.
We set count to zero, which will track how many intervals are not covered.
We set max_end to zero, representing the largest end seen so far among kept intervals.
We loop through the sorted intervals, ignoring the start value and looking only at each end.
If this end is greater than max_end, the interval reaches farther than all earlier ones, so it is not covered.
Since this interval is not covered, we add one to our count of remaining intervals.
We update max_end to this end, because it is now the farthest right endpoint seen.
After checking every interval, we return count as the number of intervals that remain.

remove-duplicates-from-sorted-list-ii.hook: Not just dedupe: any value that repeats must vanish completely. A dummy node makes it clean.
remove-duplicates-from-sorted-list-ii.ask: Given a sorted linked list, delete every node whose value appears more than once, keeping only values that were unique. Return the list, still sorted.
remove-duplicates-from-sorted-list-ii.exampleWhy: 3 and 4 each appear twice, so all their nodes go. 1, 2 and 5 were unique and stay.

brute.idea: Count every value with a hash map, then build a new list containing only values whose count is one.
steps: Walk the list counting values
Walk again, keep values with count 1
Link the kept values into a new list
brute.whySlow: Time is fine, but it needs a hash map and new nodes, ignoring that sorted input groups duplicates together.

optimal.insight: Sorted means duplicates are adjacent. Skip a whole run of equal values and link the last safe node past it, in place.
steps: Dummy node before head; prev = dummy
If cur starts a run, skip to its end
Link prev.next past the run
Otherwise prev advances to cur

pitfalls: Keep prev still after cutting a run; the next value may repeat too.
Without a dummy node, deleting the head needs special cases.

say.intro: Remove Duplicates from Sorted List two. This time, any value that appears more than once is removed completely. Not trimmed to one copy. Gone. For one, two, three, three, four, four, five, both threes and both fours disappear. That leaves one, two, five.
say.brute: The brute force counts every value with a hash map. Then a second pass builds a fresh list with only the values that appear once. It's linear time. But it uses extra memory for the map and the new nodes. And it ignores the most useful fact we got. The list is sorted.
say.insight: Because it's sorted, equal values sit next to each other in runs. So we walk with two pointers. Prev is the last node we're sure to keep. When cur starts a run, we skip to the end of it, and link prev straight past. Here's a neat trick. A dummy node in front of the head means even the head can be removed, with no special cases.
say.anim: We start with the sorted list one, two, three, three, four, four, five, plus a dummy head. Cur begins at node one, which has no duplicate neighbor, so prev just moves forward to it. Cur is now two, also unique, so prev again advances to keep it in the result. Cur reaches three, and its next is also three, so we enter the duplicate skipping loop. Cur steps through both threes, then prev links directly to four, skipping the whole run. Now cur is four, matching the next four, triggering another skip of duplicate nodes. After skipping both fours, prev points two directly to five, removing the duplicates in place. Cur becomes none, the loop ends, and the final list returned is one, two, five.
say.code: We put a dummy in front, because the head itself may be deleted. Prev starts at the dummy, cur at the head. If the next node has the same value, cur is at the start of a duplicate run. Move cur to the run's end, then cut out the entire run by linking prev past it. Otherwise it's a unique value, so prev moves up to keep it. Cur advances. Return the dummy's next.
say.outro: Linear time, constant space, in place. For linked lists, a dummy head plus a trailing pointer handles the tricky cases.

remove-duplicates-from-sorted-list-ii.title: Remove Duplicates from Sorted List II
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container LeetCode expects for the method that solves this problem.
The method deleteDuplicates takes the head of a sorted linked list and returns the new head after removing every duplicated value.
We create a dummy node pointing to head, so removing the first nodes of the list needs no special case.
We set prev to the dummy, so prev always marks the last node known to be safe in the result.
We set cur to head, and cur is the node we are currently examining as we walk the list.
We loop while cur is not empty, so every node in the list gets examined once.
We check whether the next node exists and has the same value as cur, which signals the start of a duplicate run.
Inside a duplicate run, we keep looping while the next node still has the same value as cur.
We advance cur forward until it sits on the last node of the run of equal values.
We link prev past the whole run by pointing it at the node after cur, deleting every duplicate in place.
Otherwise, cur is unique because its next value differs, so this branch handles the keep case.
We advance prev to cur, since cur is now a confirmed safe node in the result list.
We move cur to the next node, either stepping past the last duplicate or continuing after a kept node.
We return the dummy's next node, which is the true head of the cleaned list, even if the original head was removed.

remove-methods-from-project.hook: Find everything a buggy method can reach, then check if anyone outside still depends on it.
remove-methods-from-project.ask: Method k is buggy; it and every method it calls, directly or indirectly, are suspicious. Remove them only if no other method calls into that group. Return the remaining methods.
remove-methods-from-project.exampleWhy: From 0 we reach 1 and 2. Nothing outside calls them, since 3 only calls 4, so 3 and 4 remain.

brute.idea: Grow the suspicious set by sweeping all edges repeatedly until nothing new is added, then check for outside callers.
steps: Start with k suspicious
Sweep edges: caller suspicious marks callee
Repeat until no change
Any outside caller? keep everything
brute.whySlow: A long call chain needs a sweep per link: 100,000 sweeps over 200,000 edges.

optimal.insight: Suspicious methods are exactly the nodes reachable from k. One DFS finds them; one edge scan finds any outside caller.
steps: Build the call graph
DFS from k marks suspicious methods
Any edge from outside into the set? remove nothing
Else return all unmarked methods

codeNotes.note: Iterative DFS from the buggy method

codeNotes.match: if a not in bad and b in bad:
return [i for i in range(n) if i not in bad]

pitfalls: It is all or nothing: one outside caller keeps every method.
Use an iterative stack; recursion can overflow on 100,000 nodes.

say.intro: Remove Methods From Project. Method k has a bug. So k, and everything it calls directly or indirectly, is suspicious. We can delete that whole group, but only if nothing outside it calls into it. Here, zero reaches one and two. Nobody else calls them. So three and four remain.
say.brute: The brute force grows the suspicious set by sweeping all the edges. If a suspicious method calls an unmarked one, mark it. Keep sweeping until nothing changes. Then look for outside callers. So what's the catch? A long call chain can need one sweep per link. That's n times the number of edges.
say.insight: Here's the thing. Suspicious just means reachable from k in the call graph. One depth first search finds every reachable method, in linear time. And when is removal legal? Exactly when no edge goes from an unmarked method into a marked one. One more scan over the edges checks that.
say.anim: We start building a graph from the invocation list, mapping each caller to its callees. Now the graph is complete, with methods one and zero each calling others, and three calling four. We initialize bad with just k, zero, and start a stack to explore reachable methods. Popping zero, we find it calls two and one, marking both as bad and reachable. Popping one, we see it also calls two, already marked bad, so nothing new happens. Popping two, it has no outgoing calls, so the stack empties and bad is zero, one, two. We scan all invocations checking if any caller outside bad points into the bad set, but none do. Only methods three and four remain outside bad, so the final answer is three and four.
say.code: We build an adjacency list, where each edge means a calls b. Then we run an iterative depth first search from the buggy method, using a stack. Every callee we reach is suspicious, so we mark it. Next, scan every edge. An outside caller into a marked method blocks removal, so we return all methods. Otherwise, it's safe to remove the group, and we return the unmarked ones.
say.outro: Linear in nodes plus edges. The pattern? Reachability with a depth first search, then a simple boundary check.

remove-methods-from-project.title: Remove Methods From Project
lineNotes: We define the Solution class that holds the method for this problem.
The method takes the method count n, the buggy method k, and the list of invocation pairs.
We create a dictionary of lists so each method maps to the methods it directly calls.
We loop over every invocation pair, reading the caller as a and the callee as b.
We add b to the list of a, building the call graph.
We start the suspicious set with only k, since the buggy method is suspicious itself.
We seed a stack with k so a depth first search can begin from the buggy method.
We keep looping while the stack still has methods whose callees we have not explored.
We pop a method u from the stack to explore its callees next.
We go through each method v that u directly calls.
We only act if v is not yet marked suspicious, which prevents revisiting and infinite loops.
We mark v as suspicious because the buggy method reaches it through calls.
We push v onto the stack so its own callees get explored later.
Now we scan all invocations again to look for calls coming from outside the suspicious group.
If a healthy method a calls a suspicious method b, the group cannot be safely removed.
In that case we return all methods from zero to n minus one, since nothing gets removed.
Otherwise we return every method not in the suspicious set, meaning the suspicious group is removed.

remove-outermost-parentheses.hook: Peel the outer layer off each balanced chunk. A depth counter replaces the whole stack.
remove-outermost-parentheses.ask: A valid parentheses string splits into primitive balanced chunks. Remove the outermost pair of parentheses from each chunk and return the joined result.
remove-outermost-parentheses.exampleWhy: The chunks are (()()) and (()). Stripping their outer pairs leaves ()() and (), which join to ()()().

brute.idea: Find where the first primitive chunk ends, keep its inside, cut it off the string, and repeat on the rest.
steps: Scan until balance returns to zero
Append the chunk without its outer pair
Slice off the chunk and repeat
brute.whySlow: Slicing off each chunk copies the rest of the string; many small chunks make it quadratic.

optimal.insight: A parenthesis is outermost exactly when it opens at depth 0 or closes back to depth 0. Track depth; keep everything else.
steps: Open: keep it if depth > 0, then depth += 1
Close: depth -= 1, keep it if depth > 0
Join the kept characters

pitfalls: Order matters: check before incrementing, decrement before checking.
No stack needed; depth alone tells the nesting level.

say.intro: Remove Outermost Parentheses. A valid parentheses string splits into primitive pieces, each balanced on its own. We strip the outer pair from every piece. Our example has two pieces. Strip their outer pairs, and we're left with three empty pairs in a row.
say.brute: The brute force peels pieces off the front. Scan from the start, tracking balance, until it hits zero. That's the end of the first piece. Keep its inside, slice it off, and repeat on the rest. But each slice copies the rest of the string. With lots of small pieces, that's n squared.
say.insight: Here's the thing. We don't need to find the pieces at all. When is a parenthesis outermost? When an opening one starts at depth zero. Or when a closing one brings us back to depth zero. So just track depth with one counter. Everything else is inside some piece, and we keep it.
say.anim: We start with an empty result list and depth zero, ready to scan the string. The first open paren is at depth zero, so it's skipped as an outer parenthesis, depth becomes one. Next open paren at depth one gets added to result, since it's not outermost, depth rises to two. A closing paren drops depth to one, and since depth is still above zero, it's appended too. This pattern continues, appending inner parentheses while skipping ones that touch depth zero. When depth returns to zero after closing, that paren is outermost and gets dropped. The process repeats for the next group, tracking depth to find each new outer pair. Finally the kept characters join together, giving the final answer open close open close open close.
say.code: We keep a result list, and a counter for the current nesting level. For an opening bracket, we check before entering a level. Keep it only if depth is already positive, then go up one. For a closing bracket, we leave the level first, then check. Keep it only if depth is still positive. That way only inner characters survive. Join and return.
say.outro: One linear pass with a counter. It's a stack idea, squeezed into a single number, because there's only one bracket type.

remove-outermost-parentheses.title: Remove Outermost Parentheses
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container the problem expects for our method.
The method takes the string s and returns a new string with outermost parentheses removed from each chunk.
We start with an empty list called res to collect the characters we decide to keep.
We set depth to zero, since we begin outside of any open parenthesis.
We loop through each character c in the string s, one at a time.
If the character is an opening parenthesis, we handle the open case.
Only when depth is already above zero is this open parenthesis nested, so it is not outermost.
In that case we append the character to res, because inner parentheses are kept.
Either way, we increase depth by one, since we have entered one more level.
Otherwise the character is a closing parenthesis, so we handle the close case.
We decrease depth first, so it reflects the level after this parenthesis closes.
If depth is still above zero after closing, this parenthesis is not the outermost one.
Then we append it to res, since it closes an inner pair we want to keep.
Finally we join the kept characters into one string and return it.

reveal-cards-in-increasing-order.hook: Reveal one, move one to the bottom. Simulate the positions, then drop sorted cards into them.
reveal-cards-in-increasing-order.ask: Order a deck so that repeatedly revealing the top card, then moving the next top card to the bottom, reveals all cards in increasing order. Return that deck order, top first.
reveal-cards-in-increasing-order.exampleWhy: Revealing from 2,13,3,11,5,17,7 while cycling cards to the bottom shows 2, 3, 5, 7, 11, 13, 17.

brute.idea: Run the process in reverse: from the largest card down, move the bottom card to the top, then place the card on top.
steps: Sort cards from largest to smallest
Move the last card to the front
Insert the current card at the front
brute.whySlow: Each insert at the front of a list shifts every card, so n cards cost about n squared moves.

optimal.insight: The reveal order of positions does not depend on card values. Simulate it on indices with a queue, assigning sorted cards in order.
steps: Queue holds positions 0 to n-1
Pop a position; it gets the next smallest card
Move the next position to the back
Repeat until all cards placed

codeNotes.note: Next position goes to the bottom

pitfalls: Only move a position to the back if any remain.
Sorting dominates the cost; the queue work is linear.

say.intro: Reveal Cards in Increasing Order. The dealer reveals the top card, then moves the next card to the bottom, and repeats. We arrange the deck so the revealed cards come out in increasing order. For our seven cards, two, thirteen, three, eleven, five, seventeen, seven does the job.
say.brute: One approach runs the process backwards. Go from the largest card down. Before placing each card, move the bottom card to the top, undoing a move to bottom. Then put the card on top. It's correct. But inserting at the front of a list shifts everything. That's n squared.
say.insight: Here's the key insight. Which positions get revealed, and in what order, doesn't depend on the values at all. So simulate the dealer on positions instead of cards. A queue holds positions zero through n minus one. The first position popped is revealed first, so it gets the smallest card. Then the next position goes to the back, just like the dealer's move.
say.anim: We start with the deck, and build a queue holding all seven index positions in order. Cards get sorted, and we loop through them placing each into the next available position. The smallest card, two, fills position zero, since it is at the front of the queue. After placing a card, the next index moves to the back, skipping a spot for later. Card three goes into position two, then index one is pushed to the back again. This pattern continues, placing five and seven, while remaining indices keep cycling through the queue. Larger cards eleven and thirteen fill positions three and one as the queue shrinks down. Finally seventeen fills the last open spot, giving the result two, thirteen, three, eleven, five, seventeen, seven.
say.code: We simulate positions, not cards. So make a double ended queue of indices, zero to n minus one, plus a result array. Loop over the cards in sorted order, so the smallest card is revealed first. Pop the front index. This position is revealed now, so place the card there. If indices remain, the next position goes to the bottom. Return the result.
say.outro: A sort plus a linear simulation. The trick? Simulate on positions first, then fill in values in order.

reveal-cards-in-increasing-order.title: Reveal Cards In Increasing Order
lineNotes: We define a class named Solution, which holds the method that solves this card revealing problem.
The method takes the deck of cards and returns the order the deck must start in.
We store the number of cards in n, since we will need it to size our structures.
We build a queue of positions from zero up to n minus one, representing the deck's slots from top to bottom.
We create a result list of n zeros, to be filled in with cards at their proper positions.
We loop over the cards in sorted order, because they must be revealed from smallest to largest.
We take the front position from the queue, which is the next revealed spot, and place the current card there.
If any positions remain in the queue, we still need to perform the move-to-bottom step.
We move the next top position to the back of the queue, mimicking the card going to the bottom.
Finally we return the result list, which is the deck order that reveals cards in increasing order.

reverse-linked-list-ii.hook: Reverse just the middle of a linked list, in one pass, without losing either end.
reverse-linked-list-ii.ask: Given the head of a singly linked list and positions left and right, reverse only the nodes from position left to position right, counting from one, and return the head of the list.
reverse-linked-list-ii.exampleWhy: Positions 2 to 4 hold 2, 3, 4. Reversed they become 4, 3, 2; nodes 1 and 5 stay put.

brute.idea: Copy all values into an array, reverse the slice from left to right there, then write the values back into the nodes.
steps: Walk the list, collecting values
Reverse the slice left-1 to right
Walk again, overwriting node values
brute.whySlow: Same time, but it needs an O(n) copy and two passes, and it swaps values instead of relinking nodes.

optimal.insight: Stop at the node before left. Then repeatedly pull the next node out and insert it right after that anchor. Each move grows the reversed block by one.
steps: Add a dummy node so left = 1 needs no special case
Walk prev to the node just before position left
cur is the first node of the block; it ends up last
right - left times: unlink cur.next and insert it after prev

codeNotes.note: Handles reversing from the very first node
Point it at the current block front
It becomes the new block front
Real head, even if it changed

pitfalls: Without a dummy node, left = 1 needs special handling for the new head.
Keep cur fixed: it slides back naturally as nodes jump in front of it.

say.intro: Reverse Linked List two. We get a linked list and two positions, left and right. Only the nodes between them get reversed. So for one, two, three, four, five, with left two and right four, the middle becomes four, three, two. The answer is one, four, three, two, five.
say.brute: The easy way skips pointers entirely. Copy every value into an array. Reverse the slice between left and right there, then walk the list again and write the values back. It's linear time. So what's the problem? It needs a full copy and two passes. And it moves values instead of rewiring nodes, which is what interviewers want to see.
say.insight: Here's the trick. Find the node just before position left. Call it the anchor. The first node of the block, cur, is going to end up last. Now, over and over, take the node right after cur, cut it out, and insert it right after the anchor. Each move grows the reversed block by one. After right minus left moves, we're done.
say.anim: We start with list one through five, reversing the section between positions two and four. A dummy node is added before the head, and prev points to it. Prev steps forward once, landing on node one, the anchor before the reversal. Cur is set to node two, the start of the section to reverse. Node three is pulled out as nxt and linked after node four, skipping three. Nxt three is inserted right after prev, giving one, three, two, four, five. Now node four is pulled out similarly and inserted right after prev one. Final list returned is one, four, three, two, five, the reversed section complete.
say.code: We start with a dummy node before the head. That handles reversing from the very first node. Prev walks forward, stopping just before position left. Cur is the block's first node. Then, right minus left times, we unlink the node after cur. We point it at the current block front. And it becomes the new block front, hanging after prev. Finally, return the real head, dummy's next, even if it changed.
say.outro: One pass, constant space. For linked lists, a dummy node plus careful front insertion reverses a sublist in place.

reverse-linked-list-ii.title: Reverse Linked List II
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container for the method that LeetCode will call.
The method reverseBetween takes the list head plus the left and right positions, and returns the new head.
We create a dummy node pointing to head, so reversing from position one needs no special case.
We set prev to the dummy node, which will walk to just before the reversal starts.
We loop left minus one times so prev can advance to the node before position left.
Each pass moves prev forward one node along the list.
We set cur to the node after prev, which is the first node of the block and ends up its tail.
We loop right minus left times, since each pass moves one more node to the front of the block.
We save the node after cur as nxt, which is the next node to pull out.
We link cur past nxt to the node after it, removing nxt from its current spot.
We point nxt at the node after prev, which is the current front of the reversed block.
We link prev to nxt, so nxt becomes the new front of the reversed block.
We return the node after dummy, which is the true head even if the first node moved.

reverse-string-ii.hook: Reverse a string in chunks: flip k characters, skip k, flip k again.
reverse-string-ii.ask: Given a string s and a number k, walk through s in blocks of 2k characters. In each block, reverse the first k characters and leave the rest alone. If fewer than k remain at the end, reverse all of them.
reverse-string-ii.exampleWhy: Blocks of six: abc flips to cba, def stays. The last block gh has fewer than three, so it flips to hg.

brute.idea: Build the answer as a new string: for each 2k block, append the reversed first k characters, then the untouched next k.
steps: Step start through s by 2k
Slice the first k and reverse it
Append it and the next k characters
brute.whySlow: Same big O, but it creates a fresh slice and a new joined string per block instead of swapping in place.

optimal.insight: Each block is just a classic two-pointer reversal on a known range: from start to the smaller of start + k - 1 and the last index.
steps: Turn the string into a list of characters
Per block: i = start, j = min(start + k, n) - 1
Swap chars[i] and chars[j], move both inward
Join the list back into a string

codeNotes.note: Strings are immutable: work on a list

codeNotes.match: for start in range(0, len(chars), 2 * k):
i, j = start, min(start + k, len(chars)) - 1
codeNotes.note: Clamp the end for a short tail

pitfalls: Forgetting the min clamp crashes or skips the short final block.
The step is 2k, not k: every other k-chunk stays untouched.

say.intro: Reverse String two. We walk through the string in blocks of two k characters. In each block, we reverse only the first k. With a b c d e f g h and k of three, a b c becomes c b a, and d e f stays. The tail, g h, is shorter than three, so we flip both.
say.brute: A direct approach builds a brand new string. Step through the input two k characters at a time. Slice out the first k, reverse it, and append it. Then append the next k untouched. Honestly, that's linear, so it isn't slow. It just makes a fresh slice and a new string for every block, instead of editing in place.
say.insight: Here's a cleaner way to see it. Each block is just the classic two pointer reversal, on a limited range. The left pointer starts at the block start. The right pointer starts k minus one later. But what if the string runs out first? Then it starts at the very last character. Swap, move both inward, and stop when they meet.
say.anim: We start with the string abcdefgh split into individual characters, and k is three. For the first block, start is zero, so i is zero and j is two. We swap characters at positions zero and two, turning a and c into c and a. Pointers move inward, i becomes one and j becomes one, so this block is done. Next block starts at six, skipping the untouched middle, setting i to six and j to seven. We swap g and h, giving us h and g in positions six and seven. No more blocks remain, since start would exceed the string length. The final reversed-in-blocks string is cbadefhg.
say.code: Strings are immutable in Python, so we work on a list. The outer loop jumps from block to block, two k at a time. For each block, i is the start, and j is k minus one later. We clamp the end to the last index for a short tail. While i is left of j, swap the outer pair and move inward. At the end, join it back to a string.
say.outro: Linear time. The pattern is two pointers: a range reversal you can apply to any slice, here once per block.

reverse-string-ii.title: Reverse String II
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container the problem expects for our method.
The method reverseStr takes the string s and the block size k, and returns the transformed string.
We convert the string into a list of characters because strings are immutable and we want to swap in place.
We loop start across the string in jumps of two times k, so each iteration begins a new block.
We set i to the block start and j to the end of the first k characters, capped at the last index.
We keep swapping while i is still left of j, which is the classic two pointer reversal.
We swap the characters at i and j, flipping that pair into their reversed positions.
We move i one step right to approach the middle from the left.
We move j one step left to approach the middle from the right.
After all blocks are processed, we join the characters back into a string and return it.

rotate-string.hook: Every rotation of a string hides inside that string written twice.
rotate-string.ask: Given strings s and goal, a shift moves the first character of s to the end. Return true if some number of shifts turns s into goal, and false otherwise.
rotate-string.exampleWhy: Shift abcab twice: bcaba, then cabab. That is exactly goal.

brute.idea: Try every possible rotation. For each split point i, build s[i:] + s[:i] and compare it with goal.
steps: Lengths differ? Not possible
For each i, build the rotation
Equal to goal? return True
brute.whySlow: n rotations, each built and compared in O(n) time: quadratic work for long strings.

optimal.insight: s + s contains every rotation of s as a window. So goal is a rotation exactly when it appears inside s + s, which KMP finds in linear time.
steps: Lengths differ? return False
Build KMP failure table for goal
Scan s + s, extending or falling back the match
Match length reaches len(goal)? return True

codeNotes.note: Longest border of each goal prefix
Every rotation lives in s + s
Mismatch: fall back without rescanning text
Whole goal matched: it is a rotation

pitfalls: Check the lengths first: goal = "a" is inside "abab" but is not a rotation.
goal in s + s is fine to say first; KMP guarantees linear worst case.

say.intro: Rotate String. A shift takes the first character of s and moves it to the end. Can some number of shifts turn s into goal? With a b c a b, two shifts give b c a b a, then c a b a b. That equals goal. So the answer is true.
say.brute: The brute force tries every rotation. For each split point, glue the back part of s in front of the front part. Then compare with goal. Any match? Return true. Simple enough. But there are n rotations, and each costs linear time to build and compare. That's n squared.
say.insight: Here's a neat trick. Write s twice in a row. Now every rotation of s shows up as a window inside that doubled string. So goal is a rotation exactly when the lengths match, and goal appears inside s plus s. Suddenly it's just substring search. And Knuth Morris Pratt does that in linear time.
say.anim: We start with s equal abcab and goal equal cabab, same length so we continue. We build the lps array for goal, tracking prefix matches to speed up searching. Stepping through goal, the lps array fills in as zeros since no repeats appear yet. Now we scan through s plus s, looking for goal hidden inside this doubled string. Characters c, a, b, a, b match goal's letters one by one, incrementing k each time. K reaches four, meaning most of goal has matched consecutively inside s plus s. K finally equals five, the full length of goal, confirming a complete match found. The function returns true, since goal cabab is indeed a rotation of s abcab.
say.code: Rotations keep the length, so if the lengths differ, return false. Next, the failure table. For each goal prefix, it stores the longest border, a prefix that's also a suffix. Then we scan s plus s, since every rotation lives there. On a mismatch, we fall back through the table without rescanning the text. When the whole goal matches, it's a rotation. Return true.
say.outro: Linear time and space. The takeaway? Double the string, and a rotation check becomes a substring search.

rotate-string.title: Rotate String
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, as the problem platform expects, to hold our method.
The method rotateString takes the strings s and goal and returns a boolean answer.
A rotation never changes length, so we first check whether the two lengths differ.
If the lengths differ, goal can never be a rotation of s, so we return false.
We build the longest prefix suffix table for goal, starting with zeros of the same length as goal.
We set k to zero, which tracks the length of the current matched prefix inside goal.
We loop i from one through the end of goal, since the first position always has value zero.
While k is positive and goal at i mismatches goal at k, we need to fall back.
We fall back by setting k to the table value just before k, reusing the shorter border.
If goal at i now matches goal at k, the current border can be extended.
So we increase k by one to record the longer matching prefix.
We store k in the table at position i as the border length ending there.
We reset k to zero to reuse it for scanning the doubled string.
We walk through each character c of s plus s, which contains every rotation of s as a window.
While k is positive and c mismatches goal at k, we need to fall back in the pattern.
We fall back using the table, so we never move backward in the text and keep linear time.
If c matches goal at k, the partial match grows.
So we increase k by one to show one more character of goal is matched.
If k equals the length of goal, the whole goal has been found inside s plus s.
We then return true, since goal is a rotation of s.
If the scan ends without a full match, no rotation equals goal, so we return false.

scramble-string.hook: Split, maybe swap, recurse. Memoize the pairs of substrings and the explosion disappears.
scramble-string.ask: A string is scrambled by splitting it into two non-empty parts, optionally swapping them, and scrambling each part recursively. Given s1 and s2 of equal length, decide whether s2 can be produced by scrambling s1.
scramble-string.exampleWhy: Split great into gr and eat. Swap gr into rg, keep eat: that gives rgeat.

brute.idea: Try every split point. Either the halves line up without a swap, or the left part of a matches the right end of b. Recurse on both halves.
steps: Equal strings? True
Different letters? False
For each split, try no-swap and swap
Recurse on both pieces
brute.whySlow: The same substring pairs are solved again and again; the recursion tree grows exponentially with length.

optimal.insight: The answer depends only on the pair of substrings being compared. There are only O(n³) such pairs, so cache each result and every pair is solved once.
steps: Same substrings? True
Letter counts differ? False
For each split i, check no-swap halves
Then check swapped halves: a[:i] vs b[-i:]
Cache every (a, b) result

codeNotes.note: Each substring pair is solved once

codeNotes.match: if dfs(a[:i], b[:i]) and dfs(a[i:], b[i:]):
if dfs(a[:i], b[-i:]) and dfs(a[i:], b[:-i]):
codeNotes.note: Swapped: left part matches b's end

pitfalls: In the swap case, compare a[:i] with the LAST i characters of b.
Prune with letter counts first, or the search explodes even with memo.

say.intro: Scramble String. To scramble a string, split it in two, maybe swap the parts, and scramble each part again. Can the second string come from the first? With great and r g e a t, split great into g r and e a t. Swap g and r inside the first part. That gives r g e a t. True.
say.brute: The brute force follows the definition. Equal strings? True. Different letters? False. Otherwise, try every split point twice. Once with the halves lined up, once with them swapped. Recurse on both pieces. So what's the catch? The same pieces get compared again and again. The work grows exponentially with the length.
say.insight: Now, notice something. The answer for any call depends only on the two substrings being compared. How many such pairs are there? A start in each string, plus a length. That's about n cubed. So we cache every result. Each pair is solved once, with a linear loop over split points. That's about n to the fourth overall.
say.anim: We start checking if great can scramble into rgeat, caching results for each pair. At i equals one, it tries splitting into g versus r and great versus geat, but g and r fail. It also tries the swapped split, comparing g with t, which also fails since letters differ. At i equals two, it splits into gr and rg, checking both straight and swapped matches. Swapping gr into g and r matches rg's letters r and g, so this split succeeds. The remaining parts, eat and eat, are identical, so that comparison instantly returns true. Both halves at i equals two succeed, so dfs returns true for great and rgeat. The final answer is true, confirming great can scramble into rgeat.
say.code: The helper is cached, so each substring pair is solved once. If the two are equal, return true. If their sorted letters differ, they can never match, so return false. Then try each split. With no swap, the halves line up, and both left parts and both right parts must match. Swapped, the left part of a matches b's end. Finally, we start with the whole strings.
say.outro: Exponential down to about n to the fourth. The pattern is two dimensional dynamic programming: memoized recursion over pairs of substrings.

scramble-string.title: Scramble String
lineNotes: We define a class named Solution, which is the container LeetCode expects for this problem.
The method isScramble takes the two strings s1 and s2 and returns whether s2 is a scramble of s1.
We decorate the helper with cache so each distinct pair of substrings is computed only once and reused.
The helper dfs takes two substrings a and b and decides whether b is a scramble of a.
If a and b are already identical, then no scrambling is needed and the answer is clearly yes.
So we return true right away as the base case.
If the sorted letters differ, the two substrings use different characters, so no scramble could possibly match them.
In that case we return false immediately, which prunes a huge amount of useless recursion.
We try every split point i from one up to one less than the length, giving two non-empty parts.
Without swapping, the first i letters of a must scramble to the first i of b, and the rest to the rest.
If both halves match without a swap, we return true for this pair.
With a swap, the first i letters of a must match the last i of b, and the remainder must match the front of b.
If both swapped halves match, we return true because this split yields a valid scramble.
If no split point works in either arrangement, we conclude that b is not a scramble of a and return false.
Finally we call dfs on the full original strings s1 and s2 and return its answer.

search-in-a-binary-search-tree.hook: A binary search tree is a built-in decision tree: one comparison picks the side.
search-in-a-binary-search-tree.ask: Given the root of a binary search tree and a value, return the node whose value equals it, which is the subtree rooted there. If no node has that value, return null.
search-in-a-binary-search-tree.exampleWhy: 5 is less than 8, more than 4, less than 6: the path ends at leaf 5.

brute.idea: Ignore the ordering and visit every node with a stack until one has the target value.
steps: Push the root on a stack
Pop a node; matching value? return it
Otherwise push both children
brute.whySlow: It may visit all n nodes. The BST order lets us skip an entire subtree at every step.

optimal.insight: In a BST, everything smaller sits on the left and everything larger on the right. Each comparison discards one whole subtree.
steps: Start at the root
Smaller than node? Go left
Larger? Go right
Stop at a match or at null

codeNotes.note: Stop on a match or falling off
Target is smaller: it must be left
The match, or None if missing

pitfalls: h is log n only when balanced; a skewed tree makes it O(n).
Return the node itself, not its value: the answer is a subtree.

say.intro: Search in a Binary Search Tree. We get the root of a search tree and a value. We return the node holding that value, which really means the whole subtree under it. If it's not there, return null. Looking for five, we follow eight, four, six, and land on five.
say.brute: The brute force ignores the ordering completely. Put the root on a stack. Pop nodes one at a time. If a node has the value, return it. Otherwise push both children. It works on any binary tree. But it can visit all n nodes. And that throws away the one thing that makes this tree special.
say.insight: Here's the thing. In a search tree, everything on the left is smaller than the node, and everything on the right is larger. So one comparison tells us which side the target must be on. The other side? Skip it completely. We walk a single path down from the root. That's at most the height of the tree.
say.anim: We start at the root node, value eight, searching for the value five. Five is less than eight, so we move to the left child, node four. Five is greater than four, so we move to the right child, node six. Five is less than six, so we move to the left child, node five. Now node's value equals five, so the loop stops here. The function returns this matching node directly. The final answer is the node with value five.
say.code: Node starts at the root. We loop, and stop on a match or when we fall off the tree. If the target is smaller, it must be left, so we move to the left child. Otherwise it must be right. When the loop ends, node is either the match, or None if it's missing. Both are exactly what we return.
say.outro: Time proportional to the tree's height, constant space. The lesson? Let the search tree's order discard a whole subtree at every step.

search-in-a-binary-search-tree.title: Search in a Binary Search Tree
lineNotes: We define a Solution class that holds the method for searching the binary search tree.
The searchBST method takes the root of the tree and the target value to find.
We start a walker called node at the root so we can move down without recursion.
We keep looping while node exists and its value differs from the target, stopping on a match or a missing child.
If the target is smaller than the current node's value, it can only live in the left subtree.
So we move node to its left child, discarding the entire right subtree.
Otherwise the target is larger, so it can only be in the right subtree.
So we move node to its right child, discarding the entire left subtree.
We return node, which is either the matching node with its subtree or null if we ran off the tree.

search-in-rotated-sorted-array-ii.hook: Rotated and full of duplicates: binary search still works, until duplicates blind it.
search-in-rotated-sorted-array-ii.ask: A sorted array, possibly with duplicate values, was rotated at some unknown pivot. Given it and a target, return true if the target appears in the array, and false otherwise.
search-in-rotated-sorted-array-ii.exampleWhy: The array is 0, 1, 2, 4, 4, 4, 5, 6, 6, 7 rotated; 1 sits at index 6.

brute.idea: Ignore the structure and scan every element, checking for the target.
steps: Walk the array
Equal to target? return True
End reached? return False
brute.whySlow: Always linear. Binary search is logarithmic on most inputs and only degrades with heavy duplicates.

optimal.insight: One half around mid is always sorted; check if the target fits its range. If left, mid and right are equal, we cannot tell, so shrink both ends.
steps: Pick mid; match? return True
nums[l] = nums[m] = nums[r]? shrink l and r
Left half sorted? Target inside it? go left, else right
Otherwise right half is sorted: same test there

codeNotes.note: Target fits in the sorted left half
Target fits in the sorted right half

pitfalls: Without the triple-equal shrink, inputs like [1,0,1,1,1] go the wrong way.
Worst case is O(n): all duplicates force one-step shrinks.

say.intro: Search in Rotated Sorted Array two. A sorted array with duplicates got rotated at some unknown point. Is the target in it? Our array runs four, five, six, six, seven, then wraps to zero, one, two, four, four. We're looking for one. It's there, so the answer is true.
say.brute: The brute force is a plain scan. Check every element, and return true the moment one equals the target. It's simple and always correct. But it's always linear time. It ignores the fact that the array is almost sorted. And that's exactly what binary search is built to exploit.
say.insight: Here's the key. Around any middle point, at least one half is in sorted order. Compare the ends to see which one. Then ask: does the target fit inside that sorted range? If yes, search there. If not, search the other half. Now, duplicates add one catch. If left, middle and right are all equal, we can't tell which side is sorted. So we just shrink both ends.
say.anim: We start searching for target one, with left at zero and right at nine. Middle index four holds seven, which does not match our target. Left side from four to seven is sorted, but one isn't in that range, so left moves past mid. Now left is five, middle index seven holds two, still not our target. That left portion is sorted again, but one falls below it, so right shrinks to six. Middle index five holds zero, not matching, so left moves forward again. Now middle index six holds one, exactly matching our target. The function returns true, confirming the target one exists in the array.
say.code: Left and right start at the two ends. Each round, we take the middle of the live range. If it's the target, return true. If left, middle and right are equal, duplicates hide the sorted side, so step both ends inward. Else if the left half is sorted, go left when the target fits there, otherwise go right. Else the right half is sorted, and we check if the target fits there instead.
say.outro: Logarithmic on typical inputs, linear in the worst case. The pattern? In a rotated array, always find the sorted half first.

search-in-rotated-sorted-array-ii.title: Search in Rotated Sorted Array II
lineNotes: We define a Solution class that holds the search method for this problem.
The search method takes the rotated array nums and a target, and returns whether the target exists.
We set left to zero and right to the last index, covering the whole array.
We loop while left is not past right, meaning some range still remains to check.
We compute mid as the average of left and right, rounded down.
We check whether the middle value equals the target.
If it matches, we return true right away since the target was found.
If left, mid and right values are all equal, we cannot tell which half is sorted.
In that case we safely discard the left end by moving left up one.
We also discard the right end by moving right down one, shrinking the range.
Otherwise, if the left value is at most the mid value, the left half is sorted.
We check whether the target lies within the sorted left half's range, below the mid value.
If it does, we search the left half by moving right to just before mid.
Otherwise the target cannot be in the left half.
So we move left to just after mid and search the right half.
Otherwise the right half must be the sorted one.
We check whether the target lies in the sorted right half, above mid and up to the right value.
If so, we move left to just after mid to search the right half.
Otherwise the target is not in the right half.
So we move right to just before mid to search the left half.
If the loop ends with no match, we return false because the target is absent.

second-minimum-time-to-reach-destination.hook: Traffic lights punish you, but they punish every path the same way. Count edges, not minutes.
second-minimum-time-to-reach-destination.ask: Every edge takes time minutes, and every light flips between green and red every change minutes. You may only leave a vertex on green. Return the second smallest strictly larger arrival time at vertex n, starting from vertex 1.
second-minimum-time-to-reach-destination.exampleWhy: Fastest route uses 2 edges; second best uses 3. Three edges cost 2, 2, then wait until 6, then 2: total 8.

brute.idea: Expand the set of vertices reachable in exactly L edges, layer by layer. The first two layers that contain n give the two edge counts.
steps: Frontier starts as {1}
Record L whenever n is in the frontier
Next frontier = all neighbours of the frontier
Simulate the lights for the second L
brute.whySlow: Each layer touches every edge again, and there can be about n layers before n is reached.

optimal.insight: Every edge costs the same and waits follow the same clock, so more edges always arrive later. Find the second-smallest edge count: BFS keeping two distances per vertex.
steps: BFS from 1 storing (vertex, edges used)
First visit sets first[v]
A strictly longer visit sets second[v] once
Simulate time and red-light waits over second[n] edges

codeNotes.note: Fewest edges to reach each vertex
Each vertex enqueued at most twice
Odd period means the light is red

pitfalls: Second minimum must be strictly larger: reject a second visit with the same edge count.
Wait only before leaving, never after arriving at n.

say.intro: Second Minimum Time to Reach Destination. Every road takes the same number of minutes. And all the traffic lights flip between green and red together. We need the second fastest arrival time at the last vertex. Here, the fastest route uses two edges, and the next best uses three. That costs eight minutes.
say.brute: A brute force grows the set of vertices reachable in exactly one edge, then two, then three. The first two layers that contain the target give the two edge counts we want. It's correct. But each layer touches every edge again, and there can be about n layers. That's roughly n times the size of the graph.
say.insight: Here's the key. Every edge costs the same, and every path waits at lights by the same rules. So a path with more edges always arrives later. That means the second fastest time is just the second smallest number of edges. Breadth first search can find that. We just let each vertex store two distances. Its first, and a second, strictly larger one.
say.anim: We build an undirected graph from the four edges connecting nodes one through four. Starting breadth first search from node one, its first distance is set to zero. Neighbors two and three get first distance one, added to the queue. Visiting node two, node one gets a second distance of two since it's already visited. Node three also gets second distance two, and node four gets first distance two. Expanding node three again, node four gets a second distance of three. Now we simulate travel time for three edges, adding time and waiting at red lights. After accounting for the signal wait, the total travel time returned is eight.
say.code: First holds the fewest edges to reach each vertex. Second holds the second fewest, strictly more. We pop a vertex and look at its neighbours. A new neighbour gets its first distance. One reached again with a larger count gets its second. So each vertex is enqueued at most twice. Then we simulate the clock. An odd period means the light is red, so we wait for the next green, then travel.
say.outro: Linear in the size of the graph. The trick? A breadth first search that keeps the two best distances per vertex.

second-minimum-time-to-reach-destination.title: Second Minimum Time to Reach Destination
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, as the problem platform expects.
This method takes the vertex count, the edge list, the travel time per edge, and the light change interval.
We build an adjacency list as a dictionary that maps each vertex to a list of its neighbors.
We loop over every edge, reading its two endpoints u and v.
We add v to the neighbor list of u.
Since the graph is undirected, we also add u to the neighbor list of v.
The first list stores the shortest edge count to each vertex, with negative one meaning unvisited.
The second list stores the strictly larger second shortest edge count for each vertex, also starting unvisited.
Vertex one is the start, so its shortest distance is zero edges.
We start a queue with vertex one at distance zero to run the breadth first search.
We keep processing until the queue is empty.
We take the next vertex and its edge count from the front of the queue.
We look at every neighbor of the current vertex.
If this neighbor has never been reached, this is its shortest distance.
We record the shortest distance as one more than the current distance.
We push the neighbor with that distance so we can explore onward from it.
Otherwise, if no second distance exists yet and this path is strictly longer than the first, it qualifies.
We record this strictly larger distance as the neighbor's second shortest distance.
We push the neighbor again so paths through its second distance are also explored.
Now we convert the edge count to real time, starting the clock at zero.
We simulate one edge at a time, repeating for the second shortest edge count to vertex n.
If the current moment falls in a red period, meaning the interval index is odd, we must wait.
We wait by jumping to the start of the next green period.
We then travel the edge, adding time to the total.
We return the total minutes needed to arrive by the second smallest distinct route.

sequential-digits.hook: Only 36 numbers in the universe have sequential digits. Just slide a window over 123456789.
sequential-digits.ask: A number has sequential digits when each digit is exactly one more than the digit before it. Given low and high, return every such number in that range, sorted in increasing order.
sequential-digits.exampleWhy: Three-digit sequential numbers are 123, 234 and so on; only 123 and 234 fall inside 100 to 300.

brute.idea: Check every number from low to high: turn it into a string and test that each digit is one more than the previous.
steps: Loop num from low to high
Compare each adjacent digit pair
All step up by one? keep num
brute.whySlow: With low = 10 and high = 1,000,000,000 it checks about a billion numbers to find at most 36 answers.

optimal.insight: Every sequential number is a substring of 123456789. Slide windows of each length over that string; there are only 36 windows in total.
steps: Window lengths run from digits of low to digits of high
Slide the window start from left to right
Convert the window to a number
Keep it if it lies in the range

codeNotes.note: Every answer is a window of this
Shorter lengths first keeps output sorted
Keep only those inside the range

pitfalls: Loop length outermost: 89 < 123, so length-first order is already sorted.
There is no 0 and nothing after 9: 7890 is not sequential.

say.intro: Sequential Digits. A number has sequential digits when each digit is one more than the one before, like one two three. Given low and high, return every such number in that range, sorted. From one hundred to three hundred, that's one two three, and two three four.
say.brute: The brute force checks every number in the range. Turn it into a string. Compare each pair of neighbouring digits. If every step goes up by exactly one, keep it. Fine for small ranges. But the range can hold a billion numbers. And the answer never has more than thirty six of them.
say.insight: So here's the question. What do all these numbers have in common? Every one is a slice of the string one through nine. A two digit one is a window of length two. A three digit one, length three. So instead of searching, we generate. Slide a window of each length across that string, and keep what lands in range.
say.anim: We start with low 100 and high 300, and the digit string 123456789. We try window length 3 first, since low has three digits. At start 0, the window gives num 123, which fits between 100 and 300, so it's added. Next window start 1 gives num 234, also within range, so it joins the result.
