Start 2 gives 345, which is too big, so it gets skipped. The remaining windows, 456 up through 789, are all too large and skipped too. Length 3 was the only length tried since high also has three digits. The function returns the final answer: 123 and 234.
say.code: We store the string one through nine, since every answer is a window of it. The outer loop picks window lengths, shorter ones first. That keeps the output sorted. The inner loop slides through all windows of this length. Each window becomes a number. We keep only those inside the range, between low and high.
say.outro: Constant time, since there are only thirty six windows. The takeaway? Sometimes it's faster to generate answers than to test candidates.

sequential-digits.title: Sequential Digits
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which holds the method that solves the sequential digits problem.
The method takes low and high as the range bounds and returns a list of the matching integers.
We store the string one two three through nine, since every sequential number is a substring of it.
We start an empty result list to collect the valid numbers as we find them.
We loop over each possible length, from the digit count of low up to the digit count of high.
For each length we slide a window, trying every start position that still leaves room for that many digits.
We cut out the substring at this start with this length and convert it into an integer.
We check whether that number falls between low and high, inclusive, so out of range windows are skipped.
If it is in range, we append the number to the result list.
Since lengths grow and starts move right, results are already sorted, so we simply return the list.

shift-2d-grid.hook: Shifting a grid is just shifting one long array. Index arithmetic does it in one pass.
shift-2d-grid.ask: Given an m by n grid and a number k, shift every element one step to the right k times. The last element of a row moves to the next row's start, and the very last element wraps to the top-left.
shift-2d-grid.exampleWhy: Read row by row, 1 to 9 is one line. Shifting it four places moves 6, 7, 8, 9 to the front.

brute.idea: Do exactly what the statement says: perform k single shifts, each carrying every element one cell forward.
steps: Repeat k times
Carry the last element into the first cell
Each cell takes the previous cell's value
brute.whySlow: Each shift touches all m·n cells, k times over. Shifting by m·n returns the same grid, yet it still does all that work.

optimal.insight: Flatten the grid row by row. Cell (i, j) is position i·n + j, and a k-step shift sends it to (i·n + j + k) mod m·n.
steps: Reduce k modulo m·n
For each cell, compute its flat index
Add k, wrap with mod m·n
Convert back to row pos // n, column pos % n

codeNotes.note: New flat index after k shifts
Flat index back to row, column

pitfalls: Build rows with a comprehension; [[0] * n] * m makes every row the same list.
Forgetting the modulo sends large k out of range.

say.intro: Shift Two D Grid. Each element moves one cell right. The end of each row spills into the next row. And the bottom right corner wraps to the top left. Do that k times. With one through nine in a three by three grid and k of four, six, seven, eight land on top.
say.brute: The brute force just simulates each shift. Carry the last element into the first cell, and let every cell take the value before it. Then repeat k times. So what's the catch? Each shift touches the whole grid, so it's k times the grid size. Even though shifting by the full grid size gives back the original.
say.insight: Here's the thing. Read the grid row by row, and it's just one long array. The cell at row i, column j sits at position i times n plus j. Shifting by k just adds k to that position. Then we wrap around, using the remainder by the total size. Divide by n, and the quotient and remainder give the new row and column.
say.anim: We start with a 3 by 3 grid and a shift amount of 4. Total cells equal 9, and k stays 4 since it is already less than total. An empty result grid is created, ready to hold shifted values. For cell 1, position becomes 4, placing value 1 into row 1 column 1. Continuing row 0, values 2 and 3 move to positions 5 and 6, wrapping the grid. Row 1 values 4, 5, and 6 shift to positions 7, 8, and 0, wrapping around. Row 2 values 7, 8, and 9 land at positions 1, 2, and 3, finishing the shift. The final shifted grid is 6,7,8 then 9,1,2 then 3,4,5.
say.code: First, we reduce k modulo the total size, since full cycles change nothing. Then we make a fresh grid for the result. For every cell, we find its new flat index after k shifts. That's its position plus k, modulo the total. Then we turn the flat index back into a row and column, with division and remainder by n. And copy the value there.
say.outro: One pass over the grid. The pattern? Flatten two dimensions into one, and let modular arithmetic do the wrapping.

shift-2d-grid.title: Shift 2D Grid
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container the problem expects for our method.
The shiftGrid method takes the grid and the shift count k, and returns the newly shifted grid.
We read the number of rows as m and the number of columns as n from the grid.
We compute total as m times n, which is the count of cells when the grid is flattened.
We reduce k modulo total, since shifting by a full cycle returns the grid to its original state.
We build a result grid of the same size, filled with zeros, ready to receive shifted values.
The outer loop walks through each row index i of the original grid.
The inner loop walks through each column index j within that row.
We find the flattened position of this cell, add k, and wrap around with modulo total.
We convert the new position back to a row and column by dividing and taking the remainder by n, then store the value.
After every cell has been placed in its shifted spot, we return the result grid.

shifting-letters-ii.hook: Thousands of range updates, one final string. Record only where each shift starts and stops.
shifting-letters-ii.ask: Given a string and a list of shifts, each shift moves every letter between start and end one step forward or backward in the alphabet, wrapping around. Apply all shifts and return the final string.
shifting-letters-ii.exampleWhy: Net shifts per index are 0, +1, +2, +1. So a stays a, b becomes c, c becomes e, d becomes e.

brute.idea: Apply each shift directly: loop over its range and move every letter in it one step.
steps: For each shift
Walk from start to end
Add or subtract one, modulo 26
brute.whySlow: Each shift can cover the whole string: 50,000 shifts on 50,000 letters is 2.5 billion updates.

optimal.insight: Use a difference array. A range update becomes two marks: plus delta at start, minus delta just past end. One prefix sum then gives each index its total shift.
steps: For each shift, mark +delta at start
Mark -delta at end + 1
Running sum of marks = net shift here
Shift the letter by it, modulo 26

codeNotes.note: Running total = net shift at i

pitfalls: Python's % keeps negative shifts in 0 to 25; other languages need + 26.
Size the array n + 1 so end + 1 never overflows.

say.intro: Shifting Letters two. We get a string and a list of shifts. Each shift moves every letter in a range one step forward or back in the alphabet, wrapping around. With a b c d, the three shifts leave a alone, push b up one, c up two, and d up one. That gives a c e e.
say.brute: The brute force applies each shift literally. For every shift, walk from its start to its end, and move each letter one step. Easy to write. But one shift can cover the whole string. Fifty thousand shifts on a fifty thousand letter string? That's billions of updates.
say.insight: Here's the thing. We never need the string between shifts. We only need the total shift at each index. A difference array records a range update with just two marks. Add the change at the start. Subtract it right after the end. Then a single running sum, left to right, gives the net shift at every index.
say.anim: We start with a difference array of zeros, one longer than the string. The first shift is backward from zero to one, so we mark minus one at zero and plus one at two. The second shift is forward from one to three, marking plus one at one and minus one at four. The third shift is forward from zero to two, adding plus one at zero and minus one at three. The final difference array is zero, one, one, minus one, minus one, ready for prefix summing. At index zero, shift stays zero, so letter a stays a in the result. At index one, shift becomes one, turning letter b into c. After processing all letters using running shifts, the final answer shown is acee.
say.code: We make a difference array with one extra slot, for end plus one. For each shift, delta is plus or minus one. The shift begins at start, so we add delta there. It stops after end, so we subtract delta at end plus one. Then we walk the string. The running total of marks is the net shift at each index. We shift the letter, wrapping around the alphabet with modulo twenty six.
say.outro: Linear time. The takeaway? A difference array turns every range update into two point updates, plus one prefix sum.

shifting-letters-ii.title: Shifting Letters II
lineNotes: This line begins the Solution class that holds our method for the problem.
The method takes the string and the list of shifts, and returns the final shifted string.
We build a difference array of zeros, one slot longer than the string so the end plus one mark always fits.
We loop over each shift, unpacking its start index, end index, and direction value.
We turn the direction into a delta of plus one for forward and minus one for backward.
We add the delta at the start index to mark where this shift begins.
We subtract the delta just past the end index to cancel the shift after the range finishes.
We create an empty list to collect the resulting characters.
We set the running shift to zero, which will accumulate the prefix sum as we walk along.
We loop through the string, getting each index and its character.
We add the difference value at this index to the running shift, giving the total shift for this position.
We convert the letter to a zero based number, add the shift, wrap with modulo twenty six, convert back, and append it.
We join the collected characters into one string and return it as the answer.

shortest-path-in-a-grid-with-obstacles-e.hook: Walls you can smash, but only k of them. Add the budget to the BFS state.
shortest-path-in-a-grid-with-obstacles-e.ask: In a grid of empty cells and walls, move up, down, left or right from the top-left to the bottom-right corner. You may walk through at most k walls. Return the fewest steps needed, or -1 if impossible.
shortest-path-in-a-grid-with-obstacles-e.exampleWhy: A full wall splits the grid. Breaking one wall cell lets a straight 4-step path through.

brute.idea: Depth-first search over every simple path, spending one unit of k on each wall, and keep the shortest path that reaches the corner.
steps: DFS from the start, marking the path
Entering a wall spends one k
Budget below zero? abandon
At the corner, record the step count
brute.whySlow: The number of simple paths explodes exponentially; a 10 by 10 grid already has astronomically many.

optimal.insight: A cell alone is not enough state: arriving with more walls left is better. BFS over (row, column, remaining k) finds the fewest steps level by level.
steps: If k ≥ m + n - 2, the Manhattan path works
BFS from (0, 0, k)
Moving into a wall costs one from remaining
Skip states already seen
First time the corner pops, return its steps

shortest-path-in-a-grid-with-obstacles-e.optimalCode:
from collections import deque

class Solution:
    def shortestPath(self, grid: List[List[int]], k: int) -> int:
        rows = len(grid)
        cols = len(grid[0])

        # 1. If we have enough eliminations, the direct Manhattan path works
        if k >= rows + cols - 2:
            return rows + cols - 2

        # 2. BFS over (row, col, remaining walls we can still eliminate)
        queue = deque()
        queue.append((0, 0, k, 0))
        seen = set()
        seen.add((0, 0, k))

        directions = [(1, 0), (-1, 0), (0, 1), (0, -1)]

        while queue:
            row, col, remaining, steps = queue.popleft()

            # 3. First time we reach the bottom-right corner, return the steps
            if row == rows - 1 and col == cols - 1:
                return steps

            for deltaRow, deltaCol in directions:
                newRow = row + deltaRow
                newCol = col + deltaCol
                if newRow < 0 or newRow >= rows or newCol < 0 or newCol >= cols:
                    continue

                # 4. Moving into a wall costs one from the remaining count
                newRemaining = remaining - grid[newRow][newCol]
                if newRemaining < 0:
                    continue

                state = (newRow, newCol, newRemaining)
                if state in seen:
                    continue

                seen.add(state)
                queue.append((newRow, newCol, newRemaining, steps + 1))

        return -1

codeNotes.note: BFS order: first arrival is shortest

codeNotes.match: if nrem >= 0 and (nr, nc, nrem) not in seen:

pitfalls: Marking only (row, col) seen blocks later visits that have more budget.
Shortcut k ≥ m + n - 2 first; otherwise a huge k bloats the states.

say.intro: Shortest Path in a Grid with Obstacles Elimination. We walk from the top left to the bottom right, one cell at a time. We can break through at most k walls. What's the fewest steps? In our grid, a wall runs down the middle column. Break one cell, and we cross in four steps.
say.brute: The brute force tries every path. A depth first search walks the grid without revisiting cells on its current path. It spends one unit of budget per wall, and records the shortest arrival. So what's the catch? The number of simple paths grows exponentially. This falls apart even on small grids.
say.insight: Breadth first search gives shortest paths in steps. But here's the thing. A cell alone isn't enough state. Reaching a cell with two walls left is better than reaching it with none. So each state is the row, the column, and the remaining budget. We search over those states. The first time the corner comes off the queue, that step count is the answer.
say.anim: We start at the top left cell with one wall removal allowed and zero steps taken. The queue holds our start state, and we begin exploring in all four directions. Moving right into a wall uses up our remaining removal, reaching state zero one zero. Breadth first search expands outward, tracking row, column, and walls left as separate states. Cells already seen with equal or better wall counts are skipped to avoid repeats. By step three, the search has spread across most of the grid's reachable states. At step four, we finally reach row two, column two, the bottom right corner. The search returns four, the fewest steps needed eliminating at most one obstacle.
say.code: First, if k is at least the Manhattan distance, we have enough budget to go straight. Otherwise, queue the start. The state includes walls left, starting full. In breadth first order, the first arrival at the target is shortest. For each neighbour, a wall uses one elimination. If we're still within budget, and it's a new state, mark it and queue it, one step further.
say.outro: Time proportional to m times n times k. The pattern? Breadth first search, with an extra resource folded into the state.

shortest-path-in-a-grid-with-obstacles-e.title: Shortest Path in a Grid with Obstacles Elimination
lineNotes: We import deque from collections so we can use a fast double-ended queue for breadth first search.
We define a Solution class, as the problem platform expects.
This method takes the grid and the wall elimination limit k, and returns the fewest steps or negative one.
We store the number of rows in the grid.
We store the number of columns from the length of the first row.
This comment says that with enough eliminations, the direct Manhattan path is always achievable.
If k is at least rows plus columns minus two, we can walk straight through any walls.
In that case we return rows plus columns minus two, the Manhattan distance to the corner.
This comment introduces the search, whose state includes how many eliminations remain.
We create an empty queue to hold states waiting to be explored.
We start at the top-left corner with all k eliminations left and zero steps taken.
We create a set to remember states we have already visited.
We mark the starting state, including its full remaining count, as seen.
We list the four moves: down, up, right and left.
We loop while the queue still has states, so we explore level by level.
We take the oldest state from the queue, giving us its position, remaining eliminations and step count.
This comment notes that the first arrival at the goal in breadth first order is the shortest.
We check whether the current cell is the bottom-right corner.
If so, we return the steps taken, which is minimal because of breadth first order.
We try each of the four directions from the current cell.
We compute the neighbor's row by adding the row change.
We compute the neighbor's column by adding the column change.
We check whether the neighbor falls outside the grid.
If it is outside, we skip this direction.
This comment explains that stepping onto a wall uses up one elimination.
We subtract the neighbor's grid value from remaining, since walls are one and empty cells are zero.
We check whether we have gone below zero eliminations.
If so, the move is not allowed and we skip it.
We build the new state from the neighbor's position and its remaining eliminations.
We check whether this exact state was already visited.
If it was, we skip it, since an earlier visit reached it in no more steps.
Otherwise we mark the new state as seen so we never queue it again.
We add the new state to the queue with the step count increased by one.
If the queue empties without reaching the corner, the goal is unreachable, so we return negative one.

shortest-subarray-with-sum-at-least-k.hook: Negative numbers break the usual sliding window. A monotonic deque of prefix sums fixes it.
shortest-subarray-with-sum-at-least-k.ask: Given an integer array that may contain negative numbers, and a target k, return the length of the shortest non-empty contiguous subarray whose sum is at least k, or -1 if no subarray reaches k.
shortest-subarray-with-sum-at-least-k.exampleWhy: 2 + 3 = 5 reaches k = 5 in just two elements; no single element is that large.

brute.idea: Fix every start index, extend the end while keeping a running sum, and stop at the first end where the sum reaches k.
steps: For each start i
Grow j, adding nums[j]
Sum ≥ k? record j - i + 1, stop
brute.whySlow: With 100,000 elements that is up to 5 billion additions when no short subarray exists.

optimal.insight: Sum of i..j is P[j+1] - P[i]. Keep starts in a deque with increasing prefix sums: pop the front when it works, the back when a smaller prefix arrives.
steps: Build prefix sums P
Front start gives sum ≥ k? record length, pop it
Back prefix ≥ current? it can never win, pop it
Push the current index as a future start

codeNotes.note: prefix[j] = sum of the first j

codeNotes.match: while dq and p - prefix[dq[0]] >= k:
codeNotes.note: Oldest start works: shortest for it
Current index is a new start

pitfalls: A plain two-pointer window fails with negatives: sums do not grow monotonically.
Popping the front is safe: any later end would only be longer.

say.intro: Shortest Subarray with Sum at Least K. We want the shortest run of consecutive numbers that sums to at least k. And the numbers can be negative. With two, minus one, two, three, minus two, four, and k of five, two plus three reaches five. Just two elements. So the answer is two.
say.brute: The brute force tries every start. From each start, extend the end one step at a time with a running sum. Stop at the first end where the sum reaches k. That's n squared. On a hundred thousand numbers, it can mean billions of additions.
say.insight: Here's the setup. A subarray's sum is one prefix minus an earlier one. Keep candidate starts in a deque, with increasing prefix values. Does the front start already give at least k? Record it, and drop it. Later ends would only be longer. And if the back start's prefix is at least the current one, drop it too. The current index is closer, and better.
say.anim: We start building prefix sums from the array, beginning with zero. After processing all numbers, prefix becomes zero, two, one, three, six, four, eight. Best is initialized large, and we prepare an empty deque to track start indices. Indices zero, one, two, and three get pushed, keeping prefix sums increasing in the deque. At j equals four, prefix six minus prefix at index two is at least five, so best becomes four. Continuing to pop, prefix six minus prefix three gives best equals two. At j equals six, prefix eight minus prefix at index five also hits five, confirming best stays two. The function returns two, the shortest subarray length with sum at least five.
say.code: First, build the prefix sums, where each entry is the sum of the first j numbers. For each index, while the oldest start works, that's the shortest window for it. So record the length, then drop that start. Next, while the back has a prefix at least as big, a later, lower prefix dominates it. Pop it. Then the current index becomes a new start. Return the best, or minus one.
say.outro: Linear time. The pattern is a monotonic deque over prefix sums. It's a sliding window that works even with negatives.

shortest-subarray-with-sum-at-least-k.title: Shortest Subarray with Sum at Least K
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container this problem's method lives in.
The method takes the array nums and the target k, and returns the shortest qualifying subarray length.
We start the prefix sums list with zero so that subarrays beginning at the first element are covered.
We loop over every number in nums to build the running totals one at a time.
Each new prefix sum is the previous prefix sum plus the current number x.
We set best to the length of nums plus one, a sentinel meaning no valid subarray found yet.
We create an empty deque that will hold candidate start indices whose prefix sums are increasing.
We walk through every prefix index j with its value p, treating j as a possible subarray end.
While the oldest start in the deque gives a sum of at least k, we have a valid subarray.
We record the shorter length and pop that start, since any later end would only make it longer.
While the newest start has a prefix sum not smaller than p, it can never beat j as a start.
We pop those worse starts from the back, keeping the deque's prefix sums strictly increasing.
We add the current index j as a new candidate start for future ends.
If best was ever lowered to a real length we return it, otherwise we return negative one.

sign-of-the-product-of-an-array.hook: You never need the product, only its sign. Count the negatives and watch for zero.
sign-of-the-product-of-an-array.ask: Multiply all the numbers in an array together. Return 1 if the product is positive, -1 if it is negative, and 0 if it is zero.
sign-of-the-product-of-an-array.exampleWhy: No zeros, and five negative numbers. An odd count of negatives makes the product negative.

brute.idea: Multiply everything into one product, then check whether it is positive, negative or zero.
steps: Multiply all numbers together
Compare the product with zero
Return 1, -1 or 0
brute.whySlow: 1,000 numbers up to 100 give a 2,000-digit product; in fixed-width languages it simply overflows.

optimal.insight: Only two facts matter: is there a zero, and is the number of negatives odd? Track a sign that flips at each negative.
steps: Start with sign = 1
Any zero? return 0 at once
Each negative flips the sign
Return the final sign

pitfalls: In Java or C++ the real product overflows within a few dozen elements.
Return 0 immediately on a zero; do not keep flipping.

say.intro: Sign of the Product of an Array. Multiply every number, and report only the sign. One for positive, minus one for negative, zero for zero. Our array has five negative numbers and no zeros. So the product is negative, and the answer is minus one.
say.brute: The obvious approach multiplies everything, then checks the result. In Python that works, but the product gets enormous. A thousand numbers near a hundred make a number with about two thousand digits. And each multiplication gets slower as it grows. In Java or C plus plus? It overflows after a few dozen numbers, and gives a wrong sign.
say.insight: So here's the question. Do we actually need the product? No. Just its sign. Multiplying by a positive keeps the sign. Multiplying by a negative flips it. And multiplying by zero makes the whole thing zero forever. So we keep a single sign variable, and flip it on every negative.
say.anim: We start with sign set to 1, before scanning the array. x is negative one, not zero, so sign flips to negative one. x is negative two, another negative, flipping sign back to positive one. x is negative three, flipping sign to negative one again. x is negative four, flipping sign back to positive one. Values three and two are positive, so sign stays unchanged. The final x is negative one, flipping sign to negative one. With an odd number of negatives and no zeros, the function returns negative one.
say.code: Sign starts at one, because an empty product is positive. Then we loop over the numbers. One zero makes everything zero, so we return zero right away. Each negative flips the sign. Positives do nothing. When the loop ends, an odd number of negatives gives minus one. So we just return the sign.
say.outro: Linear time, constant space, and no overflow. The lesson? Track only the property you need, here the parity of negatives.

sign-of-the-product-of-an-array.title: Sign of the Product of an Array
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container the interview platform expects for our method.
The method arraySign takes a list of integers called nums and returns an integer representing the sign of their product.
We start sign at one, meaning the product so far is treated as positive before looking at any numbers.
We loop through each number x in nums, checking one value at a time without computing the real product.
If the current number x equals zero, then the whole product must be zero.
So we return zero immediately, since nothing else in the array can change that result.
If x is negative, it changes the sign of the running product, so we check for that case.
We flip sign by negating it, so an even count of negatives returns to positive and an odd count stays negative.
After the loop finishes with no zero found, we return sign, which holds the product's sign, positive or negative.

single-threaded-cpu.hook: A CPU that always picks the shortest ready job. Sort by arrival, heap by length.
single-threaded-cpu.ask: Each task has an enqueue time and a processing time. A single CPU, when idle, picks the available task with the shortest processing time, breaking ties by smaller index, and runs it to completion. Return the order tasks are processed.
single-threaded-cpu.exampleWhy: Task 0 runs alone until 3. Then 2 beats 1 on length, then 3 arrives and is shortest, then 1.

brute.idea: Simulate. Each time the CPU is free, scan all unfinished tasks for the shortest one that has arrived.
steps: Scan every unfinished task
Pick the shortest that has arrived
None ready? jump time to the next arrival
Run it and advance time
brute.whySlow: Every pick rescans all n tasks: 100,000 tasks means about 10 billion checks.

optimal.insight: Two orderings drive the simulation: by enqueue time to see what has arrived, and by processing time to pick. Sort for the first, a min-heap for the second.
steps: Sort task indexes by enqueue time
Idle with an empty heap? jump to the next arrival
Push every arrived task as (length, index)
Pop the smallest, run it, record its index

codeNotes.match: if not heap and time < tasks[order[i]][0]:
codeNotes.note: Idle: skip ahead to next arrival

pitfalls: Forgetting the idle jump leaves the heap empty and crashes the pop.
Store (length, index) so ties pick the smaller index.

say.intro: Single Threaded CPU. Each task has an arrival time and a length. Whenever the CPU is free, it picks the shortest task that's arrived. Ties go to the smaller index. Then it runs that task to the end. In our example, task zero runs first, then two, then three, then one.
say.brute: The brute force just simulates. Every time the CPU frees up, scan every unfinished task, and choose the shortest one that's arrived. If nothing has, jump the clock forward. It's correct. But every choice rescans all the tasks. That's n squared. Around ten billion checks for a hundred thousand tasks.
say.insight: Here's the thing. The simulation really needs two orderings. Which tasks have arrived? Sort by arrival time, and move a pointer forward. Which arrived task runs next? Keep them in a min heap, keyed by length, then index. Each task enters and leaves the heap once. So the whole thing costs n log n.
say.anim: We sort task indices by their enqueue times, giving us the order zero, one, two, three. Time starts at zero, and since task zero arrives at time one, time jumps to one. Task zero is pushed into the heap with processing time two, since it has arrived. We pop task zero, the only option, advance time to three, and record it first. Tasks one and two have now arrived by time three, so both enter the heap. Task two has the shorter processing time two, so it's chosen next, time becomes five. Task three arrives by time five and has the shortest processing time, so it runs next. Finally task one is the only one left, processed last, giving order zero, two, three, one.
say.code: First we sort the indexes by arrival time. If the CPU is idle and nothing has arrived, skip ahead to the next arrival. Then push every arrived task as a pair of length and index. That way ties break by index automatically. Pop the shortest available task. The CPU is busy until it finishes, so advance the clock by its length, and record its index.
say.outro: n log n time. The pattern? Sort by one key to release items, and use a heap to choose by another.

single-threaded-cpu.title: Single-Threaded CPU
lineNotes: We define the Solution class that holds our method for this problem.
The getOrder method takes the list of tasks and returns the order in which the CPU processes them.
We sort task indexes by enqueue time so we can walk through tasks in the order they arrive.
We start with an empty result list and an empty heap for the tasks that are available.
We set the current time to zero and the pointer into the sorted order to zero.
We loop until every task has been processed and added to the result.
If nothing is available and the next task has not arrived yet, the CPU is idle and must wait.
So we jump the current time forward to the enqueue time of that next task.
We keep looping while there are unseen tasks whose enqueue time is at or before the current time.
We grab the original index of the next task in enqueue order.
We push its processing time and index onto the heap, so the shortest time wins and ties go to the smaller index.
We advance the pointer to move on to the next task in enqueue order.
We pop the available task with the shortest processing time, breaking ties by smaller index.
We run that task to completion by adding its processing time to the current time.
We record the index of the finished task in the result order.
Once all tasks are processed, we return the result list.

smallest-divisible-digit-product-i.hook: The answer is always close: within ten steps, some number ends in zero.
smallest-divisible-digit-product-i.ask: Given n and t, return the smallest number that is at least n and whose digits multiply to a product divisible by t.
smallest-divisible-digit-product-i.exampleWhy: Digit products from 23: 6, 8, 10, 12, then 2 · 7 = 14, which 7 divides.

brute.idea: Compute the digit product for every number in a block of ten starting at n, collect those divisible by t, and return the smallest.
steps: Loop x over n to n + 9
Multiply the digits of x
Divisible by t? collect it
Return the minimum collected
brute.whySlow: Same bound, but it always checks all ten numbers and builds a list instead of stopping at the first hit.

optimal.insight: Among any ten consecutive numbers, one ends in 0, giving product 0, which every t divides. So simply count upward; we stop within ten tries.
steps: Take the current number
Multiply its digits
Divisible by t? return it
Otherwise try the next number

pitfalls: Zero counts as divisible by every t, so 10 works for any t.
Start at n itself, not n + 1: n may already qualify.

say.intro: Smallest Divisible Digit Product one. Given n and t, find the smallest number at least n whose digits multiply to something divisible by t. Start at twenty three with t of seven. Products go six, eight, ten, twelve. Then twenty seven gives two times seven, fourteen. Seven divides that. So the answer is twenty seven.
say.brute: A cautious approach checks a fixed block. For every number from n to n plus nine, multiply its digits. Collect the ones divisible by t, and return the smallest. It's correct, and not slower in the big picture. It just always does all ten checks and builds a list. Even when n itself works.
say.insight: Here's the key. The search is guaranteed to be short. Why? Among any ten consecutive numbers, one ends in zero. Its digit product is zero. And zero is divisible by every t. So we just count upward from n, and return the first number that works. We never need more than ten tries.
say.anim: We start checking n equals 23, looking for a digit product divisible by 7. Multiplying digits 2 and 3 gives a product of 6, not divisible by 7. Since it failed, n increases to 24, and we try digits 2 and 4, giving product 8. Next n is 25, digits 2 and 5 multiply to 10, still not divisible by 7. Now n is 26, digits 2 and 6 give product 12, again not divisible by 7. Trying n equals 27, digits 2 and 7 multiply to 14, which is divisible by 7. The loop stops and returns this value as the answer. The final smallest number found is 27.
say.code: We loop forever, which is safe, because it ends within ten numbers. For the current n, prod starts at one, and becomes the product of the digits. If prod is divisible by t, the first hit is the smallest, so we return n. Otherwise, try the next number.
say.outro: At most ten tries, each costing the number of digits. The lesson? A bound on the search can make simple counting the optimal answer.

smallest-divisible-digit-product-i.title: Smallest Divisible Digit Product I
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container the problem expects for our method.
The method smallestNumber takes n as the starting number and t as the target divisor, and returns an integer.
We loop forever, counting upward from n, which is safe because a number ending in zero appears within ten steps.
For each candidate we reset prod to one, the neutral starting value for multiplying digits.
We walk through each digit of n by turning the number into a string and reading characters one at a time.
Each character becomes an integer and is multiplied into prod, building the digit product of the current number.
We check whether prod is evenly divisible by t, meaning the remainder is zero.
If it is divisible, the current n is the smallest valid number, so we return it immediately.
Otherwise we increase n by one and try the next number in the loop.

smallest-divisible-digit-product-ii.hook: Keep the longest prefix you can, bump one digit, then fill the tail with the fewest digits possible.
smallest-divisible-digit-product-ii.ask: Given a number as a string and t, return the smallest number at least num with no zero digits whose digit product is divisible by t. Return "-1" if none exists.
smallest-divisible-digit-product-ii.exampleWhy: 1205 has a zero. Keep 12, raise 0 to 2; the product still needs 6, so the last digit is 6.

brute.idea: If t has a prime factor above 7, no digits can produce it. Otherwise count upward, testing each zero-free number's digit product.
steps: Prime factor above 7? return -1
Count up from num
Skip numbers containing 0
First product divisible by t wins
brute.whySlow: Numbers can have 200,000 digits; counting upward could take astronomically many steps.

optimal.insight: Digits supply only primes 2, 3, 5, 7. Track what t still needs per prefix; from the right, keep the longest prefix where a bigger digit plus tail fits.
steps: Factor out 2, 3, 5, 7; leftover? return -1
need[i] = part of t not covered by the first i digits
From the right, try a larger digit at i
Fill the rest: greedy digits 9 down to 2, padded with 1s
Nothing fits? Use a longer number

codeNotes.note: Fewest digits whose product covers r
What t still needs after this prefix
Minimal tail for the remaining need

pitfalls: A prefix is only usable up to the first zero digit.
Pad with 1s on the left of the tail; sort tail digits ascending.

say.intro: Smallest Divisible Digit Product two. Now the number can be huge, so it comes as a string. We want the smallest number at least num, with no zero digits, whose digit product is divisible by t. For one two zero five and t of twenty four, the answer is one two two six.
say.brute: First, a quick check. Digits only contain the primes two, three, five and seven. So if t has any other prime factor, the answer is minus one. Otherwise, the brute force counts upward from num, skipping numbers with a zero. It stops when a product divides by t. With two hundred thousand digits? That count can be astronomical.
say.insight: So let's think greedily. The answer keeps the longest possible prefix of num. Then it puts a larger digit at one position. Then it fills the rest as small as possible. After each prefix, we know what part of t is still needed. And the fewest digits covering that need? Take nines, eights, down to twos, then pad with ones.
say.anim: We start with num 1205 and target product 24, checking its prime factors. Dividing rest by 2, 3, 5, and 7 reduces it fully to 1, confirming 24 is achievable. We build the need array, tracking leftover product needed after each digit, stopping at the zero. At index 2, we try digit 1 first, needing remaining factor 12 split into tail digits. Computing digits for 12 gives tail 26, but that's too long to fit remaining positions. Trying digit 2 next at index 2, we need factor 6 and compute its digit breakdown. The digits for 6 simplify neatly to just the single digit 6. Since tail length 1 fits, the final smallest valid number is 1226.
say.code: First, if t has a prime above seven, it's impossible. Next, a helper finds the fewest digits whose product covers a need. Then we record what t still needs after each prefix. We try the longest usable prefix first, scanning from the right and bumping one digit. The minimal tail covers the remaining need. If nothing fits, the fallback is a number one digit longer.
say.outro: Close to linear in the length. The pattern is greedy: keep the longest prefix, bump one digit, and fill the tail minimally.

smallest-divisible-digit-product-ii.title: Smallest Divisible Digit Product II
lineNotes: We define the Solution class that holds the method for this problem.
The method takes the digit string num and the target t, and returns the smallest valid number as a string.
We copy t into rest, which will have its small prime factors stripped away.
We loop over the only primes digits can supply: two, three, five and seven.
While rest is still divisible by the current prime, we keep dividing it out.
Each division removes one copy of that prime factor from rest.
If anything greater than one remains, t has a larger prime factor that no digit can supply.
In that case no answer exists, so we return negative one as a string.
We define a helper that builds the fewest digits whose product is exactly r.
We start with an empty list to collect the chosen digits.
We try digits from nine down to two, so that larger digits absorb factors first and the count stays minimal.
While the digit divides r evenly, we keep using it.
We append that digit as a string to the output list.
We divide r by the digit to account for the factor we just covered.
We sort the digits ascending and join them, giving the smallest number for that digit multiset.
We store n as the length of num.
We start the need list with t, meaning what is still required before any digit is used.
We walk through each character of num to build what remains needed after each prefix.
If the character is a zero, no longer prefix can be valid.
So we stop extending the need list there.
We divide the current need by its gcd with this digit, leaving what the prefix still has to supply.
If the whole num has no zeros and nothing remains needed, num itself is the answer.
We return num unchanged since it already satisfies both conditions.
We scan positions from the rightmost usable prefix leftward, to keep the longest unchanged prefix and so the smallest result.
At position i we try each digit larger than the current one, from the smallest upward.
We compute the shortest sorted tail needed for what remains after using digit d at this position.
If that tail fits in the remaining positions after i, this choice is feasible.
We return the kept prefix, the new digit, ones as padding, then the tail, which is the smallest completion.
If no same-length number works, we build the answer from the digits needed for all of t.
We pad with ones to length at least n plus one and append the tail, giving the smallest longer number.

smallest-even-multiple.hook: The least common multiple of n and 2, in one parity check.
smallest-even-multiple.ask: Given a positive integer n, return the smallest positive integer that is a multiple of both 2 and n.
smallest-even-multiple.exampleWhy: 7 is odd, so it is not a multiple of 2. The next multiple of 7, which is 14, is even.

brute.idea: Walk through the multiples of n, starting with n itself, and return the first one that is even.
steps: Start x at n
x odd? add n
Return the first even x
brute.whySlow: It loops at most twice, so it is not slow; it just hides the one-line parity reasoning.

optimal.insight: This is lcm(n, 2). If n is even, n is already a multiple of 2. If n is odd, n and 2 share no factor, so the answer is 2n.
steps: Check whether n is even
Even: return n
Odd: return 2n

codeNotes.note: Even n is already its own answer

pitfalls: n itself counts as a multiple of n; do not start at 2n.

say.intro: Smallest Even Multiple. Given a positive number n, return the smallest positive number that's a multiple of both two and n. For seven, the multiples are seven, fourteen, twenty one, and so on. Seven is odd. So the first even one, fourteen, is the answer.
say.brute: The brute force walks through the multiples of n. First n, then two n, then three n. It returns the first one that's even. To be honest, this isn't slow. It never needs more than two tries, because two n is always even. It just loops where a single observation would do.
say.insight: So what are we really asking for? The least common multiple of n and two. And two is prime, so there are only two cases. If n is already even, two divides it, and n itself is the answer. If n is odd, n and two share no common factor. So their least common multiple is just two times n.
say.anim: We start with n equal to seven, checking if it divides evenly by two. Since seven is odd, the code skips ahead to return n times two instead. The function returns fourteen, the smallest even multiple of seven.
say.code: The answer is the least common multiple of n and two. The code is a single decision. If n modulo two is zero, then even n is already its own answer, so return n. Otherwise n is odd, and the least common multiple is two n. So return n times two. No loop, no extra memory.
say.outro: Constant time and space. The lesson? Spot the least common multiple, and when one side is two, a parity check is all you need.

smallest-even-multiple.title: Smallest Even Multiple
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container that holds the method for this problem.
This method takes a positive integer n and returns the smallest positive number that both 2 and n divide evenly.
We check whether n leaves a remainder of zero when divided by two, meaning n is even.
If n is even, it is already a multiple of two, so n itself is the answer.
Otherwise n is odd and shares no factor with two, so the smallest common multiple is n times two.

smallest-missing-integer-greater-than-se.hook: Sum the run at the start, then count upward until you hit a number that is not there.
smallest-missing-integer-greater-than-se.ask: Find the longest prefix where each element is one more than the previous, and take its sum. Return the smallest integer at least that sum which does not appear anywhere in the array.
smallest-missing-integer-greater-than-se.exampleWhy: Prefix 3, 4, 5 sums to 12. The array contains 12, 13 and 14, so 15 is the first missing.

brute.idea: Compute the prefix sum the same way, then for each candidate from the sum upward, scan the whole array to see if it is present.
steps: Sum the sequential prefix
Scan the array for the candidate
Present? add one and rescan
Absent? return it
brute.whySlow: Each membership check scans all n elements, and up to n candidates may be present.

optimal.insight: The prefix sum is one pass. The repeated question 'is x in the array?' is a hash set lookup, so each check costs O(1).
steps: Add elements while each is previous + 1
Put every number into a set
While total is in the set, add one
Return total

codeNotes.match: while i < len(nums) and nums[i] == nums[i - 1] + 1:

pitfalls: Search the whole array, not just the prefix, for missing values.
The prefix stops at the first break, even if a later run is longer.

say.intro: Smallest Missing Integer Greater Than Sequential Prefix Sum. First, find the longest starting run where each number is one more than the last, and add it up. Then return the smallest integer at least that sum that's missing from the array. Three, four, five sum to twelve. Twelve, thirteen, fourteen are present. So the answer is fifteen.
say.brute: The brute force computes the prefix sum the same way. Then, for each candidate from the sum upward, it scans the whole array. Is it there? Try the next integer and scan again. Each scan is linear, and many candidates can be taken. So the worst case is n squared.
say.insight: Here's the thing. There are really two separate jobs. The prefix sum is one pass that stops at the first break. And the repeated question, is this number in the array? That's exactly what a hash set answers in constant time. So build the set once, then count upward cheaply.
say.anim: We start with total set to nums of zero, which is three. We check if each next number continues the sequential run, adding it to total. Four and five extend the prefix, so total grows to seven then twelve. At index three, one breaks the sequence, so the prefix sum stops at twelve. We build a set of all numbers to quickly check membership later. Twelve, thirteen, and fourteen are all already in the set, so total keeps increasing. Fifteen is not in the set, so the search stops there. The function returns fifteen, the smallest missing integer beyond the prefix sum.
say.code: Total starts with the first element. While the prefix stays sequential, with each next element one more, add it to the running prefix sum. Then put all the numbers into a set, for constant time membership checks. Is total taken? Then try the next integer. The first value not in the set is our answer.
say.outro: Linear time. The takeaway? A hash set turns repeated membership checks into constant time lookups.

smallest-missing-integer-greater-than-se.title: Smallest Missing Integer Greater Than Sequential Prefix Sum
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container the problem expects for our method.
The method missingInteger takes the list nums and returns a single integer, the smallest missing value at least the prefix sum.
We start total as the first element, since a prefix of length one is always sequential.
We set i to one, pointing at the second element, where we begin checking the sequential pattern.
We keep looping while i is in range and the current element is exactly one more than the previous one.
Each element that extends the sequential run gets added into our running total.
We advance i to look at the next element in the array.
We build a hash set from nums so each membership check later costs constant time.
While total appears in the set, it is not missing, so we must keep searching upward.
We bump total up by one to test the next candidate integer.
Once total is not in the set, it is the smallest missing integer at least the prefix sum, so we return it.

smallest-palindromic-rearrangement-i.hook: A palindrome is decided by its left half. Make that half as small as possible.
smallest-palindromic-rearrangement-i.ask: Given a string that is already a palindrome, rearrange its letters into the lexicographically smallest palindrome possible and return it.
smallest-palindromic-rearrangement-i.exampleWhy: Pairs are a and c, odd one out is b. Smallest left half is ac, so the palindrome is acbca.

brute.idea: Generate every permutation of the letters, keep those that read the same backwards, and return the smallest.
steps: Generate every permutation
Keep the palindromes
Return the smallest one
brute.whySlow: Ten letters already give 3.6 million permutations; real inputs have 100,000 letters.

optimal.insight: The left half fixes the whole palindrome. Each letter contributes half its count to that half, and sorting the half alphabetically makes it smallest.
steps: Count every letter
Letters in order: add count // 2 copies to the half
The odd-count letter goes in the middle
Answer = half + middle + reversed half

codeNotes.note: Half the copies on the left
At most one odd letter: the center

pitfalls: Sorting s[:n//2] also works in O(n log n); counting is linear.
The middle letter is fixed by parity, not chosen.

say.intro: Smallest Palindromic Rearrangement one. We get a string that's already a palindrome. We rearrange its letters into the smallest palindrome in dictionary order. C a b a c has two a's, two c's and one b. The smallest arrangement is a c b c a.
say.brute: The brute force generates every permutation of the letters. It keeps the ones that read the same both ways, and returns the smallest. Clearly correct. So what's the catch? The number of permutations is factorial. Ten letters already give over three million. And the input can have a hundred thousand.
say.insight: Here's the key. A palindrome is completely decided by its left half. The right half is just the mirror. Each letter puts half its copies on the left. If one letter has an odd count, it has to sit in the middle. So to make the whole string smallest, the left half must be smallest. That means alphabetical order.
say.anim: We start with the string cabac and count each letter's occurrences. Counts are c two, a two, b one, so we prepare to build half the palindrome. Sorted letters come first, so a gets half its count, one a added. Next is b, which appears once, contributing nothing to half but becoming the middle. Then c, with count two, adds one c to the half list. Joining the half list gives us ac, the smallest left half. We combine left, middle b, and reversed left to form the full palindrome. The final smallest palindromic rearrangement is acbca.
say.code: First, we count the letter frequencies. Then we walk through letters in alphabetical order, so the smallest letters go first. Each letter puts half its copies on the left. At most one letter has an odd count, and that one becomes the center. Finally, mirror the half: return the half, the middle, and the half reversed.
say.outro: Linear time. The pattern is greedy: put the smallest letters as early as possible, using counting instead of sorting.

smallest-palindromic-rearrangement-i.title: Smallest Palindromic Rearrangement I
lineNotes: We define the solution class that holds the method for this problem.
The method takes the palindrome string s and returns the smallest palindrome we can build from its letters.
We count how many times each letter appears in s using a counter.
We start an empty list that will collect the pieces of the left half.
We start the middle character as an empty string, since an even length palindrome has no middle.
We loop over the distinct letters in alphabetical order so the left half comes out sorted and smallest.
For each letter we add half of its count copies to the half list, since the other half goes on the right.
If a letter has an odd count, one copy is left over after halving.
That leftover letter becomes the middle character, and only one letter can ever have an odd count.
We join the collected pieces into a single string for the left half.
We return the left half, then the middle, then the reversed left half, which forms the smallest palindrome.

smallest-palindromic-rearrangement-ii.hook: Find the k-th palindrome without listing them: count how many start with each letter.
smallest-palindromic-rearrangement-ii.ask: Given a palindromic string and k, return the k-th smallest distinct palindrome that uses exactly the same letters, in dictionary order. If fewer than k exist, return an empty string.
smallest-palindromic-rearrangement-ii.exampleWhy: Left halves are the 6 arrangements of abc. In order: abc, acb, bac, bca... The 4th is bca.

brute.idea: List every distinct arrangement of the left half, sort them, and pick the k-th, then mirror it.
steps: Build the multiset for the left half
Generate all distinct permutations
Sort them, take the k-th
Mirror around the middle letter
brute.whySlow: The half can have 5,000 letters: factorially many arrangements, far beyond memory or time.

optimal.insight: Build the half one letter at a time. For each candidate letter, count arrangements of the rest with a multinomial. If k exceeds that count, skip the whole block.
steps: Halve every count; odd letter is the middle
Total arrangements < k? return empty
At each position, try letters in order
Block size = multinomial of remaining counts
k > block? subtract and try next letter

codeNotes.match: half = {c: count[c] // 2 for c in sorted(count)}

codeNotes.note: Cap: we only compare against k
The k-th starts with this letter

pitfalls: Count distinct strings: use multinomials, not plain factorials.
Cap the counts at k, or the numbers get thousands of digits.

say.intro: Smallest Palindromic Rearrangement two. Given a palindrome and k, return the k-th smallest distinct palindrome with the same letters. Or an empty string if there aren't enough. For a b c c b a, the left half is any arrangement of a, b, c. The fourth one is b c a, giving b c a a c b.
say.brute: The brute force lists every distinct arrangement of the left half. Sort the list, take the k-th, and mirror it. Sounds fine, right? But the number of arrangements grows factorially with the half length. And the half can be five thousand letters. We can never actually list them.
say.insight: So here's the trick. Count instead of listing. All arrangements starting with a come first. Then all starting with b, and so on. How many start with a given letter? That's a multinomial count of the remaining letters. If k is bigger than that block, skip the whole block by subtracting it from k. Otherwise, fix that letter, and move on.
say.anim: We start with the string abccba and want the fourth smallest palindrome rearrangement. Letter counts split evenly, giving half counts of one each for a, b, and c, with no middle letter. We compute total arrangements of this half using a multinomial count, which comes to six. Building position zero, we try letter a first, but only two arrangements start with a, too few for k equals four. We subtract those two, leaving k equals two, and try letter b, which yields two valid arrangements, so b is chosen. At position one, letter a only allows one arrangement, less than k equals two, so we skip to letter c. Letter c gives exactly one arrangement, matching k, so c is appended, leaving only a for the final slot. The last letter must be a, giving left half bca, so the final palindrome is bcaacb.
say.code: We collect the left half letters, in alphabetical order, and note the middle. The counting helper builds the multinomial from binomials. And here's the cap. We only compare against k, so we stop once we reach it, keeping numbers small. At each position, try letters in order. If the count is at least k, the k-th starts with this letter. Otherwise, skip the whole block.
say.outro: The pattern is combinatorics. Rank by counting whole blocks, never by listing them.

smallest-palindromic-rearrangement-ii.title: Smallest Palindromic Rearrangement II
lineNotes: We define the Solution class that holds the method for this problem.
The method takes the palindrome string s and the rank k, and returns the k-th smallest palindrome.
We count how many times each letter appears in the string.
For each letter in sorted order, we store how many copies belong in one half, which is its count divided by two.
The middle character is the letter with an odd count, or empty if every count is even.
We define a helper that counts arrangements of the remaining half letters, capped at k.
We start the running product of arrangements at one.
We loop over each letter in the half dictionary to apply the multinomial formula.
We multiply by the ways to choose positions for this letter among the remaining total slots.
We reduce the remaining slots by the number of copies of this letter just placed.
If the product already reaches k, we can stop early since we only need to compare against k.
We return k as a cap, which avoids huge numbers and still shows there are enough arrangements.
After all letters, we return the exact number of arrangements.
We compute m, the total length of the half string we must build.
If the total number of half arrangements is less than k, the answer does not exist.
So we return an empty string in that case.
We start with an empty list that will hold the letters of the left half.
We fill the half one position at a time, from left to right.
At each position we try candidate letters in dictionary order.
If a letter has no copies left, it cannot be used here.
So we skip to the next letter.
We tentatively place this letter by using up one of its copies.
We count the arrangements of the remaining positions with the letters that are left.
If that count is at least k, the k-th palindrome starts with this letter, so we keep it.
We append this letter to the left half.
Then we break out and move on to the next position.
Otherwise the whole block is too small, so we subtract its size from k to skip it.
We restore the letter's copy and try the next larger letter.
We join the chosen letters into the left half string.
The answer is the left half, then the middle character, then the left half reversed.

smallest-range-covering-elements-from-k-.hook: Hold one pointer per list. Always advance the smallest; the window can only improve that way.
smallest-range-covering-elements-from-k-.ask: Given k sorted lists, find the smallest range [a, b] that includes at least one number from every list. A range is smaller if it is narrower, or equally wide and starts earlier.
smallest-range-covering-elements-from-k-.exampleWhy: 5 from list one, 4 from list two and 7 from list three all fit inside 4 to 7, width 3.

brute.idea: Try every pair of values as the range ends, and check each list for a member inside it. Keep the narrowest valid range.
steps: Pick a start a from all values
Grow end b through the values
Every list has a member in range? record, stop
brute.whySlow: N values total, N² ranges, each checked against all N values: cubic in the total size.

optimal.insight: Keep exactly one current element per list in a min-heap and track the max. The range is min to max; only advancing the minimum can shrink it.
steps: Heap the first element of each list; track max
Pop the minimum; update best with max - min
That list is exhausted? stop
Push its next element, update max

codeNotes.match: heap = [(row[0], i, 0) for i, row in enumerate(nums)]
hi = max(row[0] for row in nums)

codeNotes.note: Strictly narrower: earlier start wins ties
A list ran out: no more ranges
New element may raise the max

pitfalls: Stop as soon as the minimum's list is exhausted; continuing drops that list.
Use strict < so equal widths keep the earlier start.

say.intro: Smallest Range Covering Elements from K Lists. We have several sorted lists. We need the narrowest range holding at least one number from every list. With one five eight, four twelve, and seven eight ten, the range four to seven works. Five, four and seven all sit inside it.
say.brute: The brute force tries every pair of values as the two ends of a range. For each one, check whether every list has a number inside. Keep the narrowest valid range. With N values in total, that's about N squared ranges. Each one checked against all values. So cubic time.
say.insight: Here's the idea. Hold one pointer in every list. The chosen numbers always form a valid range, from their minimum to their maximum. How do we make it narrower? Moving the maximum up never helps. So the only useful move is advancing the minimum. A min heap gives us the minimum instantly. And we track the maximum as we go.
say.anim: We build a heap with the first element from each list, tracking which list and index it came from. The current max, hi, is 7, so our starting best range is 1 to 7. We pop the smallest, 1 from list 0, and since its range isn't smaller, we advance that list to 5, updating hi to 7. Next we pop 4 from list 1, giving range 4 to 7, which beats our best, so best becomes 4 and 7. We advance list 1 to 12, growing hi to 12 and pushing it back into the heap. Popping 5 from list 0 gives range 5 to 12, worse than 4 to 7, so best stays the same. Continuing, popping 7 from list 2 gives range 7 to 12, still not better than our stored best. Eventually list 0 runs out of elements, so the loop stops and we return the best range, 4 to 7.
say.code: We keep one pointer per list, by heaping each list's first element with its position. We track the max of the current picks. Then we loop: pop the minimum. Is the range strictly narrower than the best? Save it, so an earlier start wins ties. If that list ran out, there are no more ranges, so return the best. Otherwise push its next element, which may raise the max.
say.outro: N log k time. The pattern is a k-way merge with a heap, always advancing the smallest pointer.

smallest-range-covering-elements-from-k-.title: Smallest Range Covering Elements from K Lists
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container the problem expects for our method.
The method smallestRange takes the list of sorted lists and returns the best range as a two-number list.
We build a heap holding the first element of every list, each paired with its list index and position zero.
We turn that list into a min-heap so the smallest current element is always available at the top.
We compute hi, the largest of the first elements, since that is the current maximum across all lists.
We initialize best as the range from the heap's smallest value up to hi, which already covers every list.
We loop forever, because the loop ends by returning once some list runs out of elements.
We pop the smallest element, getting its value lo, its list index i, and its position j in that list.
If the current range from lo to hi is narrower than best, it is a better answer.
In that case we record the new range of lo and hi as our best.
If the popped element was the last one in its list, we cannot advance that list, so no further range can cover every list.
So we return best, since any smaller range would need to advance past the end of that list.
Otherwise we fetch the next element from the same list, which replaces the minimum we just removed.
We update hi to the larger of the old hi and the new element, keeping the maximum current.
We push the new element with its list index and position into the heap, so every list again has exactly one representative.

smallest-subsequence-of-distinct-charact.hook: Keep letters on a stack, and pop any bigger letter that will show up again later.
smallest-subsequence-of-distinct-charact.ask: Given a string, return the lexicographically smallest subsequence that contains every distinct character of the string exactly once.
smallest-subsequence-of-distinct-charact.exampleWhy: Distinct letters are a, b, c, d. Choosing a at index 2, c at 3, d at 4 and b at 6 spells acdb.

brute.idea: Try every set of positions of the right size, keep those using each distinct letter once, and return the smallest string.
steps: Count the distinct letters d
Try every d-position combination
All distinct? compare with best
brute.whySlow: Combinations of positions grow exponentially; a 1,000-letter string is hopeless.

optimal.insight: Build the answer greedily on a stack. A bigger letter on top can be removed if it appears again later, because we can take it from there instead.
steps: Record each letter's last index
Skip letters already on the stack
Pop larger tops that appear later
Push the current letter

codeNotes.match: last = {c: i for i, c in enumerate(s)}
while stack and c < stack[-1] and last[stack[-1]] > i:

pitfalls: Skip letters already in the stack, or you will pop and duplicate wrongly.
Only pop when the top appears again later, not merely when larger.

say.intro: Smallest Subsequence of Distinct Characters. From a string, pick a subsequence that uses every distinct letter exactly once. Make it as small as possible in dictionary order. From c b a c d c b c, the best choice spells a c d b.
say.brute: The brute force tries every choice of positions. With d distinct letters, it tries every set of d positions. It keeps the ones where all letters differ, and compares them to find the smallest. So what's the catch? The number of position sets grows exponentially. A thousand letter string is hopeless.
say.insight: Let's build the answer left to right, on a stack. When a smaller letter arrives and the top is bigger, we'd love to remove that top. But is that safe? Only if the top letter shows up again later. Then we can pick it up there instead. So we pop while that holds. Then we push the new letter.
say.anim: First we record the last index of each character: c at 7, b at 6, a at 2, d at 4. We scan the string, pushing c then b onto the stack as new letters appear. At b, since c is bigger and reappears later, we pop c off the stack. At a, b also reappears later and is bigger, so we pop it too, leaving just a. We keep pushing letters a, c, and d since each is smaller or won't repeat again. The second c is already used, so we simply skip it and continue. We push b again, giving the stack a, c, d, b, then skip the final repeated c. Joining the stack gives the final smallest distinct subsequence, acdb.
say.code: First, we record the last place each letter appears. We keep a stack and a used set. If a letter is already placed optimally, skip it. Otherwise, check the top. If it's bigger and reappears later, drop it, and unmark it so we can reuse it later. Then place the current letter and mark it used. Finally, join the stack.
say.outro: Linear time. The pattern is a monotonic stack. Greedily pop bigger letters when they can be replaced later.

smallest-subsequence-of-distinct-charact.title: Smallest Subsequence of Distinct Characters
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container the problem expects for our method.
The method smallestSubsequence takes the string s and will return the smallest subsequence containing each distinct character once.
We build a dictionary last that maps each character to the index of its final appearance in s.
We start with an empty stack for the answer and an empty set used to track characters already on the stack.
We loop through the string, getting each index i and character c in order.
If c is already on the stack, its place is settled, so we handle it by skipping.
We continue to the next character without changing the stack, since each letter may appear only once.
While the top of the stack is bigger than c and appears again later, removing it can make the result smaller.
We pop that bigger letter and also remove it from used, since we will add it back at its later appearance.
Now that the stack is in the best order for c, we push c onto the stack.
We mark c as used so any later copies of it get skipped.
Finally we join the stack characters into one string and return it as the smallest subsequence.

sort-characters-by-frequency.hook: Count every character, then drop each into a bucket labelled by its frequency.
sort-characters-by-frequency.ask: Given a string, rearrange its characters so that more frequent characters come first, with all copies of a character kept together. Return the result.
sort-characters-by-frequency.exampleWhy: a appears three times, n twice and b once, so the order is a's, then n's, then b.

brute.idea: Sort the characters with a key of minus their count, recounting the string for each comparison key.
steps: For each character, count it in s
Sort by count descending, then by character
Join the sorted characters
brute.whySlow: s.count(c) rescans the whole string for every character: 500,000 letters means 250 billion steps.

optimal.insight: Frequencies are between 1 and n. Count once, then bucket characters by frequency and read the buckets from high to low: no comparison sort needed.
steps: Count each character once
Put each character in bucket[frequency]
Walk buckets from n down to 1
Write each character frequency times

pitfalls: Upper and lower case are different characters: 'A' and 'a' count separately.
Sorting the Counter by count is O(k log k) and also fine to mention.

say.intro: Sort Characters By Frequency. Rearrange a string so the most frequent characters come first, with all copies of each character together. In banana, a appears three times, n twice, and b once. So the answer is three a's, two n's, then b.
say.brute: A quick approach sorts the characters by how often they appear. It calls count on the whole string to get each key. It reads nicely. But every count call rescans the string. That makes it n squared. Far too slow for half a million characters.
say.insight: So first, count each character just once, with a hash map. Now, here's the thing. A frequency is always between one and the string length. So instead of sorting, make a bucket for every possible frequency. Drop each character into its bucket. Then read the buckets from the highest frequency down. That's bucket sort. Linear time.
say.anim: We start with the string banana and count each character's frequency. Counter shows a appears three times, n twice, and b once; buckets are created to sort by frequency. We place each character into the bucket matching its frequency, no comparisons needed. Now buckets hold b at index one, n at two, and a at three. We scan frequencies from high to low, skipping empty buckets at six, five, and four. At frequency three, we append a three times, giving result aaa. At frequency two, we append n twice, extending result to aaa and nn. At frequency one, we append b once, finishing with aaannb as the final answer.
say.code: We start with one pass of counting. Frequencies range from one to n, so we make a bucket for each. Then we group characters by frequency, dropping each into its bucket. Next, walk the buckets from high to low, so the most frequent come first. For each character there, write all its copies together. Finally, join everything.
say.outro: Linear time. The takeaway? Count with a hash map, then bucket sort by frequency, no comparison sort needed.

sort-characters-by-frequency.title: Sort Characters By Frequency
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container the interview platform expects for our method.
The method frequencySort takes the string s and returns a new string with characters ordered by frequency.
We count how many times each character appears in s using a Counter, giving us frequencies in one pass.
We create one empty bucket for each possible frequency from zero up to the length of s.
We loop over each character and its frequency in the count dictionary.
We place each character into the bucket whose index equals its frequency.
We start an empty result list that will collect the repeated character chunks.
We walk frequencies from the length of s down to one, so the most frequent characters come first.
Within a bucket we go through characters in sorted order, which keeps the output deterministic for ties.
We repeat each character as many times as its frequency and append that block, keeping copies together.
Finally we join all the blocks into a single string and return it.

sorted-gcd-pair-queries.hook: Never compute a single pair. Count how many pairs have each GCD, from the top down.
sorted-gcd-pair-queries.ask: Take the GCD of every pair of numbers in the array and sort those values. For each query index, return the value at that position in the sorted list.
sorted-gcd-pair-queries.exampleWhy: Pair GCDs sorted are 1, 1, 1, 2, 2, 4. Positions 5, 3, 1, 0 give 4, 2, 1, 1.

brute.idea: Compute the GCD of every pair, sort the list, and answer each query by indexing into it.
steps: GCD of every pair i < j
Sort all pair GCDs
Look up each query index
brute.whySlow: 100,000 numbers give 5 billion pairs: too many to compute, let alone store and sort.

optimal.insight: Count pairs per GCD. C(cnt, 2) pairs are both divisible by d; subtract pairs whose GCD is a larger multiple of d. Prefix sums plus binary search answer queries.
steps: Count how many numbers equal each value
For d from max down: cnt = numbers divisible by d
exact[d] = C(cnt, 2) minus exact of multiples
Prefix sums of exact; binary search each query
optimal.time: O(M log M + Q log M)

codeNotes.note: Pairs whose GCD is a multiple of d
Remove pairs with a larger GCD
Pairs with GCD at most g

codeNotes.match: return [bisect_right(prefix, q) for q in queries]

pitfalls: Iterate d from large to small so multiples are already exact.
Use bisect_right: query q needs more than q pairs at or below g.

say.intro: Sorted GCD Pair Queries. Take the greatest common divisor of every pair. Sort those values. Then answer queries about what sits at a given position. For four, four, two, one, the sorted values are one, one, one, two, two, four. So positions five, three, one, zero give four, two, one, one.
say.brute: The brute force does exactly that. Compute the greatest common divisor of every pair, sort the list, and index into it for each query. So what's the catch? With a hundred thousand numbers, there are five billion pairs. Way too many to compute, store, or sort.
say.insight: Here's the trick. Count instead of listing. Say c numbers are divisible by d. Then c choose two pairs have a common divisor that's a multiple of d. Now subtract the pairs whose exact value is a larger multiple. Work from the largest d downward. Then we know how many pairs have each exact value. And prefix sums let binary search answer any position.
say.anim: We start with nums 4,4,2,1 and max value 4, building a frequency array. We count occurrences of each number, ending with freq showing two fours, one two, one one. Now we compute exact gcd counts for each d from 4 down to 1. For d equals 4, two numbers are divisible, giving one pair with exact gcd four. For d equals 3, no numbers are divisible, so exact stays zero. For d equals 2, three numbers qualify, minus the one already counted for four, leaving two. For d equals 1, all four numbers qualify, subtracting pairs from two, three, and four, leaving three. Prefix sums become 0,3,5,5,6, and binary search gives the final answers 4,2,1,1.
say.code: First, for each d, we count how many numbers d divides, by summing every d-th slot. Choose two of those gives the pairs whose value is a multiple of d. Then we remove pairs with a larger exact value. Prefix sums tell us how many pairs have value at most g. For each query, binary search for the first g covering index q.
say.outro: The pattern is number theory. Count pairs by divisor with inclusion and exclusion, then binary search the prefix sums.

sorted-gcd-pair-queries.title: Sorted GCD Pair Queries
lineNotes: We define the solution class that holds the method for this problem.
The method takes the numbers and the query indexes, and returns the sorted pair GCD value for each query.
We find the largest number in nums, since no GCD can exceed it and it sizes our tables.
We build a frequency array of size max plus one, starting with every count at zero.
We loop over each number in nums to count how often every value appears.
For each number x we add one to its slot in the frequency array.
We create an exact array to hold how many pairs have a GCD exactly equal to each value.
We go through candidate divisors d from the max down to one, so larger multiples are already computed.
We count how many numbers are divisible by d by summing frequencies at d, two d, three d, and so on.
Any two of those numbers share d as a divisor, so we count cnt choose two pairs and store it.
We loop over every proper multiple of d greater than d, since those GCDs were already finalized.
We subtract pairs whose GCD is exactly that larger multiple, leaving only pairs with GCD exactly d.
We build prefix sums of exact counts, so each entry says how many pairs have a GCD at most that value.
For each query we binary search with bisect right to find the first GCD whose cumulative count exceeds the query index.

special-array-i.hook: A one-pass parity check: every neighbor pair must mix one even and one odd.
special-array-i.ask: Given an array of numbers, return true if every two adjacent numbers have different parity, one even and one odd. Otherwise return false.
special-array-i.exampleWhy: Everything alternates until 7 and 9 at the end: both odd, so the array is not special.

brute.idea: Turn the array into a string of parity bits, then look for 00 or 11 anywhere in that string.
steps: Map each number to its parity bit
Join the bits into one string
Reject if 00 or 11 appears
brute.whySlow: Same linear time, but it builds a whole extra string and always scans everything, even after an early mismatch.

optimal.insight: Only neighbors matter. Compare each number's parity with the one before it and stop at the first match.
steps: Walk from index 1 to the end
Compare nums[i] % 2 with nums[i - 1] % 2
Equal parity: return False immediately
Loop finishes: return True

codeNotes.note: Every adjacent pair, left to right
Stop at the first bad pair

pitfalls: A single element has no pairs, so it is special: the loop never runs.
Compare parities, not the numbers themselves.

say.intro: Okay, Special Array One. An array is special when every pair of neighbors has different parity. One even, one odd, all the way along. Look at our example. Two and one, four and three, they alternate nicely. But the last pair is seven and nine. Both odd. So the answer is false.
say.brute: So what's a first idea? Turn the array into a string of parity bits. Zero for even, one for odd. Then the array is special if that string never has two equal bits in a row.
