And honestly, it works. It's even linear. But here's the catch. We build a whole extra string, and we always scan everything. Even when the very first pair already fails.
say.insight: Here's the thing. The rule only talks about neighbors. So why look at more than two numbers at once? We just walk the array once. At each step, compare this number's parity with the one right before it. The moment two neighbors match, we're done. We answer false and skip the rest.
say.anim: We start checking the array two at a time, comparing each number's parity to its neighbor. At index one, two and one have different parities, so we keep going. At index two, one and four also alternate between odd and even fine. We continue through indices three, four, and five, each pair still alternating correctly. At index six, eight and seven keep alternating, so the loop continues onward. At index eight, seven and nine are both odd, breaking the alternating pattern. Since two neighbors share the same parity, the function immediately returns false.
say.code: Now the code. It's a single loop, starting at index one, so every adjacent pair gets checked, left to right. Inside, we compare this number mod two with the previous number mod two. If they're equal, that pair breaks the rule. So we stop and return false right away. And if the loop finishes? Every pair alternated, so we return true. Notice a one element array skips the loop entirely. It's special by default.
say.outro: Linear time, constant space. It's arrays and hashing at its simplest. One pass, each element checked against its neighbor.

special-array-i.title: Special Array I
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container LeetCode expects for the method that solves this problem.
This method takes the list of numbers and returns a boolean saying whether the array is special.
We loop an index from one up to the end, so each number can be compared with its left neighbor.
If the current number and the previous one leave the same remainder when divided by two, they share parity.
Finding a neighboring pair with the same parity means the array is not special, so we return false immediately.
If the loop finishes without finding any matching pair, every neighbor alternates parity, so we return true.

spiral-matrix-ii.hook: Fill a square in a spiral by peeling off one ring of walls at a time.
spiral-matrix-ii.ask: Given n, build an n by n grid and write the numbers 1 up to n squared into it, moving clockwise in a spiral from the top-left corner inward.
spiral-matrix-ii.exampleWhy: 1 to 4 go across the top, 5 to 7 down the right, then left and up, then the inner ring.

brute.idea: Simulate a walker: write a number, try to step forward, and turn right whenever the next cell is off-grid or already filled.
steps: Write the value at the current cell
Peek at the next cell in this direction
Blocked? turn clockwise
Step and repeat n² times
brute.whySlow: Same n² time; it just peeks and bounds-checks before every move, which is extra work and easy to get subtly wrong.

optimal.insight: Keep four walls: top, bottom, left, right. Fill one side completely, then move that wall inward. No peeking needed.
steps: Fill the top row left to right, then top moves down
Fill the right column downward, then right moves left
Fill the bottom row right to left, then bottom moves up
Fill the left column upward, then left moves right

codeNotes.match: top, bottom, left, right = 0, n - 1, 0, n - 1
codeNotes.note: Four walls around the unfilled region

pitfalls: Shrink each wall right after its side, or corners get written twice.
For general rectangles, guard the bottom and left passes; a square never needs it.

say.intro: Okay, Spiral Matrix Two. Given a number n, we build an n by n grid, and write one up to n squared in a clockwise spiral. Take n equals four. One to four run across the top. Five to seven go down the right side. Then we sweep left, climb up, and finish the inner ring with thirteen to sixteen.
say.brute: A natural first idea is a little walker. It writes a number, then peeks at the next cell. Is that cell off the grid, or already filled? Then it turns clockwise. And that's still n squared, which is optimal, since we must write n squared cells. So what's the catch? Every single move needs a peek and a bounds check. And the turning logic is easy to get wrong.
say.insight: Think about it this way. Instead of a walker, picture four walls. Top, bottom, left and right. Fill the whole top row, then push the top wall down. Fill the right column, then pull the right wall in. Same for the bottom and the left. Each side is just a plain loop. And the walls close in until they meet in the middle.
say.anim: We start with a four by four grid of zeros and four walls marking the boundary. Filling the top row left to right, values one through four get placed, then top moves down. Next we fill the right column top to bottom with five, six, seven, then right shifts inward. The bottom row fills right to left with eight, nine, ten, then bottom moves up. The left column fills bottom to top with eleven and twelve, then left shifts inward. With walls tightened, the inner top row fills thirteen and fourteen, then top and right advance. The remaining inner cells fill with fifteen, sixteen, and seventeen, completing the spiral. Walls cross so the loop ends, returning the final spiral matrix shown on screen.
say.code: Now the code. We set up four walls around the unfilled region. While they haven't crossed, we run four loops. First, the top row, left to right, then top moves down. Next, the right column, top to bottom, then right moves in. Then the bottom row, right to left. And finally the left column, bottom to top. A counter hands out each value. Then we return the grid. Every cell was written exactly once.
say.outro: n squared time, no extra space beyond the answer. The pattern is math and geometry. Simulate the shape with shrinking boundaries.

spiral-matrix-ii.title: Spiral Matrix II
lineNotes: We define a class named Solution, as the problem platform expects.
The generateMatrix method takes n and returns the filled n by n grid as a list of lists.
We create an n by n grid filled with zeros, using a fresh row for each line.
We set four walls: top and left at zero, bottom and right at the last index, n minus one.
We start the counter val at one, since that is the first number to place.
We keep spiraling while the top wall hasn't passed the bottom and the left wall hasn't passed the right.
We walk across the top row from the left wall to the right wall, inclusive.
We write the current value into the top row at that column.
We increase val so the next cell gets the next number.
The top row is done, so we move the top wall down by one.
We walk down the right column from the new top to the bottom wall.
We write the current value into the right column at that row.
We increase val after each placement.
The right column is finished, so we move the right wall left by one.
We walk the bottom row from right to left, going back down to the left wall.
We write the current value into the bottom row at that column.
We increase val again.
The bottom row is filled, so we move the bottom wall up by one.
We walk up the left column from the new bottom to the top wall.
We write the current value into the left column at that row.
We increase val to keep the sequence going.
The left column is done, so we move the left wall right by one, completing a ring.
Once the walls cross, every cell is filled, so we return the matrix.

step-by-step-directions-from-a-binary-tr.hook: Any tree path is: climb up to the common ancestor, then walk down.
step-by-step-directions-from-a-binary-tr.ask: In a binary tree with unique values, give the shortest route from the start node to the destination node as a string of moves: L for left child, R for right child, U for parent.
step-by-step-directions-from-a-binary-tr.exampleWhy: From 3 go up to 1, up to 5, right to 2, left to 6: U U R L.

brute.idea: Treat the tree as an undirected graph: record each node's parent, then breadth-first search from start, carrying the path string along.
steps: Map every child to its parent
BFS from the start node
Neighbors are left, right and parent
Return the path when we reach dest
brute.whySlow: Each queued node carries its own copy of the path string; on a deep tree that copying grows quadratically.

optimal.insight: Record the root-to-start and root-to-dest paths. Their shared prefix leads to the common ancestor; everything after it on start's side becomes U.
steps: DFS to find the root-to-start path as L/R moves
DFS to find the root-to-dest path
Drop the common prefix
Answer: one U per leftover start move, plus leftover dest moves

codeNotes.note: Skip the shared route from root
Climb up, then follow dest's path

pitfalls: Do not climb all the way to the root; strip the common prefix first.
Reuse one path list with append and pop, not new strings per call.

say.intro: Okay, Step By Step Directions From a Binary Tree Node to Another. We want the shortest route between two nodes, as moves. L for left, R for right, U for up to the parent. From three to six? Up to one, up to five, right to two, then left to six. So the answer is U U R L.
say.brute: A first idea is to treat the tree like a graph. Record every node's parent. Then run a breadth first search from the start. Each node's neighbors are its two children and its parent. And we carry the path string along. That does find the shortest route. But here's the problem. Every queued node holds its own copy of that string. On a deep tree, that's quadratic time and memory.
say.insight: Here's the thing. In a tree, the shortest path between two nodes always climbs to their lowest common ancestor, then walks down. So write down two routes from the root. One to the start, one to the destination. The part they share leads to that ancestor. Every leftover step on the start side becomes a U. And the destination's leftover steps get copied as they are.
say.anim: We search the tree for node three, building a path of left and right moves. Going left twice reaches node three, so the start path becomes L, L. Now we search for node six, again recording left or right at each step. Backtracking tries right turns when left paths dead end, exploring other branches. From root we go right then left, finding node six with path R, L. Comparing paths, to start is L, L and to dest is R, L, sharing no prefix. Since index zero already differs, the common ancestor is the root itself. We output two ups to leave start, then right and left to reach six, giving UURL.
say.code: Now the code. A helper called find does a depth first search. It pushes an L and tries the left side first. If that fails, it switches the move to R. If neither side has the target, it pops and backtracks. We call it twice, for start and destination. Then a pointer skips their shared route from the root. Finally, we climb up with one U per leftover start move, then follow the destination's path.
say.outro: Linear time and linear space. The pattern is trees. Root paths plus the lowest common ancestor turn any route into up, then down.

step-by-step-directions-from-a-binary-tr.title: Step-By-Step Directions From a Binary Tree Node to Another
lineNotes: We define the Solution class that holds our method for solving the problem.
The method getDirections takes the tree root, a start value, and a destination value, and returns the move string.
We define a helper called find that searches for a target and records the path of moves in a list.
If the current node is empty, this branch has no target, so we handle the dead end.
We return false because the target was not found down this empty branch.
If the current node holds the target value, we have arrived at the node we want.
We return true, leaving the path as the moves taken to reach this node.
Before exploring the left child, we append L to the path as a tentative move.
We recursively search the left subtree for the target, using the same shared path list.
If the left search succeeded, we return true and keep the L move in the path.
Left failed, so we overwrite the last move with R to try the right child instead.
We search the right subtree for the target with the path now ending in R.
If the right search succeeded, we return true and keep the R move in the path.
Neither side contained the target, so we remove the tentative move to backtrack.
We return false to tell the parent this subtree does not contain the target.
We create two empty lists to hold the root-to-start path and the root-to-destination path.
We call find to fill the first list with the moves from the root to the start value.
We call find again to fill the second list with the moves from the root to the destination.
We set the index i to zero to measure how long the shared prefix of both paths is.
We loop while both paths still have moves and their moves match, which means we are still above the common ancestor.
Each matching step advances i, moving the common ancestor point one level deeper.
We return one U for each remaining start move, followed by the remaining destination moves joined as a string.

stickers-to-spell-word.hook: Search over what is still left to spell, and remember every leftover you have solved.
stickers-to-spell-word.ask: Given sticker words you can use unlimited times, cut out letters to spell the target. Return the fewest stickers needed, or -1 if some target letter appears on no sticker.
stickers-to-spell-word.exampleWhy: Two with stickers give t, h, t, h; one example sticker gives e and a. Three stickers spell thehat.

brute.idea: Recursively try every sticker that removes at least one needed letter, and take the minimum over all choices, with no memory.
steps: Count the letters still needed
Try each sticker that helps
Recurse on what is left
Keep the smallest total
brute.whySlow: The same leftover multiset is reached through many different sticker orders and solved again each time: exponential blowup.

optimal.insight: The state is just the sorted leftover letters. Memoize it, and only try stickers containing the first leftover letter, since some sticker must cover it.
steps: State: sorted string of letters still needed
Only try stickers holding its first letter
Subtract that sticker's letters to get the next state
Memo stores the best answer per state

codeNotes.note: Nothing left to spell costs zero
Must cover the first letter: prune
Sorted leftover after using this sticker
One sticker plus best for the rest

pitfalls: Without the first-letter rule, the search tries useless orders of the same stickers.
Keep the leftover canonical by sorting, or equal states get different memo keys.

say.intro: Okay, Stickers to Spell Word. We have sticker words, as many copies as we like. We cut letters out of them to spell a target. And we want the fewest stickers. Say the target is the hat, no space. Two with stickers give us t, h, t, h. One example sticker gives us e and a. That's three stickers.
say.brute: So what's the obvious approach? Keep track of the letters still needed. Try every sticker that removes at least one of them. Then recurse on what's left, and keep the smallest total. It's correct. But notice something. The same leftover letters can be reached through many different sticker orders. And each time, we solve that leftover again from scratch. That blows up exponentially.
say.insight: Two observations fix this. First, all that matters is which letters are still needed. So write them as a sorted string, and memoize the answer for it. Second, the first leftover letter must be covered by some sticker eventually. So why branch on anything else? We only try stickers that contain it. That kills all the duplicate orderings.
say.anim: We build letter counters for each sticker, like with, example, and science. The target letters are sorted into aehhtt, and we start searching with memo empty. We need two h's, two t's, one a, one e, and try stickers covering the first letter a. Sticker with works, leaving hhtt to solve, so we recurse on that smaller leftover. From hhtt, using with again leaves just ht, shrinking the problem further. Ht needs one more with sticker to clear everything, costing one sticker total. So hhtt costs two stickers, and aehhtt costs three stickers overall, using example then with twice. The final answer is three stickers needed to spell thehat.
say.code: Now the code. We seed the memo with the empty string costing zero. Nothing left to spell costs nothing. In the search, if this leftover is already solved, we reuse it. Otherwise, we skip any sticker that misses the first needed letter. For the rest, we build the sorted leftover after using that sticker. Then it's one sticker plus the best for the rest. If the answer stays infinite, we return minus one.
say.outro: At most two to the target length states, each trying every sticker. The pattern is backtracking with memoization over leftover letters.

stickers-to-spell-word.title: Stickers to Spell Word
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, as required by the problem's submission format.
The minStickers method takes the list of sticker words and the target word, and returns the fewest stickers needed.
We turn each sticker into a letter count table so we can quickly see how many of each letter it offers.
The memo starts with the empty string mapped to zero, since no stickers are needed when nothing remains.
We define a recursive helper dfs that takes rem, the sorted string of letters still needed.
If we have already solved this leftover string, we take the shortcut and skip recomputing.
We return the stored answer for that leftover string right away.
We count how many of each letter the remaining string still needs.
We start the best answer at infinity so any real solution will beat it.
We try each sticker's letter counts as the next sticker to use.
If the sticker lacks the first needed letter, it cannot cover it, so we skip it.
That skip prevents trying useless stickers and avoids duplicate orderings, since some sticker must cover that first letter.
We build the new leftover string by subtracting this sticker's letters from the need, keeping it sorted so equal states match.
We recurse on the leftover, add one for this sticker, and keep the smaller total.
We save the best result for this leftover string in the memo.
We return that best result to the caller.
We start the search from the target's letters sorted into a canonical string.
If the answer is still infinity the target is impossible, so we return negative one, otherwise the count.

stone-game-ii.hook: In a zero-sum game, your best haul is everything left minus your opponent's best haul.
stone-game-ii.ask: Alice and Bob alternately take the first X remaining piles, where X is between 1 and 2M, then M becomes max(M, X). M starts at 1. With optimal play, how many stones does Alice get?
stone-game-ii.exampleWhy: Alice takes 2, Bob takes 7 and 9, Alice takes both 4s: 2 + 4 + 4 = 10.

brute.idea: Plain minimax recursion: from position i with value M, try every legal X and keep the move that leaves the opponent the least.
steps: Sum all stones still on the table
Try every X from 1 to 2M
Subtract the opponent's best from that sum
Keep the maximum
brute.whySlow: The same (position, M) pair is reached by many move sequences and recomputed every time; it explodes beyond about 30 piles.

optimal.insight: Whoever moves from i gets suffix[i] minus what the opponent gets next. State (i, M) is small, so fill a table from the back.
steps: suffix[i] = stones from pile i to the end
If 2M reaches the end, take everything
Else try each X, leaving the opponent dp[i+X][max(M,X)]
dp[i][M] = suffix[i] minus the smallest opponent result

codeNotes.note: All stones still on the table

codeNotes.match: best = max(best, suffix[i] - dp[i + x][max(m, x)])

pitfalls: Track your own stones as total minus opponent's, not by alternating max and min.
M is part of the state; memoizing on i alone is wrong.

say.intro: Okay, Stone Game Two. Piles sit in a row. On each turn, a player takes the first X piles, where X is between one and two times M. Then M grows to at least X. M starts at one. With two, seven, nine, four, four, Alice takes two. Bob takes seven and nine. Alice takes both fours. Ten stones.
say.brute: The first idea is pure minimax. From a position and a value of M, try every legal number of piles. The opponent then plays perfectly. So our haul is everything left, minus their best haul. Keep the maximum. That's correct. So what's the catch? The same position and M get reached through many different move orders. And we recompute them every time.
say.insight: Now, notice the state is just two numbers. Where the remaining piles start, and the current M. Both are at most n. And here's the trick. Every stone ends up with someone. So our best haul is the stones left, minus the opponent's best haul from wherever we leave them. That means we can fill a table from the last pile backward.
say.anim: We start with piles two, seven, nine, four, four, and compute suffix sums from the back. Suffix now holds total stones remaining from each index, like twenty six from the start. Now we fill the table from the last pile backward, handling base cases where remaining piles fit in one turn. At index two, trying each possible move size x, we find taking two piles scores best, thirteen. Moving to index one, best is sixteen for one pile, growing as m lets us take more. At the very start, i is zero and m is one, so we try taking one, two, or three piles. Taking three piles gives best value twenty two, beating smaller moves so far. The final answer stored at dp zero one is ten, the maximum stones the first player secures.
say.code: Now the code. First, suffix sums, so we know the stones still on the table from any pile. Then, for each start from the back and each M, we ask: can we grab everything? If so, do it. Otherwise, try every X. Score it as the suffix sum minus the opponent's best reply at the new position, with M updated. The answer is Alice's entry, at pile zero with M equal to one.
say.outro: Cubic time, quadratic space. Two dimensional dynamic programming on a game. My score is what's left, minus your best.

stone-game-ii.title: Stone Game II
lineNotes: We define the Solution class that holds the method for solving Stone Game II.
The method takes the list of piles and returns the most stones Alice can collect.
We store the number of piles in n for use in loop bounds and table sizes.
We create a suffix array of size n plus one, starting at zero, to hold sums of remaining piles.
We loop index i backward from the last pile to the first so each suffix builds on a later one.
Each suffix at i equals the suffix at the next index plus the pile at i, giving the total stones from i onward.
We build a table dp where dp at i and m is the best stones the mover gets from pile i with limit m.
We fill the table from the back, looping i from the last pile down to the start, since states depend on later piles.
For each i we try every value of m from one up to n.
If the mover can take at least all remaining piles, meaning i plus two times m reaches n, the choice is simple.
In that case the mover grabs everything left, so dp at i and m equals the suffix at i.
We continue to skip the search loop because this state is already settled.
We start best at zero to track the maximum stones the mover can secure from this state.
We try every allowed number of piles x, from one up to two times m.
After taking x piles, the opponent gets dp at i plus x with the updated limit, so we subtract that from the suffix and keep the maximum.
We store the best result in dp at i and m for this state.
The answer is dp at zero with m equal to one, which is Alice's best total from the start.

stone-game-iii.hook: Track the score difference, not two scores, and the game collapses into a simple array.
stone-game-iii.ask: Players alternately take 1, 2 or 3 stones from the front of the row, scoring their values, which can be negative. With optimal play, say whether Alice wins, Bob wins, or it is a tie.
stone-game-iii.exampleWhy: With best play from both sides, Alice finishes 3 points ahead, so Alice wins.

brute.idea: Recursively let the current player try taking 1, 2 or 3 stones and maximize their lead over the opponent's best lead.
steps: At index i, try taking 1, 2 or 3
Gain their sum minus opponent's best lead
Keep the maximum lead
Sign of the lead picks the winner
brute.whySlow: Each index is re-solved for every path that reaches it; 50,000 stones means astronomically many calls.

optimal.insight: dp[i] is the best lead the player to move can get from stone i. It only depends on dp[i+1], dp[i+2], dp[i+3].
steps: dp[n] = 0: no stones, no lead
Go from the back to the front
dp[i] = max over 1 to 3 stones of their sum minus dp[next]
dp[0] > 0 Alice, < 0 Bob, else Tie

codeNotes.note: Leads can be negative: start at minus infinity
My stones minus opponent's best lead
Alice moves first: her lead decides

pitfalls: Initialize best to minus infinity, not 0: every move may lose points.
Taking fewer stones is sometimes better; always try all three.

say.intro: Okay, Stone Game Three. Stones lie in a row, and values can be negative. Players take one, two or three stones from the front. Higher total wins. Our row is three, minus two, five, one, minus four, two. With perfect play, Alice ends three points ahead. So the answer is Alice.
say.brute: The first idea is plain recursion. The player to move tries taking one, two or three stones. Then the opponent tries to maximize their own lead from what's left. So our lead is what we took, minus their best lead. That's correct. But here's the problem. Each position gets recomputed along every path that reaches it. That's exponential.
say.insight: Here's the thing. We don't need two scores. Just track one number: the lead of whoever is about to move. Why does that work? Because from position i, that lead only depends on the leads at i plus one, two and three. So one array, filled from the back, solves every position exactly once.
say.anim: We start with the stone values and an empty dp array of zeros. At index five, the only move takes stone two, giving dp of five a best of two. At index four, trying both stones gives a best lead of negative two for dp four. At index three, exploring taking one, two, or three stones yields a best of three. At index two, taking two stones nets eight, the best option found so far. At index one, after comparing options, dp one settles at six. At index zero, comparing all choices gives a final best lead of three. Since dp zero is positive at three, the game result is Alice.
say.code: Now the code. We make an array of size n plus one. The last entry is zero: an empty row, no lead. Each cell starts at minus infinity, because leads can be negative. Going backward, we try one, two or three stones. Each choice scores my stones minus the opponent's best lead after it. Finally, Alice moves first, so her lead decides. Positive means Alice, negative means Bob, zero is a tie.
say.outro: Linear time. One dimensional dynamic programming. In a zero sum game, store the mover's lead and subtract the opponent's.

stone-game-iii.title: Stone Game III
lineNotes: This starts the Solution class that holds our method for solving the problem.
The method takes the list of stone values and returns a string naming the winner.
We store n as the number of stones in the row.
We build a dp list of n plus one zeros, where the last entry means no stones left, so no lead.
We loop i backward from the last stone to the first, since each answer depends on later positions.
We set best to negative infinity so any real option will replace it when we take the maximum.
We set take to zero, which will track the running sum of stones grabbed this turn.
We try taking one, two, or three stones starting at i, never going past the end of the row.
We add the current stone's value to take, building the total for taking stones up to k.
We compare options by our take minus the opponent's best lead from the next position, keeping the maximum.
We save best as dp at i, the best lead for the player to move from stone i.
If dp at zero is positive, the first player, Alice, ends with more points.
So we return Alice in that case.
If dp at zero is negative, Alice trails even with optimal play, so Bob wins.
So we return Bob in that case.
Otherwise the lead is exactly zero, so the game is a tie.

stone-game-iv.hook: A position is winning if some move hands your opponent a losing one.
stone-game-iv.ask: Starting with n stones, players alternately remove any positive square number of stones. A player who cannot move loses. Return true if Alice, moving first, wins with perfect play.
stone-game-iv.exampleWhy: From 7 you can leave 6 or 3, and both are winning for Bob, so Alice loses.

brute.idea: Recursively: the current player wins if removing some square leaves the opponent in a losing position.
steps: Try every square k² up to the pile
Recurse on the pile minus k²
Any losing reply means we win
brute.whySlow: Without memory, the same pile size is re-solved along every route to it; that is exponential even for n around 40.

optimal.insight: Solve every pile size from 0 up to n once. dp[i] is true if some square leads to a dp value that is false.
steps: dp[0] = False: no move, you lose
For each i, try squares k² ≤ i
If dp[i - k²] is False, dp[i] = True
Return dp[n]

codeNotes.note: Leave the opponent a losing pile

pitfalls: A position is winning if ANY move wins; it is losing only if ALL moves lose.

say.intro: Okay, Stone Game Four. There are n stones. Players take turns removing a square number of them. One, four, nine, and so on. If you can't move, you lose. With seven stones, Alice can remove one or four. That leaves six or three. Both turn out to be wins for Bob. So the answer is false.
say.brute: The first idea is to ask, recursively, can I win from here? Try every square that fits. If any move leaves the opponent unable to win, we win. That's the right logic. So what's wrong? There's no memory. The same pile size gets solved again on every route to it. And the number of calls grows exponentially.
say.insight: Here's the key. Whether a pile is winning never depends on who's playing or how we got there. So solve every pile size from zero up to n, once each. Zero is losing, since you can't move. And a pile is winning if at least one square move lands on a losing pile.
say.anim: We start with n equals seven, and dp initialized to all false for piles zero through seven. For pile one, subtracting one squared gives zero, which is false, so dp of one becomes true. For pile two, no square leaves a false position, so dp of two stays false. For pile three, subtracting one leaves dp of two false, so dp of three becomes true. For pile four, subtracting two squared leaves zero, false, so dp of four becomes true. For pile five, every square tried leaves a true position, so dp of five stays false. For pile six, subtracting one leaves dp of five false, making dp of six true. Finally for pile seven, every square move leads to a true position, so dp of seven is false, meaning the first player loses.
say.code: Now the code. A boolean array of size n plus one, all false. That covers zero, where the stuck player loses. For each pile size, we try every square we may remove. If removing it leaves the opponent a losing pile, this pile wins. And one winning move is enough, so we break early. At the end, Alice faces the full pile, so we return the entry for n.
say.outro: n times root n time, linear space. One dimensional dynamic programming on game states. Win if any move leaves a loss.

stone-game-iv.title: Stone Game IV
lineNotes: We define a solution class that holds the method for solving the stone game problem.
The method takes the starting number of stones n and returns whether Alice wins with perfect play.
We create a table dp of size n plus one, starting all false, so zero stones is a losing position.
We loop over every pile size i from one up to n, solving smaller piles before larger ones.
For each pile size we start trying square moves with k equal to one.
We keep trying squares as long as k times k does not exceed the current pile size i.
If removing k squared stones leaves the opponent in a losing position, that move is good for us.
So we mark dp at i as true, meaning the player to move wins with this pile.
We break immediately because one winning move is enough to settle this pile size.
If that square did not work, we increase k to try the next larger square.
Finally we return dp at n, which tells whether Alice wins when starting with n stones.

strong-password-checker.hook: Deletions are forced when too long, so spend them where they also break repeating runs.
strong-password-checker.ask: A strong password has 6 to 20 characters, a lowercase letter, an uppercase letter, a digit, and no three identical characters in a row. Return the fewest inserts, deletes or replacements to make it strong.
strong-password-checker.exampleWhy: 27 characters forces 7 deletions; spent wisely, they cut the needed replacements from 8 to 4: 7 + 4 = 11.

brute.idea: Same rules, but simulate deletions one at a time: each time, rescan all runs and shorten the one where a deletion saves the most.
steps: Count missing character types
Split the password into runs
Repeat: delete from the run with smallest length mod 3
Add deletions to max(replacements, missing)
brute.whySlow: It rescans every run for each single deletion: quadratic. Fine for n ≤ 50, but the counting version is linear.

optimal.insight: A run of length L needs L // 3 replacements. One deletion saves a replacement on runs with L % 3 = 0, two on L % 3 = 1, three otherwise.
steps: Count missing types and replacements per run
Too short: max(6 - n, missing)
Normal length: max(replacements, missing)
Too long: spend deletions on mod-0 runs, then mod-1, then in threes
Answer: deletions + max(replacements left, missing)

codeNotes.note: How many character types are absent
Bucket runs by how cheaply deletions help
Cheapest: one delete saves one replace
Remaining deletions save one per three

pitfalls: Replacements can double as fixes for missing types, so take a max, not a sum.
Spend deletions on runs with length mod 3 = 0 first.

say.intro: Okay, Strong Password Checker. A strong password has six to twenty characters. It needs a lowercase letter, an uppercase letter, and a digit. And never three identical characters in a row. We want the fewest edits. Our example has twenty seven characters with long runs. Seven deletions are forced. Spent wisely, they cut replacements from eight to four. Eleven total.
say.brute: A slower version follows the same rules, but simulates deletions one at a time. Each time, it rescans every run, and deletes from the run where one deletion helps most. That's quadratic in the length. Honestly, with at most fifty characters, it's fine in practice. But the counting version does the same thing in one pass.
say.insight: Here's the thing. A run of length L needs L over three replacements. Now, which deletions help most? A run whose length is a multiple of three saves a replacement with just one deletion. A run one past a multiple needs two. Everything else needs three. So spend deletions in that order. And one more trick. A replacement can also add a missing type. So we take the larger of the two.
say.anim: We start with a twenty-seven character password containing all three character types, so missing is zero. The scanner finds a run of three a's, adding one needed replacement. Next it finds five A's, needing one more replacement, updating the run counts. Then seven ones are found, needing two more replacements, bringing the total to four. Finally twelve b's form the last run, pushing replacements up to eight total. Since length twenty-seven exceeds twenty, we must delete seven characters to shrink it first. Deletions target the run with remainder one first, then remainder two, cutting replacements down to four. Adding the seven deletions and four leftover replacements gives the final answer, eleven.
say.code: Now the code. First, count how many character types are missing. Then scan the runs. Each run adds one replacement per three repeats. We also bucket runs by length mod three, which tells us how cheaply deletions help. If it's too long, spend deletions on mod zero runs first, since one delete saves one replace. Remaining deletions save one per three. Finally, add the deletions to the larger of replacements and missing types.
say.outro: Linear time, constant space. The pattern is greedy. Spend forced deletions where each one saves the most replacements.

strong-password-checker.title: Strong Password Checker
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, as the problem platform expects.
The method takes a password string and returns the minimum number of edits needed to make it strong.
We store the password length in n, since the length rules drive most of the logic.
We count how many of lowercase, uppercase and digit types are absent by subtracting the present types from three.
We start replace at zero to count replacements needed to break up runs of repeated characters.
The mod list tracks how many runs have length remainder zero, one or two when divided by three.
We set i to zero to scan the password from the start.
We loop until i has moved past every character in the password.
We set j to i so we can extend it across a run of identical characters.
We advance j while the next character matches the one at i, finding the run end.
Each step of j extends the current run by one character.
The run length is the distance between j and i.
Only runs of three or more characters violate the rule and need attention.
Such a run needs the run length divided by three, rounded down, replacements, which we add up.
We record this run's remainder modulo three, since it decides how efficiently deletions can shorten it.
We jump i to j to begin scanning the next run.
If the password is too short, we handle that case first.
Inserts fix both length and missing types, so the answer is the larger of the shortage and missing types.
If the length is between six and twenty, no deletions are needed.
Replacements can also fix missing types, so the answer is the larger of replace and missing.
Otherwise the password is too long, so we must delete the excess characters beyond twenty.
Deleting one character from each run with remainder zero removes one replacement, so we use as many as possible.
We subtract those saved replacements from the total.
We track the deletions still remaining after that step.
Runs with remainder one save a replacement per two deletions, so we spend up to two per such run.
We subtract one replacement for every two deletions used here.
We reduce the remaining deletions by what we just spent.
Any leftover deletions save one replacement for every three, so we subtract that amount.
The answer is all deletions plus the larger of remaining replacements and missing character types.

subarray-sums-divisible-by-k.hook: Two prefix sums with the same remainder bracket a subarray divisible by k.
subarray-sums-divisible-by-k.ask: Given an integer array and k, count the non-empty contiguous subarrays whose sum is divisible by k.
subarray-sums-divisible-by-k.exampleWhy: Seven subarrays work, such as [5], [0], [5,0], [-2,-3] and the whole array, which sums to 5.

brute.idea: Fix every start index, extend the end one step at a time with a running sum, and count sums divisible by k.
steps: Pick a start i
Extend j, adding nums[j] to the sum
Count when sum % k == 0
brute.whySlow: 30,000 numbers means about 450 million subarrays, far too many to check one by one.

optimal.insight: sum(i..j) = prefix[j] - prefix[i-1]. It is divisible by k exactly when both prefixes leave the same remainder mod k.
steps: Keep a running prefix sum mod k
Count how often each remainder has appeared
Each earlier equal remainder makes one valid subarray
Start with remainder 0 seen once

codeNotes.note: Empty prefix: lets subarrays start at 0
Pair with every equal earlier remainder

pitfalls: In Java or C++, negative sums give negative remainders: add k before the final mod.
Forgetting the initial remainder 0 misses subarrays starting at index 0.

say.intro: Okay, Subarray Sums Divisible by K. We count contiguous subarrays whose sum is a multiple of k. Our array is four, five, zero, minus two, minus three, one, and k is five. There are seven. Five on its own. Zero on its own. Minus two and minus three together. Even the whole array.
say.brute: The first idea: pick every start index. Then extend the end one step at a time, keep a running sum, and count whenever it's divisible by k. That checks every subarray. Which means quadratic time. With thirty thousand numbers, that's around four hundred fifty million subarrays. Too slow.
say.insight: Here's the thing. Any subarray sum is one prefix sum minus an earlier one. When is that difference divisible by k? Exactly when the two prefix sums leave the same remainder. So we just count, for each remainder, how many prefixes have had it so far. Each new prefix pairs with every earlier match.
say.anim: We start with a counter tracking remainder zero once, prefix at zero, and count at zero. Adding four gives prefix four, a new remainder, so count stays zero but we record it. Adding five keeps prefix at four, matching before, so count increases to one. Adding zero keeps prefix four again, matching twice more, pushing count up to three. Adding negative two gives prefix two, a fresh remainder, no matches yet. Adding negative three brings prefix back to four, matching four prior times, count jumps to six. Adding one brings prefix to zero, matching the initial zero entry, count becomes seven. The loop ends and the function returns seven as the final answer.
say.code: Now the code. We start a counter with remainder zero seen once. That's the empty prefix, so subarrays can start at index zero. For each number, we update the prefix remainder mod k. Python's mod keeps it non-negative, which matters here, since numbers can be negative. Then we add the count of earlier prefixes with the same remainder. Finally, we record this prefix for later.
say.outro: Linear time, space bounded by k. Arrays and hashing: prefix sums plus a hash map of remainders.

subarray-sums-divisible-by-k.title: Subarray Sums Divisible by K
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container the interview platform expects for our method.
The method takes the list nums and the integer k, and returns how many subarrays have a sum divisible by k.
We make a counter of remainders seen so far, starting with remainder zero once, to represent the empty prefix.
We set prefix to zero, which will hold the running sum of the array reduced modulo k.
We set count to zero, which will accumulate the number of valid subarrays we find.
We loop over each number x in nums, extending the prefix one element at a time.
We add x to prefix and take the remainder mod k, keeping the running sum small and in range.
We add to count the number of earlier prefixes with this same remainder, since each one forms a divisible subarray ending here.
We record this remainder in the counter, so later positions can pair up with the current prefix.
We return count, the total number of non-empty subarrays whose sum is divisible by k.

subarrays-distinct-element-sum-of-square.hook: Grow each subarray one element at a time, and its distinct set grows with it.
subarrays-distinct-element-sum-of-square.ask: For every contiguous subarray, count its distinct values and square that count. Return the sum of all those squares.
subarrays-distinct-element-sum-of-square.exampleWhy: Singles add 4, pairs add 12, triples add 4 + 9, the whole array adds 9: 38 in total.

brute.idea: List every subarray, build a fresh set of its values, and add the set size squared.
steps: Pick start i and end j
Build a new set from nums[i..j]
Add its size squared
brute.whySlow: Each subarray rebuilds its set from scratch, so the work is cubic instead of quadratic.

optimal.insight: Subarrays starting at i are nested: extending the end by one only adds one value to the previous distinct set.
steps: Fix a start i with an empty set
Extend j and add nums[j] to the set
Add the current set size squared
Move to the next start

codeNotes.note: Fresh distinct set for each start
Extending by one adds one value

pitfalls: Square each subarray's count, not the total count at the end.
The n ≤ 100 limit makes quadratic fine; the Hard version II needs a segment tree.

say.intro: Okay, Subarrays Distinct Element Sum of Squares One. For every contiguous subarray, count its distinct values, square that, and add it all up. Take one, two, one, three. The four singles give four. The three pairs give twelve. The two triples give four plus nine. The whole array gives nine. Thirty eight.
say.brute: The first idea lists every subarray by start and end. For each, build a brand new set, and add its size squared. It's correct. But there are about n squared subarrays. And each set gets rebuilt from scratch, up to n steps. So the total is cubic.
say.insight: Now, notice something. Subarrays with the same start are nested. The one ending at j is just the one ending at j minus one, plus a single new value. So why rebuild? Keep one set per start, and add one number each step. The distinct count is just the set size.
say.anim: We start with the array one, two, one, three, and total at zero. For i equals zero, we build a growing set as j moves forward, squaring its size each time. After finishing i equals zero, the set reached one, two, three, and total climbed to eighteen. Now i equals one, starting fresh, adding two, then one and two, then one, two, three again. Total reaches thirty two after this inner loop, since extending the end just adds one value. For i equals two, the set grows from one to one and three, pushing total to thirty seven. Finally i equals three, the single element three gives total its last addition, reaching thirty eight. The function returns total, giving the final answer of thirty eight.
say.code: Now the code. Two loops. The outer loop picks the start, and makes a fresh, empty set. The inner loop extends the end by one. Extending adds one value to the set. Then we add the square of the distinct count to the total. Why does a duplicate do nothing? Because a set ignores it. That's exactly what distinct means.
say.outro: Quadratic time, linear space. Arrays and hashing: grow a hash set step by step instead of rebuilding it.

subarrays-distinct-element-sum-of-square.title: Subarrays Distinct Element Sum of Squares I
lineNotes: We define a class named Solution, which holds the method that solves this problem.
The method sumCounts takes the list nums and returns the sum of squared distinct counts over all subarrays.
We start total at zero to accumulate the squared distinct counts of every subarray.
The outer loop picks each starting index i, so we cover every possible subarray start.
For each start we create a fresh empty set called seen to track distinct values in the current subarray.
The inner loop extends the end index j from i to the last position, growing the subarray one element at a time.
We add the value at position j to seen, which only changes the distinct set if the value is new.
We square the current size of seen and add it to total, counting the subarray from i to j.
After all starts and ends are processed, we return total as the final answer.

subarrays-with-k-different-integers.hook: Exactly k is hard to slide over; at most k minus at most k - 1 is easy.
subarrays-with-k-different-integers.ask: Count the contiguous subarrays that contain exactly k different integers.
subarrays-with-k-different-integers.exampleWhy: [1,2], [2,1], [1,2], [2,3], [1,2,1], [2,1,2] and [1,2,1,2] each hold exactly two distinct values.

brute.idea: For every start, extend the end while tracking distinct values in a set, counting when the set size equals k.
steps: Pick a start i
Extend j and add nums[j] to a set
Count when the size is exactly k
Stop once the size exceeds k
brute.whySlow: 20,000 numbers gives up to 200 million start-end pairs to examine.

optimal.insight: Windows with at most k distinct are easy: for each right end, every start from left to right works. Exactly k = atMost(k) - atMost(k - 1).
steps: atMost(k): slide right, counting values in a map
Too many distinct? shrink from the left
Add window length: that many valid subarrays end here
Answer: atMost(k) - atMost(k - 1)

codeNotes.note: Bring the new value into the window
Too many distinct: shrink from left
Drop values that left the window
Every start in the window is valid
Exactly k = at most k minus k - 1

pitfalls: A single window for exactly k misses subarrays; subtract two at-most counts.
Delete map keys at count 0, or len(count) overstates distinct values.

say.intro: Okay, Subarrays with K Different Integers. Count the contiguous subarrays with exactly k distinct values. Our array is one, two, one, two, three, and k is two. There are seven. Things like one two, two three, and one two one two.
say.brute: The first idea fixes each start and extends the end, adding values to a set. Whenever the set has exactly k values, count it. Once it goes past k, stop. Simple and correct. But it's quadratic. For twenty thousand numbers, that can mean two hundred million pairs.
say.insight: Here's the thing. Exactly k doesn't slide nicely. A window with exactly k can grow or shrink and still be valid. But at most k does slide nicely. For each right end, shrink the left until we're at most k. Then every start inside the window works. So count at most k, subtract at most k minus one. What's left is exactly k.
say.anim: We want subarrays with exactly two distinct values, using an at most k helper twice. First call finds subarrays with at most two distinct integers, sliding right through the array. The window shrinks whenever distinct count exceeds two, trimming from the left side. At right equals four, three distinct values force left to advance until only two remain. At most two distinct integers gives a total count of twelve subarrays. Now we repeat with k equal to one, counting subarrays with at most one distinct value. Again the window shrinks whenever two distinct values appear, keeping only one type inside. Subtracting five from twelve gives exactly seven subarrays with exactly two distinct integers.
say.code: Now the code. A helper counts subarrays with at most k distinct values. Each step, we bring the new value into the window's counter. While there are too many distinct values, we shrink from the left. Values whose count hits zero get dropped from the counter. Then every start in the window is valid, so we add the window length. The answer is the helper at k, minus the helper at k minus one.
say.outro: Linear time. Sliding window, with the at most k trick turning an exact count into two easy windows.

subarrays-with-k-different-integers.title: Subarrays with K Different Integers
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container for the method that solves the problem.
The main method takes the array nums and the target k, and returns the count of subarrays with exactly k distinct integers.
We define a helper called at_most that counts subarrays having at most k distinct integers, using its own k.
We create a counter to track how many times each value appears inside the current window.
We start left at zero and the running result at zero, since the window begins empty.
We slide the right end across nums, reading each index and its value one at a time.
We add the new value to the counter, since the window now includes it.
While the window holds more than k distinct values, we must shrink it from the left.
We decrease the count of the value at the left edge because it is leaving the window.
If that value's count has dropped to zero, it no longer appears in the window.
So we delete it from the counter, which lowers the number of distinct values.
We move left forward one step to actually drop that element from the window.
Every start from left to right gives a valid subarray ending at right, so we add right minus left plus one.
After scanning everything, we return the total count of subarrays with at most k distinct values.
Exactly k equals at most k minus at most k minus one, so we subtract to isolate windows with exactly k distinct.

subtract-the-product-and-sum-of-digits-o.hook: Peel digits off with mod 10 and divide by 10, no strings needed.
subtract-the-product-and-sum-of-digits-o.ask: Given a positive integer, multiply its digits together, add its digits together, and return the product minus the sum.

brute.idea: Turn the number into a string, convert each character back into a digit, then compute product and sum from that list.
steps: Convert n to a string
Build a list of digit values
Multiply them, add them, subtract
brute.whySlow: Same speed, d digits either way, but it allocates a string and a list instead of using two integers.

optimal.insight: n % 10 is the last digit and n // 10 removes it. Loop until n is zero, updating product and sum.
steps: Start product at 1 and sum at 0
Take the last digit with n % 10
Update product and sum
Drop the digit with n //= 10

pitfalls: Starting the product at 0 makes every answer negative.

say.intro: Okay, Subtract the Product and Sum of Digits of an Integer. Multiply the digits. Add the digits. Return the difference. For two three five one four, the product is one hundred twenty. The sum is fifteen. So the answer is one hundred five.
say.brute: The most direct approach turns the number into a string. Then it converts each character back into a digit, and multiplies and adds the list. Is it actually slower? Not really. Both touch each digit once. But it allocates a string and a list for something two integers can handle. And some interviewers want the arithmetic version.
say.insight: Here's the trick. The last digit of any number is that number mod ten. And dividing by ten, rounding down, chops that digit off. So we peel digits off the right end, one at a time. We update a running product and a running sum. And we stop when the number hits zero.
say.anim: We start with n equal to 23514, product set to 1, and total set to 0. The last digit, 4, is pulled out, making product 4 and total 4. Now n becomes 2351, and the next digit, 1, updates product to 4 and total to 5. With n at 235, digit 5 multiplies in, bumping product to 20 and total to 10. n shrinks to 23, digit 3 is used, giving product 60 and total 13. Finally n is 2, the last digit 2 brings product to 120 and total to 15. Once n reaches zero, the loop ends and we return product minus total. The final answer shown is 105, from 120 minus 15.
say.code: Now the code. The product starts at one, and the sum at zero. Why one? Because multiplying by one changes nothing. While the number is positive, we grab the last digit with mod ten. We multiply it in and add it on. Then we chop off that digit by dividing by ten. When the loop ends, we return the product minus the sum.
say.outro: Time proportional to the number of digits, constant space. It's math: pull digits out with mod and division by ten.

subtract-the-product-and-sum-of-digits-o.title: Subtract the Product and Sum of Digits of an Integer
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which holds the method that solves this problem.
This method takes the integer n and returns the product of its digits minus the sum of its digits.
We start product at one, since multiplying by one changes nothing, and total at zero for the running sum.
We loop as long as n is greater than zero, meaning digits still remain to process.
We get the last digit of n by taking the remainder when dividing by ten.
We multiply product by this digit to build up the product of all digits.
We add the same digit to total to build up the sum of all digits.
We drop the last digit from n using integer division by ten, moving to the next digit.
Once all digits are processed, we return the product minus the sum as the final answer.

sum-of-subarray-minimums.hook: Flip the question: instead of each subarray's minimum, ask how many subarrays each element is the minimum of.
sum-of-subarray-minimums.ask: Add up the minimum of every contiguous subarray of the array, and return that total modulo 10^9 + 7.
sum-of-subarray-minimums.exampleWhy: The ten subarray minimums are 3, 1, 2, 4, 1, 1, 2, 1, 1, 1, which sum to 17.

brute.idea: For every start, extend the end one step at a time while tracking the running minimum, and add it each step.
steps: Pick a start i
Extend j, updating the running minimum
Add the minimum to the total
brute.whySlow: 30,000 elements means about 450 million subarrays, each touched individually.

optimal.insight: arr[m] is the minimum of (m - left) · (right - m) subarrays, where left and right are the nearest smaller elements. A monotonic stack finds both.
steps: Keep a stack of indices with increasing values
A smaller (or equal) value pops the top m
For m: left boundary is the new top, right boundary is i
Add arr[m] · (m - left) · (i - m)
A final 0 sentinel flushes the stack

codeNotes.match: cur = arr[i] if i < len(arr) else 0
codeNotes.note: Sentinel 0 pops everything at the end
Value times subarrays it is min of

pitfalls: With duplicates, use strict on one side and non-strict on the other, or you double count.
In fixed-width languages, take the modulo as you go.

say.intro: Okay, Sum of Subarray Minimums. For every contiguous subarray, take its minimum. Then add all those minimums together. Our array is three, one, two, four. That's ten subarrays, and their minimums add up to seventeen.
say.brute: The first idea picks each start, and extends the end one step at a time. Keep a running minimum, and add it to the total. It never recomputes a minimum from scratch. But it still visits every subarray. That's quadratic. With thirty thousand elements, that's around four hundred fifty million subarrays.
say.insight: Let's turn the question around. For each element, how many subarrays is it the minimum of? It stays the minimum leftward until the previous smaller element. And rightward until the next smaller one. Multiply those two distances, and that's its count. A stack of indices, with increasing values, finds both boundaries in one pass.
say.anim: We start with array 3, 1, 2, 4, an empty stack, and result zero. At index zero, value 3 has nothing smaller before it, so it just gets pushed. At index one, value 1 is smaller, so we pop index zero as the minimum. With no left boundary, element 3 contributes three, making result three. Values 2 and 4 are larger, so they simply get pushed onto the stack. At the end, cur is zero, forcing us to pop everything still on the stack. Popping 4 then 2 then 1, each contributes based on its left and right smaller boundaries. After all pops, the final result is seventeen, which is the answer.
say.code: Now the code. We loop one step past the end, using zero as a sentinel. It pops everything at the end. When the stack top is at least the current value, we've found its right boundary. We pop it. The new top is the previous smaller element. That's the left boundary, or minus one. Then we add its value times the subarrays it's the minimum of. Finally, reduce mod ten to the ninth plus seven.
say.outro: Linear time and space. It's a monotonic stack: count how far each element reigns as the minimum.

sum-of-subarray-minimums.title: Sum of Subarray Minimums
lineNotes: We define the Solution class that holds the method for this problem.
The method takes the array arr and returns the sum of all subarray minimums as an integer.
We set MOD to ten to the ninth plus seven, the modulus the answer must respect.
We start the running total res at zero.
We create an empty stack that will hold indices whose values are in increasing order.
We loop through every index, plus one extra step at the end to flush the remaining stack.
For the extra final step we use a current value of zero, which is smaller than every element, otherwise we read arr at i.
While the stack top value is at least the current value, the current index is that element's right smaller boundary.
We pop the top index and call it mid, the element whose minimum contribution we now count.
The left boundary is the new stack top after popping, or negative one if the stack is empty.
Mid is the minimum of mid minus left times i minus mid subarrays, so we add its value times that count to res.
We push the current index onto the stack, keeping values increasing from bottom to top.
We return the total taken modulo MOD, applying the modulus once at the end.

super-pow.hook: A giant exponent written digit by digit is just Horner's rule inside the exponent.
super-pow.ask: Compute a to the power b, modulo 1337, where b is a huge number given as an array of its decimal digits.
super-pow.exampleWhy: 3 to the power 201, reduced modulo 1337, leaves a remainder of 90.

brute.idea: Glue the digits back into one big integer exponent, then use fast modular power on it.
steps: Build e = e · 10 + digit for each digit
Compute pow(a, e, 1337)
brute.whySlow: Building a 2000-digit integer costs quadratic time, and most languages have no big integers to build it with.

optimal.insight: a^(10x + d) = (a^x)^10 · a^d. So scan digits left to right: raise the result to the 10th, then multiply in a^digit, all mod 1337.
steps: Reduce a modulo 1337
Start result at 1
For each digit: result = result^10 · a^digit
Keep everything modulo 1337

codeNotes.note: a to the power of nothing yet
Shift exponent one decimal place left
Then add this digit to the exponent

pitfalls: Reduce a mod 1337 first; a can be about 2 billion.
Without built-in pow, use square-and-multiply for the small powers.

say.intro: Okay, Super Pow. We compute a to the power b, mod thirteen thirty seven. The catch? b is huge. Up to two thousand digits, given as an array. For three to the power two hundred one, the remainder is ninety.
say.brute: The simplest idea glues the digits back into one giant integer. Then call fast modular power on it. Python can do that. But building a two thousand digit integer, multiplying by ten each step, costs quadratic time. And most languages have no big integer type at all. So this approach just wouldn't compile there.
say.insight: Here's the thing. Read the exponent one digit at a time. Each new digit makes the exponent ten times the old one, plus that digit. And a to the ten x plus d is a to the x, raised to the tenth, times a to the d. So we never need the exponent itself. Just raise the running result to the tenth, and multiply in a to the digit.
say.anim: We start with base three and digit list two, zero, one, mod thirteen thirty seven. Result starts at one, since we build up the power digit by digit. First digit is two, so result becomes one to the tenth times three squared, giving nine. Next digit is zero, raising nine to the tenth and multiplying by a to zero gives seven zero nine. Last digit is one, raising seven zero nine to the tenth times three mod thirteen thirty seven gives ninety. The loop finishes and the function returns the final result. The answer shown is ninety, matching the expected output.
say.code: Now the code. First, we shrink the base mod thirteen thirty seven. The result starts at one. That's a to the power of nothing yet. Then, for each digit from left to right, we raise the result to the tenth. That shifts the exponent one decimal place left. Then we multiply in a to this digit, which adds the digit to the exponent. Tiny exponents only, so constant work per digit.
say.outro: Linear in the number of digits, constant space. It's math: modular power with Horner's rule over the exponent's digits.

super-pow.title: Super Pow
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container that holds the method for this problem.
The method superPow takes the base a and the exponent b given as a list of decimal digits.
We store the modulus 1337 in a constant called MOD so every reduction uses the same value.
We reduce a modulo MOD up front so later multiplications work with small numbers.
We start result at one, which is the power of a when no digits have been processed yet.
We loop over each digit of b from left to right, building the exponent one decimal place at a time.
We raise result to the tenth power and multiply by a to the digit, all modulo MOD, following a to the ten x plus d.
After all digits are consumed, we return result, which equals a to the full exponent modulo 1337.

swapping-nodes-in-a-linked-list.hook: Find the k-th node from the end with a pointer that starts k steps behind.
swapping-nodes-in-a-linked-list.ask: Given a linked list and k, swap the values of the k-th node from the front and the k-th node from the end, then return the head.
swapping-nodes-in-a-linked-list.exampleWhy: The 2nd node from the front holds 2, the 2nd from the end holds 5; swapping gives 1,5,3,4,2,6.

brute.idea: Copy every value into an array, swap positions k - 1 and -k there, then write the values back into the list.
steps: Copy all values into a list
Swap vals[k - 1] and vals[-k]
Write values back node by node
brute.whySlow: Same linear time, but it copies the whole list into an array: O(n) extra memory and two full passes.

optimal.insight: Walk k - 1 steps to the first node. From there, a runner and a second pointer from the head move together; when the runner hits the tail, second is k-th from the end.
steps: Move first k - 1 steps from head
Start fast at first and second at head
Advance both until fast is the tail
Swap the values of first and second

codeNotes.note: Reach the k-th node from the front
Gap of k - 1 nodes between them
Stop when fast is the tail

pitfalls: The two nodes can be the same node; a value swap handles that for free.
Stop at fast.next, not fast, or second overshoots by one.

say.intro: Okay, Swapping Nodes in a Linked List. Swap the k th value from the front with the k th value from the end. Our list is one through six, and k is two. The second node holds two. The second from the end holds five. After the swap: one, five, three, four, two, six.
say.brute: The easy way copies every value into an array. Arrays let us index from both ends. So we swap the two entries, then walk the list again and write the values back. It's linear time. But it uses linear extra memory, for something a couple of pointers can do.
say.insight: Here's the trick. The k th node from the front is easy. Just walk k minus one steps. But the k th from the end? Keep a fixed gap. Put a runner on that first node, and another pointer on the head. Move both together. When the runner hits the tail, the trailing pointer is exactly k th from the end.
say.anim: We start with the list one through six and k equals two. First steps forward once, landing on node two, since k minus one is one. Now fast and second both start moving together from node two and node one. Fast and second advance in lockstep, fast reaching three, second reaching two. They keep moving together, fast now at four, second trailing at three. Fast finally reaches six, the tail, so second stops at five, the kth from end. The values at first, node two, and second, node five, get swapped. The final list returned is one, five, three, four, two, six.
say.code: Now the code. We move first k minus one steps, to reach the k th node from the front. Then fast starts at first, and second starts at the head. That gives a gap of k minus one nodes between them. While fast has a next node, both advance. So they stop when fast is the tail. Finally, we swap the two values in one line. No relinking needed.
say.outro: Linear time, constant space. Linked list two pointers: a fixed gap finds the k th node from the end in one pass.

swapping-nodes-in-a-linked-list.title: Swapping Nodes in a Linked List
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which holds the method that solves the node swapping problem.
The swapNodes method takes the head of the linked list and k, and returns the head afterward.
We start first at the head, since we need to walk forward to reach the k-th node.
We loop k minus one times, moving first forward so it lands exactly on the k-th node.
Each loop step advances first to its next node, taking one step closer to position k.
We start fast at first and second at head, so the gap between them equals k minus one nodes.
We keep looping while fast has a next node, meaning fast has not yet reached the tail.
We move fast one step forward, getting it closer to the end of the list.
We move second one step forward too, keeping the same gap behind fast.
When fast sits at the tail, second is the k-th from the end, so we swap their values.
We return head, since only values changed and the list structure stays the same.

the-number-of-good-subsets.hook: Only ten primes exist below 30, so a subset's prime factors fit in a 10-bit mask.
the-number-of-good-subsets.ask: Count subsets, by index, whose product is a product of distinct primes, with no prime repeated. Every value is at most 30. Return the count modulo 10^9 + 7.
the-number-of-good-subsets.exampleWhy: Six good choices from {2,3,4,6,15}: 2, 3, 6, 15, 2·3, 2·15. Each may include the 1 or not: 12.

brute.idea: Try every subset of indices, multiply the chosen numbers, and check that no prime squared divides the product.
steps: Enumerate all 2^n index subsets
Multiply the chosen values
Skip product 1
Count if square-free
brute.whySlow: With 100,000 numbers there are 2^100000 subsets; even 40 numbers is a trillion.

optimal.insight: Group equal values. Each square-free value 2..30 maps to a mask over 10 primes; combine values whose masks do not overlap, counting copies, then multiply by 2^(number of ones).
steps: Count how often each value appears
Skip 1 and values divisible by a prime squared
Map each value to a prime bitmask
dp[mask] += dp[old] · count when masks are disjoint
Sum non-empty masks, times 2^(ones)

codeNotes.note: Bit i set: uses prime i
Pick any one of x's copies
Each 1 is in or out freely

pitfalls: Ones never change the product; multiply by 2^count at the end instead of masking them.
Iterate over a snapshot of dp, or one value gets used twice.

say.intro: Okay, The Number of Good Subsets. A subset is good when its product is a product of distinct primes. No prime used twice. Our array is one, two, three, four, six, fifteen. Without the one, there are six good picks. Two, three, six, fifteen, two with three, and two with fifteen. Each can take the one or not. Twelve.
say.brute: The first idea tries every subset of indices. Multiply the chosen numbers, and check that no prime squared divides the product. That's two to the n subsets. With just forty numbers, that's already about a trillion. And the array can hold a hundred thousand.
say.insight: Here's the thing. Values are at most thirty, and only ten primes lie below thirty. So any usable value is just a ten bit mask of its primes. Values with a squared prime, like four, are never usable. Two values can share a subset only if their masks don't overlap. And the ones? They're free. Each one doubles the count.
say.anim: We start with nums one through six, and dp tracking zero as one way. Value one is skipped since it never contributes a prime mask. For x equals two, we find prime two divides it, giving mask one. Dp updates to include mask one, then we process x equals three similarly. X equals four fails since four squared divides it, so it's skipped as not square free. X equals six combines primes two and three into mask three, merging with existing subsets. X equals fifteen uses primes three and five, building mask six and combining with mask one. Final dp sums give total six, times two for value one, yielding answer twelve.
say.code: Now the code. We count each value, since only thirty distinct values matter. For each value, a repeated prime makes it unusable. Otherwise, we set bit i for each prime i it uses. Then we combine it with every existing mask that shares no prime, multiplying by this value's count, since any copy works. Finally, each one is in or out freely, so multiply by two to the number of ones.
say.outro: Linear in the input, plus about thirty thousand mask updates. The pattern is bit manipulation: bitmask dynamic programming over a few primes.

the-number-of-good-subsets.title: The Number of Good Subsets
lineNotes: We define a class named Solution, as the problem platform expects.
This method takes the list nums and returns the count of good subsets as an integer.
We set MOD to ten to the ninth plus seven, the modulus for the final answer.
We list the ten primes up to thirty, since every allowed value only uses these.
We count how many times each value appears, because equal values can be chosen by index in different ways.
The dp dictionary maps a prime mask to the number of ways to reach it, starting with the empty mask having one way.
We loop over the distinct values in sorted order so each value is processed exactly once.
If the value is one, we handle it separately later, so we skip it here.
We skip one because it adds no primes and only contributes a power of two at the end.
We start a fresh mask for this value with no primes set.
We assume the value is square-free until we find a repeated prime factor.
We walk through each prime along with its bit position.
If the prime exceeds the value, no further primes can divide it, so we stop checking.
This stops the scan early since larger primes are irrelevant.
If the prime squared divides the value, the value has a repeated prime and cannot be used.
We mark the value as not okay.
We stop checking, since this value is already disqualified.
If the prime divides the value, we have found one of its distinct prime factors.
We set that prime's bit in the mask.
After the loop, we check whether the value was disqualified.
We skip disqualified values, so they never enter the dp.
We iterate over a snapshot of the current dp states so updates do not disturb the loop.
We only combine when the existing mask and this value's mask share no primes.
We add ways times the count of this value to the merged mask, modulo MOD, since any copy can be chosen.
We sum all dp ways, subtract one to remove the empty subset, and take it modulo MOD.
Each of the ones can be freely included or not, so we multiply by two to the number of ones, modulo MOD.

two-city-scheduling.hook: Sort people by how much they save by flying to A instead of B.
two-city-scheduling.ask: 2n people each have a cost to fly to city A and to city B. Send exactly n people to each city at the lowest total cost.
two-city-scheduling.exampleWhy: Send the first two to A for 10 + 30, and the last two to B for 50 + 20: 110.

brute.idea: Recursively decide A or B for each person, respecting the n-per-city limit, and keep the cheapest total.
steps: For person i, try city A if A has room
Try city B if B has room
Recurse and keep the cheaper total
brute.whySlow: Up to C(100, 50) ways to split 100 people, about 10^29; hopeless without pruning.

optimal.insight: Start by imagining everyone in B. Moving a person to A changes the cost by a - b. Pick the n most negative differences.
steps: Sort people by a - b
First n people fly to A
Last n people fly to B
Sum the chosen costs

codeNotes.note: Biggest savings from flying to A first
Exactly half go to each city

codeNotes.match: total += a if i < n else b
codeNotes.note: First half A, second half B

pitfalls: Sorting by a alone is wrong; what matters is the difference a - b.

say.intro: Okay, Two City Scheduling. We have two n people. Each has a cost to fly to city A and a cost to fly to city B. Exactly half must go to each city. In our example, the first two go to A, for ten and thirty. The last two go to B, for fifty and twenty. Total, one hundred ten.
say.brute: The first idea decides each person's city recursively. If A has room, try A. If B has room, try B. Keep the cheaper total. That's correct. But it explores every balanced split. For a hundred people, that's around ten to the twenty ninth. Way too many.
say.insight: Think about it this way. Imagine sending everyone to B first. Now, moving one person to A changes the total by their A cost minus their B cost. We must move exactly n people. So which ones? The n with the smallest, most negative differences. And that's just a sort by A minus B.
say.anim: We sort costs by the difference between city A and city B prices. After sorting, the smallest differences come first, and n becomes two. For the first two entries, we add their city A cost, thirty then ten. Total climbs to forty, since the cheapest A options were chosen first. At index two, past the halfway point, we add city A cost thirty again, total hits sixty. For the last entry, index three, we add its city B cost fifty instead. Total becomes one hundred ten after adding all four scheduling costs. The function returns one hundred ten as the minimum total cost.
say.code: Now the code. We sort by A cost minus B cost. That puts the biggest savings from flying to A first. Then n is half the people, since exactly half go to each city. One loop adds the A cost for the first half, and the B cost for the second half. That's it.
say.outro: n log n time for the sort. The pattern is greedy: rank choices by how much one option saves over the other.

two-city-scheduling.title: Two City Scheduling
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container the problem expects for our method.
This method takes the list of cost pairs and returns the minimum total cost as an integer.
We sort people by the cost of A minus the cost of B, so those who benefit most from A come first.
We set n to half the number of people, since exactly that many must go to each city.
We start the running total at zero before adding any flight costs.
We loop over the sorted people with their index, unpacking each one into cost a and cost b.
The first n people fly to city A and pay a, while the rest fly to city B and pay b.
We return the total, which is the lowest possible cost with an even split between the two cities.

two-sum-iv-input-is-a-bst.hook: Two Sum, but the numbers live in a tree: traverse it and keep a hash set.
two-sum-iv-input-is-a-bst.ask: Given the root of a binary search tree and a target k, return true if two different nodes have values that add up to k.
two-sum-iv-input-is-a-bst.exampleWhy: 3 + 6 = 9, and both values are in the tree, so the answer is true.

brute.idea: Collect every value in the tree, then check every pair of values for the target sum.
steps: Traverse the tree into a list
Try every pair i < j
Return true if a pair sums to k
brute.whySlow: 10,000 nodes gives about 50 million pairs to try.

optimal.insight: Visit each node once. If k minus its value is already in a set of seen values, we have the pair.
steps: Traverse the tree with a stack
If k - val is in seen, return True
Otherwise add val to seen
Tree exhausted: return False

codeNotes.note: Remember this value for later nodes
No pair anywhere in the tree

pitfalls: Check the complement before adding the value, so a node never pairs with itself.
An in-order list plus two pointers also works, in the same O(n).

say.intro: Okay, Two Sum Four, Input is a BST. We get a binary search tree and a target. Do two different nodes add up to it? In our tree, the target is nine. Three plus six works. So the answer is true.
say.brute: The first idea collects every value into a list, then tries every pair. It's correct. It ignores the tree completely. But it's quadratic. Ten thousand nodes means about fifty million pairs to test. And almost all of them obviously fail.
