say.insight: Here's the thing. This is just classic two sum. Walk the tree once. At each node, ask: have I already seen the value that completes the pair? That's k minus this value. A hash set answers instantly. If not, add this value and keep going. Does the walk order matter? No. Every pair gets caught when its second node shows up.
say.anim: We start with an empty seen set and a stack holding just the root, node five. We pop node five, check if nine minus five, four, is seen, it isn't, so we add five to seen. Next we pop node six, nine minus six is three, not seen yet, so six joins the seen set. Now node seven is popped, nine minus seven is two, not in seen, so seven is added too. We pop several empty children in a row and simply skip past them. Finally we pop node three, and nine minus three equals six, which is already in seen. That match means we found two nodes summing to nine, so the function returns true.
say.code: Now the code. We keep a set of values visited so far, plus a stack that starts with the root. Pop a node, and skip it if it's empty. If k minus its value is already in the set, we've found a pair. Return true. Otherwise, remember this value for later nodes, and push both children. If the stack empties, there's no pair anywhere. Return false.
say.outro: Linear time and space. Trees plus hashing: any traversal with a seen set solves two sum.

two-sum-iv-input-is-a-bst.title: Two Sum IV - Input is a BST
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container the problem expects for our method.
The findTarget method takes the root of the tree and the target sum k, and returns true or false.
We start with an empty set called seen to remember every value we have already visited.
We use a stack for iterative depth first traversal, starting with just the root node.
We keep looping as long as the stack still has nodes waiting to be processed.
We pop the most recently added node off the stack to examine it next.
We check whether this node is empty, since missing children are pushed onto the stack as well.
If the node is empty we skip it and move on to the next stack item.
We check whether the complement, k minus this value, is already in seen, meaning an earlier node pairs with this one.
If the complement was seen, we have two different nodes adding to k, so we return true.
Otherwise we add this node's value to seen so later nodes can pair with it.
We push the left child onto the stack so its subtree gets visited later.
We push the right child onto the stack so its subtree also gets visited.
If the stack empties without finding any pair, no two nodes sum to k, so we return false.

ugly-number.hook: Divide out every 2, 3 and 5. Whatever is left tells you the answer.
ugly-number.ask: An ugly number is a positive integer whose only prime factors are 2, 3 and 5. Return true if n is ugly.
ugly-number.exampleWhy: 300 = 2 · 2 · 3 · 5 · 5. Every prime factor is 2, 3 or 5, so it is ugly.

brute.idea: Factor n by trial division up to its square root and reject the moment a prime factor above 5 appears.
steps: Try divisors d from 2 while d² ≤ n
Divide out each d, rejecting if d > 5
Leftover must be at most 5
brute.whySlow: For a large prime like 2,147,483,647 it tries about 46,000 divisors before giving up.

optimal.insight: We only care about 2, 3 and 5. Divide each out completely; n is ugly exactly when 1 remains.
steps: Non-positive n is never ugly
Divide by 2 while possible
Then by 3, then by 5
Ugly if what remains is 1

codeNotes.note: Zero and negatives are not ugly
Strip every copy of this prime
Anything left is a forbidden factor

pitfalls: n = 0 loops forever in the while loop; reject it first.
1 counts as ugly: it has no prime factors at all.

say.intro: Okay, Ugly Number. A number is ugly if it's positive, and its only prime factors are two, three and five. Three hundred is two times two times three times five times five. So it's ugly. Fourteen wouldn't be. Why? Because of the seven.
say.brute: The first idea fully factors the number. Try every divisor from two upward while its square is at most n. Divide it out. Fail as soon as a prime above five shows up. It works. But for a big prime near two billion, it tries about forty six thousand divisors before giving up.
say.insight: Here's the thing. We don't need the full factorization. We only care about two, three and five. So divide each of them out, as many times as possible. If the number was ugly, nothing else is left. We end at one. Anything other than one? Some other prime was hiding in there.
say.anim: We start with n equal to 300, which is positive, so we continue checking. We loop through the primes two, three, and five, dividing them out completely. Dividing by two twice shrinks n from 300 down to 75. Next we divide by three once, reducing n from 75 to 25. Now dividing by five twice brings n down from 25 to 1. All three primes are checked, and n has been fully reduced to 1. Since n equals 1, the function returns true, confirming 300 is ugly.
say.code: Now the code. First, zero and negatives are not ugly. And zero would loop forever, so this check matters. Then we loop over only the allowed primes, two, three and five. For each, we strip every copy by dividing while it divides evenly. Finally, we return whether the number is one. Anything left is a forbidden factor.
say.outro: Logarithmic time, since each division at least halves the number. Math: strip out the allowed primes and check what's left.

ugly-number.title: Ugly Number
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container that holds the method for this problem.
The method isUgly takes an integer n and will return a true or false answer.
First we check whether n is zero or negative, since ugly numbers must be positive.
If so, we return false right away, because such numbers can never be ugly.
We loop over the three allowed prime factors, two, three and five, one at a time.
While n is still evenly divisible by the current prime p, we keep going.
We divide n by p, stripping that prime factor out of n completely.
After removing all twos, threes and fives, n is ugly exactly when only one remains, so we return that check.

ugly-number-ii.hook: Every ugly number is a smaller ugly number times 2, 3 or 5.
ugly-number-ii.ask: Ugly numbers are positive integers whose only prime factors are 2, 3 and 5, starting 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 8. Return the n-th ugly number.
ugly-number-ii.exampleWhy: The first ten ugly numbers are 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 8, 9, 10, 12, so the 10th is 12.

brute.idea: Test 1, 2, 3, and so on with the isUgly check, counting ugly numbers until we reach the n-th.
steps: Test the next integer
Divide out 2, 3, 5 and check for 1
Count it if ugly
Stop at the n-th
brute.whySlow: Ugly numbers get rare: the 1690th is over 2 billion, so we would test billions of integers.

optimal.insight: Generate them in order: three pointers mark which ugly number to multiply by 2, 3 and 5 next. The smallest candidate is the next ugly number.
steps: ugly[0] = 1, all three pointers at 0
Next = min of ugly[i2]·2, ugly[i3]·3, ugly[i5]·5
Advance every pointer that produced it
Repeat until n numbers exist

codeNotes.note: Smallest candidate is next in order
Separate ifs: ties advance both pointers

pitfalls: Use separate ifs, not elif, or 6 = 2·3 = 3·2 is added twice.
A min-heap with a seen set also works, in O(n log n).

say.intro: Okay, Ugly Number Two. Ugly numbers have no prime factors besides two, three and five. The sequence starts one, two, three, four, five, six, eight, nine, ten, twelve. We want the n th one. So for n equal to ten, the answer is twelve.
say.brute: The first idea tests integers one by one. Divide out twos, threes and fives, and count the ones that reduce to one. It's correct. But ugly numbers thin out fast. The sixteen hundred ninetieth one is over two billion. So we'd test billions of numbers.
say.insight: Here's the key. Every ugly number after one is a smaller ugly number times two, three or five. So we can build the sequence in order. Keep three pointers, one per factor. Each points at the next ugly number it should multiply. The smallest of the three products comes next. And any pointer that produced it moves forward.
say.anim: We start with an array of ten ones and three pointers all at zero. The next ugly number is two, the smallest multiple from our pointers, so it's stored. Three comes next, since tripling the first ugly number beats doubling or quintupling. Four, five, and six follow in order, each time picking the smallest candidate product. Now eight and nine get added, as doubling and tripling pointers advance together. Ten is generated next, keeping all three pointers moving forward in sync. Finally twelve is chosen as the tenth ugly number, completing the sequence. The function returns twelve, confirming it as the tenth ugly number.
say.code: Now the code. An array of ones, and three pointers at zero. Each one marks the next number to multiply by two, three or five. For each new slot, the smallest candidate is next in order, so we store it. Then we use separate ifs, not else ifs. Why? Ties should advance both pointers, which removes duplicates like six. Finally, return the last element. That's the n th ugly number.
say.outro: Linear time and space. One dimensional dynamic programming: build each value from earlier ones with three merging pointers.

ugly-number-ii.title: Ugly Number II
lineNotes: We define a class named Solution, which is the container the interview platform expects for our method.
The method nthUglyNumber takes n and returns the n-th ugly number as an integer.
We create a list of n slots filled with one, since the first ugly number is one.
We start three pointers, for multiples of two, three and five, all at the first ugly number.
We loop from position one up to n minus one, filling in each remaining ugly number in increasing order.
The next ugly number is the smallest of the three candidates: each pointed-to ugly number times its own prime.
We store that smallest candidate in the list at the current position.
If the new number came from multiplying by two, we check that here.
In that case we advance the two pointer so it offers a larger candidate next time.
We run the same check for the candidate that used three.
If it matched, we advance the three pointer to the next ugly number.
We also check whether the candidate from five produced the new number.
If so, we advance the five pointer, and using separate ifs skips duplicates like six when two and three tie.
After filling the list, the last entry is the n-th ugly number, so we return it.

unique-binary-search-trees.hook: Pick the root, and the problem splits into two smaller copies of itself.
unique-binary-search-trees.ask: How many structurally different binary search trees can be built using exactly the values 1 to n?

brute.idea: Recursively try every value as the root and multiply the counts of possible left and right subtrees.
steps: Try each root r from 1 to n
Left has r - 1 nodes, right has n - r
Add count(left) · count(right)
brute.whySlow: count(k) is recomputed again and again for the same small k; the calls grow exponentially.

optimal.insight: The count only depends on how many nodes, not which values. Build dp[k] for k = 0..n, each from smaller entries.
steps: For each size k, try every root
dp[k] += dp[left size] · dp[right size]
Return dp[n]

codeNotes.note: Every value can be the root

pitfalls: dp[0] must be 1, not 0, or every one-sided tree is lost.

say.intro: Okay, Unique Binary Search Trees. How many differently shaped search trees can hold the values one to n? Take n equals four. One or four at the root gives five trees each. Two or three at the root gives two each. So fourteen in total.
say.brute: The first idea tries every value as the root. Smaller values go left, larger go right. So the count is left trees times right trees, summed over all roots. Done recursively with no memory, though? The same small sizes get recomputed over and over. And the calls grow exponentially.
say.insight: Here's the thing. The number of trees depends only on how many nodes there are. Not which values. Three consecutive values make as many shapes as one, two, three. So let dp of k be the count for k nodes. Then build it from smaller sizes, zero up to n.
say.anim: We start with n equal to four and an empty dp array of zeros. Dp of zero is set to one, representing the empty tree base case. Now nodes equals one, and we sum over possible root choices to fill dp of one. Dp of one becomes one, then nodes equals two gives dp of two equal to two. Moving to nodes equals three, we accumulate contributions until dp of three reaches five. Now nodes equals four, summing each root's left and right subtree combinations. Dp of four grows through five, seven, nine, finally reaching fourteen after all roots. The function returns dp of four, giving the final answer fourteen.
say.code: Now the code. We set dp of zero to one. An empty subtree has exactly one way. Then for each size, every value can be the root. The left side has root minus one nodes. The right side has the rest. So we add left shapes times right shapes. Finally, we return dp of n. That's the n th Catalan number.
say.outro: Quadratic time, linear space. One dimensional dynamic programming: pick a root, combine counts of smaller sizes.

unique-binary-search-trees.title: Unique Binary Search Trees
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container the problem expects for our method.
The method numTrees takes n, the number of nodes, and returns how many distinct binary search tree shapes exist.
We create a dp list of size n plus one, all zeros, where dp at k will hold the count for k nodes.
We set dp at zero to one, since an empty tree is one valid shape and serves as the base case.
We loop over nodes from one up to n, computing the answer for each tree size in increasing order.
For each size, we try every value from one to nodes as the root, since each root gives different splits.
With a chosen root, the left subtree has root minus one nodes and the right has nodes minus root, so we add the product of their counts.
After filling the table, we return dp at n, the number of unique binary search trees for n nodes.

unique-middle-element.hook: Grab the middle value, then count it in a single pass.
unique-middle-element.ask: Given an array of odd length, return true if its middle element appears exactly once in the whole array, and false otherwise.
unique-middle-element.exampleWhy: The middle element is 9 at index 3, and no other position holds 9, so it is unique.

brute.idea: Count how many times every element occurs by comparing it against every element, then look up the middle one.
steps: For each i, compare with every j
Store the count for i
Check the middle count is 1
brute.whySlow: It counts every element, but only the middle one matters: n² comparisons for one answer.

optimal.insight: Only the middle value matters. Read it at index n // 2, count its occurrences once, and compare with 1.
steps: mid = nums[n // 2]
Scan the array, counting matches
Return count == 1

pitfalls: The count includes the middle itself, so unique means count == 1, not 0.

say.intro: Okay, Unique Middle Element. The array has odd length, so it has a true middle. Return true if that middle value appears exactly once. Our array is four, one, five, nine, two, six, one. The middle is nine. Nine shows up nowhere else. So the answer is true.
say.brute: A brute force counts how often every element appears. It compares each element with every other one. Then it checks the count for the middle position. It's correct. But it's quadratic. And almost all that work is wasted. Why? Because only the middle value matters.
say.insight: Here's the thing. We only care about one value: the one at the middle index. So read it once. Then walk the array a single time, and count how many positions hold it. The middle itself counts once. So it's unique exactly when the count is one.
say.anim: We start with the array four, one, five, nine, two, six, one. The middle index is computed, giving mid equal to nine, and count starts at zero. We loop through each number, checking if it matches the middle value nine. Values four, one, and five are checked but don't match nine. When x equals nine, it matches mid, so count increases to one. The remaining values two, six, and one don't match nine either. Finally, we check if count equals one, confirming the middle value is unique. The function returns true, since nine appears exactly once in the array.
say.code: Now the code. Odd length means the exact middle index is the length divided by two. We read the value there. A counter starts at zero. For each number, if it equals the middle value, we count it. That catches every copy. Finally, we return whether the count is exactly one. Only the middle itself.
say.outro: Linear time, constant space. Arrays and hashing at its simplest: focus on the one value you need, and count it.

unique-middle-element.title: Unique Middle Element
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which holds the method that answers the unique middle element question.
This method takes the list nums and returns a boolean telling us whether the middle value appears only once.
We read the middle value by indexing at the length of nums divided by two, rounded down, and store it as mid.
We start a counter called count at zero to track how many times the middle value shows up.
We loop through every number x in nums so each element gets checked exactly once.
For each number, we check whether it equals the middle value we saved earlier.
When it matches, we add one to count, so count tallies all occurrences of the middle value.
Finally we return whether count equals one, which is true only when the middle value is unique.

unique-morse-code-words.hook: Translate every word, toss the translations into a set, and count.
unique-morse-code-words.ask: Each letter has a Morse code. Translate every word by joining its letters' codes, and return how many different translations there are.
unique-morse-code-words.exampleWhy: gin and zen both become --...-., gig and msg both become --...--., so two distinct codes.

brute.idea: Translate every word into a list, then count translations that do not equal any earlier one.
steps: Translate each word into Morse
For each, compare with all earlier translations
Count it if no earlier match
brute.whySlow: Each new code is compared with every earlier code: quadratic in the number of words.

optimal.insight: Distinct strings is exactly what a hash set counts. Insert every translation; the set size is the answer.
steps: Look up each letter's code by its alphabet index
Join the codes into one translation
Add the translation to a set
Return the set size

codeNotes.note: Morse code for a through z
Letter to alphabet index to code

pitfalls: Different words can share a translation; count translations, not words.

say.intro: Okay, Unique Morse Code Words. Every letter has a Morse code. A word's translation is its letters' codes, glued together. We count how many different translations show up. Gin and zen translate to the same code. Gig and msg share another. So the answer is two.
say.brute: The first idea translates every word into a list. Then it walks the list, and counts a translation only if it differs from every earlier one. That works. But each new code gets compared against all the ones before it. That's quadratic in the number of words.
say.insight: Here's the thing. Counting distinct strings is exactly what a hash set is for. Translate each word, and drop it in the set. Duplicates collapse on their own. And the set's size at the end is our answer. Each insert is constant time on average.
say.anim: We start with the list of words and the Morse code lookup table for each letter. An empty set called seen is created to store unique Morse translations. The loop begins, picking the first word to translate into Morse code. Gin is translated into Morse and added to the set, since duplicates are automatically ignored. Zen is translated next, producing a different code also added to the growing set. Gig is translated, but its Morse code matches gin's, so the set size stays the same. Msg is translated too, but it also duplicates an existing code already in the set. The final set holds two unique codes, so the answer returned is two.
say.code: Now the code. We store the Morse codes for a through z in a list. Then a set, so each distinct translation is kept once. For each word, every letter maps to its alphabet index, and from there to its code. We join those codes into one string, and add it to the set. Finally, we return the set's size. That's the number of different translations.
say.outro: Linear in the total length of the words. Arrays and hashing: transform each item, then count distinct results with a set.

unique-morse-code-words.title: Unique Morse Code Words
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container the interview platform expects for our method.
This method takes a list of words and returns the count of distinct Morse translations as an integer.
We store the Morse codes for letters a through z in order, so each letter's position matches its code.
We create an empty set called seen, which will automatically keep only distinct translations.
We loop over each word in the input list, one at a time.
For each letter we find its index by subtracting the letter a, join the codes into one string, and add it to seen.
Finally we return the size of the set, which equals the number of unique Morse translations.

unique-paths-ii.hook: Paths into a cell come from above or from the left, unless the cell is blocked.
unique-paths-ii.ask: A robot starts top-left and moves only right or down to the bottom-right. Cells marked 1 are obstacles. How many distinct paths avoid every obstacle?
unique-paths-ii.exampleWhy: Without the rock there are 10 paths; 6 pass through it, leaving 4.

brute.idea: Recursively walk from the start, branching right and down, counting paths that reach the corner without hitting an obstacle.
steps: Off grid or obstacle: 0 paths
At the corner: 1 path
Else: paths going down plus paths going right
brute.whySlow: The same cell is re-explored from every route that reaches it; a 100 by 100 grid is hopeless.

optimal.insight: Ways into a cell = ways into the cell above + ways into the cell to the left, or 0 on an obstacle. One row of memory is enough.
steps: dp[c] = ways to reach column c in the current row
Start with dp[0] = 1
Obstacle: dp[c] = 0
Else dp[c] += dp[c - 1]: above plus left

codeNotes.note: One way to stand at the start
Wipe the count for this cell

pitfalls: An obstacle on the start cell means 0 paths; the code handles it by zeroing dp[0].
Do not fill the first row with 1s past an obstacle.

say.intro: Okay, Unique Paths Two. A robot starts in the top left corner. It can only move right or down, and it wants the bottom right. Some cells hold obstacles. In our three by four grid, there would be ten paths. But six of them pass through the rock. So four remain.
say.brute: The first idea explores every route. Off the grid, or on an obstacle? Zero paths. At the goal? One. Otherwise, add the paths going down and the paths going right. It's correct. But the same cells get explored again from every route that reaches them. That's exponential.
say.insight: Think about it this way. The robot enters any cell from above or from the left. Nowhere else. So the ways to reach a cell are the ways to reach the cell above, plus the cell to its left. And zero if it's blocked. Filling row by row, we only need one row of counts.
say.anim: We start with a four column grid and set up a single row dp array. Dp begins as one, zero, zero, zero, since only the first cell is reachable. Processing the first row with no obstacles, each cell adds the value to its left. After row one, dp becomes one, one, one, one, meaning one path to each cell. Row two has an obstacle at column one, so dp there resets to zero. Columns two and three keep summing from the left, giving dp one, zero, one, two. The final row has no obstacles, so sums continue normally across all columns. Dp ends as one, one, two, four, so the answer is four unique paths.
say.code: Now the code. One array, one count per column. We start with one way to stand at the start. For each row and column, an obstacle means no path passes through. So we wipe that count to zero. Otherwise, the count already there is the old value from above. We add the count to its left. Finally, the last entry is the number of ways to reach the bottom right.
say.outro: Time proportional to the grid, space for one row. Two dimensional dynamic programming, squeezed into a single row.

unique-paths-ii.title: Unique Paths II
lineNotes: We define a class named Solution, which is the container the judge expects for our method.
The method takes the obstacle grid and returns the number of obstacle-free paths from top-left to bottom-right as an integer.
We record the number of columns by taking the length of the first row of the grid.
We create a single row of memory called dp, with one slot per column, all starting at zero.
We set the first slot to one, giving the starting cell exactly one way to be reached.
We walk through the grid one row at a time, reusing dp to hold the counts for the current row.
Within each row, we visit every column index from left to right so left neighbors are updated first.
If the current cell is an obstacle, we must handle it specially because no path can pass through.
We set that column's count to zero, wiping out any paths that came from above into the obstacle.
Otherwise, for any column past the first, we add the count from the left neighbor into the current cell.
The current slot already holds the ways from above, so adding the left count gives the total ways into this cell.
After processing all rows, the last slot holds the number of paths reaching the bottom-right corner, which we return.

valid-perfect-square.hook: No square root allowed. Binary search on the answer finds the root, or proves there is none.
valid-perfect-square.ask: Given a positive integer num, return true if some whole number multiplied by itself equals num, and false otherwise, without using any built-in square root function.
valid-perfect-square.exampleWhy: 12 times 12 is exactly 144, so 144 is a perfect square.

brute.idea: Try every whole number x starting from 1 until x squared reaches or passes num.
steps: Start x at 1
While x·x < num, add one to x
Return whether x·x equals num
brute.whySlow: For num near 2.1 billion that is about 46,000 tries; binary search needs about 31.

optimal.insight: x squared only grows as x grows. A sorted, monotonic answer space means binary search can find the root in logarithmic time.
steps: Search x between 1 and num
Square the middle value
Exact match: return true
Too small: go right; too big: go left
Range empty: return false

codeNotes.note: The root lies somewhere in here

pitfalls: In fixed-width languages mid * mid overflows; use 64-bit or compare mid with num / mid.

say.intro: Okay, Valid Perfect Square. We get a positive whole number. Is it some integer times itself? And no square root function allowed. Our example is one hundred forty four. That's twelve times twelve. So the answer is true.
say.brute: The first idea is just counting. Start at one, and keep stepping up while the square is still smaller than the number. When we stop, check if the square landed exactly on it. That works. But it takes about root n tries. For a number near two billion, that's around forty six thousand loops.
say.insight: Here's the key. As a number grows, its square only grows too. And that ordering is exactly what binary search needs. Guess the middle of the range, square it, and compare. Too small? The root is to the right. Too big? It's to the left. Every guess throws away half.
say.anim: We start searching for a square root of 144, with lo at 1 and hi at 144. Mid is 72, its square is 5184, too big, so hi shrinks to 71. Mid becomes 36, square is 1296, still too big, hi drops to 35. Mid is 18, square is 324, still too large, hi narrows down to 17. Mid is 9, square 81 is too small, so lo moves up to 10. Mid is 13, square 169 overshoots, hi tightens to 12. Mid is 11, square 121 undershoots, lo advances to 12, narrowing the range further. Mid becomes 12, its square equals 144, confirming the number is a perfect square.
say.code: Now the code. Low is one, high is the number. The root lies somewhere in there. While the range isn't empty, we square the middle candidate. If it equals the number, we found an exact root. Return true. Too small? Move low past the middle, discarding the left half. Too big? Move high below it. And if the range empties, no integer works. Return false.
say.outro: Logarithmic time, constant space. Binary search on the answer: when a value grows steadily, search over it instead of counting.

valid-perfect-square.title: Valid Perfect Square
lineNotes: We define a Solution class that holds the method for checking whether a number is a perfect square.
The method takes a positive integer num and returns true or false without using any square root function.
We set lo to one and hi to num, so the search range covers every possible whole number root.
We loop while lo is no greater than hi, meaning at least one candidate remains to be checked.
We pick mid as the average of lo and hi, rounded down, to test the middle candidate.
We compute sq as mid times mid, which is the square of our current guess.
We check whether sq exactly equals num, which would mean mid is a whole number root.
If it matches, we return true right away because we found a valid root.
If sq is smaller than num, the guess is too small, so we take the next branch.
We move lo up to mid plus one, discarding mid and every smaller value as too small.
Otherwise sq is larger than num, so the guess is too big.
We move hi down to mid minus one, discarding mid and every larger value.
If the loop ends with no match, no whole number squares to num, so we return false.

water-bottles.hook: Drink, trade empties for full ones, repeat. Batching the trades turns a long simulation into a few rounds.
water-bottles.ask: You start with some full water bottles. Drinking one leaves an empty bottle, and a set number of empties can be traded for one full bottle. Return the most bottles you can drink in total.
water-bottles.exampleWhy: Drink 20, trade 18 empties for 6, then 6 for 2, then 3 empties for 1: 20 + 6 + 2 + 1 = 29.

brute.idea: Simulate one bottle at a time: drink one, add an empty, and trade whenever enough empties pile up.
steps: Drink one full bottle
Count one more empty
Enough empties? trade for one full
Stop when no full bottles remain
brute.whySlow: It loops once per bottle drunk; trading in batches needs only a logarithmic number of rounds.

optimal.insight: Do not trade one bottle at a time. Each round, trade every complete group of empties at once and keep the leftovers.
steps: Drink all starting bottles
Trade empties // exchange for new full bottles
Leftover empties are empties % exchange
Drink the new ones; repeat while a trade is possible

codeNotes.note: Keep going while a trade is possible
Trade every full group at once

pitfalls: Forgetting leftover empties when updating the count undercounts the answer.
Closed form: n + (n - 1) // (e - 1), if you can justify it.

say.intro: Okay, Water Bottles. We start with some full bottles. Drinking one leaves an empty. And a fixed number of empties trade in for a fresh full bottle. How many can we drink in total? With twenty bottles and a trade rate of three, the answer is twenty nine.
say.brute: The first idea simulates bottle by bottle. Drink one, add an empty. The moment we have enough empties, swap them for a full bottle. Stop when nothing full is left. It's correct. But it loops once per bottle we drink. That's linear in the answer.
say.insight: Here's the thing. We can batch the trades. After drinking, hand in every complete group of empties at once. New bottles are the empties divided by the rate. The remainder stays in our hands. And each round shrinks the pile by about the trade rate. So only a logarithmic number of rounds remain.
say.anim: We start with 20 bottles, total and empty both set to 20, trading every 3 empties. Empty is 20, which is at least 3, so we enter the exchange loop. We trade 6 groups of empties, adding 6 new bottles, total jumps to 26. Leftover empties plus new bottles gives us 8 empties for the next round. With 8 empties we trade 2 more groups, bringing total up to 28. Remaining empties now total 4, enough for one more exchange. We trade one final group, adding one more bottle, total becomes 29. Now only 2 empties remain, not enough to trade, so the loop ends with answer 29.
say.code: Now the code. First, we drink every starting bottle, so the total starts there. Then we keep going while a trade is possible. We trade every full group at once, using integer division. Those new bottles go on the total. The empties become the leftovers, plus the bottles we just drank. When no trade is left, we return the total.
say.outro: Logarithmic time, constant space. It's math: replace a step by step simulation with division and remainder.

water-bottles.title: Water Bottles
lineNotes: We define a class named Solution, which is the container the judge expects for this problem's method.
This method takes the starting number of full bottles and the number of empties needed per exchange, and returns an integer.
We set total to the starting bottles, since we can drink every one of them right away.
We set empty to the starting bottles too, because each drunk bottle leaves one empty behind.
We keep looping as long as we hold enough empties to make at least one exchange.
We compute how many new full bottles we get by dividing empties by the exchange size, trading whole groups at once.
We add those new bottles to total, because we will drink every one of them.
Leftover empties stay, and the new bottles we drink become empties, so empty is the remainder plus new.
When we can no longer trade, we return total as the most bottles we could drink.

watering-plants.hook: Every refill means walking all the way back. Count the round trip in one formula instead of walking it.
watering-plants.ask: Plants sit at positions 0 to n - 1, the river at -1. Water them left to right, refilling only when the can cannot fully water the next plant. Return the total steps walked.
watering-plants.exampleWhy: Refills happen before plants 3, 4 and 5, costing round trips of 6, 8 and 10, plus 6 forward steps: 30.

brute.idea: Walk the gardener literally, one unit step at a time, including every trip back to the river and out again.
steps: Step forward to the next plant
Not enough water? walk back to the river
Refill, then walk back out step by step
Water the plant and continue
brute.whySlow: Each refill walks up to n unit steps back and out, so many refills cost quadratic time.

optimal.insight: A refill before plant i is a round trip from i - 1 to the river and back, which always costs exactly 2·i extra steps.
steps: Each plant costs one forward step
If water is short, add 2·i for the round trip
Refill the can
Subtract the plant's need

codeNotes.note: Start at the river, can full
One step forward to plant i

pitfalls: The round trip starts from plant i - 1, so it costs 2·i, not 2·(i + 1).

say.intro: Okay, Watering Plants. Plants stand in a row, with a river just before the first one. We water left to right. Whenever the can can't fully water the next plant, we walk back and refill. Count the total steps. Needs are one, one, one, four, two, three. The can holds four. That's thirty steps.
say.brute: The first idea walks the gardener literally. One unit at a time toward each plant. When water runs short, walk back to the river step by step, refill, and walk out again. It gives the right count. But each refill can cost up to n steps of walking. So the total is quadratic.
say.insight: Here's the thing. A refill trip always has the same shape. Standing at plant i minus one, we walk i steps to the river, and i steps back. So a refill just adds two times i. Every plant also costs one step forward. No walking needed. Just one pass, adding numbers.
say.anim: We start with zero steps and water filled to capacity, four units. For plants needing one unit each, water suffices, so steps just increment and water drains. At plant index three, needing four units, only one unit remains, triggering a refill. The refill costs two times three extra steps, a round trip back and forth. At index four, water runs out again, adding two times four steps for another refill. At index five, another refill adds two times five steps before watering the final plant. The loop finishes after watering all six plants with the needed refills. The function returns thirty, the total steps needed to water every plant.
say.code: Now the code. We start at the river, with steps at zero and a full can. For each plant, if the water is less than it needs, we can't fully water it. So we add two times the index for the round trip, and refill. Then we take one step forward to the plant. And we pour exactly what it needs. Finally, return the steps.
say.outro: Linear time, constant space. Array scanning with a running state: turn repeated walking into a formula.

watering-plants.title: Watering Plants
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container for the method the problem asks us to write.
The method takes the list of plant needs and the can capacity, and returns the total steps walked.
We start with zero steps taken and a full can, so water equals capacity.
We loop over each plant, tracking its position i and the water it needs.
Before watering, we check whether the remaining water is too little to fully water this plant.
If so, we add two times i steps, the round trip back to the river and return.
We then refill the can, setting water back to its full capacity.
Whether or not we refilled, we add one step to move forward to this plant.
We water the plant by subtracting its need from the water left in the can.
After all plants are watered, we return the total number of steps.

wiggle-sort-ii.hook: Small, big, small, big. Sort, then weave the halves backwards so equal values never touch.
wiggle-sort-ii.ask: Rearrange the array in place so the values strictly alternate: the first is less than the second, which is greater than the third, which is less than the fourth, and so on. A valid answer always exists.
wiggle-sort-ii.exampleWhy: 1 < 6 > 1 < 5 > 1 < 4: every even slot dips below both of its neighbours.

brute.idea: Backtrack: fill positions one at a time, trying each remaining value that keeps the up-down pattern valid so far.
steps: Pick a value for the next slot
Check it against the previous value
Valid? recurse; stuck? undo and try another
Full array built: copy it back
brute.whySlow: With many distinct values the search can try a factorial number of orderings before finishing.

optimal.insight: Sort, then put the smaller half on even slots and the larger half on odd slots, both reversed, so duplicates land far apart.
steps: Sort a copy of the array
Split into smaller half and larger half
Even slots take the smaller half, largest first
Odd slots take the larger half, largest first

pitfalls: Without reversing, middle duplicates can sit side by side, as in 4,5,5,6.
Follow-up O(n) uses quickselect for the median plus index mapping.

say.intro: Okay, Wiggle Sort Two. We rearrange an array so it goes down, up, down, up. Every even position is strictly smaller than its neighbors. For one, five, one, one, six, four, one valid answer is one, six, one, five, one, four.
say.brute: The first idea is backtracking. Fill the array one slot at a time. For each slot, try every remaining value that keeps the up down rule with the previous one. Stuck? Undo, and try something else. It always finds an answer. But in the worst case, it explores a factorial number of orderings.
say.insight: Here's the trick. Sort first. Then the smaller half goes into the valleys, and the larger half onto the peaks. So what's the catch? Duplicates near the median. They could end up side by side. The fix: place both halves in reverse order. Then equal middle values land at opposite ends. And they can never touch.
say.anim: We start with the array one five one one six four, about to sort it. The sorted array is one one one four five six, giving six elements to place. Small starts at index two, pointing to the middle of the smaller half. Large starts at index five, pointing to the top of the larger half. At even index zero, we take arr small, which is one, and decrement small. At odd index one, we take arr large, which is six, filling nums with one six one one six four. Continuing this pattern, even slots pull shrinking small values and odd slots pull shrinking large values. After all six slots fill, the final wiggle sorted array is one six one five one four.
say.code: Now the code. First, sort a copy, so the values are in order. One pointer starts at the end of the smaller half. When the length is odd, that half gets the extra element. Another pointer starts at the very end, the end of the larger half. Now walk every index. Valleys take the next small value, largest first. Peaks take the next large value, largest first.
say.outro: Sorting time, linear space. Greedy placement after sorting. The follow up uses quickselect for linear time.

wiggle-sort-ii.title: Wiggle Sort II
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container the problem expects for our method.
The wiggleSort method rearranges nums in place, so it returns nothing and just modifies the list.
We make a sorted copy called arr so we can read values in order while overwriting nums.
We store the length of nums in n, since we use it for indexing and looping.
Small starts at the last index of the smaller half, which includes the middle element when n is odd.
Large starts at the very last index of arr, pointing at the biggest value.
We loop over every position i in nums from zero up to n minus one.
Even positions are the low slots, so we check whether i is even.
We place the current small value into this even slot, taking from the smaller half.
We move small one step left so the next even slot gets the next smaller value.
Otherwise the position is odd, which is a high slot that must exceed its neighbors.
We place the current large value into this odd slot, taking from the larger half.
We move large one step left so the next odd slot gets the next smaller large value, keeping duplicates apart.

word-break-ii.hook: Find every way to split a string into dictionary words, without re-solving the same suffix twice.
word-break-ii.ask: Given a string and a list of dictionary words, insert spaces to form sentences where every piece is a dictionary word. Words can repeat. Return all such sentences in any order.
word-break-ii.exampleWhy: cat + sand + dog and cats + and + dog both use only dictionary words.

brute.idea: Plain backtracking: at each index try every prefix that is a word and recurse on the rest, recomputing shared suffixes.
steps: Start at index 0
Try each word that matches here
Recurse on what remains
Reaching the end records a sentence
brute.whySlow: Inputs like aaaa...ab with words a, aa, aaa re-explore the same failing suffix exponentially many times.

optimal.insight: The sentences for a suffix never depend on how we reached it. Memoize each start index's list of sentences and reuse it.
steps: dfs(i) returns all sentences for s[i:]
Try every dictionary word starting at i
Prefix that word onto each sentence of dfs(j)
Cache dfs(i) so each suffix is solved once

pitfalls: Output can be exponential, so no method beats exponential worst case; memo prunes dead suffixes.
Base case must be [''] not [], or nothing gets built.

say.intro: Okay, Word Break Two. We get a string and a dictionary. We must return every way to split the string into dictionary words. Take cats and dog, run together. With words like cat, cats, sand, and, and dog, there are two sentences. Cat sand dog. And cats and dog.
say.brute: The first idea is plain backtracking. Stand at an index, try every prefix that's a dictionary word, and recurse on the rest. Reach the end, and record a sentence. So what's the problem? Repetition. A long run of the same letter makes us revisit the same dead end suffix, an exponential number of times.
say.insight: Here's the thing. The sentences for a suffix never depend on how we got there. So write a function that returns every sentence for the string starting at index i. And cache it. Each suffix is solved once. Failing suffixes are remembered as empty lists. So we never explore them again.
say.anim: We start with the word set built, and call dfs starting at index zero. At index zero, cat matches, so we recurse into index three to find the rest. At index three, sand matches, leading us to recurse into index seven. At index seven, dog matches the end, so memo for seven becomes just dog. Back at index three, sand plus dog combines into sand dog, cached in memo. Back at index zero, cat plus sand dog gives our first full sentence. Trying cats at index four, and matches then dog, giving and dog cached at four. Combining cats with and dog produces the second sentence, cats and dog. Final answer returned: cat sand dog and cats and dog, built by reusing memoized suffixes.
say.code: Now the code. We put the words in a set. The memo starts with the end of the string. An empty suffix gives one empty sentence. In the search, if the suffix is already solved, reuse it. Otherwise, try every end index. If the prefix is a dictionary word, we take every sentence for the remainder, and attach the word in front. Then we cache this suffix's sentences, and return them.
say.outro: The pattern is backtracking with memoization. When a search keeps reaching the same suffix, cache it.

word-break-ii.title: Word Break II
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container the problem expects for our method.
The wordBreak method takes the string s and the list of dictionary words, and returns every valid sentence.
We turn the word list into a set so checking whether a piece is a word takes constant time.
We create a memo dictionary seeded so that the end of the string maps to a list holding one empty sentence.
We define a helper dfs that returns all sentences that can be built from the suffix starting at index i.
We check whether this start index is already in memo, since its answer never depends on how we arrived.
If it is cached, we return the stored list immediately and skip all repeated work.
Otherwise we start an empty list called out to collect sentences for this suffix.
We try every end position j after i, so each candidate piece runs from i up to j.
We slice out the candidate piece w from index i up to but not including j.
We only continue if that piece is an actual dictionary word.
For each sentence that the rest of the string starting at j can form, we loop over it.
We join w to that rest with a space, or use w alone when rest is empty at the string's end.
We store the finished list in memo for index i so future calls reuse it.
We return the list of sentences for this start index.
We start the search at index zero and return all sentences for the whole string.

word-ladder-ii.hook: Not one shortest path but all of them. BFS finds the layers, backtracking spells out every route.
word-ladder-ii.ask: Change beginWord into endWord one letter at a time, where every intermediate word must be in the word list. Return every shortest sequence of words, or an empty list if no sequence exists.
word-ladder-ii.exampleWhy: Both routes take four one-letter changes; no route to cog is shorter.

brute.idea: DFS every simple path from beginWord, keep those reaching endWord, then return the ones with minimum length.
steps: DFS from beginWord, marking words on the path
Try every unused word one letter away
Record each path that reaches endWord
Keep only the shortest recorded paths
brute.whySlow: It enumerates every simple path, not just shortest ones; a dense word list has exponentially many.

optimal.insight: BFS by layers gives every word its shortest distance. Record each word's parents from the previous layer, then backtrack from endWord.
steps: Bucket words by wildcard pattern, like h*t
BFS one whole layer at a time
Neighbours share a bucket; record every parent
Mark the layer seen only after finishing it
Backtrack parents from endWord to list paths

codeNotes.match: while layer and endWord not in parents:
codeNotes.note: Stop once endWord's layer is done
Keep every parent, not just one

pitfalls: Removing words as soon as they are seen loses parents in the same layer.
Backtrack only over the parent graph, never the full word graph.

say.intro: Okay, Word Ladder Two. We change one word into another, one letter at a time. Every word in between must be in the list. But this time, we return every shortest sequence. Not just its length. From hit to cog, there are two. Through dot and dog. Or through lot and log.
say.brute: The first idea is a depth first search over every simple path. From the start, step to any unused word one letter away. Record each path that reaches the target. At the end, keep only the shortest. It's correct. But it explores every path of every length. And a dense word list has exponentially many.
say.insight: Here's the trick. Split the job in two. Breadth first search moves one whole layer at a time. So the first layer that reaches a word gives its shortest distance. As we go, we record every parent in the previous layer that leads to each new word. Then a small backtracking walk over those parents spells out every shortest path.
say.anim: We start with hit as beginWord and cog as endWord, confirming cog is in the word list. The code builds wildcard buckets, grouping words like hot and dot under pattern star o t. BFS begins at layer hit, exploring one letter changes to find neighbors like hot. From hot we expand to dot and lot, recording hot as their parent in this layer. Next layer is dot and lot, which lead to dog, log, and eventually cog, their shortest distance. Parents now map dog to dot and log to lot, tracking every shortest path backward. Cog is reached, so BFS stops since endWord now has recorded parents. Backtracking from cog through dog, dot, hot, and hit, then through log, lot, and hot again, builds both shortest ladders: hit hot dot dog cog, and hit hot lot log cog.
say.code: Now the code. First, we group words that are one letter apart into wildcard buckets. Then we run layer by layer, and stop once the target's layer is done. For each word in the layer, we scan its buckets, and collect unseen words. We keep every parent, not just one. Only after the whole layer do we mark those words seen. Finally, a helper walks parents back to the start word.
say.outro: Advanced graphs: breadth first search for shortest distances, plus a parent map and backtracking to list every path.

word-ladder-ii.title: Word Ladder II
lineNotes: We define the Solution class that holds the method required by the problem.
The findLadders method takes the begin word, the end word, and the list of allowed words.
If the end word is not in the word list, no valid ladder can exist.
So we return an empty list right away in that case.
We store the word length as n, since every word has the same length.
We create a dictionary of buckets mapping each wildcard pattern to the words that match it.
We loop over every word in the word list to build those patterns.
For each position in the word, we will make one wildcard pattern.
We replace that letter with a star and add the word to the matching bucket, which lets us find neighbors quickly.
The parents dictionary will record, for each word, which previous-layer words lead to it on a shortest path.
The seen set starts with the begin word so we never revisit words from earlier layers.
The current layer starts as just the begin word.
We keep expanding layers until the layer is empty or the end word has been reached.
The next dictionary collects words discovered in this layer, mapped to their parents.
We go through each word in the current layer.
For each word, we try replacing each letter position with a wildcard.
We look up the bucket for that pattern to get all neighbor words, defaulting to empty.
We only consider neighbors that were not seen in earlier layers, which keeps paths shortest.
We add the current word as a parent of the candidate, keeping every parent so all shortest paths survive.
After the layer finishes, we mark all newly found words as seen, so same-layer words can still share parents.
We merge the new parent links into the main parents dictionary.
The next layer is the list of words just discovered.
We prepare the result list to hold all shortest ladders.
We define a recursive helper that backtracks from a word toward the begin word using parents.
When the current word equals the begin word, the path is complete.
We reverse the path, since we built it from end to start, and add it to the results.
Then we return to explore other branches.
Otherwise we loop over every parent of the current word.
We recurse into each parent, appending it to the path so each branch gets its own copy.
We only backtrack if the end word was actually reached during the search.
We start the backtracking from the end word with a path containing just it.
Finally we return all the shortest ladders found, or an empty list if none.

word-pattern.hook: a b b a versus dog cat cat dog. A one-to-one match needs two maps, not one.
word-pattern.ask: Given a pattern of letters and a string of words, return true if there is a one-to-one match: each letter always maps to the same word, and no two letters share a word.
word-pattern.exampleWhy: a always means dog, b means cat, c means fish, and no word is claimed by two letters.

brute.idea: Compare every pair of positions: two letters are equal exactly when the two words at those positions are equal.
steps: Split s into words; lengths must match
For every pair of positions i < j
Letters equal must mean words equal
Any mismatch: return False
brute.whySlow: Checking all pairs is quadratic; 300 positions means about 45,000 comparisons instead of 300.

optimal.insight: A bijection needs checking in both directions. Keep a letter-to-word map and a word-to-letter map, and reject any conflict.
steps: Split s; different counts means false
Walk letters and words together
Letter seen with a different word? false
Word seen with a different letter? false
Record both directions and continue

codeNotes.match: if c2w.get(c, w) != w or w2c.get(w, c) != c:

pitfalls: One map alone wrongly accepts abba against dog dog dog dog.
Check the word count first, or zip silently drops extras.

say.intro: Okay, Word Pattern. We get a pattern of letters, and a sentence of words. Do they match one to one? Pattern a b c b a, sentence dog cat fish cat dog. a is always dog. b is always cat. c is fish. And no word belongs to two letters. So the answer is true.
say.brute: The first idea compares every pair of positions. Two letters should be equal exactly when the two words are equal. If any pair breaks that rule, return false. It's correct, since it checks both directions at once. But it's quadratic. Three hundred positions means about forty five thousand comparisons.
say.insight: Here's the thing. A one to one match must be checked in both directions. One map, from letters to words, catches a letter changing its word. But what about two letters claiming the same word? That needs a second map, from words to letters. With both maps, one pass settles it.
say.anim: We split the sentence into five words matching the five letters in the pattern. Two empty maps are created to link letters to words and words back to letters. Letter a pairs with dog, no conflict found, so we record a maps to dog and dog maps to a. Letter b pairs with cat, again no conflict, so b maps to cat and cat maps to b. Letter c pairs with fish, still consistent, so c maps to fish and fish maps to c. Letter b reappears with cat, matching the earlier mapping, so it passes cleanly again. Letter a reappears with dog, matching the stored mapping, confirming the bijection holds. All pairs matched consistently both ways, so the function returns true.
say.code: Now the code. First, the counts must line up. If the number of words differs from the pattern length, return false. Then we make one map per direction. Walk the letters and words together. If either direction conflicts, reject. Otherwise, record letter to word, and word to letter. If we make it through, return true.
say.outro: Linear time and space. Arrays and hashing: a one to one match needs a map in each direction.

word-pattern.title: Word Pattern
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container the problem expects for our method.
The method wordPattern takes the pattern string and the string s of words, and returns true or false.
We split s on whitespace to get a list of words we can compare against pattern letters.
If the number of words differs from the pattern length, a one-to-one match is impossible.
So in that case we immediately return false.
We create two empty maps: one from letter to word, and one from word to letter.
We loop over pattern letters and words together, pairing each letter with the word in the same position.
Using default values, we reject if the letter already maps to a different word or the word already maps to a different letter.
When either mapping conflicts, the bijection is broken, so we return false.
Otherwise we record that this letter maps to this word.
We also record that this word maps back to this letter, keeping both directions in sync.
If the loop finishes with no conflicts, every pairing is consistent, so we return true.

word-subsets.hook: Every word in words2 must fit inside. Merge them into one requirement, then check each candidate once.
word-subsets.ask: A word b is a subset of word a if every letter of b, counted with repeats, appears in a. Return every word in words1 that contains every word in words2 this way, in any order.
word-subsets.exampleWhy: Both need one l, one o and one e; google and leetcode have all three, the others miss one.

brute.idea: For every word in words1, count its letters, then check every word in words2 against that count.
steps: Count letters of a word a
For each b in words2, count its letters
Any letter short? a is not universal
Otherwise keep a
brute.whySlow: 10,000 by 10,000 words means a hundred million subset checks, repeating the same words2 work each time.

optimal.insight: All of words2 collapses into one requirement: for each letter, the maximum count any single word in words2 needs.
steps: For each b, count its letters
Keep the per-letter maximum across all b
Count each word a in words1
Keep a if it meets every maximum

codeNotes.note: Merged requirement for all of words2

codeNotes.match: if all(cnt[i] >= need[i] for i in range(26)):

pitfalls: Summing counts across words2 is wrong: lo and eo need one o, not two.

say.intro: Okay, Word Subsets. A word fits inside another if every letter, counting repeats, is there. We return the words from the first list that contain every word in the second list. Our requirements are lo and eo. Only google and leetcode qualify.
say.brute: The first idea checks every pair. For each candidate, count its letters. Then count every word in the second list, and make sure the candidate has enough of each. It works. But with ten thousand words on each side, that's a hundred million checks. And we redo the same second list work over and over.
say.insight: Here's the thing. The whole second list collapses into one requirement. For each letter, we only need the largest count any single word asks for. Lo needs one o. Eo needs one o. Together? Still just one o, not two. Then each candidate gets checked once, against that merged table.
say.anim: We start building a combined requirement array, need, from every word in words2. Processing lo, we count its letters, then merge them into need by taking maximums. Now processing eo, we count its letters and merge again, updating need for o and e. With need finalized as needing one l, two o's, and one e, we scan words1 one by one. Amazon, apple, and facebook each get counted but fail to meet the required letter counts. Google's counts satisfy every requirement in need, so it gets added to the result. Leetcode also meets all letter requirements and joins google in the results list. The function returns google and leetcode as the final answer.
say.code: Now the code. We start a need array of twenty six zeros. That's the merged requirement for the whole second list. For each word there, count its letters, and take the max, not the sum, per letter. Then for each candidate, count its letters. If it meets every letter requirement, it's universal. So we add it to the result.
say.outro: Linear in the total letters, constant extra space. Arrays and hashing: merge many requirements into one frequency table.

word-subsets.title: Word Subsets
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container the problem expects for our method.
The method wordSubsets takes the two word lists and returns the words from the first list that qualify.
We create need, a list of 26 zeros, to hold the maximum count required for each letter.
We loop over every word b in words2 to fold its requirements into need.
For each word b we start a fresh count list of 26 zeros.
We walk through each letter of b to count its letters.
We convert the letter to an index from zero to twenty-five and add one to its count.
Now we go through all 26 letter positions to merge this word's counts into need.
For each letter, need keeps the larger of its current value and this word's count, since one word must cover the maximum.
We create an empty result list to collect the qualifying words.
We loop over every candidate word a in words1.
We make a fresh 26-slot count list for the letters in a.
We go through each letter of a to tally it.
We bump the count for that letter's index by one.
We check that for all 26 letters, a has at least as many as need requires.
If the check passes, a is universal, so we add it to the result.
After checking every word, we return the list of universal words.

zero-array-transformation-ii.hook: Which prefix of queries is enough? Sweep the array once, pulling in queries only when an index needs them.
zero-array-transformation-ii.ask: Each query [l, r, val] may lower every value in positions l to r by up to val. Return the smallest k so that the first k queries can turn nums into all zeros, or -1 if none can.
zero-array-transformation-ii.exampleWhy: Two queries each give positions 0 and 2 one unit, exactly covering their value 2.

brute.idea: For each k from 0 upward, add up how much the first k queries can lower each index and check every index is covered.
steps: Sum coverage of the first k queries
Every nums[i] ≤ coverage[i]? return k
No k works: return -1
brute.whySlow: Each candidate k rebuilds coverage from scratch; 100,000 queries means about ten billion operations.

optimal.insight: Sweep indices left to right with a difference array. Only when index i is under-covered, apply the next query; k never moves backward.
steps: Walk index i with running coverage
While coverage < nums[i], apply query k
Queries starting after i only fill diff
Out of queries while short? return -1
End of array: return k

codeNotes.note: Ranges ending before i are useless now
Start counting from the sweep point

pitfalls: Binary search on k with a difference array also works in O((n + q) log q).
A query starting before i must be clipped to i, not dropped.

say.intro: Okay, Zero Array Transformation Two. Each query lets us lower every value in a range by up to some amount. We want the fewest queries, taken in order from the start, that can drive the whole array to zero. For two, zero, two with these queries, the answer is two.
say.brute: The first idea tries every k from zero upward. For each one, apply the first k queries with a difference array. Sweep the coverage, and check every index. The first k that works is the answer. But each k rebuilds everything from scratch. So with many queries, the work grows quadratically.
say.insight: Here's the thing. We can sweep the indices just once. Keep a running coverage at the current index. Coverage too small? Pull in the next query. Queries are only ever added, so k never moves backward. And notice, a query ending before this index can't help anymore. The rest get clipped to start right here.
say.anim: We start with nums and queries, and build a difference array of zeros to track coverage. At index zero, nums needs two, so we apply the first query, adding one from index zero to two. Still under-covered at index zero, we apply the second query, boosting diff to two there. Now cur becomes two, matching nums at index zero, so we move on. At index one, cur already covers the required zero, no new query needed. At index two, cur plus diff already meets nums, so we skip ahead again. All indices are satisfied using only two queries, so k stops at two. The function returns two, the minimum number of queries needed to zero out nums.
say.code: Now the code. A difference array handles range adds. For each index, while it's still under covered, we take the next query. Out of queries? Then it's impossible, so return minus one. A query whose range ends before this index is useless now, so we skip it. Otherwise, we start counting its value from the sweep point. Then we update the running coverage at this index. Finally, return k.
say.outro: Linear time in the array plus the queries. Two pointers, with a sweep line and a difference array.

zero-array-transformation-ii.title: Zero Array Transformation II
lineNotes: We define the Solution class that holds the method for this problem.
The method takes nums and queries and returns the smallest number of queries needed, or negative one.
We store the length of nums in n so we can size our arrays and loop.
We create a difference array of size n plus one, all zeros, to record range additions cheaply.
We set cur, the running total of coverage, and k, the count of queries used, both to zero.
We sweep through each index i of nums from left to right.
While the coverage at index i is less than nums at i, we still need more queries.
If we have already used every query, no answer exists, so the situation is hopeless.
So we return negative one because even all queries cannot zero out this position.
We take the next query and unpack its left, right, and value.
We advance k by one, since this query now counts as used.
We only apply the query if its range reaches index i, otherwise it is useless here.
We add the value at the later of l and i, since earlier positions are already handled.
We subtract the value just past r so the effect stops after the right end.
After the loop settles, we fold diff at i into cur so coverage carries to the next index.
Once every index is covered enough, we return k as the minimum number of queries.

check-if-there-is-a-path-with-equal-numb.ask: Walk a grid of zeros and ones from the top-left corner to the bottom-right, moving only right or down. Return true if some path visits exactly as many zeros as ones.

brute.idea: Try every right-or-down path with DFS, keeping a running balance of ones minus zeros. Succeed if any path ends balanced.
steps: Start at the top-left with balance 0
Add 1 for a one, subtract 1 for a zero
Branch right and down
At the corner, check balance is 0
brute.whySlow: The number of paths explodes combinatorially: a 20 by 20 grid already has about 35 billion of them.

codeNotes.note: Odd path length can never split evenly
Fewest ones to reach this cell
Most ones to reach this cell
Half the path must be ones
Every count in between is reachable

check-if-there-is-a-path-with-equal-numb.exampleWhy: Every path covers 6 cells. Right, down, down, right, right picks up 0,1,1,0,1,0: three ones and three zeros.
check-if-there-is-a-path-with-equal-numb.hook: Track only the fewest and the most ones any path can collect. Everything in between comes free.

optimal.insight: Neighbouring paths differ by one cell, so their ones-counts differ by at most 1. Every count between the minimum and maximum is reachable.
steps: Odd path length? Equal split is impossible
lo[r][c] = fewest ones on any path to this cell
hi[r][c] = most ones on any path to this cell
Both come from the cell above or to the left
Answer: half the path length lies within lo and hi

pitfalls: Checking only the min or only the max path misses answers in between.
Forgetting the odd-length check: then no target is exactly half.

say.intro: Okay, so we have a grid of zeros and ones. We walk from the top left corner to the bottom right, only moving right or down. Can some path see exactly as many zeros as ones? Here every path covers six cells. And going right, then down twice, then right twice, picks up three ones. So the answer is true.
say.brute: The obvious approach tries every path. A depth first search branches right and down, keeping a running balance. Plus one for a one, minus one for a zero. If any path reaches the corner with balance zero, we're done. It's correct. But the number of paths explodes. A twenty by twenty grid has about thirty five billion of them.
say.insight: Here's the key observation. Take two paths that differ by swapping a single corner. Their counts of ones differ by at most one. And you can morph the lowest path into the highest path one swap at a time. So every count between the minimum and the maximum is reachable. We only need two numbers per cell. The fewest ones, and the most ones.
say.anim: We start with a 3 by 4 grid, setting up to track min and max ones counts. Lo and hi grids start at zero everywhere, tracking possible one counts per path. Moving along the top row, lo and hi both grow to 1, 1, 1 as ones accumulate. Row one begins, inheriting values from above since only one path exists at column zero. At column one, lo stays 1 but hi jumps to 2, showing two possible path counts now. Lower rows merge paths from above and left, letting lo and hi diverge further apart. By row two column two, lo reaches 2 while hi reaches 3, widening the possible range. Target is 3, and since lo is 3 and hi is 3 at the end, the function returns true.
say.code: Now the code. First, an odd path length can never split evenly, so return false. Then two tables, lo and hi. The first row only looks left, the first column only looks up. Everywhere else we take the min and the max of the two neighbours, then add the cell itself. Finally, half the path length must sit between the low and the high.
say.outro: Linear in the grid size instead of exponential. The pattern is two dimensional dynamic programming. Track the range, not every value.

check-if-there-is-a-path-with-equal-numb.title: Check if There is a Path With Equal Number of 0's And 1's
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, as the problem platform expects.
The method isThereAPath takes the grid and returns true or false depending on whether a balanced path exists.
We read the number of rows as m and the number of columns as n.
Every path visits m plus n minus one cells, so if that count is odd, no equal split is possible.
In that odd case we return false immediately.
We build a table lo, the same size as the grid, to hold the minimum ones count of any path to each cell.
We build a matching table hi to hold the maximum ones count of any path to each cell.
We loop over every row in order so earlier cells are computed before later ones.
Inside each row we loop over every column, moving left to right.
For the top row beyond the first cell, the only way in is from the left.
So lo and hi for this cell are copied from the cell on its left.
For the left column beyond the first cell, the only way in is from above.
So lo and hi here are copied from the cell directly above.
For all other cells, we can arrive from above or from the left.
The minimum ones count is the smaller of the two incoming minimums.
The maximum ones count is the larger of the two incoming maximums.
We add this cell's value to lo, counting a one if the cell holds one.
We add the same value to hi, so both bounds include the current cell.
The target is half the path length, which is the number of ones we need.
Since every count between minimum and maximum is reachable, we return whether the target lies within that range at the bottom-right cell.

design-excel-sum-formula.ask: Build a tiny spreadsheet. set writes a number into a cell, get reads a cell, and sum makes a cell equal the sum of cells and ranges. Formulas stay live: changing a source changes the total.

brute.idea: Store each formula as the raw list of strings. Every get re-parses them, expands every range and recurses on each cell.
steps: sum just saves the strings
get splits each string into a range
Recurse on every cell in every range
brute.whySlow: Every read re-parses text and walks overlapping ranges cell by cell; A1 inside A1:B2 is evaluated twice instead of once with weight 2.

codeNotes.note: A plain value overwrites any formula
Follow each edge, scaled by its weight
Duplicates merge into one weighted edge
Store the formula, not a frozen value

design-excel-sum-formula.exampleWhy: C3 = A1 + A1:B2 counts A1 twice: 2 + 2 = 4. After B2 becomes 2, C3 recomputes to 6.
design-excel-sum-formula.hook: A spreadsheet is a dependency graph. Store each formula as weighted edges and evaluate on demand.

optimal.insight: A formula is just weighted edges: cell → count. Parse ranges once at sum time, merge duplicates, and evaluate lazily through the graph.
steps: Plain cells keep a number in a grid
sum expands ranges once into a Counter of cells
get on a formula recurses: weight times source value
set deletes any formula, so the cell is plain again

pitfalls: Caching the sum as a number breaks when a source cell changes later.
set must erase the old formula, or get keeps returning the stale sum.

say.intro: Okay, Design Excel Sum Formula. We build a tiny spreadsheet. Set writes a number, get reads a cell, and sum makes a cell a live formula. In our example, A1 is two. C3 becomes A1 plus the range A1 to B2. That counts A1 twice, so four. Then B2 becomes two, and C3 reads six.
say.brute: The simplest version just saves the formula strings. Every time we read the cell, we re parse each string, expand every range, and recurse on each cell inside. It is correct. But every read repeats the parsing. And overlapping ranges walk the same cell again and again, like A1 here, evaluated twice instead of once.
say.insight: Here's the shift. A formula is really a set of edges in a dependency graph. This cell depends on that cell, some number of times. So at sum time, expand the ranges once into a counter. A1 gets weight two, B1, A2 and B2 get weight one. Reading a cell then follows each edge, multiplied by its weight.
say.anim: We create a three row, three column Excel sheet, sizing the grid for columns up to C. Set writes value 2 into cell A1, clearing any formula stored there. Sum at C3 parses tokens A1 and A1:B2, counting how many times each cell is referenced. After parsing, weights show A1 counted twice, and A2, B1, B2 each counted once. Evaluating C3 sums each weighted cell: A1 is 2, others are zero, giving total 4. Setting B2 to 2 updates the grid directly, bypassing any formula. Re-evaluating C3 reuses the same weights, now multiplying B2's new value of 2 in. The formula recomputes to 6, which is the final answer returned for get C3.
say.code: Let's walk the code. Set drops any formula, then writes the value. Evaluate checks for a formula. No formula? Just read the grid. Otherwise loop over the edges and add weight times the source's value, recursively. Sum splits each token on a colon, loops over the rectangle, and bumps each cell's weight. Then it stores the counter, and evaluates it.
say.outro: The pattern is graphs. A spreadsheet is a dependency graph, and lazy evaluation keeps every formula live.

design-excel-sum-formula.title: Design Excel Sum Formula
lineNotes: We define the Excel class, which will hold cell values and live formulas for a small spreadsheet.
The constructor takes the height and a width letter that marks the last column.
We turn the width letter into a column count by measuring its distance from the letter A, plus one.
We build a grid of zeros with one row per height and one column per column count.
We create an empty dictionary that maps formula cells to their weighted source cells.
The set method writes a plain number into a cell given a row, a column letter, and a value.
We convert the one based row and letter column into a zero based pair of row and column indexes.
We remove any formula on that cell, because a plain number should replace the formula.
We store the new value into the grid at the cell's row and column.
The get method reads the current value of a cell.
We convert the cell coordinates and evaluate it, so formulas are computed fresh each time.
The evaluate method computes a cell's value, following formula edges through the graph lazily.
If the cell has no formula, it is a plain cell.
In that case we simply return the number stored in the grid.
Otherwise we start a running total at zero for the formula's result.
We loop over each source cell in the formula along with how many times it appears.
We add the source's evaluated value times its weight, recursing so nested formulas stay live.
We return the total as the cell's value.
The sum method turns a list of cells and ranges into a formula for the target cell.
We make a counter to merge duplicate cells, so each source gets a weight equal to its count.
We go through each token, which is either a single cell or a range.
We split the token at the colon, so a single cell leaves the last part empty.
If there is no last part, we reuse the first, treating a single cell as a one cell range.
We parse the top left corner into a zero based row and column index.
We parse the bottom right corner the same way.
We loop over every row in the range.
Within each row, we loop over every column in the range.
We add one to the weight of that cell, which merges overlapping references.
We compute the zero based coordinates of the target cell that will hold the formula.
We save the weights as that cell's formula, replacing any older formula.
We evaluate the target cell and return its current sum.

employee-free-time.ask: Each employee has a sorted list of busy intervals. Return the finite intervals of time when every employee is free, sorted by start.

brute.idea: Pour every interval into one list, sort it by start, then sweep and record any gap after the running end.
steps: Flatten all employees into one list
Sort everything by start time
Gap after the running end? Record it
brute.whySlow: It throws away the fact that each employee's list is already sorted, paying a full N log N sort instead of N log K.

codeNotes.note: One entry per employee: start, who, which
Nobody busy in between: free time

employee-free-time.exampleWhy: Together they are busy from 1 to 5, 6 to 7, and 9 to 12, so everyone is free from 5 to 6 and 7 to 9.
employee-free-time.hook: Each employee's calendar is already sorted. Merge them like K sorted lists and read off the gaps.

meta.name: employeeFreeTime

optimal.insight: This is merging K sorted lists. A min-heap holding each employee's next interval yields all intervals in start order, at log K each.
steps: Seed the heap with each employee's first interval
Pop the earliest start
Start beyond the running end? That gap is free
