Extend the running end, push that employee's next

pitfalls: Use start > prev_end, not ≥: touching intervals leave no free time.
Take max for the running end; a short interval can sit inside a longer one.

say.intro: Okay, Employee Free Time. Every employee has a sorted list of busy intervals. We want the windows when nobody is busy. Here, between them, people are busy from one to five, six to seven, and nine to twelve. So the common free time is five to six, and seven to nine.
say.brute: The simple approach throws everything into one big list. Sort it by start time. Then sweep, keeping the furthest end so far. If the next start is past that end, that gap is free. It works, and it's not terrible. But it ignores something we were given for free. Each employee's list is already sorted, and we pay a full sort anyway.
say.insight: So what does that remind you of? Merging K sorted lists. Keep a min heap with just the next interval from each employee. Pop the earliest one, then push that employee's following interval. The heap never holds more than K items, so each step costs log K, not log N.
say.anim: We build a heap from each employee's first interval, tracking start time, employee, and index. The heap now holds the three earliest starts, ordered one, two, two. We pop the smallest start, one, and since it's not past prev_end, no gap yet. Prev_end updates to three, and we push employee zero's next interval, starting at six. We keep popping starts two and two, merging employees one and two, prev_end reaches five. Popping start six finds a gap since six is greater than five, so we record five to six. Popping start nine finds another gap since nine is greater than seven, recording seven to nine. The heap empties and the final free time intervals are five six and seven nine.
say.code: Now the code. The heap holds a start, the employee, and which interval. We seed the running end with the earliest start. Each loop pops the earliest interval. If its start is past the running end, nobody is busy in between, so record the gap. Then stretch the running end with max. Finally, push the same employee's next interval, if there is one.
say.outro: N log K time, K extra space. The pattern is heaps, merging K sorted lists, with an interval sweep on top.

employee-free-time.title: Employee Free Time
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, the standard wrapper for this problem's method.
The method takes each employee's sorted busy intervals and returns the gaps when everyone is free.
We build a heap holding each employee's first interval start, along with the employee index and interval index, skipping empty schedules.
Heapify turns that list into a min-heap so the earliest starting interval always comes out first.
If the heap is empty, nobody has any busy time at all.
So we return an empty list, since there are no finite free intervals.
We start with an empty free list and set prev_end to the earliest start, the beginning of busy time.
We loop until the heap is empty, which means every interval has been processed in start order.
We pop the interval with the smallest start, remembering which employee and which interval it came from.
If this start is later than prev_end, nobody is busy in between, so a gap exists.
We record that gap from prev_end to this start as common free time.
We extend prev_end to the larger of itself and this interval's end, tracking the furthest busy time so far.
If this employee has another interval, we need to feed it into the heap.
We push that employee's next interval, keyed by its start, so the heap always holds one per employee.
After all intervals are merged, we return the collected free time gaps.

find-leaves-of-binary-tree.ask: Repeatedly collect all the leaves of a binary tree and remove them, until the tree is empty. Return the values collected in each round.

brute.idea: Simulate it literally. Each round, walk the whole tree, collect the leaves and cut them off. Repeat until the root is gone.
steps: Walk the tree, collect current leaves
Detach those leaves from their parents
Repeat until the tree is empty
brute.whySlow: Each round rewalks the entire remaining tree. A chain of 100 nodes needs 100 rounds, about 5,000 node visits.

codeNotes.note: So a leaf lands at height 0
First node of a new round

find-leaves-of-binary-tree.exampleWhy: Round one removes leaves 4, 7, 6. Then 5 and 3 become leaves, then 2, then the root 1.
find-leaves-of-binary-tree.hook: Peeling leaves round by round sounds like simulation. It is really just each node's height.

optimal.insight: A node is removed in round h, where h is its height: leaves are 0, a parent is 1 + max of its children. One post-order pass.
steps: Null child has height -1
Compute both children's heights first
Height = 1 + max of the two
Append the value to result[height]

find-leaves-of-binary-tree.optimalCode:
class Solution:
    def findLeaves(self, root: Optional[TreeNode]) -> List[List[int]]:
        result = []

        def getHeight(node):
            # 1. Null child has height -1
            if not node:
                return -1

            # 2. Compute both children's heights first
            leftHeight = getHeight(node.left)
            rightHeight = getHeight(node.right)

            # 3. Height = 1 + max of the two
            height = 1 + max(leftHeight, rightHeight)

            # 4. Append the value to result[height]
            if height == len(result):
                result.append([])
            result[height].append(node.val)

            return height

        getHeight(root)
        return result
pitfalls: Depth from the root is wrong: removal round depends on distance to the deepest leaf below.
Returning 0 for null shifts every leaf into round one.

say.intro: Okay, Find Leaves of Binary Tree. We keep removing all the leaves, round after round, until the tree is gone. Here, round one takes four, seven and six. Now five and three are leaves, so they go next. Then two. Then finally the root, one.
say.brute: The literal approach just simulates it. Walk the whole tree, collect the leaves, and cut them off from their parents. Then do it again. It's correct, and the code is short. But every round rewalks everything that's left. A long chain of a hundred nodes needs a hundred rounds, around five thousand visits.
say.insight: So when does a node actually get removed? Only after everything below it is gone. A leaf goes in round zero. Its parent waits for the slower child, so its round is one plus the bigger child round. That's exactly the node's height. One post order pass computes every height, and the height is the bucket.
say.anim: We start the recursion at root node 1, with an empty result list. We dive down to node 4, whose children are null, giving it height zero. Node 4 is a leaf, so it's placed into result bucket zero. Node 7 is also a leaf, height zero, added alongside node 4. Node 5's child 7 gives it height one, so 5 joins bucket one. Node 2's higher child height two makes it go into bucket two. On the right side, leaf node 6 gets height zero, joining node 4 and 7. Node 3 gets height one from child 6, placed with node 5. Root node 1 gets height three, giving final answer four seven six, five three, two, one.
say.code: Let's walk the code. A missing child returns minus one, so a leaf comes out as zero. We compute both children first, then take one plus the max. If this height is a brand new round, we add an empty list. Then we drop the value into its round, and return the height to the parent.
say.outro: Linear time, one pass. The pattern is trees. Post order height turns a simulation into bucketing.

find-leaves-of-binary-tree.title: Find Leaves of Binary Tree
lineNotes: We define a Solution class that holds the method for solving the problem.
The findLeaves method takes the root of a binary tree and returns a list of lists of values.
We start with an empty result list where each index will hold the values removed in that round.
We define a helper called getHeight that walks the tree and returns each node's height.
This comment says a missing child has height negative one, so a leaf ends up with height zero.
If the current node is empty, we have reached past a leaf.
We return negative one so that one plus the max of the children gives zero for leaves.
This comment reminds us to handle both children before the node itself, which is post-order.
We recursively get the height of the left subtree first.
We then recursively get the height of the right subtree.
This comment states that a node's height is one more than its taller child.
We set height to one plus the larger of leftHeight and rightHeight, which is the round this node is removed.
This comment says the node's value goes into the group at index height.
If height equals the current length of result, no group exists yet for that round.
So we append a new empty list to result to hold values for this height.
We append the node's value to the group at its height index.
We return height so the parent can compute its own height from it.
We start the post-order traversal from the root, ignoring the return value since result is filled as a side effect.
Finally we return result, whose groups are ordered by removal round from leaves upward.

group-shifted-strings.ask: Shifting a string moves every letter forward by the same amount, wrapping z to a. Group together all strings that can be shifted into each other.

brute.idea: Keep a list of groups. For each string, compare it with the first member of every group, trying the implied shift.
steps: Take the next string
Compare with each group's first member
Same shift everywhere? Join that group
No match: start a new group
brute.whySlow: Every string is checked against every group. With 10,000 distinct families that is up to 100 million comparisons.

group-shifted-strings.exampleWhy: abc, bcd and xyz all step +1, +1. az and ba both step +25 with wrap-around. Single letters always match.
group-shifted-strings.hook: Shifting every letter keeps the gaps between neighbours the same. Those gaps are the group's fingerprint.

optimal.insight: A shift adds the same amount to every letter, so the gap between neighbours, mod 26, never changes. That gap tuple is a hash key.
steps: For each string, compute neighbour gaps mod 26
Use the tuple of gaps as the key
Append the string to its key's bucket
Return all buckets

pitfalls: Without mod 26, az and ba get gaps 25 and -1 and split apart.
Single letters all get the empty key, so they group together.

say.intro: Okay, Group Shifted Strings. Shifting a string moves every letter forward by the same amount, and z wraps back to a. We group strings that can shift into each other. So a b c, b c d, and x y z go together. A z and b a also match, thanks to the wrap.
say.brute: The straightforward way keeps a list of groups. For each new string, compare it with the first member of every group. Work out the shift from the first letters, then check every other letter. If it fits, join that group. Otherwise start a new one. Correct, but every string scans every group, so it's quadratic.
say.insight: Here's the trick. If you add the same shift to every letter, the gap between neighbouring letters doesn't change. A b c has gaps one and one. So does x y z. Take the gaps modulo twenty six, so the wrap is handled. That tuple of gaps is a fingerprint, and a hash map groups by it directly.
say.anim: We start with an empty groups dictionary and our list of strings to process. For abc, the letter gaps are one and one, giving key (1,1). Bcd also has gaps one and one, so it joins abc under the same key. Acef has gaps two, two, one, a unique key, starting its own group. Xyz shares key (1,1) too, since its gaps are also one and one. Az and ba both produce key (25,), the shift pattern for two letter pairs. Single letters a and z have empty keys, since there are no gaps to compare. Final answer groups them as abc bcd xyz, acef, az ba, and a z.
say.code: Now the code. A default dict maps each fingerprint to its strings. For each string, we build a tuple of neighbour gaps, each one taken modulo twenty six. Then we append the string to that key's bucket. At the end, every bucket is one group.
say.outro: Linear in the total number of characters. The pattern is arrays and hashing. Find an invariant, and use it as the key.

group-shifted-strings.title: Group Shifted Strings
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which holds the method that groups strings belonging to the same shift sequence.
The groupStrings method takes a list of strings and returns a list of groups, each group being mutually shiftable strings.
We create a default dictionary of lists, so each new key automatically starts with an empty group to append to.
We loop through every string in the input, handling each one once and placing it into the right group.
We build a key from the gaps between neighbouring letters, taken mod 26, which stays the same under any shift and handles wraparound.
We append the current string to the group stored under its gap key, so shiftable strings end up together.
Finally we return just the grouped lists from the dictionary, dropping the keys, as the required answer.

intersection-of-two-linked-lists.ask: Two singly linked lists may share a common tail. Return the first node they share, compared by identity not value, or null if they never meet. Do not modify the lists.

brute.idea: For every node of list A, walk all of list B and check whether any node is the very same object.
steps: Take node a from list A
Walk list B node by node
Same object? return a
brute.whySlow: Every node of A rescans all of B: two lists of 30,000 nodes need 900 million comparisons.

codeNotes.match: a = a.next if a else headB
codeNotes.note: Off the end: switch to B

codeNotes.match: b = b.next if b else headA
codeNotes.note: Off the end: switch to A

intersection-of-two-linked-lists.exampleWhy: After skipping 2 nodes of A and 3 of B, both reach the same node 8; the earlier 1s are different nodes.
intersection-of-two-linked-lists.hook: Two lists merge into one tail. Swap starting lines and both pointers meet at the join.

optimal.insight: Walking A then B covers the same total length as B then A. Two pointers doing that line up exactly at the junction.
steps: Start pointer a at headA, b at headB
Advance both one step at a time
When one runs off the end, restart it at the other head
They meet at the junction, or both at null

pitfalls: Comparing values fails: the two 1s are different nodes with equal values.
With no junction both pointers reach null together after n + m steps, so no infinite loop.

say.intro: Okay, so two linked lists might merge and share a tail. We return the first node they share. Same node in memory, not just an equal value. Here list A is four, one, eight, four, five. List B is five, six, one, eight, four, five. They join at node eight.
say.brute: The obvious way? For every node in A, walk the whole of B. Is any node the very same object? The first hit is the junction. No extra memory, which is nice. But it's quadratic. Two lists of thirty thousand nodes each? That's nine hundred million comparisons.
say.insight: So what's the real problem? The lists have different lengths before the junction. Here's the trick. One pointer walks A, then B. The other walks B, then A. Think about it. Both travel the same total distance. So the length difference cancels out, and they hit the junction on the same step. No junction? They both reach null together.
say.anim: Two pointers, a and b, start at the heads of list A and list B. They step forward together, comparing nodes, but they are not equal yet. When pointer a reaches the end of its list, it jumps to the start of list B. Similarly, when pointer b hits the end, it switches over to list A's head. This swap evens out the path lengths so both pointers travel the same total distance. Now a and b both point to the same node, node 8, so the loop stops. The function returns this shared node where the lists intersect. The final answer is that the lists intersect at node 8.
say.code: Let's walk the code. One pointer per list. We compare identity, not values. When a falls off the end, it switches to B. When b falls off, it switches to A. The loop stops at the junction, or at null if there isn't one.
say.outro: Linear time, constant space. Swap lists to equalise the path lengths. A neat two pointer trick, and a classic linked list pattern.

intersection-of-two-linked-lists.title: Intersection of Two Linked Lists
lineNotes: We define a solution class that holds the method for finding where two linked lists meet.
The method takes the heads of list A and list B and returns the shared node or nothing.
We start two pointers, a at the head of list A and b at the head of list B.
We loop until both pointers refer to the very same node, compared by identity, which may be null for both.
Pointer a steps forward, and when it falls off the end of A it jumps to the head of B.
Pointer b steps forward, and when it falls off the end of B it jumps to the head of A.
When the loop ends, a is either the first shared node or null, so we return it.

logger-rate-limiter.ask: Messages arrive with timestamps in order. Print a message only if the same message has not been printed in the last 10 seconds. Return true when it should print.

brute.idea: Keep a list of everything printed. For each new message, scan the whole history for the same text within 10 seconds.
steps: Scan every printed entry
Same message under 10 seconds ago? Block
Otherwise append it and print
brute.whySlow: The history only grows, so a million calls scan up to a million old entries each, almost all irrelevant.

codeNotes.note: Message → earliest time it may print
Unseen messages default to always allowed

logger-rate-limiter.exampleWhy: foo prints at 1, so it is blocked until 11. bar prints at 2 and is blocked at 8.
logger-rate-limiter.hook: You don't need the whole log. Just remember when each message is next allowed.

optimal.insight: Only one fact per message matters: the earliest time it may print again. A hash map stores exactly that, with O(1) lookups.
steps: Look up the message's next allowed time
Too early? Return false, change nothing
Otherwise set next allowed to timestamp + 10
Return true

pitfalls: Updating the time on a blocked call wrongly extends the window.
At exactly 10 seconds later the message is allowed again, so compare with <.

say.intro: Okay, Logger Rate Limiter. Messages stream in with timestamps. We print a message only if that same message hasn't printed in the last ten seconds. Here foo prints at one, so it's blocked at three and at ten. At eleven it's allowed again. Bar prints at two, and is blocked at eight.
say.brute: The obvious design keeps a list of everything we've printed. For each new message, scan the whole history. Same text, less than ten seconds ago? Block it. Otherwise append and print. It's correct. But the history only grows. After a million calls, each new call scans a million old entries, and almost all of them don't matter.
say.insight: So what do we actually need to know about a message? Just one number. The earliest time it's allowed to print again. A hash map from message to that time answers every query in constant time. And we only update it when we actually print.
say.anim: We start with an empty map tracking when each message can print again. At time one, foo has no recorded time, so it is allowed and next allowed becomes eleven. At time two, bar also has no entry, so it prints and its next allowed time becomes twelve. At time three, foo's allowed time is eleven, which is later, so it is blocked. At time eight, bar's allowed time is twelve, so it is still too early and blocked. At time ten, foo's allowed time is still eleven, so it gets blocked again. At time eleven, foo's allowed time equals eleven, so it is finally allowed to print. The final results are true, true, false, false, false, true, matching the expected output.
say.code: Now the code. The map stores, for each message, the earliest time it may print. If the timestamp is still below that, return false, and change nothing. A message we've never seen defaults to zero, so it always passes. Otherwise, open a fresh window ending ten seconds from now, and return true.
say.outro: Constant time per call. The pattern is arrays and hashing. Store only the state that decides the answer.

logger-rate-limiter.title: Logger Rate Limiter
lineNotes: We define a Logger class that will remember when each message was last printed.
The constructor runs once when a Logger is created to set up our storage.
We create an empty hash map that maps each message to the earliest time it may print again.
This method receives a timestamp and a message, and decides whether the message should be printed.
This comment says the first step is finding when this message is next allowed to print.
We look up the message in the map, defaulting to zero so unseen messages are always allowed.
This comment says that if the message comes too early, we reject it and leave the map untouched.
We check whether the timestamp is smaller than the allowed time, meaning ten seconds have not yet passed.
In that case we return false and skip updating, so the original allowed time stays in place.
This comment says that otherwise we push the next allowed time to ten seconds past now.
We store the timestamp plus ten as the message's new earliest print time in the map.
This comment says the last step is to report that the message should print.
We return true because the message passed the rate limit check and was recorded.

number-of-islands-ii.ask: An m by n grid starts as all water. Each position turns one cell into land. After every addition, report how many islands exist, where an island is land connected up, down, left or right.

brute.idea: After each addition, flood fill over all the land placed so far and count how many separate islands appear.
steps: Add the new cell to the land set
Flood fill from every unvisited land cell
Each fresh flood fill is one island
brute.whySlow: Every one of k additions re-walks all earlier land: 10,000 positions means about 50 million cell visits.

codeNotes.note: New land starts as its own island

number-of-islands-ii.exampleWhy: Cells 0,0 and 0,1 join; 1,2 and 2,1 stand alone, making three; then 1,1 touches all of them, leaving one.
number-of-islands-ii.hook: Land keeps appearing. Recounting the whole map every time is hopeless; union-find just merges.

optimal.insight: A new cell adds one island, and every merge with a different neighbouring island removes one. Union-find tells us instantly whether two cells already share an island.
steps: Skip a cell that is already land
Make it its own island: count goes up by one
For each land neighbour, find both roots
Different roots? Union them and count goes down
Record the count after each addition

pitfalls: Positions can repeat; re-adding a land cell must not bump the count.
Only decrement when roots differ: two neighbours may already share an island.

say.intro: Number of Islands two. The grid starts as all water, and land appears one cell at a time. After each new cell, how many islands are there? In our example, the first two cells join into one island. Two lonely cells push it to three. Then the centre cell touches everything, and we're back to one.
say.brute: The simple way is to recount from scratch. After every addition, flood fill over all the land so far, and count how many separate fills we start. That's correct. But every addition re-walks all the earlier land. With ten thousand additions, that's around fifty million visits.
say.insight: Here's the key. Adding a cell creates exactly one new island. Then each neighbour from a different island merges with it, and the count drops by one. So we never recount. We just need a fast way to ask, are these two cells already on the same island? That's exactly what union find answers, in nearly constant time.
say.anim: We start with an empty grid and will add land cells one at a time using union find. Cell zero zero is new land, forming its own island, so count becomes one. Cell zero one is added, but it neighbors zero zero, so the two islands merge, keeping count at one. Cell one two is isolated land, bumping the island count up to two. Cell two one is also isolated for now, raising the count to three. Cell one one joins in, then merges with neighbor two one, dropping count back to three. It also merges with zero one's island, shrinking count to two, then with one two, merging again to one. All cells connect into a single island, giving the final result one, one, two, three, one.
say.code: Find walks up to the root, halving the path as it goes. If a position is already land, we just repeat the count. Otherwise the cell becomes its own island, and the count goes up. Then for each neighbour that is land, we find both roots. If they differ, we hang the smaller tree under the larger, and the count goes down.
say.outro: Nearly constant time per addition. The pattern is graphs, with union find for connectivity that only ever grows.

number-of-islands-ii.title: Number of Islands II
lineNotes: We define a solution class that holds the method for this problem.
The method takes grid height m, width n, and the list of positions to turn into land, returning island counts.
We create two dictionaries, parent and size, which only contain cells that have become land.
We define find, which returns the representative root cell of the island containing a given cell.
We keep climbing while the current cell is not its own parent, meaning it is not yet a root.
Path compression happens here, pointing the cell to its grandparent so future lookups are shorter.
We then move up to that parent and continue the climb.
Once the loop ends we return the root, which identifies the island.
We start with an empty result list and an island count of zero.
We loop through each position, unpacking it into row r and column c.
If this cell is already land, adding it again changes nothing.
So we record the unchanged island count for this step.
Then we skip to the next position without doing any merging.
We make the new cell land by setting it as its own parent, forming a single-cell island.
We give that new island a size of one.
We add one to the island count, since the new cell starts as a separate island.
We loop over the four neighbors: down, up, right and left.
We only care about a neighbor if it is already land, meaning it appears in parent.
We find the roots of the new cell and the neighbor to see which islands they belong to.
If the roots differ, the two cells are in different islands and must be merged.
We compare island sizes so we can attach the smaller one under the larger one.
If the first is smaller, we swap a and b so that a is always the larger root.
We attach the smaller root b beneath the larger root a, merging the islands.
We add the smaller island's size to the larger one's total size.
Each real merge joins two islands into one, so we reduce the count by one.
After checking all neighbors, we record the current island count for this addition.
Finally we return the list of island counts after each operation.

serialize-and-deserialize-n-ary-tree.ask: Design a Codec for an N-ary tree, where each node can have any number of children. serialize turns the tree into a string, and deserialize turns that string back into exactly the same tree.

brute.idea: Write nested brackets, like 1[3[5[],6[]],2[],4[]], and rebuild by splitting each bracket body at top-level commas.
steps: Serialize: value, then children inside brackets
Deserialize: read value up to the first bracket
Split the body at depth-zero commas, recurse
brute.whySlow: Every level re-scans and copies its whole substring, so a deep chain of 10,000 nodes costs about 50 million character copies.

codeNotes.note: Child count pins down the shape
First token of a pair: value
Second token: how many subtrees follow

serialize-and-deserialize-n-ary-tree.exampleWhy: Root 1 has children 3, 2, 4, and 3 has children 5, 6. Serialize writes 1,3,3,2,5,0,6,0,2,0,4,0; deserialize rebuilds it.
serialize-and-deserialize-n-ary-tree.hook: Any number of children per node? Write each node's child count and the shape rebuilds itself.

meta.name: CodecDriver

optimal.insight: Write each node in preorder as a value plus its child count. The count tells the reader exactly how many subtrees to build, so no brackets or markers are needed.
steps: Serialize: preorder, write value then number of children
Join every token with commas
Deserialize: read a value and a count
Build that many children recursively, in order

pitfalls: Binary-tree null markers do not work directly; the child count replaces them.
Popping from the front of a list is O(n); use an iterator or index.

say.intro: Serialize and Deserialize an N-ary tree. Each node can have any number of children. We write the tree as a string, then read it back into the identical tree. In our example, root one has three children, and the first of those has two children of its own.
say.brute: A natural first try is nested brackets. Write the value, then its children inside square brackets. To read it back, split each bracket body at the commas that sit outside any inner brackets, and recurse. It works. But every level re-scans and copies its whole substring. On a deep tree, that's quadratic work.
say.insight: Here's the trick. Walk the tree in preorder, and next to each value write how many children it has. Now reading is easy. Take a value, take a count, then build exactly that many subtrees, one after another. The count does the job brackets did, and every token is read once.
say.anim: We start with root node 1, which has three children, about to be serialized. The depth first search writes node 1 and its child count 3 into the output list. It dives into child 3, recording value 3 then its own child count of 2. Node 5 and node 6 are written next, each followed by a 0 for no children. Back at the root, children 2 and 4 are appended with zero child counts too. The final serialized string is 1,3,3,2,5,0,6,0,2,0,4,0, encoding value then child count. Deserializing reads tokens in order, rebuilding node 1 then recursively its three children. Building finishes and returns node 1 with children 3, 2, and 4, matching the original tree.
say.code: In serialize, the depth first helper appends the value, then the number of children, then recurses into each child. We join everything with commas. In deserialize, we wrap the split tokens in an iterator, so each one is consumed exactly once. Build reads a value, makes the node, then reads the count and builds that many children.
say.outro: Linear time and space. The pattern is trees: a preorder walk, where storing the child count makes the shape unambiguous.

serialize-and-deserialize-n-ary-tree.title: Serialize and Deserialize N-ary Tree
lineNotes: We define the Codec class, which holds both the serialize and deserialize methods for the N-ary tree.
The serialize method takes the root node and will return the whole tree as a single string.
If the root is empty, there is no tree to write down.
So we return an empty string, which deserialize will later recognize as an empty tree.
We create an empty list called out to collect the pieces of text in preorder.
We define a helper called dfs that visits one node and then all of its descendants.
We append the node's value as text, since the final string is built by joining text pieces.
Right after the value we append the number of children, which tells the reader how many subtrees follow.
We loop over each child of the current node in its original order.
For each child we call dfs recursively, so its whole subtree is written before moving on to the next sibling.
We start the traversal by calling dfs on the root node.
We join all the collected pieces with commas and return that as the serialized string.
The deserialize method takes the string and must rebuild the identical tree.
An empty string means the original tree was empty.
So we return None to represent no tree.
We split the string on commas and wrap the pieces in an iterator so each read consumes the next token.
We define a recursive helper called build that reads one node and its subtree from the token stream.
We read the next token as the value and create a node with an empty children list.
We read the next token as the child count and repeat that many times, one for each child.
Each time, we recursively build a child subtree and append it to the node's children, preserving order.
Once all children are attached, we return the finished node.
We start the process by calling build, which consumes the whole stream and returns the root of the restored tree.

shortest-distance-from-all-buildings.ask: In a grid, 0 is empty land, 1 is a building and 2 is an obstacle. Find an empty cell whose total walking distance to every building is smallest, moving up, down, left or right through empty land. Return that total, or -1.

brute.idea: From every empty cell, run a BFS to measure its distance to each building, and keep the smallest total that reaches all of them.
steps: For each empty cell, BFS through empty land
Add the distance whenever a building is touched
Keep totals that reach every building
brute.whySlow: There are far more empty cells than buildings; a 50 by 50 mostly empty grid means 2,500 full searches.

codeNotes.note: Start a BFS only from buildings

shortest-distance-from-all-buildings.exampleWhy: The obstacle forces a detour: the bottom middle cell is 3 steps from each building, a total of 6, and nothing beats it.
shortest-distance-from-all-buildings.hook: Don't search from every empty lot. Flood outward from each building and add up the distances.

optimal.insight: Flip the search: BFS from each building, not each empty cell. Every BFS adds its distance into a shared total grid and bumps a reach counter.
steps: BFS outward from each building through empty land
Add the step count into dist for each cell reached
Count how many buildings reached each cell
Answer: smallest dist among cells every building reached

pitfalls: A cell some building cannot reach is invalid, even if its partial total is small.
Buildings and obstacles block movement; never walk through a 1.

say.intro: Shortest Distance from All Buildings. Ones are buildings, twos are obstacles, and zeros are empty land. Pick the empty cell with the smallest total walk to every building. Here, an obstacle sits between two buildings, so we walk around it. The bottom middle cell is three steps from each building. That's a total of six.
say.brute: The direct way is to stand on each empty cell and run a breadth first search, adding up the distance to every building it touches. Keep the smallest total that reaches them all. It works, but there are usually far more empty cells than buildings, so we repeat a whole grid search thousands of times.
say.insight: So flip it around. Run one breadth first search from each building instead. Every cell it reaches gets that distance added to a shared total, and a counter saying one more building can reach it. After all the buildings, the answer is the smallest total among cells that every building reached.
say.anim: We start with a small grid, one building at row zero, column zero, another at column four. A breadth first search begins from the first building, spreading distance and reach counts outward. Each empty cell gains the distance from this building, and reach counts one visit so far. The search keeps expanding, filling row one with increasing distances up to five at the far end. Now the second building at column four runs its own breadth first search, adding more distances. Cells visited by both buildings get reach two, meaning they're reachable from every house. Distances accumulate further, with shared cells like column one reaching total distance six. Only cells reached by both buildings qualify, and the minimum total distance found is six.
say.code: We only start a search from buildings. Each building gets a fresh visited set. For each empty neighbour, we add this building's distance into dist, and bump reach by one. At the end, we keep only cells whose reach equals the number of buildings, and return the smallest total, or minus one if there is none.
say.outro: Buildings times grid size. The pattern is graphs: multi-source breadth first search, launched from the rarer side.

shortest-distance-from-all-buildings.title: Shortest Distance from All Buildings
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, as the problem setup expects.
The method takes the grid and returns the smallest total walking distance to all buildings, or negative one.
We store the number of rows and columns of the grid as R and C.
We create a dist grid of zeros that will accumulate each cell's total distance from all buildings.
We create a reach grid of zeros that counts how many buildings can reach each cell.
We start the building count, houses, at zero.
We loop over every row index of the grid.
Inside each row we loop over every column index.
We check whether the current cell is not a building.
If it is not a building we skip it, since we only start searches from buildings.
We found a building, so we increase the houses count by one.
We start a queue with this building's position and distance zero for a breadth first search.
We create a seen set holding the building's position so we never revisit cells in this search.
We keep searching while the queue still has cells to expand.
We take the oldest cell from the queue along with its distance from the building.
We look at the four neighbors: down, up, right and left.
A neighbor qualifies if it is inside the grid, empty land, and not yet seen in this search.
We mark that neighbor as seen so it is only processed once per building.
We add the distance to this neighbor, one more than the current distance, into its running total.
We bump the neighbor's reach counter, recording that this building can reach it.
We push the neighbor with its new distance so its own neighbors get explored later.
We collect totals only for empty cells that every single building could reach.
We return the smallest total among those cells, or negative one if none qualify.

the-earliest-moment-when-everyone-become.ask: There are n people and a log of friendships, each with a timestamp. Friendship is transitive: a friend of a friend counts as acquainted. Return the earliest time when everyone is acquainted with everyone, or -1 if that never happens.

brute.idea: Sort the logs, add one friendship at a time, and after each one run a BFS to check whether everybody is connected.
steps: Sort logs by timestamp
Add the edge to the adjacency list
BFS from person 0; all reached? return time
brute.whySlow: A full graph search after every log: 10,000 logs over 100 people means millions of repeated edge visits.

codeNotes.note: Everyone starts as their own root

codeNotes.match: for t, a, b in sorted(logs):

the-earliest-moment-when-everyone-become.exampleWhy: At time 0, 2 and 0 meet; at 1, 0 and 1; at 3, 0 and 3. Now all four people share one group.
the-earliest-moment-when-everyone-become.hook: Friend groups only ever merge. Sort by time and stop the moment one group remains.

optimal.insight: Start with n separate groups. Each log that joins two different groups drops the count by one. The first time it hits one, that timestamp is the answer.
steps: Sort logs by timestamp
Each person starts as their own group
Union the pair; different roots means groups minus one
Groups equals one? Return this timestamp

pitfalls: Logs are not given in time order; forgetting to sort gives wrong answers.
Only count a merge when the roots differ; repeat friendships change nothing.

say.intro: The Earliest Moment When Everyone Become Friends. We have n people and a log of timestamped friendships. A friend of a friend counts. When is everyone connected? Here, at time zero, two meets zero. At time one, zero meets one. At time three, zero meets three, and all four are linked. So the answer is three.
say.brute: The plain way is to sort the logs, add one friendship at a time, and after each one run a full search from person zero. If it reaches everyone, return that time. It's correct, but we redo a whole graph search after every single log, which gets expensive fast.
say.insight: Notice that friend groups only ever merge, they never split. So start with n groups, one per person. Each log that links two different groups drops the count by one. The first time the count reaches one, everybody is connected. Union find tells us in nearly constant time whether two people are already in the same group.
say.anim: We start with four people, each their own group, parent array zero through three. Groups count is four, and we process logs sorted by timestamp. At time zero, friends two and zero are checked, finding roots two and zero. Different roots, so we merge them, dropping groups from four to three. At time one, zero and one merge, finding roots zero and one, groups now two. At time three, zero and three are checked, with path compression finding roots one and three. Roots differ, so they merge, and groups finally drops to one. Since everyone is now connected, the function returns the answer, three.
say.code: Everyone starts as their own root, so there are n groups. We walk the logs in sorted time order. Find both roots. If they differ, we point one root at the other and drop the group count. The moment it reaches one, we return the timestamp. If the logs run out first, we return minus one.
say.outro: Sorting dominates, so n log n in the number of logs. The pattern is graphs, with union find counting connected components.

the-earliest-moment-when-everyone-become.title: The Earliest Moment When Everyone Become Friends
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container LeetCode expects for our method.
The method earliestAcq takes the friendship logs and the number of people n, and returns the earliest time everyone is connected.
We create a parent list where each person starts as their own parent, meaning n separate groups.
We define a helper called find that returns the representative root of the group containing a person.
We loop while x is not its own parent, meaning we have not yet reached the root.
Path compression happens here, as we point x to its grandparent to flatten the tree and speed up later searches.
Then we move x up to its parent, continuing the climb toward the root.
Once x is its own parent, we return it as the root of the group.
We track the number of groups, which starts at n because nobody is connected yet.
We sort the logs by timestamp so we process friendships in chronological order, unpacking time and the two people.
For each log we find the roots of both people to see which groups they belong to.
If the roots differ, the two people are in separate groups, so this friendship merges them.
We attach the root of the first group to the root of the second, joining the groups.
Because two groups became one, we reduce the group count by one.
If only one group remains, everyone is acquainted with everyone.
We return the current timestamp, since it is the earliest moment this happened given sorted order.
If we finish all logs without reaching one group, we return negative one because full connection never happens.

time-taken-to-cross-the-door.ask: People arrive at a door in index order; state 0 means enter and 1 means exit. One person crosses per second. If the door was unused or used to exit last second, exiters go first; if used to enter, enterers go first. Ties go to the smaller index. Return each person's crossing time.

brute.idea: Tick the clock one second at a time. Each second, scan everyone who has arrived and not crossed, and pick by the rules.
steps: Collect everyone waiting at second t
Prefer the direction used last second
Nobody waiting? Door resets to exit-first
brute.whySlow: Rescanning all n people every second, plus ticking through idle gaps: 100,000 people means billions of checks.
brute.code:
class Solution:
    def timeTaken(self, arrival: List[int], state: List[int]) -> List[int]:
        n = len(arrival)
        ans = [-1] * n
        t, last, done = 0, 1, 0
        while done < n:
            waiting = [i for i in range(n) if ans[i] == -1 and arrival[i] <= t]
            if not waiting:
                last = 1
                t += 1
                continue
            same = [i for i in waiting if state[i] == last]
            person = same[0] if same else waiting[0]
            ans[person] = t
            last = state[person]
            done += 1
            t += 1
        return ans

codeNotes.match: side = last if queues[last] else 1 - last

time-taken-to-cross-the-door.exampleWhy: Person 0 enters at 0, so enterers keep priority: 2 at 1, 3 at 2. Then exiter 1 goes at 3, and 4 at 4.
time-taken-to-cross-the-door.hook: One door, two queues, and a rule about who goes next. Simulate it, but skip the idle seconds.

optimal.insight: Keep one queue per direction. The rules collapse to: same direction as last second goes first, defaulting to exit. Jump the clock over empty gaps.
steps: Push everyone arrived by time t into their queue
Both queues empty? Jump to next arrival, reset to exit
Pick last direction's queue if non-empty, else the other
Record the time, remember direction, tick one second

time-taken-to-cross-the-door.optimalCode:
class Solution:
    def timeTaken(self, arrival: List[int], state: List[int]) -> List[int]:
        n = len(arrival)
        ans = [0] * n
        queues = [collections.deque(), collections.deque()]
        t, last, i = 0, 1, 0
        while i < n or queues[0] or queues[1]:
            while i < n and arrival[i] <= t:
                queues[state[i]].append(i)
                i += 1
            if not queues[0] and not queues[1]:
                t = arrival[i]
                last = 1
                continue
            side = last if queues[last] else 1 - last
            person = queues[side].popleft()
            ans[person] = t
            last = side
            t += 1
        return ans
pitfalls: After an idle second the door resets to exit priority, not the last direction.
Ticking one second at a time through large gaps is too slow; jump instead.

say.intro: Time Taken to Cross the Door. People arrive at one door, some to enter, some to exit, and one person crosses per second. If the door was idle or just used to exit, exiters go first. If it was just used to enter, enterers go first. Here, person zero enters first, so the other enterers keep priority, and the exiters wait.
say.brute: The simple way is to tick the clock one second at a time. Each second, scan everyone who has arrived and not crossed yet, prefer last second's direction, and pick the smallest index. It's correct, but it rescans all n people every second, and wastes ticks walking through idle gaps.
say.insight: Here's the simplification. The four rules boil down to one: whoever goes the same way as last second has priority, and an idle door means exit. So keep two queues, one per direction, already in index order. Each second we pop from one of them in constant time, and when both are empty, we jump the clock straight to the next arrival.
say.anim: We start with arrival times and states for five people, and an empty answer array. At time zero, person zero enters the exit queue since their state is zero. Person zero crosses first, since last defaults to exit direction, so ans becomes zero. At time one, person one joins the entrance queue, person two joins the exit queue. Exit direction continues since last was exit, so person two crosses at time one. At time two, person three joins the exit queue and crosses immediately, continuing that direction. With exit queue empty, direction switches, so person one crosses the entrance at time three. Clock jumps to four for person four, who then crosses, giving final times zero, three, one, two, four.
say.code: We hold two deques, index zero for entering and one for exiting. Each loop, arrivals up to now join their direction's queue. If both are empty, we skip idle time and reset the door to exit first. Otherwise we take last second's direction if anyone is waiting there, else the other side. That person crosses now, and the clock ticks.
say.outro: Linear time, since each person is queued and popped once. The pattern is simulation with queues, an arrays and hashing staple.

time-taken-to-cross-the-door.title: Time Taken to Cross the Door
lineNotes: We define a Solution class that holds the method for this problem.
The method takes the arrival times and the states, and returns when each person crosses.
We store n as the number of people.
We create the answer list with one zero per person, to be filled in with crossing times.
We make two queues, one for enterers and one for exiters, indexed by state.
We start the clock at zero, set last to exit as the default, and set the next-arrival pointer i to zero.
We loop while anyone has yet to arrive or either queue still holds waiting people.
We inner-loop over everyone who has arrived by the current time t.
We add each arrived person's index to the queue that matches their state, keeping index order.
We advance i to look at the next person.
If both queues are empty, nobody is waiting, so the door sits idle.
We jump the clock straight to the next arrival time instead of ticking through the gap.
We reset last to exit, since an unused door gives exiters priority.
We continue to the top so the new arrivals get queued before anyone crosses.
We pick the same direction as last second if anyone waits there, otherwise the opposite direction.
We remove the front person from that queue, who has the smallest index among that direction.
We record the current time as this person's crossing time.
We remember this direction as last, so it gets priority next second.
We move the clock forward by one second, since one person crosses per second.
Once everyone has crossed, we return the list of crossing times.

valid-word-abbreviation.ask: An abbreviation replaces non-empty runs of letters with their lengths, written without leading zeros. Given a word and an abbreviation, return true if the abbreviation matches the word exactly.

brute.idea: Expand the abbreviation into a pattern, writing a wildcard for each skipped letter, then compare it with the word.
steps: Collect digits into a number; reject a leading zero
Write that many wildcards, then the letter
Same length and every letter matches?
brute.whySlow: S is the sum of the numbers: an abbreviation like a999999999 builds a billion-slot pattern before failing.

codeNotes.match: return i == len(word) and j == len(abbr)

valid-word-abbreviation.exampleWhy: i, then skip 12 letters, then i and z, skip 4, then n: exactly 20 letters, matching internationalization.
valid-word-abbreviation.hook: Numbers in the abbreviation are jumps. Two pointers, no expansion, and watch for leading zeros.

optimal.insight: A number is just a jump. Parse it and advance the word pointer by that much; letters must match one for one.
steps: Pointer i in word, j in abbr
Digit: reject a zero, parse the full number, jump i
Letter: must equal word[i], advance both
Valid only if both pointers end exactly at the end

pitfalls: Check the leading zero only on a number's first digit; 10 is fine, 01 is not.
A jump can overshoot the word; the final equality check catches it.

say.intro: Valid Word Abbreviation. An abbreviation swaps runs of letters for their length, and numbers can't have leading zeros. Does the abbreviation match the word? Take internationalization and i twelve i z four n. That's an i, twelve letters, i, z, four letters, then n. Exactly twenty letters, and every written letter lines up. So it's true.
say.brute: A first idea is to expand the abbreviation. Turn every number into that many wildcard slots, then compare slot by slot with the word. That's linear in what we build, but what we build can be huge. An abbreviation with a nine digit number creates a billion slots, just to discover it doesn't fit.
say.insight: Here's the thing. A number in the abbreviation is simply a jump. We keep one pointer in the word and one in the abbreviation. Hit a letter? It must match, and both pointers step. Hit a number? Parse all its digits and jump the word pointer forward. No expansion at all, and constant extra space.
say.anim: We start comparing word and abbreviation with both pointers at zero. The first abbreviation character is the letter i, matching word's letter i, so both pointers advance. Next abbr characters are digits one and two, parsed together into the number twelve. That twelve jumps the word pointer forward twelve letters, skipping straight to index thirteen. Letters i and z are compared one by one and match successfully, advancing both pointers. Another digit, four, is parsed and used to jump the word pointer ahead four spots. The final letter n matches, bringing both pointers to the end of their strings. Both pointers exhausted together, so the function returns true, confirming a valid abbreviation.
say.code: We loop while both pointers are in range. On a digit, a zero means a leading zero, so return false. Otherwise build the full number, digit by digit, and move the word pointer by that amount. On a letter, it must equal the word's letter, then both advance. Finally, both pointers must land exactly at their ends.
say.outro: Linear time, constant space. The pattern is two pointers, treating numbers as jumps instead of expanding them.

valid-word-abbreviation.title: Valid Word Abbreviation
lineNotes: We define a solution class that holds the method for checking the abbreviation.
The method takes the word and its abbreviation and returns true only if they match exactly.
We start two pointers, i for the word and j for the abbreviation, both at zero.
We loop while both pointers are still inside their strings, so we compare piece by piece.
If the current abbreviation character is a digit, we are at the start of a number to jump.
A digit zero at the start of a number is not allowed, because leading zeros are invalid.
So we return false immediately when a number begins with zero.
We start a running number at zero to collect the full jump length.
We keep reading while j is in range and the character is a digit, gathering every digit of the number.
We shift the running number left by one place and add the new digit.
We advance j past that digit so the next one is read.
Once the number is complete, we move the word pointer i forward by that many letters.
Otherwise the current abbreviation character is a letter, which must match the word directly.
We compare the word letter at i with the abbreviation letter at j to check they are the same.
If the letters differ, the abbreviation cannot match, so we return false.
On a match, we move the word pointer forward by one letter.
We also move the abbreviation pointer forward by one letter.
At the end, we return true only if both strings were consumed exactly, which also catches jumps past the word's end.

replace-elements-with-greatest-element-o.ask: Replace every element of the array with the largest element somewhere to its right. The last element has nothing to its right, so it becomes -1. Return the array.

brute.idea: For every position, scan everything to its right and keep the largest value seen.
steps: For each index i, start best at -1
Scan j from i + 1 to the end
Write the largest found into the answer
brute.whySlow: Every index rescans the whole suffix; with 10,000 numbers that is about 50 million comparisons.

codeNotes.note: Nothing right of the last cell

replace-elements-with-greatest-element-o.exampleWhy: Right of 17 the biggest is 18; right of 18, 5 and 4 it is 6; right of 6 it is 1.
replace-elements-with-greatest-element-o.hook: Walk backwards and the greatest value to your right is just one running number.

optimal.insight: Go right to left. The max to the right of i is the max to the right of i + 1, combined with arr[i + 1].
steps: Start rightMax at -1
Walk i from the last index down to 0
Save the new max of rightMax and arr[i]
Overwrite arr[i] with rightMax, then advance rightMax

pitfalls: Overwriting arr[i] before folding it into the max loses that value.
The last element must become -1, not itself.

say.intro: This is Replace Elements with Greatest Element on Right Side. Every number gets replaced by the biggest number to its right. The last one becomes minus one. In our example, seventeen becomes eighteen, the next few become six, six becomes one, and one becomes minus one.
say.brute: The direct way is two loops. For each position, scan everything to its right and keep the biggest value. Write that into the answer. It's correct, but look at the work. The first index scans almost the whole array, the next one almost all of it again. That adds up to n squared, about fifty million comparisons for ten thousand numbers.
say.insight: Here's the trick. Flip the direction. If you walk from the right end, the biggest value to your right is just a running maximum. Moving one step left only adds one new number to that region, the one you just left. So one pass and one variable are enough.
say.anim: We start with rightMax at negative one, since nothing lies right of the last element. At index five, the last element, we replace it with negative one, since nothing is to its right. At index four, rightMax is one, so arr becomes six after comparing six and one. At index three, we store rightMax six, then update rightMax to max of six and four, still six. At index two, arr becomes six again, since rightMax stays six after comparing with five. At index one, we store six, then rightMax updates to eighteen, the largest so far. At index zero, we store eighteen, since that was the max to its right. The loop ends and the function returns the final array eighteen, six, six, six, one, negative one.
say.code: Right max starts at minus one, because nothing sits right of the last cell. We loop from the last index down to zero. First we compute the new max including the current value, before we lose it. Then we overwrite the current cell with right max. Then right max takes the new value. Return the array.
say.outro: Linear time, constant extra space. The pattern is arrays, scanned from the right with a running maximum.

replace-elements-with-greatest-element-o.title: Replace Elements with Greatest Element on Right Side
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container that holds the method for this problem.
This method takes the array and will return it after replacing each element with the greatest value to its right.
We start rightMax at negative one, since the last element has nothing to its right.
We loop index i from the last position down to zero, walking the array from right to left.
We compute newMax as the larger of rightMax and the current element, which is the max for the next step left.
We overwrite the current element with rightMax, the greatest value that was strictly to its right.
We update rightMax to newMax so the next element to the left sees this element included.
After the loop finishes, we return the modified array with every element replaced.

maximum-number-of-balloons.ask: Using each character of text at most once, how many copies of the word balloon can you spell? Return that maximum number of copies.

brute.idea: Simulate it: keep pulling the letters of balloon out of the text one by one until a letter runs out.
steps: Turn text into a list of characters
Remove each letter of balloon from the list
Count a balloon when all seven letters were found
Stop when some letter is missing
brute.whySlow: Each removal searches and shifts the whole list; with 10,000 characters that is millions of operations.

codeNotes.note: Demand: l and o need two

maximum-number-of-balloons.exampleWhy: There are two b, a and n, and four l and o: exactly two balloons, no more.
maximum-number-of-balloons.hook: The scarcest letter decides everything, and l and o each count double.

optimal.insight: Count letters once. Each letter of balloon allows count divided by how many times balloon needs it. The minimum ratio wins.
steps: Count every character in text
Count the letters of balloon itself
For each letter, divide supply by demand
Return the smallest quotient

pitfalls: Forgetting that l and o are needed twice per balloon.
Missing letters count as zero, so the answer can be zero.

say.intro: This is Maximum Number of Balloons. We get a string and want to spell the word balloon as many times as possible, using each character once. Our example has two b's, two a's, two n's, and four l's and four o's. That's exactly enough for two balloons.
say.brute: The simplest idea is to simulate it. Put the characters in a list. Pull out a b, then an a, then two l's, two o's and an n. If everything was found, that's one balloon. Repeat until something is missing. It works, but every removal searches and shifts the list, so long strings cost about n squared.
say.insight: Here's the thing. We don't need to build balloons one at a time. Just count the letters. For each letter in balloon, its count divided by how many times balloon uses it says how many balloons that letter can support. The scarcest letter is the bottleneck, so take the minimum.
say.anim: First we count every letter in the input string, storing each frequency. Now we count letters needed to spell balloon, noting l and o appear twice. We initialize res to sixteen, then loop through each letter in balloon. For letter b, text has two, needed one, so res drops to two. For letter a, two available divided by one needed keeps res at two. For l, four available divided by two needed gives two, res stays two. For o, four divided by two also gives two, res unchanged. After checking n, the function returns two as the final maximum balloons.
say.code: First we count every character in the text. Then we count the letters of balloon, so l and o show up with demand two. The result starts at the text length, a safe upper bound. For each letter of balloon, we divide supply by demand and keep the minimum. Return it.
say.outro: Linear time and constant space, since the alphabet is fixed. The pattern is arrays and hashing: count once, then find the bottleneck.

maximum-number-of-balloons.title: Maximum Number of Balloons
lineNotes: We import Counter from the collections module so we can tally how often each letter appears.
We define a Solution class, which is the container the problem expects for our method.
The method takes the input text and returns an integer, the most copies of balloon we can spell.
We count every letter in text once, so later lookups for any letter are quick.
We count the letters in the word balloon, which tells us l and o are needed twice each.
We start the result at the length of text, a safe upper bound that any real ratio will beat.
We loop over each distinct letter needed by balloon, so only relevant letters matter.
For each letter we divide its available count by the needed count, and keep the smallest ratio so far.
We return the result, which is the limiting letter's ratio and so the maximum number of balloon copies.

permutations-ii.ask: Given a list of numbers that may contain repeats, return every distinct ordering of the list. Each ordering should appear exactly once, in any order.

brute.idea: Generate all n factorial orderings by position, as if every element were different, and throw them into a set to remove repeats.
steps: Pick any remaining position for the next slot
Recurse until nothing remains
Add the finished tuple to a set
Convert the set back to lists
brute.whySlow: With eight copies of one value it builds 40,320 orderings just to keep one.

permutations-ii.exampleWhy: The two ones are identical, so only three of the six orderings are actually different.
permutations-ii.hook: Duplicates make duplicate permutations, unless you branch on distinct values instead of positions.

optimal.insight: Branch on distinct values, not positions. A count map says how many of each value are left, so equal values never create twin branches.
steps: Count how many times each value appears
At each level, try each value with count left
Use it: append, decrement, recurse
Undo: pop and increment

pitfalls: Appending perm itself instead of a copy leaves every result empty.
Looping over nums instead of distinct keys brings the duplicates back.

say.intro: This is Permutations Two. We get numbers that may repeat, and we return every distinct ordering, each one exactly once. With one, one, two, the two ones look identical. So instead of six orderings, there are only three: one one two, one two one, and two one one.
say.brute: The brute force ignores the duplicates at first. Generate every ordering by position, as if all elements were different, and drop each one into a set. The set removes repeats at the end. That's correct, but wasteful. With eight equal numbers, it builds forty thousand orderings, only to keep a single one.
say.insight: The fix is to branch on values, not positions. Keep a count map: one appears twice, two appears once. At each level, try each distinct value that still has copies left. Two equal ones can never create twin branches, because they're the same key in the map. So every leaf is already unique.
say.anim: We start with nums one one two, and build a count map tracking how many of each value remain. We pick value one, decrease its count, and perm becomes one, then grows to one, one. We pick the remaining two, perm fills to one, one, two, and we record this full permutation. Backtracking undoes the last pick, letting us try a different branch like one then two then one. This new order one, two, one completes another valid permutation, added to our results. Starting fresh with two first, the distinct value branching avoids repeating the one, one, two pattern. Choosing two then one then one builds the final unique permutation, two, one, one. All branches explored, the final answer is one one two, one two one, two one one.
say.code: We build a counter from the numbers and an empty current permutation. When the permutation is full, we save a copy. Otherwise we loop over the distinct values. Skip any with a zero count. Append it, decrement its count, and recurse. When we return, pop it and restore the count, so the next sibling sees the same state.
say.outro: Still n times n factorial in the worst case, but never wasted work on duplicates. The pattern is backtracking with a count map.

permutations-ii.title: Permutations II
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container the interview platform expects for our method.
The method permuteUnique takes a list of numbers that may contain repeats and returns a list of orderings.
We start with an empty result list that will collect every distinct ordering we find.
We build a count map of how many times each distinct value appears in nums.
We keep an empty perm list that holds the ordering we are currently building.
We define a helper called backtrack that explores choices recursively, sharing result, count, and perm from the outer scope.
If perm has as many items as nums, we have placed every number and finished one ordering.
We save a copy of perm into result, since perm will keep changing as we backtrack.
We return so this branch stops and control goes back to try other choices.
We loop over each distinct value in count, so equal values never create duplicate branches.
If none of this value remain, it cannot be used at this step.
We skip to the next distinct value in that case.
We choose this value by adding it to the end of perm.
We decrease its count because one copy of it is now used.
We recurse to fill the next position with the remaining values.
After returning, we undo the choice by removing the last value from perm.
We restore the count so this value is available again for other branches.
We kick off the search with an empty perm and the full counts.
We return result, which now holds every distinct ordering exactly once.

triangle.ask: Given a triangle of numbers, go from the top to the bottom row. From index i you may step to index i or i + 1 below. Return the smallest possible path sum.

brute.idea: Recursively try both moves from every cell: the best path from a cell is its value plus the better of its two children.
steps: From cell r, c recurse into r + 1, c
Also recurse into r + 1, c + 1
Return the value plus the smaller result
brute.whySlow: Inner cells are recomputed again and again; 200 rows mean 2 to the 200 paths.

codeNotes.note: Bottom row: path is just itself

triangle.exampleWhy: The path 2, 3, 5, 1 sums to 11, and no other top-to-bottom path is smaller.
triangle.hook: Start at the bottom row and the triangle collapses to one answer at the top.

optimal.insight: Work bottom-up. Each cell's best path down is its value plus the smaller of the two best paths beneath it. One row array suffices.
steps: Copy the bottom row into dp
Go up one row at a time
dp[col] = value + min(dp[col], dp[col + 1])
dp[0] is the answer

pitfalls: Going top-down needs edge cases at both ends of each row; bottom-up avoids them.
Greedily taking the smaller neighbour can miss the true minimum.

say.intro: This is Triangle. We start at the top and walk down to the bottom row. From each spot, we can go straight down or down and to the right. We want the smallest total. In our example, the path two, three, five, one gives eleven, the best possible.
say.brute: The brute force tries everything. From each cell, recurse into both children below, and return the cell's value plus the smaller of the two results. It's correct, but every row doubles the number of paths. Inner cells get recomputed over and over, so two hundred rows would be hopeless.
say.insight: Here's the aha. Flip the direction and go bottom up. For a cell on the bottom row, the best path is just its own value. For a cell above, it's its value plus the smaller of the two cells beneath it. One row of answers is enough, and the top cell ends up holding the result.
say.anim: We start by copying the bottom row of the triangle into our dp array, four, one, eight, three. Now row two, we look at col zero, combining value six with the smaller of dp zero and dp one. Dp becomes seven, one, eight, three, then col one adds five plus the smaller neighbor below. Dp updates to seven, six, eight, three, then col two adds seven plus the smaller below it. After finishing row two, dp holds seven, six, ten, three, representing best paths from there down. Moving to row one, col zero adds three plus the smaller of dp zero and dp one. Dp becomes nine, six, ten, three, then col one adds four plus the smaller neighbor below. Finally row zero, col zero adds two plus the smaller of dp zero and dp one, giving eleven. The function returns dp zero, giving the minimum path sum of eleven.
say.code: We copy the bottom row into dp. Then we loop over rows from the second last up to the top. For every column in that row, dp at col becomes the triangle value plus the smaller of dp at col and dp at col plus one. When we reach the top, dp zero is the answer.
say.outro: Quadratic time over the whole triangle, linear space. The pattern is two dimensional dynamic programming, solved bottom up with a single row.

triangle.title: Triangle
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container the interview platform expects for our method.
The method minimumTotal takes the triangle as a list of rows and returns the smallest path sum as an integer.
We copy the last row into dp, since the best path from a bottom cell is just its own value.
We loop over rows from the second to last row up to the top, moving upward one row at a time.
For each row we loop over its columns, and row index plus one gives exactly how many cells that row has.
We set each dp entry to its cell value plus the smaller of the two best paths below, overwriting in place safely.
After reaching the top, dp at index zero holds the minimum path sum from the apex, so we return it.

jump-game-vii.ask: You stand at index 0 of a binary string. From i you may jump to any j between i + minJump and i + maxJump, but only onto a 0. Can you reach the last index?

brute.idea: Plain BFS: from each reachable index, scan its whole jump window and enqueue every unvisited 0.
steps: Start a queue at index 0
Pop i and scan i + minJump to i + maxJump
Enqueue each unvisited 0
Succeed when the last index is popped
brute.whySlow: Neighbouring windows overlap, so the same cells are rescanned; n and maxJump of 100,000 is 10 billion checks.

codeNotes.note: Everything up to here is covered

jump-game-vii.exampleWhy: Jump from 0 to 3, then from 3 to 5. Both landing spots are 0.
jump-game-vii.hook: Breadth-first search, but never look at the same index twice.

optimal.insight: Indices leave the queue in increasing order, so each new window only needs the part beyond the farthest index already scanned.
steps: Queue starts with index 0
Pop i; start scanning at max(i + minJump, farthest + 1)
Enqueue zeros up to i + maxJump
Record farthest = i + maxJump

pitfalls: Scanning each full window again makes it n times k and times out.
The last character must itself be 0 to be reachable.

say.intro: This is Jump Game Seven. We have a string of zeros and ones and start at index zero. From index i, we can jump anywhere between i plus min jump and i plus max jump, but only onto a zero. Can we reach the end? Here, zero jumps to three, and three jumps to five. So yes.
say.brute: Treat it as a graph and run breadth first search. Pop an index, scan its whole jump window, and add every unvisited zero. The visited set prevents re-adding, but we still scan overlapping windows again and again. With a big max jump, that's n times k checks, around ten billion.
say.insight: Here's the key. The queue gives indices in increasing order, so each window starts and ends further right than the last one. Anything up to the previous window's end has already been scanned. So keep a farthest pointer, and only scan the new part beyond it. Every index gets looked at once.
say.anim: We start with the string 011010, jumping between two and three steps at a time. The queue holds index zero, and farthest starts at zero, tracking scanned positions. We pop index zero and compute start as two, the earliest reachable unvisited spot. Checking index two, but it holds a one, so we skip it. Index three holds a zero, so we add it to the queue to explore later. Farthest updates to three, meaning everything up to there has been scanned already. Popping index three, start becomes five, checking the next reachable zero position. Index five is a zero and also the last character, so we return true.
say.code: The queue starts with zero, and farthest starts at zero. Each round we pop an index. The scan starts at the later of i plus min jump, or one past farthest. For each zero in range, we enqueue it, and return true if it's the last index. Then farthest becomes i plus max jump. If the queue empties, return false.
say.outro: Linear time and linear space. The pattern is graphs: breadth first search with a pointer that stops overlapping windows from being rescanned.

jump-game-vii.title: Jump Game VII
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container the problem expects for our method.
The canReach method takes the binary string s plus the minimum and maximum jump lengths, and returns true or false.
We create a queue for breadth first search and seed it with index zero, our starting position.
We set farthest to zero, tracking the highest index we have already scanned so we never rescan positions.
We keep looping as long as the queue still holds reachable indices that we have not expanded.
We pop the earliest index from the front of the queue; indices come out in increasing order.
The scan starts at the later of i plus minJump and one past farthest, skipping indices already examined.
We loop over each candidate index in the window, capped by the end of the string so we stay in bounds.
We only care about candidates holding a zero, since we can only land on zeros.
We add that landable index to the queue so we can expand jumps from it later.
We check whether this newly reached index is the last index of the string.
If it is, we return true immediately because the end is reachable.
We update farthest to i plus maxJump, marking the whole window up to there as scanned.
If the queue empties without reaching the last index, we return false because it is unreachable.

paint-house.ask: Each house in a row can be painted red, blue or green, each with its own cost. Neighbouring houses cannot share a color. Return the cheapest total cost to paint all houses.

brute.idea: Recursively try every color for every house, skipping the color used by the previous house, and keep the cheapest total.
steps: At house i, try each color but the previous one
Add its cost and recurse to house i + 1
Return the smallest total found
brute.whySlow: Each house doubles the number of colorings; 100 houses means about 10 to the 30 paths.

codeNotes.note: Best total ending in each color
Swap in all three at once
Last house can be any color

paint-house.exampleWhy: Blue for 2, green for 5, blue for 3 gives 10, and no valid choice is cheaper.
paint-house.hook: Three running totals, one per color, are all the memory this problem needs.

optimal.insight: The cheapest way to end on red only depends on the cheapest ways to end on blue or green one house earlier.
steps: dp holds the best total ending in each color
For each house, color c costs costs[i][c] plus min of the other two
Replace dp with the three new totals
Answer is the smallest of dp

pitfalls: Updating dp in place mixes old and new values.
Picking the cheapest color per house greedily can force expensive neighbours.

say.intro: This is Paint House. A row of houses, each painted red, blue or green, and each color has its own price per house. Neighbours can't share a color. What's the cheapest total? Here, blue for two, green for five, then blue for three, gives ten.
say.brute: The brute force tries every coloring. At each house, try each color except the one the previous house used, add its cost, and recurse. Keep the smallest total. It works, but every house roughly doubles the number of paths. A hundred houses would mean more paths than atoms you could ever count.
say.insight: Here's the insight. To know the cheapest way to finish on red at this house, you only need the cheapest way to finish on blue or on green at the previous house. So keep three numbers, one per color, and roll them forward house by house.
say.anim: We start with costs for each house and dp all zeros, meaning no cost yet. At house zero, we compute costs for red, blue, and green: seventeen, two, and seventeen. Dp updates to seventeen, two, seventeen, the cheapest cost ending each color so far. At house one, dp becomes eighteen, thirty three, and seven, adding new house costs. At house two, we combine previous colors' minimums, getting twenty one, ten, and thirty seven. Now dp holds twenty one, ten, and thirty seven after processing all houses. We take the minimum of these final values to find the cheapest total. The minimum is ten, so the answer returned is ten.
say.code: dp starts as three zeros. For every house, red costs its red price plus the cheaper of the previous blue and green. Blue and green work the same way. We compute all three before replacing dp, so we don't mix old and new values. At the end, return the smallest of the three.
say.outro: Linear time, constant space. The pattern is one dimensional dynamic programming, with a small state per position.

paint-house.title: Paint House
