lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container the interview platform expects for our method.
The minCost method takes the list of per-house color costs and returns the cheapest total as an integer.
We start dp as three zeros, meaning before any house is painted, ending on each color costs nothing.
We loop over every house by its index, building the best costs one house at a time.
To end house i on red, we pay its red cost plus the cheaper of blue or green before.
To end on blue, we add its blue cost to the cheaper of red or green before.
To end on green, we add its green cost to the cheaper of red or blue before.
We replace dp with the three new totals so the next house builds on this one.
After all houses, the answer is the smallest of the three totals, whichever final color is cheapest.

maximum-number-of-removable-characters.ask: Remove the characters of s at removable[0], removable[1], and so on, in order. Find the largest k such that p is still a subsequence of s after the first k removals.

brute.idea: Try k = 1, 2, 3 and so on, re-checking the subsequence each time, until it breaks.
steps: Add the next removable index to a set
Check if p is still a subsequence
Stop at the first k that fails
brute.whySlow: Up to 100,000 linear subsequence checks, each over 100,000 characters: 10 billion steps.

codeNotes.match: if i1 not in removed and s[i1] == p[i2]:

maximum-number-of-removable-characters.exampleWhy: Removing indices 3 and 1 leaves a_c_cb, still containing a then b; removing index 0 too breaks it.
maximum-number-of-removable-characters.hook: Removing more never helps, so binary search on how many you remove.

optimal.insight: If p survives k removals it survives fewer, and fails for more. That monotonic yes/no lets us binary search k.
steps: Search k between 0 and len(removable) - 1
Remove the first m + 1 indices into a set
Two-pointer check whether p is a subsequence
Success moves l right, failure moves r left

pitfalls: Off by one: m indexes removable, so m + 1 characters are removed.
Checking membership in a list instead of a set makes each check quadratic.

say.intro: This is Maximum Number of Removable Characters. We remove characters from s in the order given by the removable list. What's the most we can remove while p is still a subsequence of s? Here, removing indices three and one still leaves an a followed by a b. Removing zero as well breaks it. So the answer is two.
say.brute: The direct way grows k one at a time. Add the next index to a removed set, then re-check whether p is still a subsequence with two pointers. Stop at the first failure. Each check is linear, and there could be a hundred thousand of them, so that's ten billion steps.
say.insight: Notice that the answer is monotonic. If p survives k removals, it survives any smaller number. If it fails at k, it fails for anything larger. A yes, yes, yes, no, no shape means binary search. Pick a middle k, check once, and throw away half the range.
say.anim: We binary search over how many removals from the list we can apply, starting with res zero. At midpoint m equals one, we remove characters at indices one and three and test if p is still a subsequence. Walking through s, we skip removed positions and match a then b, successfully finding both letters of p. Since p survives, res updates to two and we search further right, hoping more removals still work. Now m equals two, removing indices zero, one, and three, we check again if p still fits. This time matching fails, i2 never reaches two, so removing three characters breaks the subsequence. We shrink the search range downward since three removals failed, keeping res at two. The search ends and the final answer returned is two, the maximum removable count.
say.code: The helper walks s and p with two pointers, skipping removed indices, and returns whether all of p matched. Then the binary search. We take the middle m and remove the first m plus one indices into a set. If p survives, record m plus one and search right. Otherwise search left.
say.outro: n log k time, linear space. The pattern is binary search on the answer, driven by a monotonic yes or no check.

maximum-number-of-removable-characters.title: Maximum Number of Removable Characters
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container LeetCode expects for our method.
The maximumRemovals method takes the string s, the pattern p, and the removable index list, and returns the largest valid k.
We define a helper called isSubseq that checks whether p is still a subsequence of s given a set of removed indices.
We start two pointers at zero, one walking through s and one walking through p.
We loop while both pointers are still inside their strings, stopping early if either one runs out.
If the current index of s is not removed and its character matches the current character of p, we have a match.
On a match we advance the pointer in p to look for the next pattern character.
We always advance the pointer in s, moving on whether or not there was a match.
We return true only if the pointer in p reached the end, meaning every character of p was matched.
We set res to zero, since removing nothing is always a valid answer.
We set the binary search bounds so left is zero and right is the last index of removable.
We keep searching while left is no greater than right, so every candidate count gets considered.
We pick the middle index m, which means we test removing the first m plus one characters.
We build a set of the first m plus one removable indices, for fast membership checks inside the helper.
We test whether p is still a subsequence of s after those removals.
If it works, we record m plus one as the best count so far, keeping the larger value.
Since this count works, we search the right half for a larger one by moving left past m.
Otherwise the removal count is too large and the check failed.
So we search the left half by moving right to just before m, trying fewer removals.
After the search ends, we return res, the largest number of removals that keeps p a subsequence.

find-unique-binary-string.ask: You get n distinct binary strings, each of length n. Return any binary string of length n that is not in the list.

brute.idea: List every binary string of length n, then return the first one that is not in the input.
steps: Put the input strings in a set
Generate all 2^n strings of length n
Return the first one missing from the set
brute.whySlow: It builds all 2^n strings up front; for n = 16 that is 65,536 strings to find one answer.

codeNotes.match: return None if res in strSet else res

find-unique-binary-string.exampleWhy: 000, 001 and 010 are taken, and 011 is the next candidate in order, so it is free.
find-unique-binary-string.hook: There are n strings but 2 to the n candidates, so one of the first n + 1 is free.

optimal.insight: Backtrack in order 0 then 1 and stop at the first miss. Only n strings are taken, so at most n + 1 leaves are ever reached.
steps: Put the input strings in a set
Fill position i with 0, then try 1
At full length, return it if not in the set
Undo position i when both choices fail

pitfalls: Cantor's diagonal trick, flipping nums[i][i], gives a linear answer; mention it.
Any missing string is accepted, so outputs may differ from the examples.

say.intro: This is Find Unique Binary String. We get n different binary strings, each n characters long, and must return any string of that length that isn't in the list. In our example, zero zero zero, zero zero one and zero one zero are taken, so zero one one works.
say.brute: The brute force lists every possible binary string of length n, all two to the n of them, and returns the first one missing from the input. It's correct, but it builds an exponential list just to find one answer. For n of sixteen, that's sixty five thousand strings.
say.insight: Here's the thing. There are only n strings in the list, but candidates come in a fixed order. Backtrack, trying zero before one at each position, and stop the moment a finished string is free. Since only n strings can be taken, we reach at most n plus one leaves.
say.anim: We start with the set of existing strings and a candidate string of all zeros. Backtracking recurses deeper, trying zero at each position first, down to index three. The candidate becomes zero zero zero, but that matches an existing string, so it fails. Backtracking flips position two to one, forming zero zero one, which also already exists. Backing up further, position one flips to one, giving candidate zero one zero, still taken. Flipping position two again gives zero one one, a string not in the original set. This unique string succeeds immediately and gets returned up through every recursive call. The final answer found is zero one one, a binary string not in the input.
say.code: We put the strings in a set and start with all zeros. At full length, we join the characters and return the string unless it's taken. Otherwise, first recurse with a zero here. If that finds an answer, pass it up. Then set a one, recurse again, and reset to zero before returning.
say.outro: Quadratic time, linear space. The pattern is backtracking with an early exit, powered by a pigeonhole argument.

find-unique-binary-string.title: Find Unique Binary String
lineNotes: We define the Solution class that holds the method for this problem.
This method takes the list of binary strings and returns one binary string that is missing from it.
We put the input strings into a set so checking membership takes constant time.
We start with a current list of n zeros, which we will modify as we build candidates.
We define a recursive backtrack function where i is the position we are currently deciding.
When i equals the length of nums, every position is decided and we have a full candidate.
We join the current characters into one string to form the candidate.
If the candidate is in the set we return nothing, otherwise we return it as the answer.
We first try leaving position i as zero and recurse to the next position.
If that recursion found a string not in the set, we have our answer.
We return that answer immediately so no further branches are explored.
Otherwise we flip position i to one to explore the other branch.
We recurse again from the next position with this one set, saving whatever it returns.
We reset position i back to zero so later branches start from a clean state.
We return the result of the one branch, which is either a valid string or nothing.
We kick off the search from position zero and return the string it finds.

minimum-difference-between-highest-and-l.ask: Pick any k scores from the array so that the gap between the highest and lowest picked score is as small as possible. Return that smallest gap.

brute.idea: Try every group of k scores and measure its highest minus lowest.
steps: Enumerate every combination of k scores
Compute max minus min for each
Keep the smallest difference
brute.whySlow: Choosing 500 of 1,000 scores has more combinations than atoms in the universe.

minimum-difference-between-highest-and-l.exampleWhy: Picking 1, 3 and 4 gives a gap of 3; every other group of three is wider.
minimum-difference-between-highest-and-l.hook: Sort first, and the best group of k is always k neighbours.

optimal.insight: After sorting, the tightest group of k is always contiguous. Slide a window of size k and compare its two ends.
steps: Sort the scores
Place a window over indices 0 to k - 1
Record nums[r] - nums[l]
Slide both ends right by one

pitfalls: Without sorting, neighbours in the array say nothing about the gap.
With k equal to 1 the answer is 0.

say.intro: This is Minimum Difference Between Highest and Lowest of K Scores. Pick any k scores so that the highest minus the lowest is as small as possible. With nine, four, one, seven, three and k of three, picking one, three and four gives a gap of three.
say.brute: The brute force tries every group of k scores, takes its max minus its min, and keeps the smallest. That's correct, but the number of groups explodes. Choosing five hundred scores out of a thousand gives an astronomically large number of combinations.
say.insight: Here's the aha. Sort the scores. Now if the best group skipped over a score in the middle, swapping that score in would never widen the gap. So the best group is always k neighbours in sorted order, and the gap is just the last minus the first. Slide a window.
say.anim: We start with the array nine, four, one, seven, three, and k equals three. After sorting, the array becomes one, three, four, seven, nine, ready for scanning. Pointers l and r mark a window of size three, starting at zero and two. The window covers one, three, four, giving a difference of three, our first result. The window slides to three, four, seven, with difference four, larger than before. Now the window covers four, seven, nine, difference five, still not better. The window would exceed the array length, so the sliding loop stops. The smallest difference found across all windows is three, our final answer.
say.code: First we sort. The window starts with l at zero and r at k minus one. While r is in range, the gap is the value at r minus the value at l, since the ends are the max and min. Keep the smallest, slide both pointers right, and return the result.
say.outro: n log n for the sort, then one linear pass. The pattern is a fixed size sliding window over sorted data.

minimum-difference-between-highest-and-l.title: Minimum Difference Between Highest and Lowest of K Scores
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container this problem's method lives in.
This method takes the list of scores and the group size k, and returns the smallest gap.
We sort the scores first so that the best group of k scores must sit side by side.
We set left to zero and right to k minus one, which marks the first window of size k.
We start the result at infinity so that any real gap found will replace it.
We keep sliding while the right edge is still inside the array, so every window gets checked.
The gap of this window is the right value minus the left value, and we keep the smaller of that and the result.
We move both edges one step right, sliding the window forward while keeping its size at k.
After all windows are checked, we return the smallest gap we found.

encode-and-decode-tinyurl.ask: Design a Codec with encode, which turns a long URL into a short one, and decode, which turns that short URL back into the original long URL.

brute.idea: Keep the URLs in a list. To encode, scan the list for the URL; the short code is its position.
steps: Scan the list for longUrl
If found, reuse its position
Otherwise append and use the new length
Decode by parsing the number back out
brute.whySlow: Every encode rescans all stored URLs; after a million URLs each call does a million comparisons.

encode-and-decode-tinyurl.exampleWhy: Each new URL gets the next number; decoding 2 returns neetcode.io, and re-encoding a known URL reuses 1.
encode-and-decode-tinyurl.hook: A URL shortener is just two hash maps and a counter.

optimal.insight: Two hash maps, long to short and short to long, make both directions O(1). A counter guarantees every short code is unique.
steps: If longUrl is new, build base plus the next number
Store it in both maps
Encode returns the long-to-short entry
Decode returns the short-to-long entry

pitfalls: Sequential codes are guessable; real systems use random or hashed base-62 keys.
Hashing the URL directly risks collisions unless you check and retry.

say.intro: This is Encode and Decode TinyURL. We design a codec. Encode turns a long URL into a short one, and decode turns the short one back. In our example, the first URL becomes slash one, the second becomes slash two, and decoding slash two gives the second URL back.
say.brute: A simple version keeps every URL in a list. To encode, scan the list. If the URL is already there, its position is the code. Otherwise append it. Decoding just parses the number. Decode is fast, but every encode rescans the whole list, so after a million URLs, each call compares a million strings.
say.insight: The fix is two hash maps. One maps long to short, the other maps short to long. A counter, the number of URLs stored so far, gives each new URL a code that can never collide. Now both directions are a single lookup.
say.anim: We start with two empty maps, encode map and decode map, ready to track urls. Encoding the leetcode url, it is not in the encode map yet, so we create a new short code. Short url becomes tinyurl dot com slash one, stored in both maps for fast lookup either direction. The encode call returns http tinyurl.com slash one as the generated short url. Encoding neetcode io similarly creates a new unique short code, slash two, since it's unseen. Decoding slash two simply looks up the decode map, instantly returning https neetcode io. Encoding the leetcode url again finds it already in the encode map, so no new code needed. It returns the same cached short url, tinyurl.com slash one, confirming consistent mapping.
say.code: The constructor makes both maps and the base address. Encode checks whether the long URL is new. If it is, the short URL is the base plus the next number. We store it in both maps. Then we return the mapped short URL. Decode is a single lookup in the reverse map.
say.outro: Constant time per call and linear space. The pattern is arrays and hashing, with a pair of maps for a two way lookup.

encode-and-decode-tinyurl.title: Encode and Decode TinyURL
lineNotes: We define a Codec class that will hold everything needed to shorten and restore web addresses.
The constructor runs once when a Codec is created, so it sets up the starting state.
We create encodeMap, an empty dictionary that will map each long URL to its short URL.
We create decodeMap, an empty dictionary that will map each short URL back to its long URL.
We store the shared base address that every short URL will start with.
The encode method takes a long URL and will return its short version.
We only build a new short URL if this long URL has not been seen before.
The short URL is the base plus one more than the number of stored entries, which keeps every code unique.
We record the long to short pairing so repeated encodes of the same URL return the same answer.
We also record the short to long pairing so decode can look it up instantly later.
We return the stored short URL, which is either the new one or the one made earlier.
The decode method takes a short URL and will return the original long URL.
We look up the short URL in decodeMap and return the long URL in constant time.

maximum-length-of-a-concatenated-string-.ask: Pick some of the strings, keeping their order, and glue them together. The result must not repeat any character. Return the longest length you can reach.

brute.idea: Try every subset of the strings, concatenate it, and keep it only if no character repeats.
steps: Loop over every bitmask of the n strings
Concatenate the chosen strings
Keep the length if all characters are distinct
brute.whySlow: Same exponential worst case, but it fully builds every subset, even ones extending a clash it already saw.

codeNotes.match: if c in charSet or c in prev:

maximum-length-of-a-concatenated-string-.exampleWhy: un plus iq gives uniq, and iq plus ue gives ique: length 4. All three repeat u.
maximum-length-of-a-concatenated-string-.hook: Include or skip each word, and prune the moment a letter repeats.

optimal.insight: Decide include or skip for each string, carrying a set of used letters. A clash kills that whole branch, so dead subsets are never built.
steps: At index i, first try to include arr[i]
Only if it has no repeat and no overlap with the set
Add its letters, recurse, then remove them
Also recurse without arr[i]; return the larger

pitfalls: A single string like aa repeats itself and can never be used.
Forgetting to remove letters after recursing corrupts sibling branches.

say.intro: This is Maximum Length of a Concatenated String with Unique Characters. We pick some strings, glue them together in order, and no character may repeat. What's the longest result? With un, iq and ue, we can make u n i q, or i q u e. Both have length four.
say.brute: The brute force tries every subset. Loop over every bitmask, concatenate the chosen strings, and keep the length if all characters are distinct. It's correct, and the worst case is exponential either way. The waste is that it rebuilds every subset in full, even ones that extend a clash it already found.
say.insight: Here's the better shape. Walk the strings one by one and decide include or skip, carrying a set of letters used so far. If a string clashes with the set, or with itself, we never include it, so every branch below that choice is pruned. Only valid combinations are ever built.
say.anim: We start with an empty character set and three strings to try combining. Checking string un, no overlap found, so we add u and n to the set. Now trying iq next, its letters i and q don't clash either, so they're added. String ue clashes with u already used, so this branch fails and backtracks. That path returns length two, worse than keeping un and iq together, giving four. Backtracking tries skipping un, combining iq and ue instead, but u still clashes. After exploring all skip and include combinations, the best overlap free total remains four. The final answer is four, the maximum length from combining un and iq.
say.code: The overlap helper checks each letter against the set and against letters already seen in this string. Backtrack returns the set size at the end. Otherwise, if the string fits, we add its letters, recurse, and remove them again. Then we also recurse without it and return the better of the two.
say.outro: Exponential in the worst case, but pruned in practice. The pattern is backtracking with include or skip choices.

maximum-length-of-a-concatenated-string-.title: Maximum Length of a Concatenated String with Unique Characters
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, as the problem platform expects.
The maxLength method takes the list of strings and returns the longest unique-character concatenation length.
We create charSet, a shared set holding every letter used by the strings chosen so far.
The overlap helper checks whether a given string clashes with charSet or repeats a letter inside itself.
We start a fresh set called prev to track letters already seen within this one string.
We walk through each character c of the string s one at a time.
If c is already in charSet or already in prev, we have a duplicate letter.
In that case we return True immediately, since this string cannot be used.
Otherwise we record c in prev so later characters in the same string can detect repeats.
If the loop finishes without finding any clash, we return False, meaning the string is safe to add.
The backtrack function takes index i and explores include or skip choices for the string at that position.
When i equals the length of arr, every string has been decided, so we reach the base case.
At the base case we return the size of charSet, which is the length of the chosen concatenation.
We set res to zero as the best result for the branch where we include the current string.
We only try including arr at i if it has no overlap, which prunes dead branches early.
We loop over each character in the current string to add it to the used letters.
Each character is added to charSet, marking it as used for deeper recursion.
We recurse to the next index with this string included and store the result in res.
Now we undo the choice by looping over the same string's characters again.
We remove each character from charSet, restoring the state so the skip branch starts clean.
We return the larger of the include result and the skip result obtained by recursing to the next index.
The top-level call starts at index zero and returns the best length found overall.

find-bottom-left-tree-value.ask: Given the root of a binary tree, return the value of the leftmost node in the deepest row of the tree.

brute.idea: Run a level-order traversal and store every level's values in a list, then return the first value of the last level.
steps: BFS one level at a time
Collect every value on the level
Return res[-1][0]
brute.whySlow: Same linear time, but it keeps every value of every level when only one number is ever needed.

find-bottom-left-tree-value.exampleWhy: The deepest row holds only 7, under 5 on the right side, so 7 is its leftmost value.
find-bottom-left-tree-value.hook: Level order: the first node of each level is a candidate, and the last level wins.

optimal.insight: In BFS, the front of the queue at the start of each level is that level's leftmost node. Remember only that, and the last one remembered is the answer.
steps: Put the root in a queue
At each level start, record q[0].val
Pop the whole level, pushing left then right children
When the queue empties, return the last record

pitfalls: The answer is the leftmost of the deepest row, not the leftmost leaf overall.
Pushing right before left would return the rightmost value instead.

say.intro: This is Find Bottom Left Tree Value. Given a binary tree, return the leftmost value in its deepest row. In our tree, the deepest row has a single node, seven, hanging under five on the right side. So the answer is seven, even though it's not on the far left of the tree.
say.brute: A straightforward approach is level order traversal that stores every level as a list. At the end, take the last level and return its first value. That's linear time, so it isn't slower. But it keeps every value of every level in memory, when we only ever need one number.
say.insight: Here's the thing. In breadth first search, when a level begins, the node at the front of the queue is that level's leftmost node. So just remember its value as each level starts. When the queue runs dry, the last value we remembered belongs to the deepest level.
say.anim: We start with a queue holding just the root node, value one. At the start of this level, res is set to one, the leftmost value. Node one's children, two and three, get added to the queue. New level begins, so res updates to two, the front of the queue. Level two processed, queue now holds four, five, and six for next level. New level starts, res becomes four, the leftmost node here. Children five and six add seven, the only node for the last level. Final level begins, res updates to seven, and it becomes the answer.
say.code: We start the queue with the root. At the start of each level, res takes the value at the front of the queue. Then we pop exactly that many nodes, pushing left children before right ones so the order stays left to right. When the queue empties, we return res.
say.outro: Linear time, and space proportional to the widest level. The pattern is trees, using level order breadth first search.

find-bottom-left-tree-value.title: Find Bottom Left Tree Value
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which holds the method that LeetCode calls to solve this problem.
This method takes the root of a binary tree and returns the leftmost value in the deepest row.
We create a queue holding just the root, so we can walk the tree level by level.
We keep looping as long as the queue still has nodes waiting in the current level.
At the start of each level, we record the value of the front node, since that is the leftmost one.
We loop exactly as many times as there were nodes in the queue when this level began.
We remove the next node from the front of the queue so we can process it.
If this node has a left child, we check for it before adding anything.
We add the left child to the back of the queue so it is handled in the next level.
Then we check whether the node has a right child too.
We add the right child after the left, which keeps each level ordered left to right.
When the queue empties, res holds the leftmost value of the last, deepest level, so we return it.

number-of-longest-increasing-subsequence.ask: Given an array of integers, count how many strictly increasing subsequences have the maximum possible length.

brute.idea: Enumerate every subsequence, keep the strictly increasing ones, and count those of maximum length.
steps: Loop over every bitmask of indices
Check the chosen values are strictly increasing
Track best length and how many reach it
brute.whySlow: With 2,000 numbers there are 2 to the 2,000 subsequences; even 40 numbers is a trillion.

codeNotes.match: return sum(c for l, c in zip(length, count) if l == best)

number-of-longest-increasing-subsequence.exampleWhy: The longest length is 4, reached by 1, 3, 5, 7 and by 1, 3, 4, 7.
number-of-longest-increasing-subsequence.hook: Track two numbers per index: the longest run from here, and how many ways reach it.

optimal.insight: For each start i, store the LIS length from i and its count. A longer extension resets the count; an equal one adds to it.
steps: Go from the right end to the left
For each larger nums[j] to the right, try extending
Longer: take length[j] + 1 and count[j]
Equal: add count[j]; finally sum counts of the max length

pitfalls: Adding counts on a longer extension instead of replacing them overcounts.
Several start indices can reach the max length; sum all of them.

say.intro: This is Number of Longest Increasing Subsequence. We don't want the length of the longest increasing subsequence. We want how many there are. In one, three, five, four, seven, the longest length is four. One three five seven, and one three four seven. So the answer is two.
say.brute: The brute force checks every subsequence. Loop over every bitmask, keep the strictly increasing ones, and track the best length and how many hit it. It's correct, but there are two to the n subsequences. Forty numbers is already a trillion, and inputs go up to two thousand.
say.insight: Here's the idea. The classic LIS dynamic program stores, for each index, the longest run starting there. Add a second number: how many runs achieve that length. When an extension through j is longer, take j's length plus one, and copy j's count. When it ties, add j's count.
say.anim: We start with the array one three five four seven, all lengths and counts set to one. At index three, four is less than seven's successor, but comparing to five extends length to two. At index two, five sees four fails but seven works, giving length three a boost to two. At index one, three beats five, extending length to three with count copied as one. Three also reaches four with equal length two, so count at index one becomes two. At index zero, one extends through three, making length four and count two there. Checking five and four from index zero confirms no better or equal extension exists. The best length found is four, and summing matching counts gives the final answer two.
say.code: Both arrays start at one. We walk i from right to left, and look at every j to its right with a bigger value. If going through j is longer, we take its length plus one and copy its count. If it ties, we add its count. Finally, sum the counts of every index whose length equals the best.
say.outro: n squared time, linear space. The pattern is one dimensional dynamic programming, carrying a count alongside the length.

number-of-longest-increasing-subsequence.title: Number of Longest Increasing Subsequence
lineNotes: We define the Solution class that holds the method for this problem.
The method findNumberOfLIS takes the list nums and returns how many longest increasing subsequences exist.
We store the size of nums in n for use in the loops.
We create a length list of ones, since every element alone is an increasing subsequence of length one.
We create a count list of ones, since each element has exactly one way to form its single-element subsequence.
We walk i from the last index down to zero, so everything to the right is already computed.
For each i, we scan every later index j that could extend a subsequence starting at i.
We only consider j when nums at j is strictly greater than nums at i, keeping the subsequence increasing.
If going through j gives a longer subsequence than the best known for i, we found a new maximum.
We then set length of i to one more than length of j and copy the count from j, resetting the old count.
Otherwise, if going through j gives a length equal to the current best for i, we have more ways.
We add the count from j to the count of i, since those subsequences are distinct paths of the same length.
After filling both lists, we find the overall longest length among all starting positions.
We sum the counts of every start whose length equals the best, giving the number of longest increasing subsequences.

wiggle-sort.ask: Reorder the array in place so it goes up, down, up, down: nums[0] ≤ nums[1] ≥ nums[2] ≤ nums[3], and so on. Any valid order is accepted.

brute.idea: Sort the array, then swap each pair after the first element so every odd index becomes a local peak.
steps: Sort ascending
Swap positions 1 and 2, 3 and 4, and so on
brute.whySlow: Sorting does far more than needed; a million numbers cost about 20 million comparisons instead of one pass.

codeNotes.note: Odd index must be a peak

wiggle-sort.exampleWhy: 3 ≤ 5 ≥ 1 ≤ 6 ≥ 2 ≤ 4: every odd index is a peak.
wiggle-sort.hook: No sorting needed: one swap per bad pair fixes the wiggle as you go.

optimal.insight: Check each adjacent pair against the rule for its position. If it is wrong, swapping fixes it without breaking the pair before.
steps: Walk i from 1 to the end
Odd i needs nums[i] ≥ nums[i - 1]
Even i needs nums[i] ≤ nums[i - 1]
If the rule fails, swap the two

pitfalls: Works because of ≤ and ≥; the strict Wiggle Sort II needs a different method.
Modify in place; the function returns nothing.

say.intro: This is Wiggle Sort. Rearrange the array in place so it goes up, down, up, down. Every odd index should be at least as big as its neighbours. Our example three, five, two, one, six, four becomes three, five, one, six, two, four.
say.brute: One easy way is to sort first, then swap each pair after the first element, so every odd index holds the bigger of two neighbours. That works, but sorting does far more than we need. It's n log n, around twenty million comparisons for a million numbers, instead of one pass.
say.insight: Here's the greedy idea. Walk left to right and check each pair. An odd index should be at least its left neighbour, an even index at most. If a pair is wrong, swap it. Why is that safe? The swap only brings in a value that makes the previous pair even more correct.
say.anim: We start with the array three, five, two, one, six, four. At index one, five is greater than three, so the odd rule already holds. At index two, two should be less than five, and it already is. At index three, one is less than two, breaking the odd position rule. We swap them, giving one and two, fixing the wiggle pattern locally. At index four, six is greater than two, violating the even position rule. Swapping fixes it, placing six before two in the array. The loop finishes, giving the final wiggled array three, five, one, six, two, four.
say.code: We loop from index one to the end. The condition says: if i is odd and the value is smaller than the one before, or i is even and it's bigger, the pair is wrong. In that case we swap the two values. Nothing is returned, since the array changes in place.
say.outro: Linear time, constant space. The pattern is greedy: fix each local violation as you go, and the global order follows.

wiggle-sort.title: Wiggle Sort
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which holds the method that reorders the array into a wiggle pattern.
The wiggleSort method takes the list nums and rearranges it in place, so it returns nothing.
We loop through every index from one to the end, comparing each element with the one just before it.
At odd positions the element must be at least its left neighbor, and at even positions at most, so we detect a violation of either.
When a pair breaks the rule we swap the two elements, which fixes this pair without breaking the earlier pair.

continuous-subarray-sum.ask: Is there a contiguous subarray of length at least two whose sum is a multiple of k? Zero counts as a multiple of k. Return true or false.

brute.idea: Try every start, extend the end one step at a time with a running sum, and test each sum against k.
steps: Fix a start index i
Extend j and add nums[j] to the sum
Return true when the sum mod k is 0
brute.whySlow: With 100,000 numbers that is 5 billion subarray sums.

continuous-subarray-sum.exampleWhy: 2 + 6 + 4 = 12, which is a multiple of 6, and the subarray has three elements.
continuous-subarray-sum.hook: Two prefix sums with the same remainder fence off a multiple of k.

optimal.insight: If two prefix sums leave the same remainder mod k, the numbers between them sum to a multiple of k. Store each remainder's first index.
steps: Seed remainder 0 at index -1
Add each number to a running total
New remainder: record its index
Seen remainder: success if at least two indices back

pitfalls: Overwriting a remainder's index with a later one can miss valid long subarrays.
Without the 0 at -1 seed, a whole prefix summing to a multiple is missed.

say.intro: This is Continuous Subarray Sum. Is there a stretch of at least two numbers whose sum is a multiple of k? In our example, with k of six, two plus six plus four is twelve. That's a multiple of six, and three elements long, so the answer is true.
say.brute: The brute force tries every start. From each one, extend the end step by step, keep a running sum, and check whether it divides by k. That's fine for small arrays, but it's n squared. With a hundred thousand numbers, that's five billion sums.
say.insight: Here's the math trick. Take running prefix sums and look at their remainders mod k. If two prefixes leave the same remainder, the part between them must be a multiple of k. So store the first index where each remainder appeared. Seeing it again, at least two steps later, means we found one.
say.anim: We start with remainder map holding zero mapped to negative one, and total zero. At index zero, we add twenty three, giving total twenty three with remainder five. Remainder five isn't seen yet, so we store index zero for it. At index one, total becomes twenty five, remainder one, newly stored at index one. At index two, total is thirty one, remainder one again, but indices differ by only one, no match yet. At index three, total reaches thirty five, remainder five, matching the earlier index zero. Since index three minus zero exceeds one, we found a valid subarray summing to a multiple of six. The function returns true, confirming such a continuous subarray exists.
say.code: We seed the map with remainder zero at index minus one, which stands for the empty prefix. For each number, we add it to the total and take the remainder. If it's new, store its index. If we've seen it, and the gap is more than one, return true. Otherwise, return false.
say.outro: Linear time, and space bounded by k. The pattern is arrays and hashing, with prefix sums and remainders.

continuous-subarray-sum.title: Continuous Subarray Sum
lineNotes: We define a Solution class that holds the method for solving this problem.
The method takes the list nums and the integer k, and returns true or false.
We make a dictionary mapping remainder to first index, seeding remainder zero at index negative one so subarrays starting at the beginning count.
We set total to zero, which will hold the running prefix sum as we scan.
We loop through nums, getting each index i and value n together.
We add the current number n into the running total.
We take total modulo k to get the current prefix remainder.
If this remainder has never appeared before, we handle it as a first occurrence.
We record the current index as the first place this remainder appeared, keeping the earliest to maximize length.
Otherwise, if the earlier index is more than one step back, the subarray between has length at least two.
In that case the sum between is a multiple of k, so we return true.
If the loop finishes with no valid subarray found, we return false.

maximum-frequency-stack.ask: Design FreqStack. push adds a value. pop removes and returns the most frequent value; if several tie, it returns the one pushed most recently.

brute.idea: Keep one plain stack. On pop, count every value, find the top frequency, and scan from the top for the first value with it.
steps: push appends to a list
pop counts all values in the list
Scan from the top for a max-frequency value
Remove and return it
brute.whySlow: Every pop recounts the whole stack; 20,000 operations can mean 200 million steps.

codeNotes.note: Next level down is never empty

maximum-frequency-stack.exampleWhy: 5 appears three times, so it pops first; then 5 and 7 tie at two, and 7 is newer.
maximum-frequency-stack.hook: Keep a separate stack for every frequency, and pop from the highest one.

optimal.insight: When a value reaches frequency f, push it onto stack number f. The top of the highest stack is always the answer, ties broken by recency.
steps: Count each value on push
Append it to the stack for its new count
Pop from the stack at maxCnt and decrement the count
Lower maxCnt when that stack empties

pitfalls: A heap keyed by count and push time also works but costs log n per call.
Do not remove the value from lower stacks on push; those copies are needed later.

say.intro: This is Maximum Frequency Stack. Push adds a value. Pop removes the most frequent value, and if there's a tie, the one pushed most recently. In our example, five is pushed three times, so it pops first. Then five and seven tie, and seven is newer. Then five, then four.
say.brute: A simple version keeps one list. On pop, count every value, find the highest frequency, and scan from the top for the first value that has it. That's correct, but every pop recounts the whole stack. With twenty thousand operations, that can be two hundred million steps.
say.insight: Here's the trick. Keep one stack per frequency. When a value reaches its second occurrence, it goes onto stack two, and its first copy stays on stack one. The top of the highest stack is always the most frequent, most recent value. When that stack empties, the next one down is waiting.
say.anim: We start with empty count and stack maps to track frequencies of each value. Pushing 5 and 7 each gets frequency 1, landing in stack number 1. Pushing 5 again raises its frequency to 2, so it moves into stack number 2. Pushing 7 again also reaches frequency 2, joining 5 in stack two. Pushing 4 starts at frequency 1, while pushing 5 once more hits frequency 3, the new maximum. Popping takes from the highest stack, frequency three, returning 5 first. Next pop checks frequency two's stack, returning the most recent entry, 7. Continuing pops return 5 again then 4, matching the expected output sequence.
say.code: Push bumps the value's count. If that beats the max, we raise the max and create a new stack. Then we append the value to the stack for its count. Pop takes from the stack at the max count, decrements that value's count, and if the stack is now empty, lowers the max. Return the value.
say.outro: Constant time for every call, linear space. The pattern is stacks, one per frequency level.

maximum-frequency-stack.title: Maximum Frequency Stack
lineNotes: We define the FreqStack class, which will support pushing values and popping the most frequent one.
The constructor sets up the starting state for an empty frequency stack.
The cnt dictionary records how many times each value currently appears in the stack.
The maxCnt variable tracks the highest frequency of any value, starting at zero.
The stacks dictionary maps each frequency number to a stack of values that reached that frequency.
The push method takes a value and adds it to the structure.
We compute valCnt as one more than the value's current count, defaulting to zero if unseen.
We store the new count for this value back into the cnt dictionary.
If this count exceeds the highest frequency seen so far, we need a new level.
We raise maxCnt to match the new highest frequency.
We create an empty stack for this new frequency level.
We append the value onto the stack for its new frequency, preserving push order for tie breaking.
The pop method removes and returns the most frequent, most recently pushed value.
We pop from the stack at the highest frequency, which gives the most recent among the most frequent.
We decrease that value's count since one occurrence was removed.
If the highest frequency stack is now empty, no value has that frequency anymore.
So we lower maxCnt by one, since the next level down must be nonempty.
We return the popped value as the result.

convert-bst-to-greater-tree.ask: Given a binary search tree, replace every key with itself plus the sum of all keys greater than it. Return the root of the modified tree.

brute.idea: Collect every value first. Then, for each node, add up all collected values larger than its own.
steps: Traverse the tree and collect all values
For each node, sum the larger values
Add that sum to the node
brute.whySlow: Each node scans all values; 10,000 nodes mean 100 million additions.

codeNotes.note: One sum shared by all calls

convert-bst-to-greater-tree.exampleWhy: 8 stays 8, 7 becomes 15, 6 becomes 21, and so on down to 0, which becomes 36.
convert-bst-to-greater-tree.hook: Visit the BST from largest to smallest, and a running sum does all the work.

optimal.insight: A reverse in-order traversal, right, node, left, visits keys from largest to smallest. A running sum is exactly what each node needs.
steps: Recurse into the right subtree first
Add the node's value to the running sum
Overwrite the node with the running sum
Then recurse into the left subtree

pitfalls: Normal in-order goes smallest first; you must visit the right subtree first.
Add to curSum before overwriting the node, or its own value is lost.

say.intro: This is Convert BST to Greater Tree. Every key becomes itself plus all keys greater than it. In our tree, eight stays eight. Seven becomes fifteen. Six becomes twenty one. And so on, until zero becomes thirty six, the sum of everything.
say.brute: The brute force ignores the ordering. Collect every value, then for each node, add up all values larger than its own. It's correct, but each node scans the whole list. That's n squared, about a hundred million additions for ten thousand nodes. And it throws away the one thing a binary search tree gives us for free, which is the sorted order of its keys.
say.insight: Here's the aha. In a binary search tree, in order traversal visits keys from smallest to largest. Flip it: right subtree, then the node, then the left subtree, and you visit keys from largest to smallest. Now a running sum, at each node, is exactly that node plus everything greater.
say.anim: We start at root node four, with the running sum curSum set to zero. We dive rightmost first, reaching node eight, the largest value in the tree. Node eight updates curSum to eight, then becomes eight itself since nothing was added before. Backing up to node seven, curSum grows to fifteen, so seven becomes fifteen. Node six adds in, making curSum twenty one, so six becomes twenty one. Moving to node five's right child, we hit five, updating curSum to twenty six. After finishing the right subtree, root four updates curSum to thirty, becoming thirty. Continuing left, node one updates curSum to thirty six, so one becomes thirty six. Traversal completes, returning the tree with final values thirty, thirty six, twenty one, and more.
say.code: We keep a running sum outside the helper. The helper returns on an empty node. Otherwise it goes right first, adds the node's value to the sum, writes the sum into the node, and then goes left. We call it on the root and return the root.
say.outro: Linear time, space equal to the tree height. The pattern is trees, with a reverse in order traversal.

convert-bst-to-greater-tree.title: Convert BST to Greater Tree
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container for the method that LeetCode will call.
The convertBST method takes the root of a binary search tree and returns the root of the modified tree.
We set curSum to zero, and it will hold the running total of all keys visited so far.
We define a helper function dfs that walks the tree recursively, starting from a given node.
We declare curSum as nonlocal so that updates inside dfs change the shared running total.
If the current node is empty, we have gone past a leaf and there is nothing to process.
We return immediately in that case, which stops the recursion along this path.
We visit the right subtree first because in a binary search tree it holds the larger keys.
We add the current node's value to curSum, so the total now covers every key at least this large.
We overwrite the node's value with curSum, which is its original key plus the sum of all greater keys.
We then visit the left subtree, whose smaller keys will build on the running total.
We start the traversal by calling dfs on the root of the tree.
We return the root, whose tree has now been modified in place into the greater tree.

non-decreasing-array.ask: Can the array become non-decreasing, each element at most the next, by changing at most one element? Return true or false.

brute.idea: Changing one element works exactly when deleting it leaves a sorted array. Try deleting each element and check.
steps: For each index i, drop nums[i]
Check the rest is non-decreasing
Return true if any deletion works
brute.whySlow: Each of n deletions copies and rechecks the array; 10,000 numbers means 100 million steps.

non-decreasing-array.exampleWhy: Changing 2 to 4 gives 1, 3, 4, 4, 5, 6, which never decreases.
non-decreasing-array.hook: At the first drop, the neighbour on the left decides which number to fix.

optimal.insight: At a drop nums[i] > nums[i + 1], lower nums[i] if nums[i - 1] allows it; otherwise raise nums[i + 1]. A second drop means false.
steps: Scan pairs left to right
On a drop, fail if we already changed one
Lower nums[i] when i is 0 or nums[i + 1] ≥ nums[i - 1]
Otherwise raise nums[i + 1] to nums[i]

pitfalls: Always lowering nums[i] fails on 3, 4, 2, 3 style inputs.
Raising nums[i + 1] too eagerly can create a new drop later.

say.intro: This is Non-decreasing Array. Can we make the array never go down by changing at most one number? In our example, one, three, four, two, five, six drops from four to two. Change the two into a four, and everything is in order. So the answer is true.
say.brute: Here's a neat brute force. Changing one number works exactly when deleting that number leaves a sorted array. So try deleting each element and check whether the rest is sorted. It's correct, but each try copies and rescans the array. That's n squared work.
say.insight: The greedy fix looks only at the first drop, where a number is bigger than the next. We can lower the left one, or raise the right one. Lowering is better, since it keeps later values small, but only if the number before still fits. If not, we must raise the right one. A second drop means false.
say.anim: We start with the array one, three, four, two, five, six, and no changes made yet. At index zero, one is less than three, so we simply continue checking. At index one, three is less than four, another smooth step, so we continue. At index two, four is greater than two, a drop, and no change made yet. Since two is not greater than nums before four, we raise two up to four instead. Now the array becomes one, three, four, four, five, six, and changed is true. The rest of the array, four, five, six, stays non decreasing with no more drops. Only one drop ever occurred, so the function returns true as the final answer.
say.code: We loop over pairs. If there's no drop, continue. If we already used our change, return false. If we're at the start, or the next value is at least the one before i, lower the current value to the next. Otherwise raise the next value. Mark changed, and return true at the end.
say.outro: Linear time, constant space. The pattern is greedy: fix each problem in the way that leaves the most room later.

non-decreasing-array.title: Non-Decreasing Array
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, as expected by the problem's submission format.
The method checkPossibility takes the list nums and returns true or false depending on whether one change can fix it.
We start with changed set to false, since we have not yet used our single allowed modification.
We loop over each index except the last, so we can always compare an element with its next neighbor.
If the current element is no larger than the next one, the pair is already in order.
In that case we continue to the next index without doing anything.
Reaching here means a drop, so if we already changed something, a second fix is impossible.
We therefore return false because more than one change would be needed.
If we are at the start or the next element is at least the previous one, lowering the current element is safe.
We lower nums at i to match the next element, which removes the drop without breaking earlier order.
Otherwise the next element is too small to lower the current one, so we must raise instead.
We raise the next element up to the current value, which keeps the order intact going forward.
We mark changed as true, recording that our one allowed modification has been used.
If the loop finishes without finding a second drop, the array can be fixed, so we return true.

merge-two-binary-trees.ask: You get two binary trees. Overlay them. Where both have a node, the merged node holds their sum. Where only one tree has a node, copy that value through. Return the merged tree.

brute.idea: Number every node by heap position, add both trees into one position map, then rebuild a tree from that map.
steps: Label nodes by heap index: children 2i+1 and 2i+2
Add both trees' values into one position map
Rebuild nodes from index 0 downward
brute.whySlow: Still linear, but heap indices double every level: a deep lopsided tree makes enormous keys, and everything is copied into a map.

codeNotes.match: if not root1 and not root2:

codeNotes.note: Merge the pair of left children

merge-two-binary-trees.exampleWhy: Roots 1 and 2 give 3, left children 3 and 1 give 4. Spots only one tree fills, like 7, copy through.
merge-two-binary-trees.hook: Lay one tree over the other: where nodes overlap, add them; where one is missing, keep the other.

optimal.insight: Recurse on both trees in lockstep. A missing node simply counts as zero, so one function handles overlap and non-overlap alike.
steps: Both nodes missing? return None
Treat a missing node's value as 0
New node holds the sum
Recurse on the left pair, then the right pair

pitfalls: Reading root1.left when root1 is None crashes; guard every child access.
Return None only when both nodes are missing; one missing still merges.

say.intro: This is Merge Two Binary Trees. Picture laying one tree on top of the other. Where two nodes overlap, the merged node gets their sum. Where only one tree has a node, that value just carries through. In our example, the roots one and two become three, and the lone seven on the right copies straight across.
say.brute: A first idea is to flatten both trees into a map. Give every node a heap number, so the root is zero and its children follow a doubling rule. Add both trees into the same map, then rebuild from position zero. It works in linear time. But positions double every level, so a deep lopsided tree creates enormous numbers, and we copy everything along the way.
say.insight: Here's the cleaner view. Walk both trees together, one pair of nodes at a time. If both are missing, there's nothing to build. Otherwise, treat a missing node as zero. Make a new node holding the sum, then do exactly the same thing for the left pair and the right pair. One small recursive function covers every case.
say.anim: We start merging the roots, values one and two, since neither is missing. Both values are read and summed, creating a new root node with value three. Now we recurse on the left children, three and one, summing to four. Next level left children are five and a missing node, so five plus zero stays five. On the right side, one tree is missing so the other node's value four passes through unchanged. Back on the right subtree, two and three combine into a node valued five. A missing left paired with seven just keeps seven, filling that branch. All recursive calls return, merging into the final tree rooted at three, matching the expected output.
say.code: In the code, the base case returns None when both nodes are missing. Next, we read each value, using zero for a missing node. We create the merged node with the sum. Then we recurse on the left children and the right children, carefully passing None whenever a parent is missing. Finally, we return the new node to its caller.
say.outro: Linear in the total number of nodes, with stack space equal to the tree height. The pattern is trees: a paired depth first search.

merge-two-binary-trees.title: Merge Two Binary Trees
lineNotes: We define a Solution class that holds the method for merging two binary trees.
The mergeTrees method takes the roots of two trees, either of which may be missing, and returns the merged root.
If both current nodes are missing, there is nothing to merge, so we handle that base case first.
In that case we return None, which ends the recursion for this branch.
We read the value of the first node, treating a missing node as zero.
We do the same for the second node, so a missing node contributes nothing to the sum.
We create a brand new node holding the sum of both values, leaving the input trees untouched.
We recursively merge the left children of both nodes, passing None when a node is missing, and attach the result as the left child.
We do the same for the right children, merging them in lockstep and attaching the result as the right child.
We return the newly built node as the merged subtree rooted at this position.

arranging-coins.ask: You have n coins. Row one needs one coin, row two needs two, and so on. Build the rows in order and return how many rows you can complete fully.

brute.idea: Build the staircase row by row, subtracting each row's coins until the next row no longer fits.
steps: Start at row 1
While coins cover this row, pay and move on
Return the last completed row
brute.whySlow: Rows grow by one each time, so two billion coins still means about 65,000 loop iterations.

arranging-coins.exampleWhy: Seven rows use 1 + 2 + ... + 7 = 28 coins. Row eight needs 8 more, but only 2 remain.
arranging-coins.hook: Stack coins in rows of one, two, three. How many full rows? Binary search the row count.

optimal.insight: k full rows need k(k+1)/2 coins, which only grows with k. So binary search for the largest k whose total fits in n.
steps: Search k between 1 and n
Coins for mid rows: mid(mid+1)/2
Too many? move the right bound left
Fits? record mid and search higher

pitfalls: Use integer math; float halves can lose precision for huge n.
Return the best mid that fit, not whatever l ends at.

say.intro: This is Arranging Coins. We build a staircase. Row one takes one coin, row two takes two, row three takes three. Given n coins, how many rows can we finish completely? With thirty coins, seven rows use twenty eight. Row eight would need eight more, but only two are left. So the answer is seven.
say.brute: The direct way is to just build it. Pay one coin for row one, two for row two, and keep going until the next row doesn't fit. That's correct, and it only loops about the square root of n times. Still, two billion coins means sixty five thousand rounds, when a few dozen guesses will do.
say.insight: Here's the key. The coins needed for k full rows is k times k plus one, over two. That total only grows as k grows. So asking whether k rows fit gives yes, yes, yes, then no forever. That's exactly what binary search is for. Guess a middle row count, check the formula, and throw away half the range.
say.anim: We start with n equal thirty, searching between l equals one and r equals thirty. Mid is fifteen, needing one hundred twenty coins, way more than thirty, so r shrinks to fourteen. Mid is seven, needing twenty eight coins, which fits, so res becomes seven and l moves to eight. Mid is eleven, needing sixty six coins, too many, so r drops to ten. Mid is nine, needing forty five coins, still too many, so r drops to eight. Mid is eight, needing thirty six coins, still too many, so r drops to seven. Now l exceeds r, so the binary search loop stops and we return res. The final answer returned is seven, the largest number of complete coin rows.
say.code: The code sets the search range from one to n. Each round we take the middle, and compute its coins with the Gauss formula, using integer math. If that's more than n, the answer is smaller, so we pull the right edge in. Otherwise mid rows fit. We record it and look for something bigger.
say.outro: Logarithmic time, constant space. The pattern is binary search on the answer, over a formula that only grows.

arranging-coins.title: Arranging Coins
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container the problem expects for our method.
The method arrangeCoins takes the number of coins n and returns how many complete rows we can build.
We set the search range with left at one and right at n, since the answer lies between those.
We start the result at zero, so we have a sensible answer if no row fits.
We keep searching while left has not passed right, meaning candidate row counts remain.
We pick the middle row count between left and right as the guess to test.
We compute the coins needed for mid full rows using the formula mid times mid plus one, divided by two.
If that total is more than n, then mid rows are too many to build.
So we move right to just below mid, discarding mid and every larger count.
Otherwise the coins needed fit within n, so mid rows are achievable.
We move left above mid to see whether even more rows could fit.
We record mid as the best answer so far, keeping the larger of the result and mid.
After the search ends, we return the largest row count that fit within n coins.

robot-bounded-in-circle.ask: A robot starts at the origin facing north and repeats a string of moves forever: G steps forward, L and R turn ninety degrees. Return true if it stays inside some circle forever.

brute.idea: Simulate the instructions four times. After four rounds all heading changes cancel, so a bounded robot must be back at the origin.
steps: Run the whole string four times
Track position and facing direction
Bounded exactly when back at the origin
brute.whySlow: Same linear time, but it does four times the work and hides the real reason the answer is what it is.

codeNotes.match: x, y = x + dirX, y + dirY

robot-bounded-in-circle.exampleWhy: One pass ends at (-1, 3) still facing north, so every repeat drifts three more steps away.
robot-bounded-in-circle.hook: One pass tells you everything: the robot escapes only if it ends away from home still facing north.

optimal.insight: After one pass, if the robot is home or no longer faces north, at most four passes bring it back. Only north-facing drift escapes.
steps: Start at the origin with direction (0, 1)
G adds the direction to the position
L and R rotate the direction vector
Bounded if home, or not facing north

pitfalls: Ending away from home is still bounded if the direction changed.
Mixing up the left and right rotation formulas mirrors the whole path.

say.intro: This is Robot Bounded in Circle. A robot starts at the origin facing north. G moves it one step, L and R turn it ninety degrees. It repeats the string forever. Does it stay trapped in some circle? In our example, one pass ends three steps up and one step left, still facing north. So it drifts away forever. False.
say.brute: One safe approach simulates four full rounds. Why four? Every turn is a multiple of ninety degrees, so after four rounds the headings cancel and so do the drifts. If the robot is bounded, it must be back at the origin. That's correct and linear, but it does four times the work and hides the reason.
say.insight: Here's the real insight. Look at just one pass. If the robot is already home, it's obviously bounded. If it ends facing any direction other than north, the next passes rotate its drift, and within four passes it walks a closed loop. The only escape is ending away from home while still facing north. Then every pass pushes it further out.
say.anim: We start facing north at the origin, with position and direction both reset. Two G moves push the robot forward, moving y up to 2. An L turns the robot left, now facing west with direction negative one, zero. Another G moves the robot west, making x equal to negative one. An R turns the robot right again, restoring it to face north. A final G moves the robot forward, landing at x negative one, y three. Since the robot isn't home and still faces north, it will drift away forever. The function returns false, meaning the robot is not bounded in a circle.
say.code: The code tracks a direction vector, starting at zero, one, which is north. On G, we add the direction to the position. Turning left maps x, y to minus y, x. Turning right maps it to y, minus x. After one pass, return true if we're at the origin, or if we're no longer facing north.
say.outro: Linear time, constant space. The pattern is math and geometry: simulate once, then reason about rotations.

robot-bounded-in-circle.title: Robot Bounded In Circle
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container the problem expects for our method.
The method takes the instruction string and returns true if the robot stays within a circle forever.
We set the direction vector to zero in x and one in y, meaning the robot faces north.
We place the robot at the origin by setting both x and y to zero.
We loop over each instruction character in the string, simulating exactly one pass of the moves.
If the instruction is G, the robot needs to step forward one unit.
We add the direction vector to the position, moving the robot one step the way it faces.
If the instruction is L, we handle a left turn in this branch.
A left turn rotates the direction ninety degrees counterclockwise, so new x is negative old y and new y is old x.
Otherwise the instruction must be R, so we handle a right turn.
A right turn rotates the direction ninety degrees clockwise, so new x is old y and new y is negative old x.
After one pass, the path is bounded if we are back at the origin or no longer facing north, since repeating then cycles within four passes.

combination-sum-iv.ask: Given distinct positive numbers and a target, count the ordered sequences of those numbers that add up to the target. Numbers may repeat, and different orders count as different sequences.

brute.idea: Recursively choose the next number: try every number in nums, subtract it from target, and count the ways to finish.
steps: Target zero? that is one way
Target negative? zero ways
Sum the ways after each possible first number
brute.whySlow: The same leftover totals are recounted again and again: target 30 with three numbers takes tens of millions of calls.

codeNotes.note: One way to make zero: pick nothing
n can be the last pick
Add the ways ending with n

combination-sum-iv.hook: Despite the name, order matters here. That makes it a staircase: count the ways to climb to target.

optimal.insight: The ways to reach a total is the sum of the ways to reach total minus each number. Build those counts from 0 up to target.
steps: dp[0] = 1: the empty sequence
For each total from 1 to target
Add dp[total - n] for every n that fits
Answer is dp[target]

pitfalls: Totals outside, numbers inside; swapping the loops counts combinations, not orders.
Skip numbers larger than the current total to avoid negative indices.

say.intro: This is Combination Sum Four. We have distinct positive numbers and a target. How many sequences add up to the target? Numbers can repeat, and order matters, so one then two, and two then one, count separately. With one, two and three, and a target of four, there are seven sequences.
say.brute: The brute force picks the first number of the sequence, then recursively counts the ways to finish the rest. A leftover of zero means one valid way. Below zero means none. It's correct, but it keeps recounting the same leftover totals. With a target of thirty and three numbers, that's tens of millions of calls, and it grows exponentially.
say.insight: Here's the key. Think about the last number in the sequence. If it's n, everything before it sums to total minus n. So the ways to reach a total is the sum, over every number, of the ways to reach total minus that number. That's a staircase. Fill the counts from zero upward, and each total takes just one pass over nums.
say.anim: We start with dp all zeros, then set dp of zero to one, the base case. Now total is one, and we check each number, adding ways to reach total minus that number. Total is two, combining dp of one and dp of zero, giving dp two a value of two. Total is three, summing dp of two, one, and zero, making dp three equal four. Total is four, now adding dp three, dp two, and dp one for each number. After all numbers, dp four becomes seven, counting every combination summing to four. Finally the function returns dp of target, giving the answer seven.
say.code: We make a dp array of size target plus one, and set the zero slot to one, for the empty sequence. Then for each total from one up to target, we try every number as the last pick. If it fits, we add the ways to reach the leftover. Loop order matters here. Totals outside, numbers inside, so different orders are counted. Return the last slot.
say.outro: Target times n time, linear space. The pattern is one dimensional dynamic programming, the same shape as climbing stairs.

combination-sum-iv.title: Combination Sum IV
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container the problem expects for our method.
The method combinationSum4 takes the list of numbers and the target, and returns how many ordered sequences sum to the target.
We create a dp list of zeros with one slot for every total from zero up to target.
We set dp at zero to one, because there is exactly one way to make zero, the empty sequence.
We loop over each total from one up to target, building the counts in increasing order.
For each total, we try every number in nums as the last number in a sequence.
We only use a number if it is not bigger than total, since otherwise the remainder would be negative.
We add the ways to reach total minus n into dp at total, which counts every sequence ending with n.
Finally we return dp at target, which holds the count of ordered sequences reaching the target.

game-of-life.ask: Given a grid of live and dead cells, apply Conway's rules once: live cells with two or three live neighbours survive, dead cells with exactly three come alive, all others die. Update the board in place.

brute.idea: Copy the board first. Count each cell's live neighbours on the untouched copy, and write the new state into the real board.
steps: Copy the whole board
Count live neighbours on the copy
Write the rule's result to the board
brute.whySlow: Same time, but the copy doubles the memory, and the follow-up explicitly asks for an in-place update.

game-of-life.exampleWhy: The vertical bar turns horizontal: the middle keeps two neighbours, and each side cell sees three.
game-of-life.hook: Update every cell at once, in place, with no copy: store the old and new state in one number.

optimal.insight: Use spare values as combined states: 3 means alive and survives, 2 means dead but born. Originally-alive cells read as 1 or 3, so counts stay correct.
steps: Count neighbours that were alive: value 1 or 3
Live cell survives? mark it 3
Dead cell with three neighbours? mark it 2
Second pass: 2 and 3 become 1, the rest 0

pitfalls: Writing plain 0 or 1 mid-pass corrupts the neighbour counts of later cells.
Skip the cell itself and anything off the board when counting.

say.intro: This is Game of Life. Each cell is live or dead. A live cell survives with two or three live neighbours. A dead cell with exactly three comes alive. Everything else is dead next round. All cells update at the same moment, in place. Our example is a vertical bar of three, which flips into a horizontal bar.
say.brute: The simple way is to copy the whole board. Count neighbours on the copy, which never changes, and write the new states into the real board. That's correct, and linear in the number of cells. The cost is a full second board in memory, and the follow up asks us to avoid exactly that.
say.insight: Here's the trick. A cell only holds zero or one, so we have spare values. Mark a live cell that survives as three. Mark a dead cell that comes alive as two. A plain one now means alive but dying. When counting, treat one and three as originally alive. A final pass turns two and three into one, and everything else into zero.
say.anim: We start with a vertical blinker, column one alive in all three rows. For cell zero zero, we scan its eight neighbors, counting only ones or threes as alive. At row one column zero, counting neighbors gives three live cells nearby. Since this dead cell has exactly three neighbors, it becomes two, meaning it will be born. Row one column one stays alive with three neighbors, so it becomes three, meaning it survives. Row two column one also gets marked two, since it has three live neighbors. Now a second pass converts coded values back to plain zero or one states. The final board shows the blinker rotated horizontally, matching the expected output.
say.code: The helper counts neighbours in the three by three box around a cell, skipping the cell itself and anything off the board, and counting values one or three. The first pass marks survivors as three and births as two. The second pass maps one to zero, and two or three to one.
say.outro: Linear time, constant extra space. The pattern is a matrix simulation, using state encoding to update in place.

game-of-life.title: Game of Life
lineNotes: We define a Solution class that holds the method for this problem.
The gameOfLife method takes the board and updates it in place without returning anything.
We store the number of rows as R and the number of columns as C.
We define a helper that counts the live neighbours of the cell at row r and column c.
We start the neighbour count at zero for this cell.
We loop the row index i from one above r to one below r.
We loop the column index j from one left of c to one right of c.
We skip the cell itself and any position that falls outside the board edges.
Skipping is done with continue, so out of range positions never get read.
A neighbour counts as live if it holds 1 or 3, since both were alive originally.
We add one to the neighbour count for each originally live neighbour.
We return the final neighbour count to the caller.
We now walk through every row of the board.
Within each row we visit every column, so each cell gets processed.
We count the live neighbours of the current cell using the helper.
If the current cell is alive, we apply the survival rules.
A live cell with two or three neighbours survives.
We mark it as 3, meaning alive now and alive next, so neighbours still see it as live.
Otherwise the cell is dead, and we check whether it has exactly three live neighbours.
We mark that dead cell as 2, meaning dead before but born next, so it still reads as dead for counting.
In the second pass we walk through every row again to finalize the board.
We visit every column in the row to decode each cell's state.
A cell still equal to 1 was alive but does not survive.
So we set that cell to zero, since it dies.
A cell holding 2 or 3 will be alive in the next generation.
So we set those cells to 1, completing the in place update.

count-sub-islands.ask: Two same-sized grids of land and water. An island in grid2 counts if every one of its cells is also land in grid1. Return how many islands in grid2 qualify.

brute.idea: Flood fill each grid2 island to collect its cells in a list. Afterwards, check that every listed cell is land in grid1.
steps: Flood fill grid2, listing each island's cells
Check every listed cell in grid1
Count the islands that pass
brute.whySlow: Same linear time, but it stores every island's cell list and walks each island twice instead of once.

codeNotes.match: if grid2[r][c] and (r, c) not in visit and dfs(r, c):

count-sub-islands.exampleWhy: grid2 has three islands. The right one reaches a cell that is water in grid1, so only two count.
count-sub-islands.hook: Flood each island in grid2, and while you flood, check that grid1 has land under every cell.

optimal.insight: Do the check during the flood. The DFS returns false if any cell sits on grid1 water, but keeps exploring so the whole island gets marked.
steps: Scan grid2 for unvisited land
DFS the island, marking cells visited
Any cell over grid1 water makes the result false
Count islands whose DFS returns true

pitfalls: Writing res and dfs(...) short-circuits, leaving half an island unvisited.
An unvisited leftover piece would later be counted as a new island.

say.intro: This is Count Sub Islands. We get two grids of land and water. An island in grid two counts if every one of its cells is also land in grid one. In our example, grid two has three islands. The one on the right reaches a cell that is water in grid one, so the answer is two.
say.brute: A straightforward approach floods each island in grid two and collects its cells into a list. Then, separately, it checks every cell in that list against grid one. That's still linear in the grid size. But it keeps a list of cells for every island, and walks each island twice, when one walk can do both jobs.
say.insight: Here's the idea. Do the check while flooding. The depth first search returns true only if every cell it touches is land in grid one. The subtle part is to keep exploring even after we find a bad cell. Otherwise the rest of that island stays unvisited, and we'd count it later as a brand new island.
say.anim: We start with grid1 and grid2, two small island grids to compare. At row 0, column 0, the algorithm begins flooding this island in grid2. Cells zero zero and zero one get visited as the flood spreads outward. Now starting row 1, column 0, the dfs explores further, checking grid1 for matching land. Visited set grows to include row2 col2, but grid1 has water there, so result turns false. At row 2, a fresh island starts flooding, marking cells two zero and two two. The first island fails the check, but the second one fully matches grid1, so count becomes two. The final answer returned is two sub islands.
say.code: The DFS returns true for water, edges and visited cells, since they can't break anything. For a land cell, we mark it visited, and set the result to false if grid one has water there. Then we recurse into all four neighbours, calling DFS first and combining after, so nothing gets skipped. The outer loop counts each new island whose DFS returns true.
say.outro: Linear time and space in the grid size. The pattern is graphs: a flood fill with the check folded in.

count-sub-islands.title: Count Sub Islands
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container the problem expects for our method.
This method takes both grids and returns the number of islands in grid2 that are sub islands of grid1.
We store the number of rows and columns, since both grids share the same dimensions.
