We create a set called visit to remember cells of grid2 we have already explored.
We define a recursive helper dfs that floods one island in grid2 and reports whether it fits inside grid1.
This condition catches cells that are out of bounds on any side.
It also stops at water in grid2 or at cells we already visited.
Such cells return true because they neither break nor contribute to the sub island condition.
We mark the current cell as visited so we never process it twice.
We start by assuming this island is valid, setting res to true.
If the matching cell in grid1 is water, this island cannot be a sub island.
So we set res to false to record that failure.
We explore upward and combine the result with res, always making the call so the whole island gets visited.
We explore downward the same way, keeping any earlier false result.
We explore to the left, again combining with res without skipping the recursive call.
We explore to the right, finishing the flood fill from this cell.
We return whether this cell and everything connected to it sit on land in grid1.
We initialize count to zero for the number of sub islands found.
We loop over every row of the grid.
Within each row we loop over every column.
If we find unvisited land in grid2 whose full island passes the dfs check, we have a sub island.
We increment count because this island is entirely covered by land in grid1.
After scanning all cells, we return the total count of sub islands.

find-the-kth-largest-integer-in-the-arra.ask: You get a list of strings, each an integer with no leading zeros, and a number k. Return the k-th largest integer, as a string. Duplicates count as separate entries.

brute.idea: Repeat k times: scan the whole list for the largest remaining number and remove it. The last one removed is the answer.
steps: Convert the strings to integers
Find and remove the current maximum
After k rounds, return the last maximum
brute.whySlow: Each removal rescans the whole list, so k near n costs n squared: ten billion steps for 100,000 numbers.

codeNotes.note: Negate: Python heaps are min heaps
Build the heap in linear time
Undo the negation, back to text

find-the-kth-largest-integer-in-the-arra.exampleWhy: Largest first: 100, 21, 12, 9, 2, 1. The third largest is 12.
find-the-kth-largest-integer-in-the-arra.hook: The numbers arrive as strings. Turn them into integers, heapify, and pop the largest k minus one times.

optimal.insight: Heapify all numbers into a max heap in linear time. Each pop then removes the current largest in log n, and we need only k - 1 pops.
steps: Negate the integers to fake a max heap
Heapify the whole list in O(n)
Pop k - 1 times
The top is the k-th largest

pitfalls: Comparing the strings directly is wrong: "9" sorts above "100".
Without big integers, compare by length first, then character by character.

say.intro: This is Find the Kth Largest Integer in the Array. The numbers come as long strings. We return the kth largest, also as a string. With two, twenty one, twelve, one, a hundred and nine, and k equal to three, the order from the top is a hundred, twenty one, twelve. So the answer is twelve.
say.brute: A simple approach finds the maximum, removes it, and repeats k times. The last maximum removed is the answer. It's correct, but every removal rescans the whole list. When k is close to n, that's n squared work, around ten billion steps for a hundred thousand numbers.
say.insight: Here's the better idea. Put everything into a max heap. Building a heap from a full list takes only linear time. After that, each pop removes the current largest in log time. So pop k minus one times, and the top of the heap is our answer. Python's heap is a min heap, so we store negated values.
say.anim: We start by negating every number, turning this into a max heap problem. After heapify, the array rearranges so the largest value sits at the root as negative hundred. K is three, meaning we need to pop the largest twice to reach third largest. We pop off negative hundred, removing the current largest element from the heap. K decreases to two, and the heap reorders with negative twenty one now on top. Another pop removes negative twenty one, the second largest value, from the heap. K drops to one, so the loop stops, leaving negative twelve at the root. Negating the root gives the answer, the third largest integer is twelve.
say.code: The first line converts each string to an integer and negates it. Heapify arranges that list into a heap in linear time. Then, while k is bigger than one, we pop the top and count k down. Finally, we read the top of the heap, flip the sign back, and return it as a string.
say.outro: Linear plus k log n time, linear space. The pattern is a heap, or priority queue, the go to tool for kth largest questions.

find-the-kth-largest-integer-in-the-arra.title: Find the Kth Largest Integer in the Array
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container for the method that LeetCode asks us to write.
This method takes the list of numeric strings and k, and it will return the kth largest number as a string.
We convert each string to an integer and negate it, since Python's heap is a min heap and negatives simulate a max heap.
We heapify the list in place, which arranges it into a valid heap in linear time.
We loop while k is greater than one, because we only need to discard the k minus one largest values.
Each pop removes the current top of the heap, which is the largest remaining number in original terms.
We decrease k by one to track how many more larger numbers still need to be removed.
Now the top of the heap is the kth largest, so we negate it back and convert it to a string.

flatten-binary-tree-to-linked-list.ask: Given a binary tree, flatten it in place into a chain: each node's right pointer goes to the next node in preorder, and every left pointer becomes null.

brute.idea: Record the nodes in preorder in a list, then walk the list and link each node's right pointer to the next one.
steps: Preorder traversal into a list
For each node, clear left
Point right at the next node in the list
brute.whySlow: Same linear time, but the list holds every node: O(n) extra memory on top of the recursion stack.

codeNotes.note: Left chain's end hooks onto right
Left chain moves to the right

codeNotes.match: return rightTail or leftTail or root

flatten-binary-tree-to-linked-list.exampleWhy: Preorder visits 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, so the chain runs in that order down the right pointers.
flatten-binary-tree-to-linked-list.hook: Rewire a tree into a right-leaning chain in preorder, by splicing each left chain in front of the right one.

optimal.insight: Flatten both subtrees first and return each chain's tail. Then splice: the left chain slots in between the node and its right chain.
steps: Flatten left and right, keeping their tails
Left tail links to the old right child
Left chain moves to the right; left becomes null
Return the last node of this subtree

pitfalls: Link the left tail to root.right before overwriting root.right, or the right side is lost.
The tail is the right tail if it exists, else the left tail, else the node.

say.intro: This is Flatten Binary Tree to Linked List. We rewire the tree in place into a chain that only uses right pointers, in preorder, and every left pointer becomes null. Our tree visits one, two, three, four, five, six in preorder. So that's the chain we build.
say.brute: The easy approach does a preorder traversal and stores every node in a list. Then it walks the list, clears each left pointer, and points right at the next node. That's linear time and correct. The cost is a list holding every node, so linear extra memory on top of the recursion stack.
say.insight: Here's the cleaner idea. Let the recursion flatten both subtrees first, and return the tail of each chain. Then splice. The end of the left chain hooks onto the start of the right chain. The left chain moves over to the right pointer, and left becomes null. Finally, return the last node, so the parent can splice too.
say.anim: We start flattening at node 1, calling dfs recursively on its left subtree. Dfs dives into node 2, then node 3, finding node 3 has no children, returning None. With both children null, node 3 itself becomes the returned tail. Dfs now processes node 4, which also has no children, returning itself as tail. Back at node 2, its left tail is 3 and right tail is 4, so we splice them. Node 3's right pointer links to node 4, then node 2's left is cleared, chaining 2 then 3 then 4. Now dfs processes the right side, flattening node 5 and node 6 similarly into a chain. Finally node 1 splices its flattened left chain before the right chain, producing the final list 1,2,3,4,5,6.
say.code: The helper returns the tail of a flattened subtree. We flatten left and right, keeping their tails. If there's a left child, the left tail points at the old right child, the right pointer takes the left child, and left is cleared. Then we return the right tail if there is one, else the left tail, else the node itself.
say.outro: Linear time, with space equal to the tree height. The pattern is trees: a post order depth first search that returns tails.

flatten-binary-tree-to-linked-list.title: Flatten Binary Tree to Linked List
lineNotes: We define a Solution class that holds the flatten method for this problem.
The flatten method takes the root of the tree and modifies it in place without returning anything.
We define a helper called dfs that flattens a subtree and returns the tail of its resulting chain.
If the current node is empty, there is nothing to flatten, so we handle the base case here.
In that base case we return None because an empty subtree has no tail.
We recursively flatten the left subtree and keep its tail, which we will need for splicing.
We recursively flatten the right subtree and keep its tail, since it may end up as the overall tail.
We only need to splice if the node actually has a left child.
We attach the original right chain after the left chain's tail, so the left chain leads into it.
We move the left chain to the right pointer so it comes right after the current node.
We set the left pointer to null, as every left pointer must be empty in the final chain.
We return the last node of the whole chain, preferring right tail, then left tail, then the node itself.
We start the process by calling dfs on the root, which flattens the whole tree in place.

grid-game.ask: A 2 by n grid of points. Robot one walks from top-left to bottom-right moving right or down, clearing cells it passes. Then robot two does the same. Robot one minimises robot two's total. Return robot two's total.

brute.idea: Try every column where robot one turns down. For each, add up the top-right and bottom-left leftovers with fresh loops.
steps: Pick the column where robot one drops down
Sum the leftovers top right and bottom left
Robot two takes the max; robot one keeps the min
brute.whySlow: Every turning column re-adds both leftovers from scratch: 50,000 columns means over a billion additions.

codeNotes.note: Robot one clears this top cell
Robot two's best; robot one minimises
Cell now left of the turn

grid-game.exampleWhy: Robot one runs the whole top row, then drops. Robot two's best is the bottom row: 1 + 3 + 3 = 7.
grid-game.hook: Robot one chooses a single column to drop down. Robot two then grabs the better leftover piece.

optimal.insight: Robot two can take only the top row right of the turn or the bottom row left of it. Two running sums give both in constant time per column.
steps: top = whole top row, bottom = 0
At each column, robot one clears its top cell
Robot two gets the larger sum; keep the minimum
Add the column's bottom cell to bottom

pitfalls: Robot two cannot take both leftovers; it is a max, not a sum.
Maximising robot one's own score does not minimise robot two's.

say.intro: This is Grid Game. Two rows of points. Robot one goes from the top left to the bottom right, moving only right or down, and clears every cell it touches. Then robot two does the same. Robot one wants robot two's score as small as possible. In our example, robot one runs the whole top row, leaving robot two seven.
say.brute: Robot one only drops down once, so its whole path is decided by one column. The brute force tries every column. For each, it adds up what's left in the top row to the right, and in the bottom row to the left, with fresh loops. That's n squared additions, over a billion for fifty thousand columns.
say.insight: Here's the observation. Robot two can't collect both leftover pieces, because it also drops down only once. So it takes the larger of the top right sum and the bottom left sum. And as the turning column moves right, each sum changes by just one cell. Keep two running sums and update them in constant time.
say.anim: We start with result set to infinity, and the grid values loaded in. Bottom starts at zero, top starts at twenty, the full top row sum. At the first column, top drops by one to nineteen after taking a equals one. We compare top and bottom, giving nineteen, our current best result. Next column, top shrinks to sixteen, and bottom grows to four, beating the old result. Third column, top falls to fifteen, bottom rises to seven, slightly improving result. Fourth column, top drops to zero after subtracting fifteen, bottom reaches eight, giving max seven. The loop ends, and the function returns the final answer seven.
say.code: We start bottom at zero and top at the whole top row. For each column, robot one picks up the top cell, so we subtract it from top. Robot two's best score is the max of the two sums, and we keep the minimum over all columns. Then the bottom cell joins the bottom sum for the next column.
say.outro: Linear time, constant space. The pattern is prefix sums, kept as two running totals.

grid-game.title: Grid Game
lineNotes: We define a solution class, which is the container the problem expects for our method.
The method gridGame takes the two row grid and returns the most points robot two can collect.
We start result at infinity so that any real candidate value will replace it when we take a minimum.
We set bottom to zero and top to the total of the top row, since robot two could initially collect everything on top.
We walk down the columns together, reading the top value a and the bottom value b for each column.
We subtract a from top, so top now holds the points in the top row strictly right of this column.
Robot two gets the larger of top remaining or bottom collected, and robot one picks the turn column minimizing that.
We then add b to bottom, so the next column's bottom sum covers all cells left of it.
After checking every turning column, we return the smallest worst case total for robot two.

trim-a-binary-search-tree.ask: Given a binary search tree and a range from low to high, remove every node outside the range while keeping the survivors' relative structure. Return the root of the trimmed tree.

brute.idea: Collect the surviving values in preorder, then build a fresh BST by inserting them one at a time from the root.
steps: Preorder walk, keeping values in range
Insert each kept value into a new BST
Preorder insertion recreates the trimmed shape
brute.whySlow: Each insert walks down from the root; on a skewed tree that is n squared work, plus a full copy of the values.

codeNotes.note: Too big: right side is too big too
Too small: drop it and its left
In range: trim children in place

trim-a-binary-search-tree.exampleWhy: 0 is too small, so its right subtree, 2 then 1, takes its place. 4 is too big and has no left side.
trim-a-binary-search-tree.hook: A node outside the range doesn't just vanish: BST order tells you which whole side survives.

optimal.insight: If a node is below low, its whole left subtree is too, so the answer comes from its right. Above high, the answer comes from its left.
steps: Empty spot? return None
Too big: return the trimmed left subtree
Too small: return the trimmed right subtree
In range: trim both children and keep the node

pitfalls: Don't just delete an out-of-range node; one of its subtrees may still hold valid values.
The replacement subtree can contain more out-of-range nodes, so trim it too.

say.intro: This is Trim a Binary Search Tree. We get a search tree and a range, low to high. Remove every node outside the range, but keep the survivors in the same relative shape. Here the range is one to three. Zero is too small, so its child two moves up into its place. Four is too big and simply disappears.
say.brute: One approach collects the surviving values in preorder, then builds a brand new search tree by inserting them one at a time. Inserting in preorder rebuilds exactly the trimmed shape. But every insert walks down from the root. On a lopsided tree, that's n squared work, plus a full copy of the values.
say.insight: Here's the key, and it comes from the search tree order. If a node is bigger than high, everything to its right is bigger too, so that whole side goes. The answer is just the trimmed left subtree. If a node is smaller than low, the answer is the trimmed right subtree. Otherwise, keep the node and trim both children.
say.anim: We start at the root, value 3, trimming to keep values between 1 and 3. Node 0 is less than low, so we skip it and recurse into its right child. Node 2 is within range, so we recurse left into node 1 to check it too. Node 1 has no children, so both recursive calls return none and it stays as is. Node 2 keeps its left child as 1, with no right child since it was none. Back at root 3, we now trim its right subtree, which is node 4. Node 4 exceeds high, so it is dropped and its left child, none, is returned instead. The final trimmed tree keeps root 3 with left child 2 and its child 1.
say.code: The base case returns None for an empty spot. If the value is above high, we return the result of trimming the left subtree, skipping this node. If it's below low, we return the trimmed right subtree. Otherwise the node stays. We reattach its trimmed left and right children, and return it.
say.outro: Linear time, with space equal to the tree height. The pattern is trees: a depth first search guided by the search tree order.

trim-a-binary-search-tree.title: Trim a Binary Search Tree
lineNotes: We define a Solution class that holds the method for trimming the tree.
The trimBST method takes the root of a tree plus the low and high bounds, and returns the trimmed root.
First we check the base case, where the current node is empty and there is nothing to trim.
If the node is empty we return None, which ends the recursion down that path.
If the node's value is greater than high, the node and its entire right subtree are out of range.
So we discard this node and return the trimmed result of its left subtree, where valid values may still live.
If the node's value is less than low, the node and its entire left subtree are out of range.
So we discard this node and return the trimmed result of its right subtree instead.
Here the node is within range, so we keep it and replace its left child with the trimmed left subtree.
Likewise we replace its right child with the trimmed right subtree, so out-of-range nodes are removed below.
Finally we return this node as the root of the trimmed subtree, passing it up to its parent.

delete-and-earn.ask: Pick a number to earn its value; then every number equal to it plus one or minus one is deleted. Repeat as often as you like. Return the maximum points you can earn.

brute.idea: Group equal values. For each distinct value in sorted order, try both: take all its copies and skip the next value, or skip it.
steps: Count each value; sort the distinct ones
Take: earn value times count, jump past value + 1
Skip: move on to the next value
Return the better of the two
brute.whySlow: Every distinct value branches two ways with no memory, so 60 distinct values already means over a billion calls.

codeNotes.note: Best two back, best one back

codeNotes.match: prev, cur = cur, max(cur, prev + p)
codeNotes.note: Skip this value, or take it

delete-and-earn.exampleWhy: Take all three 3s for 9 points. That deletes the 2s and the 4, and nothing beats it.
delete-and-earn.hook: Taking a value burns its neighbours. That is House Robber, indexed by value instead of position.

optimal.insight: Put the total points for each value in a bucket. Neighbouring buckets can't both be taken: exactly House Robber along the value line.
steps: points[v] = v times its count
Walk the buckets from 0 to the max
Best = max(skip v, take v plus best two back)
Return the final best

pitfalls: Taking a value means taking every copy, so bucket the totals first.
Gaps between values are fine: empty buckets hold zero.

say.intro: This is Delete and Earn. Pick a number and earn its value. But then every number equal to it plus one, or minus one, gets deleted. What's the most you can earn? With two, two, three, three, three, four, we take all three threes for nine points. That wipes out the twos and the four.
say.brute: The brute force groups equal values, since once you take one copy you might as well take them all. Then, for each distinct value in sorted order, it tries both choices. Take it and skip the next value up, or skip it. Without remembering results, the calls grow exponentially. Sixty distinct values already means over a billion calls.
say.insight: Here's the aha. Line the values up from zero to the max, and put the total points for each value in a bucket. Now the rule is simple. You can't take two neighbouring buckets. That's exactly House Robber. At each value, the best is either the best so far, skipping this one, or this bucket plus the best from two back.
say.anim: We start with nums and build a points bucket for each possible value. Each occurrence adds its value, so points at index two becomes four and index three reaches nine. The last value, four, adds in giving points of zero, zero, four, nine, four. Now we run house robber logic, tracking prev and cur as we scan the buckets. At bucket four, cur updates to four since that's better than taking nothing. At bucket nine, prev becomes four and cur jumps to nine, skipping the neighbor. The final bucket, four, can't beat nine, so cur stays at nine. The function returns cur, giving the final answer of nine.
say.code: We make one bucket per value up to the max, and add each number into its bucket. Then two variables, prev and cur, hold the best from two values back and one value back. For each bucket, the new best is the larger of skipping, which keeps cur, or taking, which is prev plus this bucket. Return cur.
say.outro: Linear in n plus the largest value. The pattern is one dimensional dynamic programming, House Robber in disguise.

delete-and-earn.title: Delete and Earn
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container the problem expects for our method.
The method deleteAndEarn takes a list of integers called nums and returns the maximum points we can earn.
We build a points list with one bucket for every value from zero up to the largest number in nums.
We loop through each number n in the input list nums.
We add n into its bucket, so each bucket holds the total points for taking that value.
We set prev and cur to zero, tracking the best totals from the two most recent buckets.
We walk through each bucket's total p in order along the value line, like houses in House Robber.
We update so cur is the better of skipping this bucket or taking it plus the best from two buckets back.
We return cur, which holds the maximum points after considering every bucket.

design-circular-queue.ask: Build a circular queue of capacity k with enQueue, deQueue, Front, Rear, isEmpty and isFull. enQueue fails when full, deQueue fails when empty, and Front or Rear return -1 when empty.

brute.idea: Keep a plain Python list. Append to enqueue, and pop the first element to dequeue.
steps: Append at the back if not full
Pop index 0 to dequeue
Front and Rear read the list's ends
brute.whySlow: Popping index 0 shifts every remaining element left, so each deQueue costs O(k) instead of O(1).

design-circular-queue.exampleWhy: Capacity 3: the fourth enQueue fails. After one deQueue there is room, so 4 enters and becomes the rear.
design-circular-queue.hook: A fixed-capacity queue where both ends move. Head, tail and a size counter make every operation constant time.

optimal.insight: A singly linked list with head and tail pointers plus a size counter: enqueue links at the tail, dequeue advances the head, nothing shifts.
steps: Track head, tail, size and capacity
enQueue: refuse if full, else link a node at the tail
deQueue: refuse if empty, else move head forward
Front and Rear read head and tail

pitfalls: When the queue is empty, the new node must become both head and tail.
Use the size counter for empty and full; the tail pointer can go stale.

say.intro: This is Design Circular Queue. We build a queue with a fixed capacity k. Enqueue adds at the back, but fails when full. Dequeue removes from the front, but fails when empty. Front and Rear peek, returning minus one when empty. In the example, the capacity is three, so the fourth enqueue fails.
say.brute: The quick version keeps a regular Python list. Enqueue appends to the end, and dequeue pops the first element. It behaves correctly. But popping from the front of a list shifts every remaining element one step left. So each dequeue costs time proportional to the queue's size, instead of constant time.
say.insight: Here's the cleaner design. Use a singly linked list with a head pointer, a tail pointer, and a size counter. Enqueue hangs a new node after the tail. Dequeue just moves the head to the next node. Nothing ever shifts. And the size counter answers is empty and is full instantly.
say.anim: We create a circular queue with capacity three, starting with empty head and tail pointers. Enqueueing one creates the first node, becoming both head and tail. Enqueueing two and three links new nodes at the tail, growing the list without shifting. Enqueueing four fails because size equals capacity, so the queue is full. Rear checks the tail node and correctly returns three. Dequeue advances head past node one, shrinking size to two. Now enqueueing four succeeds, linking a new node and updating the tail pointer. Rear is called again, and this time it returns four, the final answer.
say.code: The constructor stores the capacity and empty pointers. Enqueue first checks is full. For an empty queue, the new node becomes both head and tail. Otherwise we link it after the tail and move the tail. Dequeue checks is empty, then advances the head. Front and Rear return the head or tail value, or minus one.
say.outro: Constant time for every operation, and space linear in the capacity. The pattern is a linked list, used as a queue.

design-circular-queue.title: Design Circular Queue
lineNotes: We define the circular queue class, which will be backed by a singly linked list.
The constructor takes k, the maximum number of items the queue may hold.
We start with head and tail both set to nothing because the queue has no nodes yet.
We store k as the capacity so we can detect when the queue is full.
We track the number of items with a size counter starting at zero.
The enQueue method tries to add a value at the back of the queue.
We first check whether the queue is full, since enqueue must fail in that case.
If it is full, we return false to signal the insertion failed.
Otherwise we create a new list node holding the given value.
We check whether the queue is empty, which needs special handling for the pointers.
For an empty queue, the new node becomes both the head and the tail.
Otherwise the queue already has nodes, so we take the other branch.
We link the current tail's next pointer to the new node, appending it at the back.
We move the tail pointer to the new node so it stays the last element.
We increase the size by one because an item was added.
We return true to show the enqueue succeeded.
The deQueue method removes the item at the front of the queue.
If the queue is empty there is nothing to remove, so we check for that first.
In that case we return false to report failure.
We advance the head to the next node, which drops the old front without shifting anything.
We decrease the size by one since an item was removed.
We return true to show the dequeue succeeded.
The Front method returns the value at the front of the queue.
If the queue is empty we return negative one, otherwise the head's value.
The Rear method returns the value at the back of the queue.
If the queue is empty we return negative one, otherwise the tail's value.
The isEmpty method reports whether the queue holds no items.
It simply checks whether the size equals zero.
The isFull method reports whether the queue has reached its limit.
It returns true when the size equals the capacity.

push-dominoes.ask: A row of dominoes: L is pushed left, R is pushed right, a dot is standing. Each second, falling dominoes tip their standing neighbour; one pushed from both sides stays up. Return the final row.

brute.idea: Simulate one second at a time: build the next row from the current one, until a full round changes nothing.
steps: Each second, look at every standing domino
Pushed by exactly one side? it falls that way
Repeat until nothing changes
brute.whySlow: One R followed by 100,000 dots needs 100,000 rounds, each scanning the whole row.

codeNotes.note: Seed with the dominoes already falling

codeNotes.match: if d == 'L' and i > 0 and dom[i - 1] == '.':
codeNotes.note: Left push tips a standing neighbour

push-dominoes.exampleWhy: The R at index 3 and the L at 7 squeeze three dots: one falls each way and the middle stays up.
push-dominoes.hook: Every falling domino tips its neighbour one tick later. Process the ticks in order with a queue.

optimal.insight: Handle pushes in time order with a queue, like a multi-source BFS. Each domino falls once. R, dot, L is a standoff: cancel that L's turn.
steps: Queue every domino that starts falling, left to right
L tips a standing left neighbour
R tips a standing right neighbour, unless an L waits beyond it
Standoff: pop that L and leave the middle up

pitfalls: A domino pushed from both sides at the same moment stays upright.
Only standing dominoes can be tipped; never overwrite one that already fell.

say.intro: This is Push Dominoes. We get a row where L means pushed left, R means pushed right, and a dot means standing. Each second, every falling domino tips its standing neighbour. If a domino gets pushed from both sides at once, it stays up. In our example, three dots get squeezed between an R and an L.
say.brute: The brute force simulates one second at a time. For each standing domino, check its neighbours. If only a right falling domino touches it, it falls right. If only a left falling one touches it, it falls left. Repeat until nothing changes. A single R followed by a hundred thousand dots takes that many rounds, each scanning the whole row.
say.insight: Here's the better idea. Treat it like a breadth first search with many starting points. Put every initially falling domino in a queue, left to right. Pop them in order, and each tips at most one neighbour, which joins the queue. The only tricky case is R, dot, L. The middle domino is balanced, so we leave it standing and drop that L's turn from the queue.
say.anim: We start with the string of dots, L and R, converted into a list for processing. Scanning left to right, every L and R found gets queued as a starting push, like index one with L. By index eight, the queue holds forces at positions one, three, seven, eight and eleven, ready to spread. Popping position one's L pushes dot at index zero to fall left, since its neighbor was empty. At index three, R checks ahead and sees R then L two steps later, a standoff that cancels the push. Opposing forces from index six and seven both become L, since no space separates them to fight over. Position eleven's L falls left into index ten, filling that gap directly before it. Once the queue empties, the final arrangement reads LL dot RR dot LLRRLL dot dot, our answer.
say.code: We seed the queue with every falling domino and its direction. Each pop handles one push. A left push tips a standing domino on its left. A right push tips the next domino, unless the one after that is an L. In that case the middle is balanced, so we pop that L off the queue and leave the middle standing.
say.outro: Linear time, linear space. The pattern is graphs: a multi source breadth first search, played out over time.

push-dominoes.title: Push Dominoes
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, as the problem platform expects.
The method takes the dominoes string and returns the final settled arrangement as a string.
We convert the string into a list of characters so we can change dominoes in place.
We create a queue to process falling dominoes in time order, like a multi-source breadth first search.
We loop over every position and its character in the list.
We only care about dominoes that are already pushed, meaning anything that is not a dot.
We add the position and direction of each pushed domino to the queue as a starting source.
We keep processing while the queue still holds dominoes that might tip a neighbour.
We take the earliest domino from the front of the queue, getting its position and direction.
If it leans left and the left neighbour is standing, that neighbour will be tipped.
We queue that neighbour as a left falling domino so it can push onward next second.
We mark the neighbour as L in the list right away so nothing else claims it.
Otherwise, if the domino leans right, we look at how it affects its right side.
We check that the right neighbour exists and is still standing.
We also check whether the domino two places right is an L, which would form an R dot L standoff.
In that standoff the middle domino stays up, so we pop the next queue item, which is that L, to cancel its leftward push.
Otherwise there is no standoff, so the right push can safely continue.
We queue the right neighbour as a right falling domino for the next step.
We mark the right neighbour as R in the list.
When the queue empties, everything has settled, so we join the list back into a string and return it.

binary-search-tree-iterator.ask: Build an iterator over a binary search tree that returns its values in ascending order. next returns the next smallest value, and hasNext says whether any values remain. Aim for O(h) memory.

brute.idea: Do a full in-order traversal up front into a list, then hand out the values with an index.
steps: In-order traversal into a sorted list
next returns the value at the index
hasNext checks the index against the length
brute.whySlow: Calls are fast, but it stores all n values up front instead of O(h), and pays the full traversal even if you stop early.

codeNotes.note: Next values live in its right subtree

binary-search-tree-iterator.exampleWhy: In-order visits 3, 7, 9, 15, 20. hasNext is true until 20 has been returned.
binary-search-tree-iterator.hook: Pause an in-order traversal mid-walk: a stack of the left spine lets you resume one node at a time.

optimal.insight: Simulate iterative in-order traversal lazily. The stack holds the path of pending left ancestors, so it never exceeds the tree height.
steps: Constructor pushes the whole left spine
next pops the smallest pending node
Then push the left spine of its right child
hasNext: is the stack non-empty?

pitfalls: A single next can push h nodes; each node is pushed once, so it averages O(1).
Pushing the right child alone, without its left spine, breaks sorted order.

say.intro: This is Binary Search Tree Iterator. We wrap a search tree in an iterator. Next returns the next smallest value, and has next says whether anything is left. In our tree, the values come out as three, seven, nine, fifteen, twenty, and has next turns false after twenty.
say.brute: The easy approach does the whole in order traversal in the constructor and saves every value in a list. Then next just reads the list with an index. Each call is constant time. But memory grows with the whole tree, when the follow up asks for memory proportional to the height. And we pay for the full traversal even if we stop after one call.
say.insight: Here's the idea. Run the iterative in order traversal, but pause it between values. The stack holds the nodes we've passed on the way down but not yet returned. Start by pushing the left spine. Each next pops the smallest pending node, then pushes the left spine of its right child. The stack never gets taller than the tree.
say.anim: We start at root 7, pushing left ancestors 7 and 3 onto the stack. First next pops 3, its right child is empty, so it returns 3. Next pops 7, then pushes its right subtree's left path, 15 then 9, and returns 7. HasNext checks the stack size and confirms more nodes remain, returning true. Next pops 9, which has no right child, returning 9 as the next value. Next pops 15, pushes its right child 20, and returns 15. Next pops the last node 20, which has no children, returning 20. The stack is now empty, so hasNext returns false, ending traversal at order 3,7,9,15,20.
say.code: The constructor walks left from the root, pushing each node. Next pops the top node, which is the smallest one left. Then it moves to that node's right child and pushes its whole left spine. Finally it returns the popped value. Has next just checks whether the stack is empty.
say.outro: Amortized constant time per call, and height-sized memory. The pattern is a stack, used to pause an in order traversal.

binary-search-tree-iterator.title: Binary Search Tree Iterator
lineNotes: We define a class called BSTIterator that wraps the tree and hands out values in sorted order.
The constructor takes the root of the tree, which may be empty.
We start with an empty stack that will hold the pending ancestors along the left path.
We loop while the current node exists, walking down the left edge of the tree.
Each node on the way is pushed onto the stack so we can return to it later.
We move to the left child, since smaller values live there.
The next method returns the smallest value not yet returned.
We pop the top of the stack, which is the next smallest node, and call it res.
We look at the right child of res, since its subtree holds the next larger values.
While that current node exists, we descend through the right subtree's left edge.
Each node along that left edge is pushed so the smallest of them ends on top.
We step to the left child, continuing until no more left children remain.
We return the value of the popped node, which is the next in ascending order.
The hasNext method reports whether any values remain to be returned.
If the stack has anything in it, nodes remain, so we return true; otherwise false.

remove-all-adjacent-duplicates-in-string.ask: Given a string and k, repeatedly delete any k adjacent equal letters until no such group remains. Return the final string, which is guaranteed to be unique.

brute.idea: Scan for any run of k equal letters, cut it out, and restart the scan from the beginning. Stop when a full scan finds nothing.
steps: Scan for k equal adjacent letters
Cut them out, rebuilding the string
Repeat until a full scan finds nothing
brute.whySlow: Every removal rebuilds the string and restarts the scan, so many removals add up to n squared character work.

codeNotes.match: return "".join(char * count for char, count in stack)

remove-all-adjacent-duplicates-in-string.exampleWhy: Delete eee and ccc to get ddbbbdaa. Then bbb goes, giving dddaa. Then ddd goes, leaving aa.
remove-all-adjacent-duplicates-in-string.hook: Removing a run can glue two runs together. A stack of letter counts handles the chain reaction in one pass.

optimal.insight: Keep a stack of [letter, run length]. Extending the top run is O(1); when it reaches k, popping exposes the earlier run to keep growing.
steps: Same letter as the top? bump its count
Different letter? push [letter, 1]
Count reaches k? pop the run
Expand the stack back into a string

pitfalls: Store counts with the letters; recounting the top of a plain char stack is quadratic.
After a pop, the next letter may extend the run underneath.

say.intro: This is Remove All Adjacent Duplicates in String Two. Whenever k equal letters sit next to each other, delete them, and keep going until no group of k remains. With k equal to three, our string collapses in waves. First the three e's and three c's go, then three b's, then three d's. Only two a's are left.
say.brute: The brute force does exactly what the statement says. Scan for k equal letters in a row, cut them out, and start scanning again from the beginning. Stop when a whole scan finds nothing. It works, but every cut rebuilds the string and restarts the search. With many removals, that adds up to n squared work.
say.insight: Here's the insight. A deletion can only join the run just before it with the letters coming next. So keep a stack of runs, each a letter with its count. A new letter either extends the top run, or starts a new one. When a count hits k, pop it. The run underneath is now on top, ready to keep growing. One pass does it all.
say.anim: We start with an empty stack and process the string one letter at a time. Letter d is new, so it's pushed as a run of one. Letter e extends its own run, growing to two, then three e's. Once the run hits three, matching k, that run pops off entirely. The next d merges with the earlier d, forming a run of two. Letters b and c build up similarly, each reaching three and popping away. The second d also completes a run of three and gets removed. Only the two a's remain, so the final answer is aa.
say.code: Our stack holds pairs of a letter and its count. For each character, if it matches the top letter, we bump the count. Otherwise we push the letter with a count of one. If the top count reaches k, we pop that run. At the end, we expand each pair back into letters and join them.
say.outro: Linear time, linear space. The pattern is a stack that stores counts, collapsing runs in a single pass.

remove-all-adjacent-duplicates-in-string.title: Remove All Adjacent Duplicates in String II
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container the interview platform expects for our method.
The method removeDuplicates takes the string s and the group size k, and returns the reduced string.
We start with an empty stack that will hold pairs of a letter and its current run length.
We loop over each character c in the input string, processing the letters from left to right.
If the stack has something and its top letter matches c, we are extending an existing run.
In that case we add one to the run length stored on top of the stack.
Otherwise the letter is different from the top, or the stack is empty, so a new run begins.
We push a new pair holding c with a count of one onto the stack.
After updating, we check whether the top run has reached k, meaning it is a removable group.
If so, we pop that run off, which exposes the earlier run so it can keep growing.
Finally we rebuild the string by repeating each letter by its remaining count and joining everything together.

number-of-ways-to-rearrange-sticks-with-.ask: Sticks of lengths 1 to n stand in a row. A stick is visible from the left if no longer stick comes before it. Count the orders with exactly k visible sticks, modulo 10^9 + 7.

brute.idea: Recurse on the last position without remembering results: tallest last adds a visible stick; any other stick last is hidden.
steps: Tallest last: visible, recurse on n - 1, k - 1
Another stick last: hidden, recurse on n - 1, k
Stop when k = n or k = 0
brute.whySlow: The same (n, k) pairs are recomputed over and over; n = 20 already takes hundreds of thousands of calls.

codeNotes.note: No sticks, none visible: one way

codeNotes.match: for j in range(1, min(i, k) + 1):
codeNotes.note: At most i sticks can show
Tallest last, or one of i - 1 others
All n sticks, exactly k visible

number-of-ways-to-rearrange-sticks-with-.exampleWhy: Of the 24 orders of four sticks, exactly 11 show two from the left, like 3, 1, 4, 2 or 2, 4, 1, 3.
number-of-ways-to-rearrange-sticks-with-.hook: Exactly k sticks visible from the left. Decide who stands last: the tallest stick, or someone hiding.

optimal.insight: Look at the last stick. Tallest there: visible, giving dp[i-1][j-1]. Any of the i - 1 others there: hidden, giving (i-1) · dp[i-1][j].
steps: dp[i][j] = orders of i sticks with j visible
Tallest last: add dp[i-1][j-1]
Another stick last: add (i-1) · dp[i-1][j]
Fill i from 1 to n; answer dp[n][k]

pitfalls: Reason about the last stick, not the first; the tallest last is always visible.
Take the modulo inside the loop to keep the numbers small.

say.intro: This is Number of Ways to Rearrange Sticks With K Sticks Visible. Sticks of lengths one through n stand in a row. From the left, you see a stick only if nothing taller stands before it. How many orders show exactly k sticks? For four sticks and k equal to two, eleven of the twenty four orders work.
say.brute: The brute force could try every one of the n factorial orders, which is hopeless for twenty sticks. A smarter recursion uses the last position, but remembers nothing. The same pair of stick count and visible count gets solved again and again, so the calls still grow exponentially.
say.insight: Here's the aha. Ask who stands last. If the tallest stick is last, everything before it is shorter, and it's visible. That leaves i minus one sticks showing j minus one. If any other stick is last, the tallest stands somewhere in front, so it's hidden. There are i minus one choices, and the rest must still show j. That's a clean two dimensional table.
say.anim: We start with n equal 4, k equal 2, and build a dp table of zeros. Base case dp of zero zero is set to 1, meaning one way to arrange zero sticks. For i equals 1, dp of 1,1 becomes 1, since a single stick is always visible. For i equals 2, dp of 2,1 and dp of 2,2 become 1 each, using the recurrence. For i equals 3, dp of 3,1 is 2 and dp of 3,2 becomes 3. For i equals 4, dp of 4,1 reaches 6 and dp of 4,2 becomes 11. The function returns dp of 4,2, giving the final answer 11.
say.code: We build a table where each cell counts the orders of i sticks with j visible. Zero sticks with zero visible has one way. For each i, j only goes up to the smaller of i and k. Each cell adds the tallest last case, plus i minus one times the hidden case, taken modulo a billion and seven. Return the cell for n and k.
say.outro: n times k time and space. The pattern is two dimensional dynamic programming, built by choosing the last element.

number-of-ways-to-rearrange-sticks-with-.title: Number of Ways to Rearrange Sticks With K Sticks Visible
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the standard wrapper for this problem's submission.
The method takes the number of sticks n and the visible count k, and returns how many arrangements work.
We set MOD to one billion seven so every count stays small and matches the required modulus.
We build a table dp with n plus one rows and k plus one columns, all starting at zero.
The base case is that zero sticks with zero visible has exactly one arrangement, the empty row.
We loop over i from one to n, adding sticks one at a time to the row.
For each i we loop over j visible counts from one up to the smaller of i and k, since more visible than sticks is impossible.
We add the case where the last stick is the tallest, visible, plus i minus one choices for a hidden last stick, all taken modulo MOD.
Finally we return dp at n and k, the number of arrangements with exactly k visible sticks.

unique-email-addresses.ask: Each email has a local name and a domain split by @. In the local name, dots are ignored and everything after the first plus is ignored. Count how many distinct addresses actually receive mail.

brute.idea: Normalize each address, then compare it against every address already kept in a plain list before adding it.
steps: Cut the local name at the first plus
Remove the dots from the local name
Scan the kept list for a duplicate
Append it only if it is new
brute.whySlow: Each new address is compared with every earlier one, so 100 addresses mean about 5,000 string comparisons.

codeNotes.note: Drop everything after the first plus
Dots in the local name mean nothing

unique-email-addresses.exampleWhy: The first two both become testemail@leetcode.com; the third has a different domain, so two inboxes.
unique-email-addresses.hook: Different spellings, same inbox: normalize every address, then let a set count the real ones.

optimal.insight: Once every address is rewritten into its one true form, duplicates are literally equal strings, so a hash set removes them in constant time each.
steps: Split each address at the @
Keep the local name before the first plus
Delete every dot from the local name
Add local plus domain to a set
Return the size of the set

pitfalls: Only the local name loses dots; dots in the domain must stay.
Cut at the plus before removing dots, or a dot after the plus survives.

say.intro: Let's do Unique Email Addresses. Every address has a local name and a domain. In the local name, dots don't count, and anything after a plus is ignored. How many different inboxes actually get mail? In our example, the first two addresses land in the same inbox. The third has a different domain. So the answer is two.
say.brute: A simple approach cleans each address and keeps a plain list of the ones we've seen. Before adding a new address, we walk the whole list looking for a match. It gives the right count. But every new address is compared with every earlier one. That's n squared string comparisons, which hurts once the list gets long.
say.insight: Here's the key. After cleaning, two addresses go to the same inbox exactly when their strings are equal. So the whole problem is normalizing. Cut the local name at the first plus. Remove the dots. Glue the domain back on. Then drop the result into a hash set. The set ignores duplicates for us, in constant time each.
say.anim: We start with an empty set to store unique normalized email addresses. The first email splits into local part test.email+alex and domain leetcode.com. Dropping everything after plus gives local equal to test.email, since plus tags are ignored. Removing dots turns it into testemail, then we add testemail at leetcode.com to the set. The second email becomes testemail after removing dots, same domain, so it's a duplicate. The third email normalizes to testemail at lee.tcode.com, a different domain than before. Now the set holds two distinct normalized addresses after processing all three emails. Returning the set size gives the final answer, two unique email addresses.
say.code: Here's the code. We start with an empty set. For each address, we split once at the at sign. The domain is never touched. On the local name, we keep only the part before the first plus. Then we replace every dot with nothing. We join the pieces and add them to the set. The answer is just the size of the set.
say.outro: Linear in the total length of the input. The pattern is arrays and hashing: normalize each item to a canonical form, then let a set count them.

unique-email-addresses.title: Unique Email Addresses
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container this problem's method lives in.
The method numUniqueEmails takes a list of email strings and returns how many distinct receiving addresses exist.
We create an empty set called unique, so duplicate normalized addresses collapse automatically with constant time inserts.
We loop over each email in the input list so every address gets rewritten into its true form.
We split the email at the at sign, giving us the local name and the domain separately.
We split the local name at plus and keep only the first piece, discarding everything after the first plus.
We remove every dot from the local name, since dots in the local part are ignored.
We rebuild the address from cleaned local name, at sign, and domain, then add it to the set.
We return the size of the set, which equals the number of distinct normalized addresses.

baseball-game.ask: You get a list of operations. A number records that score. Plus records the sum of the last two scores, D doubles the last score, and C deletes the last score. Return the total of all remaining scores.

brute.idea: Keep every score ever written, marking cancelled ones as dead. For each rule, scan backwards to find the latest live scores.
steps: Write numbers into the log as live
C: scan back, kill the latest live score
D or +: scan back for the latest live scores
Sum the live scores at the end
brute.whySlow: Cancelled scores never leave the log, so after many C operations each backwards scan crawls past a pile of dead entries.

codeNotes.note: Plus: sum of the top two

baseball-game.exampleWhy: The record ends as 5, -2, -4, 9, 5, 14, and those add up to 27.
baseball-game.hook: Every rule only looks at the most recent scores, which is exactly what a stack hands you.

optimal.insight: Each operation only touches the newest one or two scores, and C removes the newest. Last in, first out: the record is a stack.
steps: Number: push it
D: push double the top
+: push the sum of the top two
C: pop the top
Return the sum of the stack

pitfalls: Check for the symbols before calling int, since minus two is a valid number.
Plus adds a new score; it does not replace the two it read.

say.intro: Baseball Game. We get a list of operations. A number records a score. Plus records the sum of the last two scores. D records double the last score. And C cancels the last score. Return the total. In our example, the record ends as five, minus two, minus four, nine, five and fourteen. That adds up to twenty seven.
say.brute: One clumsy way keeps every score ever written, and just marks cancelled ones as dead. Then each rule scans backwards through the log to find the latest live scores. It works. But dead entries never go away. After lots of cancels, every scan crawls past them, and the worst case turns quadratic.
say.insight: Notice that every rule only cares about the newest scores. Plus reads the top two. D reads the top one. And C removes the newest one. That's last in, first out. So the record is simply a stack. Each operation is one push or one pop, and the answer is the sum at the end.
say.anim: We start with an empty stack to record each score as we process operations. Scores five, negative two, and four are plain numbers, so each gets pushed onto the stack. The next operation is C, which removes the most recent score, popping four off the stack. D doubles the last score, so negative two becomes negative four and is pushed on. Nine is just a number, so it gets pushed directly onto the stack. The first plus adds the last two scores, nine and negative four, pushing five. The second plus adds nine and five, pushing fourteen onto the stack. Summing all the stack values together gives a final score of twenty seven.
say.code: In the code, we keep one list as our stack. For plus, we push the top two added together. For D, we push the top doubled. For C, we pop. Anything else must be a number, so we convert it and push it. We test the symbols first, because minus two is a number, not an operation. Then we return the sum.
say.outro: Linear time and space. The pattern is a stack: when every rule looks only at the most recent items, push and pop.

baseball-game.title: Baseball Game
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container this problem's method lives in.
The method calPoints takes the list of operation strings and returns the final total score as an integer.
We start with an empty stack that will hold every valid score recorded so far.
We loop over each operation in order, since each one depends on the scores before it.
If the operation is a plus, we need to add the last two scores together.
We push the sum of the top two stack entries, the newest and the one just below it.
If the operation is D, we need to double the most recent score.
We push twice the top of the stack as a new score.
If the operation is C, the most recent score must be cancelled.
We pop the top of the stack, which removes the newest score, last in first out.
Otherwise the operation must be a number written as text.
We convert that text to an integer and push it as a new score.
After all operations, we return the sum of every score still left on the stack.

reorder-routes-to-make-all-paths-lead-to.ask: There are n cities joined by n minus 1 one-way roads that form a tree. Return the fewest roads you must reverse so that every city can drive to city zero.

brute.idea: For each road, delete it and test whether its start city can still be reached from city zero. If so, the road points away and must flip.
steps: Build the undirected tree
For each road a→b, ignore it
Search from 0; reached a means flip
Count the flips
brute.whySlow: It runs a full graph search once per road, so 50,000 roads mean 50,000 searches.

codeNotes.match: edges = {(a, b) for a, b in connections}

reorder-routes-to-make-all-paths-lead-to.exampleWhy: Roads 0→1, 1→3 and 4→5 point away from city 0; reversing those three lets everyone reach 0.
reorder-routes-to-make-all-paths-lead-to.hook: Start at city zero and walk outward: every road pointing away from you must be flipped.

optimal.insight: Treat roads as undirected and DFS out from city zero. Every road you cross while moving away from zero must point back toward you; if it does not, flip it.
steps: Store original directions in a set
Build an undirected neighbor list
DFS from city 0, marking visited
Road neighbor→city missing? count a flip
Return the flip count

pitfalls: Follow only original directions and you never reach cities behind a wrong-way road.
Check the pair neighbor then city, not city then neighbor.

say.intro: Let's solve Reorder Routes to Make All Paths Lead to the City Zero. We have n cities connected by one way roads, and they form a tree. What's the fewest roads we must reverse so everyone can drive to city zero? In our example, three roads point the wrong way. So the answer is three.
say.brute: The brute force checks each road on its own. Pretend the road is gone, then search from city zero. If we can still reach the road's starting city, then the road leads away from zero, and it has to flip. That's correct. But it's one full search per road, so the work grows as n squared.
say.insight: Here's the trick. Ignore direction and walk outward from city zero. Every road we cross leads from our current city to a new one, further from zero. For traffic to flow home, the road must point from the new city back to the current one. If the original road doesn't, that's exactly one flip. One DFS counts them all.
say.anim: We build a set of original edges and an undirected neighbor map from the connections. Starting the depth first search from city zero, with visit set containing just zero. Visiting neighbor one, since edge zero to one exists, it points away from zero, so we increment changes to one. From city one we check neighbor three; edge three to one is missing, meaning it points wrong way, changes becomes two. From city three we explore neighbor two; that edge already points correctly back, so no change needed. Back at zero, we visit neighbor four; edge four to zero already points correctly, no change there. From city four we check neighbor five; edge four to five points away, so changes increases to three. The search finishes and returns three, the minimum roads that must be reversed.
say.code: In the code, a set remembers each road's true direction. Then we build an undirected neighbor list. We mark city zero visited and DFS from it. For each unvisited neighbor, we ask: is there a road from that neighbor into this city? If not, we add one change. Then we mark the neighbor and recurse.
say.outro: Linear time and space. The pattern is graphs: traverse from the target, and count edges pointing the wrong way.

reorder-routes-to-make-all-paths-lead-to.title: Reorder Routes to Make All Paths Lead to the City Zero
lineNotes: We define the Solution class that holds the method for this problem.
The method takes the city count and the list of directed connections, and returns the minimum number of reversals.
We store every original directed road in a set so we can quickly check a road's direction later.
We create a dictionary mapping each city to a list of its adjacent cities, ignoring direction.
We loop over every connection, reading its starting city a and ending city b.
We add b to the neighbor list of a so we can travel along the road forward.
We also add a to the neighbor list of b so the road can be walked in reverse.
We mark city zero as visited, since the search starts there and we must never return to it.
We set the counter of reversed roads to zero before the search begins.
We define a depth first search function that explores outward from a given city.
We declare changes as nonlocal so the inner function can update the outer counter.
We loop through every city adjacent to the current city, regardless of road direction.
If that neighbor was already visited, it is the way we came from or already handled.
So we skip it and move on to the next neighbor.
If no road goes from the neighbor to the current city, the road points away from zero and must be flipped.
We add one to the count of changes for that road.
We mark the neighbor as visited so we do not process it again.
We recurse into the neighbor to keep exploring outward through the tree.
We start the search from city zero, the destination everything must reach.
We return the total number of roads we had to reverse.

maximum-alternating-subsequence-sum.ask: The alternating sum of an array adds the elements at even positions and subtracts those at odd positions. Pick any subsequence of nums, keeping order, and return the largest alternating sum possible.

brute.idea: Recursively decide for each element whether to skip it or take it, with a plus or minus sign depending on how many we have taken.
steps: At index i, try skipping the element
Or take it with the current sign
Flip the sign after a take
Return the better branch
brute.whySlow: Every element doubles the branches; forty numbers already means about a trillion subsequences.

codeNotes.note: Skip n, or add it as a plus

maximum-alternating-subsequence-sum.exampleWhy: Take 6, 1 and 5: six minus one plus five is ten, the best possible.
maximum-alternating-subsequence-sum.hook: Two running totals, one ending on a plus and one on a minus, replace every subsequence.

optimal.insight: A future choice only needs to know whether the next taken number gets plus or minus. So keep two bests: ending on a plus, ending on a minus.
steps: even: best sum where the next sign is minus
odd: best sum where the next sign is plus
For each n, even = max(even, odd + n)
odd = max(odd, even - n), using old values
Answer is even

pitfalls: Updating sumEven first and then using it for sumOdd double-counts the same number.
The answer is sumEven; ending on a subtraction never helps.

say.intro: This one is Maximum Alternating Subsequence Sum. Pick any subsequence, keeping the order. Its score adds the first element, subtracts the second, adds the third, and so on. What's the biggest score? In our example we take six, one and five. Six minus one plus five is ten.
say.brute: The brute force tries everything. At each number we either skip it, or take it. If we take it, it gets a plus or a minus depending on how many we've taken so far. Then we keep the better branch. It's correct, but every number doubles the branches. That's two to the n.
say.insight: So what does the future actually need to know? Only whether the next number we take gets a plus or a minus. So track two values. Even is the best sum where the next sign is minus. Odd is the best sum where the next sign is plus. For each number, either skip it, or move from one state to the other.
say.anim: We start with sumEven and sumOdd both at zero for this array. Taking the first number, six, sumEven updates to six, treating it as added. With two, sumOdd stays better by adding at an even step, giving four. Number one pushes sumOdd up to five, tracking the best alternating minus ending. With two again, sumEven jumps to seven by adding onto the odd best. Four extends the pattern, raising sumEven to nine using the alternating trick. Finally five lifts sumEven to ten, the best alternating sum so far. The loop ends and the function returns ten as the final answer.
say.code: In the code, both totals start at zero, the empty choice. For each number, new even is the larger of old even, or old odd plus this number. New odd is the larger of old odd, or old even minus it. We compute both from old values, then swap them in together. The answer is even.
say.outro: Linear time, constant space. The pattern is one dimensional dynamic programming, with two states that hand off to each other.

maximum-alternating-subsequence-sum.title: Maximum Alternating Subsequence Sum
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container the interview platform expects for our method.
The method maxAlternatingSum takes a list of integers called nums and returns the largest alternating subsequence sum as an integer.
We start both sumEven and sumOdd at zero, since an empty subsequence has sum zero and is always allowed.
We loop through each number n in nums, deciding for each one whether to use it or skip it.
The new sumEven is the better of keeping the old one or taking n with a plus after an odd-length sum.
The new sumOdd is the better of keeping the old one or taking n with a minus after an even-length sum.
We update both sums together using the temporary values, so neither calculation sees the other's already-changed result.
After the loop we return sumEven, because the best alternating sum never gains by ending on a subtracted number.

process-tasks-using-servers.ask: Servers have weights, and task j arrives at second j. Each task goes to the free server with the smallest weight, ties broken by index. If none is free, it waits for the next server to finish. Return which server runs each task.

brute.idea: Track when each server becomes free. For every task, scan all servers for the best free one, jumping time forward if none is free.
steps: Time is the later of now and arrival
No free server? jump to earliest finish
Scan all servers for lightest free one
Mark it busy until time plus duration
brute.whySlow: Every task rescans every server: 200,000 tasks times 200,000 servers is forty billion checks.

codeNotes.match: available = [(w, i) for i, w in enumerate(servers)]

codeNotes.note: Task i cannot start before second i
All busy: skip to next finish

process-tasks-using-servers.exampleWhy: Server 2 is lightest, so it takes every task it is free for; servers 0 and 1 cover the gaps.
process-tasks-using-servers.hook: Two heaps: one hands out the lightest free server, the other tells you who frees up next.

optimal.insight: Keep free servers in a min-heap by weight and index, and busy servers in a min-heap by finish time. Each step only touches heap tops.
steps: Heapify free servers as weight, index
Advance time to the task's arrival
Nothing free? jump time to next finish
Release every busy server finished by now
Pop lightest free server, push it as busy

process-tasks-using-servers.optimalCode:
class Solution:
    def assignTasks(self, servers: List[int], tasks: List[int]) -> List[int]:
        res = [0] * len(tasks)
        available = [(w, i) for i, w in enumerate(servers)]
        heapq.heapify(available)
        busy = []
        time = 0
        for i in range(len(tasks)):
            time = max(time, i)
            if not available:
                time = busy[0][0]
            while busy and busy[0][0] <= time:
                _, w, idx = heapq.heappop(busy)
                heapq.heappush(available, (w, idx))
            w, idx = heapq.heappop(available)
            res[i] = idx
            heapq.heappush(busy, (time + tasks[i], w, idx))
        return res
pitfalls: When all servers are busy, time jumps forward; later tasks start from that time.
Released servers must re-enter by weight and index, not by finish time.

say.intro: Let's do Process Tasks Using Servers. Each server has a weight, and task j arrives at second j. A task goes to the lightest free server, with ties broken by the smaller index. If nobody is free, it waits. Which server runs each task? In our example, server two is the lightest, so it grabs most tasks.
say.brute: The direct approach remembers when each server becomes free. For every task, it scans all the servers to find the lightest free one. If none is free, time jumps to the earliest finish. That works, but each task scans every server. That's m times n, and with two hundred thousand of each, it's far too slow.
say.insight: Here's the thing. We only ever need two answers. Which free server is lightest? And which busy server finishes first? Those are both minimums, so use two heaps. Free servers are ordered by weight, then index. Busy servers are ordered by finish time. Each task pops and pushes a few times, and that's logarithmic.
say.anim: We start with servers of weight three, three, two, heaped by weight and index. For task zero, server two has the smallest weight, so it gets assigned, res becomes two. At time one, server two is still busy, so server one, weight three, handles task one. At time two, server zero becomes the pick, since it ties on weight but has lower index. At time three, server two finishes and frees up, taking over task three. At time four, no servers are free, so server one, still weight three, takes task four. At time five, multiple servers finish and free up together into the available heap. Server two is picked again for the last task, giving final answer two two zero two one two.
say.code: In the code, the free heap holds weight and index pairs. For each task, time is at least its arrival second. If nothing is free, we jump time to the top of the busy heap. Then we move every server finished by now back to the free heap. Finally we pop the lightest, record it, and push it as busy until now plus the duration.
say.outro: Time is n plus m, times log n. The pattern is heaps: two priority queues, one for ready items and one for items coming back.

process-tasks-using-servers.title: Process Tasks Using Servers
lineNotes: We define a class named Solution, which is the container for the method the problem expects us to write.
The method assignTasks takes the server weights and the task durations, and returns the server index chosen for each task.
We create a result list with one slot per task, all starting at zero, to record the chosen server.
We build the available heap of pairs holding weight and index, so the lightest server, with the lowest index on ties, is on top.
We heapify the available list so it becomes a valid min-heap in linear time.
We start with an empty busy heap, which will hold servers currently running tasks ordered by their finish time.
We set the current time to zero, and it will move forward only when needed.
We loop over each task index, since task i arrives at second i and must be assigned in order.
We move time forward to at least i, because a task cannot start before it arrives.
If no server is free right now, we must wait for the earliest finishing server.
We jump time to the finish time of the top busy server, skipping idle seconds directly.
While any busy servers have finished by the current time, we need to release them back to the free pool.
We pop a finished server from busy, ignoring its finish time and keeping its weight and index.
We push that server into available using weight and index, so heap ordering picks it correctly later.
We pop the best free server, the smallest weight and then smallest index, to run this task.
We record this server's index as the answer for task i.
We push the server into busy with its new finish time, the current time plus the task duration.
After all tasks are assigned, we return the result list of server indices.

splitting-a-string-into-descending-conse.ask: Given a string of digits, can you cut it into two or more pieces whose numeric values strictly descend by exactly one each step? Leading zeros are fine. Return true or false.

brute.idea: Try every way to place cuts between digits, then check whether the resulting values go down by one each time.
steps: Each gap between digits is cut or not
Skip the no-cut case: need two pieces
Convert pieces to numbers
Check each drop is exactly one
brute.whySlow: A 20-digit string has over half a million cut patterns, and each is fully checked even when its first two pieces already fail.

codeNotes.match: if val + 1 == prev and dfs(j + 1, val):

codeNotes.note: First piece leaves at least one digit

splitting-a-string-into-descending-conse.exampleWhy: Split as 05, 004, 3: the values 5, 4, 3 each drop by exactly one.
splitting-a-string-into-descending-conse.hook: Choose the first number, and every later piece is forced: it must be exactly one less.

optimal.insight: Only the first piece is a free choice. After that, the next piece must equal previous minus one, so backtracking prunes every branch the moment a value is wrong.
steps: Try each prefix as the first value
From the next index, grow a piece digit by digit
Recurse only if piece equals previous minus one
Reaching the end means success

pitfalls: The first piece cannot be the whole string; at least two pieces are required.
Leading zeros are allowed, so 004 really is four.

say.intro: This is Splitting a String Into Descending Consecutive Values. We get a string of digits. Can we cut it into at least two pieces, where each value is exactly one less than the one before? In our example, zero five, zero zero four, and three give five, four, three. So the answer is true.
say.brute: The brute force tries every cut pattern. Each gap between digits is either cut or not. For each pattern, we convert the pieces to numbers and check that each step drops by one. It's correct. But there are two to the n patterns, and we check each one fully, even when the first two pieces already fail.
say.insight: Here's the key. Once we pick the first number, nothing else is free. The next piece must equal that number minus one. So we backtrack. Grow the next piece one digit at a time. Only recurse when it hits exactly previous minus one. Every wrong branch dies immediately.
say.anim: We start with the string 050043, trying each possible first piece one by one. With i equal to zero, the first piece is just 0, so prev becomes 0 and we search for the next piece. Every candidate value like 5, 50, 500, 5004, and 50043 fails because none equals prev minus one. This whole branch returns false, so we backtrack and try i equal to one instead. Now the first piece is 05, giving prev equal to 5, and we look for the next piece starting at index 2. The piece 0 fails, but the piece 4 matches since 4 plus 1 equals 5, so recursion continues. Next the piece 3 matches since 3 plus 1 equals prev 4, moving index all the way to 6. Index now equals the string length, so recursion returns true all the way up, giving final answer true.
say.code: In the code, dfs takes an index and the previous value. If the index hits the end, we used every digit, so return true. Otherwise grow a piece from index to j. If its value plus one equals previous, and the rest also works, return true. The outer loop tries each first piece, but never the whole string.
say.outro: Polynomial instead of exponential, and instant for twenty digits. The pattern is backtracking: fix one choice, and the constraints force the rest.

splitting-a-string-into-descending-conse.title: Splitting a String Into Descending Consecutive Values
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, the standard wrapper for this problem.
The splitString method takes the digit string s and returns whether a valid descending split exists.
We define a helper dfs that takes the current index in the string and the previous piece's value.
If index has reached the length of s, every character has been used, so the split worked.
In that case we return true, since all pieces matched the descending by one rule.
Otherwise we try every possible end position j for the next piece starting at index.
We convert the substring from index through j into an integer, which handles leading zeros naturally.
If this value plus one equals prev, we recurse on the rest, with this value as the new previous.
When that recursion succeeds we return true immediately, since one valid split is enough.
If no end position led to success, we return false, which backtracks to the caller.
In the main body, we try each possible first piece, stopping before the last character so at least two pieces exist.
For each first piece we start dfs right after it, passing the first piece's integer value as prev.
If dfs finds a valid split from that starting choice, we return true.
If no first piece choice works, we return false.

eliminate-maximum-number-of-monsters.ask: Monster i starts dist[i] away and walks toward the city at speed[i]. You can shoot one monster per minute, starting at minute zero. You lose the moment a monster arrives. Return how many you can eliminate.

brute.idea: Simulate minute by minute: each minute, scan every living monster, shoot the one that will arrive soonest, and stop if any has already arrived.
steps: Scan living monsters for an arrival by now
If one arrived, the game is over
Otherwise scan again for the soonest arrival
Shoot it and advance one minute
brute.whySlow: Every minute rescans all survivors, so 100,000 monsters cost about five billion checks.

codeNotes.match: arrive = sorted(d / s for d, s in zip(dist, speed))

eliminate-maximum-number-of-monsters.exampleWhy: Sorted arrivals are 1.5, 2, 2.33, 2.5, 6; by minute 3 the fourth monster has already arrived.
eliminate-maximum-number-of-monsters.hook: Only arrival times matter: sort them and shoot whoever lands first.

optimal.insight: A monster's only property that matters is its arrival time, dist over speed. Shooting in order of arrival is optimal, so sort and check each minute.
steps: Compute arrival time dist divided by speed
Sort arrival times ascending
Minute m shoots the m-th earliest monster
If it already arrived by minute m, stop

pitfalls: Arriving exactly when the weapon recharges still loses, so compare with less-or-equal.
Use true division or ceiling math; integer division rounds arrivals too early.

say.intro: Let's do Eliminate Maximum Number of Monsters. Each monster starts some distance away and walks toward the city at its own speed. We fire one shot per minute, starting at minute zero. If any monster reaches the city, we lose. How many can we eliminate? In our example, three.
say.brute: A direct simulation goes minute by minute. Scan every living monster. If one has already arrived, the game ends. Otherwise shoot the one that will arrive soonest, and move to the next minute. It's correct, but each minute rescans everyone. That's n squared.
say.insight: Here's the key. Distance and speed only matter through one number: the arrival time, distance divided by speed. And the most urgent monster should always be shot first. So sort the arrival times. At minute m, we shoot the m th earliest monster. If it already arrived by minute m, we're done.
say.anim: We compute each monster's arrival time as distance divided by speed. Sorted arrival times are 1.5, 2.0, 2.33, 2.5, and 6.0 minutes. At minute zero, arrival time 1.5 is greater, so we can still shoot it. At minute one, arrival time 2.0 is still greater than one, safe again.
