At minute two, arrival time 2.33 beats the deadline, so we survive. At minute three, arrival time 2.5 is now less than or equal to three. That means a monster reaches us before we can shoot it. The function returns three, the maximum number of monsters we can eliminate.
say.code: In the code, we build the arrival times and sort them in one line. Then we loop over the minutes. If the monster at this position arrived at or before this minute, we return the minute, which is exactly how many shots we fired. If the loop finishes, we eliminated everyone.
say.outro: Sorting makes it n log n. The pattern is greedy: reduce each item to one deadline, then handle the earliest deadline first.

eliminate-maximum-number-of-monsters.title: Eliminate Maximum Number of Monsters
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container the judge expects for the method that solves this problem.
The method takes lists of distances and speeds and returns how many monsters we can eliminate before one reaches the city.
We compute each monster's arrival time as distance over speed, then sort so the earliest arrivals come first.
We loop over each minute from zero up to the number of monsters, firing one shot per minute.
If the monster we need to shoot at this minute has already arrived by then, we have lost.
In that case we return the current minute, since that is exactly how many monsters we shot before losing.
If the loop finishes without any monster arriving too soon, we eliminated every monster and return the total count.

maximum-product-of-the-length-of-two-pal.ask: Pick two subsequences of s that never use the same index, and both read the same forwards and backwards. Return the largest possible product of their lengths. The string has at most 12 characters.

brute.idea: Enumerate every bitmask, keep the ones whose chosen letters form a palindrome, then try every pair of palindromes that share no index.
steps: For each mask, read its chosen letters
Keep masks that form a palindrome
Pair up kept masks with no common bit
Track the largest product of lengths
brute.whySlow: Pairing all palindromic masks is quadratic in 2^n: twelve letters can mean millions of pairs.

codeNotes.match: return max(lps(m) * lps(full ^ m) for m in range(1, full))

maximum-product-of-the-length-of-two-pal.exampleWhy: Take aa from indices 0 and 2, and bb from indices 1 and 3: two times two is 4.
maximum-product-of-the-length-of-two-pal.hook: Split the indices with a bitmask; the best palindrome inside each half is a memoized lookup.

optimal.insight: Give one subsequence's indices as mask m; the other can use anything in the complement. So answer = max over m of LPS(m) · LPS(complement), with LPS memoized per mask.
steps: lps(mask): longest palindrome using only those indices
Compare the lowest and highest chosen index
Equal letters: 2 plus lps of the inside
Else drop one end and take the better
Try every split of indices into m and complement

pitfalls: Each mask's LPS must be memoized, or the recursion becomes exponential per mask.
Both halves must be non-empty: skip mask zero and the full mask.

say.intro: Maximum Product of the Length of Two Palindromic Subsequences. Pick two subsequences that never share an index, and both must be palindromes. Maximize the product of their lengths. The string has at most twelve letters. In our example, a b a b splits into a a and b b, so the answer is two times two, which is four.
say.brute: The brute force uses bitmasks. For every mask, read the chosen letters and keep it if they form a palindrome. Then try every pair of kept masks that share no bit, and multiply their lengths. It works. But pairing all those masks is like four to the n, which is millions of pairs for twelve letters.
say.insight: Flip the question around. Once the first subsequence owns some indices, the second can use anything else. So split the indices into a mask and its complement. On each side, take the longest palindromic subsequence. Compute that per mask with memoized recursion: compare the lowest and highest chosen index, just like the classic interval version.
say.anim: We start with the string abab, checking every way to split its letters into two groups. For mask 14, the ends match, so we add two and recurse on the inner bits, getting three. For mask 13, the ends differ, so we try dropping each end and take the better result. Smaller masks like 12 and 5 get solved and cached, building up longest palindromic subsequence lengths. Repeated masks like 3 and 12 are reused instantly from memo instead of recomputing. Masks like 10 and 11 combine matching or mismatched ends to produce lengths of two. More masks like 9, 7, and 6 fill in, some reaching length three for matching patterns. After checking every split, the best product of two palindromic subsequence lengths found is four.
say.code: In the code, lps of a mask with zero or one bit is zero or one. Otherwise we find the lowest and highest set bits. If their letters match, it's two plus the inside. If not, drop one end and keep the better. Results are memoized. Finally, try every mask and multiply by its complement.
say.outro: About two to the n states. The pattern is bit manipulation: bitmasks as subsets, with dynamic programming on top.

maximum-product-of-the-length-of-two-pal.title: Maximum Product of the Length of Two Palindromic Subsequences
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container the problem expects for our method.
The method maxProduct takes the string s and returns the largest product of two disjoint palindromic subsequence lengths.
We store the length of s in n, since each character index becomes one bit in a mask.
We create an empty memo dictionary to cache the longest palindromic subsequence length for each mask.
We define a helper lps that computes the longest palindromic subsequence using only the indices set in mask m.
This checks whether m has at most one bit set, using the trick that clearing the lowest bit leaves zero.
With zero bits the answer is zero, and with exactly one bit it is one, since a single character is a palindrome.
We check whether this mask was already solved, to avoid repeating work.
If so, we return the cached answer immediately.
We find the lowest set bit, which is the leftmost chosen index, by isolating it and taking its bit position.
We find the highest set bit, the rightmost chosen index, from the bit length of the mask.
If the characters at the leftmost and rightmost chosen indices match, they can wrap a palindrome.
We add two for the matching pair and recurse on the mask with both of those bits removed.
Otherwise the two ends cannot both be used, so we handle the mismatch case.
We try dropping the left end or the right end, and keep whichever gives the longer palindrome.
We save the computed result in memo under this mask for future reuse.
We return the result to the caller.
We build full, a mask with all n bits set, representing every index in the string.
We try every nonempty proper mask m, pairing it with its complement, and return the maximum product of their palindrome lengths.

flip-equivalent-binary-trees.ask: A flip swaps a node's left and right subtrees. Two binary trees are flip equivalent if some sequence of flips turns one into the other. Given both roots, return whether they are flip equivalent. Values are unique.

brute.idea: Generate every tree shape reachable by flips from the first tree, as serialized tuples, and check whether the second tree is one of them.
steps: Collect all flip variants of each subtree
Combine children straight and swapped
Serialize the second tree
Return whether it is in the set
brute.whySlow: Every internal node doubles the variants, so a tree with 30 internal nodes has a billion shapes to build.

codeNotes.note: True only if both are empty

flip-equivalent-binary-trees.exampleWhy: Flipping nodes 1, 3 and 5 in the first tree produces the second tree exactly.
flip-equivalent-binary-trees.hook: At every node, the children either line up straight or crossed. Check both, recursively.

optimal.insight: Roots must match. Then the children either match straight, left with left, or crossed, left with right. Recurse on both options; unique values keep it linear.
steps: Both empty is true; one empty is false
Different values: false
Try straight: left-left and right-right
Try crossed: left-right and right-left
Equivalent if either works

pitfalls: Handle one-empty-one-not before reading values, or you crash on None.
Short-circuit with and: a failed first pair skips the second call.

say.intro: Let's solve Flip Equivalent Binary Trees. A flip swaps a node's left and right subtrees. Can some sequence of flips turn the first tree into the second? In our example, flipping nodes one, three and five does it, so the answer is true.
say.brute: The brute force builds every shape the first tree can reach. For each node, combine every variant of its children, both straight and swapped. Then check whether the second tree is in that set. It's correct, but each internal node doubles the variants. That's exponential.
say.insight: Think locally. The two roots must have the same value. After that, either this node was not flipped, so left matches left and right matches right. Or it was flipped, so left matches right and right matches left. Recurse on both options. Since values are unique, the wrong option fails right away.
say.anim: We start comparing root one and root two, both valued one, roots match so we continue. Left subtrees two and three have different values, so straight matching fails here. Since straight failed, we try crossed matching, pairing left with the opposite right child. Deeper nodes valued four and four match straight, and their subtrees recurse down to null leaves. Straight and crossed both succeed for node four, so flip equivalence holds there. For nodes valued seven, straight matching also leads to a true crossed check. Back at node two, crossed matching links four with five and six, confirming equivalence. All subtrees align through straight or crossed matches, so the final answer is true.
say.code: In the code, if either node is empty, they're equivalent only if both are. Different values return false. Then straight checks left with left and right with right. Crossed checks left with right and right with left. The and short circuits, so a failed first call skips the second. We return straight or crossed.
say.outro: Linear time, height sized stack. The pattern is trees: compare two trees recursively, trying each allowed pairing.

flip-equivalent-binary-trees.title: Flip Equivalent Binary Trees
lineNotes: We define a solution class that holds the method for checking whether two trees are flip equivalent.
The method takes two roots and returns true or false depending on whether the trees can match after flips.
If either root is empty, we reach the base case where at least one tree has run out of nodes.
Here we return whether both are empty, since an empty tree only matches another empty tree.
If the two root values differ, the trees cannot match no matter how we flip their children.
So we return false right away without exploring any deeper.
For the straight option, we check that the left subtrees match each other and the right subtrees match each other.
This second half of the straight check compares the two right subtrees and combines it with the left result using and.
For the crossed option, we check that the first left subtree matches the second right subtree, as if a flip happened.
The second half of the crossed check compares the first right subtree with the second left subtree, and both must hold.
The trees are flip equivalent if either the straight arrangement or the crossed arrangement works.

seat-reservation-manager.ask: Design a manager for seats numbered 1 to n, all free at first. reserve takes the smallest free seat and returns its number. unreserve frees the given seat again.

brute.idea: Keep a taken flag for each seat. reserve scans from seat 1 upward for the first free one.
steps: Array of n flags, all free
reserve: scan for the first free seat
Mark it taken and return it
unreserve: clear that seat's flag
brute.whySlow: When the front seats are taken, each reserve walks past them all: 100,000 calls can cost ten billion steps.

codeNotes.note: Sorted list is already a heap

seat-reservation-manager.exampleWhy: Seats 1 and 2 go first; seat 2 comes back, so the next reserve returns 2 again before 3, 4, 5.
seat-reservation-manager.hook: Always hand out the smallest free seat number: that is a min-heap's whole job.

optimal.insight: We only ever need the minimum free seat, and seats come and go. A min-heap gives the minimum and accepts returns in log time.
steps: Start the heap with seats 1 to n
reserve: pop the smallest seat
unreserve: push the seat back

pitfalls: A sorted 1..n list is a valid heap, so no heapify call is needed.
Follow-up: a counter plus a heap of returned seats avoids building n items upfront.

say.intro: This is Seat Reservation Manager. We have seats numbered one to n, all free. Reserve must hand out the smallest free seat number. Unreserve gives a seat back. In our example, seats one and two go out. Seat two comes back, so the next reserve gets two again, then three, four and five.
say.brute: The simple design keeps a taken flag for each seat. Reserve scans from seat one upward until it finds a free seat. Unreserve just clears a flag. It works. But once the front rows fill up, every reserve walks past all of them. That's linear per call, and quadratic over many calls.
say.insight: What do we actually need? The smallest free seat, again and again, while seats keep returning. That's exactly a min heap. Put every seat in the heap. Reserve pops the minimum. Unreserve pushes the seat back. Both are logarithmic. And a sorted list from one to n is already a valid heap, so setup is free.
say.anim: We start with five seats, building a min heap holding seats one through five. Reserve pops the smallest seat from the heap, returning seat one. Reserve again pops the next smallest seat, returning seat two. Unreserve pushes seat two back into the heap, keeping it sorted. Reserve pops the smallest available seat again, returning seat two. Successive reserves pop seats three and four from the heap in order. Another reserve pops the last remaining seat, returning seat five. Unreserve pushes seat five back, matching the expected final output sequence.
say.code: The code is tiny. The constructor builds the list from one to n, which already satisfies the heap property. Reserve is one heap pop, returning the smallest free seat. Unreserve is one heap push. The heap keeps the smallest number on top for us.
say.outro: Log n per call. The pattern is heaps: whenever you repeatedly need the smallest available item, reach for a priority queue.

seat-reservation-manager.title: Seat Reservation Manager
lineNotes: We define a SeatManager class that will track which seats are free and hand out the smallest one.
The constructor takes n, the total number of seats, and sets up our starting state.
We fill a list with seats one through n, which is already sorted and so already a valid min-heap.
The reserve method will give out the lowest numbered free seat and mark it taken.
We pop the smallest value off the heap, which removes that seat from the free pool and returns its number in log time.
The unreserve method takes a seat number that a guest is releasing back to the pool.
We push that seat number back onto the heap so it can be chosen again as the smallest when appropriate.

find-missing-observations.ask: You saw m die rolls; n more were lost. The average of all n plus m rolls is mean. Return any n values from 1 to 6 that make the average work, or an empty list if impossible.

brute.idea: Backtrack over the missing dice, trying each face from 6 down to 1, until the chosen faces add up to the missing total.
steps: Compute the missing total from the mean
Pick a face for the next missing die
Recurse; undo if the total cannot be hit
Return the first full assignment
brute.whySlow: Without bounds it explores almost every combination of faces, which explodes after a dozen dice.

codeNotes.note: What the lost dice must total

codeNotes.match: if missing < n or missing > 6 * n:

codeNotes.note: Leave at least one per remaining die

find-missing-observations.exampleWhy: All seven rolls must total 21; the known ones sum to 12, so the missing four sum to 9.
find-missing-observations.hook: The mean fixes the missing total; then hand out big dice while every remaining die can still show one.

optimal.insight: Only the missing total matters, and n dice make any total from n to 6n. Check that range, then give each die the most it can, leaving one per later die.
steps: missing = mean times (n plus m) minus sum
Outside n to 6n? return empty
Each die takes min(6, missing - remaining + 1)
Subtract it and move to the next die

pitfalls: Any valid answer is accepted; an even spread with divmod works too.
Check the n to 6n range first, or the loop produces invalid faces.

say.intro: Find Missing Observations. We saw some die rolls, and n more were lost. We know the average of all of them. Return any values for the missing dice that make the average work. In our example, seven rolls averaging three must total twenty one. The known ones sum to twelve, so the four missing dice must sum to nine.
say.brute: A brute force backtracks. Try a face from six down to one for the first missing die, then recurse on the rest, undoing whenever the total can't be hit. It finds an answer, but without bounds it wanders through almost six to the n combinations.
say.insight: Here's the thing. Only the missing total matters, and n dice can make any total from n up to six n. So first check that range. If it fits, fill greedily. Give each die as much as possible, but leave at least one for every die still to come.
say.anim: We start with rolls one five six, mean three, and four missing rolls to find. The missing total is nine, which fits between four and twenty four, so it is valid. We begin building the result list, looping while rolls remain to fill. The first die takes the max possible value, six, leaving three for the rest. With three rolls left and missing now three, each remaining die just needs one. Continuing, each next die also gets one, keeping totals balanced across rolls. The last die takes the final one, using up all remaining missing total. The loop ends and the answer six, one, one, one is returned.
say.code: In the code, we compute the missing total from the mean. If it's below n or above six n, return an empty list. Otherwise loop while dice remain. Each die gets the smaller of six, or the total minus the other remaining dice. Subtract it, and count down n.
say.outro: Linear time. The pattern is math: turn the constraint into one total, check its bounds, then fill greedily.

find-missing-observations.title: Find Missing Observations
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the wrapper this problem's solution lives in.
This method takes the observed rolls, the target mean, and n, the number of lost rolls to reconstruct.
The missing total equals the mean times all rolls, minus the sum of the rolls we already saw.
If the missing total is below n or above six times n, no valid dice values can reach it.
In that impossible case we return an empty list right away.
We start an empty result list to collect the reconstructed die values.
We loop until n reaches zero, placing one die per pass.
Each die gets the largest value up to six that still leaves at least one for every remaining die.
We append that die value to the result list.
We subtract the chosen value from the missing total, since it is now accounted for.
We decrease n because one fewer die remains to be assigned.
Once all dice are assigned, we return the list of missing rolls.

partition-to-k-equal-sum-subsets.ask: Given an integer array nums and an integer k, decide whether the numbers can be split into k non-empty groups that all have the same sum. Every number must be used exactly once.

brute.idea: Assign each number to one of the k buckets in every possible way, and check whether all bucket sums come out equal.
steps: Take the next number
Try it in each of the k buckets
After the last number, compare bucket sums
Undo and try the next bucket
brute.whySlow: Sixteen numbers into four buckets is four billion assignments, with no early cutoff.

codeNotes.match: if used[j] or cur + nums[j] > target:

partition-to-k-equal-sum-subsets.exampleWhy: The total 12 split three ways is 4: groups 4, 3+1 and 2+2.
partition-to-k-equal-sum-subsets.hook: Fill one bucket at a time to the exact target, biggest numbers first, and back out on overflow.

optimal.insight: Every bucket must hit total over k exactly. Fill buckets one at a time, prune any overflow, and try big numbers first so dead ends show up early.
steps: Total not divisible by k? false
Sort descending; target is total / k
Fill the current bucket from unused numbers
Hit target: start the next bucket from index 0
Undo a choice when it leads nowhere

pitfalls: Restart the scan at index 0 for each new bucket, or leftover small numbers get missed.
Any number larger than the target makes the answer false immediately.

say.intro: Let's do Partition to K Equal Sum Subsets. Can we split the numbers into k groups that all have the same sum? Every number goes in exactly one group. In our example, the total is twelve, so three groups need four each. Four alone, three plus one, and two plus two. So the answer is true.
say.brute: The brute force drops each number into each of the k buckets in turn. After placing the last number, it checks whether all the sums are equal. It's correct, but that's k to the n assignments, with no early cutoff at all.
say.insight: Here's the better idea. We know every bucket must hit total over k exactly. So fill one bucket at a time. Pick unused numbers, and skip any that would overflow. When a bucket hits the target, start the next one from the beginning. Sort biggest first, so impossible branches die early.
say.anim: We start with numbers three, one, two, two, four, split into three equal buckets. Sorted descending to four, three, two, two, one, each bucket target becomes four. Four fills the first bucket completely, so backtracking starts a fresh bucket at zero. Three plus one makes four, completing the second bucket exactly on target. Two plus two reaches four again, filling the third bucket perfectly. All five numbers are now used, with every bucket hitting the target of four. With zero buckets left to fill, the recursion confirms success and returns true. The function returns true, confirming the array can split into three equal sum groups.
say.code: In the code, an uneven total returns false right away. Then we sort descending and mark nothing used. Backtrack takes a start index, the buckets left, and the current sum. When a bucket is full, we recurse with one fewer bucket from index zero. In the loop, we skip used or overflowing numbers, try the rest, and unmark on failure.
say.outro: Exponential in the worst case, but heavily pruned. The pattern is backtracking: build one bucket at a time and cut overflow early.

partition-to-k-equal-sum-subsets.title: Partition to K Equal Sum Subsets
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container for the method we are asked to write.
The method takes the list nums and the count k, and returns whether a valid split into k equal groups exists.
First we add up every number in nums to get the grand total.
If the total cannot be divided evenly by k, equal sums are impossible.
So in that case we immediately return false.
Otherwise each bucket must sum to the total divided by k, which we call target.
We sort nums from largest to smallest so big numbers get placed first and failures appear early.
We create a used list of false flags to track which numbers are already placed in a bucket.
We define a recursive helper that tracks a start index i, the buckets still to fill k, and the current bucket sum cur.
If no buckets remain to fill, every number has been placed properly.
So we return true.
If the current bucket has reached target exactly, we finish it and move on.
We start the next bucket by recursing with index zero, one fewer bucket, and a sum of zero.
We loop over candidate numbers from index i onward to try adding to the current bucket.
We skip numbers already used or ones that would push the bucket past target, pruning overflow.
That skip is done with continue, moving to the next candidate.
We mark this number as used because we are tentatively placing it in the bucket.
We recurse from the next index with the larger current sum, and check whether that succeeds.
If it succeeds, we pass true all the way up.
Otherwise we backtrack by marking the number as unused so other choices can be tried.
If no candidate works from this state, we return false to trigger backtracking above.
We kick off the search from index zero with all k buckets to fill and an empty current sum.

snakes-and-ladders.ask: Squares 1 to n squared zigzag up an n by n board. Each turn you roll 1 to 6 and move forward; landing on a snake or ladder sends you to its target. Return the fewest rolls to reach the last square, or -1.

brute.idea: Bellman-Ford style: keep a best roll count per square and keep relaxing every square's six rolls until nothing improves.
steps: Square 1 costs zero rolls, others infinity
Sweep every square and its six rolls
Improve the target square's count if shorter
Repeat sweeps until no count changes
brute.whySlow: Each sweep touches all n² squares, and snakes can force up to n² sweeps before counts settle.

codeNotes.note: Row 0 is now the bottom row
Odd rows run right to left
First arrival is the fewest rolls

snakes-and-ladders.exampleWhy: Roll a 3 to land on square 4, climb the ladder to 10, then roll a 6 to reach 16.
snakes-and-ladders.hook: Every square is a node and every die roll an edge: fewest rolls is a breadth-first search.

optimal.insight: All rolls cost exactly one, so the board is an unweighted graph. BFS from square 1 reaches each square first by the fewest rolls.
steps: Reverse rows so row 0 is the bottom
Map a square number to row and column
BFS from square 1, trying rolls 1 to 6
Follow a snake or ladder if present
First time we hit n squared, return rolls

pitfalls: Only one snake or ladder per roll: never chain a second jump from the target.
Get the zigzag right: odd rows from the bottom are numbered right to left.

say.intro: Let's do Snakes and Ladders. Squares are numbered in a zigzag from the bottom left. Each turn, roll one to six and move forward. Land on a snake or ladder, and you jump to its target. What's the fewest rolls to reach the last square? On our four by four board, the answer is two.
say.brute: One slow approach keeps a best roll count for every square, then sweeps the whole board, relaxing each square's six rolls. It repeats sweeps until nothing improves, like Bellman Ford. That's correct. But snakes can force many sweeps, each over every square, so the worst case grows like n to the fourth.
say.insight: Here's the key. Every roll costs exactly one move. So this is an unweighted graph: squares are nodes, and each roll is an edge, after any snake or ladder. The fewest rolls is a shortest path in an unweighted graph, which is exactly breadth first search. The first time we reach the last square, that's the answer.
say.anim: We reverse the board so square one starts at the bottom row, ready for breadth first search. Starting at square one with zero moves, we explore rolls one through six to find neighbors. Square three has a snake, redirecting it down to square ten instead. From square one we queue squares two, three, five, six, and ten, all at one move. Processing square two next, we discover square eight, reachable in two moves. Continuing breadth first search, squares nine, eleven, thirteen, and fourteen join at two moves. From square ten, rolling six lands exactly on square sixteen, the final square. The search returns two, the minimum number of moves needed to win.
say.code: In the code, we reverse the board so row zero is the bottom. Pos turns a square number into a row and column, flipping the column on odd rows. BFS starts at square one with zero moves. For each roll, we take a snake or ladder if there is one. If we hit the last square, return moves plus one. Otherwise queue unseen squares.
say.outro: Each square is visited once, so it's linear in the board size. The pattern is graphs: fewest equal cost moves means breadth first search.

snakes-and-ladders.title: Snakes and Ladders
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container the judge expects for our method.
The method takes the board grid and returns the fewest rolls needed to reach the last square, or negative one.
We store the side length of the board as n, taken from the number of rows.
We reverse the rows so the first row is the bottom, matching how squares are numbered from one.
We define a helper called pos that converts a square number into a row and column on the board.
Dividing the zero-based square index by n gives the row and the column offset within that row.
On odd rows the numbering runs right to left, so we need to flip the column.
We mirror the column by subtracting it from n minus one.
The helper returns the row and column for that square.
We start the queue with square one and zero moves, since BFS begins from the starting square.
We keep a visited set containing square one so we never process a square twice.
We loop while the queue still has squares to explore.
We pop the oldest square and its move count, so squares are handled in order of fewest rolls.
We try each die roll from one to six.
The candidate next square is the current square plus the roll.
We look up the board row and column of that candidate square.
If the cell is not negative one, it holds a snake or ladder.
We then jump to that cell's target square instead of staying put.
If we land on the last square, which is n squared, we are done.
We return the current moves plus one, since BFS guarantees this is the fewest rolls.
Otherwise we check whether this destination square has not been visited yet.
We mark it visited so later paths do not revisit it.
We enqueue it with moves plus one, to explore from there on the next level.
If the queue empties without reaching the end, the last square is unreachable, so we return negative one.

insertion-sort-list.ask: Given the head of a singly linked list, sort it using insertion sort: take nodes one at a time and insert each into its correct place in the already sorted part. Return the new head.

brute.idea: Selection sort on the list: repeatedly scan everything left for the smallest node, unlink it, and append it to a new list.
steps: Scan the remaining list for its minimum
Unlink that minimum node
Append it to the sorted tail
Repeat until the list is empty
brute.whySlow: It always scans the whole remainder, so even an already sorted list costs n squared, and it is not insertion sort.

codeNotes.note: Lets us insert before the head

insertion-sort-list.exampleWhy: Each node slides back into the sorted front: 3 goes before 5, 4 before 5, and 0 right after -1.
insertion-sort-list.hook: Grow a sorted prefix in place: unhook each out-of-order node and splice it where it belongs.

optimal.insight: If the next node is at least the previous one, the sorted prefix just grows for free. Only an out-of-order node needs a search from the front.
steps: Dummy node before head; prefix is the first node
Next node not smaller? extend the prefix
Else find the last node smaller than it
Unlink it and splice it in there
Continue from the node after prev

pitfalls: Save where to continue before rewiring, or you lose the rest of the list.
Without a dummy node, inserting a new smallest value needs a special case.

say.intro: This is Insertion Sort List. We get the head of a singly linked list, and we must sort it with insertion sort. Take nodes one by one, and slide each into place in the sorted part. In our example, minus one, five, three, four, zero becomes minus one, zero, three, four, five.
say.brute: A different quadratic sort would be selection sort. Scan the whole remaining list for its smallest node, unlink it, and append it to a new list. Repeat until nothing's left. It works in constant space. But it always scans everything, so even a sorted list costs n squared. And it's not what the problem asked for.
say.insight: Here's the thing about insertion sort. If the next node is at least as big as the last sorted one, the sorted part just grows, and that's free. Only a node that's out of order needs work. Walk from a dummy node at the front to find where it belongs. Then unhook it and splice it in, all with pointer changes.
say.anim: We start with the list negative one, five, three, four, zero, and build a dummy head. Prev is negative one and cur is five, since five is at least negative one, we just advance both. Now prev is five and cur is three, which is smaller, so we need to search from the front. Tmp walks from dummy to negative one, the right spot, and three gets inserted right after it. Cur is now four, smaller than five, so tmp searches again and four is inserted after three. Cur is zero, smaller than five, tmp finds the start again and zero slots in after negative one. Cur becomes none, so the loop ends and we return the sorted list from dummy's next. The final sorted list is negative one, zero, three, four, five, matching the expected output.
say.code: In the code, a dummy node points at the head, so we can insert even before it. Prev is the end of the sorted part, and cur is the next node. If cur is in order, both step forward. Otherwise tmp walks from the dummy while cur is bigger than the next value. Then we unhook cur, point it at tmp's next, and point tmp at cur. Cur becomes the node after prev.
say.outro: Quadratic in the worst case, linear when nearly sorted, constant space. The pattern is linked lists: a dummy node plus careful pointer splicing.

insertion-sort-list.title: Insertion Sort List
lineNotes: We define a Solution class that holds the method for this problem.
The method takes the head of a linked list and returns the head of the sorted list.
We create a dummy node pointing to head so inserting before the first real node is easy.
We set prev to the head and cur to the second node, treating the first node as a sorted prefix.
We loop until cur runs off the end of the list, meaning every node has been placed.
We check whether cur is at least as large as prev, which means it is already in order.
In that case the sorted prefix grows, so we move prev and cur one step forward.
We continue to the next iteration, skipping the insertion work since nothing needs to move.
For an out-of-order node, we start a search from the dummy node at the front of the list.
We advance tmp while cur is larger than the node after tmp, stopping right before the correct insertion spot.
Each step of that search moves tmp forward by one node.
We unlink cur from its current position by making prev skip over it to the following node.
We point cur's next at the node after tmp, so cur links into the sorted part.
We set tmp's next to cur, completing the insertion at the correct position.
We move cur to the node after prev, which is the next unsorted node to process.
Finally we return the node after dummy, which is the head of the fully sorted list.

repeated-dna-sequences.ask: A DNA string uses only A, C, G and T. Return every substring of length 10 that appears more than once in it. Any order is fine.

brute.idea: Compare every 10-letter window with every later window, and record the ones that match.
steps: Pick a window start i
Compare it with every later window j
Record a match in a result set
Return the result set as a list
brute.whySlow: With 100,000 letters that is about five billion window comparisons.

codeNotes.note: Res is a set: report each once
Every start of a full window

repeated-dna-sequences.exampleWhy: AAAAACCCCC starts at 0 and 10, and AAAACCCCCA starts at 1 and 11.
repeated-dna-sequences.hook: Slide a 10-letter window and remember every window you have seen: a second sighting is a repeat.

optimal.insight: Seeing a window twice is just a membership test. One pass with a seen set finds every repeat, and a second set reports each only once.
steps: Slide a 10-letter window across s
Already in seen? add it to the result set
Add the window to seen
Return the result set as a list

pitfalls: Use a set for the result, or a window seen three times is reported twice.
Loop to len(s) minus 9 so the last full window is included.

say.intro: This is Repeated DNA Sequences. We get a DNA string of A, C, G and T. Return every ten letter substring that appears more than once. In our example, A A A A A C C C C C shows up at position zero and again at ten. And the window starting at one repeats at eleven.
say.brute: The brute force compares every ten letter window with every later window. Whenever two match, record that sequence. It's correct, but the number of window pairs grows as n squared. With a hundred thousand letters, that's billions of comparisons.
say.insight: Here's the thing. Has this window appeared before? That's just a membership question. So slide the window once and keep a set of everything seen. If the current window is already in the set, it's a repeat. Put repeats in a second set, so a sequence that shows up three times is still reported only once.
say.anim: We start with two empty sets, seen and res, to track windows of ten letters. At i equals zero, the window AAAAACCCCC is new, so it gets added to seen. The window slides forward each step, checking each ten letter chunk against seen. By i equals six, seen holds many unique windows as we keep sliding along the string. At i equals ten, cur is AAAAACCCCC again, which is already in seen, so it's added to res. At i equals eleven, AAAACCCCCA also repeats, so it gets added to res too. Finally the function returns the result list containing both repeated sequences found.
say.code: In the code, we keep two sets: seen and result. We loop over every start where a full ten letter window fits. We slice the window. If it's already in seen, add it to the result. Either way, add it to seen. Finally, return the result as a list.
say.outro: Linear time, since each window is just ten letters. The pattern is a sliding window with a hash set for repeats.

repeated-dna-sequences.title: Repeated DNA Sequences
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the wrapper this problem's starter code expects.
This method takes the DNA string s and returns a list of repeated ten letter substrings.
We create two empty sets: seen for every window met so far, and res for repeats to report.
We loop start index i over every position where a full ten letter window still fits in s.
We slice out the ten letter window beginning at i and call it cur.
We check whether this window already appeared earlier by looking it up in the seen set.
If so, we add it to res, and since res is a set, duplicates are reported only once.
Whether or not it was a repeat, we record the window in seen for later comparisons.
After scanning everything, we convert the res set into a list and return it.

find-eventual-safe-states.ask: In a directed graph, a terminal node has no outgoing edges. A node is safe if every path from it ends at a terminal node. Return all safe nodes in increasing order.

brute.idea: For each node separately, run a fresh DFS that looks for a cycle reachable from it. No reachable cycle means safe.
steps: Pick a start node
DFS with fresh visiting and done marks
Hitting a visiting node means a cycle
No cycle found: the start is safe
brute.whySlow: Every start redoes the whole search from scratch, so shared downstream nodes are explored again and again.

codeNotes.note: Assume unsafe while on the path
Every path leads to a terminal

codeNotes.match: return [i for i in range(len(graph)) if dfs(i)]

find-eventual-safe-states.exampleWhy: Nodes 0, 1 and 3 can loop forever around 0→1→3→0; every path from 2, 4, 5 and 6 ends at a terminal.
find-eventual-safe-states.hook: A node is unsafe exactly when it can reach a cycle. One memoized DFS labels them all.

optimal.insight: Mark a node unsafe while exploring it, so a cycle looping back sees unsafe. Only when all neighbors prove safe does it flip to safe, and answers are cached.
steps: Cached answer? return it
Mark the node unsafe before exploring
Any unsafe neighbor makes it unsafe
All neighbors safe: mark it safe
Collect safe nodes in index order

pitfalls: Marking unsafe before exploring is what turns a cycle into a quick false.
Terminal nodes have no neighbors, so the loop is skipped and they become safe.

say.intro: Let's do Find Eventual Safe States. In a directed graph, a terminal node has no outgoing edges. A node is safe if every path from it ends at a terminal. Return the safe nodes in order. In our example, nodes zero, one and three can circle forever, so the safe nodes are two, four, five and six.
say.brute: The brute force checks each node on its own. Run a fresh DFS from it, looking for a cycle it can reach. If there's none, it's safe. That's correct. But every start repeats the whole search from scratch, so the work is n times the size of the graph.
say.insight: Here's the key. A node is unsafe exactly when it can reach a cycle. So during DFS, mark a node unsafe the moment we enter it. If the search loops back to it, it sees unsafe and fails. Only when every neighbor turns out safe do we flip it to safe. And we cache every answer, so each node is solved once.
say.anim: We start exploring node 0, marking it unsafe while we visit its neighbors. Node 2 leads to node 5, which has no neighbors, so node 5 becomes safe. Since all of node 2's neighbors are safe, node 2 also becomes safe. Node 1 leads to node 3, which loops back to node 0, still marked unsafe. That cycle means nodes 3, 1, and 0 all end up marked unsafe. Node 4 reaches the already safe node 5, so node 4 becomes safe too. Node 6 has no neighbors at all, so it is immediately marked safe. The final safe nodes collected are 2, 4, 5, and 6.
say.code: In the code, safe is a dictionary cache. If a node has an answer, return it. Otherwise mark it false before exploring. If any neighbor is not safe, return false, leaving the mark in place. If all neighbors pass, mark it true. Finally, keep every index whose DFS returns true, which is already sorted.
say.outro: Linear in nodes plus edges. The pattern is graphs: DFS with three states for cycle detection, cached per node.

find-eventual-safe-states.title: Find Eventual Safe States
lineNotes: We define a Solution class that holds the method for finding all eventual safe nodes in the graph.
The method takes the adjacency list called graph and returns a list of safe node numbers.
We create an empty dictionary called safe that caches whether each visited node is safe or not.
We define a helper function dfs that decides whether node i is safe using depth first search.
If node i is already in safe, we have an answer cached or a node currently being explored.
We return that stored value, which is false for a node on the current path, revealing a cycle.
Before exploring neighbors we mark node i as unsafe, so any cycle returning to it sees false.
We loop over every neighbor that node i points to in the graph.
We recursively check each neighbor, and if it is not safe then node i cannot be safe either.
We return false immediately, leaving node i marked unsafe in the cache.
If every neighbor proved safe, we flip node i to safe in the cache.
We return true to tell the caller that node i is safe.
We run dfs on every node in order and collect the safe ones, giving increasing order automatically.

check-if-a-string-contains-all-binary-co.ask: Given a binary string s and an integer k, return true if every possible binary code of length k appears somewhere in s as a substring. Otherwise return false.

brute.idea: Generate each of the 2^k binary codes and search for it in s with a substring scan.
steps: Loop over every number below 2^k
Write it as a k-bit binary string
Scan s for that substring
Any missing code means false
brute.whySlow: With k = 20 there are a million codes, and each one rescans the whole string.

codeNotes.note: Two to the k codes exist

check-if-a-string-contains-all-binary-co.exampleWhy: The windows of length 2 include 00, 01, 11 and 10, all four possible codes.
check-if-a-string-contains-all-binary-co.hook: Don't search for 2^k codes. Collect the windows you have, and count them.

optimal.insight: s has only n - k + 1 windows of length k. Put them in a set; all codes are present exactly when the set holds 2^k distinct strings.
steps: Need starts at 2^k distinct codes
Slide a k-length window across s
New window? add it and decrease need
Need hits zero: return true

pitfalls: If s has fewer than 2^k windows, the answer must be false.
Loop to len(s) minus k plus one, or the last window is skipped.

say.intro: Check If a String Contains All Binary Codes of Size K. Given a binary string and a number k, does every possible k bit code appear somewhere in the string? In our example, with k equal to two, the windows include zero zero, zero one, one one and one zero. That's all four codes, so the answer is true.
say.brute: The brute force generates every code. For each number below two to the k, write it as a k bit string, and scan the whole input for it. If any code is missing, return false. It works, but there are two to the k codes, and each one rescans the string. With k equal to twenty, that's a million scans.
say.insight: Flip it around. Instead of searching for every code, look at what the string actually has. There are only about n windows of length k. Drop each into a set. Every code is present exactly when the set reaches two to the k distinct strings. One pass over the string, and we can stop as soon as the count is reached.
say.anim: We need four distinct codes since k is 2, so need starts at 4. At i equals 0, the window gives code 00, which is new, so need drops to 3. At i equals 1, code 01 is new too, need decreases to 2. At i equals 2, code 11 appears for the first time, need becomes 1. At i equals 3, code 10 is also new, filling the last missing code. Need reaches zero, meaning all four binary codes of length two were found. The function returns true, confirming the string contains every possible binary code.
say.code: In the code, need starts at two to the k, written as one shifted left by k. We slide over every window start. If the window is new, add it to the set and decrease need. When need hits zero, every code has appeared, so return true. If the loop ends first, return false.
say.outro: Linear windows, each of length k. The pattern is arrays and hashing: count distinct windows with a set.

check-if-a-string-contains-all-binary-co.title: Check if a String Contains all Binary Codes of Size K
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container the interview platform expects for our method.
The method hasAllCodes takes the binary string s and the code length k, and returns a true or false answer.
We set need to two raised to the power k, the count of distinct binary codes we must find.
We create an empty set called seen to remember which codes of length k have already appeared.
We loop i over every window start, from zero up to the length of s minus k, inclusive.
We slice out the substring of length k starting at i and call it code.
We check whether this code is new, meaning it is not yet in the seen set.
Since it is new, we add it to the seen set so repeats are not counted again.
We decrease need by one because one more distinct code has now been found.
We check whether need has reached zero, meaning every possible code has been found.
If so, we return true immediately, since there is no reason to scan the rest of the string.
If the loop finishes with some codes still missing, we return false.

n-queens-ii.ask: Place n queens on an n by n chessboard so that no two attack each other along a row, column or diagonal. Return how many distinct arrangements exist.

brute.idea: Each row gets one queen in a different column, so try every permutation of columns and check every pair of queens for a shared diagonal.
steps: Generate each permutation of the columns
Row r puts its queen at perm[r]
Check every pair for a diagonal clash
Count the permutations with no clash
brute.whySlow: It builds complete boards before checking: for n = 9 that is 362,880 boards, each checked pair by pair.

codeNotes.match: if c in cols or r + c in pos or r - c in neg:

codeNotes.note: Undo before trying the next column

n-queens-ii.exampleWhy: On a 4 by 4 board only two layouts work: columns 1, 3, 0, 2 and their mirror 2, 0, 3, 1.
n-queens-ii.hook: One queen per row, and three sets tell you instantly which columns and diagonals are already under attack.

optimal.insight: Place queens row by row. A square is attacked if its column, its r plus c diagonal, or its r minus c diagonal is taken: three set lookups prune instantly.
steps: Recurse on row r; r equals n counts one
Skip columns whose column or diagonals are taken
Claim the column and both diagonals
Recurse to the next row
Release all three on the way back

n-queens-ii.optimalCode:
class Solution:
    def totalNQueens(self, n: int) -> int:
        cols, pos, neg = set(), set(), set()
        res = 0

        def backtrack(r):
            nonlocal res
            if r == n:
                res += 1
                return
            for c in range(n):
                if c in cols or r + c in pos or r - c in neg:
                    continue
                cols.add(c)
                pos.add(r + c)
                neg.add(r - c)
                backtrack(r + 1)
                cols.remove(c)
                pos.remove(r + c)
                neg.remove(r - c)

        backtrack(0)
        return res
pitfalls: Forgetting to remove from all three sets leaves phantom attacks for later branches.
Counting is enough here; no need to build board strings like in N-Queens I.

say.intro: Let's do N Queens Two. Place n queens on an n by n chessboard so no two attack each other, along a row, a column, or a diagonal. Return how many arrangements exist. For a four by four board, there are exactly two.
say.brute: Every row needs exactly one queen, and every column too. So the brute force tries every permutation of columns, and then checks each pair of queens for a diagonal clash. It's correct. But it builds complete boards before checking anything, so it costs n factorial times n squared.
say.insight: Here's the better idea. Place queens one row at a time, and reject a square the moment it's attacked. How do we know quickly? Squares on one diagonal share r plus c. Squares on the other share r minus c. So keep three sets: columns, plus diagonals, and minus diagonals. Three lookups, and dead branches stop right away.
say.anim: We start with three empty sets tracking used columns and diagonals for four queens. The first queen is placed at row zero, column zero, recorded in all three sets. Backtracking tries column one in row one, adding it before checking deeper rows. By row three a valid arrangement is found, so the result counter becomes one. The algorithm backtracks and restarts row zero, now trying column two instead. Another full placement through row three succeeds, raising the result counter to two. Remaining column choices like three get pruned quickly by the diagonal and column checks. All branches are explored, and the function returns the final answer, two solutions.
say.code: In the code, backtrack takes a row. If the row equals n, every queen is placed, so add one. Otherwise try each column. Skip it if the column or either diagonal is taken. Claim all three, recurse to the next row, then remove all three before trying the next column.
say.outro: Roughly n factorial, but heavily pruned. The pattern is backtracking: place, recurse, undo, with sets for constant time conflict checks.

n-queens-ii.title: N-Queens II
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container the problem expects for our method.
The method totalNQueens takes the board size n and returns the number of valid queen arrangements.
We create three empty sets to remember taken columns, taken plus diagonals, and taken minus diagonals.
We start the result counter at zero to tally each complete valid arrangement we find.
We define a recursive helper called backtrack that tries to place a queen on row r.
The nonlocal declaration lets the helper modify the outer result counter instead of making a new local one.
If r equals n, every row already holds a queen, so we have found a full solution.
We add one to the result because this arrangement is a distinct valid placement.
We return to stop going deeper and let the caller try other options.
We loop over every column c in the current row as a candidate square for the queen.
If the column, the row plus column diagonal, or the row minus column diagonal is taken, the square is attacked.
We skip that square and move on to the next column.
The square is safe, so we mark its column as occupied.
We mark the row plus column diagonal as occupied, since squares on it share that sum.
We mark the row minus column diagonal as occupied, since squares on it share that difference.
We recurse to the next row to place the following queen with this choice in place.
After returning, we undo the choice by freeing the column so other branches can use it.
We free the plus diagonal too, restoring the state before this placement.
We free the minus diagonal, completing the backtrack so the next column starts clean.
We kick off the search by calling backtrack on row zero of the empty board.
Finally we return the total count of arrangements collected in result.

path-sum.ask: Given a binary tree and a target number, return true if some path from the root down to a leaf has values adding up exactly to the target.

brute.idea: Collect every root-to-leaf path as its own list, then sum each list and check whether any equals the target.
steps: DFS, copying the path list at every node
Save the full path at each leaf
Sum every saved path and compare
brute.whySlow: Every node copies its whole path, and every path is summed again from scratch; a tall tree makes that quadratic.

codeNotes.match: if not root.left and not root.right:
codeNotes.note: Only leaves can finish a path

path-sum.exampleWhy: The path 5, 4, 11, 2 ends at a leaf and adds up to 22.
path-sum.hook: Carry the remaining target down the tree; a leaf that hits exactly zero wins.

optimal.insight: Subtract each node's value from the target on the way down. At a leaf, the path works exactly when what is left is zero.
steps: Empty tree: return false
Subtract the node's value from the target
At a leaf, check the remainder is zero
Otherwise try left, then right, with the remainder

pitfalls: A node with one child is not a leaf; do not stop there.
An empty tree returns false even when the target is zero.

say.intro: This is Path Sum. We get a binary tree and a target. Is there a path from the root all the way down to a leaf, where the values add up to the target? In our tree the target is twenty two. Five, four, eleven, two. That reaches a leaf and sums to twenty two, so the answer is true.
say.brute: The brute force writes every path down. Walk the tree, copying the path so far into a new list at each node. When we reach a leaf, save that list. At the end, add up every saved path and see if any matches. It's correct. But each node copies the whole path above it, and then every path gets summed all over again.
say.insight: Here's the trick. We never need the whole path. We only need to know how much of the target is still left. So as we step down into a node, subtract its value. When we land on a leaf, the path works exactly when the remainder is zero. One number travels down the tree, and nothing is stored.
say.anim: We start at root node five with a target sum of twenty two. Subtracting five leaves a remaining target of seventeen, not yet a leaf. Moving to node four, subtracting its value brings the target down to thirteen. At node eleven, subtracting leaves a target of two, still not a leaf. Trying node seven, subtracting gives negative five, which fails since it isn't a leaf match. Backtracking, we try node two instead, subtracting leaves exactly zero remaining. Since node two is a leaf and the remainder is zero, this path works. The true result bubbles back up through each call, confirming the final answer is true.
say.code: First, a missing node means no path, so return false. Then subtract this node's value from the target. If the node has no children, it's a leaf, and we return whether the remainder is exactly zero. Otherwise we ask the left subtree with the new remainder, or the right one. Either can succeed, and the or stops early as soon as one does.
say.outro: Linear time, and space equal to the tree height. The pattern is tree depth first search, carrying a running remainder down to the leaves.

path-sum.title: Path Sum
lineNotes: We define a Solution class that holds the method for solving the path sum problem.
The method hasPathSum takes the root of a tree and a target sum, and returns true or false.
First we check whether the current node is missing, which happens when we step past an empty child.
An empty tree has no path to a leaf, so we return false.
We subtract the current node's value from the target, so the target tracks what is still needed.
We check whether this node is a leaf, meaning it has no left child and no right child.
At a leaf the path works exactly when the remaining target is zero, so we return that comparison.
Otherwise we search both subtrees with the reduced target, and return true if either side finds a valid path.

construct-string-from-binary-tree.ask: Turn a binary tree into a string using preorder: the node's value, then its left subtree in brackets, then its right subtree in brackets. Leave out empty brackets unless dropping them would change the tree's meaning.

brute.idea: Recursively build each subtree's string, then glue strings together with brackets at every level.
steps: Return the empty string for a missing node
Wrap the left result in brackets if any child exists
Wrap the right result only if it exists
brute.whySlow: Every level copies its children's whole strings again, so a tall skewed tree recopies the same characters n times.

codeNotes.match: if not node.left and not node.right:

codeNotes.note: Left pair kept, even if empty

construct-string-from-binary-tree.exampleWhy: Node 2 has no left child but has a right one, so it needs the empty pair to show 4 is on the right.
construct-string-from-binary-tree.hook: Preorder with brackets: the only empty pair you keep is a missing left child.

optimal.insight: Append pieces to one shared list during preorder. Brackets for the left child are needed whenever any child exists; right brackets only when the right child exists.
steps: Append the node's value
Leaf? Stop, no brackets at all
Always bracket the left subtree, even if empty
Bracket the right subtree only if it exists
Join the pieces once at the end

pitfalls: Dropping the empty left pair makes a right-only child look like a left child.
Repeated string concatenation can turn linear work into quadratic.

say.intro: Construct String from Binary Tree. We write the tree in preorder. The node's value, then its left subtree in brackets, then its right subtree in brackets. Empty brackets get dropped, unless that changes the meaning. Node two has no left child but has a right child four. So it needs an empty pair to show four is on the right.
say.brute: The brute force builds a string for every subtree and returns it. Each parent glues its children's strings together with brackets. It reads nicely, and it's correct. But every level copies its children's full strings into a new one. In a tall, skewed tree, the same characters get copied over and over, and that's quadratic.
say.insight: So instead, keep one shared list and only ever append to it. The bracket rules are simple. A leaf gets no brackets at all. Otherwise the left child always gets a pair, even when it's empty, because that pair holds the right child in place. The right child gets a pair only if it exists. Then join once at the end.
say.anim: We start a preorder traversal from root node 1, building one shared result list. Node 1 is appended, then open brackets start since it has children. Node 2 is appended, and another open bracket begins for its left child. Node 2 has no left child, so nothing is added, just closing its bracket. Node 2 has a right child, so we open brackets and append node 4. Closing brackets wrap up node 2's section, completing left child of root. Root node 1 has a right child, so we open brackets and append node 3. Final brackets close everything, joining the list into one string, 1(2()(4))(3).
say.code: Inside the helper, a missing node adds nothing. Otherwise we append the value first, because it's preorder. If the node is a leaf, we stop right there. If not, we open a bracket, recurse left, and close it, even when left is empty. Then, only if a right child exists, we wrap it in its own pair. Finally we join every piece in one pass.
say.outro: Linear time and space. The pattern is tree preorder traversal, building output into one shared buffer.

construct-string-from-binary-tree.title: Construct String from Binary Tree
lineNotes: We define the Solution class that holds the method for converting a tree to a string.
The tree2str method takes the root of the tree and returns its string form.
We create one shared empty list called res to collect string pieces as we traverse.
We define a helper function dfs that visits a node and appends its pieces to res.
If the current node is empty, there is nothing to write for it.
So we return right away and add nothing, which leaves an empty left child as empty brackets.
We append the node's value as text to res, since preorder writes the node first.
If the node has neither a left nor a right child, it is a leaf and needs no brackets.
So we return early, leaving just the value for this leaf.
Since at least one child exists, we open a bracket for the left child, even if it is empty.
We recurse into the left child, which adds nothing if it is missing, giving empty brackets.
We close the left bracket, which keeps the position of a lone right child unambiguous.
Only if a right child exists do we add a second bracketed section.
We open a bracket for the right subtree.
We recurse into the right child to append its own pieces.
We close the right bracket after the right subtree is written.
We start the traversal by calling dfs on the root.
We join all collected pieces into one string and return it as the answer.

maximum-subarray-min-product.ask: The min-product of a subarray is its smallest value times its sum. Return the largest min-product over all non-empty subarrays, modulo one billion and seven.

brute.idea: Try every subarray, keeping a running minimum and running sum as the right end grows.
steps: Pick a start index
Extend the end, updating min and sum
Score min times sum and keep the best
brute.whySlow: There are about n squared over two subarrays; with a hundred thousand numbers that is billions of checks.

codeNotes.note: Modulo only at the very end

maximum-subarray-min-product.exampleWhy: Subarray 3, 3 has minimum 3 and sum 6, giving 18, the best of all.
maximum-subarray-min-product.hook: Let every value be the minimum, and stretch its window as wide as it can go.

optimal.insight: Treat each value as the minimum; its best window stretches until a smaller value on each side. A monotonic increasing stack finds those borders, and prefix sums give window sums instantly.
steps: Build prefix sums for instant range sums
Keep a stack of starts and values, increasing
Smaller value pops: popped value's window ends here
Popped start becomes the new value's start
Leftover entries extend to the array's end

pitfalls: Take the modulo only after the max; modding early breaks the comparison.
Forgetting the leftover stack entries misses windows ending at the last index.

say.intro: This is Maximum Subarray Min Product. For any subarray, multiply its smallest value by its sum. We want the biggest such product. Our array is two, three, three, one, two. Take the two threes. The minimum is three, the sum is six, so that's eighteen. Nothing beats it.
say.brute: The brute force tries every subarray. Fix a start, then slide the end to the right, keeping a running minimum and a running sum. Score each one, and keep the best. It's simple and correct. But there are about n squared over two subarrays. With a hundred thousand numbers, that's billions of checks.
say.insight: Flip the question around. For each value, pretend it's the minimum. Then the best window around it stretches until it hits something smaller on either side. A stack that stays increasing finds those borders for us. When a smaller number arrives, it pops bigger ones, and their windows end right there. Prefix sums give each window's sum instantly.
say.anim: We start with the array two three three one two, and build a prefix sum array for fast range totals. Now we scan each number, pushing increasing values onto a stack with their start index. At index three, value one is smaller, so we pop three and three, closing their windows. Popping value three with total three gives product nine, then popping the other three with total six gives eighteen. Popping value two with total eight gives sixteen, smaller than current best, so res stays eighteen. We push one and then two onto the stack as remaining increasing elements. After the loop, leftover stack entries one and two give products eleven and two, both less than eighteen. The final answer returned is eighteen, the maximum minimum product found.
say.code: First, build prefix sums. Then walk the array. Each new value starts its window at its own index. While the stack top is bigger, pop it. Its window ends just before here, so score its value times that range sum. The new value inherits the popped start, stretching left. Push it. At the end, leftovers stretch to the last index. Take the modulo only at the very end.
say.outro: Linear time and space. The pattern is a monotonic stack, finding how far each value can reach as the minimum.

maximum-subarray-min-product.title: Maximum Subarray Min-Product
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container the problem expects for our method.
The method takes the list nums and returns the largest min-product, reduced by the modulus at the very end.
We start the result at zero, since all values are positive and any real product will beat it.
The stack holds pairs of a start index and a value, kept in increasing order of value.
The prefix list starts with zero so that any window sum is a difference of two prefix entries.
We walk through each number in nums to build the running prefix sums.
Each new prefix entry is the previous entry plus the current number, so prefix holds cumulative totals.
Now a second pass goes through every index and value, treating each as a possible window boundary.
We assume the new value's window starts at its own index until we learn it can reach further left.
While the top of the stack is larger than the current number, that top value's window must end here.
We pop that entry to get its start index and its value as the window minimum.
The window sum runs from its start up to just before index i, using the difference of prefix sums.
We compare the best so far with this value times its window sum and keep the larger, without taking the modulus yet.
The current number can extend back to the popped start, since everything in between was larger, so we move newStart there.
We push the current number with its extended start, keeping the stack increasing.
Values left on the stack never met a smaller number on the right, so their windows extend to the array's end.
Each leftover window sum is the total prefix at the array's length minus the prefix at its start.
We update the result with this value times its window sum if it is larger.
Finally we return the result modulo one billion and seven, applying the modulus only now so comparisons stay accurate.

number-of-subsequences-that-satisfy-the-.ask: Count the non-empty subsequences whose smallest plus largest element is at most the target. Return the count modulo one billion and seven.

brute.idea: Generate every non-empty subsequence with a bitmask, and test its minimum plus maximum against the target.
steps: Loop over every bitmask from one up
Collect the picked numbers
Count it if min plus max fits
brute.whySlow: Twenty numbers already give a million subsequences; the limit is a hundred thousand numbers.

codeNotes.note: Order does not change subsequence sets
Largest too big with this min
Each middle element in or out

number-of-subsequences-that-satisfy-the-.exampleWhy: Of 63 non-empty subsequences, only 7 alone and 6 with 7 exceed 12, so 61 pass.
number-of-subsequences-that-satisfy-the-.hook: Only the min and max matter, so sort, then count whole families of subsequences at once.

optimal.insight: After sorting, fix the smallest element at left. Every element between left and the farthest valid right can be in or out freely: two to the gap subsequences at once.
steps: Sort the numbers
Put pointers at both ends
Sum too big: move right inward
Otherwise add two to the power right minus left
Then move left forward

pitfalls: Sorting is safe: a subsequence's min and max do not depend on order.
In fixed-width languages precompute powers of two modulo, or they overflow.

say.intro: This is Number of Subsequences That Satisfy the Given Sum Condition. Count the subsequences where the smallest plus the largest is at most the target. Our numbers are two, three, three, four, six, seven, and the target is twelve. Only seven on its own, and six with seven, go over. So sixty one of the sixty three pass.
say.brute: The brute force tries every subsequence. Each bitmask picks a subset. Gather the picked numbers, find the min and the max, and count it if they fit. It's correct, but it's exponential. Twenty numbers already make a million subsets, and the input can hold a hundred thousand.
say.insight: Here's the key. A subsequence only cares about its smallest and largest values, so we can sort. Now fix the smallest at the left pointer. Move the right pointer in until left plus right fits. Every number in between can be in or out, freely. That's two to the power of the gap, counted in one step.
say.anim: The array sorts to 2, 3, 3, 4, 6, 7, with target 12 and two pointers set. Left is 0 and right is 5; their sum 2 plus 7 is 9, within target. That means every subset of the middle elements works, adding 32 to res, now 32. Left moves to 1; sum 3 plus 7 is 10, still valid, adding 16 more, res is 48. Left is 2 now; sum 3 plus 7 is 10, valid, adding 8, making res 56. Left is 3; sum 4 plus 7 equals 11, still valid, adding 4, res becomes 60. Left is 4; sum 6 plus 7 exceeds target, so right shrinks to 4 instead. Now sum 6 plus 6 equals 12, valid, adding 1 more, giving final res 61. Left passes right, the loop ends, and the function returns the answer 61.
say.code: Sort first. Then put left at the start and right at the end. If the pair sums past the target, the right value can't be the max with this min, so move right in. Otherwise, every element after left, up to right, is optional. Add one shifted by right minus left, which is two to that power. Then move left forward. Return the total modulo.
say.outro: Sorting costs n log n, then one linear sweep. The pattern is two pointers on a sorted array, counting whole families at once.

number-of-subsequences-that-satisfy-the-.title: Number of Subsequences That Satisfy the Given Sum Condition
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container the problem expects for our method.
The method numSubseq takes the list nums and an integer target, and returns the count of valid subsequences.
We sort nums first, because then the smallest and largest of any subsequence are just its first and last chosen positions.
We start the result at zero and set the modulus to one billion and seven.
We place left at the first index and right at the last index to form a two pointer window.
We loop while left has not passed right, since a single element can still form a subsequence by itself.
If the smallest plus the largest exceeds target, this right end is too big for the current left.
So we move right one step inward to try a smaller maximum value.
Otherwise the pair fits, so every element strictly between left and right can be freely included or excluded.
We add two to the power of the gap between right and left, using a bit shift, to count those subsequences with left as the minimum.
Then we move left forward to fix the next smallest element and count its subsequences.
Finally we return the total taken modulo one billion and seven, keeping the huge count within bounds.

array-with-elements-not-equal-to-average.ask: Rearrange an array of distinct integers so that no element equals the average of its two neighbours. Any valid arrangement is accepted.

brute.idea: Try permutations one by one and return the first where no middle element equals its neighbours' average.
steps: Generate the next permutation
Check every middle position
Return the first that passes
brute.whySlow: Permutations grow factorially; even twelve numbers can mean hundreds of millions of orderings in the worst case.

codeNotes.note: Split into small and large halves
Output array to fill by slot

array-with-elements-not-equal-to-average.exampleWhy: Each middle value is bigger or smaller than both neighbours, so it cannot sit halfway between them.
array-with-elements-not-equal-to-average.hook: Make every middle element a peak or a valley, and no average can ever land there.

optimal.insight: An average sits strictly between its neighbours. Sort, put the smaller half on even slots and the larger half on odd slots: every middle is a peak or valley.
steps: Sort the numbers
Fill even indices with the smallest values
Fill odd indices with the largest values
Every element is now above or below both neighbours

pitfalls: Even slots must get the smaller half, including the extra middle for odd n.
Distinct values matter; duplicates could tie with an average.

say.intro: This is Array With Elements Not Equal to Average of Neighbors. Rearrange the numbers so no element is exactly the average of the two beside it. Any valid order works. Take six, two, zero, nine, seven. One answer is zero, seven, two, nine, six. Every middle value is either higher or lower than both its neighbours.
say.brute: The brute force tries orderings one at a time. For each permutation, check every middle position, and return the first one that passes. On small inputs it finds an answer fast. But in the worst case, permutations grow factorially. Twelve numbers can already mean hundreds of millions of orderings to scan.
say.insight: Here's the thing. An average always sits strictly between its two neighbours. So if every middle element is a peak, bigger than both sides, or a valley, smaller than both, no average can land there. Sort, then put the small half on the even slots and the large half on the odd slots. Small, big, small, big. Done in one pass.
say.anim: We start by sorting the array, giving us 0, 2, 6, 7, 9 in order. An empty answer array of five zeros is created to fill in. We place the smaller sorted values into the even positions, zero, two, and four. Now ans holds 0, 0, 2, 0, 6 after filling those even slots. Next we fill the odd positions with the larger remaining values, seven and nine. Ans becomes 0, 7, 2, 0, 6 after placing seven at index one. Finally index three gets nine, completing the alternating peak and valley pattern. The final answer returned is 0, 7, 2, 9, 6, matching the expected output.
say.code: Sort the numbers first. Make an answer array of the same size, and a pointer j into the sorted list. The first loop walks the even indices, handing out the smallest values in order. The second loop walks the odd indices, handing out what's left, which are the larger values. Every odd slot now towers over its neighbours.
say.outro: n log n time for the sort, linear extra space. The pattern is greedy interleaving, building peaks and valleys.

array-with-elements-not-equal-to-average.title: Array With Elements Not Equal to Average of Neighbors
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container the judge expects for our method.
The method rearrangeArray takes the list of distinct integers and returns a new arrangement with no element equal to its neighbors' average.
We sort the numbers first so the smaller half and the larger half are cleanly separated.
We store the length of the array in n so we can size the answer and loop bounds.
We create an answer list of n zeros to be filled slot by slot.
We set j to zero, a pointer that walks through the sorted numbers in order.
We loop over the even positions, stepping by two, starting at index zero.
Each even slot receives the next smallest unused number, so even slots hold the smaller half.
We advance j so the next slot takes the following number in sorted order.
We loop over the odd positions, stepping by two, starting at index one.
Each odd slot receives the next unused number, which comes from the larger half.
We advance j again so we keep consuming sorted numbers one at a time.
We return the answer, where every odd slot is a peak or every middle sits as a valley, so no average matches.

check-if-move-is-legal.ask: On an eight by eight Othello board, placing your colour on an empty cell is legal if, in some direction, it caps a line of one or more opponent pieces ending in your own colour. Return whether this move is legal.

brute.idea: For each of the eight directions, copy the whole ray to the board edge into a string, then check its pattern.
steps: Copy every cell along the ray into a string
Count the opponent pieces at its start
Legal if your colour follows at least one
brute.whySlow: On a fixed 8x8 board both are constant; this one copies every ray to the edge and never stops early.

check-if-move-is-legal.exampleWhy: Going up from the move, three white pieces are capped by a black piece, so the line is good.
check-if-move-is-legal.hook: Walk out in all eight directions: opponents in a row, then your own colour, means legal.

optimal.insight: A good line is a run of opponent pieces closed by your own colour. Walk each direction and stop at the first empty or own cell.
steps: Place the piece on the move square
Step outward in one of eight directions
Empty cell or board edge: this line fails
Own colour after at least one opponent: legal

pitfalls: Your own colour right next to the move is not a good line.
Stop at the board edge; running off it means no capture.

say.intro: Check if Move is Legal. It's Othello on an eight by eight board. Placing your colour is legal if, in some direction, it caps a run of opponent pieces that ends in your own colour. Black plays at row four, column three. Looking straight up, three white pieces sit under a black one. So the move is legal.
say.brute: A brute force copies each of the eight rays, all the way to the edge, into a string. Then it counts opponent pieces at the start, and checks whether your colour comes next. It's correct. Honestly, on a fixed eight by eight board, both versions take constant time. This one just copies every ray fully and keeps going after it already knows the answer.
