say.insight: The smarter walk stops early. Step outward one cell at a time. An empty cell or the edge kills the line. Your own colour ends it, and it's good only if at least one opponent piece came first. So track the line's length, counting both ends. A length of three or more means something got sandwiched.
say.anim: We place piece B at row 4, column 3 on the board. We check each of the eight directions from this move to find a legal line. Going downward, direction one zero, we hit white then empty, so this direction fails. Now trying upward, direction minus one zero, from row 4 column 3. We pass through white cells at rows three, two, and one, increasing length each step. At row zero we find another black piece, closing the line with length five. Since length five is at least three, this direction is legal, returning true. The move is confirmed legal, so the final answer is true.
say.code: First, put the piece on the board. The helper takes a direction and steps once. Length starts at one for the new piece. While we're on the board, grow the length. An empty cell returns false. Our own colour returns whether length is at least three. Otherwise keep stepping. The main loop tries all eight directions and returns true as soon as one works.
say.outro: Constant time on a fixed board. The pattern is matrix direction scanning, walking outward with eight direction vectors.

check-if-move-is-legal.title: Check if Move is Legal
lineNotes: We define the Solution class that holds the method for this problem.
The checkMove method receives the board, the move's row and column, and the colour being placed.
We store the number of rows and columns so we can check bounds while walking.
We list the eight directions: down, up, right, left, and the four diagonals.
The second half of the list finishes the diagonal directions so all eight neighbours are covered.
We place our colour on the move cell so the line's starting end counts as our own piece.
We define a helper that walks one direction and reports whether it forms a good line.
We step once from the move cell to its first neighbour in that direction.
We start the length at one, counting the placed piece, so a good line needs a length of at least three.
We keep walking while the current cell stays inside the board.
Each visited cell adds one to the length of the line so far.
If we hit an empty cell, the run has no closing piece, so this direction fails.
This returns false because an empty cell cannot cap a line of opponent pieces.
If we reach a cell of our own colour, the run is closed and we must check its size.
We return true only if length is at least three, meaning at least one opponent piece lay between.
Otherwise the cell is an opponent piece, so we step further along the same direction.
If we walk off the board without finding a closing piece, the direction is not legal.
We try each of the eight directions in turn.
We call the helper from the move cell with this direction to test for a legal line.
As soon as one direction works, the move is legal and we return true.
If no direction produced a legal line, we return false.

operations-on-tree.ask: Build a locking tree from a parent array. A user can lock a free node and unlock only their own. Upgrade locks a node and frees its whole subtree, but only if no ancestor is locked and some descendant is.

brute.idea: Store only parent pointers. To upgrade, test every node in the tree by climbing its ancestors to see if it sits under num.
steps: Climb from num to the root: any lock fails
For every locked node, climb to check it is below num
Unlock those, then lock num
brute.whySlow: Each upgrade climbs from every locked node in the whole tree, even ones far outside num's subtree.

operations-on-tree.exampleWhy: User 1 upgrades the root because node 4 is locked below it; then locking the root again fails.
operations-on-tree.hook: Locks are an array; upgrade walks up for locked ancestors, then sweeps the subtree below.

optimal.insight: Precompute a children list once. Then upgrade only climbs num's own ancestors and sweeps num's own subtree with a queue.
steps: Build children lists from the parent array
Lock and unlock just check and set one slot
Upgrade: climb ancestors, fail on any lock
Breadth first over the subtree, unlocking and counting
Lock num only if something was unlocked

pitfalls: Check the ancestor chain includes num itself: num must be unlocked.
If no descendant was locked, upgrade fails and changes nothing.

say.intro: Operations on Tree. We build a locking tree from a parent array. A user can lock a free node, and unlock only a node they locked. Upgrade is the tricky one. It locks a node and frees everything below it, but only if no ancestor is locked, and at least one descendant is. Here, user one upgrades the root.
say.brute: A brute force keeps only parent pointers. Lock and unlock are easy. But to upgrade, it checks every node in the tree. For each locked node, it climbs upward to see whether num is one of its ancestors. That works, but every upgrade climbs from locked nodes all over the tree, even ones nowhere near num.
say.insight: The fix is to also store each node's children, built once from the parent array. Now lock and unlock just check one slot. Upgrade climbs num's own ancestor chain, which is short. Then it sweeps only num's subtree with a queue, unlocking as it goes and counting. If it unlocked anything, lock num.
say.anim: We build the tree from the parent array, setting up each node's children list. Locking node two for user two succeeds, since it was unlocked before. User three tries to unlock node two but fails, since user two owns the lock. User two unlocks node two successfully, clearing its lock. Locking node four for user five succeeds immediately. Upgrading node zero checks ancestors first, but node zero has no parent, so it's fine. A queue sweep now scans node zero's subtree, searching for locked descendants to clear. Node four is found locked, so it gets unlocked and locked count becomes one. Since locked count is positive, node zero locks for user one, upgrade succeeds, and the final lock on node zero fails since it's already locked.
say.code: The constructor builds a children list for every node. Lock fails if the slot is taken, otherwise it stores the user. Unlock only works for the same user. Upgrade first climbs from num to the root, failing on any lock. Then a queue walks the subtree, clearing locks and counting them. If the count is positive, lock num and return true.
say.outro: Constant time lock and unlock, linear upgrade. The pattern is tree design with parent and children pointers, climbing up and sweeping down.

operations-on-tree.title: Operations on Tree
lineNotes: We import deque from collections so we can sweep the subtree with a fast queue later.
We define the LockingTree class that manages lock state for every node in the tree.
The constructor takes the parent array, where each entry names that node's parent and the root has negative one.
We store the parent array so upgrade can climb from a node up through its ancestors.
We create a locked list with one slot per node, where none means the node is unlocked.
We build a children dictionary giving every node an empty list, computed once so subtree sweeps are cheap.
We loop over every node except the root, since the root has no parent to attach to.
We append each node to its parent's children list, completing the downward view of the tree.
The lock method tries to lock a node for a given user.
If the node already holds a user, it is locked, so locking must fail.
We return false because a locked node cannot be locked again.
Otherwise we record the user as the owner of the lock on this node.
We return true to report that locking succeeded.
The unlock method tries to release a node for a given user.
If the stored owner is not this user, including when unlocked, we cannot unlock.
We return false because only the user who locked the node may unlock it.
We clear the slot back to none, freeing the node.
We return true to report that unlocking succeeded.
The upgrade method locks a node and clears its subtree, if all conditions hold.
We start a cursor at the node itself to check it and every ancestor above it.
We loop upward until the cursor passes the root, which is marked by negative one.
If the current node on the path is locked, the ancestor condition is violated.
We return false because upgrade requires that no ancestor, or the node itself, is locked.
We move the cursor to its parent and keep climbing.
We start a counter for how many locked descendants we find.
We create a queue seeded with the node to sweep its subtree breadth first.
We keep processing while the queue still has nodes to visit.
We pop the next node from the front of the queue.
If this node is locked, it is a locked descendant that must be released.
We unlock it by setting its slot to none, since upgrade frees the whole subtree.
We increment the counter to remember that at least one locked descendant existed.
We add this node's children to the queue so the sweep reaches the entire subtree.
After the sweep, we check whether any locked descendant was found.
If so, we lock the target node for the upgrading user.
We return true because all upgrade conditions were satisfied.
If no descendant was locked, we return false and the node stays unchanged.

brick-wall.ask: A wall has rows of bricks of equal height but different widths, and every row has the same total width. Draw one vertical line top to bottom, not on the outer edges, crossing as few bricks as possible. Return that number.

brute.idea: Try every whole-number position across the wall, and for each row check whether a brick edge lands there.
steps: Loop over every position from 1 to width minus 1
For each row, walk bricks looking for that edge
Count rows without an edge; keep the minimum
brute.whySlow: W can be billions while bricks are few, so scanning every position wastes almost all its work.

codeNotes.note: Zero gaps if no inner edges
Prefix sum is the edge position
One more row has a gap here

brick-wall.exampleWhy: Position 4 is a brick edge in four of the six rows, so a line there crosses only 2 bricks.
brick-wall.hook: Do not count bricks you cross; count the gaps you slip through.

optimal.insight: Crossed bricks equal rows minus rows with a gap at that position. So count gap positions in a hash map and use the most popular one.
steps: Walk each row with a running prefix sum
Record each inner edge position in a map
Skip the last brick: the wall's outer edge
Answer is rows minus the biggest gap count

pitfalls: Including the last brick counts the outer edge, which the line may not use.
Seed the map so single-brick rows do not crash max.

say.intro: This is Brick Wall. Each row is a list of brick widths, and every row is equally wide. We draw one vertical line, not on the outer edges, and want to cross as few bricks as possible. In our wall, position four is an edge in four of the six rows. So the line there cuts only two bricks.
say.brute: The brute force tries every position across the wall, one, two, three, and so on. For each one, it walks every row, looking for a brick edge right there. Rows without one get crossed. Keep the minimum. It works, but the wall can be billions of units wide, while there are only a few thousand bricks.
say.insight: Flip it around. A line crosses a brick in every row, except the rows where it slips through a gap. So crossed bricks equals the number of rows, minus the gaps at that spot. Now we only care about positions that are actually edges. Walk each row with a running sum, and count edge positions in a hash map.
say.anim: We start with a gap map containing only position zero, counting rows with brick edges. For each row, we track cumulative brick widths as potential gap positions, skipping the last brick. Row one adds gaps at positions one, three, and five, each counted once. Row two adds another gap at position three, making it two, plus new gaps at four. Row three increases gaps at one and four, both now counted twice. Row four only adds a gap at position two, appearing once. Rows five and six keep boosting positions three and four, which become the most common gaps. Position four has the most gaps, four rows, so six minus four gives the answer two.
say.code: We seed the map with zero, so rows of one brick still work. For each row, keep a running total. Skip the last brick, because its right side is the wall's outer edge. Each prefix total is an edge position, so bump its count. Finally, return the number of rows minus the biggest gap count.
say.outro: Linear in the number of bricks. The pattern is hashing prefix sums, counting where the edges line up.

brick-wall.title: Brick Wall
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container the problem expects for our method.
The method leastBricks takes the wall, a list of rows, and returns the fewest bricks a vertical line can cross.
We create a map from position to gap count, starting with zero at zero so the maximum is always defined.
We loop over each row of the wall, handling one row of bricks at a time.
For each row we reset total to zero, tracking how far across the wall we have measured.
We walk every brick except the last, since the last brick's edge is the wall's outer edge, which is not allowed.
We add the brick's width to total, giving the position of the gap at that brick's right edge.
We increase the count for that position by one, using zero if we have not seen it before.
The answer is the number of rows minus the most common gap count, since every row without a gap there gets crossed.

all-possible-full-binary-trees.ask: A full binary tree is one where every node has zero or two children. Given n, return every full binary tree with exactly n nodes, all values zero, in any order.

brute.idea: Recursively split the remaining nodes between left and right, and rebuild every smaller size's trees from scratch each time.
steps: Size one: a single leaf
Try every odd left size
Recompute left and right lists, then pair them
brute.whySlow: Same exponential output, but every smaller size is recomputed again and again, building duplicate nodes each time.

all-possible-full-binary-trees.exampleWhy: With five nodes, the root's extra pair of children can hang under either the left child or the right child.
all-possible-full-binary-trees.hook: A full tree is a root plus two smaller full trees; memoize every size once.

optimal.insight: Every full tree is a root with a full left tree of size l and a full right tree of size n minus one minus l. Cache each size's list and reuse it.
steps: Base cases: zero nodes none, one node a leaf
Split the other n minus 1 nodes into odd l and r
Pair every left tree with every right tree
Store the list for this size and reuse it

pitfalls: Even n has no full trees; the even splits simply return empty lists.
Cached subtrees are shared between answers, which LeetCode accepts.

say.intro: This is All Possible Full Binary Trees. In a full binary tree, every node has either zero children or two. Given n, return every full tree with n nodes. With five nodes there are two. The root has two children, and the extra pair hangs under either the left child or the right one.
say.brute: The brute force recurses directly. Pick an odd size for the left subtree, and the rest go right. Build both lists of smaller trees, and pair them up. It's correct. But the same small sizes get rebuilt over and over. Size three is recomputed inside every bigger call, creating duplicate nodes every time.
say.insight: Here's the thing. A full tree is just a root, a full left tree, and a full right tree. The two sizes add up to n minus one. So the answer for n is built purely from answers for smaller sizes. Cache each size's list the first time, then reuse it. Every root simply points at shared subtrees.
say.anim: We start with n equal to five, and base cases for zero and one node cached already. Backtrack for size three begins, trying left size one and right size n minus one minus l, also one. Both left and right subtrees of size one are fetched directly from the cache instantly. We combine the single left tree and single right tree into one new full tree of size three. Size three's result, one tree, gets cached in dp for reuse later. Now building size five, we pair left size one trees with the cached right size three tree. Next we try left size three and right size one, fetching cached trees for both again. Final answer for five nodes is two full binary trees, matching the expected output.
say.code: The cache starts with sizes zero and one. Zero has no trees, one is a single leaf. The helper returns a cached list if it has one. Otherwise, it tries every odd left size l, with the right size n minus one minus l. For every left tree and every right tree, it makes a new root over them. Then it stores the list.
say.outro: Exponential output, but each size is built once. The pattern is recursion with memoization on tree sizes.

all-possible-full-binary-trees.title: All Possible Full Binary Trees
lineNotes: We define the Solution class that holds our method for building all possible full binary trees.
The method takes n, the required node count, and returns a list of tree root nodes.
We create a cache dp where size zero maps to no trees and size one maps to a single lone node.
We define a helper called backtrack that returns every full binary tree having exactly n nodes.
If this size is already in the cache, we know the answer without recomputing.
So we return the cached list of trees straight away, which lets us reuse subtrees.
Otherwise we start an empty result list to collect the trees of this size.
We try every odd left subtree size from one up to n minus one, since full trees have odd sizes.
The right subtree size is n minus one minus l, because the root uses one node.
We recursively get all trees for the left size and the right size.
We loop over each possible left subtree to pair it with right subtrees.
We loop over each possible right subtree, so every left and right combination gets used.
For each pair we make a new root with value zero and attach the left and right trees.
We store the finished list in the cache under n so later calls can reuse it.
We return the list of all full binary trees of size n.
Finally we call backtrack with the original n and return its list of trees.

restore-ip-addresses.ask: Given a string of digits, return every valid IP address you can make by inserting three dots. Each of the four parts must be 0 to 255 with no leading zeros, and digits cannot be moved or dropped.

brute.idea: Try all three dot positions with nested loops, cut the string into four parts, and validate each part.
steps: Choose first, second, third cut positions
Slice into four parts
Keep it if all parts are valid
brute.whySlow: Same constant number of splits, but it never prunes: a bad first part still tries every later cut.

codeNotes.note: Too many digits for four parts

codeNotes.match: for j in range(i, min(i + 3, len(s))):
codeNotes.note: Piece of one to three digits

codeNotes.match: if int(s[i : j + 1]) < 256 and (i == j or s[i] != "0"):
codeNotes.note: Range check and no leading zero

restore-ip-addresses.exampleWhy: Five ways split 101023 into four valid parts; 01 or 023 would have leading zeros.
restore-ip-addresses.hook: Place four dots: each piece is one to three digits, at most 255, no leading zero.

optimal.insight: Build the address left to right. Each step tries a one, two or three digit piece and recurses only if it is valid, pruning dead branches immediately.
steps: Reject strings longer than twelve digits
From index i, try pieces of length one to three
Piece must be under 256 with no leading zero
Four pieces using every digit: record the address

pitfalls: A single 0 is fine, but 01 or 00 is not.
Must use every digit: four parts that leave digits over do not count.

say.intro: This is Restore IP Addresses. We get a string of digits, and insert three dots to make a valid IP address. Each of the four parts must be between zero and two fifty five, with no leading zeros. For one zero one zero two three, there are five ways. Something like zero one is never allowed.
say.brute: The brute force uses three nested loops, one for each dot position. Every choice slices the string into four parts, and we check each part. It's actually a constant amount of work, at most twenty seven splits. But it never prunes. Even when the first part is already invalid, it still tries every later cut.
say.insight: Backtracking builds the address one piece at a time. From the current index, try a piece of one, two, or three digits. Only recurse if it's under two fifty six and has no leading zero. The moment a piece is bad, that whole branch is cut. When we've placed four pieces and used every digit, record the address.
say.anim: We start backtracking on the string one zero one zero two three, building segments one at a time. Taking single digits, we build one then zero, forming the start one dot zero dot. Trying a two digit piece, curIP becomes one dot zero dot ten dot, three segments so far. All four segments fit exactly, so one point zero point ten point twenty three is saved as valid. Backtracking tries another split, producing one point zero point one hundred two point three as another valid address. The search backtracks further, now exploring addresses starting with ten, like ten point one point zero point twenty three. More branches are explored, adding ten point ten point two point three and ten point one zero two point three fails validity. Finally branches starting with one zero one succeed, giving one zero one point zero point two point three as the last valid result.
say.code: First, more than twelve digits can never fit. The helper tracks the index, the dots used, and the address so far. If we have four parts and no digits left, save it without the trailing dot. Too many dots means stop. Otherwise try pieces of one to three digits. Check the range and the leading zero, then recurse past the piece.
say.outro: At most three to the fourth branches, so constant time. The pattern is backtracking with pruning on each piece.

restore-ip-addresses.title: Restore IP Addresses
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container the interview platform expects for our method.
The method takes the digit string s and returns a list of valid IP address strings.
We start with an empty result list that will collect every valid address we find.
If the string has more than twelve digits, no valid address is possible, since four parts hold at most twelve.
In that case we return the empty result right away, skipping all the work.
We define a helper backtrack that tracks the current index i, how many parts we placed, and the address built so far.
If we have placed four parts and consumed every digit, we have found a complete valid address.
We save the current address without its trailing dot, since each piece added a dot after itself.
We return to stop exploring this branch, because the address is already complete.
If we have placed more than four parts, this path can never be valid.
So we return immediately, pruning this dead branch.
We try pieces of length one, two or three starting at i, never running past the end of the string.
A piece is valid if its value is under 256 and it has no leading zero, unless it is a single digit.
For a valid piece, we recurse from the next index with one more part and the piece plus a dot appended.
We kick off the search from index zero with no parts placed and an empty address.
Finally we return the list of all valid addresses collected during the search.

matchsticks-to-square.ask: Given matchstick lengths, decide whether you can use every stick exactly once, without breaking any, to form a square. Return true or false.

brute.idea: Try every way to assign each stick to one of four sides, then check at the end whether all four sides are equal.
steps: Put the next stick on side 0, 1, 2 or 3
Recurse until every stick is placed
Check all four sides equal a quarter
brute.whySlow: Same four to the n worst case, but without pruning it keeps building sides that overflowed long ago.

codeNotes.note: Undo and try the next side

matchsticks-to-square.exampleWhy: The total is 8, so each side is 2: three sides use one 2 each, and the two 1s form the fourth.
matchsticks-to-square.hook: Four buckets, each exactly a quarter of the total: drop sticks in, longest first.

optimal.insight: Every side must be exactly a quarter of the total. Never let a side exceed that, and place the longest sticks first so failures show up early.
steps: Total not divisible by four: false
Sort sticks longest first
Try the stick on each side that still fits
Undo and try the next side on failure
All sticks placed: it is a square

pitfalls: Without sorting descending, the search can blow up on large inputs.
Reaching the end means all sides equal, since none can exceed a quarter.

say.intro: This is Matchsticks to Square. We get matchstick lengths, and must use every single one, unbroken, to make a square. Our sticks are one, one, two, two, two. They add up to eight, so each side must be two. Three sides take one two each, and the two ones make the fourth. So it's true.
say.brute: The brute force tries every assignment. Each stick goes on side zero, one, two, or three, and we recurse. Only when every stick is placed do we check whether the four sides are equal. That's four to the n assignments, and it keeps building sides that went over the limit long before the end.
say.insight: We know the target side length up front. It's the total divided by four. So never let a side go past it. That one check prunes most branches. Placing the longest sticks first makes dead ends show up even sooner. And if every stick gets placed without overflowing, all four sides must be exactly full.
say.anim: The sticks sum to eight, so each side must measure exactly two. Sticks are sorted largest first, placing big pieces early to catch failures sooner. The first two goes into side zero, filling it completely to two. Next, another two is tried but skips to side one, filling it too. The third stick, size two, fills side two, now also at two. With three sides full, a size one stick adds into side three. The final one stick fills side three completely, making all sides equal two. All matchsticks placed successfully, so the function returns true, forming a square.
say.code: If the total isn't divisible by four, return false right away. The side length is a quarter of the total. Sort the sticks longest first. The helper places stick i. It tries each side where the stick still fits, adds it, and recurses. If that fails, it takes the stick back off and tries the next side. Placing every stick means success.
say.outro: Exponential in the worst case, but heavily pruned. The pattern is backtracking into buckets with a capacity limit.

matchsticks-to-square.title: Matchsticks to Square
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container the problem expects for our method.
The makesquare method takes the list of matchstick lengths and returns true or false.
We add up all stick lengths to learn the total length we have to work with.
If the total does not divide evenly by four, no square is possible.
In that case we return false right away.
Otherwise each side must equal the total divided by four, so we store that as length.
We create a list of four zeros to track how long each side currently is.
We sort sticks from longest to shortest so impossible placements fail early and prune the search.
We define a recursive helper that tries to place the stick at index i.
If i equals the number of sticks, every stick has been placed successfully.
So we return true because all four sides were built without exceeding the target.
For the current stick, we try each of the four sides in turn.
We only consider a side if adding this stick keeps it within the target length.
We place the stick by adding its length to that side.
We recurse to place the next stick and see whether the rest can be completed.
If the recursion succeeds, we pass the true result back up immediately.
Otherwise we backtrack by removing the stick from that side and try the next side.
If no side can hold this stick, we return false so earlier choices get revisited.
We start the search with the first and longest stick at index zero and return its result.

open-the-lock.ask: A lock has four wheels of digits 0 to 9, starting at 0000. One turn moves one wheel up or down by one, wrapping around. Avoiding the dead-end combinations, return the fewest turns to reach the target, or -1.

brute.idea: The same breadth first search, but remember visited codes and dead ends in plain lists, so every check is a scan.
steps: Breadth first search from 0000, one turn per level
Check each new code against the dead-end list and the seen list
Return the level when the target appears
brute.whySlow: Up to ten thousand codes, and each 'have I seen it?' scans a growing list: about fifty million comparisons.

codeNotes.note: First arrival is the fewest turns

open-the-lock.exampleWhy: Wheels two to four are blocked one turn away, but turning the first wheel up twice reaches 2000.
open-the-lock.hook: Every lock combination is a node with eight neighbours; breadth first search finds the fewest turns.

optimal.insight: Treat each combination as a graph node and generate its eight neighbours on the fly. Breadth first search reaches nodes in order of turns, so the first hit is minimal.
steps: Start at 0000 unless it is a dead end
Seed the visited set with the dead ends
Pop a code; if it is the target, return turns
Push each unvisited neighbour with turns plus one

pitfalls: Mark visited when pushing, not popping, or the queue fills with duplicates.
Check 0000 itself against the dead ends before starting.

say.intro: Open the Lock. Four wheels, each zero to nine, all starting at zero. One turn moves one wheel up or down by one, and nine wraps to zero. Some combinations are dead ends. Here, the other wheels are blocked one turn away. But turning the first wheel up twice reaches two zero zero zero, so the answer is two.
say.brute: A brute force first builds the entire graph. All ten thousand combinations, each with its eight neighbours. Then it runs a breadth first search from zero zero zero zero. It's correct, and the worst case is the same. But it always pays for all eighty thousand edges up front, even when the target is just two turns away.
say.insight: Here's the thing. Each combination is a node, and its eight neighbours are one turn away. We don't need the whole graph stored. Just generate neighbours when we pop a node. Breadth first search explores in rings, all one turn codes, then all two turn codes. So the first time we see the target, that's the fewest turns.
say.anim: We start at wheel zero zero zero zero, marking deadends and the start as visited. We generate all eight neighbors of zero zero zero zero by turning each wheel up or down. Only one zero zero zero reaches the queue since the deadends block the rest, at one turn. Now expanding one zero zero zero, we generate its neighbors including the target two zero zero zero. Two zero zero zero gets added to the queue with two turns, since breadth first search tracks turn count. Next we expand nine zero zero zero, adding its unvisited neighbors at two turns each. The queue reaches the front where wheel equals two zero zero zero with turns equal two. Since wheel matches the target, the search returns two as the minimum number of turns.
say.code: If the start itself is a dead end, return minus one. The children helper turns each wheel up and down, with wrap around. The visited set starts with the dead ends, so we never step on them. Pop a code and its turn count. If it's the target, return. Otherwise push every new neighbour with one more turn, marking it right away.
say.outro: At most ten thousand states, eight edges each. The pattern is breadth first search over an implicit state graph.

open-the-lock.title: Open the Lock
lineNotes: We import deque from collections to get a queue with fast removal from the front for breadth first search.
We define the Solution class that holds the method required by the problem.
The openLock method takes the list of dead end combinations and the target combination, and returns the fewest turns.
If the starting combination zero zero zero zero is itself a dead end, the lock is stuck immediately.
In that case we return negative one because no move can ever be made.
We define a helper called children that produces every combination reachable in one turn from a given wheel state.
We start with an empty list named res to collect the neighbouring combinations.
We loop over the four wheel positions, handling each wheel one at a time.
We compute the digit one higher at this position, wrapping nine back to zero using modulo ten.
We build the new combination by swapping that digit into position i and keep the rest unchanged, then add it to res.
We compute the digit one lower at this position, and modulo ten wraps zero around to nine.
We build and append the combination with the decremented digit, giving two neighbours per wheel.
After all four wheels we return the list of eight neighbouring combinations.
We start the queue with zero zero zero zero at zero turns, storing each wheel paired with its turn count.
We create the visited set from the dead ends so that dead combinations are never entered.
We also mark the start as visited so we never queue it again.
We keep searching while the queue still has combinations to explore.
We take the oldest entry from the queue, which guarantees we process combinations in order of turns.
If this combination equals the target, we have reached it.
We return its turn count, which is minimal because breadth first search finds the shallowest path first.
Otherwise we look at each of the eight neighbours of the current combination.
We only consider neighbours that are not dead ends and have not been visited already.
We mark the neighbour as visited right away so it cannot be added to the queue twice.
We enqueue the neighbour with one more turn than the current combination.
If the queue empties without reaching the target, it is unreachable, so we return negative one.

longest-happy-string.ask: Build the longest string using at most a letters a, b letters b and c letters c, with no three identical letters in a row. Return any longest such string.

brute.idea: Backtrack over every happy string, adding a, b or c while no triple forms, and keep the longest one found.
steps: Try appending a, b, then c
Skip a letter that would make three in a row
Record the longest string reached
brute.whySlow: It explores every happy string; with dozens of letters the number of branches explodes exponentially.

codeNotes.note: Negative counts make a max heap

codeNotes.match: if len(res) > 1 and res[-1] == res[-2] == char:
codeNotes.note: Would make three in a row

longest-happy-string.exampleWhy: Pairs of c are split by the single a and single b; a ninth letter would force ccc.
longest-happy-string.hook: Always spend the most plentiful letter, unless that would make three in a row.

optimal.insight: Greedily use the letter with the most remaining. If it would make a triple, use the second most plentiful once, then go back. A max heap gives both instantly.
steps: Push nonzero counts into a max heap
Pop the most plentiful letter
Would it make three in a row? Use the runner-up once
Otherwise append it
Push back any letter with count left

pitfalls: Push the blocked top letter back; it is still needed later.
Counts are negative in the heap, so adding one uses a letter.

say.intro: Longest Happy String. We have some a's, b's and c's. Build the longest string with no three identical letters in a row. Here we have one a, one b, and seven c's. The best is c c a c c b c c. The a and b split the c's into pairs. A ninth letter would force three c's.
say.brute: The brute force backtracks over every happy string. At each step, try adding a, then b, then c, skipping any letter that would make a triple. Keep the longest string it ever reaches. It's correct. But it explores every possible happy string, and with dozens of each letter, that tree of choices explodes.
say.insight: Think greedy. The letter we have the most of is the one most likely to get stuck at the end. So always spend it first. The only exception is when it would make three in a row. Then spend the runner up letter just once, which breaks the run, and come right back. A max heap hands us both letters instantly.
say.anim: We start with counts a equals 1, b equals 1, c equals 7, building a max heap. The heap holds c with 7, b with 1, a with 1, so c is popped first. Since result is still short, we append c, giving res equal to c, with count now 6. C is popped again, but adding it would make three c's in a row. So instead we borrow a, appending it to get res equal to c c a. We continue greedily alternating c and remaining letters, building ccaccb as letters deplete. Only c remains, so it fills in the final two spots, forming ccaccbcc. The heap empties and the function returns the final happy string ccaccbcc.
say.code: Push each nonzero count as a negative number, so the heap behaves as a max heap. Pop the top letter. If the last two characters are already that letter, we need the runner up. If there isn't one, we're finished. Otherwise append the runner up once and push it back if it has letters left. Else append the top letter. Then push the top back if it still has count.
say.outro: Linear in the total letters, since the heap holds at most three. The pattern is greedy with a max heap.

longest-happy-string.title: Longest Happy String
lineNotes: We import heapq to get a heap, which gives us the most plentiful letter quickly.
We define a Solution class, as the problem format expects.
This method takes the counts of a, b and c and returns the longest happy string.
We start with an empty result string and an empty heap that will act as a max heap.
We loop over each letter paired with its negated count, since Python's heap is a min heap.
We skip letters whose count is zero so they never enter the heap.
We push the negative count and letter onto the heap, so the largest remaining count sits on top.
We keep going while the heap still has letters available to place.
We pop the letter with the most remaining uses, along with its negative count.
If the last two characters already equal this letter, adding it would make a triple.
In that case, if the heap is empty we have no alternative letter available.
So we stop building, because any further letter would break the rule.
Otherwise we pop the second most plentiful letter to use as a separator.
We append that separator letter to the result once.
We add one to its negative count, which means one fewer copy remains.
If the separator still has copies left, we proceed to put it back.
We push the separator back onto the heap with its updated count.
This else covers the normal case where adding the top letter is safe.
We append the top letter to the result.
We add one to its negative count to record that we used a copy.
If the top letter still has copies remaining after this step, we put it back.
We push the top letter back with its updated count so it can be chosen later.
When the heap is empty or we broke out, we return the built string.

shortest-bridge.ask: A square grid of 0s and 1s holds exactly two islands of connected 1s. Return the fewest 0s you must flip to 1 to connect the two islands.

brute.idea: Collect the cells of both islands, then try every pair and take the smallest Manhattan distance minus one.
steps: Flood fill to collect the first island
Every other land cell is the second island
Minimum distance over all pairs, minus one
brute.whySlow: Two big islands can each have about n squared cells, so comparing every pair costs n to the fourth.

codeNotes.note: Multi-source BFS from the whole island

shortest-bridge.exampleWhy: The islands are at the top middle and bottom right; the shortest water path between them is two cells.
shortest-bridge.hook: Flood one island with DFS, then grow it outward ring by ring until it touches the other.

optimal.insight: Mark all of island one with DFS, then run a multi-source BFS from every one of its cells. The layer where BFS first touches land is the bridge length.
steps: Find any land cell and DFS its whole island
Put every island cell in the BFS queue
Expand one water layer at a time
First new land cell reached: return the layer count

pitfalls: Starting BFS from a single cell instead of the whole island overcounts.
Count layers, not cells popped, to get the number of flips.

say.intro: This is Shortest Bridge. A square grid has exactly two islands of ones. We can flip water cells to land. What's the fewest flips to connect the islands? Here one island is at the top middle, the other at the bottom right. The shortest water path between them is two cells, so the answer is two.
say.brute: The brute force collects the cells of both islands. Then it checks every pair, one cell from each island, and takes the smallest grid distance, minus one. That's correct, since a shortest path never needs to cross land. But two big islands can each have n squared cells, so all pairs costs n to the fourth.
say.insight: Instead, grow one island outward. First, depth first search marks every cell of island one. Then put all of those cells into a queue at once, and breadth first search outward, one ring of water at a time. The first time a ring touches land we haven't marked, that's island two. The ring number is the answer.
say.anim: We start scanning the grid looking for the first land cell to begin flood fill. At row zero column one we find land, so depth first search marks it visited. DFS explores neighbors but finds no more connected land, so island one is just that single cell. Now breadth first search expands outward from the island, layer by layer, tracking distance res. The first ring adds cells like zero zero and one one to the visited set at distance zero. Res increases to one as the search expands further outward without hitting new land yet. At distance two the search reaches cell two one, right next to the second island. Bfs returns two, meaning the shortest bridge connecting both islands is two cells long.
say.code: The scan finds the first land cell and runs the depth first search, adding every connected land cell to visit. Then BFS starts from all of visit together. Each pass of the inner loop handles one layer. For each neighbour, skip it if it's off the grid or seen. If it's land, we've reached island two, so return the layer count. Otherwise queue it as water.
say.outro: Every cell is touched a constant number of times, so n squared. The pattern is DFS to mark, then multi source BFS.

shortest-bridge.title: Shortest Bridge
lineNotes: We import deque from collections so the breadth first search can pop from the front of a queue efficiently.
We define the Solution class that holds the method the problem asks for.
The method shortestBridge takes the grid of zeros and ones and returns the minimum number of flips.
We store N as the grid side length since the grid is square.
We list the four directions, right, left, down and up, used for moving between neighboring cells.
We define a helper called invalid that checks whether a row and column fall outside the grid.
It returns true when the row or column is negative or equals N, meaning off the board.
We create a visit set that will hold every cell of the first island and later any cells the search reaches.
We define a recursive dfs function that marks all connected land cells of the first island.
We stop if the cell is out of bounds, is water, or was already visited.
Returning here ends that branch of the depth first search.
Otherwise we add the current cell to the visit set to mark it as part of island one.
We loop over each of the four directions to explore neighbors.
We recursively call dfs on each neighbor so the entire island gets marked.
We define the bfs function that expands outward from island one to find the nearest second island cell.
We set the flip count res to zero and seed the queue with every cell of the first island.
We keep looping while the queue still has cells to expand.
We process exactly the cells currently in the queue, which makes up one layer, or one more flipped zero.
We pop a cell from the front of the queue and unpack its row and column.
We try each of the four directions from this cell.
We compute the neighbor's row and column by adding the direction offsets.
We skip neighbors that are off the grid or already visited.
The continue moves on to the next direction without doing anything for that neighbor.
If the neighbor is land and not visited, it must belong to the second island.
We return res, the number of water layers crossed, which is the shortest bridge length.
Otherwise the neighbor is water, so we add it to the queue to expand from next layer.
We mark that water cell visited so we never queue it twice.
After finishing a full layer, we increase res because the bridge needs one more flipped zero.
We scan every row of the grid to find the first land cell.
We scan every column within that row.
When we hit a cell equal to one, we have found a cell of the first island.
We run dfs from that cell to mark the whole first island in visit.
We then return the result of bfs, and this also stops the scan so only one island is marked.

search-suggestions-system.ask: As each letter of the search word is typed, suggest up to three products that start with the typed prefix, choosing the alphabetically smallest. Return the list of suggestions after every letter.

brute.idea: Sort the products, then for every prefix scan the whole list for words starting with it, keeping the first three.
steps: Sort the products
Grow the prefix one letter at a time
Filter every product by that prefix; take three
brute.whySlow: Every typed letter rescans every product, even ones ruled out letters ago.

codeNotes.match: while l <= r and (len(products[l]) <= i or products[l][i] != c):
codeNotes.note: Left skips words that stopped matching

codeNotes.match: while l <= r and (len(products[r]) <= i or products[r][i] != c):

codeNotes.note: Smallest three are at the left

search-suggestions-system.exampleWhy: After m and mo every product matches, so the first three alphabetically show; from mou only mouse and mousepad remain.
search-suggestions-system.hook: Sort once, then squeeze a window from both ends as each letter is typed.

optimal.insight: In sorted order, words sharing a prefix form one contiguous block. Each new letter only shrinks that block, so two pointers move inward and never back.
steps: Sort the products alphabetically
For letter i, move left past words that mismatch at i
Move right inward past mismatching words too
Take up to three words from the left pointer

pitfalls: Check word length before indexing, or short words crash the loop.
Once the window is empty, every later letter gets an empty list.

say.intro: This is Search Suggestions System. As the user types each letter, suggest up to three products that start with what's typed so far, picking the alphabetically smallest. With the word mouse, after m and m o, everything matches, so we show the first three. From m o u on, only mouse and mousepad remain.
say.brute: The brute force sorts the products, then grows the prefix one letter at a time. For every prefix, it scans the entire list, keeps the words that start with it, and returns the first three. It's correct. But every letter rescans every product, including ones that stopped matching several letters ago.
say.insight: Here's the trick. After sorting, all words sharing a prefix sit together in one block. Typing another letter can only shrink that block. So keep two pointers, left and right. For each new letter, move left forward past words that don't match at that position, and move right backward the same way. They never move back.
say.anim: We sort the products alphabetically before searching for suggestions matching mouse. Pointers l and r start at zero and four, spanning the whole sorted product list. For letter m, both pointers already match, so the window covers all five words. We grab up to three words from the window, giving mobile, moneypot, and monitor. For letter u, l moves rightward past words lacking a u, landing on mouse at index three. Now the window only contains mouse and mousepad, so both get suggested. For s then e, the window stays fixed at mouse and mousepad as letters keep matching. Final answer: suggestions narrow each step until only mouse and mousepad remain.
say.code: Sort first. Left starts at zero, right at the end. For each letter index i, move left forward while that word is too short or has a different letter at i. Do the same for right, moving backward. The words between them all match. Take up to three, starting from left, since those are the smallest.
say.outro: Sorting dominates, then each pointer moves at most n times. The pattern is two pointers shrinking a sorted window.

search-suggestions-system.title: Search Suggestions System
lineNotes: We define a class named Solution, which holds the method that LeetCode will call.
The method takes the list of products and the search word, and returns a list of suggestion lists.
We start with an empty result list that will collect one suggestion list per typed letter.
We sort the products alphabetically so that words sharing any prefix sit together in one contiguous block.
We set left to zero and right to the last index, so the window starts as every product.
We loop over each position in the search word, representing one more typed letter each time.
We grab the current letter at position i, which every product in the window must match.
We move left forward while that product is too short or has a different letter at position i.
Each time the left product fails the check, we advance left by one to shrink the window.
We move right backward while that product is too short or has a different letter at position i.
Each time the right product fails the check, we decrement right to shrink the window from the end.
We append an empty list to the result, ready to hold suggestions for this prefix.
We compute how many products remain in the window by taking right minus left plus one.
We loop up to three times, or fewer if the window has fewer than three products.
We add the product at left plus j to the latest suggestion list, giving the smallest words in order.
After processing every letter, we return the full list of suggestion lists.

maximum-performance-of-a-team.ask: Each engineer has a speed and an efficiency. A team's performance is the sum of its speeds times its lowest efficiency. Choose at most k engineers to maximise performance, modulo one billion and seven.

brute.idea: Try every team of one up to k engineers, and score each as total speed times minimum efficiency.
steps: Loop over team sizes one to k
Enumerate every combination of that size
Score speed sum times min efficiency
brute.whySlow: Combinations explode: a hundred thousand engineers choose fifty is astronomically many teams.

maximum-performance-of-a-team.exampleWhy: Engineers with speeds 10 and 5 have efficiencies 4 and 7: total speed 15 times 4 gives 60.
maximum-performance-of-a-team.hook: Fix the slowest-efficiency member, then keep the k fastest speeds with a min heap.

optimal.insight: Sort by efficiency, highest first. When engineer i joins, their efficiency is the team minimum, so just keep the k biggest speeds seen so far in a min heap.
steps: Pair each engineer as efficiency and speed
Sort by efficiency, highest first
Heap full? Drop the slowest speed
Add the new speed and score with this efficiency

pitfalls: Take the modulo only at the end; modding inside max breaks comparisons.
Pop before pushing so the newcomer, who sets the minimum, always stays.

say.intro: This is Maximum Performance of a Team. Each engineer has a speed and an efficiency. A team scores its total speed times its lowest efficiency. Pick at most k engineers. With k equal to two, take the engineers with speed ten and speed five. Their lowest efficiency is four, and fifteen times four is sixty.
say.brute: The brute force tries every team, every combination of one engineer, then two, all the way up to k. Score each one and keep the best. It's correct, but combinations explode. Even a modest n and k give an astronomical number of teams to check.
say.insight: Here's the trick. Sort engineers by efficiency, highest first. As we walk down that list, the newest engineer always has the lowest efficiency so far. So if they're on the team, they set the minimum. Given that, we just want the fastest k minus one others seen before them. A min heap of speeds tracks that, dropping the slowest when it's full.
say.anim: We start with speeds, efficiencies, and k equal to two, building engineer pairs. Engineers are sorted by efficiency descending, so the highest efficiency comes first. With efficiency nine and speed one, the heap is empty so we just add it, giving result nine. Next efficiency seven and speed five join, heap now holds one and five, result becomes forty two. Efficiency five and speed two push out the smallest speed one, keeping heap size at two. Efficiency four and speed ten replace two, speed sum reaches fifteen, boosting result to sixty. Efficiency three and speed three, then efficiency two and speed eight, keep updating the heap but find no better result. The loop ends and the final maximum performance returned is sixty.
say.code: Pair each engineer's efficiency with their speed, and sort descending. Walk the list. If the heap already holds k speeds, pop the smallest and subtract it from the running sum. Then add the newcomer's speed and push it. Score the running sum times the newcomer's efficiency, since it's the lowest on the team. Return the best, modulo at the end.
say.outro: Sorting plus heap operations, so n log n. The pattern is sort by one dimension, heap on the other.

maximum-performance-of-a-team.title: Maximum Performance of a Team
lineNotes: We import heapq so we can use a min heap to track the team's speeds.
We define the Solution class that holds the required method for this problem.
This method takes the engineer count, the speeds, the efficiencies and the team size limit k, and returns the best performance.
We start with an empty list that will hold each engineer's efficiency and speed together.
We loop over every engineer index from zero up to n minus one.
For each index we append a pair of efficiency and speed, putting efficiency first so sorting uses it.
We sort the pairs in descending order so the highest efficiency engineers come first.
We set the best result and the running sum of team speeds both to zero.
We create an empty min heap that will store the speeds of the current team.
We walk through engineers in order, so the current efficiency is the lowest among everyone considered so far.
If the heap already holds k engineers, we must drop one to make room for the new person.
We pop the smallest speed from the heap and subtract it from the running speed sum.
We add the current engineer's speed to the running speed sum.
We push the current speed onto the heap so it can be removed later if it becomes the smallest.
We compute performance as current efficiency times speed sum and keep the larger of it and the best so far.
We return the best performance modulo one billion and seven, applying the modulus only at the end to compare true values.

populating-next-right-pointers-in-each-n.ask: In a perfect binary tree, every node has a next pointer. Point each node to the node on its right in the same level, or to null if it is the last one. Return the root.

brute.idea: Breadth first search level by level with a queue, linking each node to the next node popped in its level.
steps: Push the root into a queue
Pop a whole level, linking neighbours in order
Queue each node's children
brute.whySlow: Same linear time, but the queue holds a whole level, up to n over two nodes; the follow-up wants constant space.

codeNotes.match: cur, nxt = root, root.left if root else None
codeNotes.note: nxt remembers the next level's start

populating-next-right-pointers-in-each-n.exampleWhy: Each level becomes a left-to-right chain: 2 points to 3, and 4, 5, 6, 7 link in order.
populating-next-right-pointers-in-each-n.hook: Use the next pointers you already wired on one level to walk it and wire the level below.

optimal.insight: Once a level is linked, it is a linked list. Walk it with next pointers and wire the children: left to right, and right to the neighbour's left.
steps: Start at the root; nxt marks the next level's start
Link cur's left child to its right child
Link cur's right child to cur.next's left child
Move along cur.next; at the end, drop to nxt

pitfalls: Only works because the tree is perfect: every parent has two children.
Check cur.next before linking cousins; the last node has no neighbour.

say.intro: This is Populating Next Right Pointers in Each Node. The tree is perfect, so every level is full. Each node has a next pointer, and we point it at the node to its right on the same level, or null at the end. In our tree, two points to three, and four, five, six, seven chain together.
say.brute: The brute force does a level order traversal with a queue. Pop a whole level at a time, and link each node to the next one popped in that level. Then queue the children. That's linear time, so it isn't slower. The catch is space. The queue holds an entire level, up to half the tree, and the follow up asks for constant space.
say.insight: Here's the thing. Once a level is linked, it's just a linked list. So walk it with the next pointers, and wire up the level below as you go. Each parent links its left child to its right child. Then it links its right child to its neighbour's left child. When the level ends, drop down to the next one.
say.anim: We start at root, node one, and set next to its left child, node two. Node one links its children, so node two now points its next to node three. Cur moves to cur dot next, which is none, since one had no next. Cur resets to nxt, node two, and nxt becomes node two's left child, node four. Node two connects its children, so four points next to five. Since two has a next, five links across to three's left child, node six. Cur moves to three, which links six to seven using the same two rules. Cur drops to nxt, now four, but four has no left child, so nxt is none. The loop ends since nxt is none, and the tree returns fully connected, starting at node one.
say.code: Cur starts at the root, and nxt remembers the leftmost node of the next level. While both exist, link cur's left child to its right child. If cur has a neighbour, link cur's right child to that neighbour's left child. Then move cur along the level. When it runs off the end, jump down to nxt, and set nxt to the next level's start.
say.outro: Linear time, constant space. The pattern is tree traversal that reuses the next pointers as a linked list.

populating-next-right-pointers-in-each-n.title: Populating Next Right Pointers in Each Node
lineNotes: We define a Solution class that holds the method for this problem.
The connect method takes the root of a perfect binary tree and returns that same root afterward.
We start cur at the root and nxt at the root's left child, or none if the tree is empty.
We loop while both cur and nxt exist, meaning the current level has children that need wiring.
We point the left child's next pointer at the right child, linking siblings under the same parent.
We check whether the current node has a neighbor on its right in the same level.
If so, we link our right child to the neighbor's left child, bridging across the two parents.
We move cur one step right along the already linked level.
If we ran off the end of the level, we need to descend to the next one.
We set cur to nxt, the leftmost node of the next level down.
We update nxt to the new cur's left child, which is the start of the level below.
Finally we return the root, now with every next pointer filled in.

minimum-number-of-flips-to-make-the-bina.ask: You have a binary string. Rotating it, moving the first character to the end, is free. Flipping a character costs one. Return the fewest flips needed to make the string alternate, like 0101 or 1010.

brute.idea: Try every rotation. For each, count mismatches against both alternating patterns, and keep the smallest count.
steps: Build each of the n rotations
Count mismatches against 0101... and 1010...
Keep the minimum over everything
brute.whySlow: Each of the n rotations is rescanned from scratch: 100,000 characters means ten billion comparisons.

codeNotes.note: Every rotation is now a window
Too long: drop the left char

minimum-number-of-flips-to-make-the-bina.exampleWhy: Rotate twice to get 100011, then flip two characters to reach 101010.
minimum-number-of-flips-to-make-the-bina.hook: Rotations plus flips sounds scary. Double the string and every rotation becomes a sliding window.

optimal.insight: Every rotation of s is a length-n window of s + s. Slide that window, updating mismatch counts as one character enters and one leaves.
steps: Double the string so rotations become windows
Count the entering character's mismatch
Window longer than n? remove the leaving character
At full size, record the smaller count

pitfalls: Track both patterns; which one is cheaper changes from window to window.
Only record answers when the window is exactly length n.

say.intro: This is Minimum Number of Flips to Make the Binary String Alternating. We can rotate the string for free, moving the front character to the back. Flips cost one each. What's the fewest flips to make it alternate? For one one one zero zero zero, rotate twice and flip two characters. The answer is two.
say.brute: The brute force tries every rotation. For each one, it compares the string against both alternating patterns, zero one zero one, and one zero one zero, and counts the mismatches. Keep the smallest count. Correct, but each of the n rotations is rescanned from scratch. That's n squared, so a hundred thousand characters means ten billion comparisons.
say.insight: Here's the trick. Glue the string to itself. Now every rotation is just a window of length n inside the doubled string. So slide a window. When a character enters, add its mismatch against each pattern. When one leaves, subtract it. Every full window gives a rotation's cost in constant time.
say.anim: We start with string 111000, doubled to 111000111000, with n equal to six. A sliding window of length six moves across the doubled string, tracking mismatches in two counters. As characters enter the window, diff1 and diff2 count mismatches against alternating patterns starting with zero or one. Once the window reaches size six, res updates to the smaller of diff1 and diff2, now two. The window slides forward, removing the leftmost character and adjusting diff1 and diff2 as l increases. This process repeats, recomputing mismatches for each rotation while keeping res at its minimum value. Later rotations give diff1 values of four, never beating the current best result of two. The loop finishes and the function returns two, the minimum flips needed.
say.code: We double the string and keep two counters. For each new right character, we compare it to the zero one pattern. A mismatch bumps the first counter, otherwise the second, because the other pattern is its exact opposite. If the window grows past n, we undo the left character and move left forward. At exactly n, we record the smaller counter.
say.outro: Linear time, linear space for the doubled string. The pattern is a sliding window, with rotations turned into windows.

minimum-number-of-flips-to-make-the-bina.title: Minimum Number of Flips to Make the Binary String Alternating
lineNotes: We define the Solution class that holds our method for this problem.
The method minFlips takes the binary string s and returns the minimum number of flips needed.
We store the original length of the string as n, since every window will have this size.
We double the string by appending it to itself, so every rotation appears as a window of length n.
We start the best answer at n, which is a safe upper bound on flips.
We set two mismatch counters to zero: diff1 for the pattern starting with zero, diff2 for the pattern starting with one.
We set the left edge of the sliding window to zero.
We move the right edge across every position of the doubled string.
If the character at the right edge differs from the zero-first pattern at that index, it is a mismatch for that pattern.
So we increase diff1 because this position needs a flip to match the zero-first pattern.
Otherwise the character matches the zero-first pattern, which means it mismatches the one-first pattern.
So we increase diff2 because this position needs a flip to match the one-first pattern.
If the window has grown larger than n, we must drop the leftmost character.
We check whether the leaving character had counted as a mismatch against the zero-first pattern.
If so, we decrease diff1 to remove its contribution.
Otherwise it had counted toward the one-first pattern.
So we decrease diff2 to remove that contribution.
We advance the left edge by one to shrink the window back to size n.
When the window has exactly n characters, it represents a valid rotation to evaluate.
We update the best answer with the smaller of the current best and the two mismatch counts.
After scanning all windows, we return the smallest number of flips found.

minimum-number-of-swaps-to-make-the-stri.ask: A string has equal numbers of opening and closing square brackets. One swap exchanges any two characters. Return the fewest swaps needed to make the brackets balanced.

brute.idea: Simulate the fixes: find the first closer that has no partner, swap it with the last opener, and repeat.
steps: Scan for the first point the balance goes negative
Swap that closer with the last opener
Count the swap and rescan from the start
brute.whySlow: Every swap triggers a fresh scan of the whole string, and there can be n over four swaps.

minimum-number-of-swaps-to-make-the-stri.exampleWhy: Three closers come before any opener. Swapping the first closer with the last opener fixes two at once, so two swaps.
minimum-number-of-swaps-to-make-the-stri.hook: Count the worst pile-up of unmatched closers; each swap fixes two of them.

optimal.insight: Only the peak number of unmatched closers matters. One good swap fixes two unmatched closers, so the answer is that peak divided by two, rounded up.
steps: Closer adds one to the unmatched count
Opener cancels one unmatched closer
Track the highest unmatched count seen
Return half the peak, rounded up

pitfalls: Answer is half the peak, not the number of bad characters.
Round up: a peak of three still needs two swaps.

say.intro: This is Minimum Number of Swaps to Make the String Balanced. We have equal numbers of opening and closing brackets. A swap exchanges any two characters. What's the fewest swaps to balance it? Our string is three closers, then three openers. Swap the first closer with the last opener, and two problems vanish. So the answer is two.
say.brute: The brute force just plays it out. Scan from the left, keeping a balance. The first time it dips below zero, that closer has no partner. Swap it with the last opening bracket, count the swap, and scan again from the start. It does find the minimum. But every swap means another full scan, so it's quadratic.
say.insight: Here's the thing. We don't need to perform the swaps. Track how many closers are waiting with no opener. Only the highest point of that count matters. Why? Swapping an unmatched closer with a far opener fixes two of them at once. So the answer is the peak, divided by two, rounded up.
say.anim: We start with extraClose and maxClose both at zero for the string of brackets. Each closing bracket increases extraClose, tracking unmatched closers seen so far. After three closers, extraClose and maxClose both climb up to three. Now opening brackets appear, each one decreasing extraClose by one. ExtraClose drops to two, then one, then zero as openers balance closers. The loop finishes, with maxClose having peaked at three unmatched closers. We compute maxClose plus one divided by two, giving the minimum swaps. The final answer returned is two, matching the expected result.
say.code: We keep two numbers. Extra close counts the unmatched closers right now. Max close remembers the worst it ever got. An opening bracket cancels one waiting closer, so subtract one. A closing bracket adds one. After each character, update the peak. At the end, return the peak plus one, divided by two. That's rounding up.
say.outro: Linear time, constant space. The pattern is greedy counting. Track the worst imbalance, and let each swap fix two.

minimum-number-of-swaps-to-make-the-stri.title: Minimum Number of Swaps to Make the String Balanced
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container the problem expects for our method.
The method minSwaps takes the bracket string s and returns the minimum number of swaps as an integer.
We start both extraClose, the current surplus of closers, and maxClose, its highest value so far, at zero.
We walk through the string one character at a time, calling each character c.
If the character is an opening bracket, we have a new opener available to match later closers.
So we decrease extraClose by one, since that opener cancels out one unmatched closer.
Otherwise the character is a closing bracket, which needs an opener before it.
So we increase extraClose by one, because we now have one more closer than openers.
We update maxClose to keep the peak surplus of closers seen anywhere in the string.
We return maxClose plus one, floor divided by two, because each swap fixes two unmatched closers and odd leftovers need one more.

number-of-pairs-of-interchangeable-recta.ask: Each rectangle is a width and a height. Two rectangles are interchangeable when width divided by height is the same for both. Return the number of interchangeable pairs.

brute.idea: Compare every pair of rectangles, cross-multiplying widths and heights to test for equal ratios without division.
steps: Pick rectangle i
Compare it with every j after it
Equal cross products? count the pair
brute.whySlow: With 100,000 rectangles that is about five billion pair checks.

number-of-pairs-of-interchangeable-recta.exampleWhy: Four rectangles share ratio one half, giving 6 pairs. Two share two thirds, giving 1 more.
number-of-pairs-of-interchangeable-recta.hook: Same shape means same width-to-height ratio. Count each ratio in a hash map, then count pairs per group.

optimal.insight: Matching ratios form groups, and a group of c rectangles gives c(c-1)/2 pairs. So just count rectangles per ratio.
steps: Compute each rectangle's width / height
Count how many share each ratio
Add c(c-1)/2 for each group

pitfalls: Float ratios work at these sizes; a gcd-reduced (w, h) tuple is exact everywhere.
The count can exceed 32 bits; other languages need a long.

say.intro: This is Pairs of Interchangeable Rectangles. Two rectangles are interchangeable if width over height is the same for both. Count the pairs. In our example, four rectangles have ratio one half, which gives six pairs. Two more have ratio two thirds, which gives one more pair. So the answer is seven.
say.brute: The brute force checks every pair. To avoid fractions, it cross multiplies, so the first width times the second height must equal the second width times the first height. That's correct, but it's n squared. With a hundred thousand rectangles, that's about five billion pair checks.
say.insight: Here's the shift. We don't need to match rectangles to each other directly. We only need to know how many share each ratio. A group of c rectangles forms c times c minus one, over two, pairs. So one pass fills a hash map from ratio to count, and a second pass adds up the pairs for each group.
say.anim: We start with an empty ratio count map and six rectangles to process. Rectangle four by eight has ratio zero point five, so count becomes one. Three by six and ten by twenty also give ratio zero point five, raising count to four. Two by three introduces a new ratio, zero point six six seven, counted once. Four by six matches that second ratio too, making its count two. With four rectangles sharing a ratio, we add four times three over two, six pairs. The two matching rectangles add one more pair, bringing total to seven. The function returns seven, the total interchangeable rectangle pairs.
say.code: We keep a map from ratio to count. For each width and height, we divide, and bump that ratio's count. Then for every count c, we add c times c minus one, integer divided by two. That's the number of ways to choose two rectangles from the group. Return the total.
say.outro: Linear time, linear space. The pattern is arrays and hashing: group by a key, then count the pairs inside each group.

number-of-pairs-of-interchangeable-recta.title: Number of Pairs of Interchangeable Rectangles
lineNotes: We define a solution class that holds the method required for this problem.
This method takes the list of rectangles and returns the total number of interchangeable pairs as an integer.
We create an empty dictionary that will count how many rectangles share each width to height ratio.
We set the result to zero, since we have not counted any pairs yet.
We loop over every rectangle, unpacking its width and height into w and h.
We divide width by height to get the ratio, then increase that ratio's count by one, starting from zero if unseen.
Now we loop over the final counts, one for each distinct ratio group.
For a group of c rectangles we add c times c minus one, divided by two, which is the number of pairs.
We return the accumulated total of interchangeable pairs.

longest-string-chain.hook: Building word chains by adding one letter at a time. Sort by length, then grow each word from something smaller.
longest-string-chain.ask: Given a list of lowercase words, a word chain inserts exactly one letter at each step without reordering the rest. Return the length of the longest possible chain using words from the list.
longest-string-chain.exampleWhy: a leads to ba, ba leads to bda, bda leads to bdca. That is four words long, and nothing longer exists.

brute.idea: Sort by length, then for every pair of words check directly whether one is a predecessor of the other by scanning characters, and use recursion with memoisation to find the longest chain starting at each word.
steps: Sort words by length
For word i, scan every later word j
Check predecessor relation by walking both strings with a skip allowance
Recurse to find the best chain starting at j, memoise, take the max
brute.whySlow: Checking every pair of words directly, rather than generating candidates, wastes work comparing words that can never connect.

optimal.insight: A word's predecessors are exactly the words formed by deleting one of its own letters. So instead of searching outward for successors, look inward: delete each letter from the current word and check if that shorter word already has a known chain length.
steps: Sort words by length so shorter words are processed first
For each word, try deleting each single character to form a candidate predecessor
If that candidate exists in the map, this word's chain length is one more than it
Track the best chain length seen so far

codeNotes.note: Every word is at least a chain of one
Delete one letter to find a possible predecessor
Has that shorter word been seen?
Extend the best predecessor chain by one

pitfalls: Sorting by length is essential, otherwise a predecessor might not be processed yet when needed.
Two words of the same length can never be in a predecessor relation, so only shorter words matter.
Forgetting to initialise dp[w] to 1 breaks single word chains.

say.intro: This is Longest String Chain. You can insert one letter into a word to get a longer word. Chain as many words together as possible and return the chain length. Here, a becomes ba, ba becomes bda, bda becomes bdca. That is a chain of four.
say.brute: The obvious approach is to sort by length, then for every word check every later word directly, scanning both strings to see if one letter was inserted. With memoised recursion this finds the answer, but comparing every pair of words character by character is wasteful when most pairs can never match.
say.insight: Flip the question around. Instead of asking which later word can I extend to, ask which earlier word could have led to me. That means deleting one letter from the current word. If that shorter version is already in our map of best chain lengths, we can extend it by one. This turns a pairwise search into a simple lookup.
say.anim: Words are sorted by length so shorter chains are built first. We start with a and b, each a chain of length one by itself. Processing ba, deleting its a leaves b, which already has a chain, so ba becomes length two. For bca, deleting the b leaves ca which is unknown, but deleting the c leaves ba, giving length three. Similarly bda finds ba as a predecessor, also reaching chain length three. Finally bdca deletes its b to find bca, extending that chain to length four. Best updates to four as bdca becomes the longest chain found. The function returns four, the longest string chain length.
say.code: We sort the words by length first, so shorter words are always ready in the map. We give every word a default chain length of one. Then for each position in the word, we delete that character to form a candidate predecessor. If that candidate is already in our dictionary, we update this word's chain length to one more than it. Finally we track the best chain length seen across all words.
say.outro: This runs in roughly n times length squared time, which is fast enough even for a thousand words. The pattern here is one dimensional dynamic programming, built on the trick of looking backwards by deletion instead of forwards by insertion.

longest-string-chain.title: Longest String Chain
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container the problem expects for our method.
The method longestStrChain takes the list of words and returns the length of the longest chain as an integer.
This comment says we process shorter words first so every possible predecessor already has a known chain length.
We sort the words in place by their length, so shorter words come before longer ones.
We create an empty dictionary that will map each word to the longest chain ending at that word.
We set best to one, since any single word is already a valid chain of length one.
We loop over each word in sorted order, so all shorter words have already been handled.
This comment says we begin by treating the current word as a chain of just itself.
We record a chain length of one for the current word as a starting baseline.
This comment explains that we now look inward by deleting letters to find possible predecessors.
We loop over every position in the word, each one marking a letter we will try deleting.
We build the predecessor by joining the part before position i with the part after it, skipping that letter.
We check whether that shorter word is in our dictionary, meaning it exists in the list and has a known chain.
If so, we compute a candidate chain length by adding one to the predecessor's chain length.
We compare that candidate against the current word's best chain length found so far.
