If the candidate is larger, we update the word's chain length, since extending that predecessor gives a longer chain.
This comment says we now update the overall best answer using this word's result.
We check whether this word's final chain length beats the best answer so far.
If it does, we store this word's chain length as the new best.
After processing every word, we return the best chain length found.

maximum-profit-in-job-scheduling.hook: Jobs that pay well but overlap in time. Pick the best non-clashing set for maximum profit.
maximum-profit-in-job-scheduling.ask: Given start times, end times and profits for a set of jobs, choose a subset with no overlapping time ranges that maximises total profit. A job ending at time X can be followed immediately by one starting at time X.
maximum-profit-in-job-scheduling.exampleWhy: Taking the first job, one to three for fifty, then the fourth job, three to six for seventy, gives one hundred twenty. Nothing beats that combination.

brute.idea: Sort jobs by end time. For each job, scan backwards through earlier jobs to find the latest one that finishes at or before this job starts, then decide to take or skip.
steps: Sort jobs by end time
For each job, linearly search earlier jobs for the last compatible one
dp[i+1] = max(skip, take + dp of that compatible job]
brute.whySlow: With fifty thousand jobs the backward linear search for each job makes it far too slow.

optimal.insight: Sort jobs by end time, then for each job binary search for the last job whose end time is at or before this job's start. That turns the backward scan into a fast lookup.
steps: Sort jobs by end time
Build a dp array where dp[i] is best profit using the first i sorted jobs
For job i, binary search the sorted end times for the count of jobs ending by its start
dp[i+1] is the max of skipping this job or taking it plus the best profit before it

codeNotes.note: Sort all jobs by their end time
Precompute sorted end times for binary search
Find how many jobs finish at or before this job's start
Choose the better of skipping or taking this job
dp holds best profit using first i jobs

pitfalls: Sort by end time, not start time, or the binary search logic breaks.
Use bisect_right so a job ending exactly at the current start still counts as compatible.

say.intro: This is Maximum Profit in Job Scheduling. Each job has a start, an end, and a profit. You can only pick jobs that do not overlap. A job ending at time X can be followed by one starting at time X. With these four jobs, the best choice is job one and job four, giving a profit of one hundred twenty.
say.brute: The natural idea is to sort jobs by when they finish, then for each job look backwards for the last job that ends at or before this one starts. That backward search works, but doing it for every single job means a lot of repeated scanning. With fifty thousand jobs that quadratic behaviour becomes painfully slow.
say.insight: The fix is to replace that backward scan with a binary search. Since jobs are sorted by end time, the end times form a sorted list. For any job, we want to know how many earlier jobs finish by the time this one starts. Binary search answers that instantly. Then it is a simple decision, skip this job and keep the previous best, or take it and add its profit to the best profit available before it started.
say.anim: We start with four jobs defined by start times, end times, and profits. Each job is combined into a tuple of end, start, and profit, then sorted by end time. After sorting, we build a list of end times for fast binary searching later. Now we scan jobs in order, tracking dp as the best profit using jobs so far. For job ending at 3, binary search finds no earlier compatible job, so we take profit 50. Job ending at 5 can follow the first job, giving a combined profit of 90. The last job ending at 6 builds on dp index 1, yielding takeProfit 120, beating skipping. The final dp array shows the best total, and the function returns 120 as the answer.
say.code: We sort jobs by end time using a zip of end, start and profit. We build an array of just the end times for binary search, and a dp array one longer than the job count. For each job we binary search to find the index of the last compatible job, then set dp of i plus one to the better of skipping or taking this job using that compatible profit. The final answer sits at the end of the dp array.
say.outro: Sorting plus binary search inside a dynamic programming pass gives us n log n overall. This is a one dimensional dynamic programming pattern, dressed up with interval scheduling and a clever lookup.

maximum-profit-in-job-scheduling.title: Maximum Profit in Job Scheduling
maximum-profit-in-job-scheduling.optimalCode:
from typing import List
import bisect

class Solution:
    def jobScheduling(self, startTime: List[int], endTime: List[int], profit: List[int]) -> int:
        # 1. Combine jobs into tuples and sort by end time
        jobs = []
        for i in range(len(startTime)):
            jobs.append((endTime[i], startTime[i], profit[i]))
        jobs.sort()

        count = len(jobs)
        endTimes = []
        for i in range(count):
            endTimes.append(jobs[i][0])

        # 2. dp[i] holds the best profit using the first i sorted jobs
        dp = [0] * (count + 1)

        for i in range(count):
            end, start, currentProfit = jobs[i]

            # 3. Binary search for the last job that ends at or before this job's start
            index = bisect.bisect_right(endTimes, start, 0, i)

            # 4. Either skip this job or take it plus the best profit before it
            skipProfit = dp[i]
            takeProfit = dp[index] + currentProfit
            dp[i + 1] = max(skipProfit, takeProfit)

        return dp[count]

We import bisect to get a fast binary search over the sorted end times.
We define a Solution class, as the problem format expects.
The jobScheduling method takes start times, end times and profits, and returns the maximum total profit.

We start with an empty list that will hold one tuple per job.
We loop over every job index using the number of start times.
We append a tuple of end time, start time and profit, putting end first so sorting uses it.
We sort the jobs, which orders them by end time because end time is the first tuple entry.
We store the number of jobs in count for use in later loops.
We create an empty list to hold just the sorted end times for binary search.
We loop over each sorted job index.
We copy that job's end time into the endTimes list, keeping it in sorted order.
This comment explains that dp at index i is the best profit using only the first i sorted jobs.
We create dp with count plus one zeros, so dp at zero means no jobs and zero profit.
We loop through the sorted jobs, deciding for each one whether to take it.

Skipping the job leaves us with the best profit from the first i jobs, which is dp at i.

maximum-profit-in-job-scheduling.optimalCodeOriginal:
from typing import List
import bisect

class Solution:
    def jobScheduling(self, startTime: List[int], endTime: List[int], profit: List[int]) -> int:
        jobs = sorted(zip(endTime, startTime, profit))
        n = len(jobs)
        dp = [0] * (n + 1)
        ends = [jobs[i][0] for i in range(n)]
        for i in range(n):
            e, s, p = jobs[i]
            idx = bisect.bisect_right(ends, s, 0, i)
            dp[i+1] = max(dp[i], dp[idx] + p)
        return dp[n]

detonate-the-maximum-bombs.hook: One bomb goes off, and a chain reaction follows. Which bomb should you light first?
detonate-the-maximum-bombs.ask: You are given bombs as x, y, radius. Detonating a bomb sets off every bomb within its blast radius, and those trigger more in turn. Choose one bomb to detonate first so that the total number of bombs that go off is as large as possible.
detonate-the-maximum-bombs.exampleWhy: Bomb 0 reaches bomb 1, and bomb 1 reaches both bomb 0 and bomb 2. Starting from bomb 0 or bomb 1 sets off three bombs total. Bomb 2 and bomb 3 only ever trigger themselves.

brute.idea: For every starting bomb, simulate the chain reaction from scratch using a fresh search, checking all pairs each time.
steps: Pick a starting bomb
Run a search that checks every other bomb for being in range of any detonated bomb
Repeat until no new bombs are added
Track the biggest count across all starts
brute.whySlow: Recomputing distances inside every search for every starting bomb repeats the same geometry checks over and over.

optimal.insight: This is really a directed graph problem. Build an edge from bomb i to bomb j if j lies inside i's blast circle. Then the answer is simply the size of the largest reachable set from any single node, found with one BFS per node on the precomputed graph.
steps: Precompute a directed adjacency list using squared distances to avoid floating point square roots
For each bomb as a starting point, run BFS or DFS on this graph
Count how many bombs are reachable
Return the maximum count over all starting bombs
optimal.time: O(n^3) worst case but with a cheap precomputed graph

codeNotes.note: Adjacency list, one list per bomb
Squared distance avoids costly square roots
Bomb j lies inside bomb i's radius
Fresh visited set for each starting bomb
Track the biggest chain reaction so far

pitfalls: The relation is not symmetric. Bomb i reaching bomb j does not mean bomb j reaches bomb i, because radii differ.
Use squared distances with squared radius to avoid floating point errors from square roots.
Remember to try every bomb as the starting point, not just the first one.

say.intro: You have a pile of bombs, each with a position and a blast radius. Detonate one, and any bomb caught in its circle also goes off, then theirs do too. Pick the best bomb to start with. In our example, four bombs sit in a line with different radii. Starting from bomb zero or bomb one sets off three bombs. The other two only ever destroy themselves.
say.brute: The naive approach tries every bomb as a starting point and simulates the whole chain reaction from scratch each time, checking all pairs of bombs again and again. It works, but with a hundred bombs you are repeating the same distance calculations needlessly across every single simulation.
say.insight: The clever reframing is to see this as a directed graph problem. Draw an arrow from bomb i to bomb j if j sits inside i's blast circle. Build this graph once. Then the question becomes, from which starting node can you reach the most other nodes? That is just a breadth first search run once from every node on a graph you only built one time.
say.anim: We start with four bombs, each having a position and a blast radius. Checking bomb zero against bomb one, the distance squared is four, within range, so an edge is added. Bomb zero also reaches bomb two, but not bomb three, since that distance is too large. Now building edges from bomb one and bomb two, forming connections back to zero and two. Bomb three turns out isolated, too far from every other bomb to trigger any. Starting breadth first search from bomb zero, it reaches bombs one and two, visited set size three. Starting from bomb one gives the same reachable set, updating best to three. Bombs two and three each reach fewer bombs alone, so the final answer stays three.
say.code: We first build the graph. For every ordered pair i and j, we compare the squared distance between them against bomb i's radius squared, which avoids any square root. If j is close enough, we add a directed edge from i to j. Then, for each bomb as a starting point, we run a breadth first search using a visited set seeded with just that bomb, following edges outward and marking everything we reach. We keep the largest visited count we ever see across all starting points.
say.outro: The precomputed graph turns repeated geometry checks into cheap graph traversals. This is a graphs pattern question. Whenever detonations or infections spread through connections, build the graph first, then search from every possible starting point.

stock-price-fluctuation.hook: Stock prices arrive out of order, and corrections can arrive late. We need instant max, min and current anyway.
stock-price-fluctuation.ask: Design a class that records timestamp to price updates, where a later update can correct an earlier timestamp, and supports getting the current price, the maximum price, and the minimum price seen so far.
stock-price-fluctuation.exampleWhy: After updating timestamp 1 to 3, the max among {3,5} is 5, not 10 anymore. Then timestamp 4 brings price 2, the new minimum.

brute.idea: Store every timestamp to price mapping in a dictionary. For current, track or scan for the largest timestamp. For maximum and minimum, scan all stored prices every single call.
steps: update: prices[timestamp] = price, track latest timestamp
current: return prices[latest timestamp]
maximum: loop over all values, take the biggest
minimum: loop over all values, take the smallest
brute.time: O(n) per maximum or minimum call
brute.whySlow: With 100,000 calls, scanning the whole map on every maximum or minimum query becomes extremely slow overall.

optimal.insight: Keep a dictionary for the true current price per timestamp, plus a max heap and a min heap of (price, timestamp) pairs. Heaps never get updated in place, so when you pop the top you must check it against the dictionary. If it does not match, it is stale, throw it away and look at the next one.
steps: update: store the correct price in the dict, track the latest timestamp, push the pair onto both heaps
current: just read the dict at the latest timestamp
maximum: peek the max heap top, if it disagrees with the dict, pop it and keep peeking
minimum: same idea with the min heap
optimal.time: O(log n) amortised for update, maximum and minimum; O(1) for current

codeNotes.note: Negate price to fake a max heap
Check if heap top is still valid

pitfalls: Never delete from a heap directly, lazily verify against the dictionary instead.
Forget to negate prices for the max heap and you will get the minimum by accident.
current must use the latest timestamp, not the largest price.

say.intro: This is stock price fluctuation. Updates can arrive out of order, and a later update can correct an earlier timestamp. We still need instant access to the current price, the maximum, and the minimum.
say.brute: The simple approach is a dictionary from timestamp to price. Current is easy if you track the latest timestamp. But maximum and minimum mean scanning every single price you have stored, every single call. With a hundred thousand calls that adds up fast.
say.insight: Heaps give fast max and min, but heaps are painful to update when a value changes. The trick is laziness. Keep a max heap and a min heap of price and timestamp pairs, but never try to edit them when a correction comes in. Just push the new pair alongside the old one. When you ask for the maximum, peek the top of the max heap. Check its price against the dictionary, which always holds the truth. If they disagree, that entry is stale, so pop it and check the next one. Eventually you land on a valid, fresh maximum.
say.anim: We start with empty price map and empty max and min heaps for the stock tracker. We update timestamp one with price ten, storing it and pushing it onto both heaps. We update timestamp two with price five, again updating the dictionary and both heaps. Current looks up the latest timestamp, two, and returns its price, five. Maximum peeks the max heap, finds price ten at timestamp one matches, and returns ten. We update timestamp one to price three, pushing a fresh stale entry into both heaps. Maximum pops the stale price ten entry, then finds price five at timestamp two valid, returning five. We update timestamp four with price two, then minimum returns two, the lowest true price.
say.code: We keep a dictionary for truth, a max heap storing negated prices with timestamps, a min heap storing prices with timestamps, and a variable for the latest timestamp. Update writes to the dictionary, updates the latest timestamp, and pushes fresh pairs onto both heaps. Current just reads the dictionary at the latest timestamp. Maximum and minimum peek their heap, compare against the dictionary, and pop away anything stale until the top is trustworthy.
say.outro: Updates and queries run in amortised logarithmic time, current is instant. Pattern: heap and priority queue, with the classic lazy deletion trick for handling corrections.

find-if-path-exists-in-graph.hook: A graph question that's really just asking: are these two dots in the same blob?
find-if-path-exists-in-graph.ask: Given n vertices and a list of bi-directional edges, determine whether there is any path connecting a given source vertex to a given destination vertex.
find-if-path-exists-in-graph.exampleWhy: Vertices 0, 1, 2 form one connected group, and vertices 3, 4, 5 form another. Source 0 and destination 5 sit in different groups, so no path exists.

brute.idea: Build an adjacency list and run a breadth first search from source, marking visited vertices until destination is found or we run out of nodes.
steps: Build adjacency list from edges
BFS or DFS from source
Mark each visited vertex
If destination gets visited, return true
If the search ends without visiting it, return false
brute.whySlow: This already is the standard approach and is actually fine. The real alternative worth comparing is union-find, which avoids building an explicit adjacency list and is often faster in practice for pure connectivity checks.

optimal.insight: This is pure connectivity, nothing about shortest paths or order. Union-Find lets us merge vertices into groups as we read each edge, then just check whether source and destination ended up in the same group.
steps: Create a parent array where each vertex starts as its own parent
For every edge, union the two endpoints
After processing all edges, find the root of source
Find the root of destination
Return true if the roots match

codeNotes.note: Each vertex starts in its own group
Follows parent pointers up to the group root
Union merges two groups into one

pitfalls: Forgetting path compression makes find slow on long chains.
Comparing source and destination directly instead of their roots gives wrong answers.

say.intro: You have a bunch of vertices and some bi-directional edges. The question is simple. Can you get from source to destination somehow, following any path. Here, zero connects to one and two. Five connects to four and three. Those are two separate islands. So zero can never reach five.
say.brute: The obvious approach is breadth first search. Build a list of neighbours for every vertex, then explore outward from source, marking what you've visited, until you either hit destination or run out of places to go. This works perfectly fine and runs in linear time. Nothing wrong with it.
say.insight: But here's a neater way to think about it. We don't actually care about the path, just whether two vertices belong to the same connected group. That is exactly what union find was built for. Start with every vertex in its own group. Then for every edge, merge the two groups it connects. Once all edges are processed, just check if source and destination landed in the same group.
say.anim: We start with six nodes, each its own parent, since no unions have happened yet. Processing edge zero to one, we find both roots are different, zero and one, so we merge them. Next edge zero to two finds roots one and two, merging them into the same group. Edge three to five finds separate roots three and five, so they get unioned together. Edge five to four merges root five with root four, joining that whole chain. Edge four to three finds both already share root four, so no merge is needed here. Finally we find the roots of source zero and destination five, comparing their groups. Source resolves to root two while destination resolves to root four, so the answer is false.
say.code: We make a parent array, each vertex pointing to itself at first. The find function walks up parent pointers until it hits a root, with path compression to keep things fast. For every edge, we find both roots and merge them by pointing one at the other. After handling every edge, we just compare the root of source with the root of destination. Same root, same group, path exists.
say.outro: Nearly linear time, linear space. Pattern: graphs, specifically union find for connectivity questions. Whenever a problem only cares about groups, not actual routes, reach for union find.

number-of-flowers-in-full-bloom.hook: Flowers blooming over time windows, and people dropping in to check. Counting overlaps fast is all about splitting starts and ends.
number-of-flowers-in-full-bloom.ask: Given a list of flowers, each with a start and end day it is in full bloom, and a list of arrival times for people, return for each person how many flowers are in full bloom exactly when they arrive.
number-of-flowers-in-full-bloom.exampleWhy: At time 2 only flower [1,6] is blooming, so the answer is 1. At time 7, flowers [3,7] and [4,13] are blooming, plus [1,6] has ended, so the answer is 2, and so on.

brute.idea: For every person, scan every flower and check if the arrival time falls inside its start and end range.
steps: For each person time t
For each flower, check start <= t <= end
Count how many flowers match
brute.whySlow: With 50,000 flowers and 50,000 people that is 2.5 billion checks, far too slow.

optimal.insight: A flower is blooming at time t if its start is at or before t, and its end is at or after t. So split starts and ends into two sorted lists. The number of flowers started by time t minus the number already ended before time t gives the blooming count. Binary search finds both counts instantly.
steps: Sort all start times into one list
Sort all end times into another list
For each person t, count starts <= t using bisect right
Count ends < t using bisect left
Subtract ended count from started count

codeNotes.note: How many flowers have started by t
How many flowers have already ended before t
Started but not yet ended equals currently blooming

pitfalls: Use bisect right for starts so a flower starting exactly on t is counted.
Use bisect left for ends so a flower ending exactly on t is not counted as ended.
Keep the people in their original order in the output, do not sort them in place.

say.intro: Flowers each bloom for a window of days. People show up on certain days. For each person we want to know how many flowers are blooming right then. Person arrives at day two, only one flower is open. By day seven, two flowers are open.
say.brute: The obvious approach checks every flower for every person. Is their arrival time inside this flower's window? With tens of thousands of each, that is billions of checks. Way too slow for the limits here.
say.insight: Think about what makes a flower blooming at time t. Its start must be at or before t, and its end must be at or after t. So separate all the starts into one sorted list, and all the ends into another sorted list. Then for any arrival time, the number of flowers that have started by then, minus the number that have already finished before then, gives exactly how many are blooming. Both of those counts are just binary searches.
say.anim: We sort the flower start times into one list and end times into another. For person at time 2, one flower has started and none ended, giving one. For time 3, two flowers started and none ended yet, so the count is two. At time 7, three flowers started but one already ended, leaving two blooming. At time 11, all four flowers started and two have ended, still two blooming. The loop finishes after processing every person in the list. The final answer returned is one, two, two, two.
say.code: We sort the starts and the ends into two separate lists. For each person's time, bisect right on starts tells us how many flowers have begun by now, including one starting exactly today. Bisect left on ends tells us how many have already finished strictly before today. Subtract the two and that is the blooming count. We append results in the same order people arrived.
say.outro: Each query becomes a pair of binary searches, so the whole thing runs in about n log n time. Pattern: binary search, with a neat trick of separating starts and ends.

number-of-flowers-in-full-bloom.title: Number of Flowers in Full Bloom
number-of-flowers-in-full-bloom.optimalCode:
import bisect
from typing import List

class Solution:
    def fullBloomFlowers(self, flowers: List[List[int]], people: List[int]) -> List[int]:
        # 1. Separate all start days and all end days, each sorted
        starts = sorted(f[0] for f in flowers)
        ends = sorted(f[1] for f in flowers)

        res = []
        # 2. For each person, count started minus ended flowers
        for t in people:
            started = bisect.bisect_right(starts, t)
            ended = bisect.bisect_left(ends, t)
            res.append(started - ended)

        return res

class Solution:

        for t in people:
            started = bisect.bisect_right(starts, t)
            ended = bisect.bisect_left(ends, t)
            res.append(started - ended)

maximum-population-year.hook: Think of births and deaths as a timeline of plus ones and minus ones.
maximum-population-year.ask: Given a list of birth and death years for several people, return the earliest year with the maximum number of people alive at once. A person counts in every year from their birth up to, but not including, their death year.
maximum-population-year.exampleWhy: At year 1960 the first person is still alive (dies in 1961) and the second person has just been born. That gives two people alive, which is the peak, and 1960 is the earliest year it happens.

For each person, check birth <= year < death
Count how many match
Track the year with the highest count

optimal.insight: Treat each birth as a plus one event and each death as a minus one event on a timeline. Sweep through the years once, adding up these events as you go, and the running total is the population for that year.
steps: Create a small array covering all possible years
For each person, add one at their birth year and subtract one at their death year
Sweep the array from 1950 to 2050, keeping a running total
Track the year where the running total is highest

pitfalls: Use strictly greater than when updating the best population, so the earliest year is kept on a tie.
Remember the death year itself is excluded, so the minus one event goes exactly at the death year, not after it.

say.intro: This is Maximum Population Year. You get birth and death years for a bunch of people. You need the earliest year with the most people alive. In our example, two people are alive at once, and that first happens in 1960.
say.brute: The obvious approach checks every year from 1950 to 2050, and for each one scans through every single person to see if they were alive then. It works, but you are redoing a full scan for every candidate year, which is a lot of repeated effort.
say.insight: Here is the trick. Instead of asking how many people are alive in each year separately, think of it as a timeline of events. A birth is a plus one event, a death is a minus one event. If you sweep through the years in order, keeping a running total, that running total is exactly the population in that year. One pass does it all.
say.anim: We start with three people's birth and death years to process into a timeline. Each birth adds a plus one event and each death a minus one event in delta. Sweeping from year 1950, population becomes 1 as the first birth occurs. At year 1960 population rises to 2, becoming the new best with best year 1960. After 1960 population drops back to 1, since one person's lifespan ended. By year 1982 everyone has died, so population falls back to zero. The sweep finishes and the function returns 1960 as the maximum population year.
say.code: We build a small array covering every possible year. For each person we add one at their birth year and subtract one at their death year. Then we sweep from 1950 to 2050, adding each year's delta to a running population total. Whenever that total strictly beats our best so far, we record the new best and the year. Because we only update on strictly greater, the earliest peak year naturally wins any tie.
say.outro: This runs in time proportional to the number of people plus the fixed year range, which is effectively linear. The pattern here is a sweep line, close cousin of interval problems, turning a counting question into simple addition and subtraction over a timeline.

maximum-population-year.title: Maximum Population Year
maximum-population-year.optimalCode:
class Solution:
    def maximumPopulation(self, logs: List[List[int]]) -> int:
        delta = [0] * 2052

        # 1. Record birth as +1 event, death as -1 event
        for b, d in logs:
            delta[b] += 1
            delta[d] -= 1

        # 2. Sweep through years, tracking running population
        best_year = 1950
        best_pop = 0
        pop = 0
        for year in range(1950, 2051):
            pop += delta[year]
            if pop > best_pop:
                best_pop = pop
                best_year = year

        return best_year
lineNotes: We define a class named Solution, which holds the method that LeetCode will call for this problem.
The method takes the list of logs, each a birth and death year, and returns the best year.
We create a delta array of 2052 zeros, one slot per possible year, to hold population change events.
This comment explains that we will mark each birth as a plus one event and each death as a minus one.
We loop over every log, unpacking each person's birth year as b and death year as d.
At the birth year we add one, since this person starts being alive that year.
At the death year we subtract one, since the person is no longer counted from that year onward.
This comment says we now sweep through the years while keeping a running population total.
We start the best year at 1950, the earliest possible year, as a default answer.
We set the best population to zero so any real population will beat it.
We set the running population to zero because nobody is counted before the sweep begins.
We walk through each year from 1950 up to 2050 in increasing order, which guarantees earliest ties win.
We add that year's delta to the running population, giving the number of people alive that year.
We check whether this year's population is strictly greater than the best seen, so ties keep the earlier year.
When it is greater, we record the new best population.
We also record the current year as the new best year.
After the sweep finishes, we return the earliest year that had the maximum population.

is-graph-bipartite.hook: Colour every node with one of two colours so that no edge joins two nodes of the same colour. If that is ever impossible, the graph is not bipartite.
is-graph-bipartite.ask: Given an undirected graph as an adjacency list, decide whether its nodes can be split into two groups so that every edge connects a node from one group to a node in the other.
is-graph-bipartite.exampleWhy: Put 0 and 2 in group A, and 1 and 3 in group B. Every edge, 0 to 1, 0 to 3, 1 to 2, 2 to 3, crosses between the groups, so the graph is bipartite.

brute.idea: Try every possible way of splitting the nodes into two groups, then check if any split makes all edges cross between groups.
steps: Represent a split as a bitmask over n nodes
For each of the 2^n masks, check every edge
If every edge connects differing bits, this split works
If no split works, the graph is not bipartite
brute.whySlow: With 100 nodes there are 2^100 possible splits, utterly impossible to check.

optimal.insight: You never need to guess a split. Just colour a node, then force every neighbour to take the opposite colour. If a neighbour already has the same colour as you, the graph can't be bipartite.
steps: Keep a colour map, initially empty
For every uncoloured node, start a breadth first search and colour it 0
For each neighbour, if uncoloured give it the opposite colour and queue it
If a neighbour already shares your colour, return false immediately
If the whole search finishes without conflict, return true

codeNotes.note: Same colour on an edge means conflict

pitfalls: The graph may be disconnected, so you must start a fresh search from every uncoloured node.
Forgetting to check already coloured neighbours for a matching colour misses the conflict case.

say.intro: Is this graph bipartite. Can we split the nodes into two groups so every edge jumps between the groups. Here, zero and two go in one group, one and three in the other. Every edge crosses between them, so the answer is true.
say.brute: The naive idea is to try every possible way of splitting the nodes into two groups and check if any split works. With n nodes that's two to the power n possible splits. Even for a modest graph that number explodes instantly. We need something smarter.
say.insight: Here's the trick. You don't need to guess a split at all. Just pick a node, colour it, say, red. Then every one of its neighbours must be blue. Their neighbours must be red again, and so on. If at any point a node is forced to be both red and blue, the graph is not bipartite. This is just a colouring process using breadth first search.
say.anim: We start with four nodes and an empty color map to track assignments. Node zero isn't colored yet, so we color it zero and queue it. Processing node zero, neighbor one is uncolored, so it gets color one. Neighbor three is also uncolored, so it gets the opposite color, one. Node one's neighbor zero is already colored correctly, no conflict found. Neighbor two is uncolored, so it gets color zero, opposite of node one. Checking node three's neighbors, colors still differ properly, no conflicts appear. Remaining nodes are already colored, so the algorithm finishes and returns true.
say.code: We keep a colour map. For every node not yet coloured, we start a new search, since the graph might have separate pieces. We colour the starting node zero and push it onto a queue. For each neighbour, if it's uncoloured, we give it the opposite colour and queue it up. If it's already coloured and matches our colour, that's a contradiction, so we return false straight away. If we finish everything cleanly, the graph is bipartite.
say.outro: Linear time, linear space, one pass of breadth first search with two colours. Pattern: graphs. Whenever you see a constraint about alternating groups or colours, think two colouring with breadth first or depth first search.

is-graph-bipartite.title: Is Graph Bipartite?
lineNotes: We import deque from collections so we can use a fast double-ended queue for breadth first search.
We define a Solution class, as the problem platform expects.
The isBipartite method takes the adjacency list graph and returns true or false.
We store the number of nodes in n, taken from the length of graph.
We create an empty dictionary called color that records each visited node's colour, zero or one.
We loop over every node as a start point, so disconnected components are all checked.
If the start node already has a colour, an earlier search covered its component.
So we skip it and move on to the next start node.
Otherwise we colour the start node zero, beginning a fresh search on a new component.
We create a queue holding just the start node for breadth first traversal.
We keep processing nodes until the queue is empty, meaning the component is fully explored.
We take the next node from the front of the queue.
We look at every neighbor connected to this node by an edge.
If the neighbor has no colour yet, it hasn't been visited.
We give it the opposite colour of the current node, by subtracting that colour from one.
We add the neighbor to the queue so its own neighbors get checked later.
Otherwise the neighbor is already coloured, so we compare its colour with the current node's.
If both colours match, an edge joins two same-coloured nodes, so the graph cannot be bipartite and we return false.
If every component is coloured with no conflict, we return true because the graph is bipartite.

distant-barcodes.hook: Spread out the duplicates so no two neighbours match. The trick is to place the most common barcode first, skipping every other slot.
distant-barcodes.ask: Given a list of barcodes, rearrange them so that no two adjacent barcodes are equal. Any valid arrangement is accepted, and one is guaranteed to exist.
distant-barcodes.exampleWhy: Both 1 and 2 appear three times. Placing 1 at even positions and 2 at odd positions keeps every neighbour different.

brute.idea: Try to build the arrangement one slot at a time, backtracking whenever the next barcode would clash with the one just placed.
steps: Pick any unused barcode that differs from the last placed one
Place it and recurse
If no choice leads to a full valid arrangement, undo and try another
brute.whySlow: For large inputs the search tree explodes long before it finds a valid ordering.

optimal.insight: If you place the most frequent barcode first, filling every other slot, it is spread as far apart as possible. Then fill the remaining slots the same way with the next most frequent value, and so on.
steps: Count how many times each barcode appears
Sort barcodes by frequency, highest first
Fill even indices first, then wrap to odd indices once even ones are full
Write each barcode that many times, advancing two slots each time

codeNotes.note: Skip a slot to keep spacing

pitfalls: Forgetting to wrap the index from even to odd positions leaves gaps unfilled.
Not sorting by frequency first can bunch up the most common barcode.

say.intro: This is Distant Barcodes. You get a row of barcodes and need to rearrange them so no two neighbours match. Our barcodes are one, one, one, two, two, two. We end up with one, two, one, two, one, two, and every neighbour is different.
say.brute: The obvious idea is to build the row step by step, picking any barcode that differs from the last one placed, and backtracking if we get stuck. It works, but trying every possible order is far too slow once the list grows.
say.insight: Here's the clever bit. If a barcode appears very often, it needs the most spacing. So place the most frequent barcode first, filling every even slot. Once even slots run out, carry on into the odd slots. Then do the same for the next most frequent barcode. Because the biggest group gets spread out first, it never ends up squashed next to itself.
say.anim: We start with barcodes one one one two two two, counted as three each. Sorted by frequency, one and two tie, so items are one then two. We place value one at even indices zero, two, and four first. Result becomes one, zero, one, zero, one, zero after filling evens. Index wraps to one, so value two starts filling the odd slots. Twos are written at indices one, three, and five in sequence. Final arrangement spreads values apart, giving one, two, one, two, one, two.
say.code: We count frequencies with Counter, then sort the items by frequency descending. We prepare an empty result array. Then for each barcode, we write it into slots two apart, and if we run past the end, we jump back to index one to fill the odd gaps. Because the most frequent values go first, there is always room to spread them out.
say.outro: Sorting is the costly step, so we get n log n time with linear space. This is a greedy pattern: handle the biggest problem first and the rest falls into place.

distant-barcodes.title: Distant Barcodes
distant-barcodes.optimalCode:
class Solution:
    def rearrangeBarcodes(self, barcodes: List[int]) -> List[int]:
        # 1. Count how many times each barcode appears
        count = Counter(barcodes)
        total = len(barcodes)
        result = [0] * total

        # 2. Sort barcodes by frequency, highest first
        items = sorted(count.items(), key=lambda pair: (-pair[1], pair[0]))

        # 3. Fill even indices first, then wrap to odd indices once even ones are full
        index = 0
        for value, freq in items:
            # 4. Write each barcode that many times, advancing two slots each time
            for _ in range(freq):
                if index >= total:
                    index = 1
                result[index] = value
                index += 2

        return result
lineNotes: We define a Solution class, which is the container the problem expects for our method.
This method takes the list of barcodes and returns a rearranged list with no two equal neighbors.
This comment says our first step is to count how often each barcode appears.
We build a counter that maps each barcode value to the number of times it occurs.
We store the total number of barcodes so we know how many slots to fill.
We create a result list of the same length, filled with zeros as placeholders.
This comment says our second step is to order barcodes by frequency, most common first.
We sort the counted items by descending frequency, breaking ties by the barcode value for a stable order.
This comment explains that we fill even positions first, then wrap around to odd positions.
We start the write position at index zero, the first even slot.
We loop over each barcode value and its frequency, going from most frequent to least frequent.
This comment says we write each barcode as many times as it appears, jumping two slots each time.
We repeat once per occurrence of the current barcode, since we must place every copy.
If the index has run past the end, the even slots are full and we need to switch.
We reset the index to one, the first odd slot, to continue filling the gaps.
We place the current barcode value into the result at the current index.
We advance the index by two so copies of the same value never land next to each other.
Once every barcode is placed, we return the finished arrangement.

sum-of-mutated-array-closest-to-target.hook: Cap every number in the array at some value, and the sum lands as close to the target as possible. Binary search finds that cap in no time.
sum-of-mutated-array-closest-to-target.ask: Given an array of integers and a target, choose a value so that replacing every array element larger than it with that value makes the array's sum as close as possible to the target. If two values tie, return the smaller one.
sum-of-mutated-array-closest-to-target.exampleWhy: Capping everything at 3 gives [3,3,3], which sums to 9. That is as close to 10 as we can get, and 3 beats any other value that ties.

brute.idea: Try every possible cap value from 0 up to the largest number in the array, compute the capped sum each time, and keep the best one.
steps: For each candidate value v from 0 to max(arr)
Sum min(x, v) for every x in arr
Track the v with the smallest absolute difference from target
Break ties by preferring the smaller v
brute.whySlow: If the array holds values up to 100,000, that is up to 100,000 full passes over the array, around a billion operations in the worst case.

optimal.insight: As the cap value increases, the capped sum only ever increases, never decreases. That monotonic behaviour means we can binary search for the smallest cap whose sum reaches the target, then check whether that cap or the one just below it is closer.
steps: Binary search the cap between 0 and max(arr)
At each guess, compute the capped sum
If the sum is too small, raise the lower bound
Otherwise lower the upper bound
Once the search closes in, compare the cap found with one less than it
Return whichever gives a smaller absolute difference, preferring the smaller value on a tie

codeNotes.note: Search the cap between zero and the largest element

codeNotes.match: total = sum(min(x, mid) for x in arr)

codeNotes.note: Sum too small, cap must go higher
Sum reached target, try smaller cap
Tie rule favours the smaller value

pitfalls: The capped sum is monotonic in the cap, which is exactly what makes binary search valid here.
Remember the tie-break: always prefer the smaller value when two caps give the same distance from target.

say.intro: This one is about capping an array. Pick a value, replace every element bigger than it with that value, and you want the resulting sum to land as close as possible to a target. With four, nine, three and a target of ten, capping at three gives three, three, three, which sums to nine. That turns out to be the best we can do.
say.brute: The obvious approach is to just try every possible cap, from zero up to the biggest number in the array. For each one, work out the capped sum and see how close it gets. It always finds the right answer, but if the numbers are large, you might be trying a hundred thousand different caps, each needing a full pass over the array. That gets slow fast.
say.insight: Here's the key observation. As you raise the cap, the capped sum never goes down. It only grows or stays the same. That's a monotonic relationship, and monotonic relationships are exactly what binary search loves. So instead of checking every cap one by one, we binary search for the point where the capped sum first reaches the target.
say.anim: We start binary search with left at 0 and right at 9, the max array value. Testing mid equals 4, capping values gives a total sum of 11. Since 11 is not less than target 10, right shrinks to 4. Testing mid equals 2, the capped sum comes out to only 6. Since 6 is less than target 10, left moves up to 3. Testing mid equals 3, the capped sum is 9, still under target. Left now equals right at 4, ending the binary search loop. Comparing differences, capping at 3 or 4 both give difference 1, so the smaller value wins and the answer returned is 3.
say.code: We binary search between zero and the maximum array value. At each guess we compute the capped sum using min of each element and our guess. If the sum is too small, we need a bigger cap, so we move the lower bound up. Otherwise we pull the upper bound down. When the loop ends, we don't just trust that result blindly. We compare the sum at this cap and the sum one below it, since one might be closer to the target than the other. If they tie, we pick the smaller value, as the problem demands.
say.outro: This runs in log time over the value range rather than linear time, a huge saving for large arrays. Pattern: binary search, specifically searching over the answer rather than over the array itself.

sum-of-mutated-array-closest-to-target.title: Sum of Mutated Array Closest to Target
lineNotes: We define a class named Solution, which is the container the judge expects for this problem.
The method findBestValue takes the array and the target and returns the best cap value.
This comment says we first need a helper that computes the array sum after capping values.
We define capped_sum, which takes a cap and returns the sum of the array with every value limited to that cap.
We start a running total at zero to accumulate the capped values.
We loop over each value in the array one at a time.
If the value is smaller than the cap, it is not changed by the capping.
So we add the original value to the total.
Otherwise the value is at least the cap and would be reduced.
So we add the cap itself to the total instead.
After the loop we return the total as the capped sum.
This comment says we now binary search for the smallest cap whose capped sum reaches the target.
We set left to zero, the lowest sensible cap value.
We set right to the maximum of the array, since any larger cap changes nothing.
We loop while left is less than right, narrowing the search range until they meet.
We pick mid as the average of left and right, rounded down.
We compute the capped sum using mid as the cap.
If that sum is still below the target, the cap is too small.
So we move left up to mid plus one, discarding all caps that are too small.
Otherwise the sum reaches or passes the target, so mid might be the answer.
So we set right to mid, keeping mid as a candidate while searching lower.
This comment says we now compare the found cap with the cap just below it.
We measure how far the capped sum with left minus one is from the target.
We measure how far the capped sum with left is from the target.
This comment reminds us that ties must resolve to the smaller value.
If the lower cap is at least as close as the found cap, the lower one wins ties too.
So we return left minus one.
Otherwise the found cap is strictly closer, so we return left.

longest-happy-prefix.hook: A string hiding inside itself. Find the longest piece that is both its own beginning and its own ending.
longest-happy-prefix.ask: Given a string, return its longest happy prefix: the longest string that is both a proper prefix and a proper suffix of it. Return an empty string if none exists.
longest-happy-prefix.exampleWhy: The prefix abab and the suffix abab are both four characters long and match, which is the longest such overlap in ababab.

brute.idea: Try every prefix length from longest to shortest, and for each one check directly whether that prefix equals the suffix of the same length.
steps: Try length n-1 down to 1
Slice the prefix and the suffix of that length
Compare them character by character
Return the first length that matches
brute.whySlow: Each comparison can take O(n) time and you might try O(n) lengths, so for a 100,000 character string this blows up.

optimal.insight: This is exactly the failure function from the KMP string matching algorithm. Build an array where each position stores the length of the longest prefix that is also a suffix ending at that position. The final value of that array is the answer.
steps: Build an lps array of zeros, same length as s
Track a running length of the current matching prefix
Walk the string from index 1 with a pointer i
If s[i] matches s[length], extend the match and record it
On mismatch, fall back using the lps array itself, or reset to zero
The last entry of lps gives the answer length

codeNotes.note: lps[i] = longest prefix-suffix ending at i
Final value is the whole answer

pitfalls: On mismatch do not just reset length to zero, fall back using lps[length-1] or you lose partial matches.
The prefix and suffix must be proper, so never consider the entire string itself.

say.intro: Longest happy prefix. You get a string. Find the longest piece that is both a prefix and a suffix of it, but not the whole string. For ababab, the answer is abab, four letters, both at the start and the end.
say.brute: The obvious approach tries every possible length, starting from the longest, slicing out the prefix and the suffix, and comparing them directly. It works, but each comparison can itself take linear time, and you might do this for every length. That is quadratic, far too slow for long strings.
say.insight: This is actually the famous building block behind the KMP pattern matching algorithm, called the failure function. The idea is to build an array where each position tells you the longest prefix that is also a suffix ending right there. You grow this match incrementally, and crucially, when a mismatch happens, you do not throw everything away. You fall back to a shorter known match using the array you have already built. By the time you reach the end of the string, the very last value in that array is exactly the length of the longest happy prefix.
say.anim: We start with the string ababab and an all zero lps array of length six. At i equals one, the characters don't match, so lps at that position stays zero. At i equals two, s of i matches s of length, so length becomes one, stored in lps. Matches continue at i equals three and four, growing length to two then three. At i equals five, another match pushes length to four, filling lps completely. The loop ends since i now equals six, the length of the string. We take the prefix of length four from the last lps value. The final answer, the longest happy prefix, is abab.
say.code: We create an array lps of zeros. We track a running length of the current match, starting at zero. We walk through the string from index one. If the current character matches the character at position length, we extend the match and record it in lps. If it does not match, and length is not zero, we fall back to lps of length minus one rather than giving up entirely. If length is already zero, we just move on. At the very end, lps at the last index holds the length of our answer, so we slice that many characters from the start of the string.
say.outro: Linear time, linear space, no nested loops needed. Pattern: strings, specifically the KMP failure function. Whenever you see prefix equals suffix problems, this array is the tool to reach for.

longest-happy-prefix.title: Longest Happy Prefix
lineNotes: We define the Solution class that holds our method, as the problem platform expects.
The method longestPrefix takes the string s and returns its longest happy prefix as a string.
We store the length of s in n so we can use it for sizing and looping.
We create the lps array of n zeros, where each entry will hold the longest prefix that is also a suffix.
We set length to zero, which tracks the current matched prefix length as we scan.
We start i at one because a single character at position zero has no proper prefix match.
We loop while i is less than n, processing each character once to fill the array.
We compare the character at i with the next prefix character at position length to see if the match extends.
On a match, we increase length by one because the matching prefix has grown.
We record this new length in lps at position i.
We advance i to move on to the next character.
Otherwise the characters differ, and we need to decide how to fall back.
If length is not zero, a shorter prefix border might still match, so we try that.
We fall back by setting length to the lps value just before it, without advancing i.
If length is already zero, there is no shorter border to try.
So we set lps at i to zero, since no prefix matches the suffix here.
We then advance i to the next character.
We return the prefix of s whose length is the last lps value, which is the longest happy prefix or empty.

divide-array-in-sets-of-k-consecutive-nu.hook: Can you split this pile of numbers into perfect little straight runs? Think cards in a hand of poker.
divide-array-in-sets-of-k-consecutive-nu.ask: Given an array of integers and a positive integer k, check whether the array can be divided into groups, each containing k consecutive numbers. Return true if possible, otherwise false.
divide-array-in-sets-of-k-consecutive-nu.exampleWhy: The numbers split into [1,2,3] and [1,2,3], two runs of three consecutive numbers each.

brute.idea: Keep sorting what remains, grab the smallest number as the start of a run, then try to pull out each of the next k-1 consecutive numbers one at a time.
steps: Sort the remaining list
Take the smallest as the start of a run
Remove start, start+1, ... start+k-1 one by one
If any is missing, fail
Repeat until the list is empty
brute.whySlow: Sorting and searching after every single removal is wasteful when we could track counts directly.

optimal.insight: Count every value. Walk through the distinct values in sorted order. Whenever a value still has leftover count, it must start new runs, so consume that many copies of it and the next k-1 values. If any of those values do not have enough copies, it is impossible.
steps: If the array length is not divisible by k, return false immediately
Count all values with a hashmap
Sort the distinct keys
For each key with leftover count c, that count must start c runs
Deduct c from keys, key+1, ..., key+k-1
If any of those has fewer than c left, return false

codeNotes.note: Only start new runs from leftover values
Not enough copies to complete the run
Consume c copies for this many runs

pitfalls: Always start runs from the smallest leftover value, otherwise you might consume a number another run genuinely needed to start at.
Forgetting the length check wastes time on arrays that can never split evenly.

say.intro: This is the hand of straights problem. You get a pile of numbers and a group size k. Can you split every number into groups of k consecutive numbers? With one, one, two, two, three, three and k equals three, the answer is yes. Split it into one two three, and one two three.
say.brute: The naive way is to keep sorting what's left, grab the smallest number, and try to pull out that run of k consecutive numbers one at a time, checking the list each time. It works, but sorting and searching after every removal adds up fast on large inputs.
say.insight: Here's the better way. Count how many of each number you have. Walk through the distinct numbers from smallest to largest. If a number still has leftover copies, those copies must each start a brand new run, because nothing smaller remains to absorb them. So take that leftover count and subtract it from that number and the next k minus one numbers. If any of those don't have enough copies, it's impossible. One pass through sorted keys, no backtracking needed.
say.anim: We start with array three, three, two, two, one, one and k equals three, length divides evenly. Counting values gives us two copies each of one, two, and three. Starting with the smallest value one, which still has two leftover copies. We consume two copies each of one, two, and three to form the runs. After using them, counts for one, two, and three all drop to zero. Moving to value two, its count is now zero, so nothing left to start. Value three also has zero count left, confirming all numbers were used. All values cleared successfully, so the function returns true.
say.code: We count everything with a Counter. We sort the distinct keys so we always process the smallest leftover value first. For each key, if its count is still positive, that many runs must start here, so we check and subtract that amount from the next k values in a row. If any of them can't cover it, we return false straight away. Otherwise we finish the loop and return true.
say.outro: Linear-ish time after sorting the keys, linear space for the counts. Pattern: greedy with hashing. Always resolve the smallest leftover value first, because nothing else can ever start a run there.

divide-array-in-sets-of-k-consecutive-nu.title: Divide Array in Sets of K Consecutive Numbers
lineNotes: We import Counter from collections so we can tally how many times each value appears in the array.
We import List from typing so the method signature can describe the input as a list of integers.
We define a Solution class, which is the container the problem expects for our method.
The method isPossibleDivide takes the list nums and the group size k, and returns true or false.
If the length of nums is not a multiple of k, equal groups are impossible, so we check that first.
In that case we return false right away.
We build a counter that maps each distinct value to how many times it occurs.
We loop over the distinct values in sorted order, so the smallest remaining value always starts a run.
We read c, the current leftover count of this value.
If c is positive, this value has unused copies that must each begin a new run of k numbers.
We walk through the k consecutive values starting at num, since each of the c runs needs all of them.
If any value in the run has fewer copies than c, we cannot complete all the runs.
So we return false because the division is impossible.
Otherwise we subtract c from that value's count, using up the copies for these c runs.
If the loop finishes without any failure, every value was placed in a valid run, so we return true.

expressive-words.hook: Stretched out words like heeellooo are just normal words with extra repeated letters. The trick is to compare them group by group.
expressive-words.ask: Given a string s and a list of query words, count how many query words can become s by stretching groups of repeated letters, where a stretch must make the group at least three letters long.
expressive-words.exampleWhy: hello splits into h, e, l, l, o which matches s's groups h, eee, ll, ooo letter for letter. The e and o groups can stretch to 3, and ll already has size 2 matching exactly. helo only has one l, so its ll group can never reach size 2, it fails. hi has totally different letters, it fails too.

brute.idea: Actually try every possible way of stretching each group of a word, building candidate strings and checking if any of them equals s.
steps: Split the word into groups of repeated letters
For each group, try every possible extra amount of stretching
Build up the candidate string recursively
Check if any fully built candidate equals s
brute.time: O(n^k) in the worst case, exponential in the number of groups
brute.whySlow: With many groups and a long target string, the number of stretching combinations to try explodes very quickly.

optimal.insight: You never need to build any actual stretched string. Just compress both s and the word into groups of letter and count, then compare groups directly: same letter, and the word's count must either equal s's count, or be smaller while s's count is at least 3.
steps: Compress s into a list of (letter, count) groups
Compress the query word the same way
If the number of groups differs, reject immediately
Walk both group lists together comparing letters and counts
A group is acceptable if counts match exactly, or the word's count is smaller and s's count is at least 3
optimal.time: O(n + m) per word, where n and m are the lengths of s and the word
optimal.space: O(n + m) for the group lists

codeNotes.note: Compress the string into runs of identical letters
Different group counts can never line up
Matching groups must have the same letter

codeNotes.match: if n1 != n2 and (n1 < n2 or n1 < 3):
codeNotes.note: Word's count must stretch up to s's count, which needs to be at least 3
Every group passed, so this word is stretchy

pitfalls: Forgetting that a group only needs stretching to size 3 or more, not any size.
Missing the case where counts already match exactly, no stretch needed at all.
Comparing raw characters instead of compressed groups, which breaks on different group counts.

say.intro: This is Expressive Words. You get a string s and a list of words. A word counts if you can stretch its repeated letter groups to turn it into s. Here s is heeellooo, and only hello manages it.
say.brute: The obvious approach is to actually try stretching. Split the word into its letter groups, then try every possible extra amount you could add to each group, building up candidate strings as you go. If any candidate matches s, the word works. It's correct, but the number of combinations to try can blow up badly, especially with several groups and a long target.
say.insight: Here's the shortcut. You never need to build any string at all. Just compress s into groups of letter and count, do the same for the word, and compare group by group. The letters must match. The counts must either be identical, or the word's count is smaller while s's count is at least three, since that's the only way a stretch could have happened.
say.anim: We start by compressing the string heeellooo into letter groups for comparison. The compressed groups for s are h one, e three, l two, o three. Now we compress the first word hello into groups h, e, l, l, o with counts one, one, two, one. Comparing groups: e has count three in s but only one in hello, yet three is at least three, so it still stretches fine. All groups match the stretching rule, so hello counts as expressive, count becomes 1. Next word hi has different group lengths than s, so it fails immediately and is skipped. For helo, the l group has count one versus two in s, which breaks the stretch rule, so ok becomes false. Only hello qualified, so the function returns the final answer 1.
say.code: We write a helper that walks the string and builds a list of letter and count pairs. We compress s once outside the loop. For each word, we compress it too. If the group counts differ, we skip straight away, there's no way to align them. Otherwise we zip the two group lists together and check each pair: letters must match, and counts must either be equal or the word count is smaller with s's count being at least three. If every group survives that check, we count the word as stretchy.
say.outro: Linear time per word, nice and simple once you stop thinking about actual string building. Pattern: strings, specifically run length compression and comparison.

count-number-of-bad-pairs.hook: A pair looks bad only because the maths hides a simple pattern once you shift it.
count-number-of-bad-pairs.ask: Given an integer array, count the number of pairs of indices i and j with i less than j where the gap between the indices does not equal the gap between the values. Return the total count of such bad pairs.
count-number-of-bad-pairs.exampleWhy: Out of all six possible pairs, only the pair (1,3) has a matching gap of index and value difference, since both differ by zero once shifted. The other five pairs are bad.

brute.idea: Check every pair of indices directly against the bad pair condition.
steps: Pick index i
Try every index j greater than i
Check if j minus i differs from nums[j] minus nums[i]
Count it if so
brute.whySlow: With one hundred thousand numbers that is up to five billion comparisons, far too slow.

optimal.insight: Rearrange the bad pair condition. j minus i not equal nums[j] minus nums[i] is the same as nums[j] minus j not equal nums[i] minus i. So a pair is good exactly when nums[k] minus k is the same for both indices. Count how many pairs share that value, those are the good pairs, and subtract from the total number of pairs.
steps: Compute key = nums[k] minus k for every index
Group indices by this key using a hashmap of counts
Good pairs equal the sum over each group of count choose two
Total pairs equal n choose two
Bad pairs equal total pairs minus good pairs

codeNotes.note: The shifted key for this index
Tracks how many times each key has appeared
Each earlier match forms one good pair
Record this index under its key
Bad pairs are everything that is not good

pitfalls: Forgetting to use long arithmetic style counts, since results can exceed normal int ranges in other languages.
Mixing up which index counts as i and which as j when forming the key.

say.intro: This is Count Number of Bad Pairs. You are given a list of numbers. A pair of positions is bad if the gap between their positions does not match the gap between their values. We count how many bad pairs exist. For four, one, three, three, the answer is five.
say.brute: The obvious approach checks every single pair of positions directly. For each one you compare the index gap against the value gap. It works, but with a hundred thousand numbers that is billions of comparisons. Too slow.
say.insight: Here is the trick. Rearrange the inequality. Index gap not equal value gap becomes nums at j minus j not equal nums at i minus i. So if we define a key for each position as its value minus its index, a pair is good exactly when both positions share the same key. So instead of hunting for bad pairs directly, we count good pairs, which is much easier, then subtract from the total.
say.anim: We start with array four, one, three, three, and an empty counts map. At index zero, value four, diff is four minus zero equals four, no prior match. At index one, value one, diff is zero, no matches yet, so good stays zero. At index two, value three, diff is one, still no matching diff found. At index three, value three, diff is zero, matching the earlier zero, good becomes one. Total pairs for four elements is six, computed from four times three over two. Subtracting the one good pair from six total pairs gives five bad pairs. The final answer returned is five, matching the expected output.
say.code: We walk through the array once, computing the key for each index. We check how many times that key has appeared before and add that count to our good pairs total, since each earlier match forms a new good pair with the current index. Then we record this key in our hashmap. At the end we compute the total number of pairs using n choose two, and subtract the good pairs to get the bad pairs.
say.outro: One pass, linear time. The pattern here is arrays and hashing. Whenever a condition involves a difference between two indices and two values, try shifting it so both sides depend only on one index each.

count-number-of-bad-pairs.title: Count Number of Bad Pairs

The method countBadPairs takes the array nums and will return how many bad pairs of indices it contains.
We store the length of nums in n, which we need later to compute the total number of pairs.
We create an empty dictionary called counts to remember how many times each value of nums minus index has appeared.
We start good at zero, and it will count the pairs whose value minus index matches.
We loop through nums with both the index i and the value num available at each step.
We compute diff as num minus i, since two indices form a good pair exactly when this value matches.
We add to good the number of earlier indices that had the same diff, each forming one good pair with this index.
We then record the current diff in counts by increasing its tally by one, so later indices can pair with it.
We compute total as n times n minus one divided by two, which is the number of all pairs with i less than j.
We return total minus good, because every pair that is not good must be a bad pair.

number-of-closed-islands.hook: Islands of land hiding in a sea of water. Some are safe, some touch the edge and leak out.
number-of-closed-islands.ask: Given a grid of zeros for land and ones for water, count the islands of zeros that are fully enclosed by water, never touching the border of the grid.
number-of-closed-islands.exampleWhy: The zeros down the left edge and across the top right all touch the border, so they leak out and do not count. Only the single zero in the middle, boxed in on all four sides by ones, is a true closed island.

brute.idea: Flood fill every unvisited land cell with a breadth first search, and while flooding, check whether any cell in that island touches the border. If none do, count it as closed.
steps: Scan every cell
If it is land and unvisited, start a breadth first search
Mark visited, and flag the island as open if any visited cell is on the border
After the search finishes, count it only if the flag stayed closed
brute.whySlow: It works, but it needs a separate visited grid and a queue, plus extra bookkeeping to track the border flag during the search, when the grid itself could be reused directly.

optimal.insight: Any island touching the border can never be closed, so drown it first. Flood fill from every border land cell, turning it into water. Whatever land is left in the interior must be fully surrounded, so just count those islands directly.
steps: Loop over border cells, and flood fill any that are land, turning them to water
Loop over the interior cells only
Each remaining land cell starts a brand new closed island, flood fill it away and count it

codeNotes.note: Stop at water or off the grid
Mutate the grid itself, no extra visited array needed

codeNotes.note: Find border land and drown it first
Now only interior cells are left to check
Every remaining land patch must be enclosed

pitfalls: Forgetting to flood the border first means interior counting will wrongly include islands that actually leak out.
Grids with only one row or one column have no true interior, so the answer is always zero.

say.intro: Number of closed islands. Zero is land, one is water. We want islands of land that are completely boxed in by water, never touching the edge of the grid. In our tiny grid, the zeros along the edges leak out, but one lonely zero in the middle is fully surrounded, so the answer is one.
say.brute: The direct way is to flood fill every patch of land with a queue, mark cells visited, and while we are at it, check whether any cell in that patch sits on the border. If the whole patch stays away from the border, we count it. It works, but we need a whole extra grid just to track what we have visited, on top of the queue.
say.insight: Here is the shortcut. Any island touching the border can never be closed, no matter what. So drown those first. Walk around the edge of the grid, and for any land you find, flood fill it away into water. Once that is done, whatever land survives in the interior is guaranteed to be boxed in, because it never reached the edge. So we just sweep the interior and count fresh islands, flooding each one as we find it.
say.anim: We start with a small grid holding zeros for land and ones for water. The algorithm scans the border, starting at row zero column zero, which is border land. Flood fill marks that border land as one, draining it into the surrounding water. This border draining continues around the edges, turning all border connected zeros into ones. The scan finishes the border pass, leaving only interior cells unmarked and untouched. Now at row one column two, a leftover zero is found, so count becomes one. Flood fill drowns this interior island completely, turning the whole grid into ones. No more zeros remain, so the function returns one closed island.
say.code: We write one small flood fill function that turns a land cell and all its connected land neighbours into water, directly inside the grid. First we scan every border cell, and any land we find there gets flooded immediately, since it can never be closed. Then we only scan the interior rows and columns. Any land cell found there must be a genuine closed island, so we count it and flood it away so it is not counted twice.
say.outro: Same time and space as the breadth first version, but far tidier, since we reuse the grid itself instead of a separate visited array. Pattern: graphs, flood fill with a clever twist, clear the border threats first.

number-of-enclaves.hook: Think of it like island cells that touch the edge of the map escaping into the sea, everything left behind is trapped.
number-of-enclaves.ask: You get a grid of land and sea cells. Land cells connected to the border can walk off the grid. Count how many land cells can never reach the border no matter how they move.
number-of-enclaves.exampleWhy: The land cell in the second row, first column touches the border, so it escapes. The three remaining land cells form a cluster in the middle that never touches an edge, so they are trapped.

brute.idea: For every single land cell, flood fill outward and check if that flood ever touches the border.
steps: Pick a land cell
Flood fill to find its whole connected island
Check if any cell in that island sits on the border
If not, count it as trapped
brute.whySlow: Every land cell triggers its own flood fill over the whole grid, so work repeats massively for cells in the same island.

optimal.insight: Flip it around. Start from every border land cell and flood fill inward, sinking every cell that can escape. Whatever land is left afterwards could never reach the border.
steps: Scan the border of the grid
For every land cell on the border, flood fill and turn connected land to sea
After all flood fills, every remaining 1 is trapped
Count the remaining 1s

Mark visited by sinking it, no extra set needed

codeNotes.note: Only start flood fill from border land

pitfalls: Forgetting to check all four border edges, not just the top row.
Starting flood fill from every cell instead of only border land cells wastes time.

say.intro: This is Number of Enclaves. You have land and sea. Land touching the border can escape. Count the land that is stuck inside forever. In our small grid, one land cell sits right on the border and escapes, but three others are boxed in by sea and trapped. The answer is three.
say.brute: The obvious approach checks every land cell one at a time. Flood fill outward from it, see if that flood ever touches an edge. It works, but cells in the same island get checked again and again, wasting huge amounts of time on bigger grids.
say.insight: Flip the direction of thinking. Instead of asking each cell can I escape, start from the border itself. Any land cell sitting on the border can clearly escape, and so can anything connected to it. So flood fill inward from every border land cell, sinking all of it to sea. After that sweep, whatever land remains was never connected to the border, so it is permanently trapped.
say.anim: We start with a four by four grid containing a few land cells marked one. The code scans the border cells first, checking row zero for any land. At row one column zero, a land cell is found on the border, triggering flood fill. Flood fill sinks that connected border land, turning cell row one column two back to zero. Row two column zero is checked but it is a zero, so nothing changes there. Now the code rescans the whole grid, counting any ones that survived the flood fill. Counts increase as trapped land cells are found, reaching one, two, then three. The final answer is three enclosed land cells that could never reach the border.
say.code: We scan only the border cells of the grid. Whenever we find land there, we run a depth first search that turns every connected land cell into sea, walking in all four directions. Once we have processed the whole border, anything still marked as one could never reach the edge. We sum up all the remaining ones in the grid and that total is our answer.
say.outro: Same work as one full pass over the grid, just started from the right place. Pattern: graphs, flood fill from the boundary inward instead of checking every cell outward.
