design-hit-counter.hook: A hit counter that forgets anything older than five minutes. The trick is a queue that cleans itself.
design-hit-counter.ask: Design a hit counter that records hits with a timestamp and reports how many hits happened in the last three hundred seconds, counting back from a given timestamp. Timestamps arrive in increasing order, and several hits can share the same timestamp.
design-hit-counter.exampleWhy: At timestamp 4 the hits at 1, 2 and 3 are all within the last 300 seconds, so the count is 3. After adding a hit at 300, getHits(300) counts 1 through 300, which is 4. At 301, the hit at 1 has fallen out of the window, so it drops back to 3.

brute.idea: Store every hit timestamp in a list. For getHits, scan the whole list and count how many timestamps are within the window.
steps: Append timestamp to a list on hit
On getHits, loop through every stored timestamp
Count those greater than timestamp minus 300
brute.whySlow: If there are many hits, every single getHits call re-scans the entire history, even hits from hours ago that can never count.

optimal.insight: Since timestamps only increase, old hits at the front of a queue become stale in order too. Keep hits in a deque and simply pop off the ones that have expired whenever you touch the counter.
steps: Keep a deque of hit timestamps
On hit, append the new timestamp
On getHits, pop from the left while the front timestamp is more than 300 seconds old
Return the length of what remains
optimal.space: O(n) in the worst case, but bounded by the window

codeNotes.note: Hit just adds to the back
Drop anything outside the 300 second window
Expired hits always sit at the front
Whatever is left is within the window

pitfalls: Use strictly within 300 seconds: a hit at timestamp minus 300 exactly should be expired, not counted.
Do not clean up only on hit, getHits can be called without a preceding hit and needs fresh results too.

say.intro: Design a hit counter. You record hits by timestamp and ask how many happened in the last five minutes. In our example, after three quick hits, getHits at timestamp four returns three. Then a hit lands far later at timestamp three hundred, and the oldest hit falls out of the window one second after that.
say.brute: The obvious approach is to just remember every hit in a list. Then for every getHits call, walk through the entire list and count how many are still within the last three hundred seconds. It works, but every single query rescans the whole history, even hits from ages ago that obviously cannot count anymore. That is wasted work piling up over time.
say.insight: Here is the trick. Timestamps only ever increase. That means hits expire in exactly the order they arrived. So keep them in a queue. The oldest hit always sits at the front. Whenever you hit or check hits, just pop expired timestamps off the front until what remains is all within the window. No scanning the middle or end, ever.
say.anim: We start with an empty deque to store hit timestamps. Hits at timestamps one, two and three get appended to the queue. At timestamp four, no hits are old enough to expire yet. So getHits returns three, counting all recorded hits. A new hit at timestamp three hundred joins the queue, still within range. Checking again, nothing falls outside the window, so the count becomes four. At timestamp three hundred one, timestamp one is now stale and gets popped. After removing it, getHits returns three, the final answer.
say.code: The queue stores raw timestamps. Hit just appends to the back, that is the newest arrival. GetHits does the real work. While the front of the queue is older than timestamp minus three hundred, we pop it off the left. Once that loop finishes, everything left in the queue is within the window, so we just return its length.
say.outro: Each hit and each cleanup step only ever happens once per timestamp, so the work amortises to constant time. Pattern: queue based design, a close cousin of sliding windows.

sequence-reconstruction.hook: Topological sort with a twist: at every single step there must be exactly one choice.
sequence-reconstruction.ask: You get a permutation nums of 1 to n, and a list of sequences, each a subsequence of nums. Decide whether nums is the one and only shortest sequence that contains every one of those sequences as a subsequence.
sequence-reconstruction.exampleWhy: The sequences force one before two, one before three, and two before three. That pins down the order completely as one, two, three, so nums is the unique shortest supersequence.

brute.idea: Generate the topological order using a graph, but whenever more than one node is available at the same time, try every permutation and check all of them reconstruct validly, which is hopeless at scale, or alternatively regenerate order and separately check if a second valid order exists by brute force search.
steps: Build a graph of precedence constraints from each sequence
Try to find any topological order different from nums
If one exists, return false
If nums is the only order found, return true
brute.time: O(n!) worst case for searching alternative orders
brute.whySlow: Searching the space of all topological orderings is exponential, completely impractical for n up to ten thousand.

optimal.insight: Build a directed graph from consecutive pairs in every sequence, then run Kahn's algorithm. If at any moment more than one node has in degree zero, the order is ambiguous. If the final built order does not match nums exactly, or every sequence value was not covered, it fails too.
steps: Build adjacency list and in degree counts from consecutive pairs in each sequence
Start a queue with all nodes of in degree zero
At each step, if the queue has more than one node, return false immediately
Pop the single node, check it matches the expected position in nums
Decrease in degree of its neighbours, push any that drop to zero
After processing all nodes, return true only if everything lined up

Edge a before b from consecutive sequence pairs
Nodes ready to be placed, in degree zero
More than one candidate means order is not unique
Placed node must match expected position in nums
Move to next expected position in nums

pitfalls: Forgetting to check that the number of processed nodes equals n, which would miss disconnected or cyclic cases.
Not returning false the instant the queue has more than one ready node, waiting too long loses the ambiguity signal.

say.intro: This is sequence reconstruction. You have a permutation called nums, and a bunch of shorter sequences. Each one must appear in order inside the final answer. The question is whether nums is forced to be the only possible shortest answer. Here nums is one, two, three, and the sequences give us one before two, one before three, and two before three. That pins everything down uniquely, so the answer is true.
say.brute: The naive approach tries to generate every possible ordering of the numbers and checks which ones satisfy all the sequence constraints. If more than one ordering works, it is not unique. But generating every permutation blows up factorially. For even twenty numbers that is already astronomically large. We need something smarter.
say.insight: Think of this as building a dependency graph. Each sequence tells us that one number must come directly before another. That gives us edges in a graph. Now run a topological sort using Kahn's algorithm, where you repeatedly pick nodes with no remaining dependencies. Here is the key trick: at every step, there must be exactly one node ready to go. If ever two or more are ready at once, there are multiple valid orderings, so it cannot be unique. We also check that the order we build matches nums exactly, step by step.
say.anim: We start with nums one two three and three sequences building a dependency graph. The code scans each sequence, marking seen values and recording edges between consecutive numbers. After processing all pairs, graph edges show one points to two and three, two points to three. In degree ends up zero, zero, one, two for nodes one, two, three respectively. Only node one has in degree zero, so the queue starts with just one. Since the queue has one node, it is unambiguous, so one matches nums at index zero. Removing node one drops two's in degree to zero, queue becomes two, keeping order unique. Nodes two then three pop in sequence, matching nums exactly, so the result returns true.
say.code: We build in degree counts and an adjacency list from consecutive pairs within each sequence. We seed a queue with every node that has zero in degree. As we process, the moment the queue holds more than one node, we bail out immediately and return false, since that means ambiguity. Otherwise we pop the single node, verify it matches the next expected value in nums, then reduce in degree for its neighbours, pushing any that reach zero. If we process every node this way and they all matched nums in order, we return true.
say.outro: This runs in linear time relative to the total size of everything given. Pattern: graphs, specifically topological sorting. Whenever a problem asks about uniqueness of an order, check that only one choice is ever available at each step.

moving-average-from-data-stream.hook: Keep a running total and a queue, and the average never costs more than one pass over the window.
moving-average-from-data-stream.ask: Design a class that computes the moving average of the last size values from a stream of integers. Each call to next adds a new value and returns the average of the most recent size values seen so far.
moving-average-from-data-stream.exampleWhy: Window size is 3. After 1,10,3,5 the last call keeps 10,3,5 in the window, which averages to 6.0.

brute.idea: Store every value ever seen in a list. On each call, slice out the last size values and sum them to get the average.
steps: Append val to the full history list
Take the last min(size, len) elements
Sum them and divide by how many there are
brute.whySlow: Slicing and summing up to size elements on every single call wastes work that a running total avoids.

optimal.insight: Only the last size values matter. Keep them in a queue and a running sum. When the queue overflows, pop the oldest value and subtract it from the sum, so each call does constant work.
steps: Push val into the queue and add it to the running total
If the queue is now longer than size, pop the oldest value and subtract it from the total
Return total divided by current queue length

pitfalls: Dividing by the fixed size instead of the current queue length gives wrong early answers before the window fills.
Forgetting to subtract the evicted value corrupts the running total.

say.intro: This is Moving Average from Data Stream. You get numbers one at a time and must report the average of the most recent window each time. With a window of three, after one, ten, three, five, the last answer is the average of ten, three and five, which is six.
say.brute: The obvious approach stores every number ever seen. Each call slices out the last few values and sums them fresh. It works, but that sum gets recomputed from scratch every single time, which is wasteful once the stream gets long.
say.insight: Instead, keep a queue holding just the current window, plus a running total. When a new value arrives, add it to both. If the queue grows past the window size, pop the oldest value out and subtract it from the total. The average is just the total divided by however many values are currently in the queue.
say.anim: We set up the window size of 3, an empty queue, and a running total of 0. Value 1 is added to the queue, total becomes 1, and since the queue fits, average returns 1.0. Value 10 is added, total becomes 11, queue still fits within size 3, average returns 5.5. Value 3 is added, total becomes 14, still within size, average returns 4.666666666666667. Value 5 is added, total becomes 19, but now the queue has 4 elements, overflowing size 3. The oldest value 1 is popped and subtracted, making total 18 with 3 elements remaining. Dividing total 18 by the window length 3 gives the final moving average of 6.0.
say.code: The constructor stores the size, an empty deque, and a total of zero. In next, we append the value and add it to the total. Then we check if the queue is too long, and if so we popleft and subtract that value from the total. Finally we return the total divided by the queue length, which handles the early calls before the window is full.
say.outro: Every operation is constant time, and the space is bounded by the window size. This is a classic sliding window pattern: maintain a running aggregate instead of recomputing it.

design-search-autocomplete-system.hook: Every keystroke needs instant suggestions ranked by popularity. A trie with counts baked into every node makes that nearly free.
design-search-autocomplete-system.ask: Design a search autocomplete system. You start with a list of past sentences and how many times each was typed. As a user types one character at a time, return the top three matching sentences sorted by typed count, then by alphabetical order, for the prefix typed so far. A hash sign ends the sentence, saves it to history, and returns an empty list.
design-search-autocomplete-system.exampleWhy: All three sentences start with c, so typing c shows all of them ranked by count: car (3), cat (2), care (1). Typing a keeps the prefix ca, which still matches all three, so the ranking is unchanged. The hash saves ca as a brand new sentence and clears the buffer.

brute.idea: Keep a dictionary of sentence to count. On every typed character, rebuild the current prefix, scan every stored sentence to see if it starts with that prefix, then sort the matches.
steps: Append the new character to a buffer
Loop through every stored sentence and keep ones starting with the buffer
Sort the matches by count descending then alphabetically
Return the top three
brute.time: O(n times L) per keystroke, where n is the number of stored sentences
brute.whySlow: With thousands of keystrokes and sentences growing over time, rescanning and resorting everything on every single character wastes huge amounts of work that a trie can avoid.

optimal.insight: Build a trie of all sentences, but at every node along the way also store a small map of sentence to accumulated count. Then, as the user types, just walk one step deeper into the trie each time. The node you land on already knows every sentence passing through it and its count, so you only sort that small local list instead of rescanning everything.
steps: Insert every sentence into the trie, adding its count to every node along the path
Keep a pointer to the current trie node as the user types
On each character, step the pointer into the matching child, or mark it lost if no such child exists
Sort that node's local counts by count descending then alphabetically and return the top three
On a hash, save the typed sentence with count one and reset the pointer to the root
optimal.time: O(L) per keystroke to walk the trie, plus sorting a small local list of candidates
optimal.space: O(n times L) for the trie

If the trie pointer falls off because of an unseen prefix, every following character must also return an empty list, not crash.
Ties must break by ascii order, not insertion order, so always sort by the pair of negative count then the sentence itself.

say.intro: This is the autocomplete system problem. You start with some sentences and how many times each was typed. As someone types, you return the top three matching sentences by popularity. We start with cat, car and care, with counts two, three and one. Typing c matches all three, so car comes first with three, then cat with two, then care with one.
say.brute: The naive approach keeps a dictionary of sentence to count. Every keystroke, you rebuild the typed prefix, scan every single stored sentence to check if it starts with that prefix, then sort the matches. It works, but with thousands of keystrokes and a growing history, you are redoing that full scan and sort constantly. Painfully wasteful.
say.insight: The fix is a trie that remembers more than just which letters exist. At every node along a sentence's path, we also store a tiny map of sentence to accumulated count. Now the current typed prefix corresponds to exactly one trie node, and that node already knows every sentence running through it along with its count. Typing a new character is just one step deeper into the trie. No rescanning the whole history ever again.
say.anim: We build a trie from cat, car, and care, storing counts of each sentence at every node along its path. Inserting cat with count two updates counts at the root, c, a, and t nodes as we descend. Inserting car adds count three, so nodes c and a now track both cat and car. Inserting care adds count one, updating nodes c, a, r, and a new e node with all three sentences. Typing c moves us one step into the trie, where that node already lists cat, car, and care with totals. Sorting by count then alphabetically gives car, cat, care as the top three suggestions. Typing a moves deeper into the trie, reusing the same precomputed counts to return car, cat, care again. Typing the end marker saves the typed sentence and resets, returning an empty list as the final result.
say.code: We build a trie node class holding children and a counts dictionary. Inserting a sentence walks its characters, adding the count to the counts map at every node on the way, including the root. On input, a hash saves the buffered sentence with count one and resets everything. Otherwise we extend the buffer, step the current node into its matching child, and if that child does not exist we mark the pointer as lost. If the pointer is lost we return nothing. Otherwise we sort that node's counts by highest count first, then alphabetically, and return the top three.
say.outro: Each keystroke only costs a single trie step plus sorting a small local list, instead of scanning the whole history. Pattern: tries. Whenever you need fast prefix lookups with rankings, push the ranking data down into the trie nodes themselves.

number-of-ships-in-a-rectangle.hook: You can't see the ships, you can only ask about rectangles. Time to think like a quadtree.
number-of-ships-in-a-rectangle.ask: You are given a hidden Sea object. Calling hasShips on a rectangle tells you whether any ship lies inside it, including the boundary. Given the top right and bottom left corners of a search rectangle, return how many ships lie inside it, using no more than four hundred calls.
number-of-ships-in-a-rectangle.exampleWhy: Ships sit at (1,1), (2,2) and (3,3), all inside the rectangle from (0,0) to (4,4), so the answer is three.

brute.idea: Check every single integer point in the rectangle one at a time with its own tiny hasShips call.
steps: Loop over every x from bottomLeft to topRight
Loop over every y from bottomLeft to topRight
Call hasShips on that single point
Count the ones that return true
brute.whySlow: A 1000 by 1000 rectangle needs a million calls, but we are only allowed four hundred.

optimal.insight: If a rectangle reports no ships, skip it entirely. If it reports ships and is a single point, that point is a ship. Otherwise split the rectangle into four quadrants and recurse, only where ships were reported.
steps: If the rectangle is empty or has no ships, return 0
If it's down to a single point, return 1
Split into four quadrants around the midpoint
Recurse on each quadrant and sum the counts
optimal.time: O(log(area)) calls, bounded by the at most ten ships guarantee

say.intro: This one is interactive. There's a hidden sea full of ships, and the only tool you get is a function that tells you whether any ship sits inside a given rectangle. We start with a rectangle from zero zero to four four, and three ships sit right inside it, so the answer is three.
say.brute: The obvious idea is to check every single point in the rectangle one at a time. That works, but a thousand by thousand rectangle has a million points, and we are capped at four hundred calls. This approach gets disqualified before it even starts.
say.insight: Think like a quadtree. Ask the whole rectangle first. If there are no ships at all, you're done, skip it completely. If the rectangle has shrunk down to a single point and it says yes, that point is a ship. Otherwise, split the rectangle into four quarters around the midpoint and ask the same question of each quarter. Because there are at most ten ships total, this branching stays small and the call budget is easily met.
say.anim: We start with three ships and search the rectangle from zero zero to four four. Since ships exist in this area, we split it into four smaller quadrants around the midpoint. The bottom left quadrant shrinks down until it isolates the single point one one, a ship. That quadrant returns one ship found, adding to our running count. Next the quadrant around two two isolates another ship, bringing the count to two. The algorithm then checks the top right area and zooms into three three, finding the third ship. The final corner near four four has no ships, so it returns zero and skips further splitting. All quadrants combined give a final total of three ships found.
say.code: We first wrap the raw ships data into our Sea helper so we have the hasShips method to call. We check if the rectangle is invalid first, since splitting can produce that. Then we ask hasShips on the whole area. No ships, return zero straight away. If we're down to a single point and it said yes, that's one ship. Otherwise we compute the midpoint and recurse into all four quadrants, carefully adjusting the boundaries so they don't overlap, then sum up the results.
say.outro: This uses roughly logarithmic calls relative to the area, comfortably within the limit. Pattern: recursion and divide and conquer. When you can only ask yes or no questions about regions, keep halving the region.
